That changes the conversation.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally a religion teaching people to hate their bodies.
The biblical story is something far more beautiful.
Creation.
Fall.
Redemption.
Restoration.
God created what was good.
Sin corrupted what God created.
And Jesus came not to teach us to call corruption good, but to redeem sinners from corruption and restore us to holiness.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because there are two lies constantly competing for your soul.
One says, “If you desire it, it must be good.”
The other says, “If you experience sexual desire at all, you must be dirty.”
Scripture teaches neither.
Desire is not God.
But neither is desire automatically shameful.
In fact, anyone who thinks the Bible is embarrassed by marital desire has probably forgotten that the Bible contains the Song of Songs.
Listen to this extraordinary Hebrew declaration:
"אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ"
Ani ledodi, ve'alai teshuqato.
“I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me.” — Song of Songs 7:10.
There it is.
תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah.
Desire.
Inside Scripture.
Not hidden in some forbidden manuscript.
Not smuggled into the Bible by modern culture.
There.
In the Word of God.
The Song of Songs celebrates the longing, delight, attraction, exclusivity, and embodied affection of lovers within its poetic world.
The Bible does not need pornography to teach us that desire exists.
Pornography did not invent sexuality.
God did.
Pornography takes something profoundly human and tears it away from covenant, dignity, faithfulness, and love. It turns persons into consumable images. Lust says, “Your body exists for my appetite.”
Covenant love says something radically different.
“I give myself faithfully to you.”
That is why biblical holiness is not the destruction of sexuality.
It is sexuality brought under the lordship of God.
And that lordship gives us boundaries.
Real boundaries.
Necessary boundaries.
Scripture does not celebrate every sexual impulse simply because it feels sincere.
Paul writes:
Touto gar estin thelēma tou Theou, ho hagiasmos hymōn…
“This is the will of God, your sanctification…”
And Paul immediately connects that sanctification with abstaining from porneia—sexual immorality—and living in holiness and honor rather than uncontrolled lust. — 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5.
So Christianity does not say:
“Whatever you desire, pursue it.”
Neither does Christianity say:
“Having a body makes you filthy.”
Christianity says something infinitely more demanding and infinitely more hopeful.
Your body belongs under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Your sexuality belongs under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Your desires belong under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Your wounds belong under the healing authority of Jesus Christ.
Your memories.
Your fantasies.
Your marriage.
Your singleness.
Your temptations.
Your failures.
Your future.
All of it.
Jesus does not merely want the religious compartment of your life.
He claims you.
And this is precisely why biblical sexual ethics should never be reduced to “God hates sex.”
Hebrews says:
“Τίμιος ὁ γάμος… καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος.”
Marriage is honorable, and the marriage bed is amiantos—undefiled. — Hebrews 13:4.
Notice what Scripture does in the same verse.
It honors marriage and the marriage bed while also warning that God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
Celebration and boundary.
Gift and holiness.
Desire and covenant.
Pleasure and faithfulness.
The Bible refuses our culture's false choice between sexual indulgence and sexual shame.
And Paul becomes surprisingly direct when speaking to married Christians.

He tells husbands and wives to fulfill their marital responsibilities toward one another. Then he uses deliberately reciprocal language about their bodies and tells spouses not to deprive one another except temporarily by mutual agreement. — 1 Corinthians 7:3–5.
Read the passage carefully and something remarkable appears.
Mutuality.
Not exploitation.
Not coercion.
Not selfish entitlement.
Not one spouse treating the other like property.
The language runs both directions.
Husband toward wife.
Wife toward husband.
And even temporary abstinence in the passage is connected with mutual agreement.
That matters.
Biblical marital intimacy must never be twisted into permission for abuse, coercion, humiliation, or domination.
Sexual violence is not marital intimacy.
Coercion is not covenant love.
Using Scripture to force another person's body into submission to selfish appetite is not a defense of biblical sexuality. It is a distortion of it.
Biblical intimacy is inseparable from the wider biblical commands to love, faithfulness, self-giving, holiness, and honor.
And Paul goes even further.
When describing the “one flesh” union of husband and wife, he says:
“τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν…”
To mystērion touto mega estin.
“This mystery is profound…”
And then he says he is speaking about Christ and the church. — Ephesians 5:31–32.
Think about that.
Human marriage is not ultimate.
Christ is.
Even the deepest covenant intimacy between husband and wife becomes a signpost pointing beyond itself toward something greater—the faithful covenant love between Christ and His people.
And suddenly sexuality is neither god nor garbage.
It is not worthy of worship.
It is not worthy of contempt.
It belongs beneath the throne of Jesus.
But maybe none of that feels comforting to you yet.
Because your story did not happen in Eden.
Your story happened after the fall.
Maybe your sexual history does not feel like Song of Songs.
It feels like Genesis 3.
Hiding.
Covering.
Fear.
Maybe somebody introduced you to pornography before you were old enough to understand what it would eventually do to your mind.
Maybe curiosity became habit.
Habit became dependency.
Dependency became secrecy.
Secrecy became shame.
And shame became identity.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your marriage carries years of rejection and resentment that nobody at church sees.
Maybe someone touched you when they had no right to.
Maybe someone who should have protected you exploited you instead.
Hear this carefully:
What someone did to you was not made righteous because your body was involved.
Being sinned against does not make you the guilty party for another person's evil.
Or maybe you were the one who crossed the line.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Maybe you lived promiscuously.
Maybe you manipulated.
Maybe you used people.
Maybe you keep returning to images you promised God you would never look at again.
Maybe you crossed boundaries in a relationship and afterward stared at yourself wondering:
“How did I become this person?”
Now we have arrived at the place shame loves most.
Because shame wants to take something you did and transform it into a permanent name.
Adulterer.
Porn addict.
Impure.
Damaged.
Unwanted.
Unclean.
Unlovable.
Hypocrite.
Ruined.
Finished.
But then Paul writes one of the most breathtaking sentences in the New Testament.
After naming serious patterns of sin, including sexual immorality and adultery, he turns toward believers whose pasts were anything but spotless.
And he says:
“καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε…”
Kai tauta tines ēte.
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then come three thunderclaps of grace:
“ἀπελούσασθε…”
You were washed.
“ἡγιάσθητε…”
You were sanctified.
“ἐδικαιώθητε…”
You were justified.
“In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:9–11.
Do you see it?
Paul does not pretend sin was harmless.
He names it.
Then grace interrupts the sentence.
But.
You were this…
but you were washed.
The Gospel does not require us to rename darkness as light.
The Gospel announces that darkness does not have to own us forever.
Jesus does not save us by pretending sin never mattered.
He saves sinners at the cost of His own blood.
The cross simultaneously destroys two lies.
The first lie says:
“My sin isn't serious.”
Look at Calvary.
It is serious.
The second says:
“My sin is too serious for Jesus.”
Look again at Calvary.
His grace is greater.
This is where some Christians have accidentally confused shame with repentance.
They are not the same.
Repentance says:
“What I did was sin. Jesus, turn me around.”
Condemning shame says:
“What I did is what I am, and there is no road home.”
Repentance runs toward God.
Toxic shame hides from Him.
Repentance agrees with God's truth.
Shame often tells a different story: that Christ's blood may cleanse other people, but somehow your particular stain survived Calvary.
And if Christ has washed you, who gave shame permission to keep calling you permanently filthy?
This does not mean consequences disappear.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Marriages may require difficult conversations.
Patterns may require accountability.
Pornography may require radical changes in access, habits, secrecy, and community.
Some wounds may require wise pastoral care and qualified professional help.
Repentance is not pretending nothing happened.
Forgiveness is not calling evil good.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying yourself or someone else.
Jesus forgives sinners and calls them into transformed lives.
That balance appears vividly in the familiar account recorded in John 8.
Jesus says:
“οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω.”
“Neither do I condemn you.”
But He continues:
“πορεύου… μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε.”
“Go…and sin no more.” — John 8:11.
Grace.
And transformation.
Mercy.
And repentance.
Neither condemnation nor permission.
Jesus refuses both counterfeits.
Some churches have shouted “sin no more” so loudly that broken people never heard “neither do I condemn you.”
Others have emphasized “neither do I condemn you” while becoming uncomfortable with “sin no more.”
Jesus said both.
And we need both.
We need a Savior tender enough to receive the ashamed and holy enough to refuse to leave us enslaved.
Maybe that is what your soul has been starving for.
Not another person telling you sexual sin does not matter.
Not another person acting as though sexual struggle makes you uniquely disgusting.
You need Jesus.
The Jesus who knows everything.
Everything.
Not the edited testimony.
Not the cleaned-up version.
Not the church version.
Everything.
And still calls sinners to come.
David knew something about sexual sin.
He knew desire could become coveting.
He knew coveting could become adultery.
He knew adultery could become deception.
He knew concealed sin could spread devastation far beyond a private moment.
And after his sin was exposed, his prayer was not:
“God, help me manage my reputation.”
It was:
"לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים"
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.” — Psalm 51:10.
What a prayer.
Not:
Make me look clean.
Not:
Help everybody think I am clean.
Create in me a clean heart.
There is the difference between reputation management and repentance.
Some of us have spent years trying to make sure nobody discovers what Jesus has been asking us to surrender.
We delete.
Hide.
Minimize.
Rationalize.
Blame our marriage.
Blame loneliness.
Blame our childhood.
Blame our hormones.
Blame culture.
Blame our spouse.
Blame temptation.
And yes, circumstances matter.
Wounds matter.
Trauma matters.
Loneliness matters.
But eventually grace brings us to the place where excuses can no longer heal us.
We finally whisper:
“Jesus…this is mine.
I did this.
I have hidden this.
I need You.”
And strangely, confession—the thing shame told you would destroy you—becomes the doorway toward freedom.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people can become slightly better.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Real sinners.
Sexually broken sinners.
Proud sinners.
Religious sinners.
Secret sinners.
Public sinners.
People whose lives look respectable.
People whose stories look like scandals.
People who sinned yesterday.
People who have carried what was done to them for decades.
People who desperately need cleansing.
People who desperately need healing.
People like us.
This is why you cannot understand Christian sexuality without understanding the cross.
At the cross, Jesus does not merely tell you to try harder.
He gives Himself.
The sinless One bears sin.
The condemned sinner is offered justification.
The unclean is washed.
The enslaved can become free.
The ashamed can learn to stand before God clothed not in self-righteousness but in Christ.
And the resurrection announces that your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your ending.
That authority belongs to Jesus.
Maybe your marriage has become cold.
Jesus is not finished.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out places inside you.
Jesus is not finished.
Maybe you are single and exhausted from fighting desires nobody knows about.
Jesus is not finished.
Maybe adultery shattered your home and you would give anything to rewind time.
Jesus is not finished.
Maybe someone violated you, and for years you have confused what was done to you with who you are.
Jesus is not finished.
Maybe you have repented but cannot forgive yourself.
Then perhaps the question is no longer whether your feelings pronounce you clean.
The question is whether Christ's verdict is greater than your feelings.
The Gospel does not say your past never happened.
It says your past does not get to be your savior, your master, or your final identity.
Your scandal is not stronger than His grace.
Your temptation is not stronger than His Spirit.
Your wound is not beyond His compassion.
Your body is not beyond His claim.
Your marriage is not beneath His concern.
Your sexuality is not a room Jesus is embarrassed to enter.
Open the door.
Bring Him the truth.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Tell Him what happened.
Tell Him what you did.
Tell Him what you keep wanting.
Tell Him what you cannot seem to stop.
Tell Him what was done to you.
Tell Him why you are angry.
Tell Him why intimacy terrifies you.
Tell Him why you feel unwanted.
Tell Him why you keep going back.
Tell Him the sentence you have never dared to say in prayer.
He already knows.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek safety where abuse exists.
Seek wise help where wounds run deep.
Confess sin instead of negotiating with it.
Bring darkness into the light.
Ask trusted, mature believers for accountability rather than fighting every battle alone.
And when the accuser drags an old file across the courtroom of your mind, remember the grammar of grace:
“Such were some of you.”
Were.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Jesus Christ does not merely edit scandals.
He redeems people.
And perhaps someone reading this is shaking a little because this article touched the room inside your heart that you have kept locked for years.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your story.
But stop lying to God.
He already knows the unedited version.
Let somebody know that behind the polished profile picture there is a real human being who still needs grace.
There may also be somebody on your Facebook friends list who will never walk into a pastor's office and say, “I'm struggling sexually.”
They may never tell their family.
They may never tell you.
But they might read something you share at 1:37 in the morning when nobody else is awake.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they need it.
If this ministry is helping you know Christ more deeply, there is another way you can help carry the message farther.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not to buy forgiveness.
Not because salvation is for sale.
It never will be.
And not as a substitute for faithful generosity and responsibility in your local church.

And if God has blessed you with the ability to give, supporting Gospel work can itself be an act offered for His glory when it flows freely from faith, gratitude, love, and obedience—not fear, manipulation, or an attempt to purchase spiritual favor.
The goal is not merely more content.
The goal is deeper discipleship.
More Scripture opened.
More wounded believers reminded of grace.
More hidden battles brought into light.
More Christians strengthened to follow Jesus when nobody is applauding.
More marriages pointed toward covenant faithfulness.
More prodigals reminded that the Father's house is not closed.
More sinners hearing that repentance is possible because mercy is real.
Pray for this ministry.
And most importantly, follow Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot wash you.
A church cannot justify you.
A book cannot redeem you.
A pastor cannot carry your sin away.
A ministry cannot resurrect your heart.
Jesus can.
So when shame whispers,
“Hide…”
Jesus calls,
“Come.”
When shame says,
“You are what you did…”
the Gospel says,
“Such were some of you.”
When shame says,
“You will always be dirty…”
the Gospel says,
“You were washed.”
When shame says,
“God could never use someone with your history…”
look at the cross.
Christianity itself is filled with redeemed histories.
David had scandal.
Peter had denial.
Paul had blood on his résumé.
The Corinthian church had sexual brokenness serious enough for Paul to confront directly.
And still grace kept writing.
Not grace that excuses sin.
Grace that transforms sinners.
That is why shame does not get the final word.
Pornography does not get the final word.
Adultery does not get the final word.
Abuse does not get the final word.
Your divorce does not get the final word.
Your virginity does not save you.
Your sexual history does not automatically damn you.
Your desires are not your god.
Your wounds are not your identity.
Your failures are not your master.
Your body belongs beneath the lordship of Christ.
Your past can be confessed.
Your wounds can be brought into the light.
Your mind can be renewed.
Your life can become an offering of holiness.
Your story can still become a testimony.
Because the final word over every repentant sinner who has taken refuge in Christ is not:
Scandal.
It is:
Grace.
And maybe that is the sentence you needed tonight.
You thought Jesus was standing at the end of your story holding a red pen.
Perhaps you forgot He walked to a cross carrying scars.
The chapter you are most ashamed to let anyone read may become the very place where people someday discover how fiercely Jesus Christ knows how to redeem.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID BIBLICAL KINGS HAVE CONCUBINES—AND WHY COULD SLEEPING WITH A KING’S CONCUBINE BECOME A POLITICAL ACT?
paragraphs: WHY DID BIBLICAL KINGS HAVE CONCUBINES—AND WHY COULD SLEEPING WITH A KING’S CONCUBINE BECOME A POLITICAL ACT?

The disturbing royal custom hiding behind some of the Bible’s strangest stories—and the breathtaking difference between the kings who took women to prove their power and the King who gave Himself to save His Bride.
There is a scene in the Bible so disturbing that most people read it quickly, feel uncomfortable, and move on.
A prince walks onto a rooftop.
A tent is erected where the nation can see it.
Ten women who belonged to his father’s household are brought to him.
And then, publicly, deliberately, in an act designed to send a message across Israel, Absalom sleeps with his father David’s concubines.
It sounds like sexual depravity.
It was.
But it was also something more.
It was politics.
It was rebellion.
It was a declaration of war.
And once you understand what a royal concubine represented in the ancient world, several strange passages of Scripture suddenly begin connecting like pieces of a puzzle.
Why did Ish-bosheth become furious when Abner was accused of sleeping with Saul’s concubine Rizpah?
Why did Absalom publicly take David’s concubines?
Why did Solomon react so severely when his older brother Adonijah asked to marry Abishag?
And perhaps the uncomfortable question beneath all of them:
Why did biblical kings have concubines in the first place?
Before answering, we need to establish something Christians sometimes forget when reading the Old Testament:
The Bible faithfully recording an action does not mean God is approving that action.
Scripture is brutally honest.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not sanitize kings.
It does not pretend powerful men were righteous simply because God used them.
The Bible will show you David worshiping.
Then David lusting.
David trusting God.
Then David manipulating.
David writing psalms.
Then David destroying a family.
That honesty is one reason Scripture feels so painfully human.
God does not need to hide His servants’ scandals to protect His reputation.
He exposes human sin because ultimately the Bible is not the story of impressive men rescuing themselves.
It is the story of sinners desperately needing a Savior.
And concubinage belongs inside that broken world.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “concubine” is פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pîlegeš.

A concubine was not simply the ancient equivalent of a casual girlfriend or modern mistress. She occupied a recognized domestic and sexual relationship with a man, but generally without the full status, security, or privileges associated with a primary wife.
That distinction matters.
Because when kings accumulated wives and concubines, women could become entangled with dynasty, inheritance, alliances, prestige, household expansion, succession, and royal power.
But we must never confuse what kings practiced with what God originally designed.
Long before Israel had palaces...
before David...
before Solomon...
before royal harems...
Genesis takes us into a garden.
One man.
One woman.
A covenant union.
Genesis 2:24 declares:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד — vehayu levasar echad
“and they shall become one flesh.”
Jesus Himself later reaches back to this creation account when teaching about marriage.
That is enormously important.
When Jesus explains marriage, He does not point to Solomon’s household.
He points to Eden.
The kings are not the standard.
Creation is.
And Israel’s kings were specifically warned against multiplying wives.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says of the king that he must not יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים — yarbeh-lo nashim, multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.
God knew what human beings keep discovering the painful way:
What looks like an expansion of power can become an expansion of bondage.
What looks like possession can eventually possess you.

Solomon became perhaps the most spectacular example. The king famous for wisdom eventually became the king whose multiplied relationships helped turn his heart away from wholehearted faithfulness to God.
So when Scripture tells us that kings possessed many women, the correct conclusion is not, “God must have endorsed royal harems.”
Sometimes Scripture describes the disease before showing us the consequences.
And now the story gets darker.
Because in the royal world, a king’s women could become connected with the king’s throne.
That helps explain one explosive confrontation after Saul’s death.
Saul was gone.
His dynasty was collapsing.
David’s kingdom was rising.
Saul’s surviving son Ish-bosheth occupied a fragile throne while Abner, Saul’s powerful military commander, increasingly held enormous influence.
Then one accusation detonated between them.
Saul had possessed a concubine named Rizpah, daughter of Aiah.
Ish-bosheth confronted Abner over allegedly sleeping with her.
To modern ears, the reaction can seem disproportionate.
Why would an accusation involving one woman threaten a kingdom?
Because this was not necessarily heard merely as:
“You slept with my father’s woman.”
It could carry the terrifying political implication:
“Are you reaching for my father’s throne?”
The biblical narrative immediately turns toward royal legitimacy and transfer of the kingdom. Abner becomes enraged, breaks with Ish-bosheth, and moves toward transferring allegiance to David.
One woman stands at the center of a political earthquake.
And painfully, Rizpah herself barely gets a voice.
That should bother us.
Because one of the Bible’s recurring exposures of fallen power is how easily powerful people turn human beings into instruments.
She had a name.
Rizpah.
Not merely “Saul’s concubine.”
Not merely a royal possession.
A woman.
A mother.
A human being bearing God’s image.
Later Scripture gives us an unforgettable picture of Rizpah grieving over her dead sons, guarding their bodies with staggering maternal devotion.
The woman whom political history could reduce to somebody’s concubine emerges as a grieving mother.
That is worth remembering.
Behind the scandals of kings were real women.
Real tears.
Real consequences.
Real human beings caught inside the ambitions of powerful men.
Then comes Absalom.
And here the political symbolism becomes unmistakable.
Absalom is David’s son.
Handsome.
Charismatic.
Ambitious.
Wounded.
Dangerous.
He slowly steals the hearts of Israel, undermines his father, gathers supporters, and launches a rebellion.
David flees Jerusalem.
But David leaves ten concubines behind to maintain the palace.
Then Ahithophel gives Absalom horrifying advice.
Sleep with your father’s concubines.
Why?
Because Israel will hear about it.
That detail changes everything.
This was meant to become public knowledge.
Absalom was not merely indulging private lust.
He was making an irreversible public declaration.
So a tent was erected on the palace roof.
And Absalom went in to his father’s concubines “in the sight of all Israel.”
Think about the symbolism.
The son has entered the father’s capital.
The son occupies the father’s palace.
The son claims access to women belonging to the father’s royal household.
The message could hardly be louder:
David’s reign is finished. I am taking his place.
Sex became propaganda.
A bedroom became a battlefield.
Bodies became political territory.
And the roof itself carries a haunting irony.
Because years earlier David had walked on a rooftop and seen Bathsheba.
David’s sexual sin had begun in secrecy.
Nathan the prophet later announced that consequences would erupt publicly.
Now another rooftop appears.
Another sexual scandal.
Except this time all Israel is meant to see.
Sin has a terrible way of promising privacy while producing consequences far beyond the room where it began.
That does not mean every tragedy in a family is a direct punishment for a particular parental sin.
Scripture does not permit such simplistic conclusions.
But David’s story does show something terrifyingly real:
Our sins rarely remain as private as we imagine.
One hidden decision can wound marriages.
Children.
Trust.
Friendships.
Churches.
Generations.
You may hide the browser history.
Hide the messages.
Hide the relationship.
Hide the addiction.
Hide the bitterness.
Hide the secret account.
Hide the compromise.
Hide what happened when nobody else was watching.
But there is Someone from whom darkness cannot hide you.
And strangely...
that is not only terrifying.
For the repentant sinner, it can become the beginning of freedom.
Because the God who sees what you hide is also the God before whom you no longer have to pretend.
Maybe that is why this story is hitting you harder than you expected.
Maybe your scandal never involved a palace.
But you understand secrecy.
You understand wanting something that did not belong to you.
You understand the strange insanity of risking everything for one moment.
You understand what it feels like when desire starts whispering louder than obedience.
You understand regret.
You understand consequences.
You understand wishing you could travel backward and stop yourself before one decision became ten more decisions.
David understood that feeling too.
And this is where Christianity becomes radically different from moral theater.
The Gospel does not say:
“Good people never make terrible choices.”
The Gospel says:
Sinners need a Redeemer.
But before we reach that Redeemer, there is one more royal woman we need to meet.
Her name was Abishag.
When David became old, his servants searched for a young woman to attend him and keep him warm. They found Abishag the Shunammite.
Scripture explicitly says David did not have sexual relations with her.
Then David died.
Solomon became king.
And Solomon’s older brother Adonijah—who had previously attempted to position himself for the throne—made what sounded like a modest request.
He wanted Abishag as his wife.
Bathsheba carried the request to Solomon.
And Solomon immediately saw something beneath it.
His response was essentially:
Why ask for Abishag?
You might as well ask for the kingdom.
That sentence is one of the clearest biblical windows into the political meaning surrounding women attached to a royal household.
Whatever Adonijah’s personal motives may have been, Solomon interpreted the request politically, in the context of Adonijah’s previous royal ambitions.
And that distinction matters.
We should not claim more than Scripture gives us.
The Bible does not contain a footnote saying, “Every relationship with every royal concubine automatically transferred legal kingship.”
History is usually messier than slogans.
But Scripture itself repeatedly connects access to women of the royal household with questions of succession, royal prerogative, rebellion, and claims upon the throne.
Rizpah.
David’s concubines.
Abishag.
Different circumstances.
The same disturbing political world.
Women could become symbols inside struggles between powerful men.
And suddenly an ancient story begins sounding painfully modern.
Because human beings still do this.
We still use people to acquire power.
We still turn relationships into leverage.
We still exploit sexuality.
We still confuse possession with love.
We still sacrifice people to ambition.
We still destroy homes because we wanted something.
We still call lust “freedom.”
We still call selfishness “finding myself.”
We still call compromise “complicated.”
We still hide behind language because plain words would force us to confront what we have become.
Kings had palaces.
We have phones.
Kings had harems.
We have secret conversations.
Kings had servants protecting their scandals.
We have passwords.
Different century.
Same human heart.
That is why the Bible remains uncomfortable.
It refuses to let us stare at David, Absalom, Adonijah, or Solomon long enough to avoid looking at ourselves.
The question eventually stops being:
“How could those kings do such things?”
And becomes:
“What would I become if every desire in my heart had a throne, unlimited opportunity, and nobody powerful enough to tell me no?”
That question is harder.
Because sin is easy to condemn when someone else is wearing it.
But Scripture is a mirror before it is a window.
Maybe your sin is sexual.
Maybe it is greed.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe you crave attention.
Maybe you manipulate people.
Maybe you secretly envy somebody.
Maybe you are addicted to approval.
Maybe you are carrying bitterness against someone who wounded you years ago.
Maybe everybody thinks you are spiritually strong because you learned how to smile while your soul slowly collapsed.
Maybe you know Christian language but your heart has wandered far from Christ.
Maybe you worship on Sunday and negotiate with temptation Monday night.
Maybe you are exhausted from maintaining two versions of yourself.
One everyone knows.
And one God knows.
Be honest.
This may have started as an article about ancient concubines.
But somehow...
it found your room.
And now Jesus is standing at the door of the part of your life you hoped nobody would ever discover.
Not because He needs information.
He already knows.
He is standing there because you need redemption.
Not because typing a phrase saves you.
It does not.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops protecting the mask.
The ancient kings reveal something else too.
Power cannot cure the human heart.
David had a throne.
It could not cure lust.
Solomon had wisdom.
It could not guarantee faithfulness.
Absalom had beauty and popularity.
They could not cure rebellion.
Adonijah had royal blood.
It could not cure ambition.
And maybe you have been trying your own version.
“If I just earn more...”
“If people finally respect me...”
“If I find somebody who loves me...”
“If my ministry grows...”
“If my marriage improves...”
“If I become successful...”
“If I get enough followers...”
“If I can finally prove them wrong...”
Then I will be whole.
But there is no throne high enough to heal a sinful heart.
There is no bedroom intimate enough.
No applause loud enough.
No bank account large enough.
No relationship passionate enough.
No platform big enough.
No secret pleasure powerful enough.
Your deepest problem cannot be solved by finally getting everything your flesh wants.
You need something flesh cannot manufacture.
You need forgiveness.
You need reconciliation with God.
You need a new heart.
You need Jesus Christ.
And this is where the story of kings becomes breathtaking.
Because after centuries of flawed kings...
another King arrived.
But He was nothing like them.
Jesus did not accumulate women as trophies of royal power.
He treated women with dignity in a world that often reduced them.
He spoke with the Samaritan woman.
He defended the vulnerable.
Women followed Him as disciples.
Women stood near His cross.
Women became the first witnesses of His resurrection.
And unlike earthly kings who demonstrated power by taking...
Jesus demonstrated kingship by giving.
The kings of this world say:
“What can I take?”
Jesus says:
“I lay down My life.”
Earthly kings protected their thrones with blood.
Jesus left heavenly glory and shed His own blood for sinners.
Earthly kings used bodies to strengthen kingdoms.
Jesus gave His body to rescue people for His Kingdom.
Earthly rulers sacrificed others to preserve themselves.
Christ sacrificed Himself to save others.
Do you see the reversal?
The Gospel is not merely that Jesus is another king.
He is the King who exposes every counterfeit definition of power.
At Calvary, the One who possessed all authority allowed Himself to be stripped.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Pierced.
Crucified.
The crown placed upon Him was made of thorns.
The throne men gave Him was a cross.
And above His bleeding head was the accusation:
KING OF THE JEWS.
They thought it was mockery.
He was accomplishing redemption.
The King was dying for rebels.
For adulterers.
For liars.
For hypocrites.
For sexually broken people.
For proud people.
For people carrying secret histories.
For people whose worst moments would destroy their reputation if anyone discovered them.
For people like David.
For people like you.
For people like me.
But grace does not call evil good.
Grace calls sinners out of darkness.
Jesus did not die so we could decorate our chains with Christian vocabulary.
He died to redeem us.
Repentance means we stop defending the very thing from which Christ came to rescue us.
You cannot repent of the sin you insist on renaming.
Call lust lust.
Call adultery adultery.
Call pornography bondage.
Call greed greed.
Call manipulation manipulation.
Call pride pride.
Call bitterness bitterness.
Call unbelief unbelief.
Bring it into the light.
And then look at the cross.
Because the blood of Jesus is greater than the thing you finally found the courage to name.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
Not scandal ignored.
Not scandal celebrated.
Not scandal rebranded.
Scandal confessed.
Scandal brought beneath the cross.
Scandal met by mercy.
A sinner forgiven.
A rebel reconciled.
A heart made new.
A story rewritten by Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have spent years thinking your past disqualifies you.
David’s story should destroy that illusion without ever minimizing his sin.
David suffered consequences.
David was disciplined.
David’s family carried wounds.
Grace did not magically make every earthly consequence disappear.
But sin did not get the final word over the repentant man.
God’s mercy did.
That is why Christianity can look directly at scandal without surrendering to despair.
Our hope was never human perfection.
Our hope is Jesus.
Pray.
Even if the prayer comes out ugly.
Even if all you can say is:
“Jesus...I have sinned.”
Say it.
He already knows the chapter you are afraid to read aloud.
Bring it to Him.
Trust in Christ.
Turn from sin.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him.
Somebody reading beneath you may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people whose scars no longer belong to hopelessness.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be hiding.
Somebody may be losing a battle nobody knows they are fighting.
Somebody may have convinced themselves that God could never forgive what they did.
Somebody may know everything about church except what grace feels like.
And yes—even send it to the skeptic who thinks the Bible hides the failures of its heroes.
It does not.
Come back when temptation tries to convince you that secret sin has no public consequences.
Come back when shame tells you scandal is stronger than grace.
Come back when you need to remember the difference between the kings who took and the King who gave Himself.
Not as a replacement for your biblical responsibility to give faithfully and generously as God directs you, and not because anyone can purchase God’s favor.
Grace cannot be bought.
Your generosity does not make Jesus love you more.
But voluntary Christian generosity can help Gospel-centered work continue.
Sharing these articles publicly is another meaningful way to help the message travel.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it because you believe biblical truth should keep moving.
Do it as an act of willing generosity before God—not as a transaction with Him.
Then keep doing something even more important.
Love your church.
Help the poor.
Care for your family.
Give generously.
Serve quietly.
Forgive people.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
Open your Bible when nobody is applauding.
Pray when nobody is watching.
Obey Christ when obedience costs you.
Because Christianity was never supposed to produce spectators impressed by Christian content.
Jesus calls disciples.
And perhaps that is the final lesson hiding inside these disturbing stories of kings and concubines.
Human beings have always been tempted to turn people into possessions.
To turn sex into power.
To turn power into identity.
To turn desire into a throne.
To take.
To possess.
To conquer.
To hide.
But then Jesus entered our world.
The true King.
And instead of asking whose life He could take to preserve His throne...
He asked whose life He could save by laying down His own.
That is our King.
The King who knows your scandal.
The King who sees behind your mask.
The King who refuses to flatter your sin.
The King who calls you to repent.
The King whose wounds purchased forgiveness.
The King whose grave is empty.
The King who can take a story that should have ended in shame and write mercy across the final page.
So bring Him the chapter you keep hiding.
Bring Him the appetite you cannot control.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the wreckage.
Bring Him the crown you built for yourself.
Lay it down.
And follow Jesus.
And invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even unbelievers—to follow too.
Because the goal is not merely to understand why ancient kings had concubines.
The goal is to recognize the King standing before us now.
A King unlike David.
Unlike Solomon.
Unlike Absalom.
Unlike every ruler who used another human being to prove his power.
Jesus Christ.
The King who did not exploit His Bride.
The King who died for her.
And when every earthly crown has turned to dust, every palace has fallen, every secret has been exposed, and every human throne stands empty...
the King who gave Himself for sinners will still be standing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IT IS NOT GOOD FOR MAN TO BE ALONE” — BUT WHAT IF GENESIS 2:18 IS SAYING MORE THAN YOU WERE EVER TAUGHT?
paragraphs: “IT IS NOT GOOD FOR MAN TO BE ALONE” — BUT WHAT IF GENESIS 2:18 IS SAYING MORE THAN YOU WERE EVER TAUGHT?

We usually hear this verse at weddings. But before there was heartbreak, before there was sin, and before humanity knew what loneliness felt like, God looked at something in His perfect creation and said, “Not good.” What He saw may explain why some of us can be surrounded by people, married, successful, active in church—and still feel painfully alone.
There is a kind of loneliness nobody notices.
You answer messages.
You go to work.
You smile when somebody asks how you are.

You may sit beside your spouse at dinner. You may have children running through the house. You may attend church every Sunday, shake hands, sing worship songs, say “God bless you,” and go home with a Bible under your arm.
And still...
something inside you aches.
Because being around people is not the same thing as being known.
Having contacts is not the same thing as having community.
Sleeping beside somebody is not the same thing as being emotionally present with them.
And having thousands of Facebook friends certainly does not mean you have one person you can call at 2:13 in the morning and say:
“I am not okay.”
Maybe that is why one sentence near the beginning of Scripture still reaches into the human heart with frightening accuracy.
Before murder.
Before disease.
Before funerals.
Before betrayal.
Before depression.
Before divorce.
Before the Fall itself.
God saw a human being alone.
And for the first time in the creation account, something was called “not good.”
Genesis 2:18 records:
“וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ אֶעֱשֶׂה־לּוֹ עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ”
“Vayyomer YHWH Elohim, lo-tov heyot ha-adam levado; e'eseh-lo ezer kenegdo.”
In a close rendering:
“And the LORD God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone; I will make for him a helper corresponding to him.’”
Listen to the weight of those Hebrew words.
לֹא־טוֹב — lo tov.
“Not good.”
That should stop us.

Throughout Genesis 1, God looks at His creation and repeatedly calls it good. Light—good. Land and sea—good. Vegetation—good. Heavenly lights—good. Living creatures—good. And after humanity appears, the completed creation is described as “very good” (Genesis 1:31).
Yet Genesis 2 zooms in on the human story, and suddenly we hear:
Lo tov.
Not good.
Not because Adam had sinned.
Not because Satan had successfully corrupted him.
Not because Adam was defective.
Adam was living in Eden.
Think about that.
No bills.
No sickness.
No shame.
No pornography.
No adultery.
No social media comparison.
No family trauma.
No rejection.
No childhood wounds.
No funeral memories.
No betrayal.
And most importantly, Adam had fellowship with God.
Yet God Himself declared that something about Adam's solitary human condition was not good.
That matters enormously.
Because Christians sometimes give hurting people an answer that sounds spiritual but can actually oversimplify Scripture:
“If you have God, you shouldn't need anybody else.”
It sounds holy.
Genesis 2 makes it difficult to defend.
Adam had God.
And God said Adam should not remain alone.
That does not mean God was insufficient.
It means the God who is sufficient created human beings for relationships with other human beings.
Our need for godly human connection is not necessarily evidence that we do not love God enough. It is part of the way our Creator designed human life.
But here we need to be careful.
Genesis 2:18 absolutely does concern marriage.
We should never rip the verse out of its immediate context to make it say something completely different.
God's specific answer to Adam's situation is Eve.
The narrative moves directly toward the creation of the woman, Adam's recognition of her as “bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh,” and the institution of the one-flesh union in Genesis 2:24.
Jesus Himself later appeals to Genesis 1 and 2 when teaching about marriage (Matthew 19:4–6).
So yes.
Genesis 2:18 is profoundly about marriage.
But is its significance exhausted by marriage?
No.
And this is where some lonely Christians desperately need to hear the whole biblical story.
The Hebrew expression describing what God would provide is עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ — ezer kenegdo.
Ezer means “help” or “helper.”
Kenegdo carries the sense of corresponding to him, matching him, or standing opposite him in a fitting correspondence.
This is not the picture of an insignificant servant being handed to an important man.
In fact, the Hebrew word ezer is used elsewhere in the Old Testament for God Himself as the help of His people.
“The LORD is on my side as my helper...” (Psalm 118:7).
So biblical “helper” does not mean inferior.
Eve is the human counterpart Adam does not find among the animals.
She corresponds to him.
Equal in human dignity.
Distinct.
Suitable.
Able to enter a relationship no animal could provide.
And when Adam sees her, Scripture suddenly becomes poetry:
“This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh...” (Genesis 2:23).
You can almost feel the recognition.
At last.
Someone like me.
Someone who can know and be known.
Someone with whom life can be shared.
And yes, this culminates in marriage.
But Scripture does not consequently teach that every person must marry in order to become a complete human being.
How could it?
Jesus Christ was never married.
And no Christian can seriously argue that Jesus lived an incomplete human life.
The apostle Paul was unmarried during the ministry reflected in 1 Corinthians 7, and he actually describes singleness as possessing genuine kingdom advantages for some believers.
Paul does not tell every unmarried Christian, “Your real life begins when you find a spouse.”
Jesus does not teach that either.
That means we must hold two biblical truths together without sacrificing either one.
Marriage is God's good creation.
And marriage is not humanity's savior.
Your spouse cannot carry the weight of being your Messiah.
Your boyfriend cannot.
Your girlfriend cannot.
Your future husband cannot.
Your future wife cannot.

And if you enter marriage expecting another sinner to heal every wound, satisfy every longing, understand every silence, eliminate every insecurity, and make you whole, eventually you will discover something painful:
You asked a human being to occupy a throne built for Jesus Christ.
Maybe somebody reading this is married and lonelier than they were when they were single.
Nobody warned you that was possible.
You thought the wedding would cure loneliness.
Then came the photographs.
The congratulations.
The rings.
The home.
Maybe children.
And eventually...
silence.
Two people under one roof staring into two different screens.
Two bodies in one bed carrying two private worlds.
Two Christians attending one church while quietly becoming strangers.
That is why Genesis 2:18 cannot be reduced to the slogan:
“Lonely? Get married.”
Marriage itself requires communion.
Presence.
Sacrifice.
Truth.
Listening.
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
Service.
Vulnerability.
And ultimately grace.
A marriage can contain two people and still contain devastating loneliness.
Likewise, a single Christian can live without a spouse and yet experience profound belonging within the family of God.
The rest of Scripture makes this impossible to ignore.
Ecclesiastes says:
“Two are better than one... For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10).
Notice what the passage does not say.
“Husband and wife are better than one.”
Its wisdom is broader.
When one falls, another person can lift them.
And perhaps that is exactly where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because some of us have constructed lives where nobody is close enough to know when we fall.
We have privacy without accountability.
Followers without fellowship.
Contacts without covenant.
Church attendance without church family.
We know how to post Bible verses while hiding the battle happening behind the screen.
We know how to say, “I'm blessed.”
We know how to type, “God is good.”
We know exactly which Christian words make people stop asking questions.
But nobody knows what happened Thursday night.
Nobody knows about the relapse.
Nobody knows you cried in the bathroom so your children would not hear you.
Nobody knows your marriage is collapsing.
Nobody knows you have started questioning your faith.
Nobody knows how exhausted you are from pretending.
Nobody knows because you have perfected the art of being visible without being known.
And isolation loves that.
Sin often grows where secrecy becomes normal.
Shame whispers:
“Don't tell anybody.”
Pride whispers:
“You can handle this yourself.”
Fear whispers:
“They will judge you.”
Past wounds whisper:
“People cannot be trusted.”
And sometimes those fears come from real wounds.
Perhaps you trusted someone once.
They betrayed you.
Perhaps you confessed something, and instead of restoration you received gossip.
Perhaps somebody weaponized your vulnerability.
Perhaps the church that should have helped you became part of your wound.
So you learned something:
Keep the door locked.
Smile.
Serve.
Worship.
But never let anybody close enough to hurt you again.
And slowly, protection became imprisonment.
Please hear this carefully.
Biblical community does not mean giving everybody unrestricted access to your heart.
Jesus Himself did not relate to every person identically. Wisdom matters. Boundaries matter. Character matters. Trust should not be handed carelessly to unsafe people.
But there is a difference between wise boundaries and permanent isolation.
One protects what God is healing.
The other can prevent anyone from helping carry what is crushing you.
The New Testament does not imagine Christianity as Jesus-and-me spirituality.
Again and again we encounter a phrase:
“one another.”
Love one another.
Serve one another.
Encourage one another.
Forgive one another.
Bear with one another.
Confess to one another.
Pray for one another.
Carry one another's burdens.
Build one another up.
That is Christianity with skin on it.
Hebrews 10:24–25 tells believers to consider how to stir one another toward love and good works, not abandoning their gathering together, but encouraging one another.
Why?
Because following Jesus was never designed to be a spectator sport.
You need people who will celebrate when you rise.
But you also need people who will notice when you disappear.
People who do not merely ask:
“How are you?”
but can recognize when your “I'm fine” does not sound like you.
People who will pray when your own words are gone.
People who will lovingly confront you when sin starts sounding reasonable.
People who will remind you of grace when shame tells you to run.
People who will tell you the truth when everybody else is applauding your destruction.
And people who will stay long enough to watch Christ rebuild what sin shattered.
That is why the Gospel is so breathtaking.
Because the deepest human problem is not merely loneliness.
It is alienation from God through sin.
Genesis 2 shows humanity in fellowship before the Fall.
Genesis 3 shows fellowship ruptured.
Suddenly Adam and Eve hide.
Notice the movement.
Sin enters.
Shame enters.
Hiding follows.
God asks:
“Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9).
Humanity has been hiding ever since.
We hide behind achievements.
Behind humor.
Behind religion.
Behind relationships.
Behind sex.
Behind money.
Behind ministry.
Behind busyness.
Behind anger.
Behind carefully edited online lives.
Sometimes we even hide inside marriage.
But God did not leave humanity hiding among the trees.
The Bible moves from Eden lost toward redemption.
And eventually...
Jesus enters the story.
God with us.
The Word made flesh.
The One through whom everything was created stepped into our exile.
Jesus touched people others avoided.
He ate with people respectable society condemned.
He welcomed sinners.
He confronted hypocrites.
He wept beside a grave.
He restored failures.
He called disciples not merely into private spirituality but into a new family gathered around Himself.
Then He went somewhere infinitely darker than ordinary human loneliness.
The cross.
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46).
Christ bore judgment for sinners.
He gave Himself for our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
The Gospel is not motivational advice for lonely people.
It is the announcement that the crucified and risen Jesus Christ reconciles sinners to God.
Through Christ, guilty people can be forgiven.
The ashamed can come out of hiding.
The rebellious can repent.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
Enemies can become sons and daughters.
Strangers can become family.
Scandal can become grace.
Not because our sin was insignificant.
But because the blood of Jesus was sufficient.
This is where Genesis 2:18 ultimately forces us to ask something deeper than, “When will I get married?”
Maybe the better question is:
“Have I allowed Christ to bring me out of isolation?”
Perhaps you need a spouse someday.
Perhaps God has called you to singleness for this season—or perhaps for life.
But every Christian needs Christ.
And Christians need the body of Christ.
Paul describes believers not as disconnected religious consumers but as members of one body (1 Corinthians 12).
An eye cannot tell the hand:
“I have no need of you.”
Imagine your hand announcing independence from your body.
It would not become free.
It would die.
Some believers are spiritually starving while insisting they do not need anybody.
“I worship by myself.”
“I don't need church.”
“I don't trust Christians.”
“God knows my heart.”
Some of those statements may have pain underneath them.
But pain should be brought to Jesus for healing, not allowed to become lifelong permission for isolation.
The church is imperfect because the church contains redeemed sinners.
You may encounter disappointment.
You may need discernment.
You may sometimes need to leave an unhealthy congregation and find a faithful one.
But Christ did not redeem isolated consumers.
He is building a people.
A household.
A body.
A bride.
A family.
And maybe tonight the bravest thing you can do is stop pretending.
Tell somebody:
“I need prayer.”
Tell somebody:
“My marriage needs help.”
Tell somebody:
“I am struggling with temptation.”
Tell somebody:
“I have been drifting from Jesus.”
Tell somebody:
“I am lonely.”
Tell somebody:
“I need a Christian brother.”
“I need a Christian sister.”
“I need discipleship.”
“I need accountability.”
“I need help.”
There is no medal in heaven for suffering silently so convincingly that nobody knew you were drowning.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to write your private details publicly.
But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Or simply:
“pray for me.”
Let somebody know there is a real human being behind that screen who needs the family of Christ right now.
And when you finish reading, do something beyond commenting.
Find a mature, trustworthy believer.
Find a faithful local church.
Find someone who loves Jesus enough not merely to comfort you, but to tell you the truth.
Because sometimes the answer to “It is not good...to be alone” is marriage.
Sometimes it is friendship.
Sometimes it is discipleship.
Sometimes it is reconciliation.
Sometimes it is a small group.
Sometimes it is finally admitting to another believer that you cannot keep carrying everything yourself.
But underneath every legitimate human relationship stands a greater reality:
No human being can replace Jesus.
The goal is not merely to become less lonely.
The goal is reconciliation with God and transformation through Christ.
Maybe you came into this article expecting a debate about Genesis.
Instead, Genesis found you.
Maybe you are the husband who stopped talking.
The wife quietly starving for affection.
The widow who still instinctively reaches toward the empty side of the bed.
The single believer wondering whether God forgot you.
The divorced Christian embarrassed by a chapter you never expected to live.
The pastor surrounded by people who has nobody with whom he feels safe enough to admit he is exhausted.
The young man whose closest relationship is with a screen.
The young woman surrounded by notifications but aching to be truly known.
The believer who stopped attending church after being hurt.
Or the person who does not even know whether you believe any of this anymore.
Jesus sees you.
But please understand what that means.
He does not merely see your loneliness.
He sees your sin too.
Your secrets.
Your pride.
Your lust.
Your bitterness.
Your unbelief.
Your wounds.
Your excuses.
Your attempts to save yourself.
He sees everything we spend our lives editing out.
And still the Gospel invitation stands:
Repent.
Come to Christ.
Receive mercy.
Not cheap grace that excuses rebellion.
Grace that forgives and begins transforming the rebel.
Grace that takes people who were hiding and teaches them to walk in the light.
Grace that turns strangers into brothers and sisters.
Grace that teaches husbands to love sacrificially.
Grace that teaches wives and husbands to forgive.
Grace that gives singles an identity deeper than relationship status.
Grace that gives widows a family.
Grace that restores failures.
Grace that gives lonely people somewhere to belong without pretending another human being can become their god.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior will always come back to Jesus.
Not self-help.
Not religious performance.
Not algorithms.
Jesus.
There may be a night when you need to read it again.
That simple share costs nothing, but it may place this message in front of the person who has been quietly asking God for help.
Send it privately to the believer who stopped showing up.
Send it to the single Christian who has begun believing that being unmarried means being unwanted.
Send it to the person who needs to know that Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
But let us be biblically clear about what that means.
It does not purchase favor from God.
It does not purchase forgiveness.
It does not buy answered prayers.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
If God has blessed you and you believe this ministry is worth helping continue and expand, consider making Gospel Warrior part of your regular Christian generosity.
Not from guilt.
Not from fear.
Not because God needs your money.
Give freely because you want to participate in putting Christ-centered truth in front of another person.
Pray for the ministry.
Follow.
There are many ways to help carry the message.
But before you go, answer one question honestly.
Who knows the real you?
Not the Facebook you.
Not the Sunday-morning you.
Not the “I'm blessed” you.
Not the person everybody assumes is strong.
Who knows when you are tempted?
Who knows when your faith feels weak?
Who knows when your marriage is hurting?
Who knows when you are drifting?
Who can ask you the uncomfortable question?
Who can lift you when you fall?
And whose fall would you notice?
Maybe Genesis 2:18 is about marriage.
It certainly leads there.
But the Bible's answer to human isolation becomes far bigger than a wedding ceremony.
God forms families.
God gives friendships.
God builds His church.
God makes believers members of one body.
And above all, God gives us His Son.
So do not worship marriage.
Do not worship independence either.
Do not make another human being your savior.
And do not make isolation your fortress.
Come out of hiding.
Come back to Scripture.
Come back to faithful Christian community.
Come back to the foot of the cross.
If you have wandered, repent.
If you have fallen, reach out.
If you have been wounded, seek wise and godly healing rather than disappearing forever.
If you are lonely, do not confuse your loneliness with worthlessness.
If you are single, do not believe your life is waiting to begin.
If you are married, do not assume a ring automatically creates intimacy.
And if Jesus Christ is calling you out of darkness today, stop negotiating with grace.
Come home.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, do not ignore that name.
Because perhaps the most dangerous loneliness is not having nobody around you.
Perhaps it is spending years surrounded by people while keeping every door to your heart locked...
and then mistaking hiding for strength.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely to improve the mask.
He came to bring sinners out of hiding, reconcile us to God, and make us part of a redeemed people where grace can finally teach us to be known.
You were never meant to make peace with the darkness simply because you learned how to survive there alone.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “DELIGHT YOURSELF IN THE LORD AND HE WILL GIVE YOU THE DESIRES OF YOUR HEART” — BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN READING THE PROMISE BACKWARDS?
paragraphs: “DELIGHT YOURSELF IN THE LORD AND HE WILL GIVE YOU THE DESIRES OF YOUR HEART” — BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN READING THE PROMISE BACKWARDS?

Psalm 37:4 may be one of the most beautiful promises in Scripture—and one of the easiest to turn into something God never promised. What if the greatest gift in this verse is not God giving you everything your heart wants…but God becoming what your heart wants most?
There is a particular kind of heartbreak Christians do not always know how to talk about.
It happens when you prayed.
Believed.
Waited.
Quoted the verse.

Maybe you even wrote it on a journal page, placed it on your wall, turned it into your phone wallpaper, whispered it through tears at two in the morning, and held onto it when almost everything else seemed to be falling apart.
“Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.”
Psalm 37:4.
So you delighted.
Or at least you tried.
And somewhere inside you, perhaps without realizing it, a quiet agreement began forming:
I will pursue God…and eventually God will give me this.
The marriage.
The healing.
The successful business.
The house.
The child.
The restored relationship.
The financial breakthrough.
The ministry opportunity.
The person you cannot stop thinking about.
The future you have already rehearsed a thousand times in your imagination.
Then the months became years.
The door stayed closed.
Someone else received what you had begged God for.
The relationship ended.
The business failed.
The diagnosis did not disappear.
The opportunity went to somebody else.
The prayer seemed to disappear into heaven without returning with the answer you expected.
And suddenly Psalm 37:4 did not feel comforting anymore.
It felt confusing.
Maybe even cruel.
Because if God promised to give you the desires of your heart…
why are you still carrying desires He has not given you?
That question has quietly wounded more believers than many churches realize.
And perhaps the problem was never the promise.
Perhaps the problem was what we made the promise mean.
Read the ancient Hebrew carefully:
וְהִתְעַנַּג עַל־יְהוָה וְיִתֶּן־לְךָ מִשְׁאֲלֹת לִבֶּךָ
Ve-hit‘annag ‘al-YHWH, ve-yitten lekha mish’alot libbekha.
“Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires—the requests, the petitions—of your heart.”
The Hebrew really does say it.
The verb וְהִתְעַנַּג — ve-hit‘annag is an imperative: delight yourself, take delight, find your pleasure.
And מִשְׁאֲלֹת — mish’alot refers to requests, petitions, desires.
So we do not need to weaken the verse to protect God from difficult questions.
God said what He said.
But here is where everything changes.
David did not write Psalm 37:4 as an isolated inspirational sentence for people building their dream lives.
Psalm 37 begins with something entirely different:
Do not envy evildoers.
Trust in the LORD.
Do good.
Dwell faithfully.
Delight yourself in the LORD.
Commit your way to Him.
Trust Him.
Be still before Him.
Wait for Him.
The entire psalm is confronting the temptation to look at people who seem to be prospering without God and secretly wonder whether following God is worth it.
That context matters enormously.
Because Psalm 37 is not teaching you how to manipulate God into financing your ambitions.
It is teaching you how to remain faithful when somebody else's life makes obedience look foolish.
David even says later:
“A little that a righteous man hath is better than the riches of many wicked.”
Psalm 37:16.
Read that slowly.
A little.

Psalm 37 cannot honestly mean, “Delight in God and He will guarantee you material abundance,” when the same psalm explicitly says the righteous person's little can be better than the wicked person's abundance. The psalm contrasts temporary prosperity with lasting trust in God; it repeatedly calls God's people to faithfulness, patience, righteousness, generosity, and confidence in the LORD.
That destroys the prosperity-gospel version of Psalm 37:4.
But it does not destroy the promise.
It makes the promise infinitely more beautiful.
Because God is offering something deeper than a transaction.
He is offering Himself.
There is a dangerous way to “delight in the Lord.”
God can become the hallway we walk through because we actually want what is behind the next door.
Jesus becomes the means.
The dream becomes the destination.
We pray because we want the relationship.
We worship because we want the breakthrough.
We obey because we want the promotion.
We give because we want the hundredfold return.
We seek God because somewhere underneath our Christian vocabulary is a contract we never realized we wrote:
God, I will give You my devotion if You give me my desired outcome.
But what happens when He doesn't?
That is when the hidden contract is exposed.
And sometimes the unanswered prayer reveals something answered prayers never could:
whether we wanted God…
or merely wanted God to give us something else.
That hurts.
Because there are desires we can baptize with spiritual language while they quietly occupy the throne of our hearts.
There are things we say we are “believing God for” that we have slowly become unable to imagine living without.
There are blessings that have become functional gods.
There are dreams we would never call idols because they look innocent.
Marriage is good.
Children are good.
Health is good.
Financial stability is good.
Fruitful ministry is good.
A home can be good.
Success can be good.
Reconciliation can be beautiful.
But a good thing becomes spiritually dangerous when our heart begins saying:
Jesus plus this equals enough.
The Gospel says something radically different.
Jesus is enough before the prayer is answered.
Jesus is enough while the door remains closed.
Jesus is enough when everybody else appears to be passing you.
Jesus is enough when the thing you wanted becomes the thing God asks you to surrender.
And this is where Psalm 37:4 stops being a refrigerator magnet and becomes a knife.
“Delight yourself in the LORD…”
Not merely in what comes from His hand.
In Him.
There is an enormous difference.
Imagine a child running toward his father every evening.
The father opens his arms.
But the child runs straight past him.
“Did you bring me something?”
Again tomorrow.
“Where is my gift?”
Again next week.
“What did you buy me?”
Eventually the painful question becomes obvious:
Does the child love the father…
or the father's pockets?
Now bring that question into prayer.
If God never gives you the exact life you imagined, is Jesus still worthy?
If the person never comes back…
is Jesus still worthy?
If your bank account never reaches the number you dreamed about…
is Jesus still worthy?
If nobody ever knows your name…
is Jesus still worthy?
If the ministry remains small…
is Jesus still worthy?
If your testimony does not end the way you scripted it…
is Jesus still worthy?
If heaven itself were stripped of every image you have associated with reward, and there stood Christ alone—
would Christ be enough?
That is where delight becomes worship.
And something mysterious begins happening to the heart that truly delights in God.
Its desires begin changing.
Not because Christians stop desiring things.
Not because holiness means becoming emotionally numb.
Not because wanting marriage, provision, healing, children, meaningful work, or restored relationships is inherently sinful.
But because proximity to God rearranges what we love.
The closer you come to Christ, the harder it becomes to remain satisfied with desires that lead you away from Him.
You begin praying differently.
“Lord, give me this.”
slowly becomes…
“Lord, if this will draw me closer to You, give it to me.”
Then deeper still…
“Lord, if this will destroy what You are doing in me, keep it from me.”
And finally, perhaps trembling through tears…
“Lord, I want You more than I want this.”
That prayer costs something.
Ask Jesus.
In Gethsemane, Christ did not pretend suffering was pleasant.
He did not call agony enjoyable.
He brought His anguish before the Father.
Yet His surrender remained complete.
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.”
Luke 22:42.
Christian surrender is not pretending you do not have desires.
It is placing those desires into pierced hands.
And those hands know suffering.
That matters.
Because Psalm 37 ultimately makes fullest sense for the Christian when we stop imagining God as a cosmic vending machine and look toward Jesus Christ.
Jesus did not come primarily to make your earthly dreams come true.
He came because something far more catastrophic had happened.
Sin separated humanity from God.
Our greatest problem was never that we did not have enough money.
Our greatest problem was not singleness.
It was not career disappointment.
It was not lack of influence.
It was not the house we could not afford.
It was sin.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed righteousness we could never manufacture.
We needed rescue.
And Christ came.
The eternal Son of God entered our broken world.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He loved perfectly.
Obeyed perfectly.
And then He walked toward a Roman cross.
The hands that had healed the sick were pierced.
The voice that commanded storms was mocked.
The One through whom all things were made was treated as though He were worthless.
Jesus bore sin and shame.
And on the third day, the grave did not get the final word.
Christ rose.
That is the Gospel.
And suddenly our definition of “the desires of your heart” begins undergoing surgery.
Because grace does not merely give sinners better circumstances.
Grace gives sinners a new heart.
The scandal of Christianity is not that sufficiently faithful people eventually get everything they want.
The scandal is that guilty people can receive what they could never earn:
forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Mercy.
Adoption.
A new identity.
A new life.
Christ.
Maybe you came to God asking Him to rewrite your circumstances.
And He began by rewriting you.
Maybe you wanted Him to remove the wilderness.
He wanted to meet you inside it.
Maybe you begged Him to open the door.
He knew what was waiting behind it.
Maybe what felt like rejection was protection you could not yet recognize.
Maybe what felt like silence was an invitation to roots deeper than feelings.
Maybe the delay exposed an idol.
Maybe the loss revealed where your identity had been hiding.
Maybe the shattered dream brought you to the feet of Jesus in a way the fulfilled dream never would have.
We should be careful here.
We do not know the hidden purpose behind every unanswered prayer.
Scripture does not give us permission to invent explanations for every tragedy.
Sometimes we simply do not know.
Faith does not mean pretending to know God's secret providence.
Faith means knowing God when we do not know why.
There are prayers whose answers may not make sense this side of eternity.
There are graves beside which Christians still weep.
There are faithful believers carrying unanswered questions.
There are people reading these words who have prayed for years.
Please hear this:
Psalm 37:4 is not permission for someone to shame you because your prayer has not been answered.
Your unanswered prayer is not automatic proof that you did not “delight enough.”
Christian faith is not a spiritual formula where sufficient positive thinking forces God's hand.
God is God.
We are not.
And sometimes one of the deepest acts of faith is whispering through tears:
“I still trust You.”
Job worshiped while grieving.
Paul prayed repeatedly concerning his thorn and did not receive the removal he requested; instead, he received sufficient grace.
Jesus Himself prayed in agony before the cross.
Biblical faith has never meant getting every circumstance we desire.
Biblical faith means belonging to God through every circumstance.
And maybe that is why you needed to read this today.
Because perhaps you have been angry with God.
Perhaps you have been afraid to admit it.
You smiled at church.
You posted the verse.
You said, “God is good.”
But privately?
You were disappointed.
Confused.
Maybe jealous.
Maybe exhausted from watching somebody else live the life you asked God for.
You saw their engagement announcement.
Their pregnancy announcement.
Their new house.
Their successful ministry.
Their healing testimony.
Their promotion.
Their family photographs.
And something inside you whispered:
Why them, Lord?
Psalm 37 begins almost exactly there.
“Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious…”
David understood comparison.
He understood looking sideways.
And God's answer was not:
“Compete harder.”
It was:
Trust Me.
Do good.
Delight in Me.
Commit your way to Me.
Rest in Me.
Wait for Me.
That is the pathway surrounding Psalm 37:4.
Perhaps your heart has been exhausted because you have spent years asking God to bless a script He never wrote.
And perhaps today is not the day you abandon hope.
Perhaps today is the day you surrender authorship.
“Jesus…
rewrite my desires.
If what I want will pull me away from You, change what I want.
If what I am chasing has become my identity, expose it.
If I have loved Your gifts more than Your presence, forgive me.
If I have treated prayer like negotiation, forgive me.
If disappointment has hardened me, heal me.
If envy has poisoned my gratitude, cleanse me.
If I have made an idol out of a dream, tear down the altar.
I still have desires.
I still have prayers.
I still have hopes.
But Jesus…
I want You more.”
That is not defeat.
That is freedom.
Because when Christ becomes your treasure, unanswered prayers can still hurt without becoming your master.
You can grieve without abandoning God.
You can desire without demanding.
You can ask boldly without pretending you control the answer.
You can dream without worshiping the dream.
You can lose something precious without losing the One who is infinitely precious.
And when God does bless you?
You can enjoy the blessing without turning it into your god.
That may be one of the hidden beauties of delighting in the LORD.
The heart begins learning the difference between receiving God's gifts and replacing God with His gifts.
Maybe God will give you the marriage.
Maybe He will open the business opportunity.
Maybe reconciliation will come.
Maybe the diagnosis will change.
Maybe the financial door will open.
Maybe the prayer you have whispered for ten years will suddenly become tomorrow's testimony.
Ask.
Seek.
Knock.
Pray boldly.
God is not irritated by the cries of His children.
But hold every dream with open hands.
Because the greatest promise of Christianity is not:
“You will eventually get everything you ever wanted.”
It is something better.
In Christ, you get God.
And once you understand that, Psalm 37:4 becomes breathtaking.
וְהִתְעַנַּג עַל־יְהוָה
Ve-hit‘annag ‘al-YHWH.
Delight yourself in the LORD.
Not merely His blessings.
Not merely His answers.
Not merely His miracles.
Not merely His provision.
Him.
Then bring Him the מִשְׁאֲלֹת לִבֶּךָ — mish’alot libbekha…
the petitions of your heart.
Bring every one.
The embarrassing ones.
The enormous ones.
The broken ones.
The desires you are afraid to say aloud.
Bring them honestly.
But bring them to a Father, not a vending machine.
And trust that the God who sees what you cannot see is wiser than the version of your future you constructed in your imagination.
If this exposed something hidden inside you, do not rush past that conviction.
Maybe your prayer today is simply:
“Jesus, change what my heart wants.”
If that is you, comment those words.
Not to perform spirituality for strangers.
Let it become a confession.
“Jesus, change what my heart wants.”
Someone else reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only believer fighting through disappointment.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
It does not.
They may never tell you.
They may simply need someone to place this truth in front of them today.
Because there may come another night when the unanswered prayer hurts again, comparison returns, and you need to remember:
God never promised to become the servant of your desires.
He calls you into something infinitely better—
to find your delight in Him.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, understand difficult passages in context, confront comfortable distortions, heal through biblical truth, and keep Jesus Christ at the center, you can help this ministry continue and expand.
Not through pressure.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior earns salvation, favor, answered prayer, or spiritual status.
Scripture is too clear for manipulation.
Paul wrote:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ, μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης· ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός.
“Each one” should give according to what has been purposed in the heart, not from grief or ἀνάγκη — anankē, compulsion or necessity, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which support should be offered. Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted through spiritual coercion.

Your support helps us keep creating Scripture-centered content designed to point people away from deception, despair, shame, shallow Christianity, and spiritual confusion—and toward Jesus Christ, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, discipleship, and transformation.
And there is another way to support that costs nothing:
A share helps carry the message farther.
Both can serve the Gospel when they are done freely, prayerfully, and for God's glory rather than ours.
But the merchandise is not the heart of this.
Jesus is.
The mission is.
People are.
Souls matter more than algorithms.
Truth matters more than reach.
And if this ministry grows, may it grow for one reason above all:
that more people encounter biblical truth and are pointed toward Jesus Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend struggling with faith.
Invite the believer who has become spiritually cold.
Invite the person who has never understood the Gospel.
Invite the Christian who looks strong online but is barely holding together behind the screen.
you cannot buy God's grace.
Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Your money cannot purchase forgiveness.
Your generosity cannot erase your sin.
Only Jesus saves.
The cross is enough.
So come to Christ before you come to anything we offer.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring Him the heart you have actually been carrying—not the polished version you show everybody else.
Bring the envy.
Bring the disappointment.
Bring the unanswered prayer.
Bring the dream.
Bring the anger.
Bring the confusion.
Bring the secret resentment you felt when someone else received what you wanted.
Bring the desire you are terrified God might ask you to surrender.
And discover what countless wounded believers eventually discover:
sometimes Jesus does not begin by giving you the life you wanted.
Sometimes He begins by resurrecting the heart that wanted it.
And one day you may look backward at the prayer you thought God ignored…
the door you thought He should have opened…
the relationship you thought you could never survive without…
the season you begged Him to end…
and realize that while you were asking God to rewrite your circumstances,
Jesus was rewriting you.
That is grace.
Scandalous grace.
Grace that forgives sinners.
Grace that breaks idols.
Grace that survives disappointment.
Grace that teaches trembling hearts to trust again.
