That is why we keep building.
The Sabbath year ultimately confronted Israel with a terrifyingly simple question.
Can God be trusted when obedience requires open hands?
Maybe that is the question waiting for us too.
We spend our lives planting.
Building.
Collecting.
Protecting.
Planning.
Trying to guarantee tomorrow.
Then Scripture walks into our carefully managed field and reminds us:
The land belongs to God.
The harvest belongs to God.
Our lives belong to God.
Our salvation belongs to Christ.
And grace cannot be harvested by human effort.
It must be received.
So perhaps tonight the bravest thing you can do is stop pretending you are your own provider, your own redeemer, your own refuge, and your own god.
Open your hands.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Give where God leads you to give.
Release what He tells you to release.
Work faithfully where He tells you to work.
Care for the vulnerable.
Stop hiding.
Trust Him.
And come again to Jesus.
Because one day every field we spent our lives protecting will belong to someone else.
But the soul that belongs to Christ has found a treasure death itself cannot harvest away.
Maybe the field had to become quiet before your heart could finally hear the voice of the One who owned it all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE LOVERS HEAR EACH OTHER, SEARCH FOR EACH OTHER, MISS EACH OTHER, AND LONG FOR EACH OTHER—BIBLICAL ROMANCE IS NOT EMOTIONLESS
paragraphs: THE LOVERS HEAR EACH OTHER, SEARCH FOR EACH OTHER, MISS EACH OTHER, AND LONG FOR EACH OTHER—BIBLICAL ROMANCE IS NOT EMOTIONLESS
Somewhere along the way, some Christians became so afraid of lust that they almost became afraid of love. But Scripture never was.
There is a woman awake at night because the man she loves is absent.
She reaches for him.
He is not there.
She searches.
She cannot find him.
She gets up.
She walks through the city.
She asks the watchmen if they have seen him.
Why?
Because she misses him.
Because love has made absence painful.
And somehow this scene is sitting right there in the Bible.
Not in a secular romance novel.
Not in a Hollywood screenplay.
Not in a forbidden diary somebody hid beneath a mattress.
In Scripture.
The Song of Songs gives us these startling Hebrew words:
עַל־מִשְׁכָּבִי בַּלֵּילוֹת בִּקַּשְׁתִּי אֵת שֶׁאָהֲבָה נַפְשִׁי
ʿal-mishkavi balleilot biqqashti et she’ahavah nafshi…
“On my bed at night, I sought the one whom my soul loves…”
Then comes the ache:
בִּקַּשְׁתִּיו וְלֹא מְצָאתִיו
“I sought him, but I did not find him.”
—Song of Songs 3:1
Read that slowly.
The one whom my soul loves.
She misses him.
She searches for him.
She longs to find him.
And God did not blush and remove those words from His Bible.
Maybe we should stop pretending biblical romance is emotionless.
Because sometimes Christians have been taught a strange version of love.
Be committed—but do not be too emotional.
Be faithful—but do not be too passionate.
Marry—but somehow pretend attraction does not matter.
Love your spouse—but never speak as though you actually ache for their presence.
Desire marriage—but feel vaguely guilty for wanting to be wanted.
We rightly warn people against lust.
We rightly warn against sexual immorality.
We rightly preach holiness.
But holiness does not require emotional anesthesia.
Purity is not the absence of affection.
Biblical self-control is not the death of tenderness.
And godly romance is not two Christians signing a theological contract and then spending fifty years pretending they never desperately wanted to hold each other.
The Bible is far more human than that.
The lovers hear each other.
They search for each other.
They miss each other.
They admire each other.
They delight in each other.
They long for each other.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs permission to understand something:
Wanting to be deeply loved is not automatically carnality.
The problem is not that the human heart longs to love.
The problem is what sin does with that longing.
There is a difference.
Long before Song of Songs, there was another scene.
A man sees a woman.
And something happens inside him.
Genesis says that when God brought the woman to Adam, Adam responded:
זֹאת הַפַּעַם עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי
Zot happaʿam, ʿetsem meʿatsamai uvasar mibbesari.
“This one, at last, is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
—Genesis 2:23
Do not miss those little words:
“At last.”
There is recognition there.
Wonder.
Arrival.
Someone corresponding to him.
Then Scripture gives us the foundation of marriage:
A man leaves father and mother, clings to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
Before betrayal entered Eden…
before lust distorted desire…
before pornography commercialized bodies…
before adultery shattered homes…
before manipulation turned affection into leverage…
before people learned to use sex without covenant and covenant without tenderness…
God created man and woman.
Marriage was not Satan's invention.
Romantic love was not Hollywood's invention.
Human sexuality was not invented by pornography.
The enemy did not create these gifts.
He corrupted them.
And there is an enormous difference between creation and corruption.
Maybe that is why Song of Songs can sound almost shocking to ears accustomed to treating Christianity as emotionally sterile.
Listen.
The woman hears something.
קוֹל דּוֹדִי
Qol dodi.
“The voice of my beloved!”
—Song of Songs 2:8
You can almost hear the excitement.
He is coming.
The beloved approaches, and then she remembers his voice calling her:
קוּמִי לָךְ רַעְיָתִי יָפָתִי וּלְכִי־לָךְ
Qumi lakh, raʿyati, yafati, uleki-lakh.
“Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.”
—Song of Songs 2:10
That is not cold.
That is not mechanical.
That is not embarrassed affection.
The lovers speak.
They listen.
They notice.
They praise.
They desire presence.
They experience separation.
They experience reunion.
And sometimes they experience pain.
That matters.
Because maybe you know exactly what it means to miss somebody.
Maybe there is a name you still cannot hear casually.
Maybe there is a chair that became painful after someone left.
Maybe there are photographs you avoid because one image can resurrect an entire season.
Maybe you loved somebody who did not stay.
Maybe your marriage has become painfully quiet.
Maybe you sleep beside someone who feels a thousand miles away.
Maybe you are single, and underneath all the Christian language about “waiting on God's timing,” there are nights when you simply wish somebody would choose you.
Not use you.
Not hide you.
Not keep you as an option.
Choose you.
Maybe you are divorced.
Maybe betrayed.
Maybe widowed.
Maybe still recovering from a relationship where the person who said “I love you” slowly taught you to fear love.
And perhaps you have wondered whether your longing itself was shameful.
Scripture gives us a better answer.
Longing can be beautiful.
But longing also needs redemption.
Because we can turn a person into a god.
We can ask another human being to heal wounds only Christ can reach.
We can demand from romance what romance was never designed to provide.
We can call obsession “love.”
We can call possession “protection.”
We can call lust “chemistry.”
We can call emotional dependency “soulmates.”
We can ignore character because somebody makes our heart race.
We can stay where God is being dishonored because loneliness frightens us more than compromise.
And that is where biblical romance confronts modern romance.
The Bible celebrates love without worshiping the lover.
It celebrates desire without making desire sovereign.
It celebrates the body without separating the body from covenant, faithfulness, holiness, and responsibility.
It allows lovers to burn with affection while still insisting that God remains God.
That distinction can save your heart.
Because no husband can be Jesus.
No wife can be Jesus.
No boyfriend can be Jesus.
No girlfriend can be Jesus.
No wedding can resurrect your soul.
No human kiss can permanently silence the deepest cry inside fallen humanity.
You were created for relationship with people, yes.
But beneath every human hunger is a deeper reality:
You were created for God.
And this is where the love story becomes bigger than romance.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to teach lonely people how to find partners.
He came to rescue sinners.
He came for adulterers.
For the sexually broken.
For the abandoned.
For the ashamed.
For the lustful.
For the betrayed.
For the betrayer who repents.
For the person who gave too much away.
For the person who took what was not theirs.
For the person carrying memories they desperately wish they could erase.
For the person whose private search history would humiliate them if exposed.
For the woman who thinks her past made her unlovable.
For the man who thinks his failures permanently disqualified him.
Christ came into the scandal.
And He brought grace.
Not cheap grace that says sin does not matter.
Grace that tells the truth about sin and then pays an unimaginable price to redeem the sinner.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend our corruption was beautiful.
He bore it.
The Greek New Testament announces the heart of the Gospel with words Christians should never become numb to:
Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν
Christos hyper hēmōn apethanen.
“Christ died for us.”
See Romans 5:8.
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we became worthy romantic partners.
Not after we finally stopped struggling.
Christ moved toward sinners.
The Gospel is not the story of good people climbing toward God.
It is the story of the holy Son of God coming down to rescue people who could never save themselves.
That changes romance too.
Because when Christ becomes the center, love stops asking only:
“What can you make me feel?”
Love begins asking:
“How can I honor Christ in the way I treat you?”
That changes dating.
That changes marriage.
That changes sexuality.
That changes conflict.
That changes forgiveness.
That changes attraction.
That changes what you tolerate.
That changes what you refuse.
Biblical love is deeply emotional, but it is more than emotion.
Feelings can say, “I want you.”
Covenant says, “I will be faithful.”
Attraction can say, “You are beautiful.”
Love says, “Your soul matters to God.”
Lust asks, “How much of you can I take?”
Love asks, “How faithfully can I seek your good?”
Manipulation says, “Prove that you love me.”
Godly affection says, “I refuse to make you sin in order to keep me.”
That is romance redeemed.
And Song of Songs gives us perhaps its most unforgettable declaration:
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Ki ʿazzah khammavet ahavah.
“For love is strong as death.”
—Song of Songs 8:6
The poem continues with imagery of blazing fire and an astonishing declaration:
Many waters cannot extinguish love.
Floods cannot sweep it away.
That is powerful language.
But Scripture never tells us that every intense feeling is therefore holy.
Intensity alone proves nothing.
You can intensely desire the wrong person.
You can intensely desire someone else's spouse.
You can intensely desire what God has forbidden.
You can intensely miss somebody God rescued you from.
Your tears do not automatically make a relationship righteous.
Your chemistry does not rewrite Scripture.
Your loneliness does not turn disobedience into God's will.
That may hurt.
But sometimes grace hurts before it heals.
Sometimes Jesus loves us enough to separate us from the thing we kept calling love because He can see what it is doing to our souls.
And maybe this article found you while you are trying to return to someone you know keeps pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe you keep rereading messages.
Checking whether they are online.
Remembering the nights when everything felt alive.
Missing the person so badly that you have started editing the memories.
You remember the tenderness.
You forget the compromise.
You remember being held.
You forget how often you were spiritually disappearing.
You remember the apology.
You forget the cycle.
You remember what they promised.
You forget what they repeatedly chose.
Listen carefully:
Missing someone does not always mean you are supposed to return to them.
Sometimes grief is simply the price of finally walking away from what was destroying you.
And sometimes the person you need to run toward is not the person you lost.
It is Jesus.
Because there is another voice in Scripture calling.
Christ describes Himself as the Good Shepherd, and He says His sheep hear His voice.
He knows them.
They follow Him.
See John 10:27.
Do you see the deeper beauty?
The lovers hear each other.
But above every human voice, the redeemed learn to recognize the voice of Christ.
The lovers search for each other.
But Jesus spoke of the shepherd who searches for the lost.
The lovers ache in separation.
But sin created the separation no human romance can ultimately repair.
And the Gospel announces that God acted.
Christ came.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ calls.
Christ forgives.
Christ restores.
Christ makes sinners new.
That is why Christian romance cannot ultimately be about finding somebody who “completes” you.
Christ is not the missing decoration around your love story.
He is Lord.
And when two people belong to Him, romance can become something beautiful precisely because it is no longer required to become their god.
You can say, “I miss you,” without saying, “I cannot exist without you.”
You can say, “I desire you,” without saying, “Therefore I am entitled to you.”
You can say, “You are beautiful,” without turning a body into an object.
You can say, “Stay,” while still surrendering the future to God.
You can love fiercely and worship Christ supremely.
That is freedom.
And married couples, perhaps you need to hear this too.
Do not become so familiar with your spouse that you stop pursuing the person you once prayed God would give you.
Speak.
Listen.
Notice.
Flirt with your spouse.
Tell them they are beautiful.
Tell him you appreciate him.
Tell her what you still notice.
Reach for the hand you have held ten thousand times.
Put the phone down.
Look into the face across the table.
Ask what is happening inside their heart.
Pray together even when it feels awkward.
Repent quickly.
Forgive biblically.
Protect your marriage from secret appetites.
And please—do not outsource to strangers on a screen the desire that belongs inside your covenant.
Pornography trains the eyes to consume bodies without covenant.
Jesus teaches us to see people as souls bearing God's image.
Adultery says desire outranks faithfulness.
Christ teaches us that obedience sometimes means crucifying desires that feel overwhelmingly alive.
Christian marriage does not destroy passion.
It gives passion a holy home.
And single believer, your life is not God's waiting room.
You are not half a Christian until somebody puts a ring on your finger.
Jesus was not incomplete.
Paul was not spiritually defective.
Marriage is a gift.
Singleness can also be a gift.
And neither marital status determines your worth before God.
So do not marry simply because silence scares you.
Do not accept spiritual incompatibility because the attention feels intoxicating.
Do not trade conviction for companionship.
Do not hand your future to someone who wants your body but resents your devotion to Jesus.
You are not looking merely for someone who makes your heart beat faster.
You need character.
Truth.
Repentance.
Faithfulness.
Humility.
Someone who understands that love must eventually survive mornings when nobody feels cinematic.
Because real biblical romance is not less emotional than the world's version.
It is deeper.
It has butterflies, but it cannot survive on butterflies.
It has desire, but desire bows to holiness.
It has tenderness, but tenderness grows backbone.
It has longing, but longing refuses idolatry.
It has passion, but passion learns covenant.
It has forgiveness, but forgiveness never calls evil good.
It has sacrifice.
Patience.
Repentance.
Truth.
Grace.
And Christ at the center.
Maybe that is what your heart has actually been looking for.
Not emotionless Christianity.
Not reckless passion.
Redeemed love.
Love that can look another human being in the eyes and say:
“I desire you, but I will not worship you.”
“I love you, but I will not help you rebel against God.”
“I want you close, but I want Jesus honored more.”
“I will tell you the truth because your soul matters more than my comfort.”
And perhaps the most romantic thing a Christian can ever say is not merely:
“I cannot live without you.”
Maybe it is:
“I want to walk with you toward Jesus.”
Because eventually every beautiful face ages.
Bodies change.
Circumstances collapse.
Money disappears.
Illness comes.
Feelings fluctuate.
And unless Christ returns first, one lover may eventually stand beside the grave of the other.
That sounds unbearable.
Because love makes loss expensive.
But Christians grieve differently because death does not get the final sentence.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
And those who belong to Him possess a hope stronger than the cemetery.
Christian love can stare at mortality without surrendering to despair because the Gospel declares that Jesus rewrites endings.
That is why this message matters.
Maybe somebody on your Facebook friends list has almost given up on love.
Maybe somebody is confusing lust with intimacy.
Maybe somebody is about to return to an abusive or spiritually destructive relationship simply because loneliness became unbearable.
Maybe a married couple is quietly drifting apart.
Maybe a young believer has never been told that attraction is not automatically dirty but must be surrendered to Christ.
Maybe someone feels permanently stained by sexual sin and desperately needs to know that repentance and the blood of Jesus are stronger than their past.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody you know may need truth tonight.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not pretend it did not.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail.
Sometimes three words are enough to stop hiding.
Because feelings have short memories.
There may come a night when loneliness starts rewriting history, when temptation starts negotiating with conviction, or when disappointment whispers that biblical love does not exist.
Come back.
Read it again.
Remember what love is supposed to bow before.
Jesus Christ.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, challenging your compromises, strengthening your walk with Christ, or putting biblical truth in front of people who desperately need it, consider helping us continue and expand this mission.
Supporting Gospel Warrior is not a payment for God's favor.
It cannot purchase salvation.
It does not replace repentance.
It does not make God indebted to you.

The New Testament teaches generosity that is willing rather than coerced. Paul writes that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
So if you already give faithfully through your local church, continue honoring God with biblical generosity there.
But if you also believe this ministry is producing spiritual fruit, you can make Gospel Warrior part of your voluntary monthly giving and missionary support.

If God has given you the ability and conviction to help, your monthly support can become one practical expression of generosity toward Gospel work—not buying blessing, but helping make ministry possible.
One share can reach a marriage in trouble.
One tag can reach a friend hiding heartbreak.
One comment can make another struggling Christian realize they are not alone.
One saved article can become truth somebody returns to at 2:00 in the morning.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
Let them encounter Jesus.
But the greatest reason to stay close is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Truth.
Conviction.
Encouragement.
Accountability.
Spiritual sharpening.
And comment—not for empty engagement, but because your testimony, confession, prayer request, or declaration of faith may become the sentence another wounded person needed to see.
Because biblical romance was never emotionless.
The lovers hear each other.
They search for each other.
They miss each other.
They long for each other.
They delight in each other.
But redeemed love eventually learns something even greater:
No human being was ever meant to carry the weight of being your Savior.
So love deeply.
Desire faithfully.
Guard your heart wisely.
Honor marriage.
Flee sexual immorality.
Repent when you fall.
Forgive as Christ teaches.
Refuse counterfeit intimacy.
And never make an idol out of the person whose hand you hope to hold.
Hold their hand.
But give Jesus your throne.

Because after every heartbreak, every betrayal, every lonely night, every sinful chapter, every shattered expectation, every tear on the pillow, and every scandal you thought permanently ruined the story, there remains a Savior with nail-scarred hands who still knows how to write redemption.
And sometimes the heart spends years searching for someone to love it perfectly before discovering that Perfect Love had been calling its name all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CONTEXT CAN DESTROY A COMFORTABLE INTERPRETATION—AND SAVE YOU FROM FALSE TEACHING
paragraphs: CONTEXT CAN DESTROY A COMFORTABLE INTERPRETATION—AND SAVE YOU FROM FALSE TEACHING
The Most Dangerous Lie in the Church May Be a Bible Verse That Was Never Meant to Say What You Were Told It Says
There is something more frightening than hearing a lie.
It is hearing a lie with a Bible verse attached to it.
Because once someone says, “The Bible says…”
we lower our defenses.
We assume the argument is over.
We see chapter and verse.
We hear familiar Christian language.

We feel that little sense of recognition because we have heard the verse preached before, printed on a coffee mug, stitched onto a shirt, posted over a sunrise, turned into a caption, repeated from a pulpit, or shared thousands of times online.
So we think…
It must be true.
But what if the words are actually in the Bible…
and the interpretation still isn’t?
What if the verse is real…
but the meaning you were given is not?
What if you have spent years believing something God never actually promised you because somebody handed you one sentence while quietly leaving the paragraph behind?
That question should make every Christian uncomfortable.
And it should.
Because one of the most sobering scenes in the New Testament involves someone quoting Scripture accurately…
while using it deceptively.
And the person quoting Scripture was Satan.
Read that again.
The devil quoted the Bible.
When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, the tempter brought Him to the pinnacle of the temple and challenged Him to throw Himself down.
Then came words that should disturb every careless reader of Scripture:
“For it is written…”
Satan proceeded to quote Psalm 91.
The quotation was Scripture.
The application was wicked.
The words came from God's Word.
The interpretation was being weaponized against the Son of God.
Jesus did not respond by saying, “That verse isn't in the Bible.”
He answered Scripture with Scripture:
“It is also written…”
and pointed to the command not to put the Lord God to the test.

That encounter in Matthew 4:5–7 should permanently destroy the idea that merely quoting a Bible verse proves that someone's teaching is biblical. Satan cited Psalm 91:11–12 while tempting Jesus; Christ answered from Deuteronomy 6:16 and exposed the misuse.
Think about what that means.
You can quote Scripture…
and violate Scripture.
You can memorize Scripture…
and misunderstand Scripture.
You can preach Scripture…
and manipulate Scripture.
You can build an entire theology out of biblical words while missing the biblical message.
A verse removed from its context can become a ventriloquist's dummy.
Someone can make it say almost anything.
And perhaps this is where the knife turns toward us.
Because false teaching does not always arrive looking evil.
Sometimes it arrives carrying a Bible.
Sometimes it sounds encouraging.
Sometimes it makes you feel powerful.
Sometimes it confirms exactly what you desperately wanted to believe.
Sometimes it comes from somebody you trust.
Sometimes it comes from somebody with millions of followers.
Sometimes it comes from your favorite preacher.
And sometimes…
it comes from something you have believed so long that questioning it feels like questioning God Himself.
But those are not the same thing.
Your interpretation is not God.
My interpretation is not God.
A pastor's interpretation is not God.
A denomination's tradition is not God.
A viral Christian post is not God.
Scripture is authoritative precisely because our interpretations must remain accountable to what Scripture actually says.
That is why Acts gives us one of the healthiest pictures of biblical faith imaginable.
When Paul preached in Berea, the people did not simply swallow everything because an apostle said it.
Acts 17:11 says they were:
“ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφὰς καθ᾽ ἡμέραν”
anakrinontes tas graphas kath’ hēmeran
—examining the Scriptures day by day.
The key idea in ἀνακρίνοντες (anakrinontes) is examination, investigation, careful evaluation.
They received the message eagerly…
and then checked it.
Luke calls that noble.
Not rebellious.
Not cynical.
Not disrespectful.
Noble.
They listened eagerly and examined Scripture daily to determine whether what they were hearing was true.
That means biblical discernment is not unbelief.
Testing teaching by Scripture is obedience.
You do not honor a preacher by refusing to examine what he teaches.
You honor God by caring enough about truth to examine everything.
Paul himself later tells Timothy:
“ὀρθοτομοῦντα τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας”
orthotomounta ton logon tēs alētheias
—rightly handling the word of truth.
That language appears in 2 Timothy 2:15, where Timothy is commanded to present himself to God as an approved worker who correctly handles God's truth.
Notice the implication.
If Scripture can be handled rightly…
it can be handled wrongly.
And wrong handling does not always mean changing the words.
Sometimes it means keeping the words…
but removing everything around them.
This is where some comfortable interpretations begin to collapse.
Take one of the most famous Christian sentences in the world:
“I can do all things through Christ…”
Beautiful.
True.
Inspired.
But what are the “all things”?
If you isolate Philippians 4:13, you can turn it into a slogan about limitless achievement.
Win the championship.
Build the company.
Get the promotion.
Reach the dream.
Crush every obstacle.
Nothing can stop you.
Except Paul wasn't writing from a motivational seminar about achieving whatever ambition entered his imagination.
Read backward.
Paul says he learned contentment.
He knew abundance.
He knew need.
He knew what it was to be well fed.
He knew what it was to be hungry.
Then comes the famous declaration.
In context, the verse is not primarily a blank check for accomplishing any dream you choose.
It is a confession of Christ's sustaining strength through radically changing circumstances—including suffering and lack.
Context did not make the verse weaker.
Context made it deeper.
Without context, Philippians 4:13 can become:
“Jesus will help me achieve whatever I want.”
With context, it becomes something far more powerful:
“Whether I have much or almost nothing, Christ is enough to sustain me.”
One interpretation feeds ambition.

The other can keep a suffering believer alive at 2:17 in the morning when the bank account is empty, the diagnosis is terrifying, the job disappeared, the relationship collapsed, and there is no victory trophy waiting tomorrow.
That believer does not merely need a motivational slogan.
They need Christ.
And context gives Christ back to the verse.
Then consider Jeremiah 29:11.
You have probably seen it everywhere.
Plans.
Prosperity.
Hope.
Future.
But listen to the surrounding story.
These words were spoken to people experiencing exile.
Jeremiah speaks of seventy years connected with Babylon before restoration.
The Hebrew of Jeremiah 29:11 includes the beautiful expression:
“מַחְשְׁבוֹת שָׁלוֹם”
maḥshevot shalom
—plans/thoughts of shalom.
Shalom carries the sense of peace, welfare, well-being, wholeness.
But God's promise was not a guarantee that every individual Israelite would immediately escape hardship.
The context includes waiting.
Exile.
Discipline.
Generational time.
Seeking God.
Restoration according to God's covenant purposes.
Jeremiah 29:10–14 explicitly places the promise within Babylonian exile, the seventy-year horizon, prayer, wholehearted seeking, and eventual restoration.
Again…
context does not ruin the promise.
It rescues it from sentimentality.
The message becomes something stronger than, “God will make my immediate circumstances comfortable.”
It becomes:
God remains faithful even when His people are living through a chapter they desperately wish He would end.
Maybe somebody reading this needs that distinction.
Because you prayed.
And things did not immediately improve.
You believed.
And the door still closed.
You obeyed.
And somehow life became harder.
You quoted promises.
You cried.
You fasted.
You asked other people to pray.
And somewhere underneath all your disappointment came the terrifying whisper:
“Maybe God failed me.”
But what if God did not fail you?
What if somebody taught you to expect something from a passage that the passage never actually promised?
There is grief in discovering that.
Real grief.
Because sometimes losing a false interpretation feels like losing God.
It isn't.
Sometimes it is the beginning of finally seeing Him clearly.
There is another familiar sentence:
“Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them.”
It is often used to reassure a tiny prayer meeting that Jesus is present.
And there is certainly nothing wrong with Christians taking comfort in Christ's presence.
But read Matthew 18:15–20.

Jesus has been speaking about confronting sin, witnesses, bringing a matter before the church, binding and loosing, agreement, and then the statement concerning two or three gathered in His name appears. The immediate literary setting concerns serious matters of church discipline and communal authority, not a minimum attendance requirement for Jesus to arrive.
Context changes things.
And sometimes context destroys sermons we loved.
That hurts.
But truth is worth the pain.
Because there is something worse than having your favorite interpretation destroyed.
Building your life on something God never said.
This is why context matters.
Who is speaking?
Who is being addressed?
What happened before this sentence?
What happens afterward?
What problem is the author addressing?
What kind of literature am I reading?
Is this command, narrative, poetry, wisdom, prophecy, apocalyptic imagery, parable, lament, historical description, or doctrinal instruction?
Is this promise made to a particular person or covenant community?
Is there a principle that legitimately extends beyond that original audience?
How does this passage fit within the book?
How does the book fit within the whole biblical story?
And ultimately…
how does this lead us toward the revelation of God fulfilled in Jesus Christ?
Because the goal of biblical interpretation is not merely winning arguments.
It is knowing God truthfully.
This matters especially in an age where almost anyone can become a teacher.
A phone.
A microphone.
A ring light.
A dramatic soundtrack.
A Bible opened on a desk.
And suddenly somebody's interpretation can reach a million people before anyone asks whether the verse actually means what the video claims.
Emotional intensity is not exegesis.
Confidence is not exegesis.
Virality is not exegesis.
A large following is not exegesis.
Saying “God told me” loudly enough does not exempt a teaching from examination.
And having tears in your eyes does not transform an interpretation into truth.
The Bereans teach us something desperately needed today:
You can receive the Word eagerly while still checking the teaching carefully.
That balance matters.
Some people become so suspicious that nobody can teach them anything.
Others become so trusting that anybody holding a Bible can teach them anything.
Scripture commends neither gullibility nor cynical pride.
It calls us toward humble discernment.
Open Bible.
Open heart.
Eyes on Christ.
And courage enough to admit:
“I may have been wrong.”
Those five words can become the doorway to enormous spiritual freedom.
I may have been wrong.
Not Scripture.
Me.
Maybe I inherited an interpretation without ever checking it.
Maybe I heard it when I was twelve.
Maybe my favorite preacher said it.
Maybe everybody in my church says it.
Maybe I have quoted it myself hundreds of times.
Maybe I have taught it.
Maybe I have posted it.
Maybe I have corrected other people with it.
And maybe…
I was wrong.
What happens then?
Grace.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus does not save people because they have perfectly interpreted every verse.
He saves sinners.
Confused sinners.
Proud sinners.
Religious sinners.
Broken sinners.
Self-righteous sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
People who misunderstood.
People who ran.
People who hid.
People who thought they knew everything.
People who discovered they knew almost nothing.
Peter misunderstood.
The disciples misunderstood.
Religious leaders knew enormous amounts of Scripture and still failed to recognize the One standing before them.
Yet Christ went to the cross.
Not because we interpreted everything perfectly…
but because we desperately needed a Savior.
At Calvary, the deepest problem in your life was not merely that you had bad theology.
It was sin.
And Jesus did not solve that problem with a motivational quotation.
He gave Himself.
The sinless Son of God bore sin.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The One rejected by men became the refuge of sinners.
The tomb received Him.
Then the tomb lost Him.
Jesus Christ rose.
And suddenly Christianity was not ultimately about collecting inspirational sentences.
It was about a crucified and risen King.
That changes how we read everything.
We do not come to Scripture asking only:
“What can this verse do for my dream?”
We begin asking:
“What has God revealed?”
“What did He actually say?”
“What does this reveal about His character?”
“Where have I been resisting Him?”
“What needs to change in me?”
“How does this point me toward Christ?”
“Where do I need to repent?”
Because sometimes the interpretation we desperately want is the interpretation that leaves us exactly as we are.
And sometimes context takes that comfortable interpretation by the throat…
and kills it.
Good.
Let it die.
If an interpretation must ignore the surrounding verses to survive, it deserves to die.
If a doctrine requires us to pretend the original audience never existed, examine it.
If a teacher repeatedly needs fragments instead of passages, pay attention.
If an interpretation consistently makes you the hero, your prosperity the destination, your desires the center, and God the mechanism for getting what you want…
look again.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of God orbiting you.
It is the story of everything finding its rightful center in Christ.
And there is another uncomfortable place where context must govern us.
Money.
Giving.
Support.
Even Christian ministries can mishandle Scripture here.
The Old Testament explicitly speaks of the tithe in Israel; Leviticus 27:30 describes a tenth of the land's produce as belonging to the LORD and being holy to Him.
But when Paul addresses Christian generosity in 2 Corinthians 9, listen carefully to the language:
“μὴ ἐξ ἀνάγκης”
mē ex anankēs
—not out of compulsion.
And:
“ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός”
hilaron gar dotēn agapa ho Theos
—for God loves a cheerful giver.
Paul says giving should be purposeful and willing, “not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
So let us refuse to manipulate what we have spent this entire article warning against.
You do not purchase God's favor by supporting Gospel Warrior.
You do not buy salvation.
You do not buy answered prayers.
It does not replace belonging to and serving in a faithful local church.
It does not replace generosity toward those in need.
And we will not tell you that God will love you more if you send money.
Jesus Christ cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be bought.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
Christ paid the price.
But biblical generosity is real.
Supporting faithful Gospel work is real.
Partnership in spreading truth is real.

And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, brought you back to Christ, strengthened you during a dark night, confronted your sin, encouraged your repentance, helped restore your prayer life, or placed biblical truth in front of you when you desperately needed it…
then you can choose to become part of helping that work continue and expand.
Not under compulsion.
Not because we can promise you financial blessing in return.
But freely.
Cheerfully.
As an act of voluntary Christian generosity and partnership.
And there is something else you can give that costs nothing.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Someone may be living under false teaching.
Someone may be furious with God for breaking a promise God never made.
Someone may be following a teacher simply because that teacher sounds confident.
Someone may be one carefully explained passage away from opening the Bible again.
Send it privately to the person you know will never comment publicly but desperately needs to read it.
Because the next time a thirty-second clip gives you a life-changing doctrine from half a verse…
you may need this reminder:
Read before it.
Read after it.
Find the audience.
Find the argument.
Find the context.
Test the teaching.
Then follow the truth wherever it leads.
Even when it hurts.
Especially when it hurts.
Has there ever been a Bible verse you discovered you had misunderstood for years?
What changed when you finally saw its context?
Your story might help somebody else realize that correction is not humiliation.
Sometimes correction is mercy.
And if this struck somewhere deeper—somewhere between conviction and surrender—do not hide behind religious language.
Tell the truth.
Maybe your comment simply needs to be:
Because there are people reading the comments who need to discover they are not the only ones who have had to unlearn something.
Stay close to Scripture.
Stay teachable.
And invite someone else to follow too.
A family member.
A struggling believer.
A seeker.
A Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Even the unbelieving friend who keeps asking difficult questions.
But hear this clearly after everything we have just studied.
Never give because someone tells you God's grace has a monthly price.
The New Testament instruction itself says Christian giving must not be “under compulsion.”
Truth matters even when truth costs us conversions.
Because if we must twist Scripture to fund the preaching of Scripture…
we have already betrayed the thing we claimed to defend.
And perhaps that is the final test.
Will we still love the Bible when it destroys one of our favorite beliefs?
Will we still call God good when context removes the promise we thought guaranteed an easier life?
Will we let Jesus correct our theology?
Will we allow Scripture to disagree with us?
Because the Bible was never given merely to decorate the life you already decided to live.
The Word confronts.
Corrects.
Exposes.
Comforts.
Wounds our pride.
Strengthens our weakness.
Reveals our sin.
Announces grace.
And ultimately points us beyond ourselves toward Jesus Christ.
So open the Bible again.
Not hunting for a sentence that agrees with you.
Come hungry.
Come humble.
Come willing to repent.
Read the verse.
Then read the paragraph.
Read the chapter.
Understand the book.
Ask what the original author was communicating to the original audience.
Compare Scripture with Scripture.
Test what teachers tell you.
Test what Gospel Warrior tells you.
Test what your favorite pastor tells you.
Test what you have told yourself.
And when Scripture proves you wrong…
do not run from it.
Thank God for loving you enough to correct you.
Because discovering that your interpretation was wrong does not mean Jesus abandoned you.
Sometimes it means Jesus is leading you out of something false.
And maybe the scandal you are afraid to admit today is simply this:
“I believed something God never actually said.”
There is grace for that too.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Release what Scripture will not support.
Return to Christ.
He is not threatened by your questions.
He is not diminished when your favorite interpretation collapses.
Truth does not fear examination.
And the Jesus who meets you after your comfortable interpretation dies is infinitely better than the imaginary Christ we create from isolated verses.
Remember this when the next preacher sounds irresistible.
Remember it when the next viral Christian video gives you goosebumps.
Remember it when someone says, “The Bible clearly says…”
Remember the wilderness.
Remember the devil knew how to say:
“It is written.”
Then remember Jesus knew what came around the quotation.
Follow because none of us outgrows our need to return to Scripture.
Because sometimes the verse that destroys your comfortable theology is the very verse God uses to rescue your faith.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES THE BIBLE SHOW THE JEALOUSY, FAVORITISM, AND FAMILY CHAOS THAT SO OFTEN FOLLOW POLYGAMY?
paragraphs: WHY DOES THE BIBLE SHOW THE JEALOUSY, FAVORITISM, AND FAMILY CHAOS THAT SO OFTEN FOLLOW POLYGAMY?

Scripture never needed to hide the wreckage. The broken homes, competing wives, wounded children, divided affections, and bitter rivalries are there for a reason—and what they reveal about marriage, sin, grace, and Jesus Christ may be far more personal than we want to admit.
There is something deeply uncomfortable about the Bible.
It tells the truth about its heroes.
Not the polished truth.
Not the sanitized Sunday-school version.
The ugly truth.
Abraham believed God... and still made devastating choices.
Jacob encountered God... and still presided over a painfully fractured household.
David was called a man after God’s own heart... and his family became the scene of horrifying dysfunction.
Solomon possessed extraordinary wisdom... yet multiplied wives until the very thing God had warned Israel’s kings about happened: his heart was turned away.
And that raises a question many Christians have quietly wondered but sometimes feel afraid to ask:
If God designed marriage, why does the Bible contain so many men with multiple wives?
And why—again and again—does jealousy, favoritism, rivalry, rejection, manipulation, wounded children, divided loyalty, and spiritual disaster seem to follow?
Maybe the answer begins with something we desperately need to understand about Scripture.
The Bible recording something is not the same as the Bible approving it.
That distinction changes everything.
Scripture is brutally honest about humanity because Scripture is ultimately telling a story about humanity’s need for a Savior.
The Bible does not airbrush its families.
It lets us walk into their tents.
It lets us hear the arguments.
It lets us see the woman who knows her husband loves someone else more.
It lets us meet the wife desperately hoping another child might finally make her husband love her.
It lets us watch sisters become rivals.
It lets us watch children grow up knowing who Daddy favors.
It lets us see brothers become jealous enough to contemplate murder.
It lets us see kings acquire women as symbols of appetite, power, alliances, and prestige.
And then Scripture quietly asks us to look at the wreckage.
Go all the way back before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before Israel had kings.
Before human civilization had accumulated centuries of brokenness.
Go back to the garden.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew ends with these words:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
One flesh.
The Hebrew verb translated “cleave” is דָּבַק — dabaq, carrying the sense of clinging, holding fast, being joined.
There is something beautifully undivided about the picture.
A man.
His wife.
A covenant union.
One flesh.
Jesus Himself returned to this creation account when questioned about marriage.
He did not begin with Abraham’s household.
He did not begin with Jacob.
He did not begin with David.
He went back to creation.
In Matthew 19:4–6, Jesus said that the Creator made them male and female, and then quoted Genesis:
“For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh... Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh.”
Jesus pointed people backward...
before the compromises...
before the cultural accommodations...
before generations of sinful human behavior...
to the Creator’s design.
That matters.
Because one of our greatest mistakes when reading Scripture is assuming that every behavior practiced by a biblical character represents the biblical ideal.
It does not.
The Bible contains adultery.
That does not endorse adultery.
The Bible contains murder.
That does not endorse murder.
The Bible contains drunkenness, deception, incest, betrayal, idolatry, greed, slavery, violence, cowardice, and horrifying abuses of power.
Scripture records fallen humanity honestly.
And sometimes the consequences become part of the sermon.
Consider Abraham.
God promised Abraham descendants.
But years passed.
Sarah remained barren.
Waiting became painful.
And Genesis 16 records Sarah giving Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abraham.
Then Hagar conceived.
Immediately the household changed.
The text tells us that when Hagar realized she had conceived, Sarah became diminished in her eyes.
Sarah then complained to Abraham.
Abraham handed Hagar back into Sarah’s authority.
Sarah dealt harshly with her.
Hagar fled.
Stop there.
A woman is pregnant.
Another woman is humiliated.
A husband is caught inside the conflict.
Power is being abused.
Someone runs into the wilderness.
This is not presented like paradise.
It is a wounded household.
And yet...
God sees Hagar.
That matters too.
Because even inside human disorder, God remains merciful.
Hagar encounters the God who sees her.
Human beings created the mess.
God entered the pain.
That pattern runs throughout Scripture.
Then comes Jacob.
And if you have ever wondered what favoritism can do to a family, Jacob’s house should make you tremble.
Jacob loved Rachel.
But through Laban’s deception, Jacob first received Leah as his wife.
Genesis 29:30 states plainly that Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Then comes one of the saddest descriptions of a wife anywhere in Genesis.
Genesis 29:31 says:
וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי־שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה
“YHWH saw that Leah was hated...”
The Hebrew word שְׂנוּאָה — senu'ah can express being hated; in a comparative marital context translations sometimes render the idea “unloved” or “less loved.”
Either way, feel the sentence.
God saw Leah.
Her husband had eyes for her sister.
Imagine sleeping beside someone while knowing his heart is reaching across the household toward someone else.
Imagine wondering whether you are enough.
Imagine watching the face of the person you married change when your sister enters the room.
Leah begins having children.
And listen to the ache inside the names and words surrounding those births.
After Reuben, she hopes her husband will love her.
After Simeon, she speaks of the LORD hearing that she is unloved.
After Levi, she hopes:
“Now this time will my husband be joined unto me...”
Do you hear her?
This is not merely ancient genealogy.
This is a woman begging to be chosen.
Maybe that is why her story still hurts thousands of years later.
Because somebody reading this knows what it feels like to keep accomplishing things hoping somebody will finally decide you are worth loving.
Maybe you changed your appearance.
Maybe you became successful.
Maybe you became useful.
Maybe you became religious.
Maybe you kept saying yes because you were terrified that saying no would make somebody leave.
Maybe your heart has been whispering its own version of Leah’s sentence:
“Maybe now they will love me.”
But another child could not heal Leah's marriage.
Because children were never created to repair an adult’s wounded identity.
And eventually something changes in Leah’s language.
When Judah is born, she says:
“Now will I praise the LORD.”
Something in the story turns upward.
The husband who could not give her enough love was no longer the only direction her soul could look.
But the household rivalry did not disappear.
Rachel had her own agony.
She was loved...
but barren.
Leah had children...
but longed for Jacob’s affection.
One woman possessed what the other desperately wanted.
And both hurt.
Genesis 30:1 says Rachel envied her sister.
Think about that.
The favored wife was jealous of the unfavored wife.
That is what comparison does.
It can make you stare so intensely at what another person possesses that you become blind to what you have.
Then servants become involved.
Children become entangled in competition.
Mandrakes become bargaining chips.
Intimacy becomes negotiated.
The household becomes a battlefield of longing.
And later, favoritism reaches another generation.
Jacob especially loves Joseph, Rachel’s son.
Joseph receives the famous garment.
His brothers notice.
Genesis says they hated him.
Eventually their jealousy becomes so poisonous that they throw their own brother into a pit and sell him.
Do you see the generational echo?
Favoritism did not remain inside Jacob’s marriages.
The wounds reached the children.
That is one of sin’s most terrifying characteristics.
What parents refuse to confront can become an inheritance their children never asked to receive.
Then Scripture gives us another household.
Elkanah.
Hannah.
Peninnah.
First Samuel 1:2 tells us plainly:
“He had two wives.”
And almost immediately we encounter rivalry.
Elkanah loved Hannah.
Hannah was barren.
Peninnah had children.
Elkanah gave Hannah a special portion because he loved her.
Then Scripture calls Peninnah Hannah’s צָרָה — tsarah—her rival or adversary.
And Peninnah provoked Hannah bitterly.
Year after year.
Until Hannah wept.
Until she could not eat.
Read that slowly.
One husband.
Two wives.
One favored.
One fertile.
One wounded.
One provoking.
One crying.
And nobody appears emotionally whole.
Yet again, God meets the wounded woman.
Hannah pours out her soul before the LORD.
God eventually gives her Samuel.
The answer to Hannah’s deepest anguish does not ultimately come from winning the rivalry.
It comes through bringing her broken heart before God.
Then there is David.
David loved God.
David wrote psalms.
David defeated Goliath.
David also accumulated wives.
And Scripture refuses to pretend that spiritual gifting makes relational compromise harmless.
David’s household eventually becomes almost unbearable to read.
Sexual violation.
Hatred.
Murder.
Revenge.
Political ambition.
Betrayal.
A son rising against his father.
A kingdom shaken.
Not every tragedy in David’s household can simply be reduced to polygamy; Scripture itself connects major judgment in David’s house to his sin involving Bathsheba and Uriah.
That distinction matters.
We should never force the Bible to say more than it says.
But neither should we ignore the larger portrait of a divided and deeply troubled royal household.
Then Solomon takes multiplication to another level.
And centuries before Solomon was born, God had already given Israel’s future kings a warning.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
“He shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.”
Notice the connection.
Multiply wives.
Heart turns away.
Then read Solomon’s story.
First Kings 11 describes Solomon loving many foreign women and says his wives turned his heart after other gods when he was old.
The warning and the tragedy meet.
The wisest king in Israel could recognize wisdom intellectually and still violate it personally.
That should frighten every one of us.
Because knowing Scripture is not the same thing as surrendering to Scripture.
You can quote truth you are not obeying.
You can teach boundaries you secretly cross.
You can recognize someone else’s compromise while protecting your own.
You can know exactly where a road leads...
and still walk down it.
But now the question becomes deeper.
Why did God tolerate things in fallen societies that were not the creational ideal?
That question requires humility.

The Bible unfolds across real human history, inside deeply patriarchal ancient cultures, among sinful people whom God patiently calls, restrains, judges, teaches, redeems, and progressively reveals His purposes to.
Biblical law sometimes regulates broken realities without thereby declaring those realities the Edenic ideal.
Jesus Himself gives us a principle for understanding this when discussing divorce in Matthew 19.
Moses permitted something, Jesus explained, “because of the hardness of your hearts.”
Then Jesus says:
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
Those words are enormous.
From the beginning.
Jesus teaches us to distinguish between creation design and concessions operating within a fallen world.
So when we ask about marriage, we should not merely ask:
“What did fallen people sometimes practice?”
We should also ask:
“What did God establish in the beginning?”
And:
“Where does Jesus point us?”
That trail leads back to one flesh.
It also moves forward into something breathtaking.
Because Christian marriage ultimately becomes a signpost pointing beyond itself.
Ephesians 5 takes us to Christ and His Church.
The deepest Christian picture of covenant love is not a powerful man collecting women.
It is Christ giving Himself for His bride.
Read that again.
Jesus does not exploit His bride.
He dies for her.
He does not use covenant for self-indulgence.
He sacrifices Himself.
He does not ask, “How many people can exist for my pleasure?”
He loves sacrificially.
He cleanses.
He nourishes.
He cherishes.
He gives Himself.
Suddenly the conversation is no longer merely about ancient polygamy.
It is about us.
Because perhaps you have never had multiple spouses...
but you know something about divided affection.
Maybe Jesus has your Sunday morning...
but money has Monday.
Maybe Jesus has your vocabulary...
but pornography has your secret imagination.
Maybe Jesus has your worship playlist...
but resentment owns a locked room inside your heart.
Maybe Jesus has your public testimony...
but another master receives your private obedience.
The Bible’s broken marriages are not there merely so we can stand at a safe historical distance and criticize ancient people.
They force us to confront a deeper question:
Who has your heart?
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because spiritual adultery is one of Scripture’s recurring descriptions of idolatry.
God does not want a fragment of you.
Jesus did not bleed for your leftovers.
He did not endure the cross so He could become one interest among many.
Christ calls us to Himself.
And perhaps the deepest scandal in these stories is not that Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon, and others were flawed.
The scandal is that God continued working through deeply flawed people.
That He saw Hagar.
That He saw Leah.
That He heard Hannah.
That He preserved His promise.
That He disciplined David but did not abandon His redemptive purpose.
That even after Solomon’s catastrophic compromise, God's covenant purposes continued moving through history.
Not because sin did not matter.
But because grace is greater than the wreckage grace comes to redeem.
And eventually...
Jesus came.
Not another morally compromised patriarch.
Not another king collecting wives.
Not another ruler using people to enlarge his kingdom.
The King came to give His life for His people.
Jesus Christ entered our human scandal without participating in our sin.
He touched the rejected.
He welcomed the ashamed.
He confronted hypocrites.
He forgave repentant sinners.
He restored ruined people.
And finally He walked toward a cross carrying sins that were not His.
Ours.
Your envy.
Your lust.
Your favoritism.
Your adultery.
Your bitterness.
Your sexual sin.
Your hidden messages.
Your secret browser history.
Your manipulation.
Your broken promises.
Your pride.
Your jealousy.
Your compromises.
Your attempts to extract from human beings the love only God can ultimately satisfy.
At Calvary, Jesus did not pretend those things were harmless.
He demonstrated how serious sin truly is.
And then He demonstrated how astonishing grace truly is.
Christ died for sinners.
And He rose again.
That means your story does not have to end where your worst chapter happened.
Maybe your family is already complicated.
Maybe you grew up watching favoritism destroy siblings.
Maybe your father chose another family.
Maybe your mother spent years competing for affection.
Maybe infidelity shattered your home.
Maybe you were the favored child and only later understood what that did to your siblings.
Maybe you were the forgotten child.
Maybe you became the person who caused the damage.
Maybe you betrayed someone who trusted you.
Maybe you are carrying consequences you cannot reverse.
The Gospel does not ask you to rename darkness as light.
It offers something better.
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
A new heart.
A new direction.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything by bringing grace into the place where sin seemed to have written the final sentence.
That is the Gospel.
Repentance does not mean saying, “It wasn't that serious.”
Repentance says:
“Lord, it was sin. I have no excuse. Have mercy on me.”
And grace answers with a crucified and risen Savior.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess it.
Bring it into the light.
Turn from it.

If necessary, seek wise biblical pastoral counsel. Make restitution where appropriate. Ask forgiveness where you have wounded people. Establish boundaries where temptation keeps finding an unlocked door.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace teaches us to come home.
Somebody reading silently may need evidence that grace can reach a house like theirs too.
Do not underestimate what sharing truth can do.
Even send it to the skeptic who thinks the Bible hides the failures of its own people.
It doesn't.
That honesty is part of its power.
Some truths are not meant to be consumed once and forgotten. Return to the Scriptures mentioned here. Test what you have read against the Word of God.
It does not.
It does not.
And not because anyone can purchase a blessing from God.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But voluntary generosity can help Gospel-centered work continue.
Paul wrote that giving should be purposeful and willing, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your support helps us keep reaching people who may never walk into a church building but will stop long enough to read something about Jesus on their phone.
Because this ministry was never supposed to terminate on a screen.
Truth is meant to travel.
The wounded need to know that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
The ashamed need to know that forgiveness exists.
The compromised need to know that repentance is still possible.
The broken family needs to know that inherited dysfunction does not have to become inherited destiny.
And the Church needs to remember that the Bible's honesty about human failure is not an embarrassment to Christianity.
It is part of why grace is so breathtaking.
Scripture shows us jealous homes.
Favored wives.
Rejected wives.
Rival sisters.
Provoked women.
Competing children.
Divided fathers.
Compromised kings.
Broken households.
And hearts wandering from God.
It shows us what sin does.
But then Scripture keeps moving.
Past Abraham.
Past Jacob.
Past Hannah.
Past David.
Past Solomon.
Past every human failure.
Until eventually we arrive outside Jerusalem...
at a cross.
And there hangs the only Man in the story who never needed grace...
giving His life so the rest of us could receive it.
That is where every broken family must finally look.
Not toward perfect ancestors.
Not toward perfect parents.
Not toward perfect marriages.
Toward a perfect Savior.
Jesus Christ.
The One who tells the adulterer to leave sin.
The One who welcomes the repentant.
The One who restores the fallen.
The One who heals what human beings have shattered.
The One whose blood speaks a better word over everyone who comes to Him in faith.
So perhaps the question is no longer only:
“Why does the Bible show so much jealousy, favoritism, and family chaos around polygamy?”
Perhaps another question has been waiting beneath it all along:
Why would a holy God keep pursuing people whose lives were this messy?
And the answer has a name.
Jesus.
The Bible shows the scandal because without seeing the scandal, we may never understand the magnitude of grace.
It shows the wound because there is a Healer.
It exposes the darkness because Light has come.
It tells the truth about sinners because sinners are exactly the people Christ came to save.
And maybe tonight, the family story you thought permanently disqualified you is becoming the very place where you finally discover what grace actually means.
Your family's broken chapters may explain some of your wounds—but because of Jesus Christ, they do not get to write your final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jeremiah 29:11 Was Written to People Facing 70 Years of Exile—Now Read It Again
paragraphs: Jeremiah 29:11 Was Written to People Facing 70 Years of Exile—Now Read It Again

You may have quoted this verse when you needed God to change your circumstances. But what if its original message is even more powerful? God spoke these words to people who were not coming home tomorrow.
There is a version of Jeremiah 29:11 that fits beautifully on a coffee mug.
And then there is the Jeremiah 29:11 that had to survive Babylon.
Those are not quite the same thing.
Maybe you know the verse by heart.
“For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.”
Jeremiah 29:11, KJV.
We print it on journals.
We frame it on walls.

We send it to people graduating from school, beginning new careers, walking into interviews, waiting for breakthroughs, starting businesses, fighting illnesses, praying for marriages, and hoping that something painful is finally about to change.
And there is nothing wrong with loving this verse.
But there is something breathtaking that happens when you stop reading Jeremiah 29:11 by itself.
Because the people who first received these words were not standing on the edge of an exciting promotion.
They were exiles.
Their world had been ripped apart.
Jerusalem was behind them.
Babylon was around them.
Home was somewhere they could remember but could not simply return to.
And then God sent them a message.
But it was not the message many of them wanted.
It was essentially this:
You are going to be here longer than you hoped.
Build the house anyway.
Plant the garden anyway.
Raise your children anyway.
Pray anyway.
Seek Me anyway.
Live faithfully anyway.
Because I have not abandoned you.
That changes everything.

Jeremiah's letter tells the exiles to build houses and live in them, plant gardens and eat their produce, marry and raise families, multiply rather than disappear, and even seek the welfare of Babylon—the very place of their exile—and pray for it. God also warns them not to believe prophets offering deceptive messages. Then comes the sentence modern readers sometimes rush past:
“When seventy years are completed for Babylon…”
Only after that comes Jeremiah 29:11.
The seventy years were not hidden in the fine print.
They were part of the message.

Jeremiah had already prophesied that the nations would serve Babylon for seventy years. Jeremiah 29 places the famous promise directly against that long horizon of judgment, displacement, endurance, and eventual restoration.
Imagine hearing that.
Seventy years.
Some of the people receiving the letter could have immediately understood what that meant.
They might die in Babylon.
Some would plant trees whose mature shade would fall across somebody else's shoulders.
Some would build houses in which their grandchildren would eventually sleep.
Some would pray for restoration and grow old before seeing the answer.
Some would tell their children about Jerusalem.
And their children would tell their children.
Now read the promise again.
The Hebrew of Jeremiah 29:11 is stunning:
כִּי אָנֹכִי יָדַעְתִּי אֶת־הַמַּחֲשָׁבֹת אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי חֹשֵׁב עֲלֵיכֶם נְאֻם־יְהוָה מַחְשְׁבוֹת שָׁלוֹם וְלֹא לְרָעָה לָתֵת לָכֶם אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה
The heartbeat of it is:
“מַחְשְׁבוֹת שָׁלוֹם” — machshevot shalom.
Thoughts, intentions, purposes of shalom.
And shalom is richer than the thin idea that nothing painful will happen to you.
Peace.
Welfare.
Wholeness.
Well-being.
God's promised end for His covenant people was not destruction.
“וְלֹא לְרָעָה” — velo lera'ah.
Not for evil, calamity, or disaster as their final destiny.
And then:
“אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה” — acharit vetiqvah.
A future and a hope.
The Hebrew text itself preserves this movement: God's purposes are shalom, not disaster, giving His people an acharit—a future/end—and tiqvah—hope.
But notice what God did not say.
He did not say, “Because I have plans for you, Babylon disappears tonight.”
He did not say, “Because I love you, you will never bury anything you hoped would live.”
He did not say, “Because My purposes are good, every season will feel good.”
He did not say, “Because you prayed, there will be no waiting.”
He told people facing decades in exile that exile would not get the final word.
And maybe that is the Jeremiah 29:11 somebody reading this desperately needs.
Because perhaps you have quietly begun measuring God's goodness by the speed of your rescue.
You prayed.
Nothing moved.
You fasted.
Nothing changed.
You tried to obey.
The door still closed.
You believed God could heal the relationship.
It still fell apart.
You asked Him to save someone you loved.
You still stood beside a grave.
You thought by now you would be married.
You thought by now the marriage would be healed.
You thought by now your child would have come home.
You thought by now the addiction would have lost its voice.
You thought by now the anxiety would have stopped ambushing you at 2:17 in the morning.
You thought by now you would understand why God allowed it.
And perhaps the hardest sentence you have ever whispered was not “God doesn't exist.”
Maybe it was:
“God, I know You're there.
I just don't understand what You're doing.”
That is where Jeremiah 29:11 becomes more than decoration.
Because biblical hope is not pretending Babylon is Jerusalem.
Faith does not require you to call exile pleasant.
Faith does not demand that you rename grief as happiness.
You can cry and still trust.
You can hurt and still worship.
You can have unanswered questions and still follow Jesus.
You can wake up disappointed and still say, “Lord, where else would I go?”
You can be faithful in a place you never wanted to live.
That is what the exiles were being taught.
Build here.
Plant here.
Pray here.
Be faithful here.
Not because Babylon has become home forever.
But because Babylon cannot cancel the purposes of God.
Read that slowly.
Babylon cannot cancel the purposes of God.
Neither can the divorce papers.
Neither can the diagnosis.
Neither can the rejection letter.
Neither can the bankruptcy.
Neither can your past.
Neither can the years you wasted.
Neither can the sin you deeply regret.
Neither can the thing you did that still makes you ashamed when the room gets quiet.
And neither can the thing somebody did to you.
But there is another truth we must not soften.

Israel's exile was not merely an unfortunate interruption in an otherwise comfortable story. Jeremiah's wider message repeatedly confronted Judah's rebellion and covenant unfaithfulness. The seventy-year judgment had already been announced.
So Jeremiah 29:11 is not sentimental optimism.
Grace shines against the darkness of judgment.
God was not saying sin did not matter.
He was showing that judgment would not erase His covenant purposes.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because sometimes what we call “God's plan” has been turned into a Christian version of wish fulfillment.
We imagine:
I belong to God, therefore my plans should succeed.
I prayed, therefore this relationship should work.
I gave, therefore I should become wealthy.
I served, therefore tragedy should stay away from my family.
I believed, therefore God owes me the outcome I imagined.
But Christianity does not put God in our debt.
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
God gave Himself.
This is where Jeremiah's hope ultimately drives the Christian heart beyond Babylon and toward Jesus Christ.
The Bible's great story does not end with people merely returning geographically from Babylon.
Humanity has a deeper exile.
Sin separates us from the holy God who made us.
Our deepest problem is not that life failed to follow our five-year plan.
Our deepest problem is that sinners need reconciliation with God.
And Jesus Christ stepped into that disaster.
The innocent One stood where the guilty should have stood.
The sinless Son carried judgment.
The King wore thorns.
The Lord of glory was mocked.
Hands that healed were pierced.
The One through whom everything was made was laid inside a borrowed tomb.
If anyone standing near Calvary had judged God's plan exclusively by what could be seen on Friday afternoon, everything would have looked lost.
The Messiah was dead.
Hope appeared buried.
The stone was sealed.
Saturday was silent.
But God was not finished.
Sunday came.
Jesus rose.
The grave did not rewrite God's promise.
God rewrote what the grave appeared to mean.
That is why Christian hope is not positive thinking.
It has a name.
Jesus.
The New Testament says that through Jesus Christ, those justified by faith have peace with God.
There is the deeper shalom.
Not merely circumstances behaving themselves.
Reconciliation.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
Life with God.
So please hear this carefully.
Jeremiah 29:11 does not mean every Christian gets the career, spouse, house, healing, bank balance, ministry platform, or earthly ending they imagined.
It was originally God's promise to His exiled covenant people in a particular historical moment.
We should not steal the promise from its context and turn it into a blank check addressed individually to every ambition we have.
But neither should understanding the context make the verse smaller.
The context makes it enormous.
Because the God revealed in Jeremiah is a God whose purposes remain standing when His people cannot see how restoration could possibly happen.
And Christians know something those exiles had not yet seen in its fullness.
We know the cross.
We know the empty tomb.
We know Jesus.
We know that God's greatest act of redemption came through something that, for a terrible moment, looked like catastrophic defeat.
So perhaps you are in your own Babylon right now.
Not literally.
Not in Jeremiah's historical sense.
But emotionally, you understand exile.
You know what it feels like to wake up somewhere in life you never planned to be.
You congratulate them.
Then put the phone down.
And cry.
Maybe everybody at church thinks you're strong because you know when to smile.
You know when to say, “God is good.”
You know which verse to quote.
You know how to worship while your heart is bleeding quietly underneath your clothes.
Nobody knows how tired you are.
Nobody knows you almost gave up.
Nobody knows how many times you have asked God why.
Nobody knows that some mornings, faith feels less like soaring on eagle's wings and more like crawling toward Jesus with whatever strength you have left.
If that is you, listen.
Do not confuse waiting with abandonment.
Do not confuse God's silence with God's absence.
Do not confuse a chapter with the ending.
Do not confuse Babylon with your identity.
And do not build your theology around the false promise that genuine faith always produces immediate escape.
God told the exiles to plant gardens.
Think about how strange that command is.
Planting is an act of hope.
You bury something in the ground and trust that hiddenness is not death.
You water dirt.
For days, perhaps nothing appears.
Still you water it.
That may be what faithfulness looks like in your life right now.
Keep planting.
Keep praying.
Keep forgiving.
Keep repenting.
Keep opening Scripture.
Keep showing up for your children.
Keep loving your spouse faithfully.
Keep serving when nobody applauds.
Keep resisting the secret sin that keeps whispering your name.
Keep returning to Jesus when shame tells you to hide.
Keep planting.
Because some of the holiest things you will ever do may happen during a season you keep asking God to end.

That does not mean every painful circumstance was directly caused by God as punishment. Scripture gives us no permission to look at every suffering person and announce that their pain is God's judgment.
Job should have cured us of that arrogance.
Jesus Himself rejected simplistic equations between particular suffering and particular personal sin.
Sometimes we suffer because we live in a fallen world.
Sometimes because other people sin against us.
Sometimes because our own choices have consequences.
Sometimes obedience itself becomes costly.
Sometimes we simply do not know why.
But Christianity never promises that following Christ removes every furnace.
It promises something better than a furnace-free life.
Christ Himself.
And if the furnace lasts longer than you expected?
Christ.
If the prayer is answered differently than you begged?
Christ.
If everybody leaves?
Christ.
If your earthly plans collapse?
Christ.
If repentance costs you everything you were using to hide?
Christ.
If you have to begin again with tears running down your face?
Christ.
Jesus is not the consolation prize you receive when God refuses to give you the life you wanted.
Jesus is the treasure.
And perhaps that is what some of us need to repent of.
We wanted God's plan more than we wanted God.
We wanted the future.
We wanted the hope.
We wanted the prosperity.
We wanted restoration.
We wanted the blessing.
We wanted the breakthrough.
But did we want Him?
Because immediately after Jeremiah 29:11, the passage moves toward something profoundly personal.
God speaks about His people calling upon Him.
Praying to Him.
Seeking Him.
Finding Him.
Seeking Him with the whole heart.
The destination of biblical hope is not merely improved circumstances.
It is God.
Maybe you have spent years asking Jesus to rewrite your circumstances while resisting His desire to rewrite you.
Maybe the relationship is not the deepest problem.
Maybe the money is not the deepest problem.
Maybe the loneliness is not the deepest problem.
Maybe beneath all of it is a heart exhausted from running.
A hidden habit.
An unforgiven wound.
A secret compromise.
A carefully managed religious image.
You know how to look Christian.
But somewhere underneath the worship songs, Bible verses, Sunday clothes, and “I'm blessed” answers, something in you has been starving.
Come home.
Not to religion.
To Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of the grave you decorated until it looked like a home.
Jesus does not wait for you to clean yourself before you approach Him.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the unbelief.
Bring Him the anger you were afraid to admit.
Bring Him the church wound.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are exhausted from pretending to be.
There is grace at the cross.
Not cheap grace that tells you sin does not matter.
Costly grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that forgives and transforms.
Grace that does not merely excuse the old life but calls you into a new one.
This is why “From Scandal to Grace” is more than a phrase.
It is the shape of redemption.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace met him.
Paul persecuted the church.
Grace interrupted him.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes, not merely years.
Grace reached him.
The Gospel has always been filled with stories that looked irredeemable until Jesus entered them.
And maybe yours is next.
Not because God owes you an easy ending.
But because no repentant sinner who comes to Christ for mercy discovers that the Savior has run out of grace.
Not because typing words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing something into the light begins with refusing to pretend anymore.
Somebody reading beneath this article may be standing where you once stood.
Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another person from giving up tonight.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because someone on your Facebook friends list may be living in Babylon behind a smiling profile picture.
Send it privately to the friend who has gone quiet.
But let us say this biblically and clearly.
The New Testament says giving should come from a heart that has decided to give, “not grudgingly, or of necessity,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
He cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be bought.
Christ paid for salvation with His blood.
And perhaps that is especially fitting after Jeremiah 29.
Plant the garden.
Plant the truth.
Plant the Gospel.
Plant something whose fruit may feed somebody you never meet.
That costs nothing.
Your share may carry Scripture into a home we could never personally enter.
Your tag may reach somebody who would never search for a Christian article themselves.
Your comment can help create a community where wounded believers realize they are not struggling alone.
Your prayer matters.
Your willingness to tell somebody about Jesus matters.
The mission was never supposed to terminate with us.
The Gospel moves through people willing to carry it.
And before you leave, go back one final time.
Seventy years.
Then the promise.
That order matters.
God's people heard about the waiting before they heard the words we love printing on our walls.
And strangely, that does not weaken Jeremiah 29:11.
It makes it almost unbearably beautiful.
Because now the verse is not saying:
“Nothing painful will happen.”
It is saying:
Pain does not have sovereign authority over God's purposes.
Exile is real.
But exile is not God.
Babylon is powerful.
But Babylon is not God.
Your circumstances are real.
But your circumstances are not God.
Your failure is real.
But your failure is not God.
Your grief is real.
But your grief is not God.
Your waiting is real.
But your waiting is not God.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And because Christ walked out of His grave, Christians do not have to manufacture hope from favorable circumstances.
We have a risen Savior.
So build when you would rather run.
Plant when you cannot yet see fruit.
Pray when heaven feels silent.
Repent when pride tells you to hide.
Forgive when bitterness feels easier.
Seek Christ when you cannot understand His providence.
And when somebody offers you a counterfeit Christianity that says God's love can always be measured by how quickly He removes suffering, remember the exiles opening Jeremiah's letter in Babylon.
They were loved.
And they still had to wait.
They were remembered.
