And they still had to endure.
They had a promise.
And some of them would not personally live to see its complete historical fulfillment.
Yet God remained faithful.
Maybe you needed to know that tonight.
Maybe you are planting a garden whose fruit another generation will eat.
Maybe the prayer you are praying is shaping your children.
Maybe your repentance will break a pattern your family has carried for decades.
Maybe your faithfulness in suffering is teaching somebody watching you what Christianity actually looks like.
Maybe you cannot see what God is doing.
You do not have to pretend that you can.
You are called to trust the One who can.
Share it with somebody living through a season that has lasted much longer than they expected.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not to earn grace.
But to help put Gospel-centered truth in front of another exhausted soul who may desperately need to hear that Jesus is not finished.
Because someday you may look back at the place you begged God to remove you from…
and realize that while you were asking Him to change the scenery,
Jesus was doing something even deeper.
He was changing you.
The chapter that felt like exile may become the page where you finally discover that God never left you in Babylon alone.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHESHAN HAD NO SONS—SO HE GAVE HIS DAUGHTER TO HIS EGYPTIAN SERVANT
paragraphs: SHESHAN HAD NO SONS—SO HE GAVE HIS DAUGHTER TO HIS EGYPTIAN SERVANT

Buried inside a genealogy most Christians skip is an Egyptian servant, an unnamed daughter, an impossible family line—and a quiet reminder that God can write a future through the people everyone else would have overlooked.
There are verses in the Bible we underline.
There are verses we memorize.
There are verses we put on coffee mugs, T-shirts, phone wallpapers, and the walls of our homes.
And then there are verses like this.
Verses buried inside genealogies.
Names.
More names.
A father begat a son, who begat another son, who became the father of somebody whose name we can barely pronounce.
So we keep scrolling.
We keep turning pages.
We tell ourselves we will come back later.
But sometimes...
the verse you almost skipped is carrying a story you desperately needed to hear.
Because tucked quietly inside 1 Chronicles 2 is a family situation that should make you stop.
Sheshan had a problem.
Not a small problem in the world in which he lived.
He had no sons.
He had daughters.
And he had an Egyptian servant named Jarha.
Then Scripture records something extraordinary in its simplicity:
Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha as a wife.
And she gave birth to Attai.
That is it.
No thunder.
No angel appears.
No sea divides.
No prophet announces what is happening.
No one gives a speech.
Yet a family line that appeared to have reached a dead end...
continued.
Read the Hebrew carefully.
1 Chronicles 2:34 describes the situation:
וְלֹא־הָיָה לְשֵׁשָׁן בָּנִים כִּי אִם־בָּנוֹת וּלְשֵׁשָׁן עֶבֶד מִצְרִי וּשְׁמוֹ יַרְחָע
The heart of the statement is startlingly plain:
Sheshan had no sons, but daughters, and Sheshan had an Egyptian servant whose name was Jarha.
Then comes verse 35:
וַיִּתֵּן שֵׁשָׁן אֶת־בִּתּוֹ לְיַרְחָע עַבְדּוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וַתֵּלֶד לוֹ אֶת־עַתָּי
Literally, in its basic sense:
“And Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha his servant for a wife, and she bore him Attai.”
Look at the words Scripture refuses to erase.
עַבְדּוֹ — ‘avdo — “his servant.”
מִצְרִי — mitsri — “Egyptian.”
בִּתּוֹ — bitto — “his daughter.”
לְאִשָּׁה — le’ishshah — “for a wife.”
וַתֵּלֶד — vatteled — “and she bore.”
The Chronicler could have simply jumped from Sheshan to Attai.
He did not.
He made sure Jarha was remembered.
An Egyptian.
A servant.
A man who, at first glance, might have seemed completely outside the future of this Israelite family.
And suddenly his name was inside the genealogy.
Do not make the passage say more than God says.
The Bible does not tell us Jarha's thoughts that day.
It does not tell us the daughter's emotions.
It does not tell us whether people whispered about the marriage.
It does not give us permission to invent a romance, a scandal, or motives that Scripture never reveals.
But what Scripture does tell us is already astonishing enough.
Sheshan had no sons.
Jarha was his Egyptian servant.
Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha in marriage.
She bore Attai.
And the genealogy continued.
Maybe that hits you differently when your own life looks like it has reached a sentence containing the words:
“No sons.”
No way forward.
No second chance.
No money.
No marriage.
No child.
No ministry.
No opportunity.
No strength left.
No way that family can be restored.
No way God could still use someone with your history.
No way the pieces could possibly become something beautiful again.
You looked at what was missing and decided the story was over.
But God was not finished writing.
That does not mean God promises to give us every earthly outcome we desire. Scripture never gives us permission to turn this passage into a blank check for our dreams.
Sometimes God changes the circumstances.
Sometimes He changes us inside circumstances we desperately wanted changed.
Sometimes He opens the door.
Sometimes His grace teaches us to trust Him while the door remains closed.
The Christian hope is not that every painful situation eventually becomes the life we imagined.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
And that distinction matters.
Because Christianity is not positive thinking wearing a cross.
The Gospel is better.
The Gospel tells us that humanity had a problem far greater than a broken family line.
We had sin.
We had guilt.
We had rebellion.
We had death.
And no amount of self-improvement could repair what sin had done between humanity and a holy God.
We were not merely wounded people needing encouragement.
We were sinners needing reconciliation.
Then God did what we could never do for ourselves.
Jesus Christ came.
He lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin's judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The greatest apparent dead end in history became the doorway through which redemption was proclaimed to the world.
Friday looked like defeat.
The tomb looked final.
The stone looked like punctuation.
Heaven wrote something else.
Resurrection.
And once you understand that, you begin reading stories like Sheshan and Jarha differently.
Not because Jarha is secretly Jesus.
Scripture never says that.
Not because every detail in 1 Chronicles 2 is an allegory.
It is not.
But because the God revealed across Scripture repeatedly overturns human assumptions about who matters, who belongs, what can be redeemed, and where His purposes can go.
Jarha was Egyptian.
That detail would have meant something to an Israelite reader.
Egypt was not a neutral word in Israel's memory.
Egypt was associated with bondage.
Pharaoh.
Oppression.
Bricks.
Tears.
The cries of slaves.
The Passover.
The Red Sea.
Yet here, inside Judah's genealogy, stands an Egyptian named Jarha.
Do not miss the irony.
The label describing where a man came from did not prevent his name from appearing in the record of where this family was going.
Someone reading this right now needs that sentence.
Because you have been letting your origin become your identity.
You came from addiction.
You came from abuse.
You came from poverty.
You came from divorce.
You came from a dysfunctional home.
You came from a season you are ashamed to describe.
Maybe you were the person who caused the damage.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe you abandoned your faith.
Maybe you spent years pretending to love God while privately feeding something you knew was destroying you.
Maybe everyone at church sees the polished version of you.
But you know what happened when nobody was watching.
And somewhere along the way you began believing that your past had acquired veto power over God's grace.
It does not.
But hear this carefully:
Grace is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
Grace cost blood.
Jesus did not go to the cross because sin was insignificant.
He went because sin was deadly.
And repentance is not paying God back.
You could never pay Him back.
Repentance is turning from sin and turning toward the Savior who has already done what you could never accomplish for yourself.
That is why the Gospel is so offensive to human pride.
You cannot boast your way into it.
You cannot purchase it.
You cannot clean yourself enough to deserve it.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem a sinner.
Maybe your sentence begins:
“I was an adulterer...”
“I was addicted...”
“I lied...”
“I destroyed my marriage...”
“I walked away from God...”
“I compromised...”
“I hated myself...”
“I hurt people...”
“I knew better and did it anyway...”
Do not put the period where the blood of Jesus can put a comma.
You were that.
And if you belong to Christ, that does not have to be the final definition of who you are becoming.
This is where cheap grace must die.
Jesus does not merely make sinners feel better about remaining unchanged.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He calls.
He transforms.
He teaches forgiven people to walk differently.
You do not meet Jesus so you can become comfortable in chains.
You meet Jesus and discover that the One who forgives you also becomes your Lord.
And sometimes His rewriting begins in places nobody applauds.
That may be one of the most beautiful things about 1 Chronicles 2:34–35.
There is nothing glamorous here.
Just a genealogy.
A daughter whose name is not even preserved in these verses.
A servant from Egypt.
A marriage.
A child named Attai.
Then another name.
Then another.
Then another.
Most people would never make a movie about it.
God put it in Scripture.
Maybe you have mistaken invisibility for insignificance.
You pray where nobody sees.
You raise children and wonder whether any of it matters.
You keep choosing faithfulness while somebody else gets the platform.
You serve and nobody thanks you.
You fight temptation quietly.
You open your Bible while your emotions feel numb.
You forgive again.
You show up again.
You repent again.
You pray again.
You whisper, “Jesus, help me,” again.
And heaven does not measure significance the way social media does.
God does not need something to go viral before He can call it faithful.
The Kingdom has always contained people whose names history barely noticed but whose obedience mattered.
And there is another uncomfortable truth hiding here.
We love putting people into categories.
Insider.
Outsider.
Successful.
Failure.
Clean.
Messy.
Useful.
Damaged.
Religious.
Worldly.
Worthy.
Unworthy.
We can look at someone's current position and imagine we already know the ending.
But the Gospel destroys our right to boast.
At the foot of the cross, nobody arrives with a résumé impressive enough to make Jesus unnecessary.
The respectable church member needs Christ.
The prisoner needs Christ.
The pastor needs Christ.
The addict needs Christ.
The skeptic needs Christ.
The wealthy need Christ.
The poor need Christ.
The person who has been in church for fifty years needs Christ.
The person who does not know how to find Genesis needs Christ.
And salvation is not earned by pedigree.
It is received by grace through faith.
That is why Jesus' invitation is so devastatingly beautiful.
Come.
Not because your history is spotless.
Come because His mercy is sufficient.
Come because the cross is sufficient.
Come because Christ is sufficient.
But come ready to surrender.
There may be someone reading this who has been trying to negotiate with Jesus.
You want forgiveness without lordship.
Heaven without repentance.
Comfort without surrender.
A Savior who rescues you from consequences but never confronts your idols.
That Jesus exists only in our imagination.
The biblical Jesus loves us too much to leave our rebellion unnamed.
So perhaps the deepest question raised in your heart by this obscure genealogy is not, “What happened to Jarha?”
Maybe the question is:
What will happen to me if I finally stop hiding?
What if tonight you tell Jesus the truth He already knows?
What if you stop performing?
What if you confess the bitterness?
The pornography?
The affair?
The secret messages?
The envy?
The unforgiveness?
The pride?
The greed?
The double life?
The exhaustion?
The unbelief?
The resentment toward God you have been afraid to admit?
What if the most spiritual thing you can do right now is stop pretending?
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is 1 John 1:9.
Not because confession manipulates God into mercy.
Because Christ has made forgiveness possible.
This is the scandal of grace.
God knows the unedited story...
and still calls sinners to Himself.
Jesus knows what you did.
Jesus knows what was done to you.
Jesus knows which memories still wake you at night.
Jesus knows the version of yourself you hope nobody ever discovers.
And the cross stands there saying simultaneously:
Your sin is more serious than you wanted to believe.
And His grace is greater than you dared to hope.
That is why we say:
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin should be romanticized.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
But because Jesus Christ can take a life genuinely wrecked by sin and make forgiveness, repentance, restoration, holiness, and a new direction possible.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not always by rewriting your circumstances.
Sometimes He rewrites you.
And perhaps that is the miracle you actually need.
Maybe the marriage does not immediately repair itself.
Maybe the debt does not disappear tomorrow.
Maybe the person you hurt still needs distance.
Maybe consequences remain.
Maybe grief remains.
Grace does not make consequences imaginary.
But grace means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
There can be repentance after rebellion.
Purity after sexual sin.
Truth after deception.
Sobriety after addiction.
Humility after pride.
Service after selfishness.
Prayer after years of silence.
Faith after wandering.
A surrendered life after decades of running.
And when Christ saves you, the goal is no longer merely to become a better version of yourself.
The old throne has to be surrendered.
Jesus becomes King.
Talk to God.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Tell Him the truth.
If you need words, they do not have to be impressive.
“Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot save myself. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Change me. I believe You died and rose again. I surrender myself to You. Teach me to follow You.”
The prayer itself is not magic.
Jesus is the Savior.
Turn to Him.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But you also do not have to keep pretending you are spiritually invincible.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance is possible, healing can begin, and God is still at work.
Do not make the comment section a stage.
Make it a place where masks come down.
And think of one person who needs this message.
Not twenty random people.
One.
The friend who thinks he has gone too far.
The woman quietly rebuilding her life.
The believer who has become spiritually numb.
The prodigal who still follows you on Facebook but has not walked into a church in years.
The person whose past has become a prison.
Or send this privately.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
Not because an algorithm can advance the Kingdom of God.
God does not need an algorithm.
But because one ordinary act of sharing can place the truth of Christ in front of someone you may never know was struggling.
Sometimes evangelism begins with something as simple as refusing to keep good news to yourself.
Because eventually there may be a night when the accusations return.
A night when your past starts shouting.
A night when you look at the unfinished parts of your life and think, “There is no future here.”
Come back.
Read the names again.
Remember Jarha.
Remember Sheshan's apparent dead end.
And then look beyond them to the greater hope Scripture gives us.
Look to Jesus.
Stay close to truth.
Stay close to Scripture.
Most of all, stay close to Christ.
Use them.
Share them.
Put biblical resources into the hands of people who need them.

And if you have been wondering how you can help Gospel Warrior continue producing and expanding Christ-centered articles, biblical resources, discipleship materials, and outreach, there is a practical way to stand with the mission.
But understand what that means biblically.
It cannot buy a blessing.
It cannot buy salvation.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
Scripture teaches generosity that is willing rather than coerced: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
So pray about it.
Not your payment to God.
Not the price of grace.
Not proof that you are a better Christian.
Support for the work.
Pray.
Use the free resources.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done for you.
Because support is larger than money.
And the mission is larger than Gospel Warrior.
The mission belongs to Christ.
We are simply trying to be faithful with whatever He places in our hands.
That brings us back to a man almost nobody talks about.
Jarha.
An Egyptian servant.
One small name buried inside a chapter filled with names.
Beside him stands a woman whose personal name the passage does not even give us.
Then comes their son:
Attai.
And the genealogy moves forward.
Maybe that is why this obscure passage refuses to leave the heart once you finally notice it.
Human beings see categories.
God sees the whole story.
We see the chapter.
God sees what comes after it.
We see what is missing.
God knows what He can accomplish with what remains.
We see an Egyptian servant.
Scripture remembers his name.
We see an unnamed daughter.
God saw her life.
We see a dead end.
Then suddenly...
Attai.
Another generation.
Another name.
Another page.
So what have you already declared dead that God never told you to bury?
Your usefulness?
Your faith?
Your future?
Your ability to become a godly father?
Your ability to become a godly woman?
Your ministry?
Your testimony?
Your capacity to love again?
Your hope that you could ever become different from the person you used to be?
Do not turn this passage into a promise that God will give you the earthly ending you want.
Turn your eyes instead toward the promise Scripture actually gives to those who belong to Christ.
Your life is no longer defined merely by what happened behind you.
You belong to Jesus.
And if you have never surrendered to Him, the invitation still stands.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
You may have arrived at this article thinking your story was already written.
Maybe you thought the scandal got the final word.
Maybe shame wrote your identity in permanent ink.
Maybe failure named you.
Maybe somebody else's sin wounded you so deeply that you cannot imagine becoming whole again.
Maybe your sentence currently reads:
“There is no way forward.”
But two thousand years ago, outside Jerusalem, humanity watched a stone roll across the entrance of a tomb.
It looked like the end.
Then came Sunday.
The stone moved.
The tomb emptied.
Jesus Christ rose.
And because He lives, despair does not get to pretend it is God.
Sin does not get the final word.
Death does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
So remember this when you encounter another genealogy you are tempted to skip.
Somewhere among those difficult names is evidence that God remembers people the world forgets.
And remember this when you look into the mirror tomorrow.
You may see the scandal.
You may see the failure.
You may see what is missing.
You may see the years you cannot recover.
But if your life has been surrendered to Jesus Christ, you are looking at someone whose story is now held by a Redeemer.
And when the Redeemer holds the pen...
what looked like the end may become the place where grace begins writing something you never thought your life could say.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES GENESIS KEEP TELLING THE SHOCKING STORY OF KINGS TAKING THE PATRIARCHS’ WIVES?
paragraphs: WHY DOES GENESIS KEEP TELLING THE SHOCKING STORY OF KINGS TAKING THE PATRIARCHS’ WIVES?

Abraham did it. Then it happened again. Then Isaac repeated almost the same failure. If you have ever wondered why Scripture seems to tell the same disturbing story more than once, look closer—because buried inside these uncomfortable chapters is a devastating truth about fear, generational patterns, human failure, divine faithfulness, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
There are Bible passages we read slowly because they are beautiful.
And then there are passages we read twice because something feels wrong.
Genesis gives us one of those moments.

A patriarch enters foreign territory with his beautiful wife. He becomes afraid that the men of the land will kill him in order to take her. So he identifies her as his sister. A ruler becomes involved. The woman is endangered. God intervenes. The deception is exposed. The ruler confronts the patriarch.
Then, chapters later...
it seems to happen again.
And later still...
again.
If you have ever read Genesis and thought, “Wait. Haven’t I already read this story?” you are not imagining it.
But there is something even more interesting than the question most people ask.
People often speak of “two different stories.”
Genesis actually contains three related wife–sister episodes.
Abram and Sarai before Pharaoh in Egypt in Genesis 12:10–20.
Abraham and Sarah before Abimelech in Gerar in Genesis 20.
Isaac and Rebekah before Abimelech in Gerar in Genesis 26:6–11.
Three scenes.
Three moments of fear.
Three endangered marriages.
Three encounters with powerful rulers.
And one God who refuses to allow human fear to destroy His covenant purposes.
That last sentence changes everything.
Because perhaps the deepest question is not merely, “Why does Genesis repeat this story?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
Why does God keep protecting promises entrusted to people who keep behaving as though the promises depend entirely upon them?
That question is no longer only about Abraham.
It is about us.
Go back to the first scene.
A famine drives Abram into Egypt. As he approaches the country, fear begins talking.
Genesis 12:11–13 preserves his reasoning.
The Hebrew becomes painfully direct:
“אִמְרִי־נָא אֲחֹתִי אָתְּ”
ʾimrî-nāʾ ʾaḥōtî ʾāt
“Please say that you are my sister.”
Why?
Abram explains:
“וְחָיְתָה נַפְשִׁי בִּגְלָלֵךְ”
weḥāyetâ napšî biglālēḵ
“So that my life may be preserved because of you.”
Listen to what fear has done.
This is the man God called.
This is the man who left his homeland.
This is the man to whom God had already spoken extraordinary promises.
Yet when danger appears, the man of faith becomes a frightened man trying to control the outcome.
And Scripture does not airbrush him.
That matters.
The Bible could have turned Abraham into an untouchable religious superhero.
It does not.
It lets us watch him tremble.
It lets us hear his strategy.
It lets us see the consequences.
Sarai is taken into Pharaoh’s house.
The very woman through whom the covenant family must continue has entered another man's household because Abram's fear has helped place her there.
The tension is enormous.
Has the promise been endangered?
Has Abram ruined everything?
Will human failure cancel divine purpose?
Then God moves.
Genesis 12:17 says the LORD strikes Pharaoh and his household with severe afflictions because of Sarai.
Pharaoh eventually summons Abram.
And the pagan ruler asks the man of promise an embarrassing question:
“What is this you have done to me?”
There is something deeply uncomfortable about that scene.
The patriarch is not correcting Pharaoh.
Pharaoh is correcting the patriarch.
The man carrying God's promise has behaved in such a way that an outsider has reason to confront him.
Anyone who thinks the Bible exists to flatter its heroes has not been reading carefully.
Scripture exposes them.
No cosmetic surgery.
No spiritual Photoshop.
No carefully managed public image.
Abraham can believe God and still become afraid.
David can write psalms and commit terrible sin.
Peter can confess Jesus as the Christ and later deny knowing Him.
The Bible does not hide the scandals of its people because its ultimate Hero was never Abraham, David, Peter...
or you.
Its Hero is God.
And then Genesis 20 arrives.
Abraham is in Gerar.
Sarah is his wife.
And once again:
“אֲחֹתִי הִוא”
ʾaḥōtî hîʾ.
“She is my sister.”
Abimelech king of Gerar sends for Sarah and takes her.
If you are reading Genesis attentively, you almost want to shout into the page:
“Abraham! Again?”
That is precisely why this story reaches beyond ancient history.
Because some of us know exactly what “again” feels like.
Again you became afraid.
Again you hid.
Again you compromised.
Again you returned to the behavior you promised God you would leave behind.
Again the same insecurity spoke.
Again the same temptation found the same unlocked door.
Again the same wound produced the same reaction.
Again.
There are sins that feel less like isolated incidents and more like paths our feet somehow remember.
There are fears we thought we buried that suddenly resurrect themselves when pressure becomes strong enough.
And Genesis refuses to pretend that encountering God automatically makes a human being incapable of repeating old failures.
But Genesis 20 adds details Genesis 12 does not.
God appears to Abimelech in a dream.
And His warning is terrifyingly direct.
“הִנְּךָ מֵת”
hinnəḵā mēṯ.
Literally, something like:
“Behold—you are a dead man.”
Why?
Because Sarah is married.
The Hebrew describes her as:
“בְּעֻלַת בָּעַל”
bəʿulaṯ bāʿal—
a woman belonging in the covenant bond of marriage, a married woman.
But Genesis immediately makes something crucial clear: Abimelech has not touched her.
He protests that Abraham said she was his sister and that Sarah likewise identified Abraham as her brother.
God acknowledges Abimelech's integrity in the matter and then reveals something extraordinary:
God Himself prevented him from sinning against Him.
Think about that.
The story is not simply about God rescuing Sarah after disaster.
It is also about God restraining disaster before it occurs.
Sometimes grace is God forgiving what you did.
Sometimes grace is God preventing what you were about to do.
There may be sins in your past that Christ has forgiven.
There may also be sins absent from your past because God's providence shut doors you were foolish enough to approach.
Grace is bigger than the disasters you remember.
It includes disasters God never permitted to happen.
Then comes another uncomfortable confrontation.
Abimelech asks Abraham:
“מֶה־עָשִׂיתָ לָּנוּ”
meh-ʿāśîṯā lānû?
“What have you done to us?”
And Abraham finally explains the fear underneath his behavior.
“I thought, surely there is no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.”
There it is.
Fear.
Abraham imagined a future in which God’s promise could apparently continue only if Abraham first kept Abraham alive.
Fear had quietly rewritten his theology.
God had made the promise.
But Abraham behaved as though everything depended on his manipulation.
Have you ever done that?
We say God is sovereign...
until the medical report arrives.
We say God provides...
until money becomes tight.
We say God sees us...
until loneliness lasts longer than expected.
We say truth matters...
until telling the truth might cost us something.
Then suddenly we begin constructing our own little Egypt strategy.
Our own Gerar strategy.
Our own “just call yourself my sister” strategy.
Not necessarily because we stopped believing in God.
Sometimes because fear became louder than what we believed about Him.
Abraham then explains that Sarah really was his relative—his half-sister according to Genesis 20:12—and that they had agreed upon this arrangement during their travels.
So the statement contained truth.
But partial truth can still be used deceptively.
That should make us uncomfortable too.
A sentence does not become righteous merely because its individual words can technically be defended.
Truthfulness is not merely avoiding technically false vocabulary.
It includes refusing to weaponize selected truth to create a false impression.
Then Genesis does something remarkable.
God does not discard Abraham.
Abraham prays.
God heals Abimelech's household.
The compromised patriarch is still called a prophet in Genesis 20:7.
Not because deception suddenly became acceptable.
Not because God approves of fear.
Not because sin has stopped mattering.
But because God's calling rests finally upon God's grace rather than human perfection.
And just when we think the lesson has been learned...
Genesis 26 gives us Isaac.
Different generation.
Different wife.
Same kind of fear.
Isaac is living in Gerar.
The men ask about Rebekah.
And Genesis records:
“אֲחֹתִי הִוא”
ʾaḥōtî hîʾ.
“She is my sister.”
The exact kind of claim appears again.
Genesis even tells us why Isaac says it.
He is afraid.
“פֶּן־יַהַרְגֻנִי”
pen-yahargunî—
“lest they kill me.”
Read that again.
Abraham feared being killed because of Sarah.
Isaac fears being killed because of Rebekah.
The father’s strategy has appeared in the son's life.
We should be careful here. Genesis does not explicitly say, “Isaac learned this deception from Abraham,” so we should not claim more than Scripture gives us.
But the literary parallel is impossible to miss.
Genesis places similar failures across generations before our eyes.
And that raises a painful question.
What are we teaching the people who come after us—not merely through what we tell them, but through the patterns we normalize?
Children can inherit money.
They can inherit property.
They can inherit traditions.

But families can also repeat fears, habits, evasions, resentments, addictions, distorted ways of handling conflict, and survival strategies that existed long before the youngest generation knew where they came from.
Sometimes you wake up one day and hear your father's anger coming out of your mouth.
Sometimes you recognize your mother's fear living inside your decisions.
Sometimes you discover that something you hated watching as a child has somehow become something you now do as an adult.
Not because generational repetition is destiny.
It isn't.
But because unexamined patterns can travel frighteningly far.
Isaac is eventually exposed in an almost cinematic way.
Abimelech looks through a window and sees Isaac interacting affectionately with Rebekah in a manner revealing that she is not merely his sister.
The Hebrew uses a fascinating word:
“מְצַחֵק”
məṣaḥēq.
It comes from the same Hebrew root associated with Isaac's own name, Yiṣḥāq—“he laughs.”
The man named for laughter is exposed while “laughing,” playing, or showing intimate affection toward his wife.
The disguise cracks.
Abimelech calls him.
“So she really is your wife! Why did you say, ‘She is my sister’?”
And once again a foreign ruler confronts a patriarch.
Isaac answers with almost heartbreaking simplicity:
“Because I thought I might die because of her.”
Fear.
Again.
But notice a significant difference.
In Genesis 26, Rebekah is not actually taken into Abimelech's household.
Abimelech discovers the truth and commands his people not to harm Isaac or Rebekah.
These accounts therefore are not identical copies.
Genesis 12 involves Egypt and Pharaoh.
Genesis 20 involves Gerar, Abraham, Sarah, Abimelech, a divine dream, and explicit divine prevention of sexual contact.
Genesis 26 involves Isaac and Rebekah; Rebekah is not taken by the ruler, and the deception is discovered when Abimelech sees Isaac's behavior toward her.
The similarities are striking.
So are the differences.
Why, then, does Genesis preserve them?

Scholars have proposed different explanations for the literary relationship between these narratives. Some source-critical approaches understand the parallels as traditions transmitted or shaped through different textual streams. Other interpreters emphasize deliberate literary repetition: similar situations occurring in the patriarchal narratives in ways that expose recurring fear while developing the covenant story.
Christians do not need to pretend that scholarly questions do not exist.
Neither should we pretend Scripture says something it does not.
Whatever position one takes on the compositional history of Genesis, the canonical text we actually possess intentionally places these narratives before the reader.
And read together, they proclaim something enormous.
The covenant survives the weakness of the covenant bearers because God is faithful.
That does not excuse their failures.
It magnifies His faithfulness.
God had promised Abraham descendants.
God had attached enormous covenant significance to that family.
Yet repeatedly, the human beings carrying the promise find themselves behaving in ways that threaten the very future God promised.
And repeatedly...
God remains faithful.
Now we are getting close to the Gospel.
Because if the message of Scripture were merely, “Great people occasionally make mistakes, so try harder,” Christianity would be nothing more than moral self-improvement wearing religious clothing.
The Bible tells a far more devastating story.
Human beings cannot save themselves.
Even our heroes need rescue.
Abraham needs grace.
Isaac needs grace.
Jacob needs grace.
Judah needs grace.
David needs grace.
Peter needs grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
And none of them is Jesus.
That distinction matters.
Abraham's fear placed his wife in danger.
Jesus places Himself in danger for His Bride.
Abraham sought to preserve his own life.
Jesus willingly laid His life down.
Abraham's strategy involved concealing the true nature of his relationship.
Christ publicly claims His people even at the cost of blood.
The patriarchs reveal how fragile human faithfulness can be.
Jesus reveals what perfect faithfulness looks like.
At the cross, God does not pretend our scandals never happened.
He does something infinitely more glorious.
He deals with sin.
Jesus Christ bears judgment.
The innocent One stands in the place of the guilty.
The sinless Savior receives what sinners deserve so that sinners united to Him may receive what they could never earn.
That is why grace is not God shrugging at sin.
Grace cost blood.
And resurrection announces that sin, shame, fear, failure, and death do not get the final sentence over those who belong to Christ.
Maybe that is why these strange stories hurt so much when we finally stop reading them as ancient curiosities.
We recognize ourselves.
Maybe you have spent years calling something “wisdom” that was actually fear.
Maybe you learned to survive by hiding.
Maybe you became skilled at giving technically true answers that concealed what was really happening inside you.
Maybe your family handed you patterns nobody knew how to break.
Maybe you love God sincerely...
and still cannot understand why you keep returning to the same weakness.
Maybe your Christian life has an “again” in it that embarrasses you.
Again I failed.
Again I became angry.
Again I compromised.
Again I looked.
Again I lied.
Again I ran.
Again I doubted.
Again I hid.
Again I promised God it would be different.
And maybe you are wondering whether Jesus finally became tired of you.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is the reason repentance is possible.
Jesus does not merely cover our shame so we can continue worshiping our chains.
He calls us out of darkness.
Repentance means turning.
Confession means bringing what we have hidden into the light.
Faith means we stop trusting our own strategies for salvation and throw ourselves upon Christ.
The same God who exposed the fearful strategies in Genesis was still moving His promise toward fulfillment.
Generation after generation.
Failure after failure.
Until eventually the story arrived at another threatened Son.
Jesus Christ.
And unlike every flawed patriarch before Him...
He did not fail.
When tempted, He remained faithful.
When threatened, He did not manipulate truth to save Himself.
When suffering approached, He obeyed the Father.
When the cross stood before Him, He went willingly.
And when death swallowed Him...
death could not keep Him.
That is the real direction of the biblical story.
Not from flawed people to better people.
From fallen humanity...
to the faithful Christ.
From hiding...
to confession.
From fear...
to faith.
From guilt...
to forgiveness.
From death...
to resurrection.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed a pattern you have been hiding, don't perform for the comments.
Be honest before God.
Someone reading those two words may stop and pray for you tonight.
That is what Christian community should look like.
Not polished people pretending they never bleed.
Redeemed people carrying one another toward Jesus.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Someone is ashamed.
Someone believes repeated failure has placed them beyond grace.
Someone has inherited a family pattern they desperately want Christ to break.
Someone may never search for a sermon—but they may read something a friend cared enough to share.
It does not.
It never could.
And not because supporting this ministry replaces whatever biblical convictions you have about giving faithfully, generously, and supporting your local church and Christian ministry.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
But voluntary generosity can help Christian ministry continue.
If God has used this ministry in your life and you want to help it reach another person, your support can become one practical expression of Christian generosity and partnership in Gospel work.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person quietly questioning everything.
Invite the Christian who is tired of shallow Christianity.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the wounded.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks the Bible is only a book about religious people pretending to be perfect.
Genesis itself destroys that illusion.
These people were not saved by maintaining flawless reputations.
The Bible opens the family album and leaves the embarrassing photographs inside.
Why?
Because if Scripture erased every scandal, we might eventually believe redemption belongs only to people without one.
But the Bible keeps showing us frightened patriarchs, dysfunctional families, failures, betrayals, denials, tears, graves...
and a God whose faithfulness keeps moving through all of it toward Jesus.
So when you read Genesis 12...
then Genesis 20...
then Genesis 26...
and whisper,
“Why is this happening again?”
perhaps somewhere inside that question you will hear another one.
How many times has God been faithful to me...
again?
How many doors did He close?
How many consequences did He restrain?
How many times did He call me back?
How many times did His Word expose me?
How many times did Christ meet me in the ruins of something I thought I had destroyed beyond repair?
Do not use grace to excuse your pattern.
Bring the pattern to Jesus.
Do not hide behind half-truths.
Step into the light.
Do not surrender your future to what happened in your family before you.
In Christ, inherited patterns do not have to become inherited destinies.
Repent.
Believe.
Tell the truth.
Seek forgiveness where you have sinned.
Make restitution where righteousness requires it.
Ask for help when you cannot fight alone.
And fix your eyes on the One Abraham could never be.
The One Isaac could never be.
The One you and I could never be.
Jesus Christ.
The faithful Son.
The crucified Savior.
The risen King.
The Friend of sinners who does not leave sinners unchanged.
Because perhaps the most unforgettable truth hidden inside these uncomfortable stories is this:
Your “again” may expose how deeply you need grace—but Christ's faithfulness reveals that your failure does not have to write the final chapter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABDON HAD FORTY SONS AND THIRTY GRANDSONS—WHAT DO THESE ENORMOUS JUDGE-ERA FAMILIES TELL US?
paragraphs: ABDON HAD FORTY SONS AND THIRTY GRANDSONS—WHAT DO THESE ENORMOUS JUDGE-ERA FAMILIES TELL US?

Seventy descendants. Seventy donkeys. Eight years of leadership. Three verses. And buried inside this almost-forgotten judge’s story is a warning about success, legacy, family, influence—and the one thing none of them can save.
There are Bible verses we underline.
There are verses we memorize.
There are verses we preach from pulpits, print on coffee mugs, write inside birthday cards, and whisper through tears when life collapses.
And then there are verses like Judges 12:13–15.
We read them.
We see an unfamiliar name.
We encounter a collection of numbers.
Forty sons.
Thirty grandsons.
Seventy donkeys.
Eight years.
A burial.
Then we keep moving.
But maybe we are moving too fast.

Because Scripture suddenly introduces a man named Abdon, gives us only a few sentences about his life, surrounds him with an enormous family, tells us that seventy of his descendants rode seventy donkeys, tells us that he judged Israel for eight years...
and then tells us he died.
That last part changes everything.
Listen carefully, because what looks like an obscure genealogy may force you to ask one of the most uncomfortable questions a human being can face:
If God wrote only three verses about your life, what would actually matter enough to remain?
The Hebrew text of Judges 12:14 reads:
וַיְהִי־לוֹ אַרְבָּעִים בָּנִים וּשְׁלֹשִׁים בְּנֵי בָנִים רֹכְבִים עַל־שִׁבְעִים עֲיָרִם וַיִּשְׁפֹּט אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל שְׁמֹנֶה שָׁנִים
Vayehi-lo arba'im banim u-sheloshim benei vanim, rokhevim al-shiv'im ayarim; vayishpot et-Yisrael shemoneh shanim.
In straightforward English:
“He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys, and he judged Israel eight years.”
That is an astonishing household.
And Abdon was not the only judge whose family size receives unusual attention.
Just a few verses earlier, Ibzan is described as having thirty sons and thirty daughters. Earlier still, Jair had thirty sons who rode thirty donkeys and controlled thirty towns.
This means the detail concerning Abdon is not floating alone in the book.
There is a pattern.
Large households.
Numerous descendants.
Donkeys.
Leadership.
Influence.
Public standing.
And eventually...
death.
We should be careful here.
The Bible does not explicitly tell us, “Abdon's seventy descendants prove this exact sociological theory.” We should never make Scripture say what Scripture does not say.
But the details are clearly important enough for the inspired narrator to preserve them.

And within Judges itself, riding donkeys appears elsewhere alongside people of standing. Judges 5:10 addresses those who ride on white donkeys, while Judges 10:4 describes Jair's thirty sons riding thirty donkeys.
So when Abdon appears with forty sons, thirty grandsons, and seventy donkey-riding descendants, we are not being shown the portrait of an isolated, powerless man.
We are looking at a substantial household.
A visible family.
A man whose influence had multiplied across generations.
Try to picture it.
Not forty names printed in a genealogy.
Forty living sons.
Voices around tables.
Arguments.
Marriages.
Children.
Work.
Responsibility.
Thirty grandsons growing up underneath the shadow of the family name.
Seventy men riding out.
Seventy animals requiring care.
A household large enough that wherever the family went, people probably noticed.
And at the center of it all stood Abdon.
Judge of Israel.
For eight years.
For most of us, seventy direct male descendants sounds almost unimaginable.
We live in an age where getting four relatives into the same photograph can feel like a military operation.
Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons recorded in Scripture.
But here is where this little passage begins to hurt.
Because after all those sons...
after all those grandsons...
after all those donkeys...
after all that influence...
after eight years of judging Israel...
Judges 12:15 essentially brings the curtain down:
Abdon died.
And he was buried.
That quickly.
An entire human empire reduced to a grave.
That is not cynicism.
That is mortality.
And the Bible loves us too much to let us pretend mortality belongs only to somebody else.
You can build something impressive.
You can have children who carry your name.
You can become respected.
You can acquire property.
You can build businesses.
You can gain followers.
You can become the person everyone calls when something goes wrong.
You can accumulate achievements until your biography sounds extraordinary.
And one day...
someone else will carry your body.
Someone else will close the door to your house.
Someone else will sit in your chair.
Someone else will inherit things you spent decades acquiring.
And eventually people who never met you will walk past the place where you were buried.
That is why Abdon's seventy descendants should not merely make us curious about ancient families.
They should make us think about ours.
What exactly are we building?
Some parents are working themselves nearly to death to give their children everything except the one treasure their children desperately need.
Christ.
We give them education.
Devices.
Shoes.
Bedrooms.
Vacations.
Inheritance.
Connections.
Opportunities.
We worry about what school they attend, what career they choose, what house they eventually own, and whether they will be financially comfortable.
Those things can matter.
But somewhere between paying bills and planning futures, it is frighteningly possible to raise children who know how to survive in this world but do not know the Savior who can rescue them from sin.
Imagine succeeding everywhere...
and failing there.
Imagine leaving your child property but no prayer life.
Money but no knowledge of Scripture.
A family name but no understanding of the name above every name.
Confidence but no repentance.
Religion but no regeneration.
A Christian label but no love for Christ.
What good is an impressive family tree if its branches grow farther and farther away from God?
This is where we must resist another temptation.
Judges 12 does not tell us the spiritual condition of Abdon's forty sons and thirty grandsons.
We cannot honestly preach that they were righteous.
We cannot honestly preach that they were wicked.
The text does not tell us.
And perhaps that silence itself should humble us.
Because Scripture tells us what they rode...
but does not give us enough information to tell us where their hearts stood before God.
That distinction matters.
External prosperity is not the same thing as spiritual prosperity.
A large family is not automatically a godly family.
A successful child is not automatically a surrendered child.
A respected household is not automatically a redeemed household.
And visible blessing should never be confused with saving grace.
That distinction becomes especially powerful in the book of Judges because Judges repeatedly shows us how desperately Israel needed more than another temporary human leader.
Again and again the pattern appears.
Israel falls.
Israel suffers.
God raises a deliverer.
There is relief.
The deliverer dies.
And the deeper human problem remains.
Another judge.
Another generation.
Another crisis.
Another grave.
Abdon could judge Israel.
Abdon could not redeem Israel.
That difference leads us straight to Jesus Christ.
The judges could provide temporary deliverance.
Jesus provides the deliverance no earthly judge could accomplish.
The judges eventually died and remained among the dead.
Jesus died...
and rose.
That changes the entire story.
The Gospel does not tell us that good people climb high enough to reach God.
The Gospel tells us that the Son of God came down to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
We sinned.
Not merely “society.”
Not merely “those people.”
Us.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Envied.
Hated.
Hidden.
Manipulated.
Gossiped.
Worshiped created things.
Protected secret sins while maintaining respectable appearances.
Some of us learned how to look Christian long before we learned how to surrender.
We learned when to say “Amen.”
We learned worship songs.
We learned Christian vocabulary.
We learned how to post Bible verses.
And somehow...
we also learned how to hide.
There are people reading this article who know exactly what that means.
Everyone thinks you are okay.
You aren't.
Everyone thinks your marriage is fine.
It isn't.
Everyone thinks your faith is strong.
You feel exhausted.
Everyone thinks that habit disappeared years ago.
It followed you into last night.
Everyone sees the polished version.
Jesus sees the room nobody else enters.
And still...
He calls you.
Not because sin does not matter.
Precisely because it matters so much that He went to the cross.
Jesus does not expose our sin merely to humiliate us.
He brings darkness into the light so sinners can repent, receive mercy, and become new.
The cross destroys two lies at once.
The first lie says:
“Your sin isn't serious.”
Look at Calvary.
It is.
The second lie says:
“Your sin is too terrible for Christ to forgive.”
Look at Calvary again.
His grace is greater.
That is the scandal.
Holy God receiving guilty people through the sacrifice of His sinless Son.
The ashamed welcomed.
The rebellious invited to repent.
The unclean washed.
The guilty forgiven.
The spiritually dead made alive.
Not because they cleaned themselves first.
Because Jesus saves.
Maybe your family story is beautiful.
Maybe it is broken.
Maybe your father wounded you.
Maybe your mother disappeared emotionally when you needed her most.
Maybe your children barely speak to you.
Maybe divorce divided your home.
Maybe addiction turned childhood memories into scars.
Maybe your surname carries pain instead of honor.
Maybe your family photographs contain people who no longer sit at the same table.
Maybe you look at Abdon's enormous household and do not feel impressed.
You feel lonely.
Hear this carefully.
Your earthly family story does not get the final word over your identity.
Jesus does.
The Gospel reaches into families filled with failure and begins creating something human effort could never manufacture.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation where possible.
Repentance.
New desires.
New priorities.
New fathers who refuse to repeat what their fathers did.
New mothers who decide the cycle stops here.
Young men who choose holiness over secret pornography.
Young women who discover that their worth is not determined by whether somebody desires them.
Husbands who learn to repent instead of dominate.
Wives who learn to forgive without pretending sin is harmless.
Children who watch adults admit, “I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Families opening Bibles where arguments once dominated every evening.
That is legacy.
Not perfection.
Transformation.
Maybe that is what someone in your family has been waiting to see.
Not another sermon from you.
Repentance in you.
We spend enormous energy asking what our children will inherit from us.
Perhaps we should also ask:
What are they learning from watching us suffer?
What do they see when we are angry?
Do they see humility when we are wrong?
Do they hear us apologize?
Do they watch us forgive?
Do they know we pray when nobody is watching?
Do they know that Jesus is more than the religious decoration hanging on our wall?
Do they see Christianity changing how we speak to people who cannot benefit us?
Because eventually your children may forget many of the things you purchased for them.
But they may remember hearing you pray their name before God.
They may remember the night you apologized.
They may remember seeing your Bible open before sunrise.
They may remember that when tragedy entered the house, your faith bent...
but did not break.
And perhaps years after you are gone, one of your grandchildren will repeat something you taught their parent about Jesus.
Suddenly Abdon's seventy descendants feel less like an ancient statistic.
They feel like a mirror.
Because legacy travels.
Sin travels through families.
Patterns travel.
Words travel.
Wounds travel.
But by God's grace, so can faithfulness.
So can truth.
So can prayer.
So can repentance.
So can testimony.
And there is something else we desperately need to notice.
Abdon judged for eight years.
Eight.
Years.
Then another sentence begins.
We often behave as though our current season is permanent.
It isn't.
Your influence has an expiration date.
Your career has an expiration date.
Your physical strength has an expiration date.
Your platform has an expiration date.
Your opportunity to tell certain people about Christ has an expiration date.
There will be a last conversation with your father.
A last meal with your mother.
A last time your child runs through your front door.
A last Sunday in your familiar church seat.
A last ordinary morning.
You probably will not know it is the last one while it is happening.
That is why the Gospel creates urgency without creating panic.
You still have today.
If there is someone you need to forgive, begin praying about it today.
If there is sin you need to confess, stop feeding it in darkness.
If you have wandered from Christ, return.
If your children have never heard your testimony, tell them what Jesus has done.
If someone you love does not know the Gospel, stop assuming there will always be another convenient opportunity.
And if you are reading this while carrying secret shame...
stop trying to rewrite your story without the Author.
You cannot erase yesterday.
Jesus can redeem what yesterday became.
You cannot crucify your own guilt away.
Christ already went to the cross.
You cannot resurrect your own heart.
But the risen Christ gives life.
This is why our message will always be:
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
Not because repentance magically repairs every relationship overnight.
Not because following Jesus guarantees wealth, health, enormous families, or seventy donkeys.
The Gospel is infinitely better than that.
It gives sinners Christ Himself.
Forgiveness through His blood.
Reconciliation with God.
A new identity.
A new Lord.
A new direction.
A hope death cannot bury.
Abdon had forty sons.
Thirty grandsons.
Seventy donkey riders.
Eight years as judge.
And then a grave.
Jesus had no biological dynasty recorded like Abdon's.
Yet two thousand years later, men and women from nations Abdon never knew existed call Jesus Lord.
Kings have died.
Empires have disappeared.
Generations have returned to dust.
Christ remains.
And the question is no longer merely what Abdon's enormous family tells us.
The question is:
What will your life tell the people coming after you?
Will they inherit only your possessions?
Or will they inherit the memory of someone who loved Jesus?
Will your children remember Christianity as something you posted...
or Someone you followed?
Will your grandchildren know you accumulated things...
or that you knew how to kneel?
And if you have no children at all, do not imagine that you have no spiritual legacy to leave.
Someone is watching.
A younger believer.
A sibling.
A friend.
A neighbor.
A hurting stranger.
A person online who almost scrolled past.
Faithfulness multiplies in ways we may never live long enough to see.
That is one reason Gospel-centered work matters.
When an article reaches a person at two in the morning who is ashamed to enter a church...
when a devotional reaches someone whose faith is collapsing...
when Scripture reaches a marriage in crisis...
when biblical truth reaches someone who has been discipled more by algorithms than by the Word of God...
we may never know on this side of eternity what God chooses to do with that seed.
And that is why, if Gospel Warrior has genuinely helped you grow closer to Christ, consider helping this ministry continue and expand.
It does not.
It does not.
The New Testament calls believers to generosity that is willing rather than coerced: “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” as Paul teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7.
But voluntary financial support of Gospel ministry can be a real act of Christian generosity and partnership.

So if God has given you the desire and ability to help Gospel Warrior keep producing Scripture-centered content, reaching more people, expanding discipleship resources, and pointing wounded and wandering hearts toward Jesus Christ, we would be deeply grateful for your monthly support.
It is mission.
We want Scripture opened.
Christ proclaimed.
The wandering called home.
The wounded encouraged.
The comfortable awakened.
The ashamed reminded that grace still has a name.
Jesus.
And financial support is not the only way you can help.
Sometimes one share reaches farther than money ever could.
Not simply to increase a number beneath a post, but because somebody connected to you may desperately need the message you almost kept to yourself.
And yes...
Let them see that Christianity is not pretending Christians never fall.
It is the announcement that sinners can be forgiven because Jesus Christ died and rose again.
Come back to it when success starts convincing you that earthly accomplishments are permanent.
Come back when family disappoints you.
Come back when you are tempted to measure your life by possessions, followers, achievements, or applause.
Forty sons.
Thirty grandsons.
Seventy donkeys.
Eight years.
Then a grave.
Christ must be greater than all of it.
And if something inside you has been exposed while reading this, don't disappear silently.
No explanation required.
And if you have been hiding something from God—as though anything could actually remain hidden from Him—perhaps your comment needs to be simpler still:
Let those words become more than engagement beneath an article.
Let them become a decision.
Then take that decision somewhere deeper than a comment section.
Take it to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Ask for help.
Find mature believers who will walk with you.
Become deeply rooted in Scripture.
Be part of a faithful local church.
Do not build your entire spiritual life around online content.
Online ministry can point you toward the Shepherd.
It must never replace Him.
Give freely.
Never from fear.
Never because someone implied God would love you more.
Never because you were promised earthly prosperity in return.
Jesus cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be bought.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith”—not by building a dynasty, accumulating possessions, earning religious status, or financing a ministry.
We support Gospel work because we have already received something money could never purchase.
Christ.
And maybe that is the secret hidden beneath Abdon's seventy riders.
Not a secret code.
Not a mystical meaning attached to the number seventy.
Something far more confronting.
You can spend your entire life building something enormous...
and still eventually leave it behind.
Abdon did.
You will.
I will.
Every one of us will.
So build what death cannot finally steal.
Teach someone about Jesus.
Forgive.
Repent.
Pray with your children.
Tell your testimony.
Open your Bible.
Serve quietly.
Give generously.
Love faithfully.
Share truth.
Carry the Gospel farther than your own lifetime.

And when your final chapter comes—and somebody else closes your eyes, empties your room, sorts through your possessions, and speaks your name in the past tense—may the greatest thing you leave behind not be what you owned.
May it be evidence that Jesus Christ owned your heart.
Because one day the donkeys disappear.
The houses belong to somebody else.
The titles are reassigned.
The photographs fade.
The applause stops.
The body returns to dust.
But the life surrendered to Jesus can leave fingerprints of grace on generations its owner never lived to meet.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMEN MEN DESTROYED IN THE BIBLE — AND THE SAVIOR WHO REFUSED TO LEAVE THEM IN THE RUINS
paragraphs: THE WOMEN MEN DESTROYED IN THE BIBLE — AND THE SAVIOR WHO REFUSED TO LEAVE THEM IN THE RUINS

They were violated, used, traded, abandoned, silenced, blamed, and sometimes left without even a name. The Bible does not hide what sinful men did to women. It records the wreckage—and then leads us to Jesus Christ, the Man who never used a woman for His pleasure, never exploited her weakness, never confused lust with love, and never walked past her pain.
There is a woman lying at a doorway.
Before you read another sentence, see her.
Not as a Bible character.
Not as an illustration for a sermon.
As a woman.
Somebody's daughter.
A human being made in the image of God.
She has spent the night being brutalized by men while another man—the man who should have protected her—survived inside.
Morning comes.
The door opens.
She is there.
Her hands are at the threshold.
And Scripture gives us one of the most horrifying sentences in the Bible:
“Get up; let us be going.”
But there is no answer.
Judges 19 is not comfortable Christianity.
It is not a verse embroidered on a pillow.
It is Scripture dragging human depravity into the light and refusing to let religious people pretend evil becomes less evil merely because it happened thousands of years ago.
The Hebrew calls this woman an אִשָּׁה פִילֶגֶשׁ — ishshah pilegesh — a woman, a concubine.
Her personal name is never given.
That may be one of the most haunting details of all.
We know the Levite.
We know where he came from.
We know where they traveled.
We know what the men wanted.
We know what happened afterward.
But we do not know her name.
And perhaps that is why her story still sounds terrifyingly modern.
Because history is full of women whose pain everybody discussed while nobody remembered the woman.
Women reduced to scandals.
Women remembered by what was done to them.
Women whose stories became gossip before they became grief.
Women whose bodies became battlefields for the sins of powerful people.
And the Bible does not look away.
Neither should we.
But understand something before going further.
This is not an article declaring men evil and women innocent.
That would not be Christianity.
The Gospel says something far more devastating.
“All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
Women sin.
Men sin.
Women can abuse power. Men can abuse power.
Hagar herself was treated harshly by Sarai, a woman.
Sin does not belong to one sex.

But Scripture contains particular stories in which women suffered terribly through the lust, cowardice, selfishness, violence, negligence, or abuse of men—and those stories deserve to be heard without being softened to protect our comfort.
Because somewhere reading this is a woman who knows what it feels like to become collateral damage in somebody else's appetite.
And somewhere reading this is a man who needs enough courage to ask whether he has ever wounded a woman while calling what he felt “love.”
That question takes us into a royal house.
Her name was Tamar.
She was beautiful.
She was a daughter of David.
A princess.
And Amnon said he loved her.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 13:1 says:
וַיֶּאֱהָבֶהָ אַמְנוֹן
wayye'ehaveha Amnon.
Amnon “loved her.”
But keep reading.
Because the Bible is about to expose one of the most dangerous counterfeits of love.
Amnon becomes consumed with Tamar.
He wants access to her.
He schemes.
He manipulates circumstances.
He gets her alone.
Tamar realizes what is happening and begs him not to do it.
She reasons with him.
She resists him.
He refuses to listen.
And because he is stronger than she is, he violates her.
Then comes one of Scripture's most psychologically brutal observations.
After taking what he wanted, Amnon's supposed love becomes hatred.
The Hebrew text says:
הַשִּׂנְאָה ... מֵאַהֲבָה
ha-sin'ah ... me-ahavah.
The hatred with which he hated her became greater than the “love” with which he had loved her.
Read that slowly.
Because Scripture just exposed lust wearing love's clothing.
Real love does not destroy the person it claims to desire.
Real love does not say, “If you love me, prove it with your body.”
Real love does not manipulate vulnerability.
Real love does not punish boundaries.
Real love does not become hatred when denied gratification.
Real love “seeketh not her own” (1 Corinthians 13:5).
Amnon did not love Tamar as God defines love.
He desired possession.
And when desire had consumed what it wanted, the mask came off.
Then he threw her out.
Tamar went away grieving, with ashes upon her head.
The scandal belonged to Amnon.
But Tamar carried the shame.
How many women know that feeling?
Someone else sinned against you...
yet somehow you became ashamed.
He lied, but you wondered what was wrong with you.
He cheated, but you wondered whether you were beautiful enough.
He manipulated you, but you called yourself stupid.
He violated your boundaries, but you replayed the moment asking what you should have done differently.
He abandoned you, and you began treating his rejection as a verdict on your worth.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel never requires us to rename evil so that sinners can remain comfortable.
Grace is not pretending nothing happened.
Forgiveness is not calling darkness light.
And repentance is not saying, “I'm sorry you felt hurt.”
Biblical repentance faces the truth.
The Hebrew text later describes what Amnon did with the verb עִנָּה — 'innah—language associated here with humiliating, afflicting, or violating Tamar.
God did not inspire Scripture to disguise what happened.
Neither should the church.
And then there is Hagar.
An Egyptian servant in Abraham's household.
Before Hagar becomes part of a theological discussion, remember that she was a human being living under the authority of people more powerful than she was.
Genesis 16 calls her שִׁפְחָה מִצְרִית — shifchah mitzrit — an Egyptian female servant.
Sarai could not conceive and gave Hagar to Abram.
Abram agreed.
Hagar conceived.
Conflict followed.
Then Genesis records:
וַתְּעַנֶּהָ שָׂרַי
vatte'anneha Sarai.
Sarai dealt harshly with her, afflicted her, mistreated her.
Notice the Bible's honesty again.
The victimizer in this scene is a woman.
Scripture will not cooperate with simplistic gender warfare.

But Abram—the man with tremendous authority in this household—does not emerge as some spotless protector either. Hagar is caught inside decisions made by people with vastly greater power than she possesses.
Eventually she runs.
Pregnant.
Into the wilderness.
Imagine that journey.
No maternity ward.
No safety net.
No comfortable home waiting at the end of the road.
A pregnant servant running into a wilderness because the place called home had become unbearable.
And there...
God found her.
That sentence is worth everything.
God found her.
The woman other people treated as useful was not invisible to heaven.
The servant had a name before God.
The foreigner had a name before God.
The pregnant runaway had a name before God.
And Hagar eventually speaks of the God who sees her.
אֵל רֳאִי
El Roi.
The God who sees me.
Maybe you need that name of God tonight.
Because some wounds are made worse by the terrifying thought that nobody saw.
Nobody saw what happened after the door closed.
Nobody heard the things he said.
Nobody saw the messages.
Nobody knew how afraid you were.
Nobody understood why you changed.
Nobody noticed how much of yourself disappeared trying to keep someone else happy.
But God saw.
God saw Tamar.
God saw Hagar.
God saw the unnamed woman at the doorway.
God saw Dinah after Shechem violated her in Genesis 34.
God saw Bathsheba when David, the king, summoned her into a situation marked by an enormous imbalance of royal power and then arranged the death of her husband Uriah after she became pregnant.
And Scripture does something important in David's story.
When Nathan confronts David, he does not place the primary prophetic condemnation upon Bathsheba.
He points at David and says:
“Thou art the man.”
That is biblical accountability.
Not protecting the powerful because they are useful.
Not burying sin because the offender is gifted.
Not worrying more about a man's reputation than the people wounded by his choices.
“You are the man.”
Imagine what would happen if those words returned to Christian masculinity.
Not as hatred toward men.
As a call to holy men.
Men who protect instead of prey.
Men who repent instead of manipulate.
Men who can hear “no” without rage.
Men who keep covenant when temptation whispers.
Men who refuse pornography's education in objectification.
Men who do not use spiritual authority to control women.
Men who do not quote “wives, submit yourselves” while conveniently forgetting that Christlike husbands are commanded to love sacrificially as Christ loved the church.
Men who would rather crucify their lust than crucify somebody else's dignity.
Men who understand that masculinity is not proven by how many women desire you but by how faithfully your life resembles Jesus.
Because then Jesus arrives.
And suddenly the treatment of women becomes breathtaking.
A Samaritan woman stands beside a well in John 4.
Jesus knows her history.
He knows about the husbands.
He knows about the man presently in her life.
He knows everything.
And He speaks to her.
Not around her.
Not about her.
To her.
He does not pretend her story does not matter.
He tells her the truth.
But truth in the hands of Jesus is not a weapon for sadistic humiliation.
It becomes a doorway toward living water.
The woman who came carrying a water jar eventually leaves it behind and runs into the city talking about Christ.
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?”
The woman with a complicated past becomes a witness.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Then another woman comes crawling through a crowd.
Twelve years of bleeding.
Twelve years.
Think about what twelve years means.
Twelve years of waking up with the same problem.
Twelve years of hoping.
Twelve years of disappointment.
Twelve years of watching other people's lives move while yours seems trapped inside one relentless sentence.
She reaches for Jesus.
She touches His garment.
And the bleeding stops.
But Jesus does something more than heal her body.
He turns around.
He brings the hidden woman into the light—not to humiliate her, but to restore her.
And then He says one word that must have landed on her wounded soul like heaven itself:
Θυγάτηρ.
Thygatēr.
“Daughter.”
Daughter.
Not nuisance.
Not unclean woman.
Not embarrassing interruption.
Not damaged goods.
Daughter.
Then:
ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε
hē pistis sou sesōken se.
“Your faith has made you well”—with sesōken coming from sōzō, a word carrying the beautiful biblical field of saving, rescuing, healing, making whole.
And then:
ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην
hypage eis eirēnēn.
Go into peace.
Do you see Jesus?
This is Christianity.
Not men protecting male sin.
Not women being taught to tolerate abuse as though suffering at the hands of an unrepentant abuser were a spiritual virtue.
Not sinners weaponizing forgiveness to escape accountability.
Jesus.
Jesus touching the unclean.
Jesus dignifying women others dismissed.
Jesus receiving repentant sinners.
Jesus exposing hypocrisy.
Jesus telling truth.
Jesus forgiving sin.
Jesus restoring dignity.
Jesus making broken people whole.
And ultimately Jesus Himself being stripped, mocked, beaten, humiliated, pierced, and crucified.
Why?
Because the deepest destroyer in every one of these stories is bigger than man versus woman.
The deepest enemy is sin.
Sin corrupts desire.
Sin turns authority into domination.
Sin turns sexuality into consumption.
Sin turns people into objects.
Sin makes victims hide and perpetrators justify themselves.
And sin lives in male and female hearts alike.
That is why feminism alone cannot save us.
Masculinity movements cannot save us.
Politics cannot save us.
Self-help cannot save us.
Religious performance cannot save us.
We need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
At the cross, Christ does not merely offer traumatized people better self-esteem.
He deals with sin at its root.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
That means there is grace for the woman who has been destroyed.
And there is grace for the man who finally admits he has been doing the destroying.
But grace does not mean remaining the same.
The Gospel says repent.
Turn.
Come into the light.
If you abused someone, repent.
If you manipulated someone sexually, repent.
If you betrayed your marriage, repent.
If pornography has trained your eyes to consume human beings made in God's image, repent.
If you use anger to intimidate your wife or girlfriend, repent.
If you weaponize Scripture to control someone, repent.
If you have treated women's bodies as commodities while singing worship songs on Sunday, repent.
Do not hide behind “God knows my heart.”
He does.
That is precisely why repentance is necessary.
And if you are the woman who was wounded, please hear something equally important.
What happened to you is not the final author of who you are.
Your abuser does not get authorship rights over the rest of your life.
Your abandonment does not name you.
Your divorce does not name you.
Your assault does not name you.
Your betrayal does not name you.
Your sexual past does not possess the authority to write the last chapter.
Your worst night cannot overrule the empty tomb.
Christ can redeem what sin devastated.
That does not mean every scar disappears overnight.
It does not mean trauma is imaginary.
It does not mean justice is unnecessary.
It does not mean reconciliation is automatically safe or required where there is continuing abuse and no repentance.
And it certainly does not mean staying in immediate danger to prove you have faith.
It means evil does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Maybe you saw Tamar and suddenly remembered yourself.
Maybe Hagar's wilderness felt familiar.
Maybe you have spent years being everybody's strong woman while quietly wondering whether God still sees you.
Maybe you are a man reading this with an uncomfortable heaviness because faces are coming into your mind.
Someone you used.
Someone you lied to.
Someone whose trust you broke.
Someone you pressured.
Someone you abandoned.
Someone who still carries a wound bearing your fingerprints.
Run toward Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Where appropriate and safe, make restitution.
Accept consequences.
Stop defending the person Jesus is calling you to crucify.
There is mercy at the cross even for people who discover that they were the villain in somebody else's story.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus saves sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Real ones.
The sexually broken.
The adulterer.
The liar.
The coward.
The manipulator.
The bitter.
The abused.
The abuser who genuinely repents.
The ashamed.
The self-righteous.
The person crying in the wilderness.
The person who caused someone else to run there.
But nobody comes to Jesus clutching both salvation and the right to remain unchanged.
Grace forgives us.
Then grace begins transforming us.
That is why this is bigger than an article about women destroyed by men.
It is about what sin does to human beings...
and what Jesus Christ can do with the ruins.
Not performative.
Not religious.
Honest.
Sometimes confession begins with four words typed through trembling fingers.
And sometimes testimony begins when somebody realizes, “I am not the only one.”
Not because every sentence will feel good tomorrow.
You may never know whose midnight prayer your share answers.
And yes, even share it with the skeptic who thinks the Bible hides human ugliness.
It doesn't.
Scripture exposes human sin with frightening honesty because the Bible's Hero is not humanity.
The Hero is Christ.
I want to be careful here because biblical truth matters more than fundraising.

Scripture teaches generous support for Gospel ministry, but it also says giving should be purposeful and willing, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

If these articles glorify Christ, proclaim His Gospel, call sinners to repentance, strengthen wounded believers, and help people open their Bibles again, your monthly support becomes a practical offering toward keeping that work moving.
Scripture recognizes the legitimacy of materially supporting Gospel ministry. Paul wrote that “the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14).
Supporting faithful Christian work can therefore be an act of generosity offered to God's glory.
Not purchasing God's favor.
Not buying a blessing.
Not paying for salvation.
You could never purchase what Jesus bought with His blood.
Salvation is grace.
But redeemed people can freely choose to put their resources behind work they believe advances the Gospel.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is another morning in Scripture.
Another conviction you needed.
Another reminder when your faith feels weak.
Another opportunity to point someone toward Jesus.
Another soul encountering the Gospel.
Because this world has enough voices teaching people how to disguise their wounds.
We need Christ teaching us how to bring them into His light.
Enough Amnons calling lust love.
Enough Davids believing power can hide consequences.
Enough Hagars running into wildernesses believing nobody sees.
Enough Tamars carrying shame that belongs to somebody else's sin.
Enough unnamed women collapsing at thresholds while everybody else keeps moving.
And enough men believing repentance makes them weak.
Repentance does not emasculate a man.
It brings a sinful man to the feet of the only perfect Man who ever lived.
Jesus Christ.
The Man who possessed all authority and never abused it.
The Man who knew every woman's secret and never exploited one.
The Man who confronted sin without becoming cruel.
The Man who defended dignity without redefining holiness.
The Man who touched the unclean.
The Man who welcomed the repentant.
The Man who carried our sin.
The Man who died our death.
The Man who walked out of His grave.
The King who still looks at ruined human stories and says:
I am not finished.
So remember the woman at the doorway.
Remember Tamar in ashes.
Remember Hagar beside the spring.
Remember the bleeding woman trembling at Jesus' feet.
And then remember what He called her.
Daughter.
That is what grace does.
Sin reduces people to bodies.
Grace restores persons.
Sin uses.
Grace gives.
Sin hides.
Grace brings truth into light.
Sin wounds.
Christ saves.
And when Jesus takes the pen, the chapter that nearly destroyed you does not have permission to become the ending.
Your wound may explain some of your scars—but only Jesus Christ has the authority to write your final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Should Christians Use Images of Jesus? The Question That Becomes More Serious the Longer You Look at Him
paragraphs: Should Christians Use Images of Jesus? The Question That Becomes More Serious the Longer You Look at Him

Before you delete the picture, defend the painting, kiss the icon, condemn the icon, share the AI-generated Jesus, or accuse another Christian of idolatry… there is one question Scripture forces us to ask first: What exactly are we doing with the image—and what has happened inside our hearts?
There is a picture of Jesus on the wall.
Maybe you grew up with one.
Long hair. Gentle eyes. A carefully trimmed beard. Light falling across His face as though heaven itself had paused for the portrait.
Perhaps your grandmother had one hanging above the dining table.
Perhaps there was one in your childhood church.
Maybe you have a picture of Christ carrying a lamb, praying in Gethsemane, standing beside a frightened child, or stretching His wounded hands toward the world.
