And maybe looking at it has never bothered you.
Until someone told you:
“That is idolatry.”
Suddenly something that once seemed innocent feels dangerous.
Then another Christian responds:
“No. Jesus became a real human being. Christians have portrayed Him for centuries.”
Now you are caught between two people who both quote Scripture, both confess Christ, and both seem absolutely convinced that the other side is missing something obvious.
So what should a Christian actually believe?
Should Christians use images of Jesus?
Before answering, we need enough humility to admit something important.
The Bible never gives us a verse that simply says, “You may paint Jesus,” or, “You may never draw Jesus.”
That means we must resist the temptation to make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
But Scripture does give us powerful principles.
And once those principles are placed beside one another, this question becomes far deeper than whether a painting belongs on your wall.
Because this is ultimately a question about worship.
About conscience.
About incarnation.
About idolatry.
And about whether our hearts are satisfied with the Jesus God has revealed—or whether we quietly begin creating a Jesus of our own imagination.
Go back to Sinai.
Smoke.
Fire.
Thunder.
A trembling mountain.
And the voice of God.
Then comes the command:
“לֹא־תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל”
Lo-ta'aseh lekha pesel.
“You shall not make for yourself a carved image…”
Exodus 20:4 continues by prohibiting the making of a likeness for the purpose described immediately afterward: bowing down to them and serving them.
That context matters.

God was not giving Israel a universal prohibition against every piece of representational artwork. We know this because God Himself later commanded artistic representations to be made in connection with the tabernacle, including cherubim.
The problem was not simply that human hands could produce art.
The horror was that human beings could take something created, fashioned, carved, painted, or imagined and give it the devotion belonging to the Creator.
That distinction matters enormously.
Yet Deuteronomy adds another warning that should make every Christian slow down before dismissing concerns about religious imagery.
Moses reminds Israel that at Horeb:
“You saw no form…”
The Hebrew idea is striking.
Israel heard God.
But they were not given a visible form of God to reproduce.

Therefore Moses warns them against corrupting themselves by making an image in the likeness of male or female. Deuteronomy 4:15–16 connects their not seeing a form with the danger of manufacturing one for themselves.
God would not allow Israel to domesticate Him.
They could not shrink the invisible Creator into something their hands could control.
They could not say:
“This is what God looks like.”
And perhaps that is where this conversation first reaches into us.
Because human beings have always wanted a God we can manage.
A God we can carry.
A God we can decorate.
A God who agrees with us.
A God who never contradicts us.
A God whose face looks exactly as we imagine it should.
But the living God refuses to become the product of human imagination.
Paul makes essentially that point centuries later in Athens.
Surrounded by idols, he declares that the divine nature should not be thought of as gold, silver, or stone—
“χαράγματι τέχνης καὶ ἐνθυμήσεως ἀνθρώπου”
—something fashioned by human art and imagination.
And then Paul moves directly toward repentance.
That warning should never be trivialized.
No painting contains God.
No statue contains God.
No crucifix contains God.
No icon contains God.
No photograph-like reconstruction contains God.
No AI-generated portrait contains God.
And no artist knows the precise facial appearance of Jesus of Nazareth.
Whatever image you have seen is an artistic representation.
It is not a photograph.
It is not an eyewitness portrait supplied by Scripture.
It is not Jesus Himself.
But then Christianity makes an astonishing claim that prevents this discussion from ending there.
Something happened in Bethlehem that had never happened at Sinai.
John writes:
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh…”
John 1:14.
Read those words slowly.
The Word became flesh.
Christianity does not teach that God merely projected a human illusion.
Jesus Christ truly entered human history.
He had a human body.
Human hands.
Human eyes.
Human skin.
People saw Him.
People touched Him.
People ate with Him.
Children could be brought to Him.
John could recline near Him.
Thomas could be invited to see His wounds.
Roman soldiers could seize Him.
A crown of thorns could be pressed onto His head.
Nails could pierce His flesh.
His body could be placed inside a tomb.
And that body could rise.
This is why Christians who permit images of Jesus make an argument that deserves to be represented fairly rather than caricatured.
Their reasoning is not necessarily:
“The Second Commandment does not matter.”
Often their reasoning is exactly the opposite.
They believe the incarnation matters so profoundly that the Son of God truly became visible humanity.
Christ is not merely an invisible spiritual idea.
Paul even calls Jesus:
“εἰκὼν τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου”
eikōn tou Theou tou aoratou.
“The image of the invisible God.”
Colossians 1:15.
But we must be extraordinarily careful here.
Paul is describing Christ Himself as the image of the invisible God.
He is not saying that our painting of Christ becomes the image of God in the same sense.
Jesus is unique.
The canvas is not Jesus.
The statue is not Jesus.
The digital illustration is not Jesus.
The icon is not Jesus.
Christ is the incarnate Son.
The artwork is the work of a human being attempting to portray Him.
Confusing those categories is where spiritual danger begins.
Imagine a woman sitting alone late at night.
Her marriage is collapsing.
Her son will not speak to her.
She has prayed until she does not know what else to say.
Across the room hangs a painting of Jesus reaching toward Peter as he sinks beneath the water.
She looks at it.
And suddenly remembers:
“Lord, save me.”
She begins crying.
Not because she believes the canvas can hear her.
Not because she believes paint has supernatural power.
The image simply reminded her of a biblical truth:
Peter sank.
Peter cried out.
Christ rescued him.
Her heart moves beyond the painting to the Savior.
Is that automatically the worship of an idol?
We should be careful before saying yes.
Now change the scene.
Another person stands before an image.
He begins believing the physical object possesses spiritual power.
He trusts the object to protect his house.
He treats touching it as though touching the material object itself guarantees divine favor.
His confidence gradually moves from Christ toward the object.
The representation has become spiritually confused with the One represented.
Now we have entered very dangerous territory.
Because idolatry does not become acceptable simply because the idol has been given a Christian name.
You can write “Jesus” underneath an object and still misuse it.
You can place a cross around your neck and live as though you hate the One who died upon it.
You can own twenty Bibles and refuse to obey a single page.
You can fill your house with Christian artwork while Christ remains unwelcome in your decisions.
And you can have absolutely no religious artwork anywhere in your home while worshiping money, reputation, sexuality, political power, success, comfort, or yourself.
That is the twist we sometimes miss.
A person can remove every picture of Jesus from the house…
and still have a house full of idols.
Because idolatry ultimately reaches deeper than furniture and decoration.
It reaches the throne of the heart.
Yet that does not make physical idolatry imaginary or harmless.
Scripture repeatedly warns God's people against giving created things the worship, trust, devotion, or glory belonging to God.
So perhaps the more revealing question is not merely:
“Do you have an image of Jesus?”
Perhaps it is:
“What are you doing with it?”
Do you believe it is Jesus?
Do you attribute spiritual power to the object itself?
Does your devotion depend upon possessing or touching it?
Has an imagined face begun replacing Scripture's revelation of Christ in your mind?
Are you defending the object more passionately than you defend the Gospel?
Would losing the image feel like losing Jesus?
Those questions matter.
But there is another side.
If you reject images of Jesus, ask yourself something equally uncomfortable.
Do you believe Christians who use them are automatically idolaters even when they explicitly deny worshiping the object?
Have you turned your conviction into a weapon against brothers and sisters?
Have you begun measuring someone's faithfulness to Christ by a disputed application that Scripture does not address in one simple sentence?
Can you distinguish between someone illustrating a biblical event and someone worshiping an object?
Can you disagree without condemning someone's heart when you cannot see that heart?
Romans 14 was not written specifically about religious artwork. Its immediate disputes concerned matters such as food and days, so we should not pretend otherwise.
But Paul's principles concerning conscience, judgment, faith, and stumbling fellow believers are relevant when Christians navigate disputed practices.
He writes:
“Therefore let us not judge one another anymore…”
and urges believers not to place a proskomma or skandalon—a stumbling block or occasion for falling—in another believer's path.
Later comes an even more sobering principle:
“πᾶν δὲ ὃ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως ἁμαρτία ἐστίν.”
“Whatever is not from faith is sin.”
Romans 14:23.
That should stop both sides from behaving carelessly.
If your conscience, informed by Scripture, will not allow you to use an image of Jesus in good faith before God, do not violate your conscience merely because someone calls you legalistic.
You do not need the picture.
You need Christ.

But if another believer uses a biblical illustration as art, education, storytelling, historical imagination, or a reminder of a Gospel event without worshiping it, do not casually pronounce a judgment on that person's soul that Scripture itself has not explicitly pronounced.
And if you do use images of Jesus, hold them loosely.
Very loosely.
Never confuse imagination with revelation.
Never pretend we know Jesus' precise earthly appearance when Scripture does not give us a portrait.
Never allow an artist's face of Jesus to become more authoritative in your imagination than Scripture's revelation of Jesus.
Because Scripture gives us something infinitely better than a reconstruction of His cheekbones.
It tells us who He is.
Holy.
Merciful.
Righteous.
Compassionate.
Sinless.
Crucified.
Risen.
Lord.
King.
Savior.
The Lamb of God who takes away sin.
The image of the invisible God.
The One through whom and for whom all things were created.
The One before whom every knee will bow.
That is the Jesus we cannot afford to replace.
And perhaps this is where the argument suddenly stops being about somebody else's wall.
Because there is a far more dangerous image of Jesus than anything hanging inside a church.
It is the Jesus we manufacture inside ourselves.
The Jesus who never confronts our sin.
The Jesus who approves every desire.
The Jesus who exists to make us wealthy.
The Jesus who hates everyone we hate.
The Jesus who belongs to our political tribe.
The Jesus who never says, “Repent.”
The Jesus who gives heaven without lordship, forgiveness without repentance, Christianity without a cross, and grace without transformation.
That Jesus may never be painted.
He may never be carved.
He may never hang on a wall.
But he can still be an idol.
And perhaps some of us have spent years arguing about pictures of Jesus while worshiping a Jesus created in the image of ourselves.
That should frighten us more.
Because the Gospel does not invite us to invent Christ.
It calls us to surrender to Him.
The real Jesus does not exist to decorate our lives.
He comes to save sinners.
He comes to expose darkness.
He comes with grace for the ashamed and truth for the self-deceived.
He touches lepers.
He receives the broken.
He confronts hypocrites.
He welcomes repentant sinners.
He carries a cross.
And then, astonishingly, He carries our sin upon it.
Maybe that is why this question becomes so emotional.
Somewhere beneath the theological arguments is a human heart desperately wanting to see Jesus.
We want something tangible.
Something close.
Something we can look at when life becomes unbearable.
But Christian hope goes beyond every painting ever made.
One day faith will become sight.
Not because an artist finally produces the perfect portrait.
Not because artificial intelligence reconstructs the right face.
Not because archaeologists discover the right image.
But because Christ Himself will be seen.
Until then, Scripture calls us to know Him through the revelation God has actually given us and to worship Him in spirit and truth.
So should Christians use images of Jesus?

Scripture gives clear prohibitions against idolatry and against reducing the divine nature to the products of human art and imagination. It also gives us the astonishing reality that the eternal Son truly became flesh and was genuinely seen by human beings. What Scripture does not give us is a simple verse explicitly settling every modern use of a visual depiction of Jesus.
Therefore, Christians should approach the question with biblical conviction, humility, and a guarded conscience.
Never worship an image.
Never trust an image.
Never attribute divine power to an image.
Never confuse an artistic representation with Christ Himself.
Never allow an imagined face to replace the biblical Christ.
Never violate your conscience simply to fit in.
And never make your own conclusion on a disputed application an excuse for pride, contempt, or careless judgment toward another believer.
If an image leads you toward superstition, misplaced devotion, confusion, or violation of conscience, remove it.
Christ is infinitely more precious than the object.
If you use an image simply as illustration or art, remember every time you see it:
This is not His photograph.
This is not His presence.
This is not my mediator.
This cannot hear me.
This cannot save me.
Jesus Christ can.
And perhaps someone reading this has discovered something more painful than a theological disagreement.
Maybe you realized you have been carrying a counterfeit Jesus.
Not necessarily in your hands.
In your heart.
A convenient Jesus.
A manageable Jesus.
A Jesus who never gets close enough to touch the secret you have protected for years.
But the living Christ already knows.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The bitterness hidden behind Christian vocabulary.
The affair nobody discovered.
The resentment toward God.
The prayer life that disappeared months ago.
The church smile covering spiritual exhaustion.
The addiction.
The pride.
The secret unbelief.
The shame.
The thing you keep promising Jesus you will stop doing.
He knows.
And still the Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful.
Christ died for sinners.
Not cleaned-up sinners.
Not impressive sinners.
Sinners.
At the cross, the Holy One took the judgment His people deserved.
And the risen Christ still calls sinners to repent, believe, come into the light, and receive mercy.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending your scandal never happened.
Not by renaming sin.
Not by telling you darkness is actually light.
Grace does something far more glorious.
Grace meets the guilty person at the place where excuses finally die…
and offers forgiveness purchased by Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to perform for us.
But you can be honest.

And if you disagree about images of Jesus, let the comments demonstrate something the world rarely sees anymore: Christians capable of conviction without cruelty. Tell us what Scripture has persuaded you to believe and why. Then listen to another believer before assuming the worst about them.
Not because every sentence must become your conclusion, but because these Scriptures deserve more than a five-second reaction.
Send it to the person who once asked you whether Christian images are idols and you did not know how to answer.
It does not.
Not because giving can purchase salvation.
It cannot.
Christian generosity must never be manipulated.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be a genuine voluntary expression of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, prayerfully, cheerfully, and for the glory of God.
And sometimes supporting Gospel work costs less than we imagine.
One shared article.
One friend tagged.
One believer deciding that instead of merely consuming Christian content, they will help useful biblical content reach somebody else.

If you want to glorify God through your resources, there are many faithful ways to do that: care for your family, serve your local church, help the poor, support missions and Gospel ministry, practice hospitality, and give generously as God enables you. Supporting Gospel Warrior can be one voluntary part of that larger life of Christian generosity.
Free resources because truth should reach people who cannot afford another purchase.
And the Gospel at the center because none of this matters if people remember Gospel Warrior but forget Jesus.
But above everything else…
Follow Christ.
Because when the paintings fade, when the screens go dark, when our arguments are forgotten, when every earthly ministry has finished its assignment, there will still be Jesus.
Not an artist's Jesus.
Not your imagined Jesus.
Not my preferred Jesus.
Not a Jesus reconstructed to fit the culture.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
And coming again.
So whether there is a picture of Jesus hanging on your wall or you would never permit one inside your home, make certain there is no rival sitting on the throne that belongs to Him.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be getting the painting wrong.
It would be spending your life defending an image of Jesus while never surrendering to Jesus Himself.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE MODERN-DAY PROPHETS BIBLICAL? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE WHO YOU’VE BEEN LISTENING TO
paragraphs: ARE MODERN-DAY PROPHETS BIBLICAL? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE WHO YOU’VE BEEN LISTENING TO

Before you call someone a prophet because they predicted something correctly, gave you chills, knew something about your life, or said, “Thus says the Lord,” there is something Scripture desperately needs you to understand.
There is a sentence being spoken in churches, livestreams, conferences, prayer meetings, Facebook videos, and private messages all over the world.
“God told me…”
Sometimes those words are followed by comfort.
Sometimes by warning.
Sometimes by a prediction.
Sometimes by a request for money.
Sometimes by something so strangely accurate that the person hearing it freezes.
And sometimes those four words have been used to manipulate frightened people into decisions God never commanded them to make.
That is why this question matters more than many Christians realize:
Are modern-day prophets actually biblical?
Because there are two dangerous mistakes we can make.
We can believe everything supernatural-looking.
Or we can reject everything we cannot explain.
The Bible permits neither.
And somewhere between gullibility and cynicism stands a command many Christians have forgotten:
Test it.
Not because you hate prophecy.
Not because you are afraid of the Holy Spirit.
Not because you think God has become silent or powerless.
But because you love Jesus too much to put another human voice where only His truth belongs.
Paul wrote something remarkably balanced:
“Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies. Test all things; hold fast what is good.”
That tension matters.
Do not despise.
But test.
Receive what is good.
Reject what is false.
The Christian is not commanded to swallow every spiritual claim whole. Neither is the Christian commanded automatically to mock every claim of prophetic activity.
We are commanded to discern.
And the original language makes the point even sharper.
When John warns believers about spiritual deception, the Greek text of 1 John 4:1 says:
“Ἀγαπητοί, μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε, ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα…”
Agapētoi, mē panti pneumati pisteuete, alla dokimazete ta pneumata…
In straightforward English:
“Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits…”
The word δοκιμάζετε — dokimazete carries the idea of examining or testing something to determine whether it is genuine.
John does not say, “If somebody mentions Jesus, believe them.”
He does not say, “If they perform something impressive, believe them.”
He does not say, “If thousands follow them, believe them.”
He says:
Test.
Why?
“Because many false prophets have gone out into the world.”
That warning was not written to atheists.
It was written to believers.
And that changes everything.
Because apparently it is possible to be sincerely religious and still be deceived.
It is possible to hear someone use biblical vocabulary while teaching something unbiblical.
It is possible to mistake charisma for anointing.
Confidence for authority.
Emotion for revelation.
Popularity for fruit.
And accuracy for divine approval.
Jesus Himself warned:
“Beware of false prophets…”
Then He gave His disciples a test that reaches much deeper than performance:
“You will recognize them by their fruits.”
Not their follower count.
Not their stage.
Not their title.
Not how dramatically they say, “The Lord showed me…”
Fruit.
Character.
Doctrine.
Obedience.
What kind of life grows around their ministry?
Where does their message ultimately lead?

And perhaps most terrifyingly, Jesus later describes people saying to Him that they prophesied in His name, yet His response exposes that impressive spiritual claims are not themselves proof of belonging to Him.
Read that again.
A person can use the name of Jesus while Jesus Himself is not impressed by the spectacle.
That should put holy caution inside every Christian heart.
But now we must confront the other side.
Does the New Testament actually describe prophets after the resurrection of Jesus?
Yes.
It does.
Paul writes in Ephesians 4:11:
Kai autos edōken tous men apostolous, tous de prophētas…
“He Himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets…”
Prophets appear among the ministries Christ gave to His church.
The New Testament also speaks of prophecy as a spiritual gift. Acts records prophets in the early Christian community. Paul discusses prophecy repeatedly in 1 Corinthians.
So simply saying, “Prophets are Old Testament, therefore prophecy has nothing to do with the New Testament church,” does not account for all the biblical evidence.
But neither does that mean every modern person calling himself “Prophet” possesses the same authority as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Moses, Peter, or Paul.
That distinction is enormous.
The prophets through whom God delivered the canonical Scriptures occupied a revelatory role that cannot casually be claimed by somebody with a microphone and a social-media account.
Hebrews opens with words that should humble every Christian teacher:
“Πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως πάλαι ὁ θεὸς λαλήσας τοῖς πατράσιν ἐν τοῖς προφήταις… ἐλάλησεν ἡμῖν ἐν υἱῷ…”
Polymerōs kai polytropōs palai ho Theos lalēsas tois patrasin en tois prophētais… elalēsen hēmin en Huiō…
“In the past God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets at many times and in various ways, but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son.”
Do not miss the direction.
The climax is Jesus.
Not the prophet.
Jesus.
Christianity does not culminate in chasing people who claim secret information from heaven.
Christianity culminates in Christ.
The Word became flesh.
The Lamb was slain.
The grave was opened.
The King rose.
And if a supposed prophetic ministry continually makes you fascinated with the prophet while leaving you strangely shallow in your knowledge of Jesus, something has gone terribly wrong.
True Christian ministry does not build dependence upon the messenger.
It points beyond the messenger to the Messiah.
That is why prophecy in the New Testament church is not presented as something that automatically shuts down discernment.
Quite the opposite.
Paul says:
“προφῆται δὲ δύο ἢ τρεῖς λαλείτωσαν, καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι διακρινέτωσαν.”
Prophētai de dyo ē treis laleitōsan, kai hoi alloi diakrinetōsan.
“Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others discern.”
That final word matters.
διακρινέτωσαν — diakrinetōsan.
Let the others discern, distinguish, evaluate.
Imagine saying that in some modern religious environments.
“Pastor, I want to test that prophecy against Scripture.”
“How dare you question the anointed!”
But Paul expected evaluation.
The apostolic command was not:
“Prophecy has been spoken. Everybody stop thinking.”
It was:
Let it be weighed.
That means biblical discernment is not rebellion against the Holy Spirit.
Biblical discernment is obedience to the Holy Spirit-inspired Scriptures.
And here is where many wounded Christians need to hear something clearly.
Someone saying “God told me” does not automatically give that person authority over your life.
You are not required to marry someone because a self-proclaimed prophet said so.
You are not required to abandon medical care because somebody announced a healing.
You are not required to empty your bank account because someone promised a supernatural financial harvest.
You are not required to move cities, quit your job, end a relationship, join a ministry, or make a life-changing decision merely because somebody attached God’s name to their personal impression.
Those words should make us tremble:
“God told me.”
Because if God did not tell you…
you have just placed His name on your own words.
The Old Testament treated that offense with frightening seriousness.

Deuteronomy 18 warns against someone who presumes to speak in God's name what God did not command. It also gives Israel a concrete test regarding predictions: when a supposed word spoken in the Lord’s name does not happen, the text says that word was not spoken by the Lord.
That should destroy the casual culture of endlessly failed predictions followed by excuses.
If someone repeatedly announces specific events “from God” that do not happen, Christians should not keep moving the goalposts simply because they love the personality.
God does not need public-relations professionals to protect Him from failed prophecy.
Truth survives examination.
And Scripture gives another important picture of New Testament prophecy.
Paul says:
“ὁ δὲ προφητεύων ἀνθρώποις λαλεῖ οἰκοδομὴν καὶ παράκλησιν καὶ παραμυθίαν.”
The person prophesying speaks toward oikodomē—building up; paraklēsis—encouragement or exhortation; and paramythia—comfort or consolation.
Notice how different that can look from the celebrity-prophet culture many people have encountered.
Biblical prophecy is not primarily spiritual entertainment.
It is not fortune-telling baptized with Christian vocabulary.
It is not a machine for discovering lottery numbers, celebrity deaths, election results, romantic partners, or secret codes.
And it is certainly not permission to replace Scripture.
The purpose is connected to the building up of God's people.
That does not settle every theological debate.

Faithful Christians disagree about whether the New Testament gift of prophecy continues today in the same way it functioned in the apostolic church. Christians commonly described as continuationists believe gifts such as prophecy continue, while cessationists argue that certain revelatory gifts were particularly associated with the foundational apostolic era and have ceased or do not continue in the same form.
That debate deserves honesty.
There are serious Christians on both sides who confess the authority of Scripture and the lordship of Jesus Christ.
But here is something both sides should be able to say together:
No modern prophet outranks Scripture.
No vision corrects the Gospel.
No dream rewrites Jesus.
No “word from the Lord” gets immunity from biblical examination.
No supernatural experience gives someone permission to preach another Christ.
And nobody gets to manipulate you simply because they put “Prophet” before their name.

Even Christians very near the early centuries of the church wrestled with fraudulent prophetic ministry. The Didache, an early Christian writing outside the New Testament canon, discusses how communities should respond to itinerant apostles and prophets. Strikingly, it warns about those who exploit religious authority for personal gain and connects the credibility of a purported prophet with conduct. This document is not Scripture and must never be treated as Scripture, but historically it demonstrates that concerns about false and financially exploitative prophets are hardly a modern invention.
And maybe that is where this article becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the greatest question is not:
“Are there prophets today?”
Maybe the question beneath the question is:
“Why are we so desperate for one?”
Why do we sometimes want somebody to tell us God's secret plan when God has already told us plainly how to live?
We want a prophecy about our future…
while ignoring His command to forgive.
We want someone to reveal whom we will marry…
while refusing to become the kind of godly person Scripture tells us to be.
We want a word about financial breakthrough…
while Jesus is confronting our greed.
We want somebody to tell us that a season of promotion is coming…
while Christ is calling us to take up our cross.
We want to know what God will do next year…
while avoiding what God has already commanded today.
Sometimes chasing prophetic voices can become a way of escaping obedience.
Because mystery feels exciting.
Obedience feels expensive.
And Scripture is already painfully clear about many things we would rather have God “reveal” differently.
Love your enemies.
Forgive.
Flee sexual immorality.
Care for the poor.
Tell the truth.
Repent.
Pray.
Make disciples.
Deny yourself.
Take up your cross.
Follow Jesus.
Maybe you do not need another prediction.
Maybe you need surrender.
Maybe the word your heart has been waiting for is not hidden in somebody’s private revelation.
Maybe it has been sitting unopened on your bedside table.
And maybe the Holy Spirit is not trying to make you obsessed with tomorrow.
Maybe He is putting His finger on something in your life right now.
That secret sin.
That bitterness.
That double life.
That pride.
That relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
That addiction nobody knows about.
That religious performance hiding a starving soul.
You have watched sermons.
You have saved prophetic videos.
You have searched for signs.
You have whispered:
“God, just tell me what happens next.”
And perhaps Christ is asking something far more important:
“Will you follow Me even if I do not tell you what happens next?”
That is faith.
Not knowing every detail.
Knowing Him.
Not possessing tomorrow.
Being possessed by Christ today.
There is something profoundly liberating about realizing that your safety is not found in locating a flawless modern prophet.
Your safety is found in Jesus Christ.
The One who knew your scandal before you committed it.
The One who saw your shame before anybody else discovered it.
The One who knew exactly how far you would run.
And still went to the cross.
He did not die so that you could spend your life terrified that you missed somebody's prophecy.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
At Calvary, Jesus carried what no prophet could carry for you.
Your guilt.
Your condemnation.
Your sin.
Your rebellion.
Your shame.
The scandal of the Gospel is that the Holy One took the place of the guilty.
And the wonder of grace is that guilty people do not have to remain what sin made them.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you home.
Grace is not permission to stay chained.
Grace breaks the chains.
Forgiveness is not pretending the scandal never happened.
Forgiveness is Jesus taking the scandal into His wounds and writing redemption where judgment should have been the final sentence.
So if a prophet, preacher, apostle, pastor, evangelist, teacher, influencer, visionary, dreamer, or miracle worker makes himself the center…
look again at Jesus.
If the message contradicts Scripture…
stay with Scripture.
If someone demands unquestioning allegiance…
remember that the apostles themselves instructed Christians to discern.
If money becomes the price of blessing…
be careful.
If fear becomes the leash keeping you attached to a spiritual personality…
look to Christ.
If a prophecy fails…
do not pretend truth does not matter.
If somebody tells you that questioning their words means questioning God…
open your Bible.
And if somebody faithfully points you toward Jesus, repentance, holiness, grace, truth, love, humility, and obedience to Scripture…
do not worship the messenger.
Thank God for the servant.
Then keep your eyes on the Master.
Because the goal was never to become addicted to prophetic voices.
The goal was to know Jesus.
Maybe this article found you because you have been confused.
Maybe somebody prophesied over you and you have secretly built years of your life around those words.
Maybe the prediction never happened.
Maybe you blamed yourself.
“Perhaps I didn't have enough faith.”
Maybe someone told you your delay happened because you did not sow enough money.
Maybe you have carried guilt because you questioned a spiritual leader.
Or perhaps you have experienced something you genuinely cannot explain and you are afraid that examining it biblically somehow dishonors God.
It does not.
Truth does not fear examination.
Bring everything into the light of Scripture.
Test the teaching.
Examine the fruit.
Look at the person's relationship with money, power, correction, sexual integrity, accountability, truth, and especially Jesus Christ.
And never surrender the authority of God's written Word to somebody else's experience.
You do not have to choose between being spiritually alive and biblically discerning.
You can desire everything God genuinely gives while refusing everything God never said.
You can pray:
“Holy Spirit, I do not want counterfeit fire.
I want Christ.
If something is from You, give me humility to receive it.
If something is false, give me courage to reject it.
If I have made an idol out of a preacher, prophet, ministry, experience, or prediction, forgive me.
Bring me back to Jesus.”
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to pray something even simpler:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Somebody reading silently may realize for the first time that they are not alone.
Not because every sentence must be accepted unquestioningly—test this article too.
Open the Scriptures yourself.
Read the passages in context.
Search.
Pray.
Study.
Let God's Word correct us wherever correction is needed.
Send it privately to the person who has been afraid to question what someone supposedly “prophesied” over them.
Not to start a witch hunt.
Not to mock Christians who understand spiritual gifts differently.
Not to attack people.
But to bring the conversation back where it belongs:
Jesus Christ and His Word.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you grow deeper in Christ, you can also help this ministry continue and expand.
Supporting Gospel work can be a genuine act of Christian generosity when it is given freely, prayerfully, and without manipulation.
Never underestimate one share.
You do not know who is awake at 2:17 in the morning scrolling through Facebook while silently losing a battle nobody knows they are fighting.
You do not know whose marriage is collapsing.
Whose faith is dying.
Who feels too ashamed to enter a church.
Who has been spiritually manipulated.
Who thinks Jesus has finally given up on them.
Your share might place the Gospel in front of them at exactly the moment they were ready to stop looking for hope.
Give because you want Christ proclaimed.
Share because somebody needs truth.
But whatever you do, never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's approval.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be bought.
Christ gives it to repentant sinners who trust Him.
So…
Are modern-day prophets biblical?

The New Testament unquestionably records prophets and prophecy within the early church, while Christians disagree over how those gifts continue today. Scripture therefore gives us something wiser than gullibility and something humbler than dismissiveness:
Do not despise.
Do not blindly believe.
Test.
Discern.
Examine the fruit.
Hold tightly to what is good.
Reject what is false.
And above everything…
hold tightly to Jesus.
Because one day every prediction will become irrelevant.
Every platform will disappear.
Every microphone will go silent.
Every famous name will become history.
Every earthly ministry will end.
But Christ will remain.
And when that day comes, you will not need to tell Jesus how many prophets you followed.
The question will be whether you belonged to Him.
So listen carefully.
Test faithfully.
Repent quickly.
Love deeply.
And follow Jesus relentlessly.
Because the safest sheep is not the one who knows the name of every prophet.
It is the one who knows the voice, character, truth, and Gospel of the Shepherd.
When every other voice finally goes silent, make sure the One you learned to recognize was Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS CALL THE BLEEDING WOMAN “DAUGHTER”?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS CALL THE BLEEDING WOMAN “DAUGHTER”?
She came looking for a healing. Jesus stopped the entire crowd because He wanted to give her something even deeper: a name she may have forgotten she still had.
There is one word in Mark 5 that is dangerously easy to read too quickly.
One word.
Jesus could have simply said, “You are healed.”
He could have allowed the woman to disappear back into the crowd with her miracle.
After all, wasn’t that what she came for?
Twelve years of bleeding.
Twelve years of suffering.
Twelve years of reaching for answers and watching hope disappear.
Then one touch.
One moment.
One encounter with Jesus.
The bleeding stopped.
The miracle had already happened.
So why did Jesus stop?
Why did He turn around?
Why did He bring a frightened, trembling woman out of hiding?
And when she finally fell before Him and told Him “all the truth,” why did Jesus look at this woman and call her something extraordinarily tender?
“Daughter.”
Not “woman.”
Not “stranger.”
Not “unclean.”
Not “problem.”
Not “the bleeding woman.”
Not even “the woman who was healed.”
Daughter.
And perhaps that single word was part of the miracle.
Mark records the words of Jesus in Greek:
“Θυγάτηρ, ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην…”
Thygatēr, hē pistis sou sesōken se; hypage eis eirēnēn…
“Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace…” — Mark 5:34
The word Θυγάτηρ — Thygatēr — means “daughter.”
Do not rush past it.
Because before Jesus called her “daughter,” Mark never gives us her name.
We know Jairus.
We know that Jairus was a ruler of the synagogue.
We know Jairus had a daughter.
But this woman?
No name is recorded.
Mark introduces her simply as “a certain woman” who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years.
Twelve years.
Try to feel the weight of that before turning it into a Sunday-school story.
This was not a bad week.
Not a difficult season.
Not three months of unanswered prayer.
Twelve years.
She woke up bleeding.
She went to sleep bleeding.
Seasons changed.
People grew older.
Children became teenagers.
Life continued around her while her own body remained trapped in a nightmare that would not end.
Mark tells us that she had suffered many things from many physicians and had spent everything she possessed. Instead of improving, she became worse.
Imagine spending your money because you desperately want your old life back.
Another doctor.
Another treatment.
Another possibility.
Another disappointment.
Then another.
Until eventually the money is disappearing almost as relentlessly as the blood.
And perhaps you understand her better than you thought.
Maybe you have never bled for twelve years.
But you know what it means to carry something for so long that you stop remembering who you were before it began.
Maybe yours is grief.
Addiction.
Shame.
A marriage quietly falling apart.
A child who walked away.
A secret sin nobody knows about.
A prayer you have prayed so many times that you are almost embarrassed to pray it again.
Depression behind a smiling Facebook photograph.
A betrayal you supposedly “got over” years ago.
A past you cannot forgive yourself for.
You can become so accustomed to pain that eventually pain starts introducing you.
People stop seeing your name.
They see your scandal.
Your divorce.
Your failure.
Your addiction.
Your mistake.
Your diagnosis.
Your bankruptcy.
Your prison record.
Your breakdown.
Your past.
And if you hear those names long enough, eventually you can start calling yourself by them too.
But watch Jesus.
Because this story is about far more than blood.

According to Leviticus 15:25–27, an ongoing discharge of blood placed a woman in a state of ritual uncleanness under Israel’s covenant law. Objects on which she lay or sat were affected by that uncleanness, and those who touched such things became ceremonially unclean until evening and underwent the prescribed washing.
That needs to be understood carefully.
Ritual uncleanness was not the same thing as personal moral guilt.
The Bible does not say this woman was bleeding because she was especially sinful.
It does not tell us she was being punished for some secret wickedness.
Scripture gives us no permission to invent that accusation.
But her condition had profound religious and social consequences.
And it had lasted twelve years.
Now picture the crowd.
Bodies pressing against bodies.
People surrounding Jesus.
And somewhere inside that mass of humanity is a woman who knows what her condition means.
She does not walk toward Jesus demanding attention.
She comes from behind.
Quietly.
Almost invisibly.
“If I may touch but his clothes,” she tells herself, “I shall be whole.”
There is something painfully human about that sentence.
She does not appear to be looking for a conversation.
She does not ask for the crowd to make room.
She does not request a microphone.
She does not announce twelve years of suffering.
She just wants to touch Him and disappear.
Maybe suffering taught her to survive without being noticed.
Maybe shame taught her to keep her head down.
Maybe disappointment taught her not to expect too much.
But faith whispered one more time:
Get to Jesus.
And she did.
She reached through the crowd.
Her fingers touched His garment.
And immediately—
the bleeding stopped.
Twelve years.
Finished.
Imagine the second she realized it.
Something inside her body was different.
The thing doctors could not stop had stopped.
The thing money could not fix had been fixed.
The thing twelve years could not change changed in a moment in the presence of Christ.
She had her miracle.
She could go home.
Except Jesus stopped walking.
“Who touched my clothes?”
The disciples almost seem bewildered.
Everyone is touching You.
Look at the crowd.
People are pressing against You everywhere.
But Jesus knew this touch was different.
Many were touching Him physically.
One woman had reached for Him in faith.
And Jesus kept looking.
This is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because the woman knows.
Mark says she came “fearing and trembling.”
Then she fell down before Him.
And told Him “all the truth.”
All the truth.
Those words deserve to sit in the room for a while.
Because many of us want Jesus to heal what hurts without exposing what we hide.
We want relief without surrender.
Restoration without confession.
Grace without truth.
We want to touch His garment and quietly return to the shadows.
But sometimes Jesus loves us too deeply to leave us healed and hiding.
So she tells Him the truth.
Perhaps twelve years of it.
And Jesus listens.
Then comes the word.
Θυγάτηρ.
Daughter.
The woman the narrative has left unnamed is personally addressed by Jesus with a family word.
And Mark 5 contains a breathtaking narrative contrast.
Jesus is already on His way to help somebody else’s daughter.
Jairus has begged Jesus because his little girl is dying.
Mark tells us that Jairus’s daughter is twelve years old.
And the suffering woman has been bleeding for twelve years.
One has apparently spent twelve years growing up.
The other has spent twelve years bleeding.
One is known as the daughter of an important man.
The other woman’s father is not mentioned at all.
One has someone publicly pleading for her.
The other has apparently come alone.
Yet Jesus stops.
Because the desperate woman in the crowd is not invisible to Him.
Jairus has a daughter.
And suddenly Jesus says to this woman:
“Daughter.”
Do you see it?
She came secretly seeking power from Jesus.
Jesus responded personally.
She wanted healing.
Jesus gave her dignity.
She wanted to leave unnoticed.
Jesus allowed her to stand before the crowd no longer merely as the woman with the bleeding, but as someone publicly addressed with tenderness.
“Daughter.”
This is not sentimental decoration added to the miracle.
Jesus could have spoken without that word.
He deliberately addressed her.
And there is no need to exaggerate the passage to feel its force.
The text itself is enough.
The Greek continues:
ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε
hē pistis sou sesōken se
“Your faith has made you well.”

The crucial verb is σέσωκέν — sesōken, from σῴζω — sōzō, a word whose semantic range can include saving, rescuing, delivering, and making well depending on context. Here the woman has unquestionably experienced physical healing, and Jesus explicitly confirms it. The language is rich enough that English translations variously communicate the idea of being healed, made well, or made whole.
But notice something important.
Her faith was not magic.
The garment was not magic.
She was not healed because she discovered a spiritual technique.
Jesus was the object of her faith.
Biblical faith is not confidence in confidence.
It is not positive thinking with religious vocabulary.
The power was Christ’s.
Her faith reached for Him.
That distinction matters because somebody reading this has been blaming yourself for not having enough faith.
You prayed.
Nothing happened.
Someone told you that if your faith were stronger, the disease would disappear.
Please do not turn this woman’s story into a weapon against suffering Christians.
Mark 5 does not teach that every faithful Christian will receive immediate physical healing in this present life if only they believe intensely enough.
Paul prayed about his thorn and received sustaining grace rather than the removal he requested.
Faithful believers still become sick.
Faithful believers still suffer.
Faithful believers still die awaiting the resurrection.
Christian hope is not that believers can force God to perform the miracle they choose.
Christian hope is that Jesus Christ can be trusted even when we cannot dictate what He does.
And ultimately every person who belongs to Christ will experience a healing more complete than anything medicine can accomplish—the resurrection of the body and life with Him.
But this woman’s healing was real.
Jesus wanted her to know who had healed her.
And perhaps He wanted the crowd to know too.
She would not have to spend tomorrow wondering whether the miracle might disappear because she had stolen something from Jesus.
She had not stolen a miracle.
Christ publicly confirmed her restoration.
Then Jesus said:
ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην
hypage eis eirēnēn
“Go in peace.”
Not merely, “Stop bleeding.”
Go in peace.
There is a difference.
You can have a changed circumstance and still possess a terrified heart.
You can escape the scandal and still live expecting somebody to expose you.
You can receive forgiveness and continue punishing yourself.
You can walk out of the prison while the prison keeps living inside your mind.
Jesus did not merely address what was leaving her body.
He spoke to the woman who would have to live after the miracle.
Go in peace.
And maybe that is why this story found you today.
Because perhaps you have spent years believing the worst thing that happened to you became your name.
Maybe somebody labeled you by your darkest chapter.
Maybe you labeled yourself.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Failure.
Unwanted.
Dirty.
Abandoned.
Hypocrite.
Broken.
Too far gone.
You walk into church carrying names Jesus never gave you.
You worship while remembering what you did.
You raise your hands while wondering whether God remembers where those hands have been.
You hear people talk about grace, but somewhere inside you still believe grace is beautiful for everybody except you.
So hear the Gospel.
Jesus did not come for people who successfully cleaned themselves before approaching Him.
He came for sinners.
He touched lepers.
He ate with tax collectors and sinners.
He received the disgraced.
He confronted sin without surrendering sinners to hopelessness.
And eventually He walked toward a cross carrying something infinitely more devastating than ceremonial uncleanness.
He bore our sins.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities…” — Isaiah 53:5.
At Calvary, Jesus did not merely risk His reputation by standing near sinners.
He gave Himself for sinners.
The sinless Son of God was crucified.
Blood poured from His body.
And the One who called this suffering woman “daughter” made the way for rebellious sons and daughters to be reconciled to God through His death and resurrection.
That is the Gospel.
Not that your past was imaginary.
Not that sin does not matter.
Not that consequences disappear.
Not that everything you did was secretly okay.
The Gospel is infinitely better.
Your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die—and His grace is powerful enough that Christ willingly died to save sinners who could never save themselves.
Repentance does not mean pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace means the scandal no longer gets the final word.
Jesus does.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
Not because Jesus edits history.
He redeems people.
Peter still denied Him.
David really fell.
Paul really persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman really had a complicated history.
The thief really hung on a cross because he was guilty.
Grace does not require us to lie about the chapter.
Grace changes who writes the ending.
And maybe you have been trying to disappear into the crowd.
You are reading Christian posts.
Watching sermons.
Saving Bible verses.
Touching the edges of Christian community.
But hiding.
Jesus is not calling you out to humiliate you.
He calls sinners out of darkness because grace gives us somewhere better to live.
Tell Him the truth.
Not the polished testimony.
Not the church answer.
The truth.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
“Jesus, I am exhausted.”
“Jesus, I am angry.”
“Jesus, I am addicted.”
“Jesus, my marriage is hurting.”
“Jesus, I don't know whether I can keep fighting.”
“Jesus, I have been pretending.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
There is no confession you can make that surprises the Christ who already knew what He was carrying when He went to Calvary.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come into the light.
Reach for Christ.
Not because you deserve Him.
Because He is merciful.
Or simply write, “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Not for performance.
Not because typing words earns salvation.
It does not.
But sometimes a small public confession becomes the moment we stop protecting the mask.
Someone reading the comments may need to discover they are not fighting alone.
If you need prayer, say it plainly:
“Pray for me.”
Let believers pray with you.
And if Christ has already brought you through a chapter you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony may become another wounded person's reason to reach toward Jesus tonight.
Then think of one person who needs this story.
Not twenty random names.
One person.
The friend who has been unusually quiet.
The brother who stopped attending church.
The woman carrying a divorce she thinks disqualified her forever.
The believer secretly fighting addiction.
The person who thinks Christians would reject them if everyone knew the truth.
Sharing costs you seconds.
For somebody else, those seconds could place Scripture in front of them at exactly the moment they were preparing to give up.
There may come a night when shame starts calling you by your old name again.
Come back.
Read the word again.
Daughter.
Remember the Christ who stops for trembling people.
Remember that the crowd does not determine your worth.
Remember that your suffering does not get to rename you.
Remember that forgiveness is not purchased by your perfection.
It was purchased by Christ.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow closer to Jesus, confront sin, understand Scripture, return to prayer, and remember the Gospel when life becomes dark, consider staying close to this ministry.
But understand this carefully.
You cannot buy a blessing.
And the New Testament describes Christian giving as willing rather than coerced: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
For Christians who practice tithing through their local church, continue honoring your biblical convictions and responsibilities there.
That support matters.
So does sharing.
If financial support is not possible for you, please never believe you are less valuable here.
Pray.
Share.
Invite another person to follow.
Those acts can help Gospel truth travel far beyond what one ministry could accomplish alone.
Do it as worshipful generosity if God has genuinely placed it on your heart—not from guilt, fear, pressure, or the belief that you can purchase God's approval.
Because God does not need your money.
But Gospel ministry in this world is carried forward through ordinary believers who pray, give, serve, speak, share, sacrifice, encourage, and refuse to keep the good news to themselves.
The woman in Mark 5 thought she was reaching through a crowd for one final chance.
She did not know that millions of people would still be talking about that moment centuries later.
She thought it was private.
Jesus made it a testimony.
She thought she needed only healing.
Jesus stopped and spoke peace.
She approached anonymously.
Jesus called her Daughter.
And perhaps the most painful thing about your life right now is not simply what happened to you.
Perhaps it is what you started calling yourself because of it.
Jesus still meets people there.
At the intersection of desperation and faith.
Where masks fall.
Where truth comes out.
Where sinners repent.
Where grace becomes more than a theological word.
Where wounded people discover that Christ is not frightened by their wounds.
So come to Him.
Come trembling if you must.
Come exhausted.
Come ashamed.
Come after twelve years.
Come after twenty.
Come after the relapse.
Come after the divorce.
Come after the scandal.
Come after everybody else gave up on you.
But come to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of wounded people learning to repair themselves.
It is the story of sinners who could not save themselves being rescued by a crucified and risen Savior.
And when grace finally reaches the chapter you were certain had ruined the whole story, you may discover something breathtaking:
Jesus never needed your worst chapter erased before He could begin writing redemption across it.
Because somewhere tonight, another trembling person is hiding in another crowd, believing nobody sees the blood, nobody knows the shame, and nobody remembers their name.
But Jesus has never confused your wound with your name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS SEXUAL AROUSAL ITSELF SINFUL—or Does Scripture Care About Where Desire Is Directed?
paragraphs: IS SEXUAL AROUSAL ITSELF SINFUL—or Does Scripture Care About Where Desire Is Directed?

What if the feeling you have been ashamed to admit is not where the real spiritual battle begins? What if Scripture draws a line many Christians were never taught to see—and understanding that line could change the way you fight lust, understand your body, love your spouse, pursue holiness, and run back to Jesus after years of hiding?
There are Christians who have whispered apologies to God simply because their bodies reacted.
They noticed someone attractive.
Something stirred.
Desire appeared before they invited it.
And almost immediately came the second feeling.
Shame.
“God, forgive me.”

Sometimes they did not even know what they were asking forgiveness for. They only knew that somewhere along the way they had absorbed the idea that a Christian who was truly holy would somehow stop being sexually responsive.
So they began fighting not merely sexual sin...
but their own humanity.
Some married believers even carried that shame into marriage.
Some single believers concluded that the existence of sexual desire meant something spiritually defective was hiding inside them.
Some young Christians discovered arousal before they possessed the vocabulary to understand it and quietly decided that God must already be disappointed in them.
And some people became trapped in a devastating cycle:
desire...
fear...
shame...
secret indulgence...
repentance...
temporary relief...
then desire again.
Eventually they stopped distinguishing temptation from surrender, attraction from lust, bodily response from deliberate fantasy, and sexuality from sexual immorality.
Everything became “dirty.”
But Scripture is more careful than that.
And we must be careful too.
Because there is a difference between saying sexual desire can become sinful and saying that the mere existence of sexual arousal is itself sin.
That difference is not an excuse for lust.
It is actually one of the keys to fighting lust truthfully.
The Bible begins its theology of human sexuality before sin enters the world.
Before pornography.
Before adultery.
Before prostitution.
Before sexual exploitation.
Before shame.
Before Genesis 3 ever records humanity's fall, Genesis 2 presents a man and woman brought together by God.
The Hebrew says:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
ʿal-kēn yaʿăzāḇ-ʾîš... wəḏāḇaq bəʾištô... wəhāyû ləḇāśār ʾeḥāḏ.

A man leaves father and mother, holds fast to his wife, and the two become “one flesh”—בָשָׂר אֶחָד, basar echad. Then comes the almost startling final sentence: the man and his wife were naked and were not ashamed.
Think about that.
Nakedness existed before shame.
Marriage existed before shame.
Embodied sexuality existed before shame.
The human body was not Satan's invention.
Sexual union was not humanity's invention.
God created embodied human beings, male and female, and Scripture places marital union inside creation before it ever introduces the serpent.
So Christianity does not teach that holiness means becoming less human.
It teaches that fallen human beings must learn to bring their humanity under the lordship of Christ.
That includes sexuality.
And here is where the question becomes uncomfortable.
If sexual arousal is not automatically sinful, when does desire become sinful?
Jesus takes us directly into the heart.

In Matthew 5:27–28, He moves beyond the external act of adultery and exposes inward sexual sin. His warning is not permission to say, “As long as I never touch anyone, anything happening in my imagination is harmless.”
Far from it.
Jesus destroys that loophole.
He teaches that a person can violate sexual faithfulness internally by cultivating desire toward someone who is not rightly theirs to possess.
That means holiness cannot merely be measured by whether your clothes stayed on.
A person can remain physically untouched while feeding an entire secret sexual world.
The browser history may be clean while the imagination is not.
The conversation may look innocent while the heart is rehearsing something else.
The person across the room may never know what you are doing with their image inside your mind.
But Jesus does.
And that is precisely why we must distinguish involuntary awareness from cultivated lust.
You can notice beauty without mentally undressing someone.
You can experience bodily arousal without deciding to feed it.
You can encounter temptation without agreeing with temptation.
You can feel something before you have chosen what you will do with what you feel.
That distinction matters enormously because Hebrews says something extraordinary about Jesus:
πεπειρασμένον... χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας
He was genuinely “tempted” and yet “without sin.”

Hebrews 4:15 does not erase temptation by redefining it as sin. It distinguishes the reality of temptation from committing sin and then tells struggling believers to approach the throne of grace for mercy and help.
Read that again if you have spent years condemning yourself merely because temptation appeared.
Temptation is not identical to surrender.
A temptation may arrive at your door.
You do not have to invite it inside, pour it a drink, give it your imagination, and build it a bedroom.
James gives us an even more vivid picture.
He writes:
ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος
Each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his or her own epithymia—desire.
Then James continues:
εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν
“Then desire, having conceived, gives birth to sin.”
James intentionally uses the imagery of conception and birth. Desire is present in the sequence, temptation is real, and then desire “conceives” and gives birth to sin.
That does not make disordered desire harmless.
It means Scripture is describing movement.
A progression.
Something catches your attention.
Desire pulls.
Enticement whispers.
The imagination begins negotiating.
The will starts cooperating.
What initially appeared becomes something you intentionally entertain.
Then what you entertained begins entertaining you.
And soon you are no longer merely experiencing temptation.
You are feeding it.
That is where many believers lose the battle—not because temptation appeared, but because they mistook the appearance of temptation for total defeat.
“I already felt it. I have already sinned. I might as well continue.”
No.
That lie has dragged countless people deeper into pornography, masturbation fueled by illicit fantasy, emotional affairs, adultery, sexting, secret relationships, and obsessive fantasies.
The enemy would love to convince you that the first spark means the entire house is already burning.
Because if you believe you have already lost, why resist?
But you have not necessarily lost because you noticed.
You have not necessarily lost because your body responded.
The decisive question becomes:
Where will you take the desire now?
Paul's language in 1 Corinthians 7 is especially revealing.
Speaking to unmarried people and widows, he says that if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry, “for it is better to marry than to burn.”
The Greek reads:
κρεῖττον γάρ ἐστιν γαμῆσαι ἢ πυροῦσθαι

The verb pyrousthai carries the image of burning. Paul does not respond to sexual passion by pretending it does not exist. He acknowledges its reality and directs believers toward honorable covenant rather than sexual immorality.
That is profoundly different from saying, “If you experience sexual desire, you are filthy.”
Paul knows human beings are embodied creatures.
But he also refuses to let desire become lord.
This is the balance modern culture hates.
One side tells you:
“If you desire it, express it.”
The other distortion whispers:
“If you desire it, hate yourself.”
Jesus offers something holier than either.
Bring it under My lordship.
The Gospel neither worships desire nor requires you to pretend desire does not exist.
Jesus calls you to surrender it.
Paul writes in 1 Thessalonians that God's will is our sanctification, that believers abstain from sexual immorality and learn to live in holiness and honor—not “in the passion of lust.”
The Greek phrase is:
μὴ ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας

mē en pathei epithymias—not in a passion dominated by lustful desire. The surrounding passage speaks not merely of feelings but of holiness, bodily conduct, and refusing to wrong or exploit another person sexually.
There is something deeply important hiding there.
Biblical sexuality asks more than, “How strongly do I feel this?”
It asks:
Does this honor God?
Does this honor the other person?
Am I loving this person—or consuming them inside my imagination?
Am I treating someone created in God's image as a whole human being—or turning them into material for my gratification?
Is desire serving covenant love...
or has another human being become fuel?
That question reaches pornography with devastating clarity.
Pornography trains the eyes to consume bodies detached from covenant, responsibility, sacrificial love, and often even basic knowledge of the person being watched.
It teaches the heart to say:
“Your body exists for my experience.”
The Gospel teaches the opposite.
Love does not ask how much of another person it can privately consume.
Love asks how faithfully it can honor them before God.
That is why the answer to lust is not merely “stop being aroused.”
The deeper answer is:
Learn to see people again.
That woman is not a body delivered to your screen.
That man is not a fantasy character God placed in your workplace.
That married person is not an emotional escape hatch.
That person walking past you at the gym does not exist for your imagination.
They bear God's image.
They have a story.
A soul.
Wounds you cannot see.
A future.
Perhaps a spouse.
Perhaps children.
Perhaps loneliness.
Perhaps trauma.
Perhaps a desperate need to discover that their worth is greater than the attention their body receives.
And suddenly lust looks different.
Because lust reduces.
Love restores personhood.
But now someone reading this is frightened for another reason.
Because you did not merely experience temptation.
You fed it.
You clicked.
You watched.
You fantasized.
You returned.
Maybe for years.
Maybe you betrayed vows.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you swore you never would.
Maybe your spouse sleeps beside you without knowing what lives behind your locked phone.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong.
You serve.
You worship.
You quote Scripture.
You encourage other people.
And then midnight comes.
The room goes quiet.
The screen lights your face.
And another version of you appears.
You have asked yourself:
“If they knew, would they still respect me?”
But there is a more terrifying question.
“God knows... so how could He still want me?”
Now we have reached the place where this article was always trying to bring you.
Not merely to sexuality.
To Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of sexually pure people congratulating themselves for being cleaner than sexually broken people.
Christianity is the story of sinners who needed a Savior.
Every one of us.
The sexually immoral need Christ.
The self-righteous need Christ.
The porn-addicted need Christ.
The adulterer needs Christ.
The person who has remained physically chaste but cultivated lust needs Christ.
The ashamed teenager needs Christ.
The wounded spouse needs Christ.
The single believer burning with desire needs Christ.
The married couple trying to rediscover intimacy after betrayal needs Christ.
The person who fell last night needs Christ.
And the person who has been free for twenty years still needs Christ.

Paul tells the Corinthians to flee sexual immorality because the body belongs to the Lord. He reminds believers that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, that they were “bought with a price,” and therefore they are to glorify God in their bodies.
Notice the Gospel order.
You were bought.
Therefore glorify God.
Not:
“Make yourself clean enough so Christ might consider buying you.”
Christ's redemption becomes the foundation of holiness.
The cross does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says your sin was so serious that redemption cost blood...
and God's love was so astonishing that Christ gave Himself for sinners.
That destroys both presumption and despair.
You cannot say, “Sexual sin doesn't matter.”
Look at the cross.
Sin matters.
But you also cannot say, “My sexual sin has placed me beyond the reach of Jesus.”
Look again at the cross.
Grace matters too.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because Jesus calls darkness light.
Because He enters the darkness and brings sinners into light.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Because grace finally gives us somewhere safe enough to stop pretending.
Repentance is not God screaming, “Disgusting. Get away from Me.”
Repentance is the mercy of God calling:
“Stop running toward the thing destroying you. Turn around. Come home.”
Maybe you need to hear that tonight.
You are not called to make peace with lust.
You are called to make war against it.
But you do not fight as someone trying to persuade Jesus to love you.
You fight because in Christ you have encountered a love worth becoming free for.
So when arousal comes, do not immediately panic.
Ask where it is pointing.

If you are married and desire awakens toward your spouse, do not treat covenant desire as though marital affection itself were unclean. Scripture's vision of marriage includes one-flesh union, and the Song of Songs can speak openly and poetically about delight and desire between beloveds.
If you are single and sexual desire reminds you how deeply you long for intimacy, do not worship the longing and do not despise yourself for possessing it.
Bring it to Christ.
Practice self-control.
Refuse pornography.
Guard your imagination.
Build friendships.
Serve.
Pray.
Exercise wisdom about what you watch.
Do not intentionally remain in environments you already know inflame destructive patterns.
And if marriage is something you rightly desire, you do not need to apologize for wanting covenant intimacy.
But do not make marriage your savior either.
A wedding ring does not crucify lust.
Jesus must remain Lord of your sexuality before marriage, within marriage, and if necessary through lifelong singleness.
If you are married and become aware that another person is attractive, awareness is not permission.
Do not cultivate it.
Do not build the second glance into a private story.
Do not start comparing.
Do not manufacture reasons to message them.
Do not hide conversations from your spouse.
Do not call emotional adultery “friendship” simply because nobody has kissed yet.
Sin often asks for permission in millimeters before taking territory in miles.
And if you have already crossed the line...
bring it into the light.
Confess to God.
Seek wise pastoral accountability.
Where another person has been harmed or vows have been violated, repentance must become more than private emotion; wisdom, truth, accountability, and appropriate repair may be required.
Do not confuse feeling terrible with repenting.
Judas felt terrible.
Peter wept bitterly too.
But Peter eventually ran back into the presence of Jesus.
Shame says:
“Hide until you become worthy.”
Grace says:
“Come into the light because Christ alone can make you clean.”
And please understand this.
Grace is not Jesus standing beside your pornography habit saying, “Don't worry about it.”
Grace is Jesus refusing to abandon you to what is enslaving you.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace disciplines.
Grace restores.
Grace transforms.
Grace teaches your eyes to see differently.
Grace teaches your imagination to bow.
Grace teaches your body that it is not your master.
Grace teaches desire that it has a King.
Maybe the prayer you need tonight is not complicated.

“Jesus, my desires have been ruling me. Forgive me. Teach me to desire what You desire. Teach me to see people as You see them. Clean my imagination. Heal what I have distorted. Give me courage to confess what must be confessed. Give me strength to flee what must be fled. And when temptation comes, remind me that temptation does not own me. You do.”
Write something honest.
Not because every sentence is perfect, but because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what we believed when our minds were clear.
Come back when the battle becomes loud.
Send it privately to the husband who is struggling.
The wife who feels betrayed.
The single Christian who thinks sexual desire means God is disappointed in them.
The young believer being discipled more aggressively by pornography than by the church.
The believer who fell again last night and is wondering whether there is any road home.
There is.
His name is Jesus.
It does not.
It cannot.

And not because anyone should be pressured into giving. Scripture says giving is to come from a heart that has decided freely, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
Your support helps us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep placing the Gospel in front of people scrolling at midnight while fighting battles nobody else can see.
Sometimes your share may place biblical truth in front of the one person who desperately needed to read it that night.
Because ultimately this was never merely an article about sexual arousal.
It was about lordship.
Your body is not your god.
Your urges are not your identity.
Your temptation is not your destiny.
Your past is not your master.
Your shame does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
So when desire awakens, do not merely ask:
“Did I feel something?”
Ask:
“Where am I taking what I feel?”
Toward fantasy...
or faithfulness?
Toward consumption...
or love?
Toward secrecy...
or light?
Toward self-rule...
or surrender?
The goal of Christian holiness is not to become a person incapable of feeling.
It is to become a person whose whole life—including desire—belongs increasingly to Jesus Christ.
And if you failed yesterday...
come back.
If you failed this morning...
come back.
If you have spent ten years hiding...
come back.
Come with confession.
Come with repentance.
Come without excuses.
But come.

The throne you are approaching is called the throne of grace, and Hebrews says that because our High Priest understands temptation yet remained without sin, we may draw near to receive mercy and find grace in our time of need.
Your darkest desire does not need another hiding place.
It needs a King.
And perhaps the most unforgettable thing you can carry away from these words is this:
Jesus did not shed His blood merely to forgive what you did in the darkness—He rose again to teach you how to walk in the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS WASH HIS DISCIPLES’ FEET?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS WASH HIS DISCIPLES’ FEET?
The Night the King Knelt Before the Men Who Would Fail Him—and Revealed What the Cross Was About
There is something almost unbearable about the scene when you finally realize whose feet were in the room.
Not strangers.
Not saints standing in stained-glass windows.
Not men who had already proven themselves faithful.
These were the feet of men who were about to fail Jesus.
Feet that would run when soldiers arrived.
Feet belonging to a disciple who would swear that he did not even know Him.
Feet belonging to men who had argued about greatness.
And somewhere in that room were the feet of Judas Iscariot.
The man already moving toward betrayal.
Yet Jesus got down on the floor.
That is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because Christianity becomes much easier when Jesus stays standing.
We like the Jesus who commands storms.
The Jesus who multiplies bread.
The Jesus who casts out demons.
The Jesus who raises the dead.
The Jesus who will someday return as King.
But John takes us into a room where the King removes His outer garments, wraps a towel around Himself, pours water into a basin...
and kneels.
Before dirty feet.
And perhaps the question is not merely, “Why did Jesus wash His disciples’ feet?”
Perhaps the more dangerous question is:
What does it reveal about Jesus that He was willing to kneel before people who were about to hurt Him?
And what does it reveal about us that we often want to follow Jesus everywhere except down to the floor?
John does not begin this scene by telling us that Jesus had forgotten who He was.
He tells us almost the exact opposite.
Jesus knew.
That detail changes everything.
John says that Jesus knew His hour had come and that, having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them “εἰς τέλος”—eis telos.
To the end.
To completion.
To the uttermost.
Then John tells us that Jesus knew the Father had given all things into His hands, that He had come from God, and that He was returning to God.
Think about that.
Jesus knew exactly who He was.
He knew where He came from.
He knew where He was going.
He knew the Father had placed all things into His hands.
And what did those hands do with that authority?
They picked up a towel.
John records:
“καὶ ἤρξατο νίπτειν τοὺς πόδας τῶν μαθητῶν”
kaì ērxato níptein toùs pódas tōn mathētōn.
“And He began to wash the feet of the disciples.”
The verb John uses, νίπτειν—niptein, refers to washing, particularly washing part of the body.
The hands that held authority over creation were washing dust from human feet.
Do not rush past that.
Because the world teaches us that when you become important enough, other people serve you.
Jesus reveals a Kingdom where the One who truly possesses all authority stoops to serve.
The world says, “When you know who you are, make people recognize you.”
Jesus knew precisely who He was...
and knelt.
Real security did not make Him arrogant.
It made Him free to serve.
Some of us are exhausted because we spend our lives trying to prove that we matter.
We need recognition.
We need someone to notice.
We need the title.
The applause.
The platform.
The apology.
The respect.
The last word.
We secretly keep records of who called first, who gave more, who appreciated us, who overlooked us, who owes us something.
Then Jesus silently walks into the middle of all our calculations carrying a basin.
And suddenly our definition of greatness begins collapsing.
Peter could not handle it.
“Lord, are You washing my feet?”
You can almost hear the shock.
Not You.
Not my Lord.
Not my Master.
This is backwards.
Peter resisted because grace often feels offensive before it feels beautiful.
We want a Savior powerful enough to rescue us.
But sometimes we struggle with a Savior humble enough to touch the places we are ashamed of.
Peter told Him, in effect:
Never.
You will never wash my feet.
Jesus answered with words far more serious than Peter expected:
“Ἐὰν μὴ νίψω σε, οὐκ ἔχεις μέρος μετ’ ἐμοῦ.”
Eàn mē nípsō se, ouk écheis méros met’ emoû.
“If I do not wash you, you have no share with Me.”
Suddenly this is about more than dusty feet.
Something deeper is being revealed.
Peter's problem was not simply that his feet were dirty.
Peter needed to receive what Jesus alone could give.
That is still the scandal of grace.
You cannot clean yourself enough to make yourself worthy of Christ.
You cannot erase yesterday.
You cannot undo the words you said.
You cannot crawl backward through history and prevent your worst decision.
You cannot punish yourself long enough to purchase forgiveness.
You cannot perform enough religious activity to make the blood of Jesus unnecessary.
You must be washed.
You must receive.
And pride sometimes says, “I don't need help.”
Shame says, “I don't deserve help.”
Jesus confronts both.
Peter then swings to the other extreme.
“Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!”
And Jesus answers with another fascinating statement:
“Ὁ λελουμένος ... ἔστιν καθαρὸς ὅλος.”
Ho lelouménos ... estin katharòs holos.
“The one who has bathed ... is completely clean.”
