John's wording is striking.
In the passage, Jesus speaks of the one who has been λελουμένος—leloumenos, bathed or washed, while using the foot-washing language built from νίπτω—niptō.
There is a distinction in the imagery.
Jesus is doing something physically real, but His words reach beyond water in a basin.
Because dirt was never humanity's deepest problem.
Sin was.
And water on feet could never remove guilt from the human heart.
Only Christ could deal with that.
Only the Lamb of God could bear sin.
Only the cross could answer the accusation against us.
Only the blood of Jesus could accomplish what no amount of religious scrubbing ever could.
And this is where the towel begins pointing toward something even more terrible and beautiful.
The cross.
John 13 is not the crucifixion itself, and we should not force every detail of the foot washing into an allegory the text never gives us.
But we cannot miss the direction of Jesus' life.
The One who lays aside His garments and stoops before His disciples is moving toward the ultimate act of self-giving love.
Soon there will be no basin.
There will be blood.
No towel around His waist.
His garments will be taken from Him.
No comfortable room.
A cross.
No dust being washed from feet.
Sin being borne by the sinless Son of God.
Philippians tells us that Christ humbled Himself and became obedient unto death—even death on a cross.
Jesus did not merely preach humility.
He descended into it.
And perhaps one of the most haunting details of John 13 is the presence of Judas.
Jesus knew.
John makes that clear.
He knew who would betray Him.
Imagine knowing exactly who was going to wound you.
Imagine knowing the conversation already happening behind your back.
Imagine knowing which friend would sell you.
Imagine knowing that the person in front of you was already preparing the betrayal.
Now imagine kneeling.
This does not mean Jesus approved Judas's evil.
He did not.
Love does not require pretending sin is righteousness.
Grace does not call betrayal good.
Jesus would speak truth about the betrayal.
Judas remained responsible for what he chose.
But Judas's darkness did not turn Jesus into Judas.
That may be a word somebody desperately needs.
What they did to you was wrong.
But do not let another person's sin disciple your heart.
Do not let betrayal teach you hatred.
Do not let rejection turn you cruel.
Do not let wounds become permission to become the thing that wounded you.
Jesus knew betrayal was coming...
and remained Jesus.
Maybe you have been asking God to change the people around you while He has been trying to keep what they did from changing you.
Maybe your basin is sitting in front of the person you think least deserves it.
Not because evil should be tolerated.
Not because boundaries are unbiblical.
Not because abuse should be endured.
Not because justice does not matter.
But because followers of Jesus are not permitted to make hatred their master.
Then Jesus sat down and asked His disciples:
“Do you understand what I have done to you?”
That question has survived two thousand years.
And it is now sitting in front of us.
Do you understand?
Jesus says:
“εἰ οὖν ἐγὼ ἔνιψα ὑμῶν τοὺς πόδας ὁ κύριος καὶ ὁ διδάσκαλος, καὶ ὑμεῖς ὀφείλετε ἀλλήλων νίπτειν τοὺς πόδας.”
“If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet.”
Then comes the word that prevents us from treating this as a sentimental story:
“ὑπόδειγμα γὰρ ἔδωκα ὑμῖν”
Hypódeigma gàr édōka hymîn.
“For I have given you an example.”
Ὑπόδειγμα—hypodeigma.
An example.
A pattern.
Something placed before another person to be followed.
Jesus was not performing humility for applause.
He was showing His disciples what life under His lordship looks like.

Whether Christians understand His command as requiring literal foot washing in particular settings or as also embodying the wider pattern of humble, self-giving service, nobody gets to escape the heart of His command.
Followers of the Servant King must become servants.
And this is where Christianity stops being something we merely post and becomes something we practice.
Because it is easy to put a cross in your bio.
Harder to carry one.
Easy to share a verse about forgiveness.
Harder to forgive.
Easy to sing, “I surrender all.”
Harder when Jesus reaches for the thing you have been refusing to surrender.
Easy to say, “Jesus is Lord.”
Harder when Lord Jesus tells you to take the lower place.
Maybe your towel looks like apologizing first.
Maybe it looks like caring for an aging parent when nobody applauds.
Maybe it is serving your spouse when resentment tells you to keep score.
Maybe it is feeding someone who can never repay you.
Maybe it is cleaning a church after everybody leaves.
Maybe it is listening to the lonely person everybody else ignores.
Maybe it is forgiving while still maintaining wise boundaries.
Maybe it is admitting, “I was wrong.”
Maybe the dirtiest feet God has placed before you belong to someone whose approval will never increase your social status.
Would you still kneel?
Jesus destroys the idea that service is beneath us.
Because if washing feet was not beneath the Son of God...
who exactly are we to say it is beneath us?
And there is another layer.
Before Jesus tells the disciples to wash one another's feet, He washes theirs.
Grace comes before imitation.
Jesus does not say, “Become humble enough and perhaps I will accept you.”
He serves them first.
He loves first.
He moves toward them first.
That is the Gospel.
Christianity is not fundamentally humanity climbing toward God.
It is the staggering announcement that God came toward sinners in Jesus Christ.
The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many.
At the cross, Jesus did what none of us could do.
He bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He died.
And He rose again.
Our hope is not that we have washed enough feet.
Our hope is Christ.
Our righteousness is not our record of service.
Our righteousness is found in Him.
Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And when grace truly takes hold of a human being...
something begins changing.
The proud begin learning to kneel.
The bitter begin learning to forgive.
The selfish begin learning generosity.
The hidden sinner steps into the light.
The person who once demanded to be served begins asking:
“Who can I serve?”
That is transformation.
That is what grace does.
Maybe you have been around Christianity for years but have never actually let Jesus wash you.
You know Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say amen.
You know the songs.
You know how to look okay in church.
But there is a room inside you nobody is allowed to enter.
A secret.
An addiction.
A bitterness.
A relationship.
A wound.
A compromise.
Something you keep hiding beneath religious clothing.
And Jesus already knows.
Remember Peter.
Jesus did not wait for clean feet before He approached him.
He approached him because his feet needed washing.
Stop confusing hiding with holiness.
Bring your sin into the light.
Repent.
Confess.
Turn to Christ.
You do not need to convince Jesus that you are clean.
You need Jesus.
Maybe you failed Him this week.
Maybe last night.
Maybe five minutes before reading this.
The Gospel is not permission to remain in sin.
It is the announcement that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed because Jesus Christ died and rose again.
Repentance does not mean pretending the mud was never there.
It means turning to the One who can wash you.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest.
Not because typing words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But perhaps you need to stop hiding behind silence and let that comment become a small public confession that you are done pretending you do not need grace.
And read the other comments.
You may discover that the Church is filled with people carrying battles you could never see from their profile pictures.
Someone needs your testimony.
Someone needs to know grace reached you too.
Someone needs to know that failure does not have to be the final chapter when repentance brings us back to Christ.
This is why we say:
Because Scripture is filled with people whose worst moments looked final until God intervened.
Peter denied Jesus.
That was scandal.
Jesus restored Peter.
That was grace.
The cross looked like humiliation.
Then came resurrection.
What appeared to be defeat became the place where Christ triumphed.
And perhaps your story currently looks like it has stopped at the scandal.
It has not.
Jesus Christ is still the Redeemer.
Jesus still restores repentant sinners.
Jesus still changes hearts.
Jesus still calls prodigals home.
Jesus still turns graves into testimonies of resurrection power.
Jesus still rewrites everything.
If this article put words around something somebody you love is going through, do not keep it to yourself.
Because eventually pride comes back.
Eventually hurt returns.
Eventually somebody disappoints you.
Eventually you will need to remember again that on the night He was betrayed, Jesus chose the towel.
Invite your family.
Invite your Christian friends.
Invite the believer who has become lukewarm.
Invite the person quietly questioning everything.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who is willing to listen.
Not so we can build a crowd around a page.
May God build people around Christ.
But hear this carefully.
It cannot replace repentance.
It cannot earn forgiveness.
Christian giving must never be manipulated.
Paul wrote:
“ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ, μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης”
Let each person give as he has determined in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion.
That matters.

If you want to glorify God through your resources, supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one meaningful expression of that generosity. Others may faithfully support their local church, missionaries, the poor, Gospel workers, and other Christ-centered ministries as God leads them.
The glory belongs to God.
Always.
It is mission.
It is helping keep Scripture moving.
Helping discipleship resources reach another home.
Helping a wounded believer encounter truth.
Helping a seeker hear about Jesus.
Helping someone who thought their scandal was the end discover grace.
Pray.
Invite others to follow.
Serve your local church.
Love your neighbor.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
Because the Kingdom of God was never built by spectators admiring the towel.
It advances through disciples willing to pick it up.
And maybe that is the real reason this story refuses to leave us alone.
We began by asking why Jesus washed His disciples' feet.
Now perhaps we understand why the answer hurts.
Because Jesus was showing us Himself.
His authority did not make Him distant.
His holiness did not make Him unwilling to touch the unclean.
His knowledge of betrayal did not make Him abandon love.
His greatness did not prevent Him from kneeling.
And His love did not stop at the basin.
It carried Him all the way to the cross.
So when you picture Jesus washing those feet, do not merely see an ancient custom.
See the King.
See the towel.
See Peter's confusion.
See Judas sitting in the room.
See dirty water.
See holy hands touching human dust.
And then look toward Calvary.
The hands washing feet would soon be pierced.
The Teacher kneeling before sinners would soon die for sinners.
The Lord who told Peter, “Unless I wash you...” was moving toward the place where cleansing would cost Him His blood.
And after the cross...
the grave would not keep Him.
Jesus Christ rose.
That is why your sin does not have to write your ending.
That is why your betrayal does not have to write your ending.
That is why your shame does not have to write your ending.
That is why your failure does not have to write your ending.
Repent.
Come to Christ.
Receive grace.
Then get up...
pick up the towel...
and follow your King.

Because one day, when all our titles are forgotten, all our platforms disappear, all our applause goes silent, and everything temporary falls away, we may discover that some of the moments that looked smallest on earth were enormous in the Kingdom of Heaven.
A basin.
A towel.
A surrendered heart.
A servant who looked like Jesus.
And never forget this:
The hands that washed dirty feet were the same hands that would be pierced for dirty souls—and He did not pull either of them away.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BE ANGRY AND DO NOT SIN” — DOES THE BIBLE ACTUALLY GIVE CHRISTIANS PERMISSION TO BE ANGRY?
paragraphs: “BE ANGRY AND DO NOT SIN” — DOES THE BIBLE ACTUALLY GIVE CHRISTIANS PERMISSION TO BE ANGRY?
Maybe the emotion you have been ashamed to admit is not the real danger. Maybe what you do with it is.
There is a kind of anger you hide because you are a Christian.
You know the feeling.
Someone betrays you.
Someone lies about you.
Someone wounds your child.
Someone you trusted smiles in your face and destroys your name behind your back.
You watch injustice happen while everyone else stays quiet.
You discover something that makes your stomach turn.
Or maybe the wound is much closer than that.
A spouse broke a promise.
A parent left scars nobody sees.
A church hurt you.
A friend abandoned you when you needed them most.
Someone apologized, but something inside you still burns when you remember what happened.
And then comes the guilt.
Because Christians aren't supposed to get angry...
Right?
So you bury it.
You call it “being okay.”
You smile.
You worship.
You post the Bible verse.
You tell everyone you have forgiven.
But somewhere beneath the Christian vocabulary, something is still burning.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing about that fire is not that you feel it.
It is that you have never learned what Jesus wants you to do with it.
Because there is a sentence in Scripture that sounds almost shocking when you read it slowly.
Paul writes:
Read the first four words again.
“Be ye angry.”
The Greek is even more striking:

ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε
orgizesthe kai mē hamartanete
“Be angry, and do not sin.”
Paul does not simply write, “Never feel anger.”
He draws a line between anger and sin.
But before anyone turns that verse into a permission slip for rage, revenge, cruelty, insults, grudges, intimidation, bitterness, or the sentence, “Well, Jesus got angry too,” keep reading.
Because Paul does not leave anger unsupervised.
“Be angry...”
Then immediately:
“...and do not sin.”
Then:
“...let not the sun go down upon your wrath.”
Then the next verse lands like a warning:
“Neither give place to the devil.” — Ephesians 4:27, KJV
That changes everything.
Scripture acknowledges anger...
then immediately puts a fence around it.
Do not let anger become sin.
Do not nurture it indefinitely.
Do not let it become territory surrendered to the enemy.
The question, then, is not merely:
“Am I allowed to be angry?”
The more searching question is:
“What is my anger becoming?”
Because anger can begin as a response to something genuinely wrong and still mutate into something spiritually poisonous.
You can be right about what happened to you...
and wrong about what you are becoming because of it.
That is the part nobody wants to hear.
The betrayal may really have happened.
The injustice may really be injustice.
The lie may really be a lie.
The abuse may really have been evil.
Your tears may be justified.
Your wound may be real.
And yet Jesus loves you too much to let the person who wounded you continue shaping your heart from a distance.
That is why this verse is not permission to explode.
It is an invitation to surrender.
And Paul did not invent the language.
Behind Ephesians 4:26 stands language found in Psalm 4:4. In Hebrew, the opening words are:

רִגְזוּ וְאַל־תֶּחֱטָאוּ
rigzu ve’al-techeta’u
The wording carries the force of trembling, agitation, or being deeply disturbed, followed immediately by the prohibition against sin.
The rest of Psalm 4:4 turns the person inward before God—considering the matter upon the heart and becoming still.
That context matters.
Biblical anger is not:
“I am angry, therefore whatever I do next is justified.”
Biblical anger is closer to:
“Something has disturbed me deeply, therefore I must bring what is happening inside me under the authority of God before it becomes sin.”
That is radically different.
The Bible does not teach emotional anesthesia.
It teaches holy government of the heart.
And we see something astonishing when we look at Jesus.
Mark records a moment when Christ encountered men whose hearts were hardened while a suffering man stood before them.
Mark 3:5 says Jesus looked around at them “with anger,” while also being grieved at the hardness of their hearts.
Notice the combination.
Anger.
And grief.
Jesus' anger was not petty wounded pride.
He was not furious because someone took His seat.
He was not raging because someone failed to compliment Him.
He was not trying to win an argument on Facebook.
His anger existed alongside grief over hardened hearts, and what did He do with that anger?
He healed the suffering man.
That should stop us.
Because sinful human anger often asks:
“How can I hurt them back?”
Christlike anger asks:
“What does righteousness require?”
Our anger wants humiliation.
His moved toward restoration.
Our anger wants the last word.
His remained submitted to the Father's will.
Our anger says, “They will pay.”
The Gospel reveals the Savior who ultimately went to a cross and paid for sinners.
There is an enormous difference between being angry because God's holiness and love have been violated and being angry because our ego has been inconvenienced.
And if we are honest...
much of what we call “righteous anger” is just ordinary pride wearing a Bible verse.
That one hurts.
Because sometimes we are not defending God's honor.
We are defending ours.
Sometimes we are not angry because somebody sinned against God.
We are angry because somebody disagreed with us.
Sometimes what we call discernment is resentment.
Sometimes what we call boldness is cruelty.
Sometimes what we call “speaking truth” is the flesh enjoying the opportunity to punish someone with words.
Sometimes we say, “Jesus overturned tables,” when what we really mean is, “I want theological permission to lose control.”
But Jesus never lost control.
Jesus was not controlled by anger.
Jesus was controlled by perfect holiness, perfect love, perfect obedience to the Father.
That distinction is everything.
And Scripture refuses to romanticize human anger.
James writes that every person should be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger, because “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (James 1:19–20, KJV).
The Greek of James 1:20 is devastatingly clear:
ὀργὴ γὰρ ἀνδρὸς δικαιοσύνην θεοῦ οὐκ ἐργάζεται
Human anger does not accomplish God's righteousness.
So place Ephesians and James beside each other.
“Be angry, and do not sin.”
“Be slow to anger.”
“Human anger does not produce God's righteousness.”
There is no contradiction.
There is a warning.
Anger may arise.
But anger must never become your master.
Feeling anger is not identical to committing sin.
Yet anger is extraordinarily fertile soil for sin.
Leave it unattended long enough and things begin growing there.
Bitterness.
Contempt.
Revenge.
Hatred.
Slander.
Self-righteousness.
Cruelty.
Violence.
Unforgiveness.
And eventually you can become so accustomed to carrying the anger that you stop realizing how heavy it is.
You start calling it personality.
“I just tell it like it is.”
You call it wisdom.
“I know what people are really like now.”
You call it boundaries.
“I don't need anybody.”
You call it discernment.
“I can see straight through them.”
But sometimes underneath all of those sentences is simply a wounded person who never brought the wound completely to Jesus.
And wounds that are not surrendered have a frightening way of becoming weapons.
Maybe that is why you needed to read this today.
Not because anger makes you uniquely terrible.
But because Jesus wants the room in your heart you have kept locked.
The room where you replay the conversation.
The room where you imagine what you should have said.
The room where you secretly hope they experience what they did to you.
The room where their name changes your breathing.
The room where you insist, “I've forgiven them,” while continuing to prosecute them in the courtroom of your imagination every night.
Jesus wants that room too.
Not because what happened did not matter.
Precisely because it did.
Christian forgiveness never requires calling evil good.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending abuse was acceptable.
It does not mean refusing appropriate boundaries.
It does not mean preventing legitimate authorities from addressing crimes or wrongdoing.
It does not mean automatically restoring trust where repentance and rebuilding have not occurred.
And forgiveness certainly does not mean returning yourself or someone vulnerable to danger.
Forgiveness means vengeance no longer belongs to you.
You place judgment into hands more righteous than yours.
Paul says in Romans 12:19:
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
That is not God minimizing justice.
It is God removing the gavel from your hand.
There are things only God can judge perfectly because only God knows everything.
You don't.
I don't.
And when we demand the throne, anger begins transforming us into judges who cannot see the entire case.
But here is where the Gospel cuts deeper still.
At the cross, we discover that we are not merely victims of other people's sin.
We are sinners ourselves.
That does not erase what anyone did to us.
It destroys our illusion that grace is something only other people need.
We have lied.
We have lusted.
We have envied.
We have hated.
We have spoken words we cannot retrieve.
We have ignored God.
We have cherished pride.
We have wanted our own way.
We have failed to love God with everything we are.
We have failed to love our neighbor as ourselves.
And the holy God against whom we have sinned did something infinitely greater than suppress His justice and pretend everything was fine.
He sent His Son.
Jesus Christ lived the righteousness we could not live.
He bore sin upon the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
The Gospel is not God saying sin doesn't matter.
Calvary proves sin matters more than we imagined.
The Gospel is God revealing that His grace is greater than our guilt.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
And suddenly forgiveness is no longer a sentimental religious slogan.
It has blood on it.
Forgiveness cost Christ something.
So when Jesus calls us to forgive, He is not asking us to pretend wounds are painless.
He is calling forgiven sinners to live from the mercy they themselves have received.
Maybe somebody reading this has carried anger for ten years.
Maybe twenty.
Maybe longer.
Maybe the person who wounded you has already forgotten what happened.
But you haven't.
You remember the room.
The date.
The words.
The expression on their face.
You remember driving home.
You remember crying where nobody could see you.
You remember lying awake asking God why He allowed it.
And perhaps part of you has been waiting for permission to finally stop carrying it.
Here it is:
You do not have to pretend it never hurt.
You can bring the anger honestly to Jesus.
Tell Him.
Not the polished church version.
Tell Him the truth.
“Lord, I am angry.”
“Lord, this hurt me.”
“Lord, I don't know how to forgive.”
“Lord, part of me still wants revenge.”
“Lord, I need You to change what this pain is doing inside me.”
That prayer is more spiritually honest than smiling while resentment eats you alive.
God already knows.
The question is whether you will open the door.
Because Ephesians gives us another frightening phrase:
“Neither give place to the devil.”
The Greek word translated “place” is topos — τόπος — a place, location, opportunity, or room.
Think about that.
Paul warns Christians not to let sinful, lingering anger become territory the devil can exploit.
One wound.
One offense.
One resentment.
One door left open.
And slowly the enemy begins furnishing the room.
He puts bitterness in one corner.
Suspicion in another.
Pride on the wall.
Revenge beside the bed.
Then he whispers:
“You are justified.”
“Never trust again.”
“Make them suffer.”
“Don't forgive.”
“Keep replaying it.”
“They don't deserve mercy.”
And perhaps they don't.
That is why mercy is mercy.
Nobody earns grace.
Neither did we.
This is where Christianity becomes more than inspirational language.
Because following Jesus eventually brings you to a place where obedience costs something.
Sometimes the thing placed on the altar is your right to retaliate.
Sometimes surrender sounds like:
“Jesus, I give You my anger before my anger takes me away from You.”
And no, that does not mean becoming passive toward evil.
There are moments when love must confront.
There are moments when truth must be spoken.
There are moments when injustice must be opposed.
There are moments when vulnerable people must be defended.
There are moments when silence would itself become cowardice.
But Christian confrontation must remain Christian.
Truth without hatred.
Courage without cruelty.
Justice without vengeance.
Conviction without contempt.
Anger without sin.
And that is impossible by willpower alone.
We need the Holy Spirit.
Because anger reveals who sits on the throne.
When somebody insults you, something rises.
When somebody humiliates you, something rises.
When somebody misunderstands you, something rises.
When somebody refuses to apologize, something rises.
And in that moment the question becomes:
Who rules me now?
My wound?
My pride?
My adrenaline?
My need to win?
Or Jesus Christ?
This is why “Be angry and do not sin” is not a loophole for Christians who want permission to rage.
It is a command that exposes how desperately we need sanctification.
Anybody can explode.
Anybody can insult.
Anybody can retaliate.
Anybody can destroy.
It takes supernatural grace to have the power to wound someone and choose not to.
It takes Christ to look at the person who hurt you and say:
“I will not let your sin teach me how to sin.”
Read that again.
I will not let your sin teach me how to sin.
Maybe that is the sentence your heart needed.
What they did was wrong.
But you do not have to become what wounded you.
Their bitterness does not have to become yours.
Their cruelty does not have to reproduce itself inside you.
Their abandonment does not have to make you incapable of loving.
Their betrayal does not get to write the ending of your story.
Jesus does.
That is the scandal of grace.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
His disciples scattered.
Religious leaders mocked Him.
Soldiers struck Him.
A crowd demanded His crucifixion.
Nails went through His hands.
And the story still ended with an empty tomb.
That is what Jesus does.
He walks into stories that look ruined and writes resurrection where everyone expected a grave.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From bondage to freedom.
From bitterness to surrender.
From death to life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe today the miracle is not that the person who hurt you suddenly apologizes.
Maybe the miracle begins when they can no longer control your heart without even being in the room.
Maybe freedom begins when you stop drinking poison hoping somebody else becomes sick.
Maybe tonight, before the sun goes down, you finally say:
“Jesus, this anger belongs to You.”
And perhaps you will need to say it again tomorrow.
And again next week.
Forgiveness can involve repeated surrender as memories resurface.
But every time the wound demands the throne, bring it back to the cross.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Until one day you realize their name no longer owns your peace.
Be honest.
Or, if Christ has already delivered you from years of bitterness, tell your testimony. Somebody reading the comments may desperately need evidence that Jesus can actually heal a heart after betrayal.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend who is angry with God.
The husband carrying resentment.
The wife silently breaking.
The believer wounded by church people.
The person who was betrayed.
The person whose anger is slowly destroying everything they love.
Or send this privately if their wound should not be made public.
You may never know who reads it at 2:13 in the morning while fighting tears.
You may never know whose marriage pauses before another explosion.
You may never know who puts the phone down instead of sending the message they would regret.
You may never know who whispers for the first time in years:
“Jesus, help me forgive.”
Because anger has a way of returning when the memory returns.
Come back when it does.
Not because these words have power in themselves, but because the truth of God's Word points us back to Christ.
Scripture teaches willing, cheerful generosity rather than giving under compulsion.
But voluntary support can still become a meaningful act of Gospel partnership.
And remember this when anger rises again:
You are not required to deny that the wound hurt.
You are not commanded to call evil good.
You are not told that justice does not matter.
You are being called to something far harder.
Bring the anger to Jesus before anger becomes your master.
Confront what must be confronted without becoming consumed by hatred.
Establish boundaries where wisdom requires them.
Seek justice without worshiping revenge.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Repent when your anger crosses into sin.
And when you fail, run toward Christ rather than away from Him.
There is grace even there.
Especially there.
Because the Gospel was never the story of good people successfully controlling themselves until God finally accepted them.
It is the story of sinners who could not save themselves being rescued by a Savior who could.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
Still forgiving.
Still restoring.
Still breaking chains.
Still healing wounds nobody else can see.
Still taking stories covered in shame, rage, betrayal, failure, and regret...
and writing grace across the pages everyone else thought were ruined.
So yes...
Scripture can speak of being angry without immediately equating the emotion itself with sin.
But Scripture never gives anger permission to become your god.
Take it to the cross.
Before bitterness writes another chapter.
Because the person who wounded you does not deserve to hold the pen to the rest of your life.
Give the pen back to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES THE BIBLE TELL A MAN TO DELIGHT IN HIS WIFE’S BODY Instead of Pretending Bodies Don’t Matter?
paragraphs: WHY DOES THE BIBLE TELL A MAN TO DELIGHT IN HIS WIFE’S BODY Instead of Pretending Bodies Don’t Matter?
Proverbs 5:18–19 says something about marriage, desire, and the human body that many Christians are almost embarrassed to admit is actually in the Bible.
There are verses Christians whisper about.
Verses we read quickly when the children are in the room.
Verses that somehow never make it onto the coffee mug.
And then there is Proverbs 5:18–19.
Read it slowly, because the Bible is far less embarrassed about God’s design for married love than many of us have become.
The Hebrew says:
יְהִֽי־מְקוֹרְךָ֥ בָר֑וּךְ וּ֝שְׂמַ֗ח מֵאֵ֥שֶׁת נְעוּרֶֽךָ׃
אַיֶּ֥לֶת אֲהָבִ֗ים וְֽיַעֲלַת־חֵ֥ן דַּ֭דֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּ֣ךָ בְכָל־עֵ֑ת בְּ֝אַהֲבָתָ֗הּ תִּשְׁגֶּ֥ה תָמִֽיד׃

“Let your fountain be blessed: Find joy in the wife of your youth—a loving doe, a graceful mountain goat. Let her breasts satisfy you at all times; be infatuated with love of her always.” Proverbs 5:18–19, Revised JPS.
Yes.
The Hebrew really says that.
The word is דַּדֶּיהָ — daddeha — “her breasts.”
The text does not hide the body behind a cloud of religious euphemisms.
And perhaps that makes some of us uncomfortable because somewhere along the way, many Christians learned an idea that did not actually come from the Bible:
That holiness means pretending physical attraction does not matter.
But Proverbs does something radically different.
It does not tell the husband to become blind to his wife’s body.
It tells him where his eyes, affection, desire, delight, and covenant loyalty belong.
With her.
That changes everything.
Because Proverbs 5 is not pornography dressed up as Scripture.
It is almost the exact opposite.

The chapter begins with a father warning his son about sexual temptation. The seductive alternative initially appears sweet, but the path ends in devastation. Then comes the breathtaking counter-command: do not merely spend your entire life saying “no” to forbidden desire.
Learn the holy place where desire can say “yes.”
“Drink water from your own cistern,” Proverbs says.
Rejoice in your wife.
Delight in her.
Remain captivated by her love.
And then, immediately after these words, verse 20 asks why the son should become captivated by a forbidden woman instead. Verse 21 reminds him that his ways are before the eyes of the LORD.
That context matters enormously.
God is not teaching men to objectify women.
He is teaching a husband to direct sexual desire toward covenant faithfulness rather than adultery.
There is a difference between delighting in your wife and reducing your wife to a body.
A massive difference.
One says, “Your body exists for my consumption.”
The other says, “You are my beloved covenant companion, and I refuse to pretend that the physical dimension of our marriage is somehow beneath God.”
Biblical desire is never permission for selfishness, coercion, humiliation, comparison, entitlement, or abuse.
The woman being celebrated in Proverbs 5 is not a product.
She is “the wife of your youth.”
There is history there.
Covenant.
Years.
Memories.
Ordinary mornings.
Private laughter.
Arguments survived.
Tears witnessed.
Children perhaps raised.
Bodies that change.
Hair that changes.
Faces that change.
Strength that changes.
Seasons that change.
And Scripture still says:
Rejoice in her.
Maybe somebody needs to hear that.
Because we live in a culture trained to discard bodies when they change.
The world says youth is desirable.
God teaches covenant faithfulness.
The world says compare.
Covenant says cherish.
The world says scroll until somebody more attractive appears.
Wisdom says come home.
And suddenly Proverbs 5 becomes painfully contemporary.
The forbidden woman may not be standing at somebody’s doorway anymore.
She can appear through a glowing screen at 1:17 in the morning.
She can be an old flame rediscovered online.
A secret conversation.
A private browser.
A fantasy carefully hidden from a spouse.
A relationship at work that supposedly “isn’t anything.”
One more message.
One more picture.
One more compromise.
One more secret.
Until a man wakes up and realizes that he has been feeding his appetite everywhere except the covenant where God called him to cultivate love.
That is why this passage is not merely about breasts.
It is about direction.
Where is your desire going?
Where is your attention going?
Where is your imagination going?
Where is the tenderness going that your spouse once received?
Where are your eyes going when nobody else can see them?
Because God can.
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD.”
That comes immediately after this teaching.
Not because God despises desire.
Because He sees what desire can become when it escapes wisdom.
And here is where the Gospel has to enter this conversation.
Because some people reading this already feel condemned.
Maybe pornography has been part of your secret life.
Maybe emotional infidelity crossed lines you promised yourself you would never cross.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Maybe you have spent years comparing your spouse to edited bodies on a screen.
Maybe your marriage has become cold.
Maybe physical intimacy became transactional.
Maybe resentment entered the bedroom years ago and never left.
Maybe you are the spouse who was betrayed.
Maybe these verses hurt because your body has been criticized instead of cherished.
Maybe you cannot remember the last time you felt wanted.
Maybe you have carried shame about your body since childhood.
Maybe religious environments taught you that your body itself was dirty.
Maybe someone used “submission” or “marital duty” as religious language to pressure you, and now even biblical passages about intimacy make your body tense.
Hear this carefully.
Proverbs 5 does not give anyone permission to abuse you.
Marriage does not transform selfishness into holiness.
Sexual coercion does not become righteous because somebody attaches a Bible verse to it.
Biblical marital intimacy belongs within covenant love, faithfulness, mutual care, honor, and self-giving.

The New Testament makes that mutuality strikingly clear. In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul speaks to both husband and wife about marital affection and mutual responsibility. Neither spouse is presented as a disposable object existing merely for the gratification of the other.
And Christ gives us an even deeper pattern for love.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
That is Ephesians 5:25.
Gave Himself.
That is the shape of Christian love.
Not “How much can I take?”
“How can I give?”
Not domination.
Sacrifice.
Not consumption.
Covenant.
Not using another body.
Cherishing another person.
And suddenly Proverbs 5:19 and Ephesians 5:25 belong in the same marriage.
Desire and sacrifice.
Delight and devotion.
Attraction and covenant.
Body and soul.
This is something Christians desperately need to recover.
The body is not the enemy of spirituality.
God created human beings embodied.
Before sin entered the story, Genesis says the man and woman were naked and unashamed.
Christianity does not ultimately teach escape from embodiment. The Christian hope includes resurrection.
And at the center of Christianity stands one of the most astonishing claims imaginable:
“The Word became flesh.”
Jesus Christ did not save humanity by pretending physical existence was beneath Him.
He entered it.
Of course, none of that means every bodily appetite is automatically holy.
Hunger can become gluttony.
Anger can become violence.
Sexual desire can become lust, exploitation, adultery, pornography, selfishness, or idolatry.
The answer is not to declare the body evil.
The answer is redemption.
Desire needs discipleship.
And that is exactly what Proverbs 5 is doing.
It takes sexual desire by the shoulders, turns it away from betrayal, and points it home.
To your covenant.
To your spouse.
To faithfulness.
To gratitude.
To delight without betrayal.
There is another uncomfortable truth here.
Some married Christians have become experts at resisting adultery while forgetting to cultivate affection.
They never physically cheated.
But somewhere along the way they stopped seeing each other.
Stopped flirting.
Stopped touching without an agenda.
Stopped complimenting.
Stopped listening.
Stopped laughing.
Stopped dating.
Stopped protecting time together.
Stopped saying, “You are beautiful to me.”
Then they wonder why the marriage feels like two exhausted roommates managing bills, children, laundry, and calendars.
Proverbs does not merely say:
Do not commit adultery.
It says:
Rejoice.
That Hebrew command is וּשְׂמַח — u-semach — “and rejoice,” “be glad,” “take joy.”
That is active language.
Marital faithfulness is more than refusing to leave.
It is learning, again and again, how to come home.
And verse 19 becomes even more startling.
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד

The translations capture the intensity differently: be captivated, intoxicated, infatuated with her love continually. The Hebrew imagery is strong enough that several major translations preserve that sense of being deeply overcome or exhilarated by marital love.
Do you see what Scripture is doing?
It takes language of overwhelming desire and places it inside covenant.
Not outside marriage.
Inside it.
God is not saying attraction is irrelevant.
He is saying attraction is not your god.
It must learn covenant.
And this matters when bodies change.
Because they will.
Pregnancy changes bodies.
Childbirth changes bodies.
Illness changes bodies.
Medication changes bodies.
Stress changes bodies.
Age changes bodies.
Gravity is undefeated.
The twenty-five-year-old body will not remain twenty-five.
Neither will yours.
And if your definition of marital delight survives only while another human being looks young, then you have confused covenant love with consumer preference.
Biblical marital love can acknowledge beauty without worshiping youth.
It can celebrate physical attraction without making physical perfection the admission price for affection.
A Christian husband should never weaponize Proverbs 5:19 against a wife whose body has changed.
Think about the cruelty of that.
The woman who carried your children should not have to compete with digitally altered strangers for the eyes of the man who promised to cherish her.
The husband aging beside his wife should not have to believe his worth disappears when his hair thins, his strength changes, or his body bears the evidence of years.
Marriage says:
I know what time has done to you.
Time has touched me too.
Come here.
I still choose you.
That may be one of the most beautiful things an aging couple can say without speaking.
And maybe that is why this passage reaches deeper than sexuality.
It exposes our entire theology of faithfulness.
God does not call us to a disposable love.
And neither does the Gospel.
Jesus did not look at ruined sinners and say, “Come back when you are more desirable.”
He came for sinners.
He touched lepers.
He ate with the despised.
He called the guilty to repentance.
He carried a cross.
He shed His blood.
He rose from the grave.
And He still calls sinners home.

Be careful here: Christ’s redeeming love for His people is not identical to marital erotic desire. Scripture uses marriage imagery for Christ and the church in its own theological way, and we should not collapse those categories.
But Christian marriage can still point beyond itself.
Forgiveness points beyond itself.
Faithfulness points beyond itself.
Sacrificial love points beyond itself.
Covenant points beyond itself.
And for the person reading this who has already failed sexually, the final word of Christianity is not:
Scandal.
It is not:
Ruined.
It is not:
Unclean forever.
It is not:
Too late.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Repentance does not mean pretending the sin never happened.
Grace does not mean calling evil good.
Forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence.
But the blood of Christ is sufficient for the genuinely repentant sinner.
There is forgiveness for the adulterer.
There is forgiveness for the pornography addict.
There is forgiveness for the person who cultivated secret fantasies.
There is forgiveness for the husband who neglected his wife.
There is forgiveness for the wife who hardened herself in bitterness.
There is forgiveness for sexual sin you would rather die than let anyone discover.
Not cheap forgiveness.
Blood-bought forgiveness.
Jesus does not invite us to rename darkness.
He calls us out of it.
Repent.
Confess.
Bring what is hidden into the light.
Seek wise pastoral and professional help where necessary.
If another person has been harmed, do not use “God forgave me” as a weapon to silence their pain or escape accountability.
Grace tells the truth.
Grace kneels.
Grace repents.
Grace makes restitution where possible.
Grace learns new patterns.
Grace closes secret doors.
Grace deletes numbers.
Grace installs boundaries.
Grace asks for help.
Grace stops blaming the spouse for personal sin.
Grace says, “Jesus, I cannot keep living two lives.”
And grace gets back up after failure and keeps walking toward Christ.
Maybe you need to whisper that right now.
Jesus, forgive me.
Maybe nobody around you knows what that sentence means.
He does.
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Not because typing words into a comment section saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing a struggle into the light begins with refusing to pretend anymore.
Maybe your story is different.
Maybe you are fighting hard to stay faithful while your marriage is going through an incredibly dry season.
Maybe betrayal has left you wondering whether your heart will ever feel safe again.
Maybe you have been performing Christianity publicly while privately collapsing.
And if you cannot find many words at all, simply write:
Let believers pray for believers.
Let wounded people discover they are not the only wounded people in the room.
Let testimonies meet confession.
Let grace interrupt shame.
And husbands, hear Proverbs again.
Your wife is not invisible.
Your wife is not a household appliance.
She is not merely “the mother of the children.”
She is not supposed to spend her marriage wondering why you can notice every beautiful woman on a screen but no longer notice her.
Look at her.
Not merely at her body.
At her.
Remember the woman you prayed for.
Remember the conversations that lasted until ridiculous hours.
Remember the first time you realized you loved her.
Remember the years she has walked beside you.
Remember what the two of you survived.
And yes—within the tenderness, privacy, mutuality, and holiness of your marriage—delight in her physically too.
The Bible is not embarrassed to say it.
Neither should we be.
Wives, this is not a command to achieve some impossible beauty standard so that your husband will remain faithful.
His faithfulness is his responsibility before God.
You do not have to defeat aging to deserve covenant faithfulness.
And husbands, your wife is not responsible for becoming every image your undisciplined imagination has consumed.
Perhaps the deeper repentance for some men is not asking their wives to become more visually stimulating.
Perhaps it is retraining eyes that have been overstimulated by a world designed to monetize lust.
Come home.
Come home with your body.
Come home with your eyes.
Come home with your imagination.
Come home with your phone.
Come home with your affection.
Come home with your repentance.
Come home with your tenderness.
And above everything else—
come home to Christ.
Because your spouse cannot be your Savior.
A wonderful marriage cannot wash away your sin.
Sexual fulfillment cannot heal the deepest hunger of the human soul.
Only Jesus can reconcile sinners to God.
And perhaps this is where somebody finally realizes that the real emptiness was never merely sexual.
You kept asking bodies to satisfy a thirst they were never created to satisfy.
You wanted another image.
Another fantasy.
Another person.
Another experience.
Another secret.
Another rush.
But underneath all of it was a soul starving for God.
Jesus does not offer another temporary intoxication.
He offers Himself.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
New life.
A new heart.
A new direction.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message will always return here:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
You may need these words again when temptation whispers that covenant is boring and forbidden things are exciting.
Not for empty numbers.
Send it privately to someone fighting pornography.
Send it to the believer drowning in sexual shame.
Send it to the person who needs to know that repentance is still possible and Christ has not stopped calling sinners home.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the lukewarm.
Invite the curious.
Invite the person who does not even believe yet but cannot stop wondering whether Jesus might actually be who Christians say He is.
But hear this clearly because biblical integrity matters more than conversion numbers:
Christian generosity is not spiritual extortion.
“God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your support can help Gospel Warrior keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep building the free library.
Keep putting Christ-centered resources into the hands of people who may never be able to pay for them.
Keep carrying the message farther.
God cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is not for sale.
But Gospel work can still be generously supported by people who believe in helping it reach others.
That costs nothing.
Yet somewhere in your network may be a husband staring at temptation tonight.
A wife wondering whether she is still beautiful.
A marriage quietly bleeding.
A believer drowning in pornography.
A wounded spouse blaming herself for somebody else’s betrayal.
A Christian carrying sexual shame from years ago.
A sinner convinced Jesus could never want him back.
You do not know whose screen this will reach because you pressed “Share.”
So share it.
But whatever else you do after reading this, do not miss the point of Proverbs 5.
The world will teach you to keep looking.
God’s wisdom teaches covenant faithfulness.
The world will train you to compare.
Wisdom teaches you to cherish.
Sin whispers that forbidden water will satisfy you.
Then leaves you thirstier than before.
Jesus calls sinners out of hiding.
Back into truth.
Back into repentance.
Back into grace.
Back into the light.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you tonight is this:
Sin keeps asking you to trade what is sacred for what is exciting; grace teaches your heart to see the sacred as beautiful again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “SUSTAIN ME WITH RAISINS… FOR I AM SICK WITH LOVE”: THE PHYSICAL INTENSITY OF BIBLICAL DESIRE
paragraphs: “SUSTAIN ME WITH RAISINS… FOR I AM SICK WITH LOVE”: THE PHYSICAL INTENSITY OF BIBLICAL DESIRE

What if Scripture’s most startling picture of desire is not a warning against feeling deeply—but a revelation that God created human love with enough force to make the body tremble, the appetite disappear, and the heart ache… while still insisting that love must never be awakened outside its proper time?
There are verses in the Bible we read comfortably.
And then there are verses that almost make us look over our shoulder before reading them aloud.
Song of Songs 2:5 is one of those verses.
The woman does not merely say, “I love him.”
She does not say, “I think he is attractive.”
She does not offer us the sanitized vocabulary we sometimes prefer when discussing desire in church.
She says:

סַמְּכוּנִי בָּאֲשִׁישׁוֹת
רַפְּדוּנִי בַּתַּפּוּחִים
כִּי־חוֹלַת אַהֲבָה אָנִי
Samkhuni ba’ashishot, rapp’duni battappuchim, ki-cholat ahavah ani.
“Sustain me with raisin cakes, refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love.”
Song of Songs 2:5.
Read that last line again.
כִּי־חוֹלַת אַהֲבָה אָנִי
Ki-cholat ahavah ani.
“For I am faint with love.”
Or, more literally in its force:
“For I am sick with love.”
Not metaphorically bored.
Not mildly interested.
Not casually attracted.
Love has invaded the body.
And suddenly one of the Bible’s most beautiful love poems confronts something many Christians have spent years trying not to talk about:
Desire can become physical.
Longing can enter the stomach.
Love can disturb sleep.
Absence can ache.
Anticipation can accelerate the heart.
The human body can participate in what the heart desires.
And Scripture is not embarrassed to tell us.
Maybe we have been.
But Scripture is not.
That matters.
Because some people grew up believing that holiness meant becoming almost suspicious of being human.
They learned to distrust attraction.
To fear their bodies.
To confuse temptation with desire.
To confuse desire with sin.
To confuse sexuality with shame.
Some were taught what not to do but were never taught what God actually created.
So they entered adulthood knowing how to feel guilty about desire without knowing how to understand it.
Then Song of Songs walks into the room.
Flowers.
Fragrance.
Fruit.
Skin.
Voices.
Kisses.
Longing.
Absence.
Presence.
Anticipation.
Restraint.
Delight.
And a woman saying she is practically overwhelmed by love.
This is in your Bible.
Not hidden in an appendix.
Not smuggled into Scripture by someone who forgot Christians would eventually read it.
God permitted this astonishing celebration of covenantal human love to stand within Holy Scripture.

The woman has just described her beloved as an apple tree among the trees of the forest. She delights to sit beneath his shade. His fruit is sweet to her taste. He brings her into a place of feasting, and love is over her. Then comes the cry:
“Sustain me…”
“Refresh me…”
“I am sick with love.”
And immediately after it:
“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.”
The progression is intensely embodied.
Food.
Taste.
Weakness.
Touch.
Embrace.
Then Scripture does something extraordinarily important.
It introduces restraint.
The next verse warns the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken or arouse love until the proper time.
That changes everything.
Because the Bible does not solve the intensity of desire by declaring desire evil.
It gives desire a boundary.
That distinction is enormous.
Biblical holiness is not the murder of desire.
It is the consecration of desire.
Fire inside a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire unleashed across the living room can destroy it.
The problem is not that fire possesses heat.
The question is where the fire belongs.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years hating the fire simply because nobody taught you the fireplace.
You felt attraction and immediately felt dirty.
You wanted to be wanted and immediately felt ashamed.
You longed to be held, known, chosen, pursued, cherished—and wondered whether serious Christians were supposed to outgrow such things.
Song of Songs refuses that mutilated picture of humanity.
God created bodies.
God created affection.
God created marriage.
God created the astonishing possibility that one human being could look upon another and experience desire so intense that poetry reaches for the language of sickness.
But because God created desire, desire does not become god.
That may be where this gets painfully personal.
Because beautiful things become destructive when we ask them to save us.
Romance makes a terrible savior.
Sex makes a terrible savior.
Marriage makes a terrible savior.
Being desired makes a terrible savior.
Another human being makes a terrible savior.
And some of us have discovered that only after bleeding from the attempt.
You thought, If somebody finally chooses me, I will know I matter.
So you accepted attention that should never have been called love.
You ignored warning signs because loneliness was louder.
You stayed because leaving felt like becoming unwanted again.
You confused being pursued with being valued.
You confused chemistry with character.
You confused sexual attention with intimacy.
You confused obsession with devotion.
You confused somebody needing your body with somebody loving your soul.
Maybe you gave pieces of yourself away because for a few minutes it silenced the terrifying question:
Am I lovable?
And afterward…
silence.
Maybe shame.
Maybe another message you knew you should not answer.
Another night.
Another compromise.
Another promise that this would be the last time.
Another morning asking God whether grace still reaches people who knew better.
Listen carefully.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Because Jesus did not come only for people whose desires have always been perfectly ordered.
He came for sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with screenshots they hope nobody sees.
People with relationships they regret.
People who crossed boundaries.
People who were used.
People who used others.
People carrying secret fantasies.
People trapped in pornography.
People who have slept beside someone and still felt desperately alone.
People who made an idol out of romance.
People who cannot forgive themselves for what happened.
People who have been trying to wash yesterday off their souls for years.
The Gospel does not say your sin was imaginary.
The Gospel says Christ's mercy is greater.
At the cross, Jesus does not redefine darkness as light.
He enters the darkness to rescue sinners from it.
Repentance therefore is not God standing at a distance saying, “Clean yourself before you come closer.”
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who receives sinners.
The Christian message is not:
“Become pure enough so Jesus will want you.”
It is:
Jesus Christ came to save sinners, and His grace does not merely pardon us—it begins transforming us.
There is a difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide.”
The Gospel says:
“Come into the light.”
Shame says:
“You are what you did.”
Grace says:
“Bring what you did to Christ.”
Sin says:
“Keep feeding me and eventually I will satisfy you.”
Jesus says, in effect throughout the Gospel:
“Come to Me.”
And perhaps that is why this ancient woman’s confession—I am sick with love—can reach beyond romance and expose something deeper inside all of us.
We are creatures of desire.
We are always reaching.
Always thirsting.
Always attaching our hearts to something.
Always saying, consciously or unconsciously:
“Sustain me with this.”
“Refresh me with this.”
“Give me this person.”
“Give me this body.”
“Give me this success.”
“Give me this attention.”
“Give me this validation.”
“Give me enough likes.”
“Give me enough money.”
“Give me enough pleasure.”
“Give me enough admiration.”
“Give me something that will finally quiet this hunger.”
And eventually every created thing reaches the boundary of what it can give.
The lover cannot carry the weight of being God.
The spouse cannot heal every wound.
The sexual experience cannot produce eternal belonging.
The applause dies.
Beauty changes.
Bodies age.
Feelings fluctuate.
People disappoint us.
And beneath all those smaller hungers remains the terrifyingly beautiful truth:
Human beings were made not merely to consume gifts from God but to know God Himself.
That does not erase human romance.
It puts romance in its proper place.
The Bible can celebrate marital desire precisely because marriage does not have to become salvation.
And the New Testament takes us somewhere breathtaking.
Marriage itself becomes a sign pointing beyond itself.
Paul speaks in Ephesians 5 of husband and wife and then says that this mystery ultimately speaks of Christ and the church.
Not because Jesus is merely a larger version of romantic attraction.
He is not.
But because covenant love reaches its ultimate redemptive horizon in Christ—the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His people.
Human lovers say:
“I desire you.”
At Calvary, Christ demonstrates something infinitely deeper:
“I give Myself for you.”
That is the difference between lust and cruciform love.
Lust asks:
“What can your body give me?”
Christlike love asks:
“What can I give for your good?”
Lust consumes.
Love serves.
Lust reduces a person to appetite.
Love sees a person bearing the image of God.
Lust says, “Now.”
Wisdom can wait.
And Song of Songs, despite all its heat, understands waiting.
“Do not awaken or arouse love until it pleases.”
What a word for an age built upon instant gratification.
We awaken everything.
Immediately.
We swipe.
Click.
Watch.
Message.
Meet.
Consume.
Discard.
Repeat.
We have unprecedented access to bodies and perhaps unprecedented difficulty with intimacy.
We can see strangers naked without knowing their names.
We can simulate closeness without covenant.
We can receive sexual stimulation without sacrifice.
We can call obsession romance.
We can call exploitation empowerment.
We can call loneliness freedom.
And still, at 2:17 in the morning, the human heart whispers:
Does anybody actually know me?
Not my body.
Me.
Not my profile.
Me.
Not the version I perform.
Me.
Would anybody stay if they knew everything?
That question leads straight toward the scandal of grace.
Because Jesus already knows.
The parts you edited out of your testimony.
The thoughts you never confessed.
The relationship nobody knows about.
The search history.
The relapse.
The betrayal.
The night you wish you could erase.
The wound somebody else gave you that somehow made you feel dirty even though you were the one harmed.
He knows.
And the cross still stands.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes grace astonishing.
Christ does not redeem us by pretending rebellion does not matter.
He bears sin and calls sinners to repentance, forgiveness, new life, and holiness.
That means your past does not need to become your permanent address.
There are people reading this who need to hear that sentence again.
Your past does not need to become your permanent address.
You may have awakened love at the wrong time.
You may have awakened desire with the wrong person.
You may have offered your body where there was no covenant.
You may have broken someone else's trust.
You may have built secret habits that are slowly destroying your ability to see another person as a person.
You may have called something love that was actually dependency.
You may have been manipulated by someone who used Scripture itself to control you.
You may have believed that because something happened to your body, your body became permanently ruined.
But Christianity is a resurrection faith.
Jesus specializes in graves people assumed were permanent.
Repentance is real.
Consequences can be real.
Healing can take time.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Some relationships should not be restored.
Some doors should remain closed.
Some phone numbers should remain blocked.
Some patterns need pastoral help, accountability, counseling, and serious intervention.
Grace is not pretending damage never happened.
Grace means damage does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same heartbeat:
Not scandal to denial.
Not scandal to religious performance.
Not scandal to pretending.
Scandal to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by editing sin until it looks respectable.
By forgiving sinners who repent and making them new.
Maybe your deepest problem today is not sexual sin.
Maybe it is loneliness.
Maybe you have actually waited.
Prayed.
Tried to honor God.
Watched other people marry.
Watched pregnancy announcements appear.
Watched anniversaries accumulate.
Watched younger people find what you have begged God for.
And somewhere underneath your faithful Christian vocabulary is a sentence you are almost afraid to pray:
Lord, why not me?
Song of Songs gives you permission to acknowledge that longing is physical.
Loneliness can hurt.
Desire can ache.
Waiting can exhaust you.
Wanting marriage does not automatically mean Jesus is insufficient.
Wanting affection does not automatically mean you are spiritually immature.
But the ache becomes dangerous when you decide that God must give you another human being before life can have meaning.
No spouse can bear that burden.
No future husband can be Christ.
No future wife can be Christ.
And if God gives you marriage, one of the greatest gifts you can bring into it is refusing to demand that your spouse become your Messiah.
Love them deeply.
Desire them faithfully.
Cherish them tenderly.
Enjoy the gift without worshiping it.
Because every good human love is still creaturely love.
Christ alone is Lord.
And maybe you are married, but the fire has dimmed.
You remember when you could hardly stop thinking about each other.
Now there are bills.
Children.
Deadlines.
Fatigue.
Unresolved resentment.
Phones glowing between you in bed.
Two people who once talked until sunrise now scrolling separately in silence.
Song of Songs reminds us that covenant does not require affection to die.
Marriage is more than desire—but it need not become less than tenderness.
Sometimes spiritual maturity looks like praying together.
Sometimes it looks like repentance.
Sometimes it looks like forgiving.
Sometimes it looks like putting the phone down.
Sometimes it looks like listening again.
Sometimes it looks like remembering that the person beside you is not furniture in your life.
They are a soul.
See them again.
Not as the person who forgot the groceries.
Not merely as the mother or father of your children.
Not merely as the person sharing the mortgage.
See the human being.
The one God entrusted to your love.
And if your marriage contains coercion, violence, or abuse, do not misuse biblical language about covenant as an excuse to conceal danger. Seek wise, trustworthy help and safety.
Biblical love never needs evil to be renamed good.
And perhaps that brings us back to the woman beneath the apple tree.
“Sustain me…”
“Refresh me…”
“For I am sick with love.”
She is overwhelmed.
Desire has reached her body.
Scripture lets the sentence remain.
It does not blush.
But Scripture also refuses to let desire become sovereign.
There is a time.
There are boundaries.
There is wisdom.
There is covenant.
There is restraint.
There is love.
And above every human love stands the God who created us capable of loving at all.
So maybe the question is not whether you desire.
You will.
The question is:
What is your desire teaching you to worship?
That person you cannot stop thinking about…
Have you turned them into salvation?
That relationship you are terrified to lose…
Have you surrendered it to Christ?
That secret habit…
Is it training your eyes to consume people instead of love them?
That loneliness…
Is it driving you toward Jesus or convincing you to accept anything that temporarily numbs the ache?
That marriage…
Are you protecting it?
That wound…
Are you hiding it?
That shame…
Why are you still carrying what Christ is calling you to bring into the light?
Be honest.
This may have hit somewhere you were not expecting.
Not as performance.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when hiding ends.
And if you have spent too long pretending everything is fine:
“No more hiding.”
Someone else reading the comments may discover that they are not the only believer fighting that battle.
Not because every sentence will be needed tonight.
Because there may come a night when one of them will.
You may never know whose midnight your share enters.
It cannot.
It is not.
Not because anyone must financially support Gospel Warrior in order to glorify God.
Scripture does not give us the right to make that claim.
Biblical giving must never be reduced to spiritual pressure.
But voluntary generosity has always helped Gospel work continue.
Pray.
Send it privately to somebody who is hurting.
Because the Gospel has never depended upon finding people with spotless histories.
It announces a spotless Savior.
Song of Songs gives us a woman overwhelmed enough to say:
כִּי־חוֹלַת אַהֲבָה אָנִי
Ki-cholat ahavah ani.
“I am sick with love.”
And perhaps tonight you understand that sentence differently.
You know what it is to ache.
To want.
To wait.
To regret.
To reach.
To burn.
To break.
But whatever your history, do not make desire your god.
Do not make shame your master.
Do not make another human being your savior.
Bring your desire under the lordship of Christ.
Bring your sexuality under the lordship of Christ.
Bring your loneliness under the lordship of Christ.
Bring your marriage under the lordship of Christ.
Bring your memories under the lordship of Christ.
Bring your body under the lordship of Christ.
Bring the secret.
Bring the wound.
Bring the appetite.
Bring the failure.
Bring the part of the story you thought disqualified you.
Repent where you have sinned.
Seek help where you are wounded.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Flee what is destroying you.
Honor what God has made holy.
And come again to Jesus.
Because the deepest miracle of grace is not that God finds people who never became messy.
It is that Christ enters the stories we thought were beyond redemption and begins making all things new.
You may still remember the chapter that broke you—but in the hands of Jesus, the chapter that broke you does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN SOMEONE BE SAVED WITHOUT EVER REPENTING?
paragraphs: CAN SOMEONE BE SAVED WITHOUT EVER REPENTING?
The Question Many Christians Are Afraid to Ask—Because the Answer May Expose the Difference Between Knowing About Jesus and Actually Belonging to Him
There is a terrifying possibility hiding inside modern Christianity.
A person can know the songs.
Know when to raise a hand.
Know how to say, “God is good.”
Know John 3:16.
Own three Bibles.
Have Christian posts all over Facebook.
Have been baptized.
Have walked an aisle.
Have repeated a prayer.
Have called Jesus “Lord” for twenty years...
…and still be clinging to the very sin Christ has been calling them to surrender.
So here is the question we need enough courage to ask:
Can someone be saved without ever repenting?
Not, “Can a Christian still struggle with sin?”
They can.
Not, “Can a saved person fall badly?”
They can.
Not, “Can a believer have seasons of weakness, confusion, addiction, failure, or spiritual exhaustion?”
Absolutely.
Peter denied Jesus.
David fell catastrophically.
The Corinthian church needed severe correction.
The Bible is brutally honest about the failures of people who belong to God.
The question is more disturbing than that.
Can I spend my entire life saying I believe in Jesus while never actually turning toward Him?
Can I want forgiveness without wanting the One who forgives?
Can I want heaven while refusing the King of heaven?
Can I want Jesus as Savior while spending my entire life telling Jesus, in effect, “You will never be Lord over this part of me”?
And somewhere beneath all our theological vocabulary is an even more personal question:
What if I have mistaken regret for repentance?
That question changes everything.
Because Judas regretted.
Pharaoh regretted consequences.
People cry when sin destroys their marriages, reputations, finances, families, ministries, health, and peace.
But tears alone are not repentance.
Fear of hell is not automatically repentance.
Feeling guilty is not repentance.
Getting caught is not repentance.
Feeling embarrassed is not repentance.
Even saying “I’m sorry” is not necessarily repentance.
Repentance goes deeper.
When Jesus began publicly proclaiming the Gospel, His message was not merely, “Believe that God loves you.”
Mark 1:15 records:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
There are two Greek imperatives sitting there with enormous spiritual weight:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō
“Repent and believe in the Gospel.”
Do not rush past that.
Jesus did not place repentance against faith.
He placed repentance beside faith.

The Greek verb commonly translated “repent,” μετανοέω — metanoeō, carries the idea of changing one’s mind, reconsidering, turning in thought and orientation. But biblical repentance cannot honestly be reduced to the shallow slogan, “Just change your opinion.”
Because when the mind truly changes about God, sin, Christ, and ourselves, direction begins to change too.
That is why Peter later preached:
“Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out...” — Acts 3:19, KJV
And after the resurrection, Jesus told His disciples that:
“repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations...” — Luke 24:47, KJV
Repentance was not an embarrassing doctrine invented centuries after Jesus.
Jesus preached it.
The apostles preached it.
The early church proclaimed it.
And the Gospel still demands that we understand it.
But here is where people often make the opposite mistake.
They hear “repentance” and imagine God standing with crossed arms saying:
“Clean yourself up first. Fix everything. Stop every sin. Become worthy. Then perhaps I will save you.”
That is not the Gospel either.
You do not repent in order to make yourself worthy of Jesus.
You repent because you have finally begun to see that Jesus alone is worthy.
You do not scrub yourself clean before coming to the fountain.
You come filthy.
You come guilty.
You come exposed.
You come unable to rescue yourself.
You come with your addictions, secrets, pride, lust, bitterness, hypocrisy, wounds, religious performance, shame, and excuses.
You come because the blood of Christ—not your moral résumé—is your only hope.
Salvation is not God paying you wages because you successfully stopped sinning.
Salvation is grace.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
So repentance is not a work by which you purchase salvation.
You cannot purchase what Christ purchased with His blood.
You cannot improve upon Calvary.
You cannot add a single ounce of saving merit to the finished work of Jesus Christ.
The scandal of grace is that Jesus receives sinners who could never make themselves worthy.
But grace does something extraordinary.
It does not merely pardon the rebel.
It begins transforming the rebel.
Grace does not say, “Your sin does not matter.”
Grace says, “Your sin mattered so much that the Son of God carried its judgment—and He loves you too much to leave you enslaved to what was destroying you.”
This is where repentance becomes beautiful.
In the Hebrew Scriptures, one of the great words associated with turning back is שׁוּב — shuv, meaning “turn” or “return.”
The prophetic cry again and again is essentially:
Come back.
Return.
Stop running.
Turn toward the God you abandoned.
Repentance, then, is not merely God screaming, “You disgusting sinner, get away from Me.”
The Gospel reveals something breathtakingly different.
It is God calling the sinner home through Christ.
Think about the prodigal son.
He left his father.
He squandered what he had.
He descended into humiliation.
Then came that devastating moment of clarity.
Luke says:
“And when he came to himself...”
What a description.
Sin had taken him so far that returning to the father looked like coming back to reality.
He got up.
He went home.
And perhaps he rehearsed his confession with every painful step.
Maybe he expected anger.
Maybe rejection.
Maybe a locked door.
Maybe a father saying, “You made your decision. Live with it.”
But Jesus tells us something astonishing.
The father saw him while he was still far away.
The father ran.
The father embraced him.
The father kissed him.
Grace ran toward repentance.
And repentance discovered that the Father it feared approaching was already moving toward the returning son.
That is the Gospel.
But notice something we sometimes remove from the story.
The prodigal came home.
He did not remain in the pigpen sending messages to his father saying:
“I love you, Dad. Please continue funding this lifestyle.”
He arose.
He returned.
Not because returning purchased his father’s love.
He returned because something inside him had finally awakened to the truth about the father, himself, and the far country.
That is why the question, “Can someone be saved without ever repenting?” cannot be answered by pretending repentance is optional.
The New Testament will not allow us to do that.
When the crowd at Pentecost was “pricked in their heart” and asked what they should do, Peter answered:
Μετανοήσατε
Metanoēsate.
Repent.
Not “pretend nothing happened.”
Not “add Jesus to the life you already worship.”
Not “say religious words while intentionally reserving the throne for yourself.”
Repent.
Yet even here we must guard the Gospel carefully.
Biblical repentance does not mean sinless perfection.
If repentance meant becoming completely sinless before salvation, nobody could be saved.

If repentance meant never struggling again after conversion, the New Testament’s repeated calls for believers to confess, resist temptation, put sin to death, forgive, mature, and pursue holiness would make little sense.
A Christian can stumble.
A Christian can fall terribly.
A Christian can find himself crying over the same battlefield more than once.
The difference is not that Christians never fall.
The difference is that grace will not allow the true believer to make permanent peace with the darkness.
There is a difference between struggling against sin and surrendering yourself to sin as your rightful master.
There is a difference between falling into the mud and building your house there.
There is a difference between saying:
“Jesus, I hate what this is doing in me. Help me.”
…and saying:
“Jesus, I know what You say, but I have decided You will never have authority here.”
Perhaps you needed that distinction.
Because maybe you have been terrified that your struggle means you are beyond grace.
You fell again.
You clicked again.
You drank again.
You exploded again.
You returned to the relationship again.
You entertained the bitterness again.
You lied again.
And now shame is whispering:
“A real Christian would never struggle like this.”

But the fact that you are grieving your sin, bringing it into the light, seeking Christ, fighting, confessing, getting back up, and longing to be free is profoundly different from proudly declaring sin your king.
Do not confuse the battlefield with abandonment by God.
Run to Christ.
Again.
Confess.
Again.
Ask for help.
Again.
Cut off what feeds the sin.
Again.
Bring another mature believer into the battle if necessary.
Again.
But keep coming toward the Light.
Because repentance is not merely one dramatic emotional moment at an altar.
The Christian life remains a life of turning toward Christ.
And there is another person reading this.
Your problem is not that you are afraid you have not repented enough.
Your problem is that you do not want to repent at all.
You want reassurance.
Not surrender.
You want someone to tell you that because you prayed a prayer when you were twelve, nothing else matters.
You want eternal life without interruption of your present kingdom.
You want a Jesus who forgives but never commands.
A Savior who rescues but never rules.
A cross without death to self.
A crown without a King.
And perhaps this article is making you uncomfortable because somewhere inside, you know exactly what you have been protecting.
Nobody else knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your church does not know.
Your followers do not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
But you know.
And God knows.
There is a locked room in your heart with a sign hanging on the door:
JESUS MAY HAVE EVERYTHING EXCEPT THIS.
Maybe it is pornography.
An affair.
Greed.
Hatred.
A secret relationship.
Dishonesty.
Pride.
Unforgiveness.
A double life.
Religious hypocrisy.
An idol you have renamed “my happiness.”
And you have spent years trying to negotiate with Jesus.
But Christ did not die merely to become another accessory inside the kingdom of Self.
He came as King.
And this is precisely where the Gospel becomes unbelievably good news.
You can stop hiding.
Today.
You do not have to manufacture a cleaner past.
You cannot.
You do not have to rewrite what happened.
You cannot.
You do not have to pretend your scandal never existed.
Jesus already knows the worst chapter.
And He still went to the cross.
That is the breathtaking center of Christianity.
The sinless Son of God took the place of sinners.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Our hope is not that sinners eventually become impressive enough for God.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ is sufficient to save sinners who come to Him.
Repentance does not mean bringing Jesus your perfection.
It means bringing Him the surrender of your excuses.
Faith says:
“Jesus, You are my hope.”
Repentance says:
“And therefore sin cannot remain my king.”
They are not competing roads to salvation.
They are inseparable dimensions of turning to Christ.
This is why Paul described his ministry in Acts 20:21 as testifying of:
“repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Toward God.
Toward Christ.
That is the direction.
And perhaps the most comforting truth of all is that even repentance ultimately leaves us dependent upon grace.
Acts 11:18 speaks of God granting “repentance unto life.”
Second Timothy 2:25 similarly speaks of God granting repentance leading to the knowledge of the truth.
