Even when you turn toward God, you discover grace was already at work calling you.
Christianity gives us no room to boast.
Not even in our repentance.
We do not stand at heaven’s gates saying:
“Look how beautifully I repented.”
We stand there with one name.
Jesus.
One righteousness.
Christ’s.
One sacrifice.
Christ’s.
One cross.
Christ’s.
One empty tomb.
Christ’s.
One boast:
Christ.
So can somebody be saved without ever repenting?

If by “repenting” we mean achieving sinless perfection, fixing ourselves before approaching Jesus, earning forgiveness through sorrow, or performing enough good works to deserve salvation—no one is saved that way.

But if by repentance we mean the Gospel’s call to turn toward God, away from rebellion, and entrust ourselves to Jesus Christ—then Scripture does not present an intentionally unrepentant life as an alternative route to salvation.
Jesus said:
“except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.” — Luke 13:3, KJV
Those words are severe.
But listen carefully.
A warning from Jesus is itself an act of mercy.
If a building were burning and someone screamed, “GET OUT,” you would not accuse them of hatred because they raised their voice.
The urgency exists because the danger is real.
Jesus warns because eternity matters.
And Jesus invites because mercy is available.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Perhaps beneath all the theology, something much more personal has been happening.
You thought you were reading an article about whether someone can be saved without repentance.
Then, somewhere along the way, “someone” became...
you.
Your secret.
Your heart.
Your compromise.
Your exhaustion.
Your fear.
Your need for Christ.
So do not turn this moment into another piece of Christian content you consume, agree with, and forget.
Talk to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Tell Him the truth.
No polished Christian language.
No performance.
No pretending.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
“Jesus, I believe You died and rose again.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
“Jesus, change me.”
“Jesus, I surrender.”
And when shame says, “You are too dirty,” look toward the cross.
When pride says, “You do not need forgiveness,” look toward the cross.
When despair says, “You have gone too far,” look toward the cross.
When self-righteousness says, “At least you are better than them,” look toward the cross.
Calvary destroys both despair and boasting.
At the cross, your sin is shown to be worse than you wanted to admit...
and the love of God is shown to be greater than you dared to hope.
That is scandal becoming grace.
That is condemnation meeting substitution.
That is rebellion meeting mercy.
That is a ruined story meeting the Author who can write another ending.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, do not give us a polished religious answer. Be honest.
Somebody reading quietly at two in the morning may need evidence that chains really can break.
Do not let shame keep believers isolated.
We were never meant to fight alone.
And think of one person who needs this message.
Not twenty random people.
One.
The friend who still talks about God but has slowly wandered away.
The son who stopped going to church.
The daughter carrying shame.
The husband living two lives.
The wife quietly losing hope.
The believer who thinks repeated failure has disqualified them forever.
The person who does not believe in Jesus at all but has begun asking questions they cannot silence.
Send this privately if that would be wiser.
Save it too.
Because there may come a night when accusation gets loud, temptation returns, or somebody you love asks you the same question:
“Can someone really belong to Jesus and never repent?”
You may want these Scriptures again.
There is also a deeper way to help this work continue.

Gospel ministry should never manipulate people into giving, and money cannot purchase salvation, forgiveness, blessing, repentance, or God’s favor. Scripture teaches willing generosity rather than coerced giving.
It does not.
We will tell you something simpler.

Think of it as a voluntary offering of support—not a payment for grace, not a replacement for faithful giving according to your biblical convictions, and certainly not the price of belonging to Christ.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, creating, reaching, and putting Gospel-centered material in front of people who may desperately need it.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Grace is not behind a paywall.
The Gospel is not a product.
Forgiveness cannot be bought.
Only Jesus can save.
Pray.
Send it to somebody who needs Christ.
Sometimes the offering in your hand is money.
Sometimes it is reach.
Sometimes it is prayer.
Sometimes it is simply refusing to keep life-changing truth to yourself.
But above all...
respond to Jesus.
Because someday the number of likes beneath this article will mean nothing.
The shares will mean nothing.
The comments will mean nothing.
The merchandise will mean nothing.
The platform will mean nothing.
What will matter is Christ.
Do you know Him?
Have you stopped defending the darkness He died to rescue you from?
Are you trusting His finished work rather than your religious performance?
Have you come home?
The Father is not asking the prodigal to repair the far country before returning.
Come home filthy.
Come home crying.
Come home trembling.
Come home ashamed.
Come home with consequences you cannot reverse.
Come home with scars.
Come home with nothing impressive to offer.
But come home.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be that your story became scandalous.
The greatest tragedy would be standing within reach of grace...
and choosing the far country anyway.

Repentance is not the price you pay to make Jesus receive you; it is what happens when grace opens your eyes, you stop running from the Savior, and finally turn toward the One who has been calling you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BE INTOXICATED ALWAYS IN HER LOVE”: BIBLICAL MARRIAGE WAS NEVER SUPPOSED TO MEAN SEXUAL INDIFFERENCE
paragraphs: “BE INTOXICATED ALWAYS IN HER LOVE”: BIBLICAL MARRIAGE WAS NEVER SUPPOSED TO MEAN SEXUAL INDIFFERENCE
Proverbs 5:19 contains a sentence so passionate that if many Christians encountered it without knowing where it came from, they might hesitate to believe it came from the Bible.
“Be intoxicated always in her love.”
Not tolerate her.
Not merely provide for her.
Not simply remain legally married to her.
Not live beside her for thirty years while your hearts slowly become strangers.
Be intoxicated with her love.
The Hebrew text is even harder to domesticate:
אַיֶּלֶת אֲהָבִים וְיַעֲלַת־חֵן דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
A fairly direct sense is:
“A loving doe, a graceful deer—let her breasts satisfy you at all times; in her love be captivated continually.”
The final words are especially striking:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Be’ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
“In her love… be captivated, exhilarated, even intoxicated… continually.”

The Hebrew verb שָׁגָה, shagah, is unusually vivid. Depending upon context, it can describe wandering, reeling, going astray, or being carried away. Here, within the poetry of marital delight, translations understandably reach for language such as “captivated,” “ravished,” or “intoxicated.” The Masoretic Hebrew actually places this language directly beside the physical delight of the wife’s breasts. This is not a later attempt to make Scripture sensual. The sensuality is already there.
And that should make us confront something.
Somewhere along the way, many Christians became more comfortable talking about adultery than talking about marital desire.
We learned how to say, “Do not commit adultery.”
We did not always learn how to say, “Delight in your wife.”
We warned people against pornography, lust, affairs, fornication, temptation, and sexual immorality—and rightly so.
But sometimes we forgot that God's answer to distorted sexuality is not the destruction of sexuality.
It is its redemption.
Proverbs 5 is not embarrassed by married desire.
It protects it.
The entire chapter warns a young man against the seductive path of adultery. Then, remarkably, wisdom does not merely tell him what he must run FROM.
It reminds him what he should run TOWARD.
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
Then comes the imagery of verse 19.
And immediately afterward comes the contrast:
Why, my son, should you become intoxicated with another woman?
That contrast matters enormously.

The same verbal idea appears on both sides of the moral boundary. There is a kind of desire that destroys covenant, and there is desire that flourishes within covenant. Proverbs is not teaching the young man to become desireless.
It is teaching him where his desire belongs.
That changes the conversation.
Biblical holiness is not sexual numbness.
Faithfulness does not mean becoming indifferent toward the body of the person you married.
Purity is not pretending attraction stopped mattering after the wedding photographs were taken.
The biblical vision is much richer.
Desire is called home.
And maybe somebody reading this desperately needs to hear that because you are married, faithful on paper, sleeping under the same roof…
and starving for tenderness.
Nobody cheated.
Nobody filed for divorce.
Nobody packed a suitcase.
But something has been disappearing quietly.
The kisses became shorter.
The conversations became logistical.
“Did you pay the bill?”
“Who is picking up the kids?”
“What time are you coming home?”
“Did you lock the door?”

Then two exhausted people turn away from each other in the darkness, illuminated by separate phones, carrying separate disappointments, wondering when the person who once made their heart race became someone they barely touch.
There may have been no scandal.
But there is distance.
And distance can become its own kind of grief.
This is where Proverbs 5:19 refuses to let us reduce marriage to mere endurance.
God does not merely say, in effect, “Don't sleep with somebody else.”
Wisdom calls a husband to delight in the woman who is already his wife.
Look at her again.
Treasure her again.
Pursue her again.
Let covenant love become something warmer than shared paperwork.
But we must be equally careful here, because Scripture must never be weaponized.
Proverbs 5:19 is not permission for a husband to demand sexual access regardless of his wife's physical condition, emotional state, wounds, exhaustion, fear, illness, or dignity.
And 1 Corinthians 7 cannot honestly be used to establish one-sided male entitlement either.
Paul's language is radically reciprocal.

He says the husband should give his wife what is due to her and the wife likewise to her husband. He then makes the astonishingly symmetrical statement that the wife does not exercise authority over her body independently of her husband—and immediately says the same thing about the husband's body in relation to his wife.
Then comes:
Μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους…
“Do not deprive one another…”
And when Paul discusses temporary abstinence, he describes it as occurring ἐκ συμφώνου—by agreement, by mutual consent.
Notice the repeated idea:
One another.
Mutual.
Reciprocal.
Biblical intimacy is therefore not a license for coercion.
It is covenantal self-giving.
A husband cannot quote Scripture about his wife's body while ignoring Scripture's commands concerning his own sacrificial love.
Christ is the pattern.
Ephesians 5 does not tell a husband, “Make sure your needs are met.”
It points him toward Jesus Christ—the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His bride.
That changes everything.
Christian marriage is not two consumers asking, “What am I getting?”
It is two covenant partners increasingly learning to ask, “How can I love you faithfully, tenderly, truthfully, sacrificially?”
And yes…
that includes the bedroom.
Because God created bodies too.
Christianity does not teach that the soul is holy while the body is dirty. The scandal at the center of Christianity is that the eternal Son of God took on flesh.
Jesus touched lepers.
Jesus ate food.
Jesus wept.
Jesus grew tired.
Jesus physically rose from the grave.
Christian hope is ultimately resurrection—not escape from embodiment.
So why have some believers acted as though acknowledging physical desire between husband and wife somehow lowers marriage?
Scripture doesn't.
Song of Songs certainly doesn't.
Proverbs doesn't.
Paul doesn't.
What Scripture does is place sexuality inside a moral architecture sturdy enough to carry its tremendous power.
Covenant.
Faithfulness.
Mutuality.
Self-control.
Tenderness.
Honor.
Exclusive devotion.
Sacrificial love.
And that means this article is not telling a hurting spouse, “Just have more sex.”
Some marriages carry wounds that cannot be healed with a date night and a Bible verse.
Maybe betrayal happened.
Maybe pornography invaded the marriage.
Maybe childbirth changed her body and she no longer feels desirable.
Maybe age changed his body and he carries embarrassment he has never admitted.
Maybe one spouse repeatedly experienced rejection until asking began to feel humiliating.
Maybe intimacy became mechanical.
Maybe unresolved resentment followed both of you into the bedroom.
Maybe trauma is involved.
Maybe illness, medication, disability, hormonal changes, chronic pain, grief, depression, exhaustion, or years of unresolved conflict have affected sexual desire.
Those realities should not be mocked, minimized, or spiritually bullied.
Sometimes love looks like passion.
Sometimes love looks like patience.
Sometimes love looks like repentance.
Sometimes love looks like rebuilding trust one painfully honest conversation at a time.
Sometimes love looks like getting appropriate medical or professional help rather than accusing your spouse of spiritual failure.
And sometimes the holiest sentence spoken in a marriage is simply:
“I miss us.”
Not merely sex.
Us.
I miss laughing with you.
I miss reaching for your hand.
I miss feeling wanted.
I miss feeling safe with you.
I miss talking without defending myself.
I miss praying together.
I miss the person I married.
I miss who we were before disappointment taught us to protect ourselves from each other.
And perhaps underneath all those sentences is another confession:
“I don't know how to find our way back.”
That is where the Gospel enters.
Not as a trick for improving your sex life.
Not as religious decoration around marriage advice.
The Gospel enters because marriage involves sinners.
Two of them.
Every marriage eventually discovers this.
You married someone capable of hurting you.
And they married someone capable of hurting them.
Sin does not remain outside the wedding ceremony simply because the vows mentioned God.
Pride comes home.
Selfishness comes home.
Lust comes home.
Insecurity comes home.
Bitterness comes home.
Unforgiveness comes home.
Secret habits come home.
Old wounds come home.
And sometimes the person lying beside you becomes the person who sees most clearly what everyone else never sees.
That can feel scandalous.
But scandal does not have to be the final chapter.
Because Jesus Christ specializes in rewriting stories sin seemed determined to finish.
The cross tells the truth about us without abandoning us.
We were not rescued because we were innocent.
Christ died for sinners.
He does not heal us by pretending our sin wasn't serious. He carries its judgment, offers forgiveness to the repentant, and begins making people new.
That means a husband can repent.
A wife can repent.
The unfaithful can confess.
The addicted can seek freedom.
The cold heart can soften.
The wounded can establish wise boundaries while healing.
The ashamed can discover that their worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
And forgiveness does not mean pretending consequences do not exist.
Reconciliation after serious betrayal may require confession, accountability, transparency, patience, changed behavior, wise pastoral care, and sometimes qualified professional counseling.
Grace is not denial.
Grace tells the truth and then refuses to believe sin is more powerful than Christ.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your marriage does not need another performance.
Maybe it needs truth.
Maybe tonight, instead of silently scrolling beside each other, somebody needs to put the phone down.
Turn toward your spouse.
And speak.
“I love you, but we're drifting.”
“I have been selfish.”
“I have rejected you in ways I didn't realize were hurting you.”
“I stopped pursuing you.”
“I have been carrying resentment.”
“I have compared you to people on a screen.”
“I haven't guarded my eyes.”
“I made intimacy about myself.”
“I haven't listened to what you need.”
“I am sorry.”
“Can we begin again?”
Those sentences are terrifying because intimacy is not merely naked bodies.
Real intimacy is naked honesty.
It is being known without the costume.
It is allowing another human being to see the insecurity beneath the anger, the loneliness beneath the silence, the fear beneath the rejection.
And perhaps that is why so many people settle for counterfeit intimacy.
Pornography requires no vulnerability.
Fantasy requires no sacrifice.
An affair initially seems to offer excitement without the accumulated weight of ordinary covenant life.
But counterfeit intimacy eventually collects its price.
Proverbs 5 understands that.
That is why the chapter does not merely shout, “NO.”
It offers a better YES.
Drink from your own well.
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
Be captivated by her love.
Stay.
Pursue.
Delight.
Protect what God entrusted to you.
And hear this carefully: “always” does not mean every marriage will permanently feel like the honeymoon.
Biblical love is deeper than emotional adrenaline.

There will be pregnancies, sleepless nights, financial pressure, screaming toddlers, demanding jobs, illness, aging parents, grief, body changes, misunderstandings, seasons of low desire, and days when romance requires deliberate cultivation.
“Always” does not mean “always effortless.”
It means covenant love refuses to surrender the marriage to indifference.
You keep learning each other.
You keep speaking.
You keep touching tenderly.
You keep forgiving.
You keep repenting.
You keep protecting exclusivity.
You keep making room for delight.
You keep remembering that your spouse is not furniture in the house you built together.
They are a person.
A soul.
A body.
An image-bearer.
Someone who still needs to be seen.
And if you are unmarried, Proverbs 5 still has something urgent to say to you.
Do not train your desires on what cannot belong to you faithfully and then expect marriage magically to retrain them.
What you repeatedly feed becomes easier to hunger for.
Guard your eyes.
Guard your imagination.
Do not romanticize adultery.
Do not normalize pornography.
Do not treat another person's body as content.
Do not confuse lust with love.
Bring your sexuality beneath the lordship of Jesus before marriage, not merely after it.
And if you have already failed…
listen closely.
The Gospel is not only for people who kept themselves spotless.
The Gospel is for sinners.
Sexual sin is serious.
But sexual sin is not stronger than the blood of Jesus Christ.
Repentance is real.
Forgiveness is real.
Transformation is real.
You may carry consequences.
You may have trust to rebuild.
You may need accountability.
You may have difficult confessions ahead.
But if you come to Christ, you are not coming to a Savior surprised by what you have done.
He already knows.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
No more pretending.
No more secret browser.
No more secret conversation.
No more second life.
No more blaming your spouse for choices you made.
No more using “everybody struggles” as camouflage for refusing to repent.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could become comfortable prisoners.
He came to save.
And maybe this is where you need to stop reading for several seconds.
Because you know exactly what the Holy Spirit has been pressing on.
Maybe it is not adultery.
Maybe it is indifference.
Maybe you haven't betrayed your spouse with another body.
You betrayed your covenant with neglect.
You stopped noticing.
Stopped listening.
Stopped pursuing.
Stopped praying.
Stopped saying thank you.
Stopped saying “you're beautiful.”
Stopped reaching across the bed.
Stopped fighting for the tenderness you once promised to protect.
And now Proverbs reaches across thousands of years and whispers into a bedroom illuminated by two lonely screens:
Be captivated again.
Not by somebody new.
By the covenant you already made.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't turn conviction into shame and then run from God.
Run toward Christ.
You don't have to publish private details. You don't owe strangers your wounds.
But sometimes one honest sentence is the first crack through which light enters.
And if you know a husband or wife quietly drifting from the person they once could not wait to marry, share this with them—not as an accusation, but as an invitation home.
But hear this clearly because biblical integrity matters more than conversion numbers:
It does not purchase blessing.
It does not purchase salvation.
And we will not tell you that you cannot glorify God unless you give money to us.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
Grace is a gift.
Paul's instruction concerning Christian generosity is explicit:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ … μὴ … ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Each should give as he has determined in his heart—not from compulsion.
Then Scripture says:
ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ Θεός
“God loves a cheerful giver.”
That principle matters. Christian generosity is meant to arise from willing hearts, not spiritual pressure.
Your local-church commitments, your convictions concerning tithes and offerings, and voluntary support for a digital ministry should therefore not be deceptively collapsed into one category.
Pray.
Invite someone.
Encourage a wounded marriage.
Send Scripture to somebody fighting temptation.
Tell someone what Jesus has done for you.
There are many ways to participate in spreading truth.
Because in the end, Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Jesus can.
A book cannot resurrect your heart.
Jesus can.
A marriage article cannot manufacture reconciliation.
But Jesus can take two surrendered hearts, teach them repentance, truth, forgiveness, wisdom, patience, and sacrificial love, and begin rebuilding what sin tried to destroy.
So tonight…
before searching for somebody new…
look again at the person you promised not to abandon.
Before fantasizing about another life…
ask whether God is calling you to become different in this one.
Before saying, “The passion disappeared”…
ask whether tenderness stopped being cultivated.
Before demanding to be desired…
ask whether you have become a safe, attentive, sacrificial lover.
Before using Scripture against your spouse…
stand beneath Scripture yourself.
And before believing your marriage is too damaged for grace…
look again at the cross.
Christianity began proclaiming hope from an occupied tomb.
Never underestimate what Jesus can resurrect.
Maybe your marriage needs counseling.
Get help.
Maybe confession needs to happen.
Tell the truth.
Maybe repentance is overdue.
Repent.
Maybe forgiveness will take time.
Walk patiently.
Maybe trust has to be rebuilt brick by brick.
Start laying bricks.
Maybe the first step tonight is not sex at all.
Maybe it is sitting beside each other without phones and finally saying:
“Where did we lose each other?”
Then listen.
Really listen.

And somewhere beyond the resentment, beyond the exhaustion, beyond the years that changed both your bodies, beyond the disappointments neither of you expected on your wedding day, perhaps you will begin to see again the person God once taught your heart to recognize.
Not an object.
Not an obligation.
Not a roommate.
Your husband.
Your wife.
Your covenant companion.
And perhaps Proverbs 5:19 will no longer sound like an embarrassingly passionate ancient sentence.
Perhaps it will sound like an invitation.
Come home.
Come back to faithfulness.
Come back to tenderness.
Come back to truth.
Come back to delight without exploitation, desire without betrayal, intimacy without coercion, passion protected by covenant.
And above everything else…
come back to Jesus.
Because the deepest miracle is not that two imperfect people can remain attracted to one another forever.

The deepest miracle is that sinners can be forgiven, hardened hearts can become tender, hidden things can be brought into light, broken people can learn to love differently, and stories that appeared finished can be placed into the scarred hands of a resurrected Savior.
Your scandal may explain a chapter.
It does not have to write your ending.
Jesus still does some of His most beautiful rewriting in places everyone else thought were beyond repair.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE HAD MANY WIVES—BUT NEVER CALLED IT THE DREAM
paragraphs: THE BIBLE HAD MANY WIVES—BUT NEVER CALLED IT THE DREAM

Polygamy appears in Scripture again and again. But perhaps we have been asking the wrong question. Instead of asking, “Why did God allow it?” we should ask, “What happened every time human beings wandered from the pattern God established in the beginning?”
There is a dangerous way to read the Bible.
You can open its pages, find something a biblical character did, and quietly assume that because Scripture recorded it, Scripture approved it.
Abraham had more than one woman.
Jacob had Leah and Rachel, along with Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon had hundreds.
So the argument sounds simple:
“If these men belonged to God, and some of them practiced polygamy, how can Christians say polygamy is not God’s design?”
It sounds convincing.
Until you stop reading the Bible like a collection of isolated verses and start reading it like one unfolding story.
Because the Bible is painfully honest about its heroes.
It does not airbrush Abraham.
It does not sanitize Jacob.
It does not protect David’s reputation.
It does not hide Solomon’s collapse.
Scripture sometimes places the sins, compromises, foolish decisions, cultural accommodations, and catastrophic consequences of its greatest human characters directly in front of us.
Not so we can imitate everything they did.
Sometimes so we will never do it ourselves.
And nowhere is that distinction more important than here.
The Bible contains polygamy.
That is undeniable.
But description is not automatically prescription.
And when we follow the biblical storyline from Eden, through Israel, through Israel’s kings, into the teaching of Jesus and the apostolic church, something remarkable emerges:
Polygamy keeps appearing in the story…
but it never replaces the pattern established at creation.
Before Abraham.
Before Moses.
Before Israel.
Before kings.
Before human culture had centuries to normalize broken things…
there was a garden.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was God.
Genesis 2:24 gives us the foundational language of marriage:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew ends with two unforgettable words:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Not merely shared property.
Not merely sexual access.
Not merely a contract.
Not a man collecting women as symbols of wealth, dynasty, fertility, or power.
One flesh.
Two lives joined in covenantal union.
And centuries later, when Jesus was questioned about marriage, He did something enormously significant.
He went backward.
Past the kings.
Past David.
Past Jacob.
Past Abraham.
Past Moses.
All the way back to creation.
Jesus quoted Genesis and said:
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
kai esontai hoi duo eis sarka mian.
“And the two shall become one flesh.”
Notice the word Jesus preserved:
οἱ δύο.
hoi duo.
“The two.”
Then He continued: “So they are no longer two, but one flesh.”
Jesus did not establish His theology of marriage by pointing to Solomon’s palace.
He pointed to Eden.
That matters.
A lot.
Because sometimes people ask, “What did fallen humanity manage to practice?”
Jesus directs us toward a deeper question:
“What did the Creator establish from the beginning?”
And suddenly the biblical story begins to look different.
The first explicit polygamist named in Scripture is not Abraham.
It is Lamech.
Genesis 4:19 tells us that Lamech “took two wives.”
Read the surrounding story.
Lamech appears in Cain’s line, and shortly afterward Scripture records his violent boast about killing a man.
That does not by itself prove that his marriages caused his violence, nor does Genesis explicitly stop to pronounce, “Lamech’s polygamy was the specific sin in this paragraph.”
We should not force Scripture to say more than it says.
But neither should we miss the literary atmosphere.
The first departure from the one-man, one-woman pattern of Genesis 2 appears not in Eden’s innocence but in humanity’s increasingly fractured world.
Then comes Abraham.
God promises him descendants.
Years pass.
Sarah remains barren.
Pain begins whispering.
Waiting becomes unbearable.
And human beings do what human beings still do when God seems slow:
they try to manufacture with their own hands what God promised to provide in His time.
Sarah gives Hagar to Abraham.
A child is conceived.
And almost immediately the house fills with pain.
Genesis 16 tells us that after Hagar conceived, tension erupted between her and Sarah. Sarah dealt harshly with Hagar, and Hagar fled.
Look carefully.
A man.
Two women.
One household.
Jealousy.
Humiliation.
Bitterness.
Flight.
A child caught inside adult decisions.
Does that sound like Scripture advertising an alternative marital paradise?
Or does it sound like Scripture letting us hear the cracking of something?
Then Jacob enters the story.
He loves Rachel.
He is deceived into marrying Leah.
Eventually Rachel becomes his wife too, and Bilhah and Zilpah are drawn into the family structure.
What follows?
Competition.
Jealousy.
Women measuring their worth through children.
A husband pulled through rival affections.
Leah aching because she knows she is less loved.
Rachel envying her sister.
Servants becoming instruments in a fertility struggle.
Children eventually inheriting the fractures of the household.
Joseph becomes Jacob’s favored son.
His brothers hate him.
Eventually they sell him.
Again, we should be careful.
Scripture does not reduce every tragedy in Jacob’s household to one single cause.
Human sin is more complicated than that.
But neither can we pretend the household is presented as some peaceful advertisement for plural marriage.
It is heartbreaking.
And then we arrive at the man people most often bring into this conversation.
David.
A man after God’s own heart.
A worshiper.
A warrior.
A king.
And yes…
a man with multiple wives.
This is where shallow answers become dangerous, because 2 Samuel 12:8 must not be ignored.
Through Nathan, God reminds David that He had given David his master’s house and his master’s wives “into” his care or bosom, depending on the translation, together with the kingdom.
Someone reading that verse can reasonably ask:
“Doesn’t that mean God approved of David having multiple wives?”
That question deserves more than a slogan.
The verse exists.
We do not need to hide from it.

In its immediate context, Nathan is confronting David over Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah. The language emphasizes everything David had already received in contrast with his wicked seizure of another man’s wife. English translations themselves reflect some nuance in how the phrase concerning Saul’s wives is rendered—some use language such as “into your arms,” while others render the relationship in terms of David’s keeping or care.
But even granting the strongest reading of the verse, one historical statement cannot simply erase the broader canonical trajectory.
Because Israel’s kings had already received this warning in Deuteronomy 17:17:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
velo yarbeh-lo nashim, velo yasur levavo.
“He shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.”
Read that again.
Not because the Hebrew is magical.
But because sometimes seeing the words slows us down enough to hear them.
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים
“He shall not multiply wives for himself.”
And then comes the warning:
וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
“lest his heart turn away.”
The warning is almost prophetic.
Because eventually Solomon arrives.
The richest.
The wisest.
The king whose reputation reaches nations.
And Solomon multiplies wives on a staggering scale.
First Kings 11 records seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines.
And then Scripture tells us what happened.
His wives turned away his heart.
The warning of Deuteronomy becomes the tragedy of Kings.
The man famous for wisdom becomes evidence that knowing truth does not make someone immune to ignoring it.
Think about that.
Solomon could understand mysteries…
write proverbs…
govern a kingdom…
possess extraordinary wealth…
and still allow desire to pull his heart somewhere wisdom had warned him not to go.
Maybe that is why this subject reaches much deeper than polygamy.
Because this is really a story about all of us.
We are remarkably skilled at finding biblical characters who did what we already want permission to do.
We say:
“David did it.”
“Abraham did it.”
“Jacob did it.”
But imagine applying that method consistently.
Noah became drunk.
Should we imitate his drunkenness?
Abraham lied about Sarah.
Should deception become a Christian marriage principle?
Jacob deceived his father.
Should we teach deception because a patriarch practiced it?
David committed adultery and arranged Uriah’s death.
Should we imitate David there?
Peter denied Jesus.
Should denial become discipleship?
Of course not.
Because the Bible is not saying, “Everything these people did is holy.”
It is saying something infinitely more hopeful:
“Look what God can do with deeply flawed human beings.”
That changes everything.
The heroes of Scripture do not save Scripture.
God saves sinners.
And this is where the subject becomes uncomfortable.
Because maybe your issue is not polygamy.
Maybe you have never considered having multiple spouses.
But maybe you have done something remarkably similar with another desire.
Maybe you found one verse to defend what twenty others were confronting.
Maybe you called compromise “freedom.”
Maybe you renamed lust “love.”
Maybe you renamed greed “blessing.”
Maybe you renamed bitterness “discernment.”
Maybe you renamed vengeance “justice.”
Maybe you kept asking, “Can I technically get away with this?” when the Holy Spirit was pressing a much more frightening question into your heart:
“Does this look like Jesus?”
That question changes the room.
Because Christianity was never supposed to be a competition to discover the maximum amount of brokenness we can biblically justify.
We are being conformed to Christ.
And when Jesus discusses marriage, He returns us to the Creator’s intention:
the two becoming one flesh.
Paul later develops Christian marriage through an even more breathtaking image.
In Ephesians 5, marriage becomes a living picture of Christ and His church.
Christ loves His bride.
Christ gives Himself for His bride.
Christ sanctifies His bride.
Christ does not treat covenant love as an exercise in accumulating people for personal gratification.
He gives Himself.
That is the shape of Christian love.
Self-giving rather than self-collecting.
Covenant rather than consumption.
Faithfulness rather than appetite.
Sacrifice rather than entitlement.
Then the pastoral epistles contain another striking expression.
First Timothy 3:2 describes an overseer with the Greek phrase:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
mias gynaikos andra.

Literally, the words carry the sense of “a man/husband of one woman/wife.” The precise pastoral implications of the expression have been debated—particularly questions involving remarriage, marital faithfulness, and qualification for leadership—so we should not pretend every interpretive question disappears with a Greek phrase.
But the language certainly does not celebrate the accumulation of wives.
The New Testament movement is not toward expanding plural marriage.
It is toward covenant faithfulness, sexual holiness, sacrificial love, and a marriage shaped by Christ’s relationship with His church.
And perhaps now we can finally understand why God could work through Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon without every marital decision they made becoming an instruction for us.
Grace is not endorsement.
Please remember that sentence.
Grace is not endorsement.
God using a person does not mean God approves of everything that person does.
And thank God for that.
Because if God could only use people whose lives had never contradicted His design…
He could use none of us.
Not me.
Not you.
Not Abraham.
Not David.
Not Peter.
Nobody.
That is where this story stops being an argument about ancient marriage and becomes a mirror.
You may have scars from choices God never instructed you to make.
You may have a family history so tangled that reading stories like Jacob’s feels less like ancient history and more like reading your childhood diary.
Maybe your father divided his affection.
Maybe someone betrayed your mother.
Maybe adultery shattered your home.
Maybe you were the child wondering why you were apparently not enough to make somebody stay.
Maybe you have been the betrayer.
Maybe you crossed a line.
Maybe you broke a promise.
Maybe you have carried secret sexual sin while smiling in church.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been watching.
Nobody knows who you have been messaging.
Nobody knows what happened when the door closed.
Nobody knows the compromises hidden behind your worship songs.
But Jesus knows.
And somehow…
He has not stopped calling sinners home.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin does not matter.
Grace would be meaningless if sin did not matter.
The scandal is that Christ knew exactly what our rebellion would cost Him…
and He went to the cross anyway.
He was pierced.
He bled.
He bore shame.
He died.
And He rose.
Not so we could become better lawyers for our compromises.
So we could become new.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the burning house.
Jesus does not expose darkness because He enjoys watching sinners collapse.
He exposes darkness because He intends to bring people into light.
So if this article uncovered something deeper than a theological debate, do not run.
Come to Christ.
If there is adultery, confess it and turn from it.
If there is pornography, bring it into the light and seek serious accountability.
If there is emotional infidelity, stop feeding it.
If there is manipulation, repent.
If there is sexual sin, stop negotiating with it.
If you have wounded your spouse, do not use grace as an excuse to avoid responsibility.
And if you have been wounded by someone else’s sin, hear this carefully:
their betrayal does not determine your worth.
Christ does.
Some consequences cannot be erased overnight.
Some families are complicated.

Some people come to Christ already carrying marriages, divorces, children, betrayals, legal responsibilities, and painful histories that cannot be reduced to a social-media slogan. Difficult real-life situations deserve careful pastoral counsel, biblical wisdom, truth, compassion, and responsibility toward every person affected.
But nobody is beyond the reach of Christ.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people pretending they never fell.
To keep pointing fallen people toward the One who raises the dead.
You do not have to tell strangers every private detail of your life, but you can simply write, “Jesus, lead me back to Your design.”
If you are fighting for purity, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If your marriage needs prayer, comment, “pray for us.”
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed tonight.
Save it too.
Because sooner or later someone will say, “But David had many wives,” and you may need to return to the larger story rather than fight with isolated verses.
The goal is not to create spectators.
It is to keep bringing people close enough to the Word to encounter Jesus.
And for those asking how they can help this ministry continue and expand, there is a practical way.
It does not.
It does not.
Absolutely not.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace has no premium membership.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
Giving should never be manipulated out of fear or guilt. Scripture says God loves a cheerful giver.
So pray first.
Take care of the responsibilities God has entrusted to you.
Support your local church and faithful Gospel work according to biblical conviction.
Free resources matter because someone searching for Christ should never be treated merely as a customer.
A share costs nothing.
But somewhere beyond your screen could be a husband quietly justifying compromise.
A wife wondering whether covenant faithfulness still matters.
A young believer confused by difficult Old Testament stories.
A skeptic convinced that Christians simply ignore uncomfortable Bible passages.
A wounded child who grew up inside somebody else’s unfaithfulness.
A person one decision away from destroying something precious.
Because the final message of Scripture is not that Abraham was flawless.
He was not.
Jacob was not.
David was not.
Solomon certainly was not.
Neither are we.
The message is that human beings keep taking beautiful things and breaking them…
and God keeps pursuing broken human beings.
The Bible does not need us to sanitize its heroes.
Their failures are part of the point.
Abraham needed grace.
Jacob needed grace.
David needed grace.
Solomon needed mercy.
Peter needed restoration.
And you and I need Jesus.
So no—the existence of polygamy in Scripture is not, by itself, an instruction for Christians to reproduce it.

When the whole biblical storyline is heard, its presence often belongs to the painful world Scripture refuses to romanticize, while Jesus points His hearers back toward the Creator’s beginning: the two becoming one flesh.
Deuteronomy had already warned Israel’s king not to “multiply wives,” connecting that multiplication with the danger of the heart turning away.

And when the New Testament describes exemplary Christian leadership, it uses the striking expression μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα—language centered on singular marital faithfulness, even while interpreters debate some of its precise applications.
Scripture is not embarrassed by humanity's mess.
It tells the truth about it.
Because the Gospel only becomes breathtaking when we finally admit how desperately we need it.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this needs to hear most.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your family history does not have to become your destiny.
Your father's failure does not have to become your pattern.
Your mother's wounds do not have to become your identity.
Your own sin does not have to become the name you die carrying.
There is repentance.
There is forgiveness.
There is restoration.
There is a cross.
There is an empty tomb.
There is Jesus.
And sometimes the very chapter you wish could be ripped out of your story becomes the place where Christ begins writing something you never believed could exist.
The Bible never needed flawless heroes—because from the beginning, it was leading broken people toward a flawless Savior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD TOLD THEM TO LEAVE MONEY IN THE FIELD—AND THE REASON MAY EXPOSE WHAT WE HAVE FORGOTTEN ABOUT GRACE
paragraphs: GOD TOLD THEM TO LEAVE MONEY IN THE FIELD—AND THE REASON MAY EXPOSE WHAT WE HAVE FORGOTTEN ABOUT GRACE

Why were Israel’s farmers forbidden to harvest everything they owned—and what does an ancient command about leftover grain reveal about the heart of God, the dignity of the poor, the story of Ruth, and the grace that ultimately leads us to Jesus Christ?
Imagine spending months preparing a field.
You break the ground.
You plant the seed.
You watch the sky.
You pray for rain.
You fight insects, drought, disease, exhaustion.
Then finally...
Harvest.
Every stalk represents work.
Every bundle represents food.
Every basket represents security.
And just when you are ready to gather everything your labor produced, God says:
Stop.
Do not harvest all of it.
Leave some behind.
Not because the grain is defective.
Not because you forgot it.
Not because you are careless.
Leave it deliberately.
For somebody who has nothing.
That command appears in Leviticus, and hidden inside those few ancient sentences is something breathtaking about the character of God.
The Hebrew of Leviticus 19:9 says:
“וּבְקֻצְרְכֶם אֶת־קְצִיר אַרְצְכֶם לֹא תְכַלֶּה פְּאַת שָׂדְךָ לִקְצֹר וְלֶקֶט קְצִירְךָ לֹא תְלַקֵּט”
Transliterated:
“Uvequtzrekhem et-qetzir artzekhem, lo tekhalleh pe’at sadekha liqtzor; veleqet qetzirkha lo telaqqet.”
In plain English, the command is essentially this:
When you reap the harvest of your land, you are not to reap your field completely to its edge, and you are not to gather up every gleaning of your harvest.
Then God explains who the remainder is for:
“לֶעָנִי וְלַגֵּר תַּעֲזֹב אֹתָם”
“Le‘ani velagger ta‘azov otam.”
“You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner.”
Then comes the sentence that changes the entire weight of the command:
“אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם”
“Ani YHWH Eloheikhem.”
“I am the LORD your God.”
Leviticus 19:9–10.
God attaches His own name to the command.
Think about that.
The edge of the field mattered to God.
The grain lying on the ground mattered to God.
The widow mattered.
The poor mattered.
The foreigner living among Israel mattered.
The person without land, inheritance, savings, influence, connections, or social power mattered.
And God designed Israel’s harvest so that prosperity would contain an intentional margin for mercy.
The Hebrew word פֵּאָה—pe’ah—means an edge, extremity, or corner.
God was effectively telling the landowner:
Do not turn every available inch into personal gain.
There must be an edge you refuse to consume.
There must be something your hands could legally gather...
but choose to leave.
And then there was לֶקֶט—leqet—the gleaning, what remained or fell behind during harvesting.
The farmer was not supposed to squeeze the field until absolutely nothing remained.
Why?
Because somewhere nearby was a person praying for what someone else might consider insignificant.
One stalk to the prosperous farmer could become bread to the hungry family.
What looked like “leftovers” from one perspective could look like answered prayer from another.
And perhaps that is where this ancient command begins reaching uncomfortably into our modern hearts.
We live in a world that teaches us to maximize everything.
Maximize profit.
Maximize productivity.
Maximize possessions.
Maximize influence.
Maximize return.
Take everything the field will give you.
But God built a holy interruption into Israel’s harvest.
Leave something.
Not because provision is evil.
Not because ownership is evil.
Not because successful farmers were condemned for succeeding.
But because God refused to let His people imagine that blessing should terminate upon themselves.
There was supposed to be room at the edge.
Room for mercy.
Room for the stranger.
Room for the forgotten.
Room for somebody whose name the landowner might never even know.
And then...
a woman named Ruth walked into one of those fields.
Suddenly Leviticus stopped being ink on a scroll.
It became survival.
Ruth was a widow.
A foreigner.
A Moabite.
She had returned with Naomi, another widow whose grief had become so severe that she said, in effect, “Do not call me Naomi... call me Mara,” because her life had become bitter.
Two women.
Loss behind them.
Uncertainty in front of them.
No husband coming home with wages.
No comfortable future waiting at the door.
No guarantee that tomorrow would be easier than today.
And Ruth said something heartbreakingly simple:
Let me go to the fields and glean.
She was going to live from what harvesters left behind.
Think about the humility of that walk.
She was not entering her own field.
She was following workers who possessed what she did not.
She would bend down for what others passed over.
Piece by piece.
Stalk by stalk.
Enough grain, hopefully, to keep two grieving women alive.
Have you ever lived through a season like that?
Maybe not literally gathering barley from somebody else’s field.
But emotionally?
Spiritually?
Financially?
You used to dream about abundance.
Now you are asking God for enough strength to make it through Tuesday.
You used to imagine changing the world.
Now getting out of bed feels like warfare.
You used to pray long prayers.
Now sometimes all you can whisper is...
“Jesus, help me.”
You are gleaning.
One promise.
One breath.
One prayer.
One more morning.
One more reason not to quit.
And maybe nobody around you understands how exhausted you really are.
But God sees people in the margins.
He always has.
Ruth “happened” to enter a field belonging to a man named Boaz.
And Boaz noticed her.
That matters.
Because people who are suffering often begin to believe they have become invisible.
Grief can make you feel invisible.
Poverty can make you feel invisible.
Rejection can make you feel invisible.
Being the outsider can make you feel invisible.
Secret battles can make you sit in a crowded room while feeling as though nobody could possibly see you.
But Boaz asks about Ruth.
Then he does something beautiful.
He does not merely tolerate the minimum requirement of the law.
He becomes generous.
He tells Ruth to remain in his field.
He gives instructions concerning her safety.
He allows her access to water.
He invites her to eat.
And then Boaz tells his workers to deliberately pull grain from the bundles and leave it where Ruth can gather it.
Do not humiliate her.
Let her glean.
Boaz understood something many people still miss:
Biblical generosity is not merely about transferring resources.
It also cares about human dignity.
The poor person was not treated merely as a statistic.
The foreigner was not erased.
The vulnerable person was allowed to gather, work, participate, and eat.
And notice something else.
God’s command concerning gleaning was not an excuse for laziness.
Ruth worked.
Hard.
The narrative describes her labor from morning onward.
Grace gave her access to the field.
She still bent down and gathered.
That balance matters.
Compassion without dignity can become condescension.
Responsibility without compassion can become cruelty.
Biblical mercy refuses both extremes.
And there is another detail we should not rush past.
Ruth was precisely the kind of person Leviticus had named.
Poor.
Foreign.
Vulnerable.
God wrote provision for someone like Ruth into Israel’s law before Ruth ever entered Boaz’s field.
Before she knew where tomorrow’s food would come from...
God had already spoken about the edge.
Before she arrived...
mercy had been commanded.
Before she knew Boaz...
God knew the vulnerable would need room in the harvest.
Maybe you need to hear that today.
God can prepare provision before you recognize your need for it.
He can already be working in places you have not reached yet.
That does not mean Christians are promised painless lives, automatic wealth, or instant deliverance from every hardship.
Ruth herself is proof that faithful people can walk through bereavement, poverty, uncertainty, exhausting labor, and seasons where providence is easier to see looking backward than looking forward.
But her story reminds us that suffering does not mean God has stopped seeing.
And then the story becomes even more astonishing.
The foreign widow gleaning behind the workers becomes the wife of Boaz.
Ruth and Boaz have a son named Obed.
Obed becomes the father of Jesse.
Jesse becomes the father of David.
And generations later, the Gospel of Matthew places Ruth inside the genealogy that leads to Jesus Christ.
Do not miss the beauty.
The woman gathering leftovers becomes part of the human family line of the Messiah.
The outsider is brought near.
The widow receives a future.
The woman who entered the field with emptiness becomes woven into the story of redemption.
That does not mean Leviticus 19 was secretly a direct prediction of Jesus. We do not need to force Scripture to make it beautiful.
The real connection is already powerful enough.

The same God who revealed His concern for the poor, the outsider, the widow, and the vulnerable in Israel’s law unfolds His redemptive purpose through Ruth’s story—and the biblical story ultimately brings us to Christ.
Jesus does something infinitely greater than leaving grain at the edge of a field.
He gives Himself.
We were not merely economically poor.
Our deepest problem was sin.
We could not purchase reconciliation with God.
We could not harvest enough righteousness.
We could not accumulate enough good deeds.
We could not erase our guilt by becoming more religious.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
That is the scandal.
We want to believe we can save ourselves.
We want to believe a few good deeds can outweigh rebellion against a holy God.
We want a Savior who improves us without confronting us.
A cross without repentance.
Grace without truth.
Forgiveness without surrender.
Resurrection without death.
But the Gospel destroys that illusion.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ bore sin.
Christ rose from the grave.
And salvation is received by grace through faith, not purchased by human merit.
Jesus does not merely give you the edge of the field.
He gives Himself.
The Bread of Life was broken for hungry sinners.
The One who had every right to condemn came offering mercy to everyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
This is why grace is so offensive to human pride.
Grace means you cannot boast that you rescued yourself.
You came empty-handed.
And Christ was enough.
Maybe that is why Ruth’s posture in the field feels strangely familiar.
Bending down.
Receiving what she did not produce.
Living because mercy made room for her.
That is not a complete theological definition of salvation, and Ruth’s gleaning should not be turned into an allegory at every point.
But it gives us a beautiful picture of something every Christian eventually discovers:
We live because God is gracious.
Every breath.
Every mercy.
Every forgiveness.
Every second chance.
Every answered prayer.
Every strength we did not know we had.
Every morning after the night we thought would destroy us.
Grace.
And perhaps the question is no longer merely:
“Why were farmers told not to harvest the edges of their fields?”
Perhaps the question has become:
What edges are we harvesting that God intended us to hold with open hands?
Maybe your field is money.
Maybe it is time.
Maybe it is food.
Maybe it is knowledge.
Maybe it is influence.
Maybe it is your home.
Maybe it is your business.
Maybe it is your platform.
Maybe it is simply the ability to notice somebody everybody else walks past.
We should be careful here.
Christians today are not ancient Israelite farmers living under Israel’s land laws, so we should not pretend Leviticus establishes a mandatory modern percentage called “the edge.”
It does, however, reveal something enduring about the heart of God that the rest of Scripture repeatedly confirms:
God cares about generosity.
God cares about justice.
God cares about the poor.
God cares about strangers.
God cares about how His people use what has been entrusted to them.
And the New Testament carries voluntary generosity forward with unmistakable clarity.
Paul writes that believers should give as they have purposed in their hearts, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Notice that carefully.
Not under compulsion.
Christian generosity must never be manipulated out of somebody through spiritual threats.
You do not purchase God’s love.
You cannot buy salvation.
Jesus Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But when grace changes a heart, generosity begins to change too.
A redeemed heart begins asking:
“What has God placed in my field that can become provision for somebody else?”
That question is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Every article shared...
every biblical resource created...
every person encouraged...
every wounded believer reminded that Jesus has not abandoned them...
every seeker confronted lovingly with the truth of the Gospel...
requires people willing to leave something at the edge of their own field.
We will not twist Scripture to say something it does not say.
Your church giving, Christian generosity, and support of Gospel ministry should be approached faithfully, prayerfully, and without compulsion.
But supporting Gospel work can genuinely be an offering of generosity to God when it is given freely, wisely, and for His glory.
Paul explicitly affirmed the legitimacy of materially supporting those who proclaim the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:13–14).
So if you have been asking how you can help Gospel Warrior continue creating, reaching, teaching, encouraging, and expanding...
this can be one edge of your field.
But the greater reason is not the discount.
It is the mission.
If you want to help keep that field open...
If you want to help put biblical truth in front of another exhausted believer...
If you want to help reach the person scrolling at 2:00 in the morning wondering whether God could possibly forgive what they have done...
If you want to help strengthen families, encourage struggling Christians, confront lukewarm faith, welcome seekers toward truth, and keep pointing people back to Jesus...
Give freely.
Give prayerfully.
Never from manipulation.
Never because you believe money earns favor with God.
Let your generosity come from gratitude for the One who first gave Himself for you.
And if financially supporting this work is not possible right now, do not underestimate what sharing can do.
That costs nothing.
But someone you know may desperately need what you just read.
The person who needs it may never search for a sermon.
They may never walk into a church this week.
They may never tell you they are struggling.
But they might stop when this article appears on their screen because you shared it.
Your share can become an edge of the field.
Send this to a family member.
Send it to the person who believes their past has disqualified them forever.
Even send it—with gentleness, never pressure—to someone who does not yet believe, if you think it could help them understand the heart of the Gospel.
There may come a day when you feel empty and need to remember Ruth bending down in a field she did not own...
and the God who had already commanded that there be something waiting for her.
And before you leave...
be honest.
Which side of this story are you living right now?
Are you Boaz—with something God is calling you to leave at the edge?
Or are you Ruth—exhausted, uncertain, quietly gathering enough grace to survive another day?
Maybe you are both.
Maybe you have something to give while simultaneously carrying a wound nobody knows about.
That is why I want you to comment.
Not for empty engagement.
For honesty.
Or simply tell your testimony.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only one fighting to keep believing.
Because the Gospel has never been the story of impressive people proving how much they deserve God.
It is the story of sinners discovering how astonishingly gracious God is.
Ruth entered the field as a poor foreign widow.
She could not see the generations ahead.
She could not see David.
She could not see Bethlehem centuries later.
She could not see shepherds staring into a night filled with angels.
She could not see a manger.
She could not see a cross outside Jerusalem.
She could not see an empty tomb.
She could not see nations hearing the name of Jesus.
She was simply bending down...
picking up grain.
One piece at a time.
Maybe that is where you are.
You cannot see what God will do with the chapter you are living.
You cannot understand why so much was taken.
You cannot see how redemption could possibly grow out of this field.
You are just trying to remain faithful today.
Then remain faithful today.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Give where God calls you to give.
Receive grace where pride has kept you hiding.
Come back to Jesus if you have wandered.
And if shame keeps whispering that your scandal is the final chapter, look again at the Gospel.
Peter failed.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Ruth entered Israel as a Moabite widow.
And every one of us comes to Christ carrying something we cannot erase by ourselves.
Yet Jesus still saves sinners.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still transforms.
Jesus still takes stories that look finished and writes grace into places where shame thought it had written the final sentence.
So leave room at the edge.
Someone may be praying for what God has placed in your hands.
And when you are the one standing empty at somebody else’s field, do not confuse your season of need with your identity.
Ruth was gleaning...
but Ruth was not forgotten.
Neither is the repentant sinner who comes to Christ.
Because sometimes what looks like grain abandoned at the edge of a field is actually mercy waiting for someone God already knew was coming.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DIDN’T JESUS WRITE HIS OWN GOSPEL?
paragraphs: WHY DIDN’T JESUS WRITE HIS OWN GOSPEL?
The Answer May Change the Way You Read Every Word He Ever Spoke
There is something strangely unsettling about it once you notice it.
Moses wrote.
David wrote.
The prophets wrote.
Paul wrote letters that crossed cities, survived empires, outlived kings, and are still being read thousands of years later.
But Jesus?
The One Christians confess as the Word made flesh...
left us no surviving Gospel written in His own hand.
No autobiography.
No signed manuscript.
No parchment beginning, “I, Jesus of Nazareth, write these things to you...”
Matthew tells us about Him.
Mark tells us about Him.
Luke carefully investigates and writes about Him.
John testifies about Him.
But where is the Gospel according to Jesus...written by Jesus?
If He knew that generations would live and die before His return, why didn't He simply sit down and write the definitive account Himself?
Why entrust His words to witnesses?
Why disciples?
Why testimony?
Why four Gospel accounts rather than one autobiography bearing His own signature?
And perhaps the most important question is the one hiding beneath all the others:
If Jesus did not come primarily to write a book...
what exactly did He come to do?
Stay with that question.
Because the answer leads directly to a hill outside Jerusalem, to blood on wood, to an empty tomb—and perhaps to the reason you are reading these words right now.
We need to begin with intellectual honesty.
The Bible never gives us a verse saying, “Jesus did not write a Gospel because...”
So Christians should be careful not to manufacture an explanation and then present speculation as revelation.
Scripture gives us evidence from which we can understand the shape of Christ's mission, but where Scripture remains silent about Jesus' private reasoning, humility requires us to remain silent too.
What we can say is extraordinary enough.
Jesus came into a world where writing certainly mattered.

The Hebrew Scriptures were central to His teaching. Jesus quoted Scripture, appealed to Scripture, interpreted Scripture, confronted distortions of Scripture, and repeatedly treated Scripture as authoritative.
Yet His earthly ministry was overwhelmingly embodied.
He walked.
He spoke.
He touched.
He ate.
He wept.
He confronted.
He healed.
He called people by name.
He sat at tables with sinners.
He placed His hands on the unclean.
He stood before religious leaders.
He knelt in Gethsemane.
He carried a cross.
He died.
He rose.
Christianity begins not with the claim that God mailed humanity a new religious textbook from heaven.
It begins with the staggering confession that God came near.
John reaches for language almost too enormous for language itself:
“Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο”
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
The eternal λόγος—Logos, the Word—became σάρξ, flesh.
That is the scandal at the heart of Christianity.
The message became a Man.
Truth walked into villages.
Grace ate with sinners.
Holiness touched lepers.
The Creator entered His creation.
And salvation was not accomplished by Jesus sitting safely behind a desk explaining crucifixion.
He was crucified.
Jesus did not merely come to describe salvation.
He came to accomplish it.
That distinction changes everything.
A written autobiography could have told us what Jesus intended to do.
The cross shows us what He actually did.
A manuscript could have described sacrificial love.
Calvary displayed it.
Ink could have recorded the sentence, “I love you.”
Blood demonstrated how far that love would go.
This does not make writing unimportant. Christianity became deeply rooted in written apostolic testimony, and the New Testament itself presents written testimony as purposeful and faith-forming.
But the center of the Christian faith is not a document Jesus personally authored.
It is Jesus Christ Himself.
And then something remarkable happened.
Jesus made witnesses.
Luke begins his Gospel by acknowledging that accounts concerning Jesus had been handed down through people who had been there.
The Greek of Luke 1:2 contains two striking descriptions:
“αὐτόπται καὶ ὑπηρέται γενόμενοι τοῦ λόγου”
autoptai kai hypēretai genomenoi tou logou.
“Eyewitnesses and servants of the word.”
The word αὐτόπται—autoptai—is where English gets the idea behind “autopsy”: seeing something with one's own eyes.

Luke is not pretending Christianity emerged from anonymous spiritual imagination. His prologue deliberately roots his account in testimony handed down from those associated with the events from the beginning, and Luke says he investigated matters carefully in order to write an orderly account so that his reader could know the certainty of what he had been taught.
Think about the beauty of that.
Jesus did not merely leave information.
He formed witnesses.
Men who had seen storms become still.
Men who remembered bread multiplying in their hands.
Men who had heard Him teach.
Men who had watched Him arrested.
Men whose courage collapsed when He was taken.
Men who knew the humiliation of discovering that they were not nearly as faithful as they thought they were.
And then...
men who proclaimed that they had encountered Him alive.
Their weakness matters.
Peter was not introduced to us as a polished religious superhero.
He failed spectacularly.
He promised loyalty and then denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples misunderstood.
They argued.
They became afraid.
They ran.
And somehow this makes the Gospel painfully recognizable.
Because maybe your story isn't clean either.
Maybe you love Jesus and still know what it is to fail Him.
Maybe there are things in your browser history you would never project onto a church screen.
Maybe there is resentment living behind your worship songs.
Maybe everybody thinks your marriage is fine.
Maybe you know how to say “God is good” while privately wondering why God allowed your life to hurt this much.
Maybe you have served in church while slowly becoming spiritually numb.
Maybe you have preached grace to other people while secretly believing your own sin has disqualified you from receiving it.
Maybe you promised God, “Never again.”
And then there was an again.
And another.
And another.
You know what makes the witnesses of Jesus so uncomfortable?
They knew something about “again” too.
Peter knew.
“I will never deny You.”
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denial.
Three times.
And then the rooster.
Imagine that sound.
Not loud for everybody.
But deafening for Peter.
Because sometimes the most painful sound in your life is the moment you realize you have become the person you swore you would never become.
Maybe you know that sound.
A door closing.
A message being deleted.
A bottle opening.
A search bar.
A doctor's call.
Divorce papers.
A secret conversation.
A relapse.
A confession.
The silence after somebody discovers what you did.
The moment your carefully maintained image finally collapses.
Peter had his moment.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
And perhaps this is where the question “Why didn't Jesus write His own Gospel?” begins reaching somewhere deeper than historical curiosity.
Because the Gospel is not fundamentally the story of impressive people finding God.
It is the announcement of God coming for sinners.
Jesus said that He came to seek and save the lost.
He described Himself as a physician for the sick.
He welcomed people respectable religion preferred to keep at arm's length.
He called sinners to repentance, yes—but He did not demand that sinners repair themselves before coming to Him.
The order matters.
Grace does not tell sin that sin is harmless.
Grace tells the sinner that sin is so serious Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is so astonishing that the cross became the place where judgment and forgiveness meet.
Repentance is not pretending your chains never existed.
Repentance is turning toward the One who can break them.
And the New Testament does not present Jesus' death as an unfortunate ending to an inspiring teacher's life.
The cross is central.
Paul summarizes the Gospel he had received and passed on by pointing to Christ dying for our sins, being buried, being raised, and appearing to witnesses.
Again...
testimony.
Received.
Handed on.
Witnessed.
Proclaimed.
The Gospel moved through human mouths before most Christians could ever have possessed a personal collection of New Testament books.
People heard about Jesus from people whose lives had collided with Jesus.
That matters.
Because perhaps you have been telling yourself:
“I don't know enough.”
“I haven't studied enough.”
“My past is too ugly.”
“My testimony isn't dramatic enough.”
“Someone else should tell people about Jesus.”
But look at whom Jesus used.
Fishermen.
A tax collector.
Former doubters.
Former cowards.
Broken people.
Restored people.
People who could say, in effect:
I saw enough to know He changed everything.

The Gospel writers did not need Jesus to leave behind an autobiography for them to invent a Christ of their own choosing. The New Testament presents the Gospel tradition as rooted in eyewitness testimony and apostolic proclamation, while Luke explicitly describes careful investigation and orderly writing.
And John's Gospel gives us perhaps the clearest statement of why a Gospel was written at all.
Near the end, John says Jesus performed many other signs that were not written in his book.
Then comes this:
“ταῦτα δὲ γέγραπται ἵνα πιστεύητε...”
tauta de gegraptai hina pisteuēte...
“But these have been written so that you may believe...”
Believe what?
“ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν ὁ χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ”
“That Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.”
And why believe?
“καὶ ἵνα πιστεύοντες ζωὴν ἔχητε...”
“So that believing you may have life...”
That is John's stated purpose.
Not merely information.
Life.
The written signs point beyond themselves to Jesus so that readers may believe and have life in His name.
Read that again.
The book points to the Person.
The testimony points to the Savior.
The words point to the Word.
And suddenly the absence of a Gospel personally penned by Jesus does not leave Christianity without a center.
It exposes what the center has always been.
Christ Himself.
Christianity is not ultimately “believe in this manuscript because Jesus personally held the pen.”
It is the apostolic proclamation:
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ was buried.
Jesus Christ rose.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And now the question turns toward you.
Because it is possible to spend years debating who wrote what...
and never surrender to the One they wrote about.
You can study Greek and still refuse to repent.
You can memorize Hebrew and still hide hatred.
You can know every argument for the resurrection while living as though Jesus remained in the grave.
You can defend the Bible online while ignoring the Bible privately.
You can win an argument about Christ...
and still refuse to give Christ your heart.
That may be the most dangerous distance in Christianity.
Not the distance between atheism and church attendance.
The distance between knowing about Jesus...
and belonging to Jesus.
Maybe you have been close enough to Christianity to learn its vocabulary but never close enough to Christ to surrender.
You know “grace.”
You know “salvation.”
You know “born again.”
You know “repentance.”
You know when to say amen.
But if nobody were watching...
does Jesus actually have you?
Not your Facebook religion.
Not your Sunday clothes.
Not your Christian posts.
You.
Your private habits.
Your wounds.
Your sexuality.
Your bitterness.
Your money.
Your ambition.
Your pride.
Your secret anger.
Your unforgiveness.
Your shame.
Your plans.
Your future.
You.
This is where the Gospel stops being an interesting historical question.
Because Jesus did not come merely to leave humanity something to analyze.
He came calling people:
“Follow Me.”
Those words are frightening because they leave us nowhere to hide.
Follow Me.
Not admire Me.
Not occasionally quote Me.
Not add Me to the life you already decided to live.
Follow.
Me.
And what happens when you do?
Ask Peter.
Failure did not receive the final sentence.
Grace did.
Peter denied Jesus, but denial was not the last chapter.
The risen Christ restored him.
The man who had collapsed under fear would become a public witness to the very Christ he once denied.
That is the heartbeat behind everything we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
He does something greater.
He redeems sinners.
He forgives the repentant.
He restores the fallen.
He gives new life.
He takes stories we would rather burn and turns them into testimonies that point away from our greatness and toward His mercy.
Your worst chapter does not need to become your final chapter.
Your sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Repentance matters.
But grace is real too.
The cross is real.
The empty tomb is real.
And Jesus still receives sinners who come to Him.
Perhaps you came into this article wondering why Jesus never wrote His own Gospel.
But maybe another question has quietly been forming underneath it:
What is Jesus doing with my story?
There are pages you cannot erase.
Neither can I.
There are sentences in our histories we desperately wish had never been written.
People we wounded.
Years we wasted.
Warnings we ignored.
Promises we broke.
Things done to us that we never deserved.
Things done by us that we cannot excuse.
We cannot travel backward and rewrite those pages.
But redemption does not require pretending the past never happened.
Jesus can take a scandal and make it the backdrop against which grace becomes visible.
He can take shame and produce testimony.
He can take a denier named Peter and make him a witness.
He can take enemies and make them family.
He can take spiritually dead people and give them life.
He can take sinners and call them forgiven.
That is not self-improvement.
That is Gospel.
And if something in you has been exposed while reading this, don't rush past it.
Maybe you need to pray something much simpler than a polished religious speech.
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Maybe you need to confess what you have spent months hiding.
Maybe you need to stop negotiating with a sin Christ is calling you to abandon.
Maybe you need to return after years of running.
Maybe you need to admit:
I cannot save myself.
Christ, save me.
The Christian hope is not that good people eventually become good enough for God.
It is that sinners are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
His death.
His resurrection.
His grace.
His lordship.
His invitation.
Be honest.
If your spirit feels worn thin and you need brothers and sisters in Christ to remember you in prayer, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
And if you have lived through a chapter you thought would destroy you but Christ met you there, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needs to read tonight.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person whose name came into your mind while reading this.
The friend who has slowly disappeared from church.
The son who stopped believing.
The mother who prays while everybody sleeps.
The Christian who smiles publicly and collapses privately.
The person carrying shame.
The person who thinks Jesus wants nothing to do with them anymore.
Or send this privately if their pain should not become public.
Come back when shame tries to convince you that your worst chapter is the whole book.
But hear this clearly.
It does not purchase salvation.
It does not make someone a better Christian.
And it should not be confused with a universal biblical requirement that every believer must financially support this particular ministry.
Christ purchased redemption—not us.
Christian giving is meant to flow from grace, willingness, love, stewardship, and worship rather than spiritual coercion.

Financial generosity can certainly be one way a Christian glorifies God, but it is not the only way. Pray. Serve. Give where God leads you. Care for your family. Support faithful Gospel work. Help those in need. Share truth. Encourage somebody. Live generously.
And if Gospel Warrior is one of the ministries you freely choose to support, we are deeply grateful.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help tremendously.
Send it to someone who needs Christ.
Because the objective was never to build an audience that merely admires Gospel Warrior.
The objective is to point people to Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Back to Scripture.
Back to repentance.
Back to grace.
Back to the cross.
Back to the empty tomb.
Back to the Savior.
So why didn't Jesus write His own Gospel?
Scripture does not explicitly tell us.
And we should have enough reverence for Scripture not to pretend that it does.
But Scripture does show us something breathtaking.
Jesus came not merely to produce words about salvation.
He came to accomplish salvation.
He formed witnesses.
Their testimony was proclaimed.

The Gospel accounts were written so that people might know the truth about Him, and John's stated purpose is breathtakingly personal: that you may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in His name.
Maybe that is why this question matters so much.
Because eventually you must stop staring at the handwriting...
and look at the One the words reveal.
The carpenter.
The teacher.
The healer.
The Lamb.
The crucified King.
The risen Christ.
The Savior of sinners.
Jesus.
And somewhere between your first breath and your last, His story confronts yours.
You will bring Him scars.
He knows scars.
You will bring Him failure.
He restored failures.
You will bring Him sin.
He went to a cross for sinners.
You will bring Him a story whose pages cannot be undone.
And grace will whisper something shame never wants you to believe:
Your story may contain the scandal...
but Jesus can still write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABIMELECH GAVE SARAH SILVER AFTER RETURNING HER TO ABRAHAM—WHAT WAS THE PAYMENT FOR?
paragraphs: ABIMELECH GAVE SARAH SILVER AFTER RETURNING HER TO ABRAHAM—WHAT WAS THE PAYMENT FOR?

He had already given Sarah back. So why did King Abimelech suddenly give Abraham a thousand pieces of silver—and why does the Hebrew Bible call it a “covering of the eyes”?
