“For He Himself will save His people from their sins.”
Not merely from embarrassment.
Not merely from loneliness.
Not merely from poverty.
Not merely from difficult circumstances.
From their sins.
That is where the Christmas story becomes uncomfortable for anyone who wants a Savior without repentance.
Jesus did not enter the world merely to make bad people feel better about themselves.
He came because humanity needed rescuing.
We have sinned against a holy God.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Hated.
Envied.
Manipulated.
Hidden.
Gossiped.
Used people.
Worshiped created things instead of the Creator.
Protected secret sins while maintaining public appearances.
We have wanted grace without surrender and forgiveness without repentance.
And still...
God came near.
Matthew reaches back to Isaiah:
“Ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν...”
“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son...”
And His name would be called:
Ἐμμανουήλ—Emmanouēl.
Matthew himself explains it:
“Μεθ’ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός.”
God with us.
Read those words again.
God.
With.
Us.
With us in a world stained by sin.
With us among broken families.
With us among rumors and misunderstandings.
With us among people carrying shame.
With us among people whose lives do not look like the polished version they post online.
God with the grieving.
God with the exhausted.
God with the repentant sinner.
God with the person whispering at two in the morning, “Jesus, I don't know how to fix what I've become.”
And eventually...
God incarnate would go to a cross.
The Child Joseph was told to receive would grow into the Man humanity would reject.
Jesus would be mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
He would bear sin.
He would die.
And He would rise.
The apparent scandal surrounding His entrance into the world would eventually lead toward another scene that looked, from a human perspective, like total defeat.
A cross.
A dead Messiah.
A sealed tomb.
Again, appearances seemed to tell one story.
God was writing another.
The cross looked like defeat.
It became the place where Christ offered Himself for sinners.
The tomb looked final.
Then Sunday came.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
And perhaps this is why Matthew's account of Joseph reaches deeper than Christmas nostalgia.
It asks what you will do when obedience costs you your preferred version of the story.
Joseph woke up.
And Matthew 1:24 gives us one of the quietest descriptions of extraordinary faith:
“ἐποίησεν ὡς προσέταξεν αὐτῷ ὁ ἄγγελος κυρίου.”
He did as the angel of the Lord commanded him.
No recorded speech.
No dramatic negotiation.
No demand that God explain every future consequence first.
Joseph got up...
and obeyed.
He took Mary as his wife.
Think about what that obedience could cost.
Other people had not received Joseph's dream.
Other people had not heard the angel.
Joseph could obey God and still be misunderstood by people.
That is where many of us struggle.
We want obedience that comes with immediate vindication.
We want God to explain Himself to everyone who misunderstands us.
We want faithfulness without rumors.
Conviction without cost.
Christianity without a cross.
But sometimes obedience means being willing to look foolish to people because you trust the God who sees what they cannot.
Joseph did not need everyone to understand his obedience before he obeyed.
He needed to know what God had said.
And someone reading this right now may be living inside the space between confusion and clarity.
Maybe your life did not become what you expected.
Maybe you trusted someone and were wounded.
Maybe you were the one who caused the wound.
Maybe the scandal is not something somebody did to you.
Maybe it is yours.
Maybe nobody knows.
You still smile.
Still work.
Still attend church.
Still post verses.
Still say, “I'm okay.”
But underneath the Christian vocabulary is a secret you are terrified will eventually find daylight.
Pornography.
An affair.
A lie.
Bitterness.
Addiction.
Hidden messages.
A double life.
A heart that has slowly grown cold toward Christ.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not telling you that your sin does not matter.
It mattered enough for Jesus to go to the cross.
But your sin does not have to have the final word.
Jesus saves sinners.
That is literally the announcement embedded in His name and mission in Matthew's opening chapter.
You do not need a better disguise.
You need a Savior.
You do not need to become impressive enough for God.
You need to repent and come to Christ.
Grace is not God pretending your sin never happened.
Grace is God providing in Jesus Christ what you could never provide for yourself.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A new direction.
A new identity.
A new life.
This is where scandal can meet grace.
Not because scandal becomes good.
Not because sin becomes harmless.
But because Jesus rewrites what sin tried to make final.
Peter denied Him and was restored.
Paul persecuted the church and became a servant of Christ.
The thief beside Jesus reached the end of a ruined life and found mercy in the crucified King.
And you...
whatever chapter you are ashamed to reread...
are not beyond the reach of Christ if you will turn to Him.
Repentance means you stop defending what Jesus died to save you from.
You bring it into His light.
You call sin what God calls it.
You stop hiding.
You trust Christ.
And you follow Him.
Maybe that is why you stayed with this article this long.
Maybe underneath all the theology, one sentence has been following you:
God knows the whole story.
He knows what they did.
He knows what you did.
He knows what actually happened.
He knows where you were misunderstood.
He knows where you were guilty.
He knows which tears were real.
He knows which excuses were not.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Come to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to write the details publicly.
Your few words may become the reason another person realizes they are not the only one struggling.
And please do not keep this message trapped on your screen.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Because someone you know may be quietly living through the worst chapter of their life.
Someone may have already decided God is finished with them.
Someone may be hiding sin and desperately needs to hear the call to repentance.
Someone may be carrying shame Jesus died to redeem.
Someone may need to discover that Christianity is not about pretending you have never been broken.
It is about a crucified and risen Savior who receives repentant sinners.
There may come a night when circumstances look final and you need to remember Joseph waking from that dream...
and obeying God before everybody else understood.
And if Gospel Warrior has genuinely helped you grow closer to Christ, there is another practical way you can help this ministry continue and expand.
It does not.
Scripture does not teach that.
And we would never want financial support for an online ministry to become an excuse for neglecting faithful generosity, service, and responsibility in your local church.
Your support helps us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep building resources.
That matters because discipleship should never be reduced to buying something.
We want people in the Word.
We want marriages strengthened by Christ.
We want prodigals coming home.
We want hidden sin brought into the light.
We want wounded believers restored.
We want unbelievers hearing the Gospel.
We want Christians who do more than repost verses—we want disciples who know Jesus, love Jesus, obey Jesus, and make Jesus known.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite someone to follow.
Send it privately to the person God puts on your heart.
Faithful support takes more than one form, and the Gospel itself is not for sale.
But whatever you do, do not leave this story merely impressed by Joseph.
Leave looking at Jesus.
Because Joseph's confusion was not ultimately resolved so we could admire Joseph.
Mary's miraculous pregnancy was not recorded merely so we could admire Mary.
The angel did not appear merely to save a relationship.
He announced a Savior.
“He shall save his people from their sins.”
That includes respectable sinners.
Religious sinners.
Secret sinners.
Public sinners.
People with beautiful reputations and ugly hidden chapters.
People who have been falsely accused.
People who are genuinely guilty.
People who thought they were too far gone.
People who believed their worst chapter had already written the ending.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He died for sinners.
He rose victorious.
And He still calls sinners to repent, believe, and follow Him.
Joseph thought the story in front of him meant something had gone terribly wrong.
Then God revealed that redemption had entered the room.
Maybe your story really does contain scandal.
Maybe yours contains betrayal.
Maybe failure.
Maybe shame.
Maybe something was done to you that you never deserved.
Maybe something was done by you that you cannot undo.
The Gospel does not ask you to rename darkness as light.
It gives you something infinitely better.
It tells you darkness does not get the final word when Jesus Christ enters the story.
If God shows me that my conclusion, my fear, my sin, or my plan must surrender to Jesus...will I obey when I wake up?
Because the greatest miracle in Matthew 1 is not that Joseph's reputation survived.
It is that God came near to save His people from their sins.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you after everything else fades is this:
What looked like the end of Joseph’s future was carrying the Savior—and what looks like the end of yours may still become the place where you finally surrender the pen to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID POLYGAMY REVEAL HUMAN WEAKNESS MORE THAN GOD’S DESIGN?
paragraphs: DID POLYGAMY REVEAL HUMAN WEAKNESS MORE THAN GOD’S DESIGN?

The Bible records men with multiple wives—but Jesus did something startling when questioned about marriage. He did not point His listeners toward Abraham, Jacob, David, or Solomon. He took them all the way back to the beginning.
There is an uncomfortable question hiding in some of the most familiar pages of the Bible.
Abraham had more than one woman in his household.
Jacob married Leah and Rachel and fathered children through their servants.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon multiplied wives on a scale almost impossible to imagine.
These were not anonymous villains lurking in Scripture’s shadows.
These were patriarchs.
Kings.
Men woven into the history through which God would eventually bring the Messiah into the world.
And that leaves a question many Christians have quietly wondered but sometimes feel afraid to ask:
If monogamy was God's design, why does the Bible contain so much polygamy?
Maybe the answer is more devastating—and more beautiful—than we realize.
Because perhaps the presence of polygamy in Scripture does not reveal uncertainty in God's design.
Perhaps it reveals something painfully familiar about ours.
The human heart can receive something good from God...
and still reach for more.
The human heart can know God's intention...
and still construct alternatives.
The human heart can be blessed beyond measure...
and still believe another person, another possession, another relationship, another experience will finally make it satisfied.
And if we read these stories carefully, Scripture does not romanticize that impulse.
It exposes it.
Before there was Abraham and Hagar...
before Jacob entered the rivalry between Rachel and Leah...
before David's complicated household...
before Solomon filled palaces with wives and concubines...
there was a garden.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was God.
Genesis 2:24 gives us one of Scripture's foundational descriptions of marriage:
“עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
‘Al-ken ya‘azov-ish et-aviv ve’et-immo, vedavaq be’ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
In context, the Hebrew declares that a man leaves his father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad — “one flesh.”
One flesh.
Not merely two people sharing property.
Not merely a political arrangement.
Not merely sexual access.
Not merely a contract of convenience.
A covenantal union so profound that Scripture describes two lives becoming “one flesh.”
And notice something else.
When Jesus was confronted centuries later with a controversy about marriage and divorce, He did not settle the question by pointing to the complicated marriages of Israel's patriarchs or kings.
He went backward.
Past Solomon.
Past David.
Past Jacob.
Past Abraham.
Back to creation.
Jesus said:
“ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ κτίσας...”
ap’ archēs de ktisas...
“He who created them from the beginning...”
Then Christ invokes Genesis and declares that the two become one flesh, concluding:
“ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω.”
Ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen, anthrōpos mē chōrizetō.
What God has joined together, man must not separate.
Matthew 19:4–6.
That phrase matters:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς — ap’ archēs — “from the beginning.”
Jesus takes the argument back to God's original ordering of creation.
And that gives us an important principle for reading the Old Testament:
Everything Scripture truthfully records is not therefore something Scripture morally recommends.
The Bible is brutally honest about humanity.
That honesty is one reason its stories cut so deeply.
Noah can survive the flood and later become drunk.
Abraham can believe God and then act out of fear.
Jacob can encounter God and still carry the consequences of deception.
David can write breathtaking worship and commit devastating sin.
Peter can confess that Jesus is the Christ and later deny knowing Him.
Scripture does not airbrush its heroes.
It exposes them.

And that means when Scripture tells us that someone did something, we must still ask whether God commanded it, permitted or regulated it within a fallen world, tolerated it for a time, or condemned it.
Description is not automatically prescription.
And nowhere does this become more emotionally visible than in the households touched by polygamy.
Look at Abraham.
God promised Abraham descendants.
Years passed.
The promise seemed delayed.
Sarah suffered through barrenness.
And eventually human beings attempted to accomplish through their own arrangement what God had promised to accomplish by His faithfulness.
Hagar entered the story.
Ishmael was born.
Then the household fractured.
Genesis does not present the aftermath like a romantic picture of expanded marriage.
There is jealousy.
Pain.
Conflict.
Humiliation.
Fear.
A woman eventually wandering in the wilderness with her child.
God, in His mercy, sees Hagar.
That is one of the beautiful moments of the story.
Human beings created the broken situation.
God still saw the suffering person inside it.
That distinction matters.
God's mercy toward people living inside broken circumstances does not mean the brokenness itself was His ideal.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You made a decision God never told you to make.
Then everything became complicated.
And somewhere in the wreckage you assumed God must have abandoned you.
But Hagar's story whispers something powerful:
God can meet people in consequences without calling the consequences His design.
Maybe that is already hitting somewhere you did not expect.
Because this article may be about polygamy on the surface...
but underneath it is about us.
About what happens when waiting becomes unbearable.
When desire becomes louder than obedience.
When we start helping God accomplish something God never asked us to manufacture.
Abraham's household asks a frightening question:
How much pain begins when human impatience tries to finish God's sentence?
Then comes Jacob.
Jacob loved Rachel.
But through deception and the customs surrounding him, he first received Leah as his wife, then Rachel.
What follows?
Competition.
Jealousy.
Comparison.
Women aching to be loved.
Children being born into an atmosphere where affection, fertility, status, and rivalry become painfully intertwined.
Read those chapters slowly.
Do not merely count Jacob's sons.
Listen to their mothers.
Listen to Leah longing to be loved.
Listen to Rachel grieving her barrenness.
Listen to two sisters competing inside the same household.
The text refuses to let us pretend that multiplying relationships multiplied peace.
Sometimes what looks powerful from the outside is bleeding behind closed doors.
Then David.
A warrior.
A king.
A worshiper.
A man through whose royal line the Messiah would come.
Yet David's household becomes increasingly complicated, and Scripture never asks us to imitate every choice David made merely because God used him.
That distinction is essential to understanding grace.
God using a person does not mean God endorses everything that person does.
If that were true, grace would become meaningless.
Grace exists precisely because God works through deeply flawed people.
And then Solomon.
Perhaps nobody exposes the danger more dramatically.
Before Israel ever had a king, Deuteronomy 17:17 warned that the king must not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.
Those words eventually read almost like a prophecy over Solomon's life.
Solomon accumulated wives and concubines on an extraordinary scale.
And 1 Kings 11 tells us what happened.
His heart turned.
The man famous for wisdom became living evidence that knowing truth intellectually is not the same thing as surrendering your desires to God.
Think about that.
You can know Proverbs...
and still ignore wisdom.
You can understand theology...
and still feed an idol.
You can teach other people...
and secretly be drifting yourself.
You can look spiritually successful...
while your heart is slowly learning to live without complete devotion to God.
That may be the real warning hidden inside Solomon's palace.
The danger was not merely that Solomon had many women.
The deeper catastrophe was a divided heart.
And suddenly this ancient story walks straight into our century.
Most people reading this will never have hundreds of spouses.
But we understand divided hearts.
We know what it is to want Jesus...
and the secret habit.
Jesus...
and approval.
Jesus...
and money.
Jesus...
and pornography.
Jesus...
and revenge.
Jesus...
and the relationship we know is pulling us away from Him.
Jesus...
and the hidden life nobody at church knows exists.
We want Christ...
plus whatever we refuse to surrender.
Solomon's palace may look foreign to us.
Solomon's heart does not.
That is why this conversation cannot end with a smug judgment about ancient people.
The Gospel never allows us to stand comfortably above sinners.
It brings the mirror closer.
Polygamy reveals something larger than marital history.
It reveals the restless tendency of fallen humanity to multiply what God intended to be surrendered to Him.
More.
Another.
Again.
Not enough.
Just one more.
One more relationship.
One more purchase.
One more achievement.
One more secret pleasure.
One more person telling us we matter.
And somehow...
still empty.
Sin keeps promising addition while quietly performing subtraction.
It promises more pleasure and subtracts peace.
More freedom and subtracts self-control.
More attention and subtracts intimacy.
More choices and subtracts contentment.
More secrecy and subtracts wholeness.
Until eventually we discover that what we thought we possessed has begun possessing us.
This is why God's design cannot merely be reduced to a rulebook.
God's commands reveal something about His wisdom.
When Christ points us toward the beginning, He is not merely winning a theological argument.
He is reminding humanity that we were not created to invent truth according to appetite.
We were created by Someone.
For Someone.
And our deepest restoration comes not by asking, “How much can I get away with?”
but:
“Jesus, what did You intend?”
There is another layer here that Christians should handle carefully.

The Mosaic law contains provisions addressing situations involving multiple wives. That does not require us to conclude that polygamy represented creation's ideal. Biblical law often addressed human beings inside an already fallen social world, restraining injustice and protecting vulnerable people within realities that were not identical to Eden.
Jesus Himself gives us a principle for understanding this when discussing divorce.
Moses permitted something because of the hardness of human hearts.
Then Jesus says, in essence:
It was not that way from the beginning.
Matthew 19:8.
There it is again.
The beginning.
God's design on one side.
Human hardness on the other.
That distinction changes the question.
Instead of asking only, “Why did God allow this to exist?”
we begin asking:
“What does its existence reveal about humanity after the fall?”
And perhaps that question is far more uncomfortable.
Because suddenly we cannot keep the discussion thousands of years away.
We have to confront our own compromises.
How many things have we renamed “normal” simply because people around us practice them?
How many things have we defended because culture tolerates them?
How many desires have we baptized because surrender felt too expensive?
How often have we searched Scripture hoping God would approve what we had already decided to do?
Be honest.
Have you ever opened the Bible looking for permission instead of transformation?
That question hurts.
Because sometimes we do not want God's will.
We want God's signature underneath ours.
We want heaven to notarize decisions we made without prayer.
We want Jesus as Savior while retaining veto power over Jesus as Lord.
And then grace interrupts us.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls darkness light.
Not grace that tells us repentance is unnecessary.
Real grace.
The kind that tells the truth and then refuses to leave the sinner there.
This is where the entire Bible begins moving toward Jesus.
Because the scandal of Scripture is not that God found perfect people and rewarded them.
The scandal is that a holy God entered the history of deeply imperfect people and brought redemption through it.
Look at the genealogy leading to Christ.
Broken families.
Sexual scandal.
Foreigners.
Kings.
Failures.
People carrying stories they probably wished could be erased.
And God did not erase the history.
He entered it.
Jesus Christ came into a human story already scarred by sin.
Then He carried sin's judgment to the cross.
The Gospel is not God pretending our rebellion never happened.
The Gospel is God dealing with it completely in Christ.
At Calvary, Jesus did not say your sin was harmless.
His wounds declare the opposite.
Sin was so serious that redemption cost blood.
Yet His resurrection declares something equally staggering:
your failure does not have to write the final chapter.
That is why repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
Repentance is coming home.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia, carrying the idea of repentance, a changed mind and reorientation toward God.
It is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt anguish.
Peter wept bitterly.
But the Gospel calls us beyond regret into return.
Maybe your scandal is not polygamy.
Maybe nobody knows your scandal.
Maybe it lives behind a deleted browser history.
A hidden conversation.
A relationship you keep defending.
An addiction you keep promising to stop.
A marriage slowly suffocating under resentment.
A heart that still worships Sunday morning but belongs to ambition Monday through Saturday.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary so well that nobody realizes how exhausted your soul has become.
You smile.
You post verses.
You say, “God is good.”
But when the room gets quiet...
you know something is wrong.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your public image.
He came to resurrect what sin has killed.
He came for the adulterer.
The liar.
The sexually broken.
The religious hypocrite.
The ashamed.
The addicted.
The betrayed.
The betrayer.
The person who destroyed something precious and would give anything to rewind time.
The person whose family history looks more like Genesis than a Christian greeting card.
He came for sinners.
That includes you.
That includes me.
And there is no scandal so dark that Christ's grace becomes frightened of it.
But grace does not merely comfort us inside rebellion.
Grace calls us out.
Jesus forgives...
and Jesus transforms.
Jesus receives...
and Jesus commands repentance.
Jesus cleanses...
and Jesus becomes Lord.
That is the difference between using Christianity to soothe the conscience and actually following Christ.
Maybe the question was never merely:
“Did God approve of every marriage arrangement recorded in Scripture?”
Maybe the deeper question is:
“What will I do when God's design confronts my desire?”
Because that moment eventually comes for every disciple.
There will be something you want that Jesus asks you to surrender.
There will be something culture celebrates that Scripture calls you to examine.
There will be something your flesh calls freedom that Christ exposes as slavery.
And eventually Christianity becomes personal.
Not Abraham's obedience.
Yours.
Not David's repentance.
Yours.
Not Solomon's divided heart.
Yours.
Not Peter's tears.
Yours.
Not somebody else's cross.
Yours.
And in that moment, you discover whether Jesus is merely someone you admire...
or the Lord you follow.
If this exposed something hidden inside you, do not turn conviction into shame and run from God.
Run toward Christ.
That is enough.
Let other believers see it and pray.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because every paragraph will feel comfortable tomorrow.
It is wisdom.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the person who has not believed yet but keeps asking questions about Jesus.
Because if Gospel truth matters, it should not remain trapped inside our private feeds.
It does not.
It does not.
And not because anyone can purchase spiritual maturity.
They cannot.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But voluntary generosity has always mattered in the work of ministry.
If you want to glorify God through the resources He has entrusted to you, ask Him where and how He wants you to give.
But whether you ever give financially or not...
do not leave this article merely thinking about Abraham.
Or Jacob.
Or David.
Or Solomon.
Look at your own heart.
Where have you multiplied what God asked you to surrender?
Where have you called compromise “complicated”?
Where have you mistaken God's patience for God's approval?
Where have you allowed desire to become a throne?
And most importantly...
will you bring it to Jesus?
Because Christianity is not the story of human beings successfully hiding their scandals from God.
It is the story of God seeing everything...
coming near anyway...
calling sinners to repentance...
paying the price they could never pay...
and making broken people new through Jesus Christ.
Polygamy may reveal human weakness.
But Scripture does not end with human weakness.
It leads us toward a faithful Bridegroom.
Christ.
The One who does not betray His covenant.
The One whose heart cannot be seduced away from His people.
The One who loved His Church and gave Himself for her.
The One who takes divided hearts and calls them home.
So perhaps the final question is no longer whether the failures of biblical men disprove God's design.
Perhaps the question is whether we will allow their failures to expose our own need for grace.
Because the Bible's scandals were never preserved so we could feel superior to broken people.
They were preserved so broken people like us could discover how desperately we need a Savior.
And when Jesus gets the final word, your worst chapter does not have to become your last one.
Your scandal may explain where you have been—but only Jesus gets to decide what grace can make of what remains.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IF MY PEOPLE HUMBLE THEMSELVES…” — THE VERSE WE KEEP PUTTING ON NATIONS THAT GOD FIRST AIMED AT HIS PEOPLE
paragraphs: “IF MY PEOPLE HUMBLE THEMSELVES…” — THE VERSE WE KEEP PUTTING ON NATIONS THAT GOD FIRST AIMED AT HIS PEOPLE
Before you use 2 Chronicles 7:14 as a political slogan again, read what God actually said. The most uncomfortable word in the verse may not be “land.” It may be “My.”
There is something almost haunting about the way we use this verse.
We print it beneath flags.
We post it during elections.
We quote it when governments disappoint us.

We reach for it when society appears to be collapsing, when corruption fills the headlines, when morality seems upside down, when the candidate we fear is rising or the candidate we trusted has failed.
“If My people, which are called by My name, shall humble themselves…”
And almost immediately, our eyes move outward.
Toward politicians.
Toward political parties.
Toward the culture.
Toward unbelievers.
Toward “those people.”
We read a verse about repentance…
and somehow leave convinced that somebody else needs to repent.
Maybe that is why this verse needs to be rescued from our slogans.
Because before 2 Chronicles 7:14 ever became something Christians printed over the colors of a modern nation, it was the voice of the living God confronting a covenant people who carried His name.
And the finger was not pointing first at Babylon.
It was not pointing first at Egypt.
It was not pointing first at pagan kings.
It was pointing toward His people.
That changes everything.
The Hebrew begins:
וְיִכָּנְעוּ עַמִּי אֲשֶׁר נִקְרָא־שְׁמִי עֲלֵיהֶם
Wəyikkānəʿû ʿammî ʾăšer niqrāʾ-šəmî ʿălêhem…
“…and My people, upon whom My name is called, humble themselves…”
The Hebrew text continues:
וְיִתְפַּלְלוּ וִיבַקְשׁוּ פָנַי וְיָשֻׁבוּ מִדַּרְכֵיהֶם הָרָעִים
“…and pray, and seek My face, and turn from their evil ways…”
Then comes God's response:
וַאֲנִי אֶשְׁמַע מִן־הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֶסְלַח לְחַטָּאתָם וְאֶרְפָּא אֶת־אַרְצָם
“…then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.”
That is the Hebrew text of 2 Chronicles 7:14.
Read it slowly.
God does not begin with their enemies.
He begins with עַמִּי — ʿammî — “My people.”
And historically, we need to be precise.
The immediate audience was not America.
Not the Philippines.
Not Britain.
Not Canada.
Not Australia.
Not any modern political state.
God was speaking to Solomon in connection with Israel, the temple, the land God had given them, and the covenant consequences that could fall upon His people when they rebelled.
The previous verse matters enormously.

God speaks about shutting the heavens so there is no rain, commanding locusts to consume the land, or sending pestilence among His people. Those circumstances directly echo Solomon’s temple-dedication prayer, where he had asked God to hear His people when sin brought defeat, drought, disaster, and judgment and they turned back toward Him.
So “heal their land” was not originally a campaign promise.
It was covenant language.
That does not make the verse irrelevant to Christians.
It makes it too sacred to misuse.
Because the spiritual pattern blazing through the passage remains unmistakable:
God's people humble themselves.
God's people pray.
God's people seek Him.
God's people turn from wickedness.
And God is revealed as the God who hears, forgives, restores, and shows mercy.
Notice what the verse does not say.
“If My people can defeat the other political party…”
“If My people can expose enough corrupt politicians…”
“If My people can win enough arguments online…”
“If My people can make unbelievers behave like believers…”
“If My people can recover enough cultural influence…”
No.
Before God talks about what is wrong “out there,” the text forces His people to confront what has gone wrong in here.
That is why this verse is far more dangerous than a political slogan.
A slogan can be shouted without changing you.
This verse cannot be understood honestly without bringing you before a mirror.
Maybe the crisis is real.
Maybe the corruption is real.
Maybe the cultural decay is real.
Maybe political leaders really are lying.
Maybe institutions really have failed.
Maybe evil really is being normalized.
Christians are not commanded to become blind to injustice. Scripture repeatedly calls God's people to righteousness, justice, truth, mercy, courage, and concern for those who are vulnerable.
But there is something spiritually terrifying about becoming experts at diagnosing the sins of a nation while remaining amateurs at confessing our own.
We can rage about corruption in government while hiding corruption in our hearts.
We can demand integrity from politicians while lying to our spouse.
We can condemn sexual immorality in society while secretly feeding lust through a screen.
We can complain that the next generation has abandoned God while our children rarely see us praying.
We can demand biblical values from unbelievers while refusing biblical forgiveness to the person who wounded us.
We can talk endlessly about revival while protecting the very sin from which we need revival.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is this:
We can become politically awake while remaining spiritually asleep.
That is where 2 Chronicles 7:14 stops being comfortable.
וְיִכָּנְעוּ — wəyikkānəʿû.
Humble themselves.
Not advertise themselves.
Not defend themselves.
Not congratulate themselves.
Humble themselves.

The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, renders the opening with ἐντραπῇ ὁ λαός μου, language carrying the sense of being humbled, brought to a recognition that turns the person inward before God. It then continues with prayer, seeking God's face, and turning away from wicked ways.
This is not religious theater.
This is surrender.
And surrender hurts because pride rarely dies quietly.
Pride says, “Look what they have done.”
Humility whispers, “Lord, search me.”
Pride says, “Fix them.”
Humility says, “Change me.”
Pride says, “They are destroying the country.”
Humility asks, “Jesus, what is destroying my communion with You?”
That question is harder.
Because suddenly there is nowhere to hide.
No political party can repent for you.
No president can surrender your secret sin.
No pastor can confess your bitterness.
No Christian influencer can forgive your enemy for you.
No election can crucify your flesh.
No government can make you holy.
No legislation can regenerate the human heart.
Politics can restrain certain evils. Governments can administer justice well or badly. Laws matter. Leadership matters. Christians may participate faithfully in public life.
But government cannot accomplish what only the Gospel can accomplish.
A ballot can change an administration.
Only Christ can change a heart.
And if we forget that distinction, Christianity slowly becomes a political identity wearing a cross around its neck.
Jesus becomes useful instead of Lord.
Scripture becomes ammunition instead of revelation.
Prayer becomes strategy instead of communion.
And repentance becomes something we demand from our opponents rather than something we practice before our God.
That is not revival.
That is religion protecting itself from repentance.
Maybe this is why the next words matter so much:
וִיבַקְשׁוּ פָנַי — wîḇaqšû pānay.
“Seek My face.”
Not merely My help.
Not merely My protection.
Not merely My blessing.
Not merely My intervention in the election.
My face.
There is a difference between wanting God's hand and wanting God.
You can want God to rescue your marriage without wanting Him to confront your selfishness.
You can want God to bless your finances without wanting Him to confront your greed.
You can want God to restore your nation without wanting Him to disturb your comfortable Christianity.
You can want revival in your church while secretly hoping revival never reaches the locked room inside you.
But God says:
Seek Me.
And then comes the phrase we often rush past:
וְיָשֻׁבוּ מִדַּרְכֵיהֶם הָרָעִים
“…and turn from their wicked ways.”
The Hebrew verb behind “turn” comes from שׁוּב — shuv, one of the Old Testament's great words for turning or returning.
That is repentance with movement in it.
Not merely feeling guilty.
Not merely crying.
Not merely posting a Bible verse.
Not merely saying, “Lord, forgive me,” while planning to return tomorrow to the same cherished rebellion.
Turning.
There are prayers we pray because we want God to change our circumstances.
Then there are prayers that finally allow God to change us.
Those prayers are dangerous.
“Jesus, show me where I have become proud.”
“Show me whom I refuse to forgive.”
“Show me what I secretly worship.”
“Show me where politics has occupied emotional territory that belongs to Your Kingdom.”
“Show me whether I am more devastated when my candidate loses than when someone I love dies without knowing Christ.”
That last one hurts.
But perhaps it should.
Because Jesus did not bleed on a Roman cross so that Christians could merely win culture wars.
He came seeking sinners.
He came announcing the Kingdom of God.
He called people to repent and believe.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed the rejected.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He forgave the guilty.
He carried sin.
And at Calvary, the scandal became almost unbearable.
The Holy One hanging among criminals.
The innocent condemned.
The King mocked.
The Creator bleeding beneath His creation.
And there, human politics revealed its limitations in the most horrifying way imaginable.
Religious authorities could accuse Him.
Political authorities could sentence Him.
Soldiers could crucify Him.
Crowds could reject Him.
But none of them could keep Him in the grave.
Jesus Christ rose.
And that means our deepest hope has never lived inside a palace, parliament, congress, senate, courthouse, presidential residence, or voting booth.
Our hope walked out of a tomb.
That does not mean Christians abandon public responsibility.
It means we finally put politics back where it belongs.
Under Christ.
Not beside Him.
Certainly not above Him.
We pray for leaders.
We seek justice.
We defend truth.
We care about laws because laws affect human beings made in God's image.
We vote according to conscience shaped by Scripture.
We refuse corruption regardless of which political tribe benefits from it.
But we do not baptize a party and call it the Kingdom of God.
We do not turn candidates into messiahs.
We do not excuse wickedness merely because the person committing it promises to protect our interests.
And we never forget that the Church's ultimate mission was given by Jesus, not by a political campaign.
Make disciples.
Proclaim Christ.
Teach His commands.
Love God.
Love neighbor.
Care for the suffering.
Walk in holiness.
Speak truth.
Call sinners to repentance.
Carry the Gospel into the world.
And perhaps that is where this article becomes personal.
Because it would be easy to finish reading this and think:
“Yes. Christians really need to hear this.”
But that would allow you to escape the verse again.
Forget everybody else for thirty seconds.
Just you.
Just God.
No political parties.
No politicians.
No denominations.
No pastor.
No Facebook comments.
No person you wish were reading this.
You.
If Jesus opened every hidden room of your life tonight, what would you beg Him not to show anyone?
What bitterness have you renamed “discernment”?
What pride have you renamed “conviction”?
What hatred have you renamed “righteous anger”?
What fear have you renamed “wisdom”?
What compromise have you renamed “struggle” because “sin” feels too uncomfortable?
What idol have you protected because it wears Christian clothing?
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe people think you are strong.
Maybe you still post Scripture.
Maybe you still worship.
Maybe you still serve.
Maybe you still smile when somebody asks how you are doing.
But Jesus knows.
And strangely…
that is not only terrifying.
It is beautiful.
Because the One who knows everything is still calling you.
The Gospel is not the story of clean people being rewarded for remaining clean.
It is the announcement that guilty people can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
Through His resurrection, death was defeated.
And when a sinner comes to Him in repentance and faith, the answer is not merely self-improvement.
It is grace.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
New life.
The scandal does not have to become the final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace was not finished.
Thomas doubted.
Grace was not finished.
Paul persecuted believers.
Grace was not finished.
The thief beside Jesus had almost no life left with which to prove himself.
Grace was not finished.
And whatever brought you to these words…
Grace may not be finished with you either.
But grace never means sin does not matter.
Grace means sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and sinners were loved so deeply that He went willingly.
So perhaps the prayer our generation needs is smaller and more frightening than the slogans we have been shouting.
Not:
“God, give us our country back.”
But:
“Jesus, take my heart back.”
Take the room I locked.
Take the pride.
Take the lust.
Take the bitterness.
Take the political idolatry.
Take the hypocrisy.
Take the secret addiction.
Take the unforgiveness.
Take the Christianity I learned to perform.
Take everything that has been competing with You.
I do not merely want Your hand.
I want Your face.
I do not merely want better circumstances.
I want Christ.
That is where awakening begins.
Not with pointing.
With kneeling.
Not with “them.”
With us.
Not with outrage alone.
With repentance.
And maybe tonight there is somebody reading this who has been running from Jesus for years.
You know Christian language.
You know the songs.
You know the verses.
Maybe you even know how to look spiritual.
But beneath all of it, you know something has been dying.
Your prayer life became mechanical.
Your Bible became decorative.
Your conscience became quieter.
The compromise became easier.
And slowly you learned how to live near Christianity without actually walking closely with Christ.
Come home.
Not to a political movement.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
Not to a religious brand.
To Jesus Christ.
Confess your sin.
Turn toward Him.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Stop negotiating with the thing that is destroying you.
Stop waiting until you feel worthy.
You will never clean yourself enough to make grace unnecessary.
Come to Christ because you need mercy.
Let it become prayer.
Somebody reading silently may need evidence that grace still reaches people in ruins.
And if you know someone who loves Jesus but has slowly allowed political anger to consume his peace, tag him—not to embarrass him, but because you love him.
If you know someone who has almost given up on Christianity because all they have seen is political warfare dressed in religious language, share this with them.
Not because every sentence deserves remembering.
Because sooner or later, you may need the question again:
Am I asking God to heal everything around me while refusing to let Him confront what is inside me?
We want this space to remain centered on Jesus Christ—Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, repentance, healing, discipleship, grace, and spiritual nourishment.
It cannot buy blessing.
It cannot replace repentance.
The New Testament gives us a better way to speak about Christian generosity:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ… μὴ… ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Let each person give according to what he has purposed in his heart—not from compulsion.
Paul then says that God loves a cheerful giver.
So there is no spiritual pressure here.
But there is an invitation.
Supporting Gospel work can result in thanksgiving and glory being given to God; Paul explicitly connects generous Christian ministry with needs being supplied and thanksgiving overflowing to God.
So if you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel-centered work, do it freely, prayerfully, joyfully, and with Christ—not pressure—at the center.
If you believe this ministry should continue…
if you want these messages to reach the person sitting alone at 2:00 in the morning wondering whether Jesus could still want them…
if you want to help put biblical resources into the hands of believers hungry for truth…
if you want to stand with the work as it grows…
Pray.
Sometimes a single share travels farther than money ever could.
Because somewhere behind another screen is a human being.
A tired father.
A wounded mother.
A teenager secretly drowning.
A believer trapped in shame.
A skeptic watching Christians fight and wondering whether Jesus is anything like the people invoking His name.
A prodigal who thinks he has gone too far.
And perhaps God will use something as ordinary as your share to put the name of Jesus in front of that person one more time.
So before we ask God to fix the nation…
before we ask Him to defeat our enemies…
before we ask Him to restore the culture…
before we quote 2 Chronicles 7:14 beneath another flag…
perhaps we should finally hear the words that come before the healing:
“If My people humble themselves…”
His people.
Us.
Me.
You.
Maybe revival begins when the finger we pointed at the world finally curls back toward our own chest…
and then the hand opens in surrender before Jesus.
Because the greatest healing is not winning back a country while losing our souls.
It is sinners coming home to Christ.
And when everything you tried to hide finally stands exposed before Jesus, remember this:
The hands that uncover your sin are the same scarred hands that were pierced to redeem you from it.
The world does not need Christians who have mastered the art of identifying everybody else's wicked ways.
It needs men and women who have looked into the holiness of God, fallen to their knees, turned from their own—and discovered that Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: LEVITICUS 20 GIVES A SERIOUS PENALTY FOR SEX DURING MENSTRUATION—BUT DOES THIS LAW STILL APPLY TO CHRISTIANS?
paragraphs: LEVITICUS 20 GIVES A SERIOUS PENALTY FOR SEX DURING MENSTRUATION—BUT DOES THIS LAW STILL APPLY TO CHRISTIANS?

One disturbing verse. One severe consequence. And one question many Christians are almost afraid to ask: If we believe the whole Bible is the Word of God, what are we supposed to do with Leviticus 20:18?
There are verses in the Bible people underline.
There are verses people frame on walls.
There are verses Christians memorize when life is falling apart.
And then there are verses we quietly pass over because we are not quite sure what to do with them.
Leviticus 20:18 is one of those verses.
Read slowly what the King James Version says:

“And if a man shall lie with a woman having her sickness, and shall uncover her nakedness; he hath discovered her fountain, and she hath uncovered the fountain of her blood: and both of them shall be cut off from among their people.”
—Leviticus 20:18, KJV
That is not a comfortable verse.
And perhaps it should not be.
But discomfort is not permission to distort Scripture.
Some people will read this and immediately conclude, “See? The Old Testament is cruel.”
Others will respond from the opposite direction and say, “God said it, so Christians must still enforce it exactly as ancient Israel did.”
Both reactions can move too quickly.
Because before asking, “Do Christians have to obey this?” we need to ask a more fundamental question:
What exactly did God command, to whom did He give the command, what did the command mean within the covenant God made with Israel, and what changed when Jesus Christ established the New Covenant?
That journey takes us somewhere much deeper than menstruation.
It takes us into holiness.
Covenant.
Sin.
Blood.
Grace.
And ultimately...
Jesus.
The Hebrew text of Leviticus 20:18 begins:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִשְׁכַּב אֶת־אִשָּׁה דָּוָה
Ve’ish asher-yishkav et-ishah davah...
In straightforward terms:
“And a man who lies with a menstruating woman...”

The word דָּוָה (davah) describes the woman in connection with her menstrual condition. The verse then says that the man has “uncovered her nakedness” and exposed her מָקוֹר (maqor)—her source or fountain—and that she has uncovered the source of her blood.
Then comes the frightening conclusion:
וְנִכְרְתוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם מִקֶּרֶב עַמָּם
Venikhretu sheneihem miqqerev ‘ammam.
“And both of them shall be cut off from among their people.”
Notice something immediately.
The Hebrew does not say, “Both of them shall be stoned.”
It does not explicitly say, “Execute them.”
It says they are to be “cut off”—from the Hebrew root כרת (karat).
That distinction matters.

The expression translated “cut off” appears elsewhere in the Torah and has generated considerable discussion concerning precisely how the sanction was understood—whether exclusion from the covenant community, divine judgment, premature death, loss of descendants, or some combination depending on context.
So we should not make Leviticus 20:18 say more than it actually says.
But neither should we make it say less.
This was serious.
Very serious.
Within Israel’s covenant life, this was not presented as an insignificant private matter.
And this is where the question becomes uncomfortable for modern Christians.
Why?
Why would God care about something so intimate?
To understand that, you have to walk backward several chapters.

Leviticus 15 discusses bodily discharges and ritual uncleanness. Menstruation made a woman ceremonially unclean for a period of time. Contact with certain things associated with that condition could communicate ritual uncleanness.
That did not mean the woman was morally disgusting.
It did not mean menstruation itself was a personal sin.
That distinction is absolutely essential.
Biblical ritual uncleanness and personal moral guilt are not identical categories.

People could become ceremonially unclean through ordinary realities of embodied human life. The book of Leviticus carefully regulates how Israel approached the holy presence of God, and categories of clean and unclean formed part of that covenant system.
In fact, Leviticus 15:24 says that if a man lies with a menstruating woman and her menstrual impurity comes upon him, he becomes unclean for seven days.
Then Leviticus 18:19 goes further and explicitly commands:
“Also thou shalt not approach unto a woman to uncover her nakedness, as long as she is put apart for her uncleanness.”
Then Leviticus 20:18 gives the corresponding sanction.
So we should not flatten these passages into one sentence.
Leviticus 15 discusses ritual impurity.
Leviticus 18 gives a prohibition.
Leviticus 20 attaches a serious covenant consequence.
The Bible is doing more than saying, “Blood is gross.”
That modern caricature completely misses the theological world of Leviticus.
Blood had enormous significance in Israel’s worship.
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood...”
—Leviticus 17:11
Blood represented life.
Blood belonged profoundly within Israel’s sacrificial symbolism.
Blood was associated with purification, sacrifice, atonement, life, death, and approach to a holy God.
And Leviticus repeatedly teaches Israel something modern humanity desperately wants to forget:
God is holy.
Not casually holy.
Not symbolically holy.
Not holy only when holiness happens to agree with our preferences.
Holy.
The Hebrew word is קָדוֹשׁ—qadosh.
Set apart.
Distinct.
God was teaching Israel that approaching Him was not casual business.
Their bodies mattered.
Their sexuality mattered.
Their worship mattered.
Their relationships mattered.
Their blood mattered.
Their obedience mattered.
Their covenant mattered.
This is where many readers make a mistake.
We open Leviticus as twenty-first-century Christians and instinctively ask, “Which of these rules do I personally have to follow?”
But Leviticus was originally given within the Mosaic covenant to Israel.
It was not dropped out of heaven as an isolated collection of random regulations addressed identically to every nation in every historical covenant setting.
Israel was a covenant people.
God had redeemed them from Egypt.
He had bound Himself to them.
He gave them priesthood, sacrifices, purity regulations, civil judgments, festivals, dietary distinctions, circumcision, tabernacle worship, and laws governing life in the covenant community.
And then Jesus came.
This is where the story turns.
Not because the Old Testament was a mistake.
Not because holiness stopped mattering.
Not because God suddenly changed His personality.
Jesus came because everything toward which the Law was moving finds its ultimate fulfillment in Him.
At the Last Supper, Jesus took the cup and declared:
“This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.”
—Luke 22:20, KJV
There it is again.
Blood.
But now...
His blood.
The book of Hebrews explains the enormous covenantal significance of what Christ accomplished.
“In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old.”
—Hebrews 8:13, KJV
Christians therefore do not live under the Mosaic covenant as ancient Israel lived under it.
That does not mean Christians tear Leviticus out of the Bible.
It means we read Leviticus through the fulfillment brought by Jesus Christ.
This distinction is visible almost immediately in the early Church.
When Gentiles began coming to Christ, the apostles faced an enormous question.
Would Gentile believers have to enter the Mosaic covenant and bear its requirements in the same manner as Jewish Israel?
Acts 15 records the Jerusalem Council wrestling with that very issue.
The apostles did not command Gentile converts to become Israel under the Mosaic covenant.
Yet—and this matters enormously—they did not conclude that grace means moral chaos.
They specifically instructed believers to abstain from idolatry, blood, things strangled, and sexual immorality (Acts 15:28–29).
Grace did not erase holiness.
Grace changed our covenant relationship to the Law.
That is why the Christian response to Leviticus 20:18 cannot simply be:
“That is Old Testament. Ignore it.”
No.
Christians should never be embarrassed by something God chose to reveal.
We should study it.
Understand its covenant setting.
Ask what it reveals about God's holiness.
Recognize how the New Testament treats the Mosaic covenant.
And then bring the entire matter to Christ.
So does Leviticus 20:18 mean Christians today should “cut off” a husband and wife who have sexual intercourse during menstruation?
Christians are not authorized by the New Testament to recreate ancient Israel’s covenant sanctions and impose Leviticus 20:18 as a civil or ecclesiastical penalty.
The Church is not ancient Israel's theocratic civil government.
Jesus established the New Covenant.
The apostolic Church did not simply transfer every Mosaic purity regulation and its associated national sanctions into Christian church discipline.
But that answer should not become an excuse for another dangerous error:
“Then Leviticus has nothing to teach us.”
It has everything to teach us about the God we worship.
It reminds us that God has never treated sexuality as spiritually meaningless.
Our culture often says that what consenting adults do sexually is nobody else's concern.
Scripture never gives sexuality that kind of spiritual independence.
Your body belongs to God.
Your marriage belongs to God.
Your desires belong under the lordship of Christ.
Your sexuality is not a tiny kingdom where Jesus has no throne.
Paul would later write:
—1 Corinthians 6:19–20, KJV
Read those words again.
“You are not your own.”
That sentence collides violently with modern individualism.
We want Jesus as Savior while keeping certain rooms locked.
My money.
My body.
My sexuality.
My relationship.
My entertainment.
My secret habits.
My private messages.
My browser history.
My resentment.
My addiction.
My hidden fantasy.
My life.
And Jesus stands at the door of every room we have labeled “private.”
Not because He wants to destroy us.
Because He purchased us.
The Christian life is not Jesus decorating the parts of your old life you are willing to show Him.
It is death and resurrection.
It is surrender.
And maybe that is why a strange verse in Leviticus can suddenly become painfully personal.
Because perhaps your issue has nothing to do with Leviticus 20:18.
Perhaps your issue is the room you refuse to surrender.
The relationship you know is pulling you from Christ.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The bitterness you have baptized as “boundaries.”
The affair hidden behind deleted messages.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The secret compromise you keep promising God you will abandon “soon.”
The Sunday worship followed by Monday surrender to the same chains.
You came here wondering about menstrual sex.
And somehow Scripture turned the mirror toward you.
That is what the Word of God does.
“For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword...”
—Hebrews 4:12, KJV
It cuts through our performances.
Through religious vocabulary.
Through excuses.
Through carefully edited Christian appearances.
And eventually it reaches the place where we cannot hide.
But please hear what happens next.
Because Christianity does not end with exposure.
If exposure were the end, every one of us would be finished.
The same Bible that reveals God's holiness reveals something even more astonishing.
A holy God came looking for unholy people.
Not with lowered standards.
With pierced hands.
Jesus did not come to announce that sin had stopped mattering.
He came because sin mattered so much that redemption would cost blood.
His blood.
The ancient sacrificial system had trained generations of Israelites to understand that approaching holiness was costly.
Then outside Jerusalem, the Lamb of God was nailed to wood.
Blood ran from His wounds.
The innocent for the guilty.
The righteous for the unrighteous.
The Holy One for sinners.
And suddenly the Bible's long story of holiness, sacrifice, blood, cleansing, covenant, priesthood, and forgiveness converged on a crucified Messiah.
Jesus was not Plan B.
He was the Lamb “foreordained before the foundation of the world” (1 Peter 1:20).
At the cross, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
He dealt with it.
And when Jesus rose from the dead, grace walked out of the tomb alive.
That is why there is hope for the sexually broken.
Hope for the adulterer.
Hope for the porn addict.
Hope for the ashamed.
Hope for the religious hypocrite.
Hope for the person who knew better and did it anyway.
Hope for the person carrying memories they wish they could erase.
Hope for the person reading this quietly thinking:
“If everyone knew what I had done, they would never look at me the same.”
Jesus already knows.
Every chapter.
Every deleted scene.
Every secret.
Every night.
Every compromise.
Every wound.
Every sin.
And the Gospel is not the announcement that those things do not matter.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ is greater.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
Cleanse.
There is a word Leviticus prepares us to understand.
We spend enormous energy trying to look clean.
Jesus came to make sinners clean.
Not through ritual performance.
Not through pretending.
Not through social-media Christianity.
Through His blood.
Through repentance.
Through faith.
Through grace.
Through a Savior who died and rose again.
Maybe you have spent years hiding.
Maybe people call you strong.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
Maybe you can quote Scripture while carrying a private war nobody sees.
Then stop performing for one moment.
God already knows.
You do not have to impress the One who watched you fall.
You need to surrender to the One who can raise you.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the door through which you stop running from the only One who can actually save you.
Turn to Jesus.
Confess what needs confessing.
Leave what needs leaving.
Repair what can be repaired.
Seek help where help is needed.
Bring darkness into light.
Not because obedience purchases salvation.
Because the Savior who purchased you is worthy of your obedience.
And if you stumbled onto this article because somebody shared it...
Maybe they were not judging you.
Maybe they were thinking about you because they love you.
Maybe this is the conversation you have avoided.
Maybe God is using an uncomfortable verse from Leviticus to remind you that He still wants every part of your life.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to write the details publicly.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become another person's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Neither honors the whole biblical story.
We need the Law.
We need the prophets.
We need the apostles.
And above all, we need Jesus Christ—the One toward whom the Scriptures lead.
That share matters more than you may realize.
Someone may be drifting from Christianity because nobody ever helped them understand the Bible in context.
Someone may be drowning in secret shame.
Someone may be convinced that what they have done has permanently disqualified them from grace.
Let this reach them.
At the cross, they meet.
Help us keep going.
Christian ministry requires people willing not only to receive but also to participate—to pray, share, serve, give, and help truth travel farther than it could travel without them.
Your giving before God is a matter of faithful Christian stewardship, conscience, and conviction.
Supporting Gospel work can glorify God when it flows from love for Christ rather than pressure, appearance, or manipulation.
Paul described Christian generosity this way:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
From the heart.
That is the kind of support we want.
But the deeper reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the person who is angry with God.
Invite the seeker with questions Christians sometimes seem afraid to answer.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing intelligent to say.
And keep sharing.
Because sometimes evangelism begins with a pulpit.
Sometimes it begins across a kitchen table.
And sometimes it begins when one Christian presses “Share” and a wounded person, alone at 1:37 in the morning, finds exactly the truth they were about to stop searching for.
Leviticus 20:18 is serious.
We should let it be serious.
It belonged to the covenant God made with Israel, and Christians should neither rip it from that covenant setting nor pretend it never existed.
It reminds us that the God of Scripture is holy.
It reminds us that sexuality belongs under His authority.
It reminds us that blood, purity, covenant, and access to God's presence run deeply through the biblical story.
But Leviticus is not the end of that story.
There is another covenant.
Another Priest.
Another sacrifice.
Another blood.
Jesus Christ entered the story.
And for the sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith, the final word is no longer simply:
Unclean.
Outcast.
Condemned.
The Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful.
Forgiven.
Cleansed.
Redeemed.
Adopted.
Made new.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear more than the answer to the original question.
God's holiness is more terrifying than modern Christianity sometimes admits.
Your sin is more serious than your excuses have allowed you to believe.
But the blood of Jesus is more powerful than the darkest chapter you have ever written.
So stop hiding.
Come home.
And remember this when shame tries to introduce you by your worst moment:
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story—but when Jesus takes the pen, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HE WHO FINDS A WIFE FINDS A GOOD THING” — BUT WHAT IF WE HAVE BEEN MAKING THIS VERSE PROMISE SOMETHING GOD NEVER SAID?
paragraphs: “HE WHO FINDS A WIFE FINDS A GOOD THING” — BUT WHAT IF WE HAVE BEEN MAKING THIS VERSE PROMISE SOMETHING GOD NEVER SAID?

Proverbs 18:22 is beautiful. It is also one of the easiest verses about marriage to quote, romanticize, weaponize, and misunderstand. What God actually said is better than the fantasy we sometimes attach to it.
“He who finds a wife finds a good thing, and obtains favor from the LORD.”
Proverbs 18:22.
You have probably heard it at weddings.
You have seen it beneath engagement photographs.
You may have watched someone post it after finally meeting the person they had prayed for.
Maybe you have whispered it yourself.
Maybe you are still waiting for it.
Or maybe reading those words hurts.
Because you found a wife... and your marriage has been difficult.
Because you became a wife... and discovered that a wedding ring does not magically turn two wounded human beings into spiritually mature people.
Because you prayed, waited, dated carefully, believed you had found “the one,” and still ended up heartbroken.

Or perhaps you are single, getting older, watching other people announce engagements, pregnancies, anniversaries, and family photographs while quietly wondering whether God somehow passed over your name.
Then this verse appears:
“He who finds a wife finds a good thing...”
And suddenly a beautiful proverb begins sounding like an accusation.
If marriage is favor, does singleness mean I am less favored?
If a wife is a good thing, does that mean every woman I desire is God's choice for me?
If I marry, is happiness guaranteed?
If my marriage is painful, did I marry the wrong person?
If I have not found a spouse, has God withheld something good because something is wrong with me?
Those questions deserve more than Christian clichés.
They deserve Scripture.
And when we slow down long enough to hear what the Bible actually says, Proverbs 18:22 becomes deeper, wiser, and far more beautiful than the slogan we sometimes make it.
The Hebrew reads:
מָצָא אִשָּׁה מָצָא טוֹב וַיָּפֶק רָצוֹן מֵיְהוָה
Matza ishah, matza tov; vayafeq ratzon me-YHWH.
In straightforward sense:
The one who finds a wife finds good and receives favor from YHWH.
The word מָצָא — māṣāʾ means to find, encounter, attain, or come upon.
אִשָּׁה — ʾiššâ can mean woman or wife according to context.
טוֹב — ṭôḇ is one of Scripture's great words for that which is good, beneficial, beautiful, desirable, or fitting.
And רָצוֹן — rāṣôn carries the sense of favor, goodwill, acceptance, or pleasure.
So yes.
Do not explain the verse away.
Marriage is good.
A godly wife is good.
A faithful husband is good.
Covenant companionship is good.
There is something genuinely beautiful about two people standing before God and saying, in effect, “My life is no longer only about me.”
Scripture does not apologize for celebrating marriage.
But notice something equally important.
The verse says a wife is a good thing.
It does not say a wife is the ultimate good thing.
It says marriage may be experienced as favor from the LORD.
It does not say marriage is the only evidence of God's favor.
And it certainly does not say:
“He who finds the person he is attracted to has found God's guaranteed soulmate.”
That verse is not in your Bible.
Neither is:
“He who gets married will never feel lonely again.”
Neither is:
“He who finds a wife will automatically have a peaceful marriage.”
Neither is:
“Every romantic relationship that feels supernatural was sent by God.”
Neither is:
“If you are still single, God is withholding His favor.”
We have to stop making God responsible for promises He never made.
Because sometimes the deepest disappointment in our spiritual lives comes not from God breaking His Word...
but from us attaching our expectations to His Word and calling those expectations promises.
Read Proverbs as Proverbs.
Biblical proverbs ordinarily communicate wisdom about how life works under God's moral order. They are not magical formulas guaranteeing identical outcomes in every circumstance.
“Train up a child in the way he should go...” does not turn parents into sovereign controllers of another human being's future choices.
“A soft answer turns away wrath” does not mean every furious person will immediately become peaceful.

And “he who finds a wife finds a good thing” does not mean putting a wedding ring on someone's finger guarantees fifty years without betrayal, conflict, sickness, grief, financial pressure, temptation, misunderstanding, or tears.
Marriage is good.
Marriage is also lived by sinners.
That changes everything.
Two people do not stop needing grace because they said, “I do.”
In many ways, marriage reveals how desperately they need it.
You can love Jesus and still communicate badly.
You can pray together and still hurt one another.
You can know Bible verses and still carry childhood wounds into your bedroom.
You can worship on Sunday and fight in the car on the way home.
You can genuinely love your spouse and, in a moment of selfishness, behave in ways that do not look much like love.
Marriage does not remove the old nature.
It gives the old nature fewer places to hide.
And perhaps that is part of marriage's severe mercy.
Someone begins seeing you up close.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
Not the carefully edited version.
The tired version.
The insecure version.
The irritated version.
The version that wants its own way.
The version that sometimes says, “Nothing's wrong,” when almost everything is wrong.
The version that needs forgiveness.
That is why Christian marriage cannot survive spiritually on romance alone.
Romance can bring two people to dinner.
Only covenant teaches them to remain at the table when the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Attraction may begin a relationship.
It cannot crucify pride.
Chemistry can make your heart race.
It cannot make you holy.
A beautiful wedding can gather hundreds of people into a room.
It cannot create the character required for a beautiful marriage.
Only Christ can transform the sinner.
That is where Proverbs 18:22 becomes even more meaningful when read beside Proverbs 19:14:
“House and riches are the inheritance of fathers: and a prudent wife is from the LORD.”
There is a difference between merely finding someone and recognizing godly character.

Proverbs itself refuses to teach that every wife, simply by occupying the marital position, automatically brings peace and wisdom into a household. Elsewhere the same book warns vividly about contentious relationships.
So Proverbs 18:22 cannot reasonably mean, “Any woman you marry will necessarily produce a wonderful marriage.”
The Bible is wiser than that.
The good being celebrated is God's beautiful design of covenant companionship rightly lived.
And that means the verse is not permission to become desperate.
Please hear this if loneliness has been making decisions for you.
You do not need to turn every attractive stranger into a prophecy.
You do not need to call chemistry “confirmation.”
You do not need to ignore character because somebody said they believe in God.
You do not need to overlook manipulation, deception, uncontrolled anger, habitual unfaithfulness, or contempt because you are afraid you will never find anyone else.
And you certainly do not need to marry someone merely because being alone has become painful.
Loneliness can make red flags look pink.
Desperation can make attention feel like love.

And when you have prayed for companionship for years, sometimes simply being wanted can feel so much like being answered that you stop asking whether the relationship actually resembles the wisdom of God.
But God never asks you to abandon wisdom in order to receive His gifts.
A godly marriage is not built merely on finding someone willing to marry you.
It is built through two people continually surrendering themselves to Christ.
And there is another side of this verse that the Church must say clearly.
Single Christian...
Proverbs 18:22 is not an insult to you.
Your unmarried life is not God's waiting room.
You are not half a Christian waiting for your other half to arrive.
Jesus Christ was not incomplete.
Paul was not spiritually defective because of singleness.

In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul speaks positively about both marriage and singleness and recognizes different gifts and callings from God. He even explains that unmarried believers may possess particular freedom to devote themselves to the Lord.
That means the Bible that says marriage is good is the same Bible that can say singleness is good.
There is no contradiction.
There are different gifts under the same Lord.
Your spouse cannot become your savior because you already have One.
And perhaps that is where some marriages quietly begin collapsing.
We ask another human being to carry messianic weight.
“Make me happy.”
“Make me secure.”
“Make me feel valuable.”
“Heal what my father did.”
“Repair what my mother never gave me.”
“Convince me I am attractive.”
“Make my loneliness disappear.”
“Complete me.”
That is too much weight for human shoulders.
Your husband cannot be Jesus.
Your wife cannot be Jesus.
And whenever we demand that a spouse provide what ultimately belongs to Christ, even a good marriage can begin suffocating beneath impossible expectations.
Marriage is a gift.
Christ is the Giver.
Never worship the gift.
Because every human marriage eventually reaches places where romance cannot save it.
There will be moments when forgiveness costs something.
Moments when repentance has to become more than a theological word.
Moments when “I was wrong” becomes harder to say than “I love you.”
Moments when grace stops being something you sing about and becomes something you must give to the person who wounded you.
And suddenly...
the Gospel is standing in your living room.
Because Christian marriage, at its deepest, points beyond itself.
Scripture presents the relationship between husband and wife against the breathtaking backdrop of Christ and His Church.
Jesus does not love His people because His people have always been lovable.
Look at us.
We wander.
We doubt.
We hide.
We make promises and break them.
We sin after swearing we would never do it again.
We bring Him hearts full of contradictions.
Yet Christ went to the cross.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because it mattered so much that blood was required.
Grace is not God pretending our scandal never happened.
Grace is God meeting guilty people inside the scandal and doing what they could never do for themselves.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus paid the debt.
Jesus rose from the grave.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
That is why the Gospel is bigger than marriage.
And this may be the sentence somebody reading this desperately needs tonight:
A spouse cannot rewrite your story.
Jesus can.
Maybe your marriage is beautiful right now.
Thank God.
Do not worship it.
Steward it.
Maybe your marriage is struggling.
Do not hide behind photographs.

Bring what is broken into the light. Seek biblical wisdom, repentance, wise pastoral counsel where appropriate, and qualified professional help when needed. Forgiveness never means calling evil good, and covenant faithfulness should never be twisted into permission for abuse or danger.
Maybe your marriage ended and you carry shame every time Christians talk about “successful families.”
Bring the wreckage to Jesus.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Jesus sees you.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Do not rename your sin, but do not run from the only Savior who can forgive sinners either.
Repent.
Come into the light.
The cross was built for guilty people.
Maybe you are widowed and still instinctively reach toward the other side of the bed.
Maybe you are single and tired of pretending you never ache for companionship.
Maybe everyone keeps telling you, “God is preparing someone,” even though Scripture never promised that every Christian will marry.
You do not need another cliché.
You need Christ.
Because whether married, divorced, widowed, abandoned, betrayed, waiting, healing, or happily single, your deepest identity cannot safely rest in your relationship status.
It must rest in Jesus.
“He who finds a wife finds a good thing.”
Yes.
Believe it.
Celebrate it.
Protect it from distortion.
But never turn “a good thing” into God Himself.
Marriage is not heaven.
Your spouse is not the Holy Spirit.
A wedding is not salvation.
And being chosen romantically is not the same thing as being chosen in Christ.
There is a greater love story running through Scripture.
Humanity ran from God.
We sinned.
We hid.
We rebelled.
And God did not respond by lowering His holiness and pretending rebellion was harmless.
He came for sinners.
The Son of God entered our world.
Jesus lived the righteousness we could not live.
He carried the judgment sinners deserved.
He was crucified.
Buried.
And He rose.
The ultimate answer to human loneliness is therefore not, “Find a spouse.”
It is:
Be reconciled to God.
And when Christ becomes the center, marriage can finally stop carrying the burden of being your god.
Then a husband can love his wife without possessing her.
A wife can love her husband without worshiping him.
Two imperfect people can repent.
Forgive.
Grow.
Fall down.
Get back up.
And keep walking toward Jesus.
Not because marriage magically fixes sinners.
Because Jesus transforms sinners.
Be honest.
Maybe you have idolized marriage.
Maybe you have judged single believers.
Maybe you have stayed desperate because you thought having someone—anyone—was better than being alone with God.
Maybe you are married and have spent years demanding from your spouse what only Christ can give.
Maybe you are the one who needs to repent.
Maybe you are simply tired.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance, grace, forgiveness, wise help, and patient obedience still matter.

Not because you need another post sitting in a folder, but because feelings have short memories. There may come a day when loneliness starts preaching to you again. There may come a night when disappointment begins rewriting what God actually said.
Come back.
Read the verse again.

Following Gospel Warrior also helps you stay connected to daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment. Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who is not sure what they believe yet.
It does not.
Not because financial support can buy blessing, forgiveness, salvation, or a better standing before God.
It cannot.

And not because supporting Gospel Warrior should be presented as replacing whatever your conscience and biblical convictions lead you to give through your local church, generosity to people in need, missions, or other faithful Christian work.

But voluntary financial support can be an act of Christian generosity and stewardship when it is given freely, wisely, cheerfully, and for the advancement of work you genuinely believe is bearing good fruit.
It helps us keep reaching the person scrolling alone at two in the morning.
The marriage quietly falling apart.
The believer wrestling with temptation.
The prodigal wondering whether Jesus would still receive them.
The wounded Christian who almost gave up.
The seeker who has never understood grace.
The person who will never comment but reads every word.
And the soul we may never meet on this side of eternity.
