That matters because this was never supposed to be about building consumers.
It is about making disciples.
Come to Jesus.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have wandered, return.
If you have been hiding, step into the light.
If your marriage has become an idol, put Christ back on the throne.
If singleness has become bitterness, bring the bitterness to Him.
If heartbreak has convinced you that God abandoned you, bring Him the questions you are afraid to say aloud.
If shame keeps whispering that your story is already ruined...
look at the cross.
Christianity begins with a scandal human beings could never have invented their way out of:
sinners guilty before a holy God.
And then came grace.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Cross-shaped grace.
Empty-tomb grace.
The kind of grace that does not merely improve your public image.
The kind that raises dead things.
So yes...
“He who finds a wife finds a good thing.”
Treasure the truth.
But remember the greater truth.
The greatest thing that can happen to a man is not that he finds a wife.
The greatest thing that can happen to a woman is not that she finds a husband.
The greatest thing that can happen to either of them is that, by grace, they belong to Jesus Christ.
Because eventually every earthly marriage reaches its final day.
Every photograph ages.
Every anniversary count eventually stops.
Every hand we hold in this life must someday be released unless Christ returns first.
But the redeemed will never reach the end of Christ.
So love your spouse.
Pray for your future spouse if marriage is something you desire.
Honor marriage.
Honor faithful singleness.
Seek wisdom instead of desperation.
Repent quickly.
Forgive biblically.
Love sacrificially.
And never ask a human being to sit on a throne that belongs to Jesus.
Because sometimes the “good thing” God gives you is not meant to become the center of your story.
It is meant to lead your eyes back to the One who is.
Your wedding ring may tell the world whom you married—but only the scars in the hands of Jesus can tell you how completely you are loved.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF JESUS FULFILLED THE LAW, WHY DO BIBLICAL SEXUAL LAWS STILL FEEL SO PERSONAL?
paragraphs: IF JESUS FULFILLED THE LAW, WHY DO BIBLICAL SEXUAL LAWS STILL FEEL SO PERSONAL?

The uncomfortable question many Christians quietly ask: If we are under grace, not the Mosaic covenant, what exactly does Jesus expect us to do with the Bible’s sexual boundaries—and what happens when those boundaries reach into the most private room of our lives?
There is a moment when Christianity stops being theoretical.
It usually does not happen while you are sitting comfortably in church.
It happens when Scripture touches something you love.
Something you want.
Something you have already justified.

Something connected to your body, your relationship, your memories, your loneliness, your marriage, your attraction, your secret browser history, your private conversations, your past, your shame—or the person you cannot imagine surrendering.
Suddenly the Bible is no longer an ancient book sitting politely on a shelf.
It is standing in your bedroom.
And that is when one of the most emotionally loaded questions in Christianity comes crawling out of the shadows:
“If Jesus fulfilled the Law, why should Christians still care about biblical sexual laws?”
Maybe you have wondered it.
Maybe somebody you love has asked it.
Maybe you have heard someone say:
“Christians eat pork.”
“Christians wear mixed fabrics.”
“Christians do not offer animal sacrifices.”
“So why do Christians suddenly quote the Old Testament when sex enters the conversation?”
That question deserves more than a slogan.
It deserves more than outrage.
And it certainly deserves more than Christians throwing isolated Bible verses at hurting people as though winning an argument were the same thing as winning a soul.
Because behind many theological questions about sexuality is a human being.
Sometimes frightened.
Sometimes confused.
Sometimes wounded.
Sometimes genuinely searching.
Sometimes desperately hoping God will approve what the heart already wants.
And sometimes quietly terrified that He will not.
So before we go any further, hear this:
Jesus did fulfill the Law.
Completely.
Gloriously.
Perfectly.
But “Jesus fulfilled the Law” does not mean, “Therefore nothing God ever revealed about holiness matters anymore.”
Jesus Himself said:
“Μὴ νομίσητε ὅτι ἦλθον καταλῦσαι τὸν νόμον ἢ τοὺς προφήτας· οὐκ ἦλθον καταλῦσαι ἀλλὰ πληρῶσαι.”
“Do not think that I came to destroy the Law or the Prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.”
Matthew 5:17.
The crucial Greek word is πληρῶσαι — plērōsai, from plēroō: to fulfill, fill up, bring to completion.
And notice the word Jesus deliberately contrasts it with:
καταλῦσαι — katalysai.
To tear down. Destroy. Demolish. Abolish.
Jesus is not announcing that God's previous revelation was embarrassing and He had arrived to erase it.
He is declaring that it reaches its intended fulfillment in Him.
That distinction changes everything.
Because Christians do not approach Moses as though Jesus never came.
But neither do Christians approach Jesus as though Moses never existed.
We read the whole story through Christ.

The Torah revealed God's holiness, exposed human sin, formed Israel as God's covenant people, anticipated realities ultimately fulfilled in Christ, and carried Israel through a particular covenant administration.
Then Jesus came.
Not as another lamb standing beside the altar.
As the Lamb.
Not as another priest repeating sacrifices.
As the One to whom the sacrifices were pointing.
Not merely as another teacher interpreting God's revelation.
As the Son in whom God's redemptive purposes reach their climax.
That is why the New Testament can say things that initially seem almost contradictory.

Galatians says the Law functioned as a guardian until Christ, and that with the coming of faith God's people are no longer under that guardian. Hebrews speaks explicitly of the new covenant and describes the former covenant as obsolete.
So Christians are not ancient Israelites living under the Sinai covenant.
We do not rebuild the Levitical priesthood.
We do not return to animal sacrifices.
We do not seek justification by keeping Torah.
We do not pretend Calvary never happened.
But here comes the part that makes the question intensely personal.
When the apostles brought the Gospel to Gentiles—people who had never lived as Jews under the Mosaic covenant—they did not conclude:
“Jesus fulfilled the Law, therefore sexual conduct no longer matters.”
Quite the opposite.

At the Jerusalem Council, while explicitly refusing to require Gentile converts to take on the whole Mosaic covenant as the means of belonging to God's people, the apostles still instructed them to abstain from πορνεία — porneia, sexual immorality.
The Greek of Acts 15:20 contains the unmistakable phrase:
“ἀπέχεσθαι … τῆς πορνείας”
—to abstain from sexual immorality.
That should make us stop.
Because these are Gentile Christians.
This is after the resurrection.
After the cross.
After Christ fulfilled the Law.
And sexual holiness did not disappear.
Paul tells the Thessalonian believers:
“τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν, ἀπέχεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς πορνείας”
“For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality.”
1 Thessalonians 4:3.
Read that slowly.
Your sanctification.
Not your humiliation.
Not God's attempt to make you miserable.
Not God's embarrassment over the human body.
Sanctification.
Being made holy.
Belonging increasingly and visibly to God.
This is where many modern conversations go wrong.
We ask:
“How close can I get to the boundary without technically sinning?”
The New Testament asks something far more beautiful and far more terrifying:
“How completely can this body belong to Christ?”
That changes the conversation.
Christian sexual ethics are not ultimately built upon disgust for the body.
They are built upon the breathtaking value God gives the body.
Paul does not tell Christians that their bodies are worthless.
He says something almost shocking:
Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
You are not your own.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
There it is.
The Gospel enters the bedroom.
Not because Jesus is obsessed with catching people doing something dirty.
Because Jesus purchased the whole person.
Your Sunday morning belongs to Him.
Your bank account belongs under His lordship.
Your anger belongs under His lordship.
Your ambitions belong under His lordship.
Your mouth belongs under His lordship.
Your phone belongs under His lordship.
Your sexuality belongs under His lordship.
Your body belongs under His lordship.
Grace never meant:
“Jesus forgave me, therefore my body is irrelevant.”
Grace means something infinitely greater:
“Jesus bought me, therefore even my body can become an instrument of worship.”
And this is why simplistic arguments about “Old Testament sexual laws” often fail.

Leviticus 18 does contain sexual prohibitions. It forbids various incestuous unions, adultery, child sacrifice in connection with Molech, male-male intercourse, and bestiality, among other prohibited practices. The chapter also portrays these practices as defiling and connects them not only with Israel but with the nations occupying the land before Israel.
But Christians should not simply grab Leviticus, ignore the covenantal storyline, and declare the interpretive work finished.
We must ask what happens after Christ comes.
Does the New Testament reaffirm sexual holiness?
Yes.
Does it continue to condemn porneia?
Repeatedly.
Does the apostolic church tell Gentile Christians to abstain from sexual immorality?
Yes.
Does Paul apply an Old Testament sexual boundary involving a man's father's wife directly to a Christian congregation?

Yes. In 1 Corinthians 5, Paul condemns a relationship involving “his father's wife,” showing that at least some sexual boundaries known from Torah remain morally relevant in apostolic Christian instruction.
Does the New Testament teach that keeping Mosaic Law earns salvation?
No.
That is the distinction we desperately need.
A Christian does not refuse sexual sin in order to purchase salvation.
A Christian pursues holiness because salvation has been purchased by Christ.
Those are completely different religions.
One says:
“Obey so God might accept you.”
The Gospel says:
“In Christ, you have been received by grace; now learn to live as someone who belongs to Him.”
One produces pride when you succeed and despair when you fail.
The other produces gratitude, repentance, dependence, and transformation.
And perhaps this is where the conversation stops being theological and becomes painfully personal.
Because maybe you did not click this article because you wanted a lesson about Greek verbs.
Maybe there is a name in your head right now.
A relationship.
A habit.
A night you cannot erase.
A secret.
Maybe you already crossed boundaries you once promised God you never would.
Maybe you have been sleeping beside someone while quietly wondering whether Jesus approves.
Maybe pornography has trained your mind to consume bodies while nobody in church knows.
Maybe your marriage has become sexually cold, and temptation suddenly feels less theoretical.
Maybe somebody used Scripture to shame you so brutally that whenever Christians speak about sexual holiness, you hear condemnation before you hear Jesus.
Maybe you are carrying sexual wounds that were inflicted upon you rather than chosen by you.
Hear this distinction carefully:
Being sinned against is not the same as committing the sin done against you.
Someone else's violation does not make you spiritually contaminated beyond Christ's reach.
And if you were abused, exploited, assaulted, manipulated, or coerced, the Gospel does not ask you to carry the perpetrator's guilt as though it belonged to you.
Jesus is not standing over wounded people saying,
“Disgusting.”
He is the Savior who touched people society would not touch.
The Savior who ate with sinners.
The Savior who confronted hypocrisy.
The Savior who spoke truth without needing cruelty.
The Savior who called people to repentance while opening His arms to repentant sinners.
This is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
Because Jesus neither tells us that sin does not matter nor tells sinners that they are beyond redemption.
He does something far more astonishing.
He takes sin seriously enough to die for it.
And loves sinners deeply enough to die for them.
That is Calvary.
Truth without grace becomes a hammer in human hands.
Grace without truth becomes permission to remain imprisoned.
But in Jesus Christ, grace and truth meet.
He does not save us by pretending darkness is light.
He enters our darkness and leads us out.
That means repentance is not God demanding that you destroy yourself.
Repentance is turning toward the One who came to rescue you.
And yes...
sometimes repentance hurts.
Sometimes following Jesus means surrendering something that feels woven into your identity.
Sometimes obedience means deleting a number.
Ending a relationship.
Confessing to your spouse.
Installing accountability.
Leaving the room.
Closing the browser.
Calling a pastor.
Seeking wise Christian counseling.
Admitting that what you called “freedom” has actually been mastering you.
Sometimes discipleship feels like death because Jesus really does call us to take up a cross.
But Christianity has never taught that every desire inside us automatically possesses moral authority simply because we experience it intensely.
Every disciple eventually discovers desires that must be surrendered.
Sexual desires.
Financial desires.
Desires for revenge.
Desires for status.
Desires for control.
Desires for applause.
Desires for comfort.
Desires to hate.
Desires to hide.
The question is not merely:
“What do I desire?”
The deeper Christian question is:
“Who is Lord of what I desire?”
And the answer cannot be Moses.
It cannot be your pastor.
It cannot be your denomination.
It cannot be your political tribe.
It cannot be social media.
It cannot even be your feelings.
For the Christian, the answer is Jesus Christ.
That does not make biblical interpretation easy.

Sincere Christians and Christian traditions have disagreed over precisely how Old Testament commands should be categorized and applied under the new covenant. The familiar categories of moral, ceremonial, and civil law can be useful theological tools, but the Bible itself does not present Leviticus with modern headings marking every command with those three labels.
So humility matters.
Context matters.
Biblical theology matters.
Jesus matters.
The apostles matter.
We should neither flatten the covenants into one nor cut the Old Testament away from Christian Scripture.
We follow the storyline all the way to Christ.
And when we do, something becomes difficult to escape:
The New Testament does not lower the significance of sexual holiness after Jesus.
It roots holiness more deeply in union with Jesus.
Paul's argument is not merely:
“Moses prohibited something.”
His argument becomes:
You belong to Christ.
Your body matters because Christ redeemed you.
Your sexual conduct matters because your body is for the Lord.
Your holiness matters because the Holy Spirit dwells in God's people.
Suddenly the question changes.
Not:
“Can Christians find a technical exemption?”
But:
“Does this glorify the Jesus who bought me with His blood?”
That question reaches places legalism never can.
Because legalism wants the minimum requirement.
Love asks how much of me belongs to Him.
And the Gospel answers:
All of you.
But perhaps you are thinking:
“You don't know what I've done.”
No.
But Jesus does.
“You don't know how many times I've fallen.”
Jesus does.
“You don't know what I watched.”
He knows.
“You don't know who I slept with.”
He knows.
“You don't know the lies.”
He knows.
“You don't know what happened to me.”
He knows that too.
And still the cross stands.
That is the scandal.
The holy Son of God knew exactly what humanity was—and came anyway.

He did not wait for prostitutes, adulterers, addicts, hypocrites, liars, religious frauds, sexually broken people, sexually wounded people, and self-righteous people to become clean enough to approach Him.
He came looking for sinners.
But He loves us too much to make peace with whatever is destroying us.
Grace says:
“Come as you are.”
Discipleship says:
“You cannot remain exactly as you were.”
The cross says both.
Come.
And die.
Come.
And live.
Come with your shame.
Come with your desires.
Come with your history.
Come with your questions.
Come with your confusion.
Come with the thing you are terrified to surrender.
But come to Jesus.
Not to a Jesus redesigned to agree with us.
To the crucified and risen Christ who loves us enough to forgive us and has authority enough to transform us.
Maybe you have spent years asking God to endorse your desires.
Perhaps tonight the prayer becomes:
“Jesus, teach my desires to bow to You.”
That prayer is dangerous.
Because He may touch something.
But He may also free something.
And perhaps what you thought would be the funeral of your happiness becomes the beginning of your freedom.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sexual history publicly.
If you need prayer, simply write:

And if Christ has already rescued you from sexual bondage, shame, pornography, adultery, destructive relationships, or years of secret compromise, consider sharing what God has done without exposing details that should remain private.
Someone reading the comments may believe they are the only person Jesus could never restore.
Your testimony may become the sentence that keeps them from running away.
Not because everybody needs another religious argument on Facebook.
Someone may be trapped between desire and discipleship.
Someone may believe sexual failure permanently disqualified them from Christ.
Someone may be searching for permission when what their soul actually needs is freedom.
Someone may need to discover that holiness and grace are not enemies.
It does not.
Not because paying Gospel Warrior saves you.
Only Jesus saves.

Christians and churches differ in how they understand tithing under the new covenant, and your responsibility to support your local church and other ministries should be approached prayerfully, faithfully, and according to conscience before God.
But voluntary financial partnership with Gospel ministry is thoroughly compatible with the New Testament pattern of believers generously supporting Gospel work.
If you want your resources to glorify God, prayerfully consider whether supporting this work should become part of your voluntary Christian giving.
Your support helps keep the work moving.
Your share helps this message cross a wall money cannot cross.
Your comment tells another struggling believer, “You are not fighting alone.”
And your prayers matter more than any algorithm ever will.
Pray.
Read.
Grow.
Send it privately to somebody who needs it.
Because ultimately this article was never merely about sex.
It was about lordship.
It was about what happens when Jesus reaches the one room of our lives where we desperately want the final word.
The question is not whether you have a scandal in your story.
Some scandals are public.
Others have passwords.
Some happened because of what we chose.
Others because of what someone did to us.
Some live in bedrooms.
Some live inside memories.
Some are hidden behind wedding photographs and Sunday smiles.
The question is what happens when the scandal meets Jesus.
Because at the cross, Christ does not merely expose sin.
He pays for sin.
He does not merely command repentance.
He makes restoration possible.
He does not merely tell the sexually broken to become clean.
He gives Himself to make sinners clean.
So bring Him the relationship.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the adultery.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the confusion.
Bring Him the wounds.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the desires you understand.
Bring Him the desires you do not understand.
Bring Him the past you cannot rewrite.
Then watch what happens when the Author of resurrection takes the pen.
Your past may explain the scars—but it does not get to write the final sentence after Jesus takes hold of the story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Forgave Your Parents for What They Did. Now You Have to Grieve What They Never Gave You.
paragraphs: You Forgave Your Parents for What They Did. Now You Have to Grieve What They Never Gave You.

Some childhood wounds are not memories of what happened. They are memories of what never happened—and forgiving the people who failed you does not mean pretending you were never wounded by what was missing.
Maybe you already forgave them.
Maybe you prayed the prayer.
Maybe you stopped replaying the arguments.
Maybe you stopped demanding an apology you finally realized might never come.
Maybe you surrendered the anger to Jesus because carrying it was poisoning places inside you that your parents could no longer even see.
And perhaps you thought that was supposed to be the end of the story.
So why does something inside you still ache?
Why can a father hugging his grown daughter in an airport make your throat tighten?
Why can watching a mother speak gently to her child awaken something you cannot explain?
Why does hearing someone say, “My parents always believed in me,” sometimes make you genuinely happy for them...
and strangely sad for yourself?
You forgave what they did.
But perhaps nobody ever told you that you may still need to grieve what they never gave you.
The affection that never came.
The protection you needed but did not receive.
The words, “I’m proud of you.”
The apology.
The safety.
The consistency.
The bedtime conversations.
The father who should have shown up.
The mother who should have listened.
The home where you should not have needed to study everybody’s mood before deciding whether it was safe to speak.
The childhood where being a child should have been enough.
There are wounds caused by something terrible happening.
And there are wounds created by something beautiful never happening at all.
Sometimes the second kind is harder to explain because there is no single scene to point toward.
No photograph of absence.
No scar with a date written underneath it.
Only an empty chair inside the heart.
And sometimes that empty chair follows you into adulthood.
It follows you into friendships.
Into marriage.
Into parenting.
Into church.
Sometimes even into prayer.
You wonder why reassurance matters so much to you.
Why silence can feel like rejection.
Why conflict makes something inside you panic.
Why receiving affection feels wonderful and frightening at the same time.
Why you keep trying to prove that you are useful enough, spiritual enough, successful enough, generous enough, strong enough...
to deserve being kept.
And somewhere beneath the adult you became is still the child who learned a devastating question far too early:
“Am I worth staying for?”
Then Psalm 27:10 speaks.
Not with shallow optimism.
Not by pretending parents never fail.
Not by demanding that wounded people call abandonment love.
It says:
כִּי־אָבִי וְאִמִּי עֲזָבוּנִי וַיהוָה יַאַסְפֵנִי
Ki avi ve’immi azavuni, vaYHWH ya’asfeni.
The Hebrew expresses the thought: though father and mother forsake me, the LORD will gather or receive me.
That final word is breathtaking.
יַאַסְפֵנִי — ya’asfeni.

It comes from the Hebrew verb אָסַף — ’asaph, carrying the sense of gathering, collecting, receiving or taking in. In Psalm 27:10, the word has been understood with the beautiful implication of taking someone into care and protection.
Read that again.
The Scripture does not have to deny the abandonment in order to proclaim the faithfulness of God.
The verse contains both realities.
They may forsake me.
The LORD will gather me.
That matters.
Because biblical faith is not pretending the first half never happened so you can celebrate the second half.
David's poetry has room for both.
Human failure is named.
Divine faithfulness is named.
Loss is acknowledged.
God is trusted.
And perhaps that is where your healing has been stuck.
You thought forgiving meant you were no longer allowed to be sad.
It does not.
Forgiveness and grief are not enemies.
Forgiveness says, “I will not make vengeance my god.”
Grief says, “What was lost actually mattered.”
Forgiveness says, “I release judgment into God's hands.”
Grief says, “I wish this had been different.”
Forgiveness refuses to become consumed by the debt.
Grief acknowledges there really was a debt.
Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to leave vengeance to God. He does not tell them that evil must therefore be renamed good.
And when Paul describes forgiveness in Ephesians 4:32, the Greek says:
χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς καθὼς καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐν Χριστῷ ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν

Believers are called to forgive one another as God in Christ forgave them. The verb is related to grace—χαρίζομαι, charizomai—and Paul places Christian forgiveness squarely in the grace believers themselves have received in Christ.
But forgiveness does not require rewriting history.
Jesus never needed lies in order to produce grace.
And neither do you.
You can forgive your father and still admit that you needed him.
You can forgive your mother and still acknowledge that something important was missing.
You can love your parents and tell the truth about your childhood.
You can honor them without calling every decision they made honorable.
You can release vengeance without surrendering wisdom.
You can pray for someone and still recognize that trust, where it has been deeply damaged, is not identical to forgiveness.
You can stop demanding that yesterday change...
and still cry because it never will.
Some of you need permission to cry over something that happened thirty years ago.
Not because you want to live in the past.
Because you finally became safe enough to tell the truth about it.
You survived by minimizing.
“They did their best.”
“Other people had it worse.”
“At least I had food.”
“At least nobody hit me.”
“At least they stayed married.”
“At least they took me to church.”
Perhaps some of those things are true.
But gratitude for what you received does not require dishonesty about what you did not.
Two things can be true at once.
Your parents may have been wounded people themselves...
and they may have wounded you.
They may have loved you in the only ways they understood...
and those ways may still have been painfully insufficient.
They may have carried trauma they never learned to name...
and you may now be carrying consequences you never volunteered to inherit.
Understanding their story can produce compassion.
It does not require erasing yours.
And this is where the Gospel becomes far more beautiful than sentimental religion.
Christianity does not begin with human beings pretending nothing went wrong.
It begins with the declaration that something went catastrophically wrong—and that God came to rescue sinners.
The cross itself destroys the fantasy that love means ignoring evil.
If sin were insignificant, Calvary would be unnecessary.
At the cross, God does not pretend sin is harmless.
He deals with it.
And there Jesus Christ does something no wounded child, wounded adult, wounded parent, or wounded family could ever accomplish alone.
He bears sin.
He offers forgiveness.
He reconciles sinners to God.
He breaks condemnation.
He opens the household of God to those who come to Him.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace enters the darkness and redeems people from it.
That means Jesus does not need you to lie about your wound before He heals you.
He already knows.
He knew about the birthdays when someone important did not come.
He knew about the words you desperately wanted to hear.
He knew about the nights you cried quietly because crying loudly caused problems.
He knew every time you became the peacemaker in a home where adults should have been protecting you.
He knew when you learned to become funny so nobody noticed you were hurting.
He knew when achievement became your way of asking, “Am I worth loving now?”
He knew when you became fiercely independent because depending on people had disappointed you too many times.
He knew.
And He knows the adult version of you too.
The one who says, “I’m fine.”
The one everybody calls strong.
The one who takes care of everyone.
The one who knows how to encourage everybody except the frightened person staring back from the mirror.
Maybe nobody abandoned you physically.
Maybe they were sitting three feet away from you your entire childhood.
But emotionally...
you were alone.
That kind of loneliness can be difficult to explain.
A person can live inside a full house and still grow up starving for tenderness.
And if this is your story, hear Psalm 27 again:
יַאַסְפֵנִי.
Ya’asfeni.
The LORD gathers me.
Not because earthly family is meaningless.
Precisely because it matters so deeply, its failure hurts.
God does not mock that need.
He meets His people in it.
But there is another difficult truth.
God's fatherly care does not mean every consequence of childhood pain disappears overnight.

Sometimes Christ heals through a long process of truth, repentance, prayer, Scripture, wise pastoral care, healthy Christian community, reconciliation where genuinely possible, appropriate boundaries where necessary, and sometimes skilled professional help.
There is no shame in admitting that something still hurts.
The danger is allowing the wound to become your permanent identity.
Your parents may explain part of your story.
They do not own its ending.
Their absence does not get the final sentence.
Their failure does not get to name you forever.
Their inability to affirm you does not determine your value before God.
Their rejection does not possess authority over the verdict of Christ.
For everyone who receives Christ and believes in His name, Scripture speaks of becoming children of God.
Think about that.
The Gospel does not merely offer you techniques for surviving rejection.
It brings you into a new relationship with God through Jesus Christ.
You are not saved because you had good parents.
You are not disqualified because you had broken ones.
You are not redeemed because your family finally understands you.
You are redeemed through Christ.
Maybe your parents never said the words you needed.
Maybe they are gone now.
Maybe dementia took the conversation away.
Maybe death closed the door.
Maybe pride closed it years before death ever could.
Maybe reconciliation remains possible, and God is slowly softening hearts.
Maybe wisdom requires distance right now.
Different stories will require different forms of faithfulness.
But one truth remains:
You do not have to spend the rest of your life standing outside yesterday, knocking on a door that cannot be opened.
You can grieve.
Really grieve.
Not performatively.
Not bitterly.
Not as someone worshiping pain.
As someone finally placing the truth before Jesus.
“Lord, I wanted my father.”
“Lord, I needed my mother.”
“Lord, I needed protection.”
“I needed affection.”
“I needed someone to tell me I mattered.”
“I needed home to feel safe.”
“I needed them to notice.”
“I forgive them...
but Lord, it still hurts.”
Perhaps one of the holiest things you can do tonight is stop editing that prayer.
Jesus already knows the unedited version.
Bring Him that one.
Bring Him the disappointment.
Bring Him the anger you are ashamed of.
Bring Him the jealousy you sometimes feel when you see healthy families.
Bring Him the questions.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him the empty chair.

Repent where your pain has turned into your own sin. Forgive as Christ commands. Refuse revenge. Seek reconciliation where it is wise and possible. Refuse to let bitterness become the inheritance you pass to the next generation.
But do not confuse repentance with pretending.
Do not confuse forgiveness with amnesia.
Do not confuse honoring your parents with denying reality.
And do not confuse grieving with unbelief.
There is a difference between living inside the wound and bringing the wound to Jesus.
One imprisons you.
The other opens your hands before the One who can redeem what you cannot rewrite.
And perhaps that is why this hurts so much to read.
Because you are not merely grieving your parents.
You are grieving the version of yourself you might have been if home had felt safer.
The child who might have laughed more freely.
The teenager who might not have needed approval from dangerous people.
The adult who might not have spent years confusing attention with love.
The husband who wishes he knew how to receive tenderness.
The wife who wonders why disagreement feels like abandonment.
The parent desperately trying not to repeat what was done to them.
You may even be grieving the relationship you still wish you could have today.
And grief sometimes whispers:
“It is too late.”
But the Gospel answers with something stronger.
Not, “Nothing was lost.”
Something was.
Not, “Nothing happened.”
Something did.
The Gospel says loss does not possess the authority to determine the final outcome of a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
That is redemption.
That is why our message has never been “your scandal did not matter.”
It is:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not rewrite history by falsifying yesterday.
He rewrites what yesterday is permitted to become in the hands of grace.
What wounded you can become a place where compassion grows.
What exposed you to darkness can make you fiercely committed to bringing your own children into light.
What taught you instability can make you treasure faithfulness.
What made you ache for tenderness can become the reason someone else encounters tenderness through you.
Not because trauma is good.
Not because abandonment was God's ideal.
Not because evil secretly deserves gratitude.
But because Christ is so sovereign, so merciful, and so redemptive that even what He hates can be overruled for purposes darkness never intended.
The cross proves it.
Human beings committed the greatest injustice in history against the sinless Son of God.
Yet through that very cross, God accomplished redemption.
The scandal became the place where grace was displayed.
And then came resurrection.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Resurrection.
So maybe today is not the day you “get over it.”
Maybe today is the day you stop hiding it.
Maybe you finally say:
“Yes. I forgive them.
And yes.
I am still grieving.”
Those sentences can exist together.
Then place both into the hands of Jesus.
You do not owe strangers the details.
But you also do not have to keep pretending you are the only believer carrying this kind of ache.
Someone reading the comments may discover for the first time that they are not alone.
And if you know someone who has spent years trying to forgive complicated parents while secretly feeling guilty for still grieving, send this to them.
Save it too.
Because healing is rarely one conversation.
There may come a night when the old ache returns and you need to remember one Hebrew word:
יַאַסְפֵנִי.
Ya’asfeni.
The LORD gathers me.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, or a deeper hunger for Jesus Christ, you can also help this ministry continue and expand.

Scripture says Christian giving should be willing rather than compelled: “ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης”—each person giving as decided in the heart, not from compulsion. Paul also describes generosity that supplies ministry needs and results in thanksgiving and glory to God.
Your support helps us keep sowing.
It helps us reach farther.
It helps us keep placing the name of Jesus into timelines where despair, anger, temptation, loneliness, unbelief, and spiritual exhaustion are already competing for people's attention.
A share can become ministry.
A tag can become an invitation.
A comment can help another wounded believer realize someone understands.
A saved article can become the truth someone returns to at 2:00 in the morning.
A follow can keep Scripture appearing in a feed filled with everything except Scripture.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not believe yet.
Invite the person who quietly wants to come home to God but does not know where to begin.
It cannot.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
Not because generosity earns grace.
Grace cannot be bought.
Support because the Gospel has made you generous.
Support because you believe biblical truth should keep traveling.
Support because somebody you will never meet may encounter Jesus through something your generosity helped place before them.
You can still share.
You can still comment.
You can still follow.
You can still help carry truth into another person's darkness.
Most importantly, you can surrender yourself again to Jesus.
Because eventually every childhood story reaches a place money cannot repair.
Every apology reaches a limit.
Every parent reaches a limit.
Every human relationship reaches a limit.
But Christ does not.
So grieve what you never received.
Forgive what must be forgiven.
Repent of what your wounds taught you to do to others.
Seek wisdom where relationships remain complicated.
Tell the truth without becoming enslaved to bitterness.
And when the child inside you asks one more time—
“Who will take me in?”
Remember the ancient words:
כִּי־אָבִי וְאִמִּי עֲזָבוּנִי וַיהוָה יַאַסְפֵנִי
When even the closest human love fails...
the LORD gathers me.
You may never receive the childhood you should have had.
But in Jesus Christ, the absence that wounded you does not get to write the ending.
Some people spend their whole lives waiting for yesterday to come back and love them—when Jesus is already standing in today, calling them home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “SPREAD YOUR WINGS OVER ME”: WAS RUTH PROPOSING MARRIAGE TO BOAZ IN THE MIDDLE OF THE NIGHT?
paragraphs: “SPREAD YOUR WINGS OVER ME”: WAS RUTH PROPOSING MARRIAGE TO BOAZ IN THE MIDDLE OF THE NIGHT?

What Ruth whispered to Boaz in the darkness was far more daring than it sounds in English—and the Hebrew reveals a breathtaking connection between vulnerability, covenant, redemption, and the God who gathers broken people beneath His wings.
There are sentences in the Bible that sound almost ordinary until you read them in the language in which they were written.
Then suddenly…
the room changes.
The words become heavier.
The scene becomes more intimate.
And something you may have read a dozen times suddenly reaches through the centuries and grabs you by the heart.
Ruth 3:9 contains one of those sentences.
It happens in the middle of the night.
A man wakes unexpectedly.
A woman is lying near his feet.
He cannot immediately recognize her.
And then comes the question:
“Who are you?”
Her answer would alter the direction of her life.
“I am Ruth your servant. Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer.”
That sounds beautiful.
But the Hebrew is even more striking.
Ruth says:
אָנֹכִי רוּת אֲמָתֶךָ וּפָרַשְׂתָּ כְנָפֶךָ עַל־אֲמָתְךָ כִּי גֹאֵל אָתָּה
ʾĀnōḵî Rûṯ ʾămāṯeḵā; ûp̄āraśtā ḵənāp̄eḵā ʿal-ʾămāṯeḵā, kî gōʾēl ʾāttāh.
“I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wing over your servant, because you are a redeemer.”
כְּנָפֶךָ — kenāfekha.
“Your wing.”
That one Hebrew word unlocks the scene.
And once you see what Ruth was saying, you may never read her story the same way again.
Because Ruth was not merely asking Boaz for a blanket.
She was asking for covenant.
She was placing her vulnerable future before a man who possessed the ability—and, subject to the proper redemption process, the opportunity—to act as a family redeemer.
In the world of Ruth, this was breathtakingly bold.
Yet there is something even more beautiful happening.
Ruth was effectively returning Boaz’s own words to him.
Earlier, when Boaz first learned of Ruth’s loyalty to Naomi, he blessed her:
“The LORD repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.”
That is Ruth 2:12.
And the Hebrew word translated “wings” there comes from the same word:
כָּנָף — kānāf.
Wing.
Covering.
Extremity or edge of a garment, depending on context.
Boaz had told Ruth that she had come beneath the wings of the God of Israel.
Then, sometime later, Ruth stood—or more precisely, lay—at Boaz’s feet and essentially said:
Then become part of the answer to that prayer.
“Spread your wing over me.”
Think about that.
Boaz prayed for God to shelter Ruth beneath His wings.
God’s providence would involve calling Boaz himself to participate in that sheltering redemption.
Sometimes we pray, “Lord, help them,” and God answers:
“I intend to. Now obey Me.”
Sometimes we ask God to feed someone, encourage someone, protect someone, forgive someone, restore someone, or carry someone…
and then discover that God has placed something in our own hands that can become part of His provision.
But Ruth’s request goes deeper still.
The language of spreading a garment or wing over someone appears elsewhere in Scripture with covenant and marital imagery.
Centuries later, Ezekiel 16:8 uses strikingly similar imagery as God metaphorically describes His covenant relationship with Jerusalem:
“I spread the corner of my garment over you… and entered into a covenant with you.”
That does not mean Ruth 3 and Ezekiel 16 describe identical circumstances.
They do not.
But the shared imagery helps us understand why Ruth’s words could carry significance far beyond, “Please keep me warm.”
Ruth was asking Boaz to take the role of redeemer seriously.
She was asking for covering.
Commitment.
Covenant.
A future.
So was Ruth proposing marriage?
In substance, her request clearly points toward marriage and redemption, although we should be careful not to force a modern Western marriage proposal ceremony onto an ancient Israelite narrative.
Ruth was acting according to Naomi’s instructions within the social and legal world surrounding family redemption.
And notice what Ruth herself says:
“for you are a redeemer.”
כִּי גֹאֵל אָתָּה — kî gōʾēl ʾāttāh.
“Because you are a redeemer.”
The crucial word is:
גֹּאֵל — gōʾēl.
Redeemer.
More specifically, a family or kinsman-redeemer: someone connected to the family who could perform certain obligations of restoration or redemption under Israelite law and custom.
But this is where careful reading matters.
The book does not present the situation as though Boaz could simply say, “Yes,” and privately marry Ruth before sunrise.
There was another redeemer.
One nearer than Boaz.
Boaz himself immediately acknowledges it.
“As the LORD lives, I will redeem you. Yet there is a redeemer nearer than I.”
That detail matters enormously.
Because it reveals Boaz’s character.
He desires to help Ruth.
He responds tenderly to her.
He praises her faithfulness.
But he refuses to obtain a righteous outcome through an unrighteous shortcut.
He will not manipulate the process merely because the opportunity is standing—or lying—right in front of him.
He will do this properly.
Publicly.
Honorably.
At the city gate.
Before witnesses.
And that makes the nighttime scene even more powerful.

Because Scripture places two vulnerable people in an emotionally charged situation and then emphasizes restraint, integrity, covenant responsibility, and honorable action rather than exploiting the scene for erotic spectacle.
That is important in a culture that has trained us to confuse desire with love.
Boaz could have exploited Ruth’s vulnerability.
Ruth could have attempted manipulation.
Instead, the narrative moves toward honor.
There is attraction in this story.
There is tenderness.
There is risk.
There is extraordinary vulnerability.
But redemption refuses to turn vulnerability into exploitation.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because some of us know what it feels like to stand emotionally at someone’s feet and silently ask:
Will you cover me…
or use me?
Will you protect what I reveal…
or weaponize it later?
Will you still respect me after you discover how desperately I need help?
Will you stay when you discover the parts of my story I tried to hide?
Will you love me when there is nothing impressive left?
Ruth arrived in Bethlehem carrying very little.
She was a Moabite widow.
Her husband was dead.
Her future was uncertain.
She was living beside another grieving widow.
She gleaned behind harvesters because gathering leftover grain was how she and Naomi survived.
She did not arrive with social prestige.
She arrived with grief.
And yet God was writing something she could not see.
That may be where your story meets hers.
You expected your life to look different by now.
You thought the marriage would survive.
You thought the person would stay.
You thought the prayer would already have been answered.
You thought you would be further ahead.
You thought you would have healed by now.
You thought you would be stronger.
You thought that after everything you gave God, you would not still find yourself standing in another midnight wondering what happens next.
And perhaps nobody around you realizes how tired you are.
You smile.
You serve.
You post Scripture.
You tell people, “God is good.”
And He is.
But somewhere beneath that confession is a trembling prayer you have barely allowed yourself to say aloud:
“God…
please cover me.”
Not because you deserve it.
Not because your record is spotless.
Not because you have everything figured out.
Simply because you have nowhere safer to go.
And that is where Ruth’s story begins reaching beyond Ruth and Boaz.
Because Boaz is an important redeemer in Ruth’s story…
but he is not the ultimate Redeemer of Scripture.
Jesus Christ is.
And we must be careful here too.
Boaz should not be flattened into a simplistic allegory where every detail automatically equals Jesus.
The book of Ruth is real history and literary narrative involving real people, real customs, real loss, real decisions, and real providence.
Yet the canonical story leads somewhere astonishing.
Ruth marries Boaz.
Their family produces Obed.
Obed fathers Jesse.
Jesse fathers David.
And from David’s royal line, generations later, comes Jesus the Messiah.
Matthew deliberately includes Ruth in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Do not rush past that.
The Moabite widow gathering leftover grain in a field becomes part of the human ancestry of the Messiah.
The outsider is brought in.
The widow receives a future.
The empty household experiences restoration.
The woman whose story looked finished becomes woven into the unfolding story that leads to Christ.
That is scandalous grace.
And if you have ever believed your past disqualifies you from being used by God, Ruth’s presence in the biblical story should make you reconsider what grace can do.
Your worst chapter does not possess authorship rights over your ending.
Jesus does.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe someone betrayed you.
Maybe you walked away from God.
Maybe you became addicted to something you once swore you would never touch.
Maybe your prayer life disappeared.
Maybe you compromised.
Maybe shame became so normal that you stopped recognizing it as a prison.
Maybe you have learned how to look spiritually alive while privately becoming numb.
Maybe there are nights when you wonder whether God could possibly want you after everything you have done.
Look again at Ruth.
Not because Ruth committed every kind of sin represented in those struggles—Scripture does not say that, and we should never place sins upon her that the text does not.
Look at her because her story reminds us that desperate circumstances do not prevent divine providence from working.
Then look beyond Ruth.
Look at Christ.
Because Jesus does something infinitely greater than Boaz ever could.
Boaz could redeem property and preserve a family line within the obligations and customs of his world.
Jesus redeems sinners.
Peter writes:
The New Testament word translated “ransomed” there comes from the Greek verb λυτρόω — lytróō, carrying the idea of setting free by payment of a ransom.
Your redemption was not cheap.
Grace is free to the sinner.
But it was not free to Christ.
It cost blood.
The cross is where every illusion that God takes sin lightly collapses.
And it is also where every lie that says repentant sinners are beyond mercy collapses.
At Calvary, justice and mercy are not sentimental slogans.
Jesus bears sin.
Jesus dies.
Jesus rises.
And sinners are summoned not merely to admire Him…
but to repent and believe.
Christianity is not Jesus placing a decorative wing over the life you already intended to live without Him.
It is surrender.
It is coming out of hiding.
It is confessing that sin really is sin.
It is abandoning the fantasy that you can save yourself.
It is placing the weight of your eternity upon the crucified and risen Christ.
Some people want covering without covenant.
Comfort without repentance.
Forgiveness without surrender.
A Savior who rescues them from consequences but never confronts their idols.
But Jesus did not shed His blood merely to make our rebellion more comfortable.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.”
Grace does not merely cover the guilty person and leave the heart untouched.
Grace begins transformation.
The Gospel says you can come exactly as helpless as you truly are.
But when Christ receives you, He does not intend to leave you enslaved to what was destroying you.
That is redemption.
That is why Ruth’s midnight words are so haunting.
“Spread your wing over me.”
Perhaps you need to pray something deeper tonight.
“Jesus, I have spent years hiding underneath everything except You.”
Under relationships.
Under success.
Under church attendance.
Under pornography.
Under alcohol.
Under approval.
Under anger.
Under ministry.
Under money.
Under endless scrolling.
Under secret sin.
Under religious performance.
Under the desperate need to appear okay.
And none of it could redeem you.
You cannot hide beneath something that is drowning with you.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Tell Him the truth.
He already knows it.
There is no secret you can reveal that will cause an omniscient God to suddenly discover something about you.
The question is not whether He knows.
The question is whether you will finally stop hiding.
The cross already tells you what God thinks about your sin.
It is serious enough that Christ died.
And the cross already tells you something astonishing about His mercy.
Christ willingly came to save sinners.
So stop waiting until you become worthy of grace.
If you could make yourself worthy of grace, it would no longer be grace.
Bring Him the ruined chapter.
Bring Him the midnight.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the anger you were afraid to admit.
Bring Him the religious mask.
Bring Him the memories that still make you lower your eyes.
And ask for mercy.
Not because God owes you redemption.
Because Jesus Christ is merciful to sinners who come to Him.
Be honest.
And when you see somebody else write those words, remember that there is a human being behind that comment.
Do not judge them.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Remind them of Christ.
Because the Church should be one of the places where repentance does not become ammunition for humiliation, but an occasion to point broken people toward the grace and truth of Jesus.
And perhaps somebody on your Facebook friends list needs this story more than you realize.
Not because an algorithm deserves another post.
Because someone you love may be living through their own midnight.
Someone scrolling quietly may be one sentence away from finally admitting, “I need Jesus.”
Send this privately to the person who has become distant from God.

Supporting Christian ministry can be an act of generosity offered to God when it is done willingly, faithfully, and with the right heart. Scripture says, “Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.”
It is an invitation.
And there is something else we want people to know.
We want Scripture opened.
We want disciples strengthened.
We want prodigals reminded that the road home still leads to the Father.
We want wounded believers encouraged.
We want unbelievers to hear the Gospel.
We want people to encounter Jesus rather than merely consume religious content.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help.
Save these messages.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow along for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.
Because somebody's midnight may be happening while you are reading this.
And perhaps your share is how these words reach them.
Ruth could not see Bethlehem's entire future from the threshing floor.
She could not see Obed.
She could not see Jesse.
She could not see David.
She certainly could not stand there and see centuries ahead to Bethlehem again, where another chapter in God's redemptive plan would unfold with the birth of Jesus.
She could only stand inside the moment God had given her.
And trust.
That is often how providence feels from inside the story.
We see a field.
God sees generations.
We see an ending.
God may see a doorway.
We see a widow collecting leftover grain.
God sees a woman whose name will eventually appear in the genealogy of the Messiah.
We see midnight.
God sees morning.
And perhaps that is the word someone needs tonight.
Your life may not look redeemed yet.
The prayer may not be answered yet.
The relationship may not be restored.
The tears may still come.
The temptation may still require a daily fight.
The consequences of yesterday may still be sitting at today's table.
Following Jesus does not mean every earthly loss will be reversed exactly the way we want.

Ruth's story should never be turned into a formula promising that every widow gets another husband, every financial struggle ends in prosperity, or every painful chapter receives an immediate earthly resolution.
The Gospel promises something greater than a formula.
It gives us Christ.
Forgiveness for the repentant sinner.
Reconciliation with God through Jesus.
A risen Savior.
A living hope.
A kingdom that cannot be shaken.
And ultimately resurrection.
So when the darkness whispers that your story is already over…
remember the woman at the feet of Boaz.
Remember the wing.
Remember the redeemer.
Then look beyond Boaz to the Redeemer whose hands were pierced.
You may be standing in the chapter you would never have chosen.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, shame does not get the final sentence.
Sin does not get the final sentence.
Death does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
So come beneath His mercy.
Come out of hiding.
Repent.
Believe.
And when grace begins rewriting what sin, suffering, grief, and failure tried to make permanent, do not keep the story to yourself.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done.
Because sometimes what feels like the darkest midnight of your story is standing only a few pages away from a redemption you cannot yet see.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SAME BIBLE THAT SAYS “FLEE SEXUAL IMMORALITY” ALSO CELEBRATES SEXUAL DELIGHT—WHY ISN’T THAT A CONTRADICTION?
paragraphs: THE SAME BIBLE THAT SAYS “FLEE SEXUAL IMMORALITY” ALSO CELEBRATES SEXUAL DELIGHT—WHY ISN’T THAT A CONTRADICTION?
Maybe God Was Never Trying to Destroy Your Sexuality. Maybe He Was Trying to Rescue It From Everything That Would Eventually Destroy You.
There is a sentence in the Bible that sounds almost terrified of sexual sin.
Not “manage it.”
Not “experiment carefully.”
Not “see how close you can get without technically crossing the line.”
Run.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 6:18 is startlingly direct:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — Pheugete tēn porneian.
Flee sexual immorality.
Φεύγετε—pheugete—is an imperative. Run. Escape. Get away.
And then you turn backward in your Bible and discover something that may surprise anyone who grew up believing Christianity was embarrassed by sexual desire.
Proverbs speaks to a husband about his wife:
יְהִי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yehi-meqorkha barukh, u-semach me'eshet ne'urekha.
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
And Proverbs does not stop with a polite reference to companionship.
It becomes unmistakably intimate.
דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
Proverbs 5:18–19.
Read those passages beside each other.
One says run from sexual immorality.
The other celebrates sexual delight.
So which Bible are we supposed to believe?
Both.
Because the contradiction disappears the moment you understand what Scripture is actually protecting.
God is not against sexual desire.
God is against sexual desire becoming detached from His holy design and turning into something that consumes, deceives, exploits, enslaves, betrays, or destroys.
And that distinction changes everything.
Maybe some of us were taught Christianity as though holiness meant becoming less human.
Don’t desire.
Don’t feel.
Don’t talk about it.
Don’t admit the struggle.
Smile at church.
Sing loudly enough that nobody notices the war happening inside you.
Then Monday night comes.
The room is quiet.
The marriage is hurting.
The phone is glowing.
The memories return.
The loneliness gets louder.
The temptation knows your name.
And suddenly the sanitized Christianity we learned on Sunday seems completely unprepared for the human being staring back at us in the dark.
But Scripture is far more honest than that.
The Bible knows desire is powerful.
That is precisely why it refuses to treat desire casually.
Proverbs 5 is not a chapter written by someone frightened of sexuality. It is a father warning his son that sexual desire can lead in radically different directions.
One direction ends in devastation.
The other belongs inside faithful covenant love.

The chapter begins with warnings concerning the “strange woman,” describing seduction that initially tastes sweet but eventually becomes bitter. Then, rather than telling the young man simply to suppress every sexual impulse, Scripture redirects him.
“Drink waters out of thine own cistern.”
Then comes the breathtaking command:
וּשְׂמַח — u-semach.
Rejoice.
Delight.
Be glad with the wife of your youth.
That means biblical holiness is not merely the absence of forbidden sex.
Within marriage, Scripture can speak positively about faithful sexual delight.
God does not merely put a fence around sexuality.
He tells us why the garden inside the fence is worth protecting.
That changes the meaning of “flee.”
You are not merely running from something.
You are protecting something.
Faithfulness.
Trust.
Covenant.
Another person's dignity.
Your own body.
Your future spouse if you are unmarried.
Your present spouse if you are married.
Your conscience.
Your capacity to experience intimacy without secrecy poisoning it.
And ultimately, your life before God.
That is why Paul's language in 1 Corinthians 6 becomes so profound.
He does not simply say sexual immorality violates a rule.
He says:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Flee sexual immorality.
Then Paul brings the body itself into the argument.
Your body is not spiritually irrelevant.
Christianity does not teach that God saves some invisible “real you” while your body remains meaningless.
Paul asks believers whether they know that their bodies are members of Christ. He speaks of the believer's body as a temple of the Holy Spirit.
And then comes the sentence that changes the entire discussion:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς
Ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
“For you were bought with a price.”
Then:
δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
1 Corinthians 6:20.
Do you see what Paul just did?
He took sexual ethics all the way to the cross.
This is not ultimately about religious people obsessing over what happens in somebody's bedroom.
For the Christian, it is about belonging.
Christ bought you at a price.
And what was that price?
Not silver.
Not gold.
The Gospel takes us to Calvary.
To Christ crucified.
To the Son of God giving Himself for sinners.
Suddenly sexual holiness is no longer merely:
“What am I forbidden to do?”
A deeper question appears:
“What does it mean that even my body belongs to the Jesus who died for me?”
That is a much more uncomfortable question.
Because some of us have spent years asking how far we can go.
How much can I watch?
How much can I fantasize?
How emotionally intimate can I become with someone who is not my spouse?
How close can we get before God technically calls it sin?
Where exactly is the line?
But love asks different questions.
Love asks:
How can I honor Christ here?
How can I honor this person's body?
How can I protect my marriage?
How can I prepare myself for covenant faithfulness?
How can I stop using another human being as medication for my loneliness?
How can I glorify God with the body He redeemed?
And perhaps that is where this article stops being theological and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because maybe you already crossed the line.
Maybe many lines.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your browser history could tell stories your church friends have never heard.
Maybe pornography became the place you went whenever rejection hurt.
Maybe you slept with someone you genuinely thought you would marry.
They left.
The memories didn't.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you were cheated on.
Maybe you are married, but your marriage has become so emotionally distant that temptation no longer feels like rebellion.
It feels like relief.
Maybe you have spent years trying to convince yourself that because nobody caught you, nothing has been damaged.
Or maybe your story is different.
Maybe sexual experiences were forced upon you.
If so, hear this distinction clearly: what someone did to you was not your sexual sin.
Their wrongdoing is not your guilt.
And Christ's compassion is not frightened by your wounds.
For others, however, the Holy Spirit may be putting His finger on something you chose.
Something hidden.
Something defended.
Something renamed because calling it what Scripture calls it would require repentance.
And there is a terrible mistake Christians sometimes make at this moment.
We think exposure means God has finished with us.
But conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
Conviction says:
Come into the light.
Condemnation whispers:
Stay hidden because there is no coming back.
The Gospel says something infinitely better.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Not people with immaculate histories.
Sinners.
People whose desires became disordered.
People who betrayed.
People who lusted.
People who used others.
People who were used and later repeated destructive patterns themselves.
People carrying histories they desperately wish they could rewrite.
And this is where the Gospel becomes scandalously beautiful.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem the person who lived it.

Paul is writing 1 Corinthians to real people in a notoriously sexualized ancient environment. Immediately before this discussion, he reminds the Corinthians of sinful lives from which members of their community had come.
Then come three extraordinary words:
“You were washed.”
“You were sanctified.”
“You were justified.”
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the mud was clean.
Washing the person covered in it.
Not renaming darkness.
Bringing sinners into light.
Not saying sin does not matter.
Saying Christ matters so much that sin does not get the final word over everyone who comes to Him.
This is why Proverbs 5 and 1 Corinthians 6 are not enemies.
They are fighting the same war from different sides.
Proverbs says there is a faithful place for sexual delight.
Paul says do not surrender your body to sexual immorality.
One celebrates covenant.
The other protects covenant holiness.
Both refuse the lie that your body is meaningless.
Both refuse the lie that desire must become your master.
Both refuse the lie that freedom means obeying every appetite that becomes loud enough.
Because an appetite can promise freedom while quietly building chains.
Proverbs says exactly that.
The chapter ends with a chilling picture of a person being captured by the cords of his own sin.
Think about that.
At first, you hold the habit.
Eventually, the habit holds you.
At first, pornography is something you occasionally watch.
Then it becomes where your brain automatically runs.
At first, the secret messages feel exciting.
Then deleting them becomes routine.
At first, the affair feels like escape.
Then your entire life becomes architecture built to protect a lie.
At first, you tell yourself you can stop.
Then one night you realize you have been saying that for five years.
Sin rarely introduces itself carrying chains.
It usually introduces itself carrying a promise.
“I can make you feel wanted.”
“I can make the loneliness stop.”
“Nobody will know.”
“You deserve this.”
“Just tonight.”
And somewhere down the road, pleasure sends you an invoice you never knew you were agreeing to pay.
That is why God says flee.
Not because pleasure is evil.
Because God knows counterfeit pleasure eventually demands things from you that holy pleasure never would.
Your secrecy.
Your integrity.
Your peace.
Your spouse's trust.
Your ability to look another person in the eyes without remembering what you hid from them.
Sometimes even your family.
God's boundaries are not proof that He hates pleasure.
Sometimes the boundary is proof that God understands pleasure better than we do.
The God who says “flee” is the same God whose wisdom says “rejoice.”
The God who warns against the forbidden embrace is the God who celebrates faithful marital affection.
Biblical sexuality therefore cannot be reduced to “sex is dirty.”
Nor can it be reduced to “if it feels loving, it must be holy.”
Scripture gives us something far richer.
Sexuality under the lordship of Christ.
Desire disciplined by love.
Pleasure joined to faithfulness.
Bodies treated as meaningful.
Marriage honored.
Sin confronted.
Grace offered.
And Christ at the center.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this has needed for years.
Not another person screaming at you.
Not another excuse either.
Truth.
You are not helped when Christians pretend sexual sin is harmless.
But you are not helped when Christians behave as though sexual sinners are beyond redemption.
The cross destroys both lies.
Sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
Grace is powerful enough that Christ willingly did.
So if something hidden has been eating you alive, stop negotiating with it.
Bring it into the light.
Repentance does not mean merely feeling disgusting.
Biblical repentance turns toward God.
It brings confession instead of concealment.
It cuts off what continually feeds the sin.
It seeks wise pastoral care and mature Christian accountability where needed.
If another person is being betrayed by your secrecy, genuine repentance cannot be built forever on preserving deception.
If pornography owns your nights, stop treating access to temptation as though it were an unavoidable feature of modern life.
If you are pursuing someone else's spouse, leave the fantasy before the fantasy becomes somebody else's devastation.
If you are unmarried, do not interpret chastity as God forgetting you.
Your worth is not measured by whether somebody desires your body.
Your identity is not “unwanted.”
Your deepest identity, if you belong to Christ, is found in Him.
And if you are married, hear Proverbs again.
וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Rejoice with the wife of your youth.
Marriage is not permission to become selfish with another person's body.
Biblical intimacy includes covenant faithfulness, tenderness, honor, mutual care, patience, communication, and love.
Your spouse is not an object God assigned to satisfy you.
They bear God's image.
Love them accordingly.
And perhaps there is a married couple reading this who have almost stopped reaching for each other.
Resentment accumulated.
Words became functional.
Children became the center of every conversation.
Exhaustion moved into the bedroom.
Tenderness quietly moved out.
Maybe Proverbs 5 is not merely telling you what not to do with somebody else.
Maybe it is inviting you to remember the person you promised to love.
Talk again.
Pray together again.
Forgive.
Get help if you need it.
Become curious about one another again.
Let covenant become warm again.
Because faithfulness is more than refusing to leave.
Sometimes faithfulness means learning how to return emotionally to the person beside you.
And for the person who already failed...
Come closer.
This part is for you.
You had the affair.
You clicked again.
You lied.
You crossed boundaries.
You knew better.
You promised God it would be the last time, and then it wasn't.
Now shame is telling you not to pray until you have cleaned yourself up.
But if sinners could clean themselves before approaching Jesus, Calvary would have been unnecessary.
Come to Christ.
Not casually.
Not with excuses.
Come repentant.
Come honest.
Come without negotiating the definition of your sin.
But come.
The same Jesus who exposes darkness is the Jesus who receives repentant sinners.
The Gospel does not say your choices were insignificant.
It says your failure does not have to become your permanent name.
Adulterer does not have to be your final name.
Porn addict does not have to be your final name.
Impure does not have to be your final name.
Your worst night does not have authority to write the final chapter of a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
That authority belongs to Christ.
This is why we keep saying it:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By writing grace where shame expected the story to end.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because you need another saved post.
There is probably someone among your friends who would never walk into a church and announce, “I am losing the battle with sexual sin.”
But they may read this alone.
At 1:17 in the morning.
With nobody watching.
And God may use the truth you shared to interrupt a decision they would have regretted for years.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who says they no longer believe to follow too. Stay close to daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christian generosity is to come willingly from the heart, not through compulsion.

But voluntary financial support can help Gospel Warrior continue producing and expanding Christ-centered resources, reaching wounded people, strengthening believers, and putting the Gospel before people who may never otherwise encounter it.
If you have ever asked, “How can I help this ministry keep going?”—this is one practical way.
Pray for the ministry.
Leave a testimony.
Sometimes the share that costs you nothing financially becomes the doorway through which somebody encounters a truth worth more than money.
Because ultimately, this article was never really about sex.
It was about ownership.
Who owns your body?
Who owns your desires?
Who gets the final word over your shame?
Who gets to define freedom?
Paul's answer reaches through twenty centuries and lands directly in our generation:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς.
You were bought with a price.
Jesus did not purchase you so that shame could own you.
He did not shed His blood so pornography could own you.
He did not call you out of darkness so secret desire could become your master.
You belong to Christ.
So run when you need to run.
Repent when you need to repent.
Confess what needs to come into the light.
Protect what God has called holy.
Rebuild what can be rebuilt.
Receive forgiveness where there is genuine repentance and faith.
And when the enemy points backward and says, “Look what you did,” point to the cross and remember what Jesus did.
Because the Bible that tells you to flee sexual immorality is not contradicting the Bible that celebrates marital sexual delight.
It is revealing why holy delight is worth protecting.
God does not call you away from sexual sin because He despises joy.
He calls you away because He refuses to surrender you to a counterfeit that promises intimacy while teaching your soul how to hide.
And maybe tonight, somewhere between conviction and grace, someone will finally close the secret window.
Delete the conversation.
Tell the truth.
Ask for help.
Reach for their spouse.
Fall to their knees.
Come home to Christ.
And discover that the final sentence of their story was never written by their worst desire.
The chains may remember who you were—but the scars in Jesus' hands declare whose you are.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BE STILL” DOES NOT MEAN “NEVER MOVE” — The Forgotten Command Two Verses Later Changes Everything
paragraphs: “BE STILL” DOES NOT MEAN “NEVER MOVE” — The Forgotten Command Two Verses Later Changes Everything

Israel was trapped between Pharaoh and the sea when Moses told them to stand firm. But only moments later, God gave a command many Christians accidentally leave out: “Go forward.” Maybe faith is not choosing between trusting God and moving. Maybe biblical faith is refusing to move without Him—and refusing to stay when He says go.
There are moments when “waiting on God” sounds spiritual…
but underneath the Christian vocabulary, something else is happening.
Fear.
You know exactly what that feels like.
You have prayed.
You have cried.
You have asked God for direction until you are almost embarrassed to ask again.
You keep saying, “I’m waiting on the Lord.”
But somewhere deep inside, a quieter question keeps disturbing you:
What if God has already told me enough to take the next step?
What if the door you keep asking God to open is waiting for you to walk toward it?
What if you have turned “Be still” into permission to remain somewhere God never commanded you to remain?
And what if one of the most famous “stand still” moments in the Bible actually becomes, only two verses later, one of Scripture’s most dramatic commands to move?
Go back to the shoreline.
Not the comfortable version painted on children’s ministry walls.
Feel the sand.
Hear the screaming.
Imagine mothers pulling terrified children against their bodies.
Imagine elderly Israelites staring at a horizon filled with dust.
Behind them was Egypt.
Before them was water.
And approaching behind them was the machinery of the empire they had just escaped.
Pharaoh had changed his mind.
The Egyptians were coming.
Israel had no navy.
No bridge.
No military strategy capable of solving this.
They had spent generations making bricks, not commanding armies.
And suddenly freedom looked like a trap.
That matters.
Because sometimes the most terrifying moment comes after God has already brought you out.
You thought leaving Egypt would end the battle.
Then Egypt followed you.
You thought surrendering your life to Christ meant temptation would disappear.
It followed you.
You thought repentance meant the consequences of yesterday would instantly evaporate.
Some followed you.
You thought finally walking away from that destructive relationship, secret sin, addiction, bitterness, compromise, or old identity meant you would never hear its voice again.
Then one night…
you heard the chariots.
And the terrifying thing about old bondage is that sometimes it knows your name.
Israel panicked.
They cried to the LORD, but they also turned on Moses.
Essentially: Were there not enough graves in Egypt? Is that why you brought us here to die?
Fear has a strange ability to romanticize slavery.
When freedom becomes frightening, Egypt can suddenly look comfortable.
That relationship was destroying you—but at least it was familiar.
That addiction was enslaving you—but at least you knew what tomorrow looked like.
That compromise was killing something inside you—but obedience feels uncertain.
So the chains you once begged God to break begin looking safer than the wilderness where you have to trust Him.
That is where Moses speaks.
The Hebrew of Exodus 14:13 is powerful:
אַל־תִּירָאוּ הִתְיַצְּבוּ וּרְאוּ אֶת־יְשׁוּעַת יְהוָה
Al-tira'u, hityatzevu, ure'u et-yeshu'at YHWH.
“Do not be afraid. Stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD.”
Look carefully at that language.
אַל־תִּירָאוּ — al-tira'u.
Do not fear.
הִתְיַצְּבוּ — hityatzevu.
Stand firm. Take your stand.
וּרְאוּ — ure'u.
And see.
See what?
יְשׁוּעַת יְהוָה — yeshu'at YHWH.
The salvation—the deliverance—of the LORD.
Moses is not telling terrified people that their own strength will rescue them.
He is directing their eyes away from Pharaoh…
away from themselves…
and toward the LORD.
Then comes Exodus 14:14:
יְהוָה יִלָּחֵם לָכֶם וְאַתֶּם תַּחֲרִישׁוּן
YHWH yilachem lakhem, ve'atem tacharishun.
“The LORD will fight for you, and you will be silent.”
That final Hebrew verb comes from a word associated here with being silent or holding one’s peace.
In other words, Israel was not being commanded to manufacture its own salvation.
They were not going to defeat Pharaoh by screaming louder.
They were not going to overpower Egypt through human strength.
God would fight.
God would deliver.
God would make the impossible way.
And this is where many of us stop reading.
We underline verse 14.
We put it on the wall.
We turn it into a caption.
“The LORD will fight for you. Be still.”
Beautiful.
True.
Necessary.
But then comes verse 15.
And verse 15 refuses to let “be still” become an excuse for permanent paralysis.
God speaks to Moses:
מַה־תִּצְעַק אֵלָי דַּבֵּר אֶל־בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל וְיִסָּעוּ
Mah-titz'aq elai? Dabber el-benei Yisrael veyissa'u.
“Why are you crying out to Me? Tell the children of Israel…”
And then comes the word.
וְיִסָּעוּ — veyissa'u.
Let them set out.
Let them journey.
Go forward.
Do you see it?
“Stand firm.”
Then…
“Go forward.”
There is no contradiction.
There is a sequence.
Stop panicking.
Stop imagining Pharaoh is sovereign.
Stop believing you must manufacture your own deliverance.
Stand your ground in faith.
Watch what God does.
And when God commands movement…
move.
Biblical stillness is not spiritualized paralysis.
Trusting God does not mean refusing to obey God.
There are moments when faith looks like waiting.
There are moments when faith looks like walking.
The question is not, “Should Christians always wait or always move?”
The question is:
What has God actually said?
That changes everything.
Because some of us have been asking God to guide steps we refuse to take.
Some have been praying for freedom while keeping the phone number that repeatedly leads them back into bondage.
Some have been praying for reconciliation while refusing to apologize.
Some have been praying for victory over secret sin while protecting the environment in which that sin survives.
Some have been asking God to use them while waiting for some extraordinary sign before doing the ordinary acts of obedience Scripture has already commanded.
Some keep saying, “God, show me Your will,” while the Bible sits unopened beside the bed.
And some are exhausted because they have the opposite problem.
