They are running everywhere.
Forcing doors.
Manipulating circumstances.
Calling anxiety “discernment.”
Calling impatience “faith.”
Calling personal ambition “God’s timing.”
Exodus confronts both people.
To the frantic heart:
Stand firm.
To the paralyzed heart:
Go forward.
There is a stillness that comes from faith.
There is also a stillness that comes from fear.
They can look almost identical from the outside.
One says, “I will not run ahead of God.”
The other says, “I am terrified to obey Him.”
Only God sees the difference perfectly.
Maybe that is why this story cuts so deeply.
Because Israel could not open the sea.
Read that again.
Israel could not open the sea.
No amount of positive thinking could divide those waters.
No motivational speech could make a road appear.
No Israelite could stand at the shoreline and say, “I have enough faith,” and manufacture a miracle.
God had to do what only God could do.
But when God opened the way…
Israel still had to walk through it.
That distinction could save someone years of confusion.
You cannot do God's part.
And you must not use God's sovereignty as an excuse for refusing yours.
You cannot forgive your own sins.
Christ must save you.
You cannot resurrect your spiritually dead heart by moral effort.
Grace must reach you.
You cannot make yourself righteous before a holy God through religious performance.
Jesus Christ has accomplished what you could never accomplish.
At the cross, salvation is not something you achieve.
It is something you receive.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus shed His blood.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
Jesus saves.
Christianity begins not with humanity climbing toward God but with God coming to rescue sinners.
That is grace.
But grace does not leave rescued people facing Egypt forever.
Grace calls us out.
Repentance turns.
Faith follows.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely to make us more comfortable while we continue embracing the chains from which He came to free us.
He calls us to Himself.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly where this lands.
You have been standing at your own Red Sea.
Behind you is a version of yourself you do not want anymore.
Ahead of you is a life with Christ that you cannot completely predict.
You know Egypt.
You know its streets.
You know its voices.
You know its chains.
Strangely, bondage can feel safer than unfamiliar freedom.
And Jesus is calling you farther than comfort.
Maybe nobody knows what you are fighting.
You smile in church.
You share Bible verses.
You tell people, “God is good.”
And He is.
But at two in the morning, when nobody sees the screen…
when the memories return…
when shame starts whispering…
when the craving comes back…
when loneliness becomes unbearable…
Egypt appears on the horizon again.
And suddenly you wonder whether anything really changed.
Listen carefully.
The presence of pursuing chariots did not mean Israel's deliverance from Egypt was imaginary.
The battle after your turning point does not necessarily mean God abandoned you.
Sometimes yesterday's bondage fights hardest when it realizes you are leaving.
But your hope cannot finally rest in your ability to outrun Egypt.
Your hope is the Lord.
For Christians, our ultimate hope is Jesus Christ.
And here is where Exodus becomes even more beautiful when read within the whole biblical story.
The exodus becomes one of Scripture’s great patterns of redemption: bondage, deliverance, rescue, covenant, a people brought out so they might belong to God.
Then Christ comes.
Not merely to rescue people from an earthly Pharaoh…
but to save sinners from sin and death.
The greater rescue is not that God makes every earthly obstacle disappear.
The greater rescue is that through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, guilty sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and given new life.
That means your deepest Red Sea is not your financial problem.
Not your difficult relationship.
Not your career uncertainty.
Not even your broken dream.
Your deepest problem is sin.
And your greatest need is not a changed circumstance.
It is a Savior.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve the old you.
He came to save.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To redeem.
To make new.
Maybe you have spent years hiding behind Christianity without actually surrendering to Christ.
You know worship songs.
You know church language.
You know when to say amen.
But you also know the room inside your soul you keep locked.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The affair.
The secret messages.
The dishonesty.
The pride.
The unforgiveness.
The addiction.
The double life.
The wound you turned into an identity.
The sin you renamed so you would no longer have to repent of it.
And maybe you have been calling your refusal to confront it “waiting on God.”
What if today is not another day to hide?
What if repentance is the next step?
Not earning God's love.
Not purchasing forgiveness.
Not proving yourself worthy.
Coming empty-handed to Jesus.
Confessing the truth.
Trusting the crucified and risen Christ.
Turning from sin.
Walking into the freedom His grace gives.
Because the Gospel is not:
Fix yourself and maybe God will accept you.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
At the cross, He bore judgment.
In His resurrection, death did not have the final word.
And everyone who truly comes to Him in faith finds a Savior greater than his or her scandal.
That is why our message remains:
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because sin does not matter.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the worst chapter surrendered to Him.
Jesus rewrites everything.
He can take the chapter you thought would become your ending and make it the place where grace found you.
Peter denied Him.
Grace restored him.
Paul persecuted the church.
Grace transformed him.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
He had Christ.
Grace does not pretend the past never happened.
Grace refuses to let the past have the final word.
And perhaps your next step is frightening.
Do not confuse courage with absence of fear.
Israel walked toward a sea.
Imagine the first footsteps.
Walls of water.
Darkness.
Wind.
Children clinging to parents.
Every instinct saying, This is impossible.
Yet the road existed because God had made it.
They did not walk in order to persuade God to open the sea.
They walked because God had opened it.
That is the difference.
Christian obedience is not payment for grace.
It is a response to grace.
We do not obey so Christ will finally love us.
We obey because the One who loved us first is Lord.
So perhaps you need to stop asking God to bless the Egypt He told you to leave.
Perhaps you need to stop returning to the chains Christ broke.
Perhaps you need to stop mistaking panic for prayer.
Perhaps you need to stop forcing what God has not opened.
Or perhaps…
you need to stop standing in front of an open path asking God for another sign.
“Be still” was never permission for Israel to build houses on the shoreline.
The God who said, in effect, stand firm and see My salvation is the God who shortly afterward said:
Go forward.
And there is another detail you cannot afford to miss.
The sea did not merely represent Israel's obstacle.
Behind them stood their former master.
They crossed.
Egypt followed.
But Egypt did not come out the other side.
Some things God brings you through are meant to become graves for what once enslaved you.
You may remember Egypt.
But you do not have to return to it.
Your scars may remember.
Your nervous system may remember.
Your family may remember.
People who knew the old version of you may remember.
Satan may accuse.
But your history is not your lord.
Jesus is.

And if you belong to Christ, your identity is not ultimately defined by the worst thing you did, the worst thing done to you, the darkest night you survived, or the ugliest rumor attached to your name.
Your life belongs to Jesus Christ.
So stand firm when fear tells you to run backward.
Be silent when panic wants to become your prophet.
Pray.
Listen.
Open Scripture.
Seek wise, godly counsel.
Do not manufacture divine guidance out of your desires.
But when God's revealed truth makes the path of obedience clear…
walk.
One trembling step.
Then another.
Then another.
You may not see the entire road.
Israel probably did not need a detailed map of the seabed.
They needed enough faith to take the next step God had placed before them.
Maybe that is all you have today.
One step.
Delete the number.
Confess the sin.
Ask forgiveness.
Open the Bible.
Return what is not yours.
Tell the truth.
Seek help.
Leave the compromise.
Forgive instead of feeding revenge.
Call the person you wounded.
Pray again.
Go back to church.
Serve someone.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
Take the next faithful step that Scripture makes clear.
Not because movement itself is holy.
Not because every risk is faith.
Not because every opportunity is God's will.
But because obedience matters.
And when you cannot move because the sea is still closed?
Wait on God.
Trust Him.
Do not manufacture an opening.
But when He opens the path and His Word calls you forward?
Do not make a shrine out of the shoreline.
Walk.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person standing at a frightening shoreline.
It does not.
It does not.
And never because someone pressured you into giving.
Scripture teaches generosity from the heart rather than giving under compulsion.
But voluntary financial support has long helped Gospel ministry continue.
More importantly, your support helps us keep putting Scripture-centered material in front of people who may be standing at their own Red Sea.
Pray.
Send it privately to the person whose name came into your mind while reading.
Follow so we can keep walking through Scripture together.
And above all…
follow Jesus.
Because eventually every one of us reaches a place where human strength is not enough.
A place where yesterday is chasing us.
Tomorrow frightens us.
And the road ahead looks impossible.
There, we remember:
God never told Israel to pretend Pharaoh was not real.
He told them not to fear him.
God never told Israel that the sea was imaginary.
He opened it.
God never told Israel to save themselves.
He fought for them.
But when the road appeared…
He told them to move.
Maybe the sentence you need to carry with you is this:
Do not run back to the slavery God brought you out of just because the road to freedom requires you to trust Him with your next step.
Stand firm when He says stand.
Wait when He says wait.
And when God says go forward…
do not let fear rename disobedience “being still.”
The sea in front of you may be terrifying.
But Egypt behind you is no longer home.
And the Savior who calls you forward is still writing your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EZEKIEL EXPOSED THE BEDROOMS OF JERUSALEM—AND THE LAST WORD WASN’T SEX
paragraphs: EZEKIEL EXPOSED THE BEDROOMS OF JERUSALEM—AND THE LAST WORD WASN’T SEX

Men were taking their fathers’ wives, defiling daughters-in-law, violating sisters, betraying neighbors—and then God revealed the terrifying root beneath it all: “You have forgotten Me.” — Ezekiel 22:10–12
There are passages in the Bible people read slowly because they are beautiful.
And then there are passages people read slowly because they cannot believe God actually allowed those words onto the page.
Ezekiel 22 is one of them.
This is not a comfortable chapter.
It does not smell like polished church pews and Sunday morning perfume.
It smells like a city rotting behind closed doors.
Blood in the streets.
Corruption in positions of power.
Parents dishonored.
Foreigners exploited.
Widows and orphans mistreated.
Holy things despised.
Money obtained through oppression.
And behind doors that should have been safe...
sexual boundaries were collapsing.
Men were crossing lines so dark that thousands of years later the accusations still make a reader recoil.
A father’s bed.
A neighbor’s wife.
A daughter-in-law.
A sister.
And God told Ezekiel to expose it.
Not entertain people with it.
Not sensationalize it.
Expose it.
Because sometimes the most frightening thing about sin is not what it looks like when it begins.
It is what it becomes when nobody repents.
Listen to the Hebrew of Ezekiel 22:10:
“עֶרְוַת אָב גִּלָּה בָךְ”
‘Ervat av gillah bakh.
Literally, the language speaks of “uncovering a father’s nakedness.”
That expression requires context.
Ezekiel is drawing from the sexual holiness laws already given to Israel. Leviticus 18:8 says:
“עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ הִוא”
“The nakedness of your father’s wife you shall not uncover; it is your father’s nakedness.”
That matters.

Ezekiel 22:10 does not contain the words “father’s wife” in precisely the same expanded form as Leviticus 18:8. But the Torah itself explains the expression: violating the sexual boundary surrounding a father’s wife was described as uncovering the father’s nakedness.
This is why the accusation has historically been understood as incestuous sexual violation involving the father’s wife or bed.
And Ezekiel is nowhere near finished.
The Hebrew of verse 11 reads:
“וְאִישׁ אֶת־אֵשֶׁת רֵעֵהוּ עָשָׂה תּוֹעֵבָה וְאִישׁ אֶת־כַּלָּתוֹ טִמֵּא בְזִמָּה וְאִישׁ אֶת־אֲחֹתוֹ בַת־אָבִיו עִנָּה־בָךְ”
The accusations come one after another.
A man with his neighbor’s wife.
Another defiling his daughter-in-law.
Another violating his sister—his father’s daughter.
The ancient Greek Septuagint preserves the horror with similarly severe language:
“ἕκαστος τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ πλησίον αὐτοῦ ἠνομοῦσαν ... καὶ ἕκαστος τὴν νύμφην αὐτοῦ ἐμίαινεν ... καὶ ἕκαστος τὴν ἀδελφὴν αὐτοῦ θυγατέρα τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ ἐταπείνουν ἐν σοί.”
This was not Ezekiel exaggerating to generate attention.
God was prosecuting Jerusalem.
And that distinction matters because we live in an age where scandal has become entertainment.
Someone falls and everybody reaches for a phone.
A marriage collapses and strangers want screenshots.
A pastor sins and suddenly everyone becomes a detective.
A celebrity is exposed and millions gather around the digital wreckage.
But Ezekiel is not gossip.
Ezekiel is judgment.
There is a difference.
Gossip exposes another person so we can feel superior.
God exposes sin so sinners will understand what rebellion has done.
And if you read Ezekiel 22 only to stare at those people, you may completely miss the blade of the passage turning toward us.
Because sexual depravity was not the only charge.
Before Ezekiel ever reaches the bedroom, he talks about bloodshed.
He talks about leaders abusing power.
He talks about dishonoring fathers and mothers.
He talks about oppressing foreigners.
He talks about mistreating orphans and widows.
He talks about despising what God calls holy.
Then comes sexual corruption.
Then bribery.
Then greed.
Then extortion.
The chapter refuses to let respectable sinners stand at a safe distance from scandalous sinners.
That is uncomfortable.
We like categories.
Their sins.
Our sins.
Disgusting sins.
Acceptable sins.
Public sins.
Private sins.
The sins that destroy reputations...
and the sins that fit comfortably inside respectable clothing.
God does not play that game.
Ezekiel exposes an entire culture whose relationship with God had disintegrated so badly that human beings themselves were becoming objects to exploit.
The powerful used people.
The greedy used people.
The sexually corrupt used people.
The violent used people.
And suddenly the connection becomes painfully clear.
When God disappears from the center of human life, people eventually stop looking sacred too.
A neighbor becomes an opportunity.
A woman becomes an appetite.
A vulnerable person becomes an easy target.
Money becomes a god.
Power becomes permission.
Desire becomes authority.
And conscience becomes negotiable.
But then Ezekiel says something more terrifying than almost anything else in the chapter.
After bloodshed...
after exploitation...
after sexual corruption...
after greed...
God identifies something underneath it all.
Ezekiel 22:12 ends:
“וְאֹתִי שָׁכַחַתְּ”
Ve’oti shakhakht.
“And Me you have forgotten.”
There it is.
The sentence beneath the scandal.
“You have forgotten Me.”
Maybe that is the line we were supposed to be afraid of.
Because most people reading this have probably never committed the specific incestuous sins Ezekiel describes.
But have you forgotten Him?
That question comes much closer.
You can remember Christian vocabulary and forget Christ.
You can remember Sunday and forget Christ on Monday.
You can remember worship lyrics while forgetting the One being worshiped.
You can post Scripture and secretly live as though God cannot see your browser history.
You can tell everyone, “God is good,” while nurturing something inside you that God has repeatedly told you to surrender.
You can know theology and forget God.
You can serve in ministry and forget God.
You can preach and forget God.
You can sing and forget God.
You can build a Christian-looking life around the absence of intimate obedience to Christ.
That may be one of the most terrifying possibilities in religion.
Not atheism.
Familiarity without surrender.
Jerusalem had religious history.
Jerusalem had sacred institutions.
Jerusalem had inherited revelation.
Yet God said:
“You have forgotten Me.”
And maybe somebody reading this just became uncomfortable.
Not because Ezekiel exposed ancient Jerusalem.
Because the Holy Spirit touched a locked room inside you.
Something nobody knows.
Something you keep deleting.
Something you keep explaining.
Something you keep promising will be the last time.
The relationship you know is wrong.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The messages your spouse would be devastated to read.
The bitterness you have baptized as discernment.
The money you obtained dishonestly.
The person you refuse to forgive.
The secret appetite you feed whenever loneliness gets loud.
The double life.
The hidden account.
The private addiction.
The spiritual numbness.
The version of yourself everybody applauds...
and the version only God sees.
Be careful here.
Conviction is not an invitation to despair.
It is an invitation to stop hiding.
The Gospel does not tell us that sin is harmless.
The Gospel tells us sin is so serious that the Son of God went to a cross to save sinners from it.
That is radically different.
Jesus did not die so we could rename darkness.
He died to rescue us from darkness.
He did not shed His blood so we could make peace with the chains He came to break.
Grace is not God looking at evil and shrugging.
Grace is God doing for guilty sinners what guilty sinners could never do for themselves.
And this is where Ezekiel's nightmare drives us toward the breathtaking necessity of Jesus Christ.
Centuries after Ezekiel described sexual corruption in Jerusalem, Paul wrote to another deeply troubled community in Corinth.
He named sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, greed, drunkenness, reviling and swindling among sins incompatible with inheriting God's kingdom when they characterize an unrepentant life.
Then comes one of the most beautiful turns in Scripture.
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because they had never been guilty.
Because Jesus Christ had intervened.
Paul continues by saying they had been washed, sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).
Do not race past that.
Some of the people sitting in the Corinthian church had histories.
Ugly histories.
Sexual histories.
Idolatrous histories.
Greedy histories.
Shameful histories.
And the Gospel did not require them to pretend those histories never happened.
The Gospel gave those histories a new ending.
“And such were some of you.”
That is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves for avoiding scandal.
Dead people being made alive in Christ.
Guilty people being justified.
Dirty people being washed.
Enslaved people being liberated.
Prodigals coming home.
Enemies being reconciled.
Sinners becoming saints—not because sin suddenly became acceptable, but because Jesus Christ became their Savior and Lord.
That is why repentance matters.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is turning.
Coming into the light.
Agreeing with God about what He calls sin.
Leaving the excuses behind.
Running toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
Maybe you have been thinking:
“If people knew what I did, they would never look at me the same.”
Maybe.
People may not.
Jesus already knows.
That is the terrifying part.
And the beautiful part.
You are not informing Christ when you confess.
You are surrendering what He already sees.
The cross happened with full knowledge of human depravity.
Christ was not naïve about the people He came to save.
Romans says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and that justification comes by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:23–24).
Grace does not mean consequences magically disappear.
Some sins leave wounds requiring years of healing.
Some require confession.
Some require restitution.
Some require accountability.
Criminal abuse should not be hidden behind religious language; victims deserve protection, truth, justice and appropriate lawful intervention.
Forgiveness must never become a weapon for protecting abusers.
Repentance does not mean demanding immediate trust from the people you wounded.
A repentant heart stops protecting the sin and starts submitting to truth.
That matters especially when reading Ezekiel 22 because some of the language describes violation, exploitation and abuse—not merely private consensual indiscretion.
God sees the wounded too.
In fact, the chapter proves He does.
Why was God angry?
Because people mattered to Him.
The widow mattered.
The orphan mattered.
The foreigner mattered.
The exploited neighbor mattered.
The sexually violated mattered.
The blood that had been spilled mattered.
God's holiness is not cold perfection detached from human suffering.
His holiness means evil does not receive the final word.
And neither does your past.
That is where the theme of Gospel Warrior becomes more than a slogan.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting evil into something good.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by erasing truth.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking people whose stories appeared permanently chained to guilt and giving them something they could never manufacture:
redemption.
Peter denied Him.
Paul persecuted His people.
The Corinthian believers carried histories Paul was unafraid to name.
Yet grace entered their stories.
The Gospel does not say your scandal was imaginary.
It says your scandal does not have to be your final identity.
Your worst night does not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your worst decision is not more powerful than His mercy.
Your shame cannot crucify Jesus a second time and prove His first sacrifice insufficient.
But grace must never become permission to continue deliberately embracing what nailed Christ to the cross.
Jesus saves us from sin, not merely from embarrassment about sin.
So maybe this article did not reach you accidentally.
Maybe you started reading because the title shocked you.
Ezekiel.
Fathers’ wives.
Daughters-in-law.
Sisters.
Scandal.
But now you realize the article was never merely about what those men were doing thousands of years ago.
It became about the door inside your own heart you hoped nobody would open.
God already knows what is behind it.
And Christ is still calling.
Come out of hiding.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you become cleaner.
Not after you finally defeat everything yourself.
Come to Christ now.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Ask for help where help is needed.
Bring darkness into the light.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly.
Someone reading the comments may need your testimony more than you realize.
Maybe they think Christians are people who never broke.
Show them something better.
Show them Christians are people who know where broken sinners can go.
To Jesus.
Not because scandal gets clicks.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be quietly drowning in shame while smiling in every photograph.
Someone may believe God wants nothing to do with them anymore.
Someone may be one confession away from finally seeking help.
Someone may need to discover tonight that conviction is not God inviting them to run away—it may be mercy calling them home.

There may come a night when temptation returns, shame starts speaking, or somebody you love confesses something devastating and you need to remember the difference between excusing sin and proclaiming grace.
Invite your family.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite lukewarm Christians.
Invite the friend who says they no longer believe.
The Gospel is not afraid of complicated people.
Jesus has been rescuing complicated people for a very long time.
It cannot.
Not because money buys blessing.
It does not.
It does not.

Scripture says giving should come from the heart rather than from compulsion, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Scripture also recognizes the legitimacy of materially supporting Gospel ministry and those laboring to spread God's Word (1 Corinthians 9:14; Philippians 4:15–18).
And there is another reason your support reaches beyond a single article.
Think about that.
Someone somewhere may have no Christian bookstore nearby.
No large personal library.
Very little money for resources.
Maybe even very little encouragement.
Yet a biblical resource placed freely within reach can become something God uses in their discipleship.
A devotional during grief.
A Christian book during confusion.
A discipleship resource for someone newly following Jesus.
A biblical message arriving at exactly the moment someone was preparing to surrender to temptation.
This is why support matters.
But the deepest reason to support Gospel work is not merchandise.
It is mission.
That costs nothing.
A share can cross a boundary money cannot.
It can reach the cousin you rarely speak to.
The former church member.
The exhausted father.
The wounded mother.
The teenager silently questioning everything.
The believer secretly trapped in sexual sin.
The person convinced they have gone too far for Jesus.
Never underestimate what God can do with truth placed in front of the right person at the right moment.
Christ already settled the price of our redemption with something infinitely more precious than money.
His blood.
Support the work because you love Jesus.
Support it because you value biblical truth.
Support it because you want more people reached.
Support it because generosity can become worship when it rises from a surrendered heart.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with being saved.
Only Jesus saves.
And that brings us back to Jerusalem.
Back to Ezekiel.
Back to those horrifying accusations.
The father's bed.
The neighbor's wife.
The daughter-in-law.
The sister.
The widow.
The orphan.
The oppressed stranger.
The blood.
The money.
The corruption.
The forgotten God.
God saw all of it.
Nothing was hidden.
And that should frighten us.
But thousands of years later, standing on this side of Calvary, we know something Ezekiel's accusations make desperately necessary.
The Judge against whom humanity has sinned is the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
At the cross, justice was not mocked.
Sin was not renamed.
Holiness was not lowered.
Jesus bore sin.
And from the empty tomb came the announcement that death itself does not get the last word over those who belong to Him.
So hear this carefully.
You may have a chapter you wish could be torn from your life.
Jesus does not need you to lie about that chapter.
Bring it to Him.
You may carry memories that still make your stomach tighten.
Bring them to Him.
You may have hurt people.
Repent.
Tell the truth.
Make what restitution you rightly can.
Accept necessary consequences.
Seek accountability.
And run to Christ.
You may have been the one violated rather than the one violating.
Hear this too:
The shame belongs to the evil committed against you, not to your worth before God.
Christ sees you.
You are not invisible in Ezekiel's world.
The God who thundered against exploitation is not indifferent to your tears.
And maybe that is what somebody needed tonight.
Not another scandal.
Not another headline.
Not another Christian pretending Christians never fall.
You needed Jesus.
The One who tells the truth about sin without abandoning repentant sinners to despair.
The One who can take a confession and begin a restoration.
The One who can enter the chapter you thought ruined the entire book.
What have I been asking Jesus to forgive while secretly planning to keep?
Sit with that.
Do not answer me first.
Answer Him.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody thinks their scandal is the end of their story.
Make sure they hear the Gospel before shame writes the final sentence.
The sin God exposes is never more powerful than the Savior to whom repentance runs.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WIVES, SUBMIT TO YOUR HUSBANDS” — THE VERSE EVERYONE QUOTES WITHOUT STARTING AT EPHESIANS 5:21
paragraphs: “WIVES, SUBMIT TO YOUR HUSBANDS” — THE VERSE EVERYONE QUOTES WITHOUT STARTING AT EPHESIANS 5:21

Before a husband ever gets to quote “submit,” Scripture has already placed him beneath the cross—and what Paul actually wrote may confront both husbands and wives more deeply than the isolated verse ever could.
There is a sentence from the Bible that has entered more marriage arguments than some marriage counselors.
“Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands…”
Some men know those words by heart.
They can find Ephesians 5:22 faster than they can find the last place their wife quietly cried because she felt unheard.

Some women hear those words and immediately tense up—not necessarily because they hate Scripture, not because they reject God, but because somewhere along the way somebody may have used a holy verse with an unholy spirit.
A command meant to live beneath the shadow of Jesus Christ became a weapon.
A passage about Christlike marriage became a slogan about male control.
And sometimes the tragedy is not that the Bible was quoted incorrectly.
The tragedy is that somebody started reading one verse too late.
Because before Paul addresses wives in Ephesians 5:22, there is Ephesians 5:21.
And that changes the atmosphere of the entire conversation.
The Greek reads:
“ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ.”
Hypotassomenoi allēlois en phobō Christou.
In straightforward English:
“Submitting to one another in reverence for Christ.”
Read that again.
Slowly.
Before Paul speaks directly to wives…
before husbands are addressed…
before marriage roles become the discussion…
Christ is already standing in the middle of the room.
And everybody has to bow.
The Greek matters here.

The word translated “submitting” in verse 21 is hypotassomenoi, from hypotassō—to subject oneself, to place oneself in an ordered relationship, to submit. But notice something fascinating about the flow of the Greek text.
In an important stream of the earliest Greek textual tradition reflected in modern critical editions, verse 22 does not repeat an explicit verb for “submit.” It reads essentially:
“Αἱ γυναῖκες τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ…”
“The wives to their own husbands as to the Lord…”
The idea of submission carries forward grammatically from the preceding statement.
That does not erase verse 22.
It does not make the instruction to wives disappear.
It does not allow us to rewrite Paul because modern culture finds his words uncomfortable.
But it does force us to stop pretending verse 22 dropped out of heaven without verse 21 standing immediately before it.

Paul has been describing Spirit-filled Christian life. He tells believers to be filled with the Spirit, to worship, to give thanks—and then to live in a posture of submission toward one another out of reverence for Christ.
Then he turns toward the household.
The question is no longer merely:
“Woman, are you submitting?”
The uncomfortable question becomes:
“Is anybody in this marriage behaving like Jesus?”
Because Paul does tell wives to submit to their own husbands as to the Lord.
We should not be embarrassed by Scripture.
We should understand it faithfully.
But then Paul turns toward the husband.
And husbands…
you may want to sit down for this.
Because Paul never says:
“Husbands, make sure your wives submit.”
He does not tell the husband to enforce submission.
He gives the husband another command.
A terrifying one.
A crucifying one.
A command that leaves very little room for selfish masculinity.
“Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας…”
“Husbands, love your wives…”
And then comes the standard.
Not according to your mood.
Not according to whether she agrees with you.
Not according to whether dinner was made.
Not according to whether she gave you the respect you think you deserved.
Not according to what the men in your family taught you masculinity looked like.
Paul points to Jesus.
“καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν…”
“Just as Christ loved the church…”
And what did Christ do?
“καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.”
“He gave Himself up for her.”
There it is.
The cross.
That is where biblical husbandhood goes to die to itself.
The husband wants to talk about headship?
Paul points him toward a bloody Savior.
The husband wants authority?
Paul shows him Christ giving Himself away.
The husband wants to know what leadership looks like?
Look at Jesus.
Look at the One washing feet.
Look at the One touching lepers.
Look at the One welcoming children.
Look at the One carrying burdens.
Look at the One enduring betrayal.
Look at the One who could summon angels but stretched out His hands instead.
Look at Calvary.

Christian headship can never faithfully be used as a theological costume for selfishness, intimidation, humiliation, manipulation, violence, or domination because the model Paul gives the husband is Christ Himself.
And Christ “gave Himself up for her.”
That means a man cannot scream, “Submit to me!” while refusing to die to his pride and imagine that Ephesians 5 is on his side.
Brother…
before asking whether your wife respects your leadership, ask what your leadership is costing you.
Does she experience your strength as safety?
Can she disagree without fearing punishment?
Can she tell you that you hurt her without watching your ego immediately build a courtroom?
Do you listen?
Do you repent?
Do you apologize without adding, “but you…”
Do you pray for her?
Do you protect her dignity when she is not in the room?
Do you know what has been exhausting her lately?
Do you notice what she carries?
When was the last time you asked what her heart needed and stayed quiet long enough to hear the answer?
Because Jesus did not love the Church merely by announcing His position over her.
He gave Himself for her.
And wife…
Scripture speaks to you too.
Biblical submission is not inferiority.
The passage never says a woman is less intelligent, less valuable, less human, less spiritually significant, or somehow farther from God.
Your husband is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
Your husband is not your mediator.
Jesus is.
Your husband is not your ultimate Lord.
Jesus is.
And the words “as to the Lord” can never legitimately mean “obey a husband instead of the Lord.”
No human authority gets permission to overrule God.
The apostles themselves established the principle when commanded to violate allegiance to God: “We must obey God rather than men.”
So submission cannot mean becoming an accomplice to sin.
It cannot mean calling evil good.
It cannot mean protecting criminal behavior.
It cannot mean that a battered woman must quietly endure violence because leaving immediate danger would somehow disappoint Jesus.
It cannot mean surrendering conscience to another sinner.
And if someone has used Ephesians 5 to convince you that abuse is holiness, please hear this carefully:
Jesus does not need your destruction to prove His Word is true.
Sin remains sin even when the sinner knows Bible verses.
At the same time, we must resist the opposite temptation.
We cannot rescue Scripture from abuse by deleting whatever Scripture says that our culture dislikes.
Christian marriage is not built on two autonomous people protecting themselves from ever having to yield.
It is built on two people who belong first to Jesus Christ.
A Christian wife is called to a real posture of respect and submission toward her own husband.
A Christian husband is commanded to love his wife with the staggering pattern of Christ's self-giving love.
And both stand under the lordship of Jesus.
That is why Ephesians 5:21 matters so much.
“Submitting to one another in reverence for Christ.”
Mutual submission does not necessarily mean every relationship or responsibility becomes identical. Paul goes on to address wives and husbands distinctly. We should let him.
But neither can those distinct instructions be separated from the Spirit-filled, Christ-revering posture Paul has just established.
The wife cannot say, “His responsibility to love means I never have to yield.”
The husband cannot say, “Her responsibility to submit means I get to dominate.”
Both arguments smell suspiciously like the same thing:
self.
And Jesus came to put self on a cross.
Maybe that is why this passage hurts when we actually read all of it.
Because it is much easier to use Scripture to diagnose your spouse than to let Scripture perform surgery on you.
“Husbands, she needs to submit.”
“Wives, he needs to love.”
And Jesus stands between both accusations asking:
“What about you?”
What if tonight you stopped reading Ephesians 5 as ammunition?
What if you read it as a mirror?
Imagine the husband who has quoted verse 22 for years suddenly reaching verse 25 and realizing:
“My wife isn't the only person God is confronting.”
Imagine him putting down the Bible he had been using to win the argument.
Imagine him walking into the kitchen.
She is standing there pretending everything is fine.
Because she has become good at pretending.
He knows something is wrong.
Normally he would defend himself.
Normally he would explain what she misunderstood.
Normally he would tell her she was too emotional.
But not tonight.
Tonight he has seen Jesus in Ephesians 5.
So instead of defending his authority, he lowers his voice.
“I haven't loved you like Christ.”
Silence.
“I've wanted respect without becoming respectable.”
Her eyes begin filling.
“I've demanded that you hear me while I stopped hearing you.”
And suddenly the argument is no longer about who wins.
Something else has entered the room.
Repentance.
And repentance can do what winning never could.
It can resurrect things.
Now imagine the wife who has spent years protecting herself behind contempt.
Maybe he has failed.
Maybe he has disappointed her.
Maybe she learned to survive by making sure he knew exactly how little she respected him.
Then Christ begins working on her heart too.
Not because his failures suddenly become acceptable.
Not because accountability disappears.
But because the Gospel has exposed something inside her that needs grace.
The sarcasm.
The contempt.
The weaponized silence.
The desire to punish.
And now both are standing somewhere neither expected to stand when the argument began.
At the foot of the cross.
That is Christian marriage.
Not a flawless man ruling a flawless woman.
Not a voiceless woman orbiting an unquestionable man.
Two sinners desperately needing Jesus.
Two people learning obedience.
Two people learning repentance.
Two people learning forgiveness.
Two people discovering that marriage has a brutal way of exposing the parts of us we were able to hide while we were single.
Your spouse sees the version of you that strangers never meet.
They know whether your Sunday worship survives Monday morning.
They know whether your “fruit of the Spirit” survives financial pressure.
They know whether your theology survives being interrupted.
They know whether your kindness survives exhaustion.
They know whether the person lifting hands in church becomes cruel behind a closed door.

Marriage has a way of pulling theology out of books and putting it into kitchens, bedrooms, bank accounts, hospital rooms, arguments, disappointments, unanswered texts, crying babies, unpaid bills, aging bodies, sexual struggles, family conflicts, and whispered prayers at 2:17 in the morning.
And right there…
Jesus wants to rewrite the story.
Maybe your marriage already has scandal in it.
Betrayal.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Bitterness.
Years of emotional distance.
Words you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
Secrets.
Coldness.
Control.
Neglect.
Maybe you sleep beside each other but haven't truly been close in years.
Maybe nobody at church knows.
Your Facebook photos still look beautiful.
You still smile when somebody says, “You two are such a wonderful couple.”
And both of you know the truth.
Something is bleeding behind the photograph.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not ask you to pretend the wound isn't there.
The Gospel brings the wound into the light.
Jesus specializes in meeting people where the respectable religious world thinks the story has become too messy.
That is the heartbeat of grace.
Not pretending there was never a scandal.
Not pretending sin didn't matter.
Not renaming darkness so nobody feels uncomfortable.
Grace tells the truth about sin—and then announces that sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Because Jesus does.
From scandal…
to grace.
The adulterer can repent.
The bitter spouse can soften.
The proud husband can kneel.
The contemptuous wife can repent.
The addicted can seek help.
The wounded can begin healing.
The liar can confess.
The distant can return.
The broken can seek wise pastoral and professional help.
Forgiveness can begin.
Trust, where genuinely broken, may require time and demonstrated faithfulness to rebuild. Forgiveness is not pretending consequences do not exist.
And reconciliation cannot be manufactured by forcing an endangered person back into an unsafe situation.
Grace is not denial.
Grace is God entering reality with redemption.
And sometimes redemption begins with the most frightening sentence a human being can say:
“I was wrong.”
Maybe that sentence needs to be spoken in your house tonight.
Not by your spouse.
By you.
Stop thinking about what they need to repent of for thirty seconds.
What has Jesus been trying to confront in you?
Your pride?
Your control?
Your contempt?
Your lust?
Your bitterness?
Your refusal to forgive?
Your manipulation?
Your emotional absence?
Your obsession with winning?
Your secret life?
Your harsh words?
Your spiritual hypocrisy?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If the Holy Spirit has exposed something you've been hiding, you don't need to publish the details of your private life. But don't run from conviction either.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because nobody knows what you have been carrying…
you do not have to explain everything.
Just write:
Let somebody pray for you.
Because maybe another husband will see your comment and finally repent.
Maybe another wife will realize she isn't alone.
Maybe someone who was planning to give up tonight will discover one more reason to seek God, wise counsel, safety where needed, and healing.
This is why sharing biblical truth matters.
Not to start a gender war.
Not to humiliate your spouse.
Not to announce, “See? I was right.”
Because Ephesians 5 is one of those passages we need to return to when pride starts editing the Bible in our favor.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, challenging your compromises, strengthening your walk with Christ, or helping you return to Scripture, there is another way you can help this ministry continue.
It does not.
It cannot.
Not because anyone must give Gospel Warrior money in order to glorify God.
Absolutely not.
Christ cannot be purchased, grace cannot be bought, and the Gospel is not for sale.
Your biblical giving to your local church and your support of Gospel ministry should be approached prayerfully, willingly, and according to Scripture.
But voluntary financial partnership is one legitimate way believers can help Gospel-centered work continue and expand.
Your prayers help Gospel Warrior remain faithful.
And beyond those benefits, remember what we are trying to build together.
Come to Jesus.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
To Jesus.
Because one day husbands will not stand before God clutching Ephesians 5:22 and explaining what their wives should have done.
Wives will not stand there explaining what their husbands should have done.
We will answer to Christ.
And perhaps that is the truth hiding in plain sight inside the passage everyone keeps fighting about.
Marriage was never ultimately supposed to make you look powerful.
Paul says the mystery points beyond husband and wife.
“τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν…”
“This mystery is great…”
And then:
“ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν.”
“I am speaking with reference to Christ and the church.”
That is where the passage was going all along.
Christ.
The Church.
The Bridegroom who did not exploit His Bride.
The Savior who gave Himself for her.
The Lord who washes.
The King who serves.
The Holy One who died for sinners.
The risen Christ who takes ruined people and makes them new.
So wife, before submission becomes merely a debate, look at Jesus.
Husband, before headship becomes something you demand, look at Jesus.
And church, before we quote another verse at somebody else…
look at Jesus.

Because when Jesus becomes the center, submission stops being ammunition, leadership stops being domination, love stops being sentimentality, repentance stops being humiliation, forgiveness stops being weakness, and marriage stops being primarily about proving who has the most power.
It becomes a place where two sinners learn, imperfectly and painfully, what it means to belong to a crucified and risen King.
And maybe tonight the miracle your marriage needs will not begin when your spouse finally changes.
Maybe it begins when you stop using Scripture to win the argument…
and finally allow Scripture to win you.
But first…
go home.
Put down your pride.
Open Ephesians 5.
Start at verse 21.
And when you reach verse 25, don't look at your wife.
Look at the cross.
Because sometimes the verse we wanted to use to change somebody else becomes the Word God uses to break open our own heart.
The Gospel was never given to help you win against your spouse. It was given to bring both of you to the feet of Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE DOESN’T TEACH “SEX IS DIRTY”—It Teaches That Something Powerful Needs Faithfulness, Boundaries, and Love
paragraphs: THE BIBLE DOESN’T TEACH “SEX IS DIRTY”—It Teaches That Something Powerful Needs Faithfulness, Boundaries, and Love

Maybe the Church never needed to make sex sound disgusting. Maybe we needed to recover something far more beautiful—and far more demanding: God calls it powerful enough to protect, sacred enough for faithfulness, intimate enough for covenant, and precious enough not to be treated casually.
There are people reading this who learned about sex through shame.
Not holiness.
Shame.
Maybe nobody actually said the words, “Sex is dirty.”
They didn’t have to.
You could hear it in the uncomfortable silence.
You could feel it when the subject suddenly changed.
You could see it in the expression on someone’s face whenever desire was mentioned.
And somewhere along the way, some Christians absorbed a strange message that sounded almost biblical:
Good Christians do not really talk about sex.
Good Christians barely desire it.

And if you have struggled sexually, crossed boundaries, watched pornography, slept with someone outside marriage, committed adultery, carried secret fantasies, or simply found yourself wrestling with desires you were ashamed to admit existed...
perhaps you started wondering whether something about your body itself was disgusting to God.
But then you actually open the Bible.
And something surprising happens.
The story does not begin with sex being dirty.
It begins with God creating human beings embodied, male and female, declaring His creation “very good” (Genesis 1:27–31).
Before pornography.
Before adultery.
Before exploitation.
Before lust distorted another human being into an object.
Before sin fractured human intimacy.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
There was covenantal union.
And there was no shame.
Genesis 2:24 reaches back to the foundation:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew gives us language worth slowing down for:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ
ve-davaq be-ishto
“And he shall cling to his wife.”
That word דָּבַק — davaq — carries the sense of clinging, holding fast, remaining closely joined.
Then Scripture says:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
ve-hayu levasar echad
“And they shall become one flesh.”
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד.
Basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not introduce marital intimacy as a filthy necessity God reluctantly tolerates so humanity can reproduce.
It places “one flesh” inside the creation account itself.
That changes the conversation.
Sexuality is not evil because it is powerful.
Its power is one of the reasons Scripture refuses to treat it casually.
Fire can warm a home.
Fire can also consume one.
The problem is not that fire exists.
The question is whether it is being honored according to its nature.
And perhaps that is where both religious shame and modern sexual culture make opposite mistakes.
One side can make sex seem inherently filthy.
The other can make it seem almost meaningless.
Scripture permits neither.
The Bible does not say your body is disposable.
It says your body matters so much that what you do with it matters.
It does not say sexual union means nothing.
It says sexual union means enough that faithfulness matters.
It does not say desire itself proves you are corrupt.
It teaches that our desires, like every other part of fallen humanity, must come under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That is why biblical boundaries are not evidence that God hates sexuality.
They are evidence that God refuses to trivialize it.
Listen to the startling language of Hebrews 13:4:
Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος.
Timios ho gamos en pasin kai hē koitē amiantos.
A close rendering is:
“Let marriage be held in honor among all, and the marriage bed be undefiled.”
Τίμιος — timios.
Precious.
Valued.
Honored.
And then comes ἀμίαντος — amiantos.
Undefiled.
Unstained.
Think about that.
Scripture can speak of the marriage bed and call it undefiled.
The Bible's answer to sexual immorality, therefore, cannot simply be summarized as “sex is dirty.”
The biblical picture is more beautiful than that.
Marriage is to be honored.
The marriage bed is to remain undefiled.
And sexual immorality and adultery are treated seriously before God.
The distinction matters.
Because there is an enormous difference between saying, “This is filthy, so stay away from it,” and saying, “This is precious, so do not desecrate it.”
One produces disgust.
The other can produce reverence.
One can make a wounded person hate himself.
The other calls a sinner to repentance while showing him that God created something worth restoring.
And this is where the Bible becomes uncomfortable for almost everybody.
Because recovering the goodness of sexuality does not mean erasing biblical boundaries.
Actually, it gives us a reason for them.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:18:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not see how close you can stand to it.
Not build your secret life around it while maintaining your Christian appearance.
Flee.
The command is forceful because Paul understands that your body is not spiritually irrelevant.

Only a few verses later, he reminds believers that their bodies belong to Christ, that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, that they were bought with a price, and therefore they are to glorify God in their bodies (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).
Do you see what Christianity does here?
It refuses to say your body is worthless.
It says almost the opposite.
Your body matters to God.
Your sexuality matters to God.
Your choices matter to God.
What happens behind a locked bedroom door matters to God.
What happens on a glowing screen at 1:17 in the morning matters to God.
How you look at another human being matters.
How you treat your spouse matters.
What you do with somebody else's vulnerability matters.
Whether your desire becomes service or selfishness matters.
Whether intimacy expresses faithfulness or betrayal matters.
Whether another person's body becomes someone you love sacrificially or something you consume selfishly matters.
Not because God despises the body.
Because He created it.
That means Christian sexual ethics cannot merely be a list of things you are forbidden to do.
At its deepest level, it asks:
What does love require?
What does covenant require?
What does faithfulness require?
What honors Christ?
What protects another person's dignity instead of exploiting it?
What allows me to look at another image-bearer and remember:
You are not a product for my appetite.
You are not pixels for my private consumption.
You are not an experience for me to collect.
You belong first to God.
And so do I.
That truth changes things.
Especially when nobody else is watching.
Maybe this article is hitting somewhere you hoped nobody would touch.
Maybe your browser history tells a different story from your Sunday worship.
Maybe you keep promising God, “This is the last time.”
Then the loneliness comes.
The temptation comes.
The message arrives.
The memory comes back.
The screen lights up.
And suddenly the conviction that felt powerful Sunday morning feels very far away on Tuesday night.
Maybe you have crossed a line you once swore you never would.
Maybe you slept with someone because you desperately wanted to feel loved.
Maybe you gave your body hoping someone would give you their heart.
And they left.
Maybe you are married, but pornography has quietly trained your eyes to compare your spouse with bodies that were never yours to possess.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe they know, and trust has been shattered.
Maybe you were unfaithful.
Maybe someone was unfaithful to you.
Maybe sex was used against you.
And if someone violated, coerced, exploited, or abused you, hear this distinction clearly:
Another person's sexual sin against you is not your moral stain to carry.
Their wrongdoing does not make you dirty.
Jesus never asks victims to call evil good, pretend wounds do not exist, or accept responsibility for another person's abuse.
Perhaps your story is different.
Maybe you grew up hearing so much fear around sexuality that even within marriage you struggle to receive marital intimacy without feeling ashamed.
The Bible has room to correct that distortion too.

Paul speaks remarkably openly in 1 Corinthians 7 about mutual marital responsibility. Husband and wife are both addressed. Neither spouse is presented merely as an object existing for the gratification of the other. There is mutuality, responsibility, consideration, and belonging.
Biblical marital intimacy is not a license for selfishness.
Marriage never transforms coercion into love.
The pattern Jesus gives His people is sacrificial love.
Christ does not teach us to consume people.
He teaches us to love them.
And this is why Christian sexual holiness is far richer than virginity before a wedding.
A person can technically preserve a physical boundary while cultivating lust, manipulation, pride, objectification, cruelty, or selfishness.
Jesus goes after the heart.
He does not merely ask what your hands have done.
He confronts what your heart has learned to worship.
That is terrifying.
Until you remember who is asking.
Jesus.
The One who sat near people respectable religion preferred to avoid.
The One who knew people's histories without needing gossip to inform Him.
The One who could expose sin without exploiting sinners.
The One who could say, “Go, and from now on sin no more,” while refusing to join the mob hungry for condemnation (John 8:1–11).
Grace did not tell people sin did not matter.
Grace gave sinners somewhere to go with it.
That is the Gospel.
And somebody needs that sentence tonight.
Because perhaps you have confused conviction with hopelessness.
Conviction says:
Come into the light.
Shame says:
Hide because if anybody really knew you, they would leave.
Conviction says:
Confess.
Shame says:
Pretend.
Conviction says:
Repent.
Shame says:
You are permanently defined by what you did.
But Jesus did not go to the cross merely to improve the public behavior of people who were already clean.
Christ died for sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People who knew exactly what it meant to have something in their past they could not undo.
And Scripture does not romanticize that past.
It does something better.
It announces redemption.
Paul lists patterns of serious sin in 1 Corinthians 6, including sexual sin, and then delivers three of the most hope-filled words a broken person could hear:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because their histories vanished.
Not because consequences magically disappeared.
Not because sin suddenly became harmless.
But because Jesus Christ had intervened.
Paul continues by speaking of being washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 6:11).
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace rewriting what the scandal gets to mean.
You may have sexual sin in your story.
Sexual sin does not have to be the final author of your story.
You may have betrayed someone.
Repent.
You may need to confess.
You may need accountability.
You may need to delete something.
Block someone.
End something.
Tell the truth.
Seek wise pastoral help.
Seek professional help where trauma, compulsion, abuse, or deep relational damage is involved.
You may need to stop calling bondage “just the way I am.”
But repentance is not God standing over you demanding that you crawl back to Him while He enjoys your humiliation.
The Gospel announces that God has acted in Christ to reconcile sinners to Himself.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
Jesus saves.
And because He lives, repentance is not walking toward a grave.
It is turning toward Life.
This is where boundaries begin to look different.
“No” can become an act of love.
Waiting can become worship.
Faithfulness can become freedom.
Self-control can become evidence that desire is no longer your master.
And marriage can become more than permission to have sex.
It becomes covenant.
A place where nakedness was meant to meet faithfulness.
Where vulnerability was meant to meet safety.
Where desire was meant to learn love.
Where bodies are not merchandise.
Where intimacy is not performance.
Where neither husband nor wife is reduced to an instrument.
Where the question slowly changes from “What can I get?” to “How can I love?”
That does not make marriage effortless.
It makes it holy ground for discipleship.
And for the unmarried Christian, Scripture does not treat you as half a human waiting for sexuality to complete you.
Jesus Himself destroys that lie.
The most complete human life ever lived was not completed by sexual experience.
Christ was fully human, fully holy, and unmarried.
So your worth is not measured by whether somebody desires your body.
Your adulthood is not validated by sexual experience.
Your identity is not secured by romantic attention.
And marriage is not your savior.
Jesus is.
That matters in a culture constantly whispering that you are missing something essential unless somebody wants you sexually.
You are not a body desperately waiting for another person to give you value.
You bear God's image.
And if you belong to Christ, you have been purchased at immeasurable cost.
This is why purity cannot simply mean “never having messed up.”
If that were Christianity, enormous numbers of people would have no road home.
Biblical purity ultimately depends on something far greater than an untouched past.
It points us toward the cleansing grace of God and a present life increasingly surrendered to Him.
Maybe you cannot become the person who never sinned sexually.
But through Christ, you can become a person who no longer hides.
You can tell the truth.
You can repent.
You can receive forgiveness.
You can learn faithfulness.
You can rebuild integrity one surrendered decision at a time.
You can become trustworthy again where restoration is possible.
You can stop feeding the secret that has been feeding on you.
And perhaps tonight the bravest prayer you can pray is not impressive at all.
“Jesus, I need You.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish the details of your private life. But you also do not have to keep pretending that everything is fine.
There should be places in the Body of Christ where those words are not invitations for gossip but invitations for prayer.
And if you know someone who grew up believing Christianity teaches that the human body is disgusting, share this with them.
If you know a young believer being discipled more aggressively by pornography, hookup culture, social media, or shame than by Scripture, send this to them.
Temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction sounded like when our minds were clear.
Come back when you need to remember.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who does not yet believe to follow too. We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, repentance, grace, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
It cannot.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It never will.
Your giving before God is a matter that deserves biblical conviction, wisdom, and a willing heart.
Scripture says, “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Paul also gratefully recognized believers who financially partnered with Gospel ministry (Philippians 4:15–18).
It is partnership.
It is helping keep Scripture moving through newsfeeds filled with noise.
It is helping put truth in front of the exhausted believer.
Grace in front of the ashamed.
Conviction in front of the comfortable.
The Gospel in front of the person who thought Christianity had nothing left to say to them.
One share can place the message in front of someone we could never have reached ourselves.
One tag can become a conversation.
One comment can make another struggling Christian realize they are not the only person fighting.
One saved article can become a midnight reminder.
And one surrendered life can become evidence that Jesus Christ still transforms sinners.
Because Christianity's message about sex was never:
“Your body is disgusting.”
It is far closer to this:
Your body belongs to God.
People are not objects.
Desire is not your master.
Marriage is honorable.
Faithfulness matters.
Sexual immorality is serious.
Love refuses exploitation.
Holiness requires boundaries.
Repentance is real.
Grace is available.
Forgiveness was purchased at the cross.
And no sexual history is powerful enough to make the blood of Jesus powerless.
So stop calling what God created evil.
And stop calling what God forbids harmless.
We do not need shame without truth.
We do not need desire without boundaries.
We do not need legalism without grace.
And we do not need grace stripped of repentance.
We need Jesus.
Jesus in our marriages.
Jesus in our singleness.
Jesus in our desires.
Jesus in our bedrooms.
Jesus in our browser histories.
Jesus in our wounds.
Jesus in our secrets.
Jesus in our repentance.
Jesus in our restoration.
Jesus at the center of everything.
Perhaps your scandal is real.
But scandal does not get the last word when Jesus Christ becomes the Author of what comes next.
Your worst chapter may explain where you have been—but only Jesus gets to decide what redemption can make of the pages that remain.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN CHRISTIANS BELIEVE IN ZODIAC SIGNS “JUST FOR FUN”?
paragraphs: CAN CHRISTIANS BELIEVE IN ZODIAC SIGNS “JUST FOR FUN”?
The Question Sounds Harmless—Until You Ask Who Gets to Tell You Who You Are
“It’s not like I actually worship the stars.”
“I’m a Christian. I know Jesus is Lord.”
“I just read my horoscope for fun.”
“It’s only my zodiac sign.”
“I don’t take it that seriously.”
Maybe you have said something like that.
Maybe you have never opened an astrology book in your life, but you know exactly what people mean when they ask, “What’s your sign?”
Maybe you laugh when a post says, “That is such a Scorpio thing to do.”

Maybe somebody told you that your temper comes from being an Aries, your stubbornness comes from being a Taurus, your emotional nature comes from being a Cancer, or your indecisiveness comes from being a Libra.
You laughed.
You shared it.
You tagged somebody.
You forgot about it.
Harmless... right?
But there is a question hiding underneath that question.
A much deeper one.
When you want to know who you are, who gets the final word?
The stars?
The month you were born?
A horoscope?
An algorithm?
A personality prediction?
Or the God who formed you, knows you, sees you, calls you, judges you, loves you, and sent His Son to redeem you?
Because Christianity does not merely ask whether something is entertaining.
Christianity asks whether something is true.
And sometimes the most dangerous spiritual compromises do not walk into our lives announcing themselves as rebellion.
Sometimes they arrive as entertainment.
Sometimes they make us laugh first.
Sometimes they say, “Relax. It’s just for fun.”
And perhaps that is why this question deserves more than an angry Christian slogan or a frightened warning about demons.
It deserves Scripture.
It deserves context.
It deserves honesty.
And most of all, it deserves Jesus.
Because this is not ultimately an article about twelve zodiac signs.
It is about something much closer to your heart.
It is about whom you trust to interpret your life.
Scripture does something fascinating with the heavens.
It never teaches us to hate them.
Quite the opposite.
The heavens are magnificent because God made them.
“The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork” (Psalm 19:1, KJV).
Look carefully at the direction of that sentence.
The heavens declare God’s glory.
They are witnesses to the Creator.
They are not replacements for the Creator.
That distinction changes everything.
Genesis says God made the heavenly lights.
The sun is not your god.
The moon is not your master.
Mars does not determine your anger.
Venus does not determine whom you should love.
Mercury does not rule your communication.
Saturn does not write your destiny.
The stars are created things.
Beautiful things.
Useful things.
Astonishing things.
But still created things.
And Christianity has always begun with an enormous dividing line between Creator and creation.
The problem is not looking upward and being amazed.
The problem begins when created things start receiving authority that belongs to God.
This is why astronomy and astrology are not the same thing.
Studying stars, planets, galaxies, gravitational forces, orbits, light, and the physical universe is the study of God’s creation.

Biblical objections arise when heavenly bodies or their configurations are treated as sources of hidden knowledge, personal destiny, spiritual guidance, character authority, or predictions concerning human affairs.
And Scripture is not vague about seeking supernatural guidance through divination.
Deuteronomy 18 places divination, fortune-telling, interpreting omens, sorcery, mediums, and related practices outside the life God commanded for Israel.
That matters.
But there is another passage that becomes almost uncomfortable when read slowly.
Isaiah speaks judgment against Babylon and addresses those attempting to find security in occult practices and celestial prognostication.
The Hebrew text of Isaiah 47:13 contains this remarkable phrase:
הַחֹזִים בַּכּוֹכָבִים
haḥozim bakokhavim
Literally, it speaks of those gazing or seeing “in the stars”—star-gazers.
Then comes another expression:
מוֹדִיעִם לֶחֳדָשִׁים
Those making things known according to the months.
The picture is painfully recognizable.
People looking toward the heavens for information about what is coming.
And God essentially challenges these supposed interpreters of the heavens to stand up and save Babylon from what is coming upon her.
They cannot.
The stars cannot save.
The prognosticators cannot save.
The system cannot save.
That is the biblical humiliation of astrology.
Not merely that human beings can make ridiculous predictions.
Something deeper.
The creation cannot carry the weight of trust that belongs to the Creator.
And then the New Testament gives us another disturbing picture.
Acts 16 describes a slave girl who made money through fortune-telling.
The Greek says she had:
πνεῦμα Πύθωνα
pneuma Pythōna
A “spirit of Python,” an expression associated in that ancient context with divination.
Here is where the story becomes especially sobering.
The girl follows Paul and his companions while saying things about them that sound remarkably correct.
She identifies them as servants of the Most High God proclaiming a way of salvation.
Think about that.
Something does not become spiritually trustworthy merely because something it says sounds accurate.
That destroys one of our favorite defenses.
“But my horoscope was weirdly accurate.”
Accuracy is not the biblical test of spiritual authority.
Truth must also come from the right source and lead us toward the right Lord.
The serpent in Eden did not tempt Eve with sentences containing nothing but obvious nonsense.
Deception becomes powerful precisely because falsehood can be mixed with fragments that feel believable.
And this is where “just for fun” deserves examination.
Not panic.
Not superstition.
Examination.

There is an enormous difference between knowing, as a cultural fact, that people call you a Gemini because of your birthday and actually assigning that category interpretive authority over your personality, relationships, decisions, compatibility, future, or identity.
Those things should not be carelessly collapsed into one category.
A Christian does not need to become terrified because somebody mentions Capricorn.
A zodiac symbol printed on a coffee mug does not possess magical sovereignty over somebody.
The Christian response should not become a new superstition.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
But neither should Christians use freedom as an excuse to cultivate fascination with a system built around seeking meaning and guidance from celestial configurations.
Ask yourself something more revealing than, “Can I technically get away with this?”
Ask:
Why do I want it?
What am I receiving from it?
Do I check it because it makes me curious—or because somewhere inside me I want it to tell me something about myself?
When I am anxious about tomorrow, where do I look?
When my relationship is uncertain, whose voice do I seek?
When I do not understand myself, what defines me?
When I am afraid, what comforts me?
When I need direction, what guides me?
Because eventually the question stops being about zodiac signs.
It becomes a question about trust.
And trust is deeply spiritual.
Perhaps you say, “But I don't actually believe it.”
Then consider another question.
If you know something is spiritually unreliable, why train your heart to keep returning to it?
Paul gives us a principle in Romans 14:23:
πᾶν δὲ ὃ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως ἁμαρτία ἐστίν
pan de ho ouk ek pisteōs hamartia estin.
In context Paul is discussing disputed matters involving food and conscience, so we should not rip the sentence away from its argument and pretend Paul was specifically discussing astrology.
He was not.
But the principle remains piercing:
“Whatever is not from faith is sin.”
Christian freedom is not fundamentally the freedom to ask, “How close can I stand to something questionable without technically sinning?”
Christian freedom teaches us to ask a better question:
Can I do this from faith?
Can I place it before Jesus without hiding it?
Does it strengthen my trust in Christ?
Does it train my mind toward truth?
Does it help me love God?
Does it help me love my neighbor?
Does it make Christ larger in my imagination—or does it quietly give another voice a little room beside Him?
Maybe this is becoming uncomfortable.
Good.
Not because condemnation is the goal.
Because honesty is.
There are people reading this who did not start with horoscopes.
It started with pain.
You wanted to know whether somebody would come back.
You wanted reassurance that your relationship would survive.
You wanted to understand why you always felt different.
You wanted some explanation for the chaos inside you.
You wanted tomorrow to feel less frightening.
You wanted to hear that something good was coming.
And somewhere between curiosity and vulnerability, you began listening.
Maybe not seriously.
Then a little more seriously.
One horoscope became a compatibility reading.
One zodiac video became twenty.
One personality description became something you repeated about yourself.
“I’m like this because I’m a _____.”
Read that sentence again.
“I’m like this because I’m a _____.”
There is the deeper battle.
Identity.
Scripture offers you an identity infinitely more profound than a constellation.
If you belong to Jesus Christ, the decisive truth about you is not where the planets appeared to be when you took your first breath.
It is what happened when the sinless Son of God gave His life for sinners and rose from the grave.
Your deepest problem is not that Mercury is in retrograde.
It is sin.
And your greatest hope is not that the universe is sending you positive energy.
It is that Christ died for sinners.
Your future is not ultimately held by a horoscope.
It is held by God.
Your personality does not excuse your sin.
Grace transforms sinners.
Your wounds are not healed by discovering your cosmic compatibility.
Christ meets broken people.
Your guilt cannot be removed by understanding your birth chart.
It is washed away through the blood of Jesus.
This is why the Gospel is infinitely better news than astrology.
Astrology says, in one form or another, “Look upward and interpret the signs.”
The Gospel says:
Look to Christ.
Astrology can become an attempt to decode yourself.
Jesus calls you to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him.
Astrology may tell you why you supposedly are the way you are.
Jesus can transform who you are becoming.
And perhaps that is frightening.
Because sometimes labels are easier than repentance.
“My sign makes me jealous.”
No.
Jealousy is something Christ calls us to confront.
“My sign makes me explosive.”
No.
Your anger is not sovereign over you.
“My sign makes me unfaithful.”
No.
You are morally accountable before God, and in Christ you are not condemned to remain enslaved to your old patterns.
“My sign means we aren't compatible.”
Maybe the real question is whether the relationship is characterized by truth, wisdom, holiness, sacrificial love, shared faith, repentance, maturity, and obedience to God.
The stars make convenient excuses.
Jesus gives us something harder and better.
Truth.
And then grace.
Because perhaps you are reading this thinking:
I have been doing this for years.
I should have known better.
Have I opened some terrible door?
Is God angry with me?
Can I come back?
Listen carefully.
This is where Christianity becomes breathtaking.
The Gospel is not:
“You touched something spiritually wrong, so now Jesus wants nothing to do with you.”
The Gospel is that sinners can repent and come home.
Christ did not go to the cross for people who had successfully kept themselves spiritually spotless.
He went to the cross for sinners.
For idolaters.
For the sexually immoral.
For liars.
For the greedy.
For religious hypocrites.
For the ashamed.
For the confused.
For people who searched for life in places where life could never be found.
For people like us.
Repentance does not mean pretending you were never interested.
It means turning.
It means saying:
“Jesus, I was looking somewhere else for something I should have sought in You.”
Maybe it was guidance.
Maybe identity.
Maybe comfort.
Maybe control.
Maybe knowledge about tomorrow.
Maybe hope.
Maybe simply entertainment that you now recognize was training your curiosity in a direction you no longer want to follow.
Bring it into the light.
You do not have to perform a theatrical ritual.
You do not have to live terrified of constellations.
You do not have to become obsessed with demons.
Turn your eyes toward Christ.
Confess your sin where there has been sin.
Reject what competes with God's truth.
Fill your mind with Scripture.
Pray.
Seek wise Christian community.
And keep walking with Jesus.
There is something wonderfully ironic about all of this.
Christians do believe the heavens mean something.
They mean there is a Creator worthy of glory.
We can look into a night sky exploding with stars and feel small without feeling abandoned.
Those stars do not know your name.
God does.
Those stars did not form you.
God did.
Those stars did not hear your secret crying last night.
God did.
Those stars cannot forgive your sins.
Jesus can.
Those stars did not carry a cross for you.
Jesus did.
Those stars did not walk out of a tomb.
Jesus did.
The heavens are breathtaking.
But they make terrible saviors.
So can Christians believe in zodiac signs “just for fun”?

If by “believe” we mean assigning zodiac signs genuine authority to explain personality, determine compatibility, reveal destiny, predict events, or provide spiritual guidance, the biblical trajectory gives Christians compelling reasons to say no.
We have been given a better authority.
God's Word.
We have been given a better identity.
Christ.
We have been given a better guide.
The Holy Spirit working in harmony with the truth God has revealed.
We have been given a better hope.
The Gospel.

And if “just for fun” means casually consuming horoscope or astrology material while insisting it has no authority, then perhaps the most useful question is not merely whether every isolated encounter can be assigned the same moral weight.
The better question is:
Why deliberately feed your heart from a fountain you would never trust with your soul?
You do not need to fear astrology.
You need to treasure Christ more.
That distinction matters.
Christian holiness is not spending your entire life frightened that darkness might touch you.
It is belonging so completely to Jesus that counterfeits gradually lose their beauty.
Maybe you came here expecting an argument about zodiac signs.
Maybe God used the question to expose something deeper.
Because we all have our own versions of looking toward the stars.
Something we consult before we pray.
Something we trust before Scripture.
Something we run toward when uncertainty becomes unbearable.
Something that promises control.
Something that whispers:
“I can tell you what happens next.”
But Christianity invites us into something far more difficult than prediction.
Trust.
You may not know what happens next.
But you can know Who holds you next.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody reading this desperately needed tonight.
You don't need tomorrow's horoscope.
You need today's grace.
You need the Christ who already knows tomorrow.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't turn the comments into a theological battlefield. Turn them into a place of honesty.
No performance.
No pretending.
