And if Christ has already brought you out of something like this, tell your testimony. Somebody scrolling silently may need to discover that repentance is not the end of their story.
It can be the beginning of coming home.
Not to embarrass them.
Because you love them enough to start a conversation.
The next time a horoscope, zodiac reading, compatibility chart, or spiritual prediction starts sounding strangely persuasive, come back to the question beneath all the other questions:
Who gets to tell me who I am?
There is also another way you can help this ministry continue.
Gospel work requires people willing to pray, share, serve, give, create, teach, and support.
Jesus cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
But voluntary financial support can help Gospel-centered work continue reaching people.
If you cannot financially support the ministry, please do not carry shame.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Invite people to follow.
Faithful support is larger than money, and the body of Christ is not divided into “important people who can give” and “unimportant people who cannot.”
Everything we have belongs to God.
Whatever we do—giving, sharing, serving, speaking, creating—our desire should be to do it faithfully and for His glory.
Because in the end, your birth sign cannot redeem your past.
Your horoscope cannot carry your shame.
A constellation cannot break your chains.
A planet cannot forgive your rebellion.
The universe cannot become your Father.
But Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
Jesus gives a new identity.
Jesus gives a new heart.
Jesus gives a future no horoscope could ever write.
Maybe the stars once seemed to tell you who you were.
But the One who made the stars is calling you by a better name.
And when Jesus takes hold of a life, even the chapters written in confusion do not have to remain the ending.
The stars never wrote your destiny. The hands pierced for you are the hands you can trust with your future.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: AN OLD WOMAN AND A VIRGIN WERE PREGNANT AT THE SAME TIME—And Luke Deliberately Brings Their Stories Together
paragraphs: AN OLD WOMAN AND A VIRGIN WERE PREGNANT AT THE SAME TIME—And Luke Deliberately Brings Their Stories Together

One woman thought her season had already passed. The other had barely entered hers. One pregnancy removed decades of disgrace. The other could expose a young woman to misunderstanding and shame. Then Luke brings them into the same room—and something happens before either child is even born that tells us exactly who Jesus is.
There is a moment in Luke 1 that is easy to read too quickly.
Don't.

Because if you slow down long enough to stand inside that little house in the hill country of Judah, you begin to realize that Luke has placed two women face-to-face who, humanly speaking, should never have been pregnant at the same time.
One was too old.
The other was a virgin.
Elizabeth had lived through years when pregnancy was expected but never came.
Mary became pregnant when pregnancy was not supposed to be possible at all.
One knew the ache of waiting.
The other was suddenly carrying a calling she could never adequately explain.
And somewhere between those two impossible pregnancies stands one staggering truth:
God is not imprisoned by the seasons that imprison us.
Maybe that is why this story still reaches into places we keep hidden.
Because some of us are Elizabeth.
We have prayed until the prayer became painful.
We watched other people receive what we begged God for.
We smiled at announcements that quietly broke our hearts.
We congratulated people while wondering, “Lord… when will it be my turn?”
And eventually we stopped asking out loud.
Not necessarily because we stopped believing in God.
Sometimes because hoping started hurting too much.
Then some of us are Mary.
God has allowed something into our lives that we cannot explain to everybody.
Something costly.
Something that makes obedience look frightening from the outside.
Something that leaves us wondering whether people will misunderstand us before they ever understand what God is doing.
Elizabeth represents the prayer that seemed too late.
Mary represents the calling that seemed impossible.
And Luke brings them together.
But before their meeting, he makes sure we understand something.

Elizabeth and her husband Zechariah were not introduced as rebels being punished by God. Luke describes them as righteous before God, walking faithfully in His commandments, and then immediately tells us that they had no child.
That matters.
Because suffering is not always proof that somebody has secretly failed God.
Sometimes faithful people wait.
Sometimes righteous people cry.
Sometimes people who love God carry questions they cannot answer.
Elizabeth had carried one of those questions for years.
Then Gabriel appeared to Zechariah.
The old prayer had been heard.
Elizabeth conceived.
And suddenly the woman who had probably watched the calendar betray her year after year was carrying a son.
Not merely any son.
John.
The forerunner.
The voice who would prepare the way of the Lord.
But six months into Elizabeth's miracle, Gabriel was sent somewhere else.
Not to Jerusalem.
Not to a palace.
Not to the daughter of a king.
Nazareth.
To a virgin named Mary.
Luke uses the Greek word παρθένος — parthenos.
Virgin.
He is not vague about it.
Mary herself asks the obvious question:
“Πῶς ἔσται τοῦτο…?”
Pōs estai touto?
“How will this be?”
Her question is understandable because what Gabriel has announced cannot be accomplished by ordinary human generation.
The answer takes us directly to God.
The Holy Spirit will come upon her. The power of the Most High will overshadow her. The child to be born will be holy and called the Son of God.
Then Gabriel gives Mary something astonishing.
Elizabeth.
The young virgin is told about the old woman.
The impossible calling is pointed toward the impossible pregnancy.
And then comes the declaration hanging over everything that follows:
ὅτι οὐκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πᾶν ῥῆμα
The heart of it is unmistakable:
No word from God will be impossible.
God points Mary toward Elizabeth as living evidence that human limitation does not have the final word when God has spoken.
But notice something beautiful.
Mary still has to respond.
And she does.
Ἰδοὺ ἡ δούλη κυρίου
“Behold, the servant of the Lord.”
Then:
γένοιτό μοι κατὰ τὸ ῥῆμά σου
“Let it be to me according to your word.”
That is faith.
Not pretending there will be no consequences.
Not knowing how every conversation will go.
Not receiving a ten-page explanation of the future.
Surrender.
Mary essentially places her life underneath the word of God.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to stop here.
Because you keep asking God to explain everything before you obey anything.
You want the entire road illuminated before taking the first step.
Mary did not receive that.
She received a word.
And she surrendered.
Then Luke does something cinematic.
Mary gets up.
Ἀναστᾶσα δὲ Μαριὰμ…
“Mary arose…”
She travels into the hill country “with haste.”
Picture it.
A young woman carrying a secret almost nobody could understand is traveling toward an older woman carrying a miracle almost nobody expected.
One womb carries the prophet who will announce the Messiah.
The other carries the Messiah Himself.
John and Jesus have not preached a sermon.
Neither has performed a public ministry.
Neither has been born.
Yet redemptive history is already moving.
Mary enters Zechariah's house.
She greets Elizabeth.
And suddenly Elizabeth's unborn child leaps in her womb.
Luke writes:
ἐσκίρτησεν τὸ βρέφος ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ αὐτῆς
“The baby leaped in her womb.”
Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit.
And then she cries out.
Not quietly.
Luke describes a great cry.
“Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!”
Then Elizabeth says something so enormous that we should never hurry past it:
καὶ πόθεν μοι τοῦτο ἵνα ἔλθῃ ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ κυρίου μου πρὸς ἐμέ;
“And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”
My Lord.
τοῦ κυρίου μου — tou kyriou mou.
Elizabeth's miracle recognizes Mary's Lord.
That is the center of the scene.
John is extraordinary.
Elizabeth's pregnancy is miraculous.
But neither Elizabeth nor John is the center.
Jesus is.
That is what biblical Christianity keeps doing.
It keeps bringing us back to Jesus.
Not merely to miracles.
Not merely to blessings.
Not merely to answered prayer.
Not merely to inspirational stories.
Christ.
Elizabeth had received something she had wanted for years, yet when Mary walked through the door Elizabeth did not make the moment about herself.
Think about that.
She could have said, “Mary, look what finally happened to me!”
Instead, filled with the Holy Spirit, she recognizes what God is doing through someone else.
That kind of humility is rare.
Especially when we have waited a long time for our own miracle.
Sometimes we finally receive something from God and immediately make ourselves the center of the testimony.
Elizabeth doesn't.
Her miracle bows before the Messiah.
And John does something similar before he can even speak.
The forerunner's entire life will eventually carry one message:
Someone greater is coming.
Years later John will say of Christ:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
But Luke has already shown us the direction of John's ministry before John takes his first breath.
The messenger exists for the Messiah.
And then Elizabeth turns to Mary and says:
μακαρία ἡ πιστεύσασα
“Blessed is she who believed.”
Not blessed is she who understood everything.
Not blessed is she who controlled everything.
Not blessed is she whose obedience was guaranteed to be comfortable.
Blessed is she who believed.
Someone reading this has been trying to understand before surrendering.
You keep saying:
“God, show me how.”
“Show me when.”
“Show me why.”
“Show me what everybody will think.”
“Show me how this ends.”
And perhaps the question beneath all those questions is much simpler:
Will you trust Christ when obedience costs you control?
Mary believed.
Then she sang.
And her song—the Magnificat—is not sentimental decoration around Christmas.
It is saturated with the language, theology, memory, and hope of Israel's Scriptures.
Mary declares:
Μεγαλύνει ἡ ψυχή μου τὸν κύριον
“My soul magnifies the Lord.”
And:
ἠγαλλίασεν τὸ πνεῦμά μου ἐπὶ τῷ θεῷ τῷ σωτῆρί μου
“My spirit rejoiced in God my Savior.”
Do not miss those last words.
God my Savior.
Mary understood herself as someone who needed God's saving mercy.
Her song is not ultimately about Mary's greatness.
It is about God's greatness.
His mercy.
His holiness.
His strength.
His faithfulness.
His covenant promises.
His rescue.
She speaks of the proud being scattered, rulers being brought down, the humble being lifted, the hungry being filled, and Israel being helped according to God's mercy and His promise to Abraham.
The young woman carrying Jesus understands that what is happening inside her is bigger than her.
This is covenant history moving toward fulfillment.
The God who spoke to Abraham has not forgotten.
The God who made promises across generations has not misplaced them.
The silence between promise and fulfillment was never divine amnesia.
God remembered.
And perhaps that is where Luke 1 becomes painfully personal.
Because somebody reading this believes God has forgotten.
You have been Elizabeth for too long.
You prayed.
Waited.
Watched.
Cried.
Aged.
Adjusted.
Eventually you learned how to live around the empty space.
Or maybe you are Mary.
Something has happened that you never planned.
Your reputation feels fragile.
Your future feels uncertain.
You know what God has said, but you do not know how people will respond.
Or maybe you are Zechariah.
You prayed for something for so long that when the answer finally stood in front of you, unbelief had quietly replaced expectation.
That is one of the painful ironies of Luke 1.
Zechariah had apparently prayed for a child.
Then, when Gabriel announces the answer, Zechariah asks how he can know it is true.
Have you ever done that?
“God, please.”
“God, please.”
“God, please.”
Then God moves differently from what you imagined and suddenly:
“God… are You sure?”
We are complicated creatures.
We want miracles we can control.
Answers that arrive according to schedule.
Callings that never threaten our comfort.
Grace without surrender.
A Savior without lordship.
But Luke will not give us that Jesus.
The baby in Mary's womb is Lord.
And if Jesus is Lord, then Christianity cannot merely be something added to our existing life.
He comes to claim it.
That is where this beautiful pregnancy story becomes dangerous.
Because Jesus did not enter history merely to make December more sentimental.
He came because humanity needed saving.
The manger points toward the cross.
The child Mary carries will grow.
He will proclaim the kingdom of God.
He will touch the unclean.
Welcome sinners.
Confront hypocrisy.
Call people to repentance.
Forgive sins.
Give sight.
Raise the broken.
And eventually He will be rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
The Son Mary once carried will carry a cross.
The hands that once curled around His mother's finger will be pierced.
The One Elizabeth called “my Lord” before His birth will be crucified under the accusation of men.
And then—
the grave will lose.
Jesus Christ will rise.
This is why Christianity is not fundamentally advice about becoming a slightly better person.
It is news.
Good news.
The Gospel.
Christ died for our sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
And the risen Christ calls sinners to repent, believe, receive forgiveness, and follow Him.
Maybe that is the miracle you actually need.
Not merely for circumstances to change.
For you to change.
Because some of us have spent years asking Jesus to repair our lives while refusing to surrender our lives.
We want Him as rescuer when we are drowning but not Lord when He tells us where to walk.
We want grace without repentance.
Forgiveness without confession.
Resurrection without a cross.
But Jesus loves us too deeply to merely decorate the prison we refuse to leave.
He came to set captives free.
Maybe your scandal is not visible.
Maybe nobody knows.
The secret addiction.
The hidden messages.
The bitterness.
The pride.
The pornography.
The affair.
The dishonesty.
The resentment you have baptized as “discernment.”
The prayerlessness.
The double life.
The church face.
The private darkness.
The exhausting performance of appearing spiritually alive while something inside you is starving.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not pretending harder.
The answer is Jesus.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the grave.
Grace does not say your sin never mattered.
Grace says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is so great that your sin does not have to write your final chapter.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness as light.
Not by telling sinners they were fine all along.
He rewrites lives through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation.
He takes guilty people and washes them.
Broken people and restores them.
Proud people and humbles them.
Ashamed people and covers them with grace.
Dead hearts and makes them alive.
And sometimes the first evidence that grace is rewriting you is painfully simple:
you stop hiding.
So be honest.
Did this expose something?
Did you recognize yourself somewhere between Elizabeth's waiting, Zechariah's doubt, Mary's surrender, and your own secret struggle?
And if Jesus has already taken a chapter of your life that looked ruined and turned it into a testimony of grace, tell us what He did.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to know that restoration is possible.
Your testimony may become another wounded person's reason to look toward Christ.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be Elizabeth right now.
Somebody thinks it is too late.
Somebody is Mary, terrified by a future they did not expect.
Somebody is Zechariah, struggling to believe after years of disappointment.
Somebody looks perfectly fine in profile pictures and is privately falling apart.
Send it to someone.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, understand Christ more deeply, repent honestly, heal biblically, and keep walking when your faith feels weak, stay close.
We want this space to remain filled with Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, Gospel-centered healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.
And for those who ask how they can help this work continue and expand, there is a practical way.
But I want to say this carefully because God's Word matters more than fundraising language:
The New Testament tells believers to give willingly, deliberately, generously, and “not reluctantly or under compulsion” because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
He will not.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased redemption.
Not us.
If this ministry has strengthened you, convicted you, encouraged you, or helped bring you closer to Scripture, prayerfully consider helping us keep doing it.
Not from guilt.
Not from pressure.
Not to earn God's favor.
But from willing partnership in spreading the Gospel and building resources that continually point people back to Jesus.
Do not leave this article merely impressed by Elizabeth.
Do not leave admiring Mary's courage.
Do not leave fascinated by Greek words.
Do not leave remembering Gospel Warrior.
Leave looking at Jesus.
Elizabeth eventually died.
Mary eventually died.
John eventually died.
Every ministry will someday end.
Every platform will disappear.
Every book will decay.
Every human voice will eventually become silent.
But Jesus Christ lives.
And Luke's story was leading us toward Him from the beginning.
An old woman carried the forerunner.
A virgin carried the Messiah.
The unborn prophet leaped.
Elizabeth cried out.
Mary worshiped.
And heaven was quietly announcing:
The Lord has come near.
The question now is not whether you find the story beautiful.
The question is whether the Lord of the story has your life.
Maybe you have wasted years.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe you have hidden sin.
Come into the light.
Maybe shame has convinced you that God could never want you again.
Look at the cross.
Maybe religion taught you how to appear clean while your heart remained far away.
Repent and come home.
Maybe you are tired.
Come to Christ.
Maybe you have fallen again.
Confess it.
Get up.
Run back.
Grace is not permission to remain in chains.
Grace is the pierced hand of Christ reaching into your darkness and calling you out.
So comment if you need prayer.
Share if someone needs hope.
But above everything else—
follow Jesus.
Because Elizabeth's impossible pregnancy was never the greatest miracle in Luke 1.
Neither was Mary's virgin conception presented merely as a spectacle of divine power.
The wonder is Who came.
God kept His promise.
The Savior entered our darkness.
The Lord came near.
And because He came, because He died, because He rose, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Remember this when shame starts reading your history back to you:
The scandal may explain where you have been—but only Jesus gets to decide what grace can make of what remains.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “SHE SAT IN HER BELOVED’S SHADOW—AND DISCOVERED WHAT HER SOUL HAD BEEN STARVING FOR”
paragraphs: “SHE SAT IN HER BELOVED’S SHADOW—AND DISCOVERED WHAT HER SOUL HAD BEEN STARVING FOR”

Song of Songs 2:3 is a love poem about desire, nearness, shelter, and sweetness. But read in the light of the whole biblical story, its imagery asks a haunting question of every believer: after tasting so many things this world promised would satisfy you, have you learned where your soul can finally sit down?
There is a kind of tiredness sleep cannot cure.
You know it.

Your body may be functioning. Your smile may still appear when someone points a camera at you. You may still go to work, answer messages, attend church, post Bible verses, laugh with friends, take care of everyone else, and tell people, “I’m okay.”
But somewhere beneath all of that...
your soul is standing in the heat.
Tired.
Thirsty.
Looking for somewhere safe enough to sit down.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you became so good at surviving that people started calling you strong.
Maybe you learned how to worship while hurting, serve while empty, encourage others while quietly wondering who would encourage you.
Maybe you have loved people who wounded you.
Trusted people who betrayed you.
Prayed prayers that seemed to disappear into silence.
Fought temptations you were ashamed to admit existed.
Returned to sins you promised God you would never touch again.
And perhaps the hardest part is that you still love Jesus...
but somewhere along the road, your soul became exhausted.
Then, hidden inside one of Scripture’s most beautiful love poems, we meet a woman who says something remarkably simple.
She sat down.
Not on a throne.
Not in a palace.
Not before an applauding crowd.
She sat beneath the shadow of the one she loved.
The Hebrew of Song of Songs 2:3 reads:
“כְּתַפּוּחַ בַּעֲצֵי הַיַּעַר כֵּן דּוֹדִי בֵּין הַבָּנִים בְּצִלּוֹ חִמַּדְתִּי וְיָשַׁבְתִּי וּפִרְיוֹ מָתוֹק לְחִכִּי”
Ketappuaḥ ba‘atsei haya‘ar, ken dodi bein habbanim; betzillo ḥimmadti veyashavti, ufiryo matoq leḥikki.
A close rendering is:
“Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the young men. In his shade I delighted and sat down, and his fruit was sweet to my palate.”
The Hebrew is beautiful.
בְּצִלּוֹ — betzillo.
“In his shadow.”
חִמַּדְתִּי — ḥimmadti.
“I desired... I delighted.”
וְיָשַׁבְתִּי — veyashavti.
“And I sat.”
מָתוֹק — matoq.
“Sweet.”
לְחִכִּי — leḥikki.
“To my palate.”
Do not rush past that.
She desired.
She came near.
She sat.
She tasted.
And she discovered sweetness.
That is the movement of the verse.

In its immediate context, Song of Songs is celebrating human love. We should honor that before doing anything else with the text. The woman is speaking poetically about her beloved. Scripture does not require us to pretend that the young man in this particular verse is secretly Jesus.
But Christians also read every part of Scripture inside the greater story that reaches its fullness in Jesus Christ.
And when the imagery of this ancient love poem is placed beside the rest of Scripture, something beautiful happens.
Its language gives us a vocabulary for longing.
For refuge.
For delight.
For satisfaction.
And those themes ultimately confront us with the One in whom the deepest hunger of the human soul finds its answer.
Jesus.
Not because every romantic line in Song of Songs is a coded prophecy.

But because every legitimate human longing for faithful love, safety, belonging, beauty, intimacy, and enduring delight eventually exposes a deeper hunger that no created thing can completely satisfy.
We keep trying anyway.
That may be the tragedy behind some of your deepest wounds.
You asked temporary things to carry eternal weight.
You wanted another human being to make you whole.
You wanted success to tell you that you mattered.
You wanted money to make you secure.
You wanted attention to make you feel beautiful.
You wanted achievement to silence insecurity.
You wanted pleasure to anesthetize pain.
You wanted religious activity to quiet a conscience that only grace could cleanse.
You wanted another relationship to erase what the last relationship did.
You wanted another purchase.
Another promotion.
Another notification.
Another compliment.
Another night of pretending.
Another secret indulgence.
Another distraction.
Just something...
anything...
that could make the ache stop.
And for a moment, perhaps it worked.
That is what makes false refuges so dangerous.
They usually offer a little shade.
Just not enough to survive beneath.
Sin can give pleasure.
Scripture never requires us to lie about that.
Hebrews 11:25 even speaks about the “fleeting pleasures of sin.”
The problem is not that sin never tastes sweet.
The problem is what happens after you swallow.
The screen goes dark.
The room becomes quiet.
The person leaves.
The high disappears.
The applause ends.
The purchase becomes ordinary.
The secret becomes heavier.
And you are alone again with the soul you were trying to escape.
There is a sweetness that leaves bitterness behind.
And there is another sweetness...
the sweetness of discovering that Christ does not merely distract you from your emptiness.
He meets you inside it.
Perhaps that is why the image of Song of Songs 2:3 can speak so powerfully to a weary Christian imagination.
“In his shade I delighted and sat down.”
Some of us have been running around Jesus while rarely resting in Jesus.
We study Him.
Defend Him.
Sing about Him.
Post about Him.
Serve Him.
Argue theology about Him.
Tell others they need Him.
But quietly...
we are dying of thirst beneath religious activity because we have forgotten what it means simply to come to Him.
Jesus Himself said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
Matthew 11:28.
Come.
Not impress Me.
Come.
Not repair yourself first.
Come.
Not hide until you become worthy.
Come.
That invitation becomes breathtaking when you remember who is speaking.
The sinless Son of God is calling exhausted sinners toward Himself.
The holy One is not telling the broken to clean the blood off themselves before approaching.
He is calling them near.
This is the scandal of grace.
We expected condemnation.
Christ offered Himself.
We expected distance.
Christ came near.
We expected a ladder.
Christ gave us a cross.
We expected God to tell us how to climb out of our ruin.
Instead, the Son of God entered our world, bore sin, died, was buried, and rose again.
That changes everything.
Because the shadow beneath which the Christian finally rests is not cheap comfort.
Our peace cost blood.
At Calvary, Jesus did not merely demonstrate that suffering exists.
He bore judgment for sinners.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
The Shepherd became the Lamb.
The Judge took the place of the guilty.
The righteous One suffered for the unrighteous “that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
Do you see it?
Grace does not say your sin did not matter.
The cross says it mattered more than you ever imagined.
Grace says Jesus loved sinners enough to pay what sinners could never pay.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace makes hiding unbearable.
You finally stop defending the thing destroying you.
You stop renaming your sin.
You stop blaming everybody else.
You stop negotiating with darkness.
You stop telling God, “I can handle this.”
You come into the light.
Maybe that is where this article has found you.
Not where everyone thinks you are.
Where you actually are.
Maybe there is something on your phone nobody knows about.
Maybe resentment has been living inside you so long that bitterness now feels like part of your personality.
Maybe you are married but emotionally wandering.
Maybe you know exactly which person you keep checking online.
Maybe pornography has become the room you enter whenever loneliness becomes unbearable.
Maybe pride has disguised itself as discernment.
Maybe jealousy has disguised itself as ambition.
Maybe unforgiveness has disguised itself as self-protection.
Maybe you have become cold toward God while remaining fluent in Christian language.
Maybe you have been begging Jesus to remove consequences while refusing to surrender the sin causing them.
And perhaps nobody knows.
But He does.
Jesus already knows the version of you that you are terrified someone else might discover.
And still the Gospel says:
Come.
Not because secrecy is harmless.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because holiness does not matter.
Come because the only Physician who can heal you is standing where you have been afraid to go.
Into the light.
The woman in the Song did not merely admire the tree from a distance.
She sat beneath its shade.
There is a difference between knowing shade exists and actually sitting beneath it.
There is a difference between knowing Christ saves and trusting Him.
Between studying grace and receiving grace.
Between discussing repentance and repenting.
Between believing Jesus can forgive sinners and finally admitting:
“I am the sinner who needs forgiving.”
That moment can feel humiliating.
But heaven calls it freedom.
You do not have to maintain your own legend anymore.
You can tell the truth.
David knew something about that.
After hiding terrible sin, he eventually cried in Psalm 51:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Not a better mask.
A clean heart.
That is what grace does.
It does not improve your disguise.
It begins transforming the person beneath it.
And then comes the second half of the image:
“His fruit was sweet to my palate.”
Not merely shade.
Fruit.
Not merely relief from something.
Delight in something.
Christianity is not ultimately a life spent saying no to everything enjoyable while waiting to die.
The Gospel does not merely rescue us from sin.
It reconciles us to God.
Christ becomes more than the emergency exit from hell.
He becomes treasure.
This is why Psalm 34:8 says:
“O taste and see that the LORD is good.”
Taste.
There are truths about God that cannot remain abstract doctrines on a page.
Forgiveness becomes different when you know how guilty you were.
Mercy becomes different when you know what you deserved.
Adoption becomes different when you know what it is to feel unwanted.
The presence of God becomes different when everyone else has walked away.
The promise of resurrection becomes different when you have stood beside a grave.
The words “I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” become different at three in the morning when your world has collapsed and there is nobody left to call.
Suddenly Christianity is not merely information.
The fruit becomes sweet to your palate.
You begin discovering what millions of wounded believers have discovered before you:
Jesus is not only enough when life is beautiful.
Jesus is enough when life breaks.
That does not mean Christians never grieve.
Jesus Himself wept.
It does not mean depression disappears whenever someone quotes a verse.
It does not mean trauma becomes imaginary.
It does not mean every prayer receives the answer we wanted.
It does not mean following Christ makes suffering painless.
It means suffering no longer has the authority to tell you that you have been abandoned by God.
The cross permanently destroys that conclusion.
Because the same Christ who suffered is risen.
The tomb is empty.
Death did not get the final sentence.
Sin did not get the final sentence.
Satan did not get the final sentence.
Your worst chapter does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
That is why our message is:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your story contains pages you wish you could tear out.
Sexual failure.
Addiction.
Divorce.
Betrayal.
Abortion.
Pride.
Deception.
Greed.
Anger.
Years wasted.
Promises broken.
Faith abandoned.
Relationships destroyed.
Things done to you.
Things done by you.
Jesus does not need you to pretend those pages were never written.
Redemption is more astonishing than denial.
He can take a story that should have ended in shame and make it testify to mercy.
Ask Peter.
He denied Jesus.
Jesus restored him.
Ask Paul.
He persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed him into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
Ask the woman at the well.
Her complicated history did not prevent Jesus from meeting her in broad daylight and turning a shamed woman into someone who ran toward her town saying, “Come, see a man...”
That is what Jesus does.
He walks directly into stories respectable religion might prefer to hide.
And He begins rewriting them.
Not by calling darkness light.
By bringing people out of darkness.
That is grace.
Maybe you need to stop running today.
Maybe your prayer does not need impressive vocabulary.
Maybe all you have left is:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Pray it.
Mean it.
Bring Him the real thing.
The real addiction.
The real anger.
The real loneliness.
The real fear.
The real secret.
The real you.
Christ did not die for the imaginary version of you that never struggles.
He died for sinners.
And He rose again.
So repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come out of hiding.
Sit beneath the shadow of grace.
Taste again.
You may discover that the Savior you thought was waiting to humiliate you was the Shepherd searching for you.
Be honest.
Someone reading beneath you may be standing where you once stood.
Your scars may become someone else’s evidence that Jesus still restores people.
And think of one person who needs this tonight.
Not fifty people.
One.
The friend whose smile has changed.
The brother who stopped going to church.
The daughter who thinks she has gone too far.
The husband silently fighting something he cannot explain.
The woman carrying shame from a chapter nobody knows.
The believer who loves Jesus but feels spiritually numb.
The skeptic who thinks Christianity is only condemnation.
Send this to them.
Not because an algorithm is sacred.
Because people are.
One share can place the Gospel in front of someone Gospel Warrior may never otherwise reach.
There may come a night when you need these words again.

Our purpose is not to build admiration around a page. We want Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and above everything else the Gospel of Jesus Christ placed continually before people who desperately need Him.
And if you want to help Gospel Warrior continue creating, publishing, distributing, and expanding this work, there is another way you can stand with us.
But hear this carefully.
It cannot.
It does not.
Jesus purchased our redemption.
And Scripture teaches Christian generosity without manipulation: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Supporting Gospel work can glorify God when it flows from a willing heart seeking His glory rather than human recognition.
That does not make their love for Christ smaller.
Pray for this work.
Send these articles to hurting people.
Use what God has placed in your hands.
But the merchandise is not the heart of this.
Jesus is.
The mission is.
Souls are.
Discipleship is.
Truth is.
The person sitting alone tonight wondering whether God could possibly still want them is.
The Christian secretly losing a battle nobody knows about is.
The unbeliever who may encounter the Gospel because somebody cared enough to press “Share” is.
Do not merely admire the shade.
Sit beneath it.
Do not merely discuss the fruit.
Taste.
Do not merely agree that Jesus forgives sinners.
Bring Him your sin.
Do not merely believe that Jesus restores broken people.
Give Him your brokenness.
Do not merely say that Christ can rewrite stories.
Hand Him the pen.
There may still be consequences from yesterday.
There may still be tears tomorrow.
There may still be battles ahead.
But if you belong to Christ, your scandal is no longer the final authority over your identity.
Your shame does not own the copyright to your story.
Your failure does not get the last paragraph.
At the cross, grace entered the story.
At the empty tomb, hope received the final word.
And perhaps that is why this ancient image remains so beautiful.
A weary person.
A beloved.
A shadow.
A place to sit.
Fruit sweet upon the tongue.
After all the running...
after all the substitutes...
after all the places you tried to hide...
you discover that what your soul needed most was not another place to escape.
It was Someone to come home to.
So come to Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive forgiveness where shame has chained you.
Return where you have wandered.
Rest where you have been striving.
Taste and see that the Lord is good.
And when grace has found you beneath the burning heat of everything you thought would destroy you, leave enough room beneath the shade for another wounded soul to find Jesus too.
Because one day you may look back at the chapter you begged God to erase...
and realize it became the very place where you learned how sweet grace really is.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS CELEBRATE CHRISTMAS? THE QUESTION ISN’T WHAT YOU THINK
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS CELEBRATE CHRISTMAS? THE QUESTION ISN’T WHAT YOU THINK
Before you throw away the tree—or defend it—there is a harder question every Christian needs to answer: What does Jesus actually want from you?
Every December, it happens again.
One Christian posts a picture of a Christmas tree glowing beside a Bible.
Another Christian comments, “That’s pagan.”
Someone replies, “We’re celebrating Jesus.”
Someone else says, “Jesus wasn’t born on December 25.”
Then Jeremiah 10 gets quoted.
Romans 14 gets quoted back.
Voices rise.
Defenses go up.
Brothers and sisters who both claim the name of Christ begin treating each other like enemies over lights, trees, calendars, gifts, traditions, and a date the Bible itself never gives us.
And somewhere in the middle of all the noise...
Jesus can become almost invisible.
That may be the most uncomfortable Christmas problem of all.
Because perhaps the deepest question is not simply, “Should Christians celebrate Christmas?”
Perhaps the question underneath the question is:
Can I do what I am doing with a clear conscience before Jesus Christ—and is what I am doing actually bringing glory to Him?
That question cuts deeper.
Because you can put up a Christmas tree and forget Christ.
You can also throw away your Christmas tree and become proud of how much more “biblical” you think you are than everyone else.
You can sing about Bethlehem while refusing to forgive someone.
You can condemn December 25 while carrying bitterness in your heart.
You can buy gifts for everyone you love while ignoring the Savior who gave Himself for you.
And you can know every argument about Saturnalia, Roman festivals, calendars, shepherds, trees, and church history...
while your own heart remains miles from Jesus.
So before deciding whether Christmas belongs in your home, we need to go somewhere much older than Christmas.
Back before December 25.
Back before church calendars.
Back before decorated trees.
Back before Christmas carols.
Back to a frightened young mother.
A manger.
A dark night.
Shepherds watching their flocks.
And an announcement that shook eternity.
Luke records the angel declaring that good news had arrived because a Savior had been born, identified as Christ the Lord.
The center of the announcement was not a date.
It was a Person.
Jesus.
And John reaches even deeper into the mystery of that arrival:
Καὶ ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
John 1:14.
Those Greek words are staggering.
ὁ Λόγος — ho Logos — the Word.
σὰρξ — sarx — flesh.
ἐγένετο — egeneto — became.
The eternal Word entered human existence.
God did not merely send humanity another philosophy.
He came near.
The Son took flesh.
John continues:
καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν
kai eskēnōsen en hēmin
“and dwelt among us.”
The verb eskēnōsen carries the imagery of dwelling or pitching one’s tent among a people.
Think about that.
The Christmas story, stripped of commercialism and sentimentality, is not fundamentally about snow, presents, trees, family dinners, nostalgia, or December 25.
It is about the incomprehensible humility of Christ.
The Creator entered His creation.
The One through whom all things were made entered the world of human hunger, exhaustion, rejection, suffering, betrayal, blood, nails, and death.
Bethlehem was already pointing toward Calvary.
The Child in the manger came to become the Lamb on the cross.
That is Christianity.
And that is where our Christmas question must begin.
Not with, “What does my family normally do?”
Not with, “What does social media say?”
Not even with, “What did Christians hundreds of years ago do?”
But with Scripture.
And Scripture gives us something that frustrates people on both extremes.
The Bible does not command Christians to celebrate the birth of Jesus annually on December 25.
But neither does the New Testament issue a command forbidding Christians from setting aside a day to remember and give thanks for Christ's incarnation.
That matters.
December 25 is not identified in Scripture as Jesus' birthday. Christians therefore should not pretend the Bible tells us the exact date when Christ was born.
It doesn't.

Historical discussion about why December 25 eventually became associated with the celebration of Christ's birth is more complicated than the popular slogan “Christians simply stole a pagan holiday.” Various historical explanations have been proposed, and Christians should be careful about repeating sweeping claims as unquestionable facts when the history is debated.
But even after studying all of that history, we still have to answer the more important theological question.
What should a Christian do now?
Paul gives us a remarkably relevant principle in Romans 14.
The Greek text of Romans 14:5 reads:
ὃς μὲν γὰρ κρίνει ἡμέραν παρ’ ἡμέραν, ὃς δὲ κρίνει πᾶσαν ἡμέραν· ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω.
Hos men gar krinei hēmeran par’ hēmeran, hos de krinei pasan hēmeran; hekastos en tō idiō noi plērophoreisthō.

In context, Paul describes one believer regarding one day differently from another while another regards the days alike, and then says that each should be fully persuaded or convinced in his own mind.
The passage is not specifically about modern Christmas.
We should not pretend that it is.
But its principle concerning disputed observances of days is enormously important.
Paul continues by bringing the issue underneath one governing reality:
“to the Lord.”
The person observing a day must observe it to the Lord.
That changes everything.
The question becomes painfully personal.
When you celebrate Christmas...
is it actually to the Lord?
Not to nostalgia.
Not to consumerism.
Not because everyone else is doing it.
Not because you are terrified of disappointing relatives.
Not because you want impressive family photographs.
Not because your children need more things.
Not because December would feel strange without the traditions.
To the Lord.
And for the Christian who chooses not to celebrate Christmas, the question is equally uncomfortable.
Are you abstaining to the Lord?
Or have you quietly begun to enjoy feeling spiritually superior to Christians who celebrate it?
Because Romans 14 does not merely address liberty.
It attacks contempt.
It attacks judgmentalism.
The Christian who celebrates must not despise the Christian who abstains.
The Christian who abstains must not condemn a brother or sister merely because that believer, in sincere conscience, dedicates a day to remembering Christ's incarnation.
There are boundaries, of course.
Christian liberty does not turn idolatry into worship.
Calling something “Christian” cannot sanctify sin.
If a celebration requires drunkenness, sexual immorality, greed, occult practices, idolatry, dishonesty, or anything else Scripture condemns, attaching Jesus' name to it does not make it holy.
Paul gives another governing principle:
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.”
That principle from 1 Corinthians 10:31 reaches straight into December.
Can Christ be glorified in your celebration?
Can you thank Him for taking flesh?
Can you open Scripture with your children and tell them why Bethlehem matters?
Can you feed someone who is hungry?
Can you reconcile with someone you have wounded?
Can you give without worshiping possessions?
Can you remember the lonely?
Can you invite the forgotten person to your table?
Can you tell an unbelieving relative why Jesus came?
Can your home say something more powerful than “Merry Christmas”?
Can your life say:
Christ has come. Christ has died. Christ is risen. Christ saves sinners.
Then there is another argument that appears every year.
“The Christmas tree is condemned in Jeremiah 10.”
Read the chapter carefully.
Jeremiah is confronting idolatry. The passage describes craftsmen working material into an idol and adorning it, within a larger contrast between powerless idols and the living God.
It is not a prophecy about a modern family placing a decorated evergreen in a living room.
That does not mean Christians should never examine their traditions.
We absolutely should.
Anything can become an idol.
A tree can.
Money can.
Family can.
Tradition can.
Even theological knowledge can.
But biblical interpretation requires us to ask what a passage meant in its actual context before making it address a practice centuries removed from that context.
Ironically, a Christian could have no Christmas tree at all and still be drowning in idolatry.
Because idols are not limited to objects carved from wood.
Sometimes an idol looks like success.
Sometimes it looks like approval.
Sometimes it looks like money.
Sometimes it looks like romance.
Sometimes it looks like ministry.
Sometimes it even looks like being right.
And suddenly the Christmas debate becomes uncomfortable again.
Because maybe Jesus is not asking first about the tree standing in your living room.
Maybe He is confronting what is sitting on the throne of your heart.
Imagine celebrating the birth of Jesus while refusing His lordship.
Imagine singing:
“Christ the Savior is born,”
while secretly cherishing the sin from which the Savior came to rescue you.
Imagine defending the manger while rejecting the cross.
That is the real tragedy.
Jesus did not enter this world merely so humanity could create a beautiful holiday around His infancy.
He came to save sinners.
The manger cannot be separated from the cross.
Matthew tells us why His name would be Jesus: He would save His people from their sins.
Not decorate their sins.
Not excuse their sins.
Not rename their sins.
Save them.
Christmas without repentance can become sentimental Christianity.
A baby Jesus who never grows up is very easy for the world to tolerate.
A baby in a manger makes a beautiful decoration.
But the Jesus who grows up and says, “Follow Me”...
the Jesus who confronts hypocrisy...
the Jesus who commands repentance...
the Jesus who identifies Himself as the way, the truth, and the life...
the Jesus who willingly goes to the cross...
the Jesus who rises from the grave...
the Jesus before whom every knee will ultimately bow...
that Jesus cannot simply be placed back into a storage box when December ends.
And perhaps that is the Christmas question we have been avoiding.
Not:
“Do you celebrate Christmas?”
But:
Does Christ have you?
Because you can celebrate Christmas and belong to Jesus.
You can abstain from Christmas and belong to Jesus.
But you cannot belong to Jesus while deliberately refusing Jesus Himself.
Maybe you are reading this with Christmas memories that hurt.
Perhaps December does not feel magical to you.
Maybe there is an empty chair at your table now.
Someone died.
Someone left.
Someone betrayed you.
Maybe the family photograph changed.
Maybe the marriage ended.
Maybe your child no longer calls.
Maybe you are surrounded by Christmas lights while fighting a darkness nobody around you can see.
Everyone keeps saying, “Merry Christmas.”
And you keep smiling.
But something inside you whispers:
“I just want this month to be over.”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel was never dependent upon your circumstances being merry.
Jesus entered a broken world.
He came into political tension, poverty, danger, grief, violence, and eventually exile.
The Christmas story itself contains tears.
And Christ did not come because humanity had finally cleaned itself up enough for God.
He came because we could not save ourselves.
That is grace.
Scandalous grace.
Grace for the addict who relapsed.
Grace for the religious person hiding pride.
Grace for the husband who failed.
Grace for the wife who feels invisible.
Grace for the prodigal who thinks he has traveled too far.
Grace for the churchgoer who sings loudly but secretly wonders whether God still wants him.
Grace for the woman crying after everyone has gone to sleep.
Grace for the man who keeps telling everyone he is fine.
Grace for you.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that good people finally managed to climb high enough to reach God.
It is that God came down for sinners.
ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο.
The Word became flesh.
He came down.
And eventually...
He was lifted up on a cross.
There the hands that Mary once held were pierced.
The forehead she once kissed was wounded.
The body once wrapped in swaddling cloth was stripped and crucified.
And the One whose birth angels announced died beneath the judgment our sins deserved.
Then the grave received Him.
For three days, it appeared that darkness had won.
But Christianity does not end at a manger.
And it does not end at a cross.
The tomb became empty.
Jesus Christ rose.
That is why grace can rewrite your story.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your shame does not get the last word.
Your addiction does not get the last word.
Your betrayal does not get the last word.
Your grief does not get the last word.
Your past does not get the last word.
Death itself does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
That is what we mean when we say:
So...
should Christians celebrate Christmas?
A Christian should not pretend that Scripture commands an annual December 25 celebration when it does not.
A Christian should not condemn another believer merely for sincerely setting aside a day to remember Christ's incarnation when Scripture does not issue such a prohibition.
A Christian who celebrates should do so under the lordship of Christ, with thanksgiving and a clear conscience.
A Christian who abstains should abstain under the lordship of Christ, with thanksgiving and a clear conscience.
Neither side should turn a matter of conscience into a throne from which to look down upon the other.
And every Christian should be willing to examine traditions in the light of Scripture.
If Christmas in your home has become greed...
change it.
If it has become drunkenness...
repent.
If it has become debt-fueled competition...
change it.
If it has become an exhausting performance designed to impress people...
change it.
If Santa receives more attention than Jesus...
ask yourself why.
If your children know every detail of a fictional Christmas story but barely understand why the Son of God came into the world...
something needs to change.
You do not necessarily need to throw Christmas away.
You may need to redeem the way you observe it.
Open Luke 2.
Read Matthew 1.
Read John 1.
Tell your children about the incarnation.
Pray together.
Give quietly.
Forgive somebody.
Visit someone lonely.
Feed somebody.
Support Gospel work.
Tell somebody who does not know Christ why the manger matters.
And when the lights eventually come down...
keep following Jesus.
That is the test.
January Jesus.
February Jesus.
March Jesus.
When there are no carols playing.
When the decorations are gone.
When following Him costs something.
When obedience hurts.
When temptation whispers.
When nobody applauds.
Jesus.
Still Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Be honest.
Somebody reading it may desperately need proof that Jesus still restores people.
And perhaps even send it privately to the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is nothing more than religious tradition.
Let them discover that Christianity is not ultimately about Christmas.
It is about Christ.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It never could.
It doesn't.
Jesus purchased salvation with His blood. Grace cannot be bought.
Christians hold different convictions about tithing, while the New Testament clearly emphasizes willing, purposeful, generous giving rather than giving under compulsion.
But financial support can be a voluntary offering to help Gospel ministry continue.

If you have been asking how you can help Gospel Warrior keep producing Christ-centered content, reach hurting people, develop discipleship resources, and expand this work, monthly support is one practical way.
Scripture teaches a beautiful principle of Christian generosity: giving should come from a heart that has decided to give, “not grudgingly, or of necessity” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That matters to us.
We do not want your support because someone frightened, pressured, or spiritually manipulated you into giving.
We want Jesus to receive the glory.
So pray about it.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Because someone you know is fighting a battle they have never posted about.
Someone is smiling through spiritual exhaustion.
Someone thinks Jesus could never forgive what they have done.
Someone believes their scandal has become their identity.
Someone thinks their story is already over.
Share truth with them.
Share hope with them.
And if this ministry consistently helps you do that, prayerfully consider helping us keep doing it too.
Because after every argument about Christmas eventually fades...
after the tree comes down...
after the gifts break...
after the lights burn out...
after December becomes another memory...
one question remains.
What did you do with Jesus?
Do not merely celebrate the day people remember His birth.
Know Him.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His grace.
Follow Him.
And let the Savior who entered humanity's darkness enter every locked room of your heart.
Because the greatest Christmas miracle is not that humanity finally found its way to God.
It is that, in Jesus Christ...
God came looking for us.
And when Jesus enters the story, even the chapter you were ashamed to show anyone can become the place where grace begins writing again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS BEING A MISTRESS A SIN? THE ANSWER MAY HURT—BUT WHAT JESUS DOES WITH YOUR STORY COULD SAVE YOU
paragraphs: IS BEING A MISTRESS A SIN? THE ANSWER MAY HURT—BUT WHAT JESUS DOES WITH YOUR STORY COULD SAVE YOU

She may be the woman everyone condemns. He may be the man nobody knows is cheating. A wife may be crying somewhere while two people keep calling adultery “love.” But when Jesus enters the story, He does something neither shame nor excuses can do: He tells the truth about sin—and then opens the door to an entirely different life.
There is a question some people type into a search bar because they are curious.
And then there are questions people type because their hands are shaking.
“Is being a mistress a sin?”
Maybe you already know the answer.
Maybe you are hoping the Bible has a loophole.
Maybe he told you his marriage was already dead.
Maybe he said he was leaving her.
Maybe he said you were the person he should have married.
Maybe you never intended for this to happen.
It started with conversations.
Then messages.
Then emotional dependence.
Then secrecy.
Then the moment you crossed a boundary you once swore you would never cross.
Or perhaps you are not the mistress at all.
Perhaps you are the wife who discovered the messages.
Perhaps you are the husband who has been living two lives.
Perhaps you are the child who watched adultery tear a family apart.
Perhaps you are the Christian who knows exactly what Scripture says but has become emotionally attached to someone who belongs in a covenant with somebody else.
Whatever brought you here, stay.
Not because this article is going to excuse what God calls sin.
It will not.
But neither is this going to throw stones at people Jesus came to save.
Because the most important question is not merely, “Is being a mistress a sin?”
There is another question hiding underneath it.
What does Jesus do with someone who has already crossed the line?
And that is where this story becomes bigger than your scandal.
Yes.

If by “mistress” we mean knowingly participating in a sexual or romantic relationship with someone who is married to another person, Scripture does not leave us room to rename it simply because the feelings are real.
Adultery is sin.
God said in Exodus 20:14:
לֹא תִּנְאָף — lōʾ tinʾāf
“You shall not commit adultery.”
The Hebrew verb comes from נָאַף — nāʾaph, referring to adultery, the violation of the marriage covenant through sexual unfaithfulness.
It is remarkably brief.
No complicated paragraph.
No footnote saying, “unless you truly love each other.”
No exception saying, “unless the marriage is unhappy.”
No exemption because the relationship feels emotionally profound.
לֹא תִּנְאָף.
Do not commit adultery.
And Jesus did not weaken that command.
He drove it deeper.
In Matthew 5:27, the Greek preserves the command:
Οὐ μοιχεύσεις — Ou moicheuseis
“You shall not commit adultery.”
Then Jesus takes His listeners beyond merely avoiding the external act and confronts lustful intention within the heart (Matthew 5:27–28).
That matters because adultery rarely begins in a bedroom.
It often begins much earlier.
With permission.
With fantasy.
With secrecy.
With a message you would delete if your spouse walked into the room.
With conversations you would not have if their husband or wife were sitting beside you.
With emotional intimacy that quietly belongs somewhere else.
With the sentence, “We’re just friends,” repeated long after your conscience stopped believing it.
Jesus goes after the heart because He knows where the visible collapse begins.
And this is where we need courage enough to stop manipulating language.
Calling adultery “complicated love” does not make it holy.
Calling someone your “soulmate” does not dissolve someone else’s marriage covenant.
Feeling deeply does not automatically mean God approves.
Something can feel powerful and still be wrong.
Something can feel beautiful and still require repentance.
Something can make your heart race while slowly destroying your soul.

That does not mean every person involved is equally responsible in every circumstance. Manipulation, deception, coercion, abuse, and ignorance can profoundly affect moral responsibility and pastoral care. Someone who did not know the other person was married is not in the same position as someone knowingly pursuing a married person. And someone subjected to coercion or abuse should never be treated as though abuse were simply consensual adultery.
Truth requires those distinctions.
But when two people knowingly continue an adulterous relationship, Scripture does not sanctify it because their emotions are sincere.
And before anyone points a finger exclusively at “the mistress,” we need to say something the church sometimes fails to say loudly enough.
The married person committing adultery is responsible too.
The Bible does not create a convenient theology where the outsider carries all the shame while the unfaithful spouse somehow becomes a helpless victim of temptation.
Adultery requires accountability.
The husband cannot say, “She seduced me,” and wash his hands.
The wife cannot say, “He understood me better,” and erase covenant responsibility.
The unmarried partner cannot say, “Their marriage was already over emotionally,” and declare themselves innocent when the marriage still existed.
Sin loves excuses because excuses allow us to keep what repentance would require us to surrender.
And perhaps that sentence hurt.
Maybe because there is someone you do not want to surrender.
Maybe you have prayed, “God, if this relationship is wrong, take these feelings away.”
But the feelings remained.
So you interpreted their survival as permission.
Be careful.
The continued existence of desire is not proof of divine approval.
Jesus never said obedience would always begin when temptation disappeared.
Sometimes obedience begins while your heart is screaming in the opposite direction.
Sometimes repentance has tears running down its face.
Sometimes repentance blocks the number it desperately wants to call.
Sometimes repentance deletes the conversation.
Sometimes repentance admits the truth.
Sometimes repentance stops waiting for the married person to “eventually” leave.
Sometimes repentance walks away from something that felt like love because you finally love Christ more than you love what Christ told you to surrender.
That is not easy Christianity.
That is the cross-shaped life.
Jesus said, “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24, KJV).
Notice what He did not say.
“Follow Me as long as I never ask for the relationship you cannot imagine living without.”
There are moments when following Jesus costs something.
But there is something else you need to hear.
Especially if shame has already begun whispering that you are filthy.
Especially if religious people have made you believe there is forgiveness for everybody except “women like you.”
Especially if you have already repented but still introduce yourself internally by the worst thing you ever did.
Listen carefully.
Adultery is a sin.
But adultery is not beyond the blood of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not say sin is harmless.
The Gospel says Christ is powerful enough to save sinners.
Those are radically different messages.
Paul wrote to the Corinthians about people whose lives had been marked by serious sin, including sexual immorality and adultery. He did not pretend those things were acceptable.
Then comes one of the most beautiful reversals in Scripture:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not “such are you forever.”
Not “such will your identity always be.”
Not “Jesus forgave everything except that.”
Paul continues:
“but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV).
Read those words again.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely offer you a better reputation.
He offers cleansing.
He does not merely teach you to hide the scandal more effectively.
He calls you out of the darkness.
He does not simply help you feel better while continuing deliberately in what He calls sin.
Grace forgives.
Grace transforms.
Grace teaches us to leave what is destroying us.
And perhaps you are thinking about the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
It is one of the most emotionally arresting scenes associated with the ministry of Jesus.
A woman is dragged publicly into humiliation.
The religious leaders are ready to use her.
Everybody can see her sin.
Interestingly, the man involved is nowhere in the accusation presented before Jesus.
The woman becomes the spectacle.
And Jesus refuses to join the mob.

But we should handle this passage carefully. The account of the woman caught in adultery, traditionally found in John 7:53–8:11, is absent from many of the earliest Greek manuscripts and appears in different locations in some manuscript traditions. Many modern Bibles therefore mark the passage with a textual note.
That does not give us permission to build careless doctrine on disputed textual details.
Yet the account as traditionally received contains a striking combination that is entirely consistent with the broader New Testament portrait of Jesus:
Mercy without pretending sin is righteousness.
The famous conclusion is not merely, “Neither do I condemn thee.”
It continues:
“go, and sin no more” (John 8:11, KJV).
Mercy.
Then transformation.
Grace.
Then a different road.
Jesus does not crush the sinner.
But neither does He bless the chains.
This is what modern conversations about sexual sin often tear apart.
Some people want truth without mercy.
They want stones.
They want humiliation.
They want screenshots.
They want public destruction.
They want the adulterer permanently branded by the sin.
Others want mercy without truth.
They want affirmation without repentance.
They want God to bless whatever feels authentic.
Jesus gives us something infinitely better.
Grace and truth.
He can look directly at our sin without looking away from us.
Think about that.
The thing you are terrified God will discover...
He already knows.
The messages.
The hotel room.
The secret account.
The deleted photographs.
The lies.
The anniversaries you spent with someone else's spouse.
The promises.
The rationalizations.
The nights you cried afterward.
The times you said it would be the last time.
The times it wasn't.
God did not learn those things today.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Come home.
Not because the sin was small.
Because Christ's mercy is great.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling guilty.
The New Testament frequently uses μετάνοια — metanoia, a word associated with repentance, a changed mind and turning.
Repentance is not merely crying because you got caught.
It is not simply feeling terrible.
It is not promising God, “Never again,” and then keeping every doorway back into the relationship open.
Repentance turns.
If you knowingly remain in an adulterous relationship, repentance cannot mean asking Jesus to forgive the relationship while simultaneously planning to continue it.
There may be complicated consequences.
There may be heartbreak.
There may be practical decisions requiring mature pastoral guidance.
There may be children involved.
There may be legal questions.
There may be a wounded spouse whose trust cannot instantly be restored.
There may be consequences forgiveness does not magically erase.
Grace is not a time machine.
Forgiveness does not make every earthly consequence disappear.
But Jesus can redeem what you thought was beyond redemption.
And if you are the betrayed spouse reading this, hear this too:
You are not required to pretend betrayal did not hurt.
Forgiveness and immediate restoration of trust are not identical things.

Reconciliation, where possible and safe, requires truth, repentance, changed behavior, wisdom, and time. In situations involving abuse or danger, safety matters, and seeking qualified pastoral, legal, or professional help can be appropriate.
Do not let someone weaponize Christian language to force you into silence.
And if you are the person who committed adultery, do not weaponize grace either.
“Jesus forgave me” is never permission to demand that wounded people recover on your timetable.
Real repentance becomes humble.
It stops controlling the narrative.
It stops blaming the spouse.
It stops romanticizing the affair.
It accepts responsibility.
It makes restitution where appropriate and possible.
It submits to accountability.
It learns patience.
And it stops asking, “How much can I keep?”
Instead it begins asking:
“Jesus, what must change?”
Maybe that is where you are right now.
Phone in your hand.
Heart pounding.
Knowing exactly who you need to stop contacting.
You came here asking whether being a mistress is a sin.
But perhaps the Holy Spirit has brought you to another question.
How long will you keep asking Jesus to heal the wound while protecting the knife?
There comes a moment when information must become decision.
Not perfection.
Decision.
You may stumble during healing.
You may cry.
You may grieve the relationship.
You may wake up wanting to send the message.
You may have to rebuild your entire emotional world.
But do not confuse the pain of surrender with the absence of God.
Sometimes freedom hurts when the chains have been attached for a long time.
Bring the entire mess to Jesus.
Not the cleaned-up version.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
The real one.
Tell Him the truth.
“I love someone I should not be with.”
“I betrayed my spouse.”
“I knew they were married.”
“I did not know at first, but now I know.”
“I don't know how to leave.”
“I am ashamed.”
“I have ruined things.”
“I need mercy.”
Then remember why Jesus went to the cross.
Christ did not die for imaginary sinners with respectable histories.
He died for sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
The cross is where our excuses die...
and where our hope begins.
You do not earn your way back by hating yourself enough.
You cannot punish yourself into holiness.
You cannot undo yesterday by bleeding emotionally for the rest of your life.
You repent.
You believe the Gospel.
You receive Christ's mercy.
You obey Him.
You allow Him to rebuild what sin dismantled.
And eventually, perhaps, the sentence that once sounded impossible becomes your testimony:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
That word can become holy ground.
You were hiding.
You were living two lives.
You were someone's secret.
You were cheating.
You were trapped.
You were rationalizing.
You were ashamed.
But Jesus Christ does not specialize in making sin sound prettier.
He specializes in making sinners new.
So no, this article will not tell you adultery is acceptable.
It loves you too much to lie to you.
And no, this article will not tell you that because you committed adultery you are permanently disqualified from the mercy of God.
That would also be a lie.
The Gospel is simultaneously more confronting and more beautiful than either extreme.
Your sin may be real.
Your consequences may be real.
Your victims' pain may be real.
Your repentance must be real.
And the grace of Jesus Christ is real too.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to confess private identifying details publicly. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that repentance is not the end of a person's story.
Do not name the spouse.
Do not name the other woman.
Do not name the other man.
Let confession begin with your own heart.
Not as a weapon.
Not with, “See? I told you.”
Send it with compassion.
Temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions difficult to remember tomorrow.
Come back when your emotions begin rewriting what God already made clear.
It is about following the One who saves sinners and teaches redeemed people to walk differently.
And if this ministry has been feeding your faith, you can also help Gospel Warrior continue and expand.
Scripture says giving should not be done “grudgingly, or of necessity” because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV).
So there is no spiritual manipulation here.
If you are convicted to support your local church through your giving, continue to honor that responsibility according to your biblical convictions.
Jesus is calling sinners home.
Maybe today the person He is calling is you.
Close the secret door.
End the deception.
Tell the truth.
Seek wise, biblically faithful help.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ is teaching you to forgive.
Receive grace where shame has convinced you that grace could never reach.
And follow Jesus.
Because one day the part of your story you are most ashamed of may become the place from which you tell another broken person:
“I thought it was over for me too.”
“I thought God wanted nothing to do with me.”
“I thought my scandal had become my identity.”
“But Jesus met me there.”
And when Christ truly rewrites a life, He does not merely change the final paragraph.
He changes the person holding the pen.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final name; bring the scandal into the light, because the hands scarred on Calvary are still writing stories of grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Your Child’s Rebellion Is Not Proof You Failed—and Their Obedience Is Not Proof You Succeeded
paragraphs: Your Child’s Rebellion Is Not Proof You Failed—and Their Obedience Is Not Proof You Succeeded
The Bible gives parents a sacred responsibility—but it never gives us permission to take either total blame or total credit for another human soul.
There is a mother reading this who has replayed the same question so many times that it has almost become a form of self-punishment.
Where did I go wrong?
She remembers the bedtime prayers.
The children’s Bible with the worn corners.
The whispered prayers beside a sleeping child who never knew how many tears fell onto that pillow.
She remembers Sunday mornings when getting everyone dressed felt like spiritual warfare before they ever reached the church parking lot.
She remembers correcting attitudes. Teaching forgiveness. Saying no when saying yes would have been easier. Apologizing when she herself was wrong.
She remembers praying over that child before school.
Before graduation.
Before they drove away.
And now that child wants almost nothing to do with God.
Maybe they walked away from church.
Maybe they are living in open rebellion.
Maybe they mock the faith they were taught.
Maybe they have made choices you never imagined they would make.
Maybe your relationship has become painfully distant.
And somewhere between their decisions and your unanswered prayers, you began conducting a trial inside your own heart.
The defendant is you.
The prosecutor is you.
The witness is every parenting mistake you can remember.
And the sentence sounds something like this:
If I had been a better parent, my child would still be walking with God.
But before you pronounce yourself guilty of something Scripture has not charged you with, you need to hear what God actually says.
And before the parent whose children are walking faithfully with Christ becomes too confident that their children's obedience proves they did everything right, they need to hear it too.
Because the same truth that can release one parent from crushing guilt can rescue another parent from quiet pride.
Ezekiel 18:20 contains words that may initially sound severe, but hidden inside their severity is a profound truth about human responsibility:
“The soul that sinneth, it shall die.”
The Hebrew begins:
הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַחֹטֵאת הִיא תָמוּת
Ha-nefesh ha-chotet hi tamut.
Literally, the person—the nephesh—who sins is the one who bears responsibility.
Then comes the line every guilt-ridden parent needs to sit with:
בֵּן לֹא־יִשָּׂא בַּעֲוֹן הָאָב
Ben lo-yissa ba'avon ha'av.
“The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.”
And then Scripture turns the statement around:
“Neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.”
That sentence does not mean parents have no influence.
It does not mean parental sin cannot wound children.
It does not mean generational patterns are imaginary.
It does not mean fathers and mothers can neglect, abuse, provoke, abandon, or spiritually starve their children and then shrug, “Their choices aren't my responsibility.”
Absolutely not.
Scripture takes parenting far too seriously for that.
But Ezekiel destroys another dangerous idea:
that one human being automatically carries the moral guilt of another person's choices.
Your child is your child.
Your child is not your puppet.
Your child is not your spiritual report card.
Your child is not a trophy proving your righteousness.
And your child is not automatically evidence proving your failure.
Your child is a human soul standing before God.
That changes everything.
Because Christian parents sometimes unknowingly begin believing in a formula.
Teach them Scripture.
Pray with them.
Discipline them correctly.
Homeschool them—or send them to the right Christian school.
Keep them away from certain influences.
Find the right church.
Monitor the phone.
Choose the right friends.
Have family devotions.
Do all the correct things...
and faithful Christian adulthood will come out the other side.
Then Proverbs 22:6 gets placed over the formula like a divine warranty:
“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.”
But Proverbs are wisdom sayings, not mechanical contracts by which human beings can force predetermined spiritual outcomes from other human beings.
If Proverbs 22:6 meant that faithful parenting guaranteed faithful adult children without exception, something would become deeply confused about human responsibility.
Parents would effectively possess the ability to guarantee another person's repentance.
But Scripture never gives parents that power.
Only God changes hearts.
Only Christ saves sinners.
Only the Holy Spirit gives spiritual life.
Parents can teach truth.
Parents can model repentance.
Parents can establish boundaries.
Parents can discipline.
Parents can pray.
Parents can confess their failures.
Parents can demonstrate what forgiveness looks like.
Parents can bring children repeatedly beneath the sound of the Gospel.
Parents can plant.
Parents can water.
But there is something parents cannot do.
They cannot resurrect a spiritually dead heart.
Paul wrote:
ἐγὼ ἐφύτευσα, Ἀπολλῶς ἐπότισεν, ἀλλὰ ὁ Θεὸς ηὔξανεν.
Egō ephyteusa, Apollōs epotisen, alla ho Theos ēuxanen.
“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.”
Paul was speaking about Gospel ministry, not specifically parenting, so we should not pretend the verse was originally written as parenting advice.
But the theological principle should humble every person who disciples another human being.
We labor faithfully.
God gives life and growth.
That means faithful parenting matters enormously without making parents sovereign.
Read that again.
Faithful parenting matters enormously without making parents sovereign.
Somebody reading this has spent years confusing those two things.
You were responsible to raise your child faithfully.
You were never given the power to become their Holy Spirit.
And perhaps you did fail in significant ways.
We should not soften that possibility merely because it hurts.
Maybe you were harsh.
Maybe work always came first.
Maybe your child heard you preach grace while watching you refuse to apologize.
Maybe church became a performance.
Maybe your anger frightened them.
Maybe your marriage filled their childhood with wounds.
Maybe you disciplined behavior but rarely shepherded the heart.
Maybe you demanded respect while refusing to listen.
Maybe you were physically present but emotionally absent.
Maybe they watched a public Christianity that contradicted the private atmosphere of your home.
If God is bringing something specific to your conscience, do not hide behind Ezekiel 18.
Repent.
Not vaguely.
Specifically.
Go to your child if appropriate and say what Christian parents sometimes find terrifying to say:
“I sinned against you. I was wrong. I cannot undo what happened, and I will not excuse it. Will you forgive me?”
Because Ephesians 6:4 does not merely speak to children.
It turns toward fathers:
Καὶ οἱ πατέρες, μὴ παροργίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν, ἀλλὰ ἐκτρέφετε αὐτὰ ἐν παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ Κυρίου.
“Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.”
Notice the balance.
There is discipline.
There is instruction.
There is nurture.
And there is a warning against provoking them.
Biblical parenting is neither passive permissiveness nor authoritarian domination.
It is stewardship beneath the lordship of Christ.
So if you sinned, repent.
If restitution is possible, pursue it.
If reconciliation is possible, seek it patiently.
If your child needs to hear an apology without immediately being handed a sermon afterward, give the apology and resist the urge to control their response.
But then...
after you have honestly faced what belongs to you...
stop trying to repent for what belongs to them.
That may be one of the hardest sentences a Christian parent ever accepts.
Your repentance cannot substitute for theirs.
Your faith cannot substitute for theirs.
Your baptism cannot substitute for theirs.
Your church attendance cannot substitute for theirs.
Your tears cannot substitute for theirs.
Your obedience cannot substitute for theirs.
Every child eventually stands before God as something more than somebody's son or somebody's daughter.
They stand before Him as a person.
And that truth works in the opposite direction too.
Maybe your children love Jesus.
Maybe they serve faithfully.
Maybe people compliment your family.
Maybe someone has told you, “You raised them right.”
Receive encouragement gratefully.
