Desire still felt suspicious.
Pleasure still felt vaguely unholy.
The body still felt like the enemy.
And perhaps nobody ever told them something astonishing:
The Bible that fiercely condemns sexual sin is also the Bible that can speak beautifully, poetically, and sometimes startlingly openly about sexual desire.
Not because Scripture contradicts itself.
Because lust and sexual desire are not automatically the same thing.
That distinction matters.
It matters to the unmarried Christian fighting temptation.
It matters to the husband who has quietly learned to associate desire with shame.
It matters to the wife who wonders whether enjoying her husband's desire somehow makes intimacy less spiritual.
It matters to the believer recovering from pornography.
It matters to the person carrying sexual wounds.
It matters to anyone who has confused holiness with becoming less human.
And it matters because Jesus did not come merely to teach us how to suppress ourselves.
He came to redeem us.
Including the parts of us sin has distorted.
Go back to the words of Christ that Christians often quote when talking about lust.
Matthew 5:28 in Greek reads:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.

Jesus is speaking about looking at a woman πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν—a looking directed toward desiring her in the context Jesus identifies as adultery in the heart. The verse does not reduce holiness to the biological impossibility of ever noticing that another human being is attractive. Christ takes the command against adultery inward, exposing the heart where sin can be cultivated before the body ever acts.
That is devastatingly important.
Because Jesus is not merely policing bodies.
He is exposing hearts.
Long before the Sermon on the Mount, the Ten Commandments had already reached into that territory.
Exodus 20:17 says:
לֹא תַחְמֹד אֵשֶׁת רֵעֶךָ
Lo taḥmod eshet re‘ekha.
“You shall not covet your neighbor's wife.”

The Hebrew verb חָמַד — ḥāmad can carry the sense of desiring, coveting, taking pleasure in, or regarding something as desirable. In Exodus 20:17 the object and context make the moral boundary unmistakable: this is desire reaching toward what belongs to another.
That is different from saying every experience of attraction is inherently sinful.
And Scripture itself proves why that distinction matters.
Because only a few books away from Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the prophets sits a book that has made generations of embarrassed Bible readers wonder how it survived the church committee.
Song of Songs.
Read it slowly and the myth that the Bible is embarrassed by marital desire becomes very difficult to maintain.
The lovers notice each other.
They long for each other.
They describe each other.
They delight in one another.
There is anticipation.
Beauty.
Exclusivity.
Longing.
Desire.
In Song of Songs 7, after language celebrating the beloved's physical beauty, we eventually hear:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani le-dodi, ve‘alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.”
The Hebrew word there is תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah—desire, longing. The context is not pornography. It is not adultery. It is not exploitation. It is the poetry of lovers belonging to one another.
Notice what Scripture does not do.
It does not interrupt the poem to apologize for the human body.
God is not embarrassed that human beings have bodies.
He designed them.
Before pornography commercialized the body, God created it.
Before adultery betrayed covenant, God created covenant.
Before lust learned to consume people, God created people capable of loving and being loved.
Before sin distorted sexuality, sexuality existed within a creation God called good.
The enemy is not creativity.
Corruption is.
The enemy is not the existence of desire.
Sin is what desire can become when it stops loving the person and starts consuming the person.
That is where so much confusion begins.
Lust says, “Your body exists for my imagination.”
Love says, “You bear the image of God.”
Lust asks, “What can I take?”
Covenant asks, “How can I faithfully give?”
Lust can turn a person into pieces.
Love keeps seeing the whole person.
Lust wants pleasure detached from holiness, responsibility, covenant, and the good of the other person.
Biblical sexual desire within marriage can say, without shame, “I desire you”—while still honoring the beloved as a person rather than treating them as an object.
And Proverbs becomes astonishingly direct about this.
“May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
The Hebrew contains the imperative:
וּשְׂמַח — u-semaḥ.
Rejoice.
Not merely tolerate.
Not reluctantly endure.
Rejoice.

The context of Proverbs 5 contrasts marital faithfulness with forbidden sexual relationships, and the positive instruction directs sexual joy homeward into marriage. One translation note explicitly describes the passage as finding pleasure in a fulfilling marriage and treats that delight as God-given.
Then Paul says something equally remarkable to married Christians in Corinth.
μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους...
“Do not deprive one another...”

He allows temporary abstinence by mutual agreement for prayer, followed by reunion. Whatever else must be said about the passage—and it must never be twisted into permission for coercion—the language is reciprocal. Paul speaks to husband and wife about mutuality. Sexual intimacy in marriage is not portrayed as contamination from which spiritual people should permanently escape.
And in the very same New Testament, Paul can write:
τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν, ἀπέχεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς πορνείας...
“This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality.”
The Greek word is πορνεία — porneia, sexual immorality.
Do you see the balance?
Scripture does not solve sexual brokenness by declaring sexuality itself broken.
It draws boundaries because something valuable exists inside those boundaries.
Fire in a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire consuming the home destroys it.
The answer is not to hate fire.
The answer is to understand what it is for.
And perhaps this is where the article stops being about Greek and Hebrew and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because maybe your problem isn't that you have never understood the word lust.
Maybe you understand it far too well.
Maybe you know exactly what it is like to look at another person and deliberately turn them into fantasy.
Maybe pornography has trained your eyes to consume bodies before your heart remembers they contain souls.
Maybe you promised God you would stop.
Then failed.
Promised again.
Failed again.
Deleted everything.
Downloaded it again.
Prayed.
Cried.
Fasted.
Fell.
And somewhere between repentance and relapse, you started wondering whether Jesus could possibly still want someone like you.
Listen carefully.
Do not rename your sin.
But do not rename the Savior either.
Sin is still sin.
Jesus is still Jesus.
And grace has never meant pretending darkness is light.
Grace means Christ entered our darkness to rescue sinners from it.
The cross does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says your sin was so serious that Christ died—and His mercy so extraordinary that He willingly came for sinners anyway.
That is why biblical conviction and biblical hope must remain together.
If your desire has become coveting, repent.
If pornography has trained you to consume human beings in your imagination, repent.
If you are entertaining someone else's spouse in your heart, repent.
If you have used another person's body without honoring their soul, repent.
If you are hiding an affair, repent.
If your secret sexual life would devastate the person sleeping beside you, stop calling secrecy protection.
Bring darkness into the light.
But hear the rest of the Gospel.
Repentance is not God standing at the door waiting to humiliate you.
Repentance is turning around because Someone is calling you home.
Jesus did not tell adulterers that adultery was beautiful.
He offered sinners something far more beautiful.
Mercy.
Forgiveness.
A new life.
The Gospel does not merely say, “Stop.”
It says, “Come.”
Come out of hiding.
Come out of pornography.
Come out of adultery.
Come out of shame.
Come out of self-righteousness.
Come out of the lie that because you have fallen repeatedly, Christ must finally be finished with you.
Come to the One whose blood is sufficient for sinners.
And maybe your story is different.
Maybe you are married and faithful, but you still feel guilty for desiring your spouse.
You don't need repentance for enjoying what God permits and blesses.
You may need healing from a distorted theology of the body.
Christian holiness does not require husbands and wives to pretend they are disembodied spirits.
The Bible can tell you to flee sexual immorality and tell you to rejoice in your spouse without contradiction.
Because holiness is not the destruction of desire.
It is the surrender of desire to God.
There are desires we crucify.
There are desires we discipline.
There are desires we refuse to feed.
There are desires we redirect.
And there are good gifts we receive with thanksgiving under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That distinction is everything.
Because Satan is happy with either distortion.
He can whisper, “Whatever you desire must be good.”
Or he can whisper, “The fact that you desire anything makes you dirty.”
Both lies can separate you from truth.
The first baptizes appetite.
The second demonizes embodiment.
Jesus does neither.
He calls us to holiness without teaching us to hate God's creation.
And that means the question is deeper than, “Did I feel desire?”
Ask what your desire is doing.
Is it honoring covenant or fantasizing about violating it?
Is it seeing a person or consuming an image?
Does it seek mutual love or selfish possession?
Does it move toward faithfulness or secrecy?
Can you bring it before Christ without needing to rewrite Scripture to justify it?
That last question hurts.
Because all of us are capable of becoming brilliant theologians when defending the thing we don't want to surrender.
But Jesus loves us too much to leave our chains unnamed.
And He loves us too much to call chains freedom.
Somebody reading this needs to stop hiding tonight.
Not tomorrow.
Tonight.
You know what is on your phone.
You know the conversation you keep deleting.
You know the person whose profile you keep visiting.
You know the fantasy you keep feeding.
You know what your spouse doesn't know.
You know where innocent attraction crossed the line and became deliberate cultivation.
You know.
And Christ knows too.
Yet here you are.
Still reading.
Still breathing.
Still being called.
Grace has reached you again.
Not cheap grace that pats sin on the head.
Blood-bought grace that takes sinners to a cross, buries the old life, and raises people to walk differently.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to publish the details of your private sin. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
No performance.
No pretending.
Sometimes three honest words are the beginning of walking toward the light.
And please understand something else.
There are teenagers who desperately need this truth before pornography becomes their teacher.
There are married couples who need it before shame freezes what covenant was meant to protect.
There are single Christians who need to know that experiencing attraction does not give them permission to cultivate lust—but neither does attraction itself mean they have suddenly become filthy.
There are believers recovering from sexual sin who need someone to tell them that sanctification is possible.
There are people who have never entered a church because they assume Christians are either obsessed with sex or terrified of it.
Send it privately to someone who needs truth without public embarrassment.
Let your timeline become more than entertainment. Let it occasionally become a doorway through which somebody encounters Scripture, conviction, grace, and the name of Jesus Christ.
And for those asking how to help this ministry continue and expand, there is a practical way to stand with the work.
It doesn't.
Not because paying us is required to glorify God.
It isn't.
Your generosity before God is a matter of worship, stewardship, conscience, and biblical conviction.
But voluntary support for Gospel work can be a genuine act of generosity.
Your support helps us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep putting Scripture where wounded people may find it at two in the morning.
Keep speaking about the subjects many people are afraid to touch.
Keep pointing scandalous stories toward redeeming grace.
But whether you ever give a cent or not, do not miss the greater invitation.
Give Christ your heart.
A donation cannot reconcile you to God.
A Christian T-shirt cannot make you holy.
A theological vocabulary cannot save you.
Jesus can.

The One who exposed adultery in the heart is also the One who went to the cross for adulterers, porn addicts, sexually broken people, religious hypocrites, ashamed spouses, secret sinners—and every other kind of sinner willing to come to Him.
The scandal is not that sinners need grace.
The scandal is how much grace Christ was willing to give.
So bring Him your sexuality.
Bring Him your desires.
Bring Him your marriage.
Bring Him your singleness.
Bring Him the attraction you don't know what to do with.
Bring Him the habit you cannot seem to defeat.
Bring Him the shame you have carried for twenty years.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him the wounds.
Bring Him the nights nobody knows about.
Bring Him the browser history.
Bring Him the tears.
Bring Him the body you learned to hate.
Bring Him the heart you stopped trusting.
Bring Him everything.
And then stop asking Jesus merely to make you less tempted.
Ask Him to make you holy.
Ask Him to teach you how to see people as people again.
Ask Him to restore tenderness where pornography produced consumption.
Ask Him to restore trust where adultery produced devastation.
Ask Him to restore joy where shame poisoned marriage.
Ask Him to teach you that desire does not have to become your master.
Jesus is Lord.
Even here.
Especially here.
Maybe that is what somebody desperately needed to hear.
You are not called to worship your desires.
You are not called to obey every desire.
You are not called to pretend every desire is innocent.
But neither are you called to hate everything God created simply because sin learned how to corrupt it.
The answer to corrupted desire is not pretending we were never created to desire.
The answer is redemption.
Desire under Christ.
Bodies under Christ.
Marriage under Christ.
Singleness under Christ.
Sexuality under Christ.
Thoughts under Christ.
Eyes under Christ.
Everything under Christ.
Because Christianity is not Jesus receiving the religious-looking pieces of your life while you hide the embarrassing ones behind locked doors.
He wants the locked room too.
And when Jesus enters the room we were certain would make Him abandon us, we discover the heart of the Gospel:
He already knew what was inside.
He came anyway.
So save this for the night shame tries to rewrite your identity.
Share it with the person whose silence is getting dangerous.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“No more hiding.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or, if God has already brought you through this battlefield, tell someone there is hope.
Your testimony might become the sentence another person reads five minutes before deciding not to give up.
Because maybe the most dangerous lie shame ever told you was that Jesus would rewrite everybody's story except yours.
But the hand holding the pen still bears the scars.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IF MY PEOPLE WHO ARE CALLED BY MY NAME…” — WHO EXACTLY WAS GOD TALKING ABOUT?
paragraphs: “IF MY PEOPLE WHO ARE CALLED BY MY NAME…” — WHO EXACTLY WAS GOD TALKING ABOUT?
One of Christianity’s Most Quoted Promises Becomes Even More Powerful When You Discover Who First Heard It—and Why Jesus Changes How We Read It Today
You have probably heard the verse during elections.
During national crises.
During prayer gatherings.
After disasters.
When a country appears morally exhausted and someone stands before a congregation and says:
“If My people who are called by My name will humble themselves…”
And almost instinctively, everyone knows the rest.
But there is a question we rarely stop long enough to ask.
Who were “My people”?
Not who do we want those words to mean.
Not who have we heard preachers say they mean.
Who was God actually talking about when He spoke them?
Because sometimes the most dangerous way to mishandle Scripture is not to reject it.
It is to love a verse so much that we quietly remove it from the story God placed around it.
And when we put 2 Chronicles 7:14 back where it belongs, something extraordinary happens.
The verse does not become smaller.
It becomes sharper.
More sobering.
More beautiful.
And ultimately, it leads us toward Jesus.
Listen first to the Hebrew words preserved in 2 Chronicles 7:14:
וְיִכָּנְעוּ עַמִּי אֲשֶׁר נִקְרָא־שְׁמִי עֲלֵיהֶם וְיִתְפַּלְלוּ וִיבַקְשׁוּ פָנַי וְיָשֻׁבוּ מִדַּרְכֵיהֶם הָרָעִים וַאֲנִי אֶשְׁמַע מִן־הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֶסְלַח לְחַטָּאתָם וְאֶרְפָּא אֶת־אַרְצָם׃
Transliterated approximately:
“Weyikkāne‘û ‘ammî ’ăšer-niqrā’-šemî ‘ălêhem, weyitpallelû wîbaqšû pānay, weyāšubû middarkêhem hārā‘îm; wa’ănî ’ešma‘ min-haššāmayim, we’eslaḥ leḥaṭṭā’tām, we’erpā’ ’et-’arṣām.”
In straightforward English:
If My people, upon whom My name is called, humble themselves, pray, seek My face, and turn from their evil ways, God promises to hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.
Those words are really there.
The Hebrew really says עַמִּי—‘ammî—“My people.”
It really says וְיָשֻׁבוּ—weyāšubû—“and they turn” or “return.”
It really says וְאֶסְלַח—we’eslaḥ—“and I will forgive.”
And it really ends with אַרְצָם—’arṣām—“their land.”
But now comes the question that changes the way many people have heard this verse.
Whose land?
Whose sin?
Whose covenant?
Whose temple?
Whose people?
Go backward one chapter.
Solomon has built the temple in Jerusalem.
He stands before God and prays for Israel.
He imagines terrible days that may eventually come—defeat, drought, famine, pestilence, captivity.
And Solomon repeatedly asks God to hear His people when they repent.

He even anticipates Israel being carried away by enemies. He prays that when they recognize their sin, repent, return to God wholeheartedly, and pray toward the land God gave their fathers, toward Jerusalem, and toward the temple built for God's name, God would hear from heaven and forgive His people.
That is the prayer immediately behind the famous promise.
Then comes 2 Chronicles 7.
God answers Solomon.
That detail matters enormously.
Second Chronicles 7:14 did not descend from heaven as an isolated motivational quotation.
It is part of God's answer to Solomon's temple-dedication prayer.
And immediately before verse 14, God speaks about withholding rain, locusts consuming the land, and pestilence among “My people.”
Then:
“If My people…”
Suddenly the pieces lock together.
The people are Israel.
The land is the covenant land God had given them.
The house is the temple Solomon had built.
The king standing before God is Solomon.
And the judgments reflect the covenant warnings Israel already knew.
If any doubt remains, keep reading instead of stopping at verse 14.

God addresses Solomon concerning the Davidic throne. Then He warns that if the people turn away, forsake His commandments, and worship other gods, Israel will be uprooted from the land and the temple will become an object of astonishment.
People will ask why such devastation happened.
And the answer will be devastating:
They forsook the LORD, the God of their fathers, who brought them out of Egypt.
There is no mystery left.
God was not originally addressing America.
He was not originally addressing the Philippines.
He was not originally addressing Britain, Nigeria, Australia, Canada, South Africa, Brazil, or any other modern nation.
He was speaking within His covenant relationship with Israel.
And saying that should not frighten Christians.
It should make us trust the Bible more.
Because faithful interpretation does not begin by asking, “How can I make this verse about me?”
It begins by asking, “What did God actually say?”
Then we ask how that truth reaches us through the whole story of Scripture and ultimately through Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters.
Otherwise, we can accidentally turn the Bible into a collection of promises detached from their covenants, audiences, and redemptive setting.
We can put ourselves into every “you.”
Claim every blessing.
Ignore every context.
And eventually create a Christianity that sounds biblical because it uses Bible verses while no longer allowing the Bible to tell its own story.
But perhaps there is an even more uncomfortable question.
If 2 Chronicles 7:14 was originally spoken to covenant Israel…
does that mean Christians should close the Bible and walk away from it?
Absolutely not.
Because the God who called Israel to humility, prayer, repentance, and wholehearted return has not suddenly become fond of pride, prayerlessness, rebellion, or hidden sin.
The principle remains deeply instructive.
And the New Testament does something breathtaking.
It takes the language of belonging to God and applies it to the people redeemed in Christ.
Peter writes to believers:
And then:
“Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people.”
The church is not thereby handed every national and territorial promise made to ancient Israel as though covenant distinctions never existed.
But everyone united to Christ now belongs to God.
Jew and Gentile.
Rich and poor.
The respectable church member and the former addict.
The person raised hearing hymns and the person who whispered the name “Jesus” for the first time yesterday.
People from every tribe, language, people, and nation are being redeemed by the blood of Christ.
And this is where 2 Chronicles 7:14 stops being merely a verse we quote about what is wrong with our country…
and becomes a mirror held against what is wrong inside us.
Because notice whom God told to humble themselves.
“My people.”
Not merely the pagans.
Not merely the politicians.
Not merely the sexually immoral.
Not merely the corrupt.
Not merely the atheists.
Not merely the people on the other side of your political argument.
“My people.”
That hurts differently.
Because blaming Babylon is easier than confronting the Babylon hiding in our own hearts.
We can complain about darkness while secretly feeding darkness when nobody is watching.
We can demand repentance from society while refusing to apologize to our spouse.
We can rage about corruption in government while cheating when dishonesty benefits us.
We can condemn sexual immorality publicly while protecting pornography privately.
We can sing about surrender while clutching unforgiveness like a weapon.
We can post Bible verses and still destroy someone with gossip.
We can know Christian vocabulary and still barely know the Christ our vocabulary describes.
We can look alive online…
and be spiritually exhausted behind the screen.
Maybe that is why the word “humble” comes before so much else.
Humility stops performing.
Humility quits negotiating.
Humility stops saying, “Lord, look at them.”
And finally whispers:
“Lord…
look at me.”
That is where repentance begins.
The Hebrew idea expressed in “turn” is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is movement.
A turning.
A return.
You were facing one direction.
Now, by God's grace, you turn toward Him.
And this thread does not disappear when we reach the New Testament.
After the resurrection, Jesus declares that repentance for the forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in His name to all nations.
Peter later calls people to repent and turn back so that their sins may be wiped away.
The geography expands.
The Gospel goes to the nations.
But the human problem remains.
Sin.
And God's answer reaches its climax not in national moral improvement…
but in a crucified and risen King.
Jesus Christ.
This is where the story becomes personal.
Because perhaps you came to this article expecting an argument about whether Christians have been quoting one Old Testament verse correctly.
And somewhere along the way, the verse started reading you.
Maybe there is something you need to turn from.
Something hidden.
Something rationalized.
Something renamed so many times that you almost stopped calling it sin.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
But you know how tired you are.
Maybe people call you faithful.
But you remember when prayer was not merely something you did because Christians are supposed to pray.
You remember when His presence mattered.
You remember when opening Scripture felt like coming home.
You remember when worship could break you.
And somewhere between disappointment, distraction, wounds, responsibilities, secret compromises, unanswered prayers, and ordinary life…
your heart wandered.
Not necessarily with a slammed door.
Sometimes people leave God one inch at a time.
One neglected prayer.
One tolerated compromise.
One bitterness protected.
One conviction postponed.
One Sunday performed.
One secret defended.
Until eventually you are still wearing the language of faith…
but you cannot remember the last time you surrendered.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps Jesus will take you back.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
Christ came for sinners.
The Son of God entered our ruin.
He lived without the sin that stains every one of us.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose.
Your forgiveness is not purchased by the intensity of your tears.
Your salvation is not earned by religious performance.
Your hope is not that you can punish yourself enough to compensate for what you have done.
Jesus paid what you could not pay.
Repentance does not mean purchasing your way back to God.
It means abandoning the fantasy that life away from Him can save you and throwing yourself upon the mercy offered in Christ.
This is why grace is so scandalous.
The liar can come home.
The adulterer can come home.
The addict can come home.
The hypocrite can come home.
The bitter can come home.
The proud can come home.
The person who wasted years can come home.
The church kid with a secret life can come home.
The person who promised God “never again” and then did it again can come home.
Not because sin is insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
But grace is so astonishing that Calvary became the place where condemned sinners could find reconciliation with God.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending your scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by lowering God's holiness until your sin becomes harmless.
Jesus rewrites everything by doing what you could never do for yourself.
He redeems.
He forgives.
He restores.
He makes dead hearts alive.
He turns testimonies that should have ended in shame into evidence that mercy still reaches sinners.
So perhaps the prayer we need after reading 2 Chronicles 7:14 is not first:
“God, fix my nation.”
Perhaps it begins:
“God, humble me.”
“Expose what I have hidden.”
“Break what I have worshiped.”
“Teach me to pray again.”
“Turn my heart toward You.”
“Make Jesus more precious to me than the sin I keep defending.”
Because revival used as a slogan is easy.
Repentance is costly.
Revival points outward when it becomes rhetoric.
Repentance points inward before it ever points across the street.
And there may be someone reading this whose hands have started shaking internally because you know exactly what God is putting His finger on.
Do not run from that conviction.
Run to Christ.
There is a difference between condemnation that drives you into hopeless hiding and godly conviction that brings sin into the light and drives you toward mercy.
Jesus did not die so you could become better at pretending.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Return.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But perhaps you need to stop pretending you are fine.
Or simply comment, “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Not as magic words.
Not as public theater.
But as a small declaration that you are tired of running.
Someone else reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only believer in a battle.
And please understand something else about 2 Chronicles 7:14.

We should be careful about promising that if enough Christians perform four steps, God is contractually obligated to heal the economy, remove a particular government, eliminate every disaster, or grant a modern nation political prosperity.
That is more than this passage promises us.
Ancient Israel's covenant relationship to the land is part of the verse's original setting.
But Christians have something even greater than a slogan for national recovery.
We have Jesus Christ.
A kingdom that cannot be reduced to borders.
A Gospel commanded to go to the nations.
A Savior whose blood purchases people from every tribe and language and people and nation.
A resurrection that means death itself does not get the final sentence.
And a coming King who will finish what sin shattered.
That is our hope.
Not that Christians will eventually become powerful enough to engineer heaven on earth.
Christ Himself is our hope.
And that changes what we do after reading an article like this.
We pray.
We repent.
We seek God.
We proclaim Christ.
We love our neighbors.
We make disciples.
We practice mercy.
We tell the truth.
We serve.
We give.
We carry the Gospel farther.
And sometimes carrying it farther is as simple as pressing “Share.”
Think about the person on your Facebook friends list who would never enter a church this Sunday.
The cousin who is angry with God.
The friend whose marriage is quietly collapsing.
The believer who has been spiritually asleep for years.
The person who keeps posting jokes because silence would force them to feel how broken they really are.
The skeptic.
The prodigal.
The exhausted pastor.
The teenager questioning everything.
The person smiling in photographs while privately wondering whether God could possibly want them anymore.
Not because an algorithm is sacred.
Because there may be a human soul on the other side of that screen.
Send it privately if that would be wiser.
Use them.
Share them.
Put them into the hands of someone hungry for biblical truth.
Supporting Gospel work financially has deep New Testament precedent. Paul thanked believers who partnered with him through their giving and described their gifts as an offering pleasing to God.
But Scripture also protects your conscience.
“Not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
He will not.
It cannot.
Jesus cannot be bought.
If Gospel Warrior has fed you spiritually, consider helping us keep setting the table for someone who has not arrived yet.
Pray.
Send it to someone.
Leave a sincere comment.
Invite another person to follow.
Sometimes the article you almost did not share becomes the message someone reads alone at two in the morning when nobody else knows they are falling apart.
We may never know on this side of eternity how far one faithful act travels.
But above everything else…
remember the verse.
“If My people…”
Originally, covenant Israel.
Spoken in the setting of Solomon, the temple, the land, covenant judgment, repentance, forgiveness, and restoration.
And now, standing on this side of Calvary, Christians do not need to steal Israel's historical setting to hear the holy warning echoing through Scripture:
God opposes pride.
God calls sinners to repentance.
God hears His people.
God is merciful.
And forgiveness reaches its blazing center in Jesus Christ.
So stop asking only whether your nation needs to turn back to God.
Ask the harder question.
Have I?
Maybe the greatest distance you will ever travel is not from one country to another.
Maybe it is the distance between the life you are hiding…
and the feet of Jesus.
Come home.
There is blood enough for your guilt.
Grace enough for your shame.
Mercy enough for your failure.
And a risen Savior powerful enough to write a final chapter your worst moment never deserved.
Because the most astonishing words in your story may not be what you did when you walked away.
They may be what Jesus did when you finally turned around.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HE WENT IN TO HER”: Why Does the Bible Use This Phrase When It Means Sex?
paragraphs: “HE WENT IN TO HER”: Why Does the Bible Use This Phrase When It Means Sex?
The strange biblical expression we usually read past may reveal something far deeper about sex, intimacy, sin, covenant—and the God who refuses to leave broken people where He found them.
There are phrases in the Bible that your eyes learn to glide over.
You read them.
You think you understand them.
And then one day you stop.
Wait.
What did that just say?
“He went in to her.”

If you grew up reading older English translations of Scripture, you have probably encountered language like this without giving it much thought. Abraham “went in unto Hagar.” Judah was told to “go in unto” his brother’s wife. Samson “went in unto” a woman in Gaza.
We know what happened.
The context makes it unmistakable.
They had sexual relations.
So why doesn’t the Bible simply say that?
Why this strange language of entering, going in, knowing, lying with, becoming one flesh?
Is Scripture trying to sanitize sex?
Is it embarrassed by the human body?
Were the translators too uncomfortable to say what the Hebrew actually said?
Or have we been reading an ancient world through modern ears and therefore missing something that would have been far more natural to the Bible’s first hearers?
Because the answer takes us somewhere much deeper than an old-fashioned euphemism.
It takes us into the Hebrew language.
Into marriage.
Into human vulnerability.
Into sexual sin.
Into covenant.
Into shame.
Into the bedroom.
Into Eden.
And eventually...
to Jesus Christ.
Consider Genesis 16.
Sarai cannot conceive. Years have passed. God's promise seems painfully slow. So she gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram.
Then Genesis 16:4 says:
וַיָּבֹא אֶל־הָגָר וַתַּהַר
Vayyāvoʾ ʾel-Hāgār vattahar.
Very literally:
“And he went in to Hagar, and she conceived.”
There it is.
The Hebrew verb at the center of the expression is בּוֹא — bôʾ.
Its basic meaning is remarkably ordinary.
To come.
To go.
To enter.
The word itself does not automatically mean “have sex.”
That matters.

Biblical Hebrew frequently allows context to carry meaning that modern English expects the verb itself to spell out. When bôʾ is used in certain relational settings—someone “going in to” a woman—the surrounding narrative can make sexual intercourse unmistakable.
So when an older English Bible says that a man “went in unto her,” it is often preserving the shape of the Hebrew expression more closely than contemporary English normally would.
Modern translations frequently make the intended meaning more explicit because “went in to her” no longer naturally communicates sexual intercourse to many English readers.
But Scripture has another expression that may be even more fascinating.
Genesis 4:1 says:
וְהָאָדָם יָדַע אֶת־חַוָּה אִשְׁתּוֹ
Vehaʾadam yādaʿ ʾet-Ḥavvah ʾishtô.
The key word is:
יָדַע — yādaʿ
“To know.”
Adam “knew” Eve his wife, and she conceived Cain.
Again, the context tells us this is sexual union.
But notice something beautiful.
The Bible does not have only one mechanical vocabulary for sex.
Sometimes Scripture speaks of “lying with” someone.
Sometimes of “going in to” someone.
Genesis describes husband and wife as becoming “one flesh.”
And sometimes the Bible uses the astonishing language of “knowing.”
That does not mean every occurrence of yādaʿ is sexual. Far from it. It is an extremely common Hebrew verb for knowing.
Context determines its meaning.
But when Scripture uses it for marital intercourse, the expression is striking.
Because biblical sexuality was never meant to be reduced to two bodies consuming one another.
God created sex before pornography existed.
Before adultery.
Before prostitution.
Before lust became an industry.
Before bodies became products.
Before people learned to swipe through human beings as though they were merchandise.
Before anyone learned to separate physical nakedness from personal covenant.
Go all the way back.
Before the scandal came the garden.
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25).
Read that slowly.
Naked.
And not ashamed.
No hiding.
No comparison.
No secret browser history.
No memories of betrayal.
No fear of abandonment.
No performance.
No exploitation.
No wondering whether you are attractive enough.
No wondering whether this person will disappear tomorrow.
No shame.
Then sin entered.
And what is one of the first things humanity did?
They covered themselves.
They hid.
That is not accidental.
Sin did not merely damage humanity's relationship with God.
It fractured the human experience of being seen.
Suddenly nakedness could feel dangerous.
Exposure could produce shame.
Desire could become distorted.
What God created as good could now be exploited, weaponized, commercialized, idolized and separated from covenant faithfulness.
And maybe that is where this stops being an interesting Hebrew lesson and starts getting uncomfortably personal.
Because perhaps you clicked this article because the phrase sounded strange.
Maybe even a little provocative.
But perhaps underneath the curiosity is a story nobody knows.
Maybe sex has never felt simple to you.
Maybe somebody introduced you to pornography before you were old enough to understand what it was doing to your imagination.
Maybe you keep deleting the history and returning to the same websites.
Maybe everyone at church thinks you are doing fine.
You worship.
You quote Scripture.
You post Christian content.
You say “God bless you.”
But there is another version of you that appears when nobody is watching.
Maybe you crossed a boundary you promised God you would never cross.
Maybe you slept with someone because you desperately wanted to feel loved.
Maybe you gave your body hoping someone would give you their heart.
They didn't.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe someone cheated on you.
Maybe your marriage has been carrying sexual wounds for years, but neither of you knows how to talk about them anymore.
Maybe what should have represented tenderness now reminds you of rejection.
Maybe someone used your trust against you.
Maybe something sexual happened to you that you did not choose.
If so, another person's sin against you is not something Scripture asks you to pretend was acceptable. The Gospel does not require calling evil good in order to offer healing.
And maybe your story is different.
Maybe you were the one who sinned.
That sentence is harder.
Because Christianity is not merely about identifying what somebody else did to us.
Eventually the Gospel brings us before God without costumes.
No excuses.
No carefully cropped version of ourselves.
Just truth.
And this is where Scripture becomes terrifyingly beautiful.
God already knows.
The God who asked Adam, “Where are you?” was not suffering from a lack of information.
Adam was hiding.
God was calling him out.
Humanity has been hiding ever since.
We hide behind religion.
We hide behind humor.
We hide behind relationships.
We hide behind private browsing.
We hide behind “everybody does it.”
We hide behind trauma when trauma explains some of our wounds but cannot make every choice righteous.
We hide behind shame.
We even hide behind ministry.
But eventually Christ walks directly toward the place we desperately hoped He would avoid.
Not because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
Because He intends to save them.
Look at Jesus.

A woman caught in adultery is dragged publicly into His presence in John 8. Whatever questions surround the textual history of that passage, the scene preserved in the Christian tradition powerfully depicts something thoroughly consistent with Christ's call to both mercy and holiness.
Her accusers want condemnation.
Jesus refuses their hypocrisy.
But He does not rename sin.
Grace does not become moral indifference.
His mercy moves toward transformation.
Neither condemnation from self-righteous people nor permission to remain unchanged.
Grace.
Then holiness.
That pattern matters.
Because somewhere along the way, many people began believing that repentance means God standing over a filthy sinner saying, “Look what you did.”
The Gospel gives us something far more astonishing.
The holy Son of God takes sinners seriously enough to tell us the truth...
and loves sinners deeply enough to bear judgment Himself.
At the cross, Jesus was not pretending sin did not matter.
The cross is precisely how seriously sin matters.
Christ “suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
That includes sexual sin.
Adultery.
Fornication.
Pornography.
Lust.
Secret fantasy.
Deception.
Sexual selfishness.
Things you did.
Things you regret.
Things you wish you could erase.
But hear this carefully:
You cannot erase your past.
Jesus can redeem a sinner.
There is a difference.
Christianity does not teach that salvation gives us a time machine.
Consequences can remain.
Memories can remain.
People we hurt may still need time.
Trust may have to be rebuilt.
Repentance may require painful honesty and concrete change.
Grace does not make consequences imaginary.
Grace means consequences do not have to become your final identity before God.
Paul wrote to Christians in Corinth after naming serious patterns of sexual and other sin:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then comes the Gospel-shaped reversal:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
Some of you need that word more than another motivational speech.
Were.
Your sin may explain part of your history.
It does not have to dictate your eternity.
Your worst night does not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your hidden browser history is not more powerful than the Gospel.
Your adultery is not stronger than Christ.
Your sexual past is not stronger than Christ.
Your shame is not stronger than Christ.
But grace is not permission to keep returning lovingly to the chains from which Christ calls you.
Jesus does not merely offer relief from guilt.
He calls us to Himself.
Repentance means turning.
Sometimes trembling.
Sometimes crying.
Sometimes after falling again.
But turning.
Coming into the light.
Jesus said, “The truth shall make you free” (John 8:32).
And perhaps the truth you need tonight is this:
You have spent years trying to become clean enough to approach the One who alone can cleanse you.
Stop hiding.
Come to Christ.
Not after you fix yourself.
Now.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him your disordered desires.
Bring Him the relationship you know dishonors Him.
Bring Him the secret account.
Bring Him the messages you would panic if your spouse discovered.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the loneliness underneath the lust.
Bring Him the anger underneath the promiscuity.
Bring Him the ache underneath the pornography.
Bring Him the entire ruined story.
And repent.
Not because repentance purchases His love.
Because Jesus Christ is worthy of your whole life.
The Savior who died for sinners did not remain dead.
He rose.
And the risen Christ still makes dead things live.
That is why the Bible's sexual language matters.
“He went in to her” is not some embarrassing relic Christians need to apologize for.

It reminds us that Scripture comes to us through real human languages, cultures and literary conventions. We should resist forcing twenty-first-century English assumptions onto ancient Hebrew expressions.
The Hebrew בּוֹא — bôʾ does not secretly mean “sex” every time it appears.
Context matters.
יָדַע — yādaʿ does not secretly mean “sex” every time either.
Context matters.
Good biblical interpretation does not build theology from an English euphemism while ignoring Hebrew usage.
But once we understand the language, something larger emerges.
The Bible is extraordinarily realistic about human sexuality.
It contains marital intimacy and sexual sin.
Faithfulness and adultery.
Conception and infertility.
Desire and exploitation.
Purity and prostitution.
Broken families and restored people.
It does not give us airbrushed saints.
Abraham's household becomes painfully complicated after Hagar.
Judah's story contains sexual scandal.
David's house carries devastating consequences from sexual sin and abuse of power.
Samson's appetites repeatedly place him in danger.
Yet Scripture's central story is not humanity climbing toward moral perfection.
It is God moving toward sinners in redeeming grace.
And ultimately He comes in Jesus Christ.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
You thought this article would explain a strange phrase about sex.
Perhaps God used that curiosity to bring you somewhere else entirely.
To the locked room inside yourself.
To the thing you keep refusing to name.
To the realization that being sexually desired is not the same thing as being loved.
Being touched is not the same thing as being known.
Being wanted for one night is not the same thing as covenant.
Pornography can show you thousands of naked bodies while teaching you almost nothing about genuine intimacy.
Lust says:
What can I take from you?
Love asks:
How can I faithfully seek your good?
And the Gospel goes further.
Jesus says:
I give Myself for you.
That is why Christian sexual ethics cannot finally be understood as God arbitrarily trying to keep people from pleasure.
Our bodies belong to the Lord.
Paul's answer to sexual immorality in 1 Corinthians 6 is rooted in identity, redemption and union with Christ.
“You are not your own.”
“You are bought with a price.”
Therefore:
“Glorify God in your body.”
Your body matters because Christ matters.
Your sexuality matters because discipleship includes the body.
Your private life matters because Jesus is Lord when the church service ends.
And if this is exposing something hidden, don't turn conviction into another five minutes of religious emotion.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Get accountable.
If another person is involved, stop using spiritual language to justify what Scripture calls sin.
If pornography owns your nights, bring the battle into the light with mature, trustworthy Christian accountability and practical barriers.
If you have wounded your spouse, repentance means more than feeling terrible. Seek forgiveness, accept appropriate consequences, and begin rebuilding truthfully.

And if sexual abuse was committed against you, do not confuse somebody else's crime with your guilt. Seek safe, trustworthy pastoral and professional support. Christ's compassion toward the wounded is not diminished by what another person did.
This is where Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create another corner of the internet where Christians pretend.
But to keep pointing exhausted, wounded, tempted, ashamed and hungry people toward Scripture and toward Jesus Christ.
Use them.
Share them.
Put truth into your mind before the world fills it with something else.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns forgiveness.
It cannot.
It should not be presented that way.
Scripture specifically teaches that Christian giving must not be extracted through pressure: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That share costs nothing.
Someone may read the title because they are curious about sex...
and encounter Jesus before they reach the end.
And comment.
Not for appearances.
Not because you need to tell strangers every detail of your past.
But because sometimes one honest sentence is the moment hiding begins to lose its power.
Someone scrolling beneath you may discover they are not the only Christian fighting.
Someone may finally confess.
Someone may finally pray.
Someone may finally return.
Someone may finally discover that Christianity was never the story of spotless people congratulating themselves for being better than everybody else.
It is the story of a spotless Savior rescuing sinners.
So now we return to that strange sentence.
“He went in to her.”
At first it sounded like an awkward old expression for sex.
But behind it was a doorway into something much larger.
The Bible knows exactly how complicated human desire can become.
It knows what people do with their bodies.
It knows what people do in darkness.
It knows how families fracture.
It knows how shame makes us hide.
It knows scandal.
And still...
page after page...
God keeps moving toward fallen humanity until, in the fullness of time, the Word becomes flesh.
Jesus enters our ruined story.
Not to participate in our sin.
To carry sinners out of it.
He touches lepers.
He eats with sinners.
He confronts hypocrites.
He welcomes the repentant.
He goes to a cross.
He sheds His blood.
He rises from the grave.
And He still calls people out of darkness.
Maybe tonight...
He is calling you.
The deepest question is no longer why the Bible says, “he went in to her.”
The question is whether you will keep hiding when Christ is calling you into the light.
Because the scandal may explain how your story broke...
but grace gets the final word when the Author is Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: One Day Your Adult Children May Repeat the Words You’re Saying to Them Right Now
paragraphs: One Day Your Adult Children May Repeat the Words You’re Saying to Them Right Now
Long after they outgrow your house, they may still hear your voice inside their head. The question is whether that voice will sound like condemnation… or like truth spoken through grace.
One day, your child may be thirty-seven years old.
You will not be standing beside them.

The toys will be gone. The school uniforms will be gone. The little shoes by the door will be gone. They may have a mortgage, children of their own, responsibilities you cannot carry for them, and battles they do not tell you about.
And then something will happen.
They will fail.

They will make an embarrassing mistake at work. Their marriage will enter a difficult season. Someone will reject them. Money will become tight. Their confidence will collapse. They will stare at themselves in a bathroom mirror late at night, wondering whether they are enough.
And somewhere inside that grown man or woman…
a voice may speak.
Perhaps it will say:
“You never do anything right.”
Perhaps:
“What is wrong with you?”
Perhaps:
“You’re so lazy.”
“You’re embarrassing me.”
“You’ll never learn.”
“Why can’t you be more like your brother?”
Or perhaps another voice will rise from memory.
“You made a mistake, but a mistake is not your identity.”
“Tell me the truth. We will deal with this together.”
“What you did was wrong, but I still love you.”
“Get back up.”
“God is not finished with you.”
“You belong to Jesus. Remember who you are.”
And suddenly one of the most sobering realities of parenting becomes painfully clear:
Some words leave the room.
Others remain for decades.
Paul wrote:
“πᾶς λόγος σαπρὸς ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ὑμῶν μὴ ἐκπορευέσθω, ἀλλὰ εἴ τις ἀγαθὸς πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς χρείας, ἵνα δῷ χάριν τοῖς ἀκούουσιν.”

That is Ephesians 4:29 in Greek. A careful sense of the verse is: let no corrupting or harmful speech proceed from your mouth, but only what is good for building up according to the need, so that it may give grace to those who hear.
Read the final thought again.
“ἵνα δῷ χάριν τοῖς ἀκούουσιν.”
“So that it may give grace to those who hear.”
Grace.
Not flattery.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not refusing to discipline.
Not raising children who never hear the word “no.”
Grace.
The Greek word is χάρις—charis.
And notice something else in Paul’s language: οἰκοδομήν—oikodomēn—carries the idea of building up, edification.
That means biblical speech is not merely measured by whether the sentence was technically true.
The question is also:
What is this truth building?
Parents need to hear that.
Because it is possible to say something true in a way designed to humiliate.
It is possible to correct a child while wounding his dignity.
It is possible to win an argument with a teenager and lose an opportunity to show him what Christlike authority looks like.
It is possible to become so obsessed with correcting behavior that we forget there is a human soul standing in front of us.
And perhaps that is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because some of us were raised by words we are still trying to escape.
Maybe nobody hit you.
Maybe nobody abandoned you.
Maybe food was always on the table and clothes were always in the closet.
But words lived in your house.
Sharp words.
Mocking words.
Comparisons.
Sarcasm disguised as humor.
Anger disguised as discipline.
Shame disguised as motivation.
Maybe you learned early that mistakes made you stupid.
Tears made you weak.
Questions made you disrespectful.
Failure made you disappointing.
And now you are raising children of your own.

Then one afternoon your child spills something, forgets something, breaks something, lies about something, brings home a disappointing result, talks back, or pushes the exact emotional button you hoped nobody would ever discover.
And before you can stop yourself…
you hear it.
The sentence comes out of your mouth.
And for one horrifying second, you hear your own childhood speaking through you.
You sound like the person who wounded you.
That moment can feel devastating.
But Christian, listen carefully:
That moment does not have to become the end of the story.
This is precisely where the Gospel becomes more than something printed on a church banner.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve respectable people.
He came to redeem sinners.
He enters generations of pride, anger, fear, shame, bitterness, impatience, and inherited patterns and says that the story does not have to continue unchanged.
The cross means your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
And the cross means His grace is powerful enough that repentant sinners do not have to remain who they were.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Because sometimes the scandal is not somewhere outside our homes.
Sometimes it is us.
The father who speaks about Jesus on Sunday and destroys his son with sarcasm on Monday.
The mother who posts Bible verses but compares her daughter with another girl until the daughter begins believing she will never be enough.
The parent who demands immediate repentance from a child but almost never says:
“I was wrong.”
“I sinned against you.”
“Will you forgive me?”
There are few things more powerful than a parent who can kneel beside a child and repent without excuses.
Not:
“I’m sorry, but you made me angry.”
Not:
“I wouldn’t have yelled if you had listened.”
Just:
“What I said was sinful. I was angry, and I used my words to hurt you. That was wrong. Please forgive me. Jesus is changing me too.”
Imagine what that teaches a child.
It teaches that authority does not make someone above repentance.
It teaches that Christianity is not pretending Christians never sin.
It teaches that confession is not weakness.
It teaches that grace is not theoretical.
It teaches them what to do when they fail.
And someday, when that child is grown and realizes he has wounded someone he loves, perhaps he will remember seeing his father humble himself.
Perhaps your repentance today becomes part of his courage to repent tomorrow.
That is the strange beauty of grace.
God can even use the moment after our failure.

This does not mean parental words mechanically determine a child's future. Scripture does not teach that every sentence spoken by a parent inevitably becomes an adult child's internal voice, nor does Ephesians 4:29 specifically address parenting. Paul is instructing believers more broadly about transformed Christian speech.
But surely that makes the verse no less relevant at home.
If our speech should give grace to those who hear us, who hears us more consistently than the people living under our roof?
Your children hear what you say when company leaves.
They hear how you speak when exhausted.
They hear what comes out when the internet stops working.
They hear how you talk about their mother.
They hear how you talk about their father.
They hear how you describe people you dislike.
They hear what you say about your own body.
They hear what you call yourself when you fail.
They hear whether Jesus is merely someone you worship publicly or Someone whose lordship reaches your tongue privately.
And they hear what you say about them.
That is why correction matters.
Children need correction.
Biblical grace is not permissiveness.
Love does not look at destructive behavior and shrug.
But there is an enormous difference between:
“What you did was dishonest.”
and:
“You are a liar and I can never trust you.”
Between:
“That was irresponsible.”
and:
“You are useless.”
Between:
“You disobeyed me, and there will be consequences.”
and:
“I wish you were more like your sister.”
One addresses behavior.
The other can begin attaching shame to identity.
Correct the sin.
Teach responsibility.
Establish consequences.
Protect boundaries.
But do not make humiliation your parenting strategy.
Your child does not need to be crushed in order to understand that sin is serious.
The Gospel itself shows us something far better.
Jesus never minimizes sin.
Yet sinners continually discover that being exposed by Christ does not have to end in destruction.
It can become the doorway to repentance, forgiveness, restoration, and transformation.
That is what our homes desperately need.
Truth without cruelty.
Authority without humiliation.
Correction without rejection.
Conviction without hopelessness.
Grace without pretending sin does not exist.
Maybe you are reading this with regret.
Your children are already adults.
You remember sentences you wish you could drag backward through time and swallow before they escaped your mouth.
Maybe your son barely calls.
Maybe your daughter keeps conversations shallow.
Maybe there is distance between you, and you know at least some of it has your fingerprints on it.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ is Lord of today.
You can still repent.
You can still call.
You can still write the letter.
You can still say:

“I have been thinking about the way I spoke to you when you were growing up. I justified things that I should have confessed. I hurt you. I cannot change those years, and I am not asking you to pretend they did not happen. I am asking your forgiveness for my part in them.”
Do not attach a sermon.
Do not demand an immediate response.
Do not tell them how much worse your own parents were.
Do not make your apology another way of controlling them.
Repent.
And leave room for grace to do what you cannot force.
Perhaps reconciliation comes quickly.
Perhaps slowly.
Perhaps there are wounds requiring much more than one conversation.
Faithfulness does not mean controlling the outcome.
It means obeying Christ with the part that belongs to you.
And if your children are still small, perhaps this article has reached you before some words become memories.
Tonight, when your child walks into the room, look at them differently.
That little boy will not always be little.
That girl asking you the same question for the fifth time will not always be standing beside your chair.
One day the bedroom may be empty.
One day the toys may disappear.
One day you may desperately wish you could hear those small feet running through the hallway again.
And one day your child may stand before their child.
Frustrated.
Exhausted.
Angry.
And open their mouth.
What words will come back?
That question is not meant to condemn you.
It is meant to wake you.
Because the answer is not simply, “Try harder to become a perfect parent.”
There are no perfect parents reading this.
There are no perfect parents writing it.
There is only one perfect Savior.
And this is where Christianity becomes breathtaking.
Jesus does not merely forgive the words we wish we had never spoken.
He begins changing the heart from which our words come.
Because eventually this becomes deeper than vocabulary.
Jesus said that the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart.
So if anger continually pours from us, we must eventually stop blaming everybody around us for bumping the cup.
We must ask what is inside it.
Why am I so angry?
Why do I need control?
Why does my child's failure feel like a personal humiliation?
Why do I become cruel when I feel disrespected?
Why am I repeating the very things I swore I would never repeat?
Bring those questions to Christ.
Not to self-hatred.
To Christ.
Repentance is not standing over your own soul screaming, “You are worthless.”
Repentance is turning from sin and returning to the Savior who already knows the worst thing about you and still calls sinners to Himself.
This is why grace can rewrite families.
Not because Christians magically become flawless parents.
But because Jesus teaches sinners to repent.
To forgive.
To confess.
To restrain the tongue.
To repair what pride would rather ignore.
To speak truth in love.
To begin again.
And maybe tonight the beginning is very small.
Maybe before correcting your child, you lower your voice.
Maybe you stop the sarcastic sentence before it leaves your mouth.
Maybe instead of saying, “What is wrong with you?” you ask, “What happened?”
Maybe after discipline, you remind your child:
“There are consequences for what you did, but nothing you did today made me stop loving you.”
Maybe your teenager rolls their eyes.
Say it anyway.
Maybe they act like your encouragement means nothing.
Keep speaking life anyway.
You do not know which sentence they will remember at thirty-seven.
You do not know which ordinary night will become a permanent memory.
You do not know which words will return when they are sitting alone in a car after their first devastating failure.
So give them something worth remembering.
Not empty praise.
Not a counterfeit gospel telling them they are wonderful regardless of what they do.
Give them something stronger.
Tell them the truth.
You are loved.
Sin matters.
Character matters.
Choices have consequences.
Repentance matters.
Grace is real.
Forgiveness is possible.
Failure is not final.
And Jesus Christ still receives sinners.
Maybe somebody you know needs this tonight.
Not because they are a terrible parent.
Because they are tired.
Because they are repeating patterns they hate.
Because nobody ever taught them that correction and grace can occupy the same room.
Send this privately to the person who would never admit publicly that home has become difficult.
If this exposed something you need Jesus to change, comment, “Christ, change my words.”
If you are fighting to end a painful pattern that came through your family, comment, “It ends with grace.”
If you need prayer because parenting has exhausted your spirit, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
And if you are an adult child still healing from words spoken years ago, you can say, “Christ is still healing me.”
There is no shame in needing grace.
That is why Christ came.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront hidden places in your life, understand the Gospel more deeply, and keep your eyes on Jesus, you can also help this ministry continue and expand.
Following costs nothing.
Sharing costs nothing.
Tagging someone costs nothing.
Praying costs nothing.
And every one of those actions can help biblical truth travel farther than we could carry it alone.
Scripture says that giving should come from what a person has decided in the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
Let it be because you believe Christ-centered teaching should continue reaching people.
Let it be because you want to help us keep creating, publishing, discipling, encouraging, and pointing wounded people toward Jesus.
Let it be an offering of support—not a purchase of God's favor.
God's grace cannot be bought.
Salvation is not for sale.
If you already faithfully give through your local church or elsewhere, this invitation should not manipulate you into replacing commitments you believe God has given you.
Most importantly, stay close to truth.
Go find your child.
Or call the adult child you have been avoiding.
Apologize where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Speak truth where truth is needed.
And when correction must come, remember Ephesians 4:29.
Build.
Give grace.
Because years from now, when you are no longer standing in the room, your words may still be there.
And perhaps one day your grown child will be standing over a frightened little boy who has just broken something.
Perhaps anger will rise.
Perhaps old words will come rushing toward the mouth.
And then…
perhaps your child will remember you.
Not the perfected version of you.
The redeemed version.
The parent who learned to repent.
The parent who stopped defending every failure.
The parent who discovered that authority could kneel.
The parent who finally understood that grace does not weaken truth—it teaches us how to carry truth without using it as a weapon.
And maybe your grown child will kneel beside that frightened little boy and say:
“What you did was wrong. We are going to make it right.
But look at me.
I still love you.”
And somewhere in that moment, a sentence spoken years before will live again.
Only this time…
it will sound like grace.

Be careful what you leave echoing in your children—because long after they forget the toys you bought them, they may still remember what your voice taught them to believe about failure, forgiveness, and grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JOASH HAD TWO WIVES CHOSEN FOR HIM BY THE PRIEST WHO SAVED HIS LIFE
paragraphs: JOASH HAD TWO WIVES CHOSEN FOR HIM BY THE PRIEST WHO SAVED HIS LIFE

The strange detail in 2 Chronicles 24:2–3 is not really a story about two wives. Read what happens after the man who guided Joash dies, and suddenly this becomes one of the most disturbing warnings in Scripture about borrowed faith.
There is one sentence in the story of King Joash that is incredibly easy to read past.
“And Jehoiada took for him two wives; and he begat sons and daughters.”
That is 2 Chronicles 24:3 in the King James Version.
It sounds almost like a footnote.
Joash became king.
Joash did what was right.
Jehoiada the priest arranged his marriages.
Joash had children.
Then the story moves on.
But it is sitting beside another sentence that should make us uncomfortable:
“And Joash did that which was right in the sight of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.”
All the days of Jehoiada.
Those words are going to matter.
Because Joash had something many people would dream of having.
He had a godly man who rescued him.
Protected him.
Counseled him.
Helped establish him.
Helped shape his home.
Helped direct his kingdom.
Helped him repair the house of God.
Jehoiada had been involved in Joash’s life almost from the beginning.
And according to 2 Chronicles 24:3, Jehoiada even took two wives for him.
The Hebrew is striking:
וַיִּשָּׂא־לוֹ יְהוֹיָדָע נָשִׁים שְׁתָּיִם וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת
Vayyissa-lo Yehoyada nashim shettayim, vayyóled banim uvanot.
In straightforward English:
“Jehoiada took for him two wives, and he fathered sons and daughters.”

The Hebrew does not tell us the names of these women here. It does not tell us their feelings about the arrangement. It does not give us enough information to construct a romance, a conspiracy, or some secret theological meaning behind the number two.
So we should not invent one.
The text simply tells us that Jehoiada was deeply involved in the establishment of Joash’s household.
But that raises a far more important question.
Who was this priest that had so much influence over a king?
To understand that, you have to remember what happened when Joash was a baby.
His grandmother Athaliah seized power after the death of her son Ahaziah.
And then came one of the darkest sentences in Judah’s royal history.
She attempted to destroy the royal family.
Imagine the palace.
Doors opening.
Servants running.
Whispers becoming screams.
A royal bloodline being hunted.
And somewhere inside that nightmare was an infant who had no idea people wanted him dead.
Joash.
He could not defend himself.
He could not command soldiers.
He could not negotiate.
He could not even understand what was happening.
He survived because someone hid him.
Jehosheba took the child Joash and concealed him from the slaughter.
Second Chronicles 22 tells us that he remained hidden with them in the house of God for six years while Athaliah ruled the land.
Six years.
While a murderous queen sat on the throne, the future king was growing in hiding.
Think about that.
Athaliah thought she had eliminated the threat.
But somewhere beyond her sight, God was preserving a child.
She had the palace.
God had the promise.
She had political power.
God had providence.
She appeared to control the future.
She did not.
Somebody reading this needs that.
Because there are seasons when evil looks frighteningly successful.
You look at what happened to your family.
What happened to your marriage.
What happened to your children.
What somebody did to you.
What addiction stole.
What betrayal destroyed.
What your own sin nearly ruined.
And you wonder whether anything holy could possibly survive the wreckage.
Joash’s earliest story whispers back:
You do not know what God is preserving while darkness thinks it has won.
Eventually Jehoiada acted.
He gathered leaders.
He organized protection around the young heir.
He brought Joash out.
The crown was placed upon his head.
The testimony was given to him.
He was anointed.
And the people cried:
“God save the king.”
The boy who had once been hidden from execution was now sitting on the throne.
That is already a story of astonishing providence.
And Jehoiada remained beside him.
Second Chronicles 24 opens by telling us Joash was only seven years old when he became king.
Seven.
So picture the relationship.
This was not simply a king occasionally consulting a priest.
Joash grew into kingship under Jehoiada’s enormous influence.
The priest had helped save his life.
The priest helped secure his throne.
The priest guided him spiritually.
And eventually Scripture tells us:
“Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.”
Then immediately:
“Jehoiada took for him two wives, and he had sons and daughters.”
There is something deeply human about this scene.
A rescued boy becomes a king.
The king becomes a husband.
The husband becomes a father.
Life begins replacing the terror of childhood.
A family grows where murder once threatened to erase a family line.
And yes, the text plainly says Joash had two wives.
We should neither hide that nor pretend that every action recorded in the Old Testament is automatically presented as God’s ideal.
The Bible frequently reports human behavior without commanding Christians to reproduce it.

From the beginning, Scripture’s foundational marriage pattern is expressed in Genesis 2:24 as a man being joined to his wife and the two becoming one flesh. Jesus Himself returned to that creation pattern in Matthew 19.
So 2 Chronicles 24:3 is narrative description, not a command establishing polygamy as the Christian model for marriage.
And perhaps surprisingly, Chronicles does not stop to condemn Jehoiada’s decision here.
That means we should be careful not to condemn more than the text condemns or approve more than the text approves.
Let Scripture speak.
But if you keep reading, the two wives stop being the most startling thing in the chapter.
Because something happens to Joash that is infinitely more frightening.
Jehoiada dies.
And suddenly we discover how much of Joash’s apparent spiritual stability had depended upon another man still being in the room.
Read the wording again.
Joash did right...
“all the days of Jehoiada the priest.”
Then Jehoiada died.
The man who had protected him was gone.
The voice that had guided him was silent.
The stabilizing presence disappeared.
And the officials of Judah came to Joash.
This time, Joash listened to them.
Second Chronicles 24:17–18 records the horrifying turn: after Jehoiada’s death, Judah’s officials influenced the king, the people abandoned the house of the LORD, and idolatry followed.
Stop there.
Because now this ancient king is standing frighteningly close to some of us.
You can live beside someone else's faith for years and mistake proximity to God for knowing God.
You can have praying parents.
A faithful pastor.
A godly spouse.
A grandmother who never stopped interceding.
A church that carried you.
A mentor who answered your midnight calls.
A friend who dragged you back every time you started wandering.
And all of those people can be tremendous gifts from God.
But none of them can surrender your heart to Christ for you.
There comes a moment when borrowed conviction must become personal conviction.
Borrowed prayer must become personal prayer.
Borrowed worship must become personal worship.
Borrowed obedience must become personal obedience.
Borrowed faith must become personal trust in God.
Joash apparently knew how to behave while Jehoiada was present.
But after Jehoiada was gone, another set of voices reached his heart.
That is terrifying.
Because the question is no longer merely:
Who influences you?
The deeper question is:
Who are you when your strongest spiritual influence leaves the room?
Who are you when your pastor cannot see you?
Who are you when your Christian friends are gone?
Who are you when nobody checks your browser history?
Who are you when your spouse is asleep?
Who are you when temptation knows your name and accountability is nowhere nearby?
Who are you when obeying Jesus costs something?
Maybe you have spent years looking like Joash during Jehoiada’s lifetime.
You know Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know what to post.
You know the worship songs.
You know the verses.
You know how Christians are supposed to sound.
But somewhere beneath all of that...
you know.
There is a room in your heart you have kept locked.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
An addiction you keep renaming so you do not have to repent of it.
Bitterness you have fed for years.
Secret messages.
Secret lust.
Secret pride.
Secret jealousy.
Secret compromise.
A version of yourself nobody at church has ever met.
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence a person can say is:
“I’m okay because I still look okay.”
Joash looked okay for years.
Then the supporting voice disappeared.
And what followed was devastating.
God did not immediately abandon the people to their rebellion.
He sent prophets to bring them back.
They refused to listen.
Then something almost unbearably tragic happened.
The Spirit of God came upon Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada.
Think about who this was.
The son of the man who had stood beside Joash.
The family of the priest who had helped preserve his throne.
Zechariah confronted the people with their disobedience.
And Joash—the child whose life had once been saved through Jehoiada’s household—ordered Jehoiada’s son killed.
He was stoned.
In the courtyard of the house of the LORD.
The rescued became complicit in destroying the son of his rescuer.
Scripture explicitly says Joash “remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him.”
How does a person travel that far?
How does a rescued child become that king?
Slowly.
That is usually how spiritual collapse happens.
Not always with one dramatic declaration that says, “I reject God.”
Sometimes it begins with listening to another voice.
Then tolerating another compromise.
Then ignoring another warning.
Then protecting another sin.
Until eventually the heart that once seemed tender can defend what it once would have wept over.
And this is where Joash stops being merely an ancient king.
He becomes a mirror.
Maybe your Jehoiada is still alive.
Maybe God has placed someone near you who keeps telling you the truth.
Your mother.
Your father.
Your pastor.
Your wife.
Your husband.
Your friend.
Your brother.
Your sister.
Someone who loves Jesus enough to make you uncomfortable.
Do not despise that voice.
But do not make that person your substitute for Christ either.
Because one day every earthly mentor disappears.
Every preacher eventually leaves the pulpit.
Every parent eventually releases the hand.
Every spiritual hero eventually dies.
And when every Jehoiada is gone, Jesus must still be enough.
That is where this story becomes Gospel.
Because if Joash’s story were only telling us to “be stronger,” we would eventually become another Joash.
Our deepest problem is not insufficient mentorship.
It is sin.
We need more than someone standing beside us.
We need Someone to save us.
We need more than improved behavior.
We need a new heart.
We need more than another Jehoiada.
We need Jesus Christ.
Joash was a king who was rescued from death and eventually wandered.
Jesus is the King who willingly entered death to rescue wanderers.
Joash received a crown after another family risked everything to preserve him.
Jesus wore a crown of thorns and gave Himself to preserve people who had rebelled against Him.
Joash forgot kindness shown to him.
Christ showed kindness to enemies.
Joash participated in the death of an innocent messenger.
Jesus—the truly innocent One—allowed sinful men to crucify Him and prayed for forgiveness for His executioners.
Joash needed grace.
So do we.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people finally earned God's acceptance.
The scandal is that guilty people can be forgiven because the sinless Son of God bore sin and rose victorious.
That means your secret does not have to become your ending.
Your pornography does not have to become your ending.
Your adultery does not have to become your ending.
Your bitterness does not have to become your ending.
Your pride does not have to become your ending.
Your years of pretending do not have to become your ending.
Your spiritual coldness does not have to become your ending.
But grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace calls you into the light.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could become comfortable with the chains He came to break.
Repent.
Not because you can repair yourself enough for God to love you.
Repent because Christ is merciful.
Come into the light.
Confess what you have been protecting.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop using Christian activity to hide spiritual emptiness.
Stop borrowing somebody else's relationship with Jesus.
Run to Christ yourself.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
Let the Savior who receives sinners begin rewriting what sin tried to make permanent.
And if this is exposing something you have kept hidden, do not manufacture a polished Christian answer.
Be honest.
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle.
But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
Then send this to someone.
Not because an algorithm needs another share.
Because somebody you love may be living on borrowed faith right now.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know that repentance is still possible and Christ still receives sinners.
There may come a night when the voices around you change and you need to remember the lesson Joash learned too late:
A godly person can guide your faith, but nobody can have faith in Christ for you.
