And if Gospel Warrior has been one of those voices continually calling you back to Scripture, repentance, grace, healing, discipleship, and Jesus Christ, stay close.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even the unbeliever you have quietly been praying for—to follow too.
And if you believe this work should continue reaching more people, you can help carry it.
Not as a purchase of God's favor.
Not because giving money makes someone more loved by God.
Scripture says giving is not to be done reluctantly or under compulsion; “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary generosity really can support Gospel work.
If you decide freely and prayerfully that you want to stand with us:
Give Jesus your heart.
Money can support a ministry.
It cannot save a soul.
It cannot reconcile you to God.
Only Jesus saves.
And perhaps that is the final ache in Joash’s story.
A man can have a Jehoiada choose his household...
protect his throne...
teach him righteousness...
stand beside him...
and still reach a day when the question becomes:
Will I personally remain faithful to God when the man who carried me this far is gone?
Sooner or later, every borrowed faith reaches that question.
Your parents cannot answer it for you.
Your pastor cannot answer it for you.
Your spouse cannot answer it for you.
Gospel Warrior cannot answer it for you.
You must come to Christ.
And if you have wandered, come back.
If you have failed, come back.
If you have been pretending, come into the light.
If your story has become scandalous, do not assume Jesus has finished writing.
Peter denied Him and was restored.
Thomas doubted and was met by the risen Christ.
Paul persecuted His church and became a herald of the Gospel.
The cross stands forever as proof that God does not redeem people because their histories are spotless.
He redeems sinners through Jesus Christ.
So maybe tonight is not the night your story ends.
Maybe it is the night you finally stop borrowing someone else's faith.
Maybe it is the night you whisper the name you should have called upon long ago.
Jesus.
Save me.
Forgive me.
Change me.
Keep my heart when every other voice disappears.
And years from now, when somebody asks what happened to the person you used to be, may the answer be simple:
Jesus happened.
Because the most frightening thing about Joash was not that he needed someone to guide him.
It was that when the guiding hand disappeared, it became painfully clear whose hand his heart had never fully learned to hold.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHEN YOU PASS THROUGH THE WATERS, I WILL BE WITH YOU” — NOTICE GOD NEVER SAID YOU WOULD AVOID THE WATERS
paragraphs: “WHEN YOU PASS THROUGH THE WATERS, I WILL BE WITH YOU” — NOTICE GOD NEVER SAID YOU WOULD AVOID THE WATERS
Maybe the water around you is not proof that God abandoned you. Maybe you have misunderstood what His promise was supposed to look like.
There is a sentence in Scripture that sounds beautiful until life forces you to need it.
Not quote it.
Not post it.
Not underline it.
Need it.
“When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee…” — Isaiah 43:2.
Read that again, but this time notice the words we often hurry past.
When you pass through the waters.
Not if.
Not “I will make certain you never see deep water.”
Not “Follow Me faithfully enough and I will keep every river away from you.”
God never promised that.
And perhaps that is why somebody reading this has been quietly wondering whether God has forgotten them.
Because the water came.
You prayed.
And it still came.
You believed.
And it still came.
You tried to obey God, and somehow you still ended up standing in a place you never imagined you would have to survive.
The diagnosis came.
The marriage cracked.
The person you trusted betrayed you.
The child you prayed for wandered.
The business collapsed.
The bills kept arriving.
The grief stayed longer than everyone expected.
The temptation you thought you had defeated came knocking again.
The secret struggle followed you into another year.
You smiled at church while something inside you was drowning.
And somewhere between all the prayers that seemed unanswered and all the nights nobody knew you cried, a terrifying question entered your heart:
“God… if You are really with me, why am I in this water?”
That question deserves more than a Christian cliché.
It deserves Scripture.
And Scripture gives us something far stronger than the promise of an easy life.
The Hebrew of Isaiah 43:2 begins:
כִּי־תַעֲבֹר בַּמַּיִם אִתְּךָ־אָנִי
Ki-ta'avor bammayim, itt'kha ani.
“When you pass through the waters, I am with you.”
Look closely at the heart of it:
אִתְּךָ־אָנִי — itt'kha ani — “I am with you.”
That is the promise.
Not the absence of water.
The presence of God.
And that changes everything.

Isaiah was speaking first into the story of Jacob—Israel—a people God had created, formed, called, and redeemed. The verse was not originally written as a motivational slogan promising that every modern believer will escape every earthly disaster unharmed.
The context is richer than that.
Listen to what comes immediately before the waters:
אַל־תִּירָא כִּי גְאַלְתִּיךָ קָרָאתִי בְשִׁמְךָ לִי־אָתָּה
Al-tira, ki ge'altikha; qarati v'shimkha; li-attah.
“Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.” — Isaiah 43:1.
Before God talks about the river, He talks about belonging.
Before He describes the fire, He reminds His people who they are.
Before He tells them what they will walk through, He tells them whose they are.
“I have redeemed you.”
“I have called you by name.”
“You are Mine.”
Then comes the water.
That order matters.
Because suffering has a way of making you forget your identity.
Pain starts whispering things God never said.
“If God loved you, this wouldn't have happened.”
“If you had more faith, you wouldn't be struggling.”
“Maybe God is punishing you.”
“Maybe you went too far.”
“Maybe everybody else can be restored, but not you.”
“Maybe your scandal is bigger than His grace.”
And suddenly the river outside of you becomes a river inside of you.
Fear.
Shame.
Regret.
Anger.
Confusion.
You begin interpreting God through your circumstances instead of interpreting your circumstances through what God has revealed about Himself.
But Isaiah 43 turns the question around.
God does not begin by explaining the water.
He begins by declaring ownership.
You are Mine.
Somebody needs to hear that tonight.
You may be crying…
but if you are in Christ, your tears do not cancel His grace.
You may be struggling…
but your struggle does not make Jesus stop being Savior.
You may have fallen…
but failure does not suddenly make the cross powerless.

You may have consequences to face. You may need to repent. You may need to confess what you have hidden, make something right, seek forgiveness, receive help, or walk through a long process of restoration.
Grace is not pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is the staggering truth that sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and God's mercy is so great that sinners who come to Christ in repentance and faith can be forgiven.
That is why the Gospel is not the story of good people being rewarded for staying dry.
It is the story of guilty people being rescued by a holy and merciful Savior.
And this is where Isaiah's language becomes even more beautiful.
The word translated “redeemed” in Isaiah 43:1 comes from the Hebrew root גאל — ga'al.
It carries the language of redemption—the action of reclaiming or delivering.
God identifies Himself as the One who redeems.
And for the Christian, that great biblical story of redemption reaches its center in Jesus Christ.
We were not merely people caught in unfortunate circumstances who needed encouragement.
Our deepest problem was deeper than anxiety, deeper than financial pressure, deeper than rejection, deeper even than death.
We were sinners who needed reconciliation with God.
And Jesus did not stand safely on heaven's shoreline shouting instructions at drowning people.
He entered our world.
He took flesh.
He was rejected.
He suffered.
He was crucified.
And He bore sin so that those who trust in Him could be forgiven and brought to God.
Jesus knows what suffering costs.
The Christian faith does not give us a Savior untouched by pain.
It gives us the crucified Christ.
Think about that the next time your suffering whispers, “God could never understand this.”
Look at the cross.
The hands pierced there belong to the One Christians confess as Lord.
And then remember something else.
The cross was not the end.
The tomb was occupied…
and then it wasn't.
Jesus rose.
So Christianity does not promise that believers will never enter darkness.
It announces that darkness does not get the final word.
It does not promise there will never be a Friday that feels like everything has died.
It declares that because Christ is risen, death itself will not have the last word over those who belong to Him.
This is why you must be careful about judging God's faithfulness by the chapter you are currently living.
You are reading one page.
God sees the story.
You see water.
He sees a road through it.
You see fire.
He sees what will remain when the flames have done everything they are permitted to do.
You see an ending.
God may be writing a testimony.
And sometimes…
the miracle is not that the water disappears.
Sometimes the miracle is that you discover you are still standing in water that should have destroyed you.
You lost something and thought you would never smile again.
But one morning, somehow, you did.
You were betrayed and thought you would never trust again.
But God slowly began rebuilding your heart.
You buried someone and wondered how the world could possibly keep moving.
Yet grace met you one morning at a time.
You fell into sin and believed your story was permanently stained.
Then repentance brought you back to the feet of Jesus.
You thought your scandal would become your identity.
Jesus called you by another name.
Redeemed.
Forgiven.
His.
That does not mean every earthly story gets the ending we want.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
Some wounds leave scars.
Some relationships are not restored.
Some consequences remain even after forgiveness.
Some believers have followed Christ faithfully and still endured persecution, poverty, sickness, grief, and death.
The Bible never hides this.
Jesus Himself said, “In the world ye shall have tribulation.”
But He did not stop there.
“Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — John 16:33.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Hope.
Not pretending the fire isn't hot.
Knowing the fire isn't God.
Not claiming the river isn't deep.
Knowing the river isn't Lord.
Not pretending death doesn't hurt.
Knowing death does not have the final victory.
And perhaps that is what somebody needs tonight.
You have spent months asking God to remove the water.
Maybe tonight your prayer becomes different.
“Jesus, if You do not remove it yet… walk with me through it.”
That prayer is not surrender to defeat.
It is surrender to God.
There are seasons when faith sounds like thunder.
And there are seasons when faith barely whispers:
“Jesus… I still trust You.”
Do not despise the whisper.
A trembling hand can still reach for Christ.
A tired believer can still pray.
A wounded heart can still repent.
A person with tears running down their face can still worship.
You do not have to pretend you are okay to come to Jesus.
You simply have to come.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Maybe everybody knows the polished version of you.
They know your Sunday clothes.
Your Bible verses.
Your worship songs.
Your “God is good” posts.
But they do not know what happens when the phone goes dark and the room becomes quiet.
They don't know about the addiction.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The affair.
The resentment.
The secret messages.
The envy.
The anger.
The compromise.
The loneliness.
The shame.
The exhausting performance of looking spiritually alive while feeling spiritually numb.
And maybe your deepest water is not something somebody did to you.
Maybe it is something you did.
Listen carefully.
Grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace calls you into the light.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could become more comfortable with chains.
He came to save.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Restore.
Transform.
So repent.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you become worthy.
You will never make yourself worthy of grace.
Come now.
Confess the sin.
Turn from it.
Call upon Christ.
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
Stop protecting the secret that is poisoning your soul.
Stop assuming that because people might reject you, Jesus therefore must reject every sinner who comes to Him.
The Gospel exists precisely because sinners need mercy.
This is what makes grace scandalous.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted Christians.
The woman at the well carried a complicated past.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left with which to build an impressive religious résumé.
Again and again Scripture confronts us with people whose stories looked disqualified.
Then grace entered the story.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Grace that tells the truth about sin and then points trembling sinners toward a Savior whose mercy is greater than anything they could earn.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By refusing to let sin have the final word over the repentant sinner who belongs to Him.
Maybe your life does not look like the testimony you imagined.
Maybe you thought by this age you would be farther ahead.
Maybe you thought your marriage would be stronger.
Your children closer to God.
Your finances stable.
Your faith fearless.
Your prayers answered.
Your heart healed.
Instead, you are standing waist-deep in something you never planned for.
Then hear the promise again.
Not the promise you wish the verse made.
The promise it actually makes.
כִּי־תַעֲבֹר בַּמַּיִם אִתְּךָ־אָנִי
“When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.”
Notice one more word.
Through.
The water is real.
But it is not necessarily your address forever.
There is a difference between passing through something and belonging to it.
You may be walking through grief.
Grief does not own you.
You may be walking through temptation.
Temptation does not own you.
You may be walking through consequences.
Your worst decision does not have to become your eternal identity.
You may be walking through a season where you cannot understand God.
Your confusion does not dethrone Him.
And if you belong to Christ, even death itself becomes something the believer passes through on the way to resurrection.
That is how deep Christian hope goes.
Not “everything will become comfortable.”
Something infinitely greater:
Christ will have the final word.
So if this found you while you are in the water, stop measuring God's nearness by how dry your clothes are.
He never said you would avoid every river.
He said:
I will be with you.
And maybe years from now, you will look back at the season you begged God to erase and realize it became the place where you finally stopped knowing Him merely as information…
and began knowing Him as refuge.
Maybe you will remember the night you nearly gave up.
The night you finally confessed.
The night you stopped running.
The night you whispered the name of Jesus because you had nothing eloquent left to pray.
Maybe the testimony will not be:
“I never entered the water.”
Maybe it will be:
“I entered it convinced I would drown… and discovered Christ was there.”
If that is where you are right now, don't hide behind a polished comment.
Be honest.
Somebody reading beneath you may be standing where you once stood.
Your testimony might become somebody else's reason to hold on tonight.
Then think of one person whose water is rising.
Not twenty random people.
One person.
The friend whose smile has been hiding exhaustion.
The brother who stopped coming to church.
The sister carrying a grief she rarely mentions.
The person whose marriage is quietly breaking.
The believer who thinks falling means Jesus wants nothing more to do with them.
The skeptic who has mistaken Christianity for a promise of an easy life.
Send this to them privately.
“Where is God in this?”
Let the answer find them:
He never promised there would be no waters. He promised His presence in them.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin honestly, understand grace more deeply, and keep your eyes on Jesus, you can also help this ministry continue.

Sharing costs nothing, yet it can carry biblical truth farther than we could carry it alone. Saving this article can put it back in your hands on the night you need to remember it. Following Gospel Warrior helps you stay close to daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment—and inviting family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow can place the Gospel before people who might never search for it themselves.
Scripture teaches willing, purposeful generosity—not pressured giving. “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Grace cannot be bought.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, creating, reaching, and expanding resources centered on Jesus Christ.
Pray.
Share.
Save the truth for the night the water rises again.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done for you.
Because the mission is not to build an audience around us.
The mission is to point people toward Him.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Calling people out of darkness.
Calling the guilty to repentance.
Calling the ashamed toward grace.
Calling the exhausted to Himself.
Calling prodigals home.
And perhaps that is why you are reading this at this exact moment.
You wanted God to explain the water.
Instead, Scripture gives you something better than an explanation.
A presence.
“I will be with you.”
So when the river rises tomorrow…
when another bill arrives…
when the memories return…
when temptation whispers…
when grief sits beside you again…
when people misunderstand you…
when repentance costs you something…
when the future becomes frightening…
remember what God did not say.
He did not say you would never see water.
And remember what He did say.
אִתְּךָ־אָנִי
I am with you.
The water may become part of your testimony.
But it does not get to become your Savior.
Jesus already has that name.
And when grace has finished telling your story, the chapter you once called “the place where I drowned” may become the chapter where you whisper through tears:
“That was the place I discovered I was never walking alone.”
Never confuse deep water with an absent God—the scars on the risen Christ remind us that suffering and the presence of God were never opposites.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HAGAR THOUGHT HER SON WAS ABOUT TO DIE—Then God Opened Her Eyes to a Well
paragraphs: HAGAR THOUGHT HER SON WAS ABOUT TO DIE—Then God Opened Her Eyes to a Well

She was crying beside a dying son, staring at a wilderness that seemed empty. The water was gone. Hope was disappearing. But Genesis 21:14–19 reveals something hauntingly beautiful: sometimes God's provision is already nearer than your despair allows you to see.
There is a kind of pain that does not scream at first.
It just walks.
One exhausted step after another.
It carries yesterday on its back, uncertainty in its hands, and someone it loves more than itself somewhere beside it.
That was Hagar.
Genesis 21 does not introduce us to a woman sitting peacefully beneath a tree, reflecting on God's goodness while everything in her life makes sense.
It gives us a woman in a wilderness.
Bread.
A skin of water.
A son.
And eventually...
nothing left to drink.
She had already known rejection.
She had already known what it felt like to be caught inside the consequences of other people's decisions.
She had already fled once before and encountered the God who saw her in Genesis 16.
But now she was in the wilderness of Beersheba, and the water was gone.
Read that slowly.
The water was gone.
Not running low.
Gone.
There are moments when faith sounds beautiful because the refrigerator is full, the bills are paid, the children are healthy, and tomorrow still feels predictable.
And then there are wilderness moments.
The doctor calls.
The marriage fractures.
The person you trusted walks away.
The job disappears.
The prayer you have prayed for months seems to return unanswered.
Your child begins fighting a battle you cannot fight for them.
You smile at church while privately wondering how much longer you can keep yourself together.
You know verses.
You know sermons.
You know that God is good.
But your water is gone.
And suddenly theology is no longer something printed on a page.
It is the only thing standing between your soul and despair.
Hagar reached that place.
Genesis says that when the water in the skin was gone, she placed the boy under one of the bushes.
Then she walked away.
Not because she did not love him.
Because she loved him too much to watch what she believed was coming.
She sat about a bowshot away and said, in essence, “Do not let me see the boy die.”
Try to enter that moment without rushing toward verse 19.
Do not run to the well yet.
Sit beside Hagar first.
A mother is looking toward a bush beneath which her son is lying.
Her water is gone.
Her options are gone.
Her strength is gone.
And as far as she can see, the future is gone.
There are prayers we speak beautifully.
And there are prayers made almost entirely of tears.
Hagar wept.
But then Scripture tells us something astonishing.
God heard.
The Hebrew of Genesis 21:17 begins with words worth remembering:
“וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶת־קוֹל הַנַּעַר”
Vayishma Elohim et-qol hanna'ar.
“God heard the voice of the boy.”
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not say God finally discovered where they were.
It does not say Hagar's crying alerted an uninformed God to an emergency developing in the wilderness.
God had already spoken concerning Ishmael.

Before Hagar reached this breaking point, God had told Abraham that He would make a nation from his son. The covenant line through which God's redemptive promise would advance was through Isaac; Scripture is explicit about that. Yet God had also declared that Ishmael, because he was Abraham's offspring, would become a nation.
So when Hagar saw death approaching, God had not forgotten His word.
She simply could not see how His word could survive her circumstances.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
You can see the wilderness.
You can see the empty skin.
You can see the bush.
You can see what you lost.
You can see the diagnosis.
You can see the rejection.
You can see the bank balance.
You can see the unanswered message.
You can see the person you desperately want God to rescue.
But you cannot see what God is doing.
And when pain narrows your vision, what you cannot see can begin to feel as though it does not exist.
That is one of despair's cruelest tricks.
Despair takes limited human sight and quietly turns it into a conclusion about an unlimited God.
“I cannot see a way.”
becomes...
“There is no way.”
“I do not understand what God is doing.”
becomes...
“God is doing nothing.”
“I cannot feel Him.”
becomes...
“He has abandoned me.”
But those sentences are not the same.
Hagar could not see a future.
God had already spoken one.
Then heaven addressed her personally.
“What troubles you, Hagar?”
Her name.
In the wilderness.
Her name.
God was not dealing with an anonymous tragedy.
He knew the woman sitting there.
He knew the boy beneath the bush.
He knew the distance between them.
He knew the water was gone.
He knew the fear inside her chest.
And He knew her name.
That matters because suffering has a way of making people feel invisible.
You become “the divorced one.”
“The unemployed one.”
“The addict.”
“The widow.”
“The failure.”
“The person who fell away.”
“The one whose child is struggling.”
“The one who ruined everything.”
“The one nobody checks on anymore.”
But God does not lose your name inside your pain.
The angel of God tells Hagar not to fear because God has heard the boy where he is.
Where he is.
Not where he should have been.
Not where Hagar wished he were.
Not somewhere impressive.
Where he is.
That phrase reaches farther than the wilderness of Beersheba.
God knows where you are.
And even more importantly, the Gospel announces that God did not remain distant from suffering humanity.
The Bible's story ultimately carries us from the wilderness toward Jesus Christ.
The eternal Son of God entered our broken world.
He took on flesh.
He came near to sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He received the rejected.
He called the weary.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
And at the cross, Jesus did something infinitely greater than merely improving difficult circumstances.
He dealt with our deepest catastrophe.
Sin.
Our greatest need is not merely for God to make our wilderness comfortable.
Our greatest need is reconciliation with the God against whom we have sinned.
We do not simply need better circumstances.
We need forgiveness.
We need mercy.
We need a Savior.
And Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners and rose again.
The Gospel is not that good people eventually find enough strength to walk out of the desert.
The Gospel is that the Son of God came to save people who could never save themselves.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God dealing with sin through Christ and offering forgiveness to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
And perhaps that is the well someone reading this has never seen.
You have been asking God to fix your money, your relationship, your loneliness, your career, your anxiety about tomorrow...
while Jesus is calling you to something deeper than temporary relief.
Himself.
Because you could receive everything you have ever wanted and still die spiritually thirsty.
You could gain applause and remain empty.
You could rebuild your reputation and remain unreconciled to God.
You could fill your house and still have an empty soul.
The greatest gift God can give you is not a life in which you never enter a wilderness.
It is Himself.
Then comes one of the most unforgettable sentences in Hagar's story.
Genesis 21:19 says:
“וַיִּפְקַח אֱלֹהִים אֶת־עֵינֶיהָ”
Vayifqach Elohim et-eineha.
“Then God opened her eyes...”
And she saw a well of water.
Think about that.
The text does not describe Hagar digging the well.
It says God opened her eyes and she saw it.
One moment she believed she was sitting near the end of her son's life.
Then her eyes were opened.
Water.
A well.
Provision.
Hope.
She went to it, filled the skin with water, and gave the boy a drink.
The wilderness had not instantly disappeared.
But now she saw something in the wilderness she could not see before.
That is the line I cannot shake:
God opened her eyes.
Because sometimes the miracle you desperately need is not God explaining every unanswered question.
Sometimes it is God opening your eyes to what is true while you are still standing in the wilderness.
Maybe the well is a brother or sister in Christ you have been too ashamed to call.
Maybe it is the church community you keep avoiding because hiding feels safer than being known.
Maybe it is repentance you have postponed because surrender would mean admitting you were wrong.
Maybe it is forgiveness you know you need to seek.
Maybe it is Scripture you stopped opening because disappointment made you distant.
Maybe it is help you were too proud to ask for.
Maybe it is simply the realization that God's silence is not proof of God's absence.
But we must be careful here.
Genesis 21 is not a formula promising that every illness will be cured, every marriage restored, every financial crisis immediately reversed, or every wilderness removed in the way we want.
Faith does not mean forcing Hagar's exact outcome onto every tragedy.
Some faithful Christians have prayed through tears and still buried someone they loved.
Some have trusted God and still lost jobs.
Some have obeyed Christ and still suffered deeply.
Jesus Himself told His followers that they would have trouble in this world.
Christian hope is stronger than the promise of comfortable circumstances.
Our hope is Christ.
The crucified Christ.
The risen Christ.
The reigning Christ.
The Christ who forgives sinners.
The Christ who remains faithful.
The Christ who will finally make all things right.
The Christ who conquered death itself.
Hagar's well therefore points us toward a larger biblical reality: human vision is limited, but God's faithfulness is not.
Your empty water skin does not empty God of His power.
Your confusion does not confuse Him.
Your tears do not embarrass Him.
Your wilderness does not place you outside His sight.
And your past does not possess more saving power than the blood of Jesus Christ.
That last truth may be the one somebody desperately needs.
Because perhaps your wilderness is partly of your own making.
Maybe you did make the decision.
Maybe you did betray someone.
Maybe you did relapse.
Maybe you did lie.
Maybe you did compromise.
Maybe you did waste years.
Maybe nobody forced you.
Maybe when you look backward, you cannot blame anyone else.
The Gospel does not require us to rewrite our history and pretend our sins were virtues.
It does something far more glorious.
Jesus can redeem sinners who finally stop hiding.
Repentance says, “Lord, I have sinned.”
Grace says, “Christ is sufficient for repentant sinners.”
Faith stops defending itself and runs toward Jesus.
That is why shame does not get the final sentence.
That is why failure does not get the final sentence.
That is why your worst chapter does not automatically become your final chapter.
From scandal to grace...
because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by pretending rebellion was obedience.
Not by erasing truth.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking guilty people, washing them by grace, reconciling them to God, and transforming their lives.
He turns rebels into sons and daughters.
He turns hidden sin into confessed sin.
He turns condemnation into justification for those who are in Him.
He turns graves into places from which resurrection hope speaks.
And maybe while reading this, you realized something uncomfortable.
You have spent months asking God to change what is around you while resisting what He wants to change within you.
You want the well.
But do you want God?
You want relief.
But do you want repentance?
You want restoration.
But do you want surrender?
You want Jesus to rescue the life you designed.
But are you willing to let Jesus become Lord of it?
Because someday the things consuming you right now will no longer matter.
The applause will stop.
The money will belong to somebody else.
The house will have another owner.
Your social-media profile will become silent.
Your achievements will become memories.
And you will stand before God.
The question will not be whether you looked Christian enough online.
The question is whether you belong to Christ.
If you have been hiding, come into the light.
If you have been running, turn around.
If you have been playing with sin, repent.
If you have been trying to earn salvation, stop trying to purchase what Christ alone can provide by grace.
Call upon Jesus.
Trust Him.
Bring Him the truth about you.
Not the edited version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version everybody follows online.
You.
The frightened you.
The ashamed you.
The angry you.
The exhausted you.
The you sitting a bowshot away from something you cannot bear to watch die.
Come to Christ.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn conviction into another moment you merely consume and forget.
Someone reading beneath you may be sitting in the place where you once sat.
Your story may remind them that despair does not know everything.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person whose smile has looked different lately.
The mother fighting quietly for her child.
The father carrying pressure nobody notices.
The believer who has become distant.
The friend who says, “I'm fine,” a little too quickly.
The person who has never trusted Christ.
Saving it helps too.
There are words you understand differently when the water runs out.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith and you want to help this work continue and expand, there is another way to stand with the mission.
The New Testament says giving is not to be done reluctantly or under compulsion, but from a willing heart.
If this ministry has helped you, consider helping us keep helping others.
Not because God needs your money.
Not because salvation has a price tag.
But because ministry requires people willing to pray, share, serve, give, create, send, and stand together.
If you have been asking, “How can I help Gospel Warrior reach farther?” this is one tangible answer.
It is people.
Another exhausted believer.
Another searching soul.
Another person reading alone at 2:00 in the morning.
Another marriage desperate for biblical truth.
Another prodigal who needs to remember the Father's mercy.
Another Christian who needs discipleship instead of another empty motivational slogan.
Another person in a wilderness who cannot see the well yet.
Send it privately to someone.
Pray that Jesus Christ—not a page, not a personality, not an algorithm—would be magnified through every word.
Because the goal is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The goal is to make Christ known.
Hagar believed she was about to watch her son die.
She could see the empty container.
She could see the wilderness.
She could see the bush.
She could see everything that frightened her.
Then God opened her eyes.
And there was the well.
Perhaps tonight you still do not know how your story turns out.
Perhaps the prayer has not been answered the way you hoped.
Perhaps nothing around you has changed since you began reading.
But do not confuse what you cannot see with what God cannot do.
Do not build your theology entirely from the contents of an empty water skin.
Do not let one terrible chapter convince you that God has stopped being God.
Look again toward Christ.
Open the Scriptures again.
Pray again.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask for help.
Tell somebody the truth.
And when fear whispers, “This is where everything ends,” remember a crying woman in the wilderness whose eyes could not yet see what God already knew was there.
The water skin was empty.
God was not.
And maybe that is the sentence you need to carry into your wilderness:
What looks like the end from where you are standing may still be the place where God teaches you to open your eyes and look toward Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS DRINKING ALCOHOL A SIN—OR IS DRUNKENNESS THE SIN?
paragraphs: IS DRINKING ALCOHOL A SIN—OR IS DRUNKENNESS THE SIN?
The Bible’s answer may confront both the Christian who condemns every glass…and the Christian who keeps asking how close to the edge he can stand without falling.
There is a question Christians have argued about for generations.
Some answer it before you can even finish asking.
“Alcohol is sin.”
Others laugh.
“Jesus turned water into wine. Relax.”
One side can sound as though touching a glass makes you rebellious against God.
The other can sound as though Christian liberty means nobody is allowed to question what happens after the second, third, fourth, or fifth drink.
But what if both reactions can miss the deepest question?
Because perhaps the most revealing question is not simply:
“Am I allowed to drink this?”
Perhaps it is:
“Why do I need this?”
That question changes the room.
Because you can debate Greek words while hiding an addiction.
You can quote Jesus at Cana while ignoring what happens to you after midnight.
You can defend abstinence while secretly being proud, judgmental, and merciless toward people Christ died to save.
And you can shout “Christian freedom” while becoming increasingly enslaved to the very thing you insist you control.
So before you defend your position, put the glass down for a moment.
Not necessarily because the glass itself is the sin.
But because your reaction to putting it down may tell you something your theology has not.
Scripture deserves more from us than slogans.
And Jesus deserves more than being used as ammunition in our arguments.
The Bible does not hide wine.
Psalm 104 speaks of God providing “wine that gladdens the heart of man.” The Hebrew word is יַיִן — yayin, the ordinary Hebrew word for wine.
The New Testament likewise uses οἶνος — oinos, meaning wine. That same Greek word occurs in passages including John 2, Romans 14:21, Ephesians 5:18, and 1 Timothy 5:23.
Paul even told Timothy:
“Μηκέτι ὑδροπότει, ἀλλὰ οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ χρῶ…”
Mēketi hydropotei, alla oinō oligō chrō…
In straightforward English:
“No longer drink only water, but use a little wine…”
Notice one extremely important word:
ὀλίγῳ — oligō — “a little.”
Paul was not giving Timothy permission to lose control.
He was specifically telling him to use a little wine in connection with his stomach and frequent ailments.
That alone should make us careful about saying something broader than Scripture says.
But then comes the other side of the biblical witness.
And it is severe.
Scripture repeatedly warns about wine’s power to deceive, impair judgment, produce destructive behavior, and master the person who refuses wisdom.
Then Paul writes something that should end every Christian attempt to baptize drunkenness as harmless recreation:
Καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ… ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν Πνεύματι.
Kai mē methyskesthe oinō… alla plērousthe en Pneumati.
“Do not get drunk with wine…but be filled with the Spirit.”
The word translated “get drunk” is μεθύσκεσθε — methyskesthe, from a verb meaning to become intoxicated or drunk.
Paul does not merely say something negative about wine.
He establishes a contrast.
Do not be controlled by intoxication.
Be filled with the Spirit.
Wine is οἴνῳ — oinō.
Drunkenness is expressed through μεθύσκεσθε — methyskesthe.
They are not identical words or concepts.
And the distinction matters.
So if the question is strictly:
“Does Scripture explicitly teach that every consumption of alcohol, in every amount and circumstance, is itself sinful?”
The biblical evidence does not support making that universal statement.
But if you stop reading there, you may use half the truth to hide from the other half.
Because Scripture's question is bigger than:
“Can I?”
The Gospel teaches us to ask:
“Does this glorify Christ?”
“Does this master me?”
“Does this weaken my judgment?”
“Does this violate my conscience?”
“Does this make someone else stumble?”
“Can I surrender it without becoming defensive?”
“Am I drinking because I enjoy something in moderation—or because I cannot bear what I feel when I am sober?”
That last question may hurt.
Maybe nobody knows why you pour it.
They see the photo.
The dinner.
The celebration.
The bottle.
The smile.
They don't see what happened before the picture.
They don't know that sometimes you are not drinking to celebrate.
You are drinking to forget.
To sleep.
To numb something.
To quiet your thoughts.
To escape your marriage for a few hours without physically leaving it.
To silence memories you cannot explain.
To become outgoing because you are terrified of being yourself.
To bury loneliness.
To survive grief.
To stop feeling like the person in the mirror.
And eventually what began as something you consumed begins consuming you.
You still call it freedom.
But freedom shouldn't panic when the bottle is gone.
Freedom shouldn't need another drink to feel normal.
Freedom shouldn't make you hide receipts.
Freedom shouldn't make your children recognize the sound of your footsteps and wonder which version of you just came home.
Freedom shouldn't repeatedly leave apologies waiting for morning.
There is a frightening possibility here:
You can spend years arguing that drinking is not necessarily a sin while completely missing the fact that your drinking has become sinful.
That is why Ephesians 5:18 is so powerful.
Paul does not merely prohibit something.
He offers something infinitely greater.
Not intoxication.
Presence.
Not escape.
The Spirit.
Not numbness.
Transformation.
Not something that makes you forget your wounds for several hours.
Someone who can meet you inside them.
“Be filled with the Spirit.”
There are things alcohol can temporarily blur that only Jesus can actually heal.
There are memories a bottle can suppress but cannot redeem.
There is shame you can anesthetize without ever becoming free from it.
Christ does not merely offer a more religious coping mechanism.
He offers Himself.
And that means the real battle may not be sitting inside your glass.
It may be sitting inside your heart.
Because drunkenness is not beautiful in Scripture.
It is not portrayed as harmless loss of inhibition.
It is loss of sober judgment.
Loss of self-control.
Loss of vigilance.
And sometimes, tragically, loss of things that cannot simply be recovered the next morning.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that means.
Maybe alcohol did not destroy your life.
Maybe it destroyed somebody else's life and splashed the wreckage onto yours.
Maybe you remember a father who became someone different when he drank.
A mother whose pain became unpredictable.
A spouse whose promises lasted until the next bottle.
A crash.
An ambulance.
A betrayal.
A violent night.
A childhood spent learning how to read the atmosphere of a room before speaking.
So when another Christian casually says, “There's nothing wrong with drinking,” something inside you tightens.
Your story deserves compassion.
And Scripture has something important to say here too.
Romans 14:21 says:
“It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.”
Read that again.
Because this destroys another idol:
the idol of insisting on my rights.
Paul's vision of Christian freedom is not:
“I can do whatever isn't explicitly forbidden, and everybody else can deal with it.”
Christian freedom kneels.
Christian freedom loves.
Christian freedom can surrender something permissible for the spiritual good of another person.
That means you could theoretically be free to drink and still decide:
“For the sake of Christ, for the sake of my brother, for the sake of my family, for the sake of my testimony, I won't.”
That is not weakness.
That can be love.
There may be a recovering alcoholic sitting beside you whose freedom is worth more than your glass.
There may be a son watching you.
A daughter imitating you.
A new believer learning from you.
A wounded person fighting an addiction you cannot see.
And suddenly the question is no longer:
“What's wrong with one drink?”
It becomes:
“What is another person's soul worth to me?”
Romans 14 does not teach that another person's conscience automatically creates a universal law for every Christian everywhere.
But it absolutely destroys the selfish idea that personal liberty is the highest Christian virtue.
It isn't.
Love is greater than proving your freedom.
And sometimes the most Christlike use of freedom is voluntarily laying freedom down.
Jesus did something infinitely greater.
Philippians tells us that Christ humbled Himself.
The King stooped.
The Lord became servant.
The innocent One walked toward a cross carrying the judgment of guilty people.
That is the shape of Christianity.
Not:
“How much can I keep?”
But:
“What can I surrender because I love Him?”
And this is where the debate becomes painfully personal.
If someone asks whether you could stop drinking for a month and your first emotion is anger…
pay attention.
If the possibility of never drinking again feels unbearable…
pay attention.
If you carefully count how much Scripture allows but never ask whether the Holy Spirit is asking you to surrender it…
pay attention.
If people who love you have repeatedly expressed concern…
pay attention.
If your personality changes…
pay attention.
If you drink secretly…
pay attention.
If “just one” repeatedly becomes more…
pay attention.
If alcohol has become the place you run when life hurts…
please pay attention.
Not because Christ is standing over you eager to humiliate you.
Because He loves you too much to watch you rename chains “freedom.”
And perhaps your story is completely different.
Perhaps you drink rarely.
You do not become intoxicated.
You do not crave alcohol.
You can leave it untouched.
Your conscience is clear.
You are not using it as medicine for your soul.
Even then, Scripture gives you no permission for arrogance.
Do not mock the Christian who abstains.
Do not pressure somebody to drink.
Do not turn liberty into superiority.
Do not wave Cana in the face of someone recovering from alcoholism.
And Christian who abstains—
do not automatically treat every believer holding a glass as though you have discovered secret evidence of apostasy.
Do not create commandments God did not give simply because rules make holiness easier to measure.
Holiness is deeper than beverage selection.
A person can be completely sober from alcohol and intoxicated with pride.
You can never touch wine and still be drunk on anger.
Drunk on lust.
Drunk on greed.
Drunk on approval.
Drunk on bitterness.
Drunk on yourself.
And perhaps that is why Paul's command is so penetrating.
He does not stop with:
“Do not get drunk.”
He says:
“Be filled with the Spirit.”
Christianity is not ultimately about becoming empty enough to look respectable.
It is about becoming filled with Christ's life through the Spirit.
That is the deeper question.
What fills you?
What controls you when pressure rises?
What do you reach for when your heart breaks?
Where do you run when nobody is watching?
What gives you courage?
What makes you feel whole?
What do you believe you cannot live without?
Because whatever you repeatedly run toward for salvation will eventually begin functioning like a savior.
And alcohol is a terrible savior.
It cannot forgive sin.
It cannot reconcile you to God.
It cannot resurrect what shame killed.
It cannot wash your conscience.
It cannot call you beloved.
It cannot carry your judgment.
It cannot defeat death.
It cannot make you new.
But Jesus can.
Maybe you already crossed the line.
Maybe this article isn't theoretical for you.
Maybe you have been drunk more times than you want to remember.
Maybe alcohol helped destroy relationships.
Maybe you hurt people.
Maybe you embarrassed yourself.
Maybe you promised God, crying over a toilet at three in the morning, that you would never do it again.
Then you did.
Maybe you have lied.
Hidden bottles.
Broken promises.
Driven when you shouldn't have.
Said things your family still remembers even though you don't.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up so Jesus will finally tolerate you.”
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Real sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
Addicted sinners.
Religious sinners.
Broken sinners.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People whose yesterday would humiliate them if it appeared on a screen in church.
At the cross, Jesus did not die for the imaginary polished version of you.
He died for sinners.
He bore sin.
He rose victorious.
And repentance is not pretending the chains were never there.
Repentance turns from sin toward Christ.
Grace does not call slavery freedom.
Grace opens the prison door.
Grace does not tell the drunkard, “Nothing needs to change.”
Grace says there is a new Master now.
Jesus.
So is drinking alcohol a sin?
Scripture gives us a more careful answer than many arguments do.

The Bible explicitly condemns drunkenness. It warns seriously about alcohol's dangers. Yet Scripture does not present every use of wine as intrinsically sinful in every circumstance; Paul's instruction to Timothy to use “a little wine” makes a universal prohibition difficult to sustain from the text itself.
But that is not permission for carelessness.
A Christian's relationship with alcohol must live underneath the lordship of Jesus Christ.
If it masters you, there is a problem.
If you use it to pursue intoxication, Scripture speaks clearly.
If it repeatedly destroys your self-control, stop pretending the issue is merely theological.
If your conscience condemns what you are doing, do not violate your conscience.
If your liberty becomes another person's stumbling block, love may call you to surrender your liberty.

And if wisdom, your history, your family circumstances, recovery from addiction, medical concerns, or the Spirit-convicted application of Scripture leads you to abstain completely, then abstain gladly.
You lose nothing essential by giving up alcohol.
You lose everything essential if alcohol helps pull you away from Christ.
Maybe the question you came here asking was:
“Can Christians drink?”
But perhaps the question following you out of this article is different:
“Does Jesus truly have permission to tell me no?”
Not your pastor.
Not your denomination.
Not the internet.
Jesus.
If Christ asked you to put the bottle down forever, could you?
Bring it into the light.

Talk to a trustworthy pastor, mature Christian, counselor, physician, or recovery professional if alcohol has become difficult to control. If physical dependence may be present, seek medical guidance rather than assuming abrupt withdrawal is safe.
And bring the truth to Jesus.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary required.
Just honesty.
“Jesus, I don't know whether I'm controlling this anymore.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, free me.”
“Jesus, show me whether this is liberty or bondage.”
“Jesus, I surrender.”
That prayer may be more important than winning every argument about alcohol you will ever have.
And if this exposed something you've kept hidden, don't disappear into silence.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that chains really can break.
And if you disagree with this article, come to the comments with Scripture, humility, and love. We don't need another shouting match between Christians.
We need truth.
We need grace.
We need Jesus.
Maybe alcohol isn't their bottle.
Maybe pornography is.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe gambling.
Maybe money.
Maybe approval.
Maybe rage.
Maybe a relationship.
Different bottles.
Same throne.
And there is only one rightful King.
Jesus Christ.
Supporting Gospel ministry can be a genuine act of generosity and stewardship offered to the glory of God.
Give first because you belong to Christ.
Support because you freely choose to help the work continue.
Jesus is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The cross is enough.
So share because someone needs truth.
Tag because someone needs a friend.
Save because you may need these words again.
But above everything else—
follow Jesus.
Because someday the bottle will be empty.
The party will end.
The laughter will fade.
The argument about whether Christians can drink will become astonishingly small.
And what will matter is not whether you successfully defended your glass.
What will matter is whether your heart belonged to Christ.
So perhaps the final question was never:
“How much can I drink before it becomes sin?”
Perhaps the question was always:
“How much of me does Jesus get?”
And the only answer worthy of the One who gave all of Himself for you is—
all of me.
Remember this when temptation whispers that surrender means losing something:
Anything you cannot place at the feet of Jesus has already begun trying to take His place on the throne.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOUR BODY IS A TEMPLE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT—What Does That Have to Do With Sex?
paragraphs: YOUR BODY IS A TEMPLE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT—What Does That Have to Do With Sex?

You may have heard this verse used against tattoos, alcohol, food, or unhealthy habits. But when Paul originally wrote it, he was talking about something far more intimate—and what he said about your body, your sexuality, your shame, and the blood of Jesus changes everything.
There are some Bible verses we know so well that we can quote them without remembering why they were written.
“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.”
You have probably heard it.
Maybe someone said it while talking about smoking.
Maybe tattoos.
Maybe overeating.
Maybe exercise.
Maybe taking care of yourself.
And certainly, the truth that our bodies belong to God has implications for how we treat them.
But open your Bible.
Read what comes immediately before 1 Corinthians 6:19–20.
Suddenly the room gets uncomfortable.
Because Paul was talking about sex.
Not abstract theology.
Not gym memberships.
Not diets.
Sex.
Sexual desire.
Sexual sin.
What happens when a person who belongs to Jesus takes the body that belongs to Christ into sexual immorality.
And perhaps that makes this passage uncomfortable for you for another reason.
Because maybe you are not reading about somebody else's past.
Maybe you are remembering yours.
A bedroom.
A hotel room.
A relationship you knew was crossing boundaries.
A screen you keep returning to when nobody is watching.
Messages you delete.
Pictures you would panic if someone discovered.
A relationship you keep calling “complicated” because calling it sin would require you to make a decision.
Maybe your story is not dramatic at all.
Maybe you simply gave somebody something you thought would make them stay.
You wanted affection.
You wanted to feel chosen.
You wanted somebody to hold you.
You wanted one night where loneliness stopped screaming.
And afterward...
they left.
Or perhaps they stayed, but something inside you changed.
Now here comes Christianity talking about sexual holiness, and immediately you expect condemnation.
You expect someone to point a finger.
You expect another sermon telling you how dirty you became.
But listen carefully.
Paul's argument is far more powerful than:
“Sex is bad.”
That is not Christianity.
The Bible does not teach that sex itself is dirty.
God created human beings male and female. Genesis presents the marital union of husband and wife as “one flesh.” Scripture can speak beautifully and positively about marital intimacy.
Sex is not Satan's invention that Christianity reluctantly tolerates.
It belongs inside God's design.
And because it is sacred, Scripture refuses to treat it as meaningless.
That is where 1 Corinthians 6 becomes breathtaking.
Paul writes:
To de sōma ou tē porneia alla tō Kyriō.
“The body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord.”
Notice what Paul does NOT say.
He does not merely say:
Your body is not for sexual immorality.
He says:
Your body is for the Lord.
That changes everything.
Christian sexual holiness is not ultimately about God standing over your shoulder trying to prevent you from enjoying your body.
It begins with belonging.
Your body has a purpose greater than appetite.
Your sexuality has a purpose greater than pleasure.
Your deepest identity is greater than who desires you, who rejected you, who slept with you, who touched you, what you watched, what you did, or what was done to you.
Your body is for the Lord.
Then Paul goes further.
He asks:
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”
Think about those words.
If you belong to Christ, Christianity does not teach that Jesus merely saved some invisible spiritual portion of you while your physical body remains disconnected from Him.
Your body matters to Christ.
So much that Paul connects Christian hope to bodily resurrection.
God raised Jesus, Paul says, and He will also raise us by His power.
Your body therefore isn't disposable packaging around your soul.
God intends resurrection.
Then Paul discusses sexual union and reaches back to Genesis:
“The two shall become one flesh.”
This is why biblical Christianity cannot reduce sex to:
“Two consenting adults did something pleasurable, so what difference does it make?”
Consent matters enormously because coercion and abuse violate another person's dignity. But biblical sexual ethics asks another question too:
What did God create sexual union to mean?
Sex involves the body in a profoundly personal union.
Paul therefore commands something startlingly direct:
“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.”
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not see how close you can stand to the edge.
Not keep the conversation because you enjoy the attention.
Not keep the app because you promise yourself you will only look.
Not maintain the secret relationship while praying for God to somehow make it holy.
Flee.
The Greek verb pheugete carries exactly that force: flee, escape, get away.
And the word translated “sexual immorality” is porneia—πορνεία—a broad New Testament term for illicit sexual activity.
Paul is not embarrassed about commanding Christians to run.
Sometimes spiritual maturity looks remarkably undramatic.
Close the browser.
Delete the conversation.
Leave the room.
End the affair.
Stop feeding the fantasy.
Tell somebody trustworthy.
Put distance between yourself and what repeatedly pulls you away from Christ.
Run.
Not because sexual temptation proves you are beyond grace.
Run because you belong to Someone.
And then comes the verse so many Christians have heard outside its context:
“ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν”
Ē ouk oidate hoti to sōma hymōn naos tou en hymin hagiou pneumatos estin...
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you...?”
The word translated “temple” is ναός — naos.
Paul's language is astonishing.
He is telling believers that the Holy Spirit dwells within them.
Think about what that means.
You keep calling yourself disgusting.
God calls the redeemed body His dwelling place.
You keep defining yourself by what happened in your past.
Paul points toward Who lives within the believer now.
You keep saying:
“But you don't know what I've done.”
Maybe not.
But Jesus does.
Every hidden night.
Every compromise.
Every relapse.
Every person.
Every screen.
Every fantasy.
Every betrayal.
Every moment you promised God, “Never again,” only to find yourself crying the same prayer weeks later.
Jesus knows.
And still the Gospel says something almost impossible to believe:
There is grace for repentant sinners.
This is where sexual purity teaching can become distorted.
Some people were taught purity as though virginity itself were salvation.
As though someone who had sexual sin in their past became permanently damaged goods.
As though Jesus could forgive murderers, persecutors, thieves, liars, and rebels...
but somehow sexual sinners remained spiritually stained forever.
That is not the Gospel.
Paul had already reminded the Corinthians what some of them once were, including people whose former lives involved sexual sin.
Then comes one of the most beautiful reversals in the chapter:
“But you were washed...”
Washed.
Not tolerated.
Washed.
Not permanently labeled by the worst thing you ever did.
Washed.
Paul continues that they were sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
The church at Corinth was not a museum filled with people who had never been sexually broken.
It was a community of people Jesus was redeeming.
And maybe somebody needs that sentence desperately today.
Your sexual past does not have greater cleansing power than the blood of Jesus.
Read that again.
Your sexual past does not have greater cleansing power than the blood of Jesus.
If you have genuinely turned to Christ in repentance and faith, your identity is not “the adulterer.”
Not “the porn addict.”
Not “the promiscuous one.”
Not “the person who gave themselves away.”
Not “the person who crossed the line.”
Not “the person everybody would reject if they knew.”
And if sexual violence or abuse was committed against you, someone else's sin against your body did not make you morally guilty for what they chose to do to you.
Your identity is not what someone did to you.
Jesus Christ does not stand before broken people holding a permanent label containing their worst moment.
The Gospel announces that sinners can be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled to God, and made new through Christ.
But grace does not mean sexual sin suddenly stops mattering.
Grace is not Jesus saying:
“It doesn't matter what you do with your body.”
Grace says something infinitely greater:
“You belong to Me now.”
Paul continues:
“καὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν”
Kai ouk este heautōn.
“You are not your own.”
That sentence collides violently with modern assumptions about freedom.
“My body, my choice.”
“My desires, my rules.”
“My bedroom, nobody else's business.”
Christianity introduces another category:
Lordship.
The Christian cannot ultimately say, “My body belongs to me.”
But neither does your body belong to the boyfriend pressuring you.
Or the girlfriend threatening to leave.
Or the husband demanding what is coercive or degrading.
Or the person manipulating your loneliness.
Or pornography.
Or your impulses.
Or your past.
Your body belongs to Christ.
And Paul tells us why:
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς”
Ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
“For you were bought with a price.”
There it is.
The Cross enters the bedroom.
You were bought with a price.
What price?
Not silver.
Not gold.
The New Testament's larger Gospel witness points us toward Jesus Christ giving Himself for sinners.
His body wounded.
His blood poured out.
The sinless Son of God crucified.
Buried.
Risen.
Your body matters because His body was given for your redemption.
Suddenly Christian sexual ethics is not merely a collection of prohibitions.
It becomes worship.
Paul finishes:
“δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
Doxasate dē ton Theon en tō sōmati hymōn.
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
That is the destination.
Not merely:
“Stop having sinful sex.”
Glorify God in your body.
Your eyes can glorify God.
Your hands can glorify God.
Your sexuality can glorify God.
Your singleness can glorify God.
Your marriage can glorify God.
Your boundaries can glorify God.
Your repentance can glorify God.
Even your decision tonight to walk away from something nobody else knows about can become worship.
Maybe you already failed.
Then hear this carefully.
The answer is not pretending.
The answer is repentance.
And repentance is not self-hatred.
Biblical repentance is a turning.
You stop defending what God calls sin.
You stop renaming darkness so you can remain comfortable inside it.
You bring it into the light.
You confess.
You turn.
You receive mercy through Christ.
And you begin walking differently.
Perhaps tonight that means telling someone:
“We can't keep doing this.”
Perhaps it means confessing an affair.
Perhaps it means installing accountability around pornography and inviting a mature believer into the struggle instead of fighting alone.
Perhaps it means ending a secret online relationship.
Perhaps it means admitting that what you have called “love” has repeatedly required disobedience to Jesus.
Perhaps it simply means falling to your knees and finally saying:
“Jesus... I have been trying to belong to You while keeping this part of myself for me.”
And maybe there will be tears.
Let them come.
Because conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Conviction says:
Come out of hiding.
Condemnation whispers:
Stay hidden because God could never want you now.
The Gospel answers:
Jesus already knew exactly what kind of sinner He was rescuing.
You do not clean yourself enough to become worthy of the Cross.
You come to the Cross because you cannot clean yourself.
That is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that forgives you and then begins changing you.
Grace that meets you in the wreckage without promising to leave you there.
Grace that teaches your desires they are no longer your master.
Grace that teaches your body:
You belong to Jesus now.
Maybe you have carried sexual shame for ten years.
Twenty years.
Forty years.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you became the respectable Christian.
You serve.
You smile.
You quote Scripture.
You worship with everyone else.
But somewhere inside you is still that frightened younger version of yourself thinking:
“If everybody knew, they wouldn't look at me the same.”
Maybe they wouldn't.
But Jesus already knows.
And He went to the Cross with His eyes open.
That is why our message will always be:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Not because sin is harmless.
But because scandal does not get the final word when Jesus Christ enters the story.
Peter's denial did not get the final word.
Paul's persecution of Christians did not get the final word.
The Corinthians' former sins did not get the final word.
And if you belong to Jesus, your worst sexual failure does not get to write the final sentence either.
Jesus does.
Maybe today is the day you stop hiding.
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle. Wisdom still matters. But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And if Christ has already brought you through sexual brokenness, shame, addiction, adultery, pornography, or a past you thought would destroy you, consider commenting “Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need to know that repentance is possible.
That restoration is possible.
That obedience is possible.
That Jesus still saves.
And please don't keep this article imprisoned on your screen.
Send it privately to the person who has been trying to come back to God.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.

Christians and churches differ in how they understand the application of biblical tithing under the New Covenant, and believers should give prayerfully, willingly, generously, and without manipulation.
Support Gospel Warrior because you believe Christ-centered truth should keep reaching people.
Support it as an offering of generosity if God leads you to do so.
It is mission.

If these resources help you know Christ, understand Scripture, fight sin, strengthen your family, disciple someone else, or return to God after wandering, then helping sustain and expand that work can itself be an act of Christian generosity.
And even if you cannot financially support Gospel Warrior, you can still help.
Your share costs nothing, but it may place the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Invite the believer secretly fighting pornography.
Invite the person carrying sexual shame.
Invite the seeker who thinks Christianity is nothing but rules.
Invite even the unbeliever who has never understood why Christians believe the human body matters.
Because maybe they do not need another Christian shouting at them about sex.
Maybe they need to discover why Jesus thought sinners were worth dying for.
And perhaps that is what you needed too.
You thought this article was going to tell you what you were forbidden to do with your body.
Instead, Scripture brought us somewhere deeper.
Your body is not worthless.
Your body is not merely an appetite machine.
Your body is not merchandise.
Your body is not the property of whoever desires it.
Your body is not permanently defined by whoever violated it.
Your body is not disposable.
For the Christian, your body belongs to Christ.
The Holy Spirit dwells within you.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore...
glorify God in your body.
So when temptation whispers tonight,
“Nobody will know...”
remember:
This isn't ultimately about who is watching.
It is about Whose you are.
When shame whispers,
“After what you did, God could never use you...”
remember the Cross.
When your past whispers,
“This is who you will always be...”
remember the empty tomb.
And when Jesus calls you out of sexual sin, do not hear the voice of a God trying to steal your joy.
Hear the voice of the Savior who paid for you saying:
You were made for more than this. Come home.
Because perhaps the most devastating lie sexual sin ever told you was that after everything you had done, Jesus would no longer want you.
But the hands that were pierced for sinners are still reaching into places shame told you God would never enter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SARAH CALLED ABRAHAM “LORD”—Why Did Peter Bring That Into a Teaching About Marriage?
paragraphs: SARAH CALLED ABRAHAM “LORD”—Why Did Peter Bring That Into a Teaching About Marriage?

One word has been used to make women afraid, make men feel powerful, and turn a beautiful passage about fearless faith into something Peter never intended. But when you read what Sarah actually said—and then keep reading what Peter says to husbands—the passage becomes far more confronting to both men and women than most people realize.
There is a sentence in the New Testament that can make a modern reader stop cold.
“Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord.”
There it is.
1 Peter 3:6.
And depending on what kind of church you grew up in, what kind of marriage you witnessed, or what someone once told you “biblical submission” means, those words may sound beautiful...
or deeply uncomfortable.
Maybe somebody has even used this verse against you.
Maybe you have heard it preached as though Peter were saying, “A godly wife should treat her husband like a king.”
Maybe a husband has read it and quietly thought, “See? The Bible says I’m the boss.”
Maybe a wounded wife has read it and wondered whether following Jesus means losing her voice.
Or maybe you have simply skipped over it because you did not know what to do with it.
But there is something hiding in plain sight.
Something many readers never notice.
Peter did not invent Sarah’s words.
He reached backward roughly two thousand years before his own time and pulled a tiny sentence out of Sarah’s life.
And when you go back and find that sentence...
the scene is nothing like what you might expect.
Sarah was not kneeling before Abraham.
She was not standing before a congregation teaching women to address their husbands as “lord.”
Abraham had not commanded her to use an honorific.
In fact...
Sarah was laughing.
God had promised something so impossible that Sarah laughed inside herself.
She was old.
Abraham was old.
The promise of a son appeared biologically absurd.
And Genesis 18:12 records her inward response:
“After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?”
The Hebrew expression translated “my lord” is:
אֲדֹנִי
ʾadoni.
“My lord.”
It can function as a respectful way of referring to a human superior or one held in honor. It does not make Abraham divine. It certainly does not place Abraham where only God belongs.
And notice something extraordinary.
Sarah apparently was not even saying this to Abraham.
She was speaking within herself.
That matters.
Because respect that exists only when someone is watching is performance.
Sarah’s words reveal something about the posture she carried toward Abraham even inside the privacy of her own thoughts.
Centuries later, Peter remembers her.
His Greek reads:
ὡς Σάρρα ὑπήκουσεν τῷ Ἀβραάμ, κύριον αὐτὸν καλοῦσα
hōs Sarra hypēkousen tō Abraam, kyrion auton kalousa
“as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord...”
But stop.
Please do not build an entire theology of marriage from half a sentence.
Because Peter keeps writing.
And what comes next changes the emotional temperature of the passage.
He tells these women to do good...
and not be controlled by fear.
καὶ μὴ φοβούμεναι μηδεμίαν πτόησιν
and not fearing any terror/intimidation.
Read that again.
Peter speaks about submission...
and then speaks about fearlessness.
That should make us careful.
Biblical submission is not presented here as terrified compliance.
Peter does not tell Christian women to become frightened shadows of themselves.
He does not tell them that holiness means enduring every sinful demand without question.
He does not tell them their husband has become their god.
He points to holy women who “hoped in God.”
That is the center of gravity.
God.
Not Abraham.
Not the husband.
God.
The deepest security of the godly woman Peter describes does not come from having a perfect husband.
It comes from hoping in a perfect God.
And suddenly Sarah becomes painfully relatable.
Because Abraham was not a perfect husband.
Read Genesis carefully.
This marriage had scars.
There were moments of extraordinary faith.
There were also moments of fear.
There was displacement.
There was infertility.
There was waiting.
There was conflict.
There was Hagar.
There was heartbreak.
There were decisions Abraham made that exposed Sarah to danger.
There were years when the promise of God must have seemed almost cruel in its delay.
Sarah was not married to a flawless man.
Abraham was a man of tremendous faith who still had tremendous failures.
And Sarah was not a cardboard Bible character smiling serenely through every chapter.
She laughed at God's seemingly impossible promise.
She knew disappointment.
She knew what it was like to wait until her body appeared to have become evidence against what God had spoken.
Somebody reading this knows that feeling.
You prayed.
You waited.
You believed.
Then another year passed.
And another.
You watched other people receive what you begged God for.
Another marriage restored.
Another baby born.
Another prayer answered.
Another testimony posted online.
And you smiled for them while something inside you whispered:
“Lord... what about me?”
Sarah knew that room.
She knew the strange place where faith and disappointment can occupy the same heart.
And still...
God was writing.
That may be one of the reasons this passage is so powerful.
Peter does not point to Sarah because her life was painless.
He points to a woman whose hope ultimately had to reach beyond circumstances.
A woman living inside a story she could not yet see completed.
And perhaps that is where this passage finds you.
You do not know how your chapter ends yet.
You only know this chapter hurts.
But unfinished is not the same thing as abandoned.
Now something even more important happens.
Peter turns to husbands.
And men, we cannot suddenly close the Bible here.
The next verse begins with the same kind of relational seriousness.
Husbands are commanded to live with their wives “according to knowledge”—with understanding—and to give them honor.
Honor.
Not humiliation.
Not domination.
Not contempt.
Not spiritual intimidation.
Honor.
And then Peter says something breathtaking about husband and wife.
They are together heirs of the grace of life.
Grace has leveled the ground at the foot of the cross.
The Christian husband does not stand closer to salvation because he is male.
His wife is not spiritually second-class.
She is an heir of grace.
She belongs to Christ.
She bears God's image.
She is someone for whom Christ died.
And Peter gives husbands a warning that should make every Christian man examine how he treats his wife:
Your prayers can be hindered.
Think about the weight of that.
A man may sound spiritual in public.
He may know theology.
He may quote Scripture.
He may lead prayer.
He may raise his hands in worship.
He may post Bible verses.
He may be respected at church.
But Peter drags his Christianity through the front door of his house and asks:
How do you treat your wife?
Because heaven is not impressed by public spirituality that becomes cruelty behind closed doors.
You cannot use Scripture to crush the woman Peter commands you to honor and then imagine that quoting more Scripture makes you righteous.
You cannot demand Sarah while refusing to become a man who fears God.
You cannot demand respect while feeding contempt.
You cannot demand submission while refusing sacrificial love, understanding, repentance, gentleness, faithfulness, and honor.
And husbands should notice another detail.
Peter does not command the husband to make his wife submit.
He addresses the wife concerning her conduct...
then addresses the husband concerning his.
That means before using this passage as binoculars to inspect your spouse, use it as a mirror.
Wife...
what is Christ asking of you?
Husband...
what is Christ asking of you?
Because marriage becomes dangerous when Scripture is used primarily as ammunition against the other person.
“God says YOU have to...”
“You're supposed to...”
“The Bible says YOU...”
Meanwhile, nobody is trembling before what God said to them.
Maybe that is the word somebody's marriage needs tonight.
Put down the weaponized Bible verse.
Pick up the mirror.
The Gospel does not merely teach us how to identify someone else's sin.
It brings us face-to-face with our own.
And this is where we have to be especially careful with the word “lord.”
Sarah calling Abraham “lord” does not mean Abraham became her Lord in the ultimate sense.
There is only One before whom every Christian finally bows.
Jesus Christ.
The same New Testament that can use kyrios—“lord”—as a respectful designation for human beings uses it supremely of Jesus Christ.
A Christian marriage can have order.
It can have honor.
It can have submission.
It can have responsibility.
But it can never have two Saviors.
Husbands are not Jesus.
Wives are not Jesus.
Your spouse cannot carry the weight of being your Messiah.
And some marriages are suffocating because two broken human beings are asking each other to provide what only Christ can provide.
Perfect security.
Perfect validation.
Perfect fulfillment.
Perfect understanding.
Perfect love.
Your husband cannot save you.
Your wife cannot save you.
Jesus can.
And that is where this stops being merely an article about marriage.
Because perhaps your greatest problem tonight is not your spouse.
Perhaps your greatest problem is the same problem beneath every human scandal.
Sin.
Pride.
Fear.
Selfishness.
Control.
Resentment.
Lust.
Bitterness.
Unforgiveness.
The desperate desire to be lord of our own lives.
That is the scandal underneath all our scandals.
We want the throne.
And Jesus did not come merely to improve our relationships.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
The Son of God entered our brokenness.
He lived without sin.
He carried our guilt to the cross.
He was crucified.
He died.
And He rose again.
Grace does not pretend our sin is harmless.
Grace takes sin so seriously that Christ bore its judgment.
And grace loves sinners so deeply that Christ willingly came to save.
That changes marriage.
Because the Gospel creates a kind of person the world cannot manufacture.
A husband strong enough to repent.
A wife secure enough to hope in God.
A husband humble enough to say, “I was wrong.”
A wife free enough not to be ruled by fear.
Two sinners learning to forgive because they themselves have been forgiven.
Two wounded people refusing to make wounds their identity.
Two imperfect people kneeling before one perfect Lord.
Jesus.
Maybe you have been reading this whole article thinking about your husband.
Or your wife.
But what if the Holy Spirit has been putting His finger on you?
Not them.
You.
Your pride.
Your fear.
Your secret resentment.
Your controlling behavior.
Your coldness.
Your harsh words.
Your emotional withdrawal.
Your hidden sin.
Your refusal to apologize.
Your obsession with winning arguments.
Your habit of using Scripture to defend yourself instead of allowing Scripture to expose you.
Be honest.
Did this hit somewhere you were not expecting?
Conviction is not your enemy when it leads you to Christ.
Repentance is not humiliation.
It is the doorway home.
You do not have to protect the version of yourself Jesus is trying to transform.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can ask forgiveness.
You can begin again.
Maybe your marriage has become a place where everybody is keeping score.
Who apologized last.
Who hurt whom more.
Who initiated affection.
Who failed first.
Who deserves what.
Then look at the cross.
Jesus did not save you because your score was impressive.
He saved by grace.
That does not erase justice, wisdom, healthy boundaries, or accountability.
