We have blamed other people.
We have wanted God's blessings while resisting God's authority.
We have demanded freedom and then become slaves to the very things we called freedom.
We have run from the Father.
And this is where the Gospel enters the room.
Not as sentimental religion.
Not as God shrugging at sin.
Not as a Father saying, “Nothing matters.”
God takes sin more seriously than we do.
The cross proves it.
But the cross also reveals something breathtaking.
The judgment our sin deserved fell upon Christ.
Jesus was mocked.
Rejected.
Wounded.
Crucified.
The sinless Son stood where sinners belonged.
And the scandal of the Gospel is that rebels can come home.
Not because rebellion suddenly became acceptable.
Because Christ paid for sinners.
The answer to sin was not abandonment.
It was redemption.
The answer to guilt was not denial.
It was a cross.
The answer to our wandering was not a Father who stopped caring.
It was a Savior who came looking for the lost.
This is why grace must never be confused with permissiveness.
Grace does not say sin does not matter.
Grace says sin mattered enough for Jesus Christ to die.
And repentance is not God destroying you.
Repentance is God calling you away from what is already destroying you.
Maybe that is the piece some of us never understood.
We imagined correction meant rejection.
So whenever God exposed something in us, we ran.
Whenever Scripture confronted our sexuality, pride, bitterness, greed, dishonesty, unforgiveness, addiction, secret habits, or hidden compromise, we immediately felt condemned.
We assumed:
“God must hate me.”
But Scripture presents loving correction very differently.
A father who loves does not simply abandon his child to foolishness.
Love intervenes.
Love warns.
Love disciplines.
Love calls us home.
And sometimes God's mercy hurts before it heals because truth touches the places we spent years protecting.
Maybe this article is touching one now.
Something from childhood.
Something about your father.
Something about your mother.
Something about the way you are raising your own children.
Something you regret.
Maybe you disciplined in anger.
Maybe you said things that cannot be unsaid.
Maybe your son is grown now.
Maybe your daughter hardly calls.
Maybe you would give almost anything to return to one night and handle it differently.
You cannot.
And that realization can crush a person.
But this is exactly why Christianity is not merely a religion of better behavior.
It is the Gospel of redemption.
Jesus specializes in stories human beings think are already ruined.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted His people.
The thief beside Christ was running out of minutes, not merely years.
Yet grace entered their stories.
So if you failed as a parent, do not rewrite your failure as righteousness.
Confess it.
If necessary, go to your child—even if that child is now forty years old—and say the words pride hates:
“I was wrong.”
“I used anger when I should have used wisdom.”
“I hurt you.”
“I used Scripture badly.”
“Please forgive me.”
Do not add, “But you were difficult.”
Do not add, “But my parents did worse.”
Do not add, “But the Bible says...”
Repentance does not negotiate its confession.
Bring the sin into the light.
Because your children do not need a parent who pretends never to have failed.
They need to see what a Christian does when a Christian fails.
Imagine the Gospel lesson hidden inside an apology.
Dad sinned.
Dad confessed.
Dad asked forgiveness.
Dad changed.
Maybe your child will learn more about Jesus through your repentance than through a hundred lectures about obedience.
And if you are the wounded child reading this...
you may need another kind of courage.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending evil was good.
It does not require calling abuse discipline.
It does not mean automatically restoring unsafe access or eliminating appropriate boundaries.
Forgiveness means vengeance does not have to own your soul forever.
You can bring the wound to Christ.
You can grieve honestly.
You can tell the truth.
And healing does not require you to rewrite what happened.
Jesus already knows.
He was there when nobody else knew.
Maybe somebody needs to hear that tonight.
You survived something you still struggle to explain.
And somehow you are still here.
Still searching.
Still reading.
Still wondering whether the God whose name somebody misused could actually be good.
Look at Jesus.
Not at the person who misrepresented Him.
Look at Jesus.
The One who welcomed children.
The One who confronted hypocrites.
The One who touched the rejected.
The One who wept.
The One who told sinners the truth.
The One who forgave.
The One who carried a cross.
The One who rose.
That is where Christianity ultimately asks you to look.
Not toward a slogan.
Toward Christ.
So, no.
“Spare the rod, spoil the child” is not a Bible verse.
But do not swing the pendulum so far that you erase what Proverbs actually teaches.
Scripture takes discipline seriously.
It takes parental responsibility seriously.
It takes foolishness seriously.
It takes obedience seriously.
And it also takes the parent's heart seriously.
Christian discipline should therefore never become an excuse for uncontrolled rage, humiliation, injury, revenge, or domination.
The goal is not pain.
The goal is formation.
Not fear for fear's sake.
Wisdom.
Not parental ego.
Godliness.
Not merely a child who obeys while you are watching.
A young person gradually learning to choose what is right when nobody is watching except God.
That requires more than a rod.
It requires presence.
Consistency.
Prayer.
Instruction.
Example.
Boundaries.
Consequences.
Patience.
Self-control.
Repentance.
Grace.
And above everything else...
Christ.
Because someday your children will no longer be children.
You will not control their schedules.
You will not choose their friends.
You will not monitor every screen.
You will not stand beside every temptation.
And eventually the question will no longer be:
“Will they obey me?”
It will become:
“Have I helped them understand why Jesus is worthy of their obedience?”
That is the battle for the heart.
And perhaps you are realizing that this article was never really about a rod.
It was about love.
What does love do when somebody is walking toward destruction?
What does love do with rebellion?
What does love do with sin?
What does love do when correction hurts?
And then we look toward Calvary.
There hangs our answer.
Justice and mercy meet.
Sin is not excused.
The sinner is offered reconciliation.
The holy God does not become less holy.
The guilty are invited to become sons and daughters.
That is scandalous grace.
And maybe that is why your story does not have to end where your parents' story ended.
Generational anger can stop.
Abuse can stop.
Silence can stop.
Emotional abandonment can stop.
Religious hypocrisy can stop.
You can become the parent who apologizes.
The father who prays.
The mother who listens.
The home where discipline exists without terror.
The home where truth exists alongside tenderness.
The home where children understand that grace does not eliminate boundaries and boundaries do not eliminate love.
And perhaps one day your son or daughter will look back and say:
“My parents were not perfect.
But I watched Jesus change them.”
That testimony may be worth more than appearing perfect ever could.
If this exposed something hidden in you, do not rush past it.
And if you failed...
if there are memories you wish you could erase...
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing something into the light is the first crack in a wall we have hidden behind for years.
And someone reading your words may realize they are not alone.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
That child is a soul to disciple.
Your share may reach a father five seconds before he loses his temper.
It may reach a mother drowning in guilt.
It may reach an adult child who has spent decades believing God resembles the person who hurt them.
And perhaps even send this privately to someone who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know that Jesus Christ can redeem what happened behind closed doors.
It does not.
Not because financial support can replace repentance, obedience, generosity to your local church, or care for people in need.
It cannot.
Paul wrote:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Each person according to what he has determined in his heart—not under compulsion.
Christian generosity belongs to grace, not manipulation.
If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel work, do it freely, prayerfully, and with Christ—not pressure—at the center of your decision.
If financial support is not possible, you can still help tremendously.
A share costs nothing, but it can carry truth into a home we could never enter ourselves.
Your testimony may become somebody else's courage.
Save what strengthens you.
Because this was never merely about correcting children.
It is about what happens when the Father refuses to surrender His children to their foolishness.
It is about truth strong enough to confront us...
and grace strong enough to carry us home.
And perhaps the sentence you needed most was never “Spare the rod, spoil the child.”
Perhaps it was this:
Your past may explain the scars you carry, but at the feet of Jesus, it does not get the final sentence over the person you become.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS’ FAMILY TREE CONTAINS SCANDAL, FAILURE, OUTSIDERS—AND GRACE
paragraphs: JESUS’ FAMILY TREE CONTAINS SCANDAL, FAILURE, OUTSIDERS—AND GRACE

Before Matthew tells us about the manger, the wise men, the miracles, the cross, or the empty tomb, he opens the Gospel with a list of names. But look closer. It is not a polished family résumé. It contains broken people, painful histories, outsiders, moral failure, shattered reputations, and consequences that lasted for generations. And somehow, through that very human story, God brought the Savior of the world.
There are things families do not put in photo albums.
Names nobody brings up at Christmas dinner.
Stories that become whispers.

Divorces. Betrayals. Addiction. Prison sentences. Affairs. Abandonment. Children who walked away from God. Fathers who failed. Mothers who survived things nobody knows about. Decisions that cannot be undone.
Maybe your family has a chapter like that.
Maybe you are the chapter everybody wishes could be rewritten.
And then you open the New Testament expecting God to introduce Jesus with thunder from heaven...
Instead, Matthew gives you a family tree.
At first glance, Matthew 1 can feel like the chapter people hurry through.
Abraham begat Isaac.
Isaac begat Jacob.
Jacob begat Judah.
Name after name after name.
But don't skip it.
Because buried inside that genealogy is one of the most beautiful announcements of grace in the entire Bible.
Matthew begins:
“Βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ...”
Biblos geneseōs Iēsou Christou...
“The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ...” — Matthew 1:1.
That Greek word γενέσεως — geneseōs speaks of origin, genealogy, lineage.
Matthew is telling us where the story is going.
Jesus did not arrive disconnected from human history.
The eternal Son entered it.
He entered a real human family line.
A line containing promises and kings...
but also deception.
Sexual scandal.
Violence.
Foreigners.
National catastrophe.
Moral failure.
Broken homes.
And breathtaking mercy.
The genealogy doesn't begin by telling us that humanity finally became good enough for Jesus.
It shows us that humanity desperately needed Him.
Look at Tamar.
Matthew deliberately records her name:
“Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar...” — Matthew 1:3.
If you know Genesis 38, you know this isn't a comfortable story.

Judah had failed Tamar grievously. After the deaths of his sons, he did not fulfill the responsibility he had promised concerning her future. Tamar eventually disguised herself, Judah slept with her without realizing who she was, and she conceived Perez and Zerah.
When the truth came out, Judah himself admitted:
“She is more righteous than I.”
This is in the Messiah's genealogy.
Not hidden.
Not airbrushed.
Recorded.
Then Matthew writes another name.
Rahab.
“Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab...” — Matthew 1:5.
Rahab was from Jericho.
She was a Canaanite outsider, and Joshua 2 identifies her as a prostitute.
If human beings were constructing the Messiah's family history as a public-relations campaign, this probably would not be the name they highlighted.
But Scripture does.
And Rahab's story did not end with the label attached to her past.
She heard what Israel's God had done.
She believed.
She confessed that the LORD was God “in heaven above and on earth beneath.”
She acted upon that faith by protecting the Israelite spies.
Hebrews 11 later remembers her among examples of faith.
James 2 remembers the action produced by that faith.
Think about that.
A woman whose old life could have been used forever to shame her becomes part of the genealogy leading to Christ.
Her past was real.
Grace did not require pretending it wasn't.
But her past did not get the final word.
Maybe somebody reading this needs that sentence more than they realize.
Your past is real. But in Christ, your past does not have to get the final word.
Then comes Ruth.
“Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth...” — Matthew 1:5.
Ruth was a Moabite.
An outsider.
A widow.
A woman who knew grief.
She had buried her husband and walked into an uncertain future with Naomi.
She could not see generations ahead.
She did not know that one day people across the world would read her name.
She simply trusted.
She remained faithful.
She told Naomi:
“Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.” — Ruth 1:16.
Then God quietly began writing a story Ruth could not yet see.
Ruth married Boaz.
Boaz fathered Obed.
Obed fathered Jesse.
Jesse fathered David.
The grieving foreign widow became the great-grandmother of Israel's most famous king.
And her name eventually appears in the earthly genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Never assume the chapter you're crying through is the final chapter.
You may be standing in a field picking up leftovers, wondering whether God has forgotten you...
while heaven already knows there is more to the story.
Then Matthew reaches David.
Surely now the genealogy becomes respectable.
David.
King.
Warrior.
Psalmist.
A man associated with extraordinary faith.
And then Matthew refuses to let us romanticize him.
Instead of simply saying David fathered Solomon by Bathsheba, Matthew writes that Solomon came through “the wife of Uriah.”
Those words force us to remember 2 Samuel 11.
Uriah.
David saw Bathsheba.
David took her.
She became pregnant.
David tried to conceal what he had done.
When manipulation failed, David arranged for Uriah to be placed where the fighting was fiercest and then abandoned.
Uriah died.
This was not merely a romantic mistake.
It was devastating sin involving adultery, abuse of royal power, deception, and bloodshed.
Scripture does not protect David's image by rewriting what happened.
The prophet Nathan confronted him.
David eventually confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13.
Psalm 51 gives us the language of his repentance:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
And yet consequences followed.
Forgiveness did not turn evil into good.
Grace did not make the damage imaginary.
This matters.
Because biblical grace is not God pretending sin doesn't matter.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin matters so much that our reconciliation with God required something we could never provide for ourselves.
Jesus Christ.
The spotless Lamb.
The righteous One for the unrighteous.
And suddenly Matthew's genealogy begins looking less like a boring list and more like a mirror.
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
David.
“The wife of Uriah.”
Kings who obeyed.
Kings who rebelled.
Men whose lives contained moments of faith.
Men whose lives contained catastrophic failure.
Then exile.
Matthew specifically marks the deportation to Babylon.
A national wound enters the genealogy.
Failure had consequences.
Jerusalem fell.
People were carried away.
The kingdom's glory appeared shattered.
Generations lived under the shadow of what had been lost.
And still...
God's promise had not died.
That may be the word someone needs tonight.
You thought the exile meant God had abandoned the story.
You thought the divorce ended everything.
You thought the relapse erased everything.
You thought the betrayal made restoration impossible.
You thought because your child walked away from God that prayer had become pointless.
You thought because you wasted ten years, twenty years, forty years, there could be nothing left for God to redeem.
You thought the abortion defined you.
You thought the affair defined you.
You thought the prison record defined you.
You thought the addiction defined you.
You thought what happened to you defined you.
You thought what you did defined you.
But Matthew keeps writing names.
Generation...
after generation...
after generation.
Until finally:
Jesus.
Not because every person before Him was righteous.
Not because every family story was clean.
Not because Israel had never failed.
Jesus came because sinners needed saving.
Matthew 1:21 tells us exactly why His name would be Jesus:
“He will save his people from their sins.”
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people finally found their way to God.
It is the announcement that God came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And this is where the genealogy stops being somebody else's family history.
It starts reading yours.
Because maybe you have spent years trying to edit yourself before approaching Jesus.
Learned Christian vocabulary.
Posted Bible verses.
Went to church.
Smiled when people asked how you were doing.
Said, “I'm blessed.”
But somewhere underneath the church clothes and worship songs, there is still a room in your heart you keep locked.
Something happened there.
Something you did.
Something somebody did to you.
Something you fear would change the way people see you if they knew.
And shame keeps whispering:
If they knew everything, they wouldn't love you.
Maybe people wouldn't.
People can be cruel.
People can remember the version of you that God has already begun transforming.
But Jesus already knows.
Every page.
Every night.
Every secret.
Every browser history.
Every lie.
Every compromise.
Every tear nobody saw.
Every prayer you were too ashamed to finish.
Every time you promised God, “Never again,” and then found yourself there again.
He knows.
And the astonishing truth of the Gospel is not merely that Jesus knows your worst chapter.
It is that He came for sinners.
This does not mean everyone is automatically reconciled to God regardless of response.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
Grace is free, but grace is not permission to remain comfortably enslaved to the sin Christ came to save us from.
Jesus did not come merely to make guilty people feel better while leaving them unchanged.
He came to save.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Reconcile.
Redeem.
Transform.
The word “Christ” in Matthew 1 comes from the Greek Χριστός — Christos, “Anointed One,” corresponding to the Hebrew concept of the Messiah, מָשִׁיחַ — Mashiach.
Jesus is not simply another inspiring character added to a collection of broken family stories.
He is the promised Messiah toward whom the story moves.
Son of Abraham.
Son of David.
Christ.
King.
Savior.
And notice something breathtaking about Matthew's genealogy.
The story contains sinners...
but Jesus is not presented as another sinner among them.
The failures in His genealogy explain the world He entered.
They do not stain the One who came to rescue it.
Christ entered humanity's broken story without becoming morally broken Himself.
He bore sin without committing sin.
He entered our shame without sharing our guilt.
And eventually...
He carried a cross.
The genealogy leads us toward the Gospel.
Because the deepest scandal in Christianity is not that Jesus had scandalous people in His family tree.
It is that the sinless Son of God willingly died for scandalous people like us.
At Calvary, Jesus was publicly humiliated.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Wounded.
Crucified.
And He wasn't dying because He had finally lost control of His story.
He was giving Himself.
The One without sin bore our sins.
The innocent stood where the guilty deserved to stand.
And three days later, death discovered that it could not hold Him.
Jesus rose.
That means grace is more than God helping you manage your reputation.
Grace gives dead people life.
Grace does not merely put better wallpaper over a collapsing house.
In Christ, there is new creation.
So maybe your family tree contains things you wish weren't there.
Maybe your father failed you.
Maybe your mother abandoned you.
Maybe addiction has moved through your family like an inheritance nobody asked for.
Maybe anger passes from generation to generation.
Maybe adultery did.
Maybe abuse did.
Maybe nobody taught you how to pray.
Maybe Christianity in your childhood was rules without tenderness, religion without relationship, performance without the Gospel.
Or maybe your childhood was beautiful and you became the one who wandered.
Either way, hear this carefully:
Your bloodline does not outrank the blood of Jesus.
Your history is not stronger than His grace.
Your family's failures do not make redemption impossible.
And your own failures do not place you beyond the reach of Christ when you come to Him in repentance and faith.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
It promises something greater.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
A new identity in Christ.
A new Lord.
A new direction.
A new family.
A new future.
Maybe this article has been uncomfortable because one name kept appearing in your mind while you read.
Your own.
Don't run from that.
Bring it into the light.
There is no healing in pretending.
There is no freedom in endlessly defending what God is calling you to confess.
You don't have to tell the whole internet your private sins.
But you can stop hiding from Jesus.
Right where you are, you can pray:

“Jesus Christ, I have sinned. I cannot rewrite my own heart. I cannot save myself. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Cleanse me. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I surrender what I have been hiding. Teach me to follow You. Make my life Yours.”
Not magic words.
Not a transaction.
A cry toward the Savior.
Someone scrolling beneath you may need to discover that they aren't fighting alone.
And please...
don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Because somebody you know may be quietly drowning in shame while looking completely normal.
Send it privately to the friend who has stopped believing God could want them back.
Share it with the believer who fell.
The prodigal who wandered.
The Christian who is ashamed.
The skeptic who thinks Christianity is only for polished people.
The family member who believes their past has disqualified them forever.
There may come a night when shame returns and tries to read your old story back to you.
On that night, come back and remember:
Tamar is there.
Rahab is there.
Ruth is there.
David's failure is not concealed.
The exile is there.
Human brokenness is there.
And then...
Jesus is there.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.

Not to build another religious audience around personalities, but to keep placing biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ in front of people who desperately need it.
If this ministry is helping you grow closer to Christ, you can help us continue and expand that work.

Scripture teaches generous support for Gospel ministry, but Christian giving is never supposed to be spiritual coercion. Paul wrote that giving should come from what a person has decided in the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
He won't.
It can't.

And don't substitute supporting a Facebook ministry for faithfully following Jesus, caring for your family, serving your local church, helping people in need, and practicing the generosity Scripture teaches.
And even if you cannot financially support Gospel Warrior, you can still help enormously.
Pray for the ministry.
Save the messages you need to revisit.
Sometimes one share reaches a person we never could have reached ourselves.
One tag can find somebody at 2:00 in the morning.
One comment can tell another wounded believer, “You're not the only one fighting.”
One saved article can become a reminder when temptation returns.
One Gospel-centered conversation can point a wandering heart back toward Christ.
And one person meeting Jesus matters more than numbers on a screen ever will.
So look at the genealogy one more time.
The names are still there.
The scandal wasn't erased.
The failures weren't rewritten into imaginary victories.
The outsiders weren't removed to make the family tree look respectable.
God did something far more glorious.
He carried His promise through real human history until the genealogy arrived at Jesus Christ.
And that means you don't need a fake past to have a redeemed future.
You need a Savior.
Jesus does not need you to pretend the old chapter never happened.
He calls you to bring your sin into the light, repent, trust Him, receive His mercy, and follow Him into a life being transformed by grace.
Maybe your family handed you wounds.
Maybe you added failures of your own.
Maybe people remember your scandal.
Maybe you remember it every morning.
But if your life belongs to Jesus Christ, shame does not get to write the ending.
The page you are most ashamed of may become the very place where someone someday sees how powerful the grace of Jesus really is.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS CELEBRATE HALLOWEEN?
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS CELEBRATE HALLOWEEN?
The question is not whether you can wear the costume, carve the pumpkin, or take the candy. The question is whether Jesus can be Lord of what you are about to do.
The porch light is on.
There is a plastic skeleton hanging from somebody’s tree.
Children are running down the sidewalk dressed like superheroes, princesses, monsters, ghosts, witches, and characters they saw in movies.
Someone is laughing.
Someone is handing out candy.
Someone at church has already posted that Halloween is demonic.
Someone else has already responded that Christians need to stop being legalistic.
And somewhere between the shouting, the costumes, the church harvest festivals, the haunted houses, the candy bowls, the arguments about paganism, and the social-media debates...
a sincere Christian is sitting quietly with a question that deserves more than a meme.
“Jesus... what do You want me to do?”
That question changes everything.
Because perhaps the most dangerous thing about the Halloween debate is that we can become so obsessed with proving which Christians are wrong that we forget to ask whether Christ is being glorified.
So before you defend Halloween...
before you condemn everyone who participates...
before you call another believer compromised...
before you call another believer legalistic...
put down the argument for a moment.
Put Jesus in the center.
And ask the question that reaches much deeper than October 31:
Can I bring Christ into what I am doing without asking Him to wait outside?
Because Christianity was never supposed to be a game of discovering how close we can stand to darkness without technically sinning.
It is a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
And that means we have to begin where Scripture begins.
Not with superstition.
Not with internet folklore.
Not with fear.
Not with nostalgia.
Not with “My family has always done it.”
Not even with “My church says...”
With the Word of God.
Here is something Christians on both sides of this argument need the humility to admit:
The Bible never mentions Halloween by name.
There is no verse that says, “Thou shalt not celebrate Halloween.”
There is also no verse declaring October 31 spiritually harmless and giving Christians permission to participate in absolutely anything associated with it.
That means we must not manufacture a commandment God did not give.
But it also means we cannot use the absence of the word “Halloween” as permission to ignore commandments God most certainly did give.
And some of those commandments are unmistakable.
God told Israel:
“Let there not be found among you anyone... who practices divination... engages in witchcraft... casts spells, or who is a medium or spiritist or who consults the dead.”
That is the substance of Deuteronomy 18:10–12.
This is not ambiguous.
The Hebrew vocabulary in this passage describes actual occult practices—divination, sorcery, spell-casting, mediums, and seeking information from the dead.
God's objection was not to children eating chocolate.
It was not to the color orange.
It was not to pumpkins.
It was not to October.
It was to human beings seeking supernatural power, revelation, guidance, or communion apart from Him.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because biblical discernment refuses two opposite errors.
It refuses to call darkness light.
But it also refuses to invent darkness where Scripture has not called something darkness.
A plastic spider is not a demon.
A piece of candy is not witchcraft.
A child wearing a firefighter costume has not performed necromancy.
At the same time, actual occultism does not become innocent simply because somebody calls it entertainment.
God does not become comfortable with divination because we put decorations around it.
He does not approve of attempting to contact the dead because it happens at a party.
He does not suddenly bless spells, séances, occult rituals, spiritism, or attempts to obtain supernatural power outside of Him because someone says, “Relax. We're just having fun.”
Scripture gives Christians a real boundary.
Paul writes:
Ephesians 5:11.
The Greek is striking:
καὶ μὴ συγκοινωνεῖτε τοῖς ἔργοις τοῖς ἀκάρποις τοῦ σκότους
Kai mē synkoinōneite tois ergois tois akarpois tou skotous.
The important word is συγκοινωνεῖτε — synkoinōneite.
It carries the idea of sharing in, participating with, or becoming a partner in something.
Paul is not teaching Christians to panic whenever darkness exists around them.
If that were the command, Christians could never enter a broken world.
Jesus Himself ate with sinners.
He walked among people religious society had rejected.
He touched the unclean.
He stepped directly into human misery.
But He never participated in their darkness in order to reach them.
He brought light into it.
That difference may be the heart of the entire Halloween question.
There is a difference between being present where darkness exists and participating in darkness.
Read that again.
Because this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable for everyone.
The Christian who says, “Everything associated with Halloween is automatically demonic,” must be careful not to create a universal biblical prohibition where Scripture itself has not stated one.
But the Christian who says, “It's just fun; none of it matters,” has another problem.
For a follower of Jesus, nothing belongs in a category called “Jesus doesn't matter here.”
Not our entertainment.
Not our sexuality.
Not our money.
Not our humor.
Not our relationships.
Not our screens.
Not our traditions.
Not our holidays.
Paul gives us a breathtakingly simple test:
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.”
1 Corinthians 10:31.
And in Greek:
πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ ποιεῖτε
Panta eis doxan Theou poieite.
Do everything toward the glory of God.
Suddenly the question is no longer merely:
“Is Halloween allowed?”
Now it becomes:
“Can what I am doing honestly be directed toward the glory of God?”
That is harder.
Because rules can sometimes be manipulated.
Love for Christ cannot.
Imagine Jesus physically standing beside you on October 31.
Not angry.
Not waiting to catch you.
Just present.
The Jesus who was scourged for you.
The Jesus whose hands were pierced for you.
The Jesus who carried your shame to Calvary.
The Jesus who walked out of the grave.
The Jesus you call Lord.
Would His presence make you uncomfortable with what you planned to do?
Would you change the costume?
Turn off the movie?
Leave the party?
Avoid the occult-themed attraction?
Stop joking about something you suddenly realized should not be entertainment?
Or would you gladly say:
“Lord, stay with me. I want You here.”
That is not legalism.
That is relationship.
And there is another side Christians cannot ignore.
Romans 14 deals with believers disagreeing about matters involving food and the observance of days.
Paul writes:
Then comes an important phrase:
ὁ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν κυρίῳ φρονεῖ
Ho phronōn tēn hēmeran Kyriō phronei.
The one regarding the day regards it to the Lord.
Paul's concern is not careless relativism.
He does not say sin becomes holy when your conscience approves it.
Elsewhere Scripture clearly identifies behavior Christians cannot baptize with personal preference.
You cannot say, “My conscience is fine with adultery.”
You cannot say, “My conscience is comfortable with idolatry.”
You cannot say, “Sorcery doesn't bother me personally.”
God's explicit commands remain God's commands.
But where Scripture leaves room for conscience, Christians should be extremely careful about climbing onto God's throne and issuing universal commandments in His name.
Paul goes even further:
“Why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother?”
Romans 14:10.
That should make both camps uncomfortable.
Maybe that is good.
Because perhaps some Christians need to repent of participating in darkness.
And perhaps others need to repent of the pride with which they condemn brothers and sisters whose conduct Scripture itself does not explicitly condemn.
Conviction without love becomes cruelty.
Freedom without holiness becomes compromise.
Truth without humility becomes a weapon.
And grace without truth becomes permission.
Jesus offers something better than all four.
Truth and grace.
So should Christians celebrate Halloween?
The most biblically responsible answer requires more precision than a slogan.

A Christian should not participate in actual occult practices, divination, séances, spell-casting, attempts to contact spirits or the dead, or anything else Scripture explicitly identifies as forbidden spiritual practice.
That boundary is not negotiable simply because October 31 makes such imagery culturally popular.

Beyond those explicit boundaries, believers must examine what they are actually doing, why they are doing it, what it celebrates, what effect it has on their conscience, what it communicates to others, and whether they can genuinely offer it to Christ.
One Christian family may decide:
“We want nothing to do with Halloween. We will spend the evening differently.”
They should be free to honor Christ that way.

Another Christian family may hand candy to neighborhood children, meet parents on their street, show hospitality, give out Scripture cards, host a church gathering, or use an evening when neighbors unexpectedly arrive at their door as an opportunity to demonstrate unusual kindness.
They should not automatically be accused of worshiping demons because they handed a child a chocolate bar.
Another believer may have come out of actual occultism.
For that person, symbols other people consider harmless may carry memories, temptations, associations, and spiritual wounds others do not understand.
Love says:
I will not mock your conscience.
Another believer may have never practiced occultism at all and may see costumes and candy simply as neighborhood fun.
Love says:
I will not invent secret motives in your heart.
Romans 14 calls us toward conviction without contempt.
And that may be exactly what the modern Church desperately needs.
Because while Christians fight about pumpkins...
people are dying without Christ.
While we attack each other over costumes...
marriages are collapsing.
Teenagers are quietly wondering whether life is worth living.
Pornography is discipling millions behind locked doors.
Parents are exhausted.
Believers are secretly addicted.
Churchgoers are smiling on Sunday and crying alone at night.
People who know Christian vocabulary still do not know the Christ who makes dead people alive.
Maybe October 31 is not merely a battlefield to escape.
Maybe for some believers it can become a mission field.
Not by pretending darkness is light.
But by doing what Christians have always been called to do:
carry light into darkness.
Jesus said:
“I am the light of the world.”
And here is where this stops being an article about Halloween.
Because there is a darkness far more dangerous than any haunted house.
It is the darkness inside us.
We are extraordinarily good at spotting darkness when somebody decorates their front yard with it.
We are much less comfortable confronting the darkness we hide behind our own front door.
The bitterness nobody knows about.
The pornography deleted from the browser history.
The affair living inside text messages.
The envy behind the smile.
The resentment toward someone at church.
The addiction.
The secret account.
The unforgiveness.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The judgment disguised as holiness.
The compromise disguised as freedom.
Maybe you came here asking whether Christians should celebrate Halloween.
And somehow Jesus turned the question around.
“What are you allowing in your heart?”
Because you can refuse Halloween completely...
and still entertain darkness every night on your phone.
You can throw every horror movie away...
and still hate your brother.
You can refuse to put a pumpkin outside your house...
while hiding pornography inside it.
You can warn everybody about witches...
while worshiping money.
You can expose the darkness in culture...
while protecting the darkness in yourself.
And suddenly the costume is gone.
The argument is gone.
The Facebook debate is gone.
It is just you.
And Jesus.
And the thing you hoped nobody would mention.
This is where religion often tells you to clean yourself up.
Jesus did something far more astonishing.
He came looking for sinners.
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.”
Luke 19:10.
He did not wait for scandalous people to become respectable enough to approach Him.
He approached them.
The sexually broken.
The greedy.
The dishonest.
The ashamed.
The religious hypocrite.
The social outcast.
The person everybody else had already reduced to their worst chapter.
Jesus walked into human scandal carrying grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Grace that forgives the sinner and then calls the sinner into a new life.
That is the Gospel.
Not:
“Become good enough and maybe God will accept you.”
But:
You sinned.
You could not rescue yourself.
Christ came.
Christ lived without sin.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And the risen Jesus still saves people who come to Him in repentance and faith.
Your greatest problem was never October 31.
Your greatest problem was sin.
And your greatest hope is not avoiding a holiday.
Your greatest hope is Jesus Christ.
Maybe the Holy Spirit is putting His finger on something right now that has nothing to do with Halloween.
Something hidden.
Something you have defended for years.
Something you keep renaming because calling it what Scripture calls it would mean you have to surrender it.
Do not run.
Conviction is not Christ pushing you away.
The Gospel is Christ calling sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
You do not have to pretend anymore.
Not because typing those words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Someone reading beneath you may need to discover that they are not the only believer fighting a battle nobody sees.
Let the Body of Christ behave like a body.
Let believers pray for believers.
Let testimonies meet wounds.
Let grace interrupt shame.
And before you leave this article, ask yourself one final question about Halloween—and about everything else:
Can I thank Jesus for this, invite Jesus into this, and do this for the glory of Jesus?
If the answer is no, do not spend your life hunting for technical loopholes.
You already have your answer.
If Scripture explicitly forbids it, walk away.
If your conscience condemns your participation, do not violate your conscience.
If something is mastering you, surrender it.
If your freedom is damaging someone you should love, consider whether love is asking you to lay that freedom down.
And where faithful Christians reach different conclusions on matters Scripture does not explicitly prohibit, refuse the temptation to become someone else's Holy Spirit.
Be holy.
Be humble.
Be discerning.
Be gracious.
And above everything...
belong completely to Jesus.
You may need these questions again long after the decorations disappear.
Send it privately to the friend who is searching for Christ.
Scripture teaches willing, purposeful generosity—not spiritual transactions.
Supporting Gospel work can be one way a believer chooses to glorify God with his or her resources, but the glory belongs to God, not to the payment.
Give Christ your heart again.
Not the polished version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version wearing the Christian costume.
The real one.
The wounded one.
The tempted one.
The ashamed one.
The confused one.
The one still carrying things nobody else knows.
Bring that person to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about being the person who successfully avoided every cultural controversy.
It is about belonging to the One who entered our darkness and brought us into His light.
Halloween will come and go.
The costumes will be packed away.
The candy will disappear.
The arguments will move to something else.
But Jesus will still be standing at the center of the question that matters most:
Who has your heart?
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after October ends:
Do not become so busy identifying the darkness around you that you refuse to let Jesus illuminate the darkness within you.
And whatever you decide about October 31...
do not merely ask whether a Christian can do it.
Ask whether you can place it at the feet of the crucified and risen Christ and sincerely say, “Jesus, this is for Your glory.”
Because the goal was never merely to survive the darkness.
It was to belong to the Light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Sunday Really the Christian Sabbath?
paragraphs: Is Sunday Really the Christian Sabbath?
What if the argument over Saturday and Sunday has made Christians stare so hard at the calendar that we have almost missed the Lord standing in the middle of it?
There is a question many Christians have quietly carried for years.
Some are almost afraid to ask it.

Maybe you grew up getting dressed for church every Sunday morning. Maybe Sunday meant polished shoes, Bible under your arm, worship music in the car, lunch after service, and the familiar words, “Today is the Sabbath.”
You never questioned it.
Why would you?
Then one day someone opened Exodus 20 and pointed to a sentence you had read a hundred times but suddenly saw differently.
“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.”
Then came the uncomfortable part.
The commandment does not say the first day.
It says the seventh.
And suddenly a question entered your mind that would not leave:
Is Sunday really the Christian Sabbath?
Before anyone gets angry, defensive, or frightened, understand what we are going to do.
We are not going to defend a denomination.
We are not going to attack Saturday worshipers.
We are not going to attack Sunday worshipers.
We are not going to force Scripture to protect our traditions.
We are going to open the Bible and allow the text to speak.
Because Jesus does not need us to manipulate Scripture in order to defend Him.
Truth can survive examination.
And sometimes the most beautiful thing God can do is disturb a comfortable assumption so He can lead us deeper into Christ.
Go back to Sinai.
The Hebrew of Exodus 20:8 begins:
זָכוֹר אֶת־יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת
Zāḵôr ’et-yôm haššabbāṯ.
“Remember the Sabbath day.”

Then the command becomes unmistakably specific: six days are for labor, “but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God.” The passage grounds this pattern in creation itself—God made heaven and earth in six days and rested on the seventh, blessing and setting apart the Sabbath day.
That matters.
The biblical Sabbath was not originally Sunday.
The seventh day was the Sabbath.
We should be honest enough to say that plainly.
Trying to make the Old Testament say “Sunday” where it says “the seventh day” does not strengthen Christianity. It weakens our credibility.
But that is not the end of the story.
Because then Jesus comes.
And whenever Jesus enters a religious controversy, He has an unsettling habit of exposing what human beings have done with something God intended for good.
By the first century, Sabbath observance had become the setting for repeated conflict between Jesus and religious leaders.
They watched Him.
They questioned Him.
They accused His disciples.
They scrutinized what He did.
And then Jesus said something breathtaking:
“The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.”
Then He declared Himself Lord even of the Sabbath.
Do not rush past that.
Jesus did not speak as someone trapped underneath the Sabbath.
He spoke as its Lord.
The controversy therefore cannot finally be reduced to, “Which twenty-four-hour period proves I am more righteous than somebody else?”
The Lord of the Sabbath was standing in front of them.
And some people were so consumed with defending their interpretation of the day that they failed to recognize the Lord of the day.
That possibility should terrify every religious person.
You can defend a doctrine and miss Jesus.
You can win an argument and lose tenderness.
You can know Hebrew terminology and still have hatred in your heart.
You can attend church every Saturday and remain unrepentant.
You can attend church every Sunday and remain unrepentant.
You can know exactly when the Sabbath begins and still refuse to forgive your brother.
You can know exactly when Sunday worship developed and still be secretly addicted, bitter, proud, dishonest, lustful, greedy, or spiritually dead.
A calendar cannot crucify your flesh.
Only Christ can save you.
And then something happens that changes history.
Jesus is crucified.
The stone is rolled against the tomb.
His disciples grieve.
Hope appears buried.
Then comes the first day of the week.
The tomb is empty.
Christ is risen.
Death has been invaded.
The grave has lost its final word.
The scandal of the cross becomes the announcement of grace.
The Man rejected by the world is revealed as the risen Lord.
And from that resurrection reality, the first day of the week takes on enormous significance in Christian life.
This is where we must become careful readers rather than careless slogan-makers.
Acts 20:7 describes Christians gathering “on the first day of the week” to break bread, with Paul speaking to them before his departure.
The Greek reads:
Ἐν δὲ τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων
En de tē mia tōn sabbatōn.
In its context, it is naturally rendered, “On the first day of the week.”
The believers gathered.
They broke bread.
Paul taught them.
The gathering continued until midnight.
First Corinthians gives us another first-day reference. Paul tells believers concerning the collection for the saints:
κατὰ μίαν σαββάτου
kata mian sabbatou—
“on the first day of every week,” each believer was to set something aside according to his prosperity.
Those texts matter.
But notice what they do not say.
They do not contain a sentence declaring:
“The Sabbath has now been moved from the seventh day to the first day.”
That sentence is not in Acts 20.
It is not in 1 Corinthians 16.
So we should not pretend it is.

The New Testament gives genuine evidence of first-day Christian activity and gathering, but describing Christians gathering on the first day and explicitly renaming the first day “the Sabbath” are not identical claims.
That distinction is where many arguments become unnecessarily hostile.
One side sometimes acts as though Sunday has no biblical Christian significance whatsoever.
That goes too far.
The other side sometimes speaks as though there is a verse plainly saying, “God changed the Sabbath to Sunday.”
There is not.
And Christians should never be afraid of saying exactly as much—and exactly as little—as Scripture says.
Then there is Revelation 1:10.
John writes:
ἐν τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ
en tē kyriakē hēmera—
“on the Lord’s day.”
The adjective kyriakē means belonging to the Lord; the expression literally identifies a day as the Lord’s.

Many Christians throughout history have understood this as Sunday, associated with the resurrection. That interpretation has substantial historical support. But Revelation 1:10 itself does not stop to define the expression by saying, “that is, Sunday,” and responsible interpretation should acknowledge that distinction rather than smuggling the conclusion into the wording of the verse.
What history can show us, however, is striking.

By the middle of the second century, Justin Martyr explicitly described Christians assembling on the day called Sunday. He described Scripture being read, instruction being given, prayer, Communion, and voluntary giving for those in need. He connected Sunday both with creation and with the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
That is important historical evidence.
It means Sunday Christian worship is not some modern invention dreamed up a few generations ago.
But history is not Scripture.
History can tell us what early Christians did.
Only Scripture carries the authority of Scripture.
And that distinction protects us from exaggeration in either direction.
So is Sunday really the Christian Sabbath?
The most careful answer is more nuanced than the slogans.

Biblically, the seventh day is the day explicitly identified as the Sabbath in the fourth commandment. The New Testament gives clear evidence of first-day Christian gathering and practice connected with the resurrection-era church, and very early post-apostolic evidence shows Sunday becoming an established Christian assembly day. But the New Testament never gives us a verse simply declaring, “Sunday has replaced Saturday as the Sabbath.”
And then Paul says something that should lower the temperature of this entire conversation.
“One person considers one day more sacred than another; another considers every day alike. Each of them should be fully convinced in their own mind.”

And in Colossians he tells believers not to allow others to judge them regarding food, drink, festivals, new moons, or a Sabbath day, immediately adding that these are a shadow and that the reality is found in Christ.
Read that again slowly.
The reality is found in Christ.
There He is again.
Jesus.
At the center.
Exactly where He belongs.
Hebrews takes the imagery even deeper:
ἄρα ἀπολείπεται σαββατισμὸς τῷ λαῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ
ara apoleipetai sabbatismos tō laō tou Theou.
“There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God.”
The passage then speaks about entering God’s rest and urges believers to be diligent to enter that rest.
Suddenly this is larger than your weekend schedule.
This is about the exhausted human soul.
Maybe that is why this question reaches deeper than most people realize.
Because some of you reading this are tired.
Not sleepy.
Tired.
Tired of trying to prove that you are good enough.
Tired of promising God you will change and falling into the same sin again.
Tired of smiling at church while your marriage is bleeding.
Tired of quoting Scripture while secretly wondering whether God has finally become tired of you.
Tired of pornography you keep deleting and returning to.
Tired of bitterness you cannot seem to release.
Tired of pretending your prayer life is stronger than it really is.
Tired of carrying guilt from something nobody in your church knows happened.
Tired of being the “strong Christian.”
Tired of religious performance.
Maybe you came into this article looking for ammunition about Saturday or Sunday.
And somehow Jesus found you hiding behind the argument.
Because underneath the question about the Sabbath may be another question:
Can my soul ever rest?
Yes.
But your deepest rest is not found merely by winning a calendar debate.
Your rest has a name.
Jesus Christ.
You cannot rest yourself into salvation.
You cannot Sabbath yourself into justification.
You cannot attend enough Sunday services to erase your sin.
You cannot keep enough Saturdays to purchase forgiveness.
The Gospel destroys that illusion.
You have sinned.
So have I.
And sin is not merely weakness requiring better habits. Sin is rebellion against a holy God.
Yet the breathtaking announcement of Christianity is that the God we offended came after sinners.
Christ lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went to the cross.
He bore judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
Grace walked out of the grave.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of good people climbing high enough to reach God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue people who could never climb high enough.
Maybe your life has become a scandal.
Maybe people know what you did.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you destroyed something precious.
Maybe somebody destroyed something inside you.
Maybe religion taught you how to hide the wound but never how to bring it to Christ.
Listen carefully.
Repentance is not God asking you to clean yourself before approaching Him.
Repentance is turning from sin and turning toward the Savior who alone can cleanse you.
The cross is where your excuses die.
It is also where mercy meets the guilty.
This is why the Sabbath question must eventually bring us back to the Gospel.
Saturday cannot save you.
Sunday cannot save you.
Your denomination cannot save you.
Your pastor cannot save you.
Your theological tribe cannot save you.
Jesus saves.
And if you worship on Sunday, worship Jesus.
Do not merely attend a building.
Do not give God ninety minutes and then reclaim the remaining week for yourself.
If you conscientiously observe the seventh-day Sabbath, do it unto the Lord—not as a weapon for condemning everyone whose conviction differs.
If another believer gathers on Sunday in celebration of the risen Christ, do not assume that person therefore worships the sun, has rejected God, or loves Scripture less than you do.

And Sunday worshipers, do not mock Christians who take the seventh-day command seriously. They are asking a question rooted in an actual biblical text, and they deserve a biblical answer rather than ridicule.

Paul's counsel leaves room for serious conviction without turning conviction into contempt. Romans 14 says believers may regard days differently and calls each to be convinced before God; Colossians warns against allowing disputes over such observances to become instruments of judgment.
The cross should make arrogant Christians difficult to produce.
We all arrived at Calvary guilty.
Nobody gets to boast at the foot of a cross.
So perhaps the question you need tonight is no longer simply:
“Which day?”
Perhaps it is:
“Whose am I?”
Does Jesus have Monday?
Does He have Tuesday?
Does He have the private browser history?
Does He have the bank account?
Does He have the relationship nobody knows about?
Does He have the wound you keep protecting?
Does He have your sexuality?
Your ambition?
Your anger?
Your future?
Your reputation?
Your Sunday?
Your Saturday?
Does He have you?
Because it would be a tragedy to identify the correct day while withholding your heart from the Lord of every day.
If this exposed something in you, do not hide behind another theological argument.
Be honest.
If you have spent years judging sincere believers over disputable matters and God is confronting your pride, perhaps your response is simply: “Lord, humble me.”
Somebody scrolling beneath this article may desperately need to discover that Jesus still restores people.
Come back to the Scriptures. Test what you have been taught. Read the passages in context.
Not to embarrass them.
Invite them into the conversation.
Because the goal is not winning people to Saturday.
The goal is not winning people to Sunday.
The goal is pointing people to Jesus Christ.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you encounter Scripture more deeply, you can also help this ministry continue.
It does not.
It does not.
It doesn't.
Christian generosity should never be manufactured through spiritual guilt.
Scripture describes giving as purposeful and willing, not reluctant or compelled.
But voluntary support can still become a meaningful act of generosity.
Your monthly support helps make more biblical content, discipleship material, outreach, and resources possible.
And your support does something else.
It tells us:
Keep going. Keep opening the Bible. Keep pointing broken people toward Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting away from God.
Invite the believer quietly struggling.
Invite the person who has become lukewarm.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who thinks church people could never understand what they have done.
Because that is precisely the kind of person who needs to hear what Christianity has been announcing for two thousand years:
There is grace for sinners.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
There is restoration for the broken.
There is hope beyond religious performance.
There is a Savior whose hands still bear scars.
So…
Is Sunday really the Christian Sabbath?

The seventh day is the Sabbath explicitly named in the biblical commandment. The New Testament also bears witness to first-day Christian gathering, and early Christian history clearly documents Sunday assembly. Christians have developed differing theological understandings of how the Sabbath command relates to the new covenant, and those differences deserve careful, charitable study.
But underneath every legitimate discussion about sacred days stands something infinitely greater.
An empty tomb.
A risen Christ.
A Savior calling sinners home.
Do not become so obsessed with determining which day belongs to Jesus that you miss the far more frightening question:
Does your life belong to Jesus?
Because you can argue about the Sabbath until midnight and still wake tomorrow chained to the same sin.
Or you can come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Surrender.
Receive mercy you could never earn.
And discover that the Lord of the Sabbath is also the Savior of sinners.
Maybe you opened this article looking for the correct day.
Maybe Jesus used the question to uncover your heart.
And perhaps that was the question underneath the question all along.
The calendar may tell you when a day begins—but only the cross can tell a guilty sinner that a completely new life can begin.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHOM SHALL I SEND?” — THE TERRIFYING PART OF ISAIAH 6 WE RARELY PREACH AFTER “SEND ME”
paragraphs: “WHOM SHALL I SEND?” — THE TERRIFYING PART OF ISAIAH 6 WE RARELY PREACH AFTER “SEND ME”
Everybody loves Isaiah’s “Here am I; send me.” Far fewer people keep reading long enough to discover where God was sending him—and what obedience was going to cost.
There is a version of Isaiah 6 that fits beautifully on a coffee mug.
“Here am I. Send me!”
It sounds courageous.
It sounds adventurous.
It sounds like the beginning of something extraordinary.
And it is.
But there is something almost unsettling about the way we sometimes quote those words.
Because we stop reading.
We celebrate the surrender without reading the assignment.
We preach the availability of Isaiah, but sometimes quietly walk away before hearing what God actually told the available man to do.
And if you have ever told Jesus, “Use me,” while secretly imagining what being used by Him would look like…
Isaiah 6 may disturb you.
Because sometimes God answers, “Send me,” by sending you somewhere you never would have chosen, to people who may not applaud, carrying truth they may not want to hear.
The story begins not with Isaiah volunteering.
It begins with a death.
“In the year that king Uzziah died…”
Isaiah 6:1.
A king was gone.
A throne on earth had become empty.
But Isaiah looked higher and discovered that the ultimate throne had never been vacant.
“I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up…”
That changes everything.
Before Isaiah becomes a messenger, Isaiah becomes a witness.
Before he sees the mission, he sees the Majesty.
Before he says, “Send me,” he encounters the holiness of the One doing the sending.
Seraphim cry to one another:
“Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.”
The Hebrew is breathtaking:
קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ
Qādôš, qādôš, qādôš.
Holy.
Holy.
Holy.
Not “Isaiah, Isaiah, Isaiah.”
Not “calling, calling, calling.”
Not “success, influence, platform.”
Holy.
The center of Isaiah 6 is not the greatness of a willing prophet.
It is the holiness of an incomparable God.
The foundations shake.
The house fills with smoke.
And suddenly Isaiah does something that should make every person who wants to be “used by God” think carefully.
He does not introduce himself.
He does not announce his qualifications.
He does not tell God about his potential.
He falls apart.
“Woe is me! for I am undone…”
The Hebrew begins:
אוֹי־לִי
’Ôy-lî.
“Woe to me.”
Then comes the devastating confession:
כִּי אִישׁ טְמֵא־שְׂפָתַיִם אָנֹכִי
Ki ’ish teme-sefatayim anokhi.
In sense: “For I am a man of unclean lips.”
Isaiah had been speaking prophetic woes over others.
Then he saw God.
And suddenly the sinner he could see most clearly was himself.
That is what genuine encounters with holiness do.
They do not merely make us emotional about everybody else’s sin.
They expose ours.
Maybe that is where this story has to become personal.
It is easy to look at a collapsing culture and say, “Woe to them.”
Easy to point at the addict.
The adulterer.
The hypocrite.
The corrupt leader.
The compromised church.
The rebellious generation.
The person whose sins happen to be more visible than yours.
But then the throne comes into view.
And suddenly you remember the messages you deleted.
The bitterness you renamed “discernment.”
The lust you kept feeding.
The apology you never gave.
The forgiveness you keep withholding.
The secret habit nobody at church knows about.
The pride hidden underneath your theology.
The prayer life that has quietly become almost nonexistent.
The private version of you that would terrify the public version of you if it ever became visible.
And before a holy God, Isaiah does not say, “At least I am better than them.”
He says, essentially:
I am unclean too.
But this is where Isaiah 6 becomes Gospel-shaped long before Bethlehem.
God does not leave the confessed sinner standing there condemned.
A seraph takes a burning coal from the altar.
It touches Isaiah’s lips.
And Isaiah hears words every guilty soul longs to hear:
“Thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged.”
Do not rush past that.
Isaiah did not cleanse himself before volunteering.
Grace touched him first.
The altar came before the assignment.
Cleansing came before commissioning.
Forgiveness came before sending.
That pattern matters because Christianity is not the story of sinful people making themselves impressive enough for God to employ.
It is the story of grace reaching the unclean.
And what Isaiah experiences symbolically around the altar points us toward something infinitely greater revealed fully in Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, our hope is not a coal touching our lips.
Our hope is the crucified and risen Son of God bearing sin and accomplishing redemption.
Peter writes that Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
Paul says that in Christ “we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins” (Ephesians 1:7).
Isaiah needed cleansing.
So do you.
So do I.
And the Gospel declares that forgiveness is not found in pretending we were never dirty.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
Then—and only then—comes the question.
Isaiah hears the voice of the Lord:
אֶת־מִי אֶשְׁלַח וּמִי יֵלֶךְ־לָנוּ
’Et-mi ’eshlach, umi yelekh-lanu?
“Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?”
And Isaiah answers:
הִנְנִי שְׁלָחֵנִי
Hineni, shelacheni.
“Here am I; send me.”
Hineni.
Here I am.
Not merely, “I am standing at this geographical location.”
It is availability.
Presence.
Readiness.
Here I am.
And perhaps you have prayed something like it.
“Jesus, use me.”
“Lord, send me.”
“God, whatever You want.”
Beautiful words.
Dangerous words.
Because God answers Isaiah.
And this is where the coffee-mug version usually ends.
The Bible does not.
God tells him:
“Go.”
But what follows is not a promise that thousands will immediately repent.

Isaiah receives a severe prophetic commission to a spiritually resistant people. He is to proclaim God's word in the midst of hardened hearing and blinded perception, and Isaiah eventually asks the agonizing question:
“Lord, how long?”
Think about that.
Isaiah said, “Send me.”
God did.
And the assignment included rejection.
The man who saw the throne would now speak to people who often would not listen.
The man whose lips had been cleansed would use those lips to proclaim truth that would expose hardened hearts.
His obedience could not be measured merely by applause.
His faithfulness could not be measured merely by visible results.
And suddenly Isaiah 6 becomes painfully relevant.
Because maybe you thought obedience would make everybody understand you.
Maybe you thought following Jesus would automatically repair every relationship.
Maybe you thought sharing biblical truth would guarantee appreciation.
Maybe you thought serving faithfully meant your ministry would explode.
Maybe you thought raising your children in Christ guaranteed they would never wander.
Maybe you thought praying faithfully meant the answer would arrive quickly.
Maybe you thought, “Send me,” meant God would send you somewhere glamorous.
Instead He sent you back into that difficult home.
Into that workplace.
Into that marriage that needs patient faithfulness.
Into conversations nobody applauds.
Into years of praying for someone who still seems far from God.
Into serving when almost nobody notices.
Into telling the truth lovingly when silence would have been easier.
And somewhere inside you a question begins forming.
“Lord… how long?”
How long do I keep praying?
How long do I keep forgiving?
How long do I keep serving?
How long do I keep sharing Christ with someone who keeps rejecting Him?
How long do I remain faithful when faithfulness feels invisible?
Isaiah asked that question too.
And this is one of the truths we desperately need to recover:
Your assignment is obedience.
The results belong to God.
That does not mean results do not matter. Scripture repeatedly cares about fruit.
It means visible success is not the sovereign judge of faithfulness.
Noah preached righteousness in a wicked generation.
Jeremiah spoke while people resisted him.
The apostles suffered for proclaiming Christ.
And Jesus Himself was abandoned by many who had once followed Him.
So perhaps the question is not merely:
“Will God use me?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“Will I still obey Him when being used by Him looks nothing like what I imagined?”
Will you still say hineni when nobody claps?
Will you still say shelacheni when obedience costs something?
Will you still speak truth with love when truth becomes unpopular?
Will you still follow Christ when Christianity stops being convenient?
Will you still serve when your name is forgotten?
Will you still forgive when your flesh wants revenge?
Will you still pray when heaven seems silent?
Will you still carry the Gospel when the people you love roll their eyes?
That is where “Here am I” becomes more than Christian merchandise.
It becomes surrender.
But there is another astonishing detail.
Isaiah's story does not ultimately terminate in judgment.
The book bearing his name keeps moving.
Through warnings.
Through tears.
Through judgment.
Through promises.
Until the horizon begins glowing with Someone Isaiah could not yet see in Bethlehem but whom God was already revealing through prophecy.
A child would be born.
A Son would be given.
A Servant would suffer.
A wounded Savior would bear the sins of others.
“He was wounded for our transgressions…”
Isaiah 53:5.
Centuries later, Jesus Christ came.

And when the Gospel of John reflects on Isaiah's vision, it makes an astonishing Christ-centered connection: after quoting from Isaiah 6, John says Isaiah “saw his glory, and spake of him” (John 12:41).
The throne of Isaiah 6 and the cross of the Gospel are not competing pictures.
The Holy One we cannot domesticate is the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
The God before whom Isaiah cried “Woe is me” is not indifferent to ruined people.
In Christ, He came for them.
That includes you.
Your scandal is not stronger than His grace.
Your history is not stronger than His blood.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
Your secret sin should be confessed, not protected.
Your guilt should drive you toward Christ, not deeper into hiding.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of the grave you were decorating.
Jesus does not merely make bad people appear respectable.
He makes spiritually dead people alive.
So maybe your first response today should not be:
“Send me.”
Maybe it should be:
“Woe is me.”
Maybe before asking God for a platform, you need the altar.
Before asking Him to enlarge your influence, you need Him to expose your heart.
Before saying, “Use my mouth,” perhaps you need to surrender what your mouth has been saying.
Before asking for a calling, perhaps you need repentance.
Because God is not looking for actors who know how to appear holy.
He calls sinners.
Cleanses sinners.
Transforms sinners.
And then sends forgiven sinners to tell other sinners where mercy can be found.
That is why your past does not automatically disqualify you from becoming a testimony of grace.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
Paul had persecuted the church and became a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The woman of Samaria carried the news of Jesus back toward people who knew her complicated story.
Again and again, Scripture reveals a God whose grace does not pretend the scandal never happened.
Grace does something better.
It redeems.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by pretending sin does not matter.
Not by lowering God's holiness until nobody needs repentance.
Jesus rewrites everything by confronting sin, bearing judgment, offering forgiveness, raising the dead, restoring the broken, and creating new lives that could never have written themselves.
So here is the question Isaiah 6 leaves burning in the room:
If Jesus has forgiven you…
where is He sending you?
Maybe it is not across an ocean.
Maybe it is across the hallway.
Maybe your mission field has your last name.
Maybe it sits beside you at work.
Maybe it is the friend whose jokes hide depression.
Maybe it is the child who stopped going to church.
Maybe it is the spouse you stopped praying for because disappointment became easier than hope.
Yes.
Even there.
What if the article you share becomes the article somebody reads alone at 2:13 in the morning while trying desperately not to collapse?
You cannot save them.
Gospel Warrior cannot save them.
A preacher cannot save them.
Only Jesus saves.
But someone can carry the message.
“Whom shall I send?”
Perhaps tagging that friend is not about engagement at all.
Perhaps it is you saying, “I thought of you, and I refuse to let embarrassment keep me silent.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you have been exhausted but you refuse to abandon your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to remember you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if God is confronting you about something you already know He has been asking you to surrender, comment, “Here am I.”
Not for performance.
Not to impress strangers.
As a small public confession that you do not want to keep running.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding you with Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical teaching, and reminders that continually lead you back to Jesus, you can also help this work continue.
It does not.
It does not.
And not because anyone should be pressured into giving. Scripture says plainly that giving must not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 9:7).

But Scripture also gives us a beautiful picture of believers voluntarily partnering in Gospel work. The Philippians repeatedly supported Paul's ministry, and Paul described their generosity as “an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God” (Philippians 4:16–18).
That is the spirit in which we invite you.

Your support helps us keep creating and distributing Christ-centered content, biblical encouragement, discipleship materials, and resources designed to reach the wounded, the wandering, the curious, the struggling believer, and the person who may be one Gospel encounter away from finally crying out to Jesus.
Send it privately to the person God just brought to your mind.
Because the mission was never supposed to stop with the person who received the message.
Someone carried the Gospel until it reached you.
Now somebody else may be waiting for someone willing to carry it to them.
And perhaps that is the part of Isaiah 6 we have avoided.
“Send me” was never merely a beautiful sentence.
It was permission.
Permission for God to interrupt Isaiah's plans.
Permission to speak through cleansed lips.
Permission to send him toward difficult people.
Permission to remain faithful when visible results were painful.
Permission to keep going long enough to ask:
“Lord, how long?”
Maybe you are standing there now.
Tired.
Disappointed.
Still carrying scars from your own scandal.
Still wondering whether God could possibly use someone with your history.
Look again.
The story did not begin with Isaiah's usefulness.
It began with God's holiness.
Isaiah confessed.
God cleansed.
God called.
Isaiah answered.
And that same Gospel rhythm still destroys our excuses today.
See His holiness.
Confess your sin.
Run to Christ.
Receive the mercy purchased at the cross.
Rise in grace.
Then go wherever your King sends you.
Not because you are spotless.
Because Jesus saves sinners.
Not because you are fearless.
Because Christ is worthy.
Not because everyone will listen.
Because the One who sends you deserves your yes.
So when heaven asks…
“Whom shall I send?”
May your answer no longer be a verse you merely admire.
May it become the surrender by which you live.
And when your voice trembles as you say “Here am I,” remember: the God who sends you already knows every chapter behind you—and through Jesus Christ, grace can still write what comes next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES “LUST” SETTLE THE MASTURBATION QUESTION—or Is the Biblical Discussion More Complicated?
paragraphs: DOES “LUST” SETTLE THE MASTURBATION QUESTION—or Is the Biblical Discussion More Complicated?

Jesus spoke directly about lust. Paul spoke about sexual holiness, self-mastery, conscience, and glorifying God with the body. But the Bible never actually uses the word “masturbation.” So what happens when we stop repeating slogans, open the Scriptures, and allow the text to ask harder questions than the ones we expected?
There are sins people confess at the altar.
And then there are sins—or struggles, questions, habits, wounds, compulsions—that people carry home.
Quietly.
They worship on Sunday.
They raise their hands.
They quote Scripture.
They love Jesus.
Then midnight comes.
The bedroom door closes.
The phone lights up.
The loneliness gets louder.
The body remembers what the conscience has been trying to forget.
And afterward?
Silence.
Sometimes shame.
Sometimes repentance.
Sometimes confusion.
Sometimes the exhausted prayer of a Christian who has promised God for the fiftieth time, “Lord, I will never do this again.”
And sometimes there is another question—one many believers are almost afraid to ask because they assume merely asking it makes them rebellious:
What, precisely, does the Bible actually say about masturbation?
Not what Christian culture says.
Not what pornography says.
Not what secular culture says.
Not what your guilt says.
Not what somebody’s viral video says.
What does Scripture say?
Because there is a dangerous way to become “biblical” that actually requires putting words into the Bible that the Bible never says.
And there is an equally dangerous way to exploit biblical silence as permission to indulge whatever the flesh desires.
Neither is faithful.
So stay with me.
Because this discussion becomes much more uncomfortable before it becomes hopeful.
And somewhere underneath the question about masturbation may be another question entirely:
Who owns your body when nobody else is watching?
Jesus gives us one of the most important texts in this conversation in Matthew 5:28.
The Greek reads:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.
A close rendering is:
“But I say to you that everyone looking at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Pay attention to the expression:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι — pros to epithymēsai
The verb epithymeō can mean to desire, long for, covet, or—depending upon context—lust.
And the construction here matters.
Jesus is not teaching that noticing that another human being is physically attractive is automatically adultery.
He is going after something deeper.
The look that becomes intentional desire.
The gaze that welcomes and cultivates sexual possession in the heart.
The human being standing before you—or appearing on your screen—ceases to be treated as someone bearing God's image and becomes material for your imagination.
Jesus moves the courtroom into the heart.
That changes this entire discussion.

Because if masturbation is being fueled by pornography, deliberately cultivated fantasies about someone who is not your spouse, voyeurism, sexually exploitative imagery, or intentional fantasizing designed to produce lust, then we cannot simply isolate the physical act from what the heart is doing.
The question is no longer merely:
“Did my body experience sexual release?”
The question becomes:
What did I ask my heart to consume in order to get there?
That is harder.
Because nobody else may have been in the room.
But someone may have been in your imagination.
Someone whose body became raw material for your gratification.
Someone who never consented to occupy the sexual world you constructed inside your mind.
And Jesus cares about what happens there.
Not because sexual desire itself is dirty.

God created human beings as embodied creatures. Scripture does not teach that possessing sexual desire makes you filthy. The biblical story affirms marriage, one-flesh union, marital intimacy, desire, embodiment, and the goodness of God's creation.
The problem is not that you possess a body.
The problem is what sin can teach us to do with desire.
Paul puts the matter this way in 1 Thessalonians 4:3:
Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν, ἀπέχεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς πορνείας.
“This is the will of God—your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality.”
The word ἁγιασμός — hagiasmos speaks of holiness or sanctification.
And πορνεία — porneia refers broadly to sexual immorality.
A few verses later Paul speaks of not living:
