ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας — en pathei epithymias
“In passion of lust/desire.”
So yes.
Lust matters enormously.
But here is where Christians must resist saying more than Scripture says.
The Bible never directly names masturbation as an act.
There is no verse that says, “You shall not masturbate.”
That fact should neither frighten us nor become a loophole.
It should make us more careful interpreters.
Some people immediately run to Onan.

Genesis 38 tells how Judah commanded Onan to fulfill his obligation toward his deceased brother's wife and raise offspring for his brother. The Hebrew text speaks of raising זֶרַע — zeraʿ, “seed” or offspring, for his brother.
Onan understood that the offspring would not be reckoned as his.
So during intercourse with his brother's widow, he deliberately prevented conception rather than fulfilling the obligation placed upon him.
Genesis says what he did was wicked before the LORD.
But read the story carefully.
The text describes intercourse and Onan's deliberate refusal to provide offspring for his deceased brother.
It does not describe masturbation.

Whatever broader ethical conclusions Christians may draw from the passage, turning Genesis 38 into a straightforward verse saying “God killed Onan for masturbating” does not accurately represent what the narrative actually says.
And Christians should never need a distorted Bible verse to defend holiness.
Truth does not need our exaggeration.
But now someone may say:
“Then masturbation must be okay.”
Not so fast.
Biblical ethics often works through more than a dictionary of explicitly named behaviors.
Paul gives us a devastating principle in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει... ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος.
“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial... I will not be mastered by anything.”
That final idea deserves to sit in the room with us for a moment.
I will not be mastered by anything.
Because perhaps the question you have been asking is:
“Can I do it?”
When another question may expose much more:
“Can I stop?”
That changes things.
Can you walk away for a week?
A month?
Can you sleep without it?
Can you experience stress without running toward it?
Can you feel lonely without immediately needing sexual release?
Can you encounter temptation without opening pornography?
Can you pray when the urge comes instead of automatically obeying it?
Can you say no?
Or has what you once called relief slowly become a master?
There is an enormous difference between having an appetite and being ruled by one.
Paul does not merely ask whether something appears on a forbidden-behavior list.
He asks whether it is beneficial.
Whether it dominates.
Whether it belongs with holiness.
Whether the body is being offered to God.
Then Paul says something staggering:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς· δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν Θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.
“You were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body.”
There it is.
Perhaps the deepest question in the entire discussion.
Not merely:
“Is masturbation technically forbidden?”
But:
“Can I bring this before Jesus without hiding?”
Can I thank Him for it?
Can I practice it in faith?
Can I say, “Lord Jesus, this body belongs to You. Be glorified in what I am about to do”?
Can I do it without pornography?
Without mentally possessing another person?
Without feeding fantasies that violate Christ's teaching about the heart?
Without being mastered?
Without violating my conscience?
Without using sexual pleasure as anesthesia for wounds Jesus is asking me to bring into His light?
Those questions do not manufacture a commandment Scripture never gives.
They do something much more searching.
They bring the behavior underneath the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that may expose another uncomfortable truth.
For some people, masturbation is not primarily a sexual problem.
It has become pain medication.
You are lonely.
You do it.
Rejected.
You do it.
Anxious.
You do it.
Depressed.
You do it.
Angry with your spouse.
You do it.
Feeling unwanted.
You do it.
Unable to sleep.
You do it.
Ashamed that you did it yesterday.
And somehow...
you do it again.
The body becomes the place where an emotional wound repeatedly demands anesthesia.
And this is where shouting “STOP LUSTING!” may fail to reach the actual battlefield.
Yes, sinful lust must be resisted.
Yes, pornography must be rejected.
Yes, sexual immorality must be fled.
But sometimes discipleship must also ask:
What are you trying not to feel?
What loneliness keeps returning?
What rejection are you medicating?
What wound keeps asking for relief?
What happened to you?
What are you afraid to tell anyone?
Why does darkness feel safer than being known?
This does not excuse sin.
It helps expose where the battle is actually being fought.
Because Jesus does not merely want to take pornography out of your browser history.
He wants your heart.
He does not merely want cleaner behavior.
He wants freedom.
Paul writes in Galatians 5:16:
Πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε καὶ ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκὸς οὐ μὴ τελέσητε.
“Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desire of the flesh.”
Notice the direction.
Walk by the Spirit.
Christian holiness is not merely spending the rest of your life screaming “NO!” at your body.
It is learning to say a greater “YES” to Christ.
Yes to prayer.
Yes to truth.
Yes to bringing temptation into the light.
Yes to accountability.
Yes to removing pornography rather than negotiating with it.
Yes to getting the phone out of the bedroom if that phone repeatedly becomes a doorway.
Yes to calling a mature Christian when secrecy begins whispering again.
Yes to learning how to suffer loneliness without worshiping relief.
Yes to learning that an urge can exist without becoming your master.
And yes—even after failure—to getting up again.
Somebody reading this failed last night.
Maybe this morning.
Maybe five minutes before finding this article.
And you almost stopped reading because every paragraph felt like someone opening curtains in a room you desperately wanted dark.
Listen carefully.
Conviction says:
“Come into the light.”
Shame says:
“Hide until you become worthy of the light.”
Those voices are not saying the same thing.
The Gospel does not tell sinners to cleanse themselves enough to approach Jesus.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The cross is not God's declaration that your sin does not matter.
The cross is the terrifying proof that sin matters more than we imagined—and the breathtaking proof that God's grace reaches farther than we deserved.
“If we confess our sins,” Scripture says, “He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
And Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Do not confuse no condemnation with no transformation.
Grace does not say:
“Stay chained.”
Grace walks into the prison carrying keys.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely so you could become more comfortable hiding.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what needs confessing.
Delete what needs deleting.
Block what needs blocking.
Bring into community what secrecy has protected.
If pornography is involved, stop pretending the masturbation question can be separated from pornography.
If deliberate lustful fantasy is involved, bring the fantasy under Matthew 5:28.
If the behavior controls you, bring it under Paul's refusal to “be mastered by anything.”
If your conscience is continually accusing you, do not repeatedly bulldoze your conscience merely because you found somebody online willing to give you permission.

And if your struggle has become compulsive, entrenched, or connected to trauma, loneliness, anxiety, or other deep wounds, seeking help from a trustworthy pastor, mature Christian mentor, or qualified professional is not spiritual defeat.
Sometimes walking into the light sounds like:
“I need help.”
Perhaps you have spent years asking God:
“Why can't I stop?”
Maybe tonight the prayer needs to change.
“Jesus, show me what I have been running from.”
That prayer can become frightening.
Because He may show you the pornography.
The fantasy.
The loneliness.
The resentment.
The boredom.
The secret entitlement.
The unhealed rejection.
The habit.
The self-pity.
The craving for control.
Maybe even the religious shame that convinced you God was disgusted every time you stumbled and therefore made you hide from the only One who could heal you.
Bring all of it.
Not just the respectable pieces.
Bring the scandal.
That is what grace is for.
And no, this article cannot honestly reduce every circumstance to the simplistic sentence, “Masturbation equals lust, therefore the discussion is over.”
Scripture deserves better than that.
Neither can we say, “The Bible doesn't mention the word, therefore anything goes.”
Scripture deserves better than that too.
The faithful question reaches deeper.
What accompanies the act?
What feeds it?
What does the heart intentionally desire?
Does pornography participate?
Does another person become an object inside the imagination?
Does it strengthen self-control or weaken it?
Is it mastering you?
Can it be brought honestly before Christ?
Does it move you toward holiness or repeatedly into secrecy?
Can you genuinely seek to glorify God in your body while doing it?
Those questions may produce different pastoral complexities, but they refuse both legalistic invention and convenient loopholes.
And perhaps that is why this subject hurts.
Because eventually it stops being about winning an argument concerning masturbation.
It becomes about surrender.
Jesus does not want one sanitized corner of you.
He wants you.
Your sexuality.
Your imagination.
Your loneliness.
Your browser history.
Your memories.
Your wounds.
Your body.
Your desires.
Your failures.
Your future.
All of you.
And the hands of Christ are not the hands of a disgusted Savior reluctantly touching contaminated people.
Those hands were pierced.
For sinners.
For the ashamed.
For people with histories they wish they could erase.
For people who promised “never again” and then did it again.
For people who have become experts at worshiping publicly while bleeding privately.
The Gospel is not that you finally became strong enough to save yourself.
The Gospel is that Christ came when you could not.
Died for sinners.
Rose victorious.
Calls us to repentance.
Forgives those who come to Him.
And begins making His people new.
So if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not have to write the details publicly.
But you can stop pretending.

And please remember: the comment section should never become a confessional booth for graphic details. Protect your privacy. Protect others. Confess specific sins to God and, where appropriate, to trustworthy people who can actually walk with you.

If someone came into your mind while reading this—someone fighting pornography, shame, secret sexual habits, loneliness, or the exhausting cycle of falling and hiding—send this article to them privately.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them that there is still a door out of darkness.
It does not.
Only Jesus saves.
Christian giving is meant to come willingly from the heart, not through spiritual coercion.
Pray.
Share.
Save the teachings that help you.
Support the spread of biblical truth in whatever faithful way God enables you.
Because ultimately this ministry is not about building an audience around Gospel Warrior.
It is about pointing an audience beyond Gospel Warrior...
to Jesus.
The One who sees what happens after the bedroom door closes.
The One who knows what nobody else knows.
The One who refuses to call darkness light.
And the One whose grace is powerful enough that your darkest chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
You may be ashamed of the chapter you wrote in secret—but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are still capable of writing redemption across the page.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN PORN DAMAGE YOUR FUTURE MARRIAGE?
paragraphs: CAN PORN DAMAGE YOUR FUTURE MARRIAGE?
You may delete the history from your phone. But what happens when the images have already followed you into the way you see love, intimacy, your future spouse…and yourself?
There is a person you may not have met yet.
Maybe you know their name already.
Maybe you have been praying for them.
Maybe somewhere tonight, they are praying for you.
They may one day stand across from you with trembling hands, look into your eyes, and promise before God to love you faithfully.
They may become the person who sees you without the filters.
Without the performance.
Without the carefully selected photographs.
Without the version of yourself everyone else gets.
Your spouse will eventually meet the person you have been becoming in secret.
And that is why this conversation matters.
Because pornography rarely introduces itself by saying:
“I want to affect the way you experience your future husband.”
“I want to affect the way you experience your future wife.”
“I want to teach your eyes to wander.”
“I want to train desire to demand novelty.”
“I want secrecy to become normal.”
“I want you to compare covenant intimacy with manufactured fantasy.”
No.
It usually begins much smaller.
Curiosity.
Loneliness.
A late night.
A private browser.
A difficult week.
A relationship that ended.
A body that feels restless.
A heart that feels rejected.
A phone nobody else can see.
One click.
Then another.
And sometimes something that began as a moment slowly becomes a pattern.
A pattern becomes a hiding place.
And the hiding place begins teaching the heart.
That is where Christians must speak carefully.
Not hysterically.
Not dishonestly.
Not with fake statistics.
Not by pretending every person who has ever watched pornography will inevitably destroy a marriage.
That claim would go beyond the evidence.

Research on pornography and relationships is complicated. Some studies have found pornography use to be unassociated with certain relationship outcomes, and findings can differ according to gender, whether use is solitary or shared, whether partners know about it, attitudes toward pornography, and differences between partners. Yet large-scale and longitudinal research has repeatedly found concerning associations between pornography use—particularly certain patterns of solitary or secret use—and lower relationship satisfaction, intimacy, sexual satisfaction, commitment, or other measures of relational well-being. A 2024 meta-analysis covering 41 studies and more than 70,000 participants found a small overall negative correlation between pornography use and sexual satisfaction. Other large studies have similarly found pornography use to be either unrelated or negatively associated with many measures of relationship quality, while emphasizing that association does not automatically prove causation.
So no, pornography does not mathematically guarantee a ruined future marriage.
But yes…
it can matter.
And Scripture takes us deeper than statistics ever could.
Jesus said:
“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
Matthew 5:27–28, KJV.
Look carefully at what Jesus does.
He takes the discussion from the bedroom…
to the heart.
The Greek behind Matthew 5:28 includes the verb ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō — referring here to desiring or lusting after someone.
Jesus is not teaching that merely noticing that another human being is attractive is identical to committing physical adultery.
The construction describes a look joined to lustful desire.
That distinction matters.
Because Christianity is not a religion of pretending human sexuality does not exist.
God created sexuality.
God created marriage.
God created the body.
The Christian answer to pornography is therefore not:
“Sex is dirty.”
The Christian answer is almost the opposite.
Sexuality is too meaningful to reduce people made in God's image to consumable images.
The body matters.
Desire matters.
Faithfulness matters.
The person on the screen matters.
Your future spouse matters.
And your heart matters to Jesus.
Pornography offers something radically different from covenant.
Pornography says:
Look without knowing.
Desire without serving.
Consume without committing.
Leave without grieving.
Change the person when you become bored.
Search again when the image no longer excites you.
Covenant says:
Know me.
Stay.
Serve.
Forgive.
Be known.
Be faithful when life becomes ordinary.
Remain when bodies age.
Love when emotions fluctuate.
Choose the same person again tomorrow.
Do you see the collision?
Pornography can train consumption.
Marriage requires communion.
Pornography can revolve around novelty.
Marriage asks for fidelity.
Pornography can hide behind secrecy.
Marriage needs truth.
Pornography can turn another person's body into something viewed primarily for personal gratification.
Christian marriage calls two people toward self-giving love.
And somewhere between those two visions of sexuality stands a human heart deciding what kind of lover it is becoming.
That may be the uncomfortable question beneath the question.
Not merely:
“Will pornography damage my future marriage?”
But:
“What is pornography teaching me to become before I enter it?”
Because a wedding does not magically erase yesterday's habits.
A ring is not a reset button.
You can wear white and still carry secrets.
You can say vows while carrying expectations your spouse never created.
You can enter a marriage desperately wanting covenant while still having desires shaped by years of private consumption.
And then comes the heartbreak nobody showed you on the screen.
Your spouse is human.
Their body is human.
Their energy changes.
Their appearance changes.
Pregnancy can change bodies.
Age changes bodies.
Illness changes bodies.
Stress changes desire.
Children interrupt schedules.
Work exhausts people.
Sometimes intimacy is beautiful.
Sometimes awkward.
Sometimes hilarious.
Sometimes tender.
Sometimes deeply emotional.
Sometimes one person needs patience more than passion.
Real marital intimacy is not edited.
It does not have a production crew.
It is two vulnerable human beings learning how to give themselves faithfully to one another.
And that vulnerability can be extraordinarily beautiful precisely because it is real.
Pornography cannot teach you that kind of love.
A screen cannot make a covenant with you.
An image cannot know your wounds.
A video cannot forgive you.
A fantasy cannot grow old beside you.
And pixels cannot hold your hand when somebody you love dies.
Pornography may promise intimacy without vulnerability.
But intimacy without vulnerability is not the same thing as being known.
Perhaps that is why this struggle can become so lonely.
You see bodies…
while your soul becomes increasingly hidden.
And eventually you may discover that the deepest hunger was never simply sexual.
Maybe you wanted comfort.
Maybe you wanted escape.
Maybe you wanted to feel wanted.
Maybe rejection left a hole in you.
Maybe abuse distorted the way you understood intimacy.
Maybe loneliness became unbearable.
Maybe anxiety needed somewhere to go.
Maybe pornography became anesthesia.
And anesthesia can numb pain without healing the wound.
Jesus wants the wound too.
Not merely your browser history.
Your heart.
That is why the Gospel must enter this conversation.
Because without the Gospel, an article like this becomes nothing more than:
“Porn is bad. Try harder.”
And some of you have tried harder.
You made promises.
You deleted apps.
You installed filters.
You cried.
You prayed.
You lasted three days.
Three weeks.
Three months.
Then something happened.
Stress.
Loneliness.
Temptation.
Opportunity.
And suddenly you were staring at the same screen again.
Afterward came the familiar voice:
“You are disgusting.”
“You are fake.”
“God is finished with you.”
“You might as well stop praying.”
“You will never change.”
Listen carefully.
Conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
Conviction brings sin into the light so we can run toward Christ.
Condemnation whispers that because we sinned, we should hide from Him.
The Gospel says something far more devastating to our pride and far more beautiful to our shame:
Your sin is serious enough that Jesus had to die.
And His grace is powerful enough that He willingly came to save sinners.
The cross does not tell you pornography does not matter.
The cross tells you sin mattered so much that redemption cost blood.
Paul wrote to believers in Corinth:
“Flee fornication… What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you… and ye are not your own?
For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body…”
1 Corinthians 6:18–20, KJV.
The Greek command is striking:
φεύγετε — pheugete.
Flee.
Not negotiate.
Not see how close you can stand.
Not prove how strong you are.
Flee.

Paul's larger argument is rooted in identity: believers belong to Christ. They were “bought with a price.” Sexual holiness is therefore not presented merely as fear of consequences. It flows from redemption.
You belong to Jesus.
That changes the question.
Instead of:
“How much can I get away with?”
Grace teaches us to ask:
“How can the body Christ redeemed glorify the One who purchased me?”
That can mean doing something painfully practical.
Deleting access.
Installing accountability software.
Moving the phone out of the bedroom.
Stopping the secret account.
Unfollowing the page.
Refusing the private conversation feeding fantasy.
Telling a mature Christian you trust.
Speaking honestly with your spouse rather than building another layer of deception.
Seeking a qualified counselor when the pattern feels compulsive, traumatic, or deeply entrenched.
Getting pastoral help from someone who understands both holiness and grace.
Not because practical boundaries save you.
Jesus saves you.
But genuine repentance does not merely mourn the chains.
It begins walking away from the prison.
And maybe somebody reading this is thinking:
Too late.
You don't understand what I've watched.
Too late.
You don't know how long this has been happening.
Too late.
I'm already married.
Too late.
My spouse discovered it.
Too late.
Trust is broken.
Too late.
I promised God I would stop and went back again.
Then perhaps these are the two words your shame least wants you to hear:
Not necessarily.
Your past may have consequences.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Healing may be slow.
Your spouse may have legitimate wounds that cannot be rushed away with a Bible verse.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending betrayal did not hurt.
Repentance does not entitle us to immediate restoration of another person's trust.
Some marriages need serious counseling.
Some people need specialized help.
Some conversations will involve tears.
Some consequences cannot simply be deleted.
But Christianity is built around a Savior who walks into places human beings call hopeless.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted His people.
The Corinthian church had a deeply disordered sexual past, yet Paul could say of believers who had lived in serious sin:
“And such were some of you…”
1 Corinthians 6:11.
Were.
That little word is thunder.
Not because Christians become incapable of temptation.
Not because sanctification happens instantly.
But because sin no longer gets the final word over the identity of someone washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of Jesus Christ.
That is Gospel territory.
Scandal becoming testimony.
Shame meeting mercy.
Hiddenness meeting light.
Bondage meeting a Savior.
From scandal to grace…
because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe pornography has written chapters in your story you wish had never existed.
Jesus does not call evil good.
He does something infinitely better.
He redeems sinners.
He teaches eyes to see differently.
He teaches hearts to desire holiness.
He teaches men to see women as image-bearers rather than products.
He teaches women to see men as image-bearers rather than instruments.
He teaches husbands to love.
He teaches wives to love.
He teaches single believers that purity is not wasted waiting.
He teaches married believers that confession can be the beginning of truth rather than the end of hope.
He teaches ashamed people to walk into light.
And He teaches broken people that being tempted is not the same thing as being abandoned by God.
So perhaps your future marriage does not need a “perfect” version of you.
Perhaps it needs the version of you who learned how to repent.
The version who learned how to tell the truth.
The version who stopped protecting the secret and started protecting covenant.
The version who understands that another person's body is not merchandise.
The version who can say:
“I need help.”
The version who knows how to fall at the feet of Jesus and get back up.
The version who discovered that purity is not merely saying no to pornography.
It is learning to say yes to a better vision of people.
Yes to dignity.
Yes to covenant.
Yes to truth.
Yes to sacrificial love.
Yes to a mind increasingly occupied by what Paul calls true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, excellent, and praiseworthy in Philippians 4:8.
Maybe you are single.
Fight now.
Not because marriage will cure lust.
It won't.
Your future spouse was never designed to become your rehabilitation program.
Fight because Christ is worthy now.
Maybe you are dating.
Do not build engagement photographs over buried secrets.
Truth before vows is better than discovery after them.
Maybe you are married and hiding.

The next faithful step may be difficult, and wisdom matters greatly in how disclosure happens, especially where trauma, coercion, abuse, or serious relational instability exists. Seek mature pastoral and professional guidance when needed.
But stop calling darkness home.
Maybe you are the spouse who discovered the secret.
Your pain matters too.
You are not required to pretend betrayal did not wound you.
Healing cannot be demanded on somebody else's timetable.
Grace and truth belong together.
And if the person you love is genuinely repenting, remember this:
You are not their savior.
Jesus is.
That removes an impossible burden from both of you.
Be honest.
If confession and repentance have already begun changing your life, tell somebody what Jesus is doing.
Your testimony may become the sentence another ashamed believer desperately needed tonight.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this, don't send this article as a weapon.
Send it as an invitation.
Save it too.
Not merely for yourself.
“I think this is destroying me.”
Then you will have something to send them that says both:
Come into the light.
And…
there is still grace.
It doesn't.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It cannot.
We should never place that burden on Scripture.
Give faithfully to God according to conscience, biblical conviction, and the teaching of your local church.
But voluntary financial support of Gospel work can be a genuine expression of generosity and partnership in ministry.
One share can place the Gospel in front of a person we may never reach ourselves.
One tag can begin a conversation.
One comment can tell another struggling believer, “You are not the only person fighting.”
One saved article can resurface exactly when someone needs it.
One faithful act of generosity can help keep Christian resources moving outward.
Come to Jesus.
Not when you have finally cleaned yourself.
Now.
Bring Him the browser history.
Bring Him the fantasies.
Bring Him the loneliness underneath them.
Bring Him the marriage that is hurting.
Bring Him the engagement you are afraid to jeopardize.
Bring Him the memories you wish you could erase.
Bring Him the relapse.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the tears.
Bring Him the person you became in darkness.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Walk into the light.
Receive forgiveness through Christ.
Then begin, one obedient decision at a time, becoming the person who no longer needs darkness in order to survive.
Because pornography may have trained your eyes.
It may have distorted expectations.
It may have wounded trust.
It may have complicated intimacy.
It may even have followed you farther than you ever intended.
But pornography is not sovereign over your future.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And the hands pierced for sinners are still capable of writing redemption across pages you thought were permanently ruined.
So when your past whispers, “Look what you became,” point to the cross and remember who has the final word.
Your secret may have written yesterday—but it does not get to hold the pen forever. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “A FRIEND LOVES AT ALL TIMES” — BUT BIBLICAL FRIENDSHIP INCLUDES SOMETHING WE OFTEN AVOID
paragraphs: “A FRIEND LOVES AT ALL TIMES” — BUT BIBLICAL FRIENDSHIP INCLUDES SOMETHING WE OFTEN AVOID
Some people will sit beside you while you destroy yourself because they are too afraid to risk the friendship by telling you the truth. Scripture calls us to something deeper.
There is a kind of friendship that feels like love...
until the truth becomes uncomfortable.
It celebrates you.
Defends you.
Laughs with you.
Checks on you when you disappear.
Sits beside you when your world collapses.
Says, “I’m here no matter what.”
And those things can be beautiful.
But then comes the moment that reveals what the friendship is really made of.
Your friend sees you walking toward something dangerous.
Not necessarily a cliff anyone else can see.
Maybe an affair beginning in private messages.
Maybe bitterness becoming part of your personality.
Maybe alcohol has stopped being something you occasionally drink and has quietly become somewhere you hide.
Maybe pride has made correction almost impossible.
Maybe pornography has become a secret room in your life.
Maybe you are treating your spouse cruelly while telling everyone else how badly your spouse treats you.
Maybe you are compromising your convictions because you desperately want someone to love you.
Maybe you are drifting from Christ while continuing to post Bible verses convincing everyone—including yourself—that everything is fine.
And your friend knows.
They see it.
They feel the warning in their spirit.
They know they should say something.
But they hesitate.
Because telling you the truth could cost them access to you.
So they say nothing.
And suddenly one of the most uncomfortable questions in biblical friendship appears:
If I watch someone I love destroy something God is trying to restore, and I remain silent simply because I don't want them angry with me... is my silence really love?
That question hurts.
Because most of us want friends who love us at all times.
We are less certain that we want friends who tell us the truth at all times.
Proverbs 17:17 gives us one of Scripture's most beloved descriptions of friendship:
בְּכָל־עֵת אֹהֵב הָרֵעַ וְאָח לְצָרָה יִוָּלֵד
Bəḵāl-ʿēṯ ʾōhēḇ hārēaʿ; wəʾāḥ ləṣārāh yiwwālēḏ.
“A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.”
Look closely at those opening Hebrew words:
בְּכָל־עֵת — bəḵāl-ʿēṯ — “at every time,” “at all times.”
Not only when you are easy to love.
Not only when you are succeeding.
Not only when you agree.
Not only when friendship is convenient.
Not only when your life looks beautiful.
The friend loves through changing seasons.
But we sometimes misunderstand what that love requires.
We can reduce “a friend loves at all times” to something Scripture never actually says:
A friend agrees at all times.
A friend approves at all times.
A friend never confronts.
A friend never makes you uncomfortable.
A friend always validates your choices.
That is not what the proverb says.
It says the friend loves.
And biblical love is much more courageous than unconditional applause.
A few chapters later, Proverbs gives us words that can almost feel offensive to modern ears:
טוֹבָה תּוֹכַחַת מְגֻלָּה מֵאַהֲבָה מְסֻתָּרֶת
“Better an open rebuke than hidden love.”
And then:
נֶאֱמָנִים פִּצְעֵי אוֹהֵב
Neʾĕmānîm piṣʿê ʾōhēḇ...
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend...”
That word translated faithful, neʾĕmānîm, carries the sense of being reliable, trustworthy, dependable.
Think about the disturbing beauty of that.
There are wounds you can trust.
And there are kisses you cannot.
Because the rest of Proverbs 27:6 warns about the kisses of an enemy.
Not everyone who makes you feel good loves you.
And not everyone who makes you uncomfortable hates you.
Sometimes the person flattering you is protecting their access to you.
Sometimes the person correcting you is risking their access to you because they care about your soul.
That distinction matters.
But we need another distinction just as badly.
Because this verse has also been abused.
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend” does not give Christians permission to become cruel.
It is not a license to humiliate people.
It does not sanctify gossip.
It does not justify publicly exposing someone's private failure unnecessarily.
It does not turn harshness into holiness.
It does not mean, “I hurt you, therefore I must be a faithful friend.”
Some wounds are not faithful.
Some are simply wounds.
Some people call cruelty “truth.”
Some call arrogance “discernment.”
Some call humiliation “accountability.”
Some enjoy correcting people more than restoring them.
That is not the heart of Christ.
The New Testament gives us the missing posture.
When Paul describes what believers should do when someone is caught in sin, he writes:
καταρτίζετε τὸν τοιοῦτον ἐν πνεύματι πραΰτητος
Katartizete ton toiouton en pneumati prautētos.
“Restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness.”
That word καταρτίζετε — katartizete — restore matters.
The goal is not destruction.
Restoration.
Not embarrassment.
Restoration.
Not proving that you were right.
Restoration.
Not winning the argument.
Restoration.
Not collecting evidence so you can tell everyone what happened.
Restoration.
Biblical confrontation should have redemption in its bloodstream.
That changes everything.
Imagine someone you deeply love walking toward a collapsed bridge in the darkness.
You can see the road ends fifty feet ahead.
They cannot.
What does love do?
Love does not say:
“I support whatever decision makes you happy.”
Love screams:
“STOP!”
And if necessary, love runs after them.
Not because love wants control.
Because love sees danger.
Yet spiritual friendship requires humility because unlike God, we can be wrong.
Our interpretation can be wrong.
Our assumptions can be wrong.
Our timing can be wrong.
We may know only half the story.
So before confronting someone else, biblical friendship first looks into the mirror.
Paul's instruction continues by warning the restorer to watch himself lest he also be tempted.
That destroys spiritual superiority.
You do not approach a struggling friend saying:
“Look how righteous I am compared with you.”
You approach remembering:
Without the grace of Jesus Christ, I am not standing either.
That is the difference between condemnation and restoration.
Condemnation stands above someone.
Grace kneels beside them.
Condemnation says, “How could you?”
Grace remembers, “I also desperately need Christ.”
Truth without love can become brutality.
Love without truth can become sentimentality.
But Jesus gives us something infinitely better:
truth saturated with grace.
And perhaps you have been on the other side of this.
Maybe someone tried to warn you.
You became angry.
You stopped answering.
You said they were judging you.
You told yourself, “A real friend would support me.”
Months passed.
Then the thing they warned you about exploded.
The relationship collapsed.
The secret became public.
The addiction tightened its grip.
The compromise cost more than you imagined.
And sometime afterward, lying awake in the silence, you remembered that conversation.
They were not trying to destroy you.
They were trying to reach you before the destruction did.
Some of us owe someone an apology.
Not because they delivered everything perfectly.
Maybe they didn't.
But beneath their imperfect words was something increasingly rare:
a willingness to risk being misunderstood in order to tell us something we desperately needed to hear.
And some of us are living the opposite story.
We saw someone drifting.
We knew.
But we stayed quiet.
We watched their marriage deteriorate.
We watched their faith disappear beneath compromise.
We watched them become someone they once said they never wanted to become.
And we kept telling ourselves:
“It isn't my business.”
Sometimes that is wisdom. Not every situation belongs to us, and Scripture never appoints us as supervisors of everyone else's life.
But sometimes...
we knew silence was cowardice wearing the clothes of kindness.
We were afraid.
Afraid they would unfollow us.
Afraid they would stop calling.
Afraid the friendship would change.
Afraid they would say:
“Who are you to judge me?”
And perhaps the answer should have been:
“I am nobody better than you.
I am somebody who loves you.
And because I love you, I cannot pretend I don't see you bleeding.”
That is friendship.
But even that is still not the deepest picture.
Because eventually every Christian discussion about friendship must arrive at Jesus.
On the night before the cross, Christ told His disciples:
Αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ ἐμὴ ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους καθὼς ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς.
“This is My commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.”
Then:
μείζονα ταύτης ἀγάπην οὐδεὶς ἔχει...
“Greater love has no one than this...”
that someone lays down his life for his friends.
Jesus did not merely describe friendship.
He walked toward a cross.
And here the Gospel exposes every shallow version of love we have created.
Jesus loves sinners.
But His love does not tell sinners that sin doesn't matter.
He calls people to repentance because sin does matter.
He exposes darkness because He came to rescue us from darkness.
He forgives sin at immeasurable cost.
At Calvary, grace did not pretend our rebellion was harmless.
Grace paid for it.
Jesus Christ was crucified and rose again so guilty people could be forgiven, reconciled to God, made new, and brought from death into life.
That is why Christian friendship can never mean helping someone become comfortable in the very thing Christ came to save them from.
And it can never mean treating struggling sinners as though we ourselves never needed saving.
We all come to the cross empty-handed.
Maybe that is what someone reading this needs right now.
Not another motivational quote.
Not another person telling you everything is okay when somewhere deep inside you know it isn't.
Maybe you need a friend courageous enough to ask:
“How is your soul... really?”
Not your Facebook.
Not your career.
Not your church attendance.
Not your public image.
Your soul.
What are you hiding?
What are you feeding?
What are you becoming?
What would you immediately delete if someone asked to see your phone?
What relationship are you protecting even though you know it is pulling you away from Christ?
What resentment have you renamed “boundaries” because admitting it is bitterness would require repentance?
What habit have you renamed “struggling” even though you have stopped fighting it?
What compromise are you hoping Jesus will ignore?
And maybe the most frightening question:
Who have you pushed away because they loved you enough to notice?
Do not run from conviction.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
For those who belong to Christ, the Gospel does not end with your scandal.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
He had promised loyalty and then collapsed under pressure.
Yet the resurrected Jesus did not discard Peter.
He restored him.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Failure does not have to write the final chapter.
Your worst night does not have to become your permanent name.
Your hidden sin does not have to remain hidden until it destroys you.
Your shame does not have authority to finish your story.
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
Come back.
Receive mercy.
Let Christ restore what sin has been dismantling.
Because this is what grace does:
It tells the truth about the scandal...
and then refuses to let the scandal have the final word.
Again.
And again.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps biblical friendship means becoming the kind of person who participates in that restoration.
The friend who stays when tears become inconvenient.
The friend who listens before assuming.
The friend who refuses to gossip about what was confessed in vulnerability.
The friend who prays when everyone else speculates.
The friend who celebrates repentance rather than permanently defining someone by failure.
The friend who says, “I love you too much to lie to you.”
And then proves that love by staying nearby while healing begins.
We need friends who can celebrate with us.
But we also need friends who can sit across the table, hands trembling because they know what the conversation may cost, and whisper:
“I need to tell you something because I love you.”
We need friends who will not abandon us in adversity.
And we need friends who will sometimes tell us that we are creating our own adversity.
We need friends who will put an arm around our shoulder.
And occasionally friends who will stand in front of the door we are determined to walk through and plead:
“Please don't do this.”
If someone like that exists in your life, do not casually throw them away.
Listen.
Test their words against Scripture.
Pray.
Look for humility and godly fruit.
And if they are wrong, respond with grace.
But if they are right...
have the courage to repent.
Some of the greatest gifts God gives us do not initially feel like gifts.
Sometimes they feel like uncomfortable conversations.
If this article exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to explain your entire story publicly.
But you can take one small step out of hiding.

And if God has used a faithful friend to pull you back from something that could have destroyed you, tell that testimony. Someone reading the comments may desperately need proof that correction can become mercy when Christ is at the center of it.
Then think of one person.
You already know who.
The friend who is struggling quietly.
The believer who is drifting.
The person carrying shame.
The person who has confused affirmation with love.
The person who thinks their scandal means Jesus could never want them again.
Not merely to increase a number.
Because someday you may need to read it again before having one of the hardest conversations of your life.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases blessing, salvation, forgiveness, or spiritual status.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
Christian generosity is to come willingly, not under compulsion.
But voluntary financial support can be a meaningful way to participate in Gospel-centered work you genuinely believe is bearing good fruit.
If you believe this work should continue...
if these messages have strengthened you...
if you want more people to encounter Scripture, conviction, grace, repentance, healing, and the hope found in Jesus...
And whether or not you are able to support financially, you can still help tremendously.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite lukewarm Christians.
Invite the person who doesn't even believe yet.
Because sometimes evangelism begins with something as ordinary as pressing Share and trusting God with who sees it.
And before you leave this page, ask yourself one final question.
Not whether you have many friends.
Not whether people like you.
Not whether you have people who agree with you.
Ask:
Do I have someone in my life who loves Jesus, loves me, and loves me enough to tell me the truth—and am I humble enough to listen when they do?
Then turn the question around.
Am I becoming that kind of friend?
A friend who loves at all times.
A friend who appears in adversity.
A friend whose truth is gentle.
A friend whose correction aims at restoration.
A friend who refuses both cowardly silence and self-righteous cruelty.
A friend who keeps pointing wounded people toward the One Friend who carried wounds for them.
Jesus.
Because eventually every faithful Christian friendship should point beyond itself.
Beyond the advice.
Beyond the late-night conversations.
Beyond the tears.
Beyond the correction.
Beyond the restoration.
To the Savior who knew the ugliest truth about us and still went to the cross.
He did not flatter us into destruction.
He loved us unto death.
And He rose again so scandal would never need to be the final sentence for anyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
Sometimes the friend who loves you most is the one willing to risk losing your approval so you don't lose yourself—and the greatest Friend of all gave His life so you could finally be found.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re Still Trying to Make a Dead Parent Finally Be Proud of You.
paragraphs: You’re Still Trying to Make a Dead Parent Finally Be Proud of You.

They may have been gone for years. But somewhere inside you, the child who never heard “I’m proud of you” may still be running, achieving, proving, performing… hoping an absent voice will finally say the words death made impossible.
There is a strange kind of grief nobody warns you about.
It is not simply missing someone who died.
Sometimes it is missing what you never received from them while they were alive.
And those are two very different graves.
Maybe your mother is gone.
Maybe your father is gone.
Maybe everybody remembers them fondly. They tell stories at family gatherings. They post old photographs on birthdays. They say how much they miss them.
And you miss them too.
But buried underneath your grief is something harder to admit.
You are still waiting.
Still waiting for the conversation that never happened.
Still waiting for the apology.
Still waiting for the embrace.
Still waiting for them to notice how hard you tried.
Still waiting to hear...
“I see you.”
“You did well.”
“I’m proud of you.”
“I should have told you that more.”
Maybe you stood beside their coffin and something inside you realized with terrifying finality:
They are never going to say it now.
Yet somehow...
you kept trying to earn it.
That is the wound we need to talk about.
Because your parent may have died...
but the audition didn’t.
You got the promotion.
You bought the house.
You raised the children.
You survived things nobody knows about.
You became responsible.
Dependable.
Successful.
Useful.
Strong.
Maybe you became the person everybody calls when life falls apart.
And somewhere beneath all of that achievement is still a little boy saying, “Dad, look what I did.”
Or a little girl whispering, “Mom, did I finally become someone you could be proud of?”
Nobody hears that voice.
Maybe even you stopped hearing it.
But it may still be directing your life.
That is what makes unresolved approval so powerful.
You can bury a parent without burying your need for their blessing.
You can grieve them and still be angry with them.
You can love them and still acknowledge what they failed to give you.
You can forgive them and still discover wounds that need the healing of Christ.
You can stand at a graveside as an adult while something inside you feels eight years old again.
And perhaps the most painful realization is this:
Some of us are spending our lives trying to win an argument with someone who is no longer here.
“See? I became somebody.”
“See? I wasn’t worthless.”
“See? I proved you wrong.”
“See what I accomplished?”
“Would you love me now?”
And then Scripture walks into that room with a question that sounds almost uncomfortably direct.
Paul writes in Galatians 1:10:
The Greek presses even closer:
“Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω ἢ τὸν θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν;”
Arti gar anthrōpous peithō ē ton theon? ē zētō anthrōpois areskein?
In context, Paul is defending the Gospel he received and proclaiming that his allegiance is not governed by human approval. The issue is bigger than insecurity. It is lordship.
Who gets the final vote over who you are?
People?
Or God?
That question becomes devastating when the person whose approval controlled you was your own parent.
Because parental approval is not inherently evil.
A child should be loved.
A child should be encouraged.
A child should hear words that strengthen rather than crush.
A father telling his son, “I’m proud of the man you’re becoming,” can become a memory he carries for decades.
A mother delighting in her daughter can give that girl a sense of safety no trophy can reproduce.
Wanting those things was not weakness.
You were not wrong for wanting to be loved.
The wound began when something good became something ultimate.
When their approval became the courtroom where your worth was continually being tried.
Maybe Dad only noticed excellence.
So you became excellent.
Maybe Mom compared you with your siblings.
So life became a competition.
Maybe affection appeared only when you accomplished something.
So accomplishment became your language for asking to be loved.
Maybe mistakes brought humiliation.
So now failure feels almost unbearable.
Maybe your parent rarely praised you, and whenever you brought home something good, there was always another question.
Why not higher?
Why not first place?
Why not more?
Why can’t you be like them?
And eventually you stopped bringing home report cards.
You started bringing home a life.
Degrees.
Money.
Titles.
Ministry accomplishments.
Children who behave well.
A respectable marriage.
A carefully maintained reputation.
Even spirituality can become part of the performance.
You can serve at church because you love Jesus...
and still secretly need everybody to recognize that you matter.
You can preach Christ while craving applause.
You can give generously while needing somebody to notice.
You can become indispensable because being needed feels dangerously similar to being loved.
That is why Galatians 1:10 cannot remain a decorative Bible verse.
It asks us something.
Whose approval has become your master?
Because Paul ends with an extraordinary expression:
“Χριστοῦ δοῦλος”
Christou doulos.
A servant—a bondservant—of Christ.
That changes everything.
Paul is not saying healthy relationships do not matter.
He is saying human approval cannot occupy Christ’s throne.
And maybe that is where Jesus is meeting you right now.
Not at the polished version of your life.
Not at the awards.
Not at the career.
Not at the ministry statistics.
Not at the bank balance.
Not at the house.
Not at the image everybody else admires.
Jesus is walking toward the child underneath all of it.
The one still holding something up toward an empty chair.
“Look what I did.”
And Christ is not mocking that child.
He is not shaming your longing.
He is exposing the throne that longing quietly built.
Because He loves you too much to let a dead person remain the functional judge of a life Jesus purchased with His own blood.
Read that again.
A dead person does not get to be the final judge of a life Jesus purchased with His blood.
Your father may never tell you what you needed to hear.
Your mother may never come back and explain herself.
There may be no final conversation.
No corrected childhood.
No handwritten letter discovered in a drawer.
No hidden recording.
No miraculous earthly resolution.
Some doors really do close.
Christian hope does not require pretending otherwise.
But the Gospel gives you something infinitely greater than rewriting yesterday.
It gives you a new identity today.
Before Jesus began His public ministry, before the miracles multiplied, before Calvary, the Father declared His pleasure in His beloved Son.
And through faith, our life becomes bound to Christ.
Paul writes elsewhere that those who belong to Jesus receive adoption as God’s children.
That does not mean God becomes a sentimental replacement for whatever our earthly parents failed to be.
It means something much greater.
Your deepest identity is no longer decided by the verdict of human beings.
Not even the human beings whose voices shaped you first.
In Christ, you belong to God.
You do not become valuable because you finally perform well enough.
Grace destroys that transaction.
The Gospel says you could never perform well enough to save yourself.
Neither could I.
Sin is deeper than insecurity.
Our problem is not merely that people failed to approve of us.
Our problem is that we have sinned against a holy God.
We have worshiped created things.
We have built identities around success, approval, control, pleasure, reputation and self.
We have tried to justify ourselves.
And then Jesus Christ stepped into the scandal.
The sinless Son of God carried the judgment sinners deserved.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
Forgiveness is therefore not a trophy for people who finally became impressive.
It is grace for people who finally stop pretending they can save themselves.
That means you can stop presenting your résumé to the grave.
You can stop whispering your achievements toward someone who cannot answer.
You can stop building monuments out of accomplishments hoping they will somehow travel backward through time and change what your childhood felt like.
Jesus is not asking you to prove that you deserved more love.
He is calling you to Himself.
Maybe your father would have been proud if you earned another million.
Maybe not.
Maybe your mother would finally have approved if you became thinner, richer, more successful, more respected, more religious.
Maybe not.
There was always going to be another finish line.
But Christ does not stand at the next finish line.
Christ stands at the cross.
And the cross destroys our illusion that salvation, identity and righteousness can be achieved.
You come empty-handed.
You repent.
You believe.
You receive grace.
And suddenly the question governing your life begins to change.
Not...
“Would Dad finally be proud?”
Not...
“Would Mom finally approve?”
But...
“Lord Jesus, are You being glorified in me?”
That is freedom.
Not indifference.
Not dishonoring your parents.
Not erasing your memories.
Not pretending the wound never existed.
Freedom is being able to remember them without continuing to perform for them.
Freedom is visiting the grave without bringing your résumé.
Freedom is succeeding without needing success to prove you deserved love.
Freedom is failing without believing failure has erased your worth.
Freedom is forgiving without calling evil good.
Freedom is grieving what you never received without allowing that absence to become your god.
And perhaps forgiveness is part of what Jesus is asking from you.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending your parent did everything right.
It does not require calling neglect loving.
It does not mean abuse was acceptable.
It does not mean boundaries were sinful.
It does not require inventing an apology they never made.
Biblical forgiveness is not historical revisionism.
It is surrendering vengeance and judgment to God.
Sometimes the person who wounded us dies before reconciliation happens.
That leaves a peculiar ache because there is no longer an earthly possibility of hearing, “I was wrong.”
But you do not need their confession before you can begin bringing your wound to Christ.
You can tell Jesus the truth.
“I wanted him to love me.”
“I wanted her to choose me.”
“I wanted them to notice.”
“I wanted just one moment when I didn’t have to earn affection.”
“I am angry.”
“I miss them.”
“I forgive them.”
“I don’t know how to forgive them.”
“Jesus, help me.”
Prayer does not need impressive vocabulary when your heart is bleeding.
Maybe repentance is also necessary.
Because wounded people can turn wounds into idols.
We can spend decades demanding from success what only Christ can give.
We can punish spouses for not supplying the affirmation our parents withheld.
We can pressure children to become evidence that our lives mattered.
We can chase money because money cannot criticize us.
We can become addicted to recognition because applause temporarily silences the old voice.
We can even resent God because He did not give us the parent we thought we needed.
Bring that into the light too.
Jesus already knows.
Grace is not frightened by the truth.
This is what Christ does.
He does not merely decorate our scars.
He redeems sinners.
He confronts what enslaves us, forgives what condemns us, heals what has been wounded, and begins transforming what sin distorted.
This is why our message has always been bigger than inspiration.
From scandal to grace...
because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By refusing to let the scandal write the final sentence.
Maybe your story began with rejection.
Jesus can still write redemption.
Maybe it began with abandonment.
Jesus can still write belonging.
Maybe your father died before saying the words.
Maybe your mother left you with questions that will remain unanswered on this side of eternity.
Jesus can still write freedom.
Your history matters.
But your history is not your Messiah.
Jesus is.
And if this exposed something you have hidden even from yourself, you do not need to write your entire story publicly.
But perhaps you need to stop pretending.
Your testimony may become permission for another grieving adult to finally tell the truth.
There may be someone reading the comments tonight who has spent forty years thinking they were the only one.
Do not underestimate what honesty surrendered to Jesus can do.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because someone on your Facebook friends list may be celebrating promotions, posting family photographs, buying things, working endlessly, smiling publicly...
while privately still trying to impress a parent buried years ago.
Send it privately if tagging them publicly would expose something that is not yours to expose.
Sometimes sharing truth is ministry.
Sometimes one click puts the Gospel in front of a person who would never walk into a church asking for help.
Because old approval wounds do not always surrender in one emotional moment.
You may need these words again when you succeed.
You may need them when you fail.
You may need them on your parent’s birthday.
You may need them on the anniversary of their death.
You may need to remember:
You are no longer required to spend your life auditioning before an empty chair.
It does not.
Not because giving purchases blessing.
It does not.
Not because anyone should pressure you into proving your love for God with money.
Scripture says giving is to come from the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary generosity can genuinely support Gospel work.

Give to your local church and practice Christian generosity according to Scripture, conscience and faithful biblical conviction. If you prayerfully choose to include Gospel Warrior among the ministries you support, receive our gratitude.
It is mission.
It is helping more wounded people encounter Scripture.
Helping another exhausted believer find biblical encouragement at 2:00 in the morning.
Helping another person discover a free Christian book they could not otherwise afford.

Helping us continue writing the uncomfortable articles that do not merely tell people they are wonderful, but lovingly point sinners and sufferers toward repentance, grace, forgiveness, healing, discipleship and Jesus Christ.
Pray for the ministry.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
Because this was never supposed to end with Gospel Warrior.
It must end where the Gospel ends...
with Christ.
Maybe tonight you finally need to say something you have been afraid to say.
“Dad, I loved you. But I cannot keep living for your approval.”
“Mom, I miss you. But I cannot keep measuring myself by what you never gave me.”
“I forgive you.”
“I release what I cannot change.”
“And Jesus...
I belong to You.”
You may cry when you say it.
Let yourself cry.
Those tears do not mean you loved your parent too much.
They may mean you are finally admitting how much you wanted to be loved by them.
Then look toward Christ.
The One who knows every secret motive.
Every achievement.
Every failure.
Every childhood memory.
Every funeral.
Every sentence you wish had been spoken.
Every question that followed you home from the cemetery.
He knows.
And He is still calling you away from the exhausting courtroom of human approval and into wholehearted allegiance to Himself.
You cannot go backward and make your childhood different.
You cannot make the dead speak.
You cannot earn yesterday’s missing affirmation tomorrow.
But through Jesus Christ, yesterday does not have to own tomorrow.
So put down the trophy.
Put down the résumé.
Put down the imaginary conversation.
Put down the lifelong audition.
The chair is empty.
But the throne is not.
You spent years hoping an absent parent would finally tell you who you are. The cross is calling you to stop asking the grave for a verdict Jesus Christ has already claimed the right to give.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “I Have Plans to Prosper You” — The Jeremiah 29:11 Promise We Keep Quoting Without Hearing
paragraphs: “I Have Plans to Prosper You” — The Jeremiah 29:11 Promise We Keep Quoting Without Hearing
What if one of the most comforting verses in the Bible becomes even more powerful when you discover that God never promised what many of us thought He promised?
You have probably seen the words framed on a wall.
Printed on a graduation card.
Written beneath a photograph of someone beginning a new career.
Quoted when the business finally takes off.
Whispered when somebody desperately needs to believe that a financial breakthrough is coming.
“For I know the plans I have for you…”
We know the rest.
Plans to prosper you.
Plans not to harm you.
Plans to give you hope and a future.
Jeremiah 29:11.
Beautiful.
But imagine hearing those words while living hundreds of miles from the home you lost.
Imagine your city conquered.
Your familiar world shattered.
Your people carried into exile.
Imagine praying every night for God to change your circumstances—and then discovering that God has just told you something you never wanted to hear:
You are going to be here for a while.
Not seven days.
Not seven months.
Seventy years.
And right there…
in Babylon…
God says:
“I know the plans I have for you.”
Suddenly Jeremiah 29:11 sounds different.
And perhaps that is exactly why somebody reading this needs it tonight.
Because maybe you believed that if God really had plans for you, your life would look better by now.
Maybe you prayed.
You waited.
You stayed faithful as long as you knew how.
And still the marriage hurt.
The door stayed closed.
The diagnosis frightened you.
The person you loved walked away.
The opportunity disappeared.
The money became tighter.
The temptation returned.
The loneliness got louder.
You watched other people celebrate prayers you are still waiting for God to answer.
And somewhere beneath all the Christian language you know how to say, there is a question you have been afraid to speak aloud:
“God… if You really have good plans for me, why does my life look like Babylon?”
That question takes us closer to Jeremiah 29:11 than the prosperity slogan ever could.
Because Jeremiah was not writing to people standing on the edge of an easy promotion.
He was writing to exiles.
And before we make their promise about our comfort, we need to hear what God actually told them.
“Build houses…”
“Plant gardens…”
Marry.
Raise families.
Multiply.
Seek the welfare of the city where you have been carried.
Pray for it.
In other words:
Live faithfully here.
Not because Babylon is your ultimate home.
Not because exile is good.
Not because suffering suddenly stops hurting.
But because God has not stopped being God simply because you are living somewhere you never wanted to be.
Then comes the sentence many people skip.
Jeremiah 29:10.
Seventy years.
Only after speaking about that long period does God give the promise we love to quote.
The Hebrew text of Jeremiah 29:11 reads:
כִּי אָנֹכִי יָדַעְתִּי אֶת־הַמַּחֲשָׁבֹת אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי חֹשֵׁב עֲלֵיכֶם נְאֻם־יְהוָה מַחְשְׁבוֹת שָׁלוֹם וְלֹא לְרָעָה לָתֵת לָכֶם אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה׃
At the center is a word Christians desperately need to recover:
שָׁלוֹם
Shalom.
Many English readers encounter this through the familiar phrase “plans to prosper you.”
But shalom is far richer than “God intends to make me wealthy.”
It carries the world of peace, welfare, soundness, completeness, well-being, wholeness.
That changes everything.
God was not standing over devastated exiles promising every individual a luxury house, exploding bank account, painless life, immediate promotion, or trouble-free future.
He was declaring His faithful intention toward His covenant people.
Their disaster would not have the final word.
Babylon would not have the final word.
Exile would not have the final word.
Judgment would not have the final word.
God would.
And then comes another breathtaking Hebrew phrase:
אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה
acharit ve-tiqvah.
A future—an end, an outcome—and a hope.
The word acharit can speak of what comes afterward, the latter end, the outcome, the future.
Think about that.
They were staring at what looked like the end.
God was looking beyond it.
They could see Babylon.
God could see afterward.
They could see displacement.
God could see restoration.
They could see the chapter that had broken them.
God could already see pages they had not lived yet.
Maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because you have been judging the entire story by the page you are currently bleeding on.
You called it the ending because you could not see another chapter.
You thought God had abandoned the manuscript because the paragraph became dark.
But Jeremiah 29:11 does not teach us that faithful people never enter Babylon.
It teaches us that Babylon cannot cancel the purposes of God.
There is a difference.
Sometimes prosperity looks like getting the thing you prayed for.
Sometimes shalom looks like God keeping your soul alive when you did not get it.
Sometimes it is an open door.
Sometimes it is enough grace to stand in front of a closed one without abandoning Christ.
Sometimes it is healing.
Sometimes it is Christ holding you while you hurt.
Sometimes it is abundance.
Sometimes it is learning, like Paul, that Christ remains sufficient in abundance and in need.
Sometimes God changes the circumstances.
Sometimes, before the circumstances change, God changes the person walking through them.
And that transformation may be worth more than the comfortable life you originally asked Him to give you.
That does not mean suffering is secretly pleasant.
The Bible never requires us to pretend pain does not hurt.
Jesus wept.
Jesus grieved.
Jesus experienced rejection.
Jesus knew betrayal.
Jesus prayed in Gethsemane beneath an anguish so terrible that no shallow prosperity message could survive beside Him.
And Christianity reaches its center not at a palace but at a cross.
That matters.
Because if “prosperity” means that God’s favor guarantees the avoidance of suffering, then we would eventually have to explain the crucified Son of God.
Jesus was perfectly loved by the Father…
and He suffered.
Perfectly obedient…
and rejected.
Perfectly righteous…
and crucified.
The cross destroys the lie that suffering automatically means God has abandoned you.
Then the resurrection destroys the lie that suffering gets the last word.
There is the Gospel.
There is our hope.
Jesus does not merely offer us a better version of our old life.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
We had a deeper exile than Babylon.
Sin had separated humanity from the holy God.
Our greatest problem was never that our dreams were taking too long.
Our greatest problem was sin.
And our greatest need was never merely prosperity.
We needed forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A Savior.
Jesus Christ took upon Himself the judgment sinners deserve, died for our sins, and rose again.
Grace entered the scandal.
Mercy entered the wreckage.
The tomb received a dead Savior on Friday and stood empty on Sunday.
That is why the Christian can look at a ruined chapter and refuse to call it the whole story.
Because Jesus Christ specializes in resurrection.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From death to life.
From wandering to reconciliation.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And notice what comes immediately after Jeremiah 29:11.
The next great movement is not:
“You will become rich.”
It is:
You will call upon Me.
You will pray to Me.
You will seek Me.
And you will find Me when you seek Me with all your heart.
There it is.
Perhaps the greatest prosperity in the passage is not finally receiving something from God's hand.
It is returning to God Himself.
What if the season you keep begging God to remove is exposing how many things you wanted more than Him?
What if you wanted His blessing but barely wanted His presence?
His provision but not His holiness?
His promises but not His commands?
His rescue but not His lordship?
Heaven someday, but control today?
We can turn Jeremiah 29:11 into a promise that God will finance our dreams while completely missing the God who calls His people to seek Him with their whole heart.
And perhaps this is where the verse stops being decoration and becomes confrontation.
What are you really asking God to prosper?
Your bank account?
Your plans?
Your reputation?
Your platform?
Your comfort?
Or your soul?
Because you can have money and still be spiritually bankrupt.
You can own a beautiful house and have no peace inside it.
You can have thousands of followers and be terrified of being alone.
You can become successful enough to impress everyone who doubted you and still lie awake at night wondering why victory feels so empty.
You can gain the world and lose your soul.
Jesus warned us about that.
Biblical shalom is deeper.
It is not a Lamborghini with a Bible verse taped to the dashboard.
It is life being brought under the reign and goodness of God.
And the Gospel goes deeper still: through Christ, enemies of God are reconciled to Him.
The prosperity gospel says, in effect, “Come to Jesus and He can make your life successful.”
The Gospel says something infinitely greater:
Come to Jesus because Jesus is Lord.
Come guilty and receive mercy.
Come stained and be washed.
Come spiritually dead and receive life.
Come carrying sins you cannot undo and meet the Savior whose blood is sufficient to forgive.
Come with the chapter you are ashamed to let anybody read.
Bring Him the addiction.
The pride.
The secret messages.
The pornography.
The bitterness.
The affair.
The greed.
The religious performance.
The years you wasted.
The hidden envy.
The secret unbelief.
The version of yourself you carefully keep away from church people.
Bring the scandal into the light.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because it mattered enough for Christ to die.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the sinner finally dropping the shovel they have been using to dig their own grave and running toward the One who conquered death.
Maybe your Babylon is not merely something that happened to you.
Maybe part of it is something you created.
There are consequences you cannot blame on Satan.
Relationships you damaged.
Warnings you ignored.
Compromises you justified.
People you wounded.
Years you cannot retrieve.
And now you are asking:
“Can God still write something beautiful after what I did?”
Look at the cross.
The answer to our sin is not pretending the scandal never happened.
The answer is grace purchased at an unimaginable price.
God does not call evil good.
He forgives repentant sinners through Christ and begins transforming them.
That is better than pretending.
That is redemption.
And perhaps somebody needs to hear this without another cliché:
The chapter you hate may be real without being final.
Your tears are real.
Your consequences may be real.
Your waiting may be real.
Your grief is real.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, despair does not own the copyright to your ending.
Christ does.
This does not mean every earthly dream will eventually come true.
Jeremiah 29:11 gives us no permission to promise that.
Some prayers are answered differently from how we hoped.
Some losses remain losses this side of resurrection.
Some faithful Christians die without seeing the earthly resolution they longed for.
Christian hope is stronger than “everything will work out exactly how I want.”
Our hope is Christ.
Our sins can be forgiven.
God can be known.
Death has been defeated.
Christ is risen.
And those who belong to Him have a future no Babylon, cancer, bankruptcy, betrayal, persecution, grave, demon, failure, or earthly empire can finally steal.
That is not smaller than the popular interpretation of Jeremiah 29:11.
It is infinitely bigger.
So perhaps you do not need God to promise you that next year will make you rich.
Perhaps tonight you need something stronger:
God is still God in Babylon.
Christ is still Savior in the wreckage.
Grace is still available after the scandal.
Repentance still leads home.
The cross still speaks forgiveness.
The tomb is still empty.
And your darkest chapter does not possess authority over Jesus Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest.
Or if you are living through a season that feels like exile and you are still choosing to trust Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
Not as a performance.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending everything is fine.
And somebody reading the comments may discover they are not the only Christian who has cried in the dark.
If you know someone who has been treating suffering as proof that God abandoned them, send this to them.
The exhausted mother.
The father carrying financial pressure silently.
The believer fighting an old addiction.
The friend whose marriage collapsed.
The person who stopped going to church because disappointment hardened into distance.
The Christian who has been smiling publicly while privately asking whether God still sees them.
Let sharing become more than an algorithm.
Let it become ministry.
Because there may come a night when you need these words again.
A night when your circumstances start interpreting God for you.
A night when silence feels like abandonment.
A night when Babylon becomes so loud that you forget the God who sees beyond it.
Come back and remember:
Shalom.
God's purposes are larger than your immediate comfort.
Achariyth.
There is an afterward you cannot yet see.
Tiqvah.
There is hope.
And ultimately, for the Christian, hope has a name.
Jesus.

If Gospel Warrior has been helping you understand Scripture more deeply, return to Christ, confront sin honestly, endure suffering faithfully, and grow in biblical truth, you can also help this work continue.

Supporting Gospel ministry should never be manipulated out of anyone. Scripture teaches believers to give willingly rather than under compulsion. Your responsibilities to your local church, family, and the needs God has placed before you matter.
But hear this clearly:
The blood of Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift in Christ.

If you support, support freely, prayerfully, gratefully, and because you want to help biblical truth reach another wounded person scrolling through Facebook at midnight wondering whether God has forgotten their name.
Share.
Pray.
Save these messages.
Use them.
Share them.
Give them to somebody hungry for truth.
Let the resources travel farther than we ever could.
Because somewhere tonight, someone thinks Babylon means God has forgotten them.
Someone thinks their scandal has written the ending.
Someone believes their failure is stronger than grace.
Someone has mistaken waiting for abandonment.
Someone is one more disappointment away from giving up.

And perhaps God will use something as ordinary as your share, your comment, your invitation, your prayer, or your voluntary support to put Gospel truth in front of that person at exactly the moment they need to hear it.
Jeremiah 29:11 was never a blank check promising that every believer would become wealthy.
It was spoken into exile.
That is precisely why it is so beautiful.
God knew where His people were.
God knew how long the road would be.
God knew what Babylon looked like.
And God could see beyond what they could see.
So if you are in Babylon tonight…
build faithfully.
Pray faithfully.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek God with your whole heart.
Do not worship the blessing.
Do not worship the breakthrough.
Do not worship the future.
Seek the One who holds it.
And when your heart whispers, “This is how my story ends,” look toward the cross.
Then look toward the empty tomb.
Your hope was never that life would contain no Friday.
Your hope is that Jesus walked out of the grave on Sunday.
Remember this when the night gets long:
Babylon may be where this chapter happens, but Babylon does not get to write the final sentence.
Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BABYLON DRESSED LIKE DESIRE: Why Revelation Portrays Corrupt Power as a Prostitute—and Why Her Seduction May Be Closer Than You Think
paragraphs: BABYLON DRESSED LIKE DESIRE: Why Revelation Portrays Corrupt Power as a Prostitute—and Why Her Seduction May Be Closer Than You Think
Revelation 17 does not merely show us a wicked woman. It exposes a world that has learned how to make rebellion beautiful, compromise profitable, and spiritual adultery feel completely normal.
There is something disturbing about the woman John sees.
Not simply because she is evil.
Because she is beautiful.
She does not crawl out of the darkness looking like a monster.
She arrives dressed in purple and scarlet.
Gold glitters against her body.
Precious stones catch the light.
Pearls announce wealth, status, luxury.
There is a golden cup in her hand.
Kings want her.
Nations drink from her.
The powerful cooperate with her.
And people become intoxicated by what she offers.
Then John sees what is really inside the cup.
And suddenly the beauty becomes horrifying.
Revelation 17 opens with words deliberately designed to disturb us:
“Δεῦρο, δείξω σοι τὸ κρίμα τῆς πόρνης τῆς μεγάλης…”
Deuro, deixō soi to krima tēs pornēs tēs megalēs…
“Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute…”
The Greek word is πόρνη — pornē.
It means a prostitute.
Then Revelation speaks of πορνεία — porneia, sexual immorality or prostitution.
John is not softening the picture.
He is making it unforgettable.
But this is where we must read Revelation carefully.
The woman is not presented merely to condemn sexual sinners, and Revelation 17 is certainly not permission to despise women or people trapped in sexual sin.
The woman is a symbol.

The chapter itself eventually tells us that she represents “the great city” exercising dominion over the kings of the earth. The sexual imagery therefore becomes prophetic imagery for something much larger: corrupt civilization seducing humanity away from faithfulness to God.
And that changes everything.
Because Babylon's greatest weapon is not simply persecution.
It is seduction.
Think about that.
Satan does not always need to make you hate God.
Sometimes he only needs to give you something you begin to love more than God.
He does not always need to drag someone screaming away from Jesus.
Sometimes all he needs to do is make compromise attractive enough that the person walks away willingly.
That is Babylon.
Babylon smiles.
Babylon offers the cup.
Babylon tells you that everybody is drinking.
Babylon whispers that obedience is too expensive.
Babylon asks why you should remain faithful when compromise could make your life easier.
And perhaps this is why God chose sexual imagery.
