Because throughout Scripture, God describes His relationship with His people using the deeply personal language of covenant faithfulness.
Sin is therefore more than breaking regulations.
Idolatry is more than choosing the wrong religious object.
There is betrayal involved.
Something relational has been violated.
Long before John saw Babylon in Revelation, the prophets used similar imagery.
Isaiah cried over Jerusalem:
“How is the faithful city become an harlot!”
The Hebrew is piercing:
אֵיכָה הָיְתָה לְזוֹנָה קִרְיָה נֶאֱמָנָה
ʾÊkhāh hāyetāh lezōnāh qiryāh neʾĕmānāh.
Literally, the shock is something like:
“How has the faithful city become a prostitute?”
But notice what Isaiah immediately connects with that betrayal.
The city that should have been filled with justice had become associated with bloodshed and corruption.
In other words, biblical “prostitution” imagery can expose not only idolatrous worship but social and moral corruption—the betrayal of justice itself.
Ezekiel 16 develops the imagery even further.
God describes Jerusalem as receiving beauty, provision, clothing, jewelry, food, and honor from Him—and then taking those very gifts and turning them toward idolatry.
That is one of the terrifying patterns of Babylon.
It takes gifts from God and teaches us to worship the gifts instead of the Giver.
Beauty becomes an idol.
Money becomes an idol.
Influence becomes an idol.
Sex becomes an idol.
Politics becomes an idol.
Success becomes an idol.
Comfort becomes an idol.
Even ministry can become an idol.
Even knowledge about God can become something we use to avoid actually surrendering to God.
The tragedy is not simply that people possess good things.
The tragedy begins when good things possess people.
That is why Revelation's woman is covered in wealth.
The gold is not the sin.
The pearls are not the sin.
Purple fabric is not the sin.
The horror is what all that splendor conceals.
A golden cup can still contain poison.
That may be one of Revelation 17's most frightening warnings to modern Christians.
We have become very good at judging things by their packaging.
If something is successful, we assume God approves.
If something becomes popular, we assume it must be good.
If everyone celebrates it, we become afraid to question it.
If compromise makes us richer, more comfortable, more accepted, or more powerful, we can become remarkably talented at renaming compromise “wisdom.”
But Babylon has always understood branding.
She knows how to make chains look like jewelry.
She knows how to make slavery feel like freedom.
She knows how to make spiritual adultery feel like self-discovery.
She knows how to make greed sound like ambition.
She knows how to make pride sound like confidence.
She knows how to make revenge sound like justice.
She knows how to make cowardice sound like tolerance.
And she knows how to make surrender to the spirit of the age feel like progress.
This is why the woman rides a beast.
Beauty is sitting on brutality.
Seduction is riding violence.
Luxury is riding domination.
The glamorous surface hides something monstrous underneath.
And eventually John sees something even worse.
The woman is drunk.
Not with ordinary wine.
With blood.
Revelation says she is drunk with the blood of the saints and the witnesses of Jesus.
Now the mask falls.
The system that promised pleasure ultimately devours people who refuse to worship it.
The seductress becomes persecutor.
The cup becomes blood.
The party becomes judgment.

Historically, there are strong reasons many interpreters have understood Babylon in Revelation 17–18 as symbolically evoking imperial Rome. Revelation itself connects the woman with seven mountains and describes her as ruling over kings, while Rome was famously associated with seven hills. The anti-Roman interpretation has ancient Christian roots, although other interpretations have existed and Christians disagree about how the symbol relates to later or future fulfillment.
That historical setting matters.
But stopping with ancient Rome would make Revelation much safer than John intended it to be.
Because Babylon is not merely something Christians are supposed to identify on a map.

Babylon represents a recurring pattern of human civilization organized in arrogant independence from God—a seductive marriage of idolatry, wealth, domination, immorality, injustice, and opposition to God's faithful witnesses.
Babylon can wear different clothes.
The spirit of Babylon says:
You can have the kingdom without the King.
You can have prosperity without holiness.
You can have spirituality without repentance.
You can have influence without integrity.
You can have pleasure without covenant.
You can have Christianity without a cross.
And perhaps the most dangerous version says:
You can have Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
That is the lie we need to confront personally.
Because it is easy to read Revelation 17 looking for Babylon somewhere “out there.”
Some government.
Some institution.
Some religious organization.
Some economic system.
Some celebrity.
Some future world empire.
Anyone except us.
But Scripture has an uncomfortable habit of turning the mirror around.
What if Babylon's cup is already near your lips?
What if there is something you know Christ has been asking you to surrender—but you keep negotiating?
What if you would rather lose intimacy with God than lose a relationship?
What if you would rather compromise your conscience than lose money?
What if you would rather hide your faith than lose people's approval?
What if pornography has become the secret room you keep locked while publicly telling everyone Jesus owns the house?
What if bitterness has become so familiar that you no longer recognize it as bondage?
What if success matters more to you than holiness?
What if your Christian identity remains visible while your private devotion to Christ is slowly dying?
That is where Revelation stops being an argument about prophecy charts.
It becomes a confrontation.
Babylon is seductive precisely because she rarely introduces herself as Babylon.
She comes disguised as the thing you think you cannot live without.
And eventually every disciple faces the same terrifying question:
If following Jesus costs me what I desperately want, do I still want Jesus?
Sit with that.
Not the version of Christianity that gives you motivational quotations.
Not the Jesus who exists merely to improve your plans.
Not the Christ reconstructed by culture until He never confronts anyone.
Jesus.
The crucified King.
The risen Lord.
The One who forgives sinners and commands them to follow Him.
The One who touches lepers.
The One who receives the broken.
The One who confronted hypocrites.
The One who welcomed repentant sexual sinners without calling their sin righteousness.
The One who carried a cross.
The One who walked out of a grave.
The One before whom Babylon itself will eventually fall.
Do you still want Him?
Because Revelation ultimately presents two radically different women.
Babylon appears as the prostitute.
Later comes the Bride.
One seduces the world.
The other belongs to the Lamb.
One is clothed in extravagant earthly luxury.
The other is prepared for her Bridegroom.
One intoxicates nations.
The other celebrates the marriage supper of the Lamb.
One rides temporary worldly power.
The other belongs eternally to Jesus Christ.
And that means Revelation is asking:
Whose love has your heart?
There is grace hidden even inside that terrifying question.
Because maybe you have already drunk from cups you wish you could put back.
Maybe you compromised.
Maybe you slept with someone you should not have.
Maybe you betrayed your marriage.
Maybe pornography has scarred your mind.
Maybe money became your master.
Maybe ambition consumed years you cannot recover.
Maybe you manipulated people.
Maybe you traded convictions for acceptance.
Maybe you once burned for Christ, but something happened.
A wound.
A disappointment.
A secret sin.
A prayer that seemed unanswered.
And slowly...
almost imperceptibly...
your heart wandered.
Now you read words like prostitute, unfaithfulness, judgment, and something inside you whispers:
“That is me.”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not end in Revelation 17.
And your story does not have to end in your scandal.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Not polished sinners.
Not respectable sinners.
Not people who successfully concealed enough evidence.
Sinners.
At the cross, Christ bore judgment for everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
He did not shed His blood because your sin was small.
He shed His blood because His mercy is greater.
The cross does not tell us sin does not matter.
The cross tells us sin mattered enough for the Son of God to die—and that sinners mattered enough to Him that He willingly came to save them.
That is grace.
Not God pretending the betrayal never happened.
God paying the price Himself.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the burning city.
It is mercy shouting:
Come out.
Stop drinking.
Stop pretending.
Stop hiding.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop defending what Jesus died to free you from.
You do not have to clean yourself before approaching Christ.
You come exposed.
You come guilty.
You come exhausted.
You come with shaking hands if necessary.
But you come.
Because Babylon says, “Hide your shame.”
Jesus says, “Bring it into the light.”
Babylon says, “You need more.”
Jesus says, “Come to Me.”
Babylon says, “Sell your soul and you can belong.”
Jesus gave His life so that sinners could become His.
Babylon decorates slavery.
Jesus breaks chains.
Babylon drinks blood.
Jesus gave His own blood.
Do you see the difference?
Babylon consumes her lovers.
Christ dies for His enemies.
Babylon uses people.
Jesus redeems people.
Babylon promises pleasure and eventually gives death.
Jesus calls us to die to ourselves and ultimately gives life.
That is the scandal of grace.
The King whom we betrayed became the sacrifice by which traitors could be forgiven.
So maybe this article did not reach you because you needed another explanation of Revelation.
Maybe you needed a rescue.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess it.
Name it.
Repent.
Ask for help.
Return.
You do not owe strangers the private details of your struggle. But sometimes three honest words can become the moment someone stops suffering alone.
And if Christ has already brought you out of something that once owned you, tell somebody what His grace has done.
Your testimony may become another person's permission to believe that restoration is still possible.
Then think of one person who needs this message.
Not twenty random names.
One person.
The friend who is quietly compromising.
The believer who has grown cold.
The person drowning in shame.
The Christian who knows Bible verses but has slowly fallen in love with the world.
The unbeliever who assumes Christianity is nothing more than religious people condemning broken people.
Send this privately if that would be wiser.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because someone in your circle may desperately need to discover that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
There may come a night when Babylon's cup looks beautiful again.
Come back and remember what was inside it.
The purpose is not merely to build an audience.
It is to keep putting Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ where people can encounter it.
There is also another way to help this ministry continue and expand.

Scripture teaches that Gospel ministry may legitimately receive material support; Paul wrote that those proclaiming the Gospel may receive their living through Gospel work. Scripture also insists that Christian giving must not be manipulated: a believer gives willingly, not “under compulsion.”
So this invitation is not a purchase of God's favor.
It cannot buy grace.
It cannot buy salvation.
It does not make God love you more.
Supporting Gospel work can glorify God when it rises from a willing heart that desires His truth to spread.
But the merchandise is not the heart of this invitation.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is.
People are.
The exhausted believer who needs encouragement is.
The prodigal quietly reading at 2:00 in the morning is.
The person ashamed of yesterday who needs to discover that Christ still offers a tomorrow is.
Pray.
Share.
Save these messages.
Invite others to follow.
Put truth into circulation.
Because somewhere behind another screen may be a human being standing with Babylon's cup in one hand and unbearable emptiness in the other.
And perhaps one faithful share will put the Gospel in front of them before they take another drink.
Revelation 17 is frightening.
But Babylon does not receive the final word.
Jesus does.
The prostitute falls.
The Lamb reigns.
The kingdoms of this world do not remain forever.
The glitter fades.
The cup empties.
The beast falls.
The marketplace eventually closes.
Every counterfeit kingdom reaches its expiration date.
But Christ remains.
So do not envy Babylon.
Do not fear Babylon.
And do not become Babylon.
Come out of everything that requires you to betray Jesus in order to belong.
Come out of the secret compromise.
Come out of the double life.
Come out of the bitterness.
Come out of the addiction.
Come out of the worship of money.
Come out of the desperate hunger for human approval.
Come out of the beautiful lie.
There is a better Bridegroom.
There is a better Kingdom.
There is a better feast.
There is a better city.
There is a better ending.
His name is Jesus Christ.
And when He takes hold of a ruined story, yesterday's scandal does not have authority to write tomorrow's final sentence.
Babylon may decorate your chains with gold—but Jesus still knows how to break them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS ENJOYING YOUR SPOUSE’S BODY “LUST”?
paragraphs: IS ENJOYING YOUR SPOUSE’S BODY “LUST”?
The Bible’s Answer Requires a Better Definition of Lust—and It May Heal Something Shame Has Been Breaking Inside Christian Marriages for Years
There is a husband somewhere who looks at his wife and still thinks she is breathtaking.
Then he feels guilty for thinking it.

There is a wife somewhere who deeply desires her husband, loves his touch, notices his body, longs to be close to him—and somewhere along the way she absorbed the idea that being “spiritual” means becoming almost embarrassed by those feelings.
So they love Jesus.
They love each other.
They are married.
They are faithful.
And somehow, in the very place God designed for covenant intimacy, shame has crawled into the bedroom and started whispering...
“Maybe wanting your spouse this much is lust.”
That sentence sounds holy.
But is it biblical?
Because if every strong sexual desire is automatically lust, we have a serious problem.
The Bible itself celebrates marital desire.
Not reluctantly.
Not apologetically.
Not with its eyes closed.
It celebrates it with language so surprisingly physical that some Christians become uncomfortable reading it aloud.
And perhaps that discomfort reveals something.
Maybe some of us have spent so long fighting sexual sin that we accidentally began treating sexuality itself as sinful.
Those are not the same thing.
Jesus absolutely condemns lust.
Jesus absolutely confronts adultery of the heart.
Jesus absolutely calls His followers to sexual holiness.
But before we put something under the judgment of Christ, we should make sure we understand what Christ actually condemned.
Listen carefully to Matthew 5:28 in Greek:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν...”
A central word is ἐπιθυμέω—epithymeō.

It can mean to desire, long for, set one’s desire upon, or covet. The word itself is not a magical Greek synonym meaning that every experience of attraction is automatically sinful. Scripture can use this word-family for desires whose moral character depends upon their object and context.
That matters.
A lot.
Because Jesus is not teaching that the human ability to recognize beauty is adultery.
He is taking the command against adultery all the way into the heart.
Matthew 5 does not permit us to say, “I never physically committed adultery, therefore my heart is clean.”
Jesus destroys that loophole.
A person can cultivate an adulterous desire internally before committing an adulterous act externally.
Sin can begin before skin ever touches skin.
The eyes can become servants of covetousness.
The imagination can take what covenant has not given.
Another human being can become an object consumed inside the mind.
That is why Jesus’ teaching is so devastating.
He does not merely ask, “What did your body do?”
He asks what your heart is doing.
But now comes the distinction Christians desperately need.
Your spouse is not your neighbor’s spouse.
Covenant desire for your husband or wife is not identical to coveting someone outside that covenant.
In fact, Proverbs gives us language that would sound almost scandalous if we had not already been told it was Scripture.
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then Proverbs 5:19 becomes startlingly physical:
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is the King James Version.
Not a romance novel.
Not secular culture.
Proverbs.
The Hebrew behind the final image includes the verb שָׁגָה—shagah—a word capable of carrying the imagery of reeling, wandering, or being intoxicated or captivated.
Think about that.
God’s wisdom literature does not merely tolerate a husband delighting in his wife.
It tells him to be captivated by her love.
The text does not say, “Try not to notice her body.”
It specifically mentions her body.
And it places that physical delight inside marital faithfulness.
That changes the conversation completely.
The biblical opposite of sexual immorality is not necessarily sexual indifference.
It is sexual holiness.
And holiness is not the destruction of every desire.
Holiness puts desire where it belongs.
Fire in a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire consuming the curtains can destroy it.
The problem is not that fire possesses heat.
The question is where the fire is burning.
That is why Song of Songs can speak with such breathtaking freedom about physical beauty.
The lovers notice each other.
They desire each other.
They describe each other.
They long for each other.
Bodies are not treated as embarrassing accidents attached to otherwise spiritual people.
Why?
Because Christianity does not teach that the body is inherently dirty.
God created humanity embodied.
Genesis does not end the creation of male and female with God saying, “This is unfortunate but necessary.”
God looked upon His creation and called it very good.
Sin corrupted human sexuality.
Sin did not invent human sexuality.
There is an enormous difference.
And when Christians confuse those two truths, something painful happens.
A young man may spend years hearing, “Don’t look. Don’t desire. Don’t think sexually. Control yourself.”
Some of that instruction may be desperately necessary.
Pornography must be resisted.
Fornication must be resisted.
Adultery must be resisted.
Using people must be resisted.
Coveting must be resisted.
Sexual fantasy that violates covenant faithfulness must be resisted.
Then the young man gets married.
Suddenly he is supposed to understand that his wife’s body is not something dirty.
But nobody helped him distinguish sinful coveting from holy marital desire.
A Christian woman can carry another version of the same wound.
She may have been taught modesty in ways that unintentionally left her believing her body was primarily dangerous.
Something that caused men to stumble.
Something to cover.
Something about which good Christian women should remain embarrassed.
Then she marries a man who looks at her with affection and desire.
And instead of feeling cherished, part of her wonders...
“Is he being lustful?”
Sometimes, of course, there can be genuinely sinful behavior inside marriage.
Marriage is not a magic word that turns selfishness into holiness.
A wedding ring does not authorize cruelty.
Your spouse is a person to love, not an object to consume.
Biblical marital intimacy must never become justification for coercion, degradation, manipulation, humiliation, violence, betrayal, pornography, comparison with other people, or selfish entitlement.
And this is precisely where 1 Corinthians 7 becomes so important.
Paul speaks about marital intimacy with striking reciprocity.
The husband has obligations toward his wife.
The wife has obligations toward her husband.
And when Paul discusses temporary abstinence, he speaks of agreement—mutuality.
Notice how radically different this is from using another person's body.
Biblical intimacy says, in effect:
I belong to you, and you belong to me.
Not...
You exist for me.
There is tenderness in that difference.
There is covenant in that difference.
There is Christlike self-giving in that difference.
Healthy marital desire asks, “How can I love you?”
Lust distorted by sin asks, “How can I consume you?”
Love sees a person.
Sin reduces a person to a product.
Love can wait.
Sin demands.
Love honors boundaries.
Sin resents them.
Love remains faithful when circumstances change.
Objectification becomes angry when the object stops satisfying it.
Love cares about the soul attached to the body.
And this is where some marriages need more than a definition.
They need healing.
Maybe your spouse’s body has changed.
Pregnancy changed it.
Childbirth changed it.
Age changed it.
Illness changed it.
Medication changed it.
Stress changed it.
Work changed it.
Grief changed it.
Years changed it.
Your own body changed too.
The honeymoon photographs are somewhere in a drawer, and neither of you looks exactly like those two people anymore.
But covenant love was never supposed to survive only while gravity cooperated.
The world teaches desire to constantly search for novelty.
Jesus teaches covenant faithfulness.
The world says, “Upgrade.”
Covenant says, “I still choose you.”
The world trains the eyes to wander.
Grace teaches the eyes to come home.
Maybe that is one of the most beautiful things a husband can communicate to the wife who no longer feels beautiful:
“I still see you.”
Maybe that is something a wife can communicate to a husband quietly wondering whether age has made him undesirable:
“I still want you.”
There is nothing inherently unholy about those words.
Within faithful, loving marriage, they can become medicine.
Because sometimes what your spouse desperately needs is not another theological lecture about marriage.
Sometimes they need to know they are still cherished.
Still wanted.
Still beautiful to the person who promised to stay.
Proverbs does not tell the husband merely to endure the wife of his youth.
It tells him to rejoice in her.
To be satisfied in her.
To be captivated by her love.
That is not lust masquerading as marriage.
That is marital delight being directed toward covenant faithfulness.
Hebrews 13:4 says marriage is to be honored and the marriage bed kept undefiled.
Notice the biblical balance.
Marriage bed.
Undefiled.
Intimacy and holiness are not enemies.
The Bible refuses both distortions.
It refuses the culture that says, “If you desire it, do it.”
And it refuses the shame-based distortion that whispers, “If you desire anything sexually, you must be dirty.”
Jesus offers something better.
Desire redeemed by covenant.
Passion governed by love.
Bodies treated with honor.
Sexuality surrendered to Christ.
Faithfulness reaching all the way into the imagination.
And grace for sinners who have failed.
Because perhaps you are reading this and the conversation has suddenly stopped being theoretical.
Maybe your eyes have wandered.
Maybe pornography has trained your mind to consume bodies instead of love people.
Maybe you have mentally compared your spouse to images on a screen.
Maybe you have carried fantasies you would be terrified for your husband or wife to see.
Maybe you have used “marital rights” as an excuse for selfishness.
Maybe you have withheld affection as punishment.
Maybe you have rejected your spouse so repeatedly that they have begun wondering whether something is wrong with them.
Maybe shame has frozen something beautiful between you.
Maybe adultery was not merely in your imagination.
Maybe there was a message.
A conversation.
A secret account.
A hotel room.
A betrayal.
And now this article hurts.
Good.
Not because condemnation is the destination.
Because sometimes pain is what happens when light reaches an infected wound.
Jesus did not expose sin so sinners would have nowhere to go.
Jesus exposed sin and then walked toward the cross.
That is the Gospel.
Christianity is not the announcement that respectable people behaved themselves.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
For adulterers.
For the sexually broken.
For the ashamed.
For the addicted.
For the betrayed.
For the betrayer who genuinely repents.
For husbands who failed.
For wives who failed.
For people who have memories they wish they could erase.
For people who have spent years hiding behind church clothes while carrying secret chains.
Christ does not call darkness light.
Grace never requires God to lie about our sin.
He names it.
He judges it as sin.
And then at Calvary, the sinless Son of God bears judgment for sinners.
That is why repentance is not running away from Jesus.
Repentance is finally stopping your running from Jesus.
You turn around.
You confess.
You stop defending what is killing you.
You bring the hidden browser history.
The secret fantasy.
The bitterness.
The shame.
The betrayal.
The wounds.
The distorted understanding of sex.
The fear of intimacy.
The years of pretending.
You bring it into the light.
And you discover that the Savior standing there already knew.
He knew before the nails.
And He went to the cross anyway.
This does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
This does not make holiness optional.
Grace teaches us to leave sin, not rename it.
But your scandal does not have to write the final sentence of your story.
Jesus can.
From scandal...
to grace.
From secrecy...
to confession.
From objectification...
to honor.
From betrayal...
perhaps, through repentance and patient rebuilding, toward restoration.
From shame...
toward freedom.
From distorted desire...
toward desire surrendered to Christ.
So no—simply enjoying your spouse’s body is not what Scripture means when it condemns lust.
The Bible itself can celebrate marital physical delight.
The better question is not merely, “Do I experience desire?”
Ask:
What is my desire doing to the person I claim to love?
Does it honor covenant?
Does it remain faithful?
Does it recognize my spouse as an image-bearer rather than a possession?
Can it hear “not now” without becoming cruel?
Can it remain tender when bodies change?
Does it seek mutual good rather than selfish consumption?
Does it draw marriage toward faithfulness rather than importing other people into the imagination?
Can this desire stand honestly before Jesus Christ?
Those questions expose the difference between merely baptizing selfish appetite and receiving marital sexuality as something to steward under the lordship of Christ.
And maybe someone reading this has spent years feeling ashamed for loving their own husband or wife.
Hear this carefully.
You do not become holier by becoming ashamed of everything God created good.
You become holy by surrendering everything—including your sexuality—to Jesus Christ.
Desire does not need to become your master.
Neither does shame.
Christ is Lord over both.
You can simply write, “Jesus, purify my heart.”
If your marriage has been wounded but you believe Christ is still working, comment, “Christ is still healing us.”
If shame has followed you into your marriage and you are finally realizing that biblical holiness and marital affection are not enemies, comment, “Grace is teaching me.”
You do not have to publish the details of your private life.
But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
Then send this to your spouse.
Send it privately to the believer fighting pornography.
Send it to the couple trying to rebuild after betrayal.
Send it to the Christian who loves Jesus but has never been taught a biblical theology of marital desire.
Save it too.
Because culture will keep preaching about sex.
Shame will keep preaching about sex.
Pornography will keep preaching about sex.
Your past may keep preaching about sex.
You need to remember what Scripture actually says.
It cannot.
It does not.
And certainly not because God needs your money.
He does not.
Scripture says giving must not be “of necessity” or under compulsion, because God loves cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary financial partnership has long helped Gospel ministry travel farther than one person could carry it alone.
If you genuinely believe this work glorifies Christ, supporting it is one practical way you can participate in helping it continue and expand.
And sharing costs nothing.
You may never know what God does with that simple act.
Bring your desires to Christ.
Bring your marriage to Christ.
Bring your wounds to Christ.
Bring your sexuality to Christ.
Bring your secret failures to Christ.
Bring your shame to Christ.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ is calling you toward forgiveness.
Seek wise pastoral or professional help where wounds run deep.
Rebuild trust where trust has been shattered.
Honor your spouse.
Guard your eyes.
Guard your imagination.
Cherish the covenant God has entrusted to you.
And remember this when shame comes knocking again:
Jesus did not die to make you less human.
He died to redeem the human being sin had broken.
Your body belongs under His lordship.
Your desires belong under His lordship.
Your marriage belongs under His lordship.
And when Jesus becomes Lord even there—in the places Christians sometimes feel too embarrassed to discuss—shame no longer gets to write the ending.
Because the deepest question was never simply whether you desired.
It was whether your desire had learned to love.
And when even the most wounded places of your life are surrendered to Christ, the sentence shame thought was final can become the place where grace begins writing again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN SEXUAL TEMPTATION BECOME STRONGER AFTER MARRIAGE?
paragraphs: CAN SEXUAL TEMPTATION BECOME STRONGER AFTER MARRIAGE?
The Wedding Ring Didn’t Kill the Temptation—and Nobody Warned You What Might Happen Next
You thought marriage would silence it.

You thought once you stood before God, looked into the eyes of the person you loved, made your vows, exchanged rings, and finally entered the sacred intimacy you had waited for, sexual temptation would lose its voice.
Maybe nobody actually said those words.
But somehow you believed them.
“Once I’m married, this struggle will be over.”
Then you got married.
And one night, perhaps months or years later, something happened that frightened you.
You noticed someone.
An image stayed in your mind longer than it should have.
An old temptation returned.
Pornography whispered your name again.
A coworker began making you feel noticed in ways you had not felt noticed at home.
An old relationship suddenly appeared in your messages.
Or perhaps nothing dramatic happened at all.
You simply discovered something you were ashamed to admit:
Marriage did not make you incapable of lust.
And maybe the temptation even seemed stronger.
That can be terrifying for a Christian.
Because now there is more to lose.
Before marriage, you feared sexual sin because you wanted to honor Christ.
Now there is another heart sleeping beside you.
There are vows.
Maybe children.
A home.
Years of trust.
A testimony.
And suddenly temptation does not merely threaten your purity.
It threatens something sacred that another person entrusted to you.
So you begin wondering:
What is wrong with me?
Why am I still fighting this?
If I truly love my spouse, why can I still feel sexually tempted?
Why didn't marriage fix this?
And perhaps the question you are almost afraid to ask is the question that brought you here:
Can sexual temptation actually become stronger after marriage?
Yes.
It can.
But not because marriage is defective.
And not because sexual intimacy between husband and wife is somehow dirty.
Scripture teaches precisely the opposite.
Hebrews 13:4 says:
Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος
Timios ho gamos en pasin kai hē koitē amiantos.
Marriage is to be honored, and the marriage bed kept undefiled.
The word τίμιος — timios carries the sense of something precious, honored, valuable.
Marriage is not God's reluctant concession to human sexuality.
Marriage is honorable.
And Scripture's first portrait of marriage reaches all the way back to Eden:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vedavaq be'ishto vehayu levasar echad.
He is joined to his wife, and they become one flesh.
One flesh.
Not shame.
Not filth.
Not embarrassment.
Covenant.
Union.
Belonging.
Marriage is good.
Sexual intimacy within God's design for marriage is good.
But here is the distinction that can save someone years of confusion:
Marriage changes your covenant status. It does not instantly erase every disordered desire inside the human heart.
A wedding ceremony is not glorification.
You do not walk down the aisle and suddenly become incapable of temptation.
You are still being sanctified.
You still need the Holy Spirit.
You still need Scripture.
You still need prayer.
You still need self-control.
You still need repentance when you sin.
You still need Jesus.
And the Bible never pretends otherwise.
In fact, Paul speaks to married Christians about sexual temptation with startling realism.

In 1 Corinthians 7 he addresses marital intimacy and says husbands and wives should not deprive one another except by mutual agreement for a limited time for prayer, and afterward they should come together again.
Why?
Paul writes:
ἵνα μὴ πειράζῃ ὑμᾶς ὁ Σατανᾶς διὰ τὴν ἀκρασίαν ὑμῶν
So that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
Read that again.
Paul is talking to married people.
And he still uses the word πειράζῃ — peirazē.
Tempt.
Marriage did not make temptation impossible.
Paul did not tell them, “You're married now. Sexual temptation should no longer exist.”
He warned them to guard their marriage precisely because temptation remained possible.
That changes the conversation.

Marriage can provide a holy context for sexual intimacy. Paul explicitly acknowledges this when he writes, because of sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.
But Paul never says marriage magically cures lust.
There is an enormous difference between God giving sexual desire a covenant home and God instantly removing every sinful distortion of sexual desire from your heart.
Those are not the same thing.
And this is where many Christians become vulnerable.
They stop guarding the gates because they think the wedding ring is the gate.
It isn't.
Your ring can remind you of your covenant.
It cannot obey Christ for you.
Your spouse can love you deeply.
Your spouse cannot become your Savior.
Sex cannot crucify your flesh.
Marriage cannot regenerate your heart.
Only Christ saves.
Only the Spirit transforms.
And sometimes temptation after marriage feels stronger simply because the stakes have become higher.
Sometimes previously hidden patterns also follow people into marriage.
The secret pornography habit you never truly confronted does not necessarily disappear because you said, “I do.”
The hunger for validation does not automatically disappear.
The fantasy life does not automatically disappear.
The habit of staring does not automatically disappear.
The wounds that made sexual attention feel like proof of worth do not automatically disappear.
The inability to handle loneliness does not automatically disappear.
And marriage eventually exposes things romance allowed us to hide.
Then life becomes ordinary.
Bills arrive.
Children cry.
Bodies change.
Work becomes exhausting.
Sexual desire between spouses may not always move at identical rhythms.

There can be pregnancy, postpartum recovery, sickness, grief, stress, medication effects, emotional wounds, unresolved conflict, physical distance, aging, exhaustion, seasons of caregiving, and thousands of other realities that make marriage look nothing like the permanently romantic fantasy sold by entertainment.
Then temptation finds an exhausted heart and whispers:
You deserve more.
Your spouse doesn't understand you.
Nobody would know.
It's only an image.
It's only a conversation.
You're not actually touching anybody.
You're just looking.
You're just fantasizing.
And Jesus walks straight into that darkness.
Not to negotiate with it.
To expose it.
Christ says in Matthew 5:28:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
The one looking at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
Jesus goes deeper than behavior.
He goes to the heart.
Because adultery can begin long before two bodies touch.
It can begin when the heart starts building a secret room where someone other than your spouse is invited to live.
That room may initially contain only imagination.
Then comparison.
Then curiosity.
Then messages.
Then deleted messages.
Then passwords.
Then explanations.
Then lies.
And eventually the person who once said, “I would never do that,” is asking how everything fell apart.
James explains the progression with frightening clarity:
ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος
Each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his own desire.
The Greek word ἐπιθυμία — epithymia means desire; in this context it is desire pulling toward what God forbids.
Notice where James forces us to look.
Not first at our spouse.
Not first at the attractive coworker.
Not first at the internet.
Not first at the state of our marriage.
Our own desires.
External circumstances matter. Satan tempts. Opportunities matter. Marital problems matter and should be addressed honestly.
But Scripture refuses to let us make someone else responsible for our sin.
“My spouse doesn't satisfy me” is not permission for adultery.
“We haven't been emotionally close” is not permission for pornography.
“My husband doesn't notice me anymore” is not permission to cultivate another man's attention.
“My wife rejected me” is not permission to fantasize about another woman.
Pain may explain vulnerability.
It does not transform sin into righteousness.
And this is where grace must enter the room, because some reader has already stopped thinking about theology.
You're thinking about last night.
The browser history.
The conversation you deleted.
The person you keep searching for.
The fantasy you keep revisiting.
The emotional affair nobody knows is already happening.
Maybe you're sitting beside your spouse while reading this.
They think you're scrolling through Facebook.
But God knows exactly why your chest feels heavy right now.
Listen carefully.
Do not confuse conviction with a declaration that redemption is impossible.
Jesus exposes darkness because He calls people into light.
The Gospel is not that respectable Christians never become sexually tempted.
The Gospel is that sinners can be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled to God, and transformed through Jesus Christ.
But grace is not permission to protect the secret.
Grace teaches us to bring darkness into the light.
Maybe your next faithful act is not another promise whispered to yourself at 2:00 a.m.
Maybe it is confession.
Maybe it is deleting access.
Maybe it is ending the private conversation.
Maybe it is putting accountability around your devices.
Maybe it is telling a mature Christian who will love you enough not to flatter your sin.
Maybe your marriage needs serious counseling from a trustworthy, biblically grounded pastor or qualified marriage counselor.
Maybe your spouse deserves the honesty you have been withholding.
And if disclosure involves abuse, coercion, violence, or genuine danger, wisdom matters; seek safe, qualified pastoral and professional help rather than placing yourself recklessly in harm's way.
But whatever obedience looks like in your situation, stop feeding what you keep asking God to kill.
You cannot continually cultivate temptation and then act surprised when temptation grows.
Paul writes in 1 Thessalonians 4:3:
τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν
“This is the will of God: your sanctification.”
Then he immediately connects that sanctification with abstaining from sexual immorality.
God does not merely want you to avoid getting caught.
He wants you holy.
He wants the secret imagination.
He wants the phone.
He wants the eyes.
He wants the lonely evenings.
He wants the wounded sexuality.
He wants the desires you are embarrassed to name.
He wants the marriage.
He wants you.
This battle is not ultimately won by becoming terrified of sex.
It is fought by learning to treasure Christ above sin.
Sexual temptation promises intimacy without covenant, pleasure without holiness, excitement without consequence, and escape without healing.
It lies.
Jesus offers something infinitely deeper.
Forgiveness without pretending sin was harmless.
Grace without calling darkness light.
Mercy without abandoning holiness.
A new identity that does not depend upon being sexually desired.
A Savior who already knows the ugliest chapter and still calls sinners to repentance.
This is why you cannot make your spouse your cure.
Your husband cannot bear the weight of being your savior.
Your wife cannot carry the responsibility of preventing every lustful thought.
A healthy sexual relationship within marriage matters. Tenderness matters. Communication matters. Mutual care matters. Paul clearly treats marital intimacy seriously.
But even a wonderful marriage cannot replace discipleship.
Even frequent intimacy cannot sanctify an undisciplined imagination.
You need Jesus more than you need circumstances perfectly arranged around your desires.
And perhaps that is the uncomfortable answer to the original question.
Can sexual temptation become stronger after marriage?
Yes, it can feel stronger or become more intense in particular seasons.
Marriage introduces new pressures, vulnerabilities, responsibilities, disappointments, opportunities, and spiritual battles.
But Scripture does not teach that marriage itself causes sinful desire.
Nor does Scripture promise marriage will eliminate temptation.
Marriage is not the enemy.
Sex is not the enemy.
Your spouse is not the enemy.
And temptation itself is not identical to committing sin.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin.
The danger comes when temptation is welcomed, fed, rehearsed, concealed, rationalized, and obeyed.
So when temptation knocks, do not sit beside the door interviewing it.
Run to Christ.
Bring your weakness into prayer.
Bring Scripture into your imagination.
Protect your eyes.
Protect your conversations.
Protect your private messages.
Protect the vulnerable hours nobody else sees.
Protect your spouse's heart.
Cultivate affection at home.
Talk honestly about intimacy without manipulation, entitlement, humiliation, or coercion.
Forgive.
Seek forgiveness.
Serve one another.
Date each other again.
Pray together.
Laugh together.
Fight for tenderness.
And remember that your spouse's body is never an object you own. Biblical marital intimacy is covenantal, loving, mutual, and never an excuse for force or coercion.
If you are currently winning this battle, stay humble.
If you are currently losing it, stop hiding.
If you already crossed a line, repent.
If you destroyed trust, understand that forgiveness does not instantly erase consequences or rebuild trust overnight.
If your spouse betrayed you, their sin is not evidence that you were inadequate.
And if you are the one who betrayed them, repentance means more than feeling terrible because you were discovered.
Repentance turns around.
It tells the truth.
It accepts consequences.
It stops protecting the idol.
It seeks restoration without demanding a timetable.
And above everything else, repentance runs toward Jesus.
Because the cross tells the truth about both things we desperately need to understand:
Our sin is worse than our excuses say it is.
And...
Christ's grace is greater than our shame says it can be.
That is why Peter could fail terribly and still be restored.
That is why the sexually broken are not beyond redemption.
That is why your worst secret does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
He rose again.
And the risen Christ is still transforming people who finally stop defending what is destroying them.
Maybe you needed this article because temptation has been screaming lately.
Then be honest.
If there is something hidden and conviction is tearing through your excuses, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly.
Let those three words become a marker in the ground.
Not salvation by a Facebook comment.
Not public performance.
Just an honest declaration that secrecy will no longer be your strategy.
That is what the Body of Christ can look like even here.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Send it privately to the friend who needs it.

Never publicly expose someone's private struggle through a tag. But if there is a brother, sister, couple, or believer who would genuinely be strengthened by this truth, put it where they can find it.
Because temptation rarely announces its next appointment.
There may come a night when these words mean more than they do right now.
It doesn't.
It doesn't.
And not because anyone should pressure you into giving.
Scripture says:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Each should give as he has decided in his heart—not under compulsion.
That matters.
But voluntary generosity can become a real act of Gospel partnership.
But whether you ever give financially or not, hear this clearly:
Jesus is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
Your greatest response to this article is not sending money.
It is surrendering your life to Christ.

And perhaps tonight, somewhere behind a locked bathroom door, beneath a blanket glowing blue from a phone screen, inside an office after everyone has gone home, or beside a sleeping spouse who has no idea a battle is happening inches away...
someone will finally close the image.
Delete the conversation.
Put down the phone.
Fall to their knees.
And whisper:
“Jesus... I don't want to live like this anymore.”
That prayer may not instantly remove every temptation.
Tomorrow may still require warfare.
Trust may take time to rebuild.
Healing may hurt.
But repentance has a direction.
Toward the light.
Toward truth.
Toward holiness.
Toward home.
Toward Jesus.
So remember this when temptation tells you the secret has already written the ending:
The ring on your finger cannot save your heart—but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus can still reclaim the story you thought temptation had already stolen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN CHRISTIANS LISTEN TO SECULAR MUSIC WITHOUT COMPROMISING THEIR FAITH?
paragraphs: CAN CHRISTIANS LISTEN TO SECULAR MUSIC WITHOUT COMPROMISING THEIR FAITH?
The question may not be whether the song has Jesus’ name in it—but whether, after listening long enough, there is still room in your heart for His voice.
You know the moment.
The song starts.
Three seconds in, you recognize it.

Maybe it takes you back to high school. Maybe to someone you used to love. Maybe to a season of your life you thought you had buried. Maybe it is simply a beautiful song—brilliantly written, emotionally honest, musically breathtaking.
You turn it up.
And then somewhere between the melody and the memory, a question quietly walks into the room:
Should I even be listening to this as a Christian?
Some believers would immediately reach for the volume knob.
Others would roll their eyes.
“It’s just music.”
And perhaps that sentence is exactly where we need to begin.
Because music is almost never just music.
It can carry memory.
Desire.
Grief.
Anger.
Hope.
Lust.
Beauty.
Rebellion.
Romance.
Despair.
Truth.
Lies.
Sometimes a song gets through doors in your heart that a sermon could not open.
Sometimes four minutes of music can awaken something you spent four years trying to bury.
So the real question is deeper than:
“Is secular music allowed?”
The deeper question is:
What is this music doing to my heart while I belong to Jesus?
And that question changes everything.
Before going further, we need to destroy one dangerous myth from both sides of this debate.
The Bible does not contain the modern category “secular music” and then give Christians a command saying, “Thou shalt never listen to it.”
That verse does not exist.
We must never manufacture commandments in places where God has not spoken.
But the opposite mistake is equally dangerous.
The absence of a verse saying, “Do not listen to secular music,” does not mean every song is spiritually harmless.
Scripture gives us something more demanding than a playlist of forbidden artists.
It gives us principles by which the heart itself must be examined.
Paul writes:
Panta exestin, all’ ou panta sympherei.
“Everything is permissible”—but not everything is beneficial.
And later in the same thought:
“Everything is permissible”—but not everything builds up.
That is 1 Corinthians 10:23.
Notice what Paul does.
He moves the question beyond:
“Am I allowed?”
and toward:
“What is this producing?”
That is a much more uncomfortable question.
Because maturity in Christ is not learning how close you can stand to darkness without technically sinning.
It is learning to love Jesus enough that you care what shapes your soul.

There are songs written outside explicitly Christian worship that contain extraordinary beauty, honest grief, tenderness, sacrifice, longing, justice, family devotion, courage, or truthful observations about human life.
Christians do not need to pretend that an unbelieving musician is incapable of recognizing anything beautiful or true.
Paul himself gives us a remarkably broad test in Philippians 4:8.
The Greek reads:
“ὅσα ἐστὶν ἀληθῆ, ὅσα σεμνά, ὅσα δίκαια, ὅσα ἁγνά, ὅσα προσφιλῆ, ὅσα εὔφημα…”
Whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and commendable—these are the kinds of things upon which believers are told to direct their thinking.
One especially important word comes at the end:
“ταῦτα λογίζεσθε”
tauta logizesthe.
Think on these things.
Dwell on them.
Take them into serious account.
Paul is concerned with what repeatedly occupies the mind.
And suddenly the question becomes personal.
Not:
“Is this artist Christian?”
But:
“What am I repeatedly feeding my mind?”
Because you can delete every secular song from your phone and still fill your mind with pride, envy, gossip, bitterness, pornography, greed, and self-righteousness.
And you can listen to an instrumental piece written by someone who never confessed Christ and be moved by its beauty without worshiping its composer.
The label alone cannot do all the discernment for you.
Jesus wants the heart.
That is why some Christians desperately need to stop asking only whether a song contains profanity.
A song can contain no profanity whatsoever and still disciple your desires toward adultery.
It can romanticize revenge.
Normalize drunkenness.
Make promiscuity sound beautiful.
Turn greed into aspiration.
Make arrogance sound like confidence.
Make objectification sound like love.
Make despair feel like identity.
Make rebellion against God feel heroic.
And if you sing something often enough, you may eventually stop noticing what you are agreeing with.
That does not mean hearing a lyric automatically transforms you into what the lyric describes.
It means Christians should take seriously the cumulative formation of the heart.
There is a difference.
David once declared:
“לֹא־אָשִׁית לְנֶגֶד עֵינַי דְּבַר־בְּלִיָּעַל”
Lo-ashit leneged einai devar-beliyya‘al.
“I will set no worthless thing before my eyes.”

Psalm 101:3 is not specifically a command about modern entertainment or music; in context it belongs to David’s declaration of integrity. But its posture is still piercing: he did not want corrupt things clinging to him.
And maybe that word—clinging—is where this becomes painfully real.
Because some songs cling.
You know they do.
You haven't heard one in fifteen years, and the opening notes play in a grocery store...
and suddenly you are seventeen again.
You remember the car.
The perfume.
The breakup.
The party.
The person.
The mistake.
The night you promised yourself you would never talk about.
Music found the file your conscious mind had forgotten existed.
And opened it.
That is why the same song may affect two Christians differently.
One person hears an old song and thinks nothing of it.
Another hears that same song and is dragged emotionally toward an addiction, relationship, sexual memory, rage, or former lifestyle from which Christ has been rescuing them.
This is where Romans 14 becomes profoundly important.

Paul was dealing with disputed matters involving food and days, not writing specifically about Spotify playlists. We should respect that context. But his teaching establishes an important principle about conscience.
He writes:
pan de ho ouk ek pisteōs hamartia estin.
Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.
That means there are moments when the Holy Spirit may be pressing your conscience and the most dangerous response is not listening to the song.
It is training yourself to ignore conviction.
Maybe nobody else understands why you deleted that album.
Maybe another mature Christian can hear it without stumbling.
Maybe you cannot.
Then do not violate your conscience merely because someone else has freedom.
Your goal is not to prove how liberated you are.
Your goal is Jesus.
But hear the other side too.
Do not turn your personal conviction into a commandment God never gave to the entire Church.
Romans 14 warns believers about judging one another in disputed matters while simultaneously demanding that each person act before God with faith and a clear conscience.
That means Christian maturity has room for both conviction and humility.
You may say:
“I cannot listen to this anymore.”
Without saying:
“Therefore every Christian who listens to it is fake.”
And another Christian may say:
“My conscience is not troubled by this particular song.”
Without mocking the believer who had to walk away from it.
Grace does not eliminate discernment.
Discernment does not require legalism.
And Christian freedom was never meant to become Christian carelessness.
Paul says something even more startling in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
“Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει…”
And then:
“ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος”
He will not be mastered—or controlled—by anything.
Read that slowly.
I will not be mastered by anything.
Now bring your music into that sentence.
Can you turn it off?
Can you delete it?
Can you surrender the playlist if Christ puts His finger on it?
Can you drive without it?
Can you worship without constantly craving another sound?
Can you stop listening to an artist when their songs repeatedly awaken desires you know are pulling you away from holiness?
If your answer is,
“No. I need it.”
then perhaps the question is no longer whether the music is secular.
Perhaps the question is whether something has begun mastering you.
And anything you cannot surrender to Jesus deserves serious examination.
Not because music itself is evil.
Because Jesus is Lord.
There is also another side Christians sometimes neglect.
God created human beings with the capacity to make melody.
Scripture itself is full of music.
Celebration has music.
Lament has music.
Victory has music.
Grief has music.
Worship has music.
The Psalms contain emotional terrain ranging from ecstatic praise to crushing sorrow.
Christianity is not a religion that requires emotional numbness.
God does not need you to pretend heartbreak does not hurt.
He does not ask you to pretend beauty outside a church building is ugly.
He does not ask you to become culturally illiterate in order to become holy.
But He does call you to belong wholly to Christ.
And Scripture gives unmistakable priority to music that fills believers with Christ-centered truth.
Ephesians 5 speaks of being filled with the Spirit and then describes believers addressing one another:
“ψαλμοῖς καὶ ὕμνοις καὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς”
psalmois kai hymnois kai ōdais pneumatikais—
psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs—singing and making melody to the Lord from the heart.
Colossians 3:16 goes even deeper.
“Ὁ λόγος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐνοικείτω ἐν ὑμῖν πλουσίως…”
Ho logos tou Christou enoikeitō en hymin plousiōs.
Let the word—or message—of Christ dwell in you richly.
Then Paul connects that rich indwelling of Christ’s word with teaching, admonishing, psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, gratitude, and singing to God.
Do you see the issue now?
The Christian life cannot merely be about what you remove.
It must be about what fills the space afterward.
You can spend your entire life running from “bad music” and still never become captivated by Christ.
The Gospel offers something infinitely greater than behavior modification.
Jesus did not bleed on a Roman cross merely to clean up your playlist.
He came for you.
Your guilt.
Your rebellion.
Your secret life.
Your shame.
Your desires.
Your memories.
Your body.
Your mind.
Your worship.
Your eternity.
He came for the part of you nobody sees when the headphones go on.
Maybe that is where this article has found you.
You already know which song you are thinking about.
Nobody had to name it.
Maybe there is a playlist you only play when nobody from church is around.
Maybe there are lyrics you would never quote during Bible study, yet you have memorized every word.
Maybe you defend it publicly...
while privately knowing what it awakens in you.

Or maybe you have lived under unnecessary guilt because someone taught you that every song not explicitly labeled “Christian” is automatically sinful, and you have confused man-made rules with holiness.
Both people need freedom.
But neither person needs freedom from Jesus.
We need freedom in Jesus.
So instead of demanding a universal blacklist, bring your music honestly before Christ.
Ask:
Jesus, can I thank You while listening to this?
Jesus, is this teaching my heart to love what You call evil?
Jesus, does this awaken lust, bitterness, pride, violence, despair, greed, or rebellion in me?
Jesus, does this dominate me?
Jesus, am I defending this because it is harmless—or because I do not want to surrender it?
Jesus, would listening to this around a weaker brother or sister wound their conscience?
Jesus, after this song finishes, am I more prepared to love You and love people—or have I been feeding something I keep asking You to kill?
And then comes perhaps the hardest question:
Jesus, if You ask me to give this up, will I?
There.
That is where the argument ends and discipleship begins.
Because sometimes we do not really want biblical discernment.
We want permission.
We want someone to tell us how far we can go without technically crossing the line.
But love does not ask:
“How much darkness can I keep?”
Love asks:
“How much of me can I give to Christ?”
And if the Holy Spirit exposes something, do not run from Him.
Run to Him.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
The Gospel is not the story of Jesus standing over dirty sinners saying, “Clean yourself up and maybe I will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that Christ came for sinners.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
And those who turn to Him in repentance and faith receive forgiveness and new life—not because they finally became worthy, but because Christ is worthy.
Maybe your scandal is bigger than music.
Maybe the song is only the doorway.
Behind it is the relationship.
Behind the relationship is the wound.
Behind the wound is the loneliness.
Behind the loneliness is the thing you have never told anyone.
And suddenly you realize you were never merely listening to music.
You were medicating pain.
You were trying to feel wanted.
You were keeping an old version of yourself alive.
You were returning, three minutes at a time, to somewhere Jesus had been calling you to leave.
And He is not exposing it because He enjoys humiliating you.
He calls sinners out of darkness because grace does not merely forgive us where we are.
Grace begins transforming us.
This is the scandal of grace:
Christ already knows the playlist.
Christ already knows the memory.
Christ already knows the fantasy.
Christ already knows the relapse.
Christ already knows why that particular lyric hurts.
And still He calls:
Come.
Repent.
Receive mercy.
Follow Me.
Let Me teach your heart a new song.
So can Christians listen to secular music without compromising their faith?
There is no faithful biblical basis for declaring that every piece of non-Christian music is inherently sinful simply because it is not explicitly Christian.
But there is equally no faithful basis for pretending that every song is harmless merely because Scripture does not mention its artist by name.
The follower of Jesus must discern.
Some music can be received without violating conscience.
Some should be rejected because its message celebrates what God condemns.
Some may be harmless for one believer yet dangerously connected to temptation for another.
And some things may be technically permissible while still being spiritually unhelpful.
The Christian question is therefore not merely:
“Is it secular?”
It is:
Is it true? Is it pure? Is it beneficial? Does it build up? Is it mastering me? Can I receive it with a clear conscience before God? Can I do this under the lordship of Jesus Christ?
That kind of discernment is harder than a banned-music list.
It requires walking with Jesus.
And maybe that is precisely the point.
If this exposed something you have been defending, do not hide behind religious language.
Be honest.
Somebody reading it may discover that they are not fighting alone.
And if another believer comes to a different conclusion on a genuinely disputable matter, remember Romans 14 before turning the comment section into a courtroom.
Truth matters.
Conscience matters.
Love matters.
Jesus matters most.
It does not.
Scripture does not give us grounds to make that claim.
And not because anyone must pay Gospel Warrior in order to glorify God.
The Gospel cannot be sold like that.
But Christians are free to support Gospel ministry voluntarily and generously, and Scripture commends willing, cheerful giving rather than giving under compulsion.
Send it privately to the person who came to mind while you were reading.
Because somewhere tonight, someone will put on a song trying to drown out a pain only Jesus can heal.
Someone will replay a memory they desperately need to surrender.
Someone will be fighting a battle behind headphones nobody else can hear.
And perhaps this article reaching their screen will remind them that Christ has not stopped calling their name.
Stay close to Scripture.
Stay teachable.
Stay honest.
Stay near Jesus.
And never forget:
The song playing in your ears matters—but the Savior shaping your heart matters infinitely more.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IRON SHARPENS IRON” — THIS VERSE IS ABOUT MORE THAN HAVING CHRISTIAN FRIENDS
paragraphs: “IRON SHARPENS IRON” — THIS VERSE IS ABOUT MORE THAN HAVING CHRISTIAN FRIENDS

You can sit beside Christians every Sunday, have Bible verses in your bio, belong to three church group chats—and still have nobody close enough to tell you the truth that could save you from becoming someone you never intended to become.
There is a kind of friendship that makes you comfortable.
And there is a kind of friendship that makes you holy.
Those are not always the same thing.
Maybe that is why this verse sounds so beautiful until you actually understand what sharpening requires:
“As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another.”
Proverbs 27:17.
We print it on shirts.
Put it on men’s ministry banners.
Send it to Christian friends.
Use it to celebrate fellowship.
And yes, friendship is certainly part of its world.
But there is something far more uncomfortable hiding inside those words.
Because iron does not sharpen iron by standing beside it.
Iron sharpens iron through contact.
Pressure.
Friction.
Resistance.
Something dull meets something strong enough to affect its edge.
And suddenly Proverbs 27:17 stops sounding like a decorative friendship verse.
It starts sounding like discipleship.
The Hebrew makes the image even more striking.

בַּרְזֶל בְּבַרְזֶל יָחַד
וְאִישׁ יַחַד פְּנֵי־רֵעֵהוּ
Barzel bevarzel yachad; ve’ish yachad penei re’ehu.
The opening picture is unmistakable: iron encountering iron.

The Hebrew verb יָחַד (yachad) carries the idea of sharpening, making keen, giving an edge. The second half turns that physical picture toward human relationships: one person affects, sharpens, or brings an edge to another.
This is not merely proximity.
It is impact.
And that raises an uncomfortable question.
Who in your life is actually allowed to sharpen you?
Not entertain you.
Not agree with you.
Not applaud everything you do.
Not tell you what keeps you comfortable.
Who is allowed to look you in the eyes and say:
“Brother, something is changing in you.”
“Sister, this relationship is pulling you away from Christ.”
“You keep calling it a struggle, but you have stopped fighting it.”
“You need to forgive.”
“You need to apologize.”
“You need to confess this.”
“You are becoming proud.”
“You are hiding.”
“You are spiritually starving while pretending you are spiritually strong.”
That kind of friendship is rare.
Because most of us love encouragement until encouragement becomes correction.
We love accountability until somebody actually holds us accountable.
We want people who will pray for us.
We are less enthusiastic about people who will confront us.
We say we want Christian community, but sometimes what we really want is Christian companionship without Christian interference.
Stay close enough to make me feel loved.
Just do not come close enough to expose me.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You have mastered the appearance of being okay.
You know the Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say, “God is good.”
You know which worship songs make you cry.
You know which Bible verse to post when life gets difficult.
You know how to walk into church carrying something nobody in the room knows is crushing you.
You smile.
You shake hands.
You worship.
You go home.
And the secret goes home with you.
Again.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The private messages you would panic if your spouse saw.
The resentment toward someone you publicly claim to have forgiven.
The drinking that stopped being occasional.
The pride hiding underneath your ministry.
The envy you disguise as discernment.
The prayer life that quietly disappeared.
The Bible collecting dust while Christian content keeps filling your feed.
The relationship you already know is pulling your heart somewhere Jesus never told you to go.
The compromise you renamed so you would not have to call it sin.
And there may be Christians all around you.
But nobody knows.
That is the tragedy.
You can be surrounded by believers and remain spiritually unsharpened.
Because Proverbs 27:17 is not fulfilled merely because Christians occupy the same room.
Iron must actually touch iron.
And real biblical community eventually gets close enough to disturb something.
Look at the surrounding wisdom of Proverbs 27.
Just a few verses earlier we read:
“Better is open rebuke than hidden love.”
Then:
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend.”
Proverbs 27:5–6.
Read that again slowly.
Faithful.
Wounds.
Those words almost sound contradictory.
But Scripture understands something our culture increasingly struggles to accept:
Love does not always feel like agreement.
Sometimes love encourages.
Sometimes love comforts.
Sometimes love sits silently beside you while you cry.
And sometimes love loves you enough to risk making you angry.
A faithful friend may wound your pride to protect your soul from destruction.
That does not mean cruelty is discipleship.
It does not mean controlling people is biblical accountability.
It does not mean humiliation is holiness.
It does not give spiritually abusive people permission to dominate others while quoting Scripture.
Biblical correction must itself submit to Christ.
Truth without love can become brutality.
“Love” without truth can become cowardice.
Jesus gives us neither.
John tells us that Jesus Christ came “full of grace and truth.”
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Grace and truth.
That is the edge.
And nobody embodied it like Jesus.
Jesus could look at a woman publicly disgraced by sexual sin while religious men prepared to destroy her—and refuse to join their condemnation.
Yet His mercy did not redefine sin as righteousness.
He could say, in essence, neither do I condemn you—and call her away from sin.
Grace did not pretend the past was holy.
Grace opened a future the past could no longer control.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not merely make sinners feel better about dullness.
He transforms them.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He calls.
He corrects.
He disciplines those He loves.
He takes people whose stories look ruined beyond repair and writes redemption across pages everyone else had already thrown away.
Peter knew something about that.
Peter was bold.
Passionate.
Impulsive.
Certain he would never abandon Jesus.
Then came the courtyard.
Questions.
Fear.
Denial.
Once.
Twice.
Three times.
And somewhere in the darkness, a rooster crowed.
Imagine carrying that sound inside your memory.
The man who said he would die for Jesus could not even admit that he knew Him.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
That could have been the final paragraph of his story.
Failure.
Cowardice.
Shame.
Scandal.
But Jesus was not finished writing.
After the resurrection, beside another fire, Christ confronted Peter not merely to embarrass him but to restore him.
“Do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
The wound was being touched.
The failure was not ignored.
But neither was Peter discarded.
Jesus restored the man at the place where shame wanted to define him.
Then He gave Peter responsibility again.
“Feed my sheep.”
That is sharpening under the hands of Christ.
Not destruction.
Restoration.
Not pretending you never failed.
Becoming someone failure no longer owns.
This is why genuine Christian friendship cannot merely consist of people telling one another, “You’re amazing.”
Sometimes the most Christlike sentence a friend can give you is:
“I love you too much to help you lie to yourself.”
Because sin grows exceptionally well in secrecy.
James writes:
James 5:16.
Notice the movement.
Confession.
Prayer.
Healing.
Not confession followed by gossip.
Not confession followed by screenshots.
Not confession followed by public humiliation.
Not confession followed by someone storing your weakness as ammunition for the next argument.
Confession followed by prayer.
That is Christian community.
A place where masks can die without people being destroyed underneath them.
A place where someone can finally whisper:
“I need help.”
And instead of hearing, “I knew there was something wrong with you,” they hear:
“Then we are going to bring this into the light, and we are going to walk toward Jesus together.”
Maybe you desperately need someone like that.
Or maybe God is calling you to become someone like that.
Because there is another side to Proverbs 27:17 that is easy to miss.
You are not merely being sharpened.
You are sharpening somebody.
The question is what kind of edge your presence is producing.
When people spend time with you, do they hunger for Christ more?
Or compromise more?
Do your conversations pull people toward holiness?
Or toward gossip?
When your friend is angry at their spouse, do you help them pursue reconciliation—or feed the anger because it makes for an interesting conversation?
When somebody confesses temptation, do you help them establish boundaries—or normalize what is destroying them?
When someone begins drifting from Jesus, do you notice?
Do you care enough to speak?
Christian friendship is not merely having someone who will stand beside you when life falls apart.
It is having someone who cares where your soul is going while everything still looks fine.
That friend is priceless.
Because sometimes you cannot see your own dullness.
Pride rarely announces itself as pride.
Bitterness usually comes carrying a folder labeled “justified.”
Lust calls itself loneliness.
Greed calls itself ambition.
Cowardice calls itself keeping the peace.
Gossip calls itself concern.
Spiritual laziness calls itself being busy.
And slowly...
quietly...
almost invisibly...
the edge disappears.
That is why we need Scripture.
That is why we need the Holy Spirit.
That is why we need the local church.
That is why we need mature believers.
That is why we need brothers and sisters who love Jesus more than they love keeping us comfortable.
But hear this carefully.
Your Christian friends cannot be your Savior.
Your pastor cannot be your Savior.
Your accountability partner cannot be your Savior.
Gospel Warrior cannot be your Savior.
No ministry can sharpen a dead heart into eternal life.
Only Jesus saves.
The Gospel is not “find better friends and become a better person.”
The Gospel is that sinful humanity could not rescue itself, so God came near in Jesus Christ.
Christ lived in righteousness.
Christ went to the cross.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
And sinners who repent and trust in Him receive what friendship, discipline, self-improvement, religious performance, and moral determination could never purchase:
forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
New life.
Grace.
That is where true sharpening begins.
Not with becoming impressive.
With surrender.
Maybe the person who most needs to sharpen you today is not another human being.
Maybe you first need to stop resisting the voice of God through His Word.
Maybe Scripture has already touched the place you keep protecting.
And you know it.
You knew before reaching this sentence.
There is something you need to confess.
Someone you need to forgive.
Something you need to delete.
A relationship where boundaries need to change.
An apology you need to make.
A habit that needs to come into the light.
A church community you need to stop avoiding.
A mature believer you need to call.
A secret you need to stop feeding.
You have been asking God for freedom while protecting the chains.
And Jesus is calling you into the light.
Not because He delights in humiliating you.
Because He loves you.
Repentance is not God standing over you saying, “Look how disgusting you are.”
Repentance is God calling:
“Come home.”
Turn around.
Stop running.
Stop hiding.
Stop defending what is killing you.
There is mercy here.
There is forgiveness here.
There is a cross here.
There is an empty tomb here.
There is still a future here.
That is the Gospel.
Your scandal does not have to become your final identity.
Your worst chapter does not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your failure does not possess editorial control over the rest of your life.
Jesus does.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest.
And when you see somebody else write those words, remember: behind that comment is a human being.
Do not judge them.
Pray for them.
We need communities where confession does not become entertainment and broken people are not treated like scandals to consume.
We need believers willing to sharpen one another toward Christ.
“Walk with me. Sharpen me. And when I start drifting, love me enough to tell me.”
Not because every sentence is easy.

Because there may come a night when you need to remember that godly correction is not rejection, that conviction is not the same as condemnation, and that Jesus has not stopped working merely because something in you still needs sharpening.
You may never know which share becomes the sentence God uses to interrupt somebody’s hiding.
If Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, face uncomfortable truth, understand the Gospel, and keep your eyes on Jesus, you can also help this ministry continue and expand.
Following costs nothing.
Sharing costs nothing.
Tagging someone costs nothing.
Praying costs nothing.
And all of those things genuinely matter.
But let us be biblically clear about something especially important:
It does not.
It does not.
And we will not place a burden on your conscience that Scripture itself does not place there.
Paul writes that each believer should give what he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
That principle matters.
If you consider your support part of your personal giving, handle questions about tithes, offerings, and support for your local church prayerfully, biblically, and with a clear conscience before God.
Support Gospel Warrior because you genuinely believe the work is worth supporting.
Support because you want more people reached with Scripture.
Support because biblical discipleship matters to you.
Support because you want Gospel-centered resources to keep reaching people who may never walk into a church building but will stop long enough to read something on a screen.
And above all, support freely.
Not fearfully.
Not superstitiously.
Not because somebody manipulated you into thinking God will love you more.
Jesus already demonstrated the depth of His love at the cross.
And whether or not you can financially support us, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person quietly trying to find their way back to Jesus.
Invite the skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing left to say to their brokenness.
But after all the comments...
after all the shares...
after all the books...
after all the resources...
remember what everything is supposed to lead toward.
Not us.
Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot forgive your sins.
A Christian friend cannot die your death for you.
Only Christ went to that cross.
Only Christ conquered the grave.
Only Christ is Lord.
And perhaps that is the deepest lesson hidden inside two pieces of iron.
God never intended you to become comfortable enough with dullness that nobody is permitted to touch your edge.
So find believers who will pray with you.
Find believers who will celebrate with you.
Find believers who will sit beside you when words disappear.
But also find the rare ones who will tell you the truth.
Give them permission to ask difficult questions.
Become that kind of friend for somebody else.
And when the friction hurts, ask whether God might be using faithful people to remove something from your life that cannot accompany you where Christ is leading you.
Because sometimes the person who loves you most is not the one who helps you remain comfortable.
Sometimes it is the one who sees you becoming dull...
comes close...
refuses to abandon you...
and loves you enough to help you find your edge again.
Some wounds are not evidence that love has left you; sometimes they are evidence that love refused to leave you dull.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “Stand Still and See the Salvation of the Lord” — Sometimes Faith Stands Still Before God Says Move
paragraphs: “Stand Still and See the Salvation of the Lord” — Sometimes Faith Stands Still Before God Says Move
There are moments when everything inside you screams, “Do something.”
Fix it.
Call somebody.
Send the message.
Defend yourself.
