The Bible could have described what happened in the bedroom more explicitly. Instead, it chose a word so deep that it exposes what sex was always supposed to mean—and why so many people can share their bodies while remaining painfully unknown.
There is a sentence in the opening pages of Scripture that most people read without realizing how astonishing it is.
Adam and Eve have already fallen.
Eden is behind them.
Shame has entered the human story.
They have hidden from God.
Blame has entered their marriage.
Death has entered their future.
Paradise has been lost.
And then Genesis tells us something intensely private.
Not crudely.
Not graphically.
Not with the language our culture would probably use.
The Hebrew text says:
וְהָאָדָם יָדַע אֶת־חַוָּה אִשְׁתּוֹ
Veha’adam yada et-Chavvah ishto.
“And Adam knew Eve his wife…”
Genesis 4:1.
The word translated “knew” is יָדַע — yādaʿ.
And what happens immediately afterward removes any ambiguity about what is occurring.
Eve conceives.
Adam “knew” his wife.
She became pregnant.
Yes, Scripture is referring to sexual union.
But perhaps the question we have not asked often enough is…
Why call it knowing?
Why would the Holy Spirit preserve a word ordinarily associated with knowledge when describing something so physical?
Why not simply say they had intercourse?
Why not reduce the moment to anatomy?
Why use a word capable of carrying ideas of recognition, relationship, experience, and personal knowledge?
Maybe because the Bible refuses to treat human sexuality as merely something bodies do.
And maybe that is exactly what our generation desperately needs to hear.
Because we have become incredibly good at seeing bodies…
while becoming terribly bad at knowing souls.
We can swipe through faces.
Watch strangers expose themselves.
Flirt without commitment.
Desire without covenant.
Touch without trust.
Sleep beside somebody whose deepest fears we have never bothered to learn.
People can know another person's body and still have no idea what makes that person cry when nobody is watching.
You can memorize someone's skin while remaining a stranger to their wounds.
You can share a bed and never share your heart.
And Scripture quietly places one devastating word in front of us:
Know.

Not because every occurrence of yādaʿ means sexual intercourse. It certainly does not. The Hebrew verb has a broad range of ordinary uses involving knowing, recognizing, learning, understanding, and experiencing. Context determines its meaning.
But in Genesis 4:1, the context is unmistakably marital and sexual.
“Adam knew Eve his wife…”
Then she conceived.
And that wording becomes even more meaningful when you remember what God said before sin entered the world.
“A man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Genesis 2:24.
One flesh.
Not two consumers using one another.
Not two bodies borrowing pleasure.
Not one person conquering another.
Not intimacy detached from responsibility.
Not appetite pretending to be love.
One flesh.
The Bible's vision of marital intimacy is profoundly embodied, but never merely physical.
That is why reducing biblical sexuality to “God made rules about sex” misses something enormous.
God did not invent sexuality because He wanted humanity tormented by restrictions.
He created human beings male and female.
He created marriage.
He created the possibility of covenantal union.

And before pornography, adultery, exploitation, lust, shame, abuse, manipulation, abandonment, and heartbreak ever scarred human sexuality, Genesis presents nakedness without shame and husband and wife joined as one flesh.
Sin did not invent sex.
God did.
Sin distorted what God made.
And that changes the conversation.
Because Christianity is not teaching that the body is disgusting.
Christianity teaches something almost scandalously higher:
Your body matters.
Your sexuality matters.
What you do with another person's body matters.
What you allow another person to do with yours matters.
The promises surrounding intimacy matter.
The person attached to that body matters.
And this is where yādaʿ begins pressing somewhere uncomfortable.
Because our culture can sometimes teach people how to become sexually experienced without teaching them how to become relationally faithful.
We know techniques.
Preferences.
Bodies.
Images.
Fantasies.
But do we know how to stay?
Do we know how to forgive?
Do we know how to tell the truth when truth costs us something?
Do we know how to protect somebody else's vulnerability?
Do we know how to listen?
Do we know how to remain faithful when novelty disappears?
Do we know how to look at another human being and remember:
This is not a product.
This is not content.
This is not an experience for my consumption.
This is a person bearing the image of God.
That is why lust and love can look toward the same person while wanting completely different things.
Lust asks:
What can I take from you?
Love asks:
How can I seek your good?
Lust wants access without responsibility.
Covenant says, “I am not disappearing when this becomes difficult.”
Lust wants the body without necessarily receiving the person.
Biblical marital intimacy belongs inside something far larger than a sexual moment.
It belongs inside covenant.
And Scripture refuses to make that covenant one-sided.
Centuries after Genesis, Paul writes something that would have confronted the assumptions of his own world.
He tells husbands to fulfill their marital responsibility toward their wives…
and wives toward their husbands.
Then he makes the language astonishingly reciprocal.
The wife does not treat her body as though marriage has no claim upon it—and the husband is told the same thing about his body toward his wife.
Then Paul says temporary abstinence should be by mutual agreement.
Read 1 Corinthians 7:3–5 carefully.
The husband is not presented as a sexual dictator.
The wife is not presented as an object.
There is mutuality.
Responsibility.
Consideration.
Agreement.
The passage must never be weaponized to excuse coercion, abuse, humiliation, or sexual violence.
Biblical covenant is not permission to stop loving your spouse as a person.
And suddenly the word “know” becomes painfully beautiful.
Because genuine intimacy involves vulnerability.
To be known is dangerous.
Someone learns what embarrasses you.
What scares you.
What happened before they met you.
Where you are insecure.
Where your confidence is fake.
What memory still makes your chest tighten.
What failure you hope nobody discovers.
What part of yourself you secretly believe would make someone leave if they ever saw it clearly.
That is why being physically naked can sometimes be easier than being emotionally naked.
Clothes can come off in seconds.
Walls can take years.
And perhaps somebody reading this understands exactly what that means.
Maybe someone has touched your body without ever caring about your soul.
Maybe you gave yourself to somebody because you desperately wanted to feel chosen.
Maybe you thought sex would make them stay.
It didn't.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you promised God you would never cross.
Maybe pornography trained your imagination to consume people rather than love them.
Maybe adultery shattered something you thought could never be repaired.
Maybe your marriage still exists publicly while privately the two of you have become strangers.
Maybe intimacy became bargaining.
Maybe rejection accumulated.
Maybe resentment moved into the bedroom.
Maybe trauma made closeness frightening.
Maybe shame whispers that because of what happened to you—or because of what you willingly did—you can never again be clean.
And this is where this article cannot simply end with Hebrew vocabulary.
Because knowing what yādaʿ means cannot save you.
Knowing biblical sexual ethics cannot save you.
Marriage cannot save you.
Virginity cannot save you.
Sexual experience cannot save you.
Your record cannot save you.
Your promises to “do better next time” cannot save you.
You need Someone.
And Scripture's story eventually carries us from the nakedness of Eden…
to another place of shame.
A hill outside Jerusalem.
A cross.
Jesus Christ publicly humiliated.
Mocked.
Wounded.
Rejected.
Bearing sin.
The One who knew no sin giving Himself for sinners.
And here is the part that should stop you.
Jesus already knows.
The thing you are hiding?
He knows.
The browser history.
He knows.
The affair.
He knows.
The secret messages.
He knows.
The fantasies.
He knows.
The years of pretending.
He knows.
The shame somebody else caused you.
He knows.
The nights you cried afterward.
He knows.
The marriage nobody realizes is collapsing.
He knows.
The loneliness underneath the lust.
He knows.
The part of your story you have carefully edited before telling anyone else.
He knows.
And still the Gospel invitation comes.
Not permission to remain in sin.
Not sentimental reassurance that holiness does not matter.
Something infinitely better.
Repentance and grace.
Jesus does not expose darkness because He enjoys humiliating broken people.
He brings darkness into the light because darkness is where chains grow.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
The cross proves that sin matters terribly.
The Gospel says that sin was so serious that Christ went to the cross—and grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly went there for sinners.
So stop confusing condemnation with conviction.
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide from God. You're filthy. It's over.”
The Gospel calls:
“Come into the light. Confess. Repent. Believe. Follow Christ.”
There is a difference between regretting consequences and repenting before God.
Repentance is not merely feeling disgusting.
It is turning.
Bringing the hidden thing into the light.
Calling sin what God calls it.
Abandoning excuses.
Seeking forgiveness.
Making necessary changes.
Accepting accountability.
And trusting the mercy purchased by Jesus Christ rather than trying to scrub your own soul clean.
Maybe that is why this subject reaches deeper than sex.
We all want to be known.
And simultaneously…
we are terrified of being known.
Because somewhere inside us is the fear:
If you really knew me, you wouldn't love me.
So we curate.
Perform.
Filter.
Hide.
Smile at church.
Post the family photograph.
Say the marriage is “fine.”
Say the temptation is “under control.”
Say we have “moved on.”
Then lie awake carrying things nobody knows.
But the Gospel introduces us to the One before whom hiding is impossible.
Christ knows the sinner completely.
And the wonder of grace is not that Jesus becomes impressed after discovering how good we secretly are.
Grace begins when we stop pretending we are.
He knows.
And He calls sinners to repentance.
He knows.
And He offers mercy.
He knows.
And He transforms.
He knows.
And for everyone united to Christ, shame does not get the final sentence.
This does not make sexual sin trivial.
It makes redemption breathtaking.
There is a reason Christianity cannot be reduced to “be a better person.”
The Gospel is resurrection language.
Dead becoming alive.
Guilty receiving justification.
Enemies reconciled.
Captives freed.
Prodigals welcomed home.
Sinners washed.
Broken stories invaded by grace.
Maybe you cannot rewrite what happened.
You cannot become a virgin again.
You cannot unsend the message.
Undo the night.
Erase the affair.
Unsee the image.
Recover every year pornography stole.
Take back every piece of yourself you gave away trying to feel loved.
But Jesus Christ does something greater than pretending your past never happened.
He redeems people whose past really happened.
That is grace.
Scandal does not get the last word.
Failure does not get the last word.
Pornography does not get the last word.
Adultery does not get the last word.
Abuse does not get the last word over the person who suffered it.
Shame does not get the last word.
Your worst night does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
And perhaps Genesis 4:1 has been waiting all this time to confront a generation drowning in counterfeit intimacy.
“And Adam knew Eve his wife…”
Sex can expose a body.
Covenant invites a person to be known.
And the Gospel goes deeper still.
It brings sinners before the God who already knows everything and offers them not an excuse to continue hiding—but a way home through Jesus Christ.
Talk to Christ.
Confess honestly.
Seek help where help is needed.
If you are married, ask yourself whether you have been trying merely to possess your spouse's body while neglecting your spouse's heart.
If pornography has trained you to turn image-bearers into objects, bring that sin into the light.
If sexual shame has convinced you that Jesus wants nothing to do with you, look again at the cross.
If you sinned, repent.
If someone sinned against you, understand this clearly: another person's evil against you is not your moral stain.
And if you are exhausted from hiding…
come into the light.
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle. Wisdom still matters. But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this, send this to them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to accuse them.
Send it because maybe they have been fighting quietly.
Because temptation has a way of making us forget what conviction once made painfully clear.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, strengthening your walk with Christ, helping you understand Scripture, or putting Gospel-centered truth in front of people who desperately need it, you can help this work continue.
It does not.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior earns forgiveness.
It cannot.
Scripture does not give us permission to make that claim.
And Christian giving must never be manipulated from people through guilt or spiritual pressure. Scripture says giving should come from the heart rather than compulsion.
But believers have always been able to use their resources voluntarily to help Gospel work continue.

You may regard it as part of the resources you prayerfully choose to dedicate to Gospel ministry—but give according to conscience before God, while faithfully honoring the responsibilities and local-church commitments He has entrusted to you.
And sharing costs nothing.
One share can enter a marriage at midnight.
One share can reach somebody after relapse.
One share can reach the person sitting alone wondering whether God could possibly forgive them.
You may never know what God does with something as simple as pressing “Share.”
And there is something even more important than merchandise.
Stay close to truth.
Stay hungry for Scripture.
Stay serious about following Jesus.
But before you leave, remember the word that started all of this.
יָדַע — yādaʿ.
To know.
Human beings spend enormous portions of their lives trying to be seen…
desired…
wanted…
touched…
chosen…
followed…
admired…
and loved.
Yet underneath so many of those desires is something deeper.
Know me.
Know who I am when the lights are off.
Know what scares me.
Know where I failed.
Know what happened to me.
Know what I did.
Know the parts I cannot post.
Know the truth…
and please don't leave.
No human relationship can carry the full weight of that longing.
But Jesus Christ can.
He already knows the chapter you desperately wish could be deleted.
And if you come to Him in repentance and faith, you discover the miracle at the center of Christianity:
The God who knows the truth about you is also the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
You do not have to make your darkness invisible.
You need to bring it to the Light.
You do not need a rewritten history.
You need a redeemed life.
And maybe that is the sentence you were supposed to carry away from this article:
Jesus knows the story you are ashamed to tell—and grace means your darkest chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD CREATE SEX TO FEEL GOOD?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD CREATE SEX TO FEEL GOOD?
Does the Bible Ever Separate Pleasure From Holiness—or Have We Been Ashamed of Something God Himself Called Good?
There is a question many Christians have thought but were too embarrassed to say out loud.
If holiness matters so much to God…
why did He make sexual intimacy pleasurable?
Why create desire at all?
Why design the human body with the capacity for extraordinary physical delight if pleasure itself is supposed to make us suspicious?
Some believers grew up hearing plenty about what sex could destroy, but almost nothing about why God created it.
They heard warnings.
Don’t lust.
Don’t fornicate.
Don’t commit adultery.
Don’t look.
Don’t touch.
Don’t cross the line.

And those warnings have biblical foundations. Sexual sin is real. Scripture never trivializes it. Paul commands believers to flee sexual immorality and glorify God with their bodies, and he explicitly connects sexual holiness with sanctification. See 1 Corinthians 6:18–20 and 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5.
But somewhere along the way, some Christians accidentally learned another lesson the Bible never actually teaches:
Pleasure itself must be dirty.
Desire itself must be shameful.
Sex must somehow become less holy the moment it feels intensely good.
And that is where we need to go back.
Not to pornography.
Not to Hollywood.
Not to modern sexual ideology.
Not even to church culture.
Back farther.
Back before adultery.
Before pornography.
Before prostitution.
Before sexual exploitation.
Before lust corrupted desire.
Before shame entered the human story.
Back to Eden.
Because if you want to understand what sex became, you first have to see what sex was before sin touched it.
Genesis says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Then comes the sentence that almost feels startling after generations of sexual shame:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
Genesis 2:24–25.
The Hebrew behind “one flesh” is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
One flesh.
Not two strangers borrowing each other’s bodies.
Not consumption.
Not conquest.
Not one person using another person as an instrument for gratification.
One flesh.
And Genesis places nakedness beside something equally important:
No shame.
Before the serpent ever entered the garden, the human body was not embarrassing to God.
Marriage was not embarrassing to God.
Nakedness between husband and wife was not embarrassing to God.
Sexual union was not something humanity invented after the Fall.
God created the bodies.
God created their capacity for union.
God created marriage.
And the Creator looked upon the world He had made and called His creation “very good.”
That changes the question.
Maybe we have been asking, “How can something this pleasurable possibly be holy?”
when Scripture pushes us toward another question:
Why would holiness require God's good gifts to be joyless?
The Bible never establishes a universal equation that says pleasure equals righteousness. Plenty of sinful things can feel pleasurable for a moment.
But neither does Scripture establish the opposite equation:
Pleasure equals impurity.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because sin did not invent pleasure.
Sin distorts good things.
Hunger is good; gluttony can corrupt it.
Money can accomplish good; greed can enslave a heart.
Authority can protect; power can become abusive.
Rest is good; laziness can distort it.
Sexual desire can belong within God's good creation; lust, exploitation, adultery, pornography, selfishness and sexual immorality can twist desire away from love, covenant and holiness.
The existence of a counterfeit does not prove the original was evil.
It proves something valuable was worth counterfeiting.
And then Scripture becomes even more uncomfortable for anyone trying to pretend biblical sexuality is merely reluctant reproduction.
Read Proverbs 5.
Not a nightclub advertisement.
Not pornography.
Not an erotic novel from secular culture.
The Bible.
The father warns his son against adultery—and what is the alternative?
Coldness?
Embarrassment?
A marriage in which husband and wife tolerate intimacy solely to produce children?
No.
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then Scripture speaks openly of the husband's delight in his wife and tells him to remain captivated by her love.

The Hebrew imagery is remarkably strong. Proverbs 5:19 uses the verb רָוָה (ravah), carrying the sense of being filled, saturated, or drinking one's fill. The verse is not ashamed to describe marital attraction and satisfaction positively.
Think about that.
God could have inspired Solomon simply to say:
“Do not commit adultery.”
Period.
But biblical wisdom goes deeper.
It does not merely tell the husband what forbidden bed to avoid.
It directs his affection back toward the woman with whom he has covenant.
That means biblical holiness is not merely the absence of forbidden desire.
It includes rightly ordered delight.
The Bible does not simply say, “Don’t go there.”
It also says, in effect:
Rejoice here.
Love here.
Be faithful here.
Delight here.
And then there is Song of Songs.
A book Christians sometimes seem more embarrassed to read than God was to inspire.
Its lovers admire one another.
They desire one another.
They speak about beauty.
Longing.
Fragrance.
Touch.
Delight.

The language is poetic rather than pornographic, covenantal rather than exploitative, but its celebration of embodied marital love is unmistakable. Song of Songs can speak of love as beautiful and delightful without treating those words as enemies of holiness.
That should tell us something.
God did not create marital intimacy and then apologize for making it pleasurable.
But there is another side of this truth that our culture desperately needs.
Because saying pleasure can be good is not the same thing as saying:
“If it feels good, God approves.”
That is not Christianity.
That is appetite enthroned as god.
And appetite makes a terrible god.
The biblical question is never simply:
“Do I want this?”
The deeper question is:
“Can this desire be surrendered to Jesus Christ?”
Paul tells the Corinthians:
“Flee fornication.”
And then:
“Ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body.”
1 Corinthians 6:18, 20.
There it is.
Christian sexuality is not ultimately about how close you can walk to the edge without technically sinning.
It is about whether Jesus is Lord even here.
In your body.
In your browser history.
In your fantasies.
In your dating relationship.
In your marriage.
In your loneliness.
In your memories.
In your wounds.
In the secret places nobody at church sees.
The Gospel does not declare your spirit God's property while leaving your sexuality outside the kingdom.
Jesus claims the whole person.
And this is precisely why sexual holiness is bigger than repression.
Holiness means belonging to God.
The New Testament language of sanctification—ἁγιασμός, hagiasmos—carries the idea of holiness, consecration, being set apart to God.
Paul writes:
1 Thessalonians 4:3.
So biblical holiness does place boundaries around sexuality.
Real boundaries.
Not imaginary ones.
Not culturally convenient ones.
But those boundaries do not mean God hates sexuality.
They mean sexuality matters.
You put fences around something precious.
And perhaps this is where someone reading this feels the article suddenly getting personal.
Because we are no longer discussing theology in the abstract.
We are talking about you.
Maybe you love Jesus…
but your sexual history still whispers another name over you.
Dirty.
Used.
Addicted.
Unfaithful.
Damaged.
Hypocrite.
Too far gone.
Maybe nobody knows what you watch when you are alone.
Maybe you promised God you would stop.
Then returned.
Promised again.
Returned again.
Deleted it.
Downloaded it.
Confessed it.
Hid it.
Cried afterward.
Then walked into church on Sunday and lifted the same hands that were trembling with shame the night before.
Maybe your story is different.
Maybe somebody violated what God intended to be sacred.
And now even the word “sex” does not sound beautiful to you.
It sounds dangerous.
Maybe intimacy reminds you of betrayal.
Maybe somebody used Scripture to pressure you.
Maybe someone demanded your body and called that biblical marriage.
Then hear this carefully:
1 Corinthians 7 does not present marital intimacy as unilateral ownership.
Paul's language is strikingly reciprocal.
“The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.”
The Greek verb is ἐξουσιάζει — exousiazei, “has authority over.”
But notice Paul's symmetry.
He applies the principle in both directions.
Husband toward wife.
Wife toward husband.

The passage therefore cannot honestly be reduced to “the husband gets whatever he demands.” Paul immediately speaks of mutuality and warns spouses against depriving one another except by mutual agreement for a limited spiritual purpose.
Biblical intimacy is not permission for coercion.
It is not permission for humiliation.
It is not permission for violence.
It is not permission to treat your spouse like property.
The New Testament takes two people and places both beneath Christ.
That changes everything.
Because Christlike love does not ask merely:
“What can I get?”
It asks:
“How can I give?”
And suddenly we discover why pleasure and holiness never needed to be enemies.
Holy marital intimacy is not merely pleasure received.
It can become affection given.
Trust embodied.
Vulnerability protected.
Faithfulness expressed.
Two people saying without words:
I am not shopping for another body.
I am not comparing you to pornography.
I am not consuming you.
I am not performing for strangers.
I am here.
With you.
Faithfully.
Tenderly.
Without shame.
That is radically different from the counterfeit our culture sells.
Pornography says:
Take without covenant.
Lust says:
Imagine without responsibility.
Adultery says:
Pleasure is worth betrayal.
Exploitation says:
Your desire matters more than another person's dignity.
But covenant says:
I will not separate your body from your person.
Holiness says:
Desire will not become my master.
Love says:
Your good matters alongside mine.
And Jesus says:
Follow Me.
That last command reaches much deeper than sexual behavior.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally God giving sexually broken people a longer rulebook.
Christianity is Christ giving dead sinners life.
This is where the scandal becomes grace.
Because some of us desperately want an article about sex to end with rules.
Rules feel safer.
Rules allow us to divide everybody into two camps.
Clean people over here.
Dirty people over there.
Virgins here.
Failures there.
Faithful people here.
Adulterers there.
Porn addicts there.
Victims somewhere else.
Divorced people.
Promiscuous people.
Abused people.
People carrying secrets they have never spoken aloud.
And then Jesus walks straight through our categories.
Not calling evil good.
Not pretending sexual sin does not matter.
But doing something infinitely more astonishing.
Calling sinners to Himself.
Remember the woman caught in adultery.
Jesus did not rename adultery righteousness.
But neither did He allow her sin to become the final sentence over her existence.
Grace did not say sin was harmless.
Grace made a new future possible.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not save us because our sexual histories are spotless.
Jesus saves sinners because His blood is sufficient.
The cross is where every illusion dies.
The illusion that sexual freedom can save us.
The illusion that religious respectability can save us.
The illusion that virginity can save us.
The illusion that marriage can save us.
The illusion that being heterosexual can save us.
The illusion that avoiding one particular category of sexual sin can save us.
Only Christ saves.
And when Christ saves, He does not merely forgive us so that we can continue bowing to the same masters.
Grace begins teaching us to walk differently.
This is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God screaming, “You disgust Me.”
Repentance is God calling:
Come home.
The Greek New Testament uses μετάνοια — metanoia — for repentance, language associated with a changed mind, a turning of orientation.
Repentance says:
Jesus, my sexuality belongs to You too.
My loneliness belongs to You.
My marriage belongs to You.
My desires belong to You.
My wounds belong to You.
My future belongs to You.
Even the parts of myself I am embarrassed to bring into prayer…
belong to You.
And maybe that is what somebody needs tonight.
Not another excuse.
Not another secret browser.
Not another hookup.
Not another fantasy.
Not another performance of religious perfection.
Jesus.
You need Jesus.
Because shame says:
Hide until you are clean.
The Gospel says:
Come to Christ because you cannot clean yourself.
Shame says:
Your worst chapter is your name.
The Gospel says:
Christ can write another chapter.
Shame says:
You ruined everything.
Grace says:
The cross was built for sinners who could not undo yesterday.
And holiness says:
Now get up.
Walk with Him.
Sexual pleasure is therefore neither our savior nor our enemy.
It is a created capacity that must remain beneath the lordship of its Creator.

Within biblical marriage, Scripture can speak unapologetically of delight, satisfaction, mutuality and a marriage bed kept undefiled. Hebrews 13:4 holds those realities together: marriage is to be honored and the marriage bed kept pure, while sexual immorality and adultery remain subject to God's judgment.
That means the Bible does not force us to choose between pleasure and holiness.
It forces us to choose between worshiping pleasure and surrendering pleasure to God.
That difference changes everything.
Sex makes a terrible god.
But God is not threatened by the goodness of what He created.
So if this exposed something hidden in you, don't hide behind religious language.
Be honest.
Not because comments save anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing darkness into honest Christian community is one small way of saying:
I refuse to keep pretending.
And if you know somebody who grew up believing their body itself was dirty, share this with them.
If you know someone trapped in pornography, sexual shame, adultery, regret, loneliness or secret temptation, do not use this article as a weapon.
Send it as a lifeline.
Save it too.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget truths we were certain about yesterday.
It does not.
And not because anyone should be pressured into giving.
Scripture itself says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity.”
2 Corinthians 9:7.
The Greek is particularly important here:
μὴ ἐξ ἀνάγκης — mē ex anankēs.
Not from compulsion or necessity.
Christian generosity should come willingly from the heart.
So if you prayerfully choose to support Gospel Warrior, let it be worship expressed through willing generosity—not spiritual pressure.
And whether or not you are able to support financially, sharing matters.
So share it.
Not to make yourself look religious.
Follow if you want to keep walking deeper into Scripture.
But above everything else…
come to Jesus.
Because the deepest question was never merely:
“Why did God make sex feel good?”
The deeper question is:
“What happens when every pleasure, every desire, every wound, every failure and every hidden room of the human heart finally bows before Jesus Christ?”
That is where freedom begins.
Not when desire disappears.
When Christ becomes Lord of it.
Not when your past becomes imaginary.
When grace becomes greater than it.
Not when you finally become impressive enough for God.
When you discover that the crucified and risen Christ came for sinners who could never rewrite themselves.
You may have chapters you wish you could burn.
Jesus specializes in stories everybody else thought were already ruined.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you after this article is this:
Your darkest sexual chapter does not have to become the final author of your story—the hands that were pierced for sinners are still rewriting lives.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS BEING A PROSTITUTE A SIN?
paragraphs: IS BEING A PROSTITUTE A SIN?

The Bible does not rename sexual sin to make us comfortable. But neither does Jesus throw away the person whose life has been tangled in it. And if you think this article is only about prostitutes, you may discover before the end that Jesus has been looking straight at you.
There is a question people sometimes ask quietly because they are afraid of the answer.
“Is being a prostitute a sin?”
Maybe you are asking because of someone you know.
Maybe because of something you have done.
Maybe because there is a chapter of your life you have never told anyone.
Maybe money was involved.
Maybe desperation was involved.
Maybe abuse was involved.
Maybe somebody used you before you understood what was happening.
Maybe you were trafficked, manipulated, threatened, groomed, abandoned, or trapped.
Or maybe none of those things happened.
Maybe you chose it.
And now you are wondering whether Jesus still wants anything to do with you.
So before we go any further, hear this carefully:
Jesus Christ is not frightened by the chapter you are ashamed to read out loud.
But He loves you too much to call darkness light simply to make you feel temporarily comfortable.
That is where the Gospel becomes both painful and breathtakingly beautiful.

Biblically, prostitution involving voluntary sexual activity outside the covenant of marriage falls within what Scripture condemns as sexual immorality. The New Testament frequently uses the Greek word πορνεία — porneia — for sexual immorality. The related word πόρνη — pornē — refers to a prostitute.
Paul writes:
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
That is 1 Corinthians 6:18.
Not negotiate with it.
Not rename it.
Not build your identity around it.
Flee it.
And the context matters enormously.
Just a few verses earlier, Paul warns that the sexually immoral will not inherit the kingdom of God. Those words are serious. Christianity does not offer grace by pretending sin does not exist.
But then comes one of the most beautiful sentences ever written to people with ruined histories:
“καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε.”
Kai tauta tines ēte.
“And such were some of you.”
—1 Corinthians 6:11.
Were.
That one word carries a resurrection inside it.
You were something.
Then Jesus intervened.
Paul continues by telling these believers that they were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Do you understand what that means?
The Gospel does not merely say, “What you did was wrong.”
The Gospel says, “What you did does not have to remain who you are.”
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says, “Come out of this. Jesus has something better.”
Condemnation whispers, “Stay down. You are permanently filthy.”
One voice leads toward Christ.
The other wants your shame to become your identity.
And Jesus did not shed His blood so your worst night could have the final word over your life.

The Old Testament commonly uses the Hebrew word זֹנָה — zonah — for a prostitute. Scripture never romanticizes prostitution or sexual immorality. Yet when we actually read the biblical story, something astonishing happens.
We meet Rahab.
Rahab is explicitly identified as a prostitute.
Her history is not erased from the story.
Yet neither is she abandoned to it.
When Israel came against Jericho, Rahab recognized something others refused to recognize: the God of Israel was truly God.
She confessed:
“For the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.”
—Joshua 2:11.
Then Jericho fell.
But Rahab lived.
The woman society could have reduced to a sexual label became part of Israel's story.
And centuries later, Matthew wrote the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Names carrying generations of history.
And then...
Rahab.
Matthew 1:5 places Rahab in the genealogy leading to Jesus.
Think about that.
Her past was not strong enough to prevent God's redemptive purpose.
And Hebrews 11 remembers Rahab not primarily by the sexual history that once described her life, but by faith.
James 2 remembers her actions as evidence of living faith.
That does not mean prostitution suddenly became righteous.
It means grace is powerful enough to redeem the prostitute.
That distinction is everything.
Christianity is not the announcement that sin never mattered.
Christianity is the announcement that sin mattered so much that the Son of God went to a cross—and that His mercy is so great that sinners can be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, and transformed.
There is another uncomfortable truth we must face.
Not everyone involved in prostitution arrived there through the same road.
Some chose it.
Some were coerced.
Some were trafficked.
Some were abused.
Some were children when exploitation began.
Some were manipulated by people who learned exactly how to weaponize their hunger, poverty, loneliness, addiction, fear, immigration status, or need for affection.
So Christians must be extremely careful about throwing the word “sinner” at an exploited person while ignoring the sins of the people exploiting them.
Scripture repeatedly condemns oppression and exploitation.

If someone is being trafficked or forced into sexual acts, that person's victimization should never be treated as though it were simply a voluntary sexual decision. The guilt belongs to those committing, facilitating, purchasing, or profiting from exploitation—not to a victim merely because another person violated or controlled them.
Jesus never commanded His people to make wounded people carry the guilt of those who wounded them.
But where prostitution involves freely chosen sexual activity outside biblical marriage, Scripture does call that sexual behavior sinful.
And perhaps somebody reading this is thinking:
“Then I knew it. God doesn't want me.”
No.
Keep reading.
Because this is where the scandal gets closer.
When religious leaders brought Jesus a woman caught in adultery in John 8, they were ready to turn her sin into her death sentence.
Jesus did not pretend adultery was holy.
But neither did He hand her over to their self-righteous bloodlust.
After her accusers departed, Jesus told her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Grace...
and truth.
Mercy...
and repentance.
No condemnation...
and no permission to remain enslaved.
That is Jesus.
Modern Christianity sometimes tries to separate those things.
One version screams, “SIN!” until wounded people believe God hates them.
Another whispers, “Nothing is sin,” until wounded people never discover that Christ can actually set them free from it.
Jesus does neither.
He forgives the sinner and calls the sinner out of sin.
He does not say, “Your chains are beautiful.”
He breaks them.
And now we need to talk about the part of this story most respectable people would rather avoid.
The prostitute is not the only sinner in the room.
Neither is the adulterer.
Neither is the addict.
Neither is the woman with the scandalous history.
Neither is the man whose sexual past would destroy his reputation if everyone knew.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
The prostitute needs Jesus.
So does the pastor.
The person selling sex needs Jesus.
The person secretly consuming pornography needs Jesus.
The sexually immoral need Jesus.
The sexually proud need Jesus.
The liar needs Jesus.
The gossip needs Jesus.
The greedy need Jesus.
The self-righteous churchgoer staring down at everybody else needs Jesus.
The cross destroys our favorite illusion—that humanity is divided into respectable people and disgusting people.
The deepest division is not between “good people” and “bad people.”
It is between sinners who need grace and the Savior who possesses it.
And every one of us stands on the same side of that line.
That is why one of the most dangerous sentences a Christian can say is:
“I would never become someone like that.”
Be careful.
Grace should make us humble.
You do not know every road another person has walked.
You do not know what happened behind the door.
You do not know who first touched them.
You do not know what promises were made.
You do not know who abandoned them.
You do not know how hungry they were.
You do not know what threats they received.
You do not know how many times they tried to escape.
You do not know what happened when they were six, twelve, sixteen, or twenty.
And even where someone walked deliberately into sin, Christians still have no permission to act as though their own salvation was earned by superior morality.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith...”
—Ephesians 2:8.
Grace leaves no room for boasting.
And if you are the person carrying this particular history, there is something you desperately need to understand.
Repentance is not God demanding that you somehow become clean enough before approaching Jesus.
You come to Jesus because you cannot cleanse yourself.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō — carrying the idea of a changed mind, a turning of one's orientation.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling disgusting.
Judas felt terrible.
Shame alone does not save anyone.
Repentance turns toward God.
You stop defending what God calls sin.
You stop hiding from the One who already knows.
You bring the truth into the light.
You trust Christ.
You receive mercy that you could never purchase.
And by His grace, you begin walking in another direction.
Sometimes that road is messy.
Sometimes freedom requires help.
Sometimes someone leaving prostitution needs somewhere safe to sleep before they need another sermon.
Sometimes she needs food.
Sometimes he needs protection.
Sometimes they need trauma-informed care.
Sometimes someone needs assistance escaping a trafficker.
Sometimes somebody needs a Christian community that will sit beside them without asking for the graphic details of their past.
Sometimes restoration means learning how to work again, trust again, sleep again, pray again, look into a mirror again.
The Church should know how to say both:
“Go and sin no more.”
And:
“You don't have to walk away alone.”
That is what redemption looks like when it grows hands and feet.
And perhaps this entire article has made you uncomfortable because your scandal has another name.
Nobody knows what you watch after midnight.
Nobody knows who you message.
Nobody knows about the affair.
Nobody knows about the hotel.
Nobody knows about the browser history.
Nobody knows about the secret relationship.
Nobody knows about the money.
Nobody knows what happened years ago.
Nobody knows how far you feel from the person you pretend to be on Sunday.
But Jesus knows.
And somehow...
He is still calling you.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
Because His cross is sufficient.
Romans 5:8 says that God demonstrates His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after the scandal disappeared.
Not after we became impressive Christians.
While we were sinners.
Christ died.
That is the heartbeat of Christianity.
Jesus did not come merely to improve respectable people.
He came to save sinners.
At Calvary, Jesus carried what sinners could not carry.
He bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
The Gospel is not positive thinking.
It is news.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ offering forgiveness and reconciliation to sinners who turn to Him in faith.
So is being a prostitute a sin?
If by that we mean voluntarily engaging in prostitution and sexual activity outside the marriage covenant, Scripture places such sexual conduct within what it condemns as sexual immorality.
But that is not the end of the answer.
Because the person is not the sin.
And no human being should be reduced to the worst thing he or she has done—or to the worst thing somebody else forced upon them.
Prostitution may describe someone's occupation.
Sexual sin may describe someone's behavior.
Victimization may describe what somebody suffered.
None of those words possesses the authority to write the final sentence of a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Jesus does.
There are former prostitutes in the kingdom.
Former adulterers.
Former drunkards.
Former thieves.
Former idolaters.
Former sexually immoral people.
Former versions of people whom grace refused to leave where it found them.
“And such were some of you.”
Maybe those words were waiting for you.
Were.
Not because the past never happened.
Because Jesus can write something after it.

If you are trapped in prostitution by coercion, threats, trafficking, or violence, please understand this clearly: seek safe, trustworthy help. Being exploited is not something you should be ashamed to disclose, and immediate danger deserves immediate protection.
If you are voluntarily living in sexual sin and the Holy Spirit is convicting you, do not turn this article into another thing you read and forget.
Come to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
There is no point hiding from the God who already sees everything.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Ask for help.
Find mature believers who care more about your restoration than your reputation.
You may have consequences to face.
Relationships may need rebuilding.
Habits may need breaking.
Doors may need closing.
Numbers may need deleting.
Income may need replacing.
Healing may take time.
But do not confuse a difficult road with an absent Savior.
Jesus never promised that repentance would make every consequence disappear overnight.
He promised something greater.
Himself.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail of your story. But you can make one small declaration that darkness will not own you forever.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not fighting alone.
One share can place the Gospel in front of somebody you may never know was considering giving up.
There may come a night when shame starts talking again.
Come back and remember:
“And such were some of you.”
But support should never be purchased guilt.
Scripture says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7.
It does not.
We will not tell you that salvation comes through supporting this ministry.
It does not.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.

Christians hold differing convictions concerning how Old Testament tithing relates to New Testament giving, while the New Testament plainly emphasizes generous, willing, cheerful giving rather than giving “of necessity.”
And whether or not you are able to support financially, you can still help.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Because somewhere tonight there is a woman convinced that what men did to her made her worthless.
Somewhere there is a man convinced his sexual sin has made him unreachable.
Somewhere there is a Christian smiling in public while privately drowning in shame.
Somewhere there is a prostitute who thinks a church would never want her.
Somewhere there is a religious person who needs to discover that he needs exactly the same Savior she does.
And somewhere...
perhaps behind the eyes reading these words...
is someone waiting to discover that Jesus already knows the whole scandal.
And He is still calling your name.

The final word over a surrendered life does not belong to the bedroom, the brothel, the trafficker, the customer, the addiction, the gossip, the church that rejected you, the person who exploited you, the sin you committed, or the shame that followed you home.
The scars may explain where you have been, but only Jesus gets to decide what grace can make of what remains.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WEEPING MAY ENDURE FOR A NIGHT, BUT JOY COMES IN THE MORNING” — DOES MORNING ALWAYS MEAN TOMORROW?
paragraphs: “WEEPING MAY ENDURE FOR A NIGHT, BUT JOY COMES IN THE MORNING” — DOES MORNING ALWAYS MEAN TOMORROW?
What if you prayed all night, believed with everything left in you… and woke up to discover that nothing had changed?
There is something nobody tells you when they quote, “Joy comes in the morning.”
Sometimes…
morning comes.
The alarm rings.
Sunlight slips through the curtains.
Cars begin moving outside.
People go to work.
Coffee gets poured.
The world starts another ordinary day.
And you are still hurting.
The diagnosis is still there.
The marriage is still broken.
The person you begged God to heal is still gone.
Your child still has not come home.
The bills are still sitting on the table.
The depression did not magically disappear at sunrise.
The prayer you whispered through tears at 2:13 in the morning still seems unanswered at 7:00.
And somewhere inside you, a frightening question begins forming:
“God… You said joy comes in the morning.
It’s morning.
So where is my joy?”
Maybe nobody has ever told you this.
Maybe you desperately need to hear it tonight.
Psalm 30 was never promising that every tragedy expires at midnight.
And “morning” does not always mean tomorrow.
Sometimes morning is a date only God knows.
But morning is coming.
Listen carefully to the actual Hebrew words of the psalm:
בָּעֶרֶב יָלִין בֶּכִי וְלַבֹּקֶר רִנָּה
Ba'erev yalin bekhi, velaboker rinnah.
“Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning.”
That is the language preserved in the Hebrew text of Psalm 30:5 in common English numbering, Psalm 30:6 in the traditional Hebrew numbering.
And there is something breathtaking hiding inside those words.
The Hebrew בֶּכִי — bekhi means weeping.
Not inconvenience.
Not irritation.
Weeping.
Scripture does not sanitize suffering.
The Bible does not look at the person whose heart has been shattered and say, “Real believers don't cry.”
It gives the tears a name.
Bekhi.
Weeping.
But then comes the word יָלִין — yalin.
It carries the idea of spending the night, lodging, remaining overnight.
Read that again slowly.
Your weeping is given lodging.
Not ownership.
It may spend the night…
but it does not own the house.
Pain can be a visitor without becoming your identity.
Grief can occupy a chapter without being allowed to write the final sentence.
The night can feel endless without actually being eternal.
And perhaps that is where someone reading this has been living.
Not in rebellion.
Not because you stopped loving Jesus.
You are simply tired.
You prayed.
You waited.
You worshiped when worship felt impossible.
You told everybody, “God is good,” and you meant it.
Then you went somewhere private and cried until you had nothing left.
People saw your Sunday smile.
God saw Tuesday at 2:00 a.m.
People heard your “Amen.”
God heard the shaking breath afterward.
People saw you serving.
God saw you sitting inside your car before going home because you needed five minutes where nobody needed anything from you.
And maybe you started wondering whether your long night means God abandoned you.
It doesn't.
The Bible never says faithful people never experience long nights.
Joseph had a night that lasted through betrayal, slavery, false accusation and prison before elevation came.
David was anointed king and then spent years running from a king who wanted him dead.
Job's morning did not arrive the day after his catastrophe.
Abraham waited years for the promised son.
Israel spent generations waiting for the promised Messiah.
And when Jesus Himself entered His darkest earthly night, Gethsemane was not followed immediately by visible relief.
It was followed by betrayal.
Arrest.
False accusation.
Mockery.
Scourging.
Nails.
A cross.
A tomb.
Think about that.
Sometimes obedience to God does not immediately take you out of darkness.
Sometimes obedience carries you straight through it.
That destroys the shallow version of Christianity that tells suffering people, “If you had enough faith, this would already be over.”
Jesus had perfect faith.
And still there was Gethsemane.
Jesus perfectly obeyed the Father.
And still there was Golgotha.
Jesus was perfectly loved by the Father.
And still there was a tomb.
So your suffering is not automatic proof that God has rejected you.
Your waiting is not proof that God has forgotten your address.
Your tears are not proof that your faith failed.
Sometimes faith looks less like shouting victory and more like whispering through trembling lips:
“Jesus… I still trust You.”
That may be one of the holiest sentences a wounded human being can speak.
Because biblical hope is not pretending midnight is noon.
Biblical hope looks straight into the darkness and says:
“This is night.
But night does not get the final word.”
Psalm 30 continues toward an astonishing reversal:
הָפַכְתָּ מִסְפְּדִי לְמָחוֹל לִי
Hafakhta mispedi lemachol li.
“You turned my mourning into dancing.”
The psalmist does not say the mourning was imaginary.
It had to exist before it could be turned.
There was sackcloth before gladness.
There were cries before songs.
There was darkness before dawn.
The entire movement of Psalm 30 is not denial.
It is transformation.
And that is the Gospel.
Christianity is not the announcement that terrible things never happen.
Christianity announces that because of Jesus Christ, terrible things do not possess ultimate authority.
Sin does not.
Shame does not.
Death does not.
The grave does not.
Your past does not.
Your worst failure does not.
Your deepest wound does not.
And your darkest night does not.
Because Christianity stands or falls on the greatest Morning in history.
Friday looked like defeat.
The disciples watched the One they believed was Messiah die.
His body was placed inside a tomb.
A stone was rolled across the entrance.
Imagine Saturday.
We know Sunday is coming because we have read the story.
They were living inside it.
They did not have the next chapter in their hands.
They had promises.
And a sealed tomb.
Maybe that is exactly where you are.
You know what God has said.
But everything you can currently see looks like a stone rolled across the promise.
Saturday faith is different.
Friday has already broken your heart.
Sunday has not arrived yet.
And all you have is the character of God.
That is where some of the deepest faith is born.
Not when you understand what God is doing.
When you don't.
Not when the tomb is empty.
When the stone is still there.
Not when you can testify about the breakthrough.
When your testimony is simply:
“I haven't walked away.”
Then Sunday came.
The stone moved.
The tomb opened.
Jesus Christ rose.
And suddenly the darkest event in human history became the doorway through which God displayed redemption.
The scandal of the cross became the proclamation of grace.
The instrument of Roman execution became the symbol Christians would carry across continents and centuries.
What looked like the end became the beginning.
That is why we say:
He does not rewrite history by pretending the wounds never happened.
The risen Jesus still bore scars.
Think about that.
Resurrection did not require pretending crucifixion never happened.
Jesus conquered the grave while retaining the marks of what He had endured.
Maybe healing is not always becoming the person you were before the night.
Maybe sometimes grace makes you someone deeper afterward.
Someone gentler.
Someone who notices hurting people.
Someone who no longer casually tells grieving people to “just have faith.”
Someone who knows how to sit beside another human being without trying to explain their pain away.
Someone whose scars have become evidence that the wound did not win.
That is morning.
Sometimes morning is an answered prayer.
Sometimes morning is reconciliation.
Sometimes morning is recovery.
Sometimes morning is finally being able to breathe again.
Sometimes morning is discovering that God did not change your circumstances yet—but He changed you inside them.
And sometimes…
we must say this carefully and honestly…
the fullest morning does not arrive in this lifetime.
Christian hope reaches beyond temporary earthly relief.
There are faithful Christians who die while still carrying unanswered questions.
There are mothers who never see the child return during their lifetime.
There are believers whose bodies are never healed on this side of eternity.
There are graves beside which Christians still cry.
The Bible does not ask us to lie about that.
It gives us something greater than the promise of an easy tomorrow.
It gives us resurrection.
There is coming a morning beyond every earthly morning when death itself will lose its claim upon the redeemed.
The Christian's ultimate hope is not, “Tomorrow everything will be easy.”
It is:
Jesus Christ is risen, and therefore darkness cannot be permanent.
Your morning may come tomorrow.
It may come slowly over months.
It may arrive through circumstances changing.
It may arrive through God changing something inside you while the circumstances remain difficult.
And the final morning—the one no darkness can ever invade again—is secured not by positive thinking, but by Jesus Christ.
So if you woke up today and still hurt…
you did not miss the promise.
If you prayed last night and the situation still looks impossible…
you did not miss the promise.
If everybody keeps telling you to “move on,” but grief still catches you unexpectedly in grocery-store aisles, empty bedrooms, old photographs and familiar songs…
you did not miss the promise.
Morning is not God's deadline.
Morning is God's declaration that night is temporary.
And perhaps your greatest danger tonight is not that you are crying.
It is that you are beginning to believe the darkness is telling you the truth about who you are.
It isn't.
You are not what somebody did to you.
You are not the affair.
You are not the divorce.
You are not the relapse.
You are not the bankruptcy.
You are not the diagnosis.
You are not the abuse you survived.
You are not the secret sin Jesus is calling you to bring into the light.
You are not the worst thing you ever did.
And if you belong to Christ, your scandal does not get the final sentence.
Grace does.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace calls sinners out of hiding.
Maybe your night is not only something that happened to you.
Maybe some of the darkness came from choices you made.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe pornography has quietly taken over your private life.
Maybe bitterness has lived inside you so long that you have begun calling it discernment.
Maybe pride has been wearing church clothes.
Maybe everybody thinks you're spiritually strong while you know exactly what happens when the door closes and the screen lights up.
Then morning begins with truth.
Not performance.
Not excuses.
Repentance.
Jesus did not die so we could decorate our darkness with Christian language.
He died to save sinners.
Real sinners.
People like Peter, who denied Him.
People like Paul, who persecuted His church.
People like the thief dying beside Him who had nothing impressive left to offer.
People like us.
This is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
You do not clean yourself up enough to earn morning.
You come to Christ.
You confess.
You repent.
You believe.
You receive mercy you could never purchase.
And the blood of Jesus speaks a better word over repentant sinners than shame ever could.
So perhaps this article found you during your night for a reason.
Not so someone can promise that by tomorrow morning your bank account will change, your spouse will return, your body will be healed or every unanswered question will disappear.
Scripture does not give us permission to make those guarantees.
But it gives us permission to say something stronger:
Jesus is still Lord in the night.
Jesus is still faithful in the waiting.
Jesus is still Savior when you cannot feel Him.
Jesus is still risen when your world feels buried.
And because the tomb of Christ is empty, darkness has already been served notice:
it does not reign forever.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a spiritual answer. Be honest.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall someone has spent years building.
Someone reading beneath you may realize they are not fighting alone.
That matters.
Then think of one person whose night has lasted longer than anybody knows.
Not the person most likely to react.
The person who actually needs this.
You may never know whose 2:00 a.m. prayer God answers partly through something you shared at 6:00 p.m.
Because nights have a strange way of making us forget what we knew in daylight.
Come back when the room is quiet.
Come back when the answer has not arrived.
Come back when you need to remember:
weeping may lodge for the night.
It does not own the house.
We want this ministry to be a place where people do not merely consume inspirational words.
We want people opening Scripture.
Repenting.
Healing.
Growing.
Returning to Jesus.
Learning the Gospel.
And helping somebody else find Him.
But hear this clearly.
Do not give because you think money can purchase God's favor.
It cannot.
Do not confuse supporting this ministry with purchasing grace.
Grace was purchased at a price none of us could pay—the blood of Jesus Christ.

Scripture teaches believers to give deliberately and willingly, “not grudgingly, or of necessity,” because “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). It also shows believers intentionally setting resources aside for Christian generosity (1 Corinthians 16:2).
So pray.
Use wisdom.
Honor your responsibilities.
Practice biblical generosity faithfully.
Supporting Gospel work can be one way we use resources for God's glory—but God is glorified by willing obedience, not spiritual pressure.
And if financially supporting is not possible for you right now, please do not carry shame about that.
You can still help tremendously.
Pray.
Invite others to follow.
Carry the message farther than an algorithm ever could.
Because the mission was never ultimately about building an audience.
It is about pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
And someday—perhaps sooner than you imagine—someone who once commented “pray for me” may return and write:
Someone who whispered, “Jesus forgive me,” may become the person telling another sinner about grace.
Someone who nearly surrendered to despair may become the person holding another wounded believer through midnight.
Someone ashamed of their scandal may discover that Jesus still writes redemption stories.
Maybe that someone is you.
So cry if you need to cry tonight.
The Bible has room for tears.
Grieve what needs grieving.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent of what needs repenting.
Forgive what Christ is asking you to release.
Ask for help.
Stop pretending.
But do not crown the night king.
The night is real.
The tears are real.
The wound is real.
But so is the cross.
So is the empty tomb.
So is mercy.
So is resurrection.
So is Jesus.
And the same Christ who walked out of His grave is still writing stories in places that look completely finished.
Maybe tomorrow changes everything.
Maybe it doesn't.
But your hope was never ultimately tomorrow.
Your hope has a name.
Jesus.
And when you cannot see morning yet, remember this:
The darkness may tell you that your story ended at midnight—but somewhere beyond what you can see, God is already preparing a sunrise the night cannot stop.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY WOULD GOD FORBID BOILING A YOUNG GOAT IN ITS MOTHER’S MILK?
paragraphs: WHY WOULD GOD FORBID BOILING A YOUNG GOAT IN ITS MOTHER’S MILK?

One of the strangest commands in the Old Testament may reveal something far more serious than an ancient cooking rule—and once you see what the Hebrew actually says, you may never read this passage the same way again.
There are verses in the Bible we underline.
There are verses we memorize.
There are verses we quote when life is falling apart.
And then...
there are verses that make us stop, stare at the page, and quietly ask:
“Lord... why is that in the Bible?”
This is one of them.

Hidden among commands concerning worship, justice, festivals, firstfruits, holiness, and Israel’s covenant life is a sentence so strangely specific that countless readers have rushed past it without knowing what to do with it:
“You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.”
That is Exodus 23:19.
Then something even stranger happens.
God says it again.
Exodus 34:26 repeats essentially the same command.
And then in Deuteronomy 14:21...
again.
Three times.
Not once.
Three times.
So perhaps the question is not merely, “Why would anybody cook a goat that way?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
Why did God care enough to place this unusual sentence repeatedly inside His covenant instruction to Israel?
And this is where we have to resist something Christians sometimes do with difficult passages.
We cannot invent an explanation simply because it sounds spiritual.
We cannot turn every mysterious detail into a secret prophecy.
We cannot say, “The Hebrew really means...” and then make the Hebrew say something it never said.
If we love the Word of God, we should love it enough to let it speak before we make it preach.
So look at the words.
The Hebrew reads:
לֹא־תְבַשֵּׁל גְּדִי בַּחֲלֵב אִמּוֹ
Lo tevashel gedi bachalev immo.
The straightforward sense is:
“You shall not cook/boil a young goat in the milk of its mother.”
Lo means “not.”
Tevashel, from the Hebrew root ב־ש־ל (b-sh-l), concerns cooking or boiling.
Gedi refers to a kid, a young goat.
Bachalev means “in the milk.”
Immo means “of its mother.”
The ancient Greek Septuagint likewise understood the sentence as a prohibition involving cooking the young animal in its mother’s milk:
οὐχ ἑψήσεις ἄρνα ἐν γάλακτι μητρὸς αὐτοῦ.
The precise vocabulary differs—the Greek uses a term commonly associated with a lamb—but the ancient translators clearly understood the command as involving a young animal and its mother’s milk.
And here is an important piece of biblical honesty:
The Torah gives the command.
It repeats the command.
But it never gives us a sentence saying,
“Here is the reason I commanded this.”
That matters.

Because several explanations have been proposed throughout Jewish and Christian history, and some are more plausible than others, but we should not promote a theory to the level of inspired Scripture.
One popular explanation says this was connected with pagan Canaanite religious or fertility rituals and that God was forbidding Israel from imitating the nations surrounding them.
That interpretation has a long history, and the location of the command beside material concerning Israel’s worship has understandably encouraged it.
But we should be careful.

Claims that archaeology has conclusively discovered the exact pagan ritual behind this command go beyond what the evidence securely establishes. Proposed parallels from ancient Near Eastern texts have been debated by scholars.
So we cannot honestly say:
“We know this was a Canaanite fertility ritual.”
We do not know that with certainty.
And sometimes three of the most faithful words a Bible teacher can say are:
“We don’t know.”
That is not weakness.
That is reverence.
God has not asked us to protect Scripture from unanswered questions by manufacturing answers.
But there is something the context does tell us.
The command appears in Exodus 23 immediately after Israel is told to bring the first of the firstfruits into the house of the LORD.
In Exodus 34 it appears again in a context involving covenant worship, appointed feasts, sacrifice, and firstfruits.
Then in Deuteronomy 14 it appears in a chapter deeply concerned with Israel’s identity as a people holy to the LORD and with distinctions concerning food.
That does not solve every historical question.
But it tells us something enormously important.
This command belonged to Israel’s covenant holiness.
God was teaching a redeemed people that belonging to Him reached farther than religious ceremonies.
Their worship mattered.
Their calendar mattered.
Their harvest mattered.
Their bodies mattered.
Their tables mattered.
Even their kitchens mattered.
Holiness was not something Israel was supposed to perform for an hour and then leave at the sanctuary.
They belonged to God everywhere.
And maybe that is where this ancient command suddenly gets uncomfortably close to us.
Because we are very good at dividing life into categories.
This is spiritual.
This is ordinary.
This is worship.
This is business.
This is church.
This is private.
This belongs to Jesus.
This part belongs to me.
But Scripture repeatedly destroys that illusion.
The God of Israel was not interested in being one compartment among many.
He was Lord.
Period.
And when Jesus Christ calls people today, He does not invite them merely to add Christianity to their existing lives.
He calls them to Himself.
Jesus said:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.”
That is discipleship.
Not Jesus on Sunday and self on Monday.
Not worship songs while protecting secret sin.
Not Bible verses on Facebook while bitterness controls the heart.
Not “Lord, Lord” with lips while another throne remains hidden inside us.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that hidden throne is.
Nobody else sees it.
People think you are doing fine.
You still smile.
You still post.
You may still attend church.
You may even encourage other people.
But somewhere between the public version of you and the person God sees when everything becomes quiet...
there is a war.
Maybe it is lust.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe pride.
Maybe greed.
Maybe an addiction you promised God you would stop feeding.
Maybe unforgiveness toward someone who wounded you so deeply that part of you believes releasing the hatred would mean pretending the wound did not matter.
Maybe you have not abandoned Jesus.
You have simply been slowly giving Him smaller rooms in your life.
And suddenly an ancient command about a young goat does not feel quite as irrelevant as it did five minutes ago.
Because the God who cared about Israel’s obedience in seemingly ordinary things still cares whether His people belong to Him completely.
Not because meticulous rule-keeping can save us.
It cannot.
That is precisely where we must move carefully from Sinai to Christ.

Christians are not ancient Israelites living under the Sinai covenant, and we should not pretend every food command given to Israel transfers directly into the church unchanged. The New Testament forces us to think about the old covenant through the finished work of Jesus Christ.
But the holiness of the God who gave those commands has not disappeared.
And neither has the human problem those commands could never finally cure.
Sin.
The Law could identify it.
The Law could expose it.
The Law could condemn it.
But the Law could not turn a guilty sinner into a new creation through human effort.
We needed more than instructions.
We needed rescue.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed a Savior.
And this is where the story becomes breathtaking.
The same Bible containing commands that expose the seriousness of holiness eventually leads us to a hill outside Jerusalem where the Holy One does something no sinner could do for himself.
Jesus Christ takes our guilt.
Not because we became clean enough.
Not because we finally kept enough commandments.
Not because we gave enough money.
Not because we joined the correct ministry.
Not because we shared enough Christian posts.
Not because we looked religious enough.
Grace cannot be purchased.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith... it is the gift of God.”
Jesus went to the cross for sinners.
Real sinners.
Secret sinners.
Religious sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
Broken sinners.
People whose stories would look scandalous if every hidden chapter were suddenly projected onto a screen.
People like us.
And at Calvary, the scandal of human sin collided with the astonishing grace of God.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
And now the Gospel does not merely say:
“Try harder.”
It announces:
“Come to Christ.”
Repent.
Believe.
Be forgiven.
Be reconciled to God.
Let the One who carried your sin begin rewriting what sin tried to destroy.
That is why holiness after the cross is not an attempt to purchase God’s love.
It is the response of people who have received it.
We do not obey so Jesus will finally love us.
We learn obedience because in Christ we have encountered a love so holy, costly, and undeserved that surrender becomes worship.
And suddenly the strange command from Exodus carries a larger lesson without our having to invent a secret meaning for it.
God has always had the right to define what faithfulness looks like for His covenant people.
Israel did not get to rewrite God according to the surrounding nations.
And neither do we.
Our culture says truth should adjust itself to our desires.
Jesus calls us to bring our desires underneath truth.
Our culture says, “Follow your heart.”
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
Our culture says your greatest goal is self-expression.
The Gospel announces something far more radical:
You were made for God.
Maybe that is why this verse bothers modern readers more than we realize.
The strange part is not really the goat.
The strange part, to us, is a God who believes He has authority over details.
We are comfortable with a God who comforts.
We become nervous around a God who commands.
We love grace when grace means God receiving us.
We struggle with grace when grace begins transforming us.
But biblical grace does both.
Jesus receives sinners as they come.
And He loves them too much to leave them enslaved to what was killing them.
That is the journey from scandal to grace.
Peter knew it.
He publicly denied Jesus.
Grace rewrote him.
The Samaritan woman knew it.
Her history was complicated enough that she came to draw water beneath the heat of the day.
Grace rewrote her story.
The thief dying beside Jesus had no lifetime left with which to repair his reputation.
Grace reached him there.
Paul had persecuted the church.
Grace rewrote him.
And maybe your story contains pages you wish had never been written.
Things you did.
Things done to you.
Years wasted.
Relationships destroyed.
Promises broken.
A child who wandered.
A marriage barely breathing.
A faith that once burned brightly and now feels like embers.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say the scandal never happened.
Grace is greater than pretending.
Grace looks directly at the truth...
and then points toward a bloodstained cross and an empty tomb.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Jesus Christ still forgives.
Jesus Christ still restores.
Jesus Christ still transforms.
Jesus Christ still rewrites stories.
Bring it into the light before Christ.
You do not need to explain your entire story publicly.
Sometimes two honest words are enough to tell another believer:
“I’m still fighting.”
And sometimes another person reading those words realizes they are not the only one fighting too.
Not because every interpretation surrounding this ancient command is certain. It is not.
Truth is powerful enough.
And invite someone who feels too ashamed to return to Jesus.
They especially need to hear this:
Grace has not run out.

If Gospel Warrior has been helping you understand Scripture, grow closer to Christ, confront sin honestly, heal through biblical truth, and remain spiritually nourished, consider following and supporting this work.
Financial support should never be presented as purchasing God’s favor, buying salvation, or earning a blessing.
Scripture says giving should not be done “reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
So there is no spiritual invoice attached to this article.
No price on grace.
No payment required to glorify God.
But voluntary generosity can genuinely become an act of worship when it flows from gratitude to Christ and a sincere desire to help biblical truth reach more people.
It helps sustain the work.
It helps expand the reach.
It helps us keep placing Scripture, discipleship resources, encouragement, conviction, and the Gospel in front of people who might otherwise never encounter them.
And sharing costs nothing.
Not so we can build a crowd around ourselves.
So we can keep pointing the crowd toward Christ.
Because eventually every Bible question—whether familiar or strange—should teach us humility before the God who spoke.
We began with a young goat.
We began with milk.
We began with one of those sentences people read and wonder why God bothered putting it there.
But perhaps we end somewhere much closer to home.
God's Word is not ours to domesticate.
Sometimes we understand immediately.
Sometimes centuries of interpreters wrestle with a passage.
Sometimes archaeology illuminates the background.
Sometimes it complicates our theories.
And sometimes God has told us exactly what He requires without telling us everything we wish we knew about why.
Faithfulness means we refuse to fill God's silence with confident fiction.
And discipleship means we refuse to call Jesus Lord only when His words are easy.
So open the Scriptures again.
Ask harder questions.
Check what teachers tell you.
Study context.
Learn the history.
Examine the Hebrew and Greek when it genuinely helps.
But above everything...
look for Christ without forcing Christ into meanings the biblical authors never wrote.
Because Jesus does not need invented mysteries to be magnificent.
The real Gospel is already astonishing enough.
The holy God welcomes guilty people through His Son.
The condemned can be forgiven.
The faraway can come home.
The ashamed can lift their heads.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
And the person convinced that their story has already been ruined beyond repair can discover that the Author has not put down His pen.
So be honest before God tonight.
What part of your life have you quietly labeled:
“Jesus may enter everywhere except here”?
There.
That room.
That wound.
That habit.
That relationship.
That secret.
That fear.
That resentment.
That version of yourself you are desperately trying to keep alive.
Open the door.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive forgiveness where shame has been chaining you to sins Christ is willing to forgive.
And follow Jesus into whatever comes next.
Your testimony may become the sentence someone else desperately needs tonight.
But whatever you do...
do not leave merely fascinated by an ancient commandment.
Leave looking toward Jesus.
Because the greatest wonder in Scripture is not that God once told Israel not to boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.
The greatest wonder is that the holy God whom sinners repeatedly disobeyed still pursued redemption—and ultimately gave His Son so sinners could come home.
And when grace gets the final word, even the chapter you were ashamed to let anyone read can become the chapter where someone else discovers hope.
Your scandal may explain where you have been—but only Jesus gets to decide what grace can make of what comes next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES THE BIBLE TALK ABOUT VIRGINITY SO MUCH?
paragraphs: WHY DOES THE BIBLE TALK ABOUT VIRGINITY SO MUCH?
Maybe God Was Never Obsessed With Your Sexual History. Maybe He Was Protecting Something the World Taught You to Give Away—and Offering Grace for What You Cannot Take Back.
There is a question many Christians are afraid to ask out loud.
Why does the Bible seem to care so much about virginity?

Why does Scripture talk about sexual purity, marriage, adultery, fornication, nakedness, faithfulness, husbands, wives, wedding beds, and bodies as though these things carry enormous spiritual weight?
Why would the Creator of galaxies care about what two people do with their bodies behind a closed door?
And perhaps the more painful question is this:
