What if it is already too late for me?
Maybe you are reading this as a virgin.
Maybe you are reading this after sleeping with someone you thought you would marry.
Maybe you gave yourself away because you were lonely.
Maybe you were pressured.
Maybe you were manipulated.
Maybe you confused being wanted with being loved.
Maybe pornography became the secret room you kept returning to when nobody was watching.
Maybe you have a history you would erase tonight if God placed an eraser in your hand.
Or maybe something sexual happened to you that you never chose at all.
Before we go any further, that distinction matters enormously.
Sexual sin committed by a person and sexual violence committed against a person are not the same thing.
Someone else's sin against your body does not make you morally guilty for what they did.
And if your story contains abuse, coercion, assault, exploitation, or violation, Christianity does not require you to carry the perpetrator's shame.
Jesus does not look at the wounded and call them dirty.
He comes near.
But for those of us who did choose what God forbade, Scripture refuses another lie too.
It refuses to tell us that sin does not matter.
That is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because the modern world often asks Christianity to choose between two extremes.
Condemn people until they drown in shame...
or redefine sin until nobody needs repentance.
Jesus does neither.
He tells the truth about sin while opening His arms to sinners.
And that changes everything.

The Hebrew Scriptures use the word בְּתוּלָה—betulah—commonly referring to a virgin or maiden. In places such as Deuteronomy 22, related language about בְּתוּלִים—betulim, virginity—is connected with the serious covenantal, familial, and legal realities surrounding marriage in ancient Israel. The language should be read in its ancient context rather than reduced to the modern slogan that a person's worth equals whether they have ever had sex.
That reduction has wounded people.
Biblical sexual purity matters.
But your value as a human being does not originate in your virginity.
Read that again.
Your value does not originate in your virginity.
A virgin can be proud, cruel, dishonest, lustful, self-righteous, and spiritually dead.
A person with a catastrophic sexual past can fall before Christ in repentance and be washed, forgiven, adopted, transformed, and made new.
Virginity is not the Gospel.
Jesus is.
And once you understand that, you can finally understand why Scripture takes sex so seriously without turning sexual history into an idol.
Paul writes:

The heart of 1 Thessalonians 4:3 is straightforward: God's will for His people includes their hagiasmos—ἁγιασμός—their sanctification, holiness, consecration—and therefore abstaining from porneia—πορνεία—sexual immorality. The Greek terminology points beyond a simplistic obsession with a biological status. Paul is talking about a life being consecrated to God.
That changes the question.
The question is no longer merely:
“Have you had sex?”
The deeper question becomes:
“Who owns your body?”
And Paul gives an astonishing Christian answer.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
That is the heartbeat of 1 Corinthians 6.
Your body is not meaningless matter carrying around your “real” spiritual self.
Christianity does not teach that your soul matters while your body is disposable.
The incarnation itself destroys that idea.
The eternal Son of God took flesh.
Jesus Christ entered human history with a body.
He suffered in a body.
He shed blood from a body.
He died bodily.
He rose bodily.
And Christians await the resurrection of the body.
So Christianity cannot shrug at what we do sexually and say, “It's only physical.”
There is no “only” about the body in biblical Christianity.
That is why Paul does not tell Christians merely to manage sexual immorality.
He tells them to flee it.
The Greek word πορνεία—porneia—is used in the New Testament for prohibited sexual wrongdoing and appears repeatedly in commands to abstain from, flee, or repent of sexual immorality.
But here is where some purity teaching has gone terribly wrong.
We sometimes communicated biblical holiness using illustrations that implied sexually sinful people become permanently contaminated.
A chewed piece of gum.
A used piece of tape.
A dirty cup.
A crushed flower.
Think carefully about what those illustrations accidentally say.
They say redemption cannot restore you.
They say your sexual past has greater power to define you than the blood of Christ.
That is not the Gospel.
Sin has consequences.
Sexual sin can leave devastating consequences.
Broken trust.
Pregnancy outside marriage.
Disease.
Memories.
Attachments.
Comparison.
Betrayal.
Divorce.
Abortion.
Pornographic addiction.
Secret shame.
Families fractured by adultery.
Children caught inside adult decisions.
Some consequences do not magically disappear when somebody becomes a Christian.
Grace is not pretending the wreckage never happened.
Grace is discovering that wreckage does not get the final word.
Look at the scandalous people woven through the biblical story.
Judah's family history contains sexual scandal.
Rahab had a scandalous reputation.
David committed adultery and then orchestrated terrible evil attempting to conceal what followed.
The Samaritan woman Jesus met carried a complicated relational history.
The Corinthian church contained people rescued from lives Paul described in brutally honest terms.
And then Paul said something staggering:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because their histories vanished.
Not because their sins became acceptable.
Because Jesus had intervened.
They had been washed.
Sanctified.
Justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
This is where Christianity becomes radically different from both shame culture and hookup culture.
Hookup culture can say:
Your sexual choices do not really matter.
Shame culture can say:
Your sexual choices are all that matter.
Jesus says:
Your sin matters so much that I died for it...
and My grace is powerful enough that it does not have to define you anymore.
That is Christianity.
This is why the Bible's concern with sexual purity is ultimately not an obsession with virginity.
It is a vision of covenant.
Sex was never designed merely as recreation for two consenting bodies.

Within biblical theology, sexual union belongs inside the covenant of marriage, where a man and woman give themselves to one another in a faithful union. Jesus Himself reaches back to Genesis when discussing marriage: the two become “one flesh.”
One flesh.
That is deeper than entertainment.
Sex says something with the body.
It says, in effect:
I give myself to you.
The tragedy is that human beings learned how to make that bodily declaration while withholding covenant.
Bodies say union.
Lives say temporary.
Bodies say intimacy.
Hearts say don't get attached.
Bodies say vulnerability.
Culture says keep your options open.
And then we wonder why people can feel simultaneously desired and profoundly alone.
God's commands are not arbitrary fences erected by a celestial killjoy terrified that somebody somewhere might enjoy themselves.
His commands reveal His design.
Biblical boundaries around sex are not evidence that God hates sex.
The Bible contains the Song of Songs.
God created sexuality.
God created desire.

God invented the human body before pornography ever monetized it, before advertisers exploited it, before hookup apps commodified it, and before human beings learned to use another person's loneliness for temporary gratification.
God is not embarrassed by sex.
He is opposed to what sin does to His gifts.
Fire belongs in a fireplace.
Outside its proper boundaries, the same fire that warms a home can consume it.
And maybe that is why this subject hurts so badly.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to get burned.
You promised yourself it would happen once.
Then twice.
Then you stopped counting.
You said the relationship was serious.
Then they disappeared.
You thought sending the picture would make them stay.
It didn't.
You thought pornography would relieve the loneliness.
Instead, loneliness learned your password.
You thought sleeping together would deepen commitment.
Instead, you discovered that physical access can imitate intimacy without creating covenant.
And now perhaps you sit in church while everyone assumes you are fine.
You worship.
You smile.
You post Bible verses.
But somewhere underneath all of it lives a sentence you have never dared to say:
“If they knew what I've done, they would never look at me the same.”
Maybe.
People might not.
Jesus already knows.
That is what makes the cross so terrifyingly beautiful.
Christ did not die for the edited version of you.
He did not wait for your browser history to become respectable.
He did not wait for the affair to disappear from your memory.
He did not wait for your fantasies to become clean enough.
He did not wait until you could rewrite your past.
He went to the cross knowing the unedited manuscript.
Every chapter.
Every secret.
Every night.
Every lie.
Every body.
Every betrayal.
Every hidden search.
Every rationalization.
Every tear afterward.
And still...
He went.
This does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
Biblical grace never says, “Keep your sin.”
Grace says, “Come out of your grave.”
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could decorate our chains with Christian vocabulary.
He came to set captives free.
So if you are sexually active outside biblical marriage, repentance may require stopping.
If you are committing adultery, repentance means ending the adultery.
If pornography owns a secret room in your life, repentance means bringing darkness into light and taking concrete steps toward freedom.
If you have been using people for gratification, repentance includes learning to see human beings as image-bearers rather than bodies available for consumption.

And if you are dating someone who continually pushes you toward what Christ tells you to flee, you need to ask whether that relationship is helping you follow Jesus or teaching you to negotiate with Him.
Grace is free.
Following Jesus will cost you something.
Sometimes it costs the relationship you thought you could not live without.
Sometimes it costs the secret account.
Sometimes it costs your pride.
Sometimes it costs admitting to another mature believer that you are not doing nearly as well as everyone thinks.
Sometimes repentance sounds less like thunder and more like a trembling sentence:
“I need help.”
If that is you, say it.
Do not wait until the chains become heavier.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every private detail. But you can take one honest step.
Or comment, “pray for me” if you are exhausted from fighting the same temptation.
Not because typing words saves anybody.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when pretending ends.
And perhaps someone reading the comments needs to discover they are not the only Christian fighting for holiness with tears in their eyes.
Now we have to address the question that quietly haunts people with a sexual past.
Can I ever be pure again?
If by “virgin” you mean someone who has never engaged in sexual intercourse, Christianity does not require us to manipulate language and pretend history did not happen.
Your biography is your biography.
But Christianity offers something infinitely greater than pretending your past never occurred.
It offers redemption.
Purity in Christ is not time travel.
It is transformation.
You cannot crawl backward into yesterday and become the person who never sinned.
But Jesus can make you into someone yesterday's sin no longer owns.
There is a difference between innocence and redemption.
Innocence says:
“I have never fallen there.”
Redemption says:
“I fell there, and Jesus found me there.”
Innocence has a beautiful testimony.
Redemption does too.
Do not despise either.
And do not turn virginity into spiritual superiority.
The sexually inexperienced person desperately needs Jesus.
The sexually broken person desperately needs Jesus.
The married person needs Jesus.
The single person needs Jesus.
The addict needs Jesus.
The recovering addict needs Jesus.
The person with decades of faithfulness needs Jesus.
The person who crawled back to God last night needs Jesus.
At the foot of the cross, nobody gets to boast.
That may be the deepest reason the Bible's sexual ethic still matters.
Not because Christianity worships virginity.
Because Christianity worships Christ.
Your sexuality is therefore brought under His lordship along with your money, ambitions, anger, speech, relationships, appetites, plans, career, time, and future.
Jesus does not ask to become Lord of the religious corner of your life.
He is Lord.
Including behind the locked door.
Including when your phone is in your hand at 1:17 in the morning.
Including when nobody would ever find out.
That is where discipleship becomes real.
Not because you need another saved Facebook post.
Come back when your emotions start rewriting your theology.
“Jesus forgive me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
“No more hiding.”
Or share a testimony of how Christ brought you out.
Your honesty may become somebody else's permission to stop pretending.
And if Gospel Warrior has genuinely helped you grow closer to Christ, there is another way you can help this ministry continue.
Not because God owes you a blessing if you pay.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces generosity to your local church, care for your family, or giving to people in need.
And not because anyone should give under spiritual pressure.
Scripture says Christian giving should come from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion.
But voluntary generosity can become worship when it is offered to God with a sincere heart.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
The Gospel was never meant to terminate with us.
We receive truth...
and then we carry it.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is lying in bed convinced that what happened sexually—or what they chose sexually—has permanently disqualified them from coming home.
They need to hear the truth.
Virginity is precious.
Sexual holiness matters.
God's commands matter.
Repentance matters.
But virginity is not a savior.
Jesus is.
Your sexual history cannot bleed for your sins.
Jesus did.
Your virginity cannot resurrect you.
Jesus can.
Your shame cannot sanctify you.
Christ can.
Your past cannot pronounce the final sentence over a life Jesus has claimed.
So come to Him.
Not tomorrow when you feel cleaner.
Now.
Come ashamed.
Come trembling.
Come after the relapse.
Come after the breakup.
Come after the confession.
Come carrying the memories.
Come with the consequences you cannot reverse.
Come with a heart finally tired of negotiating.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His mercy.
Then get up and learn to walk in holiness—not so Jesus will finally love you, but because in Christ you have encountered a love too costly to keep treating casually.
And remember this when shame whispers your old name:
Jesus does not need to erase your history to redeem your story—He only needs the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID BOTH PEOPLE WASH AFTER SEX IF SEX BETWEEN THEM WASN’T FORBIDDEN?
paragraphs: WHY DID BOTH PEOPLE WASH AFTER SEX IF SEX BETWEEN THEM WASN’T FORBIDDEN?

Leviticus 15:18 sounds scandalous until you discover the difference between being “unclean” and being guilty—and that difference may completely change the way you understand holiness, intimacy, shame, and the grace of Jesus Christ.
There is one sentence buried in Leviticus that can make a modern reader stop.
Not because it condemns sexual immorality.
Not because somebody committed adultery.
Not because someone violated another person.
But because apparently nothing immoral happened at all.
And yet God told both people to wash.
Leviticus 15:18 says that when a man lies with a woman and there is an emission of semen, both are to bathe in water and remain “unclean” until evening. The Hebrew text reads:
וְאִשָּׁה אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁכַּב אִישׁ אֹתָהּ שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע וְרָחֲצוּ בַמַּיִם וְטָמְאוּ עַד־הָעָרֶב
Ve’ishshah asher yishkav ish otah shikhvat-zara, verachatsu vammayim, vetam’u ad-ha‘arev.
In straightforward English:
When a man has sexual relations with a woman involving an emission of semen, both are to bathe in water, and they remain ritually unclean until evening.

That is substantially what the Hebrew says. The surrounding verses confirm the setting: Leviticus 15:16 speaks of a man's seminal emission, verse 17 addresses material on which semen falls, and verse 18 addresses intercourse involving that emission.
But here is the question almost nobody asks:
If the sexual act itself were necessarily sinful, why doesn't the passage call for repentance?
Why isn't there a confession?
Why isn't the couple commanded to bring a sacrifice for deliberate sexual sin?
Why does the text simply say...
Wash.
Wait until evening.
Then the period of ritual impurity ends.
Because one of the biggest mistakes we can make when reading Leviticus is assuming that ritually unclean means morally sinful.
It doesn't.
And once you understand that distinction, this strange little verse becomes extraordinarily revealing.
The Hebrew word translated “unclean” comes from טָמֵא — tame’.

In Leviticus, tame’ describes ritual impurity—a condition that affected a person's participation in Israel's sacred sphere. It does not automatically mean that the person committed a moral transgression.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because Leviticus itself associates ritual impurity with things that are not inherently sinful.
A woman menstruating could become ritually unclean.
A person touching a corpse could become ritually unclean.
A man experiencing a normal seminal emission could become ritually unclean.
Childbirth was followed by a period of ritual purification.
None of those realities means that menstruation, burying the dead, involuntary bodily functions, marital intimacy, or giving birth are inherently moral sins.
That would turn ordinary human biology into rebellion against God.
The biblical categories are more careful than that.
And suddenly Leviticus 15:18 begins to make sense.
The verse is not saying:
“Sex happened, therefore somebody sinned.”
It is saying that an emission associated with intercourse placed both participants into a temporary state of ritual impurity under Israel's purity system.
Notice the duration.
Not seven years.
Not seven months.
Not even seven days.
Until evening.
Then the condition ended.
The text's own language is remarkably restrained. Both bathe. Both remain tame’ until evening.
Even the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, the Septuagint, preserves the same basic idea:
καὶ λούσονται ὕδατι καὶ ἀκάθαρτοι ἔσονται ἕως ἑσπέρας
They wash themselves with water and remain akathartoi—unclean—until evening.
This was purification language.
Not automatically condemnation language.
And that difference matters because the Bible is not embarrassed by sex within the boundaries God establishes for it.
God created humanity male and female.
God commanded the first couple to “be fruitful and multiply” in Genesis 1:28.
Genesis 2 presents the man and woman becoming “one flesh.”
Proverbs tells a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth.
Song of Songs contains some of Scripture's most passionate poetic celebration of marital desire.
Hebrews 13:4 says marriage should be honored and the marriage bed kept undefiled.
So Scripture does not teach that sex itself is dirty.
It teaches that sexuality is powerful enough to be holy when rightly ordered—and destructive when torn away from God's design.
That is a very different message.
Our culture tends to fall into opposite errors.
One side says:
“If it feels good and both people want it, nothing else matters.”
The other sometimes communicates:
“Sex is basically dirty, embarrassing, and spiritually suspicious.”
The Bible refuses both extremes.
Sex is neither god nor garbage.
It is created.
It is embodied.
It is powerful.
It belongs under God's authority.

And precisely because Scripture treats the human body seriously, Leviticus pays extraordinary attention to bodily boundaries, bodily fluids, life, death, blood, reproduction, disease, worship, and access to sacred space.
Leviticus is teaching Israel something larger than hygiene.
God is holy.
Human beings are creatures.
Life and death matter.
Bodies matter.
Worship matters.
Approaching the holy God is not casual.
That is why reading every occurrence of “unclean” as “wicked” badly distorts the book.
Imagine telling an Israelite woman that her menstrual cycle meant she had committed a moral evil.
The text does not say that.
Imagine telling parents that childbirth itself proved moral guilt.
The text does not say that either.
And imagine telling a married couple that because Leviticus 15:18 required washing after intercourse, their marital intimacy must have been sinful.
Again...
The text does not say that.
This becomes even clearer when you compare Leviticus 15 with the sexual prohibitions that follow later in Leviticus.
When Scripture intends to prohibit sexual relationships, it knows how to do so.
Leviticus 18 explicitly identifies prohibited relationships and practices.
That chapter speaks differently.
It prohibits.
It warns.
It establishes boundaries.
Leviticus 15:18, by contrast, gives a purification procedure following seminal intercourse.
Those categories must not be collapsed.
And perhaps this is where an ancient purity law suddenly reaches into something painfully modern.
Because some people reading this were taught to feel dirty about their bodies long before they understood what Scripture actually said.
Some were made to feel ashamed merely for experiencing attraction.
Some grew up believing holiness meant pretending sexuality did not exist.
Others went in the opposite direction and decided that because religious shame was destructive, every biblical sexual boundary must therefore be oppressive.
But Jesus offers something better than shame...
and something better than rebellion.
Truth.
Grace.
Holiness.
Restoration.
He does not need us to call God's gifts filthy in order to make God holy.
And He does not need us to call sin harmless in order to make grace beautiful.
Grace only becomes astonishing when truth remains truth.
Maybe that is why this obscure verse matters more than we first imagined.
It teaches us not to invent guilt where God did not pronounce guilt.
But it also teaches us not to erase boundaries where God actually established them.
Some of us desperately need to hear the first truth.
Others desperately need to hear the second.
And perhaps you need both.
Because there is another person reading this who isn't wrestling with an ancient Hebrew purity law.
You're wrestling with your past.
You clicked because the question was about sex.
But somewhere halfway through, another question started whispering.
“What about what I've done?”
What about the relationship you knew wasn't right?
What about the secret habit?
The betrayal?
The pornography nobody knows about?
The person you used?
The person who used you?
The marriage you wounded?
The boundaries you crossed?
The years you spent trying to convince yourself that God didn't care?
Or perhaps something was done to you, and someone else's sin taught you to feel ashamed of your own body.
Please hear this distinction carefully:
Being sinned against does not make you morally guilty for another person's evil.
And if you have sinned sexually, your story does not have to end where your sin occurred.
This is where Christianity becomes more than an argument about ancient vocabulary.
This is where we meet Jesus.
The Gospel does not say, “You were never dirty.”
Sometimes we were.
Not ceremonially.
Morally.
We sinned.
We rebelled.
We hid.
We rationalized.
We wanted God's gifts without God's authority.
But the Gospel also does not say:
“Clean yourself up enough and perhaps Jesus will take you back.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
Christ came for sinners.
At the cross, Jesus did what ritual water could never accomplish.
Water could wash skin.
Christ cleanses the conscience.
Water could address ceremonial impurity for a time.
Christ deals with guilt before God.

The New Testament deliberately develops this deeper cleansing imagery. Hebrews speaks of hearts being cleansed from an evil conscience and bodies washed with pure water, while 1 John 1:7 declares that the blood of Jesus cleanses believers from all sin.
Do you see the movement?
Water.
Purity.
Holiness.
Sacrifice.
Blood.
Cleansing.
And ultimately...
Christ.
The rituals were never the Savior.
Jesus is.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of people successfully washing themselves.
It is the story of a Savior who came for people who could never make themselves clean enough.
Think about the people Jesus touched.
Lepers.
The ceremonially unclean.
The bleeding woman.
The broken.
The rejected.
The publicly disgraced.
The sexually scandalized.
Jesus was repeatedly surrounded by people respectable society wanted to keep at a distance.
And something astonishing happens in the Gospel accounts.
Ordinarily, uncleanness spreads to what it touches.
But when Jesus touches the unclean...
Jesus does not become corrupted.
His wholeness overwhelms their brokenness.
His purity is not fragile.
His holiness is contagious in the opposite direction.
The leper is cleansed.
The bleeding stops.
The rejected are restored.
The guilty are called to repentance.
The ashamed discover mercy.
And sinners discover that their worst chapter does not have to become their final chapter.
Maybe that is why you needed to find this article today.
Not merely to answer:
“Why did they wash after sex?”
But to confront the deeper question:
Can Jesus still cleanse me after everything I've done?
Yes.
Not because your sin was insignificant.
Because His blood is sufficient.
Not because holiness no longer matters.
Because Jesus is holy.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Because grace finally gives sinners somewhere to turn when repentance breaks their hearts open.
Repentance is not pretending the past never happened.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Christ who already knows what happened.
You do not shock Him.
You do not surprise Him.
You cannot hand Jesus a chapter of your life He didn't know existed when He went to the cross.
The woman caught in adultery was not restored because adultery suddenly became righteous.
Jesus told her to leave her life of sin.
Grace did not rename darkness.
Grace gave the sinner a road out of it.
That is the Jesus many people desperately need to rediscover.
The Jesus who can say both:
“I do not condemn you.”
And:
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy without moral confusion.
Truth without cruelty.
Holiness without self-righteousness.
Conviction without hopelessness.
That is the Gospel.
And maybe your deepest problem has never been that you are too dirty for Jesus.
Maybe it is that you have spent years standing outside the door because you believed you had to wash yourself before entering.
You cannot.
Neither can I.
That is why we need a Savior.
Leviticus 15 had water.
The Gospel brings us to Christ.
And when Jesus cleanses a sinner, He does not merely polish the outside while leaving the grave untouched.
He makes people new.
So if this article exposed something you have been hiding, don't perform for the comments.
Be sincere before God.
Someone reading the comments may need your testimony more than you realize.
And if you're not ready to write details publicly, you don't owe strangers your private wounds.
Simply say:
“No more hiding.”
Then take that confession where it ultimately belongs...
to Jesus.
You may need to read it again.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
Share it with the seeker who thinks Christianity is merely a religion obsessed with shame.
Let them discover the Christ who tells the truth about sin while opening His arms to sinners.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you understand Scripture more deeply, consider following and supporting this ministry so this work can continue reaching people with Christ-centered biblical teaching.

Scripture describes Christian giving as willing and cheerful, not compelled (2 Corinthians 9:7), and Paul also speaks appreciatively of believers financially partnering in Gospel ministry (Philippians 4:15–18).
It should not be confused with buying God's blessing, purchasing salvation, or replacing whatever convictions and responsibilities you have concerning giving in your local church.
And there is something else many people still don't know.
Supporting this work helps us keep building.
Sharing helps us keep reaching.
Following helps you stay connected to the biblical teaching being published.
Commenting helps create a community where people stop pretending that Christians never struggle.
But whatever you do, never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Savior.
Jesus does not need your money to remain King.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot donate enough to erase yesterday.
Salvation is God's gift in Christ.
Give because you love Him.
Serve because you love Him.
Share truth because you love Him.
Support Gospel work because you want other people to encounter Him.
Because the goal was never to build an audience around Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point an audience beyond Gospel Warrior...
to Jesus Christ.
And now perhaps Leviticus 15:18 doesn't seem quite as strange.
Both people washed not because the verse declares their intercourse morally forbidden, but because under Israel's purity laws the seminal emission produced temporary ritual impurity.
The Hebrew says vetam’u—they became unclean.
It does not say in this verse that they had committed sexual sin.
That distinction is not a loophole.
It is responsible reading.
And responsible reading matters because when we call something sinful that God has not called sinful, we burden consciences unnecessarily.
When we call something harmless that God has called sinful, we numb consciences dangerously.
We need neither distortion.
We need truth.
And truth eventually leads us to the uncomfortable realization that all of us need cleansing deeper than water.
Maybe your scandal was sexual.
Maybe it wasn't.
Maybe yours was pride.
Adultery.
Bitterness.
Pornography.
Dishonesty.
Greed.
Secret resentment.
Religious hypocrisy.
A double life.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
But the Gospel does not end with the scandal.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly exposed.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes.
And still...
grace arrived.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that tells sin to stay comfortable.
Transforming grace.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that calls people out of darkness.
Grace that puts shattered lives back into the hands of their Creator.
Grace with nail scars.
So remember this when shame whispers your old name tonight:
The scandal may explain where Jesus found you—but grace determines what He can make of the life you surrender to Him.
Save that.
But above everything else...
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Walk in holiness.
And when your past tries to introduce you by the worst thing you ever did, remember that Jesus specializes in giving surrendered sinners a different ending.
Your scandal does not get the final sentence when the pen is in the hands of Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BEFORE I FORMED YOU IN THE WOMB, I KNEW YOU” — THE VERSE WE LOVE MAY BE SAYING SOMETHING EVEN MORE TERRIFYINGLY BEAUTIFUL THAN WE THOUGHT
paragraphs: “BEFORE I FORMED YOU IN THE WOMB, I KNEW YOU” — THE VERSE WE LOVE MAY BE SAYING SOMETHING EVEN MORE TERRIFYINGLY BEAUTIFUL THAN WE THOUGHT

Jeremiah 1:5 is often quoted as a comforting promise about your existence. But read the next sentence. God was not merely telling Jeremiah that he was known. He was telling a frightened young man that his life belonged to God before the world ever knew his name.
There are Bible verses we memorize because they comfort us.
And then there are Bible verses we think we know...
until we finally read what comes before them.
And what comes after.
Jeremiah 1:5 is one of them.
You have probably seen the words printed across baby announcements, photographs, wall art, social-media posts, devotionals, and inspirational graphics:
“Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee...”
Beautiful.
Personal.
Comforting.
But imagine hearing those words for the first time without knowing what comes next.
Imagine being Jeremiah.
No inspirational music.
No carefully designed background.
No audience applauding your “calling.”
Just God.
And you.
And a future you do not feel remotely qualified to face.
The Hebrew reads:

בְּטֶרֶם אֶצָּרְךָ בַבֶּטֶן יְדַעְתִּיךָ
וּבְטֶרֶם תֵּצֵא מֵרֶחֶם הִקְדַּשְׁתִּיךָ
נָבִיא לַגּוֹיִם נְתַתִּיךָ
Beterem etzorkha vabbeten yeda'tikha; uveterm tetze merechem hiqdash'tikha; navi laggoyim netattikha.
In straightforward English:
“Before I formed you in the womb I knew you; and before you came out from the womb I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
Jeremiah 1:5.
Read that last line again.
Not simply:
“I knew you.”
But:
“I appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
That changes the way we must read the verse.
God is speaking specifically to Jeremiah about Jeremiah’s prophetic calling.
This is not originally a generic motivational statement declaring that every person reading the verse has been appointed to Jeremiah’s prophetic office.
The text will not allow us to make it say that.
And strangely...
the verse becomes more powerful when we stop trying to make it about us first.
Because Jeremiah 1:5 begins with God.
“Before I formed you...”
The Hebrew verb comes from יָצַר — yatsar — “to form,” “fashion,” or “shape.”
It is language capable of evoking the work of a craftsman.
A potter does not accidentally discover the vessel taking shape beneath his hands.
He forms it.
Jeremiah's story therefore does not begin when Jeremiah recognizes God.
It begins with God.
Before Jeremiah preached...
before Jeremiah protested...
before Jeremiah suffered...
before Jeremiah became the man history remembers...
before his mother ever held him...
God says,
“I formed you.”
Then comes another astonishing expression:
יְדַעְתִּיךָ — yeda'tikha.
“I knew you.”
The root is יָדַע — yada — “to know.”
In Scripture, “knowing” can carry more weight than possessing information about someone. In contexts of divine-human relationship and election, it can express recognition, regard, or choosing.
God was not looking into the future and discovering Jeremiah as though Jeremiah surprised Him.
The initiative belongs to God.
But we must be careful here.
Jeremiah 1:5 is not giving us a scientific description of fetal development.
It is not primarily attempting to answer every philosophical question about human existence before conception.
It is a prophetic call narrative.
God is telling Jeremiah that Jeremiah’s commission did not originate in Jeremiah’s ambition.
Before Jeremiah could build a résumé...
God had already acted.
Before Jeremiah could impress anyone...
God had already acted.
Before Jeremiah could fail...
God had already acted.
Before Jeremiah could even say,
“I can't do this”...
God had already acted.
And Jeremiah does say exactly that.
Immediately.
That may be the part of the story that feels painfully familiar.
Because after receiving one of the most breathtaking declarations of calling in Scripture, Jeremiah does not respond like the hero in a movie.
He essentially says:
“Ah, Lord GOD... I don't know how to speak. I am only a youth.”
There it is.
The human response.
God speaks purpose.
Jeremiah sees inadequacy.
God speaks calling.
Jeremiah sees limitation.
God speaks mission.
Jeremiah sees himself.
And maybe that is where this ancient story suddenly gets uncomfortably close.
How many times has fear become the loudest interpreter of your life?
“I am not ready.”
“I am not educated enough.”
“I have already messed up too badly.”
“Someone else could do this better.”
“If people knew what I had done...”
“If they knew what I still struggle with...”
“If they knew what happens when the door closes and the smile disappears...”
“I cannot.”
Jeremiah knew that sentence.
But God does not answer Jeremiah by inflating Jeremiah's self-esteem.
That matters.
God does not say:
“Jeremiah, believe in yourself.”
He redirects Jeremiah's eyes away from himself.
Do not say, “I am a youth.”
You will go where I send you.
You will speak what I command you.
Do not be afraid of them.
Why?
Not because Jeremiah secretly possesses unlimited strength.
God gives him something infinitely better:
“I am with you.”
That is the center.
Not Jeremiah's greatness.
God's presence.
And that distinction reaches all the way to the Gospel.
Christianity is not ultimately the announcement that somewhere inside yourself is enough strength to become everything you were meant to be.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who could never rescue themselves have been met by a Savior who could.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve our self-image.
He came to save.
We sinned.
We wandered.
We hid.
We tried to rename rebellion as freedom and self-rule as authenticity.
Yet Christ came.
The sinless Son of God entered our broken world, bore sin upon the cross, died, and rose again.
Grace walked directly into the scandal.
And grace did not pretend the scandal was harmless.
Grace paid for it.
That is why the Gospel can look directly at the worst chapter of a repentant sinner's life without pretending it never happened.
The cross says sin is more serious than we wanted to admit.
The resurrection says Jesus is more powerful than we dared to hope.
Maybe you came to Jeremiah 1:5 wanting to hear:
“You are special.”
But perhaps God wants you to hear something deeper:
Your life is not ultimately about making yourself the center of the story.
Jeremiah's wasn't.
And ours isn't.
God is.
That is actually better news.
Because if your worth depended upon your accomplishments, your worst failure could destroy you.
If your hope depended upon maintaining the appearance that you had everything together, eventually the mask would become your prison.
If salvation depended upon becoming impressive enough for God...
none of us would survive.
But Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Not polished religious performances.
Sinners.
People carrying histories they cannot rewrite.
People who wish they could travel backward and unsay words.
Undo decisions.
Unclick something.
Unsend something.
Unbetray someone.
Unwaste years.
Uncross lines.
People who have lain awake wondering whether one terrible chapter permanently changed the ending.
And this is where the theme that has followed Gospel Warrior from the beginning becomes more than a slogan:
Not because Jesus changes history into fiction.
Grace does not call evil good.
Repentance does not mean pretending nothing happened.
Jesus does something greater.
He redeems sinners.
Peter still denied Christ.
Paul really persecuted Christians.
The thief really was hanging on a cross.
Their histories were not erased into imaginary innocence.
Grace changed what their histories ultimately meant.
And if you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is not the ugliest thing you have ever done.
It is not the name someone called you.
It is not the season when you fell apart.
It is not your addiction.
It is not your rejection.
It is not your divorce.
It is not your secret shame.
It is not the photograph you hate.
It is not the memory that still makes your stomach turn.
It is not even your ministry.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
That is why we must handle Jeremiah 1:5 carefully.
We do not honor Scripture by forcing ourselves into every sentence.
We honor Scripture by listening to what God actually said.
Jeremiah was specifically known, consecrated, and appointed for a prophetic mission to the nations.
The Hebrew word הִקְדַּשְׁתִּיךָ — hiqdash'tikha — carries the sense of consecrating or setting apart.
And נְתַתִּיךָ — netattikha — in this sentence expresses God's appointment of Jeremiah as a prophet.
The calling was real.
But so was its cost.
Keep reading Jeremiah and the inspirational poster becomes a life of tears.
Jeremiah would preach to people who often did not want to listen.
He would experience opposition.
Rejection.
Isolation.
Threats.
Grief.
His calling did not make his life painless.
Being known by God did not mean being applauded by people.
Being appointed by God did not mean being comfortable.
Sometimes obedience puts you exactly where applause disappears.
That may be one of the truths modern Christianity desperately needs to recover.
God's purpose is not synonymous with our comfort.
Calling is not celebrity.
Anointing is not popularity.
Faithfulness is not measured by followers.
And suffering does not automatically mean God abandoned you.
Jeremiah's story destroys the fantasy that being used by God means everybody will finally understand you.
Sometimes obedience costs.
Sometimes truth makes a room colder.
Sometimes following Christ means losing what compromise could have preserved.
Jesus Himself never promised His disciples an applause-filled road.
He called them to follow Him.
And the road led to a cross before it led to resurrection glory.
So what can Jeremiah 1:5 legitimately teach Christians today?
Not that every Christian should announce, “I was appointed a prophet to the nations before birth.”
That belongs to Jeremiah's commission.
But Jeremiah's story reveals something gloriously consistent with the rest of Scripture:
God's knowledge is not limited by our chronology.
God's purposes do not depend upon human applause.
God forms human life.
God calls His servants according to His will.
And when God calls, human weakness does not surprise Him.
Jeremiah's inadequacy was already known by the God who called him.
Think about that.
The God who said, “I knew you,” was not later shocked when Jeremiah said, “I cannot.”
And perhaps someone reading this needs that distinction desperately.
God already knows what you keep trying to hide from Him.
You are not protecting Him from disappointing information.
He knows.
Your fear.
Your temptation.
Your history.
Your secret exhaustion.
Your resentment.
Your questions.
Your pride.
Your wounds.
Your hypocrisy.
Your late-night battles.
He knows.
But do not turn that into cheap comfort.
The biblical response to being known by God is not:
“Then nothing needs to change.”
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace makes repentance possible without despair.
Jesus does not expose us merely to humiliate us.
He calls sinners out of darkness.
So perhaps the question today is not:
“Was Jeremiah 1:5 secretly written about me?”
Perhaps the better question is:
“What happens when the God who knows me completely confronts the parts of my life I refuse to surrender?”
That question is harder.
Because there are things we call “struggles” that we secretly intend to keep.
Things we ask God to forgive while arranging the next opportunity to repeat them.
Things we hide beneath Christian vocabulary.
We sing.
We post verses.
We say, “God knows my heart.”
Yes.
He does.
That should comfort us.
And sometimes it should terrify us.
Because the heart we hide from everyone else is completely visible to Him.
Yet here stands Jesus.
Not waiting for you to become clean enough to approach Him.
Calling you to repent and come.
The answer to your shame is not better hiding.
The answer is Christ.
The answer to sin is not self-hatred.
It is repentance and faith in Christ.
The answer to failure is not pretending it never happened.
It is bringing the truth into the light and discovering that the blood of Jesus is sufficient for sinners who come to Him.
Maybe you have spent years constructing a version of yourself that people can safely admire.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
But you know how tired you are.
Maybe people call you faithful while you quietly wonder whether your heart has become cold.
Maybe you have been around Christianity long enough to know exactly how to sound alive while spiritually running on fumes.
No more hiding.
Not from God.
Come home.
Not to a brand.
Not to a personality.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
To Jesus.
Someone reading the comments may need your testimony tonight.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be one share away from opening a Bible again.
And invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who does not yet believe to follow with you.
This ministry also needs people willing to stand behind the work.
It does not.
But voluntary financial support can genuinely help Gospel-centered work continue and expand.
If you cannot financially support the ministry, please never believe that makes your prayers, encouragement, or presence insignificant.
You can help without spending anything.
Pray.
Use what God has placed in your hands.
Because the goal is not building an audience around Gospel Warrior.
The goal is pointing people beyond us...
to Christ.
Back to Jeremiah.
A young man says:
“I cannot.”
God answers, in effect:
“I am sending you.”
Jeremiah sees youth.
God sees His commission.
Jeremiah sees weakness.
God promises His presence.
And centuries later, we still hear the trembling words of a reluctant prophet because God proved faithful even when obedience became costly.
So the next time you see Jeremiah 1:5 printed beautifully across an image, remember what surrounds it.
Remember that it was spoken into a calling.
Remember the frightened young man.
Remember the nations.
Remember the opposition.
Remember the tears.
Remember the God who knew before Jeremiah knew.
And then remember something even greater.
Jeremiah could announce God's word.
But Jesus is the Word made flesh.
Jeremiah could call a rebellious people to repentance.
Jesus could bear the judgment repentant sinners deserved.
Jeremiah could weep over brokenness.
Jesus entered ours.
Jeremiah could speak about restoration.
Jesus purchased redemption with His blood.
Your ultimate hope is therefore not discovering that Jeremiah 1:5 secretly makes you the hero.
Your hope is discovering that you never needed to be.
Jesus is.
And perhaps freedom begins when we finally stop demanding that every page of Scripture revolve around us...
and discover the breathtaking beauty of a Bible that leads us again and again toward the God who saves.
You may have arrived here asking:
“Did God know me?”
But there is another question infinitely more urgent:
Do you know Christ?
Not merely know facts about Him.
Not merely follow Christian pages.
Not merely own a Bible.
Have you entrusted yourself to Jesus Christ?
If you have been running, repent.
If you have been hiding, come into the light.
If you have fallen, do not make your failure your permanent address.
If you have become spiritually cold, cry out to Him.
If you have never trusted Christ, come to Him.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is God's astonishing answer to sinners who could never save themselves.
And when Jesus gets hold of a ruined story...
the scandal does not get the final sentence.
The chapter you are ashamed to reread may become the very place where future generations see how fiercely Christ can redeem.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THIS IS THE DAY THE LORD HAS MADE” — YOU WERE PROBABLY NEVER TOLD WHAT PSALM 118:24 COMES AFTER
paragraphs: “THIS IS THE DAY THE LORD HAS MADE” — YOU WERE PROBABLY NEVER TOLD WHAT PSALM 118:24 COMES AFTER

We quote it when the sun rises. We print it on coffee mugs. We post it over beautiful mornings. But Psalm 118:24 is surrounded by rejection, desperate cries for salvation, a rejected stone, and a stunning reversal only God could accomplish. And once you see the bigger story, “this is the day” may never sound ordinary again.
There are Bible verses we know so well that we can stop hearing them.
Psalm 118:24 may be one of them.
“This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.”
Beautiful.
Familiar.
Comforting.
You may have whispered it while opening the curtains in the morning.
You may have posted it beneath a sunrise.
Maybe your grandmother said it.
Maybe your pastor quoted it.
Maybe you have repeated it on a day when you desperately needed to convince your own heart that life was still worth facing.
And there is nothing wrong with thanking God for another day.
Every breath is mercy.
Every sunrise is undeserved.
Every heartbeat is evidence that God has permitted us another moment beneath His heaven.
But Psalm 118:24 has a larger story.
And that story becomes far more powerful when you stop isolating verse 24 and begin listening to what happens immediately before it.
The original Hebrew reads:
זֶה־הַיּוֹם עָשָׂה יְהוָה נָגִילָה וְנִשְׂמְחָה בוֹ
Zeh-hayyom asah YHWH; nagilah venismechah vo.
“This is the day the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.”
But now...
Don’t stop there.
Back up.
Because just before the psalmist announces that there is a day God has made, something has been rejected.
Psalm 118:22 says:
“The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.”
Then comes verse 23:
“This is the LORD'S doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.”
Then:
“This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.”
Do you see the movement?
Rejected.
Then exalted.
Dismissed.
Then made central.
What human builders looked at and considered unsuitable, God chose for a place of astonishing importance.
And the psalmist looks at this reversal and essentially declares:
God did this.
“This is the LORD'S doing.”
Human beings rejected.
God overturned the verdict.
Human beings said no.
God had another word.
Human judgment discarded the stone.
Divine purpose gave it honor.
And suddenly verse 24 no longer sounds like nothing more than a cheerful sentence about waking up on Tuesday morning.
There is triumph behind it.
There is deliverance behind it.
There is reversal behind it.
There is a rejected stone behind it.
And for Christians, the story becomes even more breathtaking because Jesus Himself reached into this psalm and applied the rejected-stone imagery in His teaching.
Jesus quoted Psalm 118:22–23 in Matthew 21:42.
The apostles later used the same rejected-stone language concerning Christ in Acts 4:11.
The New Testament does not leave Christians guessing about the ultimate Christ-centered significance it sees in that rejected stone.
Jesus Christ—the One despised, rejected, condemned, crucified and treated as though He could simply be removed—became the cornerstone.
The verdict of men was not the verdict of God.
That changes the emotional weight of this psalm.
Because perhaps you know something about rejection too.
Maybe somebody looked at your worst chapter and decided that chapter was your entire identity.
Maybe people know what you did ten years ago but have no idea what Jesus has been doing inside you since.
Maybe your marriage broke.
Maybe your reputation collapsed.
Maybe you disappointed people who trusted you.
Maybe you disappointed yourself.
Maybe you carry memories you wish could be burned from history.

Maybe there are things in your browser history, your private conversations, your relationships, your finances, your thoughts, your past, or your secret life that you would be terrified to see projected onto a church screen.
And sometimes the cruelest builder rejecting the stone is the person staring back at you in the mirror.
You remember.
You know what you did.
You know where you went.
You know what nobody else knows.
So when someone tells you that God can redeem your story, part of you wants to believe it...
and another part whispers,
“Not mine.”
But look again at the stone.
Rejected.
Then chosen.
Humiliated.
Then honored.
What looked finished was not finished.
And here is where we must be careful.
Psalm 118 is not promising that every rejection in your life will result in earthly fame.
It is not saying everyone who walked away will come crawling back.
It is not promising that God will make everybody who hurt you regret what they did.
Christianity is not baptized revenge.
The Gospel gives us something infinitely greater.
It tells us that human rejection cannot overturn the purposes of God.
And nowhere is that more gloriously visible than in Jesus Christ.
The cross looked like rejection at its most brutal.
The Messiah was mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Condemned.
Crucified.
His enemies saw weakness.
Rome saw another execution.
Some saw a failed claimant.
His followers watched their expectations collapse beneath the weight of a cross.
But God was not finished.
That is the heartbeat Christians hear when the New Testament reaches back to Psalm 118 and identifies Jesus with the rejected stone.
The stone was rejected.
But the builders did not have the final word.
And neither does your scandal.
Neither does your shame.
Neither does your addiction.
Neither does your failure.
Neither does your divorce.
Neither does your betrayal.
Neither does the ugliest thing you have confessed at two in the morning with tears running down your face.
Sin is serious.
Repentance is necessary.
Grace is not permission to continue comfortably in rebellion.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could decorate our chains with Christian vocabulary.
He came to save sinners.
To forgive.
To reconcile.
To transform.
To call us out of darkness and into His light.
That means the Gospel does not tell you to pretend your sin never happened.
It tells you something better:
your sin does not have to write the final sentence.
Jesus can.
That is why our message has always been:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is painless.
Not because every broken relationship is automatically restored.
But because in Christ, guilt can meet forgiveness.
Rebellion can meet mercy.
The lost can be found.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The ashamed can stop hiding.
And sinners who deserve judgment can discover that the Son of God willingly stood in the place of sinners.
But there is another detail hiding just a few verses later.
Psalm 118:25 cries:
אָנָּא יְהוָה הוֹשִׁיעָה נָּא
Anna YHWH, hoshiah na.
“O LORD, save, we beseech thee.”
Hoshiah na.
Save, please.
Save now.
That cry matters because Psalm 118:26 immediately says:
“Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD.”
Does that sound familiar?
It should.
When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the crowds drew from this very psalm.
“Hosanna.”
“Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.”
Think about that.
A psalm containing the cry for salvation...
the coming One in the name of the LORD...
the rejected stone...
the LORD’s astonishing work...
and the declaration:
“This is the day which the LORD hath made.”
And then the Gospel narratives bring language from that psalm onto the streets surrounding Jesus.
This is why context matters.
This is why we cannot live on isolated Bible quotations while ignoring the story surrounding them.
“This is the day” belongs to a song saturated with deliverance, thanksgiving, reversal, worship and salvation.
For Christians reading Psalm 118 in the light of the New Testament, its rejected-stone imagery leads directly toward Christ.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs today.
Because you woke up this morning...
but something inside you did not want to.
You smiled at people while quietly falling apart.
You answered, “I’m fine.”
You went to work.
You cooked dinner.
You answered messages.
You scrolled Facebook.
You laughed at something.
You carried on.
Nobody noticed that there was a war happening behind your eyes.
And then you found this.
Maybe what you need today is not another motivational sentence telling you to “stay positive.”
Maybe you need something stronger than positivity.
You need salvation.
You need grace.
You need Christ.
Because there comes a point when motivational quotes cannot reach the places sin has wounded.
There comes a point when self-improvement cannot resurrect a dead heart.
There comes a point when pretending becomes exhausting.
You can change your clothes.
Change your city.
Change your relationship status.
Change your career.
Change your social media profile.
Change your habits.
And still carry the same unhealed, unconfessed, unforgiven weight into every new room.
The Gospel goes deeper.
Jesus does not merely offer a better morning.
He offers Himself.
And perhaps “this is the day” needs to become personal for you in an entirely different way.
Maybe this is the day you stop running.
Maybe this is the day you confess what you have spent years defending.
Maybe this is the day you stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Maybe this is the day you forgive because Christ forgave you.
Maybe this is the day you finally admit that religion cannot save you.
Maybe this is the day you stop trying to impress God with a cleaned-up version of yourself and fall before Christ with empty hands.
Maybe this is the day you whisper:
“Jesus, save me.”
Not because the calendar possesses magical power.
Not because Psalm 118:24 guarantees that everything you want will happen today.
But because Scripture repeatedly confronts us with the urgency of responding to God rather than endlessly postponing repentance.
You are not promised unlimited tomorrows.
And perhaps the most dangerous word in your spiritual vocabulary is not “never.”
Perhaps it is...
“later.”
I’ll repent later.
I’ll forgive later.
I’ll come back to God later.
I’ll open my Bible later.
I’ll stop hiding later.
I’ll deal with that sin later.
I’ll surrender later.
Later has buried countless intentions.
But grace is standing before you now.
Christ is worthy now.
Repentance matters now.
Be honest.
There is no shame in admitting that you need grace.
The church was never supposed to be a museum of people who successfully rescued themselves.
We are people whose only hope is Jesus.
And somebody reading the comments may discover that they are not the only one fighting.
Your honesty may become the doorway through which another wounded believer finally stops pretending.
And please...
don’t let this article die on your screen.
If someone came to your mind while reading this, there may be a reason.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
Simply because sometimes people are carrying battles they never announce.
They may never search for a sermon.
They may never tell you they are struggling.
Long enough to hear about Jesus.
Long enough to remember that grace is still calling.
That share costs you nothing.
But God can use a simple act of faithfulness in ways you may never see.
Not because every day will feel victorious.
When shame starts talking again.
When your past starts introducing itself again.
When you need to remember:
the builders rejected the Stone...
but God was not finished.
And He was not confused.
The cross was not evidence that God had lost control.
The resurrection was not an emergency repair to a plan gone wrong.
Jesus Christ is the cornerstone.
If Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, grow in Christ, and remember the Gospel when life becomes unbearably loud, stay close.

We want this community to be a place where people encounter daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship and spiritual nourishment centered not on personalities...
but on Jesus Christ.
And there is another way you can help this work continue.
It does not.
Not because giving can purchase salvation.
It cannot.
It should not.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ, not a product anyone can sell.
But Christians are called to generosity, and voluntary financial support can genuinely help Gospel-centered work continue.
So if you have been asking, “How can I help Gospel Warrior keep creating, publishing, reaching, teaching, and expanding?”
This is one practical way.
Give freely.
Give prayerfully.
Give cheerfully.
Never from manipulation.
Never because you think God owes you something afterward.
And never beyond what you can responsibly give.
But whether you ever spend a single cent with us or not...
hear this clearly:
Jesus is not for sale.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
Christ paid the price sinners could never pay.
That is why financial support should flow from gratitude and willing partnership—not fear, guilt, spiritual pressure, or an attempt to purchase God's blessing.
Pray.
Share.
Save the message.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
Put truth into somebody else's feed.
Sometimes the person who cannot give money can still carry the message farther than money ever could.
And perhaps that brings us back to where we began.
“This is the day which the LORD hath made.”
You may have read those words hundreds of times.
But perhaps now you will hear the footsteps surrounding them.
The rejected stone.
The astonishing reversal.
“This is the LORD'S doing.”
The cry:
“Save now.”
The coming One.
“Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD.”
And through the New Testament, the rejected Stone has a name.
Jesus.
So tomorrow morning, when sunlight reaches your window and Psalm 118:24 comes to mind, thank God for another day.
Absolutely.
Rejoice.
Breathe.
Worship.
But remember that the verse belongs to something much bigger than beautiful weather.
Remember the God who overturns human verdicts.
Remember the rejected Stone.
Remember Christ.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember grace.
And when your past tells you that your scandal is the end of your story, do not let shame hold the pen that belongs in the hands of your Redeemer.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what needs confessing.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Seek forgiveness.
Forgive others.
Walk away from the darkness you once protected.
Come into the light.
And cling to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the story of good people congratulating themselves for having clean histories.
It is the story of sinners who desperately needed a Savior...
and discovered that the Stone the builders rejected became the cornerstone.
Your support can help us keep going.
Your share can help carry the message somewhere we cannot personally go.
Your comment may encourage somebody who thought they were fighting alone.
Your prayer matters more than analytics can measure.
But never forget the center of all of it.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not a product.
Not a platform.
Jesus Christ.
The rejected Stone.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
The only One who can take a sinner's confession, a shattered history, a ruined reputation, a prodigal heart, a life buried beneath shame...
and write something grace alone could have written.
The stone they rejected was not the end of the story—and neither is the chapter of your life that made you think God could never use you again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re Trying So Hard to Give Your Children Everything You Never Had That You May Be Forgetting What They Actually Need
paragraphs: You’re Trying So Hard to Give Your Children Everything You Never Had That You May Be Forgetting What They Actually Need

Sometimes the childhood you survived becomes the blueprint you spend adulthood trying to erase—and without realizing it, you can give your children everything your younger self wanted while overlooking what their souls need most.
Maybe nobody bought you the shoes everyone else had.
Maybe birthdays were quiet because there simply wasn’t enough money.
Maybe you learned not to ask because you already knew the answer.
Maybe you watched other children open presents while pretending you weren’t jealous.
Maybe your classmates went places your family could never afford.
Maybe you remember looking inside the refrigerator and knowing there wasn’t much there.
Or perhaps your deprivation wasn’t financial at all.
Maybe there was food on the table...
but nobody asked how you were doing.
Maybe you had clothes...
but very little affection.
Maybe you had a roof...
but never felt safe underneath it.
Maybe your father provided financially but was emotionally absent.
Maybe your mother was physically there but carrying wounds so deep that tenderness rarely reached you.
Maybe discipline came without affection.
Maybe affection came without stability.
Maybe you learned to become independent before a child should ever have needed to be.
And somewhere along the way, perhaps you made yourself a promise.
My children will never feel what I felt.
You may never have said it aloud.
But you have been keeping that promise for years.
So you work.
And work.
And work.
You buy the better shoes.
The better phone.
The birthday cake you never received.
The toys you once stared at through store windows.
The vacations you could only imagine.
You make sure there is food in the refrigerator because you remember what an almost-empty refrigerator felt like.
You say yes because you remember hearing no.
You rescue them because nobody rescued you.
You soften consequences because yours were sometimes cruel.
You give because you remember going without.
And there is something profoundly understandable about that.
A parent who suffered deprivation naturally wants to spare a child from the same pain.
But there is a question loving parents sometimes need the courage to ask:
Am I raising my child according to what my child truly needs—or according to what my wounded younger self still wishes someone had given me?
Because those are not always the same thing.
You can give your children everything you never had...
and accidentally fail to give them what God says matters most.
Moses spoke words thousands of years ago that cut straight through the noise of modern parenting.
Deuteronomy 6:6–7 reads in Hebrew:
וְהָיוּ הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוְּךָ הַיּוֹם עַל־לְבָבֶךָ׃ וְשִׁנַּנְתָּם לְבָנֶיךָ וְדִבַּרְתָּ בָּם בְּשִׁבְתְּךָ בְּבֵיתֶךָ וּבְלֶכְתְּךָ בַדֶּרֶךְ וּבְשָׁכְבְּךָ וּבְקוּמֶךָ׃
The sense is beautifully direct:
These words God commands are first to be upon your own heart, and then you are to impress them upon your children—speaking of them at home, along the way, when lying down, and when rising.
Notice the order.
Before God's truth reaches the child...
it is supposed to live in the parent.
Before instruction comes discipleship.
Before teaching comes embodiment.
Before your child hears what you believe, your child watches how you live.
And there is something especially powerful in the Hebrew verb translated “teach diligently” or “impress”: וְשִׁנַּנְתָּם — veshinnantam.
It carries the idea of impressing or inculcating these words upon your children. The underlying verb is associated with sharpening.
That gives the command an unforgettable texture.
God's truth is not supposed to be an occasional religious decoration hanging somewhere around the edges of family life.
It is to be repeatedly impressed upon the next generation.
At home.
On the road.
At bedtime.
In the morning.
In other words...
ordinary life becomes the classroom.
Your kitchen can become a classroom.
The drive to school can become a classroom.
The moment after your child fails can become a classroom.
The argument at the dinner table can become a classroom.
The moment your child catches you doing something wrong can become one of the greatest classrooms of all—if instead of defending yourself, you humble yourself and say:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Imagine what that teaches.
Your child discovers that Christianity is not pretending Christians never fail.
Christianity is knowing where sinners go when they do.
To Jesus.
This is where parenting becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the greatest inheritance you can leave your children is not a childhood containing everything you lacked.
It is a home in which they repeatedly encounter what every human being desperately needs.
Truth.
Love.
Boundaries.
Presence.
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
Grace.
And Jesus Christ at the center of it all.
Your children need food.
Provide it.
They need clothing.
Provide it.
They need education and opportunities.
Give what you responsibly can.
There is nothing inherently wrong with birthdays, toys, technology, vacations, comfortable homes, beautiful memories, or financial provision.
But never confuse giving your children more with necessarily giving them better.
A child can live in a beautiful bedroom and feel profoundly alone.
A teenager can hold the newest phone while desperately wishing Dad would put his own phone down and listen.
A child can have shelves filled with toys and still wonder whether Mom enjoys being around them.
A family can take expensive vacations and still be emotionally disconnected.
And a child can know every Christian song while having almost no idea what repentance, grace, forgiveness, holiness, or the cross actually means because those realities were rarely lived before them.
Sometimes what children desperately need cannot be purchased.
They need your eyes when they speak.
They need appropriate affection.
They need boundaries strong enough to make them feel secure.
They need correction that does not humiliate them.
They need consequences that teach rather than merely punish.
They need to know that “no” can sometimes be an expression of love.
They need to watch you forgive.
They need to watch you apologize.
They need to hear you pray when life hurts.
They need to see you open Scripture when nobody is watching.
They need to discover that Jesus is not merely Someone your family talks about on Sunday.
He is Lord on Monday morning.
Lord when money is tight.
Lord when Dad is angry.
Lord when Mom is exhausted.
Lord when somebody fails.
Lord when the diagnosis comes.
Lord when prayers seem unanswered.
Lord when nobody understands.
Lord when the family is celebrating.
Lord when the family is breaking.
Lord when there is plenty.
Lord when there is little.
Because one day your children will leave your house.
The toys will disappear.
The shoes will be outgrown.
The phones will become obsolete.
The clothes will be donated.
The bedrooms may belong to someone else.
The photographs will remain, but childhood itself will be gone.
And your children will enter a world that will not always protect them.
Their hearts may be broken.
They may experience rejection.
They may lose jobs.
Friends may betray them.
People they love will eventually die.
They may encounter temptations you cannot intercept.
They may make decisions you cannot control.
There will come a night when they are hurting somewhere you cannot reach them.
And on that night, the most important thing you gave them will not be sitting inside a bank account.
It will be what was planted inside their souls.
Do they know where to run when shame whispers, Hide?
Do they know there is grace at the feet of Jesus?
Do they know that sin destroys, but Christ receives repentant sinners?
Do they know that failure does not have to become their identity?
Do they know how to pray when Mom and Dad are not there to pray for them?
Do they know the Scriptures because they watched you treasure them?
Do they know that repentance is not humiliation but a turning homeward toward God?
Do they know the Gospel?
Not merely Christianity as culture.
Not merely church attendance.
Not merely Christian merchandise, Christian vocabulary, or Christian social media.
The Gospel.
That all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
That sin is not merely the bad behavior of other people but rebellion residing in every human heart.
That we cannot purchase, perform, inherit, or behave our way into reconciliation with a holy God.
That Jesus Christ, the Son of God, came for sinners.
That He died for sins.
That He rose again.
That forgiveness is offered through Him.
That we are called to repent and believe.
That grace does not merely excuse us—it begins transforming us.
That Jesus does not merely improve our old story.
He gives sinners a new one.
And maybe this is where your own story needs to meet His again.
Because perhaps you have been parenting from an old wound.
You weren't trying to spoil your children.
You were trying to protect them.
You weren't trying to replace love with possessions.
You were trying to make sure they never stared through the same windows you once stared through.
You weren't trying to become absent.
You were working all those hours because you remembered what poverty felt like.
You weren't trying to avoid discipline.
You simply remembered how discipline felt when anger and fear were attached to it.
You were trying to break a cycle.
But sometimes, in our determination to run away from one ditch, we run directly into another.
The answer is not shame.
The answer is surrender.
Bring the wounded child inside you to Christ.
You do not have to make your children responsible for healing the childhood you never had.
You do not need to recreate your childhood through them and then repair it by giving them everything you wanted.
Jesus can meet you there.
He can touch memories your children were never created to heal.
He can expose patterns without discarding you.
He can convict without crushing you.
He can teach you another way.
And perhaps tonight, instead of buying something else, you sit beside your child.
Ask a question.
Then actually listen.
Perhaps you tell them something you have never said enough:
“I love you.”
Perhaps you admit:
“I know I work a lot because I want to give you a better life. But I never want the things I give you to replace the time I should give you.”
Maybe your child is older now.
Maybe years have already passed.
Maybe reading this hurts because you see things you wish you had done differently.
Then remember the Gospel you are supposed to teach them.
Grace is for parents too.
Repentance means you do not have to pretend yesterday was right in order to begin walking differently today.
Perhaps one of the greatest spiritual lessons your grown son or daughter could ever receive is watching a parent become humble enough to say:
“I see things now that I didn't see then. I was trying to love you the best way I knew how, but sometimes my own wounds shaped the way I parented you. Where I failed you, please forgive me.”
That is not weakness.
That is discipleship in flesh and blood.
Your children do not need a flawless Christian parent.
They need to see what a Christian does with failure.
We confess.
We repent.
We seek forgiveness.
We receive grace.
We get back up.
We follow Jesus again.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe the scandal in your story was poverty.
Maybe abandonment.
Maybe addiction lived in your childhood home.
Maybe abuse.
Maybe emotional neglect.
Maybe divorce.
Maybe nobody taught you how healthy families communicate.
Maybe nobody prayed over you.
Maybe nobody tucked you into bed and told you that you were loved.
Maybe you are building a family without ever having seen a healthy one up close.
Then hear this carefully:
Your past can explain some of your patterns without becoming the master of your future.
Jesus Christ can interrupt what generations repeated.
The cycle does not have to continue merely because it reached you.
But breaking generational patterns requires more than giving children the opposite childhood.
It requires giving Christ access to the parent.
Because Deuteronomy does not begin:
“Put these words on your children's hearts.”
It begins with God's words upon yours.
Then teach them.
Then talk about them.
Then live them in the rhythms of ordinary life.
Your children are not merely listening to your theology.
They are studying your reactions.
They are learning what Christianity looks like when somebody irritates you.
When bills arrive.
When you are exhausted.
When somebody insults you.
When you are wrong.
When nobody is applauding.
When temptation comes.
When suffering comes.
And someday they may forget many of the things you bought them.
But they may remember seeing you on your knees.
They may remember hearing their name in your prayers.
They may remember the night you apologized.
They may remember that when everything went wrong, their mother still whispered, “Jesus, help us.”
They may remember their father opening a Bible at a kitchen table.
They may remember correction followed by an embrace.
They may remember that truth mattered in your house—but grace lived there too.
And perhaps years from now, when their own life begins falling apart, that memory will return.
Not the expensive shoes.
Not the newest phone.
Not the vacation.
Your faith.
Your presence.
Your repentance.
Your prayers.
Your Jesus.
That is why this message is worth sharing.

Some parent on your Facebook feed may be exhausting themselves trying to give their children everything they never had, and nobody has ever gently told them that their child may need them more than another thing.
Not as an accusation.
As an invitation.
Send it privately to the parent carrying childhood wounds nobody else sees.
Because parenting has a way of making us forget what matters when life becomes loud.
And if God has already begun changing the way you love your children, tell your testimony. Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that families can change.
But let us keep the language biblical.
Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης
The sense is that each should give according to what has been purposed in the heart, not under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.

So if you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel work, do it first by belonging wholly to Christ, obeying His Word, loving people, serving faithfully, giving generously where He leads you, and making the Gospel known.
And whether or not you are able to support financially, you can still help carry the message.
Save the messages you need to return to.
Because perhaps the greatest thing you can leave your children is not proof that you could afford to give them everything.
Perhaps it is the memory that when you finally understood what mattered most...
you gave them yourself.
You gave them truth.
You gave them discipline wrapped in love.
You gave them repentance without hypocrisy.
You gave them forgiveness.
You gave them the example of a life continually returning to the cross.
And above everything else, you kept pointing beyond yourself...
to Jesus.
One day your children may forget what was underneath the Christmas tree—but may they never forget who was at the center of your home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THE BATTLE IS THE LORD’S” — SO WHY IS GOD STILL TELLING YOU TO GET UP?
paragraphs: “THE BATTLE IS THE LORD’S” — SO WHY IS GOD STILL TELLING YOU TO GET UP?

You may have been calling it “faith” when God has actually been waiting for your obedience. Because trusting God does not always mean doing nothing. Sometimes it means walking straight toward the battlefield knowing the outcome was never resting on your strength.
There is a sentence Christians love to repeat when life becomes unbearable:
“The battle is the Lord’s.”
We whisper it when the diagnosis comes.
We post it when the marriage is trembling.
We repeat it when the bills are stacked on the table and the money is not there.
We say it when our child is drifting.
When temptation keeps returning.
When anxiety has been screaming louder than prayer.
When somebody wounds us and we desperately want God to defend us.
“The battle is the Lord’s.”
And it is.
But somewhere along the way, some of us quietly added words God never said.
“The battle is the Lord’s… therefore I do nothing.”
That is where a beautiful biblical truth can become an excuse for spiritual paralysis.
