Because when God originally declared that the battle belonged to Him, the people He spoke to did not crawl back into bed.
They marched toward the battlefield.
And maybe that is the word someone reading this desperately needs tonight.
The battle belongs to God.
But you still have to get up.
You still have to obey.
You still have to walk.
You still have to stand where He tells you to stand.
You still have to trust Him enough to move when everything inside you wants to hide.
The story unfolds in 2 Chronicles 20.
King Jehoshaphat receives terrifying news.
A massive coalition is coming against Judah.
Not a theoretical enemy.
Not an uncomfortable inconvenience.
An army.
A threat with faces.
Weapons.
Footsteps.
Dust rising in the distance.
Imagine being the king when the messenger arrives.
Imagine hearing that something much larger than your ability to control is moving toward everything you love.
Maybe you do not have to imagine very hard.
Because sometimes the army does not carry swords.
Sometimes it arrives inside an envelope from the hospital.
Sometimes it appears on your phone at 2:13 in the morning.
Sometimes it is the message that says, “We need to talk.”
Sometimes it is an addiction you promised Jesus you would never return to.
Sometimes it is debt.
Sometimes betrayal.
Sometimes grief.
Sometimes a private battle nobody sitting beside you at church even knows exists.
You smile.
You worship.
You shake hands.
You say, “God is good.”
Then you get home, close the door, and fall apart.
Jehoshaphat was afraid.
Scripture does not need to turn faithful people into emotionless superheroes.
He was afraid.
But fear was not allowed to become his god.
Jehoshaphat turned his face toward the LORD.
He proclaimed a fast.
Judah gathered.
Families stood before God.
Children were there.
Wives were there.
Fathers were there.
People who had absolutely no idea how tomorrow was going to work were standing before the only One who did.
And Jehoshaphat prayed one of the most painfully honest prayers in Scripture:
“We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on You.”
That is faith.
Not pretending you know.
Not manufacturing confidence.
Not shouting louder because secretly you are terrified.
Faith can sound like this:
“Jesus, I genuinely do not know what to do next.
But I know where I am looking.”
Then God answers through Jahaziel.
And here comes the sentence we love.
In Hebrew:
כִּי לֹא לָכֶם הַמִּלְחָמָה כִּי לֵאלֹהִים
Ki lo lakhem hammilchamah, ki l’Elohim.
“For the battle is not yours, but God’s.”
Look carefully.
God did not say there was no battle.
He said the battle did not belong to them.
That distinction changes everything.
The Hebrew word מִלְחָמָה — milchamah — means battle or warfare.
The danger was real.
The enemy was real.
The battlefield was real.
But ultimate responsibility for victory rested with God.
And perhaps you have been exhausting yourself because you have been trying to carry something that belongs in the hands of God.
You are trying to control another person's heart.
You cannot.
You are trying to guarantee tomorrow.
You cannot.
You are trying to make everybody understand you.
You cannot.
You are trying to heal yourself through sheer willpower.
You cannot save yourself.
You are trying to control every outcome because somewhere beneath all your Christian vocabulary is a terrified heart whispering:
“If I stop holding everything together, everything will collapse.”
But what if your clenched hands are not holding your world together?
What if they are simply exhausted?
There are burdens God never commanded you to carry.
There are outcomes He never asked you to manufacture.
There are people you cannot rescue.
There are doors you cannot force open.
There are battles where your greatest act of faith is finally admitting:
“This is bigger than me.”
But listen carefully.
God's next words destroy the idea that surrender means passivity.
In 2 Chronicles 20:17, He tells them:
לֹא לָכֶם לְהִלָּחֵם בָּזֹאת הִתְיַצְּבוּ עִמְדוּ וּרְאוּ אֶת־יְשׁוּעַת יְהוָה
Lo lakhem lehillachem bazot; hityatzevu, ‘imdu, ure’u et-yeshu‘at YHWH.
They would not need to fight this battle.
But then come the commands.
Position yourselves.
Stand.
See the salvation of the LORD.
And then something even more uncomfortable:
“Tomorrow, go out against them.”
Go out.
Think about that.
God promised to fight.
And then God told them to walk toward the place where the enemy was.
That means biblical surrender is not necessarily inactivity.
Sometimes surrender has feet.
Sometimes faith gets dressed in the morning.
Sometimes faith fills out the application.
Sometimes faith makes the apology.
Sometimes faith deletes the number.
Sometimes faith blocks the account that keeps pulling you back into sin.
Sometimes faith finally tells someone, “I need help.”
Sometimes faith opens the Bible when you feel spiritually numb.
Sometimes faith walks into counseling.
Sometimes faith forgives without pretending the wound never happened.
Sometimes faith establishes a necessary boundary.
Sometimes faith confesses the secret.
Sometimes faith walks away from the temptation you have been asking God to magically remove while continually keeping access to it.
Sometimes you pray for God to deliver you from something while He is saying:
“Get up and walk away from it.”
Do not confuse waiting on God with refusing to obey God.
There are moments when Scripture commands us to wait.
There are moments when Scripture commands us to flee.
There are moments when Scripture commands us to resist.
There are moments when Scripture commands us to speak.
There are moments when Scripture commands us to be silent.
There are moments when Scripture commands us to stand.
Faith is not choosing whichever response requires the least courage.
Faith is hearing God through His Word and obeying Him.
Judah went out.
Early.
They did not wait until the enemy looked smaller.
They moved while the threat was still real.
And then Jehoshaphat did something militarily bizarre.
He sent worshipers ahead.
Imagine being one of those singers.
You wake up knowing an enemy army is somewhere ahead of you.
And your assignment is not to lead with a sword.
It is to lead with praise.
“Give thanks to the LORD, for His steadfast love endures forever.”
They praised before they saw the victory.
That matters.
Anyone can praise after the enemy falls.
Faith praises God while the battlefield is still ahead.
Not because faith denies reality.
Because faith knows reality is larger than what human eyes can see.
And as they began to sing and praise, Scripture says the LORD acted against the invading forces.
God did what Judah could not do.
When Judah eventually reached the battlefield, the victory God had promised had been accomplished.
They obeyed.
God delivered.
Do not reverse those roles.
Your obedience does not make you God.
And God's sovereignty does not make your obedience unnecessary.
That is the tension mature faith learns to live inside.
You cannot save yourself.
But you can repent.
You cannot regenerate your own heart.
But you can come to Christ.
You cannot defeat sin through human strength alone.
But Scripture still tells you to resist the devil, flee sexual immorality, put sinful practices to death, renew your mind, pray, forgive, endure, watch, and obey.
Grace is not permission to become spiritually passive.
Grace is the reason obedience no longer has to be an attempt to purchase God's love.
Jesus already paid the price you could never pay.
And this is where the battlefield of Jehoshaphat points us toward something infinitely greater.
Because humanity had an enemy far greater than Moab or Ammon.
Sin.
Death.
Condemnation.
We did not merely need encouragement.
We needed rescue.
We could not climb our way back to God.
We could not perform enough good deeds to erase our rebellion.
We could not donate enough.
Pray enough.
Promise enough.
Cry enough.
Serve enough.
Or clean ourselves up enough.
So God came to us.
Jesus Christ entered our battlefield.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He carried sin to the cross.
He was crucified.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
The decisive victory over sin and death was not achieved because humanity finally became strong enough.
Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
That is grace.
But grace does not leave you where it found you.
Jesus does not forgive you so you can comfortably return to the chains He died to break.
He calls you.
Follow Me.
Repent.
Believe.
Come out of darkness.
Walk in newness of life.
And perhaps your greatest battle right now is not around you.
Perhaps it is inside you.
Maybe nobody knows what you looked at last night.
Nobody knows about the resentment.
Nobody knows you have been drifting from Jesus while still posting Bible verses.
Nobody knows your prayer life has almost disappeared.
Nobody knows how tired you are.
Nobody knows you keep saying, “I'm okay,” because explaining the truth feels too complicated.
But Jesus knows.
And He is not standing at the edge of your mess waiting for you to become impressive enough to approach Him.
The cross permanently destroys that illusion.
Come honestly.
Come broken.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come with trembling hands.
Come with the sentence Jehoshaphat prayed:
“I don't know what to do, but my eyes are on You.”
Maybe that is your prayer tonight.
Not twenty beautiful sentences.
Just that.
“Jesus… my eyes are on You.”
And if you have fallen again, do not turn failure into a permanent identity.
Peter denied Jesus.
David's history contained terrible sin.
Paul once persecuted Christians.
The woman caught in adultery had a scandal attached to her story.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to rebuild his reputation.
Yet throughout Scripture, grace keeps interrupting stories people would have declared finished.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls darkness light.
Grace that exposes sin, calls us to repentance, forgives the repentant sinner, and begins transforming lives.
That is why we keep saying it:
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because every earthly wound instantly heals.
Not because following Jesus guarantees an easy life.
But because your worst chapter does not possess greater authority than the crucified and risen Christ.
So what does “the battle is the Lord's” actually mean for you?
It means stop trying to be your own savior.
And stop using God's sovereignty as an excuse to disobey.
Pray like everything depends upon God because ultimately your hope does.
Then obey whatever God has actually commanded you to do.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to forgive, begin surrendering that bitterness to Christ.
If you need accountability, ask for it.
If you need to flee temptation, run.
If restitution is appropriate, make it.
If God has told you through Scripture to wait, wait without manipulating the outcome.
If you are suffering and there is nothing you can humanly change, stand.
And when you have done what obedience requires...
leave God's part to God.
You were never supposed to carry both sides of the covenant.
Somebody reading this has been fighting all night.
Not physically.
Inside.
Your mind is exhausted because you have replayed every possible outcome.
You have imagined conversations that have never happened.
You have buried yourself beneath tomorrow's hypothetical tragedies.
And maybe Jesus is calling you back to today.
Today's grace.
Today's obedience.
Today's bread.
Today's prayer.
Today's battlefield.
You do not need strength for every imaginary tomorrow tonight.
You need enough grace to obey Jesus today.
And when tomorrow comes, His mercy will already be there.
Be honest.
And if Christ has already brought you through a battle you thought would destroy you, tell someone what He did.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to quit tonight.
Do not assume they already know this truth.
Sometimes people are one shared message away from hearing exactly what their soul needed at exactly the right moment.
It does not.
Not because giving can buy blessing, forgiveness, salvation, or spiritual status.
It cannot.
And not because we want to pressure you.
Scripture explicitly teaches that Christian generosity should not be given reluctantly or under compulsion. Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ… μὴ… ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Each person is to give as he has purposed in his heart, not under compulsion.
That matters to us.

Your local church, your family responsibilities, mercy toward people in need, and whatever stewardship God has entrusted to you should never be manipulated by emotional pressure from an online ministry.
But voluntary generosity toward Gospel work is biblical.
Paul thanked believers who materially partnered with Gospel ministry, and 2 Corinthians 9 describes generosity producing thanksgiving and glory to God.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, reaching, creating, and expanding resources designed to bring people back to Scripture and ultimately to Jesus Christ.
You can still help enormously.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone struggling.
Money is not the only way to participate in spreading truth.
Sometimes your share reaches the person our page never could.
Sometimes your testimony opens a heart.
Sometimes your comment tells a stranger, “You are not the only one fighting this.”
And sometimes the smallest act of obedience travels farther than you will ever know this side of eternity.
So remember this when the enemy looks enormous.
Remember it when your hands shake.
Remember it when you cannot see how the story could possibly end well.
“The battle is the Lord's” does not always mean:
“Sit there and do nothing.”
Sometimes it means:
“Get up.
Pray.
Obey.
Walk forward.
Stand where God told you to stand.
Praise Him before you see the outcome.
And stop trying to do the part that belongs to God.”
Because the same God who told Judah, “The battle is not yours,” also told them:
“Tomorrow, go out.”
And maybe those are the words you needed.
Not “fight harder.”
Not “control everything.”
Not “save yourself.”
Just...
Trust God enough to take the next obedient step.
Then leave the impossible part in His hands.
You may still have to walk onto the battlefield—but you never have to pretend you are the Savior standing there.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES GOD USE SEXUAL DESIRE AS A METAPHOR FOR IDOLATRY?
paragraphs: WHY DOES GOD USE SEXUAL DESIRE AS A METAPHOR FOR IDOLATRY?
Because God knows there is something more dangerous than wanting the wrong person—you can give to something else the part of your heart that was created to belong to Him.
There is a reason the Bible sometimes speaks about idolatry in language so intimate that it makes modern readers uncomfortable.
Adultery.
Prostitution.
Unfaithfulness.
Jealousy.
Marriage.
Desire.
The language can feel almost scandalous.
Why would a holy God describe worship with words that sound like they belong inside a broken marriage?
Why would prophets talk about Israel chasing idols as though a spouse had climbed into another person's bed?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
What if God uses this metaphor because idolatry is far more intimate than we have allowed ourselves to believe?
Maybe an idol is not merely a statue.
Maybe idolatry begins whenever something created becomes the place where your deepest hunger kneels.
And suddenly this is not merely Israel's story.
It is ours.
Because you can sit in church while your heart sleeps with another god.
You can lift your hands during worship while secretly believing money will save you.
You can quote Scripture while craving another person's approval more desperately than God's.
You can call Jesus Lord while allowing pornography to disciple your imagination.
You can love your children so deeply that protecting the life you planned for them becomes more important than trusting the God who gave them to you.
You can desire marriage until marriage becomes your messiah.
You can desire success until success becomes your identity.
You can desire ministry until being noticed becomes more important than knowing Christ.
You can even desire theological knowledge until being right becomes more precious than becoming holy.
That is why this metaphor cuts so deeply.
Because idolatry is not simply believing the wrong thing.
Idolatry is misplaced worship.

Paul describes humanity's rebellion in Romans 1:25 with devastating simplicity: people exchanged God's truth for a lie and worshiped and served created things rather than the Creator. The Greek speaks of people who “ἐσεβάσθησαν καὶ ἐλάτρευσαν τῇ κτίσει” — who revered and served the creation instead of the One who created it.
Notice the tragedy.
The created thing may not itself be evil.
Money is not automatically evil.
Marriage is not evil.
Sex is not evil.
Achievement is not evil.
Beauty is not evil.
Food is not evil.
Human affection is not evil.
God created many things that legitimately produce pleasure, delight, longing, attachment, and gratitude.
The catastrophe begins when the gift receives what belongs to the Giver.
That is the anatomy of an idol.
And this is where sexual desire becomes such a frighteningly powerful metaphor.

Sexual intimacy was never designed to be merely mechanical. Within Scripture's vision of marriage, it belongs to a covenantal union in which two lives are joined. That is why adultery wounds differently from an ordinary disagreement.
Adultery says with the body:
“I am giving somewhere else what I covenanted to give here.”
Now listen to the prophets.
Hosea opens with language that almost feels too raw for church.
The Hebrew of Hosea 1:2 includes:
“אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים … כִּי זָנֹה תִזְנֶה הָאָרֶץ מֵאַחֲרֵי יְהוָה”
eshet zenunim … ki zanoh tizneh ha'aretz me'acharei YHWH.
The language revolves around זְנוּנִים (zenunim), sexual promiscuity or whoredom, because the land had abandoned covenant faithfulness to YHWH.
God was not saying sexual desire itself is idolatry.
That distinction matters enormously.
The Bible does not teach that possessing sexual desire makes someone dirty.
The metaphor is about exclusive covenant loyalty being transferred to another.
That is what makes adultery such an appropriate picture.
Imagine loving someone deeply.
You give yourself.
You remain faithful.
You sacrifice.
You make promises.
And then the person you love begins running after strangers.
Imagine watching them search in another person's arms for the intimacy you wanted to share with them.
Now magnify that beyond human measurement.
God created Israel.
Delivered Israel.
Fed Israel.
Protected Israel.
Entered covenant with Israel.
And Israel repeatedly ran toward gods that had never rescued them.
That is why biblical idolatry is not presented merely as an intellectual mistake.
It is covenant betrayal.
And suddenly another difficult biblical word begins making sense.
Jealousy.
Exodus 34:14 contains an extraordinary description of God:
“יְהוָה קַנָּא שְׁמוֹ אֵל קַנָּא הוּא”
YHWH qannāʾ shemo, El qannāʾ hu.
YHWH—whose name is Jealous—is a jealous God.
The Hebrew word קַנָּא (qannāʾ) means “jealous” and in this biblical usage is applied to God in the context of His demand for exclusive worship.
This is not petty insecurity.
God does not look at an idol and worry that He might lose a popularity contest.
He needs nothing from creation.
His jealousy is the rightful jealousy of covenant love.
A faithful husband is not unreasonable because he refuses to celebrate his wife's adultery.
Exclusive love necessarily says that some relationships cannot be shared.
And worship belongs to God.
This is why idolatry is so serious.
Your idol is rarely the thing you claim is your god.
It is often the thing you cannot imagine living without.
It is the thing whose loss makes life seem meaningless.
The thing you secretly believe can finally make you whole.
The thing whose approval determines whether you feel valuable.
The thing you compromise obedience to keep.
The thing you run toward when your soul hurts.
The thing you daydream about when reality disappoints you.
The thing you protect when God begins putting His finger on it.
Sometimes you discover your idol only when God threatens to remove it.
And perhaps something just came into your mind.
A person.
A relationship.
Money.
Sex.
Pornography.
Success.
Your appearance.
Your career.
Your reputation.
Your ministry.
Your political identity.
Your comfort.
Your phone.
Your audience.
Your children.
Your future.
Even your dream of finally becoming the person everyone regrets underestimating.
Anything can become an altar when your heart begins demanding from creation what only the Creator can ultimately provide.
And that is why this gets personal.
Maybe you have been asking God to bless the very thing that has quietly replaced Him.
Maybe you call it ambition.
God calls you deeper.
Maybe you call it love.
God sees dependency.
Maybe you call it harmless entertainment.
But you know what happens when nobody is watching.
Maybe you have whispered, “I can stop whenever I want.”
But you have said that before.
Maybe the browser history gets deleted.
Maybe the messages disappear.
Maybe nobody knows about the fantasy.
Maybe everybody at church thinks you are doing beautifully.
But God does not expose idols because He enjoys humiliating people.
He exposes idols because idols eventually devour their worshipers.
They always promise more than they can deliver.
Pornography says, “I will satisfy you.”
Then it asks for another image.
And another.
And another.
Approval says, “I will make you feel worthy.”
Then one criticism ruins your entire week.
Money says, “I will make you secure.”
Then you finally get more money and discover another number you supposedly need before you can breathe.
Romance says, “Once somebody loves you, you will finally be complete.”
Then another broken human being is forced to carry expectations no human being was created to bear.
Success whispers, “Just one more achievement.”
You reach it.
Celebrate.
Then wake up hungry again.
That is the cruelty of idols.
They accept sacrifices.
They never climb onto the altar for you.
But Jesus did.
And this is where the entire story turns.
Christianity does not merely announce that humanity has been unfaithful.
It announces something almost unbelievable:
The betrayed Bridegroom came looking for His unfaithful bride.
Read the words surrounding Christ and His church.
Paul writes:
ho Christos ēgapēsen tēn ekklēsian kai heauton paredōken hyper autēs.
Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Do not rush past that.
We betrayed Him.
He gave Himself.
We wandered.
He came searching.
We worshiped created things.
The Creator entered creation.
We deserved judgment.
Christ carried judgment.
We brought the scandal.
Jesus brought grace.
At the cross, the faithful Bridegroom did something no earthly love story could have prepared us to comprehend.
He died for people who had loved other gods.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because it mattered enough to require blood.
Not because God shrugged at spiritual adultery.
Because Jesus bore the judgment sinners could never remove from themselves.
That is the Gospel.
Not “clean yourself up until God can tolerate you.”
Not “hide your scandal well enough that Christians never discover it.”
Not “become religious enough to compensate for what you did.”
Repent.
Come home.
Trust Christ.
The Gospel does not pretend your idols were harmless.
It announces that they do not have to own you anymore.
Maybe pornography has had your imagination for fifteen years.
Jesus is still calling.
Maybe another person's approval has controlled every decision.
Jesus is still calling.
Maybe money has been your security.
Jesus is still calling.
Maybe you compromised your marriage.
Jesus is still calling you to repentance.
Maybe you have worshiped your own body, your career, your status, your pain, your sexuality, your reputation, your dreams—or even your ministry.
Jesus is still calling.
But hear this carefully:
Grace is not God's permission to keep sleeping beside your idols.
Grace is God's invitation to come home.
James uses language that would have sounded familiar to people who knew the prophets.
“μοιχαλίδες…”
Moichalides.
“Adulteresses.”
Then comes the piercing question about friendship with the world being hostility toward God.
Why such strong language?
Because God wants your heart.
Not because He lacks something.
Because He knows what happens when you give yourself to gods that cannot love you back.
And perhaps this explains something about your own restlessness.
You thought you needed stronger pleasure.
Maybe what your soul needs is a greater Treasure.
You thought Christianity meant learning how to desire nothing.
It doesn't.
Christian discipleship is not the extermination of desire.
It is the redemption and reordering of desire.
The problem is not that human beings hunger.
The problem is that fallen hearts keep trying to make meals out of things that were only supposed to be appetizers pointing beyond themselves.
C. S. Lewis famously explored this idea in his own way, but Scripture gets there first.
The biblical story is overflowing with desire.
“Whom have I in heaven but you?”
“As the deer pants for streams of water…”
“My soul thirsts for God…”
“Taste and see…”
Jesus does not merely say, “Stop wanting.”
He changes what the heart considers worthy.
And that is why defeating idolatry requires more than removing statues.
You need a greater love.
You can remove an app and still worship lust.
You can lose money and still worship money.
You can end a relationship and still worship romance.
You can leave social media and still worship human approval.
You can walk away from fame while spending every night imagining being famous.
An idol can survive without its physical altar because the real altar is inside us.
Repentance therefore goes deeper than behavior modification.
Repentance says:
“Jesus, I have been asking something created to do what only You can do.”
That confession changes everything.
Because the answer to idolatry is not merely deprivation.
It is restoration.
Paul could describe believers as betrothed to one Husband—Christ.
And Revelation carries that image toward the end of history:
“ἦλθεν ὁ γάμος τοῦ ἀρνίου”
ēlthen ho gamos tou arniou.
“The marriage of the Lamb has come.”
Do you see the story?
The Bible begins with a marriage.
Humanity rebels.
The prophets describe God's people as an unfaithful spouse.
Christ arrives.
The Bridegroom gives Himself for His bride.
And Scripture moves toward a wedding.
This was never merely a story about sexual desire.
It was a story about belonging.
Your deepest desires reveal where you believe life can be found.
God uses marital and sexual unfaithfulness as a metaphor for idolatry because few human experiences communicate covenant exclusivity, longing, intimacy, betrayal, and belonging with comparable force.
The metaphor is supposed to hurt.
But it is also supposed to lead you home.
So ask yourself something you may not want to answer.
What receives the first hunger of your heart?
Where do you run when you are lonely?
What do you fantasize about when you imagine finally being happy?
What loss would make you wonder whether life was still worth living?
What command of Jesus are you currently negotiating because obedience might cost you something you love?
That place may be where your altar is hiding.
Do not hide it.
Bring it into the light.
Jesus already knows.
Repentance is not informing Christ of something He failed to discover.
It is finally agreeing with Him about what is killing you.
Be honest.
Someone reading your words tonight may discover that they are not the only believer fighting.
The Gospel is.
Because idols rarely die after one confrontation.
Sometimes you need to return and remember why your heart cannot safely give God's throne to anything He created.
There is also a deeper way to partner with this work.
It does not.
It does not.
And we will not tell you that paying Gospel Warrior is what makes you faithful to Jesus.
Grace cannot be bought.
But voluntary generosity can be one way Christians participate in Gospel work.
Send it privately to the person who is struggling.
Your share may reach someone our page never could.
Do not mistake supporting a ministry for surrendering your heart to Christ.
He wants you.
The secret places.
The competing loves.
The desires you are embarrassed to name.
The idol you keep defending.
The wound underneath the addiction.
The hunger underneath the fantasy.
The loneliness underneath the compromise.
Bring all of it.
Because the scandal of Scripture is not merely that God's people behaved like an unfaithful bride.
The greater scandal is that the faithful Bridegroom loved them enough to bleed for their redemption.
You may have wandered farther than anyone knows.
You may have kissed idols in rooms where nobody saw you.
You may have given years of your life to something that promised heaven and slowly turned your soul into a prison.
But if you are breathing, the invitation to repent is still in front of you.
Come home.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you finally become respectable.
Not after you prove you can stay clean for thirty days.
Come to Christ with empty hands.
There is forgiveness in Him.
There is cleansing in Him.
There is freedom in Him.
There is a new identity in Him.
There is a Bridegroom who does not merely expose the unfaithful.
He died to redeem them.

And one day every counterfeit lover, every secret altar, every false promise, every shame-filled night, every chain Christ broke, and every tear He wiped away will disappear beneath the joy of the Lamb and His redeemed people.
Until then, guard your heart.
Watch what you worship.
Pay attention to what you desire.
And when something created begins demanding what belongs to the Creator alone, remember the cross.
Because the idol will always ask you to sacrifice yourself for it—but Jesus is the Bridegroom who sacrificed Himself for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS SPEAK IN PARABLES? THE TERRIFYING ANSWER MOST PEOPLE NEVER NOTICE
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS SPEAK IN PARABLES? THE TERRIFYING ANSWER MOST PEOPLE NEVER NOTICE
They sounded like simple stories about seeds, sheep, coins, weeds, fathers, sons, servants, weddings, vineyards, lamps, fishermen, and ordinary people.
But Jesus was doing something far more serious than telling memorable stories.
His parables were revealing hearts.
And once you understand why Jesus actually spoke in parables, you may never hear His words the same way again.
Because there is something frightening hidden inside the question the disciples once asked Him:
“Why speakest thou unto them in parables?” — Matthew 13:10, KJV
They noticed it.
Jesus could have spoken plainly.
He could have explained everything immediately.
Instead, He told a story.
A farmer walked into a field carrying seed.
Some seed fell beside the road.
Some landed on rocky ground.
Some fell among thorns.
Some landed in good soil.
Then Jesus said something that almost sounds unnecessary:
“Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.” — Matthew 13:9, KJV
Everyone standing there physically had ears.
So Jesus was obviously talking about something deeper.
There is hearing...
and then there is hearing.
There is seeing...
and then there is seeing.
There is being close enough to Jesus to hear His voice while remaining far enough from Him that His words never penetrate the heart.
That possibility should disturb every religious person.
Because one of the most dangerous places a human being can stand is close enough to Christianity to recognize its vocabulary while remaining untouched by Christ.
You can know the stories.
You can quote verses.
You can attend church.
You can sing worship songs.
You can post Christian content.
You can even explain theology.
And still have soil inside you where the seed refuses to take root.
That is where the parables become uncomfortable.
The Greek word translated “parable” is παραβολή — parabolē.

The idea involves placing something alongside something else for comparison. Jesus would take something familiar—seed, soil, bread, money, sheep, vineyards, weddings—and place alongside it a spiritual reality.
Earthly pictures opened windows into eternal truth.
But those windows did not produce the same response in everyone.
To some people, a parable became a doorway.
To others, it became a mirror.
And some looked into the mirror and walked away.
When the disciples asked Jesus why He spoke in parables, His answer was astonishing:
“Because it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given.” — Matthew 13:11, KJV
The Greek word translated “mysteries” is μυστήρια — mystēria.
This does not mean Christianity is a secret society in which clever people discover hidden codes.
In the biblical sense, a mystery is truth belonging to God that must be revealed by God.
The Kingdom cannot simply be conquered intellectually.
Jesus must open our eyes.
And suddenly the parables stop being cute Sunday school stories.
They become a spiritual diagnosis.
Jesus continued:
“Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.” — Matthew 13:13, KJV
Then Jesus reached backward centuries into the prophet Isaiah.
The Hebrew of Isaiah 6:9 contains the haunting words:
שִׁמְעוּ שָׁמוֹעַ וְאַל־תָּבִינוּ
Shim‘u shamoa‘ ve’al-tavinu.
The construction intensifies the act of hearing—hear and keep hearing—yet without understanding.
And then:
וּרְאוּ רָאוֹ וְאַל־תֵּדָעוּ
See and keep seeing—yet without perceiving.
That was the tragedy Jesus was exposing.
The problem was not merely that people lacked information.
Their hearts had become resistant to the truth standing directly in front of them.
Imagine that.
God had taken on flesh.
The One through whom all things were made was standing within hearing distance.
They could see His face.
Hear His voice.
Watch His works.
Yet proximity to Jesus did not automatically produce surrender to Jesus.
And that should make us ask a painful question.
How many times has God spoken to us through His Word while we quietly decided which parts we were willing to obey?
We say we want Jesus to speak...
until He speaks about forgiveness.
Until He touches our secret sin.
Until He confronts our pride.
Until He tells us to love the person who wounded us.
Until He exposes our greed.
Until He confronts our lust.
Until He challenges the bitterness we have protected for years.
Until He asks for the room in our heart whose door we have kept locked.
Then suddenly the issue is no longer whether God has spoken.
The issue is whether we actually wanted to hear Him.
That is why the parables are dangerous.
They do not merely ask, “Do you understand this story?”
They ask:
“What kind of heart are you bringing to Jesus?”
Consider the parable of the sower.
The same seed falls on different soils.
The seed is not defective.
The difference is the soil.
One heart is hardened.
Another receives quickly but has no depth.
Another allows the Word to grow, only to have it suffocated by competing desires.
Another receives it and bears fruit.
And before pointing at anyone else, we should ask:
Which soil looks like me?
Maybe you once burned for Christ.
Maybe there was a season when opening your Bible felt like opening a letter from home.
Prayer was not an obligation.
Worship was not background music.
You wanted Jesus.
But slowly...
something changed.
Pain came.
Disappointment came.
Success came.
Money came.
Temptation came.
Busyness came.
Your phone became louder.
Your schedule became fuller.
Your prayers became shorter.
Your Bible stayed closed longer.
And somewhere between surviving life and chasing life, the voice you once treasured became easier to ignore.
You did not necessarily wake up one morning and decide to abandon Jesus.
You simply allowed other things to become louder than Him.
That is exactly why Christ's parables still reach across two thousand years and grab us by the soul.
The thorns do not have to destroy the seed violently.
They only have to choke it slowly.
And maybe that sentence exposed something.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Not because typing a comment saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we stop pretending.
Sometimes another exhausted believer needs to discover that he or she is not the only person fighting to keep faith alive.
And sometimes your honesty becomes the sentence God uses to encourage someone else not to walk away.
There is another side to Jesus' parables that is breathtakingly beautiful.
Jesus did not merely expose hardened hearts.
He welcomed seekers closer.
Mark tells us that Jesus spoke publicly in parables and then, when He was alone with His disciples, explained things to them.
Think about that scene.
The crowds disappear.
The noise fades.
A smaller group remains.
They do not understand everything.
They are confused.
They have questions.
But they stay with Jesus.
And Jesus teaches them.
That may be one of the most beautiful pictures of discipleship in the Gospels.
The disciples were not rewarded because they were intellectual geniuses.
Read the Gospels carefully and you will discover how often they misunderstood Him.
They asked foolish questions.
They argued about greatness.
They panicked.
They doubted.
They failed.
Peter would deny Him.
Others would flee.
Yet they kept coming back.
“Explain this to us.”
That is discipleship.
Not pretending you understand everything.
Staying close enough to Jesus to keep asking.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this needs to hear tonight.
You do not need to understand everything before coming to Christ.
Come confused.
Come wounded.
Come ashamed.
Come with questions.
Come after failure.
Come after years away.
Come carrying the secret you promised yourself nobody would ever know.
Just come.
Because Christianity is not the story of impressive people climbing high enough to reach God.
The Gospel is the story of God coming down to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And this is where every parable ultimately finds its center.
Jesus Christ.
The Shepherd searching for the lost.
The King inviting people into His Kingdom.
The Bridegroom whose arrival demands readiness.
The One announcing forgiveness.
The One seeking fruit.
The One calling sinners home.
The One who would eventually stop telling stories long enough to become the center of the greatest story ever told.
He would be betrayed.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And buried.
Human beings looked at the Son of God and treated Him like a scandal.
But heaven was writing redemption.
At the cross, Jesus carried sin's judgment.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
The Shepherd gave His life for the sheep.
And on the third day, the tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately about becoming slightly better people.
It is about dead people receiving life.
Guilty people receiving pardon.
Lost people being found.
Enemies being reconciled.
Prodigals coming home.
Sinners being transformed by grace.
And perhaps that explains why one of Jesus' most unforgettable parables still breaks hearts.
A son demands his inheritance.
Leaves home.
Wastes everything.
Falls into humiliation.
And eventually comes to himself.
He prepares his confession.
He starts walking home.
And then something happens.
The father sees him from a distance.
Runs.
Embraces him.
Receives him.
The son returns carrying scandal.
The father meets him with grace.
Do you see it?
From scandal...
to grace.
That is what Jesus does.
Maybe your story contains chapters you wish could be burned.
Maybe there are decisions you cannot undo.
Relationships you damaged.
Years you wasted.
People you hurt.
Promises you broke.
Things you watched.
Things you said.
Things nobody knows.
Things you still cannot forgive yourself for.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more than we could imagine.
But the cross also proves something else:
God's grace is greater than the sinner who comes to Christ in repentance and faith.
Jesus did not die so we could decorate our old lives with religious language.
He died and rose so sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you home.
Grace is not permission to remain in the pigpen.
Grace opens the road back to the Father.
So perhaps the deepest question is no longer:
“Why did Jesus speak in parables?”
Perhaps the question has become:
“What is Jesus saying to me through them?”
Because the parables reveal something about the Kingdom...
but they also reveal something about us.
The lost sheep asks whether we know we are lost.
The unforgiving servant asks whether receiving mercy has made us merciful.
The rich fool asks what possesses our hearts.
The Good Samaritan asks whether our love crosses inconvenient boundaries.
The Pharisee and tax collector ask whether we approach God with pride or repentance.
The prodigal son asks whether we will come home.
The sower asks whether the Word is actually taking root.
And the wise and foolish builders leave us with nowhere to hide.
Jesus says the person who hears His words and does them is like someone building on rock.
Notice the difference.
Both hear.
Only one obeys.
That may be the dividing line running through this entire article.
Not information.
Response.
Not exposure to Jesus.
Surrender to Jesus.
Not merely hearing His words.
Receiving them.
And perhaps you have spent years around Christianity without ever truly surrendering yourself to Christ.
You know about Him.
But do you know Him?
You admire Him.
But have you surrendered to Him?
You want His comfort.
But do you want His Lordship?
You want heaven.
But do you want Jesus?
No article can answer that question for you.
No pastor can repent for you.
No parent can believe for you.
No church membership can substitute for Christ.
No religious performance can erase your guilt.
Jesus is the Savior.
Turn to Him.
Confess your sin.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
Ask Him for mercy.
And if you already belong to Christ but your heart has grown cold, stop pretending coldness is maturity.
Come back.
Open the Scriptures again.
Pray again.
Confess again.
Forgive again.
Obey again.
Not to purchase God's love...
but because in Christ you have encountered a love worth surrendering everything to.
And when you see someone else's comment, do not treat it like content.
Pray for them.
There is a human soul behind that screen.
Not to embarrass them.
Because you love them.
There may come a night when the noise becomes overwhelming and you need to remember the question Jesus keeps asking beneath every parable:
Do you have ears to hear?
There is another practical way you can help this work continue.
But hear this clearly because biblical integrity matters more than conversion numbers:
It does not purchase God's favor.
It does not make God love you more.
It is not a substitute for obedience to Christ, generosity toward those in need, or faithful giving in the life of the church.
And it should not be called a required biblical tithe.
Scripture says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
The Greek is equally direct:
μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Not reluctantly or from compulsion.

Your monthly support can help Gospel Warrior continue creating and distributing Christ-centered content, biblical encouragement, discipleship materials, and resources designed to reach people with the truth of Scripture.
It does not.
You can still help tremendously.
Pray.
Save these messages.
Invite your family and friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite the person who thinks God could never want them.
Even invite the unbeliever who is willing to listen.
Because this was never supposed to be about building an audience for its own sake.
It must remain about pointing human beings toward Jesus.
That brings us back to the shoreline.
The crowd is listening.
Jesus is speaking.
Seeds are falling.
Some hearts are hard.
Some are shallow.
Some are crowded with thorns.
And somewhere...
there is good soil.
Maybe that soil is a person reading something you shared.
Maybe someone you tag tonight has been quietly considering giving up.
Maybe someone scrolling Facebook at 2:17 in the morning feels too dirty to pray.
Maybe someone believes the worst chapter of their life has already written the ending.
And perhaps God will use something as ordinary as a shared article to remind them of something eternal:
Jesus still receives sinners.
So share it.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because a soul may need the Gospel.
Follow because truth deserves more room in your life than endless noise.
But whatever you do...
do not merely admire the parable.
Hear the King.
Because the most tragic person in Jesus' audience was never the one who did not understand immediately.
It was the one who heard the voice of Christ...
and decided not to follow.
And the most beautiful story is still the sinner who finally turns around and discovers that grace has been calling them home.
Your scandal does not have to write your final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU HAVE A WIFE—SO WHY ARE YOU STILL COURTING OTHER WOMEN?
paragraphs: YOU HAVE A WIFE—SO WHY ARE YOU STILL COURTING OTHER WOMEN?

You may never have touched her. You may never have kissed her. But if you are deliberately pursuing another woman’s heart while your wife is waiting for yours, Jesus has something painfully serious to say.
There is a kind of betrayal that happens long before two bodies ever meet.
It begins with a message you would rather your wife not see.
A conversation you delete.
A compliment that carries more intention than you want to admit.
A “good morning” message that somehow became daily.
An inside joke your wife knows nothing about.
A woman whose notification makes something inside you come alive.
You tell yourself, “We’re only talking.”
“She’s just a friend.”
“I haven’t slept with anybody.”
“I know my limits.”
But perhaps that is not the most important question.
The question is this:
Why are you trying to awaken in another woman something that belongs inside the covenant you already made with your wife?
That question hurts because sometimes we rename sin before we repent of it.
We call lust “admiration.”
We call flirting “being friendly.”
We call emotional dependency “just talking.”
We call secrecy “privacy.”
We call pursuing another woman “nothing serious.”
And sometimes the person most skilled at convincing us that we are innocent...
is us.
Jesus refuses to let us hide behind the technicalities.

In Matthew 5:27–28, Christ takes His listeners beyond the outward act of adultery and confronts what can happen within the heart. The crucial Greek expression includes the words “πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν” — language describing looking with lustful desire or intent.
Jesus is not teaching that noticing someone is attractive automatically makes a married person an adulterer.
He is exposing something deeper.
Intentional, cultivated lust matters before God.
There is a difference between temptation arriving at your door and you inviting it inside, feeding it dinner, giving it a password, and wondering why it refuses to leave.
There is a difference between encountering an attractive woman and deliberately pursuing her attention.
There is a difference between an ordinary conversation and secretly building romantic intimacy.
There is a difference between temptation...
and courtship.

If you already have a wife and you are intentionally courting another woman—seeking her romantic affection, cultivating sexual desire, feeding emotional intimacy that belongs within your marriage, or positioning yourself as though you were available—then you cannot make the problem disappear simply by saying, “But we never had sex.”
Jesus goes after the heart because eventually the feet tend to follow where the heart has been permitted to wander.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that your wife may not know.
But God does.
Malachi 2:14 gives marriage language that should make every married man stop.
The Hebrew text describes the wife as the wife of your “בְּרִיתֶךָ” — beritekha — “your covenant.”
Not merely your girlfriend.
Not merely the woman sharing your surname.
Not merely the mother of your children.
Your covenant wife.
Malachi says that the LORD Himself was witness between a man and “the wife of your youth,” condemning treachery against that covenant relationship.
Think about that.
When nobody sees the messages...
God sees.
When your wife believes you are merely busy...
God knows where your attention is going.
When you carefully choose words that allow you to say, “Technically, I didn't lie”...
God knows the truth you were trying not to say.
When you erase the conversation...
you have erased nothing from His sight.
Marriage is not simply an arrangement between two people.
It is covenant.
And covenant changes the question.
The question is no longer merely, “How far can I go before it technically becomes adultery?”
The better question is:
“How faithfully can I love the woman I promised to love?”
That sounds completely different.
Hebrews 13:4 tells believers to hold marriage in honor and warns that God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
Honor.
That word leaves very little room for secret romantic auditions.
A faithful husband does not need to hate every other woman.
He does not need to avoid ordinary human interaction.
He does not become sinful merely because temptation occurs.
But he must learn where his heart belongs.
Because fidelity is bigger than avoiding somebody else's bed.
Faithfulness says:
My wife does not have to compete with women who were never supposed to have access to my romantic heart.
And Scripture does not merely tell husbands what to avoid.
It tells them whom to pursue.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.” — Ephesians 5:25.
Read that slowly.
Christ did not call you merely to remain technically married.
He called you to love.
Sacrificially.
Deliberately.
Faithfully.
Christlike love asks something radically different from the wandering heart.
While lust asks, “What can she give me?”
Christlike love asks, “What can I give for her good?”
While secret courtship searches for another woman's admiration, covenant love turns home and asks, “How can I cherish the woman God has entrusted to me?”
While lust wants novelty, Christlike love learns faithfulness.
While temptation whispers, “You deserve something new,” covenant says, “Remember what you promised.”
And Proverbs gives married desire somewhere beautiful to go.
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
The passage continues by telling the husband to remain captivated by her love.
Notice what Scripture does.
It does not merely say, “Stop looking elsewhere.”
It says, in effect:
Come home.
Rejoice again.
Remember her.
Pursue her.
Cherish her.
Perhaps somewhere along the years, something changed.
Bills arrived.
Children cried.
Bodies aged.
Arguments accumulated.
Affection became routine.
You stopped dating each other.
You became excellent partners in surviving life but terrible students of one another's hearts.
Then another woman laughed at your jokes.
She noticed you.
She listened.
She complimented you.
And suddenly you felt twenty-five again.
Be careful.
Feeling alive is not always evidence that something is from God.
Sometimes temptation feels exhilarating precisely because sin is offering pleasure without showing you the invoice.
It shows you the secret messages.
It does not show you your wife crying in the bathroom.
It shows you the excitement.
It does not show you your children asking why Daddy doesn't live there anymore.
It shows you a woman at her most attractive.
It does not show you two damaged families sorting through consequences.
Sin is a terrible salesman.
It advertises the moment and hides the aftermath.
And maybe you are reading this thinking:
Too late.
Maybe it has already gone beyond messages.
Maybe there was a kiss.
Maybe there was a hotel.
Maybe there has been another relationship for months.
Maybe your wife already discovered it.
Maybe your marriage is hanging by a thread.
Maybe the man reading these words is not merely tempted.
Maybe you already fell.
Then hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not permission to continue sinning.
But neither is your sin greater than the blood of Jesus Christ.
This is where Christianity becomes breathtaking.
Jesus does not expose sin because He delights in destroying sinners.
He exposes darkness so sinners can come into the light.
Repentance is not saying, “I'm sorry I got caught.”
Repentance is not crying tonight and messaging her again next week.
Repentance is not asking God to remove consequences while protecting the secret relationship that created them.
Repentance turns.
It tells the truth.
It stops feeding the sin.
It stops romanticizing what God calls you to forsake.
It seeks forgiveness.
It accepts accountability.
It begins rebuilding what deception damaged.
And where necessary, it seeks wise pastoral and professional help to walk through the wreckage honestly.
Grace does not tell you that betrayal did not matter.
Grace tells you that betrayal does not have to write the final chapter.
Look at the cross.
There you see both the seriousness of sin and the magnitude of mercy.
Jesus did not die because sin was harmless.
He died because sin was deadly.
And He rose because death would not have the last word.
Maybe you became the scandal.
Maybe everybody thought you were the faithful husband.
Maybe you served at church.
Posted Bible verses.
Said grace before meals.
Called yourself a Christian.
And still entertained another woman's heart behind your wife's back.
There may be no comfortable way to hear this:
religious appearance cannot substitute for repentance.
But neither should shame convince you to run away from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Cut off what keeps pulling you back.
Stop protecting your reputation more fiercely than your marriage.
Stop asking whether you can keep the other woman “as a friend” when you know exactly what that relationship has become inside your heart.
Stop asking God to bless the very doorway through which temptation keeps entering.
And then...
go home.
Not merely to the house.
Go home with your heart.
Look at your wife again.
Not as the obstacle standing between you and excitement.
Not as the woman who became ordinary.
Not as the person whose weaknesses you have memorized while another woman's weaknesses remain conveniently hidden.
See her as a human being who trusted you with something precious.
Her heart.
Her years.
Her vulnerability.
Her covenant.
And if you have wounded her, understand this too:
you cannot demand that she heal according to your timetable.
Forgiveness and restored trust are related, but they are not identical.
You may confess in one evening.
Trust may take much longer to rebuild.
Real repentance is willing to walk that road without complaining that the consequences are inconvenient.
Because repentance does not ask only, “How can I feel forgiven?”
It also asks, “How can I begin becoming trustworthy?”
And husbands, Scripture gives us a terrifyingly beautiful standard:
Christ.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Not Hollywood.
Not pornography.
Not your coworkers.
Not your divorced friends.
Not the algorithm feeding you endless images of women who never ask anything difficult from you.
Christ.
The One who gave Himself.
The One whose love was faithful.
The One whose love was sacrificial.
The One who did not abandon His bride when loving her became costly.
That is the direction.
And perhaps this article was not meant only for the man already cheating.
Perhaps it found the man standing three steps before the cliff.
You have her number.
The conversations are getting personal.
Your wife doesn't know.
Nothing physical has happened.
Yet.
Then brother...
this may be mercy arriving before catastrophe.
Delete what needs deleting.
End what needs ending.
Establish boundaries.
Tell the truth where truth must be told.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Pray.
Open Scripture.
Court your wife again.
Take her somewhere.
Listen without holding your phone.
Learn what has been hurting her.
Ask what makes her feel loved.
Repent of the distance you helped create.
And remember why you chose her.
Do not wait until another man appreciates what you neglected before realizing what was sitting across the dinner table all along.
And wives reading this...
this is not permission to carry responsibility for your husband's choices.
You cannot manufacture another person's faithfulness by becoming prettier, quieter, thinner, more sexual, less emotional, or endlessly accommodating.
Each person answers before God for his or her own choices.
Marriage needs grace from both people.
But adultery is not cured by making the betrayed spouse responsible for preventing betrayal.
The unfaithful heart must repent.
And the wounded heart deserves truth, patience, and care.
Be honest before God first.
Or perhaps:
“No more hiding.”
Maybe you have not crossed the physical line, but you know your heart has been wandering.
Say it:
“Guard my marriage, Lord.”
Someone reading the same comment section may discover that they are not the only person fighting for repentance, restoration, and a marriage that nearly disappeared beneath secrecy.
Not because saving a post makes anyone holy.
Come back when the message arrives.
Come back when loneliness starts negotiating.
Come back when your mind whispers, “Nobody will ever know.”
And remember:
God already does.
Your share might reach him before the hotel room does.
Send it privately if that is wiser.

And if you know a couple struggling beneath betrayal, don't weaponize these words against them. Pray for them. Walk with them. Encourage wise pastoral care, accountability, and appropriate counseling.
Truth should perform surgery, not become another weapon.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep putting Christ-centered biblical truth where wounded, wandering, curious, and spiritually hungry people can encounter it.

Scripture teaches that Gospel ministry may receive material support; Paul writes that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from Gospel ministry. But Scripture also protects giving from manipulation: believers are to give according to what they have decided in their hearts, “not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
It does not purchase salvation.
It does not replace repentance.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is not for sale.

But if this ministry is feeding you spiritually and you genuinely want to glorify God by helping biblical truth reach farther, supporting Gospel Warrior is one practical way you can participate in that work.
Pray.
Follow.
Save.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Sometimes one share reaches a marriage you will never know you helped protect.
One comment tells a struggling believer, “You are not fighting alone.”
One saved article becomes tomorrow's reminder.
One invitation brings somebody closer to Scripture.
And one honest moment of repentance can change the direction of a family.
But after all of this, do not leave remembering Gospel Warrior more than you remember Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save your marriage.
A comment cannot forgive adultery.
A shared post cannot regenerate your heart.
Only Christ saves.
Only His blood atones for sin.
Only His grace can take guilty people who genuinely repent and begin rewriting lives that seemed beyond repair.
So if you are married and courting another woman, stop asking how close you can stand to adultery without technically falling into it.
Turn around.
There is a covenant behind you.
There may still be a wife waiting for the man who once promised himself to her.
And above everything else, there is a Savior calling sinners out of darkness—not merely into better behavior, but into Himself.
The story does not have to end with deleted messages.
It does not have to end with another woman's perfume.
It does not have to end with children divided between homes.
It does not have to end with your wife wondering why she was not enough.
It does not have to end with you becoming permanently defined by the worst thing you ever did.
But something must die.
The secrecy.
The excuses.
The double life.
The fantasy.
The entitlement.
The version of you that keeps asking Jesus to forgive what you are still planning to continue.
Bring that man to the cross.
And let Christ begin making something new from what sin nearly destroyed.
Because sometimes the greatest love story is not finding another woman.
Sometimes it is becoming faithful again to the woman whose hand you already promised never to let go.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “NO GOOD THING DOES HE WITHHOLD” — SO WHY DID GOD WITHHOLD THE ONE THING YOU BEGGED HIM FOR?
paragraphs: “NO GOOD THING DOES HE WITHHOLD” — SO WHY DID GOD WITHHOLD THE ONE THING YOU BEGGED HIM FOR?

Psalm 84:11 was never a promise that God would give you everything you wanted. It was something far deeper—and if you have ever cried over a prayer God did not answer the way you begged Him to, you need to know what these words actually mean.
There is a particular kind of pain that only praying people understand.
It is the pain of asking God for something that seemed good...
and watching Him not give it.
You prayed for the relationship to survive.
It ended.
You prayed for the door to open.
It slammed shut.
You prayed for the opportunity.
Someone else received it.
You prayed for restoration.
Nothing changed.
You prayed until your vocabulary disappeared and all you had left were tears.
Then one day, while scrolling through your phone or turning the thin pages of your Bible, you encountered a verse that almost felt cruel in that moment:
“For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.”
Psalm 84:11, KJV.
No good thing?
Then what was that?
What do you call the marriage you wanted?
The child you prayed for?
The healing you pleaded for?
The job you needed?
The person you loved?
The future you imagined?
The answer that never came?
If God withholds no good thing, and He withheld this...
there are only a few conclusions the wounded heart instinctively reaches.
Maybe God is not really good.
Maybe the Bible's promise failed.
Maybe you did something wrong.
Maybe God loves other people more.
Maybe you did not pray hard enough.
Maybe you did not have enough faith.
Or perhaps—and this possibility changes everything—we have been making Psalm 84:11 promise something it never promised.
Because the original Hebrew does not say:
“God will give you whatever feels good to you.”
It says:
לֹא יִמְנַע־טוֹב לַהֹלְכִים בְּתָמִים
Lo yimna-tov laholkhim betamim.
“No good will He withhold from those walking in integrity.”

The Hebrew word טוֹב — tov means good, pleasant, beneficial, fitting, that which is genuinely good. It has a broad semantic range, but nowhere in the word itself is there a promise that whatever you intensely desire automatically qualifies as tov.
And then comes a phrase we sometimes rush past:
לַהֹלְכִים בְּתָמִים — laholkhim betamim.
Those walking in tamim.
The Hebrew תָּמִים — tamim carries the sense of wholeness, completeness, integrity, blamelessness or uprightness.
So Psalm 84:11 is not handing fallen human desire a blank check.
It is describing the goodness of God toward people whose lives are oriented toward Him.
And the context makes that impossible to miss.
Psalm 84 is not the song of someone standing in a mansion surrounded by everything he ever requested.
It is the song of someone desperate for God.
“My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD.”
The psalmist's great hunger is not first for possessions.
It is for Presence.
He longs for God's courts.
He calls those who dwell in God's house blessed.
He describes people whose strength is in God.
And then something astonishing happens.
They walk through the Valley of Baca—a poetic landscape associated with weeping—and keep moving toward God.
“They go from strength to strength.”
Only after all of that do we arrive at the words:
כִּי שֶׁמֶשׁ וּמָגֵן יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים
Ki shemesh u'magen YHWH Elohim.
“For the LORD God is a sun and shield.”
Then:
חֵן וְכָבוֹד יִתֵּן יְהוָה
“Grace and glory the LORD will give.”
Then:
לֹא יִמְנַע־טוֹב לַהֹלְכִים בְּתָמִים
“No good will He withhold from those walking in integrity.”
And how does the psalm end?
Not:
“Blessed is the person who receives everything he asks for.”
But:
אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם בֹּטֵחַ בָּךְ
“Blessed is the person who trusts in You.”
That is the destination of Psalm 84.
Trust.
The Hebrew text itself moves through longing, pilgrimage, tears, strength, prayer, God's presence, God's goodness...
and finally trust.
And suddenly the verse becomes both more difficult and more beautiful.
Because God is not promising to give you everything you call good.
He is promising that His goodness toward His people is not defective.
There is a difference.
A massive one.
Sometimes the most dangerous thing God could give you is exactly what you are begging Him to give you.
You cannot see ten years from now.
He can.
You cannot see someone's heart completely.
He can.
You cannot see every consequence attached to the opportunity you desperately want.
He can.
You cannot see what success might awaken inside you.
He can.
You cannot see the temptation hidden inside the blessing.
He can.
You cannot see whether the door you are pounding on opens into freedom...
or into a prison decorated like an answered prayer.
He can.
And this is where faith becomes painful.
We love trusting God when His wisdom agrees with ours.
We sing about surrender when surrender still produces the outcome we wanted.
But eventually every serious disciple of Jesus reaches a place where obedience asks:
“Do you still believe He is good when His answer is no?”
That question reaches places prosperity slogans cannot reach.
James destroys the idea that prayer automatically guarantees whatever the petitioner desires:
“You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions.”
James 4:3.
Scripture therefore explicitly acknowledges prayers that do not receive the requested answer because the request itself may be disordered.
But sometimes the request is not obviously selfish.
Sometimes you can ask for something honorable...
and God still does not give you the outcome you requested.
Paul knew that pain.
He pleaded repeatedly concerning his thorn.
God did not remove it.
The answer was grace.
“My grace is sufficient for thee.”
Think about that.
Paul asked for removal.
Christ answered with sufficiency.
Paul requested changed circumstances.
Christ gave sustaining grace.
Was something good withheld from Paul?
If Psalm 84 means “God always gives believers whatever outcome they sincerely consider good,” then Paul's experience becomes extremely difficult to explain.

But if Psalm 84 means God will never ultimately deprive His faithful people of what His perfect wisdom knows to be truly good for them, Paul's unanswered request suddenly belongs inside the promise rather than contradicting it.
Sometimes grace gives.
Sometimes grace removes.
Sometimes grace restores.
Sometimes grace closes the door.
Sometimes grace says yes.
Sometimes grace says wait.
And sometimes the grace of God looks you directly in the soul and says:
No.
Not because God stopped loving you.
But because divine love is not divine indulgence.
A father who gives his child everything the child demands is not necessarily loving that child well.
And our Father sees infinitely farther than we do.
But there is something even deeper.
Something that takes Psalm 84 all the way to the cross.
Because Christianity does not ask you to trust the goodness of a distant God who has never suffered.
Christianity points you toward Jesus Christ.
Look at Gethsemane.
The Son of God is on His knees.
The cross is approaching.
The agony is real.
Jesus prays concerning the cup before Him.
Yet His prayer bends beneath the Father's will.
Not My will.
Yours.
And the Father did not remove the cross.
Sit with that.
If getting what we want were the definition of God's goodness, then what would we do with Calvary?
The greatest good in human history came through an answer that passed through suffering.
Christ was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
And from what looked like catastrophic loss came the redemption of sinners.
The cross is God's eternal warning against judging His goodness too early.
Friday looked like defeat.
Sunday revealed what God was doing.
And perhaps somebody reading this is living somewhere between Friday and Sunday.
Something has died.
Something makes no sense.
Something you prayed for did not happen.
You are standing before a sealed tomb wondering why Jesus did not write the story the way you asked Him to.
Do not call the story finished yet.
That does not mean every earthly tragedy will be reversed exactly as we desire during this life.
Christian hope is bigger than that.
Our ultimate hope is resurrection.
It is Christ.
It is reconciliation with God.
It is a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
It is the promise that sin and death do not receive the final sentence.
Paul asks in Romans 8:32:
πῶς οὐχὶ καὶ σὺν αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα ἡμῖν χαρίσεται;

The thought is staggering: the God who did not spare His own Son but delivered Him up for us will also graciously give His people “all things” with Him. The logic begins not with possessions but with Christ.
God has already given the Gift against which every other gift must finally be measured.
Jesus.
So perhaps the deepest question is no longer:
“Why didn't God give me what I wanted?”
Perhaps eventually another question emerges:
“If God gave me Christ, can I trust Him with what He did not give me?”
That does not make grief disappear.
Faith is not pretending disappointment does not hurt.
You can trust God and cry.
You can believe Scripture and still whisper, “Lord, I don't understand.”
You can worship with swollen eyes.
You can obey while your heart is still learning how to release what it wanted.
Biblical faith is not emotional anesthesia.
It is wounded trust refusing to run away from God.
Maybe you have been angry with Him.
Tell Him.
Maybe you have been pretending you are fine.
Stop pretending.
Maybe disappointment quietly became bitterness.
Bring it into the light.
Maybe you began treating God like a transaction:
I prayed.
I obeyed.
I gave.
I served.
Therefore You owe me.
But the Gospel demolishes that arrangement.
God does not owe sinners salvation.
Yet in Christ He offers mercy.
We did not purchase the blood of Jesus with our obedience.
We are rescued by grace.
And when grace gets hold of us, obedience becomes gratitude rather than currency.
This is why Psalm 84:11 cannot become a prosperity formula.
The Gospel is not:
Come to Jesus and He will make your preferred future happen.
The Gospel is:

You were separated from God by sin, unable to save yourself, and Jesus Christ came for sinners. He lived in righteousness, died for our sins, and rose again. Through repentance and faith in Him there is forgiveness, reconciliation, new life and everlasting hope.
Sometimes Jesus rewrites your circumstances.
Sometimes He rewrites you while the circumstances remain painful.
And sometimes that second miracle is the one you needed more.
Maybe the relationship you lost exposed the idol you had made of being loved.
Maybe the closed door revealed how much identity you had buried inside success.
Maybe the season of waiting uncovered a version of Christianity built around receiving rather than knowing Christ.
Maybe the unanswered prayer brought you to a place where you finally stopped saying, “Jesus, give me what I need to build my life,” and started saying:
“Jesus... You are my life.”
That is not defeat.
That is discipleship.
And if these words exposed something hidden in you—resentment toward God, disappointment you were afraid to admit, anger over an unanswered prayer—do not hide behind religious language.
Be honest.
There is no shame in admitting the battle is real.
Sometimes another believer needs to know that faith can tremble without completely letting go.
And if you know someone who has been silently asking, “If God is good, why didn't He answer me?”
Send this to them.
One share may place Scripture in front of someone on the exact night they were preparing to give up on God.
Save this too.
Because eventually another prayer may receive an answer you did not expect.
And when emotions become loud, you may need to return to what Scripture actually says.
“No good thing does He withhold” does not mean:
God will give me everything I want.
It means I can trust the goodness and wisdom of the God who sees what I cannot see.
And Gospel Warrior exists for moments exactly like this—to keep bringing people beyond isolated inspirational verses and back into context, Scripture, repentance, grace, the cross, and Jesus Christ.
If this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, return to Christ, endure a dark season, repent, heal, or grow deeper in the Gospel, you can help this work continue and expand.
Following costs nothing.
Sharing costs nothing.
Tagging someone costs nothing.
And the Gospel itself can never be purchased.
But producing and expanding ministry resources does require real-world support.
Scripture guards giving from manipulation: Paul teaches believers to give as they have purposed in their hearts, “not grudgingly, or of necessity,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
Never give because you think money can purchase an answered prayer.
Never give to bargain with God.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Grace is not behind a paywall.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Christ purchased His people with something infinitely more precious than money.
His blood.
So follow if you want to keep walking with us through Scripture.
Save the teachings you know you will need again.
Share truth beyond the walls of this page.
But above everything...
follow Jesus.
Because one day you may discover that some of the things you accused God of withholding were things from which He was protecting you.
Some closed doors were mercy.
Some delays were formation.
Some losses drove roots deeper into Christ.
Some unanswered prayers exposed idols you could not see.
And some chapters you would never have chosen became the very places where you learned that Jesus was enough.
We are often desperate for God to rewrite our circumstances.
Jesus is determined to rewrite us.
That is the scandal of grace.
Peter failed spectacularly—and Jesus restored him.
Thomas doubted—and Jesus met him.
Paul persecuted Christians—and Jesus transformed him into a herald of the Gospel.
The thief reached the cross with nothing left to offer—and received a promise from the King hanging beside him.
And you?
Your disappointment is not too complicated.
Your questions are not too frightening.
Your failure is not too filthy.
Your past is not too scandalous.
Your unanswered prayer is not proof that Christ abandoned you.
Come back.
Repent where you need to repent.
Grieve what you need to grieve.
Release what you have been demanding God explain.
Ask boldly.
Pray honestly.
Trust tremblingly if trembling is all you can manage today.
And keep walking toward Jesus.
Because the greatest evidence that God did not withhold good from His people is not the house, the promotion, the relationship, the healing, the money, or the comfortable life.
It is the cross.
He gave us His Son.
And when you cannot understand the hand of God...
look again at the wounds of Christ.
The thing God withheld may have broken your heart—but the Christ God gave you can hold your heart until you finally understand what you could not see.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID RUTH HAVE THE RIGHT TO GLEAN IN BOAZ’S FIELD?
paragraphs: WHY DID RUTH HAVE THE RIGHT TO GLEAN IN BOAZ’S FIELD?
The Forgotten Law That Turned a Poor Widow’s Hunger Into a Story of Redemption—and Revealed the Heart of the God Who Refuses to Harvest His Field Empty
There is a detail in the story of Ruth that is so easy to romanticize that we can completely miss what God was showing us.
Ruth did not walk into Boaz’s field looking for romance.
She walked into that field because she was hungry.
No beautiful dress.
No secret plan to meet a wealthy landowner.
No guarantee that someone would notice her.
No certainty that tomorrow would be easier than today.
She was a widow.
A foreigner.
A Moabite woman living among Israelites.

She had left her homeland behind. Her husband was dead. Naomi, the woman she refused to abandon, was also a widow. There was no husband bringing home wages, no son providing security, no overflowing pantry waiting when Ruth returned home.
There was just a field.
A harvest.
Some grain lying behind the workers.
And one ancient command from God standing between vulnerable people and absolute destitution.
That changes the way you read Ruth 2.
Because when Ruth said to Naomi:
“אֵלְכָה־נָּא הַשָּׂדֶה וַאֲלַקֳטָה בַשִּׁבֳּלִים”
’Elkhah-na hassadeh va’alaqotah vashibbolim...
“I would like to go to the fields and glean among the ears of grain...” — Ruth 2:2

she was stepping into something God had established long before Ruth ever arrived in Bethlehem. The Hebrew text describes her going into the field to laqet—to glean, to gather what remained behind the harvesters. Ruth 2:2 explicitly presents Ruth seeking permission or favor as she goes to glean behind the reapers.
But why was grain being left there in the first place?
That is where this story becomes much bigger than Ruth and Boaz.
Centuries before that morning in Bethlehem, God had spoken to Israel about what they were allowed to do with their own harvest.
And what God commanded was astonishing.
“וּבְקֻצְרְכֶם אֶת־קְצִיר אַרְצְכֶם לֹא תְכַלֶּה פְּאַת שָׂדְךָ לִקְצֹר וְלֶקֶט קְצִירְךָ לֹא תְלַקֵּט”
Uv’qutzrekhem et-qetzir artzekhem, lo tekhalleh pe’at sadekha liqtzor; veleqet qetzirkha lo telaqqet.
“When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap all the way to the edges of your field, or gather the gleanings of your harvest.” — Leviticus 19:9
The Hebrew word לֶקֶט — leqet refers to the gleanings of the harvest.
God was commanding His people not to squeeze every possible piece of produce out of the land for themselves.
Leave something.
Do not harvest everything.
Do not turn every stalk into personal profit.
Do not make efficiency your god.
Leave room at the edges.
Leave what falls.
Why?
The next verse answers:
“...you shall leave them for the poor and the stranger.”
Then comes the breathtaking signature behind the command:
“I am the LORD your God.”

Leviticus 19:9–10 connects holiness with how Israel treated vulnerable people. The field belonged to the landowner in an ordinary human sense, but the landowner lived under the authority of the God who had commanded that part of the harvest be left accessible to the poor and the foreigner.
Read that slowly.
God built mercy into the harvest.
Before Ruth became hungry, God had already written provision for people like Ruth into Israel’s covenant life.
Before Ruth crossed into Bethlehem...
before she knew Boaz existed...
before she bent down for her first stalk of barley...
God had already spoken.
Leave something for her.
And maybe somebody reading this knows exactly what it feels like to survive on what seems to have been “left over.”
You thought your life would look different by now.
You thought the marriage would survive.
