You thought the job would last.
You thought your children would remain close.
You thought you would be stronger.
You thought the prayer would have been answered already.
Instead, you find yourself walking through a season you never planned, picking up enough grace to survive another day.
And somewhere inside you whispers:
“Is this all I am now?”
Ruth could have asked the same question.
A widow.
A foreigner.
A gleaner walking behind everybody else.
But heaven did not call her worthless.
And God had not forgotten her.
Deuteronomy makes the purpose of the gleaning laws even clearer.
“כִּי תִקְצֹר קְצִירְךָ בְשָׂדֶךָ וְשָׁכַחְתָּ עֹמֶר בַּשָּׂדֶה לֹא תָשׁוּב לְקַחְתּוֹ לַגֵּר לַיָּתוֹם וְלָאַלְמָנָה יִהְיֶה”
Ki tiqtzor qetzirkha vesadekha, veshakhahta ‘omer bassadeh, lo tashuv leqahto; lager, layatom vela’almanah yihyeh.
When an Israelite harvested his field and forgot a sheaf, he was commanded not to return and retrieve it.
It was to be for לַגֵּר — lager, the sojourner or resident foreigner;
לַיָּתוֹם — layatom, the fatherless;
and וְלָאַלְמָנָה — vela’almanah, the widow.
Deuteronomy 24:19 says explicitly that the forgotten sheaf was to belong to these vulnerable people.
Now look at Ruth.
She was a foreigner.
She was a widow.
She was standing almost directly inside the categories God had named.
That means Ruth’s presence in the field was not an embarrassing interruption to God's economy.
God had anticipated people like her.
The poor were not supposed to be invisible.
The foreigner was not supposed to be forgotten.
The widow was not supposed to starve while wealthy fields were stripped clean.
The God of Israel had commanded His people to leave margins where vulnerable human beings could gather food with dignity.
And there is something beautiful about the way this provision worked.
Ruth still worked.
She went into the field.
She bent down.
She gathered.
She carried.
She labored through the heat.
Biblical compassion did not treat her as useless, nor did it leave her helpless.
It created space for a vulnerable woman to work and eat.
Mercy protected dignity.
Then Boaz arrived.
And suddenly the story moved beyond what the law merely required.
Boaz noticed Ruth.
He asked about her.
He learned what she had done for Naomi.
He told Ruth to remain in his field.
He ordered the young men not to harm or harass her.
He gave her access to water.
He welcomed her at mealtime.
Then he did something extraordinary.
After Ruth returned to gleaning, Boaz commanded his workers:
“גַּם בֵּין הָעֳמָרִים תְּלַקֵּט וְלֹא תַכְלִימוּהָ”
Gam bein ha’omarim telaqqet velo takhlimuha.
Let her glean even among the sheaves—and do not humiliate her.
That final thought matters.
Do not shame her.
Do not embarrass her.
Do not make her feel dirty because she needs help.
Do not use your position to crush someone already carrying grief.
Boaz then instructed his workers to deliberately pull grain from the bundles and leave it where Ruth could gather it.
The law required generosity.
Boaz chose generosity beyond the minimum.
Ruth came looking for gleanings.
Boaz started leaving handfuls on purpose.
Ruth 2:15 preserves Boaz's command that she be permitted to glean even among the sheaves and not be humiliated.
And there are people reading this who need those words:
Do not humiliate her.
Because some of the deepest wounds people carry were inflicted when they were already vulnerable.
They needed help and somebody made them feel ashamed for needing it.
They confessed their struggle and someone used it against them.
They admitted their financial hardship and were treated like failures.
They admitted their addiction and were reduced to their worst day.
They admitted their marriage was collapsing and became gossip.
They admitted they were spiritually exhausted and were told they simply did not have enough faith.
But look at the heart reflected in Boaz.
Protection without humiliation.
Provision without exploitation.
Kindness without demanding repayment.
And yet even Boaz is not the ultimate hero of Scripture.
Jesus is.
Boaz is an important redeemer figure within Ruth's story, but the biblical storyline does not terminate with him.
Keep reading Scripture.
Ruth eventually becomes the wife of Boaz.
Their son is Obed.
Obed becomes the father of Jesse.
Jesse becomes the father of David.
And from David's royal line, according to the Gospel of Matthew, comes Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
The foreign widow who once bent down gathering leftover barley becomes part of the family line through which the Messiah enters history.
The woman who looked insignificant was carrying a future she could not see.
The woman who had buried her husband had not buried God's purpose.
The woman collecting fallen grain would become an ancestor of the King.
That is why you should be careful about deciding that the chapter you are living in right now is the conclusion of your story.
Ruth 1 looked like tragedy.
Ruth 2 looked like survival.
But God was writing redemption.
You may only see the field.
God sees generations.
You see the grain you need for tonight.
God sees what He is doing beyond what you can presently understand.
You see what died.
God sees what grace can still redeem.
And this is where Ruth's story begins pressing painfully close to the Gospel.
Because all of us come to God spiritually bankrupt.
Sin has left humanity with a debt we cannot erase through moral effort.
We do not negotiate our way into salvation.
We do not impress God into forgiving us.
We do not earn the blood of Christ.
We come needy.
And the astonishing announcement of Christianity is not that sinful people managed to climb their way back to God.
It is that God came down to rescue sinners.
Jesus Christ entered our broken world.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is offered through Him.
Grace does not tell us that sin never mattered.
The cross proves that sin mattered terribly.
Grace tells us that Christ was willing to bear what we could never bear ourselves.
That is why repentance is not humiliation before a cruel God.
It is coming home to a holy and merciful One.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Maybe there is something you keep deleting from your testimony.
Something you hope nobody discovers.
Something that makes you wonder whether God could still want you.
Look again at Ruth.
Scripture never hides where she came from.
It repeatedly calls her Ruth the Moabite.
Her outsider identity is not airbrushed away.
And still grace brings her near.
Still redemption writes another chapter.
Still her name enters the genealogy.
Still her story moves toward Christ.
That does not mean every detail of Ruth's experience should be allegorized into ours.
It means the God revealed throughout Scripture truly does work through broken histories, outsiders, widows, failures, impossible circumstances, and people who cannot see what He is doing yet.
Your scandal does not have greater authority than the grace of Jesus Christ.
Your past does not become good simply because Christ forgives you.
Something better happens.
Christ redeems sinners.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He transforms.
He calls us away from sin and toward Himself.
He writes holiness where rebellion once lived.
He writes testimony where shame once ruled.
He writes restoration where devastation seemed final.
From scandal to grace...
because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps that is why the field of Boaz still speaks so loudly.
There was grain at the edge because God had commanded His people to remember the vulnerable.
There was safety because Boaz feared God enough to protect Ruth.
There was abundance because Boaz's generosity went beyond minimum obedience.
There was redemption because providence was working through ordinary decisions that probably did not look miraculous while they were happening.
No thunder.
No fire falling from heaven.
No sea splitting open.
Just a grieving woman waking up and going to work.
A field.
A landowner.
Some barley.
A command written generations earlier.
And the invisible providence of God quietly moving history toward Jesus Christ.
Maybe your miracle does not look dramatic either.
Maybe today your miracle is simply that you did not give up.
Maybe grace looks like getting out of bed.
Maybe it looks like opening your Bible again after months of spiritual numbness.
Maybe it looks like finally confessing the sin you have hidden.
Maybe it looks like saying, “Jesus, I need You,” without pretending you have everything together.
Maybe it looks like forgiving someone.
Maybe it looks like asking somebody to pray for you.
Maybe you are still in the field.
Still bending down.
Still tired.
Still wondering why everybody else seems to have armfuls while you are gathering one stalk at a time.
Do not confuse your current position with your final identity.
Ruth entered the field as a poor foreign widow.
She did not remain there forever.
And more importantly, the God who met Ruth in her vulnerability is still the God whose character is revealed supremely in Jesus Christ.
Bring it to Christ.
And if you have spent years pretending everything is okay when it is not, maybe today your confession is simply:
“No more hiding.”
Someone reading those words may realize they are not fighting alone.
That is part of why Gospel truth should travel.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not—but because somebody connected to you may desperately need the truth you almost scrolled past.
But hear this clearly.
It does not.
Scripture does not give us authority to make that claim.

And we do not want anyone supporting this work through fear, guilt, or spiritual pressure. The New Testament says giving should be purposeful and willing, “not grudgingly or of necessity,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
That support helps keep the field open.
And there is another way you can help that costs nothing.
Share.
A share helps carry the message farther.
Both can matter enormously, but neither earns salvation, buys favor from God, or replaces the Gospel.
Salvation is in Jesus Christ.
Open Ruth again.
Read the field differently.
Look at the edges.
Look at the grain.
Look at the widow bending down.
Look at the man refusing to humiliate her.
Look at the God who commanded that room be left for the vulnerable.
Then follow the story through Obed...
through Jesse...
through David...
until Scripture brings you to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most beautiful thing lying in Boaz's field was never the barley.
It was evidence.
Evidence that God had already made provision before Ruth knew where she was going.
Evidence that obedience can become somebody else's answered prayer.
Evidence that kindness can preserve another person's dignity.
Evidence that what looks like an ordinary field can become the setting for extraordinary providence.
And evidence that the woman everybody could have dismissed as merely a poor foreign widow was standing inside a story that would eventually point generations toward Christ.
So when you find yourself living on the edge of a field you never wanted to enter, do not assume God has abandoned the story.
Sometimes you are gathering what looks like scattered grain while God is quietly gathering the pieces of a future you cannot yet see.
Ruth thought she was walking into a field to find enough bread for another day; she had no idea she was walking into a redemption story that would echo all the way to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EPHESIANS 5 IS NOT A LICENSE FOR A HUSBAND TO CONTROL HIS WIFE
paragraphs: EPHESIANS 5 IS NOT A LICENSE FOR A HUSBAND TO CONTROL HIS WIFE
If Your Version of “Biblical Headship” Makes a Woman Afraid of Her Husband, You May Be Defending Something Jesus Never Commanded
There is a frightening way to hold a Bible.
You can hold it open while your heart remains closed.
You can underline a verse and still violate the God who inspired it.
You can say, “The Bible says the husband is the head,” while conveniently forgetting what the Bible says the Head did for His bride.
He died for her.
And that changes everything.
Somewhere tonight, a Christian wife may be sitting silently beside a man who knows Ephesians 5:22 but seems strangely unfamiliar with Ephesians 5:25.
She has heard the word “submit” more times than she has heard, “I was wrong.”
She has been reminded of his authority more often than she has experienced his sacrifice.
Maybe he controls the money.
Maybe he monitors every conversation.
Maybe disagreement is called rebellion.
Maybe questions are called disrespect.
Maybe Scripture gets pulled out whenever she refuses to surrender something God never commanded her to surrender—her conscience, her dignity, her safety, her voice, or her obedience to Christ.
And perhaps the most painful part is that Jesus keeps getting blamed for it.
So we need to open Ephesians 5 again.
Not to attack marriage.
Not to erase every distinction Paul makes between husbands and wives.
Not to bend Scripture around modern preferences.
And not to force the passage into whichever side of today's cultural argument makes us comfortable.
We need to read it because Scripture deserves better than being turned into ammunition for our egos.
And so do the people wounded by our misuse of it.
Paul does speak about wives submitting to their husbands. We should not pretend otherwise.
But that is not all Paul says.
The passage comes in a larger context of Spirit-filled Christian living. Immediately before addressing wives and husbands, Paul writes:
—Ephesians 5:21.
The key expression, “ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις,” carries the sense of “submitting to one another,” followed by “in the fear/reverence of Christ.”
And then comes verse 22.
This detail matters.
In an important early textual form of the Greek, verse 22 reads:
“Αἱ γυναῖκες τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ”
Literally, it gives us something like:
“Wives, to their own husbands, as to the Lord.”
Notice something?

There is no independently stated verb for “submit” in that form of verse 22. The thought is grammatically carried forward from the preceding verse. Other manuscripts supply a form of the verb explicitly, which is why translations naturally include it, but the textual history itself reminds us that verses 21 and 22 belong closely together.
Paul did not drop a disconnected command into the middle of nowhere.
He was describing relationships transformed by the lordship of Christ.
And then Paul turns toward husbands.
This is where any man tempted to use the passage as a throne should feel the throne begin to disappear beneath him.
“Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας…”
“Husbands, love your wives…”
But Paul does not stop with “love.”
He gives the husband a terrifyingly beautiful standard:
“καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς”
“As Christ also loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
—Ephesians 5:25.
Read that again.
The model is not Caesar.
The model is not a dictator.
The model is not an angry father whose word could never be questioned.
The model is Jesus Christ.
And what does Jesus do?
“ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν.”
He gave Himself up.
Paul points the husband toward the crucified Christ.
So if a husband wants to talk about being “head,” he cannot separate that language from the Christ to whom Paul points.
And Christlike headship can never become an excuse for selfish domination.
Jesus does not tell husbands, “Make sure she knows who is boss.”
Paul tells husbands to love as Christ loved.
Jesus washed feet.
Jesus welcomed the overlooked.
Jesus confronted hypocrisy.
Jesus protected the vulnerable.
Jesus laid down His life.
At Calvary, Christ did not use His power to save Himself at His bride's expense.
He used His power in sacrificial love.
That is why Ephesians 5 becomes devastating when someone tries to use it to baptize domination.
Because the husband who keeps asking, “How much must my wife submit to me?” may be asking the wrong first question.
The passage forces another question onto him:
“How much am I willing to die to myself for her good?”
Your pride.
Your selfishness.
Your need to win every argument.
Your obsession with being obeyed.
Your defensiveness when corrected.
Your appetite for control.
Your refusal to apologize.
Your habit of demanding respect while giving very little tenderness.
Put those things at the foot of the cross.
Because Paul continues:
“οὕτως ὀφείλουσιν καὶ οἱ ἄνδρες ἀγαπᾶν τὰς ἑαυτῶν γυναῖκας ὡς τὰ ἑαυτῶν σώματα”
“So husbands also ought to love their own wives as their own bodies.”
—Ephesians 5:28.
Then comes another extraordinary description:
“ἀλλὰ ἐκτρέφει καὶ θάλπει αὐτήν”
He “nourishes and cherishes” it.
—Ephesians 5:29.
Nourishes.
Cherishes.
Those are difficult words to reconcile with humiliation, intimidation, coercion, cruelty, manipulation, or fear.
A wife is not an employee in her husband's private kingdom.
She is not property.
She is not a supporting character in the story of his greatness.
She is a woman bearing the image of God, a fellow heir of the grace of life, and—if she belongs to Christ—someone for whom the same Savior shed His blood.
Peter likewise tells husbands to live with their wives with understanding and to show them honor as “heirs together of the grace of life” (1 Peter 3:7).
Honor.
Not erasure.
Understanding.
Not intimidation.
And this needs to be said carefully because people have been hurt on both sides of these conversations.

Saying that Ephesians 5 does not authorize controlling or abusive behavior is not the same as saying Scripture contains no meaningful teaching about marital order, submission, headship, or the responsibilities of husbands and wives.

Christians disagree over precisely how biblical headship and submission should be understood and practiced. Faithful believers have defended complementarian and egalitarian readings while attempting to take Scripture seriously.
But there is something no Christian interpretation should need to defend:
sin.
Whatever theological label we use, cruelty does not become holiness because somebody puts the word “headship” over it.
Manipulation does not become leadership because the manipulator can quote Paul.
Sin does not become biblical because it happens inside a Christian home.
And submission to a husband is never permission to disobey God.
The apostles themselves declared:
“We must obey God rather than men.”
—Acts 5:29.
Christ remains Lord.
Always.
No husband replaces Him.
No pastor replaces Him.
No ministry replaces Him.
No marriage replaces Him.
Jesus Christ possesses an authority no human spouse possesses.
That means a husband cannot legitimately demand that his wife participate in sin and then call her refusal “rebellion.”

It also means a woman facing violence, threats, coercion, or abuse should not be told that quietly enduring danger is what faithfulness to Ephesians 5 requires. Seeking safety, wise pastoral counsel, trustworthy support, professional help, or lawful protection is not automatically a rejection of biblical marriage.
Sometimes the sentence “You just need to submit more” has been spoken to someone who desperately needed somebody to ask:
“Are you safe?”
That should grieve the Church.
But husbands are not the only people who should feel conviction here.
Wives can sin against husbands.
Husbands can be wounded, manipulated, belittled, betrayed, or abused too.
None of us gets to weaponize Scripture.
The Gospel does not divide humanity into one gender that needs repentance and another that does not.
All have sinned.
All need grace.
All need Christ.
The deepest problem in marriage is ultimately the same disease found everywhere else in the human heart:
sin.
We want our way.
We defend ourselves.
We keep records.
We punish.
We withdraw.
We manipulate.
We crave control.
We demand from another human being what only Christ can give us.
Then two sinners stand in the same house wondering why love hurts.
And into that house walks Jesus.
Not merely as a marriage counselor.
As Savior.
This is where Ephesians 5 becomes far more beautiful than a debate about who gets the final word.
Paul eventually tells us what he has been pointing toward:
“τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν…”
“This mystery is great…”
Then he says he is speaking about Christ and the Church.
Marriage is pointing beyond itself.
The husband is not the savior.
The wife is not the savior.
Marriage is not the savior.
Jesus is.
And the Gospel says that Jesus came for controlling husbands.
For bitter wives.
For arrogant men.
For manipulative women.
For marriages suffocating under resentment.
For people carrying secrets.
For people ashamed of what they have become.
For the religious person who memorized Scripture without allowing Scripture to crucify his pride.
For the wounded person who wonders whether God saw what happened behind the closed door.
He saw.
And the cross tells us something astonishing about both sin and grace.
Our sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
His grace is great enough that Christ willingly did.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending.
Not image management.
Not posting photographs of a perfect Christian marriage while two people quietly bleed behind them.
Repentance.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
Transformation.
Maybe you are a husband reading this and something inside you has gone quiet.
Because you recognize yourself.
Not in every sentence.
But enough.
You have called control “leadership.”
You have used silence as punishment.
You have demanded an apology while refusing to give one.
You have quoted “wives, submit” without trembling before “husbands, love.”
Then don't run from conviction.
Run to Christ.
Repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
It is the mercy of God opening a prison door.
Tell the truth.
Confess your sin to God.
Ask your wife to forgive you without explaining away what you did.
Seek mature accountability.
Learn to listen.
Get help where help is needed.
And do not announce that you have changed.
Live differently long enough that the fruit begins speaking for you.
Maybe you are the wife reading this with tears forming because somebody finally put words around something you have been afraid to name.
Please hear this carefully:
Your husband's sin is not proof that Jesus has abandoned you.
Jesus is not identical to the man who misused His name.
Do not measure the character of Christ by somebody's failure to imitate Him.
Look at Jesus.
The real Jesus.
The One who sees.
The One who knows.
The One who tells the truth about sin.
The One who receives the broken.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who went to the cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still saves.
And perhaps you are neither the controlling spouse nor the wounded spouse.
Maybe you simply know someone whose marriage looks different behind closed doors than it does on Sunday morning.
Be careful with their heart.
Don't gossip.
Don't become judge and jury based on fragments.
But don't use “submission” as an excuse to ignore credible cries for help either.
Truth and love are not enemies.
Sometimes love listens.
Sometimes love confronts.
Sometimes love stays beside someone through repentance and restoration.
Sometimes love helps someone reach safety.
Sometimes love says what everyone else was too uncomfortable to say.
The Church should be one of the safest places on earth to tell the truth.
Because Christians are people who already know that everyone needs grace.
Imagine what our homes could look like if we stopped asking Scripture to defend us and started allowing Scripture to expose us.
Imagine husbands who read Ephesians 5:25 and think first about the cross rather than their authority.

Imagine wives loved so consistently that “cherish” is not merely a Greek word explained during a sermon but something they experience at breakfast, in disagreements, in financial decisions, in exhaustion, in intimacy, in sickness, in parenting, and in ordinary Tuesday-night conversations.
Imagine marriages where “I was wrong” is not defeat.
Where “forgive me” is not weakness.
Where disagreement is not treason.
Where strength protects instead of intimidates.
Where both husband and wife remember that another throne stands above their marriage.
And Jesus Christ sits on it.
That is where scandal can become grace.
Not because we rewrite Scripture.
Because Scripture, rightly received, allows Jesus to rewrite us.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to tell strangers the details. But you can refuse to keep pretending.
Somebody who thinks their story is beyond redemption may need to hear that repentance is real, forgiveness is real, and Jesus is still at work.
And if this article made you think of someone, don't weaponize it against them.
Don't send it with, “See? I told you.”
Send it with love.
Save it too.
Because one day you may encounter Ephesians 5 being reduced to a slogan again, and you may need to return to the cross at the center of the passage.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well. Not because following a page saves anyone—only Christ saves—but because filling our lives with reminders of truth can continually point us back toward the One who does.
Biblical giving is worship offered to God willingly, not money extracted through spiritual pressure.
But voluntary financial support can be a genuine form of Gospel partnership.
If this ministry is bearing good fruit in your life, prayerfully consider supporting that work as part of your generosity after honoring your biblical convictions and responsibilities.
One share can place biblical truth in front of someone we may never personally reach.
One share.
One conversation.
One wounded person realizing Jesus is not the monster somebody made Him out to be.
One proud heart finally surrendering.
One husband repenting.
One wife discovering she has been seen.
One marriage beginning the long road toward truth.
One sinner looking toward the cross.
We cannot manufacture what God will do with a seed.
We can simply plant faithfully.
So share it.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because sometimes confession is where hiding begins to die.
Husband or wife.
Married or single.
Wounded or guilty.
Religious or running.
There is room at the cross for the truth about you.
And there is grace there too.
Because the final message of Ephesians 5 is not that husbands get a throne.
It is that marriage points toward a Bridegroom who went to a cross.
Jesus does not need your marriage to look perfect.
He wants your heart surrendered enough that He can make it truthful, holy, tender, repentant, forgiving, and increasingly like Him.
And perhaps that is the sentence worth carrying with you after everything else fades:
Never use the Bible to build yourself a throne when the Jesus standing at the center of that Bible chose a cross.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HAGAR BECAME PREGNANT—And Suddenly the Relationship Between the Two Women Exploded
paragraphs: HAGAR BECAME PREGNANT—And Suddenly the Relationship Between the Two Women Exploded

Genesis 16:4–6 is not merely the story of two women who could no longer live peacefully under the same roof. It is the terrifying story of what can happen when wounded people try to accomplish God's promise without waiting for God's way—and the breathtaking reminder that even when human decisions create a wilderness, God still knows how to find people there.
There are some Bible stories we have read so many times that we no longer feel the tension.
We already know the ending.
We know Abraham will become the father of nations.
We know Sarah will eventually laugh while holding Isaac.
We know God will keep His promise.
But Sarai did not yet have Isaac in her arms.
She had a promise...
and an empty womb.
And somewhere inside that unbearable space between what God had said and what Sarai could see, something began to break.
Then Hagar became pregnant.
And suddenly everything changed.
The Hebrew of Genesis 16:4 captures the moment with devastating simplicity:
“וַיָּבֹא אֶל־הָגָר וַתַּהַר”
Vayyavo el-Hagar vattahar.
“And he went in to Hagar, and she conceived.”
Then comes the sentence that turns the household into a battlefield:
“וַתֵּקַל גְּבִרְתָּהּ בְּעֵינֶיהָ”
Vatteqal gevirtah be'eineha.
Literally, the idea is that her mistress became “light” or diminished in her eyes.
The woman Hagar had once served no longer carried the same weight in Hagar's estimation.
Pregnancy had changed the atmosphere.

The biblical text says that after Hagar realized she had conceived, she regarded her mistress with contempt. Genesis does not ask us to imagine details it never gives us. It does not tell us every conversation, facial expression, insult, or private thought.
It simply tells us enough.
Something had changed in Hagar's eyes.
And Sarai felt it.
Deeply.
Maybe that is why this ancient story feels disturbingly modern.
Because sometimes relationships do not collapse when somebody fails.
Sometimes they collapse when somebody succeeds.
Someone gets what you have prayed for.
Someone receives what you have waited years to receive.
Someone announces the pregnancy while you are still crying over infertility.
Someone gets married while you are wondering whether anybody will ever choose you.
Someone's ministry grows while yours feels invisible.
Someone gets promoted.
Someone heals.
Someone buys the house.
Someone's child returns to God.
Someone receives the opportunity you secretly believed should have been yours.
You smile.
You congratulate them.
You type, “So happy for you.”
And then you put the phone down...
and something inside you hurts.
Not necessarily because you hate them.
Sometimes because their blessing touched your wound.
That is where Sarai was living.

Long before Hagar conceived, God had already spoken extraordinary promises concerning Abram. Yet years had passed, and Sarai remained childless. Genesis 16 tells us Abram had already lived in Canaan ten years when Sarai gave Hagar to him.
Ten years.
Ten years is enough time for hope to become exhausting.
Enough time to wonder whether you misunderstood God.
Enough time to begin asking questions you are almost afraid to say aloud.
“Lord, did You forget me?”
“Did I hear You incorrectly?”
“Why is everyone moving forward except me?”
“How long am I supposed to wait?”
And this is where Genesis 16 becomes painfully personal.
Sarai tried to solve through human strategy what God intended to fulfill through divine promise.
Hagar was brought into the arrangement.
Abram agreed.
Hagar conceived.
And the solution became another problem.
That is one of Scripture's recurring warnings:
Not everything we can make happen is something God told us to make happen.
Sometimes impatience dresses itself like wisdom.
Sometimes fear calls itself practicality.
Sometimes we become so desperate for God's promise that we begin manufacturing our own version of it.
And then we ask God to bless what anxiety built.

That does not mean every difficult circumstance in our lives exists because we failed to wait correctly. Scripture never gives us permission to make that simplistic accusation against suffering people.
But Genesis 16 absolutely confronts us with this question:
What happens when we stop trusting God's timing and start trying to control the outcome?
Look at the wreckage.
Sarai is wounded.
Hagar becomes contemptuous.
Abram becomes passive.
The household fractures.
Nobody walks away untouched.
Sarai turns toward Abram and says:
“חֲמָסִי עָלֶיךָ”
Chamasi aleikha.
The sense is powerful: “The wrong done to me be upon you.”
She is hurting.
And hurting people can begin looking for somewhere to put their pain.
Abram responds by placing Hagar back into Sarai's power.
Then Genesis 16:6 says Sarai treated Hagar harshly.
The Hebrew uses the verb:
Vatte'anneha.
The language communicates affliction, harsh treatment, humiliation or oppression.
And Hagar runs.
Stop there.
Because if we rush too quickly toward the theological lesson, we can miss the human being disappearing into the wilderness.
Hagar is pregnant.
Hagar is vulnerable.
Hagar is away from home.
Hagar is Egyptian.
Hagar is a servant.
Hagar has been pulled into a complicated family arrangement involving people with far more power than she possesses.
Yes, Scripture tells us that Hagar looked upon Sarai with contempt.
It does not excuse that.
But Scripture also refuses to erase what Sarai did afterward.
The Bible is remarkably honest about its people.
It does not airbrush them simply because God has chosen them.
Abram can have faith and still fail.
Sarai can belong inside God's covenant purposes and still mistreat another human being.
Hagar can be wrong in one moment and wounded in another.
That should humble every one of us.
Because we love simple categories.
Hero.
Villain.
Victim.
Offender.
Good person.
Bad person.
But Genesis 16 gives us something painfully recognizable.
Broken people hurting broken people.
A wounded woman wounds another wounded woman.
A passive man allows the conflict to deepen.
Pride meets insecurity.
Jealousy meets contempt.
Fear meets fear.
And a pregnant woman runs toward the desert.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
Maybe your wilderness did not have sand.
Maybe it looked like a bedroom door closing behind you while everybody else thought you were fine.
Maybe it looked like sitting inside your car for another ten minutes because you did not want to walk into the house.
Maybe it looked like church hurt.
A marriage collapsing.
A friendship ending.
A betrayal you still cannot talk about without your chest tightening.
Maybe you were mistreated.
Maybe you did some of the mistreating.
Maybe the hardest truth is that you were both wounded and wrong.
And perhaps you have spent years trying to decide which part of your story disqualifies you from being seen by God.
Then Genesis does something astonishing.
Hagar runs...
but God comes looking.
The angel of the LORD finds her beside a spring in the wilderness.
Not Sarai.
Not Abram.
Hagar.
The servant.
The foreigner.
The pregnant runaway.
The woman caught inside somebody else's broken attempt to secure a promise.
He finds her.
Please do not read that too quickly.
He.
Finds.
Her.
Before Hagar had cleaned up the situation...
God saw her.
Before the family conflict was resolved...
God saw her.
Before she knew what tomorrow would look like...
God saw her.
And later in Genesis 16, Hagar responds with one of the most unforgettable declarations in Scripture:
“אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי”
Attah El Ro'i.
“You are a God who sees me.”
El Roi.
The God who sees.
Imagine what those words meant coming from Hagar.
People may have seen a servant.
God saw Hagar.
People may have seen a problem.
God saw Hagar.
People may have seen pregnancy, scandal, conflict, usefulness, inconvenience, status...
God saw a person.
And maybe that is exactly what somebody reading this needs tonight.
God sees you.
Not the version of you that knows how to behave around Christians.
You.
The exhausted you.
The jealous you.
The wounded you.
The ashamed you.
The person who made the decision you desperately wish you could undo.
The person who has been mistreated.
The person who has also mistreated others.
The person still wondering how life became this complicated.
God sees you.
But being seen by God does not mean being told that everything we have done is acceptable.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace tells the truth.
Hagar's contempt mattered.
Sarai's harsh treatment mattered.
Abram's choices mattered.
Our sin matters too.
And this is exactly why the Gospel is so beautiful.
Because Jesus did not come merely to reassure reasonably good people that they were already fine.
He came to save sinners.
He came for people whose stories contain chapters they would rather tear out.
People who have manipulated.
People who have envied.
People who have lusted.
People who have lied.
People who have hated.
People who have compromised.
People who have been cruel.
People who have tried to control what only God could accomplish.
People who have run into wildernesses of their own making.
People like us.
The scandal of Christianity is not that Christians are morally impressive enough to deserve God.
The scandal is grace.
Jesus Christ entered our broken human story, lived the righteousness we could never produce, carried sin to the cross, died, and rose again.
At Calvary, God did not minimize sin.
He demonstrated how serious it is.
And He demonstrated how immeasurable His mercy is.
The cross tells us simultaneously:
Your sin is worse than your excuses admit...
and the grace of Christ is greater than your shame believes.
That changes how we read Genesis 16.
Because the ultimate answer to human brokenness is not learning to become slightly better versions of Sarai, Abram, or Hagar.
We need redemption.
We need hearts transformed by God.
We need Jesus.
Maybe you are Sarai today.
You have waited so long that another person's blessing has started feeling like God's rejection of you.
Repent of envy.
But do not run from God in shame.
Bring the wound underneath the envy to Him.
Maybe you are Hagar.
Something changed when life began going well, and without realizing it, you started looking down upon someone who had what you once wanted.
Repent of pride.
Success does not make another human being smaller.
Maybe you are Abram.
You hate conflict so much that you keep surrendering responsibility just to make the immediate tension disappear.
God is calling you into truth, courage and responsibility.
Or maybe you are simply in the wilderness.
Tired.
Confused.
Wounded.
Wondering whether anybody sees you.
He does.
And there is something even more beautiful for those who belong to Jesus Christ.
The God who sees you is not merely observing you from a distance.
In Christ, He came near.
Jesus touched lepers.
Jesus welcomed sinners who came to Him.
Jesus noticed people crowds overlooked.
Jesus received the repentant.
Jesus carried our sin.
Jesus walked willingly toward a cross.
And the risen Christ still calls sinners out of hiding.
Not toward religious performance.
Toward Himself.
Maybe this article found you while you are carrying something nobody knows about.
Do not hide behind Christian vocabulary.
Talk to God.
Confess the sin.
Name the wound.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Get help where help is needed.
Stop trying to manufacture outcomes God never asked you to manufacture.
Stop measuring God's love by somebody else's timeline.
And stop assuming your wilderness means God has lost your address.
Hagar ran into a desert and discovered that heaven knew exactly where she was.
What if the place you thought proved you had been forgotten becomes the place where you finally understand that God sees you?
That does not mean every painful situation will resolve exactly as you want.
Biblical faith never promises that.
It means something far greater.
Your hope is not ultimately an outcome.
Your hope is Christ.
Be honest before God.
And if you are willing, be honest with this community too.
Or tell us what God showed you through Hagar's story. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
And before you leave, think of one person.
Not twenty.
One.
The woman silently struggling with infertility.
The friend carrying jealousy and ashamed to admit it.
The believer who made a terrible decision and thinks God no longer wants them.
The person wounded by church people.
The exhausted mother.
The husband who has become passive.
The believer who has been waiting so long that God's promise feels painfully distant.
It does not.
It cannot.
And not because anyone should be pressured into giving.
Scripture says giving should come from what a person has decided in the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
But voluntary financial support can become one practical expression of generosity toward Gospel work.
It is mission.
It is helping put Scripture in front of the person scrolling at 2:00 in the morning who is thinking about giving up.
It is helping reach the believer drifting away.
The marriage under pressure.
The person hiding an addiction.
The skeptic quietly asking whether Jesus could possibly want someone like them.
The Christian who has forgotten how astonishing grace really is.
Pray.
Invite people to follow.
Carry the Gospel farther than this page could ever carry it alone.
Use them. Share them. Put biblical truth into the hands of someone who needs it.
Because there are Hagars everywhere.
People running.
People hurting.
People carrying consequences.
People carrying wounds somebody else gave them.
People who have sinned.
People who have been sinned against.
People hiding behind smiles.
And they need more than inspirational Christianity.
They need the Gospel.
They need to know that repentance is still possible.
Forgiveness is still available in Christ.
Grace is still greater than shame.
Jesus still receives sinners who come to Him.
And God still sees people in the wilderness.
Maybe that is why this story has survived thousands of years.
Not so we could stand safely outside it and decide which character was worst.
But so Scripture could hold up a mirror.
There is something of Sarai's impatience in us.
Something of Hagar's pride in us.
Something of Abram's weakness in us.
And something in all of us desperately needing mercy.
Then Jesus enters the story.
Not to congratulate our dysfunction.
To redeem us from sin.
Not to baptize our bitterness.
To transform us.
Not to tell us that hiding is acceptable.
To call us into the light.
Not merely to make our circumstances comfortable.
To make us His.
So when your promise seems delayed...
when somebody else's blessing touches your deepest wound...
when relationships fracture...
when your own decisions create consequences...
when shame tells you to run...
remember the pregnant woman beside the spring.
Remember the wilderness.
Remember El Roi.
Remember the cross.
And remember this:

You may have run into the wilderness carrying a story you wish you could erase—but Jesus is still writing, and grace can make the chapter you were most ashamed of become the place where you finally discovered the God who sees you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EZEKIEL PUT THIS SEXUAL ACT ON JERUSALEM’S LIST OF COVENANT VIOLATIONS—AND ALMOST NOBODY TALKS ABOUT IT
paragraphs: EZEKIEL PUT THIS SEXUAL ACT ON JERUSALEM’S LIST OF COVENANT VIOLATIONS—AND ALMOST NOBODY TALKS ABOUT IT

Ezekiel 18:6 and 22:10 mention sexual relations during menstruation in passages about covenant faithfulness and Jerusalem’s corruption. But before turning an uncomfortable Bible passage into either a weapon or an embarrassment, we need to hear what God was actually saying—and then follow the story all the way to Jesus Christ.
There are Bible verses we underline.
There are Bible verses we quote when life hurts.
There are verses we put on coffee mugs, phone wallpapers, T-shirts, and church walls.
And then there are verses we quietly walk past.
Ezekiel 18:6 is one of them.
You can read Ezekiel for years, remember the valley of dry bones, remember the watchman, remember the strange visions, remember the promise of a new heart...
...and somehow never remember this sentence.
In describing a righteous man, Ezekiel says:
וְאֶל אִשָּׁה נִדָּה לֹא יִקְרָב
ve’el ishshah niddah lo yiqrav.
Literally, in straightforward terms:
“And he does not approach a menstruating woman.”
The context makes the sexual meaning clear.

Ezekiel is describing a man who practices righteousness. He does not participate in idolatrous worship. He does not defile his neighbor’s wife. He does not approach a woman during her menstrual impurity. He does not oppress people. He restores what he has taken in pledge. He does not rob. He feeds the hungry. He clothes the naked. He refuses unjust gain. He practices justice. He walks faithfully in God’s statutes.
Then comes the verdict:
“He is righteous; he shall surely live.”
That matters.
Because the menstruation statement is not floating alone in Scripture as some bizarre divine obsession with a woman’s biology.
It sits inside a much larger picture of covenant faithfulness.
Idolatry.
Adultery.
Sexual boundaries.
Oppression.
Robbery.
Exploitation.
Hunger.
Poverty.
Economic injustice.
Truth.
Faithfulness.
Ezekiel refuses to let people divide life into the “religious” things God cares about and the “private” things God supposedly ignores.
God cared about the altar.
God cared about the bedroom.
God cared about the hungry person outside your door.
God cared about what you did with money.
God cared about how you treated your neighbor.
God cared about what happened when nobody else was watching.
And that is where this uncomfortable verse suddenly becomes uncomfortable for reasons much deeper than menstruation.
Because Ezekiel is confronting one of humanity’s oldest spiritual lies:
“This part of my life belongs to me.”
My money belongs to me.
My sexuality belongs to me.
My anger belongs to me.
My private messages belong to me.
My fantasies belong to me.
My relationships belong to me.
My business practices belong to me.
My secret browser history belongs to me.
My body belongs to me.
My revenge belongs to me.
My hidden life belongs to me.
And God keeps walking into the rooms we labeled PRIVATE.
Not because He delights in humiliation.
Because He is Lord.
The wording in Ezekiel deliberately echoes the Torah.
Leviticus 18:19 reads:
וְאֶל־אִשָּׁה בְּנִדַּת טֻמְאָתָהּ לֹא תִקְרַב לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ
Ve’el ishshah beniddat tum’atah lo tiqrav legalot ervatah.
In sense:
You shall not approach a woman during her menstrual impurity to uncover her nakedness.
That final expression removes much of the ambiguity. “Uncovering nakedness” is sexual language in this context.
Leviticus 20:18 addresses the matter again, describing a man lying with a menstruating woman and attaching a covenant sanction to the violation.
So Ezekiel did not invent a new sexual ethic.
He was calling Israel back to a covenant command Israel already possessed.
But then Ezekiel says something even darker.
Jerusalem had become so corrupt that the prophet indicts the city in Ezekiel 22.
Bloodshed.
Idolatry.
Contempt for parents.
Oppression of foreigners.
Mistreatment of orphans and widows.
Profaning holy things.
Sabbath desecration.
Slander.
Sexual corruption.
Bribery.
Extortion.
Greed.
And forgetting God.
Then Ezekiel 22:10 says:
עֶרְוַת־אָב גִּלָּה־בָךְ טְמֵאַת הַנִּדָּה עִנּוּ־בָךְ
ʿervat-av gillah-vakh; teme’at hanniddah ʿinnu-vakh.
The first half concerns uncovering a father’s nakedness—an idiom connected with illicit sexual relations involving a father’s wife.
Then comes the chilling second accusation.
Women in menstrual impurity were עִנּוּ — ʿinnû.
The verb can carry the sense of humiliating, afflicting, humbling, or violating.
That is why responsible English translations differ in exactly how forcefully they render the verse.
And that distinction matters.
Ezekiel 18:6 describes the righteous man refusing the forbidden sexual approach.
Ezekiel 22:10 portrays Jerusalem’s corruption with darker language of humiliation or violation.
We should not make Scripture say less than it says.
But neither should we make it say more.
And we certainly should not turn these passages into permission to degrade women.
Menstruation itself is not presented as a moral sin committed by a woman.
A woman did not become morally wicked because her body menstruated.
The Torah contains an entire system of ritual purity and impurity, and ritual impurity must not automatically be equated with personal moral guilt.
That distinction is essential.
A corpse could render someone unclean.
Childbirth involved purification regulations.
Bodily discharges involved impurity regulations.
None of that means a dead body had sinned, childbirth was wicked, or normal biological processes made someone morally evil.
So if someone uses Ezekiel 18:6 to tell a woman that menstruation makes her disgusting to God...
they have missed the text.
And if someone uses this passage to humiliate women...
they have managed to weaponize a passage that actually places responsibility upon covenant obedience.
The Bible is not ashamed of the human body.
God created the human body.
The scandal in Ezekiel is not that women menstruate.
The scandal is that God's covenant people repeatedly treated His boundaries as though they were suggestions.
And suddenly this ancient text is standing much closer to us than we expected.
Because maybe your specific hidden compromise is not the one Ezekiel names.
Maybe yours has another name.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Emotional infidelity.
Secret conversations.
Greed.
Bitterness.
Dishonest business.
Cruelty inside the home.
Religious performance.
Gossip disguised as concern.
Pride disguised as discernment.
Lust disguised as loneliness.
Control disguised as leadership.
Unforgiveness disguised as wisdom.
Self-righteousness disguised as holiness.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody at church thinks you are strong.
Maybe you know exactly when to lift your hands during worship.
Maybe you know Christian vocabulary so well that you can describe surrender without actually surrendering.
Maybe you post Scripture publicly while negotiating with sin privately.
And maybe that is why Ezekiel feels invasive.
Because God is not merely asking whether Jerusalem still had religion.
Jerusalem had religious history.
Jerusalem had sacred vocabulary.
Jerusalem had priests.
Jerusalem had prophets.
Jerusalem had a temple.
What Jerusalem increasingly lacked was covenant faithfulness.
And eventually God says something devastating in Ezekiel 22:12:
“You have forgotten Me.”
There it is.
Underneath the greed.
Underneath the exploitation.
Underneath the sexual corruption.
Underneath the violence.
Underneath the religious hypocrisy.
God identifies the deeper catastrophe:
You forgot Me.
That is what sin eventually does.
It does not always begin with someone screaming, “I hate God.”
Sometimes it begins much more quietly.
You stop praying.
You stop trembling at His Word.
You stop confessing quickly.
You start explaining away what once convicted you.
You become more concerned with being exposed than being holy.
You learn how to live with what once made you weep.
You still say “Jesus.”
You just stop letting Jesus enter certain rooms.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You love Christ.
At least you desperately want to.
But there is something you have been hiding.
Something happened.
Something you did.
Something someone did to you.
Something sexual.
Something shameful.
Something complicated.
Something you cannot imagine telling another believer because you are terrified they will never look at you the same way again.
So you carry it.
Sunday after Sunday.
Month after month.
Smile after smile.
And eventually shame starts preaching its own gospel to you.
“You are filthy.”
“You are disqualified.”
“God might forgive other people, but not this.”
“If people knew the real story, they would leave.”
“You crossed the line.”
“You ruined everything.”
But shame is a terrible theologian.
Because Ezekiel does not end with Jerusalem’s scandal.
Keep reading.
The same prophetic book that exposes defilement also announces astonishing restoration.
God promises cleansing.
God promises a new heart.
God promises a new spirit.
God promises that the heart of stone will be removed.
And centuries later, Jesus Christ comes.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not rewriting evil into goodness.
Not calling darkness light.
He comes bearing something infinitely more costly.
A cross.
This is where Christianity becomes unlike cheap spirituality.
God does not save us by announcing that sin was never serious.
God saves sinners at enormous cost.
At Calvary, Jesus bears judgment.
The innocent One suffers for the guilty.
The Holy One gives Himself for sinners.
The One without scandal steps into ours.
And the Gospel says something shame never expected:
your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Repentance is not God asking you to pretend the wound never happened.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the God who can actually cleanse sinners.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace breaks chains.
Grace does not say, “Sin does not matter.”
Grace says, “Sin mattered enough for Christ to bleed—and you matter enough that He calls you out of it.”
That is why Jesus can look at people carrying histories that would make religious crowds whisper...
and offer cleansing.
Forgiveness.
Restoration.
A new identity.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Because repentance finally has somewhere to run.
To Him.
Maybe that is what you need tonight.
Not another argument.
Not another excuse.
Not another promise that you will fix yourself next week.
Jesus.
You may need to close the door.
Put the phone down.
Stop performing.
And tell Him the truth.
“Jesus, this is what I did.”
“Jesus, this is what I became.”
“Jesus, this is what I keep returning to.”
“Jesus, this is what happened to me.”
“Jesus, I cannot carry this anymore.”
There is no benefit in hiding from the One who already knows.
And there is breathtaking hope in discovering that the One who already knows is the One whose hands were pierced for sinners.
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to publish the details of your private sin for strangers.
But you can make a simple declaration of surrender.
Not as a ritual.
Not because typing words saves anybody.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes a small public confession that we need Christ becomes the moment we stop protecting the mask.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover they are not the only believer fighting for holiness.
And please hear this carefully.
If you were sexually violated, coerced, abused, or assaulted, the sin committed against you is not transformed into your guilt simply because your body was involved.
Do not let somebody misuse Ezekiel 22:10 to place an offender’s guilt upon the wounded.
God sees oppression.
God sees violation.
God sees what happened behind closed doors.
The Lord who condemns exploitation is not confused about the difference between committing evil and suffering evil at someone else's hands.
Bring the wound to Christ.
Seek wise, trustworthy help.
Healing may take time.
But what happened to you does not place you beyond the reach of Jesus.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody needed to survive tonight.
And maybe someone you know needs this entire message.
Your share may put it in front of them.
We do not need to hide difficult Scripture.
We need to read it carefully, faithfully, humbly, and ultimately through the redemptive story that leads us to Christ.
Because temptation has a way of making yesterday's convictions feel distant.
Shame has a way of making grace feel impossible.
And there may come a night when you need to read again that God exposes darkness not because darkness is stronger than Him...
but because He calls people into the light.
There is enough shallow Christianity online.
We want to keep opening the Bible.
Even the uncomfortable pages.
Especially the uncomfortable pages.
And for believers who want to help Gospel Warrior continue and expand this work, there is another practical way to stand with the mission.
But I want to say this without manipulating your conscience:

Scripture explicitly teaches that Christian giving should not be extracted through compulsion. Paul says giving should come from what a person has purposed in the heart, because God loves a cheerful giver.
It cannot.
Christ cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
It helps us keep writing.
Keep researching.
Keep teaching.
Keep confronting deception.
Keep encouraging exhausted believers.
Keep reaching people scrolling alone at midnight who may never walk through a church door but will stop when a sentence suddenly sounds like God is calling them home.
And if you cannot financially support Gospel Warrior, please do not disappear.
Read.
Pray.
Share.
Save the articles.
Invite people to follow.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
A sincere share can travel farther than money sometimes can.
Because this was never supposed to be about building an audience that admires Gospel Warrior.
It is about pointing an audience toward Jesus Christ.
Back to the difficult verse.
Ezekiel named what Jerusalem wanted to normalize.
He exposed what people wanted left in darkness.
But Scripture does not expose sin merely so sinners can stand naked beneath accusation forever.
The biblical story keeps moving.
Toward cleansing.
Toward a new heart.
Toward a new spirit.
Toward Bethlehem.
Toward Golgotha.
Toward an empty tomb.
Toward Jesus.
Maybe you came into this article because the title shocked you.
Maybe you stayed because you wanted to know what Ezekiel actually meant.
But perhaps somewhere along the way the question changed.
It stopped being:
“Why does the Bible mention sex during menstruation?”
And became:
“What part of my life have I been telling Jesus He cannot touch?”
That is the question worth carrying into prayer.
Because the God who sees Jerusalem's corruption also sees ours.
The God who named Israel's hidden violations knows every hidden thing in us.
Yet the Gospel announces that judgment does not have to be the final word for the sinner who turns to Christ.
There is repentance.
There is mercy.
There is cleansing.
There is forgiveness.
There is restoration.
There is a Savior.
His name is Jesus.
So come out of hiding.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the wound.
Bring Him the memory.
Bring Him the relationship.
Bring Him the bedroom.
Bring Him the money.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the thing you were praying nobody would ever discover.
He already knows.
And still He calls sinners to come.
“No more hiding.”
Because maybe the most terrifying thing about Ezekiel is that God sees what we hide.
But maybe the most beautiful thing about the Gospel is exactly the same:
Jesus saw the chapter you were desperately trying to hide—and He still walked toward the cross to make redemption possible.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN SEXUAL DESIRE ACTUALLY HONOR GOD? PROVERBS 5 GIVES MARRIED DESIRE A SURPRISING PLACE
paragraphs: CAN SEXUAL DESIRE ACTUALLY HONOR GOD? PROVERBS 5 GIVES MARRIED DESIRE A SURPRISING PLACE

What if the desire some Christians learned to feel ashamed of is something Scripture itself celebrates—when it is surrendered to God, protected by covenant, and directed toward the husband or wife He has given you?
There are Bible verses people quote in church.
And then there are Bible verses people quietly hope the pastor never explains while their children are sitting beside them.
Proverbs 5:18–19 belongs to the second category.
Read it slowly.
Not through the embarrassment of modern church culture. Not through pornography. Not through Hollywood. Not through the wounds of your past.
Read it as Scripture.

“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth. Let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is Proverbs 5:18–19 in the King James Version.
Yes.
That is in the Bible.
And perhaps the surprising thing is not that Scripture speaks so openly about married desire.
Perhaps the surprising thing is how many Christians have unknowingly allowed the world to define sexuality more loudly than the God who created it.
The Hebrew is even more striking.
Proverbs 5:18 says:
יְהִֽי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yehi meqorkha barukh, usmach me'eshet ne'urekha.
“May your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
Then comes verse 19:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Be'ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The thought is powerful: be continually captivated, exhilarated, even intoxicated by her love.
This is not language imported into Scripture by a sexually obsessed culture.
It is sitting there in the Hebrew text of Proverbs.
And suddenly an uncomfortable question becomes unavoidable.
Can sexual desire actually honor God?
Yes—but Scripture's answer is far more beautiful, and far more demanding, than simply saying desire is good.
Because Proverbs 5 is not permission to worship desire.
It is a command to give desire a holy home.
Look at the chapter.

Before Solomon speaks about delighting in one's wife, he warns his son about sexual temptation. What initially tastes like honey eventually becomes bitter. He describes the devastating consequences of adultery and then tells his son to stay far from the door that leads toward it.
Then the imagery changes.
“Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well.”
Then:
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then:
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
And immediately afterward comes the contrast:
“And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?”
The structure matters.
The Bible is not saying, “Desire doesn't matter.”
It is essentially saying:
Your desire matters so much that you must guard where you take it.
Your sexuality matters so much that it must not be scattered among strangers.
Your spouse matters so much that faithfulness should be more than merely refusing adultery.
There should also be delight.

The contrast in Proverbs 5:15–21 is unmistakable: one's own cistern, one's own well, one's own covenant relationship—rather than the forbidden embrace outside it. Multiple English translations preserve the unusually strong language of satisfaction, delight, captivation, exhilaration, or intoxication within that marital context.
That changes something.
Because some people grew up believing holiness meant becoming almost embarrassed by the fact that they possessed sexual desire at all.
So they entered marriage carrying shame into a place God intended for covenant intimacy.
Others went in the opposite direction.
They were taught by pornography, casual relationships, fantasies, affairs, entertainment, social media, and a culture of endless comparison that desire should never be denied anything.
One message says:
“Your desire is dirty.”
The other says:
“Your desire is your master.”
Scripture bows to neither.
God says your desire needs redemption.
That distinction is enormous.
Sexual desire was never meant to sit on the throne.
Jesus belongs there.
But when Christ is Lord, human desires can be reordered beneath His authority.
And within biblical marriage, sexual intimacy does not have to be treated as an embarrassing concession to human weakness.
It can become part of covenant delight.
Part of tenderness.
Part of exclusivity.
Part of knowing and being known.
Part of two people repeatedly saying with their bodies what their vows already declared with their mouths:
I choose you.
Still you.
Only you.
This is why Proverbs 5 is simultaneously sensual and severe.
The same chapter that celebrates a husband's delight in his wife warns that sin eventually becomes a rope.
“His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins.”
Proverbs 5:22.
That is frighteningly accurate to the nature of habitual sexual sin.
At first, you hold it.
Eventually, it holds you.
At first, you visit the fantasy.
Eventually, the fantasy follows you home.
At first, it is only a message.
Only a look.
Only a private search.
Only a conversation your spouse doesn't know about.
Only one more video.
Only one more secret.
Only one more compromise.
Until one day you realize the thing you insisted you controlled has begun controlling you.
Scripture describes sin as cords.
And cords are rarely frightening when they are still individual threads.
That may be where someone reading this needs to stop pretending.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your family doesn't know.
Your church doesn't know.
Your friends would never suspect it.
Your browser history tells one story.
Your public Christianity tells another.
You know exactly when to close the screen.
You know exactly what to delete.
You know exactly how to smile afterward.
But Proverbs 5:21 quietly walks into the room:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.”
God sees.
Not merely the scandal if it becomes public.
He sees the road toward it.
And that sentence can feel terrifying until you remember who the Gospel reveals God to be.
The God who sees is also the God who calls sinners home.
This is where Christianity is radically different from merely telling sexually broken people to behave better.
The Gospel does not begin with pretending your history never happened.
It begins with Jesus Christ entering the story you cannot rewrite yourself.
Maybe your story includes pornography.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe years of lust.
Maybe emotional infidelity.
Maybe promiscuity.
Maybe secret messages.
Maybe fantasies you have fed for so long that you no longer remember what freedom felt like.

Maybe you are married and the passion that once seemed effortless has been buried underneath children, exhaustion, arguments, disappointment, aging, rejection, resentment, illness, schedules, bills, and years of things neither of you ever properly said.
Maybe the problem isn't forbidden desire.
Maybe you barely desire each other anymore.

And perhaps reading Proverbs 5 hurts because “rejoice with the wife of thy youth” sounds beautiful until you remember that you and your spouse hardly recognize the people you were when you first made those vows.
Listen carefully.
Proverbs 5 is wisdom, not a weapon.

It should never be used to pressure a spouse into sexual activity, excuse selfishness, ignore consent, minimize pain, or demand intimacy while refusing tenderness, faithfulness, patience, repentance, and love.
Biblical marital intimacy is not permission to use another person's body.
Covenant love is not consumption.
Your husband is not a machine built to satisfy you.
Your wife is not an object God handed you.
They bear God's image.
And Christian marriage ultimately belongs underneath the lordship of Jesus Christ.
This is why the deepest question is not merely:
“What am I allowed to desire?”
It is:
“Does Jesus rule what I desire?”
Because Christ does not merely want access to the religious section of your life.
He wants the locked rooms too.
The browser.
The fantasy.
The resentment.
The marriage bed.
The loneliness.
The memories.
The wounds.
The hunger for validation.
The secret attraction.
The private messages.
The part of you that desperately wants to be wanted.
The part of you that is ashamed of wanting anything at all.
All of it.
And this is where grace becomes almost scandalous.
Jesus does not wait for sexually broken people to become spotless before calling them toward Himself.
He calls sinners to repent.
Repentance does not mean pretending the sin was harmless.
It means agreeing with God about it and turning toward Him.
Grace does not rename bondage as freedom.
Grace breaks the chains and teaches the captive how to walk again.
Forgiveness is not God saying your sin did not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more than we wanted to admit.
Forgiveness is God saying Christ's blood is sufficient for repentant sinners who come to Him.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe somebody betrayed you.
Maybe your sexuality has been tangled with shame for decades.
Maybe you learned desire from pornography before anyone taught you covenant.
Maybe nobody ever told you that God designed sexual faithfulness not merely as a list of prohibitions but as protection for something precious.
You cannot travel backward.
You cannot become the person who never clicked it.
Never watched it.
Never sent it.
Never touched.
Never cheated.
Never lied.
Never crossed the boundary.
Never shattered the trust.
But Jesus Christ is not limited to editing your past.
He redeems people.
And redeemed people can begin walking differently today.
That may mean confession.
That may mean ending the secret relationship.
That may mean deleting the hidden account.
That may mean getting serious pastoral counsel and professional help for entrenched patterns.
That may mean rebuilding trust slowly instead of demanding immediate forgiveness from the person you wounded.
That may mean learning to pursue your spouse again without entitlement.
That may mean having an awkward conversation tonight instead of living another silent year.
That may mean telling Jesus the truth you have been disguising with religious language.
And for some reading this, the first honest prayer may contain only four words:
Jesus, have mercy on me.
That is enough honesty to begin.
And if Christ has already rescued you from sexual sin or restored something you thought was permanently destroyed, perhaps your comment needs to become somebody else's reason not to give up:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading underneath you may desperately need that testimony.
Because the world already knows how to make sex scandalous.
Jesus knows how to take scandal and lead sinners toward grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that celebrates adultery.
Not grace that baptizes lust.
Not grace that tells us holiness no longer matters.
Transforming grace.
Grace that teaches wandering eyes to come home.
Grace that teaches wounded spouses how to pursue healing wisely.
Grace that teaches desire that it has a Master.
Grace that takes what sin distorted and brings it back beneath the authority of Christ.
And perhaps that is the great surprise hiding inside Proverbs 5.
God is not anti-desire.
He is against the destruction caused when desire rebels against its Creator.

Within the covenant of marriage, Scripture can speak positively and remarkably openly about delight between husband and wife. Outside covenant faithfulness, that same chapter warns of consequences, captivity, and ruin.
God's answer to destructive desire is therefore not merely suppression.
It is sanctification.
Desire surrendered.
Desire disciplined.
Desire faithful.
Desire that refuses to turn another human being into an object.
Desire that learns the difference between consuming someone and loving someone.
Desire that can look at a spouse after years of ordinary mornings, arguments, wrinkles, responsibilities, disappointments, forgiveness, laughter, children, grief, and survival and still whisper:
I choose you.
There is something profoundly holy about that.
Not because sexual desire itself saves anybody.
It doesn't.
Jesus saves.
Not because marriage makes anyone righteous.
It doesn't.
Christ's righteousness is our hope.

But because when every part of human life is brought beneath the lordship of Jesus, even desires that sin has grotesquely distorted can be reordered toward faithfulness, gratitude, tenderness, and covenant love.
So husbands and wives...
Do not let pornography teach you how to see the person you promised to love.
Do not let algorithms convince you that someone else's body is more deserving of your attention than the person whose heart you vowed to protect.
Do not let familiarity become contempt.
Do not let resentment quietly murder tenderness.
Do not outsource to strangers what belongs inside your covenant.
Talk.
Repent.
Forgive wisely.
Seek help when needed.
Flirt again.
Laugh again.
Pray together.
Hold hands when nobody is watching.
Pursue one another without coercion.
Protect the covenant before you have to rescue it from catastrophe.
And remember that the God who commands faithfulness is also the God who created delight.
There may come a night when temptation is louder than wisdom, and you will need to remember that God is not merely calling you away from something destructive.
He is calling you toward something holy.
Send this privately to the believer who thinks one sexual failure has disqualified them forever.
It cannot.
It does not.
And not because Christians should ever be manipulated into giving.
Paul's language in 2 Corinthians 9:7 is explicit:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Give as one has purposed in the heart—not “under compulsion.”
“For God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Christian generosity is meant to rise from a willing heart, not spiritual pressure.
A share can still carry Scripture into a home we could never enter.
A comment can tell a struggling believer they are not fighting alone.
A tag can place truth in front of someone at precisely the moment they need it.
A saved article can become tomorrow night's reminder when temptation returns.
And a life surrendered to Jesus can become something infinitely greater than engagement statistics could ever measure.
So before you leave this article, ask yourself one question that no algorithm can answer for you:
What part of my desire have I still refused to surrender to Jesus?
Do not answer quickly.
Let it become prayer.
Because perhaps the real scandal was never that the Bible speaks openly about desire.
Perhaps the scandal is that Christ knows everything we have desired wrongly...
everything we have hidden...
every boundary we crossed...
every person we wounded...
every promise we broke...
and still calls sinners out of darkness, toward repentance, into grace, and onward into transformation.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It does not have authority to become your savior.
Your desires may speak loudly.
They do not get to become your lord.
Your sin may have written pages you would give anything to erase.
But the pen is not ultimately in sin's hand.
Bring Jesus the chapter you are most ashamed to let anyone read—because grace is still writing where you thought the story had already ended.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JEREMIAH CALLED UNFAITHFUL MEN “WELL-FED STALLIONS”—AND WHAT GOD SAW BEHIND THEIR CLOSED DOORS SHOULD TERRIFY US
paragraphs: JEREMIAH CALLED UNFAITHFUL MEN “WELL-FED STALLIONS”—AND WHAT GOD SAW BEHIND THEIR CLOSED DOORS SHOULD TERRIFY US

They had been fed by God, blessed by God, and satisfied by God—yet they were still craving what belonged to someone else. Jeremiah 5:7–8 is not merely an ancient warning about adultery. It is a mirror held in front of the human heart…and the reflection may be closer to us than we want to admit.
There are Bible verses people underline because they comfort them.
There are verses they frame on walls because they inspire them.
And then there are verses like this.
Verses that do not knock politely.
They kick the door open.
They walk into the secret room.
They turn on the light.
And suddenly, the God who sees everything is speaking about what people thought nobody knew.
Jeremiah wrote:
סוּסִים מְיֻזָּנִים מַשְׁכִּים הָיוּ אִישׁ אֶל־אֵשֶׁת רֵעֵהוּ יִצְהָלוּ
Susim meyuzzanim mashkim hayu; ish el-eshet re‘ehu yitzhalu.
The imagery is deliberately humiliating and shocking.
“They were well-fed, lusty stallions, each neighing at another’s wife.” — Jeremiah 5:8

That is essentially what the Hebrew picture communicates, although one of the descriptive Hebrew terms in the verse has some lexical uncertainty, which is why English translations vary slightly in how they render the horses.
But Jeremiah’s central image is unmistakable.
God compares these unfaithful men to horses driven by appetite.
Not husbands protecting covenant.
Not men governing desire.
Not worshipers whose bodies belonged to God.
Stallions.
Fed.
Restless.
Neighing.
Looking over the fence.
Wanting what belonged to somebody else.
And before anyone turns this into an excuse to point at adulterers, pornography addicts, unfaithful spouses, or “those people” in society, there is something uncomfortable we need to understand.
Jeremiah is exposing something much deeper than sexual appetite.
He is exposing the insanity of a heart that has been fed by God and still believes sin has something better to offer.
Read the verse immediately before it.
God says, in essence, that His people abandoned Him, pursued false gods, and then, after He had fed them to fullness, committed adultery.
That sequence matters.
God provided.
They wandered.
God filled.
They lusted.
God remained faithful.
They became unfaithful.
The scandal was not simply that people desired something forbidden.
The scandal was that people who had received so much from God behaved as though God were not enough.
And suddenly Jeremiah 5 does not feel so ancient anymore.
Because you can have food in your refrigerator and still hunger for somebody else's life.
You can have a spouse who loves you and still entertain somebody else's attention.
You can have children calling you Mom or Dad while secretly feeding fantasies that could devastate their home.
You can sing worship songs on Sunday and erase browser history on Monday.
You can know Scripture and still keep a conversation on your phone that you would panic to see projected onto the church wall.
You can say, “God has been good to me,” while secretly negotiating with the very sin that could destroy what His goodness gave you.
You can be full…
and still live hungry.
That is the horror Jeremiah exposes.
The problem was never merely that the horses were hungry.
They were well-fed.
Think about that.
Sometimes our greatest spiritual danger does not arrive when life gives us nothing.
Sometimes it arrives after God has given us much.
Comfort can make us careless.
Blessing can become ordinary.
The spouse you once prayed for becomes familiar.
The home you once dreamed about becomes background scenery.
The ministry opportunity you once begged God for becomes something you take for granted.
The salvation that once brought you to tears becomes vocabulary.
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, gratitude becomes entitlement.
Then the fence starts looking interesting.
Someone else's marriage.
Someone else's body.
Someone else's success.
Someone else's possessions.
Someone else's attention.
Someone else's life.
The heart whispers:
Maybe over there.
Maybe happiness is over there.
Maybe excitement is over there.
Maybe fulfillment is over there.
Maybe if I could just have that person…
that experience…
that secret…
that little forbidden thing…
I would finally feel alive again.
And God says:
Look at what sin has reduced you to.
A creature controlled by appetite.
Jeremiah's language is severe because sin is severe.
Adultery is not romantic rebellion.
It breaks covenants.
It devastates spouses.
It confuses children.
It fractures trust.
It can leave wounds people carry for decades.
And Jesus did not soften the moral seriousness of adultery.
He drove the issue deeper.
He moved from the hotel room to the heart.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” — Matthew 5:27–28
Jesus knew something we desperately try to forget.
The body usually arrives somewhere the heart has already visited.
Long before certain betrayals become physical, something has been rehearsing them internally.
A glance that became a second glance.
A fantasy that was invited back.
A message that should have ended.
A conversation hidden from a spouse.
A friendship that stopped being innocent.
A screen used in darkness.
A secret account.
An emotional attachment defended with the words, “Nothing happened.”
Maybe nothing happened physically.
Yet.
But Jesus cares about what is being cultivated in the heart.
And perhaps that is where somebody reading this needs to stop pretending.
Not tomorrow.
Here.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe your children believe everything is fine.
Maybe the people sitting beside you at church would never imagine what you fight when nobody is looking.
But God knows.
