“I'm disgusting.”
“God must be tired of me.”
Listen carefully.
Your sin should never be trivialized.
But neither should the cross.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that your worst night could become your permanent name.
Repentance means sin is taken seriously precisely because grace is real.
Bring the browser history.
Bring the fantasy.
Bring the relapse.
Bring the loneliness.
Bring the compulsive behavior.
Bring the shame you've been carrying since adolescence.
Bring the secret nobody at church knows.
Bring all of it into the light of Christ.
And if the pattern has become compulsive, don't fight completely alone.
Find a mature, trustworthy Christian.
A pastor.
A mentor.
An accountability partner.
If necessary, a qualified counselor.
Remove easy access to pornography.
Change routines.
Stop negotiating with triggers you already recognize.
Put distance between yourself and whatever repeatedly pulls you toward sin.

Jesus' language immediately after His teaching about lust is intentionally severe: if your eye causes you to stumble, remove the source of stumbling. His point is not casual self-harm; it is radical seriousness toward sin.
Sometimes we pray:
“Jesus, deliver me.”
And Jesus begins showing us doors we need to close.
Apps we need to delete.
Accounts we need to unfollow.
Conversations we need to have.
Secrets we need to confess.
Patterns we need to interrupt.
Hours of the night we need to stop spending alone with a phone.
Freedom can become painfully practical.
But do not confuse fighting with earning salvation.
You do not defeat sin so Jesus will finally love you.
You fight sin because in Christ you are being called out of slavery and into holiness.
The cross is not permission to make peace with bondage.
The cross is where bondage loses its claim to be your master.
So can the Bible answer questions about masturbation when it never directly names the act?
Yes—but we must state carefully how.
Not by pretending there is a verse explicitly naming masturbation.
There isn't.
Not by forcing Genesis 38 to say something it does not say.
But by allowing the whole counsel of Scripture to examine the desires, fantasies, habits, mastery, motives, conscience, and fruit surrounding the behavior.

Where masturbation is joined to pornography, deliberate lust, sexually immoral fantasy, objectification, or an appetite that has become master rather than servant, Scripture gives substantial reason for the Christian to reject what is happening.

Where those factors are claimed to be absent, Christians have disagreed about the moral status of the physical act considered entirely by itself. Scripture's silence about the specific act means we should be cautious about claiming more explicit biblical certainty than the text itself gives.
But biblical silence about a particular word does not mean biblical silence about your heart.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody needed tonight.
Because God is interested in something bigger than whether you can locate a loophole.
He wants you.
Not merely your church attendance.
Not merely your Christian Facebook posts.
Not merely your worship playlist.
You.
Your body.
Your thoughts.
Your desires.
Your wounds.
Your sexuality.
Your secret life.
Your midnight life.
The version of you nobody else sees.
Jesus wants Lordship there too.
And if this article exposed something you've been hiding, you don't need to perform for us.
But you can stop pretending.
Maybe your comment becomes the moment another Christian realizes:
I'm not the only one.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this—someone struggling quietly, someone drowning in pornography, someone convinced God wants nothing more to do with them—send this article to them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose them.
Send it because sometimes love knocks on a locked door.
It doesn't.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces generosity to your local church or automatically constitutes the biblical tithe.
It doesn't.
We will never sell you grace.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
But voluntary Christian generosity can help Gospel-centered ministry continue.
Your support can help the message travel farther.
More articles.
More discipleship resources.
More biblical teaching.
More opportunities for a wounded person scrolling alone at midnight to encounter something that points them away from despair and toward Jesus Christ.
And sharing costs nothing.
Every time you share Gospel Warrior content publicly, you help carry the message beyond the people we could reach alone.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not merchandise.
Jesus.
We exist to point toward Him.

And if all this article accomplishes is making one person close the pornography, come out of hiding, confess the truth, seek help, repent, and discover again that the arms of Christ are still open to the repentant sinner...
then praise belongs to God.
Because your scandal does not get the final sentence.
Your secret does not get the final sentence.
Your relapse does not get the final sentence.
Your shame does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
So tonight, when the room becomes quiet again...
when nobody is watching...
when temptation begins negotiating...
remember:
You are not merely deciding what to do with your body.
You are deciding what kind of desire you will feed, what kind of person you are becoming, and whether even this hidden room of your life will be surrendered to the Lord who bought you with a price.
And if you fall?
Don't build a house in the dirt.
Come home.
Repent.
Get up.
Reach for Christ again.
Grace does not tell you that bondage doesn't matter.
Grace tells you bondage doesn't have to be the end of your story.
The secret you thought would make Jesus walk away may become the very place where you finally discover how desperately you need His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE TATTOOS SINFUL FOR CHRISTIANS TODAY?
paragraphs: ARE TATTOOS SINFUL FOR CHRISTIANS TODAY?
The Bible’s Answer May Expose a Much Deeper Question About Your Heart
Maybe the tattoo is already on your skin.
Maybe you're sitting in a tattoo shop scrolling through designs.
Maybe your son came home with one and you're furious.
Maybe your daughter wants a tiny cross on her wrist.
Maybe you've been a Christian for twenty years and somebody looked at the ink covering your arm, looked you straight in the eyes, and said:
“You know the Bible says that's a sin, right?”
And suddenly you weren't discussing ink anymore.
You were discussing whether God was disappointed in you.
That's where this gets personal.

Because somewhere between Leviticus, Christian tradition, personal conviction, modern culture, and our tendency to judge what we can see, a surprisingly complicated biblical question has sometimes been reduced to one sentence:
“Christians aren't supposed to have tattoos.”
But is that actually what Scripture teaches?
Before you answer, stay with me.
Because this article isn't ultimately about tattoos.
It's about something much closer to your heart.
And by the end, you may discover that the most dangerous mark a Christian can carry isn't necessarily the one everybody can see.
The verse almost everyone reaches for is Leviticus 19:28.
The Hebrew reads:
"וְשֶׂרֶט לָנֶפֶשׁ לֹא תִתְּנוּ בִּבְשַׂרְכֶם וּכְתֹבֶת קַעֲקַע לֹא תִתְּנוּ בָּכֶם"
Transliterated in part:
...u-khetovet qa‘aqa lo tittenu bakhem...
The traditional sense is:
You shall not make cuts in your flesh for the dead or put tattoo marks upon yourselves.

The unusual Hebrew expression כְּתֹבֶת קַעֲקַע — ketovet qa‘aqa refers to an inscribed or tattooed mark. Ancient Jewish interpretation likewise understood the prohibition as involving writing or marking impressed into the flesh.
So let's not dodge the uncomfortable part.
Yes.
There really is a biblical verse prohibiting tattoo-like markings.
We don't need to pretend it isn't there.
But responsible Bible reading asks another question:
What covenant is being addressed?
What is happening in the surrounding passage?
And how does a command given to ancient Israel relate to followers of Jesus under the New Covenant?
Leviticus 19 contains commands covering worship, holiness, agriculture, social justice, sexual morality, treatment of neighbors, pagan practices, and Israel's distinct life as God's covenant people.
And notice something easily overlooked in verse 28.
The tattoo prohibition appears alongside:
“cuttings in your flesh for the dead.”
That matters.

The surrounding material is concerned with Israel remaining distinct from practices associated with the nations around them, including practices connected with the dead and forbidden religious customs.
That doesn't make Leviticus irrelevant.
Far from it.
“All Scripture is breathed out by God” (2 Timothy 3:16).
But Christians do not faithfully interpret the Old Testament merely by finding a command and transferring it unchanged into the church.
If we did, consistency would require Christians to observe Israel's entire covenant legislation in precisely the same manner.
The New Testament itself forces us to think more carefully than that.
Jesus fulfilled the Law.
The apostles wrestled explicitly with which requirements were to be imposed upon Gentile believers.
And nowhere in the New Testament do Jesus or the apostles issue a universal command saying:
“You shall never receive a tattoo.”
That distinction is important.
But don't run to the tattoo shop yet.
Because “the New Testament doesn't explicitly prohibit this” is not the same thing as “therefore anything I want is automatically wise and pleasing to God.”
And this is where the question becomes uncomfortable for everybody.
The person with tattoos.
The person without tattoos.
The pastor.
The rebellious teenager.
The conservative grandmother.
The Christian influencer.
You.
Me.
Paul writes:
The Greek contains the striking words:
τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς... ἁγίου πνεύματος
to sōma hymōn naos... hagiou pneumatos
Your σῶμα — sōma, your body, is a ναός — naos, a sanctuary or temple, of the Holy Spirit.
And Paul continues:
“You are not your own.”
Then:
“You were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.”
That is the principle Christians cannot escape.
But even here we must respect context.
First Corinthians 6 is addressing sexual immorality. Paul did not write this passage as a tattoo regulation.
So using “your body is a temple” as though Paul were specifically saying “therefore tattoos are sinful” goes beyond what the passage itself says.
Yet the underlying truth absolutely matters.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Which means the Christian question isn't merely:
“Am I allowed to tattoo this body?”
It is:
“Jesus, what do You want me to do with the body You redeemed?”
That changes everything.
Christian freedom isn't:
“I can do whatever I want.”
Christian freedom is being liberated from slavery to sin so that your life can belong joyfully to Jesus.
Sometimes we desperately want Christianity to give us a giant list.
Allowed.
Forbidden.
Allowed.
Forbidden.
Because lists can be easier than surrender.
But discipleship often asks a more penetrating question:
Why do you want it?
That's where the ink reaches the heart.
Maybe you want a tattoo commemorating someone you loved.
Maybe it's artistic.
Maybe it's cultural.
Maybe you want Scripture permanently written somewhere you can see it.
Maybe you survived something horrific and the tattoo represents the fact that you're still here.
Maybe you're getting one because everybody around you has one.
Maybe you're trying to prove you're not like your Christian parents.
Maybe you're trying to look dangerous.
Maybe you're desperate for somebody to notice you.
Maybe you're putting something on your body that celebrates darkness, sexual immorality, violence, occult spirituality, hatred, idolatry, or something else clearly contrary to Christ.
Those are not morally identical situations.
The needle can look the same.
The heart beneath it can be completely different.
Scripture repeatedly moves believers beyond mere external appearance toward motives, conscience, love, holiness, witness, and God's glory.
Paul gives another principle:
“Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.”
Whatever you do.
That reaches considerably farther than tattoos.
Can I place this image on my body to the glory of God?
Can I choose it with a clear conscience?
Does it celebrate something Christ calls evil?
Am I acting from faith?
Am I being driven by rebellion?
Am I seeking attention because somewhere inside I desperately need people to tell me I'm valuable?
Could this unnecessarily damage my witness in the community or ministry where God has placed me?
Am I ignoring wise counsel because I have already decided what I want?
And perhaps the most revealing question:
If Jesus told me no, would I still want Jesus more than I want the tattoo?
There it is.
Because now we aren't really talking about ink anymore.
We're talking about lordship.
Romans 14 deals with disputed matters among believers, particularly food and days. It should not simply be turned into a “tattoo chapter.”
But its principles concerning conscience and faith are deeply relevant to decisions where Scripture does not provide the kind of direct New Testament prohibition some Christians wish it did.
Paul concludes:
“Whatever is not from faith is sin.”
The Greek centers upon πίστις — pistis, faith. In its actual context Paul is warning someone against acting while doubting whether the action is right before God.
So if your conscience is screaming,
“Don't do this,”
don't bulldoze your conscience simply because somebody on social media gave you permission.
Stop.
Pray.
Search Scripture.
Seek mature counsel.
Examine your motive.
You don't need to prove your freedom.
And sometimes maturity means having the freedom to do something and choosing not to do it because love, wisdom, witness, or conscience matters more.
But now we need to speak to another person.
The Christian looking at somebody covered in tattoos and quietly deciding:
“They can't really know Jesus.”
Be careful.
You may be committing a much older sin while condemning somebody else's skin.
Humans are remarkably good at measuring spirituality by visible things.
We see the tattoo.
God sees the heart.
We see sleeves of ink.
God sees pride.
We see piercings.
God sees unforgiveness.
We see somebody walk into church looking completely unlike us, and before they've reached their seat we've written a biography about their spiritual condition.
Meanwhile, somebody else walks in wearing a beautiful suit, carrying an expensive Bible, knowing every worship lyric...
and secretly hasn't spoken honestly to God in months.
One person's scars are visible.
Another person's idols wear church clothes.
Jesus reserved some of His strongest rebukes not for people whose brokenness was obvious, but for religious people who polished the outside while corruption remained within.
That should frighten every Christian who has learned how to look holy.
Because a clean arm does not equal a clean heart.
And tattooed skin does not put somebody beyond the blood of Jesus Christ.
Maybe that's exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
Perhaps you got tattoos before Christ.
Maybe some of them represent a life you don't live anymore.
Maybe there's an old symbol on your body connected to addiction, a relationship, a gang, an occult practice, hatred, rebellion, sexuality, or a version of yourself you wish you could bury forever.
And every time you look in the mirror, your past looks back.
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not intimidated by your history.
The Gospel does not say:
“Clean your skin and perhaps God will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that sinners are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ died for our sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
Repentance isn't pretending the past didn't happen.
Grace isn't calling evil good.
Grace is God meeting guilty people with forgiveness through Christ and transforming those who turn to Him.
Maybe the tattoo remains.
But the person wearing it doesn't have to remain the same.
That's Gospel.
Your body can carry evidence of yesterday while your life carries evidence of resurrection.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church contained people with deeply sinful histories.
Yet Paul could write of believers who had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace rewrites what the scandal gets to become.
A testimony.
A warning.
A scar.
A place where someone else sees that Jesus still saves people.

And perhaps that's why this question cannot end with a simplistic universal declaration that every modern tattoo is automatically sinful—or with the equally careless declaration that tattoos never matter spiritually.
Scripture demands something deeper.
If the tattoo itself contains or celebrates what God condemns, the issue is clear.
If your motivation is rebellion against God, the issue is deeper than the ink.
If you cannot proceed in faith and with a clear conscience, don't violate your conscience.
If your choice disregards love, wisdom, stewardship, or your Christian witness, those things deserve serious consideration.
If you're merely asking, “How close can I get to sin without technically sinning?” your question has already exposed something.

But if you're asking whether the Bible explicitly declares every modern tattoo on every Christian inherently sinful simply because pigment has been permanently placed beneath the skin, Scripture does not give us grounds to make that sweeping New Covenant declaration.
And if you already have tattoos?
Don't spend another night imagining that Jesus is standing outside the door of salvation inspecting your skin before deciding whether His blood is sufficient for you.
Come to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Bring Him the beautiful parts.
Bring Him the embarrassing parts.
Bring Him your addictions.
Bring Him your pride.
Bring Him the secret browser history.
Bring Him the religious hypocrisy.
Bring Him the anger nobody knows about.
Bring Him the tattoo you love.
Bring Him the tattoo you regret.
Bring Him the memory attached to it.
Bring Him everything.
Repentance means turning from sin toward God.
Faith means trusting Christ rather than yourself to save you.
Grace means you stop pretending you can erase your own record.
Jesus didn't go to the cross because humanity needed better cosmetics.
He went because humanity needed resurrection.
And maybe you've spent years hiding because Christians saw your appearance before they saw your humanity.
I'm sorry that happened.
But don't confuse Jesus with people who represented Him badly.
Look at Christ Himself.
The crucified Savior knows what it is to have His body wounded.
He knows rejection.
He knows public shame.
He knows what it means to be stared at.
And He willingly bore our sins so sinners could be reconciled to God.
The deepest mark defining the Christian isn't ink.
It is ownership.
“You were bought at a price.”
Christ's.
Redeemed.
Forgiven.
Being transformed.
So perhaps the better question tonight isn't:
“Can Christians get tattoos?”
Perhaps it's:
Does Jesus have all of me?
My body.
My image.
My sexuality.
My money.
My ambition.
My phone.
My relationships.
My hidden habits.
My wounds.
My reputation.
My past.
My future.
Everything.
Because you can have John 3:16 tattooed across your chest and still refuse to surrender your heart to Christ.
And you can have no tattoo anywhere on your body while pride quietly writes its name across your soul.
Jesus wants deeper than skin.
He wants you.
If this exposed something you've been hiding, don't turn the comments into another theological battlefield.
Turn them into testimony.
Someone reading silently may need to discover that there are other people whom grace found in places they thought God would never enter.

Share it not because every Christian must agree on every disputed matter, but because Christians desperately need to learn how to open the Bible, respect its context, examine their hearts, and keep Jesus Christ at the center.
You may need to read it again when this question stops being theoretical and becomes personal.
It doesn't.
Not because supporting this ministry saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
Scripture says Christian giving should come from the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

If you already give your tithes and offerings through your local church or elsewhere, supporting Gospel Warrior need not replace that stewardship. Consider this simply another opportunity for voluntary generosity toward Gospel work you believe is bearing fruit.
If you feel led to stand with us:
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help tremendously.
Send it privately to someone wrestling with this question.
Pray for the ministry.
Because sometimes the article you almost didn't share becomes the article somebody reads alone at 2:00 in the morning while wondering whether God could possibly still want them.
And perhaps that's the sentence they need tonight:
The marks of your past may remain on your skin, but they do not get the final word over your soul—Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE THERE SEXUAL ACTS BETWEEN HUSBAND AND WIFE THAT SCRIPTURE EXPLICITLY FORBIDS?
paragraphs: ARE THERE SEXUAL ACTS BETWEEN HUSBAND AND WIFE THAT SCRIPTURE EXPLICITLY FORBIDS?
What the Bible actually says about the marriage bed may confront both the legalist who invented rules God never wrote—and the spouse who has used “we’re married” to excuse what love should never do.
There are questions Christians whisper because they are afraid somebody will hear them.
This is one of them.
Maybe you have wondered about it but never dared ask your pastor.
Maybe you searched online and found two opposite worlds waiting for you.
One says almost everything between husband and wife is sinful.
The other says almost nothing can be sinful once two people are married.
One produces shame.
The other can produce license.
And somewhere between them sits a husband and wife who genuinely love Jesus, genuinely love each other, and simply want to know:
What does God actually say?
Not what somebody's grandmother said.
Not what pornography taught.
Not what secular culture celebrates.
Not what a preacher personally dislikes.
Not what social media normalizes.
What does Scripture say?
And here is where we have to be unusually careful, because Christians should never place words in God's mouth.

The Bible explicitly condemns sexual immorality and adultery. It commands faithfulness, holiness, honor, sacrificial love, and marital responsibility. Yet Scripture does not give married couples an exhaustive catalogue naming every conceivable intimate act and placing each into a column marked “permitted” or “forbidden.”
That distinction matters.
Because calling something sin when God has not called it sin is dangerous.
But using God's silence as permission to violate everything else He has said is dangerous too.
Hebrews 13:4 gives us one of the clearest boundaries:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
The Greek is striking:
Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος…
Timios ho gamos en pasin kai hē koitē amiantos…
Marriage is to be held in honor, and the marriage bed is to remain undefiled.
The word koitē—κοίτη—literally refers to a bed and, in this context, carries the intimate sense of the marriage bed.
But notice something Christians sometimes miss.
The verse does not say, “Marriage makes everything automatically holy.”
It tells us to honor marriage and keep the marriage bed undefiled, while warning that God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
Marriage is sacred.
It is not a moral loophole.
A wedding ring does not turn sin into righteousness.
At the same time, neither should Christians invent commandments that Scripture itself never gives.
That is where wisdom begins.
The question is therefore bigger than, “Does the Bible mention this particular act by name?”
We also have to ask:
Does this honor the covenant?
Does this involve another person, physically or through cultivated sexual infidelity?
Does it feed lust directed outside the marriage?
Does it violate holiness?
Does it degrade my spouse?
Does it cause harm?
Is there coercion, intimidation, manipulation, humiliation, or fear?
Can husband and wife approach this with a clear conscience before Christ?
Does it express covenant love—or merely use another person's body to satisfy selfish desire?
Those questions matter because Christian sexual ethics are not merely about anatomy.
They are about worship.
Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “fornication” in the KJV is porneia—πορνεία—a broad New Testament term for sexual immorality.
Notice Paul's destination:
Sanctification.
Holiness.
God is not merely interested in where your body has been.
He is interested in what your desires are becoming.
Jesus drove that truth all the way into the heart when He confronted adultery of the heart. Sexual purity cannot be reduced to the technical defense, “But I never physically cheated.”
You can remain physically beside your spouse while allowing your imagination to become unfaithful.
You can bring another person into your marriage without that person ever walking through your bedroom door.
A screen can do it.
Pornography can do it.
Secret fantasies deliberately cultivated around someone else can do it.
Comparison can do it.
An emotional or sexual fixation outside your covenant can begin turning the person God gave you into a substitute for somebody living inside your imagination.
And suddenly the question is no longer simply:
“What acts are allowed?”
The more frightening question becomes:
“Who is actually present in my heart when I touch my spouse?”
Jesus does not merely want outward technical compliance.
He wants truth in the inward person.
Then Paul says something in 1 Corinthians 7 that was astonishingly reciprocal in its wording.
“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.”

Then Paul deliberately mirrors the language in both directions: the wife does not possess unilateral authority over her body, and neither does the husband over his. He follows that reciprocal statement by saying that spouses should not deprive one another except temporarily and by agreement for prayer.
The Greek phrase in verse 5 is revealing:
ἐκ συμφώνου
ek symphōnou.
By agreement.
Together.
The word is related to the idea from which we get “symphony”—voices sounding together.
Do not twist this passage into a weapon.
Paul is not handing one spouse a divine permission slip to force the other.
The grammar is reciprocal.
The obligations are reciprocal.
The giving is reciprocal.
Even temporary abstinence in the circumstance Paul describes is ek symphōnou—by mutual agreement.
Christian marriage therefore cannot transform coercion into love merely because vows were once spoken at an altar.
A spouse is not property.
A spouse is a person made in God's image.

If someone is frightened, pressured, threatened, deliberately hurt, degraded against his or her will, manipulated with Scripture, or told, “God says you owe me this, so you cannot say no,” something has gone terribly wrong.
Do not baptize selfishness with Bible verses.
And husbands especially need to hear the standard Scripture places before them.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
That is Ephesians 5:25.
Look carefully at the direction of Christlike love.
Christ “gave himself up.”
The husband modeled after Jesus is not asking, “How much can I get?”
He is learning to ask, “How faithfully can I love?”
He does not use strength to frighten.
He uses strength to serve.
He does not weaponize authority.
He lays himself down.
He does not make his wife's vulnerability dangerous.
He protects it.
Ephesians continues by telling husbands to love their wives as their own bodies.
That destroys the theology of sexual selfishness.
If your pleasure requires your spouse's terror, something is wrong.
If your satisfaction depends upon your spouse feeling degraded, something is wrong.
If you are deliberately causing injury, something is wrong.
If pornography has become the scriptwriter of your marriage, something is wrong.
If another person is being brought into the sexual covenant, adultery and sexual immorality do not become righteous because husband and wife agreed to redefine marriage.
Consent matters profoundly.
But mutual consent is not the only category in Christian ethics.
Two people can mutually agree to something God has forbidden.
Agreement cannot sanctify adultery.
Agreement cannot turn pornography into purity.
Agreement cannot make exploitation holy.
Agreement cannot make idolatry worship.
And agreement cannot overrule Christ.
Jesus remains Lord of the bedroom too.
But now we must turn the blade in the other direction.
Some Christians have suffered beneath unnecessary shame because somebody taught personal preference as though it were Scripture.
This also must stop.

If Scripture does not explicitly identify a particular act between husband and wife as sinful, we should be cautious about announcing, “God forbids this,” merely because we personally find it strange, culturally unfamiliar, or uncomfortable.
Christians do not possess legislative authority over God's conscience.
Where God has spoken, obey Him.
Where biblical principles clearly apply, apply them faithfully.
Where Scripture has not specifically spoken, do not manufacture a verse that does not exist.
This is why the better question for many married Christians is not simply:
“Where is the verse forbidding this exact thing?”
Ask something deeper.
Can we thank God for this?
Can we approach it without violating either conscience?
Is it mutually welcomed rather than pressured?
Does it preserve exclusivity?
Does it honor rather than degrade?
Does it protect rather than injure?
Does it strengthen intimacy rather than train us to objectify one another?
Is pornography or another person's image necessary to make it desirable?
Does either spouse secretly feel used afterward?
Would bringing this honestly before Christ fill us with peace—or make us desperately search for theological loopholes?
And perhaps the most revealing question:
Does this resemble the character of Jesus?
Because Christianity is not fundamentally about discovering the maximum amount of behavior we can technically defend.
It is about becoming like Christ.
That changes everything.
Suddenly sex is no longer a consumer transaction.
It becomes covenant intimacy.
Not “What can I extract from you?”
But “How can I love you?”
Not performance.
Presence.
Not comparison.
Faithfulness.
Not coercion.
Tenderness.
Not secret resentment.
Honesty.
Not pornographic imitation.
Covenant reality.
Not shame.
Grace.
And perhaps this article is hurting because your story is already complicated.
Maybe pornography entered your marriage years ago.
Maybe you pressured your spouse.
Maybe you agreed to things because you were terrified that saying no would make your spouse leave.
Maybe somebody taught you that being a “good Christian wife” meant never having boundaries.
Maybe somebody taught you that being a husband gave you ownership rather than responsibility.
Maybe you crossed lines.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe your marriage bed became cold.
Maybe intimacy became transactional.
Maybe there are memories you wish you could erase.
Maybe you are reading this beside the very person you wounded.
And now shame is whispering:
Too late.
Look at what you became.
Look at what you did.
God must be disgusted with you.
But shame has forgotten the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come only for people with clean histories.
He came for sinners.
The cross is not God's monument to people who never became sexually broken.
It is God's declaration that sin is so serious Christ had to die—and grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly did.
Repentance does not mean pretending nothing happened.
It means bringing what happened into the light.
Naming sin as sin.
Ending what must end.
Confessing what must be confessed.
Seeking forgiveness.
Accepting appropriate boundaries and consequences.
Getting wise pastoral and professional help where trauma, coercion, abuse, addiction, or betrayal are involved.
And turning toward Jesus.
Not toward better hiding.
Toward Jesus.
There is a difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation says, “Hide from God.”
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “Your scandal is your identity.”
The Gospel says, “Your sin is real—but Jesus Christ is greater.”
This is why our heartbeat remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness as light.

He rewrites everything by meeting guilty people with truth, calling sinners to repentance, carrying sin to a bloody cross, rising from the grave, forgiving those who trust Him, and beginning the long work of making broken people new.
Maybe your marriage needs that grace tonight.
Not another argument about who is right.
Not another secret browser window.
Not another demand.
Not another night pretending everything is fine.
Maybe it begins with two terrifyingly simple sentences:
“I haven't loved you like Christ.”
“Will you forgive me?”
And perhaps another:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
That prayer is not weakness.
It may be the first honest thing your heart has said in years.
So, are there sexual acts between husband and wife that Scripture explicitly forbids?

Scripture clearly forbids sexual immorality and adultery and commands holiness, marital faithfulness, honor, Christlike love, and reciprocal marital responsibility. It does not hand us an exhaustive catalogue naming every conceivable intimate act. Therefore we must neither invent prohibitions God did not give nor use biblical silence to excuse conduct that violates what He plainly commanded. Hebrews commands that marriage be honored and its bed remain undefiled; Paul calls believers away from porneia toward sanctification; 1 Corinthians presents marital intimacy in profoundly reciprocal language; and Ephesians places Christ's self-giving love over the marriage covenant.
The Christian question is ultimately not:
“How close can we get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
It is:
“How can our marriage—including our most private life—belong completely to Jesus?”
That question changes a bedroom.
It changes a husband.
It changes a wife.
It can change a marriage.
And Christ can change the people inside it.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish the details of your private life. But you can make one honest confession of need.
There is no shame in admitting that you need the mercy of Jesus.
Not because everybody needs to know their private story—but because somebody scrolling tonight may desperately need to discover that biblical holiness and biblical grace are not enemies.
These are conversations worth returning to slowly, prayerfully, with an open Bible.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers—and even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say about real human brokenness—to follow as well.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, there is another way you can help this ministry continue and expand.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.
But voluntary financial support is a real and biblical way believers can participate in Gospel work.
But the greatest reason to support Gospel ministry is not merchandise.
It is people.
Somewhere tonight, someone is hiding.
Someone thinks sexual sin has disqualified them forever.
Someone's marriage is bleeding behind smiling Facebook photographs.
Someone is wondering whether Jesus could possibly want them after what they have done.
Someone needs truth strong enough to confront them...
and grace strong enough to keep them from running away afterward.
If supporting Gospel Warrior helps us reach that person, then your generosity becomes more than support for content.
It helps carry a message.
Tag wisely.
Save what you need to revisit.
Follow so truth remains close.
But above everything else...
Come back to Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that you were wrong about something in the bedroom.
The greatest tragedy would be defending your desires so fiercely that you refused the Savior who came to transform your heart.

And the greatest miracle may begin when the door closes, the excuses stop, the secrets come into the light, and two broken people discover that Jesus Christ is still standing there with enough truth to expose them...
and enough grace to rebuild them.
Your darkest chapter does not have to become your final sentence when the pen is surrendered to Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GIDEON HAD SEVENTY SONS BECAUSE HE HAD MANY WIVES—Then His Concubine’s Son Nearly Wiped Them Out
paragraphs: GIDEON HAD SEVENTY SONS BECAUSE HE HAD MANY WIVES—Then His Concubine’s Son Nearly Wiped Them Out
The frightening story hidden between Gideon’s victory and Abimelech’s massacre—and the warning every Christian family needs to hear before private compromise becomes somebody else’s inheritance.
There is a sentence in the Bible that is frightening precisely because of how quietly it appears.
No thunder.
No prophet screaming judgment.
No army approaching.
Just one sentence about a famous man’s private life.
And then, one chapter later, bodies begin falling.
Gideon had survived something most people never survive.
Fear.
War.
Impossible odds.

He had watched God reduce his army until only three hundred men remained. He had heard the Midianites described as numerous as locusts. He had carried the insecurity of the man who once said his clan was the weakest and he was the least in his father’s house.
Yet God used him.
That is the Gideon many of us remember.
The fleece.
The torches.
The jars.
The trumpets.
The three hundred.
The victory.
But if you stop reading when Gideon becomes victorious, you miss one of the most disturbing lessons of his entire life.
Because sometimes the most dangerous chapter of a person's life begins after the miracle.
Sometimes we know how to depend on God when we are terrified...
but we do not know how to remain humble when we become successful.
And tucked near the end of Judges 8 is the sentence that should make every parent, leader, pastor, husband, wife, and believer slow down:
“Gideon had seventy sons of his own issue, for he had many wives.”
The Hebrew is painfully direct.
וּלְגִדְעוֹן הָיוּ שִׁבְעִים בָּנִים יֹצְאֵי יְרֵכוֹ כִּי־נָשִׁים רַבּוֹת הָיוּ לוֹ
The essential sense is unmistakable:
Gideon had seventy biological sons...
because he had many wives.
Then Scripture adds another detail.
There was also a woman in Shechem.
She was his concubine.
And she bore Gideon another son.
His name was Abimelech.
At first, that can sound like an ancient genealogical footnote.
It isn't.
It is the fuse.
Judges 8:31 records that Gideon’s concubine in Shechem bore him a son whom he named Abimelech.
And then Gideon died.
That is when the consequences he could no longer control began walking around in the bodies of his children.
Read that again.
Gideon was gone.
But Gideon’s household remained.
His victories remained.
His reputation remained.
His decisions remained.
His sons remained.
And Abimelech remained.
This is where Scripture becomes uncomfortable because it refuses to give us cardboard heroes.
The Bible does not need to erase Gideon’s victories to tell us about Gideon’s failures.
Nor should we.
God genuinely used Gideon.
God genuinely delivered Israel through him.
And Gideon nevertheless made choices whose consequences extended beyond his lifetime.
That should terrify us just enough to make us honest.
Because perhaps you have been assuming that yesterday's obedience makes today's compromise harmless.
It doesn't.
You can have a testimony and still need repentance.
You can have been mightily used by God and still have places in your life that desperately need surrender.
You can defeat Midian publicly while allowing something dangerous to grow privately.
And this is where the story turns bloody.

After Gideon died, Israel again turned toward the Baals. They forgot the LORD who had delivered them, and they failed to show covenant loyalty toward Gideon's household. Then Abimelech went directly to his mother’s relatives in Shechem.
He understood something powerful.
Blood loyalty.
Family identity.
Political resentment.
Ambition.
He asked the leaders of Shechem, essentially, which was better: seventy sons of Gideon ruling over them, or one man?
Then came the sentence designed to close the sale:
Remember...
I am your flesh and blood.
Abimelech knew exactly which wound to touch.
He presented the seventy as outsiders and himself as family.
And Shechem listened.
Money was taken from the temple of Baal-berith and given to Abimelech.
He used it to hire reckless men.
Then he went to his father's house.
Imagine the scene before you read the next sentence too quickly.
These weren't statistics.
They had names.
Faces.
Childhood memories.
They were sons who had grown up beneath the shadow of the same father.
Perhaps some had eaten together.
Perhaps some had played together.
Perhaps some had argued over things brothers argue about.
Perhaps some remembered Gideon's stories of trumpets, torches, shattered jars and Midianites fleeing through the night.
Then their brother arrived.
Not to reconcile.
Not to talk.
Not to mourn their father.
To kill them.
Judges 9 tells us that Abimelech murdered his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, on one stone.
Seventy sons.
Almost.
Because one escaped.
Jotham.
The youngest hid himself.
One survivor.
One witness.
One voice left alive to speak.
And suddenly that seemingly insignificant sentence from the previous chapter feels much heavier:
Gideon had many wives.

This does not mean Scripture teaches a simplistic equation that polygamy mechanically caused Abimelech's murders. Abimelech was morally responsible for his own wickedness, as were the leaders of Shechem who supported him.
But Scripture deliberately places Gideon's complicated household immediately before the violent struggle that erupted among his sons.
That matters.
And we should never confuse biblical description with biblical approval.
The Bible records many things human beings did without commanding us to imitate them.

Polygamy appears repeatedly in the Old Testament, but Genesis establishes God's foundational marriage pattern with one man and one woman becoming “one flesh,” a pattern Jesus Himself returned to when teaching about marriage.
So Judges is not inviting us to admire Gideon's collection of wives.
It is showing us a broken world.
And brokenness has descendants.
That is where Gideon's story stops being ancient history.
Because you may not have seventy sons.
You may not have many wives.
You may never become a military leader.
But every one of us is building something somebody else may have to live inside.
Your children may inherit consequences from decisions they never made.
Your spouse may carry wounds produced by battles they never started.
People around you may eventually encounter the mature version of something you keep calling “small.”
A hidden addiction.
A secret relationship.
Uncontrolled anger.
Pornography.
Pride.
Bitterness.
Greed.
Emotional neglect.
Dishonesty.
Spiritual hypocrisy.
An obsession with status.
A refusal to forgive.
A private compromise nobody knows about.
We comfort ourselves with one dangerous sentence:
“It isn't hurting anybody.”
Gideon's story whispers back:
Not yet.
Sin rarely sends you an invoice on the day you purchase it.
Sometimes the bill arrives years later.
Sometimes it arrives at your children's door.
That does not mean every suffering child is being punished for a parent's particular sin. Scripture does not permit us to make that cruel assumption.
It means something simpler and more sobering:
Our choices affect other people.
And some consequences outlive us.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because some of us know what it feels like to inherit a war.
You did not create the alcoholism in your family.
You inherited its aftermath.
You did not create your father's anger.
But you learned to flinch because of it.
You did not create your mother's wounds.
But somehow you became responsible for navigating them.
You did not choose the divorce.
The betrayal.
The abandonment.
The dysfunction.
The silence.
The secrets.
Yet you grew up among their ruins.
And now perhaps you are terrified that you will become what hurt you.
Listen carefully.
Judges 9 is not the end of the Bible.
Abimelech is not the final Son Scripture wants you looking toward.
Another Son is coming.
Not the son of Gideon.
The Son of God.
And He does something Abimelech never could.
Abimelech destroyed his brothers to obtain a throne.
Jesus left His throne to save His enemies.
Abimelech shed the blood of others to make himself king.
Jesus allowed His own blood to be shed to rescue sinners.
Abimelech's kingdom was built through death.
Christ's Kingdom brings life through His death and resurrection.
Abimelech climbed toward power over the bodies of his brothers.
Jesus descended into humiliation and gave Himself for people who had rebelled against Him.
Do you see Him?
This is why Christianity is not merely advice about becoming a slightly better version of yourself.
You need more than advice.
So do I.
We need a Savior.
Because eventually the Bible stops allowing us to blame only what our parents handed us.
Maybe you inherited wounds.
But eventually you make choices.
Maybe somebody sinned against you.
But bitterness can still become your sin.
Maybe your childhood explains why you struggle.
But explanation is not transformation.
Jesus does not merely want to help you manage the family darkness.
He came to bring you out of darkness.
Maybe your father failed.
Maybe your mother failed.
Maybe your marriage failed.
Maybe you failed your children.
Maybe you crossed lines you swore you would never cross.
Maybe the person everyone sees at church looks nothing like the person staring at your phone at 2:13 in the morning.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret.
And somewhere underneath all the religious language is one exhausted thought:
If people knew everything about me, would Jesus still want me?
Look at the cross.
That is your answer.
Christ did not die for an edited version of you.
He died for sinners.
Repentance does not mean pretending your past never happened.
It means turning from sin toward the One who already knows what happened.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace looks evil directly in the face, calls it what it is, and announces that the blood of Jesus is sufficient to forgive the repentant sinner.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because every broken relationship immediately repairs itself.
Not because repentance erases history.
But because history does not have to remain your master.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the previous chapters weren't written...
but by changing where the story is going.
That means your father's sin does not have to become your identity.
Your mother's brokenness does not have to become your destiny.
Your divorce does not have to become your definition.
Your addiction does not have to become your name.
Your secret does not have to become your grave.
Your family's pattern does not have to become your children's inheritance.
In Christ, cycles can end.
Not through motivational slogans.
Through repentance.
Through truth.
Through forgiveness.
Through the Holy Spirit.
Through obedience.
Through the Gospel.
Perhaps your greatest spiritual victory will never be witnessed by thousands.
Perhaps it will happen tonight when you finally confess what you have been hiding.
Perhaps it happens when you delete the number.
Close the browser.
Tell your spouse the truth.
Ask your child to forgive you.
Call the person you wounded.
Seek biblical counsel.
Return what wasn't yours.
Walk away from the affair.
Pour out the bottle.
Stop feeding the resentment.
Open the Bible again.
Get on your knees.
And whisper the prayer pride has prevented you from praying:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Because sometimes breaking a generational cycle does not look dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like one trembling person deciding:
The darkness stops with me.
Be honest.
And if Christ has already broken something that once seemed impossible to break, tell somebody.
Your testimony might become another person's evidence that chains really can fall.
Not because every sentence will feel comfortable tomorrow, but because temptation has a remarkable ability to make yesterday's conviction feel distant.
Come back when compromise starts negotiating again.
Not as a trick for an algorithm.
Think about one person scrolling tonight who is silently becoming exhausted from carrying a family pattern they don't know how to break.
One father.
One mother.
One teenager.
One struggling Christian.
One prodigal.
One person who still thinks they are too dirty to come home.
Your share could put the Gospel in front of them at exactly the moment they are finally willing to listen.
It doesn't.
They don't.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces faithful giving to your local church or the other acts of generosity God may call you to.
It doesn't.
Scripture says giving should come from a heart that has decided freely, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
Pray.
Follow.
Save the teaching.
Share it publicly.
Send it privately.
Put the Gospel where somebody hurting might find it.
Because Gideon's story leaves us with a question far more personal than what happened to seventy sons thousands of years ago.
What are you building that will remain when you are gone?
What are you tolerating today that somebody you love may encounter tomorrow?
And what needs to be surrendered to Jesus while there is still time to change the inheritance?
Gideon could defeat an army.
But military victory could not redeem his household.
You cannot save yourself either.
But Jesus can save sinners.
Jesus can forgive what you confess.
Jesus can transform what you surrender.
Jesus can teach a wounded father how to become gentle.
Jesus can teach an abandoned daughter that abandonment is not her identity.

Jesus can take the addict, the adulterer, the angry, the ashamed, the religious hypocrite, the exhausted believer, the prodigal who smells like the far country—and write a chapter grace alone could have authored.
So don't merely finish this article.
Respond to Christ.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Confess what darkness has taught you to conceal.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
And then live differently.
Because perhaps the most beautiful inheritance you can leave your children is not money.
Not property.
Not your surname.
Not even stories about everything you accomplished.
Perhaps it is the memory of a mother or father who finally became humble enough to say:
“I was wrong.”
“Jesus forgave me.”
“And by His grace, the cycle ended here.”
Tell the truth.
What cycle are you asking Jesus to end with you?
Even if all you can write is:
That is enough to remind another wounded person that they are not the only one still fighting.
Because the stone where Abimelech murdered his brothers is not the final stone in Scripture.
There was another stone.
A stone rolled across the entrance of a tomb.
And on the third day, that stone could not keep Jesus Christ inside.
Death did not get the final word.
Sin did not get the final word.
The grave did not get the final word.
And if you belong to Christ...
neither does your family's darkest chapter.
You may have inherited the ruins—but in Jesus Christ, you do not have to hand them to the next generation.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “TRAIN UP A CHILD”—AND HE STILL WALKED AWAY: DID GOD BREAK HIS PROMISE?
paragraphs: “TRAIN UP A CHILD”—AND HE STILL WALKED AWAY: DID GOD BREAK HIS PROMISE?
What Proverbs 22:6 Really Says to the Parent Who Did Everything They Knew to Do… and Is Still Waiting for Their Child to Come Home
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that happens quietly.
No funeral.
No hospital room.
No sympathy cards arriving at the door.
Just an empty chair.
A bedroom that does not feel the same anymore.
A Bible you once bought for a child whose hands no longer open it.
A mother scrolling through photographs from years ago, stopping at the one where her little boy was smiling in church.
A father remembering the night his daughter folded tiny hands beside her bed and whispered a prayer to Jesus.
You taught them Scripture.
You brought them to church.
You prayed over them.
You corrected them.
You forgave them.
You tried to model Christ.
You failed sometimes too—and those failures still visit you at two in the morning.
But you tried.
And now?
Maybe they want nothing to do with God.
Maybe they laugh at what they once believed.
Maybe they are living in a way that terrifies you.
Maybe they still call themselves Christian, but Christ seems to have become a distant accessory rather than Lord.
And somewhere in the middle of all that grief, someone quotes the verse.
“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.”
Proverbs 22:6.
And suddenly a verse that was supposed to comfort you feels almost like an accusation.
So you begin asking questions you are afraid to say aloud.
Did I fail?
Did I not pray enough?
Was my faith fake?
Did I somehow ruin my child?
And perhaps the question underneath every other question is even harder:
Did God promise me something He has not done?
That is where we need to stop repeating Proverbs 22:6 like a Christian slogan and actually listen to what Scripture says.
Because God does not need us to exaggerate His Word in order to defend Him.
The Hebrew text reads:
חֲנֹךְ לַנַּעַר עַל־פִּי דַרְכּוֹ גַּם כִּי־יַזְקִין לֹא־יָסוּר מִמֶּנָּה׃
Ḥănōḵ lannaʿar ʿal-pî darkô; gam kî-yazqîn, lō-yāsûr mimmennāh.
Traditionally:
“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.”
But there is more happening underneath the English than many of us realize.
The opening word, חֲנֹךְ—ḥănōḵ—comes from the Hebrew verb חנך, ḥānak.
It carries the idea of training, initiating, or dedicating.
That matters.
Biblical parenting is not merely controlling behavior long enough to produce a respectable adult.
It is formation.
Dedication.
Direction.
It is repeatedly placing truth before a young human heart while knowing that you cannot climb inside that heart and make it worship God.
And the person being trained is called הַנַּעַר—hannaʿar.
Naʿar can describe a child or youth across a surprisingly broad range of young life.
Then comes the phrase that has produced enormous discussion:
עַל־פִּי דַרְכּוֹ
ʿal-pî darkô.
Literally, something close to “according to the mouth of his way,” an idiomatic expression commonly understood along the lines of “according to his way.”
Some have interpreted this as training a child according to his individual disposition, temperament, or natural bent.
That may contain useful parenting wisdom, but we should be careful about claiming that this is certainly what Solomon meant.
Within Proverbs, “way” is deeply moral.
There is a way of wisdom.
A way of righteousness.
A way of folly.
A way that appears right to a person yet ends in death.
Proverbs is relentlessly concerned with which road a human being walks.
So Proverbs 22:6 is not giving parents a magical technique for programming children.
It is wisdom about formation.
Set the young person upon the path.
Teach.
Correct.
Model.
Repeat.
Live the truth in front of them.
Make wisdom familiar.
Make righteousness a road their feet know well.
And here is where devastated parents need to hear something that may remove years of unnecessary shame:
A proverb is not the same literary form as an unconditional covenant promise.
Proverbs gives us wisdom—truthful observations about the way God has ordered life and the ordinary consequences of wisdom and foolishness.
Consider other proverbs.
Proverbs teaches that diligent hands tend toward prosperity.
That is true.
But Scripture also contains righteous people who suffer poverty.
Proverbs teaches that a gentle answer turns away wrath.
That is true.
But sometimes you can answer gently and the angry person becomes angrier anyway.
Why?
Because Proverbs teaches wisdom for living in God's world. It is not presenting every maxim as a mechanical formula that eliminates human choice, suffering, providence, or every possible exception.
And that changes how we hear Proverbs 22:6.
It gives parents enormous reason to take spiritual formation seriously.
What children repeatedly receive matters.
What they repeatedly watch matters.
What becomes normal in their home matters.
The prayers matter.
The conversations matter.
The apologies matter.
The correction matters.
The nights when you are exhausted but sit beside the bed anyway matter.
The Sunday mornings when getting everyone out the door feels like a small military campaign matter.
The moments when your child catches you praying when you did not know anyone was watching matter.
But the proverb should not be weaponized against a grieving mother or father as though an adult child's rebellion mathematically proves parental failure.
Because your child is not a machine.
Your child bears the dignity—and terrible responsibility—of being a human being who makes real moral choices before God.
Think about Scripture itself.
God's Word never hides the scandals inside families.
Adam had Cain.
Isaac had Esau.
Samuel's sons did not walk in his ways.
David's household became a landscape of terrible consequences, sin, grief, violence, rebellion, and regret.
Scripture refuses to give us sanitized families.
And maybe that is because God knew we would eventually need a Bible honest enough to survive our own homes.
Some parents need to hear this with tears running down their faces:
Your child's present rebellion does not automatically prove that every seed you planted was worthless.
And it certainly does not mean you should stop praying.
Seeds can disappear beneath the soil long before anything green appears above it.
But we must be equally careful here.
We cannot turn Proverbs 22:6 into another guarantee by saying, “Don't worry. Every wandering child definitely returns before death.”
Scripture does not give us permission to promise that either.
We pray.
We plead.
We love.
We speak truth.
We keep the door of appropriate reconciliation open.
We trust God's power.
But salvation belongs to the Lord.
No parent can repent on behalf of an adult child.
No mother can believe the Gospel for her son.
No father can surrender his daughter's heart to Christ in her place.
Christian parents are called to faithfulness.
They are not granted sovereignty.
And strangely enough, that truth can become freedom.
Because some of you have been trying to carry a responsibility that belongs to God.
You replay everything.
Maybe if I had been more patient.
Maybe if I had disciplined differently.
Maybe if we had chosen another church.
Maybe if I had noticed sooner.
Maybe if I had worked less.
Maybe if I had prayed more.
Maybe.
Maybe.
Maybe.
There may indeed be things to repent of.
Good parents are still sinners.
Sometimes our children carry wounds connected to things we did.
When that is true, Christianity does not teach us to hide behind Proverbs 22:6.
It teaches us to confess.
To apologize without excuses.
To seek forgiveness.
To make restitution where appropriate.
To say the words some parents find almost impossible to say:
“I was wrong.”
That can be holy ground.
But repentance is different from endless self-condemnation.
The Gospel does not ask you to pretend you were a perfect parent.
It tells you something infinitely better.
There is a perfect Savior for imperfect parents.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross because respectable Christian families had managed to get everything right.
He went because none of us had.
Parents need grace.
Children need grace.
Prodigals need grace.
Preachers need grace.
The son who ran away needs grace.
The mother crying in the kitchen needs grace.
The father wondering where he went wrong needs grace.
And the child who grew up in church but learned how to hide sin beneath Christian language needs grace too.
This is why the deepest answer to Proverbs 22:6 is not a parenting technique.
It is Jesus Christ.
Parenting can expose a child to truth.
Parenting can model truth.
Parenting can teach truth.
Parenting can discipline toward wisdom.
But parenting cannot regenerate a human heart.
Only God saves.
That realization should not make parents passive.
It should drive them to their knees.
Teach your children about Jesus.
Not merely how to behave in church.
Jesus.
Teach them why sin is deadly.
Teach them why grace is astonishing.
Teach them that repentance is not humiliation before an angry God but turning from sin toward the God who calls sinners home.
Let them see that Christianity is not Dad pretending he never struggles.
It is Dad repenting when he sins.
It is not Mom maintaining the appearance of the perfect Christian household.
It is Mom depending upon Christ when the household is breaking her heart.
Let them discover that the Gospel is strong enough for questions.
Strong enough for failure.
Strong enough for confession.
Strong enough for shame.
Strong enough for scandal.
Strong enough for the day somebody in the family does the thing nobody imagined they would ever do.
Because this is what Jesus does.
He walks into stories human beings think are already ruined.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted His people.
The thief beside Him had no lifetime left in which to repair his reputation.
Yet grace kept writing.
That does not make sin insignificant.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough for the Son of God to bleed.
But look again at the cross.
The sinner mattered enough for the Son of God to bleed.
That is the Gospel.
So if your child is wandering tonight, pray.
Do not pray merely, “God, make my child behave again.”
Pray for resurrection.
“Jesus, reveal Yourself to them.”
“Convict them.”
“Protect them from deception.”
“Bring people into their life who will speak truth.”
“Destroy the lies they have believed.”
“Give me wisdom to know when to speak and when to remain quiet.”
“Show me anything in myself that needs repentance.”
“And Lord, do what I cannot do.”
Then love them without calling darkness light.
Grace does not require approving what God calls sin.
Truth does not require becoming cruel.
Jesus was full of grace and truth.
Christian parents are called toward that same difficult intersection.
And if you are reading this as the child rather than the parent—perhaps you are the one who walked away—listen carefully.
Your mother's prayers cannot save you.
Your father's faith cannot save you.
Your Christian childhood cannot save you.
Being baptized years ago cannot substitute for knowing Christ.
Having Bible verses buried somewhere in your memory is not the same thing as surrendering your life to Jesus.
Maybe you have spent years running because Christianity became tangled in your mind with hypocrisy, pain, control, disappointment, or people who represented Jesus badly.
What happened to you matters.
But the failures of Christians do not change who Christ is.
Do not reject Jesus because somebody wearing His name wounded you.
Look at Him for yourself.
Look at the Christ who touched lepers.
Look at the Christ who ate with sinners.
Look at the Christ who confronted religious hypocrisy.
Look at the Christ who welcomed the broken.
Look at the Christ who carried a cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Then decide what you will do with Him.
Maybe Proverbs 22:6 has been sitting somewhere inside you for years.
Maybe you remember Scripture you thought you had forgotten.
A hymn suddenly returns.
A sentence from your grandmother.
Your father's voice praying.
Your mother's Bible open on the table.
A Sunday school teacher saying the name Jesus.
Do not confuse those memories with salvation.
But do not dismiss them either.
Perhaps someone planted.
Someone watered.
And even now, God is confronting you with the Gospel again.
Come home to Christ.
Not merely to church culture.
Not merely to your parents.
Not merely to the person you used to be.
To Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop negotiating with the sin that is destroying you.
Stop assuming there will always be another year.
Jesus still receives sinners.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this desperately needed tonight.
Jesus still receives sinners.
Someone else reading may realize they are not alone because you were brave enough to say it.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
There may be a father secretly wondering whether God broke His promise.
Jesus Christ.
And not because anyone should manipulate you into giving.
Scripture says giving should come from the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary generosity can genuinely help Christian ministry continue.
Your giving does not buy grace.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
Your support simply helps put the message of that grace in front of another human being who may desperately need to hear it.
So what does Proverbs 22:6 ultimately leave us with?
Not a formula.
Not permission for careless parenting.
Not a weapon for condemning grieving parents.
And not an excuse to stop praying.
It leaves us with wisdom.
Train them.
Teach them.
Dedicate yourself to showing them the way of truth.
Repent when you fail.
Keep praying when they wander.
Keep believing that no sinner is beyond the reach of Christ.
And leave the throne to God.
Maybe you are staring at an unfinished story.
Good.
Then do not write “The End” where God has placed only a comma.
You do not know what the next phone call will contain.
You do not know what conviction may already be stirring in a heart far away.
You do not know what remembered Scripture may return in the middle of somebody's darkest night.
You do not know what God may yet do.
But you know who Jesus is.
And sometimes faith is simply refusing to mistake the chapter you are crying through for the final page.
The child may have wandered far from the road you showed them—but Jesus has never lost the address.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WIVES, SUBMIT TO YOUR HUSBANDS”—BUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU START READING ONE VERSE EARLIER?
paragraphs: “WIVES, SUBMIT TO YOUR HUSBANDS”—BUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU START READING ONE VERSE EARLIER?
The verse that has started arguments, wounded marriages, been weaponized by controlling men, rejected by wounded women—and sometimes quoted without the sentence that comes immediately before it.
There are Bible verses people whisper when they are hurting.
And there are Bible verses people shout when they want to win.
Ephesians 5:22 has sometimes become the second kind.
“Wives, submit to your own husbands…”
Some women hear those words and feel peace because they have seen biblical marriage lived beautifully.
Others hear them and their stomach tightens.
Because somebody once used those words against them.
Maybe a husband quoted “submission” while refusing correction.
Maybe a pastor told her to endure what should never have been called godly.
Maybe a man demanded obedience while giving very little resemblance to Jesus.
And maybe somewhere along the way, she quietly began wondering…
Is this really what God intended?
But there is something painfully important we need to notice.
Before Paul speaks directly to wives…
before he tells husbands how to love…
before we build an entire theology of marriage from verse 22…
there is verse 21.
And once you see it, you cannot pretend it isn't there.
The Greek reads:
“ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ”
hypotassomenoi allēlois en phobō Christou.
“Submitting to one another in the fear [or reverence] of Christ.”
That is Ephesians 5:21.
And the grammatical connection matters.
Paul's thought did not originally arrive with modern chapter headings, paragraph titles, bold print, or verse numbers separating verse 21 from verse 22.

Even more striking, significant early Greek witnesses of Ephesians 5:22 contain no independently expressed verb for “submit” in verse 22; the idea is supplied from the preceding context. Other manuscripts contain an explicit form of the verb, which is why careful textual discussion matters.
Either way, verse 21 and verse 22 are not strangers living on opposite sides of a theological wall.
They belong to the same flow of thought.
And the flow begins even earlier.
Paul has been describing what Spirit-filled Christian life looks like.
“Be filled with the Spirit…”
Then come speaking, singing, thanksgiving…
and submission.
Not domination.
Not ego.
Not “How much authority can I exercise?”
But a community increasingly transformed by Jesus Christ.
And suddenly the marriage passage begins to feel different.
Not because “wives, submit” disappears.
It doesn't.
We do not honor Scripture by erasing words that make modern people uncomfortable.
But neither do we honor Scripture by isolating words that make controlling people comfortable.
Read the whole passage.
The wife is addressed.
Then the husband is addressed.
And what does Paul tell the husband?
“Husbands, love your wives…”
That sounds gentle enough until you keep reading.
“…as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Read that again.
Gave.
Himself.
Up.
Paul does not hand the Christian husband a throne.
He points him toward a cross.
The standard is not, “Make sure she knows who's boss.”
The standard is Christ.
The Christ who washed feet.
The Christ who welcomed the broken.
The Christ who touched people society avoided.
The Christ who laid aside privilege.
The Christ who endured nails.
The Christ who bled.
The Christ who gave Himself for His bride.
So before any Christian husband pounds his fist on the table demanding, “Submit to me,” perhaps he should first look toward Calvary and hear another question:
Are you loving her like THAT?
Because biblical headship can never legitimately become permission for cruelty.
Christ does not brutalize His bride.
Christ does not humiliate His bride for entertainment.
Christ does not manipulate His bride to protect His ego.
Christ does not use Scripture as a weapon to make His bride afraid of Him.
He gives Himself for her.
And that changes everything.
The Greek word translated “submit” in verse 21 comes from ὑποτάσσω—hypotassō.
But whatever debates Christians may have about the precise implications of that word for marital roles, one fact cannot be escaped:
Paul places the entire discussion under allegiance to Christ.
The marriage is not ultimately about the supremacy of the husband.
It is not ultimately about the independence of the wife.
It is about Jesus.
That is why Christian marriage cannot simply become a baptized version of a power struggle.
The Gospel invades the home.
Pride meets the cross.
Selfishness meets the cross.
Control meets the cross.
Bitterness meets the cross.
Entitlement meets the cross.
The wife belongs to Jesus before she belongs to her husband.
The husband belongs to Jesus before he exercises any responsibility toward his wife.
Both stand beneath the lordship of Christ.
Both need grace.
Both need repentance.
Both need forgiveness.
Both need the Holy Spirit.
And both will eventually discover something uncomfortable:
The greatest enemy inside many marriages isn't sitting on the opposite side of the bed.
It is the sin still fighting for control inside both human hearts.
That is why this passage cannot merely become ammunition for gender arguments.
It is supposed to become a mirror.
Husband…
when was the last time you apologized without defending yourself?
When was the last time you sacrificed something you genuinely wanted because loving your wife mattered more?
When was the last time she felt emotionally safe enough to tell you that you hurt her?
When was the last time you asked whether your “leadership” actually resembles the crucified Savior you claim to follow?
And wife…
has disappointment slowly hardened into contempt?
Have years of hurt made respect almost impossible?
Have you begun punishing him emotionally for wounds you have never honestly brought into the light?
Are you asking Jesus to transform your marriage while quietly refusing to let Him transform you?
Those questions sting.
They are supposed to.
Not because Christianity is trying to crush us…
but because Jesus loves us too much to leave our hidden idols untouched.
And sometimes the idol is control.
Sometimes it is pride.
Sometimes it is being right.
Sometimes it is being obeyed.
Sometimes it is refusing to forgive.
Sometimes it is maintaining the appearance of a Christian marriage while two people are spiritually bleeding behind a closed door.
Maybe that is where this article found you.
Not inside a theological debate.
Inside a hurting marriage.
Maybe nobody knows.
You still attend church.
You still smile.
You still upload the anniversary photo.
People comment, “Beautiful couple!”
And you stare at those words knowing how quiet the drive home was.
Knowing what was said last night.
Knowing how long it has been since either of you felt truly seen.
Maybe your marriage isn't collapsing dramatically.
Maybe it is dying politely.
One unanswered wound at a time.
One sarcastic remark.
One withheld apology.
One night facing opposite directions.
One more prayer neither of you prayed together.
And somehow you became roommates carrying wedding rings.
Please hear this:
Jesus is not intimidated by what your marriage has become.
The same Gospel that raises spiritually dead sinners can enter rooms where love seems dead too.
That does not mean every story becomes easy.
It does not mean reconciliation can be forced by one spouse.
And it absolutely does not mean a person experiencing abuse should silently endure danger because someone quoted the word “submit.”
Sin should not be renamed submission.
Coercion should not be renamed leadership.
Fear should not be renamed respect.
And protecting someone from genuine harm is not rebellion against Jesus.
The biblical picture is infinitely more beautiful than that.
Paul eventually reaches Genesis:
“The two shall become one flesh.”
Then he says something astonishing.
This mystery is profound…
and he is speaking about Christ and the church.
There it is.
The secret beneath the marriage passage.
Jesus.
Christian marriage points beyond itself.
A husband and wife are sinners standing inside a living picture of something far greater than themselves—the covenant love of Christ for His people.
That is why marriage exposes us so deeply.
Marriage eventually introduces another human being to versions of you the church crowd never sees.
They see the worshipper.
Your spouse sees the temper.
They see the Bible verse you posted.
Your spouse heard the sentence you wish you could take back.
They see the ministry.
Your spouse sees whether the Gospel reaches the kitchen.
They see your Sunday clothes.
Your spouse sees Monday night.
And perhaps that is where real discipleship begins.
Not when everybody thinks you're spiritual.
But when Jesus is allowed into the places where nobody is applauding.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter failed Jesus publicly.
David's sin brought devastation.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly exposed.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated history.
Paul himself had persecuted the church.
Scripture is filled with human beings whose stories could have ended at their worst chapter.
But Jesus has always been in the business of rewriting stories.
Not by pretending sin never happened.
By confronting it.
Forgiving it.
Redeeming sinners from it.
And transforming those who surrender to Him.
That is grace.
Grace does not say, “It doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “It mattered enough for Jesus to bleed for it.”
The cross simultaneously tells us how terrible sin is and how astonishing God's mercy is.
So maybe the question after reading Ephesians 5 should not merely be:
“Who is supposed to submit?”
Maybe another necessary question is:
“Where have I refused to become like Jesus?”
Because you can win the argument about marriage and still lose your marriage to pride.
You can memorize Ephesians 5 and never imitate Ephesians 5.
You can demand biblical order while living with an unbiblical heart.
You can insist that somebody fulfill their role while quietly refusing the cross-shaped responsibilities Scripture gives you.
And Jesus is after something deeper than outward compliance.
He wants hearts.
Husbands surrendered to Christ.
Wives surrendered to Christ.
Homes surrendered to Christ.
Pride surrendered to Christ.
Sexuality surrendered to Christ.
Money surrendered to Christ.
Arguments surrendered to Christ.
Trauma brought honestly before Christ.
Sin confessed before Christ.
Forgiveness received through Christ.
Because Christianity is not ultimately behavior management.
It is resurrection.
Maybe your marriage needs counseling.
Get help.
Maybe you owe someone an apology.
Give it without excuses.
Maybe you have been controlling.
Repent.
Maybe you have become cruel.
Repent.
Maybe bitterness has become your emotional shelter.
Bring it to Jesus.
Maybe there is serious abuse or danger.
Seek safety and trustworthy pastoral, professional, and—when necessary—legal help. No interpretation of Ephesians 5 requires someone to cooperate with violence or conceal criminal behavior.
And maybe you are reading this unmarried.
Because Ephesians 5 is exposing something bigger than marriage.
Every Christian is being called away from self-rule and toward Christ.
“Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.”
Imagine churches shaped by that.
Imagine marriages shaped by that.
Imagine men who measure strength by how much of themselves they can sacrificially give rather than how much control they can obtain.
Imagine women cherished rather than silenced.
Imagine disagreements where winning matters less than holiness.
Imagine children growing up watching Daddy apologize.
Watching Mommy forgive.
Watching both parents kneel before Jesus.
Not perfection.
Repentance.
Not performance.
Grace.
Not pretending wounds don't exist.
Healing.
That is the home the Gospel begins creating when Jesus becomes more than decoration on the wall and actually becomes Lord of the people living beneath that roof.
And maybe somebody you know desperately needs this tonight.
And if this exposed something in your own heart, don't hide behind a reaction button.
And if you are not comfortable telling your story publicly, simply comment, “Jesus, have Your way.”
There is no shame in admitting you need grace.
The entire Christian faith begins with people admitting exactly that.
Because there may come a night after an argument when you need to read it again—not to find ammunition against your spouse, but to remember the cross.
It doesn't.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It never could.
Salvation is by God's grace.
And your local church, its needs, and your convictions about biblical giving should not be casually displaced by an online ministry.
But voluntary support of Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical way of participating in work you believe is bearing spiritual fruit.
