If you want to glorify God through supporting this particular work, you can do so freely and prayerfully—not under pressure, but as an act of willing generosity.
Send it privately to the couple nobody realizes is struggling.
Pray for this ministry.
Help truth travel farther than an algorithm would naturally carry it.
Because somewhere tonight a woman may be wondering whether Christianity requires her to disappear.
Somewhere a husband may finally realize that biblical leadership looks much more like dying to himself than demanding his way.
Somewhere a couple may be one honest conversation away from asking for help.
Somewhere someone has heard Ephesians 5:22 shouted at them for years…
and desperately needs to discover the Christ whose cross stands over the entire passage.
So read verse 22.
Believe verse 22.
But don't amputate it from verse 21.
And don't stop before verse 25.
Keep reading until the husband meets the cross.
Keep reading until husband and wife meet Christ.
Keep reading until authority loses its appetite for domination.
Keep reading until submission cannot be confused with enabling evil.
Keep reading until marriage becomes something larger than two people fighting for control.
Keep reading until you reach the mystery.
Christ.
And His church.
The Bridegroom who did not save His bride by overpowering her…
but by giving Himself for her.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody needs to carry into their marriage tonight:
Before you use Scripture to ask what your spouse owes you, stand beneath the cross and ask Jesus what love requires of you.
That question could change an argument.
It could change a marriage.
It could change a family.
And by the grace of Christ…
it could change generations.
Because the Gospel does not merely tell wives to submit or husbands to love.
The Gospel brings proud, wounded, sinful human beings to the feet of a crucified and risen King…
until both finally realize that Jesus was never asking them to use Scripture to conquer each other.
He was calling them to belong completely to Him.
And when Jesus becomes Lord of the home, the goal is no longer to determine who can force the other person lower.
The question becomes who is willing to kneel before Christ.
Remember this when the argument starts again:
The safest marriage is not one where somebody finally wins the war for control—it is one where two sinners keep surrendering the throne to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Did Jesus Spend 30 Years in Obscurity?
paragraphs: Why Did Jesus Spend 30 Years in Obscurity?
Before Jesus Changed the World in Public, He Spent Decades Where Almost Nobody Was Watching—and That May Be the Word Your Hidden Heart Needs Right Now
Thirty years.
Think about that.
The Son of God entered the world…
and He did not immediately gather crowds.
He did not immediately preach the Sermon on the Mount.
He did not immediately heal the blind.
He did not immediately walk across the sea.
He did not immediately confront religious hypocrisy in Jerusalem.
He did not immediately stand before Pilate.
He did not immediately carry the cross.
For most of the earthly life of Jesus before His public ministry, Scripture gives us surprisingly little detail.
And maybe that bothers us because we live in a world obsessed with being seen.
We announce beginnings before anything has been built.
We measure significance by followers.
We measure influence by reach.
We measure success by applause, numbers, recognition, invitations, promotions, platforms, titles, and whether somebody important finally notices us.
Then we meet Jesus.
The One through whom all things were made…
living quietly in Nazareth.
And suddenly our definition of an important life begins to collapse.

Scripture does not actually say, “Jesus spent exactly thirty years in total obscurity.” We should not make the Bible say more than it says. Jesus was known by His family and community. Luke records His presentation at the Temple, the testimony surrounding His infancy, and the remarkable episode when He was twelve years old among the teachers in Jerusalem.
But after that extraordinary glimpse into His childhood, the Gospel narrative becomes remarkably quiet until the beginning of His public ministry.
Luke tells us:
“Jesus himself, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age…”
In Greek:
“Καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν Ἰησοῦς ἀρχόμενος ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα…”
—Luke 3:23
The crucial expression is “ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα”—about thirty years of age.
Not exactly thirty according to a modern birthday calculation.
About thirty.
That matters because biblical faithfulness matters.
But what also matters is what happened before the crowds came.
Jesus grew.
Jesus submitted.
Jesus waited.
Jesus lived an ordinary human life without ceasing to be the extraordinary Son of God.
And there is something almost painfully beautiful about that.
Because perhaps you are living there right now.
In the years nobody celebrates.
The years nobody photographs.
The years when you are faithful but unnoticed.
Praying but still waiting.
Serving but still overlooked.
Obeying God while watching somebody else receive the opportunity you thought would finally be yours.
Maybe you have whispered something you were almost ashamed to say:
“Lord… when is my life actually going to begin?”
But what if it already has?
What if the hidden years are not wasted years?
Look carefully at what Luke tells us after twelve-year-old Jesus returned with Mary and Joseph:
“And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them.”
The Greek carries a striking expression:
“ἦν ὑποτασσόμενος αὐτοῖς”
—Luke 2:51
He was submitting Himself to them.
Sit with that.
The eternal Son entered genuine human life and willingly lived within the humble structures of a human family.
The One who would command storms submitted.
The One before whom demons would tremble submitted.
The One whom angels worship submitted.
The One who possessed authority beyond anything Caesar could imagine went home to Nazareth.
There was no social media announcement.
No crowd waiting outside.
No earthly coronation.
Nazareth.
Home.
Ordinary responsibilities.
Ordinary days.
And then Luke gives us one of the most important sentences for understanding those hidden years:
“Καὶ Ἰησοῦς προέκοπτεν ἐν τῇ σοφίᾳ καὶ ἡλικίᾳ καὶ χάριτι παρὰ θεῷ καὶ ἀνθρώποις.”
“And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man.”
—Luke 2:52
The Greek verb προέκοπτεν—proekopten—carries the idea of advancing or progressing.
Jesus truly entered human development.
Christianity does not teach that God merely appeared to be human.
“The Word became flesh,” John 1:14 declares.
Jesus Christ was truly God and truly human.
He knew hunger.
Fatigue.
Family life.
Work.
Community.
Waiting.
And Hebrews says something staggering about the incarnate Son:
“Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered.”
—Hebrews 5:8
That does not mean Jesus moved from disobedience into obedience.
He was without sin.
Hebrews itself declares that He was tempted as we are, “yet without sin.”
It means the eternal Son experienced obedience within real human circumstances.
He did not merely teach faithfulness.
He lived it.
Before the wilderness, there was Nazareth.
Before the miracles, there was ordinary work.
Before the crowds, there was family.
Before Calvary, there were thousands of ordinary mornings.
Before the world heard His voice, heaven had already declared its pleasure in Him.
And this is where the story becomes personal.
Because some of us secretly believe visibility proves value.
If nobody sees what we are doing, we wonder whether it matters.
If the prayer has not been answered, we wonder whether God heard it.
If the ministry has not grown, we wonder whether God called us.
If the business struggles, we question ourselves.
If marriage has not come…
if the child has not returned…
if healing has not happened…
if the door remains closed…
if the dream keeps taking longer than expected…
we begin interpreting waiting as rejection.
But Nazareth will not allow us to make that equation.
Hidden does not mean abandoned.
Ordinary does not mean meaningless.
Waiting does not necessarily mean God has forgotten you.
And obscurity certainly does not mean God is absent.
Sometimes we want God to give us a platform when He is forming something inside us that a platform cannot produce.
We want the microphone.
God is concerned with the heart holding it.
We want influence.
God is concerned with character.
We want the next assignment.
God is still teaching us faithfulness in this one.
We ask, “When will people finally see me?”
Jesus quietly confronts us with another question:
“Will you still obey the Father when nobody applauds?”
That question hurts.
Because some of us do not merely want to serve God.
We want to be seen serving God.
There is a difference.
And Jesus warned about it.
In Matthew 6, He spoke about people who performed righteous acts “to be seen” by others. He spoke instead of giving, praying, and fasting before the Father who sees what is done in secret.
Maybe the greatest battle of your hidden season is not getting God to reveal you.
Maybe it is allowing God to free you from needing everyone else to see you.
Because there is a terrifying possibility:
You can become famous while your soul becomes empty.
You can become visible while becoming spiritually hollow.
You can have thousands of followers and quietly stop following Jesus.
And you can also be almost completely unknown to the world while living a life that heaven calls faithful.
Jesus did not need human applause to know who He was.
At His baptism, before the great public works recorded throughout His ministry unfolded, the Father declared:
“You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.”
—Luke 3:22
Identity came before public ministry.
Beloved before achievement.
Son before spectacle.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years trying to earn through achievement what can only be received through grace.
You thought:
If I become successful enough, I will matter.
If enough people love me, I will finally love myself.
If I accomplish enough for God, maybe God will finally be pleased with me.
If I pray harder…
serve longer…
give more…
work more…
prove more…
maybe then I will become worthy.
But Christianity does not announce that sinners can perform their way into God's family.
It announces that salvation is a gift of grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God…”
—Ephesians 2:8
And this is where the hidden years begin pointing beyond themselves.
Because Jesus did not eventually leave Nazareth merely to become famous.
He came to save sinners.
The carpenter would become the crucified King.
The hands acquainted with ordinary human labor would one day be pierced.
The feet that walked the roads of Galilee would be nailed to a Roman cross.
The face unnoticed by much of the empire would be mocked and struck.
The One who deserved every throne accepted a cross.
Why?
Not because humanity had earned Him.
Because humanity desperately needed Him.
Sin is not merely a mistake needing improvement.
It separates us from the holy God.
And Jesus came into the scandal of human rebellion carrying something sinners could never manufacture for themselves:
grace.
He lived the sinless life we have not lived.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The hidden years eventually moved toward public ministry.
The public ministry eventually moved toward Jerusalem.
Jerusalem moved toward Golgotha.
But Golgotha was not the end.
The tomb became empty.
Death did not get the final sentence.
Sin did not get the final sentence.
Shame did not get the final sentence.
Your worst chapter does not have to get the final sentence either.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is why you found this article while your own life feels painfully unfinished.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been carrying.
Maybe you smile at church and cry somewhere nobody can hear you.
Maybe you know exactly which browser history you keep deleting.
Maybe there is a relationship you cannot seem to surrender.
Maybe resentment has lived inside you so long that you have started calling it discernment.
Maybe you have been performing Christianity publicly while starving spiritually in private.
Maybe your Bible has been closed.
Prayer has become rare.
Worship feels distant.
And you keep telling everyone:
“I’m okay.”
But you know you are not.
Jesus does not call you to become better at hiding.
He calls you to come into the light.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who already knows the truth about you.
You do not have to clean yourself enough to approach Christ.
You come because you need Christ.
And grace does not mean sin does not matter.
Grace means sin mattered so terribly that Christ went to the cross—and God's mercy is so astonishing that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled, and transformed through Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not “believe in yourself.”
Not “manifest your destiny.”
Not “God will make you famous.”
Jesus never promised His followers celebrity.
He promised Himself.
And sometimes He meets us most deeply in places nobody else notices.
Nazareth teaches us that a quiet season can still be sacred.
The cross teaches us that what looks like defeat can stand at the center of redemption.
The resurrection teaches us that God can bring life where human beings see only endings.
So perhaps your prayer tonight should not merely be:
“God, get me out of this hidden season.”
Maybe it becomes:
“Jesus, make me faithful here.”
Faithful while waiting.
Faithful while healing.
Faithful while unnoticed.
Faithful when there is no applause.
Faithful when obedience costs something.
Faithful when everybody else seems to be moving faster.
Faithful when your name is not called.
Faithful when all you have is another ordinary Monday and a Savior who promised never to leave His people.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not pretend it did not.
Be honest.
Your comment might become the sentence another exhausted believer sees at two in the morning and realizes:
“I am not the only one fighting this.”
And if one person came into your mind while reading this, do not ignore that name.
Send this to them.
Come back when obscurity begins lying to you again.
Come back when comparison becomes loud.
Come back when you start believing that God cannot use ordinary days.
There is also a practical way to stand with this work.

Gospel ministry requires real resources. Writing, publishing, producing Christian resources, maintaining platforms, expanding outreach, and making discipleship materials available all carry real costs.
It does not.
Not because paying money makes someone more spiritual.
It does not.
Scripture does not teach that.

But voluntary financial support can be one practical expression of generosity toward Gospel work. Paul wrote of believers participating in the advance of the Gospel, and Scripture repeatedly treats generous Christian giving as something willing rather than coerced:
“Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7
That is the spirit in which this invitation is made.
No manipulation.
No purchasing blessings.
No buying access to Jesus.
Just believers freely helping Gospel-centered work reach farther.
And if you cannot financially support the ministry, please never believe that makes your presence meaningless.
You can pray.
You can share.
You can comment.
You can point one wounded person toward Jesus.
The Gospel itself is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Maybe that is the final lesson of those quiet years in Nazareth.
The world teaches us to fear being unseen.
Jesus shows us how to be faithful when we are unseen.
The world tells us to build a name.
Jesus calls us to follow His.
The world says visibility creates significance.
The Gospel tells us that our deepest hope is not that the world finally notices us…
but that the Savior knows His own.
So if you are in your Nazareth season right now, do not despise it.
Do not worship it either.
Do not romanticize the pain.
Just give it to Christ.
Let Him expose what needs repentance.
Let Him heal what has been wounded.
Let Him remove what cannot follow you into obedience.
Let Him teach you to serve without applause.
Let Him remind you that your identity cannot safely rest in recognition.
And when the door finally opens, may you walk through it not desperate to prove that you matter…
but already anchored in the One who matters most.
Because someday you may look back at the years you begged God to erase and discover that they were the years in which He taught you what applause never could.
You thought nothing was happening because nobody was watching—but heaven never needed an audience to make an ordinary day part of a redeemed life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE CALLED HERSELF “A ROSE OF SHARON”—But Her Lover Answered With an Even Stronger Compliment
paragraphs: SHE CALLED HERSELF “A ROSE OF SHARON”—But Her Lover Answered With an Even Stronger Compliment
She thought she was only one flower in an enormous field. Then the man who loved her answered—and suddenly the entire field disappeared.
There are some sentences you read in the Bible.
And then there are sentences that read you.
Song of Songs 2:1–2 is only two verses long, but hidden inside those few ancient Hebrew words is something painfully familiar to anyone who has ever looked in the mirror and wondered...
Am I actually enough?
Beautiful enough.
Important enough.
Wanted enough.
Worth choosing.
Worth keeping.
Worth loving after someone knows the whole story.
Maybe that question has followed you longer than you admit.
Maybe people see your smile, your church posts, your family photographs, your accomplishments, your ministry, your jokes, your confidence...
but they do not hear what happens inside your head when the room becomes quiet.
You compare.
You remember.
You notice everyone who seems prettier, stronger, younger, more successful, more spiritual, more disciplined, more loved.
And somewhere between what everyone else sees and what you secretly believe about yourself, your heart whispers:
I'm nothing special.
Then you arrive at this strange little conversation in the Song of Songs.
The woman speaks first:
“I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys.”
Then her beloved answers:
“As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.”
—Song of Songs 2:1–2, KJV
But slow down.
Because the English is beautiful...
and the Hebrew makes the exchange even more fascinating.
Her words are:
אֲנִי חֲבַצֶּלֶת הַשָּׁרוֹן שׁוֹשַׁנַּת הָעֲמָקִים
ʾĂnî ḥăḇaṣṣeleṯ haššārôn, šôšannaṯ hāʿămāqîm.
Literally, the sense is approximately:
“I am a flower of Sharon, a lily of the valleys.”

That first Hebrew word for the flower, חֲבַצֶּלֶת — ḥăḇaṣṣeleṯ, is difficult to identify botanically with certainty. “Rose” is the famous traditional English rendering, but scholars have proposed crocus, meadow-saffron, asphodel, narcissus, or simply “flower.”
And that matters.
Because we should never make Scripture say something merely because the traditional English wording sounds romantic.
We honor God by loving what the text actually says.

There is also good reason to understand her statement not necessarily as, “I am THE magnificent Rose of Sharon,” as though she were declaring herself the unrivaled flower of the region, but something closer to:
“I am a flower of Sharon...
a lily of the valleys.”
One among many.
Picture it.
A woman surrounded by beauty.
A countryside scattered with flowers.
And she essentially places herself among them.
A flower.
A lily.
Lovely, perhaps.
But ordinary.
One in a field full of others.
Then he answers.
And this is where the conversation changes.
כְּשׁוֹשַׁנָּה בֵּין הַחוֹחִים כֵּן רַעְיָתִי בֵּין הַבָּנוֹת
Kəšôšannâ bên haḥôḥîm, kēn raʿyātî bên habbānôṯ.
“Like a lily among the thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.”
She says:
I am a flower among flowers.
He essentially answers:
No.
You don't understand how I see you.
You are a lily among thorns.
He takes her own image...
and intensifies it.
The flower she considered ordinary becomes extraordinary when seen through the eyes of the one who loves her.
That is breathtaking.
But we need to be careful here.
Song of Songs is, in its immediate literary context, Hebrew love poetry celebrating human love. We should not erase that meaning and pretend every sentence is secretly a coded prophecy about Jesus.
Christians sometimes jump immediately from “Rose of Sharon” to Jesus Christ.
Yet in Song of Songs 2:1, within the flow of the poem, the words are spoken by the woman.
That doesn't make the passage less spiritual.
It makes it more honest.
God considered faithful covenant love, attraction, delight, tenderness, longing, and the dignity of being cherished worthy of a place in His Word.
And from there, the whole Bible gives us something even greater to contemplate.
Because the ache underneath this woman's words is an ache nearly every human being eventually recognizes.
We want to be known...
and still loved.
Not loved because someone has seen only the edited version.
Known.
Completely.
And still wanted.
Human love can give us a beautiful glimpse of this.
But it cannot carry the entire weight of the human soul.
Eventually every human lover discovers limitations.
People misunderstand us.
People disappoint us.
Some leave.
Some betray.
Some die.
And some of the deepest wounds in our lives come precisely from people whose voices once made us feel chosen.
So where does the heart go when the person who once called you beautiful becomes the person who made you question your worth?
Where do you go when the marriage breaks?
When the relationship disappears?
When betrayal rewrites memories you thought were safe?
When you gave someone your heart and received scars in return?
Where do you go when the thorn isn't around you anymore...
but inside you?
You go deeper than romance.
You go to the Gospel.
Because Christianity does not ultimately tell you to save yourself by repeating, “I am beautiful. I am worthy. I am enough.”
The Gospel says something far more confronting...
and far more liberating.
You were never enough to save yourself.
Neither was I.
Our deepest problem was never low self-esteem.
It was sin.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23
That includes the secret sin.
The respectable sin.
The religious sin.
The lust nobody knows about.
The bitterness hidden underneath politeness.
The pride disguised as confidence.
The envy hidden behind scrolling.
The unforgiveness we keep justifying.
The compromise we renamed “normal.”
The prayerlessness.
The hypocrisy.
The nights we would erase if heaven handed us an eraser.
The things we did.
The things done to us.
And the things we became while trying to survive them.
This is where Christianity becomes radically different from sentimental spirituality.
Jesus did not come merely to make damaged people feel prettier.
He came to save sinners.
The cross is not God whispering that sin didn't matter.
The cross is God showing exactly how seriously sin mattered...
and how astonishingly far His love would go to redeem sinners.
Christ “died for our sins according to the scriptures.”
—1 Corinthians 15:3
Jesus Christ carried what we could never remove by self-improvement.
Our guilt.
Our condemnation.
Our debt before God.
And He rose again.
Christian hope is therefore not:
Someone finally noticed how wonderful I was.
It is:
Someone knew exactly how sinful I was—and loved me enough to die to rescue me.
Do you feel the difference?
Grace is not God discovering that you were innocent all along.
Grace is God rescuing the guilty through Christ.
That means your scandal does not have to be the final chapter.
Your affair does not have to be the final chapter.
Your addiction does not have to be the final chapter.
Your divorce does not have to be the final chapter.
Your failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Your shame does not have to be the final chapter.
Your years away from God do not have to be the final chapter.
Even your religious pretending does not have to be the final chapter.
Repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is possible.
Restoration is possible.
A new life is possible.
Not because sin is small.
Because Jesus is greater.
Maybe you have spent years living like that flower in the valley.
One person among billions.
One face in a congregation.
One account in an endless feed.
One exhausted mother washing dishes while nobody notices.
One father quietly carrying financial pressure while everyone assumes he is strong.
One teenager comparing a real body to edited photographs.
One widow sleeping on one side of a bed that suddenly feels enormous.
One believer worshiping on Sunday and fighting temptation alone on Monday night.
One prodigal wondering whether you have gone too far to come home.
You look across the field and think:
Why would God notice me?
Listen carefully.
The God revealed in Scripture does not love His people because they managed to outperform everyone standing beside them.
The Gospel destroys that competition.
At the foot of the cross, nobody gets to boast.
Your neighbor's beauty cannot cancel God's grace toward you.
Another person's success cannot diminish your place in Christ.
Someone else's testimony does not make yours insignificant.
Someone else's calling does not erase yours.
You do not have to become somebody else to come to Jesus.
You come as the sinner you actually are.
You repent.
You believe.
You surrender.
And grace begins rewriting what sin tried to make permanent.
This is why perhaps the most dangerous mirror isn't hanging in your bathroom.
It's the human heart.
Because mirrors can show your face.
People can tell you whether they find you attractive.
Algorithms can count your likes.
Employers can measure your performance.
Banks can calculate your assets.
Strangers can judge your mistakes.
But none of them has authority to pronounce the final verdict over your soul.
That belongs to God.
And for those who are in Christ, Scripture says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 8:1
No condemnation.
Read that again.
Not reduced condemnation.
Not postponed condemnation.
Not condemnation waiting for the next time your past gets mentioned.
No condemnation in Christ.
This does not mean there are no consequences for sin.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It does not mean Christians become perfect overnight.
It means Christ's saving work is sufficient for those who belong to Him.
Your identity is no longer chained to the worst thing you've done.
And neither should your identity be chained to the nicest compliment another human being has ever given you.
Because people can call you a rose today...
and treat you like a thorn tomorrow.
Christ must be deeper than applause.
Deeper than romance.
Deeper than followers.
Deeper than beauty.
Deeper than your reputation.
Perhaps that is the word somebody desperately needed tonight.
You have spent years asking:
Who will choose me?
But the deeper question is:
Have I surrendered to Christ?
You have spent years asking:
Am I attractive enough?
Jesus asks for something infinitely more important:
Will you follow Me?
You have spent years trying to convince people that you are worth keeping.
The Gospel invites you to stop performing and come honestly before the One from whom nothing has ever been hidden.
Maybe even now there is something you are hiding.
Something beneath the Christian vocabulary.
Something underneath “I'm fine.”
Something you haven't confessed because you're terrified of what honesty will cost.
Bring it into the light.
Not into the hands of gossip.
Into the light of Christ.
Repentance may hurt your pride.
Grace will heal what pride could never heal.
You may have walked into this article believing you were simply reading about a woman who called herself a Rose of Sharon.
Maybe now you realize the story touched something else.
That quiet place inside you that desperately wants somebody to say:
I see you.
God sees more than the version of you anyone else has ever seen.
And that should humble us before it comforts us.
He sees the sin too.
Yet the same God who exposes sin offers mercy through His Son.
That is why Jesus is better than shallow affirmation.
He doesn't flatter you into destruction.
He calls you to repentance...
and loves you toward resurrection.
Be honest.
Sometimes one honest sentence is the first crack through which light enters a room we've kept locked for years.
And think of one person who needs this tonight.
Not twenty random people.
One.
The friend who keeps making jokes because admitting loneliness feels dangerous.
The woman rebuilding after betrayal.
The man carrying shame nobody knows about.
The believer drifting quietly from God.
The person convinced their scandal disqualified them permanently.
Send this privately if their story is too tender to expose publicly.
That simple share genuinely helps this ministry's message travel farther without turning another wounded soul into a statistic.
Because there may come a night when comparison starts screaming again.
When rejection returns.
When an old failure crawls out of memory.
When somebody's opinion of you changes.
Come back and remember:
Human voices are powerful.
But they are not God.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin honestly, understand grace more deeply, and keep your eyes on Jesus Christ, consider staying close to this mission.
It doesn't.
It doesn't.
And we will not tell you that giving money earns salvation, forgiveness, blessing, or a higher place in God's Kingdom.
Grace cannot be bought.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
But Scripture does teach cheerful, willing generosity in support of Gospel work.
It should flow from it.
But merchandise isn't the heart of this.
Jesus is.
Books eventually wear.
Mugs break.
Shirts fade.
Algorithms change.
Platforms disappear.
Christ remains.
Share because someone needs the Gospel.
Tag because somebody you love may be silently drowning.
Save because you may need these words again.
Follow because your soul needs more than an endless feed of noise.
But above everything...
follow Jesus.
Because the greatest love story in Scripture is not ultimately about finding a human being who finally recognizes your beauty.
It is about the holy God pursuing sinners with a mercy they could never deserve, sending His Son, calling them to repentance and faith, forgiving them through Christ, and transforming them by grace.
The woman said she was a flower in the valley.
Her beloved looked at the same flower and saw something extraordinary.
But the Gospel takes us farther still.
Jesus does not merely improve the way we see ourselves.
He gives repentant sinners something self-esteem never could:
a new life.
So when your past whispers your old name...
when shame shows you photographs from chapters you wish had never existed...
when rejection tells you nobody will ever choose you...
when comparison points toward a thousand other flowers and asks what makes you special...
look toward the cross.
Then look toward the empty tomb.
Your hope was never supposed to rest in being the prettiest flower in the field.
Your hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is what your wounded heart needed more than another compliment.
Not someone telling you that you were always perfect.
But a Savior telling sinners everywhere that repentance can lead home.
The thorns may explain where you have been—but in Christ, they do not get to write how your story ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS CHOOSE ORDINARY PEOPLE AS DISCIPLES?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS CHOOSE ORDINARY PEOPLE AS DISCIPLES?

He Could Have Chosen the Religious Elite, the Powerful, and the Impressive. Instead, He Walked Toward Fishermen, Outsiders, Doubters, and Broken Men—and the Reason May Change the Way You See Yourself.
There is something almost scandalous about the people Jesus chose.
Think about it.
If you knew you had only a few years to establish a movement that would eventually carry your message across nations, languages, cultures, persecution, imprisonment, and death...
Who would you recruit?
You would probably look for influence.
Education.
Connections.
Money.
Charisma.
People with spotless reputations.
People who already knew how to speak before crowds.
People who could open doors.
People whose names carried weight.
But Jesus walked past the kinds of credentials human beings tend to admire...
and called fishermen.
He called ordinary working men whose clothes probably smelled like the Sea of Galilee.
He called a tax collector—a member of a profession despised by many of his own people.
He called men who would misunderstand Him.
Men who would argue.
Men who would become afraid.
A man who would doubt.
A man who would eventually deny three times that he even knew Jesus.
And among the Twelve was even Judas Iscariot, who would betray Him.
That should make us uncomfortable.
Because somewhere along the way, many of us quietly began believing that God uses people who already have everything together.
And perhaps that is why you sometimes look at yourself and think:
God could never really use someone like me.
Not after what I did.
Not with my past.
Not with my weaknesses.
Not with how little Scripture I know.
Not with my temper.
Not with my failures.
Not with the things nobody knows about me.
Not after the promises I made to God and broke.
Maybe somebody else.
But not me.
And then Jesus walks onto the shoreline.
Suddenly, Christianity begins with something completely different from what our insecurity expected.
Matthew tells us that Jesus saw Simon Peter and Andrew casting a net into the sea because they were fishermen.
Then Jesus said:
Δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου, καὶ ποιήσω ὑμᾶς ἁλιεῖς ἀνθρώπων.
Deute opisō mou, kai poiēsō hymas halieis anthrōpōn.
“Come after Me, and I will make you fishers of people.”
Matthew 4:19.
Do not rush past those words.
Especially these:
ποιήσω ὑμᾶς — poiēsō hymas.
“I will make you.”
Jesus did not say:
“Become impressive enough, then follow Me.”
He did not say:
“Fix yourself first.”
He did not say:
“Acquire the right reputation and come back.”
He called them...
and promised to make them.
That changes everything.
Because discipleship is not primarily the story of impressive people offering their abilities to Jesus.
It is the story of Jesus transforming people who surrender themselves to Him.
The qualification was never that Peter was already Peter.
Jesus knew the man standing beside those fishing nets was still impulsive.
Still unfinished.
Still capable of enormous failure.
Jesus knew there was a courtyard coming.
A charcoal fire.
Questions from strangers.
Fear.
And three denials.
Jesus knew Peter would eventually insist that he would never abandon Him—and then crumble when the pressure became real.
And Jesus called him anyway.
Not because Peter's failure did not matter.
Not because sin was irrelevant.
But because Jesus already knew something Peter did not yet understand:
Grace was going to write a chapter after his failure.
Maybe somebody reading this desperately needs to hear that.
Your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your entire story.
Peter denied Christ.
But denial was not the end.
There would eventually be another charcoal fire beside another shore.
There would be a risen Savior.
There would be restoration.
There would be a question repeated to the wounded disciple:
Do you love Me?
And there would be another commission.
Feed My sheep.
That is the Gospel pattern.
Sin is real.
Failure is real.
Repentance is necessary.
But grace is real too.
And Jesus is still in the business of taking people whose stories appear ruined and writing redemption where everyone expected a period.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Look again at the Twelve.
These were not twelve polished religious celebrities assembled for a publicity campaign.
Mark tells us something extraordinary about why Jesus appointed them.
The Greek of Mark 3:14 says:
ἵνα ὦσιν μετ’ αὐτοῦ
Hina ōsin met' autou.
“That they might be with Him.”
Then Mark continues:
καὶ ἵνα ἀποστέλλῃ αὐτοὺς κηρύσσειν
“And that He might send them out to preach.”
Notice the order.
Before they were sent...
they were with Him.
Before ministry came presence.
Before preaching came proximity.
Before public usefulness came private fellowship with Jesus.
This is where modern Christianity can become dangerously confused.
We can become fascinated with being used by God while neglecting simply being with God.
We want platforms.
Jesus wants disciples.
We want reach.
Jesus wants surrender.
We want influence.
Jesus wants obedience.
We want God to enlarge our audience.
Jesus wants to transform our hearts.
The Twelve did not change the world because they discovered some secret formula for personal greatness.
They had been with Jesus.
Years later, after the resurrection, something remarkable happened.
Peter and John stood before powerful religious authorities.
Acts 4:13 describes them with two Greek words:
ἀγράμματοι — agrammatoi
and
ἰδιῶται — idiōtai.
The first points to their lack of formal scholarly or rabbinic training. The second refers to ordinary or nonprofessional people—not specialists belonging to the religious establishment.
Yet the authorities were astonished by their boldness.
And then came the observation that explains everything:
ἐπεγίνωσκόν τε αὐτοὺς ὅτι σὺν τῷ Ἰησοῦ ἦσαν
They recognized that these men had been with Jesus.
There it is.
Not:
They recognized that these men attended the finest academy.
Not:
They recognized their impressive social status.
Not:
They recognized their wealth.
Not:
They recognized their political influence.
They recognized...
Jesus.
Something had happened to these ordinary men because they had been with an extraordinary Savior.
And perhaps that is the answer to the question.
Why did Jesus choose ordinary people?
Because the power of Christianity was never supposed to rest upon the greatness of the disciple.
It rests upon the greatness of Christ.
God does not need human weakness, as though weakness itself were a virtue. Scripture never teaches us to celebrate ignorance, incompetence, laziness, or spiritual immaturity.
Jesus trained His disciples.
Corrected them.
Rebuked them.
Taught them.
Sent them.
And through the Holy Spirit, transformed them.
Ordinary was not their excuse to remain unchanged.
Ordinary was the raw material grace transformed.
That distinction matters.
Following Jesus does not mean saying, “This is just who I am.”
Peter could not remain the fisherman who constantly spoke before thinking.
Matthew could not remain at his tax booth.
Thomas could not build his entire life around doubt.
James and John could not remain ruled by misguided ambition.
Jesus did not call them because transformation was unnecessary.
He called them into transformation.
And that may be exactly where this becomes personal.
Maybe you have been telling yourself:
“This is just how I am.”
“I've always had this addiction.”
“I've always had this temper.”
“I've always been bitter.”
“I've always struggled with lust.”
“I've always been jealous.”
“I've always been afraid.”
“My family is like this.”
“My past made me like this.”
And Jesus does not stand before you merely saying, “Try harder.”
He says:
Follow Me.
The Gospel is not self-improvement with religious vocabulary.
It is death and resurrection.
The old life confronted.
Sin confessed.
Pride broken.
Grace received.
A sinner forgiven through the blood of Jesus Christ.
A new life beginning because the Son of God died and rose again.
Jesus does not merely decorate the old person.
He saves.
He restores.
He transforms.
And suddenly the question changes.
You came here asking:
“Why did Jesus choose ordinary people?”
But perhaps the more frightening question is:
If Jesus deliberately called ordinary, imperfect people...
what excuse are you still using to keep yourself from fully following Him?
Maybe you believed you were too insignificant.
Peter was a fisherman.
Maybe you believed your past disqualified you.
Matthew collected taxes.
Maybe you believed your questions disqualified you.
Thomas wrestled with doubt.
Maybe you failed Jesus publicly—or privately.
Peter denied Him.
Maybe you have spent years watching other Christians and thinking:
“They're stronger than me.”
“They understand Scripture better than me.”
“They pray better than me.”
“They haven't made the mistakes I've made.”
Listen carefully.
Christianity has never been about convincing God that you are worthy of salvation.
You cannot.
Neither could Peter.
Neither could Matthew.
Neither could John.
Neither could Paul.
Neither can I.
That is precisely why the cross stands at the center of Christianity.
Jesus Christ did what sinners could never do for themselves.
He lived without sin.
He willingly gave Himself.
He died.
He bore judgment.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is not God's trophy for impressive people.
It is grace given to sinners who come to Christ in repentance and faith.
That means your weakness does not have to drive you away from Jesus.
It can become the place where you finally stop pretending you do not need Him.
There is an enormous difference between saying:
“I am weak, therefore sin does not matter,”
and saying:
“I am weak, therefore I desperately need Christ.”
The first makes weakness an excuse.
The second makes weakness a doorway to dependence.
Maybe that is why this story hurts a little.
Because some of us have become professionals at hiding.
Sunday smile.
Bible verse on Facebook.
Christian music playing.
But behind the screen...
you are exhausted.
Your prayer life has become almost silent.
There is something you keep returning to that you know you need to surrender.
You love Jesus, but lately you barely recognize the person you have become.
You are carrying shame nobody knows about.
And you are terrified that if people discovered the truth, they would see you differently.
Jesus already knows.
Every hidden room.
Every midnight thought.
Every compromise.
Every wound.
Every failure.
And His response is not permission to remain there.
It is a call to come out of hiding.
Repentance is not Jesus humiliating you.
Repentance is Jesus calling you away from the thing destroying you.
Grace does not whisper:
“Stay exactly where you are.”
Grace says:
“Come follow Me.”
Maybe today your prayer does not need impressive vocabulary.
Maybe it simply needs honesty.
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I cannot change myself.”
“Jesus, make me what You want me to become.”
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
But because sometimes publicly admitting our need for Christ becomes a small act of refusing to hide any longer.
You do not owe strangers the details.
God knows them.
This is what ordinary disciples still do.
We carry one another.
We remind each other where grace is found.
And we keep pointing each other back to Jesus.
Because perhaps the greatest lie ordinary believers have accepted is that only extraordinary Christians can make an extraordinary difference.
But think about the first disciples again.
A handful of people followed Jesus.
They listened.
Failed.
Learned.
Repented.
Witnessed the risen Christ.
Received the Holy Spirit.
And went.
The Gospel traveled from person to person.
House to house.
City to city.
Life to life.
And that means you do not need a pulpit to point somebody toward Jesus.
Sometimes discipleship begins with pressing “share.”
but they might read an article you shared.
Someone quietly losing faith.
Someone hiding an addiction.
Someone grieving.
Someone convinced God could never want them again.
Someone who needs to discover that Jesus did not build His Church from people who had never failed.
Not for numbers.
Not for applause.
Send this privately to the friend who keeps saying, “God could never use me.”
Save it too.
Because there may come a night when you are the person who needs to remember what you just read.
And for those who want to help Gospel Warrior continue producing and expanding Christ-centered resources, there is another way to stand with this mission.
But hear this clearly because biblical integrity matters:
Scripture says giving should come from a heart that has freely decided—not reluctantly and not under compulsion.
That kind of voluntary generosity can glorify God when it flows from love for Christ rather than pressure.
And sharing costs nothing.
Pray.
Share.
Encourage somebody.
Point someone toward Jesus.
Those things matter deeply.
It should be partnership.
More biblical nourishment.
More discipleship.
More Gospel-centered resources.
More opportunities to reach the person sitting alone behind a glowing screen wondering whether Jesus could possibly still want them.
Tell somebody what Christ has done.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the person who walked away from church.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who has questions.
Let them know there is room here to encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, grace, repentance, discipleship, and the truth about Jesus Christ.
And before you leave, answer one question honestly.
What is the thing that has made you believe God could never use you?
Your past?
Your education?
Your addiction?
Your fear?
Your failure?
Your age?
Your lack of confidence?
Your broken family?
Your secret shame?
You do not need to tell the entire story.
And if Christ has already taken something broken in your life and begun turning it into testimony, tell us what He has done.
Someone reading your comment may be standing where you once stood.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reminder that the story is not finished.
Because Jesus is still calling ordinary people.
Still forgiving sinners.
Still restoring failures.
Still confronting sin.
Still healing wounded hearts.
Still turning frightened disciples into courageous witnesses.
Still taking people nobody expected...
and displaying what grace can do.
Peter was not powerful because Peter was extraordinary.
Peter became useful because Jesus was extraordinary.
And that means perhaps the greatest thing about your life will never be what you managed to become by yourself.
Perhaps it will be what Jesus made of the life you finally surrendered to Him.
The nets are still lying on the shore.
The old life is still calling your name.
Jesus is still saying:
Follow Me.
And somewhere between who you were...
and who Christ is making you...
grace is writing a story you could never have written alone.
Never confuse being ordinary with being unusable—the hands of Jesus have always known what to do with surrendered lives.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES THE BIBLE SOMETIMES USE PROSTITUTION AS A METAPHOR FOR SPIRITUAL BETRAYAL?
paragraphs: WHY DOES THE BIBLE SOMETIMES USE PROSTITUTION AS A METAPHOR FOR SPIRITUAL BETRAYAL?
The language sounds scandalous—until you realize God was describing something far more personal than sexual sin: what happens when a heart that belongs to Him secretly gives itself to another lover.
There are passages in the Bible that make modern readers uncomfortable.
Not because they are difficult to translate.
Because they are almost painfully easy to understand.

God speaks through His prophets about His people abandoning Him, chasing idols, trusting foreign powers, loving money, pursuing pleasure, and giving their allegiance to things that could never save them.
And sometimes Scripture describes that betrayal with startling sexual imagery.
Prostitution.
Adultery.
Unfaithfulness.
Whoredom, as older English translations sometimes put it.
The words can sound so severe that some readers quietly wonder:
Why would God speak this way?
Is Scripture degrading women?
Is God particularly angry at people who have been sexually broken?
Or is something much deeper happening in the biblical story?
Stay with this question.
Because once you understand what the metaphor actually means, the uncomfortable person standing inside these passages may no longer be someone else.
It may be you.
It may be me.
And strangely enough, that is where the beauty begins.

When the prophet Hosea enters the biblical story, God gives him one of Scripture's most painful prophetic assignments. Hosea's marriage becomes a living picture of the covenant relationship between God and Israel.
The Hebrew of Hosea 1:2 is deliberately confronting:
אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים — ʾeshet zenunim

The expression uses זְנוּנִים (zenunim), language associated with prostitution, harlotry, or repeated sexual unfaithfulness. The verse intensifies the image with זָנֹה תִזְנֶה — zanoh tizneh, essentially stressing that the land has acted in profound unfaithfulness by departing from YHWH.
But notice the target of the metaphor.
God is not simply delivering a lecture about prostitutes.
He says:
הָאָרֶץ — ha'aretz.
“The land.”
Israel.
God's covenant people.
The scandal in Hosea is Israel's betrayal of the God who loved her.
The metaphor is sexual because the relationship being betrayed is covenantal.

Marriage provides Scripture with one of humanity's clearest pictures of exclusive covenant love. Two people belong to one another in a relationship of pledged faithfulness. Therefore adultery is not merely about an illicit physical act.
It is covenant intimacy given somewhere it does not belong.
That is why the prophets reached for this devastating metaphor.
Israel belonged to YHWH.
He had delivered them.
Fed them.
Protected them.
Led them.
Made covenant with them.
Yet again and again they pursued other gods.
They wanted God's protection while embracing idols.
God's blessings without God's lordship.
God's covenant while courting the values of the nations around them.
And suddenly the prophetic metaphor makes terrible sense.
Idolatry was not merely choosing the wrong religious philosophy.
It was betrayal.
God was saying, in effect:
You were loved.
You were rescued.
You belonged to Me.
And you gave your heart to another.
That is why reducing these passages to sexual morality misses much of their force. The metaphor is not primarily designed to let respectable religious people point accusing fingers at prostitutes.
It turns the accusation toward the supposedly religious.
Toward God's own covenant people.
Toward us.
And the New Testament proves that the metaphor did not disappear with the prophets.
James writes:
μοιχαλίδες — moichalides.
“Adulteresses.”
Then he asks whether his readers understand that friendship with the world is hostility toward God.
The Greek is striking:
μοιχαλίδες, οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ἡ φιλία τοῦ κόσμου ἔχθρα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν;
The point is spiritual infidelity.

James is drawing from the same covenant world inhabited by prophets such as Hosea and Jeremiah. He can call a community of believers “adulteresses” because the image is not fundamentally about biological sex or gender.
It is about divided allegiance.
Your lips can say, “Jesus is Lord,” while your ambitions whisper, “Money is lord.”
Your worship songs can say, “Christ is enough,” while your private life says, “Approval is enough.”
Your Bible can sit beside your bed while pornography owns your imagination.
You can post Scripture publicly while jealousy consumes you privately.
You can pray for God's will and quietly resent Him whenever His will interrupts yours.
You can want heaven without holiness.
Forgiveness without repentance.
A Savior without a King.
A cross that removes guilt without a cross that crucifies the old self.
And this is where the ancient metaphor stops feeling ancient.
Because spiritual betrayal rarely begins with someone announcing:
“I have decided to abandon God.”
It usually begins much more quietly.
One compromise.
One secret.
One appetite we refuse to surrender.
One relationship we know is pulling us away.
One obsession.
One resentment.
One little idol we insist we can control.
We still attend church.
Still say grace.
Still share Christian posts.
Still know the vocabulary.
But something else has slowly acquired the affection, obedience, fear, trust, time, money, imagination, or devotion that belongs ultimately to God.
That is idolatry.
And Scripture refuses to describe idolatry as harmless distraction because God refuses to pretend covenant love is meaningless.
Imagine a husband discovering that his wife has been secretly meeting another man.
Would anyone tell him:
“Relax. Why are you being so emotional?”
Imagine a wife discovering years of hidden betrayal on her husband's phone.
Would we tell her:
“It is merely a technical violation.”
No.
Because love makes betrayal hurt.
Indifference shrugs.
Love grieves.
That helps us understand something frequently misunderstood about God's jealousy in Scripture.
God's covenant jealousy is not the insecure jealousy of a fragile human ego desperate for validation.
God needs nothing from us to complete Him.
Rather, biblical jealousy reflects the rightful exclusivity of covenant love.
The God who knows that every idol will eventually devour us refuses to pretend our idols are harmless.
Money promises security and then demands your life.
Lust promises intimacy and leaves people emptier.
Approval promises belonging and turns you into a prisoner of everybody's opinion.
Power promises significance and eventually makes everyone around you expendable.
Pleasure promises freedom and can quietly become a master.
Even ministry can become an idol.
Even theology can become an idol.
Even being admired for loving Jesus can become more precious than Jesus Himself.
That is the frightening part.
Sometimes the rival lover does not look evil.
Sometimes it looks successful.
Sometimes it looks respectable.
Sometimes it walks into church carrying a Bible.
And if you are feeling exposed right now, do not run from the discomfort too quickly.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
The Bible exposes spiritual adultery because God intends to call adulterous hearts home.
That distinction matters enormously.

Scripture's prostitution imagery must never become an excuse for Christians to humiliate actual women or men who have been involved in prostitution, sexual exploitation, promiscuity, pornography, adultery, or other sexual sin.
Jesus never gave self-righteous people permission to weaponize somebody else's sexual history.
In fact, the Gospel destroys the fantasy that respectable sinners occupy some superior moral category.
Some sins happen in bedrooms.
Others happen in boardrooms.
Some are visible.
Others sit in church pews wearing expensive clothes.
Some people sell their bodies.
Others sell their integrity.
Some chase sexual pleasure.
Others prostitute their convictions for popularity, money, influence, political access, applause, or power.
All of us need grace.
That is why the biblical metaphor ultimately becomes so devastating.
We are not merely observing Israel's unfaithfulness.
We recognize ourselves in it.
How many times has God been faithful to us while we have been inconsistent toward Him?
How many prayers have we prayed only after everything else failed?
How often have we wanted God's hand more than God's heart?
How often have we negotiated obedience?
“Lord, I surrender everything…”
Except this relationship.
Except this habit.
Except my money.
Except my reputation.
Except my anger.
Except my sexuality.
Except my plans.
Except the thing I am afraid You might ask me to release.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody reading this has been avoiding:
You cannot surrender everything while permanently reserving one room of your heart where Jesus is forbidden to enter.
He is not asking to become another decoration in your life.
Jesus is Lord.
And here comes the Gospel.
Because if Scripture ended merely by exposing the unfaithful bride, none of us would have much hope.
But the Bible does not end with betrayal.
It moves toward a Bridegroom.
Jesus Christ.
And the astonishing message of Christianity is not that spiritually faithful people managed to climb their way into God's favor.
The Gospel announces that Christ came for sinners.
For rebels.
For idolaters.
For adulterers.
For religious hypocrites.
For sexually broken people.
For respectable people hiding respectable idols.
For people whose lives became scandals.
For people who ruined things they cannot repair.
For people who promised God, “Never again,” and then did it again.
Jesus came.
And He did not come merely to improve our reputation.
He came to reconcile us to God.
At the cross, Christ bore sin's judgment.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
The faithful Son died for the unfaithful.
And resurrection morning announced that sin, death, and the grave would not have the final word.
That is grace.
Not God pretending betrayal does not matter.
Grace is God dealing with sin at unimaginable cost and opening the way for sinners to come home through Christ.
Repentance, then, is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning.
Leaving the rival lovers.
Dropping the idols.
Stopping the negotiations.
Coming into the light.
Confessing what you have been protecting.
And returning to the One you were created to know.
Maybe your spiritual betrayal does not have a dramatic name.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe it is simply that Jesus used to be the center, and somewhere along the way He became an accessory.
Your career grew.
Your responsibilities multiplied.
Your phone became louder.
Your prayers became shorter.
Your Bible stayed closed longer.
Worship became background noise.
Sin stopped frightening you.
Conviction became irritating.
And gradually you learned how to live a Christian-looking life while surviving on yesterday's intimacy with God.
Nobody noticed.
But you did.
Some nights, when everything becomes quiet…
you still do.
Maybe this article is not here so you can learn why ancient prophets used uncomfortable language.
Maybe the question underneath the question is:
Who has your heart now?
Not your church attendance.
Not your Facebook biography.
Not the verse printed on your wall.
Your heart.
What controls your decisions?
What are you terrified to lose?
What do you run toward when you hurt?
Whose approval determines whether you feel valuable?
What occupies your imagination when nobody is watching?
What could God ask you to surrender that would make you hesitate?
Sometimes your answer reveals your altar.
And maybe there is something you need to tell Jesus right now without polishing it into religious language.
Tell Him.
No performance.
No hiding.
No pretending.
“Lord Jesus, I have loved things more than I have loved You.”
“I have been divided.”
“I have protected what You told me to surrender.”
“I have called compromise freedom.”
“I have wanted Your blessings while resisting Your authority.”
“Have mercy on me.”
There is mercy in Christ.
Real mercy.
But mercy is not permission to keep running toward the idol that is killing you.
Grace calls you home.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your private sin. But you can draw a line in the sand.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only believer fighting to return.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this—someone drifting, someone wounded, someone who thinks they have gone too far—send this to them.
You may never know which person stopped scrolling.
Which person finally prayed.
Which person returned to Christ.
Which person realized that their scandal did not have to become their final chapter.
Because idols rarely surrender territory after one confrontation.
There may come a night when you need these words again.
We want this ministry to remain a place of daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Salvation cannot be purchased. Grace cannot be bought.
But voluntary generosity can glorify God when it flows from faith, gratitude, love, and a willing heart.
Think of it as a voluntary ministry offering—your personal decision to stand behind work you believe should continue reaching people.
And if financial support is not possible, please do not feel lesser.
Pray.
Share.
Those actions can carry truth into places we could never reach alone.
Because ultimately Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
A ministry is not the Bridegroom.
Jesus is.
And that brings us back to the disturbing metaphor with which we began.
Why does the Bible sometimes use prostitution as a picture of spiritual betrayal?
Because sin is more personal than rule-breaking.
God created humanity for Himself.
Idolatry gives sacred allegiance to another.
The prophets wanted Israel to feel the horror of that betrayal.
James wanted Christians to feel it too.
Not so broken sinners would believe themselves permanently filthy.
But so wandering hearts would finally understand what they were abandoning…
and Who was calling them home.
The Bible's shocking language is therefore not merely the vocabulary of judgment.
Hidden inside it is the ache of covenant love.
The God who exposes betrayal is also the God who calls sinners to repentance.
The God who names the wound is the God who offers redemption.
And Jesus Christ stands at the center of that redemption.
So perhaps the final question is not:
“Why would the Bible use such an uncomfortable metaphor?”
Perhaps the question is:
What have I been giving to another lover that belongs to Jesus?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Because every share can become a doorway.
Every sincere comment can tell another struggling believer, you are not fighting alone.
Every prayer matters.
Every willing act of generosity can help good work continue.
But never forget what all of it is supposed to point toward.
Not us.
Not a page.
Not merchandise.
Jesus Christ.
The faithful Bridegroom.
The crucified Savior.
The risen King.
The One who still receives repentant sinners.
And here is the line I hope follows you long after you close this article:
Your betrayal may explain how far you wandered—but the scars in the hands of Jesus reveal how far Love came to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THEY THAT WAIT UPON THE LORD SHALL RENEW THEIR STRENGTH” — YOU MAY HAVE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT GOD MEANT BY “WAIT”
paragraphs: “THEY THAT WAIT UPON THE LORD SHALL RENEW THEIR STRENGTH” — YOU MAY HAVE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT GOD MEANT BY “WAIT”
Biblical waiting is not sitting still while your life falls apart. Sometimes the waiting room is the very place where God is rebuilding the person who will eventually walk through the door.
There is a kind of tired that sleep cannot fix.
You know it if you have ever stared at the ceiling after midnight while everyone else seemed to be sleeping peacefully.
Your body was lying down.
But your mind was running.
You prayed.
You waited.
You tried to believe.
Then you prayed again.
And somewhere between the unanswered prayer and another disappointing morning, a question slipped into your heart that you were almost afraid to say aloud:
“God… have You forgotten me?”
Maybe you have been waiting for healing.
Waiting for work.
Waiting for your marriage to change.
Waiting for your child to come back to God.
Waiting for a door to open.
Waiting for the financial pressure to break.
Waiting for freedom from something you have fought privately for years.
Waiting for the grief to become bearable.
Waiting for an answer.
Waiting for direction.
Waiting for God to do something—anything—that proves this painful chapter is not the end of your story.
And perhaps the hardest part is not simply that you are waiting.
It is watching other people move while you remain where you are.
Someone else gets the opportunity.
Someone else announces the pregnancy.
Someone else gets married.
Someone else's ministry grows.
Someone else's prayer appears to be answered.
Someone else posts the testimony you desperately wanted to be yours.
You congratulate them.
You press the heart button.
You tell them, “Praise God.”
And you mean it.
Mostly.
Then you put down the phone, stare into the silence, and whisper something Christians sometimes feel ashamed to admit:
“Lord… when will it be my turn?”
If that sentence has ever lived inside you, Isaiah 40 was written closer to your pain than you may realize.
Because before Isaiah gives us the soaring eagle, he gives us an exhausted people.
Before the promise comes the complaint.
Israel says:
“My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God.”
That is Isaiah 40:27.
In other words:
God does not see what is happening to me.
God has overlooked my case.
God has forgotten where I am.
Sound familiar?
Then comes God's answer.
Not an explanation of every delay.
Not a timetable.
Not a date circled on a calendar.
God gives them something greater.
He gives them a revelation of Himself.
The everlasting God does not grow tired.
The Creator has not lost control.
His understanding has not reached its limit.
And the God who never runs out of strength gives strength to people who have none left.
Then Isaiah arrives at one of the most beloved promises in Scripture:
“וְקוֹיֵ יְהוָה יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ”
Ve-qovei YHWH yachalifu koach.
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength…”
—Isaiah 40:31
The Hebrew matters.
The word translated “wait” comes from קָוָה — qavah.
It carries the sense of waiting, looking for, hoping, expecting.
That changes something.
Biblical waiting is not spiritual laziness.
It is not folding your arms and saying, “Well, I guess God will handle everything.”
It is not refusing responsibility.
It is not abandoning obedience.
It is not doing nothing.
Biblical waiting is living in active dependence upon God when you cannot yet see what God is doing.
It is obedience without visible results.
Prayer without immediate answers.
Faithfulness without applause.
Hope without evidence you can hold in your hands.
It is planting when the ground still looks empty.
It is obeying God today while trusting Him with tomorrow.
That is why waiting can hurt so much.
Because real waiting requires surrender.
And surrender means admitting something our flesh hates admitting:
“I cannot control this.”
You cannot force somebody to love you.
You cannot manufacture God's timing.
You cannot manipulate a prodigal home.
You cannot command tomorrow to arrive today.
You cannot bully a closed door into becoming God's will.
You cannot hurry God.
And sometimes what feels like God withholding something from you is actually God removing your illusion that you were ever in control.
That hurts.
But it can also become holy ground.
Because some of the deepest work God performs in us happens while nothing appears to be happening around us.
Think about Joseph.
He had a dream before he had a prison.
God showed him something about his future, and then Joseph's circumstances seemed to move in precisely the opposite direction.
Betrayed.
Sold.
Falsely accused.
Imprisoned.
Forgotten by a man he had helped.
If Joseph had judged God's faithfulness only by his immediate circumstances, he could have concluded that the dream had died.
But the prison was not the conclusion.
God was still writing.
Think about David.
Anointed as king… then chased through the wilderness.
There was oil on his head while there was still a cave over his head.
Promise did not eliminate process.
David had opportunities to seize what God had promised through sinful means, yet waiting required him to refuse shortcuts.
That is one of the great tests of waiting:
Will you still want God's promise if receiving it requires God's way?
Because desperation can make counterfeits look like answered prayers.
Loneliness can make the wrong relationship look providential.
Financial pressure can make dishonest money look like provision.
Ambition can make compromise look like opportunity.
Impatience can convince you that because God has not moved quickly, you are permitted to move without Him.
But faith says:
I would rather wait with God than arrive somewhere God never sent me.
Maybe somebody reading this needs that sentence tonight.
Do not destroy tomorrow because today feels unbearable.
Do not trade obedience for relief.
Do not call something God's answer merely because it ended your waiting.
Not every open door was opened by God.
Not every opportunity deserves your yes.
Not every relationship is worth keeping.
Not every shortcut leads toward the promise.
Sometimes faith looks less like soaring and more like refusing to leave the place where God told you to stand.
And Isaiah's promise becomes even more beautiful when you notice its progression.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles…”
Wonderful.
“They shall run, and not be weary…”
Powerful.
“They shall walk, and not faint.”
Walk?
After soaring?
After running?
Why finish with walking?
Perhaps because most of the Christian life is lived there.
Not every day feels like an eagle day.
Not every morning feels supernatural.
Sometimes there is no dramatic breakthrough.
No emotional worship moment.
No miraculous phone call.
No sudden answer.
You simply get out of bed.
You pray again.
You open your Bible again.
You forgive again.
You resist temptation again.
You go to work again.
You care for your children again.
You choose honesty again.
You refuse bitterness again.
You repent again.
You trust again.
You take one more step.
And heaven calls that faithfulness.
We celebrate soaring because everyone can see it.
God also sees walking.
Especially when walking costs you everything.
Maybe you are not soaring right now.
Maybe you are barely walking.
Do not despise the walk.
The promise includes you too.
“They shall walk, and not faint.”
Notice also what Isaiah does not say.
He does not say those who wait upon the Lord will never become tired.
Verse 30 has already admitted that even youths become weary and young men stumble.
Human strength has limits.
Your exhaustion does not automatically mean you have failed God.
Sometimes you are exhausted because you have been carrying something heavy for a very long time.
The promise is not that Christians become emotionally indestructible.
The promise points us away from self-sufficiency toward the inexhaustible God.
“יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ — yachalifu koach.”
They will renew their strength.
The strength you need does not have to originate in you.
That is good news for the person who has reached the terrifying sentence:
“I don't think I have anything left.”
Maybe you don't.
But God does.
And perhaps that is exactly where grace becomes more than religious vocabulary.
The Gospel itself confronts our obsession with saving ourselves.
We could not climb our way back to God.
We could not outwork our sin.
We could not perform ourselves into righteousness.
We could not wash away our guilt.
So Jesus Christ came to us.
The sinless Son of God entered our broken world.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of exhausted human beings finally becoming strong enough to reach God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue people who could never rescue themselves.
That is grace.
And perhaps there is another kind of waiting happening right now.
Maybe God has been waiting on you.
You have been asking Him to change your circumstances while He has been exposing your heart.
You want the door opened.
He wants the sin surrendered.
You want relief.
He wants repentance.
You want Him to remove the consequences while you keep protecting the compromise.
You want a new chapter without letting Jesus rewrite the old one.
There are things waiting cannot heal if what God is calling for is repentance.
There are moments when “waiting on God” becomes a spiritual phrase we use to postpone obedience.
If God has already told you to forgive, you do not need another sign.
If Scripture has already called something sin, you do not need another confirmation.
If you know you need to repent, tomorrow is not more holy than today.
Grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace is God's invitation to come out of hiding.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the dishonest money.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the religious performance.
Bring Him the thing you keep deleting from your history but cannot delete from your conscience.
Jesus already knows.
And still He calls sinners to Himself.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you home.
The cross means your scandal does not have to become your final identity.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet grace entered their stories.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes Christ magnificent.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your waiting season has exposed things you did not know were inside you.
Jealousy.
Fear.
Control.
Anger at God.
Envy of other people's blessings.
A dependence on people's approval.
A faith that was strong as long as God behaved according to your timetable.
Do not waste the exposure.
God can use waiting like a mirror.
Not to destroy you.
To show you what needs surrender.
And perhaps years from now you will realize that while you were begging God to change your situation, He was transforming you into someone who could survive the answer.
You thought nothing was happening.
But roots were growing where nobody could see them.
Character was forming.
Discernment was sharpening.
Pride was dying.
Prayer was deepening.
False dependencies were breaking.
Your theology was moving from slogans into scars.
You were learning that God is still God when the prayer is unanswered.
Still good when the door remains closed.
Still worthy when you cannot understand Him.
That kind of faith cannot be manufactured in comfort.
There are things you learn about God in the dark that daylight could never have taught you.
So if you are waiting tonight, do not confuse God's silence with God's absence.
Isaiah's exhausted people feared that their way was hidden from God.
God's response was essentially: I have not become tired. I have not stopped seeing. I have not ceased being God.
Your life is not hidden from Him.
Your tears are not invisible.
Your obedience is not wasted.
Your prayers are not meaningless because the answer has not arrived on your schedule.
Keep walking.
And when you cannot run…
walk.
When you cannot soar…
walk.
When your prayers sound beautiful…
walk.
When your prayers are only, “Jesus, help me”…
walk.
When you feel strong…
walk.
When you are trembling…
walk.
Not because walking earns God's love.
But because grace has given you somewhere to walk toward.
Jesus.
And if you fall?
Return to Jesus.
If you sin?
Repent and return to Jesus.
If you become exhausted?
Return to Jesus.
If you realize you have been running ahead of God?
Stop.
Return to Jesus.
Your hope is not ultimately in your ability to wait perfectly.
Your hope is in the One upon whom you wait.
That distinction can save an exhausted believer from despair.
Be honest.
What are you waiting for?
What has this season exposed in you?
Somebody reading beneath this article may need the evidence of God's faithfulness that your scars can provide.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
You may never know whose midnight prayer meets this message because you pressed Share.
Send it privately to the believer who is exhausted.

Supporting Gospel work can be one expression of Christian generosity, but it should never be given through manipulation or compulsion. Scripture says, “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Everyone can pray.
Many can share.
Someone you know may desperately need what you nearly scrolled past.
But before you leave, remember this:
The eagle is breathtaking.
The running is inspiring.
But maybe the miracle God is giving you today is simpler.
You are still walking.
After everything that tried to break you…
you are still walking.
After prayers that seemed unanswered…
still walking.
After betrayal…
still walking.
After failure…
still walking.
After nights when you wondered whether God could possibly still want you…
still walking.
And perhaps one day you will look behind you and finally understand:
What felt like God making you wait was sometimes God teaching you that when your strength ended, His never did.
Keep your eyes on Jesus.
Your waiting room is not your grave.
And your weakest chapter does not get the final sentence when Christ is holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE FORGOTTEN VERSE BEFORE JEREMIAH 29:11 CHANGES THE ENTIRE MESSAGE
paragraphs: THE FORGOTTEN VERSE BEFORE JEREMIAH 29:11 CHANGES THE ENTIRE MESSAGE
You were probably told, “God has plans to prosper you.” But almost nobody told you what God said one verse earlier—and once you see it, Jeremiah 29:11 may never sound the same again.
There is a verse Christians put on graduation cards.
We print it on mugs.
We frame it.
We underline it when life falls apart.
We whisper it when the doctor calls.
We post it when the relationship ends.
We cling to it when the bank account is nearly empty and heaven seems painfully quiet.
“For I know the plans I have for you…”
Jeremiah 29:11.
Beautiful.
True.
Inspired by God.
But there is something uncomfortable sitting immediately before it.
Something we rarely put on the mug.
Something that changes the emotional weight of the promise without changing its truth.
Jeremiah 29:10.
And once you read verse 10 before verse 11, you realize something breathtaking:
God's promise was not, “You will never enter Babylon.”
It was not, “Believe hard enough and Babylon will disappear.”
It was not, “Your breakthrough is coming next Tuesday.”
God essentially told His people…
You are going to be here for a while.
That changes everything.
The Hebrew text of Jeremiah 29:10 reads:
“כִּי־כֹה אָמַר יְהוָה כִּי לְפִי מְלֹאת לְבָבֶל שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה אֶפְקֹד אֶתְכֶם…”
Ki-kho amar YHWH, ki lefi melot le-Vavel shiv'im shanah, efqod etkhem…
In context:
“For thus says the LORD: When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will attend to you and establish My good word toward you, bringing you back to this place.”
Seventy years.
Now read the famous promise that follows:
“כִּי אָנֹכִי יָדַעְתִּי אֶת־הַמַּחֲשָׁבֹת אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי חֹשֵׁב עֲלֵיכֶם…”
Ki anokhi yada'ti et-hamachashavot asher anokhi khoshev aleikhem…
“For I know the thoughts I am thinking concerning you…”
Then come these extraordinary words:
“מַחְשְׁבוֹת שָׁלוֹם וְלֹא לְרָעָה”
Machshevot shalom velo lera'ah.
Thoughts of shalom, and not of evil or calamity.
“לָתֵת לָכֶם אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה”
Latet lakhem acharit vetiqvah.
“To give you a future and a hope.”
Jeremiah 29:11.
Do you see it?
The promise did not erase the seventy years.
The seventy years stood directly beside the promise.
That means Jeremiah 29:11 was never God's guarantee that His people would experience immediate comfort.
It was God's assurance that their suffering had not canceled His covenant purposes.
They were in Babylon.
And God still knew.
They had lost what was familiar.
And God still knew.
Jerusalem was behind them.
The future looked nothing like the life they had imagined.
And God still knew.
Maybe that is why this verse needs to be rescued from the coffee mug and returned to the exile.
Because perhaps you are living in your own kind of Babylon right now.
Not ancient Babylon.
Your Babylon has a hospital room.
An empty chair.
