Divorce papers.
A child who stopped calling.
A prayer you have prayed so many times that you barely have the strength to pray it again.
A private addiction nobody at church knows about.
A marriage that looks beautiful in photographs but feels painfully lonely behind closed doors.
A ministry wound.
A betrayal.
A funeral.
A diagnosis.
A season where everybody keeps telling you, “God has a plan,” and somewhere deep inside you want to scream:
“Then why does His plan hurt this much?”
Jeremiah 29 does not shame you for asking.
But it does destroy one dangerous assumption:
That if God has good purposes for you, every chapter must feel good while you are living it.
The original recipients of this letter were exiles.
Jeremiah 29:1 identifies the message as a letter sent to people Nebuchadnezzar had carried from Jerusalem to Babylon.
They were displaced.
Homes had been lost.
Their national life had been shattered.
And false prophets were offering something terribly attractive:
A quicker ending.
That detail matters.
Because immediately before the seventy-year statement, God warns His people not to be deceived by prophets speaking falsely in His name.
They wanted a shorter exile.
God gave them the truth.
And sometimes the truth of God hurts before it heals.
The false message says:
“This will all be over immediately.”
The faithful message says:
“God will not abandon you even if it isn't.”
Read that again.
God will not abandon you even if it isn't over quickly.
That may be the Jeremiah 29:11 someone desperately needs tonight.
Because some of us have quietly concluded that God's delay means God's absence.
We prayed.
Nothing moved.
We fasted.
Nothing changed.
We worshiped through tears.
The door stayed closed.
So eventually a poisonous thought crawled into the silence:
“Maybe God forgot me.”
But the people receiving Jeremiah's letter were being told something almost unimaginably difficult.
Build houses.
Plant gardens.
Eat what they produce.
Marry.
Have children.
Multiply.
Seek the shalom of the city where you are living.
Pray for it.
In other words:
Live faithfully in the place you desperately wish God would remove you from.
That is not the Christianity many of us were sold.
We were taught how to celebrate deliverance.
Nobody taught us how to plant gardens in Babylon.
We know how to testify when the cancer disappears.
But what happens when chemotherapy continues?
We know how to praise God when the marriage is restored.
What happens when you prayed and the other person still walked away?
We know how to celebrate when the prodigal comes home.
What happens when another Christmas passes and their chair is still empty?
What happens when obedience doesn't immediately change your circumstances?
You plant.
You pray.
You remain faithful.
You refuse the lie that God's goodness can only be measured by how quickly He changes your situation.
And you remember:
Babylon is not proof that God has forgotten your address.
Sometimes faith looks less like escaping the fire and more like discovering that God has not left you inside it.
Ask Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
Ask Daniel.
Ask Joseph in prison.
Ask Paul and Silas singing with their feet fastened.
And ultimately…
Look at Jesus.
Because if we misunderstand suffering, we will eventually misunderstand the cross.
At Calvary, anyone measuring God's goodness by immediate circumstances would have reached the wrong conclusion.
The Messiah was bleeding.
His disciples were scattering.
Darkness covered the land.
The innocent Son of God hung between criminals.
His enemies appeared victorious.
Hope appeared dead.
And yet God was accomplishing redemption precisely where human eyes could see only catastrophe.
The cross looked like scandal.
God was writing grace.
The tomb looked final.
God was preparing resurrection.
Friday looked like the end.
Sunday exposed how little Friday understood.

This does not mean every painful event in your life is directly equivalent to Israel's exile, nor does it mean Jeremiah 29:11 was originally written as an individualized promise of earthly success to every Christian.
We should not steal the verse from its context to make it say something easier.
The promise was spoken to God's covenant people in a specific historical exile.
But Christians read Jeremiah inside the larger story of the God who keeps His promises—a story culminating in Jesus Christ.
And the pattern is unmistakable:
God's faithfulness is not defeated by waiting.
His sovereignty is not canceled by suffering.
His purposes do not collapse because His people cannot yet see the ending.
And in Christ, the believer's ultimate hope is even greater than returning from Babylon.
It is reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness of sin.
Resurrection.
A kingdom that cannot be shaken.
Eternal life with Christ.
This is why biblical hope is so different from positive thinking.
Positive thinking says, “Everything will work out the way I want.”
Biblical hope says, “Even when it doesn't, Christ is still Lord.”
Positive thinking needs circumstances to cooperate.
Biblical hope survived a crucifixion.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
What if the thing destroying your faith is not that God broke His promise…
but that you unknowingly added a deadline He never gave you?
You thought you would be married by now.
You thought the prayer would be answered by now.
You thought your child would return by now.
You thought you would be healed by now.
You thought the depression of the soul would lift by now.
You thought the ministry would grow by now.
You thought you would understand why by now.
You thought your “Babylon” would be over by now.
And because it isn't, you have begun wondering whether God is still good.
Jeremiah 29:10 whispers into that ache:
The waiting was part of the message.
Not because waiting is pleasant.
Not because suffering is something Christians should romanticize.
Not because pain itself is holy.
But because God's faithfulness is larger than your preferred timeline.
And there is another detail people often stop reading before they reach.
Jeremiah 29:11 is followed by verses 12 and 13.
God does not merely talk about a future.
He talks about Himself.
“You will call upon Me…”
“You will pray to Me…”
“I will hear you…”
“You will seek Me…”
“You will find Me…”
“When you search for Me with all your heart.”
Maybe the greatest promise in Jeremiah 29 was never merely that their circumstances would change.
Maybe the beating heart of the passage is that in exile, they would seek God—and God would allow Himself to be found.
We often want God's plan.
God wants our heart.
We want the future.
God says, “Seek Me.”
We want the door.
God says, “Call upon Me.”
We want Babylon removed.
God says, “I am still here.”
And suddenly Jeremiah 29:11 becomes far more beautiful than the shallow version.
God was not saying:
“I promise nothing painful will happen to you.”
He was revealing:
“Pain will not have the final word over what I have purposed.”
There is a difference.
A massive one.
And the Gospel takes us even deeper.
Your greatest Babylon is not financial hardship.
It is not singleness.
It is not sickness.
It is not rejection.
Our deepest human catastrophe is sin—the rebellion that alienates us from the holy God who made us.
We do not merely need improved circumstances.
We need reconciliation.
We need forgiveness.
We need rescue.
We need a Savior.
And Jesus did not come merely to improve your temporary situation.
He came to save sinners.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Grace does not pretend your scandal never happened.
Grace takes guilty people and gives them a new story through Christ.
Peter denied Him.
Grace rewrote the story.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace rewrote the story.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes, not merely opportunities.
Grace reached him there.
And maybe your story contains pages you wish you could tear out.
Things you did.
Things done to you.
Years wasted.
Promises broken.
Secret compromises.
Private shame.
A version of yourself you hope nobody ever discovers.
Listen carefully.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross because respectable people needed minor improvements.
He went because sinners needed resurrection.
Your sin is serious.
Repentance is necessary.
Judgment is real.
But grace is not a rumor.
The blood of Jesus is enough.
Turn to Him.
Confess what you have hidden.
Stop negotiating with the sin Christ died to free you from.
Stop calling bondage a personality trait.
Stop making peace with what is destroying your communion with God.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
Because the God who spoke hope to exiles is the God whose redemptive story reaches its climax in Jesus Christ.
Maybe you are still in Babylon.
But if you belong to Christ, Babylon does not own the ending.
Maybe you are waiting.
But waiting is not the same thing as being forgotten.
Maybe you cannot see the future.
God never required you to.
He asked you to trust the One who can.
So build faithfully.
Plant faithfully.
Pray faithfully.
Love faithfully.
Repent quickly.
Forgive deeply.
Serve Christ where you are.
Seek God before you seek escape.
And when the enemy whispers, “God abandoned you because this is taking too long,” remember the forgotten verse before Jeremiah 29:11.
Seventy years.
Then the promise.
Waiting…
then restoration.
Exile…
then homecoming.
And centuries later:
A cross…
then an empty tomb.
Scandal…
then grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding behind a smile, don't manufacture a polished Christian answer.
Be honest.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that believers can walk through darkness without Christ abandoning them.
Don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not for an algorithm.
For the person scrolling at 1:17 in the morning who has been asking God whether He forgot them.
Send it to the believer living through their own Babylon.
Send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity promises an easy life.
Send it to the person who knows Jeremiah 29:11 by heart but has never been shown Jeremiah 29:10.
Because there may come a night when you need to read it again.
Not as a purchase of God's favor.
Not as a payment for prayer.
Not as a guarantee of blessing.
And not as a replacement for faithful generosity and responsibility in your local church.

The New Testament teaches that Christian giving is to be willing rather than coerced—“not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Supporting Gospel Warrior should therefore come from conviction and generosity, never spiritual pressure.

But if you genuinely believe this ministry is helping proclaim Christ, strengthen believers, reach struggling people, and put biblical resources into more hands, your voluntary monthly support can help us continue and expand that work.
If you desire to glorify God with your resources, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one expression of Christian generosity—but giving never purchases God's approval.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, you can still help.
Sometimes supporting the spread of the Gospel begins simply by refusing to keep truth to yourself.
Somewhere tonight, somebody is standing in Babylon holding Jeremiah 29:11 and wondering why it doesn't seem to be working.
Give them verse 10.
Give them the context.
Give them the cross.
Give them Jesus.
Because maybe the sentence you thought God forgot to finish is only a chapter He has not finished writing.
Babylon can delay what you see, but it cannot erase what God has spoken—and the cross proves that the darkest page is not necessarily the final page.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: RAHAB WENT FROM JERICHO’S SHAME TO THE GENEALOGY OF JESUS
paragraphs: RAHAB WENT FROM JERICHO’S SHAME TO THE GENEALOGY OF JESUS

They knew her by what she had done. God knew her by what His grace was about to do. And somewhere between a condemned city, a scarlet cord, and the genealogy of Jesus Christ, Rahab became living proof that your worst chapter does not get to write your final sentence.
There are names people whisper.
Names attached to stories nobody wants told at church.
Names carrying reputations.
Names followed by that uncomfortable silence when somebody discovers what the person used to be.
Rahab had one of those names.

Before Scripture remembers her as a woman of faith, before James points to her as an example of faith expressed through action, before Matthew places her name inside the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ...
the Bible introduces her with words that hurt.
The Hebrew text of Joshua 2:1 says:
בֵּית־אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה וּשְׁמָהּ רָחָב
beit-ishshah zonah, u-shemah Rachav.
Literally, the spies entered the house of “a woman, a prostitute, and her name was Rahab.”
The word זוֹנָה — zonah is not sentimental.
Scripture does not airbrush her history.
It does not pretend the scandal never existed.
It does not rewrite the beginning to make the ending more respectable.
Her name was Rahab.
And she was known as a prostitute.
That is where the story introduces her.
But thank God...
that is not where God leaves her.
Maybe that is why her story still reaches into places polished religious language sometimes cannot reach.
Because some people reading this know what it is like to have a past.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe everybody does.
Maybe you have done things you would give anything to undo.
Maybe people remember the version of you that you are desperately trying to leave behind.
Maybe you still hear old accusations when the room gets quiet.
Maybe you love Jesus now, but occasionally you look backward and wonder...
“Can God really use someone who has been where I have been?”
Rahab's answer is written across thousands of years of redemption.
Yes.
But the answer is even more beautiful than that.
God does not merely tolerate repentant sinners at the edge of His story.
Through His grace, He brings sinners near.
Jericho was waiting for judgment.
Israel had crossed into a new generation. The people of Canaan had heard what the LORD had done. The reputation of Israel's God had traveled ahead of Israel's armies.
And inside the walls of Jericho lived Rahab.
When two Israelite spies entered the city, they came to her house.
The king learned that spies were there and demanded that Rahab surrender them.
Suddenly the woman with the scandalous reputation stood at the intersection of two kingdoms.
Jericho was on one side.
The God of Israel was on the other.
And Rahab had to decide whom she believed.
That is the moment beneath the moment.
This story is not powerful merely because Rahab hid two spies.
It is powerful because something had already happened inside her heart.
Listen to what she confessed in Joshua 2:9–11.
She had heard what the LORD had done.
She knew about the Red Sea.
She knew about the defeat of the kings east of the Jordan.
Jericho had heard the same reports.
But Rahab responded differently.
Others heard and trembled.
Rahab heard...
and believed.
Then came her extraordinary confession:
“The LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath.”
Think about who said that.
Not an Israelite priest.
Not Joshua.
Not someone raised around the tabernacle.
Rahab.
A Canaanite woman.
A prostitute.
A woman living inside a city marked for judgment looked beyond the walls surrounding her and recognized the sovereignty of the living God.
She did not have a spotless résumé.
She had faith.
And generations later, when Hebrews 11 assembled that breathtaking gallery of men and women remembered for faith, Scripture did something Jericho probably never would have imagined.
It put Rahab there.
The Greek begins:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη...
Pistei Rhaab hē pornē...
“By faith, Rahab the prostitute...”
There is something almost painfully beautiful about those words.
Πίστει — pistei — “by faith.”
Scripture still acknowledges where she came from.
But now another description stands in front of her name.
By faith.
Her history had not magically become good.
Grace does not call evil good.
Redemption is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The Gospel is infinitely more powerful than denial.
God deals with sin so seriously that the Son of God went to the cross.
Jesus did not die to convince us that sin was harmless.
He died because sin was deadly.
At Calvary, justice and mercy meet.
Christ bears the judgment sinners deserve, and everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives something no human being can earn:
forgiveness.
Grace.
Reconciliation.
A new identity in Christ.
This is why Rahab's story should never become a shallow slogan saying, “Your past doesn't matter.”
Your past does matter.
Sin matters.
Wounds matter.
Consequences matter.
Truth matters.
But your past is not more powerful than the grace of God.
That changes everything.
Rahab asked the spies to spare her family.
They gave her a sign.
A scarlet cord.
She was to tie it in the window through which she helped them escape.
Then came the waiting.
Imagine it.
A scarlet cord hanging from the window.
Outside, Israel approached.
Inside, Rahab gathered her family.
Then Israel marched.
Once.
Again.
Again.
Day after day.
Jericho's walls still looked invincible.
Perhaps someone inside Rahab's house looked through that window and wondered whether trusting the God of Israel had been madness.
But the cord remained.
Then came the seventh day.
The priests.
The trumpets.
The shout.
The walls collapsed.
Jericho fell.
Judgment came.
But Rahab and those gathered with her were brought out alive.
Do not rush past that.
The woman who once belonged to Jericho survived Jericho's fall because she had placed herself in faith with the God whom Jericho resisted.
Hebrews 11:31 remembers it:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη οὐ συναπώλετο...
“By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish...”
By faith.
Not because prostitution saved her.
Not because deception saved her.
Not because she accumulated enough moral achievements to erase her history.
Her faith was in the true God, and that faith did not remain theoretical.
It moved.
It acted.
It risked.
It obeyed.
That is why James reaches back to Rahab when teaching that genuine faith is demonstrated by works.
James 2:25 calls her:
Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη
Rhaab hē pornē.
Rahab the prostitute.
Then James points to what she did—receiving the messengers and sending them out another way.
James is not teaching that Rahab purchased salvation with a courageous deed.
He is showing us the character of living faith.
Real faith does not remain a religious sentence in your mouth while nothing changes in your life.
Living faith bears fruit.
Rahab believed...
and then she acted like what she believed was actually true.
That is where her story becomes uncomfortable for us.
Because it is possible to know Christian vocabulary without surrendering to Christ.
It is possible to share Bible verses while hiding cherished sin.
It is possible to attend church while maintaining a secret life.
It is possible to say “Lord, Lord” and still resist His lordship.
Rahab did not have generations of Christian tradition behind her.
She heard.
She believed.
And when the moment arrived, her allegiance changed.
Maybe that is the question this story has been quietly carrying toward you.
Has yours?
Not, “Are you religious?”
Not, “Do you believe God exists?”
Not, “Do you occasionally read Christian posts?”
Who owns your allegiance?
Because Jesus did not come merely to decorate your old life with religious language.
He came to save sinners.
To call us to repentance.
To reconcile us to God.
To make us new.
There comes a moment when faith must become more than admiration for Jesus.
The King calls us to Himself.
Maybe your Jericho is not a physical city.
Maybe it is the life you have built around something God has been asking you to surrender.
A hidden addiction.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Dishonesty.
Greed.
Secret compromise.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A carefully maintained Christian image covering a starving soul.
Everybody sees the walls.
Only you and God know what is happening inside them.
And perhaps you have been thinking:
“I'll come back when I clean myself up.”
Rahab destroys that excuse.
She did not become an Israelite with an impressive history and then decide to trust God.
She trusted the God who could give her a future she did not deserve.
That is grace.
And then...
Matthew opens his Gospel.
Most people are tempted to hurry through the genealogy.
Abraham begat Isaac.
Isaac begat Jacob.
Name after name.
Generation after generation.
Until suddenly...
there she is.
Matthew 1:5 in Greek reads:
Σαλμὼν δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Βόες ἐκ τῆς Ῥαχάβ...
“Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab...”
Rahab.
Read it again.
Rahab.
The woman introduced in Joshua as אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה — ishshah zonah, a woman who was a prostitute...
is now named in Matthew's genealogy.
She became the mother of Boaz.
Boaz became the father of Obed through Ruth.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
And through the unfolding messianic line recorded by Matthew...
comes Jesus Christ.
Do you understand how staggering that is?
Jericho would have known her scandal.
Scripture records her faith.
And Matthew records her name in the family line leading to the Messiah.
She went from a house in the wall of a condemned city...
to the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Only God writes stories like that.
From scandal...
to grace.
Not because Rahab became the hero of the Bible.
Jesus is the Hero.
Rahab needed mercy.
David needed mercy.
Ruth needed redemption.
Abraham needed grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
Every road of biblical redemption eventually forces our eyes away from human achievement and toward the faithfulness of God.
And ultimately toward Christ.
Jesus entered a human family line filled with complicated people and broken stories.
Then the sinless Son of God walked toward a cross.
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Pierced.
Crucified.
And there He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel does not tell you to save yourself.
It announces that the Savior has come.
That means the deepest question is not whether your past is ugly.
The question is what you will do with Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have spent years believing your scandal disqualified you.
Maybe someone called you filthy.
Maybe someone used your worst season as your permanent name.
Maybe you did it to yourself.
You remember what you were.
God knows too.
And still the Gospel calls sinners to come.
Not to pretend.
Not to perform.
Not to hide.
To repent.
To believe.
To receive mercy through Jesus Christ.
Rahab's story does not give us permission to celebrate sin.
It gives sinners a reason to run toward God.
There is a difference.
Grace is not God approving the chains.
Grace is God breaking them.
Grace does not say, “Stay where you are.”
Grace says, “Come out.”
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace makes restoration possible.
And perhaps someone reading this has reached that exact moment.
You are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of carrying two identities.
Tired of telling everybody that you are okay.
Tired of hiding something that is quietly consuming you.
Then stop running from the One who already knows.
Jesus is not shocked by the chapter you are afraid to show Him.
Bring it into His light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to write the details publicly.
Or simply:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Let that comment become more than engagement.
Let it mark a moment of honesty.
Somebody scrolling beneath you may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people whose hope is Jesus.
And before you leave, think of one person who believes their past has made them unreachable.
You know who they are.
Maybe they walked away from church.
Maybe shame convinced them God does not want them anymore.
Maybe they are smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Or send this privately with four words:
“Please read this tonight.”

Not merely because sharing helps this ministry reach more people—although it genuinely does—but because somewhere in your circle may be a Rahab standing inside their own Jericho, convinced judgment is the only ending available to them.
Let them hear about Jesus.
There may come a night when your old accusations return and you need to remember that Scripture itself contains the name Rahab in Hebrews 11's testimony of faith and in Matthew's genealogy of Christ.
Not as a purchase of God's favor.
Not as proof that you love Jesus.
Not as a replacement for faithful stewardship, generosity, or giving according to biblical conviction.
Grace cannot be bought.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
But voluntary generosity can help Gospel-centered ministry continue.
do not miss Jesus while reading Rahab.
That would be the greatest tragedy.
Rahab's story is not ultimately about becoming respectable.
It is about the mercy of God toward someone who believed Him.
It is about faith that moved.
It is about judgment escaped through God's mercy.
It is about an outsider brought near.
It is about a ruined reputation that could not prevent divine redemption.
And it points beyond Rahab to the greater rescue found in Jesus Christ.
So when shame tells you, “Look what you did”...
look to the cross.
When the enemy whispers, “Look where you came from”...
remember where grace can take a surrendered life.
When people insist on introducing you by an old chapter...
remember that Jesus Christ is Lord over the pages still unwritten.
Rahab was once known by Jericho for her shame.
Scripture remembers her for faith.
Matthew records her in the genealogy leading to Christ.
And the Savior who came through that unfolding redemptive history still receives sinners today.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Jesus.
Then live like His grace actually changed something.
Because somewhere tonight...
someone thinks their story is already over.
Rahab's name whispers otherwise.
The walls that witnessed your shame do not get to decide what Jesus can do with your surrendered life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HUSBANDS, STOP HURTING THE WOMAN YOU SAY YOU LOVE.”
paragraphs: “HUSBANDS, STOP HURTING THE WOMAN YOU SAY YOU LOVE.”
Colossians 3:19 contains only a handful of words—but one of them confronts a kind of marital cruelty that can hide behind closed doors, Christian language, and even a man’s claim to “lead” his home.
There is a kind of pain nobody sees on Sunday morning.
She walks into church beside him.
She smiles.
He shakes hands.
They sit together.
They may even open the same Bible.
Nobody knows what happened in the car.
Nobody heard his tone last night.

Nobody saw her standing silently in the kitchen after another cutting remark, wondering how the man who once promised to cherish her became the person whose footsteps make her emotionally brace herself.
There may be no bruise anyone can photograph.
No shattered furniture.
No police report.
Just words.
Coldness.
Contempt.
Mockery.
Constant criticism.
A temper everyone in the house has learned to navigate.
A wife slowly discovering that silence sometimes feels safer than honesty.
And then, sitting quietly in Scripture, comes a command so direct that a husband cannot honestly read it and pretend God has nothing to say about how he treats his wife:
“Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.”
—Colossians 3:19, KJV
The Greek is even more revealing:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας καὶ μὴ πικραίνεσθε πρὸς αὐτάς.
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas kai mē pikrainesthe pros autas.
“Husbands, love your wives, and do not be embittered toward them.”
That word matters.
πικραίνεσθε — pikrainesthe.
It comes from language associated with becoming bitter, embittered, irritated, or harsh.
Paul does not merely tell a husband what he must do.
He confronts what he must refuse to become.
Because sometimes the destruction of a marriage does not begin when a husband stops saying, “I love you.”
Sometimes it begins when his love becomes mixed with bitterness.
When tenderness becomes irritation.
When correction becomes humiliation.
When leadership becomes control.
When disagreement becomes punishment.
When silence becomes a weapon.
When sarcasm becomes normal.
When she has to study his face before deciding whether it is safe to speak.
And a man can call himself a Christian while slowly becoming harsh toward the very woman God commanded him to love.
Read the verse again.
“Husbands, love your wives…”
The command is ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate, from ἀγαπάω — agapaō.
This is not merely romantic emotion.
Biblical love is not reduced to butterflies, chemistry, attraction, or the feeling a man had when he first pursued her.
This love acts.
This love gives.
This love seeks another person’s good.
This love refuses to make selfishness its master.
And the New Testament gives husbands an even more staggering picture of what marital love should resemble.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
—Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Read that slowly.
Not:
“Husbands, make sure she knows who is boss.”
Not:
“Husbands, win every argument.”
Not:
“Husbands, demand respect while refusing tenderness.”
Not:
“Husbands, use Scripture to make your wife afraid of disagreeing with you.”
Christ.
Loved.
The church.
And gave Himself.
The model placed before a Christian husband is a crucified Savior.
That changes everything.
Jesus did not demonstrate His authority by selfishly crushing His bride.
He gave Himself for her.
So whenever biblical headship is twisted into permission for intimidation, degradation, coercion, selfish domination, or cruelty, something has gone terribly wrong.
The cross does not give a husband permission to become a tyrant.
The cross calls him to die to himself.
And maybe that sentence hurts.
Maybe you are the husband reading this and remembering things you said that you wish you could pull back out of the air.
Maybe you remember her face changing after you said them.
Maybe you knew exactly where she was vulnerable…
and you aimed there anyway.
Maybe afterward you justified it.
“She started it.”
“She knows how to push my buttons.”
“She should respect me.”
“I was angry.”
“She needed to hear the truth.”
But truth does not need cruelty to become true.
And anger does not magically turn sin into righteousness.
Scripture says:
“Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.”
—James 1:19–20, KJV
Your anger is not automatically God’s anger.
Your volume is not spiritual authority.
Winning an argument is not the same as loving your wife.
Being the husband does not make every reaction righteous.
And saying “I provide for this family” cannot purchase permission to wound the people living inside it.
You can pay every bill and still leave an emotional debt your wife has been carrying for years.
You can put food on the table while starving a marriage of tenderness.
You can protect your house from strangers while making your own family afraid of your temper.
You can know theology and still fail to sound like Jesus when you are angry.
That is what makes Colossians 3:19 so uncomfortable.
God does not merely care whether a marriage remains legally intact.
He cares about what kind of man a husband is becoming inside that marriage.
But husbands are not the only people who need to hear this.
Some wife reading this has spent years wondering whether she is simply “too sensitive.”
Someone repeatedly told you that his cruelty was your fault.
Perhaps every confrontation somehow ended with you apologizing.
Perhaps Scripture itself was thrown at you whenever you tried to describe what was hurting you.
Hear this carefully:
Colossians 3:19 exists because God cares how a husband treats his wife.
Christian marriage is never a biblical excuse for abuse.
A command to love cannot honestly be transformed into permission to terrorize.
And forgiveness does not require pretending evil never happened.
Reconciliation and restored trust are not produced by demanding that an injured person immediately behave as though nothing occurred. Genuine repentance bears fruit.
John the Baptist said:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.”
—Matthew 3:8, KJV
Real repentance is more than:
“Fine. Sorry.”
It is more than tears after consequences arrive.
It is more than flowers after another explosion.
It is more than quoting Scripture when your marriage begins falling apart.
Repentance turns.
Repentance confesses.
Repentance stops defending what God is confronting.
Repentance seeks forgiveness without demanding immediate restoration of trust.
Repentance accepts accountability.
Repentance asks, “How have I wounded you?” and develops enough humility to listen to the answer.

And when patterns involve abuse, threats, violence, coercion, or genuine danger, seeking appropriate outside help and immediate safety is not rebellion against biblical marriage. No person should be pressured to remain in immediate danger simply to preserve appearances.
But there is another husband reading this.
You are not hitting your wife.
You do not threaten her.
You would never describe yourself as abusive.
Yet something inside you knows the Holy Spirit is pressing on an area you have tried not to examine.
The eye rolls.
The dismissive sigh.
The way you speak to her as though she is stupid.
The jokes at her expense.
The constant corrections.
The affection you withhold when she disappoints you.
The days of cold silence.
The comparison to another woman.
The phone receiving more of your attention than your wife.
The apology you refuse to give because your pride cannot survive three words:
I was wrong.
Brother…
what if your marriage does not primarily need you to prove that you are right?
What if it needs you to become more like Christ?
There was a time when you looked at this woman and thanked God she chose you.
You waited for her messages.
You wanted another hour with her.
You noticed things.
You listened.
You were gentle.

Somewhere between courtship and mortgages, children, exhaustion, disappointments, responsibilities, unanswered expectations, and accumulated wounds, familiarity may have turned something precious into something you began taking for granted.
Now imagine losing what you stopped appreciating.
Imagine the empty chair.
The silent room.
The photographs.
The memories.
The realization that there were a thousand ordinary evenings when you could have reached across the distance and said:
“Come here.”
“I’m listening.”
“I’m sorry.”
“Forgive me.”
“I still choose you.”
Do not wait for a funeral to become tender.
Do not wait for separation to become attentive.
Do not wait until her heart has spent years bleeding before deciding her pain matters.
Love her now.
Not because she is flawless.
She isn't.
Neither are you.
Love her because Jesus is teaching you how redeemed men love.
And that is where this becomes Gospel.
Because Colossians 3:19 is not merely another rule for men who need to try harder.
The entire Christian life collapses if all we have is human willpower.
We need Christ.
We need the Savior who does not merely expose sin but saves sinners.
We need the Jesus who walked toward a cross carrying the judgment our sin deserved.
We need grace.
Because some husbands will read this and feel conviction.
Good.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Conviction says:
Bring it into the light.
Condemnation whispers:
Hide. You are beyond redemption.
The Gospel says something far more powerful.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
Not excuse.
Not minimize.
Not rename.
Confess.
There is mercy at the feet of Jesus for the husband finally willing to tell the truth.
There is grace for the proud man who becomes humble.
There is forgiveness for the man who has failed.
There is transformation for the man who stops asking Jesus merely to improve his marriage and begins asking Jesus to transform him.
Maybe tonight your first act of leadership should not be another lecture.
Maybe it should be repentance.
Put the phone down.
Look at your wife.
Do not explain yourself first.
Do not tell her what she did wrong.
Do not attach “but” to your apology.
Tell the truth.
“I have been harsh with you.”
“I have not loved you the way Christ calls me to love you.”
“I have hurt you.”
“I am sorry.”
“Will you forgive me?”
Then understand something important:
She may cry.
She may not immediately believe you.
She may have heard apologies before.
Do not punish her for needing time.
Become the apology.
Let repentance become visible in the way you speak tomorrow.
And next week.
And six months from now.
Let the Gospel reach your tone.
Your temper.
Your jokes.
Your disagreements.
Your spending.
Your sexuality.
Your attention.
Your phone.
Your priorities.
Your pride.
Your private behavior.
Your treatment of the woman you vowed to love.
Because Christianity that transforms a man at church but never reaches the way he speaks to his wife at home has left one of the most important rooms of his discipleship untouched.
And wife…
if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you wish your husband understood these words, Jesus sees you.
Your worth is not determined by another human being’s inability to recognize it.
You were not created merely to absorb someone else’s bitterness.
Bring your pain to Christ, and where serious harm is occurring, bring it into the light with trustworthy, mature help rather than carrying it entirely alone.
And to every unmarried man reading this:
Do not wait until marriage to learn gentleness.
The wedding ring will not crucify your ego for you.
Become now the kind of man who can hear correction without exploding.
Become now the kind of man who can apologize without manipulating.
Become now the kind of man whose strength makes people feel protected rather than intimidated.
Follow Jesus now.
Because someday somebody may place her heart frighteningly close to yours.
Handle it like something God can see.
And He can.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want Scripture to enter the places people hide.
The marriage nobody knows is hurting.
The believer quietly drifting.
The husband fighting pride.
The wife needing biblical encouragement.
The Christian who has learned church language but desperately needs Jesus to invade ordinary life again.
If this article exposed something in you, do not rush past the conviction.
Sit with God.
Pray.
Open Colossians 3 again.
And if necessary, go find the person you wounded.
Be honest.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your pain. But sometimes three honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not fighting alone.
You may never know whose marriage is sitting one conversation away from repentance.
It does not purchase a blessing.
It does not replace obedience to Christ, generosity toward people in need, or faithful giving according to your conscience and biblical convictions.
Christian giving is not supposed to be extracted by spiritual pressure.
Paul wrote:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That is exactly why support should come freely.
Pray.
Share truth.
Live the Gospel.
Send this to someone who needs it.
It would be another heart surrendered to Christ.
Another husband repenting.
Another wife being treated with Christlike tenderness.

Another family discovering that the Gospel is not merely something we believe on Sunday—it is something Jesus intends to carry into the kitchen, the bedroom, the argument, the apology, and every ordinary moment behind the closed doors nobody else sees.
Maybe your story contains chapters you are ashamed of.
Maybe your marriage does too.
Words you cannot retrieve.
Nights you cannot rewrite.
Years you wish you could recover.
But this is the breathtaking scandal of grace:
Jesus Christ specializes in meeting sinners inside stories they cannot repair by themselves.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
And sometimes the first sentence of a redeemed marriage sounds nothing like a sermon.
Sometimes it is simply a husband standing before the woman he wounded, with no excuses left, whispering:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me. Jesus, teach me how to love her.”
Because the strongest husband in the room may not be the man who never bends.
It may be the man finally humble enough to kneel before Christ.
The Gospel does not merely change where a man will spend eternity—it changes how he treats the woman sitting beside him tonight.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A CHRISTIAN HUSBAND BE “INTOXICATED” WITH HIS WIFE’S LOVE?
paragraphs: CAN A CHRISTIAN HUSBAND BE “INTOXICATED” WITH HIS WIFE’S LOVE?
Proverbs Literally Uses That Kind of Language—and What God Says Next Could Rescue a Marriage Before Another Heart Gets Broken
There is a sentence in the Bible that sounds almost too passionate to be sitting in Proverbs.
Not whispered by Hollywood.
Not borrowed from a romance novel.
Not invented by modern relationship culture.
It is Scripture.

And it tells a husband, in language startlingly intimate and unapologetically passionate, to become so captivated by the love of his own wife that some English translations reach for words such as “ravished,” “exhilarated,” “captivated,” or “infatuated” to communicate the Hebrew.
Read that again.
God is not embarrassed by marital desire.
And somewhere there may be a husband who desperately needs to hear that.
Because maybe you still love your wife...
but somewhere between bills, children, exhaustion, disagreements, disappointments, ministry, work, phones, responsibilities, aging bodies, unresolved wounds, and ordinary Tuesday nights...
you stopped delighting in her.
You became roommates who remember being lovers.
You became business partners managing a household.
You can discuss groceries.
School fees.
Schedules.
Problems.
Church.
Children.
Money.
But somewhere along the road, something disappeared.
The laughter became less frequent.
The touches became predictable.
The conversations became functional.
And the woman you once could barely stop thinking about became someone you sometimes barely notice.
Then Proverbs 5 walks into that quiet distance and says something astonishing.
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then comes verse 19:
“...let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is the language of the King James Version.
But look underneath the English.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 5:18 reads:
יְהִֽי־מְקוֹרְךָ֥ בָר֑וּךְ וּ֝שְׂמַ֗ח מֵאֵ֥שֶׁת נְעוּרֶֽךָ׃
Yəhi məqorkha barukh, usəmaḥ me’eshet nə‘urekha.
In straightforward English:
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
Then Proverbs 5:19 says:
אַיֶּ֥לֶת אֲהָבִ֗ים וְֽיַעֲלַת־חֵ֥ן דַּ֭דֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּ֣ךָ בְכָל־עֵ֑ת בְּ֝אַהֲבָתָ֗הּ תִּשְׁגֶּ֥ה תָמִֽיד׃
And that final phrase deserves our attention:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Bə’ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
“In her love... tishgeh... continually.”
That word matters.
תִּשְׁגֶּה — tishgeh — comes from the Hebrew root שׁגה (shagah).

It can carry the sense of wandering, reeling, being led away, or being deeply carried along. That is one reason faithful English translations differ in how they express the force of the poetry. The KJV says “ravished.” Other translations use ideas such as being captivated, exhilarated, lost in love, or infatuated.
The Hebrew text unquestionably uses unusually intense language.
But here is what makes it even more powerful.
The same verb appears immediately afterward.
Proverbs 5:20 asks why the son should tishgeh with another woman.
Do you see the contrast?
Scripture is not merely saying,
“Don't commit adultery.”
It gives something richer.
Don't become intoxicated with what does not belong to you.
Become captivated again by the covenant love God has already placed beside you.
That changes the conversation.
Biblical faithfulness is not merely refusing another woman's bed.
It is learning again to treasure your own wife.
It is possible for a man to be physically faithful while becoming emotionally absent.
He never committed adultery.
He never left.
He still pays the bills.
He still comes home.
But his eyes stopped lingering on his wife with affection.
His words stopped making her feel treasured.
His curiosity about her disappeared.
His tenderness slowly died.
And sometimes another kind of betrayal begins long before two bodies ever touch.
It begins when attention wanders.
When imagination wanders.
When private messages become exciting.
When pornography teaches a man to consume bodies instead of cherishing a person.
When comparison quietly poisons gratitude.
When a husband begins giving strangers the emotional energy his wife has been begging to receive.
Proverbs 5 refuses to reduce marital holiness to merely staying out of somebody else's bedroom.
God calls husbands toward something beautiful:
Rejoice in her.
Delight in her.
Return your attention to her.
Cherish her.
Become captivated by covenant love.
And yes...
desire her.
Christianity does not teach that marital sexuality is dirty and reluctantly tolerated by God.
God invented marriage before pornography corrupted desire.
God created the human body before lust distorted it.
God created marital intimacy before entertainment industries commercialized sexuality.
Sin did not invent sex.
God did.
Sin takes God's gifts and tears them away from God's purposes.
And Proverbs 5 does something our culture desperately needs: it places passionate sexuality inside covenant faithfulness.
Not lust without responsibility.
Not bodies without promises.
Not pleasure without holiness.
Not desire without love.
Covenant.
One man.
One woman.
Faithfulness.
Delight.
Belonging.
Joy.
And there is something especially tender about the phrase “the wife of your youth.”
Because youth doesn't remain.
Her face changes.
So does yours.
The body you married at twenty-five will not look identical at fifty-five.
Pregnancy may leave marks.
Illness may leave scars.
Stress may leave evidence.
Gray hairs arrive.
Skin changes.
Strength changes.
Seasons change.
And biblical love says:
I still see you.
Not because time stopped.
Because covenant didn't.
That may be one of the most beautiful things an aging Christian marriage can preach without ever standing behind a pulpit.
“I knew you when we were young...
and I am still choosing you now.”
Imagine being loved like that.
Imagine your wife knowing that she does not have to compete with edited bodies on a screen.
Imagine your husband knowing affection has not been replaced entirely by criticism.
Imagine children growing up watching two imperfect parents repent, forgive, laugh, touch, pray, disagree, reconcile, and keep choosing one another.
That does not mean pretending marriage is always romantic.
Sometimes marriage hurts.
Sometimes trust has been damaged.
Sometimes resentment has accumulated for years.

Sometimes sexual intimacy is complicated by trauma, illness, childbirth, medication, disability, emotional wounds, exhaustion, betrayal, or seasons where professional and pastoral help may be necessary.
Proverbs 5 must never be weaponized to pressure a spouse sexually.
Biblical intimacy is not entitlement.
Love does not demand that another person's body become an instrument for selfish gratification.
Christlike love gives itself.
It listens.
It protects.
It honors.
It serves.
It is patient.
That is where Jesus changes everything.
Because eventually every Christian marriage discovers an uncomfortable truth:
You married a sinner.
And your spouse did too.
Two people enter marriage carrying expectations, insecurities, histories, temptations, wounds, selfishness, and blind spots.
Sooner or later, somebody fails.
Somebody says the cruel thing.
Somebody withdraws.
Somebody forgets.
Somebody becomes selfish.
Sometimes the wound is small.
Sometimes it is devastating.
And this is where a merely romantic vision of marriage collapses.
Because romance alone cannot carry the weight of two sinners for a lifetime.
You need grace.
You need repentance.
You need forgiveness.
You need the Cross.
You need Jesus.
The Gospel does not tell husbands, “Try harder to become perfect men so God will finally love you.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely greater.
Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we could not live.
He bore sin at the Cross.
He died.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him receives forgiveness and new life.
That Gospel changes the way a husband comes home.
Because a man who understands grace can finally say:
“I was wrong.”
No excuses.
No manipulation.
No “but you also...”
Just repentance.
A wife transformed by grace can also repent when she has sinned.
Neither spouse becomes the savior of the marriage.
Jesus remains Savior.
And suddenly marriage becomes something deeper than two people desperately demanding that the other person complete them.
It becomes two forgiven sinners learning how to give away the grace they themselves continually need.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this needs tonight.
Not another marriage hack.
Not another seductive stranger.
Not another secret conversation.
Not another pornography tab.
Not another fantasy about somebody else's spouse.
Not another silent week sleeping beside someone whose heart you no longer know.
Maybe you need to turn around.
Go home emotionally.
Look at the person God entrusted to you.
And begin again.
Not because everything is easy.
Because covenant is worth fighting for.
Husband...
when was the last time you looked at your wife without looking through her?
When was the last time you told her something beautiful that had nothing to do with what she accomplished for you?
When was the last time you asked what was happening inside her heart and actually stayed quiet long enough to hear the answer?
When was the last time you held her without immediately asking for anything?
When was the last time you prayed over her?
When was the last time you thanked God for her?
And wife...
when was the last time your husband knew that you still saw the man inside the responsibilities?
Marriage can become so familiar that we stop being amazed by the person standing beside us.
Proverbs says:
Rejoice again.
Not merely tolerate.
Not merely coexist.
Rejoice.
And notice what comes after Proverbs 5:19.
The chapter does not end with romance.
It returns to accountability before God.
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD...”
That changes everything.
The husband scrolling secretly at midnight is seen.
The private conversation is seen.
The fantasy is seen.
The rationalization is seen.
The lonely wife crying quietly is seen.
The husband starving for affection is seen.
The repentance nobody else knows about is seen.
The couple trying desperately to rebuild is seen.
The person who closed the pornography page and cried out to Jesus is seen.
The husband who confessed what he had hidden is seen.
The wife who chose forgiveness while still establishing wise boundaries is seen.
God sees.
And that truth is terrifying when we want darkness.
But breathtaking when we want restoration.
Because the God who exposes sin is also the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
Maybe your marriage has become a scandal.
Maybe there was adultery.
Pornography.
Deception.
Emotional abandonment.
Bitterness.
Words you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
Years you cannot recover.
Maybe you're reading this thinking,
“You don't understand what happened in our house.”
I probably don't.
But Jesus does.
And grace does not mean pretending the wound never happened.
Forgiveness does not make evil good.
Reconciliation does not eliminate the need for truth, repentance, safety, wisdom, accountability, or consequences.
But the Gospel means your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your entire story.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Cross itself looked like history's darkest defeat.
Then Sunday morning came.
That is what Jesus does.
He walks into graves and starts rewriting endings.
So maybe the first step tonight is not dramatic.
Maybe it is a confession.
“I have been distant.”
“I've been comparing you.”
“I've been selfish.”
“I've stopped pursuing you.”
“I need help.”
“I sinned against you.”
“Please forgive me.”
“I want Jesus to rebuild what I helped damage.”
Those sentences can feel terrifying.
Say them anyway when they are true.
Because hiding feeds darkness.
Grace brings sinners into the light.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, don't turn conviction into shame and run from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Not because typing three words magically changes anything.
But because sometimes honesty begins when someone finally stops pretending.
Someone reading beneath you may realize they are not the only one.
Somebody desperately needs evidence that repentance is still possible, forgiveness is still real, and God is still working in ordinary homes.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
Not because every sentence will apply to every marriage, but because there may come a night when resentment whispers louder than covenant and you need to remember what Scripture actually said:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Be captivated continually by her love.
Send this to your husband.
Send it to your wife.
Send it privately to the brother drifting toward temptation before temptation becomes destruction.
Share it with the couple trying to rebuild.
And yes, share it with the single believer too, because the time to develop a biblical theology of marriage is not after temptation arrives.
If Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, stay close.

We want this community to remain a place where Scripture is opened honestly, sin is confronted without hiding the Cross, wounded people are pointed toward Christ, and believers are continually called deeper into repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation.
Scripture permits Gospel ministry to receive material support, but biblical giving must never be manipulated or coerced. Give freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully.
Jesus cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
But Gospel work can be supported.
Your support helps us keep creating.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
And sharing costs nothing.
Send it to someone. Pray for the ministry. Tell someone about Jesus.
Those things matter deeply too.
do not leave this article merely thinking about Gospel Warrior.
Think about Jesus.
Think about your covenant.
Think about the person sleeping beside you.
Think about what has quietly stolen your attention.
Think about what needs confession.
Think about what needs forgiveness.
Think about what needs rebuilding.
Then remember the strange, beautiful, startling command buried inside Proverbs:
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
Be captivated by her love.
Because the world will continuously offer counterfeit intoxications.
A different body.
A secret screen.
A forbidden conversation.
A fantasy.
An escape.
Something new.
Something hidden.
Something that promises pleasure without covenant and eventually demands a price it never mentioned at the beginning.
But wisdom points home.
Back to covenant.
Back to faithfulness.
Back to repentance.
Back to grace.
Back to the woman you promised to love.
Back to the husband you promised to honor.
And above both of you...
back to Christ.
Maybe the miracle your marriage needs does not begin when your spouse finally becomes everything you wanted.
Maybe it begins when Jesus becomes Lord again over the parts of your heart you quietly took back from Him.
Because sometimes the most dangerous affair begins long before another person enters the room.
It begins when your heart leaves home.
And sometimes restoration begins with something equally quiet:
Your heart comes home again.
The world says the thrill is somewhere else. Wisdom whispers: look again at the covenant God placed beside you—and let Christ teach your wandering heart how to come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID PAUL TELL THE THESSALONIANS TO LEARN HOW TO CONTROL THEIR OWN BODY IN HOLINESS?
paragraphs: WHY DID PAUL TELL THE THESSALONIANS TO LEARN HOW TO CONTROL THEIR OWN BODY IN HOLINESS?
Because the Gospel Was Never Meant to Save Your Soul While Leaving Your Secret Life Untouched — 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5
There is a version of you almost nobody sees.
Not the version that walks into church.
Not the version that posts the Bible verse.
Not the version that says, “God is good” when somebody asks how life is going.
The other one.
The version alone with a phone after midnight.
The version nobody hears negotiating with temptation.

The version that knows exactly which image to search for, which conversation to reopen, which memory to entertain, which person to fantasize about, which door should stay closed—but sometimes reaches for the handle anyway.
And into that private room, the apostle Paul speaks words that can feel painfully direct:
“Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν, ἀπέχεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς πορνείας…”
Touto gar estin thelēma tou Theou, ho hagiasmos hymōn…
“For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality…” — 1 Thessalonians 4:3
Then Paul continues:
“εἰδέναι ἕκαστον ὑμῶν τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι ἐν ἁγιασμῷ καὶ τιμῇ…”
That each of you should know how to possess, govern, or control his own skeuos—his “vessel”—in sanctification and honor.
Then comes the contrast:
“μὴ ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας…”
Not in pathei epithymias—not in the passion of lust—like those who do not know God.
Paul is not merely giving Christians an ancient lesson in sexual etiquette.
He is exposing a battlefield.
And the battlefield is terrifyingly close.
Your body.
Your appetites.
Your imagination.
Your private choices.
Your desires when nobody is watching.

Paul uses the word hagiasmos—sanctification, holiness, consecration. It carries the idea of being set apart for God. He is not describing cosmetic Christianity. He is describing a life increasingly brought under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, “Your body is evil.”
He does not say, “Sexual desire itself makes you filthy.”
He does not say, “If you have ever fallen sexually, God could never want you again.”
He says something far more demanding—and far more beautiful.
Learn.
Learn how to live differently.
Learn how to handle your body in holiness and honor.
That word matters because holiness is not merely something you admire in mature Christians.
It is something the grace of God teaches you to practice.

There is an important translation question here. The Greek word skeuos literally means a “vessel” or “instrument.” Interpreters have historically debated whether Paul means controlling or possessing one’s own body, or whether the expression refers to acquiring or living honorably with one’s wife. The “body” interpretation fits many modern translations and makes strong sense in a passage addressed to believers concerning sexual self-control; the marital interpretation also has historical arguments behind it.
But whichever interpretive question you examine, Paul’s larger point does not become blurry.
Sexuality is not exempt from holiness.
The Christian cannot say, “Jesus has my heart, but my body belongs to me.”
Paul will say elsewhere:

“Flee fornication… What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you… and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body…” — 1 Corinthians 6:18–20, KJV
Read those words again.
“You are not your own.”
That sentence collides violently with the spirit of our age.
Our culture tells us that freedom means obeying whatever desire feels most authentic.
Jesus offers something radically different.
Freedom is no longer being enslaved by what once commanded you.
There is an enormous difference between having a desire and surrendering your throne to it.
You can feel temptation without making temptation your master.
You can experience attraction without turning another human being into an object.
You can have a sexual past without allowing your past to write your future.
You can have fallen last night and still fall before Christ today.
That is where this passage stops being merely uncomfortable and becomes breathtakingly hopeful.
Because Paul is writing to Christians.
People being sanctified.
People learning.
People whose old world had not magically disappeared simply because they believed the Gospel.
Paul does not tell them merely to feel ashamed.
He calls them forward.
Maybe that is exactly what somebody reading this needs to hear.
You hate what you keep doing.
You promised God you would stop.
Then you returned.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You blocked the person.
Then searched the name again.
You cried during worship.
Then lost the battle in private.
And now shame has begun preaching its own gospel to you.
“You are disgusting.”
“You are fake.”
“God must be tired of you.”
“You might as well stop trying.”
Listen carefully.
That is not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not call sin harmless.
But neither does the Gospel tell the sinner that Christ is powerless.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could rename our chains “freedom.”
And He did not rise from the grave so repentant sinners would spend the rest of their lives believing their worst moment has more authority than His cross.
This is why holiness matters.
Not because holiness purchases salvation.
Jesus purchases sinners.
Not because controlling your body earns the love of God.
The cross demonstrates a love you could never earn.
Not because Christians become acceptable to God by constructing an impressive record of sexual purity.
We are reconciled to God through Christ.
Holiness is not the entrance fee for grace.
Holiness is what grace begins producing in the person grace has rescued.
That changes everything.
Paul says God’s will is your hagiasmos.
Your sanctification.
Not simply your reputation.
Not simply that nobody catches you.
Not simply that you become better at deleting browser histories.
God wants something deeper than concealed behavior.
He wants transformed desire.
He wants the secret room too.
Because Jesus is not interested in becoming the decorative Savior hanging on the wall of your public life while another master occupies your private life.
He is Lord.
And perhaps that explains why Paul immediately contrasts holiness with people who live “in the passion of lust” and “do not know God.”
Paul connects sexual ethics with knowing God.
That is enormous.
Christian holiness is not merely gritting your teeth harder than everybody else.
It grows from knowing Someone.
When God becomes more than an idea…
when Christ becomes more precious than the appetite…
when you begin seeing another person not as material for your fantasy but as someone bearing God-given dignity…
when your body becomes something entrusted to you rather than something whose impulses must always be obeyed…
the battle begins changing.
Not always instantly.
Sometimes painfully.
Sometimes with tears.
Sometimes through confession.
Sometimes through accountability.
Sometimes by fleeing instead of pretending you are strong enough to stand beside temptation and negotiate.
Sometimes holiness looks surprisingly unspiritual.
Turning the phone off.
Leaving the room.
Ending the conversation.
Blocking the account.
Refusing the second glance.
Confessing to a mature believer.
Installing accountability.
Changing the routine.
Ending a relationship that continually drags you away from Christ.
Jesus Himself spoke radically about removing occasions of sin. Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible after falling.
Repentance turns.
And some of us have been asking God to remove a temptation while continuing to feed it every night.
We pray, “Lord, make me strong.”
Then keep the doorway unlocked.
We pray, “Jesus, deliver me.”
Then preserve the secret access.
We pray for freedom while protecting the chain.
Paul says learn to govern your vessel in holiness and honor.
There is dignity in that word timē—honor.
Biblical sexual holiness is not hatred of the body.
It is honor.
Your body is not garbage.
The body matters so much to Christianity that the Son of God took on flesh.
Christ was bodily crucified.
Christ bodily rose.
And Christians await resurrection.
Christianity is not the story of God rescuing spirits from meaningless bodies.
God cares what we do with them.
That means your eyes matter.
Your hands matter.
Your bed matters.
Your messages matter.
Your search history matters.
Your relationships matter.
What you do with another person’s body matters.
And what you do with your own matters.
But perhaps your chest tightens reading that because your history is already written.
Maybe purity sounds beautiful until you remember yourself.
The affair.
The pornography.
The hookup.
The secret relationship.
The years of compromise.
The messages you hope nobody ever discovers.
The things done to you.
The things you willingly did.
The line you crossed.
Then crossed again.
Maybe you are wondering whether an article about holiness has anything left to say to somebody whose story already contains scandal.
Yes.
It has one Name left to say.
Jesus.
Jesus Christ does not specialize in polishing people who already look clean.
He saves sinners.
The woman exposed in adultery encountered both mercy and a summons away from sin.

The sexually immoral in Corinth were reminded that some of them had once been defined by patterns of sin—but they had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Not condemnation without hope.
Not grace without transformation.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Jesus does not look at repentance and say, “Pretend it never happened.”
He says, in effect, “It does not have to own you anymore.”
That is why your scandal does not get the final sentence.
Grace does.
But grace does not merely erase guilt and then return you unchanged to the same prison.
Grace opens the door and says:
Come out.
Maybe you have fallen a hundred times.
Then repentance begins again today.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Stop making peace with what crucified your Savior.
Stop calling bondage a personality trait.
Stop measuring the power of Christ by the number of times you have failed.
Your repeated failure proves your weakness.
It does not prove His weakness.
And do not confuse conviction with condemnation.
Conviction says, “This is killing you. Come back to Christ.”
Condemnation says, “You are beyond Christ. Hide.”
One leads toward Jesus.
The other drives you deeper into darkness.
There is no healing in pretending.
There is no freedom in renaming sin.
But there is astonishing mercy for the person who finally stops hiding.
So be honest.
Has your body been leading your discipleship instead of Christ?
Has an appetite quietly become a master?
Have you learned how to look Christian while protecting something you know is destroying your communion with God?
Talk to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
If necessary, tell a trustworthy mature Christian today.
If your struggle has become compulsive, seek wise pastoral and professional help rather than fighting indefinitely in isolation.
There is no trophy for hiding successfully.
And there is no shame in needing brothers and sisters to help you walk toward the light.

Paul later says in this same passage that God did not call His people to impurity, but to holiness, and that rejecting this instruction ultimately means rejecting God, who gives believers His Holy Spirit.
Do not miss that final part.
God gives His Holy Spirit.
The command toward holiness comes with the presence of the Holy One.
Christian self-control is therefore not merely self-improvement.
You are not being told to save yourself through discipline.
You are being called to walk by the Spirit because Christ has already accomplished what your moral performance could never accomplish.
The cross deals with guilt.
The resurrection announces a new creation.
The Spirit works transformation.
And sanctification continues.
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes through brutal battles.
But genuinely.
So when temptation whispers, “This is who you are,” remember your identity is not finally determined by your appetite.
When shame whispers, “After everything you've done, you cannot come home,” remember the cross.
When your flesh whispers, “You need this,” remember the empty tomb.
When the enemy whispers, “Hide,” run into the light.
And when you fall, do not build a house on the ground.
Get up.
Confess.
Repent.
Return to Jesus.
Again.
And keep walking.

And if Christ has already been restoring an area of your life you once thought was hopeless, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to interrupt someone else’s despair.
Not because saving a post makes anyone holy, but because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction sounded like when our minds were clear.
Come back to these words when compromise starts sounding reasonable again.
You may never know who reads it at 2:13 in the morning.
You may never know whose finger stops scrolling.
You may never know who was one decision away from returning to an old bondage when these words reminded them that Jesus is still calling them toward the light.
Some battles deserve privacy, dignity, and compassion.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to explore the Gospel.
Let that support be voluntary worship—not pressure.
Scripture says Christian giving should come from what a person has decided in the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
It is not.
It does not.
Your obedience belongs to Christ, not to this ministry.
Do not admire holiness from a distance.
Do not merely share an article about surrender while refusing to surrender.
Do not publicly defend biblical purity while privately feeding what is destroying you.
Go to Christ.
Because Paul’s command was never merely, “Control yourself better.”
It was a summons to become what the Gospel says you now are:
Someone who belongs to God.
Someone whose body matters.
Someone whose desires no longer deserve the throne.
Someone being sanctified.
Someone purchased at a price.
Someone in whom the Holy Spirit is at work.
Someone whose worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
And perhaps tonight, somewhere behind a locked door, with tears nobody else will ever see, the most powerful prayer you can pray is not eloquent at all.
“Jesus… this part too.
You can have this part too.”
Because the secret you surrender to Christ today does not have to become the scandal that destroys you tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THERE IS A WAY THAT SEEMS RIGHT TO A MAN…” — THE TERRIFYING DANGER OF TRUSTING WHAT FEELS RIGHT
paragraphs: “THERE IS A WAY THAT SEEMS RIGHT TO A MAN…” — THE TERRIFYING DANGER OF TRUSTING WHAT FEELS RIGHT
The most dangerous road may not look evil. It may feel peaceful, reasonable, justified—even blessed. And that is exactly why Scripture warns us about it.
There are decisions you regret because you knew they were wrong when you made them.
And then there are decisions that frighten you years later because, at the time, they felt completely right.
You had peace about it.
You prayed about it.
You talked yourself through it.
Your friends agreed with you.
Your emotions confirmed it.
Every door seemed to be opening.
You told yourself, “Surely God wouldn’t let me feel this strongly if this weren’t His will.”
And then somewhere down the road, everything began falling apart.
Not because God failed you.
Not because Scripture stopped being true.
But because there is something the Bible has been warning humanity about for thousands of years:
You can be completely sincere…
and completely wrong.
That sentence should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because one of the most dangerous lies of our generation is also one of the most comforting:
“Follow your heart.”
It sounds beautiful.
It fits on coffee mugs.
It belongs underneath sunset photographs.
It feels compassionate, empowering, liberating.
But there is a problem.
God never told you that your heart was qualified to be your god.
And the book of Proverbs gives us a warning so serious that Scripture records essentially the same proverb twice, in Proverbs 14:12 and Proverbs 16:25:
“יֵשׁ דֶּרֶךְ יָשָׁר לִפְנֵי־אִישׁ וְאַחֲרִיתָהּ דַּרְכֵי־מָוֶת”
Yesh derekh yashar lifnei-ish, ve’acharitah darkhei-mavet.
There is a way that is right before a man…
but its end is the ways of death.
Look carefully at what God does not say.
He does not merely warn about a way that looks wicked.
He warns about a way that appears יָשָׁר — yashar.
Straight.
Right.
Upright.
Correct.
That is what makes this verse terrifying.
The road does not necessarily have a skull painted on the entrance.
Sometimes it has flowers.
Sometimes it has applause.
Sometimes it has opportunity.
Sometimes it has chemistry.
Sometimes it has money.
Sometimes it has relief.
Sometimes it has religious language.
Sometimes it even feels like peace.
And still…
it can end in death.
Maybe you know that road.
Maybe you stayed in something because leaving felt cruel.
Maybe you entered a relationship because loneliness hurt more than compromise did.
Maybe you walked away from someone because your anger felt justified.
Maybe you withheld forgiveness because what they did really was terrible.
Maybe you kept the secret because telling the truth threatened everything you had built.
Maybe you called lust “love.”
Maybe you called greed “ambition.”
Maybe you called gossip “concern.”
Maybe you called bitterness “discernment.”
Maybe you called cowardice “protecting my peace.”
Maybe you called disobedience “following my heart.”
Maybe you even found people who would agree with you.
That is the frightening thing about deception.
If deception felt like deception, very few people would embrace it.
Deception succeeds because falsehood can feel true.
The first great human rebellion in Genesis did not begin because Eve looked at the forbidden fruit and thought, “I want destruction.”
She saw something desirable.
Something that appeared beneficial.
Something that seemed capable of making her wise.
The serpent did not need to convince humanity to hate goodness.
He only needed humanity to redefine goodness apart from God.
And we have been doing it ever since.
“I feel…”
“I think…”
“I deserve…”
“I don’t see anything wrong with…”
“This makes me happy…”
“This is my truth…”
Listen carefully.
Your feelings are real.
But real feelings are not necessarily reliable authorities.
Pain is real.
Attraction is real.
Anger is real.
Fear is real.
Desire is real.
Loneliness is real.
Confusion is real.
None of that means those feelings should sit on the throne.
Feelings can tell you something is happening inside you.
They cannot, by themselves, tell you what is holy.
That belongs to God.
Jeremiah 17:9 describes the human heart with uncomfortable honesty:
“עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל”
‘Aqov halev mikkol…
The heart is deceitful above all.
That does not mean every emotion you experience is sinful.
It means fallen human beings cannot safely treat inner desire as an infallible compass.
We need revelation.
We need truth outside ourselves.
We need the Word of God.
And ultimately, we need Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the story of good people learning to trust themselves more.
It is the story of lost people being rescued by Someone they desperately needed.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your instincts.
He came to save you.
There is a difference.
And perhaps this is where the knife turns.
Because sometimes what “feels right” is exactly what keeps us from repentance.
Repentance has never depended on whether confession feels comfortable.
Forgiving someone may not feel fair.
Walking away from sin may not feel liberating at first.
Ending an ungodly relationship may feel like your heart is being ripped apart.
Confessing what you have hidden may feel terrifying.
Returning what does not belong to you may feel humiliating.
Apologizing when your pride has built an entire courtroom proving you were justified may feel unbearable.
Obeying God sometimes hurts before it heals.
Ask Peter.
Jesus told His disciples that He would suffer, be killed, and rise again.
Peter did what probably felt loving.
He objected.
Surely protecting Jesus was the right thing.
Surely suffering could not be God's plan.
Surely preventing the cross was compassionate.
Yet Peter's human reasoning collided with the redemptive purpose of God.
Imagine that.
A man could love Jesus…
and in the same moment oppose the road Jesus had come to walk.
That should humble every Christian who has ever said, “But I have peace about it.”
Peace matters.
But “I feel peaceful” is not a replacement for “It is written.”
Circumstances matter.
Counsel matters.
Wisdom matters.
Conscience matters.
But none of them outrank the revealed character and Word of God.
Sometimes an open door is simply an open door.
Jonah found a ship going exactly where he wanted to go while running from what God had commanded him to do.
Availability is not automatically approval.
Convenience is not confirmation.
Difficulty is not automatically prohibition.
And emotional relief is not always the peace of Christ.
There are moments when obedience will cost you the very thing your flesh is begging you to keep.
And then there is Jesus in Gethsemane.
This is where our shallow definition of “follow your heart” collapses.
Jesus knew what was coming.
Betrayal.
Mockery.
Scourging.
Nails.
Suffocation.
Blood.
The cross.
And in the anguish of Gethsemane, He prayed in submission to the Father’s will.
Jesus did not teach us that holiness means doing whatever feels easiest.
He showed us obedience.
And He walked toward Calvary.
For us.
Think about that.
The road that looked like defeat became the road of victory.
The cross looked like scandal.
God turned it into the place where grace was proclaimed to sinners.
The tomb looked final.
Then Sunday morning came.
And suddenly the entire story changed.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely make bad people behave better.
He raises the spiritually dead.
He forgives the guilty.
He cleanses the stained.
He welcomes the repentant.
He restores the broken.
He takes stories people thought were permanently ruined and writes grace across pages soaked in shame.
That is why you cannot build your life on what merely seems right.
You need the One who is right.
Jesus did not say, “Discover whatever path feels true to you.”
He said:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”
The Christian faith is radically Christ-centered because salvation is not found by looking deeper into ourselves until we discover our own truth.
We look to Christ.
And perhaps you are reading this with something already burning in your conscience.
You know what it is.
Nobody else needs to know for this moment to matter.
That relationship.
That conversation.
That hidden browser history.
That bitterness.
That habit.
That secret.
That compromise.
That private justification you keep rehearsing because somewhere beneath all the excuses you already know what obedience would require.
Maybe you have been asking God to approve something He has already addressed.
Maybe you have been asking for another sign because you do not like the answer Scripture already gave you.
Maybe you have confused God's patience with God's permission.
