That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus does not say your sin is insignificant.
He says His blood is sufficient.
Repentance is not pretending nothing happened.
Repentance brings what happened into the light and turns toward Christ.
Grace does not say, “Keep playing with fire because Jesus forgives.”
Grace says:
“You don't have to live beside the fire anymore.”
Maybe you need to end a conversation.
Maybe you need to confess something to your spouse.
Maybe you owe someone an apology because you knowingly played with their emotions.
Maybe you need to stop calling lust “chemistry.”
Maybe you need to stop calling emotional infidelity “friendship.”
Maybe you need to stop calling manipulation “flirting.”
Or maybe your situation is genuinely innocent, and what you need is not guilt but wisdom.
Then walk in wisdom.
Be honest.
Be honorable.
Be clear.
If you like someone and both of you are free to pursue a relationship, you do not need manipulation.
You do not need sexual pressure.
You do not need mind games.
You do not need to manufacture jealousy.
You do not need to keep three other people emotionally interested in case your first choice fails.
Christian romance should increasingly produce clarity, honor, self-control, truthfulness, and love—not confusion deliberately maintained for attention.
And if you are married, guard what belongs to your covenant.
Your spouse should not have to compete with a secret emotional world you built with somebody else.
Marriage rarely collapses because two strangers suddenly wake up one morning and commit adultery without anything preceding it.
Boundaries are often crossed in inches before they are crossed in miles.
A joke.
A private message.
A personal confession.
A compliment you should not have needed from them.
A conversation you begin hiding.
A connection you defend more passionately than you protect your marriage.
Then one day someone says:
“We never meant for this to happen.”
Perhaps not.
But wisdom asks whether we kept walking toward the place where it could.
This is why guarding your heart is not legalism.
It is love.
You guard your heart because Christ purchased you.
You guard another person's heart because Christ loves them.
You guard your marriage because covenant matters.
You guard your sexuality because your body belongs to the Lord.
You guard your intentions because holiness is not merely what people see.
So...
Is flirting a sin?
There is no biblical command that declares every behavior we call “flirting” inherently sinful.

But flirting becomes morally dangerous—and may become sinful—when it cultivates lust, deception, sexual impurity, manipulation, marital unfaithfulness, dishonorable intentions, or knowingly exploits another person's emotions.
The better question is not simply:
“Can a Christian flirt?”
Ask instead:
“Can I do this before Jesus with a clean conscience, truthful intentions, self-control, love for this person's soul, and genuine concern for their holiness as well as mine?”
That question is harder.
It is also safer.
And perhaps tonight there is one name already sitting inside your mind.
You know exactly why.
Don't run from conviction.
Run to Christ.
There is mercy there.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to tell strangers every private detail. But you can make a simple confession of dependence on Christ.
And if you feel spiritually exhausted and need other believers to pray for you, simply write:
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become reminders that Christians do not have to fight hidden battles alone.
Then think of one person who needs this conversation.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Someone you love.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions feel negotiable tomorrow.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen.
It does not.
Not because anyone should be pressured into giving.
Scripture says giving should come from a heart that has freely decided to give, “not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
But voluntary generosity can be one genuine way believers support Gospel work they believe is bearing fruit.
Pray.
Send it privately to somebody whose heart may need it tonight.
Because sometimes the message you almost didn't share becomes the message somebody desperately needed before making a decision they could regret for years.
And above everything else...
come back to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Now.
Bring Him the flirtation.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the broken marriage.
Bring Him the secret conversation.
Bring Him the hunger to be desired.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the person you have become when nobody is watching.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive grace where grace is offered.
Make restitution where love requires it.
Set boundaries where wisdom demands them.
Then get up and walk with Christ again.
Because your worst conversation does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Your failure does not have to become your identity.
Your scandal does not have to become your ending.
The heart that once chased attention can become the heart that finally learns it was Christ it was hungry for all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “PRIDE GOES BEFORE A FALL”—THAT’S NOT EXACTLY WHAT PROVERBS 16:18 SAYS
paragraphs: “PRIDE GOES BEFORE A FALL”—THAT’S NOT EXACTLY WHAT PROVERBS 16:18 SAYS
You’ve probably quoted it. But the words we shortened may be warning us about something far more terrifying than embarrassment.
There is a sentence almost everyone knows—even people who rarely open a Bible.
“Pride goes before a fall.”
We say it when someone gets arrogant and loses.
We say it when a celebrity destroys his reputation.
We whisper it when the person who thought he was untouchable suddenly discovers that he wasn’t.
Sometimes we even say it with a little satisfaction.
See?
Pride goes before a fall.
Except that is not exactly what Proverbs 16:18 says.
And when you read what the Hebrew actually says, the warning becomes heavier.
Much heavier.
Because Scripture is not merely warning you that arrogance might eventually embarrass you.
It is warning you that there is a posture of the soul that can quietly walk in front of destruction.
And perhaps the most frightening thing about pride is that you can recognize it immediately in somebody else...
while remaining almost completely blind to it in yourself.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 16:18 reads:
לִפְנֵי־שֶׁבֶר גָּאוֹן וְלִפְנֵי כִשָּׁלוֹן גֹּבַהּ רוּחַ
Lifnei-shever ga'on; velifnei kishalon govah ruach.
A close rendering is:
“Before destruction is pride, and before stumbling, a haughty spirit.”
The familiar English wording “pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” captures the Hebrew parallelism well. But notice what our shortened proverb usually loses.
Destruction.
The Hebrew word is שֶׁבֶר — shever.
It carries the idea of breaking, fracture, ruin, destruction.
Not merely embarrassment.
Not simply losing an argument.
Breaking.
Then comes the second line.
גֹּבַהּ רוּחַ — govah ruach.
Literally, something like “height of spirit”—an elevated, haughty spirit.
And before what?
כִשָּׁלוֹן — kishalon.
Stumbling. Falling. Collapse.
The proverb is Hebrew poetry. The two lines illuminate each other.
Pride.
Haughtiness.
Breaking.
Stumbling.
Do you feel the weight of it now?
The verse is not a clever ancient way of saying, “Don’t get too confident or life might humble you.”
It is exposing something spiritually dangerous.
Sometimes destruction has footsteps.
And pride may be walking just ahead of it.
That should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because pride does not always look proud.
Sometimes pride walks into church carrying a Bible.
Sometimes it knows theology.
Sometimes it serves.
Sometimes it gives.
Sometimes it posts Scripture.
Sometimes it says, “God told me,” when what it really means is, “Nobody is allowed to question me.”
Sometimes pride does not boast aloud.
It simply refuses correction.
Sometimes pride sounds like:
“I know.”
“I don’t need help.”
“They’re the problem.”
“I already apologized.”
“They should come to me.”
“I deserve better.”
“I would never do what they did.”
And sometimes the most dangerous form of pride is the one wearing religious clothing.
“I’m not like those people.”
Do you hear it?
Jesus did.
He told a story about two men who went to pray.
One was a Pharisee.
One was a tax collector.
The Pharisee was outwardly religious. He fasted. He gave. He could point to visible evidence of moral discipline.
And then came the sentence that exposed him:
“God, I thank you that I am not like other people...” (Luke 18:11).
That is terrifying because his prayer contained the word “God.”
His religion was real enough to get him into the temple...
but his pride was strong enough to make his prayer revolve around himself.
Then, somewhere at a distance, stood the scandalous man.
The tax collector.
The compromised man.
The man respectable religious society had reasons to despise.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beat his chest.
And his prayer was painfully small.
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
No résumé.
No comparison.
No defense.
No list of people worse than him.
Mercy.
That was all he had left.
And Jesus said that man went home justified rather than the other.
That is the scandal of grace.
The man who arrived with nothing but sin and repentance went home with mercy.
The man who arrived impressed with his own righteousness went home exposed by the very righteousness he thought made him superior.
Maybe this is where Proverbs 16:18 stops being something we quote about other people.
Maybe now it begins reading us.
Because pride does not begin when everyone else notices.
Pride begins in hidden rooms.
It begins when correction feels insulting instead of loving.
It begins when apologizing feels like losing.
It begins when someone else’s success feels like your diminishment.
It begins when you secretly enjoy watching someone who hurt you fail.
It begins when you cannot celebrate another person without comparing yourself.
It begins when you become more concerned about appearing holy than becoming holy.
It begins when confession disappears from your prayers because repentance has slowly been replaced by explanation.
It begins when you stop asking, “Lord, search me,” and start asking, “Lord, deal with them.”
And this is why the next verse matters so much.
Proverbs 16:19 immediately gives us the contrast:
“Better to be of a humble spirit with the lowly than to divide the spoil with the proud.”
Better.
God says there is something better than standing among winners if winning requires becoming proud.
Better to kneel with the humble than celebrate with the arrogant.
Better to lose status and keep your soul tender.
Better to be corrected than celebrated into destruction.
Better to say, “I was wrong.”
Better to confess.
Better to repent.
Better to come home.
And now we arrive at Jesus.
Because if this article ends merely with “Try harder to be humble,” we have missed the Gospel.
Christianity is not self-improvement for arrogant people.
The Gospel is much more devastating...
and much more beautiful.
Scripture does not simply tell us to manufacture humility.
It shows us Humility Himself.
Jesus Christ.
Paul writes of Him in Philippians 2.
Christ did not cling selfishly to status. He humbled Himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient even to death on a cross.
Think about that.
The One who had every legitimate reason to be exalted humbled Himself.
We, who have every reason to humble ourselves, spend our lives trying to be exalted.
He descended.
We climb.
He served.
We demand recognition.
He washed feet.
We protect reputations.
He accepted humiliation.
We can barely survive being corrected.
He carried a cross.
We carry grudges.
And still...
He came for us.
That is grace.
Jesus did not go to Calvary because humble people had finally made themselves worthy of salvation.
He went because sinners could not save themselves.
The cross destroys human boasting because nobody stands at Calvary and says, “Jesus needed to do this, but only a little. I handled the rest.”
No.
At the cross, every résumé falls from our hands.
Our morality cannot purchase forgiveness.
Our church attendance cannot erase sin.
Our theological knowledge cannot reconcile us to God.
Our ministry cannot save us.
Our generosity cannot save us.
Our reputation cannot save us.
Our followers cannot save us.
Our accomplishments cannot save us.
Jesus saves.
This is why pride hates grace.
Grace says you need rescue.
Pride says you can manage.
Grace says confess.
Pride says explain.
Grace says surrender.
Pride says control.
Grace says receive.
Pride says earn.
Grace says, “Come empty.”
Pride whispers, “Make sure everybody thinks you're full.”
Maybe your fall has already happened.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe something broke.
A marriage.
A friendship.
A ministry.
A reputation.
A career.
Trust.
Maybe you made choices you once swore you would never make.
Maybe you became someone you barely recognize.
Maybe your secret finally became public.
Or perhaps nobody knows yet.
Perhaps the collapse has happened entirely inside you.
You still smile.
Still work.
Still post.
Still say, “I’m okay.”
But somewhere underneath the performance, you know.
Something is cracking.
Listen carefully.
Being broken is not the same thing as being beyond redemption.
Peter learned that.
Hours before Jesus' crucifixion, Peter sounded extraordinarily confident.
Even if others fell away...
he would not.
Even if dying became necessary...
he was ready.
Then a servant girl asked him a question.
And the fearless disciple started collapsing.
Denial.
Again.
Again.
Then the rooster.
Imagine that moment.
The man who thought he would die beside Jesus discovered that he could not even admit knowing Jesus.
Peter fell.
Hard.
But Peter's failure was not the final sentence of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus went after him.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Not to rename sin as harmless.
Not to tell Peter that repentance was unnecessary.
Jesus restored him.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Three denials.
Three questions.
A disgraced disciple sitting beside the risen Christ.
Scandal meeting grace.
Failure meeting mercy.
A broken man discovering that Jesus can write another chapter.
That is the Gospel.
Maybe pride brought you somewhere you never intended to go.
Maybe you refused counsel.
Maybe you hurt people.
Maybe you thought you could control the temptation.
Maybe you were certain you would never become addicted.
Never cheat.
Never lie.
Never compromise.
Never walk away.
Never become cold.
Never become bitter.
Never become “one of those people.”
And then you did.
What now?
You stop hiding.
You stop blaming.
You stop polishing the story.
You stop trying to make your sin sound respectable.
You come to Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you for entertainment.
Repentance is surrendering the lie so grace can meet you in the truth.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Notice who is faithful.
He is.
Your hope is not the perfection of your repentance.
Your hope is the perfection of your Savior.
And maybe somebody needs to hear this before another night passes:
Your scandal does not have to become the last word over your life.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still breaks chains.
Jesus still receives prodigals.
Jesus still transforms hearts.
Jesus still takes people whose stories look ruined and turns their scars into testimonies of mercy.
But grace is not permission to remain proud.
Grace brings us to our knees.
So ask yourself the question most of us would rather ask about somebody else:
Where is pride hiding in me?
Not them.
Me.
Where have I become unteachable?
Whose correction have I automatically dismissed?
Who am I refusing to forgive because forgiving them feels like letting them “win”?
Where am I defending something God is asking me to confess?
Where am I more concerned about looking right than becoming right?
Where have I confused influence with spiritual maturity?
Where have I secretly believed that because God uses me, God must approve of everything in me?
Where have I begun needing applause?
Where have I stopped trembling at His Word?
Where have I started looking down on the very sinners Jesus died to save?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Talk to Jesus.
Right now.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary necessary.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Sometimes revival begins with four honest words.
Not to perform repentance publicly.
Not to prove anything to strangers.
But if you are willing, let those words become your small declaration that you are finished pretending you have nothing to surrender.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not fighting alone.
Let the people of God do what pride so often prevents us from doing:
carry one another.
And send this article to the person you love enough not to flatter.
Because pride has a strange way of returning after the tears dry.
You may need these words again.

Scripture gives real grounds for supporting Gospel ministry. Paul taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support from Gospel work (1 Corinthians 9:14). But Scripture also guards the heart of giving: “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
So this is not a spiritual tax.
It is not a payment for God's favor.
It does not purchase blessing, salvation, answered prayer, or a higher place in God's kingdom.
It is simply an opportunity for willing partnership.
But the deepest reason to support Gospel work should never be merchandise.
It should be love.
Love for Christ.
Love for truth.
Love for souls.
Love for the person you may never meet who encounters one Gospel message on the night they desperately need it.
Pray.
Share.
Save the message.
Follow.
A share costs nothing, but it can place the truth of Jesus Christ in front of someone Gospel Warrior could never reach alone.
The goal is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The goal is to make Jesus known.
Because one day, every platform disappears.
Every follower count becomes meaningless.
Every possession changes hands.
Every human reputation fades.
Every proud empire falls.
And only what belongs to Christ will ultimately matter.
So perhaps the old saying needs to become personal.
Not:
“Pride goes before their fall.”
But:
“Lord, expose the pride in me before it carries me somewhere I never wanted to go.”
Because the safest place for a sinner is not standing tall while pretending to have no weakness.
It is kneeling before Jesus with nothing left to defend.
Peter fell...
and Jesus restored him.
The tax collector confessed...
and Jesus said he went home justified.
The proud can humble themselves.
The wandering can return.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The broken can be restored.
The scandal does not have to have the final word.
Christ does.
And perhaps the very place where your pride finally breaks will become the place where you discover just how breathtaking His grace has always been.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PAUL SAYS SEXUAL IMMORALITY CAN WRONG ANOTHER PERSON—Sexual Sin Isn’t Always “Just Between Two Adults”
paragraphs: PAUL SAYS SEXUAL IMMORALITY CAN WRONG ANOTHER PERSON—Sexual Sin Isn’t Always “Just Between Two Adults”
We call it private. Paul calls it something that can cross a boundary, take advantage of another human being, and bring God Himself into the matter.
There is a sentence our culture has learned to say almost automatically whenever sexual morality becomes uncomfortable:
“What two consenting adults do in private is nobody else’s business.”
It sounds reasonable.
It sounds compassionate.
It sounds like the perfect way to end an argument.
Nobody was forced.
Nobody was physically attacked.
Both people agreed.
So what could possibly be wrong?
Then the apostle Paul writes one sentence that refuses to let the conversation remain that simple.
In the middle of one of the New Testament’s clearest passages about sexual holiness, Paul says:
“that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter…”
—1 Thessalonians 4:6
Read that again.
Not merely:
“Do not hurt yourself.”
Not merely:
“Do not break a religious rule.”
Not merely:
“Try to avoid feeling guilty afterward.”
Paul introduces another person.
Someone can be wronged.
And suddenly sexual sin is no longer only about what two people wanted in a moment.
It becomes a question of what one human being may have taken from another.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because some of us have spent years calling something “love” that Scripture may force us to examine as something much more complicated.
Paul originally wrote these words in Greek:
“τὸ μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν ἐν τῷ πράγματι τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ…”
The words deserve our attention.
ὑπερβαίνειν — hyperbainein
It carries the idea of stepping beyond, going beyond a boundary, transgressing.
Then comes:
πλεονεκτεῖν — pleonektein
To overreach.
To gain an advantage.
To exploit.
To take advantage of another.
Paul is describing conduct that does not merely happen with another person.
It can happen against another person.
And that changes the question.
The modern question is often:
“Did we both want it?”
Paul forces a deeper question:
“Did I honor this person before God?”
Those are not necessarily the same question.
Because two people can mutually agree to something and still mutually participate in something destructive.
Two people can consent to bitterness.
Two people can cooperate in dishonesty.
Two people can encourage one another toward drunkenness.
Two people can participate willingly in adultery.
Mutual willingness does not automatically transform everything people choose into righteousness.
Biblical love asks something deeper than:
“Will you let me?”
Biblical love asks:
“Will this help me honor you as someone who belongs to God?”
And perhaps that is the question many of us never asked.
We asked whether they wanted us.
We asked whether there was chemistry.
We asked whether anyone would discover it.
We asked whether we were technically dating.
We asked whether everybody else was doing it.
We asked how far was “too far.”
We asked whether God would really care.
But we rarely stopped in the heat of desire and asked:
“Am I helping this person become holy?”
Because lust does not naturally ask that question.
Love does.
And Paul refuses to separate sexuality from holiness.
Listen to the entire movement of his argument:
“For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality…”
—1 Thessalonians 4:3
The Greek word translated “sexual immorality” is:
πορνεία — porneia
It is a broad New Testament term for sexual immorality—sexual behavior outside the boundaries God establishes for sexual faithfulness.
Paul continues by telling believers to live in holiness and honor rather than being ruled by “the passion of lust.”
Then comes verse 6.
Do not cross the boundary.
Do not take advantage of your brother or sister “in this matter.”
Then Paul says something even heavier:
“because the Lord is an avenger in all these things…”
This is not casual language.
And yet we need to read it carefully.

There has been interpretive discussion over precisely how Paul’s wording in verse 6 should be understood, particularly the expression ἐν τῷ πράγματι — en tō pragmati, “in the matter.” But the immediate passage unmistakably moves through sanctification, sexual immorality, bodily holiness, lust, wrongdoing toward another person, impurity, holiness, and the Holy Spirit.
So whatever excuses we bring to the text, we cannot honestly pretend Paul thinks sexual conduct is spiritually insignificant.
He does not.
Sex matters because people matter.
Bodies matter because people bearing God’s image matter.
Holiness matters because God matters.
And suddenly another uncomfortable possibility emerges.
Maybe sexual sin sometimes takes something even when the other person willingly gives it.
Maybe you can receive someone’s body while refusing them covenant.
Maybe you can awaken intimacy without accepting responsibility.
Maybe you can whisper permanence while intending something temporary.
Maybe you can enjoy somebody’s vulnerability and disappear when vulnerability becomes inconvenient.
Maybe you can tell yourself, “They wanted it too,” while never asking whether you were leading someone God loves toward holiness or away from it.
And maybe sometimes both people are doing that to each other.
That is what makes sexual sin so deceptive.
It can feel extraordinarily intimate while producing extraordinarily deep loneliness.
Two bodies can be close while two souls remain terrified of being truly known.
Someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You thought giving more of yourself would finally make them stay.
So you crossed another boundary.
Then another.
You told yourself this was what love required.
You were afraid that saying no would mean losing them.
Maybe nobody physically forced you.
But fear was sitting in the room.
Loneliness was sitting in the room.
Insecurity was sitting in the room.
The desperate need to be chosen was sitting in the room.
And afterward…
they still left.
Or perhaps you stayed together, but something changed inside you.
What promised closeness created anxiety.
What promised freedom produced secrecy.
What promised affirmation made you wonder whether you were loved…
or merely desired.
And perhaps you have carried the shame ever since.
But there is another person who needs to keep reading.
The person who did the using.
Maybe you never called it that.
You said:
“We both knew what this was.”
You said:
“They could have said no.”
You said:
“We weren't married.”
You said:
“It was consensual.”
You said:
“I never promised anything.”
Maybe technically, according to the rules you created for yourself, you can construct a defense.
But stand before Jesus for a moment and ask a different question.
Did you love them?
Not:
Did you desire them?
Not:
Did they desire you?
Did you love them with a love that sought their holiness, dignity, spiritual good, and eternal good?
Because Scripture’s definition of love is far more demanding than desire with permission.
Love “does no wrong to a neighbor.”
—Romans 13:10
Love does not ask:
“How much can I take without technically becoming the villain?”
Love asks:
“How can I honor you because Christ died for sinners like both of us?”
That changes everything.
And before anyone turns this article into ammunition against someone else, hear this carefully.
Paul is not giving religious people permission to stand over sexually broken people with stones in their hands.
Christianity begins with the devastating realization that we are the sinners who need mercy.
Sexual sin is real.
But so is sexual shame.
And shame has convinced millions of people that their worst night became their permanent name.
Adulterer.
Porn addict.
Used.
Dirty.
Unfaithful.
Promiscuous.
Unworthy.
Damaged.
Hypocrite.
Maybe nobody knows.
You sing worship songs.
You post Bible verses.
You go to church.
You smile when people ask how you are.
But somewhere underneath the Christian vocabulary is a memory you desperately hope never becomes public.
A browser history.
A hotel room.
A message thread.
A relationship nobody knew about.
Someone else's husband.
Someone else's wife.
A secret addiction.
A compromise you promised God would happen only once.
Then twice.
Then again.
And perhaps the hardest part is not merely remembering what someone did to you.
It is remembering what you did to someone else.
That is where the Gospel becomes more than inspirational language.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make respectable people feel spiritually encouraged.
Jesus came for sinners.
Real sinners.
Guilty sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
People who were wronged.
And people who did the wronging.
People whose sexuality was exploited.
And people who selfishly exploited others.
People who crossed boundaries.
People who broke vows.
People who hid.
People who lied.
People who cannot rewind what happened.
The Gospel does not say your sin was harmless.
The Gospel says something infinitely better:
your sin does not have to have the final word.
At the cross, Jesus does not rename darkness as light so we can avoid repentance.
He brings darkness into the light so sinners can be forgiven and transformed.
Grace is not God pretending nothing happened.
Grace is God doing for guilty people what guilty people could never do for themselves.
Jesus bears sin.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus changes hearts.
And Jesus calls us out of the darkness we once defended.
That is why Paul does not stop at prohibition.
Just one verse later he says:
“For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness.”
—1 Thessalonians 4:7
Called.
Do you see it?
Christian sexual ethics are not merely about what God tells you to run from.
They are about what God is calling you into.
Holiness.
Freedom.
Integrity.
A life where your body no longer controls your master.
A life where another person's body is not something to consume.
A life where desire learns to bow before Jesus.
A life where you stop asking how close you can walk to the cliff and start asking how closely you can walk with Christ.
And then Paul writes:
—1 Thessalonians 4:8
Notice that final phrase.
God gives His Holy Spirit.
Paul does not leave struggling believers standing before an impossible command with nothing but willpower.
God gives Himself.
The Spirit who convicts is also the Spirit who empowers.
So if you have fallen sexually, the answer is not pretending it never mattered.
And the answer is not spending the rest of your life believing you are too filthy for Jesus.
The answer is repentance.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
End what needs ending.
Block what needs blocking.
Flee what needs fleeing.
Seek pastoral or mature Christian accountability where needed.

If you have seriously wronged someone, repentance may involve accepting consequences and seeking wise counsel about appropriate restitution rather than demanding immediate forgiveness or renewed access to the person you hurt.

And where abuse, coercion, assault, exploitation, or criminal conduct has occurred, do not hide it behind vague religious language about “mutual sin.” Victims are not morally responsible for another person's abuse against them, and serious wrongdoing may require professional, pastoral, safeguarding, and legal intervention.
Biblical grace never requires calling evil good.
Grace tells the truth…
and then opens the door home.
Perhaps that is why this message hurts.
You did not expect 1 Thessalonians 4:6 to expose that memory.
You did not expect one Greek verb to make you reconsider a relationship you have spent years justifying.
You did not expect to wonder whether something you called “consensual” was nevertheless selfish.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide from God.”
Conviction says:
“Come back to God.”
Condemnation says:
“You are what you did.”
The Gospel says:
“There is redemption in Jesus Christ.”
The woman caught in adultery encountered a Savior who neither celebrated her sin nor abandoned her to her accusers.
Grace did not say sin was meaningless.
Grace gave the sinner somewhere to go.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Maybe you have been carrying sexual shame for ten years.
Maybe twenty.
Maybe what happened was last night.
Maybe you are still inside the relationship you know you need to surrender.
Maybe you are reading this beside the person with whom you keep compromising.
Maybe you have confessed the same sin so many times that you are embarrassed to pray again.
Pray anyway.
Run to Christ again.
Not because sin is small.
Because His mercy is greater.
Repentance means turning.
And sometimes turning begins with one trembling sentence:
“Jesus, I cannot keep living like this.”
If that is you, do not perform for the comments.

And if Christ has already been restoring an area of your life you once believed could never be healed, tell someone what grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to give another wounded person enough courage to seek help.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Not because you need another saved post buried in your phone, but because temptation has an extraordinary ability to make us forget what conviction once made painfully clear.
Not to publicly shame anyone. Not to throw stones.
Truth should be carried with love.
We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Give because you freely want to help the work continue.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help enormously.
Leave a meaningful comment.
Invite someone to follow.
Send it privately to the person whose name came into your heart while reading.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is calling bondage freedom.
Someone is calling lust love.
Someone is calling shame their identity.
Someone is convinced they have gone too far for Jesus to want them anymore.
And they need to discover what the Gospel has been saying all along.
Sin may explain part of your story.
It does not have the authority to write the ending.
The night you thought permanently stained your name may become the very place where the mercy of Jesus teaches you what it means to be made new.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID CHURCH LEADERSHIP QUALIFICATIONS TALK ABOUT A MAN’S MARRIAGE?
paragraphs: WHY DID CHURCH LEADERSHIP QUALIFICATIONS TALK ABOUT A MAN’S MARRIAGE?
Because God Was Never Only Examining the Man Behind the Pulpit—He Was Looking at the Man Who Came Home After the Sermon
There is a frightening possibility in Christianity.
A man can know how to hold a Bible...
and still not know how to hold his marriage together.
He can preach about grace while starving his wife of tenderness.
He can counsel broken couples while refusing to apologize in his own home.
He can speak beautifully about Christ’s faithfulness while secretly becoming comfortable with lust, flirtation, deception, emotional infidelity, pornography, manipulation, or betrayal.
He can be impressive under church lights...
and unbearable behind his own front door.
And perhaps that helps explain why, when the apostle Paul described the kind of character expected of church leadership, he did something remarkably personal.
He talked about the man's marriage.
Not merely his theology.
Not merely his charisma.
Not merely whether he could command a room.
Paul went home with him.
“Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife...” — 1 Timothy 3:2.
Then, writing to Titus about appointing elders, Paul returned to essentially the same qualification:
“...the husband of one wife...” — Titus 1:6.
But underneath those familiar English words is a Greek expression worth slowing down long enough to hear:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα — mias gynaikos andra.
Literally, the words carry the sense of a “man of one woman.”
That matters.

The expression appears in 1 Timothy 3:2 and substantially the same wording appears in Titus 1:6. English translations render it in different ways. “Husband of one wife” is traditional. Some translations emphasize being “faithful to his wife.” The NET notes that interpretations have included being married only once or being devoted solely to one’s wife. Scholars have long debated precisely how broadly the phrase should be applied, particularly to questions involving widowhood, remarriage, divorce, and marital history.
So we should be careful.
We should never make Scripture say less than it says.
But we should also never make Scripture say more than it says.
Paul's words should not be turned into a weapon for settling every complicated marital history with one careless sentence.
But neither should we escape the unmistakable moral force of what he is describing.
Whatever else μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα entails, the picture is not of a sexually reckless, relationally duplicitous man whose public ministry hides private unfaithfulness.
Paul is describing recognizable Christian character.
A man whose life can withstand examination.
A man whose sexuality is submitted to Christ.
A man whose relationships do not contradict his preaching.
A man whose closest relationships provide evidence that the Gospel he proclaims publicly is actually governing him privately.
And suddenly this passage becomes uncomfortable.
Because Paul does not begin his qualifications by asking whether the man can build a platform.
He asks whether his life is above reproach.
He does not ask how many people follow him.
He asks what kind of man people are following.
He does not ask whether his sermons go viral.
He asks whether his character survives when nobody is recording.
That distinction matters because Christianity has always been vulnerable to confusing giftedness with godliness.
Gifted people can gather crowds.
Gifted people can speak eloquently.
Gifted people can build organizations.
Gifted people can quote Scripture.
Gifted people can make people cry.
Gifted people can even preach true things while living dangerously inconsistent lives.
But spiritual leadership in the New Testament is never presented merely as talent.
It is character carrying responsibility.
Paul continues:
The overseer must be sober-minded.
Self-controlled.
Respectable.
Hospitable.
Able to teach.
Not controlled by drunkenness.
Not violent.
Gentle.
Not quarrelsome.
Not a lover of money.
And then Paul walks straight through the leader's front door.
He speaks about how the man manages his household.
Why?
Paul himself gives the reasoning in 1 Timothy 3:5:
If someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?
There it is.
The home is not an inconvenient interruption to ministry.
The home reveals something about ministry.
That does not mean a pastor's family must perform artificial perfection for the congregation.
It does not mean a wife becomes responsible for protecting her husband's reputation.
It certainly does not mean children cease to be morally responsible human beings with wills of their own.
And it does not give churches permission to demand an Instagram-perfect family.
It means leadership begins much closer to home than we sometimes want to admit.
Because anyone can behave differently for an audience.
Home removes the microphone.
Home removes the stage.
Home removes the applause.
Home is where your family discovers whether the patience you preach belongs only to your sermon notes.
Your spouse knows whether “gentleness” is something you teach or something you practice.
Your children know whether your Christianity disappears when you're angry.
The people closest to you eventually discover whether Jesus is merely part of your vocabulary...
or Lord of your life.
And this is where the passage stops being merely about pastors.
Because perhaps you clicked this article expecting an argument about whether divorced men can become pastors.
Perhaps you expected a denominational debate.
Perhaps you expected another theological fight.
But Scripture has quietly turned the mirror around.
What kind of person are you when nobody from church is watching?
What does your spouse experience?
What does your family experience?
What happens to your Christianity when the door closes?
There are husbands who have never committed physical adultery but have abandoned their wives emotionally.
There are marriages sharing an address while two hearts live miles apart.
There are men who would never bring another woman into their bedroom but carry thousands of women into it through a screen.
There are wives silently wondering why the man who is compassionate toward everyone at church has no tenderness left when he gets home.
There are children who know a version of their father the congregation has never met.
And there are leaders terrified that if anyone discovers the truth, everything they built will collapse.
Maybe someone reading this knows exactly what that fear feels like.
You love Jesus.
But something is wrong.
The messages became inappropriate.
The pornography came back.
The emotional attachment crossed a line.
The marriage has become cold.
The secret has grown.
The public version of you and the private version of you are becoming two different people.
And maintaining both identities is exhausting you.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not better hiding.
The answer is repentance.
Not reputation management.
Repentance.
Not deleting evidence while protecting the heart that produced it.
Repentance.
Not blaming your spouse.
Not blaming loneliness.
Not blaming ministry pressure.
Not blaming temptation.
Not saying, “Nobody understands what I've been going through.”
Bring it into the light.
Because Jesus did not shed His blood so you could become better at hiding.
He shed His blood to redeem sinners.
That is where this becomes Gospel.
Christian leadership qualifications were never instructions for manufacturing flawless human beings.
There has only ever been one flawless Shepherd.
Jesus Christ.
Every elder needs Him.
Every pastor needs Him.
Every husband needs Him.
Every wife needs Him.
Every wounded marriage needs Him.
Every sexually broken person needs Him.
Every hypocrite who finally realizes he has been pretending needs Him.
Every believer carrying a secret needs Him.
The Gospel does not say, “Become spotless enough and then approach Christ.”
The Gospel announces that Christ came for sinners.
Jesus carried sin to the cross.
He bore judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now the scandalous announcement of Christianity is that forgiveness is available to people who cannot rewrite yesterday.
Christ can forgive what you cannot undo.
But grace is not permission to continue destroying what sin has already wounded.
Grace calls us out.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace brings confession into rooms where secrecy used to live.
Grace can lead someone to accountability.
Grace can make a proud husband apologize.
Grace can make an adulterer stop hiding.

Grace can make someone close the browser, end the affair, confess the deception, seek pastoral help, pursue counseling where appropriate, accept consequences, rebuild trust patiently, and stop demanding instant restoration from people they wounded.
Grace does not merely soothe.
Grace transforms.
And that is why the phrase μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα reaches deeper than a checkbox beside the word “married.”
It confronts integrity.
It confronts fidelity.
It confronts the terrifying gap that can grow between who people think we are and who we actually are.
The church does not need leaders who have mastered looking holy.
The church needs leaders increasingly surrendered to the Holy One.
And perhaps one of the greatest tragedies in modern Christian culture is that we sometimes become more impressed by a man's platform than concerned about his soul.
Thousands of followers?
Wonderful.
Powerful preacher?
Wonderful.
Brilliant theologian?
Wonderful.
Growing ministry?
Wonderful.
But how does he treat people who cannot advance his career?
How does he treat his wife?
How does he respond when corrected?
What happens when he is angry?
What happens when temptation arrives?
What happens when nobody applauds?
What happens when he sins?
Does he conceal?
Manipulate?
Intimidate?
Blame?
Or does he confess, repent, seek accountability, and submit himself again to Christ?
That is not glamorous Christianity.
That is Christianity where character actually costs something.
And maybe this is hitting closer to home than you expected.
Maybe you are not a pastor.
Maybe nobody calls you “elder.”
Maybe you will never stand behind a pulpit.
But there is someone watching your Christianity from closer than the congregation ever could.
Your spouse.
Your children.
Your family.
Your friends.
And beneath all their observations stands Someone infinitely more important.
Christ.
He already knows.
The browser history.
The deleted conversation.
The resentment.
The fantasy.
The bitterness.
The emotional distance.
The lie.
The thing you promised would happen only once.
He knows.
And still the invitation of the Gospel stands:
Come into the light.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because it matters enough that Christ died for it.
This is where scandal can become grace.
Not when Christians pretend the scandal never happened.
Not when churches protect powerful people at the expense of wounded people.
Not when repentance becomes a public-relations statement.
But when sinners stop running from the truth and run toward Jesus Christ.
There may still be consequences.
Forgiveness does not automatically erase every earthly consequence, restore every leadership position, rebuild trust overnight, or guarantee restoration to a particular office.
The New Testament takes leadership qualifications seriously.
Churches must take them seriously too.
Grace and qualification are not identical questions.
A person can be completely loved by God, genuinely forgiven in Christ, and restored to fellowship with Him without thereby being automatically entitled to a particular position of church leadership.
That distinction protects both grace and the church.
Because ministry is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Your title is not your identity.
Jesus is.
Your platform is not your redemption.
Jesus is.
And if losing a position is what finally drives a person into honest surrender before Christ, then losing the platform may expose how desperately the soul needed the Savior.
Maybe that sentence hurts.
Let it.
Some wounds are invitations to stop pretending.
If you are a husband reading this, love your wife when nobody celebrates you for it.
Be faithful when nobody would discover the alternative.
Guard your eyes.
Guard your phone.
Guard your conversations.
Guard your heart.
Apologize when you are wrong.
Do not use “headship” as permission for domination. Christian authority is never permission to imitate tyranny. Look at Christ, who loved His church sacrificially.

If you are a wife carrying the pain of a husband's hypocrisy, Scripture does not require you to call evil good. Forgiveness does not mean pretending betrayal did not happen, and Christian submission should never be twisted into permission for abuse.
If you are a church leader, remember that the people in your congregation do not ultimately need a celebrity.
They need shepherds who remember they belong to the Chief Shepherd.
And if you are the person whose secret life is collapsing while reading this...
please stop running.
Tell the truth.
Seek trustworthy, mature Christian help.
If another person has been harmed, prioritize their safety and wellbeing rather than merely protecting your reputation.
Repent before God.
Turn away from what you know is destroying you.
And believe the Gospel you may have spent years explaining to everyone else.
Jesus still saves sinners.
Even religious sinners.
Even respected sinners.
Even leaders.
Even you.
That is the scandal of grace.
And that is why Jesus Christ remains the center of everything we do at Gospel Warrior.
We want Scripture opened.
Christ proclaimed.
Sin confronted.
Wounded believers strengthened.
Prodigals called home.
Marriages pointed toward biblical faithfulness.
Leaders reminded that character matters.
And ordinary Christians equipped to follow Jesus when nobody is watching.
And if financially supporting Gospel Warrior is not something you can do, please never believe that makes your participation meaningless.
You can help carry the message without spending anything.
Send this privately to a church leader you love.
Be honest.
Or, if Christ has already carried you through failure and repentance, tell somebody beneath this article what His grace has done.
Your testimony may become someone else's reason to believe that repentance is still possible.
Because somewhere tonight, another Christian may be sitting alone with a glowing phone in a dark room, wondering whether the secret they carry means their story is over.
Tell them what the Gospel says.
The story does not have to end where the scandal happened.
The hands that were pierced for sinners are still capable of writing redemption across the pages we thought we had ruined forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PAUL TOLD HUSBANDS TO LOVE THEIR WIVES AS THEIR OWN BODIES — AND THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING
paragraphs: PAUL TOLD HUSBANDS TO LOVE THEIR WIVES AS THEIR OWN BODIES — AND THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING
What if the verse many husbands have read casually is actually a mirror—and what if, when you finally understand what Paul said, you can no longer look at your marriage the same way?
There is a woman somewhere tonight lying beside the man she married...
and feeling completely alone.
He is there.
His body is inches away.
His breathing fills the room.
His wedding ring is still on his hand.
But somehow, somewhere between the vows and the bills, between raising children and surviving disappointments, between unanswered conversations and wounds neither of them knew how to heal...
she began wondering whether she was still cherished.
And somewhere else, there is a husband sitting quietly in his car before walking into his own house.
He loves his wife.
At least he believes he does.
He works.
He provides.
He stays.
He has sacrificed things nobody notices.
But something inside their marriage is dying, and he doesn't know how to reach for her anymore.
Maybe he thinks love means paying the bills.
Maybe she thinks his silence means indifference.
Maybe both of them are hurting.
Maybe both of them have become experts at sleeping beside pain.
Then Paul writes words that refuse to leave a husband comfortable:
“οὕτως ὀφείλουσιν καὶ οἱ ἄνδρες ἀγαπᾶν τὰς ἑαυτῶν γυναῖκας ὡς τὰ ἑαυτῶν σώματα...”
Houtōs opheilousin kai hoi andres agapan tas heautōn gynaikas hōs ta heautōn sōmata.
“In the same way husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies.”
Ephesians 5:28.
Read it again.
Slowly.
Because Paul is not giving husbands a romantic suggestion.
The Greek verb ὀφείλουσιν — opheilousin carries the sense of ought, of being obligated or indebted.
And the word translated “love” is ἀγαπᾶν — agapan, from agapaō.
Paul is describing a love that is not merely an emotion that survives only while the marriage feels easy.
But there is something even more confronting here.
Paul tells the husband to love his wife ὡς τὰ ἑαυτῶν σώματα — hōs ta heautōn sōmata...
“as their own bodies.”
Then he says:
ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἑαυτὸν ἀγαπᾷ
“The one loving his own wife loves himself.”
That changes the question.
The question is no longer merely:
“Do I love my wife?”
The question becomes:
“Does the way I treat her look like the way Christ is teaching me to understand love?”
Because Ephesians 5:28 did not fall out of heaven by itself.
Just three verses earlier, Paul gives husbands the terrifyingly beautiful standard:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Ephesians 5:25.
There it is.
The Cross standing in the middle of the marriage.
Christ.
Not Hollywood.
Not culture.
Not masculinity defined by domination.
Not romance defined by butterflies.
Not whatever our fathers did.
Not whatever our wounds taught us.
Christ.
Paul does not tell the husband, “Make sure she deserves your love today.”
He points toward Jesus.
And Jesus loved sacrificially.

That means Christian headship can never honestly be used as permission for selfishness, intimidation, cruelty, humiliation, coercion, manipulation, violence, or treating a wife as spiritually inferior.
The model Paul gives the husband is the crucified Christ.
The One who gives Himself.
The One who serves.
The One whose strength does not need to crush someone weaker to prove that it is strength.
And suddenly the verse becomes uncomfortable.
Because husbands...
we know how quickly we respond when our own bodies hurt.
A tooth starts throbbing?
We notice.
A finger gets cut?
We protect it.
Our stomach is starving?
We feed it.
Our body is exhausted?
We want rest.
Our reputation gets wounded?
We defend it.
But what happens when she hurts?
Do you notice?
When she says, “I'm tired,” do you hear weakness...
or do you hear the woman who has been carrying things you may never have noticed?
When she tries to tell you something is wrong, do you immediately defend yourself?
Or can you listen long enough to understand the wound before explaining your intention?
When you embarrass her in front of other people, do you dismiss it because you thought it was funny?
When she is emotionally bleeding, do you call her dramatic because you cannot see the wound?
You would not knowingly leave your own hand pressed against a burning stove.
So why would you knowingly leave the woman God joined to you burning in loneliness?
This is where Scripture stops being something we post...
and becomes something that examines us.
Some husbands know every argument necessary to defend biblical marriage...
but have forgotten to kiss their wives goodnight.
Some can explain submission...
but have barely studied sacrifice.
Some know how to demand respect...
but have forgotten tenderness.
Some will fight strangers for dishonoring their wives while dishonoring those same wives with their words behind closed doors.
And some men are reading this with tears forming because they already know.
You remember what you said.
You remember the night she cried.
You remember the apology you never gave.
You remember how affectionate you were when you were trying to win her heart...
and how ordinary you allowed her heart to become once you had it.
But husband...
do not stop reading at conviction.
Because condemnation whispers:
“You ruined everything.”
The Gospel says:
“Bring everything into the light.”
Jesus did not die only for respectable sins.
He died for the ugly ones too.
Pride.
Lust.
Neglect.
Bitterness.
Selfishness.
Pornography.
Cruel words.
Emotional distance.
Secret resentment.
The cold silence designed to punish.
The ego that refuses to say, “I was wrong.”
The heart that wants forgiveness from God while withholding tenderness from the person sleeping beside it.
The Cross is where excuses die...
but it is also where sinners find mercy.
Maybe your marriage has become something neither of you imagined on your wedding day.
Maybe trust was shattered.
Maybe affection disappeared.
Maybe adultery entered the story.
Maybe pornography poisoned intimacy.
Maybe years of unresolved anger built walls so high that you no longer remember how to climb them.
Maybe you are still married legally...
but emotionally you have been living like strangers.
And perhaps the most frightening sentence in your house has become:
“We're fine.”
No.
You don't have to pretend.
Jesus already knows.
And the scandal of grace is that Christ is not frightened by the chapter you are ashamed to admit exists.
Repentance does not mean pretending the damage never happened.
It means turning.
It means bringing sin into God's light.
It means confession without excuses.
It means seeking forgiveness without demanding immediate trust.
It means accepting consequences.
It means getting help when help is needed.
It means understanding that saying “I'm sorry” is not always the completion of repentance.
Sometimes it is only its first sentence.
A husband shaped by Christ does not say:
“I apologized. Why aren't you over it?”
He asks:
“What does faithfulness look like now?”
And sometimes love looks surprisingly ordinary.
Putting the phone down.
Listening.
Helping without being applauded.
Remembering.
Praying together.
Speaking gently when anger would be easier.
Protecting her dignity when she is not in the room.
Refusing pornography.
Being transparent.
Keeping promises.
Coming home.
Holding her while she cries even when you cannot fix what hurts.
Saying the words pride hates:
“I was wrong.”
“I hurt you.”
“There is no excuse.”
“Please forgive me.”
“What do you need from me?”
“I want Christ to change me.”
And wives reading this...
this passage is not permission to weaponize Scripture against your husband either.
The Gospel does not hand either spouse ammunition.
It calls both toward Christ.
Ephesians eventually speaks of the profound mystery of marriage in relation to Christ and the church.
That means Christian marriage was never designed merely to make two people look successful.
It points beyond itself.
Toward Jesus.
Toward covenant.
Toward sacrificial love.
Toward grace.
And perhaps that is why the enemy delights in destroying marriages.
Because a marriage being transformed by Christ becomes a living testimony that broken things do not have to remain what sin made them.
But hear this carefully.
Biblical teaching about marriage must never be twisted into telling someone experiencing abuse that faithfulness requires silently enduring danger.
Sacrificial love is not the same thing as enabling evil.
Forgiveness does not make violence righteous.
Grace does not require pretending abuse did not occur.
Bringing darkness into the light may include seeking trustworthy pastoral counsel, professional help, legal protection, or immediate safety when necessary.
Jesus does not need us to rename evil “love” in order to defend marriage.
Truth and grace belong together.
And maybe right now this article is no longer about somebody else's marriage.
Maybe it found yours.
Maybe you're the husband realizing:
I have been physically present and emotionally absent.
Maybe you're the wife thinking:
I wish he understood how lonely I've been.
Maybe you're divorced and reading this through tears, wondering where these words were ten years ago.
Maybe you're single and suddenly realizing that biblical marriage requires far more than finding somebody attractive.
Maybe you're engaged.
Maybe you're newly married.
Maybe you've survived forty years together.
Maybe your marriage is beautiful.
Maybe it is hanging by a thread.
Wherever this found you...
look at Jesus.
Because ultimately Ephesians 5 is bigger than marriage.
Marriage becomes a window.
Christ is the destination.
The husband who is commanded to love eventually discovers that he himself survives only because Christ loved first.
Before you could clean yourself up.
Before you could repair your reputation.
Before you could promise never to fail again.
Jesus moved toward sinners.
At Calvary, love was not a slogan.
Love bled.
Love carried a cross.
Love wore thorns.
Love opened wounded hands.
And the risen Christ still calls sinners out of hiding.
So perhaps the most important thing a husband can do tonight is not send this article to his wife and say:
“Look how much I agree with this.”
Perhaps he should put the phone down.
Find her.
Look into the eyes he once promised to cherish.
And ask a dangerous question:
“Have I been loving you in a way that makes you feel cherished, safe, heard, and valued—and where have I failed?”
Then...
listen.
Don't prepare your defense.
Don't correct every detail.
Don't explain every motive.
Listen.
And if the Holy Spirit exposes something...
repent.
Not theatrically.
Not temporarily.
Actually turn.
Because your wife does not need another inspirational quote from a husband unwilling to change.
She needs the fruit of repentance.
And husband, if you are already loving faithfully, quietly, sacrificially...
keep going.
When nobody applauds.
Keep going.
When marriage feels ordinary.
Keep going.
When you're exhausted.
Keep going.
When affection requires intentionality.
Keep going.
Not because your wife is flawless.
Not because you are flawless.
But because marriage can become one of the places where the Gospel trains us to stop worshiping ourselves.
Maybe you know a husband who desperately needs these words but would never search for them.
Not to shame somebody.
Not to start a gender war.
Send it privately to someone who needs hope rather than public embarrassment.
Because there may come a night when anger makes you forget what love requires.
If this exposed something in you, don't hide behind religious language.
“Jesus, teach me to love like You.”
No explanations required.
Your testimony may become oxygen for someone else's faith.
It doesn't.
It doesn't.
And not because anyone should give under pressure.
Scripture teaches that Christian generosity is to come willingly from the heart, not through compulsion.

But voluntary financial support can help Gospel Warrior continue reaching people with Scripture-centered content and expanding resources designed to point wounded, wandering, growing, and searching people toward Jesus.
Sometimes support looks like giving.
Sometimes it looks like sharing.
Sometimes it looks like tagging the one person God placed on your heart.
Sometimes it looks like leaving a testimony that reminds another believer that Jesus still restores broken people.
And sometimes it means helping keep biblical truth moving through a digital world desperately hungry for something deeper than another scroll.
do not miss Jesus.
Because someday the shirts fade.
The mugs break.
The books gather dust.
The algorithms change.
The platforms disappear.
But Christ remains.
And perhaps tonight, somewhere behind a closed bedroom door, a husband will finally whisper:
“I have not loved you the way I should have.”
And perhaps a wife who stopped expecting those words will begin to cry.
Perhaps there will be confession.
Perhaps there will be prayer.
Perhaps healing will begin slowly.
Perhaps professional counseling will be needed.
Perhaps trust will take months or years to rebuild.
Grace does not promise an effortless ending.
But grace tells the truth...
and then walks toward redemption.
So husband...
when Paul tells you to love your wife as your own body, don't reduce those words to something suitable for a wedding card.
Let them disturb you.
Let them examine you.
Let them drive you to Christ.
Then get up tomorrow...
and love her again.
When you fail, repent.
When you're wounded, bring it to Jesus.
When pride rises, crucify it.
When marriage becomes difficult, remember the Cross.
When you forget what love looks like...
look again at Christ.
Because the deepest miracle is not that two imperfect people somehow build a perfect marriage.
The miracle is that two sinners can continually be brought back beneath the mercy of a perfect Savior.
And maybe the marriage you thought had reached its final chapter is standing one surrendered heart away from a sentence you never expected God to write.
The scar may remain—but in the hands of Jesus, even a scar can become evidence that the wound did not get the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES PAUL SAY SEXUAL SIN IS “AGAINST” YOUR OWN BODY?
paragraphs: WHY DOES PAUL SAY SEXUAL SIN IS “AGAINST” YOUR OWN BODY?
What if the sin you thought was happening only in secret was touching something Jesus purchased with His own blood?
There are sins you can hide from your family.
Sins you can delete from your phone.
Sins you can bury beneath browser history, private messages, locked doors, hotel rooms, secret relationships, late-night searches, and a carefully maintained Christian smile.
You can sing on Sunday and struggle on Monday night.
You can lift your hands in worship while carrying memories you desperately wish you could erase.
You can know Bible verses and still feel your pulse change when temptation appears.
You can love Jesus and still be ashamed of what you did with your body.
And then Paul writes one sentence that refuses to leave us alone:
“Flee sexual immorality.”
In Greek:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — pheugete tēn porneian.
Run from sexual immorality.
Not manage it.
Not negotiate with it.
Not see how close you can stand without falling.
Run.
But then Paul says something even more disturbing:
ὁ δὲ πορνεύων εἰς τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα ἁμαρτάνει
Literally, the person practicing sexual immorality sins εἰς τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα — eis to idion sōma — against his own body.
Why?
Why does Paul speak this way about sexual sin?
Is he saying sexual sin is the unforgivable sin?
No.
Is he saying sexual sinners are uniquely disgusting to God?
Absolutely not.
Is he saying that greed, hatred, drunkenness, pride, lying, violence, idolatry, and every other sin somehow do not affect the body?
That cannot be Paul's point either.
To understand the sentence, you have to resist the temptation to pull verse 18 away from everything Paul has just said.
Because Paul's argument did not begin with sex.
It began with something much deeper.
Who owns your body?
That is where this gets personal.
Our culture often treats the body as private property.
My body.
My choice.
My appetite.
My pleasure.
My rules.

And Corinth had its own versions of bodily autonomy and sexual permissiveness. Paul confronts the mentality that bodily appetites are spiritually insignificant. He writes that the body is not for sexual immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
Then he says something astonishing.
Your body is a member of Christ.
Read that again.
Your body.
Not merely your soul.
Not merely the part of you that sings worship songs.
Not merely your theological beliefs.
Your body belongs to Christ.
And that completely changes the question.
Christian sexual ethics is not fundamentally God standing outside your bedroom shouting arbitrary restrictions.
It is God declaring something breathtaking about what redemption has done to you.
You belong to Jesus.
Paul then reaches back to Genesis and quotes the mystery of sexual union:
“The two shall become one flesh.”
That is the doorway into understanding 1 Corinthians 6:18.
Sex, biblically understood, is never presented as merely recreational contact between two biological machines.
Something covenant-shaped is written into it.
Something unitive.
Something bodily.
Something profoundly personal.
Paul says that the one who joins himself sexually becomes “one body” with the other person, while the believer who is joined to the Lord is “one spirit” with Him.
And suddenly Paul's command makes sense:
φεύγετε — FLEE.
Sexual sin uniquely takes the body that belongs to Christ and involves that very body in a union contrary to God's design.
That is why Paul does not merely say sexual immorality happens with your body.
He says it is a sin against your own body.
The Greek phrase is striking:
εἰς τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα — against one's own body.
The word σῶμα — sōma — body is not incidental to Paul's argument.
It keeps appearing.
Body.
Body.
Body.
Because Christianity does not teach that your body is disposable packaging around your “real” spiritual self.
God created the body.
Christ took on a body.
Christ died bodily.
Christ rose bodily.
And Paul has just reminded the Corinthians that God will also raise us by His power.
Your body therefore has a destiny.
Resurrection.
That means your body is not meaningless.
And that means what you do with it matters.
This is where Paul's words become uncomfortable, because sexual temptation whispers the exact opposite.
“It is only physical.”
“It doesn't mean anything.”
“Nobody knows.”
“Everyone does it.”
“You need this.”
“You deserve this.”
“Just this once.”
“You can repent afterward.”
But Scripture refuses to reduce your sexuality to appetite.
Your body is connected to your identity as someone who belongs to Christ.
Sexual sin therefore does something profoundly contradictory.
It asks the body purchased for Christ to participate in something outside Christ's design.
And Paul is about to make the reason even clearer.
Listen to the Greek of the next verse:
τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς... ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν
“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.”
The word Paul uses is ναός — naos.
Temple.
Sacred dwelling.
Paul is not telling Christians that their bodies are valuable because they are attractive.
Or young.
Or sexually desirable.
Or strong.
Or thin.
Or healthy.
Your body possesses a dignity far deeper than appearance.
For the believer, Paul says the Holy Spirit dwells within you.
Then comes the sentence that destroys the illusion of absolute self-ownership:
καὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν
“You are not your own.”
And immediately:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς
“For you were bought with a price.”
There is the Gospel.
Paul does not ultimately fight sexual immorality by screaming, “You are filthy.”
He fights it by announcing:
You were purchased.
There was a price.
And the price was not silver.
Not gold.
Not religious performance.
Not your promise that you would never fail again.
The Gospel takes us to Jesus Christ.
The Son of God who entered our broken world.
The Savior who touched the unclean.
The Christ who welcomed repentant sinners.
The Lamb who carried sin to the cross.
Jesus did not shed His blood because humanity was sexually pure.
He shed His blood because humanity was not.
He came for sinners.
Which means perhaps the most important person reading this article is not the person who has remained sexually pure.
Maybe it is the person reading with tears in their eyes.
The person who remembers the affair.
The pornography.
The hookups.
The relationship nobody knows about.
The compromises.
The messages.
The fantasies.
The night you wish you could erase.
The years you cannot recover.
Maybe you crossed boundaries willingly.
Maybe you knew Scripture and did it anyway.
Maybe you promised God, “Never again,” and then returned.
And now every time somebody talks about sexual purity, you do not hear hope.
You hear accusation.
You hear one word:
Dirty.
But hear another word.
A better word.
A blood-bought word.
Redeemed.
Paul's message is not that sexual sin places you beyond the reach of Jesus.
The context proves exactly the opposite.
Only a few verses earlier, Paul lists patterns of sinful life, including sexual sin, and then turns to the Corinthian believers and says, in effect:
That is what some of you were.
Were.
Then comes one of the most beautiful reversals in the chapter.
You were washed.
You were sanctified.
You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Do you see it?
The church at Corinth was not a museum filled with people who had never been sexually broken.
It was a family containing people whose pasts had been rewritten by grace.
People with histories.
People with scars.
People who had done things.
People who had been things.
And then Jesus entered the sentence.
But you were washed.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the stain never existed.
Being washed.
Not redefining darkness until it becomes light.
Being brought into the light.
Not saying sin does not matter.
Saying the blood of Christ matters more.
That is why grace never means, “Keep sinning; God doesn't care.”
Grace says something infinitely more beautiful:
“You don't have to live there anymore.”
Maybe that is why this hurts.
Because somewhere beneath the lust, beneath the pornography, beneath the secret relationship, beneath the fantasy, beneath the compulsive scrolling, beneath the repeated compromise...
you were looking for something.
To be wanted.
To feel close to somebody.
To escape loneliness.
To numb pain.
To quiet anxiety.
To feel desirable.
To forget rejection.
To feel alive for a few minutes.
Sin often makes enormous promises before asking for payment.
It promises intimacy and leaves isolation.
Promises freedom and builds habits.
Promises pleasure and sometimes leaves shame.
Promises control and eventually begins controlling you.
And afterward...
the screen goes dark.
The person leaves.
The adrenaline fades.
The room becomes quiet.
And you are still there.
Sometimes wondering why something that promised so much gave so little.
Jesus does not merely want to take something away from you.
He wants you.
That distinction matters.
Christian holiness is not God stealing pleasure from His children.
It is a Father refusing to surrender His children to things that promise life while pulling them away from Him.
This is why Paul says:
Flee.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is leave.
Close the app.
Delete the number.
End the conversation.
Walk out.
Install accountability.
Confess to a mature believer.
Stop revisiting the relationship.
Stop calling temptation “friendship.”
Stop calling bondage “privacy.”
Stop keeping a doorway open that you keep asking God to help you stop walking through.
Joseph did not stand in Potiphar's house trying to prove how spiritually strong he was.
He ran.
There are battles won on your knees.
There are also battles won with your feet.
But perhaps you did not run.
Perhaps you fell.
Then hear this carefully.
Do not turn conviction into hopelessness.
There is a difference between the Holy Spirit exposing sin and shame telling you to hide from God.
Adam hid.
The Gospel calls us into the light.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The answer to sexual sin is not pretending.
It is repentance.
And biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is turning.
Turning from sin.
Turning toward Christ.
Bringing darkness into light.
Receiving forgiveness while beginning to walk in obedience.
Some consequences may remain.
Some relationships may require difficult decisions.
Some patterns may require accountability, pastoral help, wise counseling, boundaries, and time.
Grace does not always erase earthly consequences.
But grace can redeem the person walking through them.
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter of your story you are most ashamed to read aloud.
At the cross, He already knew.
And still He stayed.
Nails through His hands.
Blood running down His body.
Mockery in His ears.
Sin laid upon Him.
And He stayed.
That is the price behind Paul's words:
“You were bought with a price.”
So when Paul finally says:
δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
“Therefore glorify God in your body,”
this is not merely a prohibition against sex outside God's design.
It is an invitation to worship.
Your body can worship.
Your boundaries can worship.
Your singleness can worship.
Your marriage can worship.
Your repentance can worship.
Your decision to close the laptop can worship.
Your decision to confess can worship.
Your decision to walk away from the relationship can worship.
Your decision to stop hiding can worship.
And yes...
even a body with a history can worship.
That may be the sentence somebody desperately needed.
Your past does not get the final word over a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
The cross does.
The resurrection does.
Grace does.
Jesus does.
Talk to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
Come into the light.
Not as a performance for strangers.
As a confession that you are done pretending darkness is freedom.
And if you are finally tired of having one version of yourself in public and another version behind closed doors...
“No more hiding.”
Someone reading those words may discover that they are not the only believer fighting.
Someone may finally ask for prayer.
Someone may finally confess.
Someone may finally come home.
And that is also why sharing matters.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Send this privately to the believer who disappeared because shame convinced them they could never come back.
Come back and remember:
You are not your own. You were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money purchases forgiveness.
It never could.
And not because anyone should give under spiritual pressure. Scripture says Christian generosity should come from a willing heart, not compulsion.
But supporting Gospel ministry is one genuine way believers may choose to steward what God has entrusted to them.
give Jesus what Paul was ultimately asking for.
Your body.
Your desires.
Your wounds.
Your sexuality.
Your secrets.
Your failures.
Your future.
Your whole life.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally the story of sexually clean people congratulating themselves while sexually broken people hide outside.
It is the story of sinners being washed.
Slaves being liberated.
The ashamed being brought into the light.
The guilty being justified.
The broken being sanctified.
And people who once belonged to sin discovering that they now belong to Jesus Christ.
And comment.
Be honest.
What are you asking Jesus to reclaim today?
Your mind?
Your body?
Your relationship?
Your secret life?
Your purity?
Your future?
Maybe your answer needs only three words:
“Jesus, reclaim me.”
Because the body you thought your sin had permanently ruined may become the very place where the world sees what redemption looks like.
Your scandal may explain where you have been. Grace declares you do not have to stay there.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: REVELATION SAYS THE 144,000 “HAVE NOT DEFILED THEMSELVES WITH WOMEN”—But It Does NOT Mean What Many People Think
paragraphs: REVELATION SAYS THE 144,000 “HAVE NOT DEFILED THEMSELVES WITH WOMEN”—But It Does NOT Mean What Many People Think

Revelation 14:4 contains one of the Bible’s most unsettling descriptions of the redeemed. Read carelessly, it can sound as though women, marriage, or sexual intimacy itself contaminates a person before God. But read in the world of Revelation—and beside the Lamb who stands at the center of the vision—the verse becomes something far deeper: a terrifyingly beautiful picture of people whose allegiance cannot be bought.
There is a sentence in Revelation that can stop you cold.
Not because it is difficult to pronounce.
Because it is difficult to understand.
John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion.
With Him are 144,000 bearing His name and His Father’s name on their foreheads.
Heaven erupts with a sound like rushing waters and thunder.
A new song rises.
Then John tells us who these people are.
The Greek of Revelation 14:4 reads:
οὗτοί εἰσιν οἳ μετὰ γυναικῶν οὐκ ἐμολύνθησαν, παρθένοι γάρ εἰσιν
houtoi eisin hoi meta gynaikōn ouk emolynthēsan, parthenoi gar eisin
In straightforward English:
“These are those who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins.”
And immediately the questions begin.
Does Revelation teach that women are defiling?
Is marriage somehow spiritually inferior?
Is sexual intimacy—even within marriage—unclean?
Are the 144,000 literally unmarried virgin men?
Does this mean married Christians cannot belong among the faithful pictured here?
And perhaps underneath all those theological questions is a quieter, more personal one.
What kind of purity does Jesus actually want from me?
That is where this passage becomes uncomfortable.
Because Revelation 14:4 may not be attacking what some people think it is attacking.
It may be attacking something much closer to us.
Our divided allegiance.
Our secret compromises.
Our willingness to belong publicly to Jesus while privately sleeping with Babylon.
Before going further, we need to protect this text from a dangerous misunderstanding.
Women are not spiritually contaminating.
Marriage is not a stain.

God Himself instituted marriage in Genesis. Jesus affirmed marriage. The New Testament honors marriage, and Revelation itself ultimately celebrates salvation using the imagery of a wedding—the marriage supper of the Lamb and the Bride prepared for her Husband.
So whatever Revelation 14:4 means, it cannot responsibly be turned into the claim that touching a woman, loving a wife, or participating in faithful marital intimacy makes someone spiritually dirty.
The language is much richer than that.
The word translated “defiled” comes from the Greek verb μολύνω — molynō, carrying the sense of staining, soiling, or defiling.
Then comes another striking word:
παρθένοι — parthenoi.
Virgins.
The language is undeniably sexual.
That must not be explained away.
