And the story moved toward redemption.
But Ruth’s go’el can only whisper ahead to the greater Redeemer.
Boaz could redeem a family situation.
Jesus redeems sinners.
Boaz could offer Ruth a household.
Jesus brings repentant sinners into the household of God.
Boaz could change Ruth’s circumstances.
Only Christ can give eternal life.
So when your soul reaches its midnight, do not merely ask God for a better chapter.
Ask for Christ.
When shame tells you to hide…
come to Christ.
When sin tells you there is no way home…
come to Christ.
When grief says the story is finished…
come to Christ.
When you have nothing impressive left to offer…
come to Christ.
Come honestly.
Come repentant.
Come empty-handed.
Come needing mercy.
Because the Gospel was never the story of impressive people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of the holy God coming to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And maybe that is why Ruth’s midnight still speaks after thousands of years.
Because sometimes redemption begins when a person finally stops pretending they do not need a Redeemer.
The chapter you are ashamed to let anyone read may become the very place where grace teaches you that Jesus still knows how to write an ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN SOCIAL MEDIA QUIETLY FEED LUST?
paragraphs: CAN SOCIAL MEDIA QUIETLY FEED LUST?
The Sin You Never Searched For May Still Be Training Your Heart—and Jesus Cares About What Happens in the Seconds Nobody Else Sees
You didn't search for pornography.
You didn't type anything dirty.
You weren't planning to lust.
You were just scrolling.
One video.
Swipe.
A friend's vacation.
Swipe.
A Bible verse.
Swipe.
A funny meme.
Swipe.
Then suddenly...
there she was.
Or there he was.
A body positioned for attention. A thumbnail designed to make you stop. A reel that showed just enough skin to awaken something you thought you had under control.
And for one second, your thumb stopped.
Nobody noticed.
Your spouse didn't see it.
Your pastor didn't know.
Your Christian friends will never hear about it.
Maybe you didn't even click the profile.
You just looked.
Then looked a little longer.
Then you scrolled away.
So...
was anything really happening?
That question matters more than many Christians realize, because some of the most dangerous battles for purity today don't begin in bedrooms, hotel rooms, adult websites, or secret relationships.
Sometimes they begin with a thumb hovering over a screen.
And Jesus said something nearly two thousand years before smartphones existed that reaches straight through the glass and confronts what happens behind our eyes.
In Matthew 5:28, the Greek text includes these sobering words:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι...”

The crucial expression is pros to epithymēsai—πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι—looking with the purpose or direction of desiring lustfully. Jesus continues by locating the adultery “ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ”—en tē kardia autou—“in his heart.”
Read that carefully.
Jesus was not teaching that merely noticing an attractive person is identical to adultery.
He was going deeper.
There is a difference between seeing and choosing to keep looking in order to feed desire.
There is a difference between temptation arriving at your door...
and inviting it inside.
And social media has created an environment where that distinction can become frighteningly easy to blur.
You don't always have to go looking for temptation anymore.
Temptation can scroll toward you.
It can arrive between a worship song and a cooking video.
It can appear after a sermon clip.
It can wear the disguise of fitness.
Fashion.
Entertainment.
Humor.
Influencer culture.
Celebrity news.
Even seemingly innocent curiosity.
And suddenly the battle isn't simply about what appeared on your screen.
The battle becomes what you chose to do after it appeared.
Did you scroll?
Or did you return?
Did you dismiss it?
Or visit the profile?
Did you recognize temptation?
Or quietly negotiate with it?
Did you tell yourself, “I'm not doing anything”?
Because perhaps that's exactly where somebody reading this has been living.
Not in open sexual rebellion.
Not necessarily in pornography.
Not necessarily in adultery.
But in tiny compromises nobody can see.
Five seconds here.
Ten seconds there.
Another profile.
Another reel.
Another glance.
Another late-night scroll when everyone else is asleep.
And eventually you realize something uncomfortable.
Your feed isn't merely showing you things anymore.
It may be training what you desire.
But before shame starts screaming at you, hear the Gospel clearly.
Jesus did not come merely to expose dirty hearts.
Jesus came to redeem sinners.
That distinction changes everything.
Because Christianity isn't the story of clean people congratulating themselves for never struggling.
It is the story of sinners who desperately needed a Savior.
And sexual temptation is not proof that Christ has abandoned you.
Temptation itself is not identical to surrendering to temptation.
Jesus Himself “was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” according to Hebrews 4:15.
So don't confuse being tempted with being defeated.
But don't confuse repeatedly feeding temptation with innocence either.
James describes the progression with disturbing precision.
“ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος.”
Each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his own desire.
The Greek uses epithymia—ἐπιθυμία—for desire, while exelkomenos carries the sense of being drawn away and deleazomenos of being enticed or lured.
That imagery should make every Christian who owns a smartphone think.
A lure does not usually look dangerous to the fish.
That's why it works.
It looks desirable.
Interesting.
Beautiful.
Worth investigating.
The hook isn't what catches the eye.
The bait is.
And temptation still works that way.
The enemy rarely announces:
“Hello. I'm here to destroy your purity.”
Instead...
“Just look.”
“It's not pornography.”
“Everybody watches this.”
“You're only curious.”
“One more reel.”
“Visit the profile.”
“You can stop whenever you want.”
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence of all:
“Nobody will ever know.”
But God knows.
Not as a voyeur waiting eagerly to humiliate you.
As the holy God who loves you too much to pretend the thing poisoning you is harmless.
There is another uncomfortable reality.

What you repeatedly interact with online can shape what appears before you next. Platforms use engagement and other signals to personalize recommendations. So even without consciously deciding, “I want a feed filled with sexualized content,” repeated viewing and engagement can help create a digital environment increasingly populated by the very material that weakens you.
Your scrolling habits can begin constructing tomorrow's temptations.
Think about that.
What you linger over today may influence what is offered to you tomorrow.
So maybe the question isn't only:
“Did I commit some obvious sexual sin?”
Maybe another question needs asking:
“What am I teaching my attention to love?”
Because lust rarely begins with the body.
It begins in desire.
In imagination.
In attention.
In what we allow ourselves to mentally consume.
And this is where Jesus' words become breathtakingly relevant.
Christ does not merely want custody of your church attendance.
He wants your heart.
Your eyes.
Your imagination.
Your private life.
Your phone.
Your midnight scrolling.
Your secret searches.
Your saved posts.
Your second glances.
Not because salvation is earned by having a perfectly sanitized social-media account.
It isn't.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works.
But the grace that forgives us also begins changing us.
Jesus doesn't rescue us so that we can comfortably remain chained to what enslaved us.
He rescues us to make us free.
Maybe you're reading this and something inside you is getting uncomfortable.
Maybe you know exactly which account needs unfollowing.
Which app becomes dangerous after midnight.
Which person you keep checking.
Which reels you pretend are innocent.
Which saved images you wouldn't want your husband or wife to discover.
Which conversations have started becoming flirtatious.
Which private habit has slowly become stronger than you expected.
Don't run from conviction.
Run toward Christ.
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “Hide because you're filthy.”
The Gospel says something radically different.
You were already a sinner when Jesus went to the cross.
Your darkest secret did not surprise Him.
Your failure did not catch heaven unprepared.
Christ did not shed His blood for the imaginary version of you who never struggled.
He died for sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People who fell again after promising God they wouldn't.
People who cried during worship and still struggled later that night.
People who genuinely love Jesus and yet discover that old desires can still wage war against their souls.
The answer isn't pretending the war doesn't exist.
The answer is bringing the war to Jesus.
Repentance isn't merely feeling horrible about yourself.
Biblical repentance turns.
It brings darkness into light.
It stops protecting what Christ is calling us to surrender.
Sometimes repentance looks dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like deleting an app.
Unfollowing an account.
Turning off recommendations.
Moving the phone outside the bedroom.
Installing accountability software.
Confessing the struggle to a mature believer.
Handing somebody permission to ask uncomfortable questions.
Refusing to take your phone into the bathroom.
Choosing not to scroll when you're lonely, angry, rejected, stressed, or sexually vulnerable.
Sometimes one of the most spiritual things you can do is press “unfollow.”

Jesus used deliberately radical language immediately after His warning about lust, speaking of tearing out an offending eye or cutting off an offending hand. Christians have historically understood this as forceful imagery demanding decisive action against sin, not a command for bodily mutilation.
In modern language?
Stop negotiating with whatever keeps dragging you toward the cliff.
You don't prove spiritual maturity by standing one inch from temptation and boasting that you haven't fallen.
Sometimes wisdom walks away.
Paul's command concerning sexual immorality is strikingly short:
“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.”
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not study how close you can get.
Not flirt with it.
Not manage it while keeping your favorite pieces.
Flee.
There are battles you win by standing.
There are temptations you defeat by running.
Joseph ran from Potiphar's wife.
And sometimes twenty-first-century Joseph needs to close Instagram.
There is no shame in knowing where you're weak.
The danger is knowing where you're weak and deliberately building a house there.
Maybe this isn't only about men either.
Women struggle with lust.
Married people struggle.
Singles struggle.
Pastors can struggle.
Worship leaders can struggle.
People who have followed Jesus for thirty years can struggle.
Young believers struggle.
People recovering from pornography struggle.

People who have never visited a pornographic website can still discover that social media has become a softer, socially acceptable doorway into the same inward patterns of objectification and fantasy.
And we desperately need churches where people can confess temptation without being treated like monsters...
while still being challenged not to make peace with sin.
Grace without truth becomes permission.
Truth without grace becomes crushing.
Jesus brings both.
Maybe you failed yesterday.
Come back.
Maybe you failed an hour ago.
Come back.
Maybe you were reading this article while switching between tabs you know you shouldn't have open.
Come back.
You don't have to clean yourself before approaching the One whose blood cleanses sinners.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Then take practical action.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Delete what needs deleting.
Unfollow what needs unfollowing.
Confess what needs confessing.
End the conversation that needs ending.
Ask for accountability.
And when temptation comes again—and it may—remember that holiness is not merely saying no to something beautiful.
It is discovering Someone infinitely more beautiful.
Jesus Christ.
You were created for more than endless stimulation.
More than secret fantasy.
More than comparing bodies.
More than reducing another image-bearer into something to consume.
More than becoming enslaved to an algorithm that knows exactly how long your eyes hesitate.
Paul tells believers why their bodies matter:
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς... δοξάσατε... τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
“You were bought with a price... therefore glorify God in your body.”
The verb doxasate—δοξάσατε—means “glorify.” Paul grounds the command in redemption: believers belong to the Christ who purchased them at a price.
The deepest Christian motivation for purity isn't:
“I don't want to get caught.”
It is:
“I belong to Jesus.”
Those eyes belong to Jesus.
That imagination belongs to Jesus.
That sexuality belongs to Jesus.
That lonely Friday night belongs to Jesus.
That phone in your hand can belong to Jesus too.
Not because phones are inherently evil.
Not because every attractive image is sinful.
Not because Christians should become terrified of beauty.
But because anything capable of discipling your desires deserves your attention.
And perhaps that's the question we should have asked from the beginning.
Can social media quietly feed lust?
Yes, it can.
But the deeper question is whether we will quietly keep feeding it back.
You cannot always control what unexpectedly appears before your eyes.
You can increasingly learn, by grace and discipline, what you do next.
Turn away.
Pray.
Run.
Bring the struggle into light.
Remember whose you are.
And when you fail, don't let failure become permission to surrender completely.
Run back to Jesus.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Not to abuse grace.
But because grace is precisely where repentant sinners learn to stand again.
If this exposed something you've been hiding, don't write a polished Christian answer.
Be honest.
Your confession may become the sentence that gives somebody else courage to stop pretending.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this—not somebody you want to embarrass, but somebody you genuinely love—send this to them privately.
Not because you expect never to struggle again.
There is also a deeper way to help this ministry continue and expand.
It doesn't.
Not because money can buy blessing, forgiveness, salvation, or spiritual status.
It cannot.
Christian generosity must never be manipulated.
Scripture says:
“ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης.”
Each should give as he has purposed in his heart, not from compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That matters.
Support should come from willingness, gratitude, and love for the work of the Gospel—not spiritual pressure.
Your support helps us keep going.
Your sharing helps us keep reaching.
Your prayers help us keep standing.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
Jesus is the One who forgives.
Jesus is the One who restores.
Jesus is the One who can take the person who whispered, “I'll never change,” and begin writing a completely different ending.
So tonight, when the screen lights up...
when nobody is watching...
when temptation whispers that five seconds don't matter...
remember the cross.
Remember the price.
Remember whose you are.
And remember this:
The screen may know what keeps you watching—but only Jesus knows who you can become when you finally surrender what you've been hiding.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS HAVE TO BECOME HUMAN?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS HAVE TO BECOME HUMAN?
The answer is more terrifying than Christmas—and more beautiful than you may have ever realized: to rescue humanity, the Son of God entered the very flesh that would bleed for us.
There is something almost scandalous about Christianity that familiarity can make us forget.
God became human.
Not merely appearing human.
Not pretending to suffer.
Not watching our pain safely from heaven.
The eternal Son entered it.
He became small enough to be carried.
Hungry enough to need food.
Tired enough to sleep.
Human enough to bleed.
And mortal enough to die.
Stop there for a moment.
The One through whom the universe was made entered His own creation as a baby.
Why?
Why would the eternal Son of God take on human flesh?
Why Bethlehem?
Why hunger?
Why exhaustion?
Why tears?
Why nails?
Why blood?
Why did Jesus have to become one of us?
Because our problem was far deeper than bad behavior.
We did not merely need better advice.
We needed rescue.
And the rescue God planned required something no ordinary human being could accomplish.
John reaches for words that should still make us tremble:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“The Word became flesh.”
John 1:14.
Look carefully at that word:
σὰρξ — sarx — flesh.
John does not tell us merely that the Word looked human.
The eternal Word truly entered human existence.
The One whom John has already identified as existing “in the beginning” and as God became flesh.
Not by ceasing to be God.
But by truly becoming human.
Christianity therefore makes an astonishing confession: Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man.
The eternal Son did not exchange deity for humanity.
He took humanity to Himself.
And suddenly Christmas stops being sentimental.
The manger becomes the beginning of a rescue mission.
Because humanity had a problem humanity could not repair.
Sin had entered our story.
And sin was not merely a collection of embarrassing mistakes.
Sin separated rebellious humanity from the holy God who gave us life.
We had broken what we could not restore.
We had accumulated a debt we could not pay.
We were guilty before a holiness we could never manufacture for ourselves.
And death stood at the end of the road.
You know something about this even if you have never studied theology.
You have felt the fracture.
That moment after you did the thing you promised yourself you would never do again.
That secret you hope nobody discovers.
That resentment you keep feeding.
That browser history.
That affair.
That addiction.
That lie.
That bitterness.
That pride disguised as strength.
That religious performance hiding a heart that has quietly wandered from God.
Maybe everybody around you thinks you are doing fine.
You smile.
You work.
You post.
You worship.
You say, “God is good.”
And He is.
But somewhere beneath the Christian vocabulary there may be a room inside you that you desperately hope God never opens.
Except He already knows what is inside.
That is what makes grace so shocking.
Jesus did not become human because humanity was impressive.
He came because humanity needed saving.
He did not wait for us to clean ourselves before coming near.
He came into the wreckage.
The scandal came first.
Then grace walked into it wearing human flesh.
Hebrews explains why His humanity mattered:
Ἐπεὶ οὖν τὰ παιδία κεκοινώνηκεν αἵματος καὶ σαρκός, καὶ αὐτὸς παραπλησίως μετέσχεν τῶν αὐτῶν...
Because human beings share in flesh and blood, Christ Himself likewise shared in them.
Hebrews 2:14.
And then Scripture gives the breathtaking purpose:
through death He would break the power of the one who held the power of death—the devil—and deliver those enslaved by the fear of death.
Think about the logic.
To die, the Son entered mortality.
To shed blood, He took flesh and blood.
To stand in humanity's place, He became truly human.
To conquer death, He entered death.
Jesus did not defeat death by avoiding it.
He defeated death by going through it.
This is why the incarnation cannot be separated from the cross.
Bethlehem is already pointing toward Calvary.
Those tiny hands would someday be pierced.
Those infant lungs drawing their first breaths would someday cry out from a cross.
The body Mary wrapped in cloth would one day be wrapped for burial.
But the grave would discover something it had never encountered before.
A victim it could not keep.
Jesus had to be truly human because humanity needed a faithful representative.
Where humanity rebelled, Christ obeyed.
Where Adam's disobedience brought condemnation and death into the human story, Christ's obedience opened the way of righteousness and life for those united to Him.
Jesus lived the human life we have failed to live.
Not sinlessly because temptation was imaginary.
Scripture says He was tempted, yet without sin.
He knew hunger.
He knew exhaustion.
He knew rejection.
He knew grief.
He knew betrayal.
He knew what it was to have people misunderstand Him, abandon Him and falsely accuse Him.
He wept.
Jesus did not observe human suffering from a celestial balcony.
He stepped onto the battlefield.
And this matters when you are hurting.
When you whisper, “Nobody understands,” Christianity answers with a wounded Savior.
Not with the claim that every human experience Jesus faced was identical to yours, but with something deeper:
your Savior truly entered human weakness and suffering.
Hebrews says He can sympathize with our weaknesses.
He is not cold toward your tears.
He is not disgusted by the fact that you are weak.
And He is not asking you to pretend that you are stronger than you are.
But Jesus becoming human was not merely so that He could understand our suffering.
He came to save sinners.
That distinction matters.
Jesus is more than an example.
More than a therapist.
More than an inspirational teacher.
More than a revolutionary moral voice.
More than a Christmas baby.
The incarnation moves relentlessly toward substitution.
Sin deserves judgment.
Humanity sinned.
And humanity needed a righteous representative.
Yet no merely ordinary descendant of Adam could provide the spotless sacrifice humanity needed, because every one of us stands in need of grace ourselves.
Then came Jesus.
Fully human.
Without sin.
And fully divine.
The worth of the One offering Himself cannot be separated from who He is.
This is where the mystery becomes breathtaking.
The Judge entered the world of the guilty.
The Creator walked among His creatures.
The King took the form of a servant.
Paul writes of Christ:
ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων
existing in the form of God...
yet
ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν μορφὴν δούλου λαβών
He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant.
Philippians 2:6–7.
This does not mean Jesus stopped being God.
Paul's own words describe the “emptying” through taking the form of a servant and becoming human.
His humiliation was not the abandonment of deity.
It was the astonishing descent of the divine Son into servanthood and human lowliness.
Then Paul takes us lower.
Jesus
ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν
“humbled Himself,”
becoming obedient unto death—
even death on a cross.
The road runs downward.
Glory.
Servanthood.
Humanity.
Humiliation.
Death.
Cross.
And then God highly exalts Him.
This is the Gospel.
Not humanity climbing its way toward God.
God came down.
You could not reach Him.
So Christ came for sinners.
You could not pay your debt.
So Christ gave Himself.
You could not defeat death.
So Christ entered the grave.
You could not manufacture righteousness sufficient to reconcile yourself to a holy God.
So the righteous One stood where sinners deserved to stand.
And then came Sunday.
The stone moved.
The grave emptied.
Death lost its claim over the risen Christ.
Jesus did not merely survive death.
He conquered it.
And this is where the question “Why did Jesus have to become human?” stops being a theological curiosity.
Because this is about you.
Your sin.
Your death.
Your eternity.
Your hope.
Your Savior.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to become acceptable enough for God.
Maybe you think Christianity means behaving well enough that Jesus will finally love you.
But the incarnation destroys that illusion.
Christ came because you could not save yourself.
Grace begins where self-salvation dies.
You don't need to impress Jesus.
You need Jesus.
You don't need another religious mask.
You need repentance.
You don't need to convince God that your sin was not that serious.
You need to confess that it was serious enough for Christ to go to the cross—and then believe that His grace is greater than your guilt.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself up so God will tolerate you.
It is turning from sin and turning toward the Savior who has already done what you could never do for yourself.
Maybe this article found you while you are hiding something.
Maybe everyone thinks your faith is strong.
But you know.
You know how tired you are.
You know what keeps defeating you.
You know how far your heart has wandered.
You know the prayer you stopped praying because you became ashamed of failing again.
Listen carefully.
The incarnation means God did not save humanity from a distance.
Jesus came near.
And the cross means He came near enough to carry sin's judgment.
The resurrection means your darkest chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
This is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is more honest than that.
The Gospel looks directly at sin and calls it sin.
It looks directly at guilt and calls it guilt.
It looks directly at death and calls it an enemy.
Then it points to Jesus.
Crucified.
Buried.
Risen.
And says:
There is forgiveness here.
There is reconciliation here.
There is a new beginning here.
There is a Savior here.
If something inside you has been hiding from God, stop running.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Christ did not become human so that you could admire Christianity from a distance.
He came calling sinners to Himself.
Not as a magic formula.
Not because a Facebook comment saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need mercy is one small way of refusing to keep hiding.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only believer in the battle.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose them.
It rests upon the goodness of the Savior.
One share can place the Gospel before someone we may never reach otherwise.
Save it too.
There may come a night when shame returns and whispers that your past has the final word.
Come back and remember:
Jesus does.
We want this community to remain a place of daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship and spiritual nourishment centered upon Jesus Christ.
And for those asking how they can help Gospel Warrior continue and expand this work, there is another way.
Grace cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price we never could.
But Scripture does show believers voluntarily and generously supporting Gospel ministry and those laboring to spread the Word.
Your support helps us keep going.
It helps us reach farther.
It helps us create more.
It helps put biblical encouragement before people who may be quietly drowning behind smiling profile pictures.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The invitation of Jesus remains grace.
And you can still help tremendously.
Pray.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done for you.
Because perhaps the most important person reached through this article will never be someone whose name we know.
Maybe tonight there is a man sitting alone convinced his secret sin has made him unreachable.
Maybe there is a woman scrolling through Facebook after everybody else has gone to sleep, wondering whether God could still want her after what happened.
Maybe there is a believer who fell again and is considering walking away because shame has convinced him that Jesus must finally be tired of him.
And maybe your share places one sentence in front of that person:
The Word became flesh.
God came near.
Christ entered our humanity.
He carried the cross.
He entered death.
He rose victorious.
And sinners who repent and trust in Him can be forgiven, reconciled to God and given new life.
That is why Jesus became human.
Not so Christmas could become a holiday.
So sinners could come home.
Not merely so we could have a manger scene.
So there could be a cross.
Not merely so there could be a cross.
So there could be an empty tomb.
And not merely so there could be an empty tomb.
So people once dead in sin could become alive in Christ.
So the ashamed could discover grace.
So rebels could become children.
So the guilty could be forgiven.
So those terrified of death could belong to the One who conquered it.
So your story would not have to end where your scandal began.
The hands that were small enough for Mary to hold became the hands stretched upon the cross for sinners.
And the Christ who walked out of the grave is still rewriting human stories.
Maybe yours is next.
Your scandal may explain where you have been—but because of Jesus, it does not have the authority to decide where your story ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “FLEE SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY DOES PAUL SAY RUN INSTEAD OF “SEE HOW CLOSE YOU CAN GET”?
paragraphs: “FLEE SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY DOES PAUL SAY RUN INSTEAD OF “SEE HOW CLOSE YOU CAN GET”?
Maybe the reason you keep losing the battle isn’t because temptation is stronger than you. Maybe it’s because you keep standing beside the fire God told you to run from.
There is a moment before almost every sexual fall when you still could have walked away.
Before the deleted messages.
Before the hidden browser history.
Before the second account.
Before the conversation became flirtation.
Before flirtation became fantasy.
Before fantasy became secrecy.
Before secrecy became a meeting.
Before “I would never do that” became “How did I get here?”
There was usually a door.
And for a few seconds, you were standing in front of it.
You knew.
Your conscience whispered.
The Holy Spirit convicted.
Something inside you said, Leave.
But another voice answered:
Just one more look.
Just one more message.
We’re only talking.
I can handle this.
Nothing is going to happen.
I know where my boundaries are.
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence of all:
How close can I get without actually sinning?
Then Paul enters the conversation with two words that destroy the entire strategy.
In the Greek text of 1 Corinthians 6:18:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not study it.
Not negotiate with it.
Not prove how spiritually mature you are by standing beside it.
Not see how close you can get.
Flee.

The verb φεύγετε — pheugete carries the idea of fleeing, escaping, getting away. Paul does not portray sexual temptation as something believers should deliberately keep within arm’s reach so they can demonstrate their self-control.
He tells them to create distance.
And πορνεία — porneia, translated “sexual immorality,” was a broad Greek term for sexual activity outside the boundaries God established for sexual faithfulness.
Paul’s sentence is almost violently simple.
Run from it.
And maybe somebody reading this already knows exactly why.
Because you tried staying.
You told yourself you were strong enough.
You told yourself you were only curious.
You told yourself nobody would know.
You told yourself it was only pornography.
Only fantasy.
Only flirting.
Only messages.
Only emotional intimacy.
Only one night.
Only one secret.
But sin has always loved the word only.
Because “only” makes chains look small enough to wear.
Paul knew something about sexual sin that modern culture desperately wants us to forget.
Your body matters to God.
Read the surrounding passage.
Paul does not merely say, “Stop doing bad things.”
He says something breathtaking about the Christian body.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Your body is for the Lord.
The believer is united with Christ.
Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
That changes everything.
Christian sexual holiness is not based on the idea that sex is dirty.
It is based on the truth that the body is sacred.
Sexual desire itself is not the enemy. God created humanity male and female. Scripture celebrates covenant marriage. Sexual intimacy within God's design is not something Christianity apologizes for.
The problem is not that human beings desire intimacy.
The problem begins when desire tries to become lord.
Paul had already written:
“All things are lawful for me”—but not all things are helpful.
And then:
“I will not be dominated by anything.”
There it is.
The question is no longer merely:
Can I do this?
The deeper question becomes:
Is this beginning to own me?
That is a terrifying question when asked honestly.
Because some people reading this know what it feels like to be owned by something they once thought they controlled.
You controlled the pornography.
Until pornography started deciding when you slept.
You controlled the flirting.
Until you began waiting for that person's message.
You controlled the fantasy.
Until your spouse could no longer compete with the imaginary world inside your head.
You controlled the secret relationship.
Until deleting evidence became part of your daily routine.
You controlled the desire.
Until desire started controlling you.
And suddenly Paul's command does not sound prudish.
It sounds like rescue.
φεύγετε.
Flee.
Run while your legs still remember freedom.
There is another biblical story that makes Paul's command almost impossible to read casually.
Joseph.
Genesis 39.
A young man far from home.
No father watching.
No brothers watching.
No accountability group.
No smartphone location sharing.
No wife waiting at home.
And Potiphar's wife repeatedly pressures him sexually.
Then one day she grabs his garment.
“Lie with me.”
Joseph does something remarkably unmodern.
He does not stay to demonstrate his willpower.
He does not explain that they need healthier boundaries.
He does not remain in the room for another conversation.
Scripture says he left his garment in her hand and fled.
He ran outside.
Joseph would rather lose his coat than lose his integrity.
Some of us keep trying to preserve the coat.
The relationship.
The contact.
The app.
The private conversation.
The friendship that stopped being innocent months ago.
The phone beside the bed.
The account nobody knows about.
The connection with the ex.
The person who keeps awakening something you know should be buried.
We want holiness without inconvenience.
We want purity without losing access.
We want freedom without closing doors.
We want God to deliver us from temptation while reserving the right to keep temptation's phone number.
Then we wonder why the battle never ends.
There are battles you win by standing.
Scripture says, “Resist the devil.”
But sexual immorality receives remarkably practical language:
Flee.
Sometimes courage looks like standing your ground.
Sometimes courage looks like running as fast as obedience can carry you.
This is not cowardice.
It is wisdom.
A person running out of a burning building is not weak because he refuses to prove how much smoke he can inhale.
And perhaps that is the picture somebody needs tonight.
You have been calling the flames “warmth.”
God calls them danger.
You have been asking:
How far is too far?
Maybe that is already the wrong question.
Love asks something different.
Not:
How much sin can I approach without crossing the line?
But:
How closely can I walk with Jesus?
That changes the direction of the entire Christian life.
Because holiness is not merely backing away from hell.
It is moving toward Christ.
And this is where Paul's argument becomes stunningly beautiful.
Immediately after commanding believers to flee sexual immorality, he asks:
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you...?”
Then comes the sentence shame desperately wants you to forget:
“You were bought with a price.”
Read that again.
Bought.
With.
A price.
What price?
Not silver.
Not religious performance.
Not enough clean days on your calendar.
Not enough promises that you will never do it again.
The price was Christ Himself.
His blood.
His cross.
His life given for sinners.
And suddenly this passage is no longer merely about sexual behavior.
It is about ownership.
Identity.
Redemption.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely to improve your habits.
He came to redeem you.
That means when Christ says, “Flee,” He is not a tyrant trying to steal pleasure.
He is the Savior who paid for your freedom warning you not to walk willingly back toward your chains.
But there is another person reading this.
You already crossed the line.
Maybe years ago.
Maybe last night.
Maybe ten minutes before opening this article.
And while reading these words, something inside you has been sinking.
Because you do not need anyone to explain conviction.
You feel it.
You remember the promise you made God.
You remember crying the last time.
You remember saying:
“Jesus, I swear I'll never do it again.”
Then you did.
And now shame is preaching its own gospel to you.
Filthy.
Hypocrite.
Fake Christian.
God must be finished with you.
Listen carefully.
Conviction says, Come into the light.
Shame says, Hide from God.
The Gospel says something shame never wants sinners to hear:
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Real ones.
Not imaginary sinners whose sins are socially acceptable.
Not polished church people who merely needed minor adjustments.
Sinners.
The sexually broken.
The adulterer.
The porn-addicted.
The sexually exploited.
The exploiter who truly repents.
The person carrying memories they wish they could erase.
The person whose secret would shock everyone who knows them.
Paul knew the Corinthian church was not populated by people with spotless histories.
Earlier in this very chapter he names serious patterns of sin, including sexual immorality.
Then he says:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Some.
Of.
You.
Then comes grace:
You were washed.
You were sanctified.
You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
That may be one of the most beautiful sentences ever written to people with scandal in their past.
Your past can describe where Jesus found you without being allowed to dictate where Jesus is taking you.
That is Gospel Warrior territory.
Not because scandal was imaginary.
Not because sin does not matter.
Not because God changed His definition of holiness.
But because Jesus Christ rewrites everything.
Repentance does not mean pretending the chapter never happened.
Grace means the chapter does not have to be the ending.
Maybe your story contains adultery.
Jesus can still write repentance.
Maybe pornography has occupied years of your life.
Jesus can still write freedom.
Maybe you surrendered your body trying to feel loved.
Jesus can still write restoration.
Maybe somebody violated you and you have spent years confusing what was done to you with something that made you dirty.
What another person did against you does not make their sin your guilt.
Christ is not disgusted by the wounded person coming to Him for healing.
Maybe you have hidden sexual sin beneath Christian vocabulary, ministry activity, worship songs, Bible verses and Sunday smiles.
Then perhaps today is the day the hiding ends.
Not because exposure is comfortable.
Because darkness cannot heal what it insists on hiding.
Bring it to Jesus.
Repent honestly.
Where another person has been harmed, take responsibility rather than manipulating them with spiritual language.
Seek wise pastoral help and trustworthy accountability.
If necessary, remove access.
Delete the account.
Block the number.
Move the device.
End the secret conversation.
Stop visiting the place.
Tell somebody mature enough to help you walk in truth.
Do not merely pray for God to close a door while keeping your hand wrapped around the handle.
Run.
And when temptation returns tomorrow?
Run again.
If it returns next week?
Run again.
If your flesh screams?
Run again.
Not toward emptiness.
Toward Christ.
Because biblical purity is not ultimately the worship of self-control.
It is the worship of Jesus.
You are not trying to become clean enough for Christ to love you.
If you belong to Him, you fight because you have been loved at unimaginable cost.
“You were bought with a price.”
The cross settles your worth.
The resurrection announces that sin and death do not get the final word.
The Holy Spirit means you do not fight alone.
And grace means failure does not have to become identity.
So perhaps you need to stop asking:
“How close can I get?”
Perhaps tonight you need a different prayer.
“Jesus, how far do I need to run?”
And when He shows you...
Run.
Somebody else needs this message before tonight becomes another regret.
You do not have to fight alone.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to surrender tonight.
Not because temptation disappears after one emotional moment.
Come back.
Read Paul's words again.
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Flee sexual immorality.
Then remember why.
You belong to Jesus.

Scripture gives genuine warrant for believers materially supporting Gospel ministry. Paul taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living through Gospel work. But Scripture also teaches that Christian giving should not be manipulated or forced; each believer should give willingly rather than “under compulsion.”
We can tell you this:

If these messages are feeding you spiritually, and you want to glorify God with your resources, prayerfully consider supporting Gospel work—including your local church and faithful ministries God has placed on your heart. If Gospel Warrior is one of those ministries for you, we would be deeply grateful to have you standing with us.
Your support helps us keep reaching people who may never walk through a church door but will stop long enough to read something about Jesus on their phone.
And whether or not you can financially support the ministry right now, you can still help tremendously.
Send it privately to someone fighting temptation.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is standing at a door.
One more click.
One more message.
One more secret.
One more compromise.
And perhaps God allowed these words to reach them before they touched the handle.
If that person is you...
You do not need to find out what is waiting on the other side.
Turn around.
Run.
Not because Jesus is waiting behind you with condemnation.
Run because Jesus is ahead of you with freedom.
You do not have to see how close you can get to the darkness when the One who bought you with His blood is calling you back into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT HAPPENED IF A MAN HAD SEX WITH A WOMAN DURING HER MENSTRUAL PERIOD?
paragraphs: WHAT HAPPENED IF A MAN HAD SEX WITH A WOMAN DURING HER MENSTRUAL PERIOD?

Leviticus gives an answer severe enough to disturb modern readers—but if you stop at the punishment, you may completely miss what the blood, the boundary, and ultimately Jesus Christ were pointing toward.
There are verses in the Bible people quietly skip.
Not because they are difficult to read.
Because they are difficult to explain.
Leviticus 18:19 and Leviticus 20:18 belong to that category.
Maybe you have read them and wondered, Why would God care about this?
Maybe someone used these passages to argue that the Bible treats a woman’s menstrual cycle as shameful.
Maybe you have personally done what these verses prohibit, and now the question is no longer academic.
Did I commit some unforgivable sin?
Is menstruation somehow dirty before God?
Does this command still apply to Christians today?
And what exactly happened under the Law of Moses if a man knowingly had sexual intercourse with a woman during her menstrual period?
Those questions deserve something better than embarrassment, mockery, fear, or a convenient answer designed to make Scripture say whatever we want.
So stay with the text.
Because there is blood in this story.
There is holiness in this story.
There is judgment in this story.
But before we reach the end, there will be another kind of blood.
Blood that does not make the sinner unclean.
Blood that cleanses the unclean.
And that changes everything.
Leviticus 18:19 reads:
“You shall not approach a woman to uncover her nakedness while she is in her menstrual uncleanness.”
The Hebrew is striking:
וְאֶל־אִשָּׁה בְּנִדַּת טֻמְאָתָהּ לֹא תִקְרַב לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ
Ve’el-ishshah beniddat tum’atah lo tiqrav legalot ervatah.
In straightforward sense:
You shall not approach a woman during the menstrual state of her uncleanness to uncover her nakedness.
One important word is נִדָּה — niddah.
In this context it refers to the menstrual condition or period of separation associated with ritual impurity.
And immediately we need to destroy a damaging misunderstanding.
The Bible does not say that a woman sins simply by menstruating.
Read Leviticus 15 carefully.

Menstruation is treated within Israel’s system of ritual purity. Bodily discharges could produce a state of ceremonial uncleanness, and ceremonial uncleanness was not automatically the same thing as committing a moral transgression.
That distinction matters enormously.
A menstruating Israelite woman was not being accused of rebellion against God merely because her body was functioning naturally.
Her menstrual flow placed her in a condition described by the Hebrew vocabulary of ritual impurity.
That is different from saying:
She is disgusting.
Different from saying:
Her womanhood is sinful.
Different from saying:
God is ashamed of her body.
Scripture says none of those things.

In fact, the woman herself was not the only person who could become ritually unclean in Leviticus. Men experienced bodily discharges. People became unclean through contact with corpses. Childbirth involved purification regulations. Various physical conditions intersected with Israel’s elaborate system of clean and unclean.
God was teaching Israel to live with an extraordinary consciousness of distinction.
Holy and common.
Clean and unclean.
Life and death.
Approach and separation.
And blood occupied an especially important place in that world.
Leviticus 17:11 declares that the life of the flesh is in the blood.
So when we arrive at Leviticus 18:19, we are not reading an isolated sentence dropped randomly into the Bible.
We are standing inside Israel’s covenant world.
Then comes the verse that makes people uncomfortable.
Leviticus 20:18.
The Hebrew begins:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִשְׁכַּב אֶת־אִשָּׁה דָּוָה
Ve’ish asher-yishkav et-ishshah davah...
It describes a man lying sexually with a menstruating woman.
The text says that he has exposed her flow and she has uncovered the flow of her blood, and then comes the consequence:
וְנִכְרְתוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם מִקֶּרֶב עַמָּם
Venikhretu sheneihem miqqerev ammam.
“Both of them shall be cut off from among their people.”
There is the uncomfortable answer.

Under the Mosaic covenant, Leviticus 18:19 prohibited sexual intercourse during menstruation, and Leviticus 20:18 attaches the serious covenant sanction of being “cut off” from the people to the prohibited act.
Notice something else.
The text does not place responsibility only upon the woman.
It says:
שְׁנֵיהֶם — sheneihem.
“Both of them.”
The man cannot point at the woman and say, “She was the unclean one.”
Both are addressed.
Both crossed the stated boundary.
Both are accountable.
But then somebody who has actually read Leviticus may raise an important objection.
“What about Leviticus 15:24?”
Good question.
That passage says that if a man lies with a menstruating woman and her menstrual impurity comes upon him, he becomes unclean for seven days, and the bed on which he lies becomes unclean.
So why does one passage speak about seven days of uncleanness while another speaks about being cut off?

Interpreters have wrestled with the relationship between these texts. One common distinction understands Leviticus 15 within regulations governing ritual impurity and Leviticus 18 and 20 as addressing the prohibited sexual act itself within the holiness laws.
Whatever interpretive details are debated, we should not erase either passage.
Leviticus 15 describes ritual consequences associated with menstrual impurity.
Leviticus 18 explicitly says not to approach for sexual relations during that condition.
Leviticus 20 assigns a severe covenant consequence to violating that prohibition.
We have to let all three texts speak.
But now comes the question Christians cannot avoid:
Does that mean Christians today are living under the exact civil and ceremonial sanctions of ancient Israel?
No.
And understanding why does not require throwing Leviticus away.
Jesus did not come because the Old Testament was an embarrassing mistake that needed to disappear.
He came as its fulfillment.

The Law was part of God’s covenant dealings with Israel, containing moral instruction alongside sacrificial, priestly, purity, dietary, national, and ceremonial regulations that shaped Israel as a people set apart for God.
The New Testament does not simply transfer Israel’s entire ritual-purity system and its national covenant penalties unchanged onto the Church.
That is why Christians do not become ceremonially unclean for seven days because they touched something that Leviticus declared unclean.
That is why the Church does not maintain the Levitical sacrificial system.
That is why Christians do not bring animals to a Levitical priest after bodily discharges.
And most importantly, the New Testament never teaches that the ordinary biological process of menstruation makes a Christian woman spiritually condemned before God.
So we must be careful here.
A Christian should not take Leviticus 20:18 and announce that Christians who have intercourse during menstruation must now be expelled from society under ancient Israel’s covenant sanction.
That would ignore the covenantal setting of the command and the New Testament’s teaching concerning Christ and the Law.
At the same time, we should not become so desperate to escape an uncomfortable verse that we refuse to learn anything from it.
Because underneath this difficult passage stands a truth modern culture desperately resists:
God has authority even over the parts of our lives we call private.
Including sexuality.
That is where this ancient verse suddenly stops feeling ancient.
We live in a world that repeatedly whispers:
My body.
My desire.
My bedroom.
My rules.
But Scripture keeps confronting humanity with another reality.
You belong to your Creator.
And for the Christian, Paul makes the claim even more personal:
“You are not your own.”
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
—1 Corinthians 6:19–20
That principle reaches much further than one question about menstruation.
Because the deeper question is not merely:
What am I technically allowed to do?
The deeper question is:
Does Jesus have authority here too?
In my bedroom?
In my browser history?
In my secret fantasies?
In the relationship nobody knows about?
In what I do with another person’s body?
In what I do with my own?
In the desires I excuse because nobody sees them?
That is where Leviticus stops being a strange ancient book and starts becoming a mirror.
We love a Jesus who enters the visible parts of our lives.
Our Sunday mornings.
Our worship playlists.
Our inspirational posts.
Our Bible verses.
Our public testimonies.
But Jesus does not stand outside the locked rooms of human existence.
He is Lord there too.
And maybe that is why this subject makes us uncomfortable.
Sometimes the verses we most want to avoid are standing closest to the doors we most want to keep locked.
But hear this carefully.
Conviction is not the same thing as hopelessness.
If you crossed sexual boundaries in your past...
If you crossed them last night...
If your sexual history contains things you are ashamed even to name...
If you have lived for years believing that God could forgive everybody except you...
Do not turn an Old Testament purity passage into a declaration that Christ cannot cleanse you.
Because the Gospel moves us toward another scene involving blood.
A hill.
A cross.
A wounded Savior.
And suddenly the imagery becomes almost unbearable.
Throughout Scripture, blood is associated with life.
Sacrificial blood stood at the center of Israel’s worship.
And then Jesus Christ came.
Not as another sinner searching for cleansing.
But as the spotless Lamb.
At the Last Supper He spoke of His blood of the covenant.
At Calvary, He gave Himself.
Hebrews tells us that the sacrificial system found its decisive fulfillment in Christ, whose sacrifice does what repeated animal sacrifices could never finally accomplish.
And 1 John 1:7 gives sinners one of the most beautiful sentences ever written:
“The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.”
Do you see the reversal?
Human beings spend their lives trying to hide their uncleanness.
Jesus walks toward unclean people.
Human beings say, “Do not touch me. If you knew what I had done, you would leave.”
Jesus touches lepers.
Receives sinners.
Restores failures.
Calls the ashamed out of hiding.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because His grace is greater than the sinner’s ability to save himself.
The Gospel is not:
Your sin was never serious.
The Gospel is:
Your sin was so serious that Christ went to the cross—and His grace is so powerful that the cross is enough.
That distinction can change a life.
Maybe you came to this article because you wanted an answer about sex during menstruation.
You got the answer.

Ancient Israel was expressly forbidden from that sexual act in Leviticus 18:19, and Leviticus 20:18 describes both participants being “cut off” from their people for violating the prohibition. Leviticus 15 also provides the broader ritual-purity background.
But perhaps God allowed an uncomfortable question to bring you somewhere deeper.
Because maybe your real problem was never Leviticus.
Maybe your real question was:
Can Jesus still want me after everything I have done?
Yes.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus receives sinners and transforms sinners.
Biblical repentance is not learning better vocabulary for excusing what God calls sin.
It is turning toward God.
Confessing.
Surrendering.
Trusting Christ.
Walking differently because the One who forgave you is now the One you love.
And if something in this article exposed an area you have been hiding, do not perform spirituality for the comments.
Be honest before God.

And if Jesus has already brought you out of a place you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what Christ has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another ashamed person needs to read tonight.
Not everybody who needs this will search for it.
Sometimes they need a friend courageous enough to put it where they can find it.
Supporting Gospel work can be a genuine way of using what God has entrusted to us for ministry, teaching, discipleship, and the spread of biblical truth.
Paul wrote:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός.
Hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia... hilaron gar dotēn agapa ho Theos.
In essence: each should give as he has determined in his heart, not under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
—2 Corinthians 9:7
That is how Christian support should work.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Joyfully.
For God’s glory.
And there is something else we want people to know.
Share.
Pray.

Put biblical truth in front of the struggling believer who is quietly slipping away, the Christian trapped in shame, the seeker afraid to ask difficult questions, the lukewarm believer who needs awakening, or even the unbelieving friend who has never understood what Christianity is actually about.
Because the purpose was never merely to win an argument about Leviticus.
The purpose is to lead people through Scripture to Jesus.
And perhaps that is the truth worth carrying away from this uncomfortable passage:
God is holy.
Sin matters.
Our bodies matter.
Sexuality matters.
Obedience matters.
But your worst chapter does not possess greater authority than the cross of Jesus Christ.
You may have crossed boundaries.
You may have ignored God.
You may carry memories you wish you could erase.
You may feel unclean in places nobody else can see.
But if you come to Christ in repentance and faith, your scandal does not get the final sentence.

The blood that makes us ashamed of our humanity is not the blood that defines our eternity; for the repentant sinner, the final word belongs to the blood of Jesus Christ that cleanses, redeems, and brings us home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PAUL SAYS SEX WITH A PROSTITUTE CREATES A KIND OF “ONE FLESH” UNION—Why Is That So Serious?
paragraphs: PAUL SAYS SEX WITH A PROSTITUTE CREATES A KIND OF “ONE FLESH” UNION—Why Is That So Serious?
What if the sexual encounter you called “just physical” was never merely physical at all?
There are verses in the Bible we read quickly because slowing down would make us uncomfortable.
This is one of them.
Paul asks:
“Do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute is one body with her?”
Then he reaches all the way back to Genesis:
“The two will become one flesh.”
—1 Corinthians 6:16
Read that again.
Not because sex is dirty.
Not because the human body is shameful.
Not because Christianity is terrified of sexuality.
Precisely the opposite.
Paul's warning is so severe because, in the biblical vision, the body matters enormously.
Your body matters to God.
And that changes everything.
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 6:16 is startling:
ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν
ho kollōmenos tē pornē hen sōma estin
In straightforward English:
“The one joining himself to the prostitute is one body with her.”
Paul then explains why:
Οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
Hoi duo eis sarka mian.
“The two [will become] one flesh.”
That language did not originate with Paul.
He is deliberately reaching backward into the opening chapters of Scripture.
Genesis 2:24 describes God's design for marriage: a man leaves father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Paul takes that sacred Genesis language and applies it somewhere his readers probably did not expect:
to a man having sex with a prostitute.
Why?
Because apparently the body cannot simply say, “This means nothing,” when God designed sexual union to mean something profound.
That is where this passage begins to hurt.
Because modern culture has taught us to separate what Scripture repeatedly holds together.
Body from soul.
Sex from covenant.
Pleasure from responsibility.
Desire from holiness.
What happens in private from who we are before God.
We have learned phrases that make everything sound harmless.
“It was only one night.”
“There weren't any feelings.”
“We both wanted it.”
“It didn't mean anything.”
“It was only physical.”
Paul walks directly into that reasoning and says, in effect:
Do you understand what your body is?
Because this is not merely about what you did with somebody else's body.
It is about whose body you brought into the encounter.
Paul begins verse 15 with something even more shocking than verse 16:
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”
That is his starting point.
Not disgust.
Not humiliation.
Not “your body is filthy.”
Christ.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Paul's argument is that the Christian cannot compartmentalize the body as though Jesus owns Sunday morning while sexual desire owns Saturday night.
You cannot put Christ in one room of your life and lock the bedroom door.
Paul asks whether he should take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute.
His answer in Greek is explosive:
μὴ γένοιτο — mē genoito.
It carries the force of:
Absolutely not. May it never be.
And suddenly this passage becomes much bigger than prostitution.
It reaches the secret relationship.
The hotel room.
The affair nobody discovered.
The pornography hidden behind browser history.
The hookup you told yourself you had forgotten.
The person you keep returning to even though you know the relationship keeps pulling you farther from Christ.
The messages you delete.
The compromise you renamed “love” because calling it sin would require you to change.
And perhaps, for someone reading this, it reaches into something years behind you.
Something you deeply regret.
Something nobody at church knows.
Something you have confessed to God repeatedly because part of you still wonders whether Jesus actually forgave you the first time.
Listen carefully.
Paul is not teaching that every act of sexual intercourse automatically creates a biblical marriage covenant.
That would go beyond his argument.
Marriage in Scripture cannot simply be reduced to intercourse.
But neither does Paul permit the opposite error—the modern fantasy that intercourse is merely recreational contact between two unrelated bodies.
Sex possesses a genuine one-flesh reality.
That is exactly why Paul can use Genesis 2:24 while condemning prostitution.
The sexual act can participate in one-flesh bodily union without thereby transforming sexual immorality into a righteous marriage covenant.
That distinction is crucial.
The prostitute does not become the man's covenant wife merely because he sinned with her.
But neither can the man dismiss what happened as meaningless physical contact.
Something profoundly bodily happened.
And your body matters because your body belongs to Christ.
This is why biblical sexual holiness is not God standing outside human happiness shouting, “Stop enjoying yourselves.”
It is the Creator saying:
You do not understand how valuable you are.
The world says your body is merchandise.
Christ says it was purchased.
The world says desire determines identity.
Christ says you belong to Him.
The world says sexual freedom means nobody gets to tell you what to do with your body.
Paul says something radically different:
“You are not your own.”
Those words can sound restrictive until you read the next sentence.
“You were bought at a price.”
There is Calvary hiding inside Paul's sexual ethic.
Blood.
Nails.
A wounded Savior.
A cross outside Jerusalem.
Jesus did not purchase you because you were spotless.
He purchased sinners.
People with histories.
People with cravings.
People who crossed lines.
People who knew better and still did it.
People who promised God they would stop and returned again.
People whose bodies carry memories they wish they could erase.
People who have been sexually used.
People who have sexually used others.
People who were betrayed.
People who became the betrayer.
People whose sexual past is complicated enough that they are afraid Christianity has no category for them except “unclean.”
But Christianity does.
There is a word for guilty people who come to Christ.
Forgiven.
There is a word for people enslaved by sin whom Christ begins setting free.
Redeemed.
There is a word for the person who thought his or her worst chapter had become the final chapter.
Grace.
And Paul knew exactly what kind of church he was writing to.
Immediately before this passage, he reminds the Corinthians of lives characterized by sexual immorality, adultery, greed, drunkenness and other sins.
Then comes one of the most beautiful turns in the entire letter:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because their histories disappeared.
Not because their sins suddenly became acceptable.
Because Jesus had entered the story.
Paul continues by saying they were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Do you see it?
The Gospel does not say:
Your sin wasn't serious.
The Gospel says:
Your Savior is greater.
Grace does not minimize sin.
Grace looks directly at the full horror of sin and announces that Christ's blood is sufficient for repentant sinners.
That is why cheap grace is not grace.
And hopeless shame is not the Gospel either.
One says, “It doesn't matter.”
The other says, “You can never come home.”
Jesus destroys both lies.
Sin matters.
And you can come home.
Maybe that is what someone reading this desperately needs to hear.
Your sexual past may explain some wounds.
It may carry consequences.
Repentance may require difficult decisions.

There may be relationships you need to leave, boundaries you need to establish, accountability you need to seek, pornography you need to stop feeding, secrets you need to bring into the light, forgiveness you need to ask for, or professional and pastoral help you need to pursue.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
Paul therefore does not say:
“Manage sexual immorality.”
He says:
“Flee sexual immorality.”
The Greek is brutally simple:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Run.
Not negotiate.
Not flirt with it.
Not see how close you can get before technically crossing a line.
Flee.
There are battles Scripture tells us to stand and fight.
This is one Scripture tells us to run from.
Because sometimes the most courageous spiritual decision you can make is admitting:
I am not strong enough to keep standing this close to what keeps destroying me.
Delete the number.
End the secret conversation.
Walk out.
Install the accountability.
Tell somebody mature in Christ.
Stop revisiting the profile.
Stop calling temptation “closure.”
Stop treating pornography as harmless because no physical prostitute is standing in the room.
Stop assuming secrecy makes something spiritually insignificant.
Run toward Christ.
Because Paul's destination is not merely sexual avoidance.
His destination is worship.
He ends:
“Therefore glorify God with your body.”
That is the destination.
Not merely “Don't have immoral sex.”
Glorify God.
With your eyes.
With your hands.
With your sexuality.
With your singleness.
With your marriage.
With your desires.
With your phone.
With your private life.
With the body Jesus purchased.
And if you have already failed?
Glorify Him through repentance.
If you fell yesterday?
Come back today.
If you have been hiding for ten years?
Bring it into His light.
If somebody else's sin left wounds in your body and memories you never asked for, hear this clearly: another person's sin against you does not make you morally guilty for what was done to you.
Christ receives the wounded too.
And if you were the one who sinned?
Do not rename it.
Do not excuse it.
Do not blame everybody else.
Confess it.
Repent.
Come to Jesus.
Because confession is not informing God of something He somehow missed.
It is finally agreeing with Him about the thing you have been hiding.
And repentance is not paying Jesus back.
You cannot.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who already paid a price you could never pay.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not when the scandal is denied.
When Jesus enters it.
Peter had denial.
The woman at the well had a shattered relational history.
The Corinthian church had sexual brokenness.
Paul himself carried memories of persecuting Christ's people.
Christianity is not a museum displaying people who never needed mercy.
It is a redeemed people gathered around a crucified and risen Savior.
So perhaps the question is no longer merely:
“Why is sex with a prostitute so serious?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
Why does God care so much about what happens to my body?
Paul's answer is breathtaking.
Because your body was made for the Lord.
Because your body is a member of Christ.
Because your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
Because you are not your own.
Because you were bought at a price.
And because God intends ultimately to redeem His people completely—not merely invisible souls floating away from physical existence, but human beings raised in Christ.
Your body is not disposable.
Your sexuality is not meaningless.
Your secret life is not disconnected from discipleship.
And your past is not more powerful than the blood of Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your sin publicly.
But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Let believers pray for believers.
Somebody reading the comments may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be the end.
Not because you need another post sitting in a folder.
Come back and remember:
You were bought at a price.
Someone may believe sexual sin has permanently disqualified them from Jesus.
Someone may have reduced sex to recreation because nobody ever showed them Paul's astonishing theology of the body.
Someone may be one shared article away from confronting something they have hidden for years.
Not as a replacement for biblical tithes or offerings, and never as a way of purchasing God's favor.
Grace cannot be bought.
But voluntary generosity can be an act through which Christians glorify God when it flows from faith, love, gratitude, and a willing heart.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it because you believe the Gospel should keep traveling.

Do it because biblical truth should keep reaching exhausted believers, wounded Christians, seekers, prodigals, struggling families, and people who have not yet understood what Jesus Christ has done for sinners.
And then keep sharing.
Keep tagging.
Keep commenting.
Keep praying.
Keep pointing people beyond Gospel Warrior to Jesus Himself.
Because ultimately this article is not about prostitution.
It is not even primarily about sex.
It is about ownership.
Who has your body?
Who has your desires?
Who has your secret life?
Who gets the final word over your past?
Sin will say, “You belong to me.”
Shame will whisper, “You will always be what you did.”
Culture will tell you, “Your body belongs only to your appetite.”
But over the repentant sinner stands a blood-stained cross and an empty tomb.
Jesus says there is another story available.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Purchased.
Indwelt.
Redeemed.
His.
So flee what is killing you.
Run toward the One who died to save you.
And remember this when your past tries to introduce you by the name of your worst night:
Your scandal may be part of your history—but when Jesus Christ takes hold of your story, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Pray for Your Family Every Day. Do They Experience the Jesus You’re Praying To?
paragraphs: You Pray for Your Family Every Day. Do They Experience the Jesus You’re Praying To?

You can pray for Jesus to transform your family every morning—but what happens when the prayer ends, everyone stands up, and the people you love have to live with the version of you that walks away from the prayer?
There is a kind of silence that happens after a family prayer.
Someone says, “Amen.”
Heads lift.
Hands separate.
The Bible closes.
The phone gets picked up again.
Breakfast continues. Children get ready. Someone is running late. Somebody forgot something. A spouse says the wrong thing. A child spills something. A parent becomes irritated.
And suddenly…
the real sermon begins.
Not the one preached at church.
Not the devotional you shared online.
Not the beautiful prayer you prayed five minutes ago.
You.
Your tone.
Your patience.
Your reaction when you are inconvenienced.
Your willingness to apologize when you were wrong.
The tenderness—or coldness—in your voice.
The way you treat the people who cannot unfollow you, applaud you, or walk away easily.
That is where this question becomes uncomfortable:
You pray for your family every day. But do they experience the Jesus you’re praying to?
Maybe you have prayed for your son to come back to God.
Maybe you whisper your daughter’s name before the Lord at night.
Maybe you have begged Jesus to save your spouse.
Maybe you have fasted for your parents.
Maybe you have prayed over your children while they were sleeping because you are terrified of what this world could do to them.
Those prayers matter.
Please don’t stop praying.
But Scripture confronts us with something deeper than having prayer in the house.
It asks what happens when prayer gets up from its knees and starts walking around the house.
Paul writes in Colossians 3:12–14:
The language is beautiful.
And devastating.
Ἐνδύσασθε — endysasthe.
“Put on.”
It carries the picture of clothing yourself.
Paul is saying, in effect, that because God’s people are chosen, holy, and loved, there are things that should now be visible on them.
Compassion.
Kindness.
Humility.
Gentleness.
Patience.
Forgiveness.
Love.
Not merely discussed.
Not merely prayed about.
Worn.
Visible.
Experienced.
Paul uses the striking expression σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ — splanchna oiktirmou, describing deep, heartfelt compassion.
Then comes μακροθυμίαν — makrothymian: patience, longsuffering.
And then Paul enters the territory where Christianity becomes painfully practical:
χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς — charizomenoi heautois.
Forgiving one another.
The verb is related to χάρις — charis, grace.
Paul does not merely tell Christians to tolerate each other from a distance. He anchors forgiveness in something far greater:
As the Lord forgave you, you also forgive.
Then comes love—ἀγάπην, agapēn—which Paul calls σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος, the bond that binds everything together in completeness.
That is Christianity inside a house.
And that is where some of us need to stop reading for a moment.
Because maybe the greatest spiritual contradiction in your home is not that your family refuses to pray.
Maybe it is that they have heard you pray beautifully…
and then watched you live harshly.
You pray, “Lord, give my children grace.”
Then your child makes a mistake and receives fury.
You pray, “Jesus, bring peace into this home.”
Then everyone walks carefully around your temper.
You pray, “Father, forgive us our sins.”
Then your spouse mentions an old wound and you reach for a list of everything they have ever done wrong.
You pray for your teenager to know the love of Christ.
But when that teenager disappoints you, affection becomes conditional.
You pray for your unbelieving husband.
Then use Christianity as a weapon against him.
You pray for your wife.
Then speak to her with a contempt you would never use toward someone at church.
You pray for your parents.
But bitterness has become so familiar that you no longer recognize it as bitterness.
You post Scripture.
You say grace before meals.
There is a Bible somewhere in the living room.
Christian music plays in the car.
You attend church.
You know when to say “Praise God.”
But the people closest to you may quietly be asking a question they are afraid to say aloud:
Is Jesus really like this?
That question should break something in us.
Because sometimes people are not rejecting the Jesus of Scripture.
They are struggling with the Jesus they think they have seen represented in us.
That does not excuse anyone’s unbelief. Every person ultimately answers to God for his or her own response to Christ.
But it should make every Christian tremble at the responsibility of representation.
Paul does not allow faith to remain theoretical.
Immediately after describing compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, forgiveness, and love, he begins addressing households.
Wives.
Husbands.
Children.
Fathers.
That context matters.
The Christianity of Colossians 3 is not designed merely for Sunday morning.
It comes home.
It walks through the front door.
It sits at the dinner table.
It enters the marriage.
It enters parenting.
It enters conflict.
It enters the moment someone is disrespectful.
It enters the moment you are exhausted.
It enters the argument nobody else will ever hear.
It enters the kitchen at 7:13 in the morning when everybody is late and somebody knocks over the coffee.
Because anyone can appear patient when nothing is testing their patience.
Anyone can talk about forgiveness before being wounded.
Anyone can sing about grace when nobody needs grace from them.
The question is what comes out of us when life squeezes us.
And perhaps this is where someone reading needs to become very quiet.
Maybe you have spent years asking God to change your family.
But today the Holy Spirit is putting His finger somewhere unexpected.
You.
Not because every family problem is your fault.
It isn't.
Not because godly character guarantees that your children will never rebel, your marriage will never struggle, or your relatives will automatically believe.
Scripture promises none of those things.
But perhaps you have been praying, “Lord, change them,” while God has been patiently sanctifying you.
Maybe the next answer to your family prayer begins with three words:
I was wrong.
Imagine what could happen if your child heard that.
Not an excuse afterward.
Not, “I’m sorry, but you made me angry.”
Just:
“I was wrong. The way I spoke to you did not honor Jesus. Please forgive me.”
Some parents fear that admitting wrongdoing will weaken their authority.
But there is another possibility.
Your child may finally see that Christianity is not pretending Christians never sin.
Christianity is knowing what to do when we do.
We come into the light.
We confess.
We repent.
We receive mercy.
We make things right where we can.
We return to Christ.
That is the Gospel lived where your family can see it.
Your children do not need a father who pretends to be Jesus.
They need a father who desperately needs Jesus.
Your spouse does not need a wife who never fails.
Your spouse needs to see what grace does when failure happens.
Your family does not need a flawless Christian performance.
They need evidence that Christ actually transforms sinners.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Colossians 3 does not begin with Paul screaming at broken people, “Become better so God will finally love you.”
Look carefully at the order.
Paul calls them God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved—then tells them what to put on.
Loved first.
Then transformed.
Identity before clothing.
Grace before obedience.
We do not become compassionate enough to purchase God’s love.
We do not forgive enough to earn the cross.
We do not become patient enough to make Jesus accept us.
The Christian life flows in the opposite direction.
Christ loved us.
Christ came for sinners.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ forgives those who come to Him in repentant faith.
And because we have received mercy we could never deserve, that mercy begins leaking into the rooms where we live.
That changes everything.
Because perhaps you are reading this and conviction is becoming shame.
You are remembering things.
The look on your daughter’s face.
The night you screamed.
The apology you refused to give.
The years of coldness.
The marriage where both of you learned how to punish each other with silence.
The son who stopped talking to you about his struggles because every confession became a lecture.
The family member you keep bringing before God while refusing to forgive them.
And now something inside you whispers:
I ruined too much.
Listen carefully.
That voice does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted His people.
The cross itself was surrounded by human scandal, betrayal, cowardice, violence, and sin.
Yet resurrection came.
This is what Jesus does.
He enters stories that look irredeemable and writes grace where we expected only an ending.
That does not erase consequences.
Grace is not pretending wounds never happened.
Repentance is not saying, “God forgave me, so everybody else should get over it.”
Sometimes rebuilding trust takes time.
Sometimes an apology will not immediately repair years of damage.
Sometimes the most Christlike thing you can do after asking forgiveness is patiently accept that the person you hurt may need time.
Real repentance does not demand immediate emotional payment for saying sorry.
It changes direction.
Again.
And again.
And again.
This is why your family does not merely need to hear you pray.
They need to watch prayer reshape you.
Let them see you stop halfway through an angry sentence.
Let them hear you apologize.
Let them watch you forgive without keeping score.
