Let your children discover that Dad can kneel before God and also kneel beside their bed and say, “I hurt you.”
Let your spouse discover that winning the argument matters less to you than honoring Christ.
Let your parents see bitterness losing its grip.
Let your siblings see old grudges dying.
Let your home become the place where the Gospel is not merely explained but rehearsed in ordinary human relationships.
Compassion when someone fails.
Kindness when irritation would be easier.
Humility when pride wants the final word.
Gentleness when power could crush.
Patience when change takes longer than you wanted.
Forgiveness because you remember how much you have been forgiven.
Love binding all of it together.
And tomorrow morning…
pray again.
Please.
Pray for your family.
Pray harder.
Pray longer.
Pray Scripture over them.
Cry if you need to.
Fast if God leads you.
Call their names before the throne of grace.
But when you finally whisper “Amen”…
do not leave Jesus in the prayer.
Take Him into breakfast.
Take Him into the disagreement.
Take Him into the bills.
Take Him into the car.
Take Him into discipline.
Take Him into the marriage.
Take Him into the uncomfortable conversation.
Take Him into the moment when someone disappoints you for the hundredth time.
Not as a religious weapon.
As Lord.
And when you fail—and you will—run back to Him.
Confess quickly.
Repent sincerely.
Receive grace gratefully.
Then extend the grace you just received.
Maybe your family has heard a thousand prayers from you.
Perhaps what they desperately need now is to experience the character those prayers have been asking Christ to produce.
Be honest.
Let believers who see it pray with you.
Not because sharing an article proves your faith.
It doesn't.
But someone in your circle may be praying desperately for a family member while never realizing that God also wants to transform the person doing the praying.
And stay close to Gospel Warrior if you want daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
But hear this clearly:
It does not purchase His favor.
It does not replace obedience, generosity to those in need, or faithful giving as your conscience is shaped by Scripture.
And no Christian should be pressured into giving.
Paul wrote:
“ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ, μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης…”
Each person should give as determined in the heart—not reluctantly or under compulsion—because God loves a cheerful giver. (2 Corinthians 9:7)
Pray.
Send it privately to someone whose family is struggling.
The Gospel was never meant to terminate with us.
We receive grace…
and then grace moves through us.
Into another person.
Into another home.
Into another generation.
Because maybe the prayer your family remembers most will not be the eloquent one you prayed with your eyes closed.
Maybe it will be the prayer they watched God answer when you opened your eyes…
stood up…
walked toward the person you wounded…
and said:
“Please forgive me.”
Then they saw something they could not dismiss.
Not a perfect Christian.
A repentant one.
Not religious performance.
Grace.
Not someone pretending never to fall.
Someone continually returning to Jesus.
And perhaps years from now, when your children remember the faith that lived inside their childhood home, they will not merely say:
“My mother prayed.”
“My father knew the Bible.”
“My family went to church.”
Perhaps, by the grace of God, they will be able to say:
“I saw what Jesus did to them.”
Because the most unforgettable family prayer may be the one your family watches Christ answer in you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES SONG OF SONGS DESCRIBE ORAL SEX?
paragraphs: DOES SONG OF SONGS DESCRIBE ORAL SEX?
Why Some Readers Think So—and Why We Shouldn’t Claim More Than the Poetry Says
There is a sentence in the Bible that would probably make some Christians uncomfortable if they heard it read slowly from a pulpit.
Not because it is sinful.
Not because it is vulgar.
But because it is sensual.
Very sensual.
A woman is describing the man she loves, and in the Hebrew text of Song of Songs 2:3 she says:

וּפִרְיוֹ מָתוֹק לְחִכִּי
u-firyō māthōq leḥikkî
Literally:
“And his fruit was sweet to my palate.”
Not merely “nice.”
Not merely “beautiful.”
Fruit.
Sweetness.
Palate.
Desire.
And that has caused some readers to ask a question Christians sometimes whisper but rarely say publicly:
Is Song of Songs describing oral sex?
The question itself is not automatically dirty.
But the answer requires something desperately missing from many conversations about Scripture:
Humility.
Because there are two mistakes we can make with a passage like this.
One is becoming so embarrassed by sexuality that we sterilize the Bible.
The other is becoming so fascinated by sexuality that we force the Bible to say something more explicit than God actually caused it to say.
And somewhere between those two mistakes is a breathtaking biblical vision of human intimacy that many believers have never been taught.
So stay with me.
Because this is not ultimately an article about one sexual act.
It is about something much deeper.
It is about whether Christians are willing to let God define sexuality instead of pornography, shame, culture, trauma, religious embarrassment, or our own imagination.
Song of Songs does not blush nearly as easily as we do.
The woman says of her beloved:
“In his shade I delighted and sat down, and his fruit was sweet to my palate.”
The Hebrew word translated “palate” is חֵךְ, ḥēkh. In this verse it appears as לְחִכִּי, leḥikkî—“to my palate.” The word can refer to the palate or interior of the mouth.
That matters.
But it does not settle the question.
Poetry works through imagery.
A metaphor may carry erotic force without functioning like an anatomical diagram.
And Song of Songs is saturated with metaphor.
Bodies become gardens.
Breasts become fawns and clusters.
Love becomes wine.
Fragrance fills the air.
Lips drip honey.
The beloved becomes an orchard.
The woman becomes a garden.
The man becomes a tree.
Desire becomes hunger.
Intimacy becomes eating and drinking.
Then the poetry becomes even more suggestive.
The woman says:
“Let my beloved come into his garden and eat its choice fruits.”
The Hebrew of Song of Songs 4:16 contains the unmistakable invitation:
יָבֹא דוֹדִי לְגַנּוֹ וְיֹאכַל פְּרִי מְגָדָיו
Yāḇō dōḏî legannō weyōʾkhal perî megāḏāw.
“Let my beloved come into his garden and eat its choice fruits.”
Then immediately afterward the man responds in Song of Songs 5:1:
בָּאתִי לְגַנִּי אֲחֹתִי כַלָּה
Bāʾtî legannî, ʾaḥōtî kallāh.
“I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride.”
He continues with imagery of gathering spices, eating honey and honeycomb, and drinking wine and milk.
Something has happened.
The invitation has been answered.
The garden has been entered.
The lovers delight in one another.
The poetry does not apologize for it.
And neither should we.
Yet notice something equally important.
The poet still does not stop and give us a clinical description of a particular sexual technique.
That silence matters too.
This is where interpretation requires restraint.
Some readers see “his fruit was sweet to my palate” and conclude that the woman is describing oral stimulation of the man.
Some see the invitation to “eat” the fruits of the woman’s garden and understand it as potentially including oral sexual pleasure.
Those interpretations are understandable.
The imagery can carry erotic possibilities.
But possibility is not the same thing as certainty.
The Hebrew never simply says, “They performed oral sex.”
There is no explicit anatomical description identifying those metaphors with that specific act.
And therefore we should be extremely careful about saying:
“The Bible clearly teaches oral sex in Song of Songs.”
Clearly?
That goes beyond the text.
A more responsible conclusion is:

Song of Songs celebrates passionate, embodied, mutually desired intimacy between lovers with remarkably sensual imagery. Some of that imagery can reasonably be understood as suggestive of oral eroticism, but the poetry does not explicitly identify a particular sexual act.
That answer may disappoint people looking for an easy yes.
It may also disappoint people demanding an easy no.
But Scripture deserves something better than our need for easy answers.
It deserves honesty.
Consider another passage.

Song of Songs 7 describes the woman with extraordinary physical intensity. Her breasts are compared to clusters of the vine. Her breath carries the fragrance of apples. Her mouth—or palate—is compared with fine wine.
The Hebrew again uses חֵךְ, ḥēkh, the word connected with the palate or mouth.
The poem moves through breasts...
breath...
mouth...
wine...
lips...
desire.
Nobody reading that honestly should pretend the Song is embarrassed by physical attraction.
It isn't.
But neither should we treat every metaphor as a secret code in which every fruit, garden, pomegranate, vineyard, or cup must correspond to one precise sexual organ or technique.
That is not careful interpretation.
That is decoding poetry as though Solomon left us an encrypted bedroom manual.
He didn't.
He gave us poetry.
And poetry can sometimes communicate more by refusing to describe everything.
Maybe that is part of its wisdom.
Because our culture has done the opposite.
We have seen almost everything.
Bodies displayed.
Bodies sold.
Bodies filtered.
Bodies rated.
Bodies consumed through screens.
Sex detached from covenant.
Desire detached from responsibility.
Pleasure detached from holiness.
People can know the mechanics of sex before they understand the meaning of love.
A teenager can encounter pornography before experiencing a first kiss.
A husband can know a thousand images of strangers while becoming emotionally distant from the woman sleeping beside him.
A wife can carry shame about her body for decades because somebody taught her that holiness meant pretending she did not have one.
And into that confused world comes this strange little biblical book...
with gardens.
Perfume.
Wine.
Skin.
Breasts.
Kisses.
Longing.
Absence.
Frustration.
Delight.
And lovers who actually desire one another.
That should tell us something.
Christianity is not at war with the human body.
God created it.
The scandal is not that Scripture can speak beautifully about sexual desire.
The scandal is how often sin has taught us either to worship sexuality or to despise it.
The Gospel does neither.
Jesus came in a body.
The eternal Son took flesh.
He was born.
He hungered.
He thirsted.
He suffered physically.
His hands were pierced.
His side was wounded.
His body was laid in a tomb.
And He rose bodily from the dead.
Christianity is not salvation from embodiment.
It is the redemption of the whole person.
That means Christ does not merely care about what happens during church.
He cares about what happens inside your imagination.
Inside your marriage.
Inside your loneliness.
Inside your browser history.
Inside the secret places nobody else sees.
Maybe that is where this article suddenly stops being about Song of Songs.
Because perhaps you clicked because the title made you curious.
But now there is another question sitting quietly beneath the first one.
Not:
“Does Song of Songs describe oral sex?”
But:
“What has happened to my own sexuality?”
Maybe nobody ever taught you that desire could exist without shame.
Maybe pornography became your teacher.
Maybe abuse distorted what intimacy meant.
Maybe church culture made you feel dirty simply for having a body.
Maybe you crossed boundaries and still carry the memory.
Maybe you are married but lonely.
Maybe you are single and exhausted from pretending sexual temptation never hurts.
Maybe you love Jesus...
and there is still a hidden tab you keep reopening.
A secret conversation.
A fantasy.
An addiction.
A memory.
A wound.
Something you would never want projected onto the screen at church.
And this is where the Gospel becomes infinitely more beautiful than either sexual permissiveness or religious shame.
Jesus already knows.
Not the polished version.
You.
And He does not call sexual sin holy simply because our culture celebrates it.
But neither does He tell repentant sinners that their worst chapter has become their permanent name.
At the cross, Jesus Christ carried real guilt.
Real shame.
Real rebellion.
Real sexual sin.
Real secret sin.
Real brokenness.
He did not die because sin was insignificant.
He died because sin was deadly.
And He rose because grace would have the final word for everyone who belongs to Him.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the grave.
Grace does not mean Jesus shrugs at whatever is destroying you.
Grace means Jesus loves you too much to leave you enslaved to it.
There are people reading this who need to stop arguing about what ancient lovers may have done and finally surrender what they themselves are doing.
That secret relationship.
That pornography.
That adultery.
That bitterness toward your spouse.
That manipulation.
That hidden shame.
That belief that because someone violated you, you became permanently dirty.
Listen carefully.
What somebody did against you is not the same thing as what you chose.
And what you have chosen sinfully does not place you beyond the reach of Christ when you come to Him in repentance and faith.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is transformation.
There is a Savior.
His name is Jesus.
And maybe this is the most beautiful lesson hidden beneath all the gardens and perfume and kisses of Song of Songs:
God is not embarrassed by redeemed love.
Sin takes good things and corrupts them.
Christ takes broken people and makes them new.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So does Song of Songs describe oral sex?
Perhaps some of its imagery allows that possibility.
We should not mock Christians who see erotic implications there.
The Hebrew genuinely uses language involving fruit, palate, gardens, eating, breasts, breath, mouth, wine, and physical longing.
But we should not pretend Scripture explicitly names an act that the poetry leaves metaphorical.
Where God has spoken clearly, speak clearly.
Where God has left poetry, do not turn metaphor into legislation.
And where Scripture celebrates marital desire, do not manufacture shame that God Himself did not put there.
That principle matters far beyond sexuality.
We are servants of Scripture.
Scripture is not a servant of our agenda.
Sometimes faithfulness means saying:
“This is what the text says.”
“This may be what the imagery suggests.”
“And this is where I must stop.”
There is profound freedom in those three sentences.
If this exposed something hidden in your heart, don't hide behind theology.
Somebody reading the comments may discover that they are not the only believer fighting for holiness.
Somebody may decide tonight not to return to pornography.
Somebody may confess something to a spouse.
Somebody may seek wise pastoral counsel or professional help.
Somebody may finally believe that repentance is still possible.
Somebody may come back to Jesus.
That is why these conversations matter.
If you know a married couple who needs a healthier biblical vision of intimacy, send this privately.
If you know a believer trapped between pornography on one side and religious shame on the other, share this with them.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because someone in your circle may desperately need the truth you almost scrolled past.
Questions about Scripture, sexuality, holiness, marriage, shame, grace, and interpretation will come again. When they do, return to the text rather than the noise surrounding it.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you grow closer to Christ and you want to help this ministry continue and expand, there is another way you can stand with the mission.
It doesn't.
Not because salvation can be bought.
It cannot.
Scripture does not permit us to place that burden on anyone.
But Scripture does teach believers to give willingly rather than under compulsion, and it celebrates generosity that supports Gospel ministry and produces thanksgiving to God.
So if you have prayed about how you can use part of what God has entrusted to you for Gospel work, consider making Gospel Warrior one of the ministries you voluntarily support.
Give freely.
Share freely.
Serve freely.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's love.
The greatest gift in Christianity is not something we give to God.
It is Someone God gave to us.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the grave.
Calling the ashamed out of hiding.
Calling the addicted into freedom.
Calling the wounded toward healing.
Calling the sexually broken toward holiness.
Calling sinners toward repentance.
Calling the lost home.
Maybe you opened this article wondering what two ancient lovers were doing in a garden.
Maybe God used it to ask what has been growing in yours.
Because the most dangerous secret is not the one Scripture refuses to describe—it is the one we refuse to surrender to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD TOLD ABIMELECH, “I KEPT YOU FROM SINNING AGAINST ME”
paragraphs: GOD TOLD ABIMELECH, “I KEPT YOU FROM SINNING AGAINST ME”
What if some of the sins you never committed were not proof of how strong you were—but evidence of how merciful God had been when you never even knew He was protecting you?
There is a sentence in Genesis that should make every believer sit still for a moment.
Not because it is difficult to understand.
Because once you understand it, you may never look at your own past the same way again.
God said to Abimelech:
“I kept you from sinning against Me.”
Genesis 20:6.
Read those words again.
Slowly.
I kept you.
There are sins you remember committing.
There are nights you wish you could erase.
There are words you would give almost anything to take back.
There are decisions that still make your stomach tighten when your mind wanders too far into yesterday.
You know the shame of what you did.
But have you ever thanked God for what you almost did?
For the relationship that collapsed before it could destroy you.
For the opportunity that mysteriously disappeared.
For the door you were furious God would not open.
For the person who stopped answering.
For the plan that failed.
For the temptation that somehow lost its opportunity.
For the night circumstances changed.
For the moment something inside you suddenly screamed, Don’t.
What if some of the interruptions you called bad luck were actually mercy?
What if some of your disappointments were restraints?
What if Heaven has rescued you from sins you never even realized you were about to commit?
That is part of what makes Genesis 20 so unsettling.
Abraham—the man of faith, the man carrying God's covenant promise—entered Gerar and became afraid.
Sarah was his wife.
But Abraham said of her, “She is my sister.”
Technically, there was a family relationship behind Abraham's statement, as Abraham later explained in Genesis 20:12. But he concealed the crucial truth that Sarah was also his wife.
And Abimelech, king of Gerar, took Sarah.
Then God entered the story.
Not quietly.
Not ambiguously.
God came to Abimelech in a dream and confronted him over another man's wife.
Abimelech protested that he had acted without knowing the full truth. And then comes the astonishing response of God:
“Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart, and it was I who kept you from sinning against me. Therefore I did not let you touch her.”
The Hebrew makes the force of the statement unmistakable.
וָאֶחְשֹׂךְ גַּם־אָנֹכִי אֹתְךָ מֵחֲטֹו־לִי
Va'echsokh gam-anokhi otkha mechat'o-li.
In straightforward sense:
“And I also withheld you from sinning against Me.”
The verb וָאֶחְשֹׂךְ — va'echsokh carries the idea of withholding or restraining.
And מֵחֲטֹו־לִי — mechat'o-li means “from sinning against Me.”
God did not merely say, “You happened to make the right decision.”
He said, in effect:
I restrained you.
Then God explains the practical result:
“I did not let you touch her.”
That changes something.
Because we love testimonies about the grace that forgave us after we fell.
And we should.
The Gospel is gloriously about sinners being forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, redeemed, and made new through Jesus Christ.
But there is another kind of mercy we rarely talk about.
Preventing mercy.
Mercy that does not merely pull you out of the pit.
Mercy that sometimes keeps you from falling into it.
Think about your life.
Really think.
How many times have you credited yourself for victories that may have contained far more divine mercy than you realized?
“I would never do that.”
Be careful.
Peter once sounded certain too.
“Even if everyone else falls away…”
Not Peter.
He was sure of himself.
Then came the courtyard.
Then came the questions.
Then came the denials.
Then came the rooster.
And suddenly the man who believed himself incapable of abandoning Jesus discovered what fear could uncover inside him.
That is one reason Genesis 20:6 is so humbling.
It destroys the fantasy that the only thing separating us from catastrophic sin is superior character.
Yes, human choices matter.
Yes, Scripture commands self-control, holiness, vigilance, obedience, fleeing temptation, resisting the devil, renewing our minds, and putting sin to death.
Genesis 20:6 does not erase human responsibility.
But it reveals something else alongside it:
God can intervene.
God can restrain.
God can close a door.
God can interrupt circumstances.
God can prevent an action from reaching completion.
Abimelech had not touched Sarah because God had not permitted him to do so.
And perhaps that should change the way we tell our stories.
Maybe instead of saying only,
“I was strong enough to walk away,”
sometimes we should whisper,
“God, thank You for giving me the strength to leave.”
Instead of,
“I knew better,”
perhaps,
“Lord, thank You for reminding me of what I knew before desire made me forget.”
Instead of,
“I would never become that person,”
perhaps,
“Jesus, keep my heart close to You, because apart from Your grace I dare not trust myself.”
There is something terrifying about discovering what human beings are capable of.
But there is something breathtaking about discovering how relentlessly merciful God can be.
Somebody reading this remembers a door that closed.
You cried over it.
You prayed for God to reopen it.
You wondered why He seemed silent.
Maybe you watched somebody else receive what you wanted and secretly wondered whether God had forgotten you.
Years later, you discovered what was behind that door.
And suddenly your unanswered prayer looked different.
The rejection became protection.
The delay became mercy.
The “no” became rescue.
Not every disappointment means God was specifically preventing a particular sin. Scripture does not give us permission to interpret every inconvenience as a secret divine intervention.
But Genesis 20 gives us permission to recognize something equally important:
Sometimes God really does restrain people from sin.
And because we cannot see every movement of providence, there may be mercies in our histories whose names we will not know this side of eternity.
Imagine discovering in Heaven how many times God protected you when you thought nothing was happening.
How many temptations never reached you.
How many circumstances were rearranged.
How many disasters were interrupted.
How many times the Spirit convicted you before one more decision changed everything.
How many times Scripture returned to your memory at exactly the right moment.
How many times a brother or sister called when you were about to collapse.
How many times exposure frightened you back toward wisdom.
How many times God provided an escape from temptation and you barely recognized the exit.
You remember the scars.
God remembers the cliffs He kept you from reaching.
But there is another detail in Genesis 20 that cannot be missed.
God says Abimelech would have been sinning against Him.
Not merely against Abraham.
Not merely against Sarah.
Against God.
That is the seriousness of sin.
David understood this after his own horrifying moral collapse. His sin devastated real human beings, yet in Psalm 51 he recognized that ultimately his rebellion was against God.
Sin is not merely breaking an impersonal rule.
It is rebellion against the holy God who made us.
That is why Christianity cannot be reduced to becoming nicer people.
Our deepest problem requires more than improvement.
We need reconciliation.
We need forgiveness.
We need redemption.
We need Christ.
Because eventually every one of us reaches the place where the testimony cannot be:
“God kept me from every sin.”
He didn't.
Look at your own history.
Neither did you.
Neither did I.
There are lines we crossed.
Things we actually said.
Things we actually watched.
Things we actually desired.
People we actually wounded.
Lies we actually told.
Secrets we actually kept.
Moments when God provided a way out and we chose the temptation anyway.
And this is where the story becomes even more beautiful.
Because the God who can restrain sinners before they fall is also the God who can redeem sinners after they fall.
That road leads us to Jesus.
At the cross, Christ did not die for imaginary sinners.
He died for the guilty.
The ashamed.
The exposed.
The religious hypocrite.
The sexually broken.
The angry.
The addicted.
The greedy.
The self-righteous.
The liar.
The person whose secret would horrify everyone who thinks they know them.
Jesus did not wait for humanity to become respectable.
Christ came for sinners.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Christian Gospel is not that good people managed to climb high enough to reach God.
It is that God came down to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
And maybe that is why this verse hits so deeply.
There are two testimonies of grace.
“God kept me from it.”
And:
“God rescued me after I did it.”
Both leave us with empty hands.
Neither allows boasting.
The first says, “I stood because God was merciful.”
The second says, “I fell, but Christ was merciful.”
Either way…
grace gets the final word.
Maybe you are reading this with tears forming because you are not thinking about a sin God prevented.
You are thinking about one He didn't.
You did it.
You crossed the line.
You became the person you swore you would never become.
And perhaps you have spent years believing that your worst chapter disqualified you from ever having a beautiful ending.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you to pretend your sin wasn't serious.
Grace does something far more powerful.
Grace tells you that Jesus is greater.
Repentance is not pretending the scandal never happened.
Repentance turns from sin and runs toward the Savior.
Confession brings darkness into light.
And the blood of Jesus does what your shame never could.
It cleanses.
You do not need to rewrite your history to be redeemed.
You need Jesus to rewrite what your history means.
The betrayal can become the place where repentance began.
The addiction can become the battlefield where dependence on Christ became real.
The failure can become the grave where pride finally died.
The exposed secret can become the moment hiding ended.
The broken years can become a testimony that screams:
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
This is why we say:
Not because scandal doesn't matter.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because the cross means your sin does not have to write the final sentence of your life.
Jesus does.
So perhaps your prayer tonight should not merely be:
“God, forgive me for what I have done.”
Pray that.
But maybe add something you have rarely prayed:
“Father, thank You for the sins You kept me from committing.”
“Thank You for doors You closed.”
“Thank You for convictions I almost ignored.”
“Thank You for people You sent.”
“Thank You for exposing what needed exposure.”
“Thank You for interruptions I resented.”
“Thank You for every escape from temptation I recognized—and every one I never knew You provided.”
“And Lord… please keep me again.”
Because maturity is not reaching the point where you no longer need grace.
Maturity is realizing how desperately you have always needed it.
Be honest.
Somebody reading may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be final.
Do not let shame convince you that silence is holiness.
Sometimes another wounded believer needs to hear:
“I've been there too. And Jesus met me there.”
Come back and remember:
You are never too mature to pray, “Lord, keep me.”

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too. Sometimes one Scripture appearing on someone's screen at the right moment can begin a conversation that eternity remembers.

Scripture gives real warrant for materially supporting Gospel ministry. Paul wrote that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel. But Scripture is equally clear that Christian giving must not be manipulated: each believer should give as he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
It cannot purchase blessing.
It cannot purchase salvation.
It does not replace obedience, membership in a faithful local church, or whatever giving before God your conscience and biblical convictions lead you to practice.
If you want to glorify God through generosity toward Gospel work, this is one practical opportunity to participate.
Pray.
Follow.
Invite someone else to encounter the Gospel.
Because ministry is not ultimately about building an audience.
It is about pointing an audience to Jesus.
And perhaps somewhere tonight, someone is seconds away from making a decision they will regret for years.
Maybe God will use a Scripture.
A conviction.
A phone call.
A closed door.
A Christian friend.
Even an article someone cared enough to share.
And years from now, that person may finally understand:
“That interruption wasn't God ruining my life.
That was God protecting it.”
Never forget this:
Some of the greatest testimonies of grace may be stories you will never be able to tell—because God, in His mercy, never let the story happen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID MATTHEW COUNT TO FOURTEEN THREE TIMES? THE SECRET HIDING IN JESUS’ FAMILY TREE
paragraphs: WHY DID MATTHEW COUNT TO FOURTEEN THREE TIMES? THE SECRET HIDING IN JESUS’ FAMILY TREE

You may have skipped Matthew’s genealogy your entire life. But hidden inside those names is a message about kings, collapse, scandal, exile, grace—and a King who entered a broken family line to rewrite everything.
Most people have done it.
You open the Gospel of Matthew determined to read about Jesus.
Then you meet a wall of names.
Abraham begot Isaac. Isaac begot Jacob. Jacob begot Judah.
Name after name.
Generation after generation.
Your eyes begin moving faster.
Maybe you quietly think, I already know where this is going.
So you skip ahead.
You want Bethlehem.
You want angels.
You want miracles.
You want the Sermon on the Mount.
You want the cross.
You want the empty tomb.
But Matthew refuses to begin there.
Before he shows you Jesus healing the sick, forgiving sinners, confronting hypocrisy, calming storms, carrying a cross, and walking out of a grave...
Matthew gives you a family tree.
And then, almost as though he knows you might miss what he has done, he stops at Matthew 1:17 and essentially tells you:
Count it.
The Greek reads:
Πᾶσαι οὖν αἱ γενεαὶ ἀπὸ Ἀβραὰμ ἕως Δαυὶδ γενεαὶ δεκατέσσαρες, καὶ ἀπὸ Δαυὶδ ἕως τῆς μετοικεσίας Βαβυλῶνος γενεαὶ δεκατέσσαρες, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς μετοικεσίας Βαβυλῶνος ἕως τοῦ Χριστοῦ γενεαὶ δεκατέσσαρες.
Matthew 1:17.
In straightforward English:
All the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; from David to the Babylonian exile, fourteen; and from the exile to the Christ, fourteen.
Fourteen.
Fourteen.
Fourteen.
Why?
Why would Matthew deliberately arrange the opening genealogy of Jesus into three groups built around the same number?
It was not because Israel's history naturally fell into three mathematically perfect blocks of fourteen biological generations.
Matthew's genealogy is selective.
That is important.

Comparison with the Old Testament genealogical records shows that Matthew omits some names. For example, between Joram and Uzziah, the Old Testament records Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah. Ancient genealogies could be telescoped: “fathered” or “begot” could describe ancestral descent without requiring that every intervening generation be named. Matthew has therefore arranged his genealogy purposefully rather than attempting to provide an exhaustive modern-style family registry.
So Matthew is doing theology through genealogy.
He is telling you something before Jesus ever speaks.
And one of the strongest clues is sitting inside a Hebrew name.
דוד
David.
Hebrew originally writes the name with the consonants:
ד ו ד
Dalet.
Vav.
Dalet.
In the traditional numerical values of Hebrew letters:
And:

This connection between David's Hebrew name and Matthew's fourteen-generation structure has long been proposed by interpreters and is widely regarded as a compelling explanation of Matthew's arrangement, though we should distinguish that strong scholarly interpretation from something Matthew explicitly states. Matthew never writes, “I chose fourteen because David's Hebrew name equals fourteen.” Scholars infer the connection from the genealogy's structure, Matthew's extraordinary emphasis on David, and ancient numerical practices. Scholarly work continues to examine precisely how numerical composition operates in Matthew's genealogy.
But now go back to Matthew's first sentence.
Before the list even begins, he announces:
Jesus Christ...
“the son of David, the son of Abraham.”
Matthew 1:1.
David is not buried somewhere deep inside the genealogy.
Matthew puts him at the front door.
Then he structures the genealogy around fourteen.
Then he explicitly calls David “the king” in Matthew 1:6.
Matthew is practically ringing a bell over the genealogy.
David.
Fourteen.
David.
Fourteen.
David.
King.
And then comes Jesus.
Matthew wants his readers to understand that the story they are entering is the story of the promised Messiah, the royal Son of David.
But there is something even more beautiful happening.
Because Matthew's three movements do not merely count people.
They tell Israel's story.
Abraham to David.
Promise moving toward a kingdom.
David to Babylon.
A kingdom moving toward catastrophe.
Babylon to Christ.
Exile moving toward Messiah.
Read those movements slowly.
Promise.
Kingdom.
Collapse.
Exile.
Waiting.
Christ.
That is not merely somebody's ancestry.
That is the Gospel hiding inside a family tree.
And maybe that is why this genealogy feels strangely personal when you finally stop skipping it.
Because perhaps your life has had those movements too.
There was a season when everything seemed full of promise.
Then something broke.
Maybe you broke it.
Maybe somebody else did.
Maybe your marriage entered a place you never imagined.
Maybe an addiction became stronger than you wanted anyone to know.
Maybe you became excellent at looking Christian while privately becoming spiritually numb.
Maybe people know the version of you that smiles at church...
but they do not know the version of you that cries in the car.
They do not know what you search for when nobody is watching.
They do not know about the resentment.
The secret relationship.
The relapse.
The pornography.
The anger.
The shame.
The questions about God you are afraid to say aloud.
The prayer life that slowly disappeared.
The Bible collecting dust beside your bed.
The terrifying thought that sometimes whispers:
Maybe I have gone too far.
Matthew's genealogy has something to say to that person.
Because Jesus did not arrive at the end of a spotless family history.
Look carefully at the names.
There is Judah.
There is Tamar.
There is Rahab.
There is Ruth.
There is David.
And Matthew does something startling when he reaches Solomon.
He could simply have moved to the next generation.
Instead he reminds the reader that Solomon's mother had been “the wife of Uriah.”
Matthew refuses to airbrush David's history.
Behind that phrase stands one of the darkest episodes in David's life: Bathsheba, Uriah, adultery, abuse of royal power, deception, and bloodshed.
The royal line contains glory.
And scandal.
Faith.
And failure.
Promise.
And human wreckage.

Matthew's genealogy also unusually draws attention to women including Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, “the wife of Uriah,” and finally Mary. Scholars have long debated precisely why Matthew selected these women, and reducing all of them simply to “scandalous women” is too simplistic; serious scholarship notes their varied situations, marginality, and important roles within the biblical story.
Matthew is not telling us that sin does not matter.
The Bible never calls darkness light.
David's sin mattered.
Israel's rebellion mattered.
Babylon mattered.
Exile mattered.
Your sin matters too.
Grace is not God pretending sin is harmless.
Grace is far more astonishing.
God enters a history damaged by sin...
and redemption keeps moving.
That may be the message somebody reading this desperately needs.
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write the final chapter.
Jesus does.
Matthew's genealogy begins with Abraham because God made promises.
It moves through David because God made promises.
It passes through exile because human failure did not cancel God's faithfulness.
And eventually...
after kings had died...
after Jerusalem had fallen...
after families had lived and died waiting...
after generations wondered whether God had forgotten...
Matthew writes a name.
Jesus.
The genealogy does not terminate in another political dynasty.
It arrives at ὁ Χριστός — ho Christos — the Christ, the Anointed One.
“Christ” is not Jesus' surname.
Christos is the Greek designation corresponding to “Messiah,” the Anointed One.
The genealogy has been moving toward Him.
Abraham could not save us.
David could not save us.
Solomon could not save us.
The kings could not save us.
Religious ancestry could not save us.
Human achievement could not save us.
We needed Jesus.
And suddenly those three fourteens become more than an interesting biblical pattern.
They become a drumbeat.
Promise.
Failure.
Waiting.
Jesus.
Promise.
Failure.
Waiting.
Jesus.
Your story may contain failure.
But failure does not have to be your final destination.
Your story may contain exile—the feeling that you have wandered so far from God that you barely recognize the person you have become.
But exile does not have to be the last word.
There is a name waiting at the end of Matthew's genealogy.
Jesus.
And there is a cross waiting at the end of Matthew's Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to improve respectable people.
He came to save sinners.
He came to call people to repentance.
He came to bear sin.
He came to reconcile the guilty to God.
He came to make disciples.
And He rose.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings climbing their way toward God.
It is the announcement that in Jesus Christ, God came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Maybe you have spent years editing your own genealogy.
Not the names.
The memories.
You tell people the acceptable chapters.
You hide Babylon.
You hide Uriah.
You hide the night everything collapsed.
You hide what happened after everybody went to sleep.
You hide the person you became when grief changed you.
You hide the doubt.
You hide the wound.
You hide the sin.
You hide because somewhere deep inside you believe that if people knew the entire story, they might walk away.
But Christ already knows the entire story.
Every chapter.
Every secret.
Every motive.
Every scar.
Every sin requiring repentance.
And the Gospel still calls you toward Him.
Not toward pretending.
Toward repentance.
Not toward self-salvation.
Toward grace.
Not toward hiding.
Toward the light.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
David was forgiven, yet his sin produced devastating consequences.
Biblical grace is not cheap.
The cross itself tells us how costly sin is.
But the cross also tells us how far God was willing to go to redeem sinners.
So if this article has uncovered something you have been hiding, do not merely feel emotional for five minutes and continue living exactly the same way.
Bring it to Christ.
Confess it.
Repent.
Ask for mercy.
Seek reconciliation where Scripture requires it.
Get accountable.
Return to the Word.
Return to prayer.
Return to Jesus.
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Let another believer know you need prayer.
Maybe somebody reading the comments has survived the valley you are walking through right now.
Maybe your honesty will become somebody else's permission to stop hiding.
And perhaps there is someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this genealogy more than you realized.
Not because they are fascinated by biblical numerology.
Because they believe their scandal has disqualified them from grace.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to hear that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Save it too.

Because there may come a night when Babylon feels louder than Bethlehem, when failure feels stronger than promise, and you need to remember that Matthew deliberately carried the story through exile all the way to Christ.

We want this ministry to remain a place where Scripture is opened carefully, Jesus Christ remains central, sin is taken seriously, grace is never cheapened, and broken people are continually pointed toward repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through the Gospel.
It does not.
It does not.
And never because anyone should pressure you into giving.
Paul wrote:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ, μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης...
“Each one” should give according to what has been purposed in the heart, not reluctantly or “under compulsion”—ἐξ ἀνάγκης—because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That is the spirit in which we invite your support.
Your support helps make continued Christian content, biblical teaching, discipleship materials, encouragement, and Gospel-centered resources possible.
Pray.
Read.
Grow.
Invite people into the Scriptures.
Sometimes the person who cannot financially support a ministry can still help the truth travel farther than money ever could.
Because in the end, Gospel Warrior is not the hero of this story.
Matthew is not the hero.
David certainly is not the hero.
You are not the hero.
Neither am I.
Jesus is.
Matthew begins his Gospel with generations of imperfect people because Christianity was never supposed to be a museum displaying perfect human beings.
It is the announcement of a perfect Savior entering a world of sinners.
And perhaps that is why Matthew's genealogy begins to feel less like a list once you understand it.
Abraham...
David...
Babylon...
Christ.
Promise...
glory...
collapse...
exile...
waiting...
Jesus.
Fourteen.
Fourteen.
Fourteen.
And at the end of all that waiting stands the One Matthew wanted you to see from his very first sentence:
The Son of Abraham.
The Son of David.
The Messiah.
Jesus Christ.
So when you look at the wreckage behind you, remember this:
Babylon may appear in your history, but when Jesus takes hold of a repentant sinner, Babylon does not have to write the ending.
Because the genealogy Matthew expected people to remember was never merely about where Jesus came from.
It was announcing Who had finally come.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your past—but the scars in Christ's hands declare that your sin does not have to own your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE CHRISTMAS TREES INNOCENT TRADITION—OR SOMETHING CHRISTIANS SHOULD AVOID?
paragraphs: ARE CHRISTMAS TREES INNOCENT TRADITION—OR SOMETHING CHRISTIANS SHOULD AVOID?
Before you throw the tree away—or defend it as harmless—there is a question far more dangerous than the tree standing in your living room: What has actually captured your heart?
There it stands.
Lights glowing softly against the darkness.
Ornaments carrying memories from years you wish you could relive.
Children staring upward.
Presents waiting underneath.
A star, perhaps, resting at the top.
For millions of Christian families, the Christmas tree feels almost inseparable from December.
Then someone sends you a verse.
Jeremiah 10.
Suddenly the warm lights do not feel quite as innocent.
You read about a tree being cut from the forest. You read about a craftsman. You read about silver and gold. You read about something being fastened so that it cannot move.
And the question begins crawling into your conscience:
Have Christians unknowingly brought a pagan object into their homes?
Maybe someone has even told you, “The Bible specifically condemns Christmas trees.”
Now you are caught between two fears.
One fear says, What if I have been dishonoring God without realizing it?
The other says, What if people are using Scripture to condemn something Scripture never actually condemns?
Both questions deserve more than a meme.
More than a viral video.
More than, “My pastor said…”
More than, “My family has always done it…”
More than, “Everybody knows Christmas trees are pagan…”
Because Christians are not called to inherit their convictions from algorithms, traditions, nostalgia, or outrage.
We are called to submit them to the Word of God.
So open Jeremiah 10 and look carefully.
The Hebrew begins describing the practices of the nations as empty or futile. Jeremiah 10:3 contains these words:
“כִּי־חֻקּוֹת הָעַמִּים הֶבֶל הוּא כִּי־עֵץ מִיַּעַר כְּרָתוֹ מַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵי־חָרָשׁ בַּמַּעֲצָד”

The crucial picture is of ʿēṣ mîyaʿar—wood or a tree from the forest—being cut and then worked by the hands of a ḥārāš, a craftsman or artisan. The surrounding passage does not stop with somebody cutting down a tree. The material is fashioned by human hands, decorated, secured, and treated as an object that cannot speak or walk and must be carried. Jeremiah contrasts these powerless man-made objects with Yahweh, the living God.
That context matters enormously.
Jeremiah is not watching a family in a twenty-first-century living room hang lights on an evergreen while children sing about the birth of Christ.
He is exposing idolatry.
The tree or wood becomes material in the hands of a craftsman. The resulting object cannot speak. It cannot walk. It must be carried.
The prophet's target is not botany.
It is false worship.
That means saying, “Jeremiah 10 is explicitly a prophecy condemning modern Christmas trees,” goes beyond what the passage itself says.
But do not close your Bible yet.
Because that does not mean the Christian should shrug and say, “Then anything goes.”
Scripture gives us another warning.
Deuteronomy 12:30 warns Israel not to become ensnared by asking how the surrounding nations served their gods and then imitating that worship.
The Hebrew contains the sobering question:
“אֵיכָה יַעַבְדוּ הַגּוֹיִם הָאֵלֶּה אֶת־אֱלֹהֵיהֶם”
Essentially: How did these nations serve their gods?
The warning is against adopting idolatrous worship and offering it to the Lord as though God were indifferent to how He is worshiped.
So Scripture gives us boundaries.
Do not worship idols.
Do not imitate idolatry.
Do not call evil holy.
Do not give to created things the devotion belonging to the Creator.
But now comes the uncomfortable question.
Is putting an evergreen tree in your house automatically an act of worship?
Scripture never says that it is.
And this is where Christians must be very careful not to manufacture commandments in God's name.
There is a strange temptation among religious people.
Sometimes we fear breaking God's commandments so deeply that we begin creating commandments God never gave.
Then our personal conviction slowly becomes everybody else's law.
And before long, we are no longer merely saying, “My conscience will not allow me to do this.”
We are saying, “If you do this, you are disobeying God.”
Those are not the same statement.
Paul understood how quickly sincere believers could wound each other over disputed practices.
Romans 14:5 says:
“Ὃς μὲν κρίνει ἡμέραν παρ’ ἡμέραν, ὃς δὲ κρίνει πᾶσαν ἡμέραν· ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω.”
One person regards one day differently from another; another regards the days alike. Paul then tells each person to be fully convinced in his own mind.
Notice what Paul does not do.
He does not command every believer to observe the same optional day.
Neither does he command every believer to reject it.
He moves the discussion toward the Lord.
That changes the Christmas-tree question.
The deepest question is no longer simply:
“Tree or no tree?”
It becomes:
Can I do what I am doing unto the Lord with a clear conscience, without idolatry, without violating Scripture, and without despising another believer?
That question reaches far beyond Christmas.
Because you can remove every Christmas tree from your house and still have idols everywhere.
Your idol might fit inside your pocket.
Your idol might have a screen.
Your idol might be your career.
Your reputation.
Your relationship.
Your money.
Your body.
Your ministry.
Your political identity.
Even your obsession with appearing more spiritually pure than everybody else.
You can have an empty living room and an overcrowded heart.
And that is where this discussion becomes painful.
Because God has never been fooled by exterior religious cleanliness.
Human beings are fascinated with visible objects.
God searches hearts.
Someone may decorate a tree while sincerely thanking Christ for His incarnation, knowing perfectly well that the tree possesses no spiritual power whatsoever.
Another believer may refuse to have one because his conscience associates it with practices from which he believes he should remain separate.
Neither person has permission to worship an idol.
But neither person should pretend that Scripture contains the sentence, “Thou shalt have a Christmas tree,” or, “Thou shalt not have a Christmas tree.”
It contains neither.
This is where humility becomes holy.
If your conscience before God tells you not to have one, do not violate your conscience simply because your relatives laugh at you.
You do not need a Christmas tree to celebrate Jesus.
You do not need one to have a joyful home.
You do not need one to prove that you possess Christian liberty.
If removing it helps you focus more completely on Christ, remove it.
Not dramatically.
Not self-righteously.
Not while announcing that everyone who still owns one is compromised.
Just obey God with a clean conscience.
But if you have a tree, do not imagine that decorating an evergreen somehow honors Christ automatically.
A Christmas tree cannot make Christmas Christian.
Only Christ can be the center of Christian worship.
And perhaps that is the sentence we have been avoiding.
Because some homes will spend hours decorating a tree and barely minutes opening Scripture.
Some parents will spend more energy maintaining the illusion of Santa Claus than teaching their children why the Son of God came into the world.
Some families will sing about peace while refusing to forgive each other.
Some will exchange expensive gifts while carrying resentment into Christmas dinner.
Some will photograph the manger while ignoring the Messiah.
Some will write “Jesus is the reason for the season” and still live as though Jesus is an accessory to the season.
And suddenly the tree is not the most disturbing thing in the room.
We are.
Because Christianity was never supposed to be a seasonal aesthetic.
Jesus did not come merely to make December feel warmer.
He came because humanity was lost.
He came because sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Our guilt is real.
And grace is astonishingly real.
The Child in Bethlehem came to become the crucified Christ.
The hands that Mary once held would one day be pierced.
The infant laid in a manger would become the Lamb of God.
Christmas without the cross becomes sentimentality.
The cross without the resurrection becomes tragedy.
But Jesus Christ crucified and risen is the Gospel.
This is why Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 10:31 are such a devastatingly simple test:
“Εἴτε οὖν ἐσθίετε εἴτε πίνετε εἴτε τι ποιεῖτε, πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ ποιεῖτε.”
Whether you eat, drink, or whatever you do—do everything for the glory of God.
Πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ.
Everything toward the glory of God.
Everything.
That reaches your Christmas tree.
And your Christmas spending.
And your Christmas parties.
And your family arguments.
And your social media.
And your generosity.
And your traditions.
And the things nobody else knows about.
So perhaps the better question is not merely, “Is the Christmas tree pagan?”
Ask:
Does this help me remember Christ, or has Christ become background decoration to everything else?
Ask:
Am I practicing something that I genuinely believe dishonors God?
Ask:
Am I judging another servant of Christ where Scripture has not given me authority to condemn?
Ask:
Have I become more passionate about winning arguments over Christmas than telling lost people about Jesus?
That last one hurts.
Imagine proving someone wrong about a tree while never telling them how to be reconciled to God.
Imagine knowing every disputed historical claim about Christmas while barely knowing Christ.
Imagine winning the Christmas debate...
and losing the person standing in front of you.
Christian, our mission was never to produce people who agree with us about December decorations.
Our mission is to make disciples of Jesus Christ.
So if you keep the tree, keep Christ infinitely above it.
If you remove the tree, remove it for Christ—not spiritual pride.
If another faithful believer reaches a different conclusion on a matter Scripture does not explicitly command or forbid, speak truth without contempt.
And if something has genuinely become an idol...
do not decorate it.
Destroy its throne in your heart.
Maybe this article exposed something you were not expecting.
Maybe you came here expecting ammunition for a Christmas argument and discovered that God was asking questions about you.
Then do not run from that conviction.

Were you taught that Christmas trees were sinful? Did you grow up celebrating Christmas? Have your convictions changed? Speak with grace. Listen before attacking. Christians do not need another comment section filled with brothers and sisters tearing each other apart.
Save it too.
The Christmas-tree argument returns every year. When it does, come back to the Scriptures rather than relying on fragments you remember from social media.
Invite your family, your Christian friends, the believer who is struggling, the person who has grown lukewarm, the seeker asking difficult questions—and even the unbeliever who is willing to listen.
There is also another way to help this work continue.
Scripture says giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion; God loves cheerful giving.
But voluntary support can still become an act of Christian generosity when it is offered freely to help Gospel-centered work continue.
Pray.
Share.
Save the message.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
No one should ever be made to feel that money purchases a place in this mission. The Gospel itself cannot be bought.
Christ already paid the price we never could.
And perhaps that brings us back to the tree.
Should every Christian have a Christmas tree?
Scripture does not command it.
Must every Christian avoid one?
Jeremiah 10 does not explicitly establish such a command.

Should every Christian examine every tradition under the authority of Scripture, reject idolatry, guard the conscience, refuse pagan worship, love fellow believers, and seek the glory of God in everything?
Absolutely.
So tonight, when the lights are glowing...
when the house becomes quiet...
when everybody has gone to sleep...
look past the tree.
Past the decorations.
Past the presents.
Past the arguments.
Past the traditions.
Look toward Bethlehem.
Then keep looking.
Follow that Child through Galilee.
Watch Him touch lepers.
Forgive sinners.
Confront hypocrites.
Call the broken.
Walk toward Jerusalem.
See the cross.
See the nails.
See the blood.
See the stone rolled across the tomb.
Then see the tomb empty.
That is Christianity.
Not a tree.
Not the absence of a tree.
Christ.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
Coming again.
And when He has truly captured your heart, you begin discovering that the greatest danger was never an evergreen standing in your living room.
It was anything—tradition, pride, possessions, religion, approval, arguments, or even yourself—that tried to sit on the throne belonging only to Him.
So keep the tree if you can keep it with a clear conscience unto the Lord.
Leave it behind if faithfulness to Christ requires that of your conscience.
But whatever you decide...
do not miss Jesus while arguing about Christmas.
Because one day every decoration comes down.
Every light goes dark.
Every present grows old.
Every December becomes a memory.
But the Savior who entered our darkness is still the Light—and when Jesus owns the heart, even our traditions must bow before the King.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EVERYBODY MAKES MISTAKES… BUT WHEN DOES A MISTAKE BECOME A CHOICE?
paragraphs: EVERYBODY MAKES MISTAKES… BUT WHEN DOES A MISTAKE BECOME A CHOICE?
Grace will forgive the sinner who falls—but grace was never given to make peace with the sin that keeps pulling us back.
There is a sentence we use when the truth gets too close.
When the guilt becomes uncomfortable.
When somebody confronts what we did.
When our conscience starts whispering the thing we desperately do not want to hear.
“Everybody makes mistakes.”
And it is true.
Painfully true.
Every one of us has failed.
Every one of us has said something we wish we could pull back into our mouths.
Every one of us has entertained thoughts we would never want projected onto a screen.
Every one of us has disappointed someone.
Every one of us has looked into the mirror and seen a version of ourselves we promised we would never become.
Scripture does not flatter humanity.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
Not some.
All.
The religious person.
The addict.
The pastor.
The skeptic.
The person reading this while quietly carrying something nobody knows.
Me.
You.
Everybody.
But here is where one of the most dangerous lies can quietly enter the Christian life.
Because “everybody makes mistakes” can begin as an admission of human weakness…
and slowly become permission to keep choosing what Jesus died to free us from.
There is a difference between falling into sin and making a home there.
There is a difference between weakness that drives you toward Christ and rebellion that uses Christ as an excuse.
There is a difference between saying, “Jesus, I fell again. Please help me,” and saying, “Jesus will forgive me anyway, so why stop?”
And that difference matters.
More than we may want to admit.
Imagine someone standing at the edge of the same hole for the hundredth time.
The first time, he fell.
The second time, perhaps he stumbled.
But eventually he memorized the road.
He knows where the hole is.
He knows what leads there.
He knows what happens afterward.
He knows the shame.
He knows the tears.
He knows the promises he will make at 2:00 in the morning.
He knows the prayer he will pray.
And still…
he keeps walking toward it.
At some point we have to ask the terrifying question:
Am I merely making a mistake…
or have I started protecting the sin I keep asking God to forgive?
Paul anticipated almost exactly this distortion of grace.
After explaining the astonishing abundance of God's grace, he asks in Romans 6:1:
“Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ;”
In plain English:
“What then shall we say? Should we continue in sin so that grace may increase?”
The crucial word is ἐπιμένωμεν — epimenōmen, from epimenō.
It carries the idea of remaining, continuing, persisting.
Paul is not asking whether a Christian will ever stumble again.
He is confronting the idea of continuing in sin because grace is available.
And his answer is explosive:
“μὴ γένοιτο.”
Absolutely not.
May it never be.
Then Paul asks how those who died to sin can still live in it (Romans 6:2). The Greek text itself makes the contrast unmistakable: grace is not Paul's permission slip for remaining under sin's rule.
Grace is not God's way of saying sin does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough that Christ bled.
Grace is God's astonishing answer to sin.
And that means grace does not merely say,
“You are forgiven.”
Grace begins teaching the forgiven sinner,
“You don't have to remain who you were.”
That distinction changes everything.
Because someone reading this has probably been fighting the same battle for years.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe lust.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe drunkenness.
Maybe gossip.
Maybe dishonesty.
Maybe rage behind closed doors.
Maybe greed dressed up as ambition.
Maybe pride disguised as discernment.
Maybe jealousy you would never admit publicly.
Maybe you keep returning to someone you know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your church friends don't know.
Your family doesn't know.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your followers certainly don't know.
Your Sunday face looks fine.
But God has seen every midnight.
Every deleted message.
Every secret search.
Every rationalization.
Every “last time.”
Every promise.
Every relapse.
Every tear.
And here is where this message could become cruel if we stopped too soon.
Because conviction without the Gospel would leave us staring at our filth.
But Jesus does not expose darkness merely to humiliate people.
He brings darkness into the light so captives can become free.
Listen carefully to the balance Scripture gives us.
John writes:
“My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin.”
Then immediately:
“καὶ ἐάν τις ἁμάρτῃ, παράκλητον ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν δίκαιον.”
“But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” (1 John 2:1)
Do you see it?
That single verse destroys two lies at once.
The first lie says:
“Sin doesn't matter because grace exists.”
John says no.
“I write… so that you may not sin.”
The second lie says:
“You sinned again. God must be finished with you.”
John says no again.
“If anyone does sin, we have an Advocate.”
Jesus Christ the righteous.
This is Christianity.
Not permission.
Not perfectionism.
Not pretending.
Christ.
The goal is holiness.
The reality is that believers can still fall.
And the hope of the fallen believer is not his flawless performance.
His hope is Jesus Christ.
That means your failure does not have to become your identity.
But neither should grace become your alibi.
There is a devastating difference between struggling against sin and surrendering to it.
A struggling believer may fall repeatedly and hate that he keeps falling.
He confesses.
He seeks help.
He cuts off access.
He gets back up.
He cries.
He prays.
He asks trusted believers to walk with him.
Sometimes his progress feels painfully slow.
But somewhere inside him there is still war.
The person making peace with sin begins doing something different.
He stops fighting and starts defending.
“It isn't really hurting anybody.”
“God knows my heart.”
“Nobody is perfect.”
“Everybody does it.”
“I can repent later.”
“Jesus forgives.”
And suddenly grace—the very grace purchased at immeasurable cost—has been turned into camouflage for rebellion.
Please hear this without running into the opposite ditch.
Repeated failure does not automatically prove that your repentance is fake.
Some battles are long.
Some habits have roots that reach deep into wounds, patterns, environments, relationships, and years of practiced behavior.
Sanctification is real, but Christians do not mature at identical speeds.
The answer to repeated failure is therefore not hopelessness.
It is deeper surrender.
Bring the sin into the light.
Confess it to God.
Stop romanticizing it.
Stop renaming it.
Stop protecting the doorway through which it keeps entering.
Seek wise Christian accountability.
Remove access where necessary.
Repair what your sin has damaged where possible.
Run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
Because repentance is more than feeling horrible after sin.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a changed mind and turning that produces a changed direction.
Repentance does not mean you will never stumble again.
It means you can no longer comfortably call darkness home.
Think about Peter.
He did not merely make an embarrassing mistake.
He denied Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
He had walked with Christ.
He had heard His teaching.
He had seen miracles.
He had sworn loyalty.
And when pressure came, Peter collapsed.
Imagine the moment the rooster crowed.
Imagine realizing that the warning you thought you were strong enough to overcome had just become reality.
Luke tells us Peter went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).
That could have been the final chapter.
Failure.
Coward.
Hypocrite.
Finished.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, Christ met the disciple who had denied Him.
Jesus restored him.
“Feed my sheep.”
Peter's scandal was real.
His failure was real.
His tears were real.
But so was grace.
And grace did not restore Peter so Peter could return comfortably to denying Jesus.
Grace restored Peter so he could follow Jesus.
That is the part we sometimes miss.
Restoration has a direction.
Jesus does not rescue us so we can lovingly carry our chains back into the prison.
He calls us out.
And maybe that is why this hurts.
Because perhaps the Holy Spirit has already put something in your mind while you have been reading.
You know what it is.
You didn't need me to name it.
The relationship.
The website.
The substance.
The resentment.
The secret conversation.
The dishonest money.
The hidden appetite.
The unforgiveness.
The private compromise.
The habit you keep calling “a mistake” even though you have been planning when you will do it again.
Be honest.
Not with Facebook.
Not with me.
With God.
What are you asking Jesus to forgive that you are still arranging your life to repeat?
That question is uncomfortable.
But perhaps uncomfortable is exactly where healing begins.
There is no Gospel in pretending you never sinned.
There is also no Gospel in deciding sin owns you forever.
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we could not produce.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin's judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is not offered because you finally became impressive enough for God.
Forgiveness is offered through Christ.
So stop trying to clean yourself enough to approach Him.
Come.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
And when you fall, do not run away from the only One who can restore you.
Run toward Him.
But don't crawl toward Jesus asking Him to forgive the chain while your other hand refuses to let it go.
Open your hand.
Even if it shakes.
This is where scandal meets grace.
This is where the person you became collides with the Savior who already knows what you did.
This is where Satan whispers, “You're finished,” while the Gospel declares that Christ still saves sinners.
This is where shame says, “Hide.”
Jesus says, “Come.”
Sin says, “One more time.”
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
And maybe today you need to stop saying, “Everybody makes mistakes.”
Maybe today the prayer becomes:
“Jesus, I have sinned.
I don't want to defend it anymore.
I don't want to hide it anymore.
I don't want to use Your grace as permission to remain unchanged.
Have mercy on me.
Forgive me.
Change me.
Teach me to hate what is destroying me and love what draws me closer to You.
When I fall, bring me back.
When I am tempted, give me strength.
When I begin making excuses, expose them.
I belong to You.
Jesus, rewrite everything.”
Be honest.
You do not have to publish the details of private sin. God does not require public oversharing to prove repentance. But sometimes three honest words can become the moment someone stops pretending.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't weaponize this article against them.
Love them.
Pray for them.
Not because you expect to fail, but because temptation has a way of making us forget what we knew clearly yesterday.
Come back when “just once more” begins sounding reasonable.
Come back when shame tells you not to pray.
Come back when you need to remember:
Grace is not permission to remain in chains.
Grace opens the prison door.
It does not.
It cannot.
And not because somebody who truly loves God must prove that love by paying us.
The Gospel cannot be bought.

But voluntary financial support can help Gospel-centered work continue, reach more people, develop more resources, and put biblical encouragement in front of people who may never walk voluntarily through a church door.
Give freely, prayerfully, and never from manipulation or guilt. As Paul teaches concerning Christian generosity, giving is not to be done reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Jesus Christ is still the message.
His Gospel is still the hope.
Repentance is still necessary.
Grace is still astonishing.
Forgiveness is still available.
The cross is still enough.
The tomb is still empty.
So share if it may reach somebody.
Follow if you want to keep walking through Scripture with us.
But above everything else…
follow Jesus.
Because the most dangerous thing about repeated sin is not that you made another mistake.
It is that, little by little, you may stop calling darkness darkness.
And the most beautiful thing about grace is not that Jesus gives you permission to keep returning to the grave.
It is that the risen Christ calls you out of it.
You may have returned to the same sin a hundred times—but today does not have to become one hundred and one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HOSEA EXPOSED THE MEN TOO: While Their Daughters Bore the Shame, God Revealed What the Fathers Were Doing in Secret
paragraphs: HOSEA EXPOSED THE MEN TOO: While Their Daughters Bore the Shame, God Revealed What the Fathers Were Doing in Secret

Hosea 4:13–14 is not merely a warning about sexual sin. It is a terrifying exposure of religious hypocrisy—and a reminder that before we condemn the scandal in somebody else’s life, God may first uncover the altar we have hidden in our own.
There is something almost unbearable about Hosea 4.
Not because the Bible mentions prostitution.
Not because it talks openly about adultery.
Not even because an entire nation had become spiritually unfaithful.
What makes the passage so uncomfortable is where God turns the light.
Toward the men.
Toward the people who could have looked at the younger generation and shaken their heads.
Toward people who could see sexual corruption spreading through their families while somehow failing to recognize their own participation in the darkness.
And suddenly Hosea stops sounding like an ancient prophet shouting at ancient Israel.
He sounds frighteningly close.
Because human beings have always been remarkably skilled at being disgusted by sins that look uglier on somebody else.
We can condemn publicly what we entertain privately.
We can grieve over what our children are becoming while refusing to examine what they learned from the world we helped create.
We can speak about morality while secretly negotiating with temptation.
We can worship on Sunday and feed an addiction on Monday.
We can quote Scripture while hiding messages.
Preach purity while nurturing fantasy.
Demand repentance while refusing to repent.
And then God speaks.

Hosea 4:13 describes Israel sacrificing on mountaintops and burning offerings beneath trees. This is not merely a story about sexual misconduct. The chapter is describing covenant unfaithfulness, idolatry, corrupted worship, and a people abandoning the knowledge of God.
Then come the devastating words:
“Therefore your daughters play the whore, and your brides commit adultery.”
But God does not stop there.
The next verse changes the direction of the accusation.
The Hebrew says:
לֹא־אֶפְקוֹד עַל־בְּנוֹתֵיכֶם כִּי תִזְנֶינָה וְעַל־כַּלּוֹתֵיכֶם כִּי תְנָאַפְנָה כִּי־הֵם עִם־הַזֹּנוֹת יְפָרֵדוּ וְעִם־הַקְּדֵשׁוֹת יְזַבֵּחוּ וְעָם לֹא־יָבִין יִלָּבֵט
In context, the force of the verse is devastating:

God says He will not single out the daughters for their prostitution or the daughters-in-law for adultery, because the men themselves are going aside with prostitutes and sacrificing with women associated with the corrupted worship.
Read that again.
The women were not being presented as the only problem.
The men themselves were involved.

Different English translations describe the women in the latter part of verse 14 as “cult prostitutes,” “shrine prostitutes,” “temple women,” or “ritual harlot.” We should be careful not to pretend every historical detail is beyond scholarly discussion.
But Hosea’s central accusation is not difficult to see.
The men were participants in the corruption they could so easily have blamed on the women.
And that is where this ancient passage walks through the front door of the modern church.
Imagine a father discovering sexual content on his daughter’s phone...
while pornography sits hidden behind the password on his own.
Imagine a husband raging about adultery in society...
while maintaining conversations his wife would be devastated to read.
Imagine parents horrified by the sexual confusion surrounding their children...

while those same children have spent years watching marriages without tenderness, apologies without repentance, Christianity without transformation, and church attendance without Christlike character.
Imagine condemning the generation beneath us for wandering...
while refusing to ask who showed them the road.
That does not remove anyone’s personal responsibility before God.
Children are responsible for their choices.
Parents are responsible for theirs.
Women are responsible for theirs.
Men are responsible for theirs.
Hosea is not exchanging one form of partiality for another.
God does not excuse sexual sin.
He exposes hypocrisy.
And there is a difference.
The frightening thing about hypocrisy is that eventually you become better at seeing everyone else than seeing yourself.
Jesus confronted exactly that instinct centuries later.
Why notice the speck in another person’s eye while ignoring the log in your own?
That question is devastating because the hypocrite is not necessarily blind to sin.
Sometimes he sees sin extremely well.
Just selectively.
He can identify it across the room.
In another denomination.
In another political tribe.
In another family.
In another generation.
In another gender.
In his spouse.
In his children.
But somehow the flashlight never turns around.
Hosea turns it around.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to stop here.
Not because you need another theological argument.
Because there is something you already know.
A browser history.
A relationship.
A conversation.
A habit.
A second account.
A secret meeting.
A fantasy you keep feeding.
A compromise you keep renaming.
Something you promised God would happen “only once.”
Something you have confessed repeatedly without actually fleeing from it.
Something you desperately hope nobody discovers.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong.
Maybe your children think you are strong.
Maybe your spouse thinks you are strong.
Maybe people at church ask you for prayer.
And somewhere behind the public version of you is another person fighting desperately to remain undiscovered.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not require you to remain undiscovered.
It invites you to become forgiven.
There is an enormous difference.
Satan says, “Hide it.”
Jesus says, “Come into the light.”
Shame says, “If they knew everything, you would be finished.”
Grace says, “Christ already knew everything when He went to the cross.”
Religion teaches people how to manage appearances.
Jesus raises dead people.
This is why Hosea cannot ultimately be reduced to a sensational story about sex.
The deepest prostitution in Hosea is spiritual.
Israel belonged to Yahweh and chased other gods.
The bedroom scandal exposed an altar scandal.
Their bodies revealed what had already happened in their hearts.
They had exchanged faithfulness for idols.
And before modern Christians distance ourselves from them, we should remember that idols no longer require carved statues.
Anything can become an altar when we give it what belongs to God.
Sex can.
Money can.
Success can.
Attention can.
Pornography can.
Approval can.
A career can.
A relationship can.
A ministry can.
Even religious reputation can.
You can spend your entire life protecting the appearance of being a Christian while slowly losing intimacy with Christ.
That may be the most frightening scandal of all.
Not that someone falls publicly.
But that someone can decay privately while appearing spiritually alive.
You can know worship songs and not worship.
Know Bible verses and not obey.
Know Christian vocabulary and not know surrender.
Know how to say “God bless you” while your secret life is destroying you.
And Hosea refuses to let us hide behind somebody else’s scandal.
Your daughter’s sin cannot repent for yours.
Your husband’s failure cannot justify yours.
Your wife’s failure cannot excuse yours.
Your pastor’s hypocrisy cannot cleanse yours.
The corruption of society cannot become camouflage for the corruption of your heart.
Eventually every one of us stands before God without another sinner available to use as a shield.
Just us.
And Him.
That sounds terrifying.
Until you remember who stands between guilty sinners and holy judgment.
Jesus Christ.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Because Christianity does not announce that good people can repair themselves.
It announces that guilty people can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
The cross destroys both pride and despair.
Pride cannot survive there because our sin was serious enough that the Son of God had to die.
Despair cannot have the final word there because His sacrifice was sufficient to save sinners who come to Him.
At Calvary, nobody gets to boast.
And nobody who truly comes to Christ needs to believe his scandal is stronger than Christ’s grace.
Jesus did not shed His blood only for respectable sins.
He died for adulterers.
Liars.
The sexually broken.
The religious hypocrite.
The ashamed.
The addicted.
The person who has spent years pretending.
The father who failed.
The mother who wandered.
The son who rebelled.
The daughter carrying a history she wishes she could erase.
The churchgoer whose public Christianity and private life have become almost unrecognizable from each other.
But grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace calls us out.
Repentance is not saying, “I feel terrible.”
Repentance turns.
It stops negotiating.
It stops blaming.
It stops saying, “Everybody does it.”
It stops asking how close to darkness we can walk while still calling ourselves children of light.
Sometimes repentance means deleting something.
Ending something.
Confessing something.
Returning something.
Seeking accountability.
Asking forgiveness.
Accepting consequences.
Getting away from the environment feeding the sin.
And sometimes the most spiritual sentence a person can finally say is:
“I have been blaming everyone except myself.”
Maybe that is why Hosea 4:14 hurts.
