God will not permit us to build moral platforms on top of secret altars.
Imagine what could happen in families if fathers stopped merely demanding purity and started modeling repentance.
Imagine a father looking his children in the eyes and saying:
“I have failed too. I need Jesus too. I have sinned. I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Imagine mothers who do not need to maintain the illusion of perfection.
Imagine husbands confessing before being caught.
Imagine wives choosing truth before secrecy hardens into bondage.
Imagine churches where testimony is not merely a performance about what God delivered us from twenty years ago, but where believers can say:
“I need prayer today.”
Imagine Christians who become known not because they never fail, but because when they fail they run toward Christ instead of deeper into darkness.
That kind of Christianity would confuse a world built on image management.
Because the Gospel gives us something the world cannot manufacture:
the freedom to tell the truth about ourselves because our hope is no longer ourselves.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Then stop running.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
You do not need to clean yourself enough to approach Jesus.
You approach Jesus because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Confess your sin to God.
Turn from it.
Trust Christ.
Where appropriate and safe, seek mature Christian accountability and make right what your sin has damaged.
There may still be consequences.
Grace does not magically erase every earthly consequence of our choices.
But consequences are not the same thing as condemnation.
For those who belong to Christ, shame no longer gets to write the final chapter.
Jesus does.
That is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior:
Not because scandal is entertaining.
Because grace is astonishing.
We are not building a community of people pretending they have never fallen.
We want a community of people continually being brought back to Jesus—back to Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, holiness, healing, discipleship, and the transforming truth of the Gospel.
Not performative.
Not religious.
Honest.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only person fighting.
Someone may finally confess.
Someone may finally pray.
Someone may finally come home.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Because somebody in your circle may be smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
There may come a night when temptation returns and you need to remember:
being exposed by God can become the beginning of being restored by God.
It does not.
Not because anyone should pressure you into giving.
Scripture teaches that Christian generosity should come from a willing heart, not compulsion.
But voluntary, regular generosity can absolutely become one practical way of supporting Gospel work you believe is bearing fruit.
And even if you cannot financially support Gospel Warrior, you can still help.
Pray.
Share.
Save the message.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that perfect people found God.
It is the announcement that while sinners were lost, God came looking for them.
Hosea exposed a nation whose worship had become corrupted and whose private compromises were producing public devastation.
And perhaps that is the question left hanging over us now:
What are we condemning in the next generation while quietly feeding its roots in ourselves?
Fathers, come home.
Mothers, come home.
Husbands, come home.
Wives, come home.
Sons and daughters, come home.
Pastors, leaders, wounded believers, secret strugglers...
come home.
Not to religion.
Not to appearances.
Not to another mask.
To Jesus.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the adultery.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the hypocrisy.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the person you became while everybody thought you were okay.
Repent.
Believe.
Step into the light.
And discover that the hands capable of exposing your sin are also the hands that were pierced to save sinners.
The secret you thought would become the final sentence of your story may become the very place where Jesus begins writing redemption.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LET HER BREASTS SATISFY YOU”: Why Would God Put a Sentence Like This in Scripture?
paragraphs: “LET HER BREASTS SATISFY YOU”: Why Would God Put a Sentence Like This in Scripture?
We have spent generations whispering about something the Bible was never embarrassed to say out loud—and Proverbs 5:19 may expose far more than our discomfort with sex.
There are verses people frame and hang on walls.
There are verses printed on coffee mugs.
There are verses whispered beside hospital beds, preached at funerals, written inside wedding cards, and highlighted until the paper nearly tears.
And then there is Proverbs 5:19.
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
Yes.
That is in the Bible.
Not in an ancient piece of erotic literature somebody accidentally slipped between Ecclesiastes and Isaiah.
Not in some modern paraphrase trying to make Scripture provocative.
It is Proverbs.
Wisdom literature.
Holy Scripture.
And perhaps the question is not, “Why would God allow something like that in His Word?”
Perhaps the more uncomfortable question is...
Why does it embarrass us more than it apparently embarrassed God?
Stay with me, because this verse is not permission for lust.
It is almost the exact opposite.

And if you have ever struggled with pornography, adultery, wandering eyes, sexual shame, a wounded marriage, secret fantasy, loneliness, temptation, or the feeling that Christianity treats human desire as something filthy, Proverbs 5 may be far more beautiful—and far more confronting—than you were ever told.
The Hebrew does not sanitize the verse.
It says:
אַיֶּלֶת אֲהָבִים וְיַעֲלַת־חֵן דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Ayyélet ahavim veya'alat-chen, daddeha yeravvukha bekhol-et; be'ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The language is tender, poetic—and unmistakably physical.
The woman is pictured as a loving doe, a graceful deer. Her husband is told to find satisfaction in her breasts and to remain continually captivated, even intoxicated, by her love.
The Hebrew does not apologize.
But neither does it isolate her body from covenant love.
That is where our culture—and sometimes even Christians reading this verse too quickly—can completely miss the point.
Because Proverbs 5:19 did not fall out of heaven as a random sentence about breasts.
Read what comes immediately before it.
“Drink water from your own cistern, and running water out of thine own well.”
Then:
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
And immediately after the famous verse comes the question:
“And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?”
Do you see it?
This is not God telling a man to objectify women.
This is a father warning his son not to destroy himself through sexual unfaithfulness.

The chapter begins with warnings concerning forbidden sexual relationships. It describes temptation as something that can initially seem sweet and attractive but eventually become bitter and destructive.
Then Scripture does something remarkable.
It does not merely say:
Don’t.
Don’t desire.
Don’t feel.
Don’t touch.
Don’t enjoy.
Instead, biblical wisdom redirects desire toward covenant.
Rejoice in your wife.
Delight in her.
Be captivated by her.
Remain intoxicated with her love.
In other words, God does not answer destructive desire merely by commanding the death of desire.
He teaches desire where to go.
That changes everything.
Because somewhere along the way many believers absorbed an idea the Bible itself never teaches:
That holiness means becoming almost embarrassed by the body.
Yet the first human body was not invented by pornography.
God invented it.
Sexuality was not created in a nightclub.
God created male and female.
Marriage was not invented by Hollywood.
God established covenant companionship before humanity's fall.
Sin did not create desire.
Sin distorts desire.
And there is an enormous difference.
Pornography takes something capable of covenant intimacy and removes covenant.
Lust takes a person and reduces that person to consumption.
Adultery takes desire outside the boundaries of faithfulness.
Sexual exploitation takes what should involve dignity and turns another human being into an instrument.
But Proverbs 5 paints another picture.
A husband.
A wife.
A covenant.
Exclusive affection.
Joy without betrayal.
Desire without theft.
Intimacy without strangers.
A body cherished within faithful love.
That is why verse 19 cannot honestly be separated from verse 18:
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
And it cannot be separated from verse 20:
Why become captivated by another woman?
The entire contrast is between covenant faithfulness and covenant betrayal.
And then comes a sentence that should sober anyone living a secret sexual life:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD.”
The browser history nobody knows about.
The conversation you keep deleting.
The emotional affair you keep renaming “friendship.”
The private messages.
The second account.
The fantasies you deliberately feed.
The person at work whose attention you have begun craving.
The marriage you have emotionally abandoned while continuing to occupy the same house.
God sees.
Not because He is some cosmic voyeur waiting eagerly to humiliate you.
He sees because nothing that is destroying you is invisible to Him.
And this is where Proverbs 5 becomes painfully personal.
Maybe the scandal is not that God mentions a woman's breasts.
Maybe the scandal is that we live in a culture drowning in sexual imagery while starving for covenant intimacy.
Bodies everywhere.
Faithfulness becoming rare.
Sex everywhere.
Tenderness disappearing.
Access everywhere.
Intimacy nowhere.
People learning thousands of ways to stimulate themselves while forgetting how to give themselves faithfully to another human being.
And pornography may be one of the clearest examples.
Porn promises intimacy without vulnerability.
Pleasure without covenant.
Bodies without responsibility.
Excitement without faithfulness.
It trains the eyes to consume while Proverbs trains the heart to cherish.
Porn says:
More.
Different.
Next.
Someone else.
Proverbs says:
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
There is something profoundly countercultural about that.
Biblical sexuality is not built around endless novelty.
It is built around faithful rediscovery.
The same covenant.
The same person.
Years passing.
Bodies changing.
Hair graying.
Scars appearing.
Children coming—or perhaps never coming.
Illness.
Arguments.
Forgiveness.
Ordinary mornings.
Difficult seasons.
And somehow...
“Rejoice.”
That may be more radical than anything our hypersexual culture has imagined.
Because lust asks:
“What can I take?”
Covenant asks:
“How can I love?”
Lust consumes bodies.
Love knows names.
Lust hides.
Covenant remains.
Lust continually needs another image.
Faithful love learns to see the same person more deeply.
And maybe someone reading this already feels the shame rising.
Because you crossed the line.
Maybe years ago.
Maybe last night.
Maybe ten minutes before you found this article.
Perhaps your marriage is wounded because of what you did.
Perhaps nobody knows.
Perhaps everybody knows.
Maybe pornography has become the secret room you enter whenever loneliness becomes unbearable.
Maybe you promised God a hundred times:
“Never again.”
And then again happened.
And again.
And again.
Eventually you stopped making promises because breaking them hurt too much.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not pretending sin does not matter.
Jesus never needed to minimize sin in order to maximize grace.
The cross proves precisely how serious sin is.
But the cross also proves something else.
Your sin does not get the final sentence if you belong to Christ.
There is repentance.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is a Savior who already knew the ugliest chapter before He called your name.
Christianity does not announce:
Clean yourself until Jesus can tolerate you.
The Gospel announces that sinners can come to Christ, repent, believe, be forgiven, and begin becoming new.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
Trust may need rebuilding.
A wounded spouse may need time.
Secret patterns may need confession, accountability, pastoral care, counseling, boundaries, and radical changes in behavior.
Repentance is more than feeling terrible after sin.
Repentance turns around.
But shame says:
Hide.
Jesus says:
Come.
Shame says:
You are what you did.
Grace says:
Christ can make you new.
Shame says:
This chapter ruined the entire story.
Then Jesus walks into stories everybody else thought were finished.
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because sin is cute.
Not because consequences are imaginary.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps that is why Proverbs 5:19 matters so much.
It reveals a God who is not embarrassed by faithful marital intimacy.
A God who created human beings as embodied creatures.
A God who condemns adultery while honoring covenant delight.
A God whose answer to sexual chaos is not shame but holiness.
Not repression, but rightly ordered love.
Not exploitation, but covenant.
Not secrecy, but truth.
Not endless consumption, but faithful delight.
And ultimately...
not merely behavior modification.
Christ.
Because you can install every filter and still have a heart that wants darkness.
You can throw away your phone and still carry lust inside you.
You can learn religious vocabulary while remaining inwardly enslaved.
We need more than restraint.
We need redemption.
We need new hearts.
We need the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Maybe this article found you while you are fighting something nobody knows about.
Then stop pretending with God.
He already knows.
Bring it into the light.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to confess, confess wisely.
If you need accountability, seek it.
If you have wounded your spouse, stop defending yourself and begin rebuilding truthfully.

If your marriage has become emotionally cold, do not use Proverbs 5:19 as a demand for sex. The verse is not a weapon for coercing a spouse. Biblical marital intimacy belongs inside love, honor, mutual care, faithfulness, and dignity.
Your spouse is not an entitlement.
Your spouse is a person to love.
And if you are unmarried, this passage is not telling you that you are incomplete.
Christ is not a consolation prize until marriage arrives.
The deepest identity of a Christian is not husband, wife, boyfriend, girlfriend, virgin, divorced, widowed, betrayed, or sexually broken.
It is found in Christ.
Maybe you have spent years believing your sexual past disqualified you from being deeply loved by God.
It does not.
Repentance does not rewrite history.
Jesus redeems sinners within history.
The scars may remain.
But scars are not always evidence that the story ended badly.
Sometimes scars prove the wound did not kill you.
Look at the risen Christ.
Even resurrection did not erase every scar.
And maybe somebody you know desperately needs to hear that.
Send this privately to the friend drowning in pornography.
Send it to the believer carrying sexual shame.
Send it to the marriage trying to rebuild after betrayal.
Because temptation has a strange ability to make us forget in the moment what we knew clearly yesterday.
If this exposed something hidden, you do not need to write the details publicly.

And if Christ has already brought you out of sexual bondage, shame, adultery, pornography, or a broken season, consider leaving a testimony—not to glorify the darkness you escaped, but to tell somebody still trapped inside it that chains really can break.
No performance.
No pretending.
Just truth.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, grow deeper in Christ, confront sin, understand grace, and walk more faithfully with Jesus, stay close.
But hear this clearly:
It does not replace obedience to Christ.
It does not buy blessing.
Scripture says Christian generosity should come from the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
And sometimes supporting Gospel work is not only financial.
Leave thinking about faithfulness.
About what your eyes belong to.
About what your heart has been feeding.
About the person you promised to love.
About the secrets you need to bring into the light.
About the grace you thought you had exhausted.
About the Savior who still receives repentant sinners.
Because one day the secret tab closes.
The fantasy ends.
The body ages.
The applause disappears.
The temptation that once seemed irresistible becomes dust.
And what remains is the question beneath Proverbs 5 all along:
What kind of person are you becoming when nobody else is watching?
God is not embarrassed by holy desire.
He wants to rescue desire from everything that turns love into consumption and people into objects.
And perhaps tonight, the most intimate thing you can do is not touch another body.
Perhaps it is finally to stop hiding your soul.
Come into the light.
Come back to covenant.
Come back to truth.
Come back to Jesus.
Because the chapter you are most ashamed of may become the place where someone else finally discovers what grace actually means.
The sin that told you to hide may become the scar through which somebody else finally sees the light of Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JUDAS NEED TO IDENTIFY JESUS WITH A KISS?
paragraphs: WHY DID JUDAS NEED TO IDENTIFY JESUS WITH A KISS?

They came with lanterns, weapons, and enough men to arrest a dangerous criminal. Yet Judas told them to watch for something strangely intimate: a kiss. Why? The answer takes us beyond the darkness of Gethsemane and frighteningly close to our own hearts.
There is something about the betrayal of Jesus that becomes more disturbing the longer you look at it.
It wasn't merely that Judas betrayed Him.
It was how.
He could have pointed.
He could have shouted, “There He is.”
He could have approached the soldiers beforehand and described Jesus.
He could have stood at a distance and indicated which man they wanted.
Instead, Judas walked through the darkness toward the Man whose feet he had followed for years.
Toward the Rabbi whose miracles he had witnessed.
Toward the One who had fed the hungry, touched lepers, confronted demons, raised the dead, washed His disciples' feet—and only hours earlier had shared a table with him.
And Judas came close enough to kiss Him.
That raises a haunting question.
Why?
Why did Judas need to identify Jesus at all?
And why with a kiss?
Mark preserves the chilling arrangement Judas had made beforehand:
“Ὃν ἂν φιλήσω αὐτός ἐστιν· κρατήσατε αὐτόν…”

Literally, in context: “Whomever I kiss, He is the one; seize Him…” Mark 14:44. The Greek text describes the kiss as a σύσσημον (syssēmon)—an agreed or distinguishing signal. Judas had arranged the sign in advance.
That detail matters.
The kiss wasn't spontaneous emotion.
It was a signal.
An act normally associated with affection became the mechanism of betrayal.
Think about that.
Judas weaponized intimacy.
And perhaps that is why this scene still feels so painfully modern.
Some of the deepest wounds you will ever carry will not come from enemies who hated you openly.
They will come from people who knew how to get close.
People who knew where you were vulnerable.
People who knew your routines.
People who knew what mattered to you.
People whose voices once made you feel safe.
A stranger can attack your reputation.
But only someone close can betray your trust.
And Judas knew where Jesus would be.
John tells us something easy to overlook: Judas knew the garden because Jesus had often gathered there with His disciples.
Read that again emotionally.
Judas used his knowledge of Jesus' place of prayer to help His enemies find Him.
A place associated with fellowship became the location of betrayal.
He knew where Jesus went because he had been there before.
This wasn't merely information.
It was access.
And suddenly Judas becomes much more uncomfortable to read about, because the story begins asking questions we would rather ask about somebody else.
How close can a person get to Jesus without actually surrendering to Jesus?
Apparently...
terrifyingly close.
Judas had traveled with Christ.
He had heard teaching from the mouth of the Son of God.
He had witnessed what generations before him had longed to see.
He belonged outwardly to the Twelve.
People looking at the group would have counted Judas among the followers of Jesus.
Yet proximity to Christ was not the same thing as surrender to Christ.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still conceal rebellion.
You can know worship songs and still protect a secret idol.
You can carry a Bible and refuse to let the Bible confront you.
You can know where Jesus is discussed without wanting Jesus to rule you.
You can even look like a disciple while slowly negotiating with the very things that are pulling your heart away from Him.
That is why Judas should never merely become the villain we stare at from a safe distance.
His story is a warning.
But we still haven't answered the original question.
Why was identification necessary?

The Gospel accounts tell us that Judas arrived with an armed group. Mark says the people accompanying him came with swords and clubs from the chief priests, scribes, and elders. John adds that the arresting party arrived carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons.
Mark explicitly tells us that Judas had already arranged a signal identifying the intended man: the one he kissed was the one they were to seize and lead away securely.
The text therefore gives us the central answer without requiring speculation:
The kiss was a prearranged arrest signal identifying Jesus.
Why choose such a signal?

The Gospels do not explicitly give Judas' private reasoning, so we should not pretend Scripture tells us more than it does. In the nighttime setting, among Jesus and His disciples, a close-range signal would provide an unmistakable identification for members of the arresting party who needed to know precisely whom Judas meant. Judas, unlike them, knew Jesus personally.
But then John adds something extraordinary.
When the group arrived, Jesus did not hide behind Peter.
He did not disappear into the trees.
He did not wait helplessly for Judas to expose Him.
Jesus stepped forward.
John says Jesus knew what was coming and went out to meet them.
“Whom are you seeking?”
“Jesus of Nazareth.”
Jesus answered:
“ἐγώ εἰμι.”
“I am.”
English translations commonly render the statement in context as “I am he.” John then says the arresting party drew back and fell to the ground.
Now the scene becomes even more remarkable.
Judas had arranged the kiss as identification.
But Jesus was not ultimately captured because Judas managed to outsmart Him.
Jesus identified Himself.
He stepped forward.
The traitor arrived with a signal...
and the Savior walked toward His captors.
That changes the emotional center of Gethsemane.
Jesus wasn't wondering what Judas was doing.
He wasn't caught by surprise.
John explicitly says He knew what was coming.
The tragedy of the kiss, therefore, is not that Judas successfully revealed something Jesus desperately wanted hidden.
The horror is that a disciple turned an expression of relationship into an instrument of betrayal.

Mark 14:45 says Judas approached Jesus, called Him “Rabbi,” and kissed Him. The Greek uses κατεφίλησεν (katephilēsen), a form that can carry the sense of kissing warmly or earnestly, though we should be careful not to build more theology on the verb than the context warrants.
Still, the narrative itself is devastating enough.
“Rabbi.”
A kiss.
Then arrest.
His mouth performed affection while his actions delivered betrayal.
And this is where Gethsemane stops being ancient history.
Because there is a kind of Christianity that still knows how to kiss Jesus without surrendering to Jesus.
We can call Him “Lord” while refusing His authority.
We can sing about surrender while negotiating with sin.
We can post Scripture while harboring bitterness.
We can defend Christianity publicly while neglecting Christ privately.
We can lift our hands in worship and use those same hands to hide what we hope nobody discovers.
We can look close to Jesus...
without belonging wholly to Jesus.
That should disturb us.
Not so we become obsessed with whether somebody else is a Judas.
So we examine ourselves.
The most dangerous question this story produces is not:
“Who around me might betray me?”
It is:
“Jesus, is there anything in me that claims intimacy with You while secretly resisting You?”
That question reaches deeper.
Maybe your kiss is religious appearance.
Maybe yours is a hidden addiction you keep promising God you will eventually surrender.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe pride.
Maybe sexual sin.
Maybe unforgiveness.
Maybe you know exactly how to appear spiritually healthy while your private life is collapsing.
Maybe everybody thinks you are close to God because they see what you post.
But only you know how long it has been since you spoke honestly with Him.
No performance.
No audience.
No pretending.
Just you and Christ.
And perhaps the most frightening part of Judas' story is that betrayal did not begin when his lips touched Jesus.
The kiss revealed something that had already been happening in his heart.
That is how spiritual collapse often works.
Long before people see the public fall, there have been private compromises.
Tiny permissions.
Quiet negotiations.
Secret rationalizations.
Things once resisted become tolerated.
Things tolerated become defended.
Things defended eventually become chains.
And then one day everyone asks:
“How did this happen?”
But heaven saw the road long before the world saw the wreckage.
If something hidden in you is slowly pulling you away from Jesus, do not wait until your private compromise becomes your public catastrophe.
Bring it into the light now.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is an invitation to stop running toward destruction and come home.
And this is where Judas' story becomes even more heartbreaking.
Because while Judas was betraying Jesus...
Jesus was moving toward the cross for sinners.
The hands about to be bound would soon be pierced.
The face Judas kissed would soon be struck.
The Teacher he called “Rabbi” would be mocked.
The One being arrested like a criminal would bear the judgment sinners deserved.
And He would do it willingly.
That is the scandal.
And then comes grace.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that decent people can make themselves acceptable to God.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners need a Savior—and that Jesus Christ died and rose again.
The cross exposes how serious sin really is.
Grace reveals how astonishing God's mercy really is.
And maybe you need to hear this tonight:
Your story does not have to end where your worst chapter began.
Your secret does not have to become your identity.
Your failure does not possess greater authority than the blood of Christ.
Your shame does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
But grace is not permission to continue hiding.
Grace calls us out of hiding.
Christ does not merely offer us a better public image.
He calls us to repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life.
So stop pretending.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to confess sin to God, confess it.
If you have wounded someone and restitution is possible and appropriate, begin making things right.
If you have drifted from Christ, return.
You do not need another religious kiss.
You need surrender.
Maybe that is why this story hurts so deeply.
Judas reminds us that a person can stand astonishingly close to Jesus and still have a heart moving away from Him.
But the rest of the Gospel reminds us of something greater:
Jesus went willingly toward the cross to save sinners.
Be honest.
You don't have to explain everything publicly. God already knows the whole story.
Not as religious decoration.
Someone may need to discover tonight that Christianity is not about pretending to have no scars.
It is about bringing sinners to the Savior who was wounded for them.
There may come a night when the person who needs to reread it is you.
The purpose is simple: keep placing biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ where people can encounter it.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Jesus already paid the price we never could.
Your financial support helps.
Your prayers help.
Your comments help this message reach people.
Your shares help.
But never confuse supporting Gospel Warrior with supporting Jesus Himself.
Give freely, prayerfully, cheerfully, and without compulsion. Support your local church and faithful Gospel work as God leads you.
Because ultimately this article isn't about Judas' lips.
It is about our hearts.
The question is not merely why Judas needed a kiss to identify Jesus.
The deeper question is whether our outward affection for Christ matches the inward allegiance of our lives.
Judas came close enough to kiss Him.
But closeness without surrender was not discipleship.
So don't settle for appearing close to Jesus.
Know Him.
Trust Him.
Repent when you fall.
Run toward Him when shame tells you to run away.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
Follow the Savior who knew exactly what waited for Him in that garden...
and stepped forward anyway.
They came looking for Jesus with lanterns because the night was dark.
But they were arresting the Light of the world.
And the darkness would not have the final word.
The cross was coming.
The tomb was coming.
But so was Sunday.
And if Christ can take history's most infamous betrayal and place it inside the story of redemption, imagine what He can do with the chapter of your life you thought could never be redeemed.
Your darkest chapter may know your name—but it does not get to write your ending when your life is surrendered to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABIMELECH LOOKED THROUGH A WINDOW AND REALIZED ISAAC AND REBEKAH WERE DEFINITELY NOT ACTING LIKE BROTHER AND SISTER
paragraphs: ABIMELECH LOOKED THROUGH A WINDOW AND REALIZED ISAAC AND REBEKAH WERE DEFINITELY NOT ACTING LIKE BROTHER AND SISTER

One glance through a window exposed the lie Isaac had been living—and Genesis 26 may be asking what would happen if somebody looked through the window of your life long enough to discover what fear has made you hide.
There was a window.
There was a king.
There was a husband who had been calling his wife his sister.
And then there was one ordinary moment when the truth could no longer remain hidden.
Genesis does not tell us that Abimelech launched an investigation.
It does not say somebody betrayed Isaac.
It does not describe spies following him through Gerar.
Abimelech simply looked through a window.
And what he saw changed everything.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 26:8 reads:
“וַיְהִי כִּי אָרְכוּ־לוֹ שָׁם הַיָּמִים וַיַּשְׁקֵף אֲבִימֶלֶךְ מֶלֶךְ פְּלִשְׁתִּים בְּעַד הַחַלּוֹן וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה יִצְחָק מְצַחֵק אֵת רִבְקָה אִשְׁתּוֹ׃”
Abimelech looked through the window and saw Isaac מְצַחֵק — metzacheq with Rebekah.
That one Hebrew word matters.

Its root, צחק — tsachaq — carries the sense of laughing, playing, sporting, or making merry. Here the form is metzacheq. English translations variously render the scene with words such as “sporting,” “caressing,” or “playing.”
We should be careful not to make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
Genesis does not give us a graphic description of what Abimelech witnessed.
It does not need to.
Whatever Isaac was doing, the interaction communicated something unmistakable to the king.
This was not how Isaac behaved toward a sister.
This was his wife.
And suddenly the story becomes painfully human.
Because Isaac had spent his time in Gerar trying to control what everybody believed about him.
He had introduced Rebekah as his sister.
Why?
Fear.
Earlier in the chapter, the men of that place asked Isaac about Rebekah, and he said, “She is my sister.”
Genesis immediately tells us what was happening inside him.
He was afraid.
He believed the men might kill him because Rebekah was beautiful.
Think about that.
This is Isaac.
The promised son.
The miracle child Abraham and Sarah waited decades to hold.
The boy who had once been bound upon an altar and had experienced God's provision when the ram appeared.
The man through whom the covenant promises would continue.
Yet here he is...
afraid.
And fear convinces him to hide the true nature of his relationship with the woman God gave him.
That should destroy one dangerous illusion many Christians quietly carry:
Walking with God does not make you incapable of fear.
Having a calling does not make you incapable of failure.
Receiving promises does not mean you will never panic.
Being used by God does not mean every decision you make will demonstrate perfect faith.
Isaac knew something about God's faithfulness.
And Isaac still became afraid.
Maybe that is why this strange little window scene belongs in Scripture.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to trust God on Sunday and panic on Tuesday.
You know the verses.
You know the worship songs.
You know the testimonies.
You know God has carried you before.
And then something threatens your security...
your reputation...
your marriage...
your finances...
your future...
your children...
your health...
and suddenly fear begins preaching its own gospel.
“Protect yourself.”
“Hide this.”
“Don't tell them.”
“Control the story.”
“God may not come through this time.”
And little by little, fear begins rewriting your behavior.
Isaac's deception was not born in a theological classroom.
It was born in survival mode.
He feared death.
Genesis 26:9 records Isaac's explanation after Abimelech confronted him:
“כִּי אָמַרְתִּי פֶּן־אָמ֖וּת עָלֶיהָ”
Ki amarti pen-amuth aleha.
Essentially:
“I thought... lest I die because of her.”
There it is.
Not arrogance.
Not atheism.
Fear.
And fear can make otherwise faithful people do strange things.
Fear can make you hide the marriage that needs help.
Fear can make you pretend the addiction is under control.
Fear can make you smile in church while falling apart inside.
Fear can make you tell everybody, “I'm blessed,” because admitting “I'm exhausted” feels too vulnerable.
Fear can make you protect an image while your soul quietly bleeds behind it.
Fear can make a Christian construct an entire version of life designed around one desperate objective:
Don't let anybody see what is really happening.
But Isaac eventually discovered something every person hiding behind appearances eventually discovers.
You can manage people's perception for a while.
But eventually...
there is a window.
Somewhere.
Somehow.
Truth finds daylight.
Abimelech looked.
And Scripture says:
וְהִנֵּה — vehinneh.
“Behold.”
Look.
There it is.
Isaac was metzacheq with Rebekah.
The carefully maintained story collapsed in one glance.
And Abimelech summoned him.
His words in Hebrew are almost startling in their directness:
“אַךְ הִנֵּה אִשְׁתְּךָ הִוא”
Akh hinneh ishtecha hi.
“Surely—behold—she is your wife.”
Then came the question Isaac could no longer escape:
How could you say she was your sister?
Imagine standing there.
No more explanations prepared.
No more image to maintain.
No more hiding.
The king knew.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of the story is that a pagan ruler had to confront the covenant man about behavior that could have endangered other people.
Abimelech understood how serious Isaac's deception could have become.
Someone might have taken Rebekah.
Someone could have incurred guilt.
Isaac's fear had consequences beyond Isaac.
That is another truth we desperately need.
The things we hide rarely affect only us.
Secret bitterness eventually touches somebody.
Secret lust eventually touches somebody.
Secret dishonesty eventually touches somebody.
Secret pride eventually touches somebody.
Secret compromise eventually touches somebody.
Fear whispers:
“Keep this hidden and nobody gets hurt.”
Scripture repeatedly shows us something different.
Darkness grows when protected.
Sin grows when defended.
Deception multiplies when maintained.
But exposure can become the doorway to grace.
And maybe right now you are uncomfortable because you stopped reading about Isaac several paragraphs ago.
Now you're thinking about yourself.
Your own window.
Your own secret.
Your own carefully maintained explanation.
The thing everybody believes about you...
and the thing God knows.
Maybe people see the Christian posts.
God sees the private browser history.
People see the marriage anniversary picture.
God hears the silence inside the house.
People see the ministry.
God sees the ego attached to it.
People see generosity.
God sees whether applause is secretly required.
People hear, “I'm okay.”
God hears the prayer you cannot bring yourself to pray.
People see someone who appears strong.
God sees someone who is tired of pretending.
And here is where this story could become terrifying...
unless you understand the Gospel.
Because Christianity is not the story of people successfully hiding their scandals from God.
Christianity is the story of a holy God who already knows everything...
and came looking for sinners anyway.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity had successfully convinced Him we were righteous.
He went because we weren't.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
Abraham needed grace.
Isaac needed grace.
Jacob needed grace.
David needed grace.
Peter needed grace.
Paul needed grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
And grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough for Christ to bleed.
Grace means the judgment our sin deserved fell upon the sinless Son of God, and forgiveness is offered to sinners who could never purchase it for themselves.
Jesus did not die to help us become better actors.
He died to make sinners new.
That is why repentance is not humiliation for the Christian.
Repentance is coming home.
You stop running.
Stop editing the story.
Stop blaming everybody else.
Stop calling darkness light.
Stop calling bondage personality.
Stop calling compromise weakness.
Stop saying “everybody does it.”
Stop pretending.
You come before Jesus with empty hands and tell Him the truth He already knows.
“Lord, I sinned.”
And the astonishing message of the Gospel is not that Jesus says, “I had no idea.”
The astonishing message is that He knew before you confessed...
and the cross was already standing in history.
Maybe your deepest fear is this:
“If people knew everything about me, would anybody still love me?”
Look toward Calvary.
Christ knew.
Christ came.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
And Christ still calls sinners to Himself.
Not so they can remain enslaved to what He forgives...
but so grace can transform them.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create another corner of Christianity where everybody pretends to have everything together.
We need places where Scripture can confront us.
Where Jesus remains the center.
Where repentance is not treated like a dirty word.
Where wounded believers can remember that failure does not have to write the final chapter.
Where seekers can discover that Christianity is not fundamentally “good people proving how good they are.”
It is guilty sinners discovering how glorious Jesus is.
And if this article has opened a window in your own heart, don't immediately close it.
Stay there for a moment.
What are you hiding?
What fear has been making decisions for you?
What have you been calling “wisdom” that is actually unbelief?
What relationship needs truth?
What secret needs confession?
What compromise needs repentance?
What burden needs to be brought into the light?
You don't need to confess private details publicly in a Facebook comment.
Some things belong before God and, where appropriate, with a trusted pastor, mature believer, counselor, spouse, or person directly affected.
But you can mark this moment.
And if God has been restoring you after failure, somebody reading this may desperately need your testimony.
Sometimes another believer needs to discover that they are not the only person fighting to come back into the light.
And please don't let this article die on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Christ earned what we never could.
someone smiling...
someone functioning...
someone posting...
someone quietly terrified...
someone hiding behind a version of themselves they can no longer maintain.
They may never tell you this article reached them.
Share it anyway.
Because the day may come when fear starts rewriting your decisions again, and you need to remember the window.
Stay close to truth.
Stay close to Scripture.
Most of all, stay close to Christ.
It cannot.
And not because anyone should pressure you into giving.
Scripture says Christian generosity should not be given reluctantly or under compulsion.
Think of it as voluntary monthly partnership in the work—an offering of support freely chosen, not a payment to God and not a purchase of spiritual favor.
But the merchandise isn't the heart of it.
Jesus is.
The mission is.
The Gospel is.
Pray.
Follow.
Invite others to follow.
There are many ways to help truth travel.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is still hiding.
Someone thinks their scandal disqualifies them forever.
Someone believes Jesus would walk away if the window opened and everything became visible.
Someone believes the worst chapter they ever wrote must also become the ending.
But the Gospel says otherwise.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
Paul persecuted the church and became a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The cross itself looked like history's darkest defeat...
until Sunday morning.
That is what Jesus does.
He enters graves and produces resurrection.
He enters shame and brings redemption.
He enters guilt and announces forgiveness.
He enters ruined stories and begins writing sentences grace alone could compose.
Isaac's fear was exposed through a window.
But his story did not end at that window.
God remained faithful to His covenant purposes despite Isaac's weakness.
That does not excuse Isaac's deception.
It magnifies God's faithfulness.
And perhaps that is the sentence you needed tonight.
Your failure is real.
Your sin matters.
Repentance is necessary.
Consequences may still have to be faced.
But if you belong to Christ, your worst moment does not possess greater authority over your future than the blood of Jesus Christ.
So open the window yourself.
Bring it into the light.
Tell Jesus the truth.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Make what needs to be made right.
And walk forward differently.
Because one day the question will not be whether you managed to convince everybody that you never struggled.
The question will be what you did when grace found you in the middle of it.
The window may expose what fear made you hide—but the cross reveals how far Jesus was willing to go to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “GOD IS WITHIN HER; SHE WILL NOT FALL” — THE VERSE MILLIONS OF WOMEN LOVE WAS NEVER ORIGINALLY ABOUT A WOMAN
paragraphs: “GOD IS WITHIN HER; SHE WILL NOT FALL” — THE VERSE MILLIONS OF WOMEN LOVE WAS NEVER ORIGINALLY ABOUT A WOMAN
Psalm 46:5 is beautiful. It is powerful. It is true. But when you discover who the “her” actually is, the verse does not become smaller. It becomes breathtaking.
You have probably seen the words before.
On a coffee mug.
Across a T-shirt.
Printed beneath flowers in a Christian journal.
Written underneath a photograph of a woman who survived betrayal, divorce, grief, depression, abandonment, or a season she thought would destroy her.
“God is within her; she will not fall.” — Psalm 46:5
And perhaps those words found you when you desperately needed them.
Maybe you whispered them through tears.
Maybe you sent them to your daughter.
Maybe you held onto them when your marriage was breaking, when someone walked away, when the diagnosis came, when the bills kept arriving, when nobody knew how exhausted you really were.
Maybe you looked into the mirror and told the trembling woman staring back at you:
“God is within her. She will not fall.”
There is something you need to know.
Something beautiful.
Something uncomfortable.
Something that does not destroy the verse but opens it.
The “her” in Psalm 46:5 was not originally a woman.
Because the truth is better than the slogan.
Much better.
Psalm 46 does not begin with a confident woman standing triumphantly against the world.
It begins with catastrophe.
“God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.”
Then the earth changes.
Mountains collapse.
Waters roar.
Nations rage.
Kingdoms shake.
The imagery feels almost apocalyptic.
This is not a Psalm written from the comfort of an untouched life.
This is a song for people watching everything they thought was permanent begin to move.
And perhaps that is why you need its real meaning.
Because sometimes your life moves too.
The person you thought would stay leaves.
The prayer you thought would be answered remains unanswered.
The child you raised makes choices that break your heart.
The church hurt you.
The person who quoted Scripture to you betrayed you.
You smiled on Sunday while privately wondering whether God could still hear you.
You told everyone, “I’m okay.”
You weren't.
And then you found that sentence:
God is within her.
She will not fall.
But look at what immediately precedes it.
In Hebrew, Psalm 46 speaks of:
עִיר־אֱלֹהִים — ʿir Elohim
“The city of God.”
Then comes:
אֱלֹהִים בְּקִרְבָּהּ בַּל־תִּמּוֹט
Elohim beqirbah, bal-timmot.
Literally, in sense:
“God is in her midst; she shall not be moved.”
And then:
יַעְזְרֶהָ אֱלֹהִים לִפְנוֹת בֹּקֶר
Yaʿz'reha Elohim lifnot boqer.
God will help her as morning appears.
The feminine language is really there.
The Hebrew does say “her.”
But grammar matters.
Context matters.
And the previous line tells us who “her” is.
The city of God.
The psalmist is poetically speaking of God's city—Zion/Jerusalem—as feminine.
The ancient Greek translation preserves the same idea:
ὁ θεὸς ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῆς, οὐ σαλευθήσεται
ho theos en mesō autēs, ou saleuthēsetai
“God is in her midst; she shall not be shaken.”
So the problem was never the word “her.”
The problem comes when we detach “her” from the sentence before it and quietly replace the city with ourselves.
Psalm 46:5 was not originally written as:
“God lives inside a strong Christian woman, therefore nothing bad will happen to her.”
That may fit beautifully on merchandise.
But it is not what the psalmist was saying.
And we should love Scripture too much to make it say something merely because that something sounds encouraging.
Because biblical encouragement is stronger than inspirational misquotation.
The Psalm is saying something enormous.
The world around God's people can shake while God's presence remains unshaken.
Read that again.
The security of the city is not found in the strength of the city.
It is found in the presence of God.
That changes everything.
Because perhaps you have been reading Psalm 46:5 as though the hero of the verse were “her.”
She is strong.
She is resilient.
She cannot fall.
She survives.
But look again.
God is the hero.
The city does not remain because the city is impressive.
The city remains because:
God is in her midst.
That is the heartbeat of Psalm 46.
Not human invincibility.
Divine presence.
And suddenly this becomes much more personal—not because we have stolen a promise from ancient Jerusalem, but because the entire biblical story eventually brings us to something even greater.
God came near.
Not merely symbolically.
Not merely poetically.
God came to us in Jesus Christ.
“The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).
The God whose presence made Zion secure entered human history.
He walked dusty roads.
Touched lepers.
Ate with sinners.
Welcomed the rejected.
Confronted religious hypocrisy.
Forgave the guilty.
Wept beside a grave.
And then He walked willingly toward a cross.
This is where Psalm 46 must eventually push the Christian heart—not toward self-celebration, but toward God.
And for us, toward Christ.
Because Christianity is not the story of strong people learning how to become unshakeable.
Christianity is the story of sinners discovering that their only true refuge is an unshakeable Savior.
Maybe that disappoints the version of you who wanted the verse to say:
“You are unstoppable.”
But the Gospel gives you something infinitely better.
You don't have to be.
You are allowed to tremble.
You are allowed to admit that the betrayal nearly destroyed you.
You are allowed to say that losing them hurt.
You are allowed to confess that some mornings faith feels harder than it used to.
You are allowed to admit that you have questioned God.
You are allowed to stop pretending that Christian maturity means never crying in the bathroom where nobody can hear you.
Psalm 46 never says everything around God's people remains stable.
Quite the opposite.
The earth moves.
Mountains fall.
Waters roar.
Nations rage.
Kingdoms collapse.
And God remains.
Maybe somebody reading this has been blaming herself because she fell.
You thought Psalm 46:5 promised that you wouldn't.
But you did.
You broke down.
You relapsed into an old sin.
You went back to someone you knew was destroying you.
You lost your temper.
You stopped praying.
You wandered.
You compromised.
You became someone you promised God you would never become again.
And now the words “she will not fall” almost accuse you.
Because you fell.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel was never built upon your ability not to fall.
It was built upon Christ's power to save sinners who have.
Peter fell.
David fell.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples ran.
The thief beside Jesus reached the final hours of a ruined life with nothing left to offer Christ except desperate faith.
And grace still reached him.
This is why Jesus is more beautiful than Christian motivational language.
Motivational religion says:
“Become strong enough that you never fall.”
Jesus says to broken sinners:
“Come unto me.”
There is a difference.
The cross does not celebrate our spiritual résumé.
It destroys our boasting.
At Calvary, the holy Son of God carried sin He never committed for sinners who could never rescue themselves.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, Jesus Christ rose from the grave.
The Christian hope is therefore not:
“I am powerful enough to survive everything.”
It is:
“Christ is enough even when I discover that I am not.”
That does not make you passive.
Grace never gives sin permission to remain comfortable.
Jesus does not merely comfort us in our ruins.
He calls us out of them.
Repent.
Come home.
Confess what you have hidden.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop decorating the chains Jesus died to break.
Stop using grace as permission to remain where Christ is calling you to leave.
Maybe the greatest shaking in your life right now is not happening around you.
Maybe it is happening inside you.
Maybe God is exposing what you carefully concealed.
The secret relationship.
The private messages.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The pride.
The jealousy.
The addiction.
The resentment.
The religious performance.
The secret habit nobody at church knows exists.
And perhaps you have mistaken God's conviction for God's rejection.
But conviction can be mercy.
Because the Savior who exposes darkness is the Savior who died to bring sinners into light.
There is forgiveness in Jesus.
Real forgiveness.
Not pretending your sin did not matter.
The cross proves that it mattered terribly.
And the cross simultaneously proves that God's mercy is greater than your ability to clean yourself.
That is scandalous grace.
The guilty forgiven.
The ashamed covered.
The wandering welcomed home.
The sinner transformed.
The spiritually dead made alive.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And now we can return to the woman who first found Psalm 46:5 on that coffee mug.
Can she still love this verse?
Absolutely.
But now she can love it truthfully.
She does not need to pretend the original “her” was secretly written about her personally.
She can say something richer:
“The God who was the refuge of His people is still my refuge.”
She can read the whole Psalm.
She can hear:
“God is our refuge and strength.”
She can hear:
“The LORD of hosts is with us.”
She can hear:
“Be still, and know that I am God.”
She can see that the entire song is relentlessly God-centered.
And then, as someone united to Christ, she can remember the extraordinary promises actually given to believers in the New Testament.
Christ is with His people.
Nothing can separate those who belong to Him from the love of God in Christ.
The Holy Spirit dwells in believers.
Christ will never abandon His own.
Those are not weaker truths.
They are magnificent ones.
And notice something else.
Psalm 46 does not say:
“I will never experience shaking.”
It teaches:
When everything shakes, God remains God.
There will be mornings when you feel strong.
There will be mornings when getting out of bed feels like warfare.
There will be seasons when your prayers pour out easily.
There may be seasons when all you can manage is:
“Jesus, help me.”
Say it.
There are worse prayers than the desperate cry of somebody who finally understands she cannot save herself.
Maybe that is you tonight.
Jesus, help me.
Jesus, forgive me.
Jesus, bring me home.
Jesus, I cannot keep pretending.
Jesus, I have sinned.
Jesus, I need You.
You do not need a slogan nearly as much as you need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
Not because commenting saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is the first crack in the wall of isolation.
And somebody reading your words may realize they are not fighting alone.
Not because you need to win Bible arguments.
Truth matters.
God's Word deserves more than captions detached from their meaning.
And the next time you see “God is within her; she will not fall,” remember the city.
Remember the chaos.
Remember the raging nations.
Remember the trembling earth.
Remember that the great comfort of Psalm 46 was never that “she” was extraordinarily powerful.
God was in her midst.
Send it to the believer who feels ashamed because life shook them harder than they expected.
Send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is nothing more than motivational quotations.
Let them see the Gospel.
Let them see Jesus.
Scripture teaches generosity without compulsion.
Support should come freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully.
Your support helps us keep reaching people with Scripture and pointing wounded, wandering, skeptical, struggling, and hungry hearts toward Jesus Christ.
And sharing this article publicly costs nothing, yet it can help put biblical truth in front of someone we may never otherwise reach.
You cannot buy God's grace.
You cannot donate enough money to erase one sin.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Salvation is found in Christ.
Save what strengthens you.
Share what may reach somebody else.
But above all...
Follow Jesus.
Because someday every mug will break.
Every shirt will wear out.
Every social-media post will disappear beneath another thousand posts.
Every human platform will eventually become irrelevant.
But the Word of our God stands.
And when your world shakes—and sooner or later, something will—you will discover why Psalm 46 was never really celebrating the strength of “her.”
It was celebrating the presence of Him.
The strongest thing about “her” was never her strength. It was that God was there.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF GRACE FORGIVES EVERY SIN… WHY NOT JUST KEEP SINNING?
paragraphs: IF GRACE FORGIVES EVERY SIN… WHY NOT JUST KEEP SINNING?
The question almost sounds offensive. But if we are honest, some of us have quietly lived as though the answer were yes.
There is a dangerous sentence a Christian can learn to say without ever speaking it aloud.
“God will forgive me.”
You know it is wrong.
You know what Scripture says.

You know that conversation should not be happening. You know that relationship is pulling you somewhere dark. You know what you keep watching when nobody is around. You know what you keep hiding from your spouse. You know about the bitterness you have carefully renamed “discernment.” You know about the pride you disguise as confidence. You know about the secret habit you delete from your history but cannot erase from your conscience.
And somewhere between temptation and surrender, a thought whispers:
There is always grace.
So you do it.
Again.
Then Sunday comes.
You sing.
You pray.
Maybe you cry.
You ask Jesus to forgive you.
And He is merciful.
Then Monday comes...
and somehow the mercy that should have made you love Him more becomes the excuse you use to walk back toward the thing that wounded your relationship with Him.
If that sentence made you uncomfortable, keep reading.
Because nearly two thousand years ago, the apostle Paul anticipated exactly this question.
And his answer was explosive.
“Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ;”
Ti oun eroumen? Epimenōmen tē hamartia, hina hē charis pleonasē?
“What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase?”
Then Paul answers:
“μὴ γένοιτο.”
Mē genoito.
Absolutely not.
May it never be.
The Greek is forceful. Paul is not cautiously suggesting that continuing in sin might be spiritually unhelpful.
He recoils from the idea.
Why?
Because grace was never given so that sin could become comfortable.
Grace was given because sinners needed to be rescued.
Paul continues:
“οἵτινες ἀπεθάνομεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, πῶς ἔτι ζήσομεν ἐν αὐτῇ;”
“We who died to sin, how can we still live in it?”

That is Romans 6:1–2, and the Greek text preserves the force of Paul's argument: the Gospel does not merely change the punishment awaiting the sinner. Union with Christ changes the believer's relationship to sin itself. Romans 6 goes on to describe believers as united with Christ in His death and called to walk in “καινότητι ζωῆς” — kainotēti zōēs — “newness of life.”
Read those words again.
Newness of life.
Not perfection overnight.
Not pretending temptation disappeared.
Not becoming incapable of stumbling.
But something has changed.
Someone has changed.
You have encountered Jesus Christ.
And when Christ saves a sinner, He does not merely forgive the old life so that the old life can continue undisturbed.
He begins making the sinner new.
That distinction may expose something many Christians desperately need to confront:
There is a difference between falling into sin while fighting it and planning to remain in sin because you expect grace to cover it.
A Christian can stumble.
A Christian can fall terribly.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
David committed devastating sins.
The Corinthian church had serious moral failures.
The Bible does not sanitize its heroes because Scripture is not ultimately the story of impressive human beings.
It is the story of a holy God rescuing desperately sinful people.
But grace never turns rebellion into righteousness.
Grace never calls darkness light.
Grace never looks at the chains around your wrists and says, “Stay there.”
Grace opens the prison door.
That is why Paul says something astonishing later in Romans 6:
“ἁμαρτία γὰρ ὑμῶν οὐ κυριεύσει.”
Hamartia gar hymōn ou kyrieusei.
“Sin will not have dominion over you.”
Then comes the reason:
“οὐ γάρ ἐστε ὑπὸ νόμον ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ χάριν.”
“You are not under law but under grace.”
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say:
“You are under grace, therefore sin does not matter.”
He says essentially the opposite.
You are under grace...
therefore sin is no longer your master.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace is the announcement that Jesus Christ has broken the chains.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Some of us do not actually want freedom from certain sins.
We want freedom from the consequences.
We want Jesus to remove guilt without touching the idol.
We want forgiveness without surrender.
We want heaven without holiness.
We want the Savior...
but we secretly negotiate with the Lordship.
“Jesus, You can have my Sundays.”
“But not this relationship.”
“You can have my worship.”
“But not my sexuality.”
“You can have my prayers.”
“But not my money.”
“You can have my public image.”
“But please don't enter the locked room.”
And Jesus loves us too deeply to participate in that arrangement.
The Gospel is not Christ standing outside your prison cell whispering, “I forgive you for being inside.”
The Gospel is Christ entering our death, bearing our sin, suffering the judgment we deserved, rising victorious from the grave, and calling us out of captivity into life with Him.
That is why the cross destroys both pride and presumption.
Pride says:
“I am good enough.”
The cross says:
No. Your sin was so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
Presumption says:
“Then sin doesn't matter because Jesus paid for it.”
The cross answers:
Look again at what your sin cost.
Grace is free to us.
It was not cheap.
There were nails.
There was blood.
There was a crown of thorns.
There was a cross.
And there was Jesus.
The spotless Lamb of God carrying what sinners could never carry themselves.
So when temptation whispers, “It doesn't matter; God will forgive you,” look toward Calvary.
Grace does not make sin smaller.
Grace shows us how unimaginably great God's love is toward sinners.
Maybe you failed last night.
Maybe you failed ten minutes ago.
Maybe you are reading this with shame still sitting in your chest.
Then hear this carefully:
The answer is not to run away from Jesus until you become respectable enough to return.
Run toward Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Bring the hidden thing into His light.
First John 1:9 tells believers that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Repentance does not mean you somehow purchase forgiveness by feeling terrible enough.
Jesus purchased redemption.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that finally stops defending what Christ came to save us from.
And sometimes repentance sounds less impressive than we imagine.
Sometimes it is simply:
“Jesus... I did it again.”
“No excuses.”
“No blaming.”
“No pretending.”
“I need You.”
That prayer may be spoken through tears.
It may be spoken by someone who has prayed something similar before.
But the question is not whether you have ever fallen twice.
The question is:
When you fall, where are you running?
Are you running deeper into darkness?
Or are you running toward Christ?
Because there is a world of difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
A person drowning will thrash desperately for air.
A person living underwater has accepted another environment.
The Christian life contains warfare.
Temptation.
Failure.
Confession.
Discipline.
Growth.
Sometimes painful growth.
But the direction matters.

Paul eventually describes the outcome of liberation from sin as fruit leading toward holiness, with eternal life as its end. Then Romans 6 closes with one of Scripture's most devastating and beautiful contrasts:
“τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος...”
“The wages of sin is death...”
But the sentence does not stop there.
“τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.”
“But the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
Death earned.
Life given.
Sin pays wages.
God gives a gift.
And the gift has a name.
Jesus.
That is grace.
Grace is not God pretending you never sinned.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves through Jesus Christ.
Grace does not say, “Your rebellion doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Your rebellion was deadly, but My Son went into death for you.”
Grace does not whisper, “Keep sinning.”
Grace announces:
You don't belong to that master anymore.
Maybe somebody reading this has been using grace as anesthesia.
You keep numbing conviction with theological vocabulary.
“Nobody is perfect.”
True.
“We are all sinners.”
True.
“God knows my heart.”
Absolutely.
But none of those truths were given to help us protect the sin Christ calls us to surrender.
“We are all sinners” is not the end of the Gospel.
Christ saves sinners.
He forgives sinners.
He justifies sinners.
He reconciles sinners to God.
And He begins transforming those He saves.
You may still have scars.
You may still have battles.
You may have mornings when temptation feels louder than worship.
You may stumble so badly that you wonder whether you have ruined everything.
But do not confuse the presence of a battle with permission to surrender to the enemy.
Get up.
Confess.
Repent.
Cut off access to what repeatedly drags you back.
Ask another mature believer for help.
Open Scripture.
Pray when you do not feel spiritual.
Run toward Christ when shame tells you to hide.
Especially then.
Because the devil loves two lies.
Before sin, he whispers:
“It's not that serious.”
After sin, he whispers:
“It's too serious for Jesus to forgive.”
Both lies are designed to keep you from the cross.
The Gospel destroys both.
Sin is more serious than you wanted to believe.
And Christ is more merciful than you dared to hope.
That is the scandal.
That is the grace.
And that is why Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail.
But you can stop pretending.
There is no trophy for pretending.
There is grace for coming into the light.
And somebody you know may desperately need this truth tonight.
Send it privately to the believer who stopped attending church because shame convinced them Jesus no longer wanted them.
Send it to the person who thinks grace means sin doesn't matter.
Send it to the person who thinks their sin means grace is no longer available.
Because temptation has an interesting way of making us forget tomorrow what conviction made painfully clear today.

Scripture gives us a beautiful framework for Christian generosity. Paul instructed believers to give deliberately rather than impulsively, and he wrote that each person should give what he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver. Christian generosity is therefore worship offered freely to God, not a payment used to purchase His favor.
It does not buy salvation.
It does not purchase forgiveness.
It does not make God love you more.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
Let your local-church giving, generosity toward people in need, and support of Gospel ministry be matters of faithful stewardship before God.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help tremendously.
Pray that every word points beyond a page, beyond a ministry, beyond a personality...
straight to Jesus Christ.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
A devotional is not the Savior.
A church building is not the Savior.
Your good behavior is not the Savior.
Jesus Christ is.
And perhaps after everything you have just read, one question remains.
“If I am saved by grace, do I have to keep sinning?”
No.
You may still stumble.
You will still need grace every day.
You will still need confession, repentance, Scripture, prayer, Christian community, correction, perseverance, and the mercy of God.
But sin does not have to remain your king.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ saves.
Christ forgives.
Christ transforms.
And the same grace that meets you covered in the dirt is the grace that refuses to leave you comfortably lying there.
So come home.
Again, if necessary.
Come bleeding.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come with the confession you promised yourself you would never have to make again.
But come to Jesus.
There is mercy at His feet.
There is cleansing in His blood.
There is life in His resurrection.
There is freedom under His Lordship.
And there is a future beyond the chapter you thought ruined your entire story.
The sin you thought would become the final sentence may become the very place where the world sees what Jesus can rewrite.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A CHRISTIAN REMARRY AFTER A SPOUSE DIES? PAUL GIVES A DIRECT ANSWER
paragraphs: CAN A CHRISTIAN REMARRY AFTER A SPOUSE DIES? PAUL GIVES A DIRECT ANSWER

You buried the person you promised to love until death. Now your heart is beating again—and somehow that feels like betrayal. But what if Scripture says something grief has made difficult for you to believe?
There is a kind of guilt nobody warns you about.
It does not always arrive at the funeral.
Sometimes it arrives months later.
Years later.
After the casseroles stop coming. After everyone else seems to have returned to normal. After you have learned how to sleep on one side of the bed because looking at the empty side still hurts.
Then one day, something happens.
You laugh with someone.
Really laugh.
And immediately afterward, you feel guilty.
Or somebody makes you feel safe again.
You notice their kindness. You begin looking forward to their messages. You catch yourself wondering what it would feel like to have someone sitting across the dinner table again.
And suddenly the questions begin.
“Am I betraying my husband?”
“Am I dishonoring my wife?”
“If I truly loved my spouse, shouldn’t that love be enough for the rest of my life?”
“Would God be disappointed if I remarried?”
And perhaps the hardest question of all:
“Can a Christian actually fall in love and marry again after a spouse dies?”
Paul does not leave the grieving believer trapped in uncertainty.
His answer is remarkably direct.
In 1 Corinthians 7:39, the Greek text reads:
Γυνὴ δέδεται ἐφ’ ὅσον χρόνον ζῇ ὁ ἀνὴρ αὐτῆς· ἐὰν δὲ κοιμηθῇ ὁ ἀνήρ, ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶν ᾧ θέλει γαμηθῆναι, μόνον ἐν κυρίῳ.
A careful translation is:
“A wife is bound for as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.”
Read those words again.
She is free.
Not unfaithful.
Not spiritually second-class.
Not guilty of betraying the dead.
Free.
And there is something extraordinarily tender hidden inside Paul's Greek.
He begins with δέδεται — dedetai.
It means “is bound.”
The marriage covenant is real. Scripture does not treat marriage like a disposable contract that lasts only while two people remain happy with each other. Paul treats the marriage bond seriously.
While both spouses live, that covenant matters.
But then Paul says:
ἐὰν δὲ κοιμηθῇ ὁ ἀνήρ
Literally, “but if the husband should fall asleep.”
Paul uses the language of sleep for death.
Not because death is imaginary.
Not because grief is painless.
But because for those who belong to Christ, death does not have the final word.
The grave is not the end of the Christian story.
Jesus Christ walked into death Himself.
He was crucified.
Buried.
And on the third day, the stone did not keep Him.
Christ rose.
That changes everything about how Christians understand the cemetery.
We still cry.
We still ache.
We still miss them.
But we do not grieve as though the grave owns them forever.
And then Paul writes words some grieving believers desperately need permission to believe:
ἐλευθέρα ἐστίν — eleuthera estin.
“She is free.”
There is no ambiguity in the central point.
Death ends the earthly marriage bond.
Paul makes essentially the same point in Romans 7:2, where he explains that a married woman is bound to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies, she is released from that marital bond.
That means remarriage after the death of a spouse is not adultery.
It is not automatically evidence that the first marriage meant less.
It does not erase the years you shared.
It does not delete photographs.
It does not rewrite anniversaries.
It does not mean you stopped loving the person who died.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs these next words more than everything else in this article:
Loving again does not require you to pretend you never loved before.
You can treasure what God gave you in one season without refusing what He may give you in another.
Your first spouse does not become disposable because you remarry.
And a future spouse does not have to live forever in competition with someone who died.
There can be gratitude for yesterday and faithfulness today.
There can be grief and joy occupying the same human heart.
That is one of the strange realities of surviving loss.
You can cry at a photograph in the morning and laugh with someone new that evening.
You can visit a grave and still imagine another wedding.
You can remember the hand you once held without believing your hand must remain empty forever.
Grief is not adultery against joy.
And joy is not adultery against grief.
Paul says:
ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶν ᾧ θέλει γαμηθῆναι
“She is free to be married to whom she wishes.”
Notice that Paul gives the widow genuine agency.
He does not say she must remarry.
He does not say she must not remarry.
In fact, the following verse expresses Paul's judgment that remaining unmarried may be advantageous in the circumstances he is addressing.
So Scripture leaves room for both callings.
Some widows and widowers may remain single and discover a beautiful season of undivided devotion to Christ.
Others may eventually desire marriage again.
Neither choice should automatically become a weapon for judging the other.
There is no biblical command requiring a surviving Christian spouse to remain unmarried for life.
But Paul does give one crucial boundary.
Four Greek words:
μόνον ἐν κυρίῳ — monon en Kyriō.
“Only in the Lord.”
That changes everything.
Christian freedom is never freedom from Christ.
You may be free to marry again.
But you are not free to remove Jesus from the center of the decision.
“Only in the Lord” has historically and widely been understood as requiring the contemplated marriage to remain within Christian allegiance—including marriage to a fellow believer.
So the question cannot merely be:
“Do I love this person?”
There are deeper questions.
Does this relationship draw me toward Christ or quietly pull me away from Him?
Can we pray together?
Can we worship together?
Can we build a home where Jesus is not merely mentioned but obeyed?
Will this person encourage holiness?
Do they actually belong to Christ—or have I convinced myself that vague spirituality is enough because loneliness hurts?
Because loneliness can become loud.
Very loud.
And lonely people sometimes negotiate with convictions they once thought were immovable.
That is why Paul's final phrase matters so much.
Only in the Lord.
Your loneliness does not need to become your lord.
Your memories do not need to become your lord.
Your desire to feel wanted again does not need to become your lord.
Your fear of growing old alone does not need to become your lord.
Jesus remains Lord.
Even here.
Especially here.
And there is another truth that deserves to be said carefully.
If your spouse died, you do not need to apologize for surviving.
Some people carry survivor's guilt into places God never commanded it.
You wake up.
They don't.
You eat another meal.
They don't.
Another birthday comes.
Another Christmas.
Another sunrise.
And sometimes continuing to live feels strangely disloyal.
Then love unexpectedly appears again, and the guilt becomes almost unbearable.
“How can I love somebody else when I promised forever?”
But Christian marriage vows have traditionally recognized the earthly boundary Scripture itself recognizes:
until death.
You kept your covenant.
Death did not prove your marriage failed.
Death completed the earthly duration of that covenant.
Paul's language is explicit: the surviving spouse is ἐλευθέρα — free.
Freedom does not mean forgetting.
Freedom means you are no longer bound by the marital covenant to the spouse who died.
And perhaps this is where grace needs to enter a room grief has kept locked.
Your spouse's death was not the death of your capacity to love.
Your story did not end beside a hospital bed.
It did not end when the monitor went silent.
It did not end when someone handed you a folded flag, a death certificate, an urn, or a box containing a wedding ring you could barely bring yourself to touch.
It did not end when the coffin disappeared beneath the ground.
Your life belongs to Jesus.
And as long as Christ gives you breath, there are still pages He may write.
Maybe those pages include singleness.
Maybe they include extraordinary ministry.
Maybe grandchildren.
Maybe friendships deeper than anything you expected.
Maybe quiet years of serving Jesus.
And yes...
Maybe one day they include another wedding.
Another nervous smile.
Another hand trembling while holding yours.
Another person promising to walk beside you for whatever years God gives.
If that happens in the Lord, you do not have to walk toward the altar ashamed.
You are not replacing somebody.
Human beings are not replacement parts.
You are entering another chapter of a life still surrendered to Jesus Christ.
And if you are not ready?
Then don't let anybody rush you.
There is no biblical stopwatch counting down the days until you are permitted to feel again.
Grief does not obey calendars.
You do not owe relatives a timetable.
You do not owe friends an explanation because you still wear your wedding ring.
And you do not owe anybody an apology if someday you decide to take it off.
Bring the entire journey to Jesus.
The loneliness.
The memories.
The desire.
The fear.
The guilt.
The possibility of loving again.
Lay all of it before the One who knows exactly what it means to weep at a tomb.

And if you have already remarried after your spouse died and somebody made you feel as though your second marriage were inherently sinful simply because you loved before, hear Paul's actual words rather than human accusation:
ἐλευθέρα ἐστίν.
You are free.
Free does not mean careless.
Free does not mean Christless.
Free does not mean every possible relationship is wise.
Paul immediately adds:
μόνον ἐν κυρίῳ.
Only in the Lord.
That is the balance.
Biblical covenant.
Biblical freedom.
Biblical boundaries.
And Christ over all of it.
Maybe you know somebody who has been quietly wrestling with this question.
A widow who feels guilty because someone made her smile again.
A widower sitting alone every evening, wondering whether wanting companionship somehow dishonors his wife.
A parent.
A grandparent.
A friend.
A believer carrying guilt God never commanded them to carry.
Not to pressure them into remarriage.
Not to tell them how quickly they should grieve.
Send it so they can open Scripture for themselves and hear what Paul actually said.
Grief has a way of making us forget truths we thought we understood when life was easier.
If this touched a place in you that you normally keep hidden, you don't have to pretend here.
Let other believers pray with you rather than forcing you to carry everything privately.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, helping you understand Scripture, strengthening you through grief, confronting sin, pointing you toward repentance, or reminding you that Jesus Christ is still present in the places where life hurts most, you can help this ministry continue.
Scripture recognizes the legitimacy of materially supporting Gospel ministry; Paul says that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living through that Gospel work.
But biblical giving must never be manipulated.
Paul also teaches that giving should come from a heart that has freely decided—not reluctantly or “under compulsion.”
It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased redemption with His blood, not our money.
